A school of espei rasboras, or pork chop rasboras, flashing their bright orange and deep black colors in a tight pack makes a nice display in small aquariums, or big ones with small fish. Quick Facts Scientific Name Trigonostigma espei Origin Thailand and Cambodia Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1¼" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 6 Shipping Size Approx. ½–¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a dark substrate. Soft, slightly acidic water and gentle filtration bring out their best color. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as tetras, other rasboras, danios, corydoras, gouramis and dwarf shrimp. Avoid large predatory fish that could eat them. Good to know: In a well-planted tank a school of rasboras swims together in the middle of the tank, and their colors deepen as they settle in.

The black tails of the Blue Wag Platy are quite a sight with four of them swimming together in the tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name Xiphophorus maculatus Origin Southern Mexico and Central America Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 3–4 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 70–80°F pH 7.0–8.2 Breeding Livebearer – breeds easily in the aquarium Group Size Sold as a school of 4 Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Platies are hardy and easy to keep. Give them a filter, a lid and plenty of plants. Use a heater to keep the water steady in the 70s. They prefer harder, slightly alkaline water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. Platies also need some plant matter, so a vegetable flake is a good choice. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Platies get along with most peaceful community fish, such as other livebearers (mollies, guppies and swordtails), tetras, rasboras and corydoras. Avoid large or aggressive fish that may bully or eat them. Breeding: Platies are livebearers, so a tank with males and females will almost certainly have babies (fry). Adults will eat fry, so add dense plants or use a breeding box if you want to raise them. Keeping more females than males gives the females a break from the males' attention. Good to know: Platies are one of the easiest fish to keep, which makes them a great choice for a first aquarium.

Zebra Danios are one of the most playful species in the fish tank, and a school of 6 will be chasing each other throughout the fish tank for hours. Quick Facts Scientific Name Danio rerio (long-fin variety) Origin India, Bangladesh and Nepal (Ganges region) (captive-bred) Care Level Very easy, great for beginners Temperament Peaceful, very active Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 64–77°F (often fine without a heater) pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 6 Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Danios are fast swimmers, so give them open swimming space, a filter, plants around the edges and a tight-fitting lid, since they jump. Make sure the tank is fully cycled (which takes several weeks) before adding fish. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Danios get along with most peaceful community fish, such as tetras, rasboras, barbs, corydoras and livebearers. Their speed can stress slow, long-finned fish like bettas and fancy guppies, and large predatory fish will eat them. Good to know: Long fins make these danios a little slower than regular zebras, so avoid fin-nipping tankmates like tiger barbs.

A zippy little gang of three bronze cory will be easy to follow, even in a well-grown planted aquarium. Quick Facts Scientific Name Corydoras aeneus Origin South America (widespread) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 5–10 years Diet Omnivore (bottom feeder) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–8.0 Group Size Sold as a group of 3 Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and a soft sand or smooth, fine gravel bottom. Plants, driftwood and a few shady spots help them feel secure. Corys are sensitive to salt and some medications (especially copper), so check labels before treating the tank. Feeding: Corys need their own food, not just leftovers. Feed sinking pellets or wafers once or twice a day so food reaches the bottom. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Corys get along with almost any peaceful community fish, such as tetras, rasboras, livebearers, gouramis, angelfish and bettas. Avoid large fish that could swallow them and aggressive bottom dwellers. Good to know: Corys sift through the substrate with their sensitive barbels, so soft sand or smooth, fine gravel keeps those barbels healthy.

The pom pom crab is a rare find in the high mountains of Taiwan and seldom exported to the USA. These small crabs are fully aquatic, but they will still try to escape the aquarium so there needs to be a good cover or several inches of glass so they cannot climb out. Pom pom crabs use their "pom pom" filaments to catch detritus for feeding and are quite a little spectacle when they do feed. Sinking pellets and scavenging should keep these guys happy. Quick Facts Scientific Name Ptychognathus barbatus Origin Taiwan Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1½" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Scavenger (sinking pellets, leftover food) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Sold as a group of 3 Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a mature, planted tank with rocks and hiding places, and keep a lid on the tank. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets or shrimp food once a day. They also scavenge leftover food. Tankmates: They are peaceful and do well with shrimp, snails and small peaceful fish. Good to know: Pom pom crabs are named for the fuzzy tufts on their claws, which they use to catch tiny bits of food.

A group of these fish makes a very pretty school in the fish tank. The bloodfin tetra is a peaceful, very active and hardy species. Long-lived for a small fish and active most of the day. Quick Facts Scientific Name Aphyocharax anisitsi Origin Paraná basin (Argentina, Paraguay, Brazil) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 64–82°F (tolerates cooler water) pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 5 Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a dark substrate, which brings out their color. Keep a lid on the tank, since tetras can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, rasboras, danios, corydoras, dwarf cichlids, gouramis and livebearers. Good to know: Tetras feel safer and show better color in a group. A larger school also spreads out any chasing.

listings.commonName: Red Tail Gold Line Rasbora (School of 5)
listings.description: Rasboras look best in small planted aquariums, and they get along with fancy shrimp and other gentle tank mates, along with tougher species such as angelfish. Quick Facts Scientific Name Rasbora borapetensis Origin Thailand, Cambodia, Laos and Malaysia Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 5 Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a dark substrate. Soft, slightly acidic water and gentle filtration bring out their best color. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as tetras, other rasboras, danios, corydoras, gouramis and dwarf shrimp. Avoid large predatory fish that could eat them. Good to know: In a well-planted tank a school of rasboras swims together in the middle of the tank, and their colors deepen as they settle in.

A set of ten bullfrog tadpoles is a perfect pack to add to an outdoor decorative pond. And they eat mosquito larvae. Quick Facts Scientific Name Lithobates catesbeianus Origin North America Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful as tadpoles Adult Size Tadpoles up to 6"; adult frogs 6–8" Lifespan Tadpole stage 1–3 years; adult frogs 8–10 years Diet Herbivore (algae and plant matter) Water Temperature 50–80°F pH 6.5–8.0 Group Size Sold as a group of 10 Shipping Size Approx. 1–2" Care Guide Tank setup: Bullfrog tadpoles are best suited to outdoor ponds with plants and algae. Once they grow legs and turn into frogs, they need a way to climb out of the water, and adult bullfrogs often leave the pond. Feeding: Tadpoles graze on algae and plant matter. Also feed algae wafers or a sinking pellet. Tankmates: Tadpoles are peaceful, but adult bullfrogs will eat anything that fits in their mouth, including fish. Good to know: Bullfrog tadpoles can take one to three years to turn into frogs, so they stay in the pond as tadpoles for a long time.

Start these small colorful rainbows out right by introducing them into the aquarium in a school. The Gertrudae will be more likely to swim in the open waters and not hide from potential predators (hopefully there aren't any). Quick Facts Scientific Name Pseudomugil gertrudae Origin Northern Australia and New Guinea Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1¼" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 6 Shipping Size Approx. ½–¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a planted tank with gentle filtration, some floating plants and a lid. They are small, so a sponge over the filter intake keeps them safe. Feeding: Feed crushed flake or micro pellets once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Blue-eyes are small and gentle, so keep them with other small, peaceful fish such as rasboras, small tetras, pygmy corydoras and shrimp. Good to know: Males have spotted, sail-like fins they flare at each other to show off. Their bright blue eyes stand out in a planted tank.

Just imagine a school of sparkling diamonds highlighted with red and blue colors swimming about. A school of these flashy diamonds might be more appealing than a diamond ring; think of the money one would save. Quick Facts Scientific Name Paracheirodon innesi (diamond head variety) Origin Aquarium-bred (Singapore) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1¼" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 5.5–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 6 Shipping Size Approx. ½–¾" Care Guide Tank setup: These small tetras do best in a planted tank with soft, slightly acidic water, a dark substrate, driftwood, floating plants and gentle filtration. A larger school makes them more confident and colorful. Feeding: Feed small amounts of micro pellets or crushed flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other small, peaceful fish like rasboras, small tetras, pencilfish, pygmy corydoras, otocinclus and dwarf shrimp. Avoid large or boisterous fish that could eat or bully them. Good to know: Small tetras show their best color in a large school in a planted tank with soft lighting.

Micro crabs are small, but small or large, any group of crabs is still called a consortium. Quick Facts Scientific Name Limnopilos naiyanetri Origin Thailand Care Level Moderate Temperament Very peaceful Adult Size Up to ½" Lifespan 1–2 years Diet Scavenger (fine foods) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Sold as a group of 5 Shipping Size Approx. ¼–½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a mature, planted tank with rocks and hiding places, and keep a lid on the tank. Feeding: Micro crabs pick tiny bits of food from plants and moss. In a mature tank they find much of their own food; also offer a little crushed flake or powdered food. Tankmates: Micro crabs are tiny and very peaceful. Keep them with shrimp, snails and small, gentle fish that won't eat them. Good to know: These are among the smallest crabs in the hobby. They are fully aquatic and spend most of their time hiding in moss and plant roots.

Since Albino Cherry Barbs have a little cherry color and light pink, a small school of these fish will create a very colorful display. Each order comes with 6 fish. Quick Facts Scientific Name Puntius titteya Origin Sri Lanka Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful, a bit shy Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 4–6 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 73–81°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 6 Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a filter, a heater and plenty of plants. They feel safest with places to hide and show more color in a planted tank. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other small, peaceful fish such as rasboras, small tetras, corydoras and dwarf shrimp. Avoid large or boisterous fish and fin-nippers. Good to know: Cherry barbs are one of the most peaceful barbs, so they mix well with small community fish and shrimp-safe planted tanks. Males color up most when a few females are around.

Each Rainbow Endler has a unique color pattern and a group of them will bring quite a bit of diverse color to the tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name Poecilia wingei Origin Venezuela (captive-bred in Florida) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1" (males about ¾") Lifespan 2–4 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Sold as a group of 6 Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and plenty of plants. Endlers are small, so a sponge filter or a sponge over the filter intake keeps them safe. Feeding: Feed a quality flake, crushed small, or micro pellets once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Endlers do well with other small, peaceful fish such as small rasboras, corydoras, otocinclus and shrimp. Avoid larger fish that could eat them. Good to know: Each rainbow endler has a slightly different color pattern, so a group gives a lot of variety.

All danios are so active and playful in a group, it's a shame to just order a few. Quick Facts Scientific Name Danio albolineatus Origin Myanmar, Thailand and Sumatra Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful, very active Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 68–79°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 6 Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Danios are fast swimmers, so give them open swimming space, a filter, plants around the edges and a tight-fitting lid, since they jump. Make sure the tank is fully cycled (which takes several weeks) before adding fish. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Danios get along with most peaceful community fish, such as tetras, rasboras, barbs, corydoras and livebearers. Their speed can stress slow, long-finned fish like bettas and fancy guppies, and large predatory fish will eat them. Good to know: Pearl danios have a pinkish-blue mother-of-pearl shimmer that shows best with side lighting and a dark background. Danios are fast and jump when startled, so keep a lid on the tank.

Any group of frogs is called an army. But a little pack of blonds sounds more like a sorority. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hymenochirus boettgeri Origin Central Africa (captive-bred) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1½" Lifespan 5 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 72–78°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Sold as a group of 3 Shipping Size Approx. ¾–1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a fully aquatic tank with plants and hiding spots, gentle filtration and a lid. They breathe air, so keep the water shallow enough for them to reach the surface easily. Feeding: Feed sinking frog pellets or frozen bloodworms once a day. They eat slowly, so make sure faster fish don't take all the food. Tankmates: Dwarf frogs are peaceful and do best with other small, gentle fish such as small tetras and rasboras, or with their own kind. Good to know: Blond dwarf frogs are a light-colored form of the African dwarf frog. They are fully aquatic and never need to leave the water.

Unlike writing utensils, Beckford Pencilfish are schoolers and need a few colleagues to swim with to keep a low stress level. Otherwise, they are just like pencils. Quick Facts Scientific Name Nannostomus beckfordi Origin Northern South America Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 6 Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a planted tank with floating plants, gentle filtration and a lid, since they can jump. Soft, slightly acidic water brings out their best color. Feeding: Feed crushed flake or micro pellets once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Pencilfish are shy and peaceful, so keep them with other small, gentle fish such as small tetras, rasboras, pygmy corydoras and shrimp. Good to know: Red beckford pencilfish show the most red when they are settled in a planted tank. At night their pattern changes to a blotchy "night" look, which is normal.

With their large fins and little bodies, who could resist the purchase of six? Quick Facts Scientific Name Gymnocorymbus ternetzi Origin Paraguay and Guaporé basins (Brazil, Bolivia, Paraguay); farm-raised Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful (may nip long fins) Adult Size Up to 2¼" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 6 Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a dark substrate, which brings out their color. Keep a lid on the tank, since tetras can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, rasboras, danios, corydoras, dwarf cichlids, gouramis and livebearers. Good to know: Tetras feel safer and show better color in a group. A larger school also spreads out any chasing.

These are very pretty corys and make great packs to keep the bottom of the aquarium clean. Quick Facts Scientific Name Corydoras aeneus (Venezuelan color form) Origin Venezuela Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 5–10 years Diet Omnivore (bottom feeder) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a group of 3 Shipping Size Approx. ¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and a soft sand or smooth, fine gravel bottom. Plants, driftwood and a few shady spots help them feel secure. Corys are sensitive to salt and some medications (especially copper), so check labels before treating the tank. Feeding: Corys need their own food, not just leftovers. Feed sinking pellets or wafers once or twice a day so food reaches the bottom. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Corys get along with almost any peaceful community fish, such as tetras, rasboras, livebearers, gouramis, angelfish and bettas. Avoid large fish that could swallow them and aggressive bottom dwellers. Good to know: The orange color develops as they grow past about an inch, so young fish may look plain at first.

In Asia, schools of ricefish are introduced to the rice paddies to keep the population of mosquitoes in check. Do you want mosquitoes in your house? Quick Facts Scientific Name Oryzias woworae Origin Sulawesi, Indonesia Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1¼" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F (tropical; use a heater) pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 5 Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a planted tank with floating plants, gentle filtration and a lid. Daisy's ricefish are tropical, so keep the water heated to 75–82°F. Feeding: Feed crushed flake or micro pellets once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Daisy's ricefish are a great fit for peaceful community tanks with small rasboras, tetras, pygmy corydoras and shrimp. Avoid large or aggressive fish. Good to know: Daisy's ricefish come from Sulawesi, Indonesia, and were first described in 2010. Males show the brightest blue and red on their fins.

Gold tetras are caught in the wild in very large schools. These shy tetras should be kept in groups, or they tend to hide. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hemigrammus rodwayi Origin Guyana, Suriname, French Guiana and Brazil Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 6 Shipping Size Approx. ¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a dark substrate, which brings out their color. Keep a lid on the tank, since tetras can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, rasboras, danios, corydoras, dwarf cichlids, gouramis and livebearers. Good to know: Tetras feel safer and show better color in a group. A larger school also spreads out any chasing.

The distinguishing feature of the green fire tetra is the green and orange body colors. The more fish, the more green and blue body colors. Quick Facts Scientific Name Aphyocharax rathbuni Origin Paraguay and Paraná basins (Paraguay, Brazil) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1¾" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 6 Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a dark substrate, which brings out their color. Keep a lid on the tank, since tetras can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, rasboras, danios, corydoras, dwarf cichlids, gouramis and livebearers. Good to know: Tetras feel safer and show better color in a group. A larger school also spreads out any chasing.

The blue king tetra, or simply the blue tetra, is prolific in the Amazon basin and very hardy for a wild-caught fish. These tetras grow to nearly two inches and feature a pale blue body with black and white caudal (tail) fins. The color of the fins does not stand out until the fish is about one year of age. Asian imports are cheaper, but these fish tend to be washed out in color. Blue tetras from AquariumFish.com are imported from the Amazon basin through Belém, Brazil. Quick Facts Scientific Name Boehlkea fredcochui Origin Upper Amazon (Peru, Colombia) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful but active Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 5–10 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 5 Shipping Size Approx. 1¼" Care Guide Tank setup: These are larger, active schooling fish, so give them open swimming space, plants or driftwood along the back and a tight-fitting lid, since they jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They do well with other active, similar-size fish such as larger tetras, barbs, rainbowfish, peaceful cichlids, corydoras and plecos. Very small fish may be eaten or bullied. Good to know: Larger tetras are hardy and long-lived, and a big school makes a striking display.

listings.commonName: Long Fin White Cloud Minnow (School of 6)
listings.description: The carefully bred long fin white cloud in a pack will be a sight as the fins start to grow out as the fish mature in their school. However, fish are one group of the animal kingdom that never graduates from school. Quick Facts Scientific Name Tanichthys albonubes (long fin variety) Origin Southern China and northern Vietnam (aquarium-bred) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1½" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 64–75°F (no heater needed in most homes) pH 6.5–8.0 Group Size Sold as a school of 6 Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants and gentle filtration. These are cool-water fish that do fine at room temperature, and they also do well in outdoor ponds and patio tubs in warm months. Keep a lid on the tank. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with other small, peaceful fish like ricefish, danios, small rasboras, and dwarf shrimp, and can share an unheated tank with other cool-water species. Avoid large fish (including goldfish) that may eat them. Good to know: White clouds have been kept in aquariums since the 1930s and are one of the hardiest small fish in the hobby. Males show the brightest color when they display to each other.

A school kid in China discovered this species and named it after the mountain where he found it, so why not keep these in a school? Quick Facts Scientific Name Tanichthys albonubes Origin Southern China and northern Vietnam (aquarium-bred) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1½" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 64–75°F (no heater needed in most homes) pH 6.5–8.0 Group Size Sold as a school of 6 Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants and gentle filtration. These are cool-water fish that do fine at room temperature, and they also do well in outdoor ponds and patio tubs in warm months. Keep a lid on the tank. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with other small, peaceful fish like ricefish, danios, small rasboras, and dwarf shrimp, and can share an unheated tank with other cool-water species. Avoid large fish (including goldfish) that may eat them. Good to know: White clouds have been kept in aquariums since the 1930s and are one of the hardiest small fish in the hobby. Males show the brightest color when they display to each other.

Dr. Choprae advises we keep these in schools. And five is a nice number. Quick Facts Scientific Name Danio choprae Origin Myanmar Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1¼" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 68–79°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 5 Shipping Size Approx. ¾–1" Care Guide Tank setup: Danios are fast swimmers, so give them open swimming space, plants around the edges and a tight-fitting lid, since they jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish, such as other danios, rasboras, tetras, barbs, corydoras and livebearers. Good to know: Glowlight danios have bright orange and blue-green bars that look their best in a planted tank.

Celestials are some of the most popular small schooling fish in the aquarium trade, extremely popular for planted and nano tanks. These rasboras (technically danios) look best in small planted aquariums, and they get along with fancy shrimp and other gentle tank mates. Quick Facts Scientific Name Danio margaritatus Origin Myanmar (Shan Plateau) Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 72–78°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 5 Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: These fish come from cool, clear, hard-water lakes and ponds in Myanmar. Give them dense plants, gentle filtration and plenty of cover. They do not need very warm water, and stable, slightly alkaline water suits them. Feeding: Feed crushed flake or micro pellets once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other small, peaceful fish that like similar water, such as celestial pearl danios, micro rasboras, small livebearers and dwarf shrimp. Avoid large or boisterous fish. Good to know: They are a little shy at first; plenty of plants and a group of their own kind help them settle in and color up.

A group of four scavenging Chinese algae eaters will keep that fish tank clean and active. Quick Facts Scientific Name Gyrinocheilus aymonieri Origin Thailand, Laos, Cambodia and Vietnam Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful when young; territorial and aggressive as adults Adult Size Up to 10–11" Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore (grazes on algae) Water Temperature 74–80°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 4 Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them driftwood, rocks, caves and good current. Keep a lid on the tank. Feeding: Young fish graze on algae, but adults eat less algae and more prepared food. Feed algae wafers and sinking pellets daily. Well-fed adults are less likely to bother other fish. Tankmates: Chinese algae eaters do best with fast, robust fish like larger barbs, danios and semi-aggressive cichlids. Avoid slow, flat-sided fish like angelfish, discus and goldfish, which adults may latch onto and harm. Good to know: Chinese algae eaters are not from China; most come from Thailand and nearby countries. Their algae-eating slows as they grow.

The siamensis is an active scavenger and algae eater, so four of these workers will make a nice cleaning crew. Quick Facts Scientific Name Crossocheilus oblongus Origin Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 6" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore (grazes on algae) Water Temperature 75–79°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Sold as a group of 4 Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Siamese algae eaters are active swimmers. Give them plants, driftwood and smooth rocks to graze, some current and a tight lid, since they can jump. Feeding: They graze on algae, but don't rely on algae alone. Feed algae wafers, sinking pellets or flake daily. Adults eat less algae and more prepared food. Tankmates: Siamese algae eaters get along with most peaceful community fish, such as tetras, rasboras, gouramis, barbs, corydoras and rainbowfish. Adults may squabble with each other or with red-tailed and rainbow sharks. Good to know: True Siamese algae eaters are one of the few fish that eat black beard algae. Look for the black stripe running all the way into the tail fin.

Unless the emperor tetra is an adult male in heat, the blues are subtle. A pretty school will be less subtle. Quick Facts Scientific Name Inpaichthys kerri (blue variety) Origin Brazil (wild form); bred in Singapore Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1½" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 5 Shipping Size Approx. ¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a dark substrate, which brings out their color. Keep a lid on the tank, since tetras can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, rasboras, danios, corydoras, dwarf cichlids, gouramis and livebearers. Good to know: Tetras feel safer and show better color in a group. A larger school also spreads out any chasing.

Dwarf Glass Fish are shy schoolers and even if they are see-through, other fish can still see them. Allowing them to swim in a small group will greatly improve their disposition. Quick Facts Scientific Name Parambassis ranga Origin South and Southeast Asia Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Sold as a school of 5 Shipping Size Approx. ¾–1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants, hiding places and gentle filtration. They like slightly hard water, and a little aquarium salt is optional. Feeding: Feed small amounts of flake or micro pellets once or twice a day. They also enjoy small frozen foods like brine shrimp and bloodworms. Tankmates: Glassfish are peaceful and get along with other small community fish such as rasboras, danios, livebearers and corydoras. Good to know: Glassfish are see-through, and their bodies have a soft gold or silver sheen under good lighting.

Juvenile Cacatuoides (or Cockatoo) can be hard to sex. To ensure a nice mix of sexes and to keep these little dwarf cichlids feeling more at home, a small group of four might be a good purchase for a larger community tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name Apistogramma cacatuoides Origin Peru, Colombia and Brazil (Amazon basin) Care Level Easy, a good first apisto Temperament Peaceful (males territorial with each other) Adult Size Males up to 3"; females about 2" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 75–84°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 4 Shipping Size Approx. ¾–1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter, dim lighting and lots of plants, driftwood and leaf litter. Add a cave (a coconut shell or small clay pot) for each female. Most apistos prefer soft, slightly acidic water. Feeding: Feed small pellets or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with small, peaceful fish such as tetras, rasboras, pencilfish, otocinclus and corydoras. A calm school of small "dither" fish helps apistos feel safe enough to come out. Keep one male per tank unless it is large and well planted, and avoid large or boisterous fish. Adults may eat small shrimp and baby shrimp. Breeding: Apistos are cave spawners. The female lays her eggs inside a cave and guards the fry, while the male patrols the territory. One male with several females works well in a planted tank. Good to know: Cockatoo apistos are among the hardiest apistogrammas and handle a wider range of water than most, which makes them a great first dwarf cichlid.

A group of four Ghost Catfish will appear to hover together in various areas of the fish tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name Kryptopterus vitreolus Origin Thailand Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–80°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 4 Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants, driftwood and gentle current, with some open swimming space in the middle of the tank. They feel safest with others of their kind. Feeding: Feed small amounts of a quality flake or micro pellet once or twice a day. They also enjoy small frozen foods like brine shrimp and bloodworms. Tankmates: Ghost glass catfish are peaceful and shy. Keep them with other gentle community fish such as tetras, rasboras and corydoras. Good to know: Ghost catfish are almost completely clear, so you can see their skeleton. They hover together in midwater, often facing into the current.

Three approximately 2-inch barbs will quickly grow to nearly 6 inches but remain compatible with medium to large species. Quick Facts Scientific Name Sahyadria denisonii Origin Southwestern India Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful, very active Adult Size Up to 6" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 64–77°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 3 Shipping Size Approx. 2–3" Care Guide Tank setup: These barbs grow large and swim fast, so give them lots of open space, strong filtration and a tight-fitting lid, since they can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with similar-sized, active fish such as rainbowfish, larger barbs, larger tetras, loaches and peaceful cichlids. Very small fish may be eaten or stressed. Good to know: Denison barbs are fast swimmers that need strong filtration, lots of oxygen and a tight lid, since they can jump.

Three medium-size roseline sharks will tend to swim in a tight group about the middle of the aquarium. These fish are peaceful and adapt well to medium and large aquariums. Quick Facts Scientific Name Sahyadria denisonii (formerly Puntius denisonii ) Origin Western Ghats, India (mostly captive-bred) Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful but active Adult Size Up to 5–6" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 68–77°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 3 Shipping Size Small: 1–1½" · Medium: 2–3" · X-Large: 4" Care Guide Tank setup: Roselines are active schoolers that like cool, clean, well-oxygenated water with some current. Give them open swimming space, plants along the back and a tight lid. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet with some vegetable content once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Roselines get along with most active, peaceful fish of similar size, such as other barbs, danios, rainbowfish, larger tetras, loaches and gouramis. Avoid slow, long-finned fish. Good to know: Roselines are endangered in the wild in India; most in the trade today are captive-bred.

These little guys will be all over the tank nibbling on whatever they can find. Quick Facts Scientific Name Otocinclus affinis Origin Amazon basin, South America Care Level Moderate (needs a mature tank) Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Algae eater (also eats algae wafers) Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a cleaning crew of 4 Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a mature, planted tank with algae to graze, gentle filtration and stable, clean water. Feeding: Otocinclus graze on soft algae, but don't rely on algae alone. Also feed algae wafers. Tankmates: Otos are very peaceful and get along with almost any small community fish, plus shrimp and snails. Good to know: Otos are social and feel safest with others of their kind. Make sure there is algae or algae wafers available, since they can go hungry in very clean tanks.

If the tank is large at all, with lots of hiding places, a group of four vampires might be best to ensure a couple can be spotted at any time. A group will need to be fed a small amount once per day of blood worms or similar foods. But they can go for a bit without feeding; these crabs are great scavengers. Quick Facts Scientific Name Geosesarma sp. Origin Indonesia Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Omnivore (scavenger) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Sold as a group of 4 Shipping Size Approx. ½–1" Care Guide Tank setup: These crabs need land as well as water. Use a paludarium or a tank with a large land area and a shallow water section. Keep a tight lid on the tank, since they are escape artists. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets or shrimp food once a day. They also eat vegetables and small bits of fish food. Tankmates: They are best kept in a species-only setup, since they may catch small fish. Good to know: Vampire crabs get their name from their glowing yellow or purple eyes. They hide a lot, so more hiding places mean more confident crabs.

Bumblebee gobies are notorious hiders; keep three so you are bound to catch sight of them from time to time. Quick Facts Scientific Name Brachygobius doriae Origin Malaysia and Indonesia (Borneo, Sumatra) Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful with other fish; territorial with its own kind Adult Size Up to 1–1½" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Carnivore (small meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.5–8.5 Group Size Sold as a group of 3 Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: These small gobies do best with plenty of caves and hiding spots (small shells and rocks work well) and hard, alkaline water. Many do best with a little marine salt in the water (brackish, specific gravity about 1.002–1.008). Feeding: Feed small amounts once or twice a day. They prefer small frozen foods like brine shrimp and bloodworms, and some will not eat flake reliably. Tankmates: Keep them in a species tank or with other small, peaceful brackish fish such as mollies, glassfish and small livebearers. Avoid larger fish that could eat them. Good to know: These tiny gobies are full of personality and often perch on rocks or glass to watch their surroundings.

The Scarlet Gem Badis, or simply the Scarlet Gem, is a bright red striped nano fish that needs a peaceful fish tank. These fish are small and more sociable in a small group of four. Quick Facts Scientific Name Dario dario Origin India Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful (males spar with each other) Adult Size Up to ¾" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Carnivore (tiny meaty foods) Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 4 Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a planted tank with caves, leaf litter and gentle filtration. They are shy and like plenty of hiding places. Feeding: Badis are shy eaters that prefer small frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Some will learn to take small pellets once settled. Feed small amounts once or twice a day. Tankmates: Keep them with small, calm fish such as rasboras, pygmy corydoras and shrimp. Avoid fast, pushy fish that would outcompete them for food. Good to know: Males are bright red with blue fins; females are plain silver. Their tiny size and shy nature make them a great fit for planted tanks.

A group of four mixed-sex solid gold lyretail mollies will school, chase and pair up in their new home. They just need someone to take them home. Quick Facts Scientific Name Poecilia sphenops (aquarium-bred hybrids) Origin Mexico and Central America (wild ancestors); aquarium-bred Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 3–4" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (needs plant matter) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.5–8.5 (hard water) Group Size Sold as a group of 4 Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Mollies like hard, alkaline water. Give them plants, open swimming space and good filtration, since they are active and produce a fair amount of waste. Aquarium salt is optional; they also do well in brackish tanks. Feeding: Mollies graze on algae, so feed a quality flake that includes vegetable matter once or twice a day. They also enjoy algae wafers and frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Mollies get along with most peaceful community fish that like similar hard water, such as platies, swordtails, guppies, danios, rainbowfish, corydoras and plecos. Avoid fin-nippers and soft-water specialists. Keeping more females than males keeps any one female from being harassed. Good to know: Mollies are livebearers that breed readily. Fry are born free-swimming and will be eaten unless there are dense plants or a breeding box for them to hide in.

The Flagfish will not normally school together, but appear to work in coordination as they explore their own little areas for food and hair algae. Quick Facts Scientific Name Jordanella floridae Origin Florida, USA Care Level Easy Temperament Semi-aggressive (males are territorial) Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (needs plant matter) Water Temperature 68–79°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Sold as a school of 4 Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plenty of plants and some algae to graze. They are hardy and do fine at room temperature in most homes. Feeding: Feed a quality flake that includes vegetable matter once or twice a day. They also graze on algae, including hair algae. Tankmates: Flagfish can be a little nippy and territorial, so keep them with other hardy, active fish rather than slow, long-finned fish. Good to know: Flagfish are named for the male's red-and-blue pattern, which looks a bit like the American flag. They are great at eating hair algae.

The Panda Cory has enough black on the dorsal fin and the body to give it its common name. Fortunately, these cory do not require bamboo shoots, but scavenge uneaten food at the bottom of the aquarium. Panda cory do not grow very large and are tank-raised in the aquatic trade. Wild Panda Cory from Venezuela are quite expensive but are rarely available. AquariumFish.com imports our tank-raised panda cory from Singapore. Quick Facts Scientific Name Corydoras panda Origin Peru (captive-bred in Singapore) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 5–10 years Diet Omnivore (bottom feeder) Water Temperature 72–77°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a group of 3 Shipping Size Approx. ¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and a soft sand or smooth, fine gravel bottom. Plants, driftwood and a few shady spots help them feel secure. Corys are sensitive to salt and some medications (especially copper), so check labels before treating the tank. Feeding: Corys need their own food, not just leftovers. Feed sinking pellets or wafers once or twice a day so food reaches the bottom. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Corys get along with almost any peaceful community fish, such as tetras, rasboras, livebearers, gouramis, angelfish and bettas. Avoid large fish that could swallow them and aggressive bottom dwellers. Good to know: Panda corys prefer slightly cooler, very clean water and are happiest in a group.

Technically, any group of fish, including Corydoras, is called a school, but when you put a few of these little Corys together, the word "pack" seems more appropriate. Each order comes with three Albino Corys. Quick Facts Scientific Name Corydoras aeneus (albino variety) Origin Captive-bred Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 5–10 years Diet Omnivore (bottom feeder) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–8.0 Group Size Sold as a pack of 3 Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and a soft sand or smooth, fine gravel bottom. Plants, driftwood and a few shady spots help them feel secure. Corys are sensitive to salt and some medications (especially copper), so check labels before treating the tank. Feeding: Corys need their own food, not just leftovers. Feed sinking pellets or wafers once or twice a day so food reaches the bottom. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Corys get along with almost any peaceful community fish, such as tetras, rasboras, livebearers, gouramis, angelfish and bettas. Avoid large fish that could swallow them and aggressive bottom dwellers. Good to know: Albino corys are among the hardiest corys and stand out against dark sand. Corys sometimes dart to the surface to gulp a bit of air. That's normal behavior, not a sign of trouble.

Though a platy can survive without undue stress alone, these are social fish and do better in small groups. Honestly, one platy just swimming around by himself just sounds sad. Quick Facts Scientific Name Xiphophorus maculatus Origin Southern Mexico and Central America Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 3–4 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 70–80°F pH 7.0–8.2 Breeding Livebearer – breeds easily in the aquarium Group Size Sold as a school of 4 Care Guide Tank setup: Platies are hardy and easy to keep. Give them a filter, a lid and plenty of plants. Use a heater to keep the water steady in the 70s. They prefer harder, slightly alkaline water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. Platies also need some plant matter, so a vegetable flake is a good choice. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Platies get along with most peaceful community fish, such as other livebearers (mollies, guppies and swordtails), tetras, rasboras and corydoras. Avoid large or aggressive fish that may bully or eat them. Breeding: Platies are livebearers, so a tank with males and females will almost certainly have babies (fry). Adults will eat fry, so add dense plants or use a breeding box if you want to raise them. Keeping more females than males gives the females a break from the males' attention. Good to know: Platies are one of the easiest fish to keep, which makes them a great choice for a first aquarium.

The Coral Red Platy is so bright, but small. Make a bigger bright red spectacle with five. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. Platies also need some plant matter, so a vegetable flake is a good choice. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Platies get along with most peaceful community fish, such as other livebearers (mollies, guppies and swordtails), tetras, rasboras and corydoras. Avoid large or aggressive fish that may bully or eat them. Breeding: Platies are livebearers, so a tank with males and females will almost certainly have babies (fry). Adults will eat fry, so add dense plants or use a breeding box if you want to raise them. Keeping more females than males gives the females a break from the males' attention. Good to know: Dwarf platies are small and easily intimidated, so keep them with other small, gentle fish.

The deep blue rasboras, often called "neon blue rasboras", make a beautiful school in a small aquarium. It's fortunate Dr. Axelrod discovered them. Quick Facts Scientific Name Sundadanio axelrodi (blue form) Origin Borneo and nearby islands, Indonesia Care Level Moderate (needs soft, acidic water) Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to ¾" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 5.0–7.0 Group Size Sold as a school of 5 Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them dense plants, floating plants, a dark substrate and gentle filtration (a sponge filter is ideal, since they are small enough to be pulled into strong intakes). Soft, slightly acidic water brings out their best color. Feeding: Feed crushed flake or micro pellets once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other tiny, peaceful fish such as other micro rasboras, small tetras, pygmy corydoras, otocinclus and dwarf shrimp. Avoid large or boisterous fish, which can eat or stress them. Good to know: Micro rasboras show their best color and natural schooling behavior in larger groups and well-planted tanks.

Extremely hardy and adaptable to peaceful community fish tanks and semi-aggressive cichlid tanks, a school of scissortails makes a nice attraction. Quick Facts Scientific Name Rasbora trilineata Origin Thailand, Cambodia, Malaysia, Sumatra and Borneo Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful but very active Adult Size Up to 4–5" (often smaller in aquariums) Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 6 Shipping Size Approx. 1¼" Care Guide Tank setup: These are active, fast swimmers, so give them open swimming space, plants along the back and sides, and a tight-fitting lid, since they can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They do well with other active, peaceful to semi-aggressive fish of similar size, such as barbs, larger tetras, danios, rainbowfish, gouramis and corydoras. Their speed can stress slow, long-finned fish. Good to know: They are hardy, active schoolers that look best with open swimming space where the group can move together.

This stunning school of neon green will highlight the middle region of any fish tank. Similar to the chili rasbora with a little less red but more dominant spots, a group of these will bring out the patterns of these very nice nano rasboras. Soft, slightly acidic water brings out their best color. Feeding: Feed crushed flake or micro pellets once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. Avoid large or boisterous fish, which can eat or stress them. Good to know: Micro rasboras show their best color and natural schooling behavior in larger groups and well-planted tanks.

The brilliant reflective long horizontal line on this rasbora is dramatic when a group is swimming and reflecting light together. Soft, slightly acidic water and gentle filtration bring out their best color. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as tetras, other rasboras, danios, corydoras, gouramis and dwarf shrimp. Avoid large predatory fish that could eat them. Good to know: In a well-planted tank a school of rasboras swims together in the middle of the tank, and their colors deepen as they settle in.

Chili, or brigittae, rasboras are very small and really need to be kept in small schools. Six should be a good minimum number. Please note these wild fish are sent as chili, but sometimes on closer inspection they are strawberry or phoenix rasboras. They come in and out of our warehouse pretty quickly, so if you want to ensure that they are not a similar fish, please add "MUST BE TRUE" to the order. A small group of these pearl danios will look like a quick-moving translucent orb. Quick Facts Scientific Name Danio albolineatus Origin Myanmar, Thailand and Sumatra Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful, very active Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 68–79°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 6 Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Danios are fast swimmers, so give them open swimming space, a filter, plants around the edges and a tight-fitting lid, since they jump. Make sure the tank is fully cycled (which takes several weeks) before adding fish. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Danios get along with most peaceful community fish, such as tetras, rasboras, barbs, corydoras and livebearers. Their speed can stress slow, long-finned fish like bettas and fancy guppies, and large predatory fish will eat them. Good to know: Pearl danios have a pinkish-blue mother-of-pearl shimmer that shows best with side lighting and a dark background. Danios are fast and jump when startled, so keep a lid on the tank.

Each order comes with 6 barbs. A school of these very active fish will explore the entire tank space. Quick Facts Scientific Name Puntigrus tetrazona Origin Indonesia (Sumatra, Borneo) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Semi-aggressive (fin-nipper) Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 5–7 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 6 Shipping Size Approx. ¾–1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a filter, a heater and plenty of open swimming space. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Pick fast, sturdy tankmates such as other barbs, danios, loaches, corydoras and larger tetras. Avoid slow, long-finned fish like bettas, angelfish, gouramis and guppies. Good to know: Tiger barbs nip fins mostly when kept in small numbers. Keeping them in a group keeps the chasing within the school.

The purple and black hues of the ruby barb will almost shimmer as these active schoolers swim in a tight group about the tank. Tankmates: They do well with other active fish of similar size, such as other barbs, danios, larger tetras, rainbowfish, corydoras and loaches. Avoid slow, long-finned fish like bettas and fancy guppies. Good to know: A color-enhancing flake and a darker substrate bring out the males' deep red and black.

It's likely a coincidence, but these five-banded barbs do well in groups (or bands) of 5. Avoid large or boisterous fish that can outcompete them. Good to know: Penta barbs prefer soft, slightly acidic water and a well-planted tank. They are calmer and more colorful in a group.

Rosy Barbs are fast, tight schoolers, and with the bright red males and the flashy copper females, this is a very reflective moving spectacle. A school of Rosy Barbs will need at least a ten-gallon aquarium. More would be better. A group of angelfish is called a school or herd, but why confuse the issue? We just stick with good old school. Each order comes with three medium albino angelfish, unsexed. So who knows what will happen when these juveniles grow up. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pterophyllum scalare (albino variety) Origin Amazon basin, South America (captive-bred) Care Level Easy Temperament Semi-aggressive (territorial when pairing) Adult Size Up to 6" long and 8" tall Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 3 Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them tall plants or driftwood, a heater and a gentle filter. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Choose peaceful fish too large to swallow, such as larger tetras, corydoras, plecos, rams, gouramis and peaceful barbs. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs, and small fish like neon tetras that adult angels may eat. Breeding: Angelfish pair off and lay eggs on flat surfaces like broad leaves or slate. A breeding pair can become territorial, so give them room and places for other fish to retreat. Good to know: Albino angelfish have light-sensitive eyes, so moderate lighting and a few floating plants help keep them comfortable.

These three small to medium angelfish will grow to a nice size together, and eventually two of them will pair up (happens to all of us).
