Tankmates: Choose peaceful fish too large to swallow, such as larger tetras, corydoras, plecos, rams, gouramis and peaceful barbs. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs, and small fish like neon tetras that adult angels may eat. Breeding: Angelfish pair off and lay eggs on flat surfaces like broad leaves or slate. A breeding pair can become territorial, so give them room and places for other fish to retreat. Good to know: In a group, two angelfish often pair off and claim part of the tank. If a pair forms and starts chasing the others, add more hiding places or rehome the extras.

The hardy red and blue Colombian tetra will grow to 3 inches, so this group needs a midsize to large tank at maturity. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hyphessobrycon columbianus Origin Northern Colombia (Caribbean slope) Care Level Easy Temperament Semi-aggressive (may nip fins if kept in small groups) Adult Size Up to 2½–3" Lifespan 5–10 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 6 Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: These are larger, active schooling fish, so give them open swimming space, plants or driftwood along the back and a tight-fitting lid, since they jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They do well with other active, similar-size fish such as larger tetras, barbs, rainbowfish, peaceful cichlids, corydoras and plecos. Very small fish may be eaten or bullied. Good to know: Larger tetras are hardy and long-lived, and a big school makes a striking display.

Elegant clear bodies and bright red tails create a splendid school for any aquarium. Quick Facts Scientific Name Prionobrama filigera Origin Amazon and Paraná basins Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 6 Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a dark substrate, which brings out their color. Keep a lid on the tank, since tetras can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, rasboras, danios, corydoras, dwarf cichlids, gouramis and livebearers. Good to know: Tetras feel safer and show better color in a group. A larger school also spreads out any chasing.

Though Kribensis are not schoolers, they do form a communal area in the aquarium (and the lake), so keeping them in small groups keeps them happy. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pelvicachromis pulcher Origin Nigeria and Cameroon (coastal rivers) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful (territorial when breeding) Adult Size Up to 3–4" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a group of 3 Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: West African cichlids prefer soft to neutral water. Use a sand or fine gravel bottom with plants, driftwood and caves or flowerpots for spawning. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with peaceful community fish like tetras, barbs, rasboras, corydoras and plecos. Give each pair its own territory, and expect more defensiveness when breeding. Good to know: Kribs are cave spawners. A pair will claim a cave and guard their fry, and can become pushy while breeding.

Three Bolivian rams are a nice grouping for a small or mid-size fish tank where you can easily observe the social interactions. Quick Facts Scientific Name Mikrogeophagus altispinosus Origin Bolivia and Brazil (Mamoré and Guaporé basins) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 4–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a group of 3 Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a sand bottom, plants, driftwood and flat stones or caves for spawning. Bolivian rams tolerate cooler and harder water than blue rams. Feeding: Feed a quality small cichlid pellet or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Bolivian rams do well with peaceful community fish like tetras, rasboras, barbs, corydoras and other peaceful dwarf cichlids. They may eat small shrimp. Good to know: Bolivian rams are hardier and more forgiving than blue rams, making them a great first dwarf cichlid.

A small group of veil rams in a large tank is always a good idea. Individuals tend to stress, so a couple of colleagues, even if they butt heads from time to time, will allow these dwarf cichlids to settle in the aquarium. Quick Facts Scientific Name Mikrogeophagus ramirezi (balloon veil variety) Origin Venezuela and Colombia (Orinoco basin); aquarium-bred Care Level Moderate (needs warm, clean, soft water) Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 2–4 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 80–86°F pH 5.0–7.0 Group Size Sold as a school of 3 Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Rams need warm, very clean, soft water. Give them a sand bottom, plants, driftwood, leaf litter and flat stones for spawning. Rams are sensitive to poor water quality. Feeding: Feed small amounts of quality micro pellets or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Rams do well with small, peaceful fish that like warm, soft water, such as tetras, rasboras, hatchetfish, corydoras and discus. They may eat small shrimp. Avoid large or boisterous fish. Good to know: Rams often form pairs and lay eggs on flat stones. Stable, warm water is the key to keeping them healthy.

When black convicts get to their adult stage they turn aggressive, so if a few of them grow up together, at least they can have a couple of adult friends in the tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name Amatitlania nigrofasciata Origin Central America (Guatemala to Panama); aquarium-bred Care Level Easy Temperament Semi-aggressive (territorial, especially when breeding) Adult Size Up to 5–6" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Sold as a school of 3 Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a sand or gravel bottom, rocks, caves and driftwood to create territories. Anchor decorations well, since they like to dig. Strong filtration is important. Feeding: Feed a quality cichlid pellet or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other robust Central American cichlids of similar size, plus larger catfish and plecos. Give each fish its own territory, and avoid small or timid fish. Good to know: Central American cichlids are hardy and easy to breed. Pairs become very protective of their eggs and fry.

Technically not schooling fish, two of these fish will eventually pair up. The interactions of a small group of angels make an aquarium a heavenly place. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pterophyllum scalare Origin Amazon basin, South America (captive-bred) Care Level Easy Temperament Semi-aggressive (territorial when pairing) Adult Size Up to 6" long and 8" tall Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 3 Shipping Size Approx. 1½–4" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them tall plants or driftwood, a heater and a gentle filter. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Choose peaceful fish too large to swallow, such as larger tetras, corydoras, plecos, rams, gouramis and peaceful barbs. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs, and small fish like neon tetras that adult angels may eat. Breeding: Angelfish pair off and lay eggs on flat surfaces like broad leaves or slate. A breeding pair can become territorial, so give them room and places for other fish to retreat. Good to know: The blue color develops with age and is often hard to see until the fish reach about 3", so young fish may look mostly silver or black.

The rummynose tetra is a tight schooling fish, which makes for some dramatic motions as all six of these fish move about in unison. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hemigrammus rhodostomus Origin Lower Amazon and Orinoco basins Care Level Moderate (needs soft, clean water) Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 6 Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a dark substrate, which brings out their color. Keep a lid on the tank, since tetras can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, rasboras, danios, corydoras, dwarf cichlids, gouramis and livebearers. Good to know: Tetras feel safer and show better color in a group. A larger school also spreads out any chasing.

The most prevalent theory as to how this color came about for the Yellow Parrot Cichlid from Taiwan is through selective breeding of Midas and Severum Cichlids, but there is probably more to the story. Regardless, these bright yellow hybrids offer a beautiful alternative to an already big menu of exotic hybrid parrot cichlids. Like most parrots, their behavior is unpredictable and can run from peaceful to aggressive. Hybrids are a mixed bag in more ways than one. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hybrid cichlid Origin Captive-bred hybrid (Taiwan) Care Level Easy Temperament Semi-aggressive Adult Size Up to 8" Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 76–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 3" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them caves, rocks or driftwood, a smooth bottom and good filtration. Feeding: Feed a quality floating cichlid pellet once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Parrot cichlids are usually peaceful for cichlids. Keep them with other fish of similar size, such as other parrots, silver dollars, larger tetras, plecos and peaceful cichlids. Good to know: Hybrid parrots vary in personality from fish to fish, so watch new arrivals closely as they settle in.

Spot-tail Mantis Shrimp: The Spearer Predator The Spot-tail Mantis Shrimp (Squilla mantis), also known by its regional names Canocchia or Pacchero, is a large, highly specialized crustacean belonging to the order Stomatopoda. Unlike the brightly colored 'smasher' mantis shrimp often seen in the hobby, S. mantis is a 'spearer' type, characterized by a flattened, segmented body and long, spiny, raptorial appendages designed to impale soft-bodied prey. Native to the shallow coastal areas of the Mediterranean Sea and the Eastern Atlantic, this species is typically a drabber color, often pale green or translucent with a distinctive dark spot (ocellus) on its tail or telson. It is an ambush predator that spends the vast majority of its time hidden within elaborate, U-shaped burrows excavated in deep mud or fine sand. The Spot-tail Mantis Shrimp is an opportunistic, territorial, and extremely effective hunter. It should never be kept in a reef or mixed-species tank, as it will systematically prey on and kill fish, shrimp, crabs, and other invertebrates. It must be housed in a species-specific aquarium with secure, non-glass walls (or very thick glass) to prevent potential damage from its powerful strike. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: This mantis shrimp is a dedicated Carnivore / Opportunistic Predator. In the wild, it feeds on smaller crustaceans, fish, worms (polychaetes), and mollusks (bivalves and squid). Feeding: In captivity, feed it 3-4 times per week with meaty foods, such as frozen shrimp, thawed clams, squid, or pieces of fish. They are intelligent and can be target-fed using tongs, which is safer for the keeper. Providing food with a hard outer shell (like whole frozen shrimp) allows them to exercise their hunting skills. Reef Compatibility: No. Mantis shrimps are completely incompatible with nearly all other aquarium life, including corals, fish, and invertebrates. They are notorious for killing tank mates and can destabilize rockwork. Temperament: Extremely Aggressive and Predatory. They are highly territorial and must be kept singly. Their "spearing" strike is powerful and fast enough to severely injure human fingers (earning them the nickname "thumb splitters"). Extreme caution and protective gloves are mandatory when performing tank maintenance. Tank Requirements: Requires a minimum 30-gallon species-only tank with a deep substrate (at least 6-8 inches) of fine sand mixed with rubble to allow for proper burrow construction. PVC pipes can be buried in the substrate to provide a pre-made, stable home. The tank should have thick acrylic or tempered glass walls and a tight-fitting lid (as they are known jumpers). Quick Facts Scientific Name: Squilla mantis Primary Common Name: Spot-tail Mantis Shrimp Other Common Names: Canocchia, Pacchero, Sea Locust, Thumb Splitter Origin: Mediterranean Sea, Eastern Atlantic Ocean Max Size: 7-10 inches (18-25 cm) Temperament: Extremely Aggressive / Predatory (Spearer) Diet: Carnivore (Crustaceans, fish, worms) Minimum Tank Size: 30 Gallons (Species-Only) Reef Compatibility: No (Will destroy tank life) Danger: Highly Dangerous (Spearing appendage can cause deep lacerations)

Java Fern on Driftwood Thin deep green to black leaves of the Java Fern accent the brown wood colors and the plant hold to the wood tightly. Low to mid level lighting is fine for these hardy plants. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Leptochilus pteropus Max Height (Submerged): 10 inches Care Level: Beginner / Very Easy Lighting: Low to Moderate CO₂ Injection: Not Required (Benefits from CO2, but thrives without it) Growth Rate: Very Slow Temperature Range: 68−86 ° F ( 20−30 ° C ) Water pH: 5.5 - 8.0 (Highly Adaptable) Placement: Anywhere

Java Fern on Lava Rock The rusty red color of lava rock goes together with the deep green color of the hardy Java Fern. Porous surface of lava rock offers a haven for roots and allows beneficial bacteria to grow within the pores. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Leptochilus pteropus Max Height (Submerged): 10 inches Care Level: Beginner / Very Easy Lighting: Low to Moderate CO₂ Injection: Not Required (Benefits from CO2, but thrives without it) Growth Rate: Very Slow Temperature Range: 68−86 ° F ( 20−30 ° C ) Water pH: 5.5 - 8.0 (Highly Adaptable) Placement: Anywhere

Bali Green Slimer Acropora: The Fast-Growing SPS The Bali Green Slimer Acropora (Acropora yongei) is one of the most popular and iconic Small Polyp Stony (SPS) corals in the reef aquarium hobby. Prized for its exceptionally fast growth rate and striking, consistent coloration, this coral grows in a dense, branching or staghorn morphology. It is a highly valued coral, as it is one of the easiest Acropora species to frag and propagate. The Green Slimer is characterized by its vibrant neon green color across its body and polyps, and it often has purple or blue growth tips when thriving under intense light. Its name "Slimer" comes from the copious amounts of mucus it produces when stressed or handled, a defense mechanism common among Acropora species. This coral demands expert care, requiring immaculate and highly stable water chemistry, intense light, and turbulent water flow. As a true Scleractinia (reef-building) coral, the Bali Green Slimer is a showpiece, but it is highly sensitive to fluctuations in alkalinity and is prone to various types of coral tissue necrosis (STN/RTN) if stressed. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: This coral is primarily Photosynthetic. It hosts symbiotic zooxanthellae algae, which provide the vast majority of its energy needs through light. Feeding: While photosynthesis is key, supplemental feeding is highly beneficial due to its fast growth. Target feed the coral polyps 2-3 times per week with high-quality, fine particulate foods, such as cyclops, rotifers, or commercial coral powders. Shut off powerheads briefly during target feeding to allow the food to settle. Reef Compatibility: It is Reef Safe but requires careful placement. Like most Acropora, it can extend stinging mesenterial filaments to defend territory. It needs 6 inches or more of separation from soft corals and Large Polyp Stony (LPS) corals, as it will likely be chemically or physically damaged by them. Temperament: Peaceful toward fish and motile invertebrates, but Highly Aggressive/Territorial toward other corals. It thrives best in a dedicated SPS-dominant system. Water Requirements: Requires expert-level water stability with unwavering parameters: Alkalinity (dKH 8.0-9.0), Calcium (420-450 ppm), and Magnesium (1300-1400 ppm). Demands intense lighting (PAR 300-550+) and very strong, turbulent water flow to keep tissue healthy and prevent dead spots. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Acropora yongei (often incorrectly sold as Acropora muricata) Primary Common Name: Bali Green Slimer Acropora Other Common Names: Green Slimer Acro, Green Staghorn Acropora, Acropora yongei Origin: Indo-Pacific (Bali, Fiji, Australia, Indonesia) Max Size: Can grow into large colonies (12+ inches in captivity) Temperament: Peaceful (Aggressive/Territorial toward other corals) Diet: Photosynthetic (Zooxanthellate; benefits from feeding) Minimum Tank Size: 75 Gallons (established, stable reef) Reef Compatibility: Yes, but requires expert-level spacing and stability. Care Level: Advanced / Expert

Bubble Yum Acropora: The Pink and Green Delight The Bubble Yum Acropora (Acropora species, likely a variety of A. microclados or A. loripes) is a highly sought-after and collectible Small Polyp Stony (SPS) coral in the reef aquarium hobby. This coral is a prized specimen known for its unique and stunning dual coloration: a vibrant neon green body that beautifully contrasts with bright pink to magenta growth tips and occasionally pink polyps, reminiscent of bubblegum. Like many designer Acropora strains, the Bubble Yum grows in a dense, branching or bottlebrush morphology, demanding specific environmental conditions to display its signature colors. This coral is considered Expert Only due to its extreme sensitivity. It is a true Scleractinia (reef-building) coral that requires pristine, unwavering water chemistry, high calcium/alkalinity levels, intense lighting, and robust, turbulent flow. Maintaining the intense pink and green coloration requires precise control over lighting spectrum (often demanding higher blue spectrum light) and nutrients, making it a true showpiece coral for the dedicated, advanced hobbyist. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: This coral is primarily Photosynthetic. It hosts symbiotic zooxanthellae algae, which provide the vast majority of its energy needs through high light absorption. Feeding: Supplemental feeding is highly recommended to encourage optimal growth and color saturation. Target feed the polyps 2-3 times per week with high-quality, fine particulate foods, such as cyclops, rotifers, or commercial amino acid solutions and coral powders. Reef Compatibility: It is Reef Safe but extremely Territorial. Like all Acropora species, it may extend stinging mesenterial filaments or sweeper tentacles. It requires at least 6-8 inches of distance from all other corals (both SPS and LPS), as contact will result in tissue loss for both parties. Temperament: Peaceful toward fish and motile invertebrates, but Highly Aggressive/Territorial toward other corals. It should be placed in the upper portion of the tank to maximize light and flow exposure, away from competitors. Water Requirements: Requires expert-level water stability; any fluctuation in alkalinity (dKH) can cause immediate stress. Critical parameters: Alkalinity (dKH 8.0-9.5), Calcium (420-450 ppm), and Magnesium (1300-1400 ppm). Demands intense lighting (PAR 350-550+) and very strong, turbulent water flow to prevent detritus buildup. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Acropora sp. (Likely A. microclados or A. loripes variant) Primary Common Name: Bubble Yum Acropora Other Common Names: Bubblegum Acro, Pink Tip Green Acro, Pink & Green Acropora Origin: Cultured/Maricultured (Originals from the Indo-Pacific) Max Size: Can grow into large colonies (6-12+ inches) Temperament: Peaceful (Aggressive/Territorial toward other corals) Diet: Photosynthetic (Zooxanthellate; benefits heavily from feeding) Minimum Tank Size: 75 Gallons (Established, dedicated SPS reef) Reef Compatibility: Yes, but requires expert-level spacing and stability. Care Level: Expert

Red Dragon Acropora: The Deep Red Icon The Red Dragon Acropora (Acropora species, widely recognized as a strain of Acropora formosa or A. caroliniana) is arguably the most famous and highly coveted Small Polyp Stony (SPS) coral in the reef aquarium hobby. This coral is renowned for its unmatched deep red or burgundy coloration on its branches and polyps, combined with brilliant white or pale pink growth tips, creating a fiery, almost metallic appearance. The Red Dragon grows in a delicate, open, and slightly straggly branching morphology, unlike the denser structures of many other Acropora strains. Its dramatic color is due to a high concentration of non-fluorescent red pigmentation (chromoprotein), which requires a specific set of environmental factors—most notably ultra-low nutrient levels and high-intensity lighting—to fully develop. This is an Expert-Only coral. It is extremely sensitive to changes in water chemistry and is often used as a canary in the coal mine for water quality, as the deep red color will quickly fade to brown if nutrients (nitrate/phosphate) rise above trace levels or if alkalinity fluctuates. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: This coral is primarily Photosynthetic. It relies heavily on the energy produced by its symbiotic zooxanthellae algae, which requires intense light. Feeding: While light is critical, supplemental feeding is recommended, especially for frag growth. Target feed the coral polyps 2-3 times per week with high-quality, fine planktonic foods, such as amino acid solutions, coral powders, or fine rotifers. Nutrient control is paramount, so feeding must be balanced with filtration. Reef Compatibility: It is Reef Safe but extremely Territorial. Like all Acropora species, it is a hard coral and is chemically or physically aggressive toward its neighbors. It requires at least 6-8 inches of clearance from all other corals to prevent tissue loss from stinging or chemical aggression. Temperament: Peaceful toward fish and motile invertebrates, but Highly Aggressive/Territorial toward other corals. It demands placement in the upper half of the aquarium under the strongest lighting and flow. Water Requirements: Requires zero tolerance for instability. The tank must be biologically mature with ultra-low nutrient levels (Nitrate < 5 ppm, Phosphate < 0.05 ppm). Critical parameters: Alkalinity (dKH 8.0-8.5), Calcium (420-450 ppm), and Magnesium (1300-1400 ppm). Demands very intense, high-quality lighting (PAR 400-600+) and very strong, laminar water flow to prevent dead spots and enhance color. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Acropora sp. (Likely a variant of A. formosa) Primary Common Name: Red Dragon Acropora Other Common Names: Red Dragon Acro, Deep Red Acropora Origin: Cultured/Maricultured (Originals from the Indo-Pacific) Max Size: Can grow into large, intricate colonies (8-15+ inches) Temperament: Peaceful (Aggressive/Territorial toward other corals) Diet: Photosynthetic (Zooxanthellate; benefits from plankton/aminos) Minimum Tank Size: 75 Gallons (Established, dedicated SPS reef) Reef Compatibility: Yes, but requires expert-level spacing and stability. Care Level: Expert Only

Ice Cap Acropora: The Blue Tipped Showpiece The Ice Cap Acropora (Acropora millepora) is one of the most recognized and sought-after Small Polyp Stony (SPS) corals, valued for its compact growth structure and stunning coloration. This specific strain of A. millepora is characterized by a dense, bottlebrush or tabling morphology with thick branches covered in fuzzy, extended polyps, giving it a soft appearance despite its hard, calcareous skeleton. The name "Ice Cap" is derived from its signature look: a vibrant, uniform body color—typically a rich emerald green or deep teal—that contrasts dramatically with its intense, electric blue or white growth tips. This high-contrast coloration makes it a centerpiece in any dedicated SPS reef tank. The color intensity is heavily dependent on the quality and spectrum of lighting provided. While considered slightly hardier than some other Acropora species, the Ice Cap Acropora still requires advanced care, demanding exceptional water stability, intense light, and rigorous adherence to calcium, alkalinity, and magnesium supplementation to support its dense skeleton. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: This coral is primarily Photosynthetic. It relies almost entirely on the energy produced by its symbiotic zooxanthellae algae, thriving under high light intensity. Feeding: Supplemental feeding is highly beneficial for faster and denser growth. Target feed the coral polyps 2-3 times per week with very fine particulate foods, such as cyclops, rotifers, or high-quality amino acid solutions and commercial coral powders. A. millepora polyps are known to extend well, making them receptive to feeding. Reef Compatibility: It is Reef Safe but fiercely Territorial. Like all Acropora, it is a hard coral and is aggressive toward neighboring corals. It requires 6 inches or more of clearance from other corals (SPS and LPS) to prevent damage from stinging cells or chemical warfare. Temperament: Peaceful toward fish and motile invertebrates, but Highly Aggressive/Territorial toward other corals. Place it in the middle to upper half of the tank to maximize light and ensure it receives turbulent flow. Water Requirements: Requires advanced water stability. The tank must be mature with low nutrients (Nitrate < 10 ppm, Phosphate < 0.1 ppm). Critical parameters: Alkalinity (dKH 8.0-9.5), Calcium (420-450 ppm), and Magnesium (1300-1400 ppm). Demands intense, high-PAR lighting (PAR 300-500+) and strong, turbulent water flow to prevent detritus buildup within the dense branches. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Acropora millepora (Specific strain) Primary Common Name: Ice Cap Acropora Other Common Names: Ice Cap Milly, Blue Tip Millepora Origin: Cultured/Maricultured (Originals from the Indo-Pacific) Max Size:** Can grow into large, dense colonies (6-12+ inches) Temperament: Peaceful (Aggressive/Territorial toward other corals) Diet: Photosynthetic (Zooxanthellate; benefits from feeding) Minimum Tank Size: 75 Gallons (Established, dedicated SPS reef) Reef Compatibility: Yes, but requires expert-level spacing and stability.Care Level: Advanced

Indo Queen Acropora: The Deep Water Beauty The Indo Queen Acropora (Acropora species, often believed to be a deeper water variant of A. tenuis or a similar branching species) is a highly desirable and relatively rare strain of Small Polyp Stony (SPS) coral. This coral is admired for its beautiful and complex color pattern, typically featuring a dark blue or purple base with striking bright green or neon yellow polyps that contrast vividly against the skeletal body. Unlike some shallower water Acropora that grow densely, the Indo Queen often exhibits a more open, delicately branching structure, characteristic of corals found in lower-light environments. However, to maintain its intense color saturation in the aquarium, it still requires controlled, high-quality lighting, often emphasizing the blue spectrum. Like all collector Acropora strains, the Indo Queen demands advanced to expert care. It requires pristine, stable water chemistry, especially consistent alkalinity and ultra-low nutrient levels (ULNS), to prevent the dark base from fading or the coral from browning (browning out). Diet & Compatibility: Diet: This coral is primarily Photosynthetic. It hosts symbiotic zooxanthellae algae, which provide the vast majority of its energy needs through light absorption. Feeding: Supplemental feeding is strongly recommended to support its nutritional needs and growth. Target feed the coral polyps 2-3 times per week with fine, high-quality particulate foods, such as amino acid solutions, cyclops, or commercial coral powders. Nutrient control (ULNS) must be maintained even while feeding. Reef Compatibility: It is Reef Safe but intensely Territorial. As a true Scleractinia, it is highly aggressive toward adjacent corals. It requires 6 inches or more of clearance from all other corals to prevent chemical or physical warfare via stinging cells. Temperament: Peaceful toward fish and motile invertebrates, but Highly Aggressive/Territorial toward other corals. Placement should be in the mid-to-upper tank area under controlled lighting and moderate to strong, turbulent water flow. Water Requirements: Requires expert-level water stability and ultra-low nutrient levels. Any fluctuations in alkalinity (dKH) can cause rapid tissue loss (RTN/STN). Critical parameters: Alkalinity (dKH 8.0-9.0), Calcium (420-450 ppm), and Magnesium (1300-1400 ppm). Demands intense, high-quality lighting (PAR 300-450+) and strong water flow. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Acropora sp. (Likely a variant of A. tenuis or similar) Primary Common Name: Indo Queen Acropora Other Common Names: Blue Base Green Tip Acro, Deepwater Blue Acropora Origin: Cultured/Maricultured (Originals from Indonesia/Indo-Pacific) Max Size: Can grow into large, open colonies (8-15+ inches) Temperament: Peaceful (Aggressive/Territorial toward other corals) Diet: Photosynthetic (Zooxanthellate; benefits from feeding) Minimum Tank Size: 75 Gallons (Established, dedicated SPS reef) Reef Compatibility: Yes, but requires expert-level spacing and stability. Care Level: Advanced / Expert

Lilac Attack Acropora: The Purple and Green Masterpiece The Lilac Attack Acropora (Acropora species, often considered a variation of A. tortuosa or a similar branching strain) is a premium, high-value, and deeply sought-after Small Polyp Stony (SPS) coral. This designer strain is celebrated for its incredible contrast: a vibrant, dense electric purple or lilac-colored base and branches that are tipped with striking neon green or yellow growth tips and polyps. The intense, saturated purple coloration of the Lilac Attack is dependent on specific conditions, usually requiring ultra-low nutrient levels (ULNS) and high-intensity, blue-spectrum lighting. It typically grows in a tight, twisting, or clustered branching formation. This coral is often used as a benchmark for water quality in advanced reef systems. Due to its high sensitivity and reliance on precise environmental control to maintain its signature colors, the Lilac Attack Acropora is strictly reserved for the Expert-Only hobbyist who can consistently maintain highly stable water parameters without fluctuations. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: This coral is primarily Photosynthetic. It relies almost entirely on the energy derived from its symbiotic zooxanthellae algae, thriving under strong light. Feeding: Supplemental feeding is beneficial but must be balanced carefully against nutrient levels. Target feed the coral polyps 2-3 times per week with high-quality, fine particulate foods, such as amino acid solutions, cyclops, or fine coral powders. In a ULNS system, feeding is often necessary to support the polyps. Reef Compatibility: It is Reef Safe but fiercely Territorial. Like all Acropora, it possesses stinging cells and is chemically aggressive toward neighbors. It requires a generous 6-8 inches or more of clearance from all other corals to prevent damage. Temperament: Peaceful toward fish and motile invertebrates, but Highly Aggressive/Territorial toward other corals. This specific strain is named for its mesmerizing, iridescent deep blue or violet base that coats the walls (septa/coenosteum), often contrasted by bright green or neon yellow centers (corallite mouths). The "Skull" name may refer to the recessed, pitted appearance of the corallites against the smooth blue tissue. The blue coloration is highly dependent on blue-spectrum lighting. The Blue Skull Favia grows in an encrusting and massive or dome-shaped morphology, with individual corallites clearly separated by pronounced walls. It is considered a Hardy LPS coral, making it an excellent choice for intermediate hobbyists. It requires stable water parameters and protection from high light, which can cause its vibrant blue to fade or bleach. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: This coral is a Mixotroph, meaning it is primarily Photosynthetic but is also an effective Carnivore. It relies on zooxanthellae for most of its energy. Feeding: Supplemental target feeding is highly beneficial for faster growth and maintaining health. Its mouths are visible and receptive, especially at night. Feed 2-3 times per week with meaty foods, such as mysis shrimp, brine shrimp, cyclops, or fine coral foods like Reef Roids and amino acid solutions. Reef Compatibility: It is Reef Safe but is Aggressive. Favia corals, like many other brain corals, extend long, potent sweeper tentacles at night to defend their territory. It is essential to give the Blue Skull Favia at least 3-4 inches of clear space from all neighboring corals, particularly when placed near passive or delicate species. Temperament: Peaceful toward fish and motile invertebrates, but Aggressive/Territorial toward other corals. It should be positioned on mid-to-lower rockwork where it receives moderate, indirect light and moderate water flow. Avoid excessive flow directly on the tissue. Water Requirements: Requires stable parameters. The tank should be mature with low to moderate nutrient levels (Nitrate 5-10 ppm, Phosphate 0.05-0.1 ppm). Critical parameters: Alkalinity (dKH 8.0-9.5), Calcium (400-450 ppm), and Magnesium (1250-1350 ppm). Demands Moderate PAR lighting (100-200 PAR). Quick Facts Scientific Name: Favia sp. (Specific Strain) Primary Common Name: Fruit Loops Zoa Other Common Names: Polychromatic Zoa, Rainbow Zoanthid Origin: Cultured/Maricultured (Originals from the Indo-Pacific) Max Size: Polyps typically 0.5 to 1 inch in diameter, forms large mats Temperament: Peaceful ( Competitive via overgrowth; potentially toxic ) Diet: Photosynthetic and Carnivore (Benefits from target feeding) Minimum Tank Size: 10 Gallons (Established reef) Reef Compatibility: Yes (Excellent, durable beginner coral) Care Level: Easy

Halle Berry Zoa: The Dramatic Black and Red Beauty The Halle Berry Zoa (Zoanthus species) is an iconic and highly collectible strain of Zoanthid (Colonial Anemone/Polyp). Zoanthids are prized for their ease of care, resilience, and unique, high-contrast coloration. This specific strain is named for its striking and intense beauty, characterized by a powerful contrast between dark and bright colors. It typically features a deep, dark black, brown, or purplish skirt (tentacles) that forms a dramatic backdrop. This is offset by a highly visible, contrasting oral disk (face) in bright metallic red, deep orange, or cherry red. The dark base makes the fluorescent center glow intensely, creating a captivating focal point. The Halle Berry Zoa grows in a colonial, matting morphology, spreading over rockwork and forming dense clusters. It is considered an Easy care coral and is highly durable, thriving in a variety of established reef tank conditions. ⚠️ CRITICAL SAFETY WARNING: PALYTOXIN ⚠️ Zoanthids, especially certain species, may contain Palytoxin, which can be extremely hazardous if it enters the bloodstream, is ingested, or becomes aerosolized (e.g., by handling damaged polyps, scrubbing rocks, or boiling). Always wear appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE), including gloves and eye protection, when handling Zoanthids. Never use boiling water or tools that may atomize the coral material. Consult a physician immediately if exposed. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: This coral is primarily Photosynthetic (deriving energy from symbiotic algae, zooxanthellae) but is also a highly efficient Filter Feeder/Carnivore. Feeding: Zoanthids feed readily and greatly benefit from targeted feeding, which encourages larger polyp size and faster colony growth. Target feed 2-3 times per week with shrimp eggs, rotifers, brine shrimp, or fine coral food powders. Reef Compatibility: It is Reef Safe and generally Passive. Zoanthids do not actively sting neighbors, but they will aggressively compete for space by growing over other corals. Provide space to prevent overgrowth. Temperament: Peaceful toward fish and motile invertebrates, and Competitive toward other corals. It should be positioned on low to mid-rockwork where it receives Moderate PAR lighting (75-150 PAR), which is often ideal for maximizing the color contrast, and moderate, non-turbulent water flow to keep the colony clean and deliver food. Water Requirements:** Requires stable parameters. Zoanthids are tolerant of slightly higher nutrient levels than SPS. Target ranges: Alkalinity (dKH 7.5-10.0), Calcium (400-450 ppm), and Magnesium (1250-1400 ppm). Quick Facts Scientific Name: Zoanthus sp. (Specific Strain) Primary Common Name: Halle Berry Zoa Other Common Names: Black Skirt Red Face Zoa, Metallic Red Zoanthid Origin: Cultured/Maricultured (Originals from the Indo-Pacific) Max Size: Polyps typically 0.5 to 0.75 inches in diameter, forms large mats Temperament: Peaceful ( Competitive via overgrowth; potentially toxic ) Diet: Photosynthetic and Carnivore (Benefits from target feeding) Minimum Tank Size: 10 Gallons (Established reef) Reef Compatibility: Yes (Excellent, durable beginner coral) Care Level: Easy

Not beautiful, but rare and unusual, the African knifefish has large eyes, barbs, and a long, thin, light chocolate body. Wild-caught in Nigeria, they are quite hardy and prefer live or frozen blood worms and similar food. These guys like to school in the wild, and if you have three in your fish tank they will always stick together. Quick Facts Scientific Name Xenomystus nigri Origin West and Central Africa Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 8" Lifespan 10+ years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 5" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants, driftwood and tubes or caves to hide in, plus dim lighting. They are most active at night. Feeding: Feed frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp once a day. Some learn to take sinking pellets. Tankmates: They are shy and peaceful, so keep them with calm community fish too large to fit in their mouth. Good to know: African knifefish can make soft barking sounds and swim backward as easily as forward.

Pintail Fairy Wrasse: The Elegant & Peaceful Pin-tail The Pintail Fairy Wrasse (Cirrhilabrus lanceolatus), also known as the Lanceolate Wrasse , is a captivating and elegant species known for its stunning colors and peaceful nature. This beautiful wrasse showcases a brilliant mix of hues, with a sleek body that transitions from a deep blue on its back to a vibrant reddish-orange on its underside. Its defining feature is its unique, elongated, and pointed lanceolate tail , which sets it apart from other wrasses. The Pintail Fairy Wrasse is an active, open-water swimmer that adds a dynamic and mesmerizing presence to a well-established marine aquarium . It is a fantastic choice for a community tank, as it is completely reef-safe and will not harm corals or most invertebrates. Why the Lanceolate Wrasse is a Great Choice: Unique Appearance: Its elongated, pointed tail and brilliant colors make it a true showpiece. Completely Reef-Safe: It will not harm corals, clams, or most other invertebrates. Peaceful Temperament: It is a non-aggressive species that coexists well with other peaceful fish. Active & Mesmerizing: It constantly swims in the water column, adding life and movement to the tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Cirrhilabrus lanceolatus Origin: Indo-Pacific Reefs Max Size: 4.5 inches Lifespan: 5-7 years Diet: Carnivore. Primarily feeds on meaty foods such as shrimp, krill, and prepared foods. Shipping Size: 2-3 inches

Bucephalandra theia Buce plants, or bucephalandra, became popular for planted aquariums about a decade ago and are favored by beginner and advanced aquarium aquascapers. The buce plant grows slow, does not need special lighting or CO2 and handles cooler temperatures. Bucephalandra will not tolerate high temperatures so warmer tropical fish tanks that are 80 degrees are not a good fit. Each order comes with one small loose bunch. Look to purchase binder, or just use rubberbands for the short term to attach the buce plant to a rock or driftwood. Scientific Name: Bucephalandra theia Shipping Size: Small bunch ready to attach to plant on rock or wood subtrate

Mangrove: The Rhizophora Propagule The Mangrove (Rhizophora mangle), often referred to simply by its genus Rhizophora , is the most common mangrove species kept in the marine aquarium hobby. Famous for its "walking" roots, this salt-tolerant tree is typically acquired as a long, cigar-shaped propagule (seed pod). It is an excellent choice for aquarists looking to create a lagoon biotope or enhance their filtration system naturally. In the wild, Rhizophora trees form dense coastal forests that protect shorelines. In the home aquarium, they are prized for their aesthetic appeal and their utility as a nutrient export mechanism. As the plant grows, it consumes Nitrates and Phosphates from the water column, helping to outcompete nuisance algae. Unlike macroalgae, mangroves are vascular plants that grow slowly and require their leaves to be exposed to the air. Successful care of Rhizophora requires understanding its unique biology. It is not fully aquatic; the roots must be submerged in saltwater (or rooted in sand/mud), but the leaves and upper stem must remain above the waterline . If fully submerged, the plant will eventually perish. They are architectural beauties that can eventually develop complex prop roots, adding a dramatic, naturalistic look to open-top tanks or refugiums. Care & Compatibility: Nutrient Control: This plant is a Phosphate and Nitrate sponge . It incorporates these nutrients into its tissue as it grows. Because it is a slow grower compared to algae like Chaetomorpha, it is best used for maintenance and stability rather than rapid nutrient crashes. Placement: Place the propagule in the sump, overflow box, or directly in the display tank. You can use a floating raft or wedge the pod between rocks. Ensure the growth tip is strictly emergent (in the air). Lighting: Rhizophora requires moderate to strong illumination to thrive. A standard reef light is often sufficient if the plant is positioned correctly, but a dedicated 6,500K freshwater plant light or daylight bulb focused on the leaves will yield the best growth rates. Magnesium Dependency: Mangroves utilize Magnesium to regulate their salt processing. In systems with many mangroves, magnesium levels can drop significantly. Regular testing and dosing are required to prevent the leaves from yellowing. Salt Spray Removal: The plant excretes excess salt through pores in its leaves. This manifests as white crystals. You must mist the leaves with fresh water 2-3 times a week to wash this salt away, or the leaves will burn and drop. Root System: The root system is robust and can damage silicone seals or plastic baffles if allowed to grow unchecked in a tight space. Trimming roots is possible but should be done carefully. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Rhizophora mangle Common Name: Mangrove, Walking Tree Plant Type: Vascular Marine Plant (Halophyte) Origin: Tropical Atlantic / Indo-Pacific Max Size: Can grow into a tree (bonsai techniques required in captivity) Placement: Roots submerged, Leaves in air Lighting: Moderate to High (Daylight spectrum) Supplements: Requires Magnesium Reef Compatibility: Reef Safe (Excellent for refugiums)

Clown Grouper: The Vibrant Ambush Predator The Clown Grouper (Pogonoperca punctata), also widely known as the Spotted Soapfish or Leaflike Grouper , is an extraordinary marine species coveted for its striking patterns and unique behavioral adaptations. Characterized by a deep brown or black body covered in fine white spots and punctuated by large, irregular white blotches, this fish serves as a master of camouflage in the reef environment. Native to the Indo-Pacific , from the Red Sea to the Line Islands, the Clown Grouper is a medium-sized predator that can reach a maximum length of approximately 13 inches (33 cm). It is often found hiding in caves or under ledges during the day. A distinctive feature of this species is its ability to exude a toxic mucus (grammistin) from its skin when stressed or threatened, which can be lethal to tankmates in confined spaces. For this reason, a minimum aquarium size of 100 to 125 gallons with high-quality protein skimming is essential. While juveniles are exceptionally beautiful and resemble drifting leaves, the Clown Grouper is a dedicated predator that grows quickly. It is generally peaceful toward any fish it cannot fit into its mouth, but its ambush-predatory nature must always be considered when choosing tankmates. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: This species is a Carnivore . In the wild, it feeds on small fish and crustaceans. In the home aquarium, it should be offered a variety of meaty seafood, including chopped shrimp , scallops, marine fish flesh, and frozen preparations like silversides. It is best to avoid feeder goldfish to prevent long-term nutritional issues. Feeding: Feed 3-4 times a week for adults. They are ambush hunters and may wait for food to drift near their hiding spot before striking with surprising speed. Reef Compatibility: It is Reef Safe With Caution . The Clown Grouper will not bother corals or anemones, but it will consume any ornamental shrimp , crabs, or small fish (such as blennies or gobies) that it can swallow. Temperament: It is Semi-Aggressive . It is generally shy and reclusive but highly predatory toward smaller inhabitants. Ideal tankmates include larger angels, tangs, and other robust semi-aggressive fish. Avoid keeping it with overly aggressive species that might stress it, triggering its toxic mucus defense. Special Note: The "Soapfish" toxin (grammistin) can "soap" an aquarium if the fish is severely harassed or dies, potentially killing all other inhabitants. Ensure a stress-free environment and heavy carbon filtration . Quick Facts Scientific Name: Pogonoperca punctata Primary Common Name: Clown Grouper Other Common Names: Spotted Soapfish, Leaflike Grouper, Snowflake Soapfish Origin: Indo-Pacific Max Size: 13 inches (33 cm) Temperament: Semi-Aggressive / Predatory ( Toxic Mucus ) Diet: Carnivore (Meaty seafood and frozen preparations) Minimum Tank Size: 100+ Gallons Reef Compatibility: With Caution (Will eat small fish and invertebrates)

Just like a little gold marble, these guys will roll about the waters of your fish tank. Not the most agile of fish, they sure are cute. And hardy, and they like to breed. Quick Facts Scientific Name Poecilia sphenops (balloon-bodied aquarium strain) Origin Mexico and Central America (wild ancestors); aquarium-bred Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2½–3" Lifespan 3–4 years Diet Omnivore (needs plant matter) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.5–8.5 (hard water) Group Size Keep more females than males Shipping Size Approx. 1¼" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them hard, alkaline water with plants and gentle filtration, since balloon mollies are slower swimmers than other mollies. Aquarium salt is optional; they also do well in brackish tanks. Feeding: Feed small amounts of a quality flake that includes vegetable matter once or twice a day. They also enjoy algae wafers. Avoid overfeeding, since balloon mollies are prone to bloating. Tankmates: Mollies get along with most peaceful community fish that like similar hard water, such as platies, swordtails, guppies, danios, rainbowfish, corydoras and plecos. Avoid fin-nippers and soft-water specialists. Keeping more females than males keeps any one female from being harassed. Good to know: The balloon shape comes from a shortened, curved spine bred into this strain, so they swim more slowly. Feed them where they can reach food easily and don't house them with fast, pushy eaters.

The Dalmatian sailfin molly is best kept with two females to one male, so the male does not "harass" the female to a stressful level. A purchase of a single molly or a small school avoids this situation, but if you really want an active pair, we offer that too. Quick Facts Scientific Name Poecilia latipinna / P. velifera (aquarium-bred) Origin Southeastern U.S. and Mexico (wild ancestors); aquarium-bred Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Peaceful (males can chase females and rival males) Adult Size Up to 4–5" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (needs plant matter) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.5–8.5 (hard water) Group Size Keep more females than males Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give sailfins hard, alkaline water with plants, open swimming space and good filtration. Aquarium salt is optional; they also do well in brackish tanks. Feeding: Mollies graze on algae, so feed a quality flake that includes vegetable matter once or twice a day. They also enjoy algae wafers and frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Mollies get along with most peaceful community fish that like similar hard water, such as platies, swordtails, guppies, danios, rainbowfish, corydoras and plecos. Avoid fin-nippers and soft-water specialists. Keeping more females than males keeps any one female from being harassed. Good to know: Male sailfins raise their tall dorsal fin to show off to females and rival males. Their sails grow fuller as they mature, so juveniles may not show a full sail yet.

Green sailfin mollies are the closest relatives to the original sailfin mollies of Central America, and males can be quite aggressive. To keep peace in the aquarium, or at least peace for a lone female, two females to one male is recommended, or a small school. Purple variegated guppies have very large, flowing fins and deep purple highlights on the body with lavender spotted tails. Females not so much. These guppies come from Thailand and the breeder is often out, so when we can stock them we make sure we do! Quick Facts Scientific Name Poecilia reticulata Origin Northern South America (captive-bred in Thailand) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Sold as a pair (1 male + 1 female) Shipping Size Approx. 1¼" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and plenty of plants, including some floating plants where babies can hide. Guppies like slightly hard water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Guppies get along with other small, peaceful fish such as platies, mollies, corydoras, small tetras and rasboras. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs and larger fish that could eat them. Breeding: Guppies are livebearers and breed easily. Females give birth to live babies about once a month, and adults will eat the babies, so thick plants give them a place to hide. Good to know: Males carry the big fins and purple color; females are plainer but needed for breeding.

Green Foxtail Green foxtail, or green myrio, is native to Central America and can tolerate a wide temperature range. The plant is feathery and delicate, provides a good refuge for smaller species. Lighting moderate. Scientific Name: Myriophyllum pinnatum Shipping Size: Bunched five plants with lead weight, approx. six inches tall

Of course, all freshwater angelfish originated in South America, but this particular color variety was developed by fish breeder Ken Kennedy in Pinoy, Philippine Islands. Hence, this angelfish originated there and will always be considered a Filipino angel. These fish have a nice, subtle blue color gene that gets more and more dominant as the angelfish ages. This variety, to be called a Pinoy Angelfish, must be related to the original strain from Pinoy. (Please do not confuse these with lower-priced blue zebra angelfish. For reasons unknown (well, probably to help sell them), sites are calling simple blue zebra angelfish "pinoy blue zebra angelfish." They aren't.) Quick Facts Scientific Name Pterophyllum scalare Origin Philippines (originally South America) Care Level Easy Temperament Semi-aggressive (territorial when pairing) Adult Size Up to 6" long and 8" tall Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them tall plants or driftwood, a heater and a gentle filter. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Choose peaceful fish too large to swallow, such as larger tetras, corydoras, plecos, rams, gouramis and peaceful barbs. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs, and small fish like neon tetras that adult angels may eat. Breeding: Angelfish pair off and lay eggs on flat surfaces like broad leaves or slate. A breeding pair can become territorial, so give them room and places for other fish to retreat. Good to know: The blue color develops with age and is often hard to see until the fish reach about 3", so young fish may look mostly silver or black.

These little leopard cats like to swim around in a gang. Three is perfect for nearly any size aquarium. Quick Facts Scientific Name Corydoras julii Origin Brazil (lower Amazon) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 5–10 years Diet Omnivore (bottom feeder) Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a group of 3 Shipping Size Approx. 1–1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and a soft sand or smooth, fine gravel bottom. Plants, driftwood and a few shady spots help them feel secure. Corys are sensitive to salt and some medications (especially copper), so check labels before treating the tank. Feeding: Corys need their own food, not just leftovers. Feed sinking pellets or wafers once or twice a day so food reaches the bottom. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Corys get along with almost any peaceful community fish, such as tetras, rasboras, livebearers, gouramis, angelfish and bettas. Avoid large fish that could swallow them and aggressive bottom dwellers. Good to know: Most "julii" corys in the trade are actually the near-identical false julii (C. trilineatus); care is the same for both.

Goldfish feeders are comprised of shortfin comets and are the same type of goldfish you would win at a circus. Bright red and white, and YUMMY. Quick Facts Scientific Name Carassius auratus Origin China (captive-bred) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 8–10" Lifespan 10–20 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 50–75°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Sold as a pack of 20 Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Comets are fast, active swimmers that grow big and produce a lot of waste. They do very well in outdoor ponds; indoors, use a strong filter. Feeding: Feed a quality goldfish flake or pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp and bloodworms. Tankmates: Keep them with other comets, shubunkins and pond fish. Good to know: These are common comet goldfish. If kept as pets rather than feeders, they grow quickly and do well in ponds.

Phoenix rasbora, or rasbora merah, with its bright red highlights, is nevertheless a small fish, just like its cousin the chili rasbora. A group of six would make them feel safer and much easier to follow in the fish tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name Boraras merah Origin Borneo (Kalimantan), Indonesia Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to ¾" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.0 Group Size Sold as a school of 6 Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them dense plants, floating plants, a dark substrate and gentle filtration (a sponge filter is ideal, since they are small enough to be pulled into strong intakes). Soft, slightly acidic water brings out their best color. Feeding: Feed crushed flake or micro pellets once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other tiny, peaceful fish such as other micro rasboras, small tetras, pygmy corydoras, otocinclus and dwarf shrimp. Avoid large or boisterous fish, which can eat or stress them. Good to know: Micro rasboras show their best color and natural schooling behavior in larger groups and well-planted tanks.

When these fish move together the visuals are attractive, and with a mix of males and females you will see much more activity. Quick Facts Scientific Name Nematobrycon palmeri Origin Pacific slope of Colombia (San Juan and Atrato rivers) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 5 Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a dark substrate, which brings out their color. Keep a lid on the tank, since tetras can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, rasboras, danios, corydoras, dwarf cichlids, gouramis and livebearers. Good to know: Tetras feel safer and show better color in a group. A larger school also spreads out any chasing.

The latest gene-spliced treat from the Spectrum company (via their secret lab in Singapore) is the Starfire Red Gourami. The parent of the red gourami is a pearl gourami, but with genetic magic, this gourami is a super bright fluorescent red. These fish are peaceful and can be added to any aquarium that would be suitable for a standard pearl gourami. Quick Facts Scientific Name Trichopodus leerii (genetically modified) Origin Farm-raised (genetically modified) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 4–5" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 77–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Breathes Air Yes – labyrinth fish take air from the surface Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and plenty of plants, with some open space for swimming. Keep a lid on the tank and leave a gap of air above the water, since gouramis breathe from the surface. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as tetras, rasboras, corydoras and peaceful barbs. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs. Good to know: GloFish colors look brightest under a blue or actinic LED light. Care is the same as for a regular pearl gourami.

Guppy Grass Just as the common name implies, this floating green mass provides a perfect haven for baby guppies. Found throughout North America, now it can be found in your fish tank. Scientific Name: Najas guadalupensis Shipping Size: One two inch cup Approx. 4 oz

Reds and blues are some of the prettiest and easiest-to-spot colors in an aquarium. That is just one of the reasons these fish are so popular. Quick Facts Scientific Name Paracheirodon innesi Origin Upper Amazon (Peru, Colombia, Brazil); mostly farm-raised Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1¼" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 5.5–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 8 Shipping Size Approx. ½–1" Care Guide Tank setup: These small tetras do best in a planted tank with soft, slightly acidic water, a dark substrate, driftwood, floating plants and gentle filtration. A larger school makes them more confident and colorful. Feeding: Feed small amounts of micro pellets or crushed flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other small, peaceful fish like rasboras, small tetras, pencilfish, pygmy corydoras, otocinclus and dwarf shrimp. Avoid large or boisterous fish that could eat or bully them. Good to know: Small tetras show their best color in a large school in a planted tank with soft lighting.

Despite the name, angelfish can be quite territorial, particularly when they pair up to breed in the aquarium. At that time, these fish do not act like angels. Gold Marble Angelfish are hardy and easy to care for. Each order comes with four angelfish, which are generally marble, silver, gold, and gold marble. Fish pictured here are representative only. If you are looking for a specific coloration, add a note to the order or simply allow us to choose one of our favorites for you! Quick Facts Scientific Name Pterophyllum scalare Origin Amazon basin, South America (captive-bred) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Semi-aggressive (territorial when pairing) Adult Size Up to 6" long and 8" tall Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 6 Shipping Size Approx. 1½–4" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them tall plants or driftwood, a heater and a gentle filter. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Choose peaceful fish too large to swallow, such as larger tetras, corydoras, plecos, rams, gouramis and peaceful barbs. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs, and small fish like neon tetras that adult angels may eat. Breeding: Angelfish pair off and lay eggs on flat surfaces like broad leaves or slate. A breeding pair can become territorial, so give them room and places for other fish to retreat. Good to know: In a group, two angelfish often pair off and claim part of the tank. If a pair forms and starts chasing the others, add more hiding places or rehome the extras.

Of course, all freshwater angelfish originated in South America, but this particular color variety was developed by fish breeder Ken Kennedy in Pinoy, Philippine Islands. Hence, this angelfish originated there and will always be considered a Filipino angel. These fish have a nice, subtle blue color gene that gets more and more dominant as the angelfish ages. This variety, to be called a Pinoy Angelfish, must be related to the original strain from Pinoy. (Please do not confuse these with lower-priced blue zebra angelfish. For reasons unknown (well, probably to help sell them), sites are calling simple blue zebra angelfish "pinoy blue zebra angelfish." They aren't.) Quick Facts Scientific Name Pterophyllum scalare Origin Philippines (originally South America) Care Level Easy Temperament Semi-aggressive (territorial when pairing) Adult Size Up to 6" long and 8" tall Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a group of 3 Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them tall plants or driftwood, a heater and a gentle filter. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Choose peaceful fish too large to swallow, such as larger tetras, corydoras, plecos, rams, gouramis and peaceful barbs. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs, and small fish like neon tetras that adult angels may eat. Breeding: Angelfish pair off and lay eggs on flat surfaces like broad leaves or slate. A breeding pair can become territorial, so give them room and places for other fish to retreat. Good to know: The blue color develops with age and is often hard to see until the fish reach about 3", so young fish may look mostly silver or black.

Angelfish are a hardy, popular species found in rivers all throughout South America, primarily the Amazon River and its tributaries. This family of aquarium fish all have the tall, wing-size fins giving the fish their namesake. Full black angels are bred to show a smoky to solid dark black body and fins, which makes a remarkable contrast in a planted aquarium. Our black angelfish are captive-bred in the USA and in Taiwan. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pterophyllum scalare Origin Amazon basin (bred in the USA and Taiwan) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Semi-aggressive (territorial when pairing) Adult Size Up to 6" long and 8" tall Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a group of 3 Shipping Size Approx. 1–4" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them tall plants or driftwood, a heater and a gentle filter. A breeding pair can become territorial, so give them room and places for other fish to retreat. Good to know: In a group, two angelfish often pair off and claim part of the tank. If a pair forms and starts chasing the others, add more hiding places or rehome the extras.

The German blue ram was bred in Germany a generation ago to provide a more colorful and hardier ram for the aquarium trade. Ram is short for the species name “ramirezi”, but it is also reminiscent of their tendency to butt heads like a terrestrial ram. These are beautiful fish whether captive-bred for color, such as German blue rams, or wild, such as Bolivian rams. They are peaceful, hardy and get along with other community species (except colorful fancy shrimp; they like them so much they eat them). Quick Facts Scientific Name Mikrogeophagus ramirezi (German blue variety) Origin Venezuela and Colombia (Orinoco basin); aquarium-bred Care Level Moderate (needs warm, clean, soft water) Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 2–4 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 80–86°F pH 5.0–7.0 Group Size Sold as a group of 4 Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Rams need warm, very clean, soft water. Give them a sand bottom, plants, driftwood, leaf litter and flat stones for spawning. Rams are sensitive to poor water quality. Feeding: Feed small amounts of quality micro pellets or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Rams do well with small, peaceful fish that like warm, soft water, such as tetras, rasboras, hatchetfish, corydoras and discus. They may eat small shrimp. Avoid large or boisterous fish. Good to know: Rams often form pairs and lay eggs on flat stones. Stable, warm water is the key to keeping them healthy.

Gold rams have a regal gold body with blue highlights. Ram is short for the species name “ramirezi”, but it is also reminiscent of their tendency to butt heads like a terrestrial ram. These are beautiful fish whether captive-bred for color, such as German blue rams, or wild, such as Bolivian rams. They are peaceful, hardy and get along with other species. Angelfish are a very popular species found in rivers all throughout the Amazon River basin. They are unique in appearance, very thin with long dorsal and ventral fins that can grow more than 6 inches long and 8 inches tall. Freshwater angels come in a variety of colors and patterns and get along with many other species, though it's best to keep them with fish too large for them to eat. Koi Angelfish have a marble pattern with an orange to red-orange head, named after the pond koi fish with a similar color pattern. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pterophyllum scalare Origin Amazon basin, South America (captive-bred) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Semi-aggressive (territorial when pairing) Adult Size Up to 6" long and 8" tall Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a group of 3 Shipping Size Approx. 1–4" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them tall plants or driftwood, a heater and a gentle filter. The Licorice Gourami is a beautiful species but requires low-pH water (under 7.0 would be fine) and is only one inch in size. This fish can be kept with other fish that can tolerate low pH and cannot be in the same aquarium as larger, aggressive fish. These gourami are wild-caught in ponds in Indonesia, and many come in and out of the trade as new ponds are discovered and old ponds are paved over. Unfortunately. But they are active breeders, and there are many in the wild. The colors vary on these small creatures, depending on the pond in which they are caught. Quick Facts Scientific Name Parosphromenus sp. Origin Malaysia and Indonesia (peat swamps) Care Level Difficult (for experienced keepers) Temperament Peaceful, shy Adult Size About 1–1½" Lifespan 3–4 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 4.0–6.5 (very soft water) Breathes Air Yes – labyrinth fish take air from the surface Group Size Sold as a group of 5 Shipping Size Approx. ¾" Care Guide Tank setup: These are blackwater fish: they need very soft, acidic water, dim lighting, a gentle filter and lots of plants and leaf litter. Peat or Indian almond leaves help tint and soften the water. Keep a lid on the tank and leave a gap of air above the water, since gouramis breathe from the surface and warm, humid air protects their labyrinth organ. Change small amounts of water often rather than large amounts at once. Feeding: Feed small amounts once or twice a day. Many will learn to take fine flake or micro pellets once settled. They also enjoy small frozen foods like brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them only with tiny, gentle fish that like the same soft, acidic water, such as small rasboras and pygmy corydoras. Avoid anything boisterous or larger. Good to know: Wild-caught licorice gouramis may ignore flake at first. Offer small frozen foods like brine shrimp until they settle in.

Marble angelfish are a very popular color variation due to their distinct black and white color pattern and hardy disposition. These fish grow to about six to eight inches in the aquarium. Angelfish are very adaptable to the aquarium environment and will mate when they reach three inches or more. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pterophyllum scalare Origin Amazon basin, South America (captive-bred) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Semi-aggressive (territorial when pairing) Adult Size Up to 6" long and 8" tall Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a group of 3 Shipping Size Medium: approx. 1–2" · Large: approx. 2–3" · Jumbo: approx. 4" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them tall plants or driftwood, a heater and a gentle filter.
