If a pair forms and starts chasing the others, add more hiding places or rehome the extras.

Two breeders are responsible for this special color variation of the wild blue ram, one in Taiwan and one in the Czech Republic. We select from either one when they become available, which is not very often. The black ram, or sometimes the 2x black ram, has the same behavior and care requirements as the German blue ram and is a peaceful aquarium fish. Though the body is dark, the fins display iridescent colors. These very difficult-to-breed fish are the most expensive ram on the market, but a great addition to any peaceful fish tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name Mikrogeophagus ramirezi (black variety) Origin Wild ancestors from Venezuela and Colombia; bred in Taiwan and the Czech Republic Care Level Moderate (needs warm, clean, soft water) Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 2–4 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 80–86°F pH 5.0–7.0 Group Size Sold as a group of 3 Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Rams need warm, very clean, soft water. Give them a sand bottom, plants, driftwood, leaf litter and flat stones for spawning. Rams are sensitive to poor water quality. Feeding: Feed small amounts of quality micro pellets or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Rams do well with small, peaceful fish that like warm, soft water, such as tetras, rasboras, hatchetfish, corydoras and discus. They may eat small shrimp. Avoid large or boisterous fish. Good to know: Rams often form pairs and lay eggs on flat stones. Stable, warm water is the key to keeping them healthy.

Angelfish are a very popular species found in rivers all throughout South America. The platinum angelfish is a popular color variant due to the bright, solid white reflective color of the fins and body. In an aquarium with dark woods and natural gravel, these fish stand out. The color just gets more vibrant as the platinum angelfish grows to its maximum size of 6 inches. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pterophyllum scalare Origin Amazon basin, South America (captive-bred) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Semi-aggressive (territorial when pairing) Adult Size Up to 6" long and 8" tall Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a group of 3 Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them tall plants or driftwood, a heater and a gentle filter. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Choose peaceful fish too large to swallow, such as larger tetras, corydoras, plecos, rams, gouramis and peaceful barbs. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs, and small fish like neon tetras that adult angels may eat. Breeding: Angelfish pair off and lay eggs on flat surfaces like broad leaves or slate. A breeding pair can become territorial, so give them room and places for other fish to retreat. Good to know: In a group, two angelfish often pair off and claim part of the tank. If a pair forms and starts chasing the others, add more hiding places or rehome the extras.

Banded kuhli loaches aren't schoolers, but in the evening a small group of these banded kuhli loaches will move all over the fish tank in their own individual patterns. During the day the whole pack of them will just rest. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pangio kuhlii / P. semicincta Origin Southeast Asia (Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful (shy, nocturnal) Adult Size Up to 3–4" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore (sinking foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 5.5–7.0 Group Size Sold as a group of 3 Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Kuhlis love to burrow, so use a soft sand bottom with plants, leaf litter and hiding spots. Cover filter intakes with a sponge, since they can squeeze into small gaps, and keep a lid on the tank. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets or wafers, ideally in the evening when kuhlis are most active. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Kuhlis do well with peaceful fish like tetras, rasboras, corydoras, danios and dwarf shrimp. Avoid large or aggressive fish that could eat them. Good to know: Kuhlis are shy during the day; a larger group and plenty of cover help them come out more often.

Demasoni are beautiful and curious fish, continuously exploring the nooks around the aquarium. They only get to 4", so they are a good fit with other mid-size and smaller cichlids. Slow growers and a bit more difficult to breed, they are priced accordingly. Demasoni are distinguished by the bold reflective blue vertical stripes along the entire body of the fish. Small samples of these can be found at PetSmart for as low as $9.00 for a 1/2-inch fish, but we believe superior breeding and better size will improve the aquatic experience. Hence, a bigger fish at a bigger price. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pseudotropheus demasoni Origin Lake Malawi, Africa Care Level Moderate Temperament Aggressive (territorial rock-dweller) Adult Size Up to 4" Lifespan 6–10 years Diet Omnivore (needs plant matter) Water Temperature 76–82°F pH 7.8–8.6 Group Size Sold as a group of 3 Shipping Size Small: approx. 1–1½" · Medium: approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Use a sand or crushed-coral bottom and stack plenty of rockwork with caves and hiding spots so each male can claim a territory and others can escape. Lake Malawi and Lake Tanganyika cichlids need hard, alkaline water; crushed coral or aragonite sand helps hold the pH up. Feeding: Mbuna are mostly plant eaters. Feed a vegetable-based flake or pellet once or twice a day, and avoid high-protein foods, which can upset their digestion. Tankmates: Keep mbuna with other mbuna of similar size and temperament, stocked in a group to spread out aggression. Avoid mixing them with peaceful peacocks and haps unless the tank is large, and avoid closely related species that look alike, which can crossbreed. Good to know: Demasoni are small but very aggressive with each other. Keep them in a large group, or as a single fish, so the aggression is spread out.

Ram is short for the species name “ramirezi”, but also reminiscent of their tendency to butt heads like a terrestrial ram. These are beautiful fish whether captive-bred for color, such as German Blue Rams, or wild such as Bolivian Rams. They are peaceful, hardy, and get along with other species. The Electric Blue Balloon Rams are bred to be a dwarf little metallic blue ball. These fish look striking in a planted tank and the species is peaceful and hardy. Quick Facts Scientific Name Mikrogeophagus ramirezi Origin South America (captive-bred) Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 2–4 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 78–85°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a group of 4 Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Rams need warm, clean, soft water. Give them a sand bottom, plants, driftwood and flat stones for spawning. Feeding: Feed a quality cichlid pellet or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Rams get along with peaceful community fish such as tetras, rasboras, corydoras and peaceful gouramis. Good to know: Balloon rams are bred for a short, round body, so they swim a little slower than regular rams and do best with calm tankmates.

Freshwater gobies have quite a bit of personality and unusual movement, so they are a great addition to the aquarium. They are bottom dwellers and a bit territorial, but easy to keep and feed. Stiphodons are a group of smaller gobies that go well with smaller-species fish tanks and planted aquariums. The neon blue stiphodon has a bright, reflective blue horizontal stripe along the body. Quick Facts Scientific Name Stiphodon atropurpureus / S. semoni Origin Indo-Pacific island streams (Indonesia, Philippines, Taiwan) Care Level Moderate (needs clean, oxygen-rich, flowing water) Temperament Peaceful with other fish; males territorial with each other Adult Size Up to 1½–2" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Algae eater Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Sold as a group of 3 Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: These gobies come from clear, fast-flowing island streams. Give them a mature tank with strong current, high oxygen, smooth rocks covered in algae and biofilm, and a tight lid, since they can climb out. Feeding: These gobies graze on algae off rocks, so they do best in a mature tank. Also feed algae wafers. They may go hungry in a very clean, new tank. Tankmates: They do well with small, peaceful fish that like cool, flowing water, such as danios, rasboras, hillstream loaches and dwarf shrimp. Males may spar with each other. Good to know: Stream gobies cling to rocks with a sucker formed by their pelvic fins. Their larvae drift to the sea to develop, so they rarely breed in aquariums.

Color morphs of the popular algae-eating amano shrimp are becoming more accessible. The orange amano is a light orange variation of the parent amano shrimp, and the color deepens as the shrimp grows out. Quick Facts Scientific Name Caridina multidentata (orange variety) Origin Taiwan Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Omnivore (excellent algae eater) Water Temperature 65–80°F pH 6.5–7.8 Water Hardness GH 6–12 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ½–1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a cycled, planted tank with moss, driftwood and hiding spots. Cover filter intakes with a sponge and keep a lid on the tank, since amanos can climb out. Feeding: Amanos eat algae and leftover food. If algae runs low, feed algae wafers or shrimp pellets. Tankmates: Amanos do well with most peaceful community fish, plus other shrimp and snails. Avoid cichlids, goldfish, loaches and other fish large enough to eat them. Good to know: Amano shrimp breed in captivity, but their larvae need brackish water to develop, so they will not overpopulate a freshwater tank.

Picture a bright red and blue neon tetra with long, draping fins. Well, you don't have to; we have plenty of them and even included a picture of some. This exceptional variation was developed in Taiwan, and we get them from time to time. They behave just like a regular neon tetra. Quick Facts Scientific Name Paracheirodon innesi (long fin variety) Origin Aquarium-bred (Taiwan) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1¼" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 5.5–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ¾" Care Guide Tank setup: These small tetras do best in a planted tank with soft, slightly acidic water, a dark substrate, driftwood, floating plants and gentle filtration. A larger school makes them more confident and colorful. Feeding: Feed small amounts of micro pellets or crushed flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other small, peaceful fish like rasboras, small tetras, pencilfish, pygmy corydoras, otocinclus and dwarf shrimp. Avoid large or boisterous fish that could eat or bully them. Good to know: Small tetras show their best color in a large school in a planted tank with soft lighting.

Marine Hydrometer Marine fish and invertebrates need a density of 1.022 to 1.024 g/ml assuming a common temperature of 77 degrees. Sera Marine Hydrometer is German craftsmanship at its finest. You will know exactly where your marine aquarium stands - in regards to the salt level, not where it stands on the stand. You should already know that.

A popular fish for many freshwater aquarium hobbyists, the clown loach is peaceful and gets along well with many fish tank mates. The clown loach is amazing to watch and care for. Quick Facts Scientific Name Chromobotia macracanthus Origin Borneo and Sumatra, Indonesia Care Level Moderate (grows large; prone to ich) Temperament Peaceful, playful Adult Size Up to 8–12" Lifespan 15–20+ years Diet Omnivore (bottom feeder; eats snails) Water Temperature 77–86°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a group of 4 Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Clown loaches grow slowly but eventually reach 8–12 inches. Give them a sand bottom, plenty of caves and driftwood, warm, clean water and good filtration. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets or wafers once or twice a day so food reaches the bottom. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Clown loaches love snails and help control pest snails. Tankmates: Clown loaches get along with most peaceful community fish, such as tetras, barbs, rasboras, gouramis, angelfish and other loaches. They eat snails and may eat small shrimp. Good to know: Clown loaches are social and long-lived; they often rest on their sides or in a pile, which is normal. They are also prone to ich, so quarantine new fish.

listings.commonName: Assorted Neocaridina Fancy Color Shrimp (Colony of 10)
listings.description: Add a splash of color to your aquarium or shrimp tank. Selection will be random, but we always try to mix it up. Quick Facts Scientific Name Neocaridina davidi (assorted colors) Origin East Asia (aquarium-bred, mostly Taiwan) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1–1¼" Lifespan 1–2 years Diet Omnivore (grazes on algae) Water Temperature 65–80°F pH 6.5–8.0 Water Hardness GH 6–12 (moderately hard) Group Size Sold as a colony of 10 Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Neocaridina are hardy and ideal for beginners. Use a cycled, planted tank with moss, plants and hiding spots, and a sponge filter or a sponge over the filter intake so shrimp aren't pulled in. Keep the water stable. Feeding: Shrimp graze on algae all day. Feed a small amount of quality shrimp food once a day and remove anything uneaten after a few hours. Tankmates: Keep shrimp alone or with tiny, peaceful fish like small rasboras, ember tetras, otocinclus and pygmy corydoras, plus snails. Most fish will eat baby shrimp, and cichlids (even dwarf cichlids like rams and apistogrammas) and larger fish will eat adults. Different Neocaridina colors will crossbreed and lose their color over time. Good to know: Shrimp are very sensitive to copper and many medications. Never treat a tank with shrimp, and check plant fertilizers and treatments for copper.

The Barbatus Cory is also called the Bearded Cory for the long whiskers of older specimens and the Banded Cory for the vivid black and white banding on the body. This rare cory was discovered in Brazil by Joseph Gaimard in 1824. Seldom caught, most in the hobby are tank-raised in Singapore. Our Barbatus Cory are tank-raised. When the small catfish reach two inches, a bright orange or gold line appears on the top of the body. Barbatus Cory feed in the same way as other cory and are very suitable for most fish tanks. The exception would be nano tanks, since this cory can grow to three inches. Quick Facts Scientific Name Scleromystax barbatus Origin Southeastern Brazil (coastal streams) Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 3–4" Lifespan 5–10 years Diet Omnivore (bottom feeder) Water Temperature 64–75°F (prefers cool water) pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and a soft sand or smooth, fine gravel bottom. Plants, driftwood and a few shady spots help them feel secure. Corys are sensitive to salt and some medications (especially copper), so check labels before treating the tank. Feeding: Corys need their own food, not just leftovers. Feed sinking pellets or wafers once or twice a day so food reaches the bottom. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Corys get along with almost any peaceful community fish, such as tetras, rasboras, livebearers, gouramis, angelfish and bettas. Avoid large fish that could swallow them and aggressive bottom dwellers. Good to know: Barbatus come from cool coastal streams, so keep them below the mid 70s with good water flow and oxygen.

Purple lace guppies are bred for show by our Thailand breeder. Their true purple colors on the tail take time to develop, unlike most guppy varieties. Females, as usual, do not have the same beautiful tails, but if you want handsome babies, you're going to need one. Each Purple Lace pair has one purple lace female and one purple lace male. Green sailfin mollies are the closest relatives to the original sailfin mollies of Central America, and males can be quite aggressive. To keep peace in the aquarium, or at least peace for a lone female, two females to one male is recommended, or a small school. Quick Facts Scientific Name Poecilia latipinna / P. velifera (aquarium-bred) Origin Southeastern U.S. and Mexico (wild ancestors); aquarium-bred Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Peaceful (males can chase females and rival males) Adult Size Up to 4–5" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (needs plant matter) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.5–8.5 (hard water) Group Size Sold as a pack of 4 Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give sailfins hard, alkaline water with plants, open swimming space and good filtration. Aquarium salt is optional; they also do well in brackish tanks. Feeding: Mollies graze on algae, so feed a quality flake that includes vegetable matter once or twice a day. They also enjoy algae wafers and frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Mollies get along with most peaceful community fish that like similar hard water, such as platies, swordtails, guppies, danios, rainbowfish, corydoras and plecos. Bushynose plecos are found all over the Amazon basin and are good tankmates, as they eat algae and scavenge uneaten food and only grow to five inches in the fish tank. Though these are plentiful and affordable plecos, they have a very unique appearance. They are also called bristlenose plecos for the antler-like growths at the top of their nose, which get larger and larger as the fish ages. Quick Facts Scientific Name Ancistrus sp. Origin Amazon basin (wild form); aquarium-bred Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful (males guard caves) Adult Size Up to 5" Lifespan 10–12 years Diet Herbivore (algae and plant-based foods) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Sold as a pack of 3 Shipping Size Approx. 1–1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Bristlenose plecos do well in most community tanks. Give them driftwood to rasp on, caves or hiding spots, and good filtration. They keep glass, rocks and plants clean of algae. Feeding: They graze on algae, but also feed algae wafers. Tankmates: Bristlenose plecos get along with nearly all community fish, plus shrimp and snails. Avoid large aggressive fish that might harass them. Good to know: Males grow larger, bushier "bristles" on the snout than females. Bristlenose plecos stay small and are one of the best algae-eaters for home aquariums.

Plecostomus are a specialty of AquariumFish.com. These catfish originate in South America, and many colors, sizes and patterns can be found; so many that common names often aren’t enough to identify one pleco from another, so in 1988 a tropical fish magazine in Germany called DATZ assigned “L” numbers to distinguish species. Though not exactly scientific, the system works. We carry a couple of plecos that have not been assigned their L number, but the Germans are a cautious folk, and we are sure they will get around to it in a precise and correct manner. Medium size is 2” to 3”. Most plecos do better with a little driftwood in the tank. The clown pleco has an orange stripe pattern to earn the name. These little catfish are not scary clowns; the species is compatible with pretty much all other fish in the aquarium, except those that can eat them. One advantage of the clown pleco is that it will not outgrow even a small aquarium. Quick Facts Scientific Name Panaqolus maccus (L-104) Origin Orinoco basin (Venezuela and Colombia) Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Peaceful (territorial with other plecos) Adult Size Up to 3½–4" Lifespan 10–12+ years Diet Herbivore (driftwood, algae wafers) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a pack of 2 Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: These small plecos rasp and digest wood, so driftwood is essential, not just decoration. Give them caves, driftwood and good filtration, since wood-eaters produce a lot of waste. Feeding: Feed algae wafers and sinking pellets, and always keep driftwood in the tank, since they rasp on it as part of their diet. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish. Keep only one per cave, since plecos can be territorial with each other. Good to know: Wood-eating plecos produce fine "wood dust" waste, which is normal.

In the aquatic trade the word wag refers to a black tail fin. When the red wag swordtail swims about the aquarium, it does appear to wag a tail. Unlike the deep red body of the velvet red swordtail, the red and red wag swordtails have a little orange in the red color of the body. If you need to have a specific sex, please request it in the note section when placing the order. Fry are born free-swimming and will be eaten unless there are dense plants or a breeding box for them to hide in. Only males grow the "sword" on the tail.

Engineer Goby (3-Pack) The Engineer Goby (Pholidichthys leucotaenia), also widely known as the Convict Goby or Convict Blenny , is one of the most intriguing and unique marine fish available to hobbyists. Despite its common names, this species is neither a true goby nor a blenny; it belongs to its own distinct family, Pholidichthyidae. Juveniles feature striking black-and-white horizontal stripes reminiscent of a convict's uniform or a coral cat shark, while adults undergo a dramatic visual transformation into a pattern of dark, vertical bars and marbling on an elongated, eel-like body. Native to the Central Indo-Pacific, from the Philippines to the Solomon Islands, the Engineer Goby is famous for its tireless burrowing behavior. In the wild and in home aquariums, it creates extensive network tunnels beneath rockwork and sand. Individuals can reach an impressive maximum length of 10 to 12 inches (25-30 cm). Because of their constant digging and adult size, a minimum aquarium size of 55 gallons is required, along with a deep sand bed and rockwork secured directly to the bottom glass to prevent structural collapses. The Engineer Goby is an exceptionally peaceful and hardy species that adds tremendous character to a marine setup. While completely harmless to corals and fish, its endless engineering projects mean aquarists must ensure all rock formations are completely stable. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: This species is a dedicated Carnivore . In captivity, it readily accepts a wide variety of frozen meaty foods such as mysis shrimp , chopped brine shrimp, krill, finely chopped squid, and high-quality carnivore pellets or flakes. Juveniles are active feeders in the water column, while secretive adults often wait near their burrow entrances for food to drift past. Feeding: Feed 1-2 times daily. Target feeding near their primary burrow entrance using a pipette or feeding tongs can ensure timid or shy individuals receive sufficient nutrition. Reef Compatibility: It is Reef Safe with minor caveats. The Engineer Goby will never nip at or consume hard or soft corals. However, its digging can undermine rock bases, potentially tipping corals over or smothering low-lying species (like brain corals or acans) in sand dust clouds. Temperament: It is Peaceful . They are non-aggressive toward other fish species and can easily be kept individually, in pairs, or in small groups (provided there is ample sand bed space and hiding spots for each individual). Substrate & Safety: Always place your live rock directly on the bottom glass panel before adding sand. If rockwork rests on top of the substrate, the Engineer Goby's tunneling will cause the structure to shift, collapse, or crack the glass. A fine-to-medium sand bed of at least 2 to 3 inches is essential for their natural digging behavior. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Pholidichthys leucotaenia Primary Common Name: Engineer Goby Other Common Names: Convict Goby, Convict Blenny, Pacific Eel Goby Origin: Indo-Pacific (Philippines, Indonesia, Solomon Islands) Max Size: 10-12 inches (25-30 cm) Temperament: Peaceful Diet: Carnivore (Frozen meaty foods, mysis, marine pelleted diets) Minimum Tank Size: 55+ Gallons Reef Compatibility: Reef Safe (With caution for rockwork stability)

The most striking feature of this freshwater loach, besides its unusually flat profile, is the fine-line color pattern, called reticulation. Normally hillstream loaches are gathered on rocks of swift-flowing streams in China, and their unusual flat, wide fins are perfectly suited to this environment. Freshwater loaches are hardy and feed on just about anything and are quite the sight hanging on the other side of the aquarium glass. Quick Facts Scientific Name Sewellia lineolata Origin Central Vietnam Care Level Moderate (needs cool, fast, oxygen-rich water) Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Algae eater Water Temperature 68–75°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Sold as a pack of 3 Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Hillstream loaches come from fast, clear mountain streams. Also feed algae wafers or sinking pellets. Tankmates: Hillstream loaches do well with peaceful fish that like cool, flowing water, such as white clouds, danios, rasboras and dwarf shrimp. Avoid tropical fish that need warm water. Good to know: Hillstream loaches cling to rocks and glass with their flat, sucker-like bodies, just like they do in fast mountain streams.

Yellow Leaf Scorpionfish: The Master of Camouflage The Yellow Leaf Scorpionfish (Taenianotus triacanthus), also widely known as the Leaf Fish or Paperfish , is one of the most intriguing and unique species available to marine aquarium enthusiasts. Characterized by its bright yellow coloration and extremely laterally compressed (paper-thin) body, this fascinating ambush predator blends seamlessly into its surrounding habitat. Its ability to sway gently back and forth with the water current allows it to mimic a dead leaf or a piece of macroalgae, perfectly fooling both prey and potential predators. Native to the tropical waters of the Indo-Pacific, the Yellow Leaf Scorpionfish is a relatively small species, typically reaching a maximum body length of 3 to 4 inches (7.5-10 cm). Despite its smaller size, it possesses venomous dorsal spines that require careful handling. Because of its sedentary nature and slow swimming habits, a massive aquarium is not required; a minimum tank size of 30 gallons is sufficient, provided the water quality is kept pristine and plenty of live rock or branching coral structures are available for perching. The Yellow Leaf Scorpionfish is a peaceful, slow-moving predator that will not harass tankmates too large to be consumed. However, like other scorpionfish species, caution must be taken when placing hands in the aquarium due to its painful venomous sting. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: This species is a strict Carnivore and specialized ambush predator. In the wild, it feeds on small marine fish, shrimp, and other invertebrates that swim too close to its mouth. In captivity, initial feeding can be challenging, often requiring live foods like ghost shrimp or small feeder fish to initiate a feeding response. With patience, it can often be trained to accept non-living, frozen meaty foods like mysis shrimp , krill, and chopped marine meats presented on a feeding stick. Feeding: Feed 2 to 3 times per week. Target feeding with long tongs or a feeding stick is highly recommended to ensure it receives adequate food, as faster tankmates will easily outcompete it. Reef Compatibility: It is Reef Safe With Caution . The leaf scorpionfish is completely safe around corals, anemones, and sessile invertebrates. However, it will opportunistically consume small ornamental shrimp, crabs, and tiny fish that fit into its cavernous mouth. Temperament: It is Peaceful / Predatory . It is entirely non-aggressive toward fish it cannot swallow. Ideal tankmates include slow-moving, peaceful species such as pipefish, smaller peaceful wrasses, cardinalfish, and dartfish (provided they are larger than the leafish's mouth). Avoid keeping it with fast, aggressive feeders or fin-nipping species like triggers, large angels, or aggressive wrasses. Venomous Spines: The dorsal spines contain a protein-based venom that causes severe localized pain and swelling. If accidentally stung, immediately submerge the affected area in hot water (as hot as can be tolerated without burning) for 30 to 90 minutes to break down the venom, and seek medical attention . Quick Facts Scientific Name: Taenianotus triacanthus Primary Common Name: Yellow Leaf Scorpionfish Other Common Names: Leaf Fish, Paperfish, Leaf Scorpionfish Origin: Indo-Pacific Max Size: 3-4 inches (7.5-10 cm) Temperament: Peaceful / Predatory ( Venomous ) Diet: Carnivore (Prefers live food, can be stick-fed) Minimum Tank Size: 30 Gallons Reef Compatibility: With Caution (Will eat small shrimp and small fish)

Fiji Multicolor Zoanthid: Vibrant WYSIWYG Colony The Fiji Multicolor Zoanthid ( Zoanthus sp.) is a striking soft coral prized for its incredible variety of colors, dense polyp growth, and ability to transform reef rockwork into a living field of color. Zoanthids are among the most recognizable corals in the reef hobby and are especially popular for the enormous variety of color combinations found across different colonies. This WYSIWYG specimen is a large, established multicolor colony featuring numerous polyps with a diverse mix of green, yellow, red, and orange tones. Rather than featuring a single uniform color morph, this colony displays multiple contrasting patterns across the rock, giving it a unique appearance from nearly every angle. Under blue-spectrum reef lighting, the fluorescent greens, yellows, and warmer colors become especially vivid. Zoanthids grow as colonies of individual polyps connected by a shared mat of tissue. Zoanthids are generally considered hardy and adaptable compared with many stony corals, making them suitable for a wide range of established reef aquariums. They typically thrive under moderate lighting and low-to-moderate water flow that keeps debris from settling on the colony without preventing the polyps from fully opening. Never boil or expose zoanthid-covered rock to hot water or steam. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Zoanthus sp. listings.description: XL Red Aussie Lobo Coral: A Bold, Fleshy LPS Showpiece The XL Red Aussie Lobo Coral is a striking Large Polyp Stony (LPS) coral featuring thick, fleshy polyps, pronounced ridges, and rich red coloration. This substantial Australian specimen is approximately fist-sized, giving it the presence of an established colony rather than a small frag. Under blue-spectrum reef lighting, its red coloration and contrasting details become especially vivid. Its large, inflated polyps create the characteristic folded appearance that makes Lobophyllia corals such impressive centerpiece specimens. Lobophyllia corals are photosynthetic but are also active feeders. They may extend feeding tentacles, particularly after lights out or when food is introduced. Stable reef parameters, moderate lighting, gentle-to-moderate water movement, and occasional supplemental feeding can help maintain healthy tissue and strong coloration. WYSIWYG: The XL Red Aussie Lobo pictured is the exact coral you will receive. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: Mixotroph. Primarily photosynthetic but readily captures meaty foods. Feeding: Supplemental target feeding can support growth and tissue development. Offer small portions of mysis shrimp, enriched brine shrimp, finely chopped marine foods, or quality LPS foods approximately 1–2 times per week. Reef Compatibility: Reef Safe, but should be provided adequate space from neighboring corals. Temperament: Semi-Aggressive toward neighboring corals. Placement: Best positioned on the sand bed or lower rockwork with enough room for its fleshy tissue to fully expand without rubbing against sharp surfaces. Water Requirements: Maintain stable reef conditions with consistent alkalinity, calcium, and magnesium. Avoid rapid fluctuations in salinity, temperature, or other major parameters. Water Flow: Low to Moderate, preferably indirect. Lighting: Moderate reef lighting is generally appropriate. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Lobophyllia sp. Primary Common Name: Red Aussie Lobo Coral Other Common Names: Red Lobophyllia, Lobo Brain Coral, Australian Lobo Origin: Australia / Indo-Pacific Size: XL – Approximately Fist-Sized Temperament: Semi-Aggressive Diet: Photosynthetic / Carnivorous Feeding: Supplemental target feeding beneficial Placement: Sand Bed to Lower Rockwork Water Flow: Low to Moderate Lighting: Moderate Reef Compatibility: Yes Care Level: Moderate

The roseline shark, or Denison barb, is a schooling shark in the barb family. The roseline shark grows to about six inches and is not aggressive, so these fish can be put with almost any other freshwater aquarium fish. Originating in India, AquariumFish.com collects from the Karnataka region, where roselines tend to have more color. Quick Facts Scientific Name Sahyadria denisonii (formerly Puntius denisonii ) Origin Western Ghats (Kerala and Karnataka), India Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful but active Adult Size Up to 5–6" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 68–77°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Medium: 1" · Large: 2–3½" · X-Large: 4" Care Guide Tank setup: Roselines are active schoolers that like cool, clean, well-oxygenated water with some current. Give them open swimming space, plants along the back and a tight lid. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet with some vegetable content once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Roselines get along with most active, peaceful fish of similar size, such as other barbs, danios, rainbowfish, larger tetras, loaches and gouramis. Avoid slow, long-finned fish. Good to know: Roselines are endangered in the wild in India; most in the trade today are captive-bred.

Denisoni barbs are also known as the red-line torpedo barb, Denison barb, or roseline shark. These fish are active swimmers and get more and more color as they age, showing bright reds and yellows. We recommend a school of three or more. Roseline sharks are hardy and eat flake and live foods. A school of roseline sharks is a nice addition to planted tanks, peaceful community tanks, and larger species fish tanks, but these fish do require well-filtered aquarium water. Quick Facts Scientific Name Sahyadria denisonii Origin Southwestern India Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful, very active Adult Size Up to 6" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 64–77°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 2–3" Care Guide Tank setup: These barbs grow large and swim fast, so give them lots of open space, strong filtration and a tight-fitting lid, since they can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with similar-sized, active fish such as rainbowfish, larger barbs, larger tetras, loaches and peaceful cichlids. Very small fish may be eaten or stressed. Good to know: Denison barbs are fast swimmers that need strong filtration, lots of oxygen and a tight lid, since they can jump.

The silver dollar is a larger schooling fish of the streams and rivers of the Amazon basin. Silver dollars are one of the hardiest fish in the aquarium trade and have been sold in the trade since the late 1890s. These fish will outgrow small aquariums, so be prepared to move up. Known as a peaceful community fish, the general rule applies: do not keep with fish that can fit in their mouths. A school of four makes a nice, flashy display. Silver in body, many of the wild schools also have a muted spotted pattern, but without the green hue of the "spotted silver dollar". Quick Facts Scientific Name Metynnis argenteus Origin Amazon basin, South America Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 6" Lifespan 10+ years Diet Herbivore (plant-based foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Silver dollars are active schooling fish. Give them open swimming space, a tight lid and sturdy or artificial plants, since they eat soft plants. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or pellet with vegetable content once or twice a day. They also enjoy vegetable foods like peas. Tankmates: They are peaceful and get along with other medium to large fish such as larger tetras, plecos, parrots and peaceful cichlids. Good to know: Silver dollars are a calm schooling fish that look best in a group with open swimming space.

Glass catfish, also known as ghost catfish, come from Indonesia and grow to about four inches. These fish are great in a community fish tank and will create an eerie see-through school. Glass catfish are shy and do better in a group than by themselves, but are hardy and will eat community pellet or flake food. Glass catfish like to school around the middle of the fish tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name Kryptopterus vitreolus Origin Southeast Asia Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–80°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants, driftwood and gentle current, with some open swimming space in the middle of the tank. They feel safest with others of their kind. Feeding: Feed small amounts of a quality flake or micro pellet once or twice a day. They also enjoy small frozen foods like brine shrimp and bloodworms. Tankmates: Ghost glass catfish are peaceful and shy. Keep them with other gentle community fish such as tetras, rasboras and corydoras. Good to know: Ghost catfish are almost completely clear, so you can see their skeleton. They hover together in midwater, often facing into the current.

The long nose farlowella is an unusual-looking and prolific catfish from South America. The snout is often as long as an inch, and the body is shaped like a twig for camouflage. Farlowellas tend to stick to the side of the fish tank and swim slowly from time to time in search of scraps. Quick Facts Scientific Name Farlowella acus Origin Venezuela and the Amazon basin Care Level Moderate Temperament Very peaceful Adult Size Up to 6–8" Lifespan 6–10 years Diet Algae eater (also eats algae wafers) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 3–4" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a mature tank with driftwood, plants and gentle current. They need clean, stable water. Feeding: They graze on algae. Also feed algae wafers and sinking pellets. Tankmates: They are very peaceful and slow, so keep them with calm community fish that won't outcompete them for food. Good to know: Farlowellas look like twigs and often sit perfectly still on plants, wood or the glass.

False Lemonpeel Angelfish: A Brilliant Pop of Yellow for Your Tank The False Lemonpeel Angelfish (Centropyge heraldi), also known as the Herald's Angelfish and the Yellow Angelfish , is a beautiful and exceptionally small species that adds a brilliant pop of solid yellow to any marine aquarium . It is highly sought after for its vibrant coloration and graceful swimming, without the blue markings found on the true Lemonpeel Angelfish. Known for its hardiness and active personality, the Herald's Angelfish is a great choice for both beginner and experienced hobbyists. It is a constant forager, exploring rockwork and adding a lively presence to your tank without overwhelming a small space. Why the Herald's Angelfish is a Great Choice: Ideal for Smaller Tanks: Its compact size makes it one of the few angelfish suitable for nano reef aquariums. Vibrant Color: Its stunning, solid yellow coloration makes it a highly visible and attractive inhabitant. Exceptional Hardiness: This species is incredibly resilient and easy to care for, making it a perfect first angelfish. Generally Reef-Safe: While its behavior should be monitored, this species is a great candidate for many reef tanks and is less prone to nipping corals than larger angelfish. Important Note: Like most dwarf angelfish, this species can be territorial, especially towards other angelfish. It is best to introduce it into a tank with a well-established aquascape to give it a place to hide and claim as its own. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Centropyge heraldi Origin: Western Pacific Ocean and Caribbean Max Size: 4 inches Lifespan: 5 years or more Diet: Omnivore. A varied diet of high-quality flakes, pellets, and frozen foods. Shipping Size: 1.5-2 inches

Most fish are known as juveniles to have unusually beautiful coloration, only to loose this bright coloration as an adult and become drab. This is not the case with the Vlamingii Tang. As a matter of fact this case is quite the opposite. Though drab as a juvenile with simple blue spots on a gray body, the Vlamingii Tang quickly grows to an enormous size and gains markings that include greens, blues and purples. Males will usually grow long streamers on their tails in addition to their unusual coloration. Normally non-aggressive toward tankmates, with the exception of other Vlamingii Tangs, this fish is one of the largest of the Tangs and needs an especially large aquarium. Vlamingii Tangs will spend their day picking at rockwork and occasionally sand in search for hair algae to eat.

White Tail Kole Tang: The Peaceful & Hardworking Algae Grazer The White Tail Kole Tang (Ctenochaetus flavicauda) also called the White Tail Bristletooth Tang , is a popular and highly beneficial addition to a marine aquarium . This tang is prized for its unique coloration: a beautiful brownish body with a striking white caudal fin and a subtle yellow line around its eye. Unlike some of its more aggressive cousins, the White Tail Bristletooth Tang is generally peaceful with other fish, making it an excellent community tank resident. As a specialized herbivore, it uses its bristle-like teeth to tirelessly graze on nuisance algae and detritus, making it a fantastic member of any clean-up crew. It is completely reef-safe and will not harm corals or invertebrates. Why the Whitetail Bristletooth Tang is a Great Choice: Generally Peaceful: It coexists well with other fish, making it a great community tank addition. Excellent Algae Control: It is a fantastic algae-eater, helping to keep the tank clean and healthy. Completely Reef-Safe: It will not harm corals, clams, or other invertebrates. Unique Appearance: Its distinctive coloration and graceful swimming make it a standout fish. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Ctenochaetus flavicauda Origin: Pacific Ocean Max Size: 6 inches Lifespan: 10+ years Diet: Herbivore. Primarily feeds on marine algae and detritus. Shipping Size: 2-3 inches

Flame Fin Tomini Tang: The Peaceful & Hardworking Algae Grazer The Orange Fin Tomini Tang (Ctenochaetus tominiensis), also known as the Flame Fin Tang or the Tomini Bristletooth Tang , is a very popular and highly beneficial addition to a marine aquarium . This tang is prized for its unique coloration: a beautiful brownish-orange body with a striking yellow dorsal fin and a pale blue stripe above its eyes. Unlike some of its more aggressive cousins, the Tomini Tang is generally peaceful with other fish, making it an excellent community tank resident. As a specialized herbivore, it uses its bristle-like teeth to tirelessly graze on nuisance algae and detritus, making it a fantastic member of any clean-up crew. It is completely reef-safe and will not harm corals or invertebrates. Why the Tomini Tang is a Great Choice: Generally Peaceful: It coexists well with other fish, making it a great community tank addition. Excellent Algae Control: It is a fantastic algae-eater, helping to keep the tank clean and healthy. Completely Reef-Safe: It will not harm corals, clams, or other invertebrates. Unique Appearance: Its distinctive coloration and graceful swimming make it a standout fish. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Ctenochaetus tominiensis Origin: Indo-Pacific Reefs Max Size: 6 inches Lifespan: 10+ years Diet: Herbivore. Primarily feeds on marine algae and detritus. Shipping Size: 2-3 inches

Chocolate-Yellow Mimic Tang: The Chameleon of the Reef The Chocolate-Yellow Mimic Tang (Acanthurus pyroferus), or Mimic Surgeonfish, is one of the most fascinating fish available to hobbyists, famous for its ability to mimic other species. As a juvenile, it adopts the coloration and patterns of unpalatable Dwarf Angelfish ( Centropyge species) to deter predators. The juvenile coloration is typically a vibrant yellow or two-toned mix. As it matures, the fish transitions into a beautiful adult with an overall rich, dark brown or black body and striking yellow accents on its face, gills, and fins, particularly around the eye. This species is an excellent algae-grazer and is fully reef-safe , making it a highly desirable addition for controlling nuisance algae. While generally peaceful, like all surgeonfish, it can be territorial towards other tangs, especially those of a similar shape. A large tank with plenty of live rock for grazing is essential for its long-term health. Why the Chocolate Mimic Tang is a Great Choice: Unique Mimicry: Its ability to change color and mimic other fish makes it a captivating, evolving centerpiece. Algae Control: It is a voracious algae-grazer, helping to keep your live rock and glass clean. Fully Reef-Safe: It will not harm corals or sessile invertebrates. Hardy Species: Tangs are generally robust and resilient once acclimated to a large, well-established aquarium. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Acanthurus pyroferus Origin: Indo-Pacific Reefs Max Size: 8 inches Lifespan: 10+ years Diet: Herbivore. Requires a steady supply of marine algae, supplemented with quality pellets and frozen foods. Shipping Size: 2-4 inches

Philippine Tang: A Master of Disguise for Your Reef Tank The Philippine Yellow Tang (Acanthurus pyroferus) also called a Mimic Yellow Tang , is a highly sought-after and captivating species known for its remarkable ability to mimic angelfish. As a juvenile, this fish closely resembles angelfish like the Lemonpeel Angelfish , allowing it to safely graze on the reef without being seen as a threat. As it matures, the Mimic Tang undergoes a dramatic color change, shedding its disguise to reveal a solid chocolate-brown body with a vibrant yellow or orange tail and a brilliant blue ring around its eyes. This tang is a tireless algae grazer, making it a fantastic addition to a marine aquarium with plenty of live rock for foraging. Its generally peaceful nature and unique life cycle make it a fascinating and beneficial centerpiece for a well-established, larger tank. Why the Philippine Tang is a Great Choice: Fascinating Behavior: Its ability to mimic other species is a captivating natural behavior to witness in your tank. Stunning Adult Colors: The dramatic color change to a deep brown with a vibrant tail creates a beautiful visual pop. Natural Algae Control: It constantly grazes on algae, helping to maintain a clean and healthy environment. Peaceful Temperament: It is generally non-aggressive with other tangs and fish, making it a great community tank addition. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Acanthurus pyroferus Origin: Indo-Pacific Reefs Max Size: 9 inches Lifespan: 10+ years Diet: Herbivore. Primarily feeds on marine algae and prepared foods. Shipping Size: 2-4 inches

Chocolate Tang: The Master of Disguise The Chocolate Tang (Acanthurus pyroferus), also known as the Mimic Tang , is a truly fascinating and unique addition to any marine aquarium . This species is famous for its incredible ability to mimic the coloration of various angelfish species as a juvenile to protect itself from predators. You may find juveniles sporting the vibrant yellow of a Lemonpeel Angelfish or the striking black and white of a Half-black Angelfish. As it matures, the Chocolate Tang undergoes a dramatic transformation, developing a solid brown or gray body. It is a peaceful fish but can be territorial towards other tangs, making it a great last addition to a tank. As a herbivore, it is a fantastic algae-eater and is completely reef-safe . Why the Chocolate Tang is a Great Choice: Unique Mimicry Behavior: Its ability to change appearance is a captivating and rare sight. Excellent Algae Control: As a herbivore, it helps keep nuisance algae in check. Completely Reef-Safe: It will not harm corals, clams, or other invertebrates. Graceful Swimmer: Its elegant swimming motion adds a graceful dynamic to the tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Acanthurus pyroferus Origin: Indo-Pacific Reefs Max Size: 8 inches Lifespan: 10+ years Diet: Herbivore. Feeds on marine algae. Shipping Size: 2-3 inches

Clown Tang: The Striking & Dominant Algae Grazer The Clown Tang (Acanthurus lineatus), also known as the Lined Tang , is a truly magnificent and visually stunning addition to a marine aquarium . This tang is prized for its intricate pattern of vibrant blue, black, and yellow stripes that run horizontally across its body. While its beauty is undeniable, it is crucial to understand that the Clown Tang is one of the most highly aggressive and territorial species in the aquarium hobby. It requires a very large tank with plenty of open swimming space and should be kept with other assertive species. It is completely reef-safe and an excellent algae-eater , but its temperament is the primary consideration for potential owners. Why the Clown Tang is a Great Choice: Stunning Coloration: Its brilliant and complex striped pattern makes it a true showpiece. Excellent Algae Control: As a herbivore, it helps keep nuisance algae in check. Completely Reef-Safe: It will not harm corals, clams, or other invertebrates. Active Swimmer: It adds a lot of energy and graceful movement to a very large aquarium. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Acanthurus lineatus Origin: Indo-Pacific Reefs Max Size: 12 inches Lifespan: 10+ years Diet: Herbivore. Primarily feeds on marine algae. Shipping Size: 2-4 inches

The Black Shoulder Tang The black shoulder tang grows to 15 inches so the fish will eventually require a very large aquarium. This species is rare and aggressive and intended for the serious hobbyist. The fish will fight other black shoulder tangs but will be compatible with other large species. Scientific Name: Acanthurus nigricaudus Origin: Indo-Pacific, Australia Diet: Omnivore Max Size: 16 inches Required Tank Size: 250+ gallons Shipping Size: 3 to 4 Inches

Eight Lined Wrasse: The Bold and Striped Hunter The Eight Lined Wrasse (Pseudocheilinus octotaenia) is a striking and robust species of "Line Wrasse" known for its bold, territorial nature and vibrant color pattern. Native to the vast Indo-Pacific, this fish is characterized by a body that varies in hue from whitish-pink to reddish-purple, adorned with eight thin, strong, horizontal red or purplish stripes running the length of its body. As one of the larger members of its genus, it requires thoughtful tankmate selection due to its moderately aggressive temperament, especially toward smaller or similarly shaped fish. The Eight Lined Wrasse is an active diurnal fish that spends its time patrolling the rockwork of the aquarium, hunting for small invertebrates. This makes it a popular choice for reef keepers looking for a natural pest controller, as it is known to prey upon common aquarium pests like pyramidellid snails (parasites of Tridacna clams) and some species of flatworms and bristleworms. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: This fish is a Carnivore that feeds primarily on benthic crustaceans, worms, and mollusks in the wild. In captivity, it readily accepts a variety of meaty foods, including frozen mysis shrimp, enriched brine shrimp, finely chopped seafood, and high-quality marine pellets or flakes. Feeding 2-4 times daily is recommended to maintain optimal health and coloration. An established tank with ample live rock provides crucial supplemental foraging opportunities. Habitat: A minimum of 50–55 gallons is recommended, with a larger tank preferred to mitigate territorial aggression. The tank must be richly decorated with live rock to create numerous caves, crevices, and hiding spots. Like all Pseudocheilinus species, the Eight Lined Wrasse is an exceptional jumper and requires a tight-fitting, weighted lid or mesh screen cover to prevent escape. Reef Compatibility: It is Reef Safe with Caution. While generally harmless to corals and large sessile invertebrates, its natural diet means it will opportunistically prey on small ornamental shrimp (such as Peppermint or Cleaner Shrimp, especially when molting), small crabs, and snails. It is an excellent control for some aquarium pests. Temperament: It is generally considered Aggressive/Semi-Aggressive, particularly toward its own species, other wrasses (especially other Line Wrasses like the Six Line), and smaller, more docile fish (like dartfish, smaller gobies, and certain dottybacks) that share rock-dwelling niches. It is best kept singly and introduced to the aquarium last to prevent excessive bullying. Sleeping Habit: This wrasse does not typically bury in the sand. Instead, it forms a mucus cocoon or wedges itself securely into a tight rock crevice to sleep at night. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Pseudocheilinus octotaenia Primary Common Name: Eight Lined Wrasse Other Common Names: Eight Stripe Wrasse, Eight-lined Wrasse Origin: Indo-Pacific (East Africa to Hawaii) Max Size: Up to 5.5 inches (14 cm) Temperament: Aggressive/Territorial (Especially towards congeners) Care Level: Moderate Diet: Carnivore/Pest Controller Minimum Tank Size: 55 Gallons Reef Compatibility: Safe with Caution (May eat small inverts)

Yellow Banded Possum Wrasse: The Shy Reef Dweller The Yellow Banded Possum Wrasse (Wetmorella nigropinnata) is a small, secretive, and highly valued fish in the marine aquarium hobby. It is also known by the common names Sharpnose Wrasse , Blackspot Pygmy Wrasse , or simply Possum Wrasse . Native to the vast Indo-Pacific, from the Red Sea to the Marquesas, this wrasse is a cryptic reef-dweller, preferring to spend its time hovering near caves, under ledges, and within the dark crevices of live rock. Its small, streamlined body (reaching only about 3 inches , or 8 cm) is typically a deep reddish-brown to rusty color, contrasted by two distinct vertical yellow bands : one behind the eye and another near the caudal peduncle (tail base). The soft dorsal and anal fins often feature a small, conspicuous black eyespot (ocellus) . Due to its diminutive size and timid nature, the Yellow Banded Possum Wrasse is an excellent candidate for peaceful nano or community reef tanks, requiring a minimum size of just 15 to 25 gallons . This wrasse is a known jumper , so a tight-fitting lid or screen top is essential to prevent escape. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: This wrasse is a Carnivore , feeding primarily on small benthic invertebrates (tiny crustaceans and worms) in the wild. In captivity, it must be offered a varied diet of fine, meaty frozen foods several times a day to sustain its high metabolism. Good options include nutritionally-enriched mysis shrimp , copepods, cyclops, and finely chopped clam or shrimp. It is highly beneficial to house this wrasse in a well-established aquarium with a natural supply of live copepods and amphipods , which it will actively hunt among the rockwork. Feeding: Due to its shy nature, ensure it is getting enough food and is not being outcompeted by more aggressive or fast-feeding tankmates. Reef Compatibility: It is Completely Reef Safe . The Yellow Banded Possum Wrasse will not bother corals or anemones. Its small mouth and diet mean it generally leaves ornamental shrimp and snails alone, though very tiny, prized micro-invertebrates may be at risk. Temperament: It is exceptionally Peaceful and Timid . It should only be housed with similarly small and peaceful tankmates (e.g., small gobies, cardinalfish, and small blennies). It is easily stressed and bullied by aggressive or overly active fish, which can cause it to hide permanently. It can be kept singly or in a male-female pair/harem in larger tanks, provided all are introduced simultaneously. Sleeping Habit: Unlike some other wrasse genera, Wetmorella wrasses do not require a deep sand bed to sleep. They seek shelter in rock crevices or caves at night. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Wetmorella nigropinnata Primary Common Name: Yellow Banded Possum Wrasse Other Common Names: Sharpnose Wrasse, Blackspot Pygmy Wrasse Origin: Indo-Pacific (Widespread, including Red Sea) Max Size: 3 inches (8 cm) Temperament: Peaceful / Timid ( Shy ) Diet: Carnivore (Planktivore/Benthic Invertebrates) Minimum Tank Size: 15-25+ Gallons (Nano-Reef suitable) Reef Compatibility: Yes (Completely safe with corals)

Labout's Wrasse Labouts Wrasse is a species of wrasse native to the coral reefs of New Caledonia and Australia, where it occurs at depths of 7 to 55 m. This species can reach a total length of 5 to 6 inches. Almost unreal in coloration and markings, the Labouti Fairy Wrasse is a sought after fish for it’s unusual appearance. Relatively easy to adapt in captivity but less frequently collected, the Labouti Fairy Wrasse will be shy upon introduction but become more bold in time and spend more time actively in the water column. Will hide and never feed if continually harassed. If you will have more than one, add all females and other fairy wrasses first as the male Labouti Fairy Wrasse might behave aggressively to any new introductions. Scientific Name: Cirrhilabrus laboutei, Family: Labridae Diet: Vitamin enriched frozen mysis shrimp, vitamin enriched frozen brine shrimp, and other meaty foods along with a high quality marine flake and marine pellet food. Origin: Australia, Vanuatu Max Size: 5 to 6 inches Shipping Size: Approx. Sm 2 to 2 1/2 inches , Med 3inches, Lg 4 inches

Tricolor Fairy Wrasse: The Hardy, Colorful Reef Flasher The Tricolor Fairy Wrasse (Cirrhilabrus solorensis), also widely known as the Redheaded Fairy Wrasse , Solar Fairy Wrasse , or Solon Wrasse , is a popular and relatively hardy member of the Cirrhilabrus genus. It is highly prized by reef enthusiasts for its brilliant, shifting colors, peaceful nature, and complete safety within coral and invertebrate setups. Like all Fairy Wrasses, this species displays significant sexual dimorphism and a spectacular "flashing" behavior (temporary, intense color changes used for courtship or display): Males are the most commonly seen in the trade, exhibiting a complex mix of colors: an orangish-red head/face, often a blue-green to purple body, and fins edged in blue, red, or yellow, giving it the "Tricolor" appearance. The color intensity and pattern can vary significantly based on mood and maturity. Females/Juveniles are generally more subdued, often having a reddish-brown or dull orange body. This species is a non-stop, mid-water swimmer, adding vibrant activity and color to the aquarium. Care & Compatibility Size: Reaches a manageable size of 4.5–5 inches (11–13 cm). Minimum Tank Size: A tank of 60–90 gallons is recommended to provide ample swimming room, as they are extremely active. Temperament: Peaceful and Active. The Tricolor Fairy Wrasse is a community fish. It is not aggressive towards other non-wrasse tankmates but will be aggressive toward other male Cirrhilabrus species or its own kind. It is best kept singly, or in a harem of one male and multiple females if the tank is large enough (100+ gallons). Reef Compatibility: 100% Reef Safe. This wrasse is a zooplankton feeder with a small mouth and will not bother corals, clams, or sessile invertebrates. It is generally safe with ornamental shrimp and snails. Diet: Carnivore/Zooplankton Feeder. This wrasse has a high metabolism and requires a varied diet of tiny, meaty foods 3-4 times per day. Feed high-quality enriched frozen foods like mysis shrimp, brine shrimp, copepods, fish eggs, and small marine pellets or flakes. Constant feeding is crucial for health and color retention. Tank Requirements: Lid: A tight-fitting lid is absolutely essential, as all Fairy Wrasses are notorious jumpers, particularly when startled or newly introduced. Hiding Spots: Provide abundant live rock structure with caves and crevices for security and sleeping. Fairy Wrasses do not burrow in the sand; they typically wedge themselves into rock crevices or form a mucus cocoon to sleep. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Cirrhilabrus solorensis Primary Common Name: Tricolor Fairy Wrasse Other Common Names: Redheaded Fairy Wrasse, Solar Fairy Wrasse, Solon Wrasse Origin: Western Central Pacific (Indonesia, Philippines) Max Size: 5 inches (13 cm) Temperament: Peaceful / Active (Aggressive toward other male Fairy Wrasses) Diet: Carnivore/Zooplankton Feeder (Needs multiple daily feedings) Minimum Tank Size: 60–90 Gallons Reef Compatibility: Yes (Safe with all corals and most invertebrates)

Scott's Fairy Wrasse: The Bold & Brilliant Reef Gem The Scott's Fairy Wrasse (Cirrhilabrus scottorum) is a popular and captivating species known for its stunning colors and peaceful nature. This beautiful wrasse showcases a brilliant mix of hues, with a sleek body that transitions from a deep green to a vibrant blue or purple on its fins. Males often display even more intense coloration, especially during courtship, with a bright yellow or orange wash over their heads. The Scott's Fairy Wrasse is an active, open-water swimmer that adds a dynamic and mesmerizing presence to a well-established marine aquarium . It is a fantastic choice for a community tank, as it is completely reef-safe and will not harm corals or most invertebrates. Why the Scott's Fairy Wrasse is a Great Choice: Stunning Coloration: Its brilliant and ever-changing hues make it a true showpiece. Completely Reef-Safe: It will not harm corals, clams, or most other invertebrates. Peaceful Temperament: It is a non-aggressive species that coexists well with other peaceful fish. Active & Mesmerizing: It constantly swims in the water column, adding life and movement to the tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Cirrhilabrus scottorum Origin: Indo-Pacific Reefs Max Size: 4.5 inches Lifespan: 5-7 years Diet: Carnivore. Primarily feeds on meaty foods such as shrimp, krill, and prepared foods. Shipping Size: 2-3 inches

Exquisite Wrasse: The Dazzling & Peaceful Reef Flash The Exquisite Wrasse (Cirrhilabrus exquisitus) is a popular and captivating species known for its stunning colors and peaceful nature. This beautiful wrasse showcases a brilliant mix of hues, with a sleek body that transitions from a deep blue on its back to a vibrant reddish-orange on its underside. Males often display even more intense coloration, especially during courtship, with a yellow line running down the body and a black spot near the tail. The Exquisite Wrasse is an active, open-water swimmer that adds a dynamic and mesmerizing presence to a well-established marine aquarium . It is a fantastic choice for a community tank, as it is completely reef-safe and will not harm corals or most invertebrates. Why the Exquisite Wrasse is a Great Choice: Stunning Coloration: Its brilliant and ever-changing hues make it a true showpiece. Completely Reef-Safe: It will not harm corals, clams, or most other invertebrates. Peaceful Temperament: It is a non-aggressive species that coexists well with other peaceful fish. Active & Mesmerizing: It constantly swims in the water column, adding life and movement to the tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Cirrhilabrus exquisitus Origin: Indo-Pacific Reefs, Africa Max Size: 4 inches Lifespan: 5-7 years Diet: Carnivore. Primarily feeds on meaty foods such as shrimp, krill, and prepared foods. Shipping Size: 2-3 inches

Orange-Back Fairy Wrasse: The Reef Jewel The Orange-Back Fairy Wrasse (Cirrhilabrus aurantidorsalis) is a beautiful and active marine fish, prized for its vivid, contrasting colors. Originating from the waters of Indonesia, particularly Tomini Bay, Sulawesi, this species is a dazzling sight in the aquarium. The male displays a magnificent pattern: a brilliant, shining orange or golden-yellow stripe runs along the entire length of its back, set against a lower body that fades into a vibrant blue, purple, or magenta. Males will also develop a dark red "crown" marking on the head and intensify their coloration dramatically during courtship displays, a behavior known as "flashing." This species is moderately small, reaching a maximum adult size of approximately 3.5 to 4.5 inches (9-11 cm). Due to its active nature and constant foraging for food, a minimum aquarium size of 50 to 90 gallons is recommended. Like all fairy wrasses, the Orange-Back Fairy Wrasse is a jumper , so a tight-fitting lid or screen cover is mandatory to prevent escape. Its peaceful temperament and reef-safe status make it an ideal centerpiece for most established marine community and reef tanks. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: The Orange-Back Fairy Wrasse is a dedicated Carnivore and a zooplankton feeder. It requires a diet rich in small, meaty foods, and due to its high metabolism, it must be fed two to three small feedings per day . Offer a variety of vitamin-enriched frozen foods, such as mysis shrimp, brine shrimp, copepods, and cyclops, supplemented with high-quality marine pellets or flakes. Sleeping Behavior: Fairy wrasses do not burrow into the sand. At night, they seek refuge within the rockwork or crevices, where they secrete a protective mucus cocoon to conceal their scent from nocturnal predators. Reef Compatibility: It is Reef Safe . This wrasse is generally safe with all corals (soft and hard) and most ornamental invertebrates. It may consume the smallest zooplankton and tiny benthic invertebrates living on the rockwork. Temperament: It is Peaceful and Active . It should be kept with other peaceful to semi-aggressive fish. It can be aggressive toward male wrasses of the same or very similar species (e.g., other Cirrhilabrus species). For best results, keep only one male per tank, or house a single male with multiple females (a harem) introduced simultaneously. It is not recommended to house this species with large, highly aggressive, or predatory fish. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Cirrhilabrus aurantidorsalis Primary Common Name: Orange-Back Fairy Wrasse Other Common Names: Orangeback Wrasse Origin: Western Central Pacific (Indonesia, Philippines) Max Size: 3.5-4.5 inches (9-11 cm) Temperament: Peaceful / Active ( Jumping risk ) Diet: Carnivore (Zooplankton Feeder, needs multiple daily feedings) Minimum Tank Size: 50+ Gallons Reef Compatibility: Yes (Safe with all corals)

Green Coris Wrasse The Green Coris is a durable fish that is safe with corals but will eat fanworms, small snails and small ornamental shrimps. Also called simply the green wrasse, Green Wrasses eat pyramidillid snails and flatworms. They require sand to sleep and hide in. They may tend to harass other small non-aggressive wrasses as adults so it is best to obtain juveniles as they assimilate to your own little aquatic melting pot. Scientific Name: Halichoeres chloropterus Family: Labridae Origin: Indonesia Max Size: 8 inches Diet: frozen mysis shrimp, vitamin enriched frozen brine shrimp, and other meaty foods along with a high quality marine flake and marine pellet food. Approximate Size: Small 1 to 2 inches, Medium 3 to 4 inches

Yellow Coris Wrasse: A Brilliant Yellow & Peaceful Reef Fish The Yellow Coris Wrasse (Halichoeres chrysus), also known as the Golden Wrasse or Canary Wrasse, is a dazzling and highly beneficial species that adds a touch of bold, vibrant yellow to any marine aquarium . Its stunning appearance features a beautiful, solid canary-yellow body that remains consistent throughout its life. This fish is known for its peaceful temperament and constant, active swimming behavior. It's an excellent choice for a community reef tank and is prized by hobbyists for its natural tendency to hunt and eat common pests, including bristleworms and pyramid snails that plague Tridacna clams. Why the Yellow Coris Wrasse is a Great Choice: Brilliant Color: Its vibrant, all-over yellow hue creates a beautiful, eye-catching display. Peaceful Temperament: It is a non-aggressive species that coexists well with other peaceful tank mates. Natural Pest Control: It helps control populations of nuisance pests, a valuable service for any tank. Reef-Safe: The Yellow Coris Wrasse is completely safe to keep with all types of corals and invertebrates. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Halichoeres chrysus Origin: Indo-Pacific Reefs, Sri Lanka Max Size: 5 inches Lifespan: 5 years or more Diet: Carnivore. A varied diet of high-quality frozen foods and pest invertebrates found in the tank. Shipping Size: 2-3 inches

Marble Wrasse The Marble Wrasse, also known as the Checkerboard Wrasse, is white with stripes, dots, and patches of black. With maturity, it becomes silver with a distinctive black checkerboard pattern on the body. The dorsal fin and tail are yellow, and the face is light green with orange to pink striped markings. These are peaceful aquarium wrasse and hardy. Reef safe, the Marble Wrasse will even eat nuisance critters in the marine tank. Scientific Name: Halichoeres hortulanus Origin: Fiji Diet: vitamin enriched frozen mysis shrimp, vitamin enriched frozen brine shrimp, and other meaty foods along with a high quality marine flake and marine pellet food. Max Size: 10 inches Shipping Size: Approx. 3 to 4 inches

Dragon Wrasse: The Rockmover Architect The Dragon Wrasse (Novaculichthys taeniourus), also widely known as the Rockmover Wrasse or Reindeer Wrasse (juvenile phase), is a captivating and dynamic species renowned for its dramatic change in appearance and its assertive personality. As a juvenile, this fish is strikingly patterned in greens, browns, and whites, with elongated dorsal fin rays that resemble "antlers"—hence the name Reindeer Wrasse. As it matures, it transforms into a robust, deep greenish-brown adult with a lighter head and intricate lines radiating from the eyes. Native to the Indo-Pacific, the Dragon Wrasse is a powerful, active fish capable of reaching a maximum length of up to 12 inches (30 cm). Its common name, Rockmover Wrasse, is well-earned: this fish is a diligent and often destructive forager that systematically flips over rocks, rubble, and even small corals in search of prey. For this reason, a secure, stable rock structure is essential. Due to its size and energetic nature, a minimum aquarium size of 120 gallons is highly recommended. Like many wrasses, the Dragon Wrasse is a known jumper, requiring a tight-fitting lid. It also requires a deep sand bed, at least 3-4 inches, as it buries itself in the substrate for protection and to sleep at night. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: This wrasse is a dedicated Carnivore with a high metabolism. In the wild, it consumes a wide variety of small, benthic invertebrates such as snails, crabs, shrimp, worms, and brittle stars. In captivity, it must be fed a varied diet of meaty foods several times a day, including frozen mysis shrimp, krill, enriched brine shrimp, and chopped seafood like clam, mussel, and table shrimp. Rock-Moving Behavior: Hobbyists must ensure all live rock is placed directly on the bottom glass before adding any sand to prevent the fish from undermining the structure and causing a rock slide. This fish can be highly entertaining to watch as it forages. Reef Compatibility: It is NOT Reef Safe . The Dragon Wrasse will actively hunt and consume virtually all ornamental and cleanup-crew invertebrates (snails, shrimp, crabs, and sea stars). Furthermore, its habit of flipping rocks and coral rubble makes it unsuitable for maintaining a pristine reef environment. It is best suited for a Fish Only With Live Rock (FOWLR) system. Temperament: It is Semi-Aggressive / Assertive . While juveniles are generally docile, adults can be assertive and territorial. They should only be housed with similarly sized, robust, and moderately aggressive tankmates such as large Tangs, Triggerfish, Groupers, and marine Angels. It is best kept singly, as it may become aggressive towards other wrasses or its own species. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Novaculichthys taeniourus Primary Common Name: Dragon Wrasse Other Common Names: Rockmover Wrasse, Reindeer Wrasse, Striped Wrasse Origin: Indo-Pacific (Widespread) Max Size: 12 inches (30 cm) Temperament: Semi-Aggressive / Assertive ( Highly Active Rockmover ) Diet: Carnivore (Feeds on motile invertebrates) Minimum Tank Size: 120+ Gallons Reef Compatibility: No (Predatory and destructive)

Melanurus Wrasse: The Colorful Reef Cleaner The Melanurus Wrasse (Halichoeres melanurus), also widely known as the Tail-spot Wrasse, Hoeven's Wrasse, or Pinstripe Wrasse, is a highly active and sought-after fish for the marine aquarium. It is celebrated for its stunning coloration and its beneficial role as a natural pest controller in reef systems. This species displays moderate sexual dimorphism and intense coloration: Males (Terminal Phase) feature a vibrant blue-green body with numerous striking orange, red, and yellow horizontal stripes. They have a distinctive, black spot ringed in yellow/blue at the base of the tail fin (caudal peduncle). Females/Juveniles (Initial Phase) are typically paler with a prominent black eyespot (ocellus) on the dorsal fin, in addition to the tail spot. Growing to a manageable size of 4.5–6 inches (11–15 cm), the Melanurus Wrasse is a non-stop daytime forager that adds movement and brilliant color to any tank. It is an excellent choice for intermediate hobbyists. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: This is an active Carnivore/Micropredator with a high metabolism. It requires multiple small feedings (2-3 times) per day of varied, meaty foods, including enriched frozen preparations like mysis shrimp, brine shrimp, copepods, and high-quality pellets. Its constant foraging habit means it hunts micro-invertebrates throughout the day. Pest Control: The Melanurus Wrasse is famous for its natural predatory skills against aquarium pests. It is a known consumer of nuisance organisms such as Planaria flatworms, Pyramidellid snails (which parasitize Tridacna clams), and small bristle worms. Substrate Requirement: A minimum of a 2–3 inch deep bed of fine, soft sand is mandatory. This fish is a dedicated sand-burrower, diving into the sand to sleep at night or when startled. Without this, the wrasse can become highly stressed or sustain injuries. Reef Compatibility: It is generally considered Reef Safe With Caution. It will not harm corals but will hunt and consume tiny ornamental invertebrates like small snails, hermit crabs, and perhaps the smallest ornamental shrimp. Larger shrimp (e.g., Cleaner Shrimp) are generally safe. Temperament: It is Peaceful toward most tankmates. However, it can be aggressive toward its own species or other similar-looking Halichoeres wrasses. It is generally best kept singly. Avoid pairing it with very small, timid, or slow-moving fish that may be stressed by its high energy level. Tank Environment: A tight-fitting lid is essential, as this wrasse, like all Halichoeres species, is a notorious jumper. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Halichoeres melanurus Primary Common Name: Melanurus Wrasse Other Common Names: Tail-spot Wrasse, Hoeven's Wrasse, Pinstripe Wrasse Origin: Western Pacific (Japan to Great Barrier Reef and Samoa) Max Size: 4.5–6 inches (11–15 cm) Temperament: Peaceful / Active (Caution with other wrasses) Diet: Carnivore (Micropredator - Needs multiple daily feedings) Minimum Tank Size: 55+ Gallons Reef Compatibility: With Caution (Great for pest control; may eat small inverts)

Leopard Wrasse Female Leopard Wrasse is also known as the Guinea Fowl Wrasse, or Blackspotted Wrasse. This species has two different appearances depending on gender. Females are white with multiple black or brown irregular spots with white to blue margins covering the entire body. The female's fins may have accents of yellow or tan. The males have an orangish-red background color with green mottling covering the body. Scientific Name: Macropharyngodon meleagris Family: Labridae Origin: Cook Islands, Coral Sea, Fiji, Sri Lanka, Tahiti, Tonga Diet: vitamin enriched frozen mysis shrimp, vitamin enriched frozen brine shrimp, and other meaty foods along with a high quality marine flake and marine pellet food Shipping Size: 1 to 3 inches

Wrasses are very beautiful and a real fun addition to a marine aquarium. They are usually very hardy and peaceful, however there are exceptions to every rule. A few species are extremely difficult to sustain in captivity, such as those in the genera Labroides. Some wrasse fish are social their entire lives, others are social as juveniles and become aggressive as adults, and yet others are aggressive their entire lives. Then there are species that are territorial just with members of their own kind. Scientific Name : Cheilio inermis Origin: Red Sea Max Size: 20 inches Diet: includes crustaceans , mollusks, sea urchins , and other hard-shelled prey. Shipping Size: Whatever can be found, generally 4 inches

Bluehead Wrasse: The Dazzling & Dynamic Reef-Dweller The Bluehead Wrasse (Thalassoma bifasciatum) is a popular and very active species that brings a splash of color and energy to any marine aquarium . This wrasse is a true marvel of nature, undergoing a dramatic color change from a juvenile with a yellow body and horizontal stripes to a breathtaking terminal male with a brilliant blue head , a striking black band, and a green body. The Bluehead Wrasse is a non-stop swimmer, darting in and out of rockwork, and is known for its beneficial habit of hunting small invertebrates, including some parasites, making it a valuable part of the cleanup crew. Its energetic nature and stunning coloration make it a captivating centerpiece for a well-established, larger tank with a secure lid. Why the Bluehead Wrasse is a Great Choice: Dramatic Coloration: It provides a captivating visual spectacle as it matures and changes color. Active & Energetic: Its constant swimming and foraging add a dynamic presence to the entire tank. Natural Cleaner: It naturally helps to control small pests and invertebrates on live rock and tank inhabitants. Reef-Safe: It is generally safe to keep with corals and most invertebrates. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Thalassoma bifasciatum Origin: Western Atlantic Ocean Max Size: 6 inches Lifespan: 5-7 years Diet: Carnivore. It feeds on a wide range of meaty foods and live invertebrates. Shipping Size: 2-3 inches

Orange Saddle Wrasse The Orange Saddle Wrasse, or simply the Saddle Wrasse, is a dark green-grey wrasse with an orange "saddle" just behind the pectoral fins. Its head may be purple depending on region and maturity. The wrasse is active by day and needs to hide in rock crevices to sleep at night. Also, an area of sand for the wrasse to bury itself will ease its stress. Scientific Name: Thalassoma duperreyi Origin: Hawaii Max Size: 10 inches Diet: Marine flake and pellets, meaty treat live and frozen Shipping Size: Approx. 3 inches
