Brown Bird Wrasse The Bird Wrasse Gomphosus varius is a beautiful emerald green fish in its male form, known as the Green Bird Wrasse. As a female it is white, sprinkled with tiny black spots in front that fades to a dark brown or black mid body to the tail, and is called the Brown Bird Wrasse or Black Bird Wrasse. They also reach an impressive size, up to 12 inches in length, though females are a bit smaller. Scientific Name: Gomphosus varius Max Size: 11 inches Diet: should include vitamin enriched frozen mysis shrimp, vitamin enriched frozen brine shrimp, and other meaty foods along with a high quality marine flake and marine pellet food Require Tank Size: 125+ gallons Shipping Size: 3 to 4 inches

Green Birdmouth Wrasse: The Fast, Beaked Hunter The Green Birdmouth Wrasse (Gomphosus caeruleus) is a large, vibrant, and extremely active wrasse species known for its distinctive, elongated, beak-like snout, which gives the genus the common name "Bird Wrasse." It is sometimes referred to as the Blue-Green Bird Wrasse or Indian Ocean Bird Wrasse , as it is native to the Indian Ocean. This species exhibits strong sexual dimorphism (difference between sexes): Males (Terminal Phase): Are typically a large, solid, brilliant blue-green or emerald green color with a prominent beak. Females (Initial Phase): Are generally smaller with a darker body, often featuring a black back, a yellowish-white belly, and a dark stripe running through the eye. Reaching a substantial size of up to 12 inches (32 cm), this wrasse is a constant, fast-moving daytime swimmer that requires a large amount of open water to thrive. Like other wrasses, it is a protogynous sequential hermaphrodite, meaning females can change sex to become males if the dominant male is removed. Diet & Compatibility: Size: This is a large fish, reaching a maximum length of up to 12 inches (32 cm). Minimum Tank Size: A minimum of 100 gallons is required, but a larger system of 150+ gallons is highly recommended due to its constant, frantic swimming activity. Temperament: Semi-Aggressive and Boisterous . It is generally peaceful toward larger, equally active fish but is an aggressive predator toward small tankmates. Reef Compatibility: Not Invertebrate Safe . Its long snout and carnivorous diet mean it will actively hunt and consume ornamental shrimp, crabs, snails, and small clams (including Tridacna species). It uses its beak to probe rocks and corals, which can disturb the aquascape. It is generally safe with sessile corals but is considered unsuitable for a typical reef tank setup. Diet: Carnivore . It has a high metabolism and should be fed a varied, meaty diet several times daily. Foods should include vitamin-enriched frozen preparations like mysis shrimp, krill, chopped seafood (fish, clam, shrimp), and high-quality pellets. Tank Environment: The aquarium must have a tight-fitting lid , as Bird Wrasses are notorious jumpers. It requires a long tank with large, open swimming areas and secure rockwork for shelter when sleeping. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Gomphosus caeruleus Primary Common Name: Green Birdmouth Wrasse Other Common Names: Blue-Green Bird Wrasse, Indian Ocean Bird Wrasse, Birdfish Origin: Indian Ocean (East Africa to the Andaman Sea) Max Size: Up to 12 inches (32 cm) Temperament: Semi-Aggressive / Predatory Diet: Carnivore (Crustaceans, mollusks, small fish) Minimum Tank Size: 100+ Gallons (Larger recommended) Reef Compatibility: No (Eats small invertebrates and can disturb the aquascape)

Zebra Moray Eel: The Peaceful & Striking Cracker The Zebra Moray Eel (Gymnomuraena zebra) is a unique and sought-after eel known for its distinctive pattern of black and white bands that run the length of its body, giving it a striking appearance. Unlike many larger, more aggressive morays, this species is known for its peaceful and shy demeanor, making it an ideal choice for a community aquarium with fish. The Zebra Moray has a relatively small mouth with blunt, pavement-like teeth adapted for crushing the shells of its favorite prey: crabs and shrimp. This makes it fully reef-safe with fish , but not with crustaceans or other invertebrates it can consume. Providing plenty of secure hiding spots is crucial for its well-being, as it will spend most of its time nestled in the crevices of your rockwork. Why the Zebra Moray Eel is a Great Choice: Unique Appearance: Its striking black and white bands make it a visually appealing centerpiece. Peaceful Temperament: It is one of the most docile moray eels, making it safe for a fish-only community tank. Fish-Reef Safe: Unlike most morays, its diet is primarily invertebrates, so it will not prey on your other fish. Hardy & Resilient: This is a very durable and adaptable species that thrives in a wide range of water conditions. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Gymnomuraena zebra Origin: Indo-Pacific Reefs Max Size: 30 inches Lifespan: 10+ years Diet: Carnivore. Feeds on a varied diet of meaty frozen foods with shells, such as crab, snails, and krill. Shipping Size: 8-12 inches

Alligator Pipefish The Alligator Pipefish (Syngnathoides biaculeatus), also known as the Crocodile Pipefish or Double-ended Pipefish , is one of the largest and most captivating species in the Syngnathidae family (which includes seahorses). Named for its elongated, often green-to-brown body that resembles a small crocodile or alligator, this fish is a slow-moving, stealth predator highly adapted to life in seagrass meadows and floating macroalgae beds. Native to the tropical and subtropical Indo-Pacific (from East Africa to Australia and Japan), the Alligator Pipefish is technically a "pipehorse" because, unlike true pipefish, its tail is prehensile—it can be used to grasp and anchor itself to vegetation, much like a seahorse. This large pipefish can reach an impressive maximum length of 11 to 14 inches (28-35 cm), requiring a specialized and spacious aquarium. Keeping this species is challenging (moderate to expert care level) due to its specialized feeding requirements and need for a low-flow, peaceful environment. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: This fish is a dedicated Carnivore with a tube-like snout used to suck small prey into its mouth. In the wild, it feeds exclusively on small crustaceans like amphipods and copepods ('pods') and zooplankton. In the aquarium, the biggest challenge is providing a consistent food source. They often must be trained to accept frozen, vitamin-enriched meaty foods such as frozen mysis shrimp , enriched brine shrimp, and copepods, but many specimens will only thrive on a continuous supply of live prey. A tank with an established refugium for live copepod production is essential. Feeding: They are weak competitors and slow eaters. They require multiple small feedings daily (2-3 times) of enriched food delivered directly to them, often with the help of a target feeder or pipette. Uneaten food must be removed immediately. Reef Compatibility: It is Reef Safe, as it will not bother corals. However, it is an Invertebrate Predator and will systematically hunt and consume smaller ornamental shrimp and crabs. It requires a specialized tank environment that mimics its natural seagrass/algae habitat. Temperament: It is Peaceful, but should only be housed with equally slow-moving, non-aggressive tankmates that pose no threat of competition for food. Ideal companions include seahorses, peaceful gobies (like Firefish), and dragonets (if the tank is large enough to support multiple pod feeders). Avoid all fast-swimming, aggressive, or stinging species (e.g., anemones, large corals). Sexing & Breeding: Males are slightly larger and possess the brood pouch on the underside of their abdomen where they carry the female's eggs until they hatch. They can be kept in pairs or small groups. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Syngnathoides biaculeatus Primary Common Name: Alligator Pipefish Other Common Names: Crocodile Pipefish, Double-ended Pipefish, Pipehorse Origin: Indo-Pacific (Widespread) Max Size: 11-14 inches (28-35 cm) Temperament: Peaceful / Specialized (Target Feeding Required) Diet: Carnivore (Live Copepods/Amphipods, Frozen Mysis) Minimum Tank Size: 60-100+ Gallons (Specialized System) Reef Compatibility: Reef Safe (Avoid most ornamental inverts) Unique Feature: Prehensile tail (lacks a caudal fin) and male brooding.

Cat Shark The Black Banded Cat Shark is known as a Cat Shark because the barbs at the mouth look like cat whiskers. It is also referred to as the Brown banded Bamboo Shark, and has a cream-colored body with broad dark black stripes. There may be large, muted brown spots between the stripes when the fish gets larger. The black banded shark, or cat shark, will grow to nearly three feet so at some point this fish will require a very very large aquarium. Scientific name: Chiloscyllium puntactus Max Size: 42 inches Diet: whole cockle in the shell, fresh shrimp and squid, and frozen mussel are ideal. Shipping Size: 4 to 8 inches

BAMBOO SHARK The Bamboo Shark or White spotted Bamboo Shark or Brown-spotted Cat Shark is one of the more popular exotic pet fish in the saltwater aquarium trade. Bamboo sharks grow to three feet and adapt well to large aquariums. The shark feeds on meaty foods, small feeders and generally leaves tank mates along - unless they look pieces of meaty food or small feeders. The Bamboo Shark is a bottom dwelling shark and it will eat any crustacean in the aquarium. It stays relatively small, but requires at least a 300 gallon or larger aquarium as an adult. It requires sand as the substrate as the abdomen is easily scratched by a coarser substrate, which may lead to an infection. It should never be exposed to copper-based medications. Scientific name: Chilscyllium plagiosum Origin: Japan Max Size: 36 inches Diet: Squid parts, clams, and similar food Shipping Size: 8 to 12 inches

Bluefin Angelfish: A Hardy and Resilient Dwarf Angelfish The Bluefin Angelfish (Centropyge multispinis), also known as a Bluefin Dwarf, Brown Pygmy Angelfish, Dusky Angelfish, Dusky Cherub, Many-Spined Angelfish, and Multi-Spined Angelfish , is a beautiful and exceptionally resilient dwarf angelfish that makes a great addition to most marine aquariums. It is characterized by its subtle but appealing coloration, which is typically a deep brown or black with delicate, often indistinct, horizontal stripes. Known for its incredible hardiness and active personality, the Many-Spined Angelfish is a perfect choice for beginner and experienced hobbyists alike. It is a constant forager, exploring rockwork and adding a lively presence to your tank. Why the Many-Spined Angelfish is a Great Choice: Exceptional Hardiness: This species is incredibly resilient and easy to care for, making it a perfect first fish for a new tank. Active and Engaging: Its constant movement and foraging behavior add a sense of energy and life to your rockwork. Generally Reef-Safe: While its behavior should be monitored, this species is a great candidate for many reef tanks and is less prone to nipping corals than larger angelfish. Compact Size: Its small size makes it suitable for a wider range of tank sizes. Important Note: Like most dwarf angelfish, this species can be territorial. It is best to introduce it into a tank with a well-established aquascape to give it a place to hide and claim as its own. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Centropyge multispinis Origin: Indo-Pacific and Indian Ocean Max Size: 4.5 inches Lifespan: 5 years or more Diet: Omnivore. A varied diet of high-quality flakes, pellets, and frozen foods. Shipping Size: 2-3.5 inches

Blue Ring Angelfish: A Magnificent and Iconic Angelfish The Blue Ring Angelfish (Pomacanthus annularis) also called the Annularisis Angelfish is a breathtakingly beautiful species, renowned for its majestic appearance and graceful swimming. While juveniles display a stunning pattern of concentric white and light blue stripes on a dark body, the adult form is a true showstopper. It features a predominantly yellow to brownish body covered in delicate horizontal blue stripes, with the iconic and vibrant blue ring behind its gill plate. Its intelligence and commanding presence make the Bluering Angelfish a prized centerpiece for any large, well-established marine aquarium . Why the Blue Ring Angelfish is a Great Choice: Iconic Appearance: The vibrant colors and distinct blue ring make this angelfish instantly recognizable and highly sought-after. Fascinating Transformation: Watching its dramatic change from juvenile to adult colors is a rewarding experience for any aquarist. Graceful and Stately: Its elegant swimming and large size add a sense of majesty and calm to your display. Intelligent and Active: Its engaging personality and constant exploration add a lively dynamic to your tank. Important Note: The Blue Ring Angelfish is a large fish that requires a minimum tank size of 180 gallons due to its adult size and need for ample swimming room. It is not generally considered consistently reef-safe and is best suited for experienced aquarists. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Pomacanthus annularis Origin: Indo-Pacific Reefs Max Size: 12 inches Lifespan: 10 years or more Diet: A varied diet of high-quality angelfish pellets, flakes, and a variety of frozen foods. Shipping Size: 2-5 inches

Chrysurus Angelfish: The Elegant & Regal Showpiece The Chrysurus Angelfish (Pomacanthus chrysurus), also known as the Earspot Angelfish, is a beautiful and unique fish that serves as a stunning centerpiece in a large marine aquarium . This angelfish is easily recognized by its elegant coloration: a deep purplish-black body adorned with small white spots and a prominent yellow "earspot" behind its gill plate. Its tail is also a beautiful contrast of white and yellow. It is an active and graceful swimmer that requires plenty of open space and rockwork to feel secure. While it is a generally peaceful angelfish, it can be territorial towards other angelfish and some other tank mates. It is considered reef-safe with caution , meaning it may occasionally nip at soft corals or clams. Why the Chrysurus Angelfish is a Great Choice: Stunning Appearance: Its unique high-contrast coloration and regal presence make it a true showpiece. Adds Energy to the Tank: It adds a lot of energy and graceful movement to a spacious aquarium. Impressive Size: It grows to a large size, making it a commanding and impressive fish. Reef-Safe with Caution: It can be successfully housed in many reef tanks if well-fed and monitored. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Pomacanthus chrysurus Origin: Western Indian Ocean and East Africa Max Size: 14 inches Lifespan: 10+ years Diet: Omnivore. Feeds on a varied diet of angelfish formulas, sponges, and marine algae. Shipping Size: 2-4 inches

Goldflake Angelfish This was once a very rare Angelfish to the hobby and has recently become available. Little is known about the reproductive behaviors of this fish. Goldflake Angelfish, also known as the Gold-spangled Angelfish, displays beautiful gold spots throughout the body. The mouth region of this angel is brightly colored in blue and the fins, which are black in color, are bordered by a striking blue.Once established, may become territorial. This Angelfish is one of the safer choices of the large Angels for the reef aquarium, and has proven not to pick on sessile invertebrates. Scientific Name: Apolemichthys xanthopunctatus Origin: Christmas Island Max Size: 10 inches Diet: Onmivore Shipping Size: 2 to 3 inches

Carberri Anthias Semi-aggressive Canberryi Anthias, Nemanthias carberryi , also known as the Canberry Anthias, Canberry's Anthias or Threadfin Anthias, is native to Indian Ocean waters off the coast of east Africa. They have a pink front half of their body that gradiates into a beautiful yellow back half. There is a distinctive yellow marking that bisects the Canberryi Anthias' face. As an active fish, the Canberryi Anthias is best kept in a Group of one dominant male and multiple females. If the male dies, one of the females will assume leadership of the group and turn into a male. Scientific Name: Nemanthias carberryi Origin: Maldives Max Size: 3 inches Diet: Carnivore Shipping Size: 1¾ to 2 inches

Dispar Anthias: A Stunning & Energetic Reef Fish The Dispar Anthias (Pseudanthias dispar), also known as the Redfin Anthias, is a captivating and highly sought-after species that adds a touch of graceful energy to any marine aquarium . Its stunning appearance features a beautiful orange body that transitions to a vibrant red or purple tail . These fish are known for their graceful, constant swimming in the water column and their peaceful, shoaling behavior. Keeping them in a group adds a dynamic and mesmerizing display of constant motion. It is an excellent choice for a community reef tank, where it will leave corals and invertebrates completely unharmed. Why the Dispar Anthias is a Great Choice: Stunning Coloration: Its vibrant orange and red hues create a beautiful, eye-catching display. Peaceful & Active: It is a non-aggressive species that adds constant, peaceful movement to the tank. Shoaling Behavior: Keeping them in a small group creates a mesmerizing display of synchronized swimming. Reef-Safe: The Dispar Anthias is completely safe to keep with all types of corals and invertebrates. Important Note: To thrive, this fish requires multiple daily feedings of high-quality, meaty foods. It is a very active fish and needs ample swimming space. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Pseudanthias dispar Origin: Indo-Pacific Reefs Max Size: 3.5 inches Lifespan: 5 years or more Diet: Carnivore. A varied diet of high-quality frozen foods like brine shrimp and mysis shrimp. Shipping Size: 1.5-2 inches

Princess Anthias A gorgeous deepwater anthias sure to be a prized addition for the devoted anthias keeper. The Princess Anthias sports a rich, sapphire pink coloration beautifully accentuated with golden-yellow flecks that immediately captures the eye. The careful observer will notice that the golden-yellow spots appear on each scale (except those on the ventrum) as though meticulously hand-painted by a piscine Picasso. With its vibrant jewel-like coloration, it's easy to see why the Princess Anthias achieves royal status among anthias aficionados. Scientific Name : Pseudanthias smithvanizi Origin: Indonesia, Fiji Max Size: 3½ inches Required Tank Size: 70+ gallons Diet: Carnivore Shipping Size: 1½ to 2½ inches

Sunburst Butterflyfish Sunburst Butterflyfish is also known as Klein's Butterflyfish, Black-lipped Butterfly, and Orange Butterflyfish. The Klein's Butterflyfish should only be with the same species if introduced to a tank together. Otherwise fist come first dibs and they will see the newcomer as competition. This is a good fish for a reef aquarium....but they do have the tendency to eat leather and soft corals. Scientific Name: Chaetodon kleinii Family: Chaetodontidae Origin: Hawaii Max Size: 6 inches Diet: crustaceans, mysis shrimp, and frozen marine preparations Required Tank Size: 120+ gallons Shipping Size: 1 to 3 inches

Lemon Butterflyfish: The Vibrant & Schooling Butterflyfish The Lemon Butterflyfish (Chaetodon miliaris) also called the Milletseed Butterflyfish is a beautiful and unique fish that makes an excellent addition to a large fish-only marine aquarium . This butterflyfish is easily recognized by its vibrant coloration: a lemon yellow body covered in countless small, black dots, giving it its common name. It also has a distinct black eye-band. It is an active and graceful swimmer that requires plenty of open space and is known for its schooling behavior in the wild. While generally peaceful, it is not considered reef-safe , as it is an opportunistic feeder that will eat a variety of invertebrates and may nip at stony corals. Why the Lemon Butterflyfish is a Great Choice: Stunning Appearance: Its vibrant lemon coloration and unique spotted pattern make it a true showpiece. Adds Energy to the Tank: It adds a lot of energy and graceful movement to a spacious aquarium. Peaceful Temperament: It is a generally non-aggressive fish and can be kept with a variety of other tank mates. Hardy & Resilient: It is known to be a very durable and adaptable species. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Chaetodon miliaris Origin: Hawaiian Islands and Central Pacific Max Size: 7 inches Lifespan: 10+ years Diet: Omnivore. Feeds on a varied diet of butterflyfish formulas and frozen foods. Shipping Size: 2-4 inches

Pebble Butterflyfish The Pebble Butterflyfish is also known as the Multiband Butterflyfish, Pebbled Butterflyfish, Many Banded Butterfly Fish, and Hawaiian Pebble Butterflyfish. It has a subtle color pattern. Its body is a creamy white with five or six tan bands running vertically. There is also a dark vertical eye bar and a black band in the tail fin. If keeping a pair, they should be added at the same time to avoid aggression. The tank should also be decorated with rocks creating many caves for hiding places and lots of rocky rubble. Also make sure there is plenty of open swimming space, as it swims freely and usually spends a good deal of its time in the open water, moving in and out of crevices. Pebbled Butterflyfish are not considered reef safe. Scientific Name: Chaetodon multicinctus Origin: Hawaii Max Size: 5 inches Diet: Omnivore Shipping Size: 1 1/2 to 3 inches

Four Spot Butterlfyfish The Four Spot Butterflyfish, or Fourspot Buttlerflyfish, has a dark yellow and brown body with two white patches on each side. The Four Spot Butterfly can sometimes be difficult to keep in an aquarium setting for a beginner aquarist. They require at least 50 gallons, can nibble on certain coral species, and can become territorial with smaller fish and other butterfly species. Further, the Four Spot Butterfly will pick on sessile invertebrates and even small hermits and crabs if not fed well. The aquarium should have a temperature range between 72 - 80 degrees Fahrenheit and a pH level of about 8.1 - 8.4. Good neighbor, easy to keep in the right conditions, and even good in reef tanks if well fed. Scientific Name: Chaetodon quadrimaculatus Origin: Pacific Ocean Max Size: 8" Diet: mysis or brine shrimp combined with algae and other meaty foods. Some Butterfly species, though not the Four Spot, will only eat fleshy coral polyps. Shipping Size: Approximate 2 to 3" inches

Yellow Zoster Butterflyfish (Peaceful) The Zoster Butterfly is also known as the Yellow Zoster Butterflyfish or Yellow Pyramid Butterflyfish, this saltwater aquarium fish occurs in large numbers among the reefs of the Indian Ocean. The fins are yellow in color, and the body is mostly white. The white coloration forms a triangle with the yellow fins, lending it its common name. The head area is black helping these fish camouflage themselves in the wild. The Pyramid Butterfly feeds upon plankton in the wild, and is safe for reef aquariums. The Pyramid Butterflyfish is quite shy at first, and should be provided multiple hiding places. Scientific Name: Hemitaurichthys polylepis Origin: Hawaii Max Size : 7 inches Required Tank Size: 125+ gallons Diet: Omnivore Shipping Size: 2¼ to 3½ inches

Blue Damselfish: A Brilliant Blue & Hardy Reef Fish The Blue Damselfish (Chrysiptera cyanea), also known as the Sapphire Devil, is a highly popular species that adds a touch of bold, vibrant blue to any marine aquarium . Its stunning appearance features a beautiful, solid electric-blue body that remains consistent throughout its life. This fish is known for its constant swimming and its incredible hardiness, making it a classic "beginner" fish. It's an excellent choice for a community reef tank, but be aware of its semi-aggressive and territorial nature, especially towards new or smaller tank mates. Why the Blue Damselfish is a Great Choice: Brilliant Color: Its vibrant, all-over blue hue creates a beautiful, eye-catching display. Highly Hardy: This species is known for its resilience and adaptability, making it an excellent choice for new hobbyists and tank cycling. Active Behavior: It adds constant, darting movement and energy to the water column. Reef-Safe: The Blue Damselfish is completely safe to keep with all types of corals and invertebrates. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Chrysiptera cyanea Origin: Indo-Pacific Reefs Max Size: 3 inches Lifespan: 5 years or more Diet: Omnivore. A varied diet of high-quality frozen foods, marine pellets, and algae. Shipping Size: 1-2 inches

Pink Damselfish The Pink Smith Damselfish has a shiny silver to white body with a pink fringe. A small group should live in a 30 gallon or larger aquarium with live rock and other hiding places to break up the territories. The Pink Damselfish eats variety of foods including frozen brine and mysis shrimp, dried seaweed, and flake foods. . Scientific Name: Pomacentrus smithi Max SIze: 3" Diet: variety of foods including frozen brine and mysis shrimp, dried seaweed, and flake foods. Shipping Size: 1 to 2 inches

Blue Velvet Damselfish The Blue Velvet Damselfish, or Blue Devil, features flashy neon colored electric-blue horizontal stripes dashed across its face and upper body. Also called the Japanese Damselfish, the center stripe fades as the fish ages. The Blue Devil is an easy fish for a beginner but requires clean water and needs its own territory unless kept in a larger tank. The Damsel is an omnivore and can be fed on all kinds of live, frozen, and flake foods and algae, and also is best to feed small amounts several times a day. Javanese Damsels require some rocky areas for hiding and grazing. Scientific Name: Paraglyphidodon oxyodon Diet: meaty foods, herbivore preparations, and flaked foods Max Size: 2 1/2 inches Approximate size: 1 to 1-1/2 inches

Domino Damselfish The Domino Damselfish, Snowball Damsel or Three Spot Damsel is only found around the Hawaiian Islands and Johnston Island. These territorial damsels forage among the shallows of reefs and need some rocks in the aquarium. Juveniles are black with one to three large white spots near the dorsal fin. This spot starts small on younger fish but gradually spreads as the fish matures and may cover most of the adult fish in dark-edged white scales. Scientific name: Dascyllus albisella Origin: Hawaii Max Size: 5 inches Diet: Frozen foods and marine pellets and flakes Shipping Size: Approx. 1 to 3 inches

Yellowtail Blenny The Yellowtail Blenny has a black or very dark body with yellow on its tail. Blennies can be kept with most other community tankmates like damsels, clownfish and angels but they may become territorial with time and will defend against trespassers. Blennies typically do not tolerate others of the same species except in very large aquariums with enough territory to accommodate their need for space. They are safe for reef aquariums and will not harm most invertebrates, with the possible exception of small crustaceans like Sexy Shrimp. They spend most of the time on or around the bottom, or perching in the rockwork of the aquarium. Scientific Name: Ecsenius flavipes Origin: Indonesia Max Size: 4 inches Diet: Omnivore Shipping Size: Approx. 1 to 2 inches

Sergeant Major Damselfish: A Bold & Resilient Tank Inhabitant The Sergeant Major Damselfish (Abudefduf saxatilis) is a popular and exceptionally hardy species that adds a touch of bold contrast to any marine aquarium . Its striking appearance features a grayish-white body with five prominent black vertical bands . This species is well-regarded for its resilience and active personality, making it a great choice for beginner aquarists. It is generally a reef-safe inhabitant, leaving corals and invertebrates alone. Why the Sergeant Major Damselfish is a Great Choice: Bold Coloration: Its iconic black-and-white striped pattern makes it a striking and attractive inhabitant. Highly Hardy: This species is incredibly resilient and easy to care for, making it a perfect first fish for a new tank. Reef-Safe: The Sergeant Major Damselfish is generally safe to keep with corals and invertebrates. Engaging Behavior: Its active and alert nature makes it a rewarding fish to watch. Important Note: The Sergeant Major Damselfish can become very territorial and aggressive as it matures, especially towards other fish. It is best to introduce it to the tank last and to avoid keeping it with very shy or passive fish. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Abudefduf saxatilis Origin: Atlantic and Indo-Pacific Oceans Max Size: 6 inches Lifespan: 6-10 years Diet: Omnivore. A varied diet of high-quality flakes, pellets, and frozen foods. Shipping Size: 1-2 inches

Orange Honey Damselfish Honey Damselfish, or Red Honey Chromis are small pretty damselfish, The Honey Damselfish have a red/orange colored body with an electric blue horizontal band across their body. Though they are a smaller damsel, they can be equally aggressive. Overall, the Orange Honey Damsel is quite hardy and easy to care for and will thrive in a reef tank as long as they are kept with suitable partners. Scientific Name: Neoglyphidodon crossi Max Size: 3 inches Origin: Caribbean Diet: Omnivorous - pellets, frozen foods Shipping Size: Approx. 2 inches

Harptail Blenny: The Peaceful and Elegant Sentinel The Harptail Blenny (Meiacanthus mossambicus) also known as a Blackline Blenny , or Mozambique Fang Blenny , is a graceful and highly sought-after species that adds a touch of elegance to any peaceful marine aquarium . Its unique appearance features a sleek, elongated body with a prominent black line running from its eye down the length of its body. This blenny is known for its serene, non-aggressive demeanor and its interesting behavior of hovering in the water column and perching on live rock. The Harptail Blenny possesses a fascinating defense mechanism: a set of venomous fangs that it uses to deter predators. Because of this, it is rarely bothered by larger fish, making it a confident and lively inhabitant. It's an excellent choice for a community reef tank due to its peaceful nature and hardiness. Why the Harptail Blenny is a Great Choice: Elegant Appearance: Its streamlined body and striking black stripe provide a unique aesthetic to any tank. Peaceful Temperament: It is a non-aggressive species that coexists well with other peaceful tank mates. Hardy & Resilient: This species is known for its resilience and adaptability, making it an excellent choice for a variety of tank conditions. Reef-Safe: The Harptail Blenny is completely safe to keep with all types of corals and invertebrates. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Meiacanthus mossambicus Origin: Western Indian Ocean Max Size: 4 inches Lifespan: 3-5 years Diet: Omnivore. It feeds on small invertebrates and prepared foods like mysis shrimp, brine shrimp, and high-quality pellets. Shipping Size: 1.5-2.5 inches

Green Banded Goby Greenbanded Goby formerly known as Gobiosoma multifasciatum , has since been reclassified as Tigrigobius multifasciatus . This beautiful fish makes a wonderful addition to the smaller reef or fish only aquarium. This small peaceful species is a vivid green with thin iridescent green bands running vertically down the body. A white head with a brownish red band runs across each red eye.It is common for the Greenbanded Goby to spawn in an aquarium, laying its eggs in a crevice or empty shell. Seasonal fish some what rare to find. Scientific Name: Tigrigobius Multifasciatus Family: Gobiidae Origin: Puerto Rico Diet: frozen brine shrimp, frozen mysis shrimp, table shrimp, and frozen food preparations for carnivores. Approximate Size: Up to 1 inch

Wheeler's Shrimp Goby: The Symbiotic Sentinel The Wheeler's Shrimp Goby (Amblyeleotris wheeleri), also known as the Gorgeous Prawn-Goby or Wheeler's Watchman Goby, is a captivating and highly sought-after species due to its beautiful coloration and fascinating natural behavior. This goby's slender body is marked with a striking pattern of white or pale yellow featuring distinct reddish-brown to red vertical bands and small blue dots scattered across its face and body, giving it a vibrant, "candy cane" appearance. The primary appeal of the Wheeler's Shrimp Goby is its tendency to form a symbiotic relationship with a pistol shrimp (such as the Candy Pistol Shrimp, Alpheus randalli ). The nearly blind shrimp diligently excavates and maintains a shared burrow within the sand bed, while the goby acts as the vigilant lookout , resting near the entrance and warning the shrimp of danger with a flick of its tail. This partnership is a stunning natural display for any home aquarium. Given its small size, maxing out at about 3.5 inches , the Wheeler's Shrimp Goby is suitable for a minimum tank size of **20 to 30 gallons**. A deep bed of fine sand and rubble is essential to allow for proper burrow construction. Ensure all rockwork is placed directly on the tank bottom, not the sand, to prevent cave-ins from burrowing activity. It is completely reef safe and peaceful, but prone to jumping when startled, so a tight-fitting lid is a must . This carnivore requires a varied diet of meaty foods; target-feeding frozen or live mysis shrimp, enriched brine shrimp, or copepods near its burrow entrance may be necessary. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Amblyeleotris wheeleri Common Names: Wheeler's Shrimp Goby, Gorgeous Prawn-Goby, Wheeler's Watchman Goby Origin: Indo-Pacific Max Size: 3.5 inches Temperament: Peaceful (Territorial toward other similar gobies) Diet: Carnivore. Feeds on small benthic invertebrates. Requires frozen/live meaty foods. Minimum Tank Size: 20 gallons Special Feature: Forms a symbiotic bond with pistol shrimp.

Black-ray Goby The Black-ray Goby, also called the Antenna Goby and the Hi-fin Red Banded Goby i s a peaceful saltwater aquarium addition that requires peaceful tankmates. The Antenna Goby is distinguished by a big black dorsal fin on a small colorful body. The body is purple and white, they are friendly enough to share burrows with Pistol Shrimp. The goby is small enough for nano tanks and have been known to spawn under the right conditions in the aquarium. Scientific Name: Stonogobiops nematodes Origin: Indo-Pacific Max Size: 2 inches Shipping Size: Approx. 1 to 1 1/2 inches

Naso Tang Streamer: The Elegant & Unique Unicornfish The Naso Tang Streamer (Naso brevirostris), also known as the Short-horned Unicornfish, is an elegant and highly sought-after fish for the spacious marine aquarium . This tang is easily identified by its unique features: a brownish or grayish body covered in numerous small black spots, a short horn-like protrusion on its forehead, and, most notably, the long filaments or "streamers" that extend from its caudal fin as it matures. While it is generally peaceful with most other species, it can be territorial towards other tangs. As a herbivore, it is a fantastic algae-eater , making it a valuable and hardworking member of any clean-up crew. It is completely reef-safe and will not harm corals or invertebrates. Why the Naso Tang Streamer is a Great Choice: Elegant Appearance: Its unique coloration, "horn," and caudal streamers make it a true showpiece. Excellent Algae Control: It tirelessly grazes on nuisance algae, helping to keep the tank clean and healthy. Completely Reef-Safe: It will not harm corals, clams, or other invertebrates. Adds Energy to the Tank: It adds a lot of energy and graceful movement to a spacious aquarium. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Naso brevirostris Origin: Indo-Pacific Reefs Max Size: 20 inches Lifespan: 10+ years Diet: Herbivore. Primarily feeds on marine algae. Shipping Size: 3-5 inches

Flagtail Goby The Flagtail Goby is a member of the shrimp gobies which form symbiotic relationships with snapping shrimps. The Gobies stand guard while the shrimps play "housekeeper" to their burrow, continually digging and cleaning the sand. The Shrimp Goby will signal when predators are near. Scientific name: Amblyeleotris yanoi Origin: Indonesia Max Size: 5 inches Diet: Meaty frozen foods Shipping Size: Approx. 2 inches

Yellow Clown Goby: The Pint-sized Pop of Yellow The Yellow Clown Goby (Gobiodon okinawae) is a delightful and unique species that adds a splash of vibrant color and a gentle presence to any marine aquarium . This charming fish has a truly distinct appearance, with a vibrant, solid yellow body and a comically stout body shape. The Yellow Clown Goby is a very peaceful and timid species that is completely reef-safe and will not harm corals, clams, or other invertebrates. Unlike other fish that swim constantly, it prefers to perch among the branches of hard corals, making it a fantastic and quirky addition to your tank's landscape. It's a great choice for both nano aquariums and larger community tanks. Why the Yellow Clown Goby is a Great Choice: Stunning Appearance: Its vibrant, solid yellow body makes it a true showpiece. Completely Reef-Safe: It will not harm corals, clams, or most other invertebrates. Peaceful Temperament: It is a non-aggressive species that coexists well with other peaceful fish. Unique Behavior: Its habit of perching on corals adds a unique and interesting dynamic to the tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Gobiodon okinawae Origin: Indo-Pacific Reefs Max Size: 2 inches Lifespan: 5-7 years Diet: Carnivore. Primarily feeds on meaty foods such as shrimp, krill, and prepared foods. Shipping Size: 1-1.5 inches

Dragon Goby: The Sand Sifting Specialist The Dragon Goby (Amblygobius phalaena), also known as the Sleeper Banded or Bullet Goby, is a highly functional and handsome fish for the marine aquarium. This goby is easily recognized by its elongated, torpedo-shaped body featuring a pattern of dark brown or black vertical bands over a pale yellow-green base, often highlighted by brilliant blue markings on the face and fins. The Dragon Goby is most valued for its dedication to tank maintenance. It is a tireless sand sifter , constantly taking mouthfuls of substrate, filtering out detritus, small invertebrates, and microalgae through its gills, and expelling the clean sand. This aeration process is excellent for preventing detritus buildup and maintaining a healthy sand bed. They are also known consumers of nuisance flatworms . Given its size, which can reach up to 6 inches , and its need for ample foraging space, the Dragon Goby requires a minimum of a 55-gallon aquarium with a deep, established sand bed (2-4 inches). While generally Reef Safe and peaceful toward most tank mates, aquarists should note that their constant digging can bury low-lying corals or disrupt unsecured rockwork. Due to their tendency to jump when startled, a secure, tight-fitting lid is essential. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Amblygobius phalaena Common Names: Dragon Goby, Sleeper Banded Goby, Bullet Goby Origin: Indo-Pacific Max Size: Up to 6 inches Temperament: Peaceful (but territorial toward other sand-sifting gobies) Diet: Omnivore/Carnivore. Needs meaty foods (mysis, brine shrimp, pellets) and a well-established sand bed for micro-fauna. Minimum Tank Size: 55 gallons (for best long-term success)

Orange Spotted Watchman Goby: The Polka-Dot Watchman The Orange Spotted Watchman Goby (Amblyeleotris guttata), also known as the Spotted Prawn Goby, is one of the most vibrant and engaging species for the home reef aquarium. This beautiful fish has a pale white or gray body generously dusted with brilliant orange spots that are often outlined in brown, giving it a captivating, polka-dotted appearance. Like all Watchman Gobies , the Orange Spotted Watchman Goby is highly valued for its natural behavior. It forms a classic symbiotic relationship with an Alpheus genus Pistol Shrimp. The shrimp digs and maintains a shared burrow deep within the substrate, while the goby remains at the entrance, acting as the vigilant "watchman" and warning the shrimp of danger. This fish is Reef Safe and peaceful, thriving in community tanks. Ensure you provide a deep sand bed (at least 3 inches) with ample rubble for construction. Due to their tendency to jump when startled, a secure, tight-fitting lid is essential. Why the Orange Spotted Watchman Goby is a Great Choice: Vibrant Coloration: Its bright orange spots stand out beautifully against a white background. Symbiotic Behavior: Provides a fascinating, educational display when paired with a Pistol Shrimp. Excellent Sand Sifter: Helps aerate the substrate and prevent detritus buildup as it scavenges for food. Peaceful: An ideal, non-aggressive addition to most community reef tanks. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Amblyeleotris guttata Common Names: Spotted Prawn Goby, Orange Spotted Shrimp Goby Origin: Indo-Pacific Max Size: Up to 4.5 inches Temperament: Peaceful (but territorial towards other gobies/blennies) Diet: Carnivore. Requires small, meaty foods like mysis shrimp and finely chopped seafood. Minimum Tank Size: 30 gallons

Harlequin Basslet Scientifically speaking, the basslets are members of the family Grammatidae. Within the marine fish hobby world this category also includes members of the family Serranidae. These typically smaller fish pack a Lot of options in a small package. Basslets can be found in a dazzling array of super bright colors, but they are often territorial and aggressive, so keeping more than one male is often ill advised. Scientific Name: Serranus tigrinus Origin: Caribbean Max Size: 11 1/2 inches Diet: variety of chopped live meaty items and frozen foods. Required Tank Size: 75+ gallons Shipping Size: 2 to 3 inches

Yellow Dottyback This is a fish that balances beautiful, sunflower yellow coloration with an equally intense attitude. Confident around aggressive fish several times larger than itself, the ORA Yellow Dottyback will defend its rockwork home and do well in systems typically reserved for boisterous triggers, wrasses and puffers. While our broodstock doesn’t seem to have the same assertive personality as their reputation suggests , we do not recommend this species for peaceful aquariums . T his very hardy dottyback is best housed in systems where only the strongest survive. Reaching a size of up to 4”, it will readily consume a wide range of food from pellets and flakes to frozen mysis and chopped shrimp. Scientific Name: Pseudochromis fuscus Origin: Indonesia Max Size: 4 inches Diet: Carnivore Shipping Size: 1 to 2 inches

Lantern Basslet Takes a great aquarium addition given the correct aquarium mates. The Lantern Basslet is attractive and hardy, but may be harmful to some smaller fish and ornamental fish. Growing to only three inches in length, it is a fish of appropriate size for all but the smallest of aquariums. If more than one is to be present in the same aquarium, it is recommended to introduce them at the same time. The Lantern Basslet spends it time swimming actively and occasionally digging in the substrate using its somewhat elongated snout. Its deep red, marbled body is accented by a yellow lateral line running down the body in healthy specimens. A bright white may be visible at times on the ventral fins. Scientific Name: Serranus baldwini Origin: Caribbean Max Size: 4 1/2 inches Diet: Carnivore Shipping Size: 1 to 2 inches

Blue Line Grouper Blue line groupers are beautiful ambush predators with vivid patterns enabling the groupers to blend with the bright corals. Groupers spend much of their time hiding and watching for easy prey and require large aquariums with good filtration. Caution should be considered when adding this animal to a community tank as it will eat any fish or crustacean that may fit in it’s mouth. Scientific Name: Cephalopholis formosa Origin: Indonesia Max Size: 12 inches Diet: Carnivore Shipping Size: 2 to 3 inches

Dampiera Dottyback Grouper: The Fiery, Aggressive Centerpiece The Dampiera Dottyback Grouper (Labracinus cyclophthalmus), also widely known as the Firetail Dottyback , Red Dottyback , or Fire-tail Devil , is a large, colorful, and notoriously aggressive marine fish from the Dottyback (Pseudochromidae) family. The "Grouper" designation in its common name is historical (referring to its former genus Dampieria) and reflects its incredibly belligerent, bass-like temperament and predatory nature, which is unusual for a fish of its size. Native to the Western Pacific, throughout the Indo-Malayan Archipelago, this Dottyback can grow significantly larger than its more peaceful relatives, reaching an impressive maximum size of up to 9 inches (23 cm). Its body coloration is typically dark red-brown with several pale vertical stripes, sharply contrasted by a striking, bright red or orange tail fin, which gives it one of its most common names. Due to its territoriality and active swimming, a minimum aquarium size of 75 gallons is recommended, though a 120-gallon tank is preferred for a mature specimen to reduce aggression. The Dampiera Dottyback Grouper is a fantastic showpiece for a Fish-Only-With-Live-Rock (FOWLR) system, but its aggressive nature makes careful tankmate selection essential. It is a highly hardy species and an excellent choice for experienced aquarists looking for a bold personality. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: This fish is a dedicated Carnivore and a highly efficient predator. In the wild, it hunts small fish and crustaceans. In captivity, it readily accepts most frozen, meaty marine foods, including krill, silversides, mysis shrimp, and chopped squid. A varied diet of high-quality frozen foods should be offered once daily. Feeding: Due to its aggressive metabolism and territorial defense, ensure this fish receives ample food. Its appetite can make it difficult for shyer tankmates to compete for food. Reef Compatibility: It is Reef Safe With Caution. While this species will ignore corals, anemones, and large sessile invertebrates, it will aggressively prey upon and consume nearly all ornamental shrimp, small crabs, and snails. It will also eat any fish small enough to fit into its mouth. Temperament: It is Aggressive / Predatory. This Dottyback is highly territorial and should only be housed with large, robust, and moderately aggressive fish that can defend themselves. Good tankmates include large angelfish, puffers, lionfish, tangs, and certain triggerfish. Avoid housing with smaller, peaceful, or passive fish, as they will be constantly harassed or eaten. It is generally kept singly, but can be kept as a mated pair if introduced simultaneously to a large system. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Labracinus cyclophthalmus Primary Common Name: Dampiera Dottyback Grouper Other Common Names: Firetail Dottyback, Red Dottyback, Fire-tail Devil, Red Grouper Origin: Western Pacific (Indo-Malayan Archipelago) Max Size: 9 inches (23 cm) Temperament: Aggressive / Predatory (Highly territorial) Diet: Carnivore (Meaty frozen foods) Minimum Tank Size: 75 Gallons (120+ Gallons recommended) Reef Compatibility: With Caution (Will eat shrimp and small inverts/fish)

Red Hawkfish The armatus hawkfish is a great little fish for most saltwater reef tanks. It spends most of its time just waiting for its next meal to swim, crawl or walk by as it sits perched on a coral head or rock outcropping. Scientific Name: Neocirrhitus armatus Origin: Tahiti, Fiji Max Size: 4 inches Diet: Carnivore Shipping Size: 1 to 3 inches

Freckled Hawkfish: The Unique & Watchful Reef Guardian The Freckled Hawkfish (Paracirrhites forsteri), also known as Forster's Hawkfish , Spotted or Blackside Hawkfish , is a captivating and unique species that adds a touch of personality and a watchful presence to any marine aquarium . This intriguing fish is easily identified by its striking two-tone body: a reddish-brown head and anterior section that transitions to a dark black posterior, often speckled with white spots. The Freckled Hawkfish is known for its fascinating perching behavior; it uses its thick pectoral fins to rest on live rock or coral branches, keeping a keen eye on its surroundings. While generally a peaceful addition to a community tank, caution should be taken with very small invertebrates as they can be seen as a food source. Why the Freckled Hawkfish is a Great Choice: Unique Appearance: Its two-tone body and mottled pattern make it a true showpiece. Interesting Perching Behavior: Its habit of perching on rocks adds a unique and engaging dynamic to the tank. Peaceful Temperament: It is a non-aggressive species that coexists well with other peaceful fish. Reef-Safe with Caution: It will not harm corals, but may prey on small shrimp or crabs. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Paracirrhites forsteri Origin: Indo-Pacific Reefs Max Size: 8.5 inches Lifespan: 5-7 years Diet: Carnivore. Primarily feeds on meaty foods such as shrimp, krill, and small invertebrates. Shipping Size: 2-3 inches

Volitan Lionfish: The Venomous Predator The Volitan Lionfish (Pterois volitans), also commonly known as the Black Lionfish, Red Lionfish , Common Lionfish , or Turkeyfish , is one of the most popular and striking venomous marine fish. This fish is a magnificent, though challenging, addition to the large marine aquarium. Native to the Indo-Pacific, the Volitan Lionfish is a large predator, capable of reaching an impressive body length of 12 to 15 inches (30-38 cm). Its elaborate fins, which include 13 long, venomous dorsal spines , make it a true showpiece. Due to its size and high bioload, a minimum aquarium size of 120 gallons is required, and larger is always better. The Volitan Lionfish is generally peaceful toward tankmates too large to be eaten but poses a significant risk to the hobbyist due to its highly venomous spines. Extreme caution must be exercised during all tank maintenance. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: This fish is a dedicated Carnivore and a highly effective predator. In the wild, it hunts small fish and crustaceans. In captivity, it must be trained to eat non-living, meaty foods such as frozen krill, silversides , chunks of squid, and marine shrimp. Avoid feeding freshwater feeder fish (like guppies or goldfish) as this leads to nutritional deficiencies (fatty liver disease). Feeding: Lionfish can be easily trained to recognize their owner. Feed every 2-3 days as an adult until its stomach shows a slight bulge. Reef Compatibility: It is Reef Safe With Caution . While the Lionfish will generally ignore corals, it will systematically hunt and eat nearly all ornamental invertebrates (shrimp, crabs, snails, etc.) and any fish that can fit into its surprisingly large mouth (roughly half its body size). Temperament: It is Semi-Aggressive / Predatory . It should only be housed with large, robust, and fast-moving tankmates that are at least half its body length. Good choices include large tangs, groupers, and aggressive marine angels. It is solitary and should be kept singly or in mated pairs. Venomous Spines: The sting is extremely painful but rarely fatal to humans. If stung, immediately immerse the affected area in the hottest water you can tolerate (not scalding) for 30-90 minutes, as heat breaks down the protein-based venom. Seek medical attention immediately. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Pterois volitans Primary Common Name: Black or Red Volitan Lionfish Other Common Names: Red Lionfish, Turkeyfish, Butterfly Cod Origin: Indo-Pacific (Widespread) Max Size: 12-15 inches (30-38 cm) Temperament: Semi-Aggressive / Predatory ( Venomous ) Diet: Carnivore (Must be converted to frozen meaty foods) Minimum Tank Size: 120+ Gallons Reef Compatibility: With Caution (Will eat invertebrates and small fish)

Black Box Fish Boxfish are strikingly distinctive fish that requires special care, but whose coloration and personality make it worth the effort. Of utmost importance, this fish must be kept with peaceful aquarium mates that will not cause undue stress. Scientific Name: Ostracion meleagris Origin: Hawaii Max Size: 10 inches Diet: Omnivore Required Tank Size: 180+ gallons Shipping Size: 1 to 3 inches

Boxfish and Cowfish are thought by some hobbyists to be too difficult to keep. While theses fishes do require careful attention in their dietary and habitat needs, they can and do make personable and fascinating aquarium specimens. Scientific Name: Ostracion meleagris Max Size: 10 inches Required Tank Size: 180+ gallons Diet: When first introduced, feed a diet of live brine shrimp or blood worms. After acclimatization, chopped squid, clams, mussels, and herbivore preparations. Shipping Size: 3 to 4 Inches

Yellow Belly Dogface Puffer: The Interactive Giant The Yellow Belly Dogface Puffer (Arothron nigropunctatus) is a highly sought-after color variant of the standard Dogface Puffer , which is also known as the Blackspotted Puffer . This variant is characterized by a bright, attractive golden-yellow underside (ventrally), contrasted by a grey or dark grey upper body (dorsally) and the characteristic black markings around the mouth and eyes that give it its "dog-like" expression. Hailing from the Indo-Pacific, this large, robust puffer is known for its intelligence and often develops a highly interactive, "pet-like" personality with its owner. It is a substantial fish, reaching an adult length of up to 13 inches (33 cm). Due to its size and exceptionally high bioload (messy eating), a minimum aquarium size of 125 to 180 gallons is required for long-term health, with larger tanks (200+ gallons) highly recommended for adults. Like all puffers, the Yellow Belly Dogface Puffer is able to rapidly inflate its body with water (or air) when threatened, forming a sphere nearly twice its size. This fish also possesses a potent neurotoxin, Tetrodotoxin (TTX) , in its skin and organs, making it poisonous to eat. NEVER intentionally provoke a puffer to inflate, and when moving it, always use a rigid container submerged in water to prevent it from swallowing air, which can be fatal. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: This is a dedicated Carnivore/Omnivore with a powerful beak-like mouth (fused teeth). Its natural diet includes hard-shelled invertebrates and corals. In captivity, a varied, meaty diet is essential, including frozen krill, whole shrimp, squid, scallops, and chunks of marine fish flesh. Beak Maintenance: Puffers' teeth grow continuously. It is CRITICAL to provide hard-shelled foods such as whole, in-shell clams, mussels, or oysters at least a couple of times a week to naturally wear down the beak. Failure to do so will result in an overgrown beak, making the fish unable to eat and requiring stressful manual trimming. Reef Compatibility: It is NOT Reef Safe . This puffer will systematically eat ornamental invertebrates (shrimp, crabs, snails, sea urchins, etc.) and will nip at or consume corals, especially Acropora tips. It is best suited for a Fish-Only With Live Rock (FOWLR) system with robust filtration. Temperament: It is Semi-Aggressive / Predatory . It is generally peaceful toward large, fast-moving, and robust tankmates (e.g., large tangs, eels, some triggerfish, and angelfish) but may nip the fins of slower or long-finned fish. It is best kept as the sole puffer in the tank, as they may quarrel with other puffers of the same genus. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Arothron nigropunctatus Primary Common Name: Yellow Belly Dogface Puffer Other Common Names: Blackspotted Puffer, Dogface Puffer, Black-spotted Pufferfish Origin: Indo-Pacific (Widespread) Max Size: 13 inches (33 cm) Temperament: Semi-Aggressive / Predatory ( Poisonous ) Diet: Carnivore (Requires hard-shelled foods for beak wear) Minimum Tank Size: 125-180+ Gallons Reef Compatibility: Not Reef Safe (Will eat invertebrates and corals)

Arothron meleagris , commonly known as the guineafowl puffer or golden puffer. Guineafowl puffers have heavy rounded bodies that are uniformly black with numerous small white spots (black puffer or botete negro ), bright yellow spots (golden puffer or botete dorado ) or a mixture of the two morphologies with bright yellow spots and black patches. They have large blunt heads with short snouts and are equipped with a set of massive teeth. They have small and similarly shaped anal and dorsal fins that are well back on their body. Their caudal fin base is long and deep and their caudal fin is rounded. Their body is covered with small denticles that resemble coarse sandpaper. When this fish is scared or frightened, they inflate and make themselves larger, exposing the denticles.

Porcupine Puffer: The Spiny Personality The Porcupine Puffer (Diodon holocanthus), also known as the Long-spine Porcupinefish or Balloonfish, is one of the most charismatic and intelligent fish in the marine hobby. Renowned for its endearing, "dog-like" personality, this puffer quickly learns to recognize and interact with its owner. As a nocturnal predator, the Porcupine Puffer requires an ample amount of robust rockwork to provide hiding places during the day, as well as significant open swimming space. Due to its large adult size of up to 20 inches and extremely messy eating habits, a minimum aquarium size of **180-200 gallons** is essential, supported by powerful filtration and a high-quality protein skimmer. Dietary Warning: The puffer’s beak-like teeth grow continuously. It is critical to provide a regular diet of hard-shelled, meaty foods (such as clams-in-shell, mussels, and krill with shells) to naturally wear down its beak. Failure to do so will result in overgrown teeth that prevent the fish from feeding. Defense Mechanism & Compatibility: Defense: When stressed or threatened, the Porcupine Puffer can inflate its body with water (or air, which is dangerous) to nearly twice its normal size, causing its long spines to stand erect. Its flesh contains **Tetrodotoxin**, making it toxic if consumed. Compatibility: This species is a relentless hunter of invertebrates and is **NOT Reef Safe**. It is best kept in a Fish Only With Live Rock (FOWLR) system with large, boisterous tank mates (like large Angelfish or Tangs) that can withstand occasional nipping. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Diodon holocanthus Common Names: Porcupine Puffer, Balloonfish, Long-spine Porcupinefish Origin: Circumtropical (worldwide) Max Size: Up to 20 inches (50 cm) Temperament: Semi-Aggressive (predatory) Diet: Carnivore (Must include hard-shelled food) Minimum Tank Size: 180+ Gallons

The Whitespotted Puffer has a tan body and a white belly. It's many white spots from the middle to the back half of the body are outlined by thin black lines. The spots near the front half of the body and area around the snout have a light turquoise hue to them. It has a dark, almost black spot or area at the base of the dorsal fin. All of these species have a sharp, pointed snout, thus named Sharp-Nosed Puffers. Scientific name: Canthigaster jactator Maximum size: 4 inches Shipping Size: Approx. 2 inches

Honey puffer is also known as the Honeycomb Toby. Members of the Canthigaster genus are called Sharp-nosed Puffers or Tobies. It lacks pelvic fins, but has learned to use the pectoral fins to move about the aquarium.Its teeth are actually a fused beak-like structure. It may eat invertebrates found in a reef tank. It becomes alarmed when in a net, therefore, use a container to transfer it. Scientific Name: Canthigaster Janthinoptera Max Size: 4 inches Diet: Carnivore Approximate Size: 1-1/2 to 2 inches

Emperor Red Snapper: The Giant Banded Predator The Emperor Red Snapper (Lutjanus sebae), also known as the Red Emperor or Sebae Snapper , is a large, predatory marine fish highly prized for its beauty as a juvenile. Juveniles exhibit a striking pattern of three bold, oblique dark-red to black bands over a white or pink body, including a band that passes directly through the eye. Native to the vast Indo-West Pacific, this species is a fast-growing fish that reaches an immense size. In the wild, they can grow up to 46 inches (116 cm), though they commonly reach about 24 inches. As they mature, the distinct juvenile bands fade, and the fish assumes a more uniform reddish-pink or red coloration. Due to its size, predatory nature, and heavy bio-load, the Emperor Red Snapper is suitable only for the most experienced aquarists with massive, specialized aquariums, often of a size typically found in public displays. A bare minimum tank size of 300 gallons is required for a small juvenile, with an upgrade to 1,000+ gallons being necessary for the long-term health and welfare of a sub-adult or adult specimen. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: This fish is a dedicated Carnivore and a ferocious predator in the wild. Its diet consists of fish, crabs, shrimps, and cephalopods. In captivity, it should be fed a protein-rich diet of fresh or frozen meaty foods, such as chunks of silversides, squid, clam, and marine shrimp. Supplementing with a high-quality marine carnivore pellet is also recommended. Avoid fatty freshwater foods like beefheart. Feeding: Feed once daily to several times per week. The Emperor Snapper has a heavy bio-load, so powerful filtration and careful feeding are essential to maintaining excellent water quality. Reef Compatibility: It is Not Reef Safe . While it generally ignores corals, it is a formidable predator and will systematically consume any ornamental crustaceans (shrimp, crabs) and any fish small enough to fit into its surprisingly large mouth. Temperament: It is Aggressive / Predatory . As an adult, it is best kept as a solitary specimen in a large Fish-Only (FO) or Fish-Only-With-Live-Rock (FOWLR) system. It should only be housed with large, robust, and similarly semi-aggressive fish like groupers, triggers, and large marine angels. Juveniles may school, but adults become aggressive towards conspecifics. Aquarium Note: Due to its speed and power, the aquarium must have a secure and reinforced lid to prevent the fish from jumping out. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Lutjanus sebae Primary Common Name: Emperor Red Snapper Other Common Names: Red Emperor, Sebae Snapper, African Red Snapper Origin: Indo-West Pacific (Widespread) Max Size: Up to 46 inches (116 cm) Temperament: Aggressive / Predatory Diet: Carnivore (Meaty foods: fish, squid, shrimp) Minimum Tank Size: 300 Gallons (Juvenile), 1000+ Gallons (Adult) Reef Compatibility: No (Will eat invertebrates and small fish)

Also known as the Trevally Pilotfish or Golden Jack, is shimmering metallic-gold with black vertical bands across the body. The pilot fish is a schooling fish that can grow to four feet! So remember you will need a big aquarium are a public aquarium for fish adoption. In the wild Pilot Fish are pelagic and school in open water as they will in the aquarium. Golden Trevally Juveniles are a gold/yellow color with thin black stripes that run down the side of the body; these black lines fade a little as the fish matures. Scientific Name: Gnathanodon speciosus Origin: Caribbean Max Size: 4 feet Diet: Carnivore Shipping Size: 1 to 4 inches

Indigo Hamlet: The Striped Caribbean Beauty The Indigo Hamlet (Hypoplectrus indigo) is a striking and hardy marine fish belonging to the Grouper/Sea Bass family (Serranidae). It is highly prized in the aquarium trade for its dramatic and unique coloration, featuring a deep, rich blue to indigo body adorned with several bold, vertical electric blue or white bars. This beautiful pattern helps conceal it in its natural reef habitat. Native to the Western Central Atlantic, specifically the Caribbean, Bahamas, and Florida Keys, the Indigo Hamlet is a manageable size for many home aquariums, typically reaching a maximum adult length of 5 to 6 inches (13-15 cm). Given its need for territory and swimming space, a minimum tank size of 50 to 75 gallons is recommended. The aquarium should include ample, stable live rock with numerous caves and crevices, as this fish is naturally shy and will establish a small territory to retreat to when threatened. As with all Hamlets, the Indigo Hamlet is a simultaneous hermaphrodite, possessing both male and female sex organs, and has been successfully bred in captivity. It is a long-lived species, often thriving for 15-20 years with proper care. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: The Indigo Hamlet is a dedicated Carnivore. In the wild, adults primarily feed on small fish (such as Blue Chromis) and crustaceans. In the aquarium, it should be fed a varied, protein-rich diet of frozen meaty foods, including enriched mysis shrimp, krill, brine shrimp, chopped clam, squid, and finely cut fish flesh. Feed once or twice daily. Due to its predatory nature, avoid using low-nutrition "feeder fish." Feeding: Hamlets are voracious eaters but may be shy initially. Ensure food reaches their hiding spots until they become comfortable feeding in the open. Reef Compatibility: It is generally considered Reef Safe With Caution. The Indigo Hamlet will not harm sessile invertebrates like corals or anemones. However, it is a known predator of small, ornamental crustaceans (shrimp and small crabs) and any fish small enough to fit in its surprisingly large mouth (generally less than 2 inches). Temperament: It is Semi-Aggressive / Territorial. Hamlets are generally peaceful toward non-aggressive fish that are significantly larger than its mouth, but they can be territorial toward similar-sized species, especially other Hamlets. They should be kept singly unless the tank is very large (>100 gallons) and multiple specimens (or Hamlets of different species) are introduced simultaneously to prevent aggressive pairing conflicts. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Hypoplectrus indigo Primary Common Name: Indigo Hamlet Other Common Names: Blue Hamlet, Caribbean Hamlet Origin: Western Central Atlantic (Caribbean, Florida, Bahamas, Belize) Max Size: 5-6 inches (13-15 cm) Temperament: Semi-Aggressive / Territorial Diet: Carnivore (Small fish and crustaceans) Minimum Tank Size: 50-75 Gallons Reef Compatibility: With Caution (Will eat small fish and ornamental shrimp/crabs)

Hypoplectrus (Hamlets) are a colorful and relatively small predatory fish which are well suited to tank life. All the species are very alike, when not taking color and habitat into account. They will eat small fish and crustaceans which can be swallowed, but are otherwise not a threat to the other animals in the aquarium. Hamlets are fairly hardy and easy fish, but are not very good at adjusting to tank life. They should therefore be bought as young as feasible, and should be moved around as little as possible. They are easy to feed and do not require live food, so a varied diet of frozen fish, crustaceans and the like is sufficient. Needs to be fed once a day.

Flounder Known as a flatfish which is a very fitting name because its body is laterally compressed and it lays on its side, often burrowing into the substrate. Flounder have two bubble eyes on one side of their head and it typically feeds by camouflaging itself and lying in wait for prey to come by. For the most part, flounder are semi-aggressive fish and they need to be kept in very large aquariums. Do not keep these fish with any species small enough to be viewed as prey. Scientific Name: Brachirus panoides

The Frontosa Cichlid lives twenty-five years and grows to a foot long. These are splendid cichlids, and males grow a distinctive hump on their head. These fish are appropriate for a large species community or cichlid tank. Since they are difficult to breed and grow slowly like most Tanganyikans, they are a bit more expensive than their Lake Malawi cousins. The word frontosa is Latin for "big forehead". Many of the African species we know toady were named after Belgium zoologist George Boulenge. Central Africa was part of the Belgium empire in 1906 when George came upon the fish. Quick Facts Scientific Name Cyphotilapia frontosa Origin Lake Tanganyika, Africa Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful for its size, but eats small fish Adult Size Up to 12–14" Lifespan 20+ years Diet Carnivore Water Temperature 75–80°F pH 7.8–9.0 Shipping Size Small: approx. 1" · Medium: approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Frontosa need a sand bottom, a few large, stable rock caves and lots of open water. Keep the lighting moderate. Lake Malawi and Lake Tanganyika cichlids need hard, alkaline water; crushed coral or aragonite sand helps hold the pH up. Feeding: Feed a quality sinking cichlid pellet once a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like shrimp. Avoid feeder fish, which can carry disease. Tankmates: Frontosa do best in a group with other peaceful, large Tanganyikans like calvus and cyprichromis (adult frontosa will eat small fish), plus synodontis catfish. Good to know: Frontosa grow slowly and can live 20 years or more, so they are a long-term commitment.

The male Cockatoo or Apistogramma Cacatuoides dwarf cichlid is truly magnificent when he grows to his full two-inch size. Females are a bit drabber but still have nice yellow and red coloration. AquariumFish.com tries to pair when shipping more than one item; males just never display all their colors without a female around. These apistogrammas, like all apistos, are great additions to gentle community tanks, nano tanks, and planted aquariums. Quick Facts Scientific Name Apistogramma cacatuoides Origin Peru, Colombia and Brazil (Amazon basin) Care Level Easy, a good first apisto Temperament Peaceful (males territorial with each other) Adult Size Males up to 3"; females about 2" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 75–84°F pH 6.0–7.5 Shipping Size Approx. ¾–1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter, dim lighting and lots of plants, driftwood and leaf litter. Add a cave (a coconut shell or small clay pot) for each female. Most apistos prefer soft, slightly acidic water. Feeding: Feed small pellets or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with small, peaceful fish such as tetras, rasboras, pencilfish, otocinclus and corydoras. A calm school of small "dither" fish helps apistos feel safe enough to come out. Keep one male per tank unless it is large and well planted, and avoid large or boisterous fish. Adults may eat small shrimp and baby shrimp. Breeding: Apistos are cave spawners. The female lays her eggs inside a cave and guards the fry, while the male patrols the territory. One male with several females works well in a planted tank. Good to know: Cockatoo apistos are among the hardiest apistogrammas and handle a wider range of water than most, which makes them a great first dwarf cichlid.

The albino tiger oscar will grow into a large, aggressive aquarium fish and should be kept alone or with similar-size species when it gets larger. This oscar color morph is beautiful, and the species is easy to keep and will be tolerant of other large, aggressive freshwater species. Quick Facts Scientific Name Astronotus ocellatus (albino tiger variety) Origin Amazon basin, South America; aquarium-bred Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Semi-aggressive; eats smaller fish Adult Size Up to 12–14" Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods; takes pellets) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single or pair Shipping Size Approx. 2–3" Care Guide Tank setup: Use a sand bottom, a few large rocks or driftwood, strong filtration and a tight lid, since they can jump. Oscars often rearrange decorations and uproot plants. Feeding: Feed a quality cichlid pellet once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like shrimp. Avoid feeder goldfish, which can carry disease. Tankmates: Oscars can live with other large, peaceful-to-semi-aggressive fish like silver dollars, large plecos, severums and other oscars. They will eat any fish that fits in their mouth. Good to know: Oscars are known as "water puppies" for their personality and often learn to recognize their owners and beg for food.

The bala shark, or minnow shark, is one of the most popular schooling fish for aquariums. These freshwater sharks are great in community tanks when small but will grow to 12 inches in about two years, and then these freshwater sharks are great for larger species tanks. Shipping size is about 2 inches to 3 inches. We recommend a school of three to six. Like most shark fish, bala sharks are hardy at two inches but weak (though very cheap!) at smaller sizes. These sharks tend to be less hardy under two inches, so we do our best to import the proper size. Quick Facts Scientific Name Balantiocheilos melanopterus Origin Thailand, Malaysia, Sumatra and Borneo (farm-raised) Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful but very active Adult Size Up to 12–14" Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Small: 1½" · Medium: 2–3" Care Guide Tank setup: These are fast, schooling fish that grow large, so give them plenty of open swimming space, strong filtration and a heavy, tight-fitting lid, since they jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or pellet once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other large, peaceful to semi-aggressive fish such as silver dollars, tinfoil barbs, larger gouramis, plecos and peaceful cichlids. They will eat very small fish once they are large. Good to know: These "sharks" are members of the carp family, not true sharks. They grow quickly, so check their adult size before buying.

The black tip shark is also called the white tip shark, and the names are so mixed up we felt compelled to list this fish under both names. The brackish black tip shark is also called the Colombian shark after the Amazon basin from which it originates. These fish can handle fresh, brackish and even full saltwater tanks. Quick Facts Scientific Name Ariopsis seemanni (formerly Arius jordani ) Origin Pacific coast of Central and South America (Mexico to Peru) Care Level Moderate (needs brackish water as it matures) Temperament Peaceful schooler; eats small fish Adult Size Up to 12–14" Lifespan 10+ years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods, pellets) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 7.5–8.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 2–4" Care Guide Tank setup: Colombian sharks are active schoolers that need lots of swimming space and strong filtration. Juveniles can live in fresh or lightly brackish water, but as they mature (over about 5 inches) they need brackish water, rising to a specific gravity of about 1.010–1.015; many keepers eventually move them to full marine. Keep a lid on the tank. Feeding: Feed sinking carnivore pellets once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like shrimp and bloodworms. Tankmates: Keep them with other brackish fish that are too large to swallow, such as monos, scats and larger archerfish. Their fin spines are venomous, so handle them with care. Good to know: Colombian sharks are catfish with venomous fin spines. They are true brackish fish and do poorly long-term in pure freshwater.

Rainbow sharks from Indonesia have deep red fins on a silver body. These sharks are actually catfish and are hardy and easy to keep and peaceful. The rainbow shark grows to about six inches. Quick Facts Scientific Name Epalzeorhynchos frenatum Origin Mekong basin (Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam); aquarium-bred Care Level Moderate Temperament Semi-aggressive, territorial (especially toward other sharks) Adult Size Up to 6" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Keep one per tank Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give a rainbow-type shark caves, driftwood and plants to break up sight lines, plus a tight lid, since they jump. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets or wafers and a quality flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy algae wafers and frozen bloodworms. Tankmates: Keep only one rainbow-type shark per tank, and avoid other bottom-dwelling sharks and territorial fish like red-tailed sharks. They do best with fast, mid- to upper-level swimmers such as danios, barbs, rainbowfish and larger tetras. Good to know: Despite the name, these "sharks" are members of the carp family, not true sharks or catfish. They claim a territory near the bottom and chase other bottom dwellers, so give them caves and keep only one per tank.

The red tail shark is an active scavenger in the aquarium and is very easy to keep. These "sharks" are actually catfish and will eat anything they can fit in their mouths, which are fortunately small. Red tail sharks only grow to about four inches. The shark pictured is show quality; few red tail sharks get color that deep. Quick Facts Scientific Name Epalzeorhynchos bicolor Origin Thailand (aquarium-bred; critically endangered in the wild) Care Level Moderate Temperament Semi-aggressive, territorial (especially toward other sharks) Adult Size Up to 5–6" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Keep one per tank Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give a rainbow-type shark caves, driftwood and plants to break up sight lines, plus a tight lid, since they jump. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets or wafers and a quality flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy algae wafers and frozen bloodworms. Tankmates: Keep only one rainbow-type shark per tank, and avoid other bottom-dwelling sharks and territorial fish like red-tailed sharks. They do best with fast, mid- to upper-level swimmers such as danios, barbs, rainbowfish and larger tetras. Good to know: Despite the name, these "sharks" are members of the carp family, not true sharks or catfish. They claim a territory near the bottom and chase other bottom dwellers, so give them caves and keep only one per tank.

The Indian glass fish, or dwarf glass fish, is a popular aquarium classic. You can see right through them! These community schooling fish never get large and eat flake foods and get along with other fish in a peaceful community fish tank. Glass fish prefer to swim in a school of three or more, and are more apt to swim in the middle of the tank than hide in the corner if they have school mates. Quick Facts Scientific Name Parambassis ranga Origin South and Southeast Asia Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ¾–1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants, hiding places and gentle filtration. They like slightly hard water, and a little aquarium salt is optional. Feeding: Feed small amounts of flake or micro pellets once or twice a day. They also enjoy small frozen foods like brine shrimp and bloodworms. Tankmates: Glassfish are peaceful and get along with other small community fish such as rasboras, danios, livebearers and corydoras. Good to know: Glassfish are see-through, and their bodies have a soft gold or silver sheen under good lighting.

The Tiger Shovelnose Catfish has a classic sleek body with broad tiger stripes and they will grow to two feet in the aquarium over time, so this fish should be kept only with larger species. These are beautiful catfish with a long flowing body and are caught in the upper Amazonian basin of Peru. These fish come in pattern variations from spotted to striped depending upon the stream they are caught in. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pseudoplatystoma fasciatum Origin Amazon and Orinoco basins, South America Care Level Moderate (grows very large) Temperament Predatory Adult Size Up to 2 feet in aquariums Lifespan 15–20 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 4–8" Care Guide Tank setup: Shovelnose catfish grow large and are strong swimmers. Give them open swimming space, a sand bottom, strong filtration and a heavy, tight lid. Feeding: Feed meaty foods like quality carnivore pellets and frozen shrimp or fish. Many learn to take pellets once settled. Avoid feeder fish, which can carry disease. Tankmates: They will eat any fish that fits in their mouth. Keep them only with large, robust fish.
