Good to know: Tiger shovelnose catfish are fast swimmers and can startle easily, so a heavy, secure lid is important.

These beautiful veil angelfish are truly unique, with a silver front and a solid black rear. Long fins are characteristic of all "veil" type angelfish. The black half of the half-black veil angelfish will get deeper and darker as the fish grows, and the fins, like all veils, will get much longer than the standard angelfish. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pterophyllum scalare (veil-fin variety) Origin Amazon basin, South America (captive-bred) Care Level Easy Temperament Semi-aggressive (territorial when pairing) Adult Size Up to 6" long, with extra-long fins Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Shipping Size Approx. 2–3" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them tall plants or driftwood, a heater and a gentle filter. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Choose peaceful fish too large to swallow, such as larger tetras, corydoras, plecos, rams, gouramis and peaceful barbs. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs, and small fish like neon tetras that adult angels may eat. Breeding: Angelfish pair off and lay eggs on flat surfaces like broad leaves or slate. A breeding pair can become territorial, so give them room and places for other fish to retreat. Good to know: Long veil fins are easy targets for fin-nippers and can get infected in dirty water, so keep the water clean and skip nippy tankmates.

The albino lemon tetra is a species that originates from South America and was then bred in Thailand to provide this beautiful albino color morph. It is a small tetra growing to 2 inches in length. The parent lemon tetra was first brought to the trade in 1932, but the albino version was not seen until the movie Back to the Future . Quick Facts Scientific Name Hyphessobrycon pulchripinnis (albino variety) Origin Aquarium-bred (Thailand); wild form from Brazil Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a dark substrate, which brings out their color. Keep a lid on the tank, since tetras can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, rasboras, danios, corydoras, dwarf cichlids, gouramis and livebearers. Good to know: Tetras feel safer and show better color in a group. A larger school also spreads out any chasing.

The blue emperor tetra is a rare tank-bred variety developed from the parent wild purple emperor tetra. Super blue, or royal blue, emperor tetras display a solid blue body and light blue highlights on the classic extended fins. Male emperor tetras have slightly larger fins than the females, but like most other species, they display their colors better with both sexes present. We import our blue emperors from a breeder in Singapore whenever they become available! Pictured is a mature male in heat, but some blue and black is featured in all the fish. Available in a group Quick Facts Scientific Name Inpaichthys kerri (blue variety) Origin Brazil (wild form); bred in Singapore Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1½" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a dark substrate, which brings out their color. Keep a lid on the tank, since tetras can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, rasboras, danios, corydoras, dwarf cichlids, gouramis and livebearers. Good to know: Tetras feel safer and show better color in a group. A larger school also spreads out any chasing.

Yes, the goonch catfish, also called the giant devil cat, was featured on River Monsters as the fish that swallows men in India. Why someone wants this in an aquarium where they can grow up and eat their owner is questionable, but once in a while we'll get them in and they sell pretty fast! Goonch cats require a good size tank and good aeration and a varied diet. We guarantee to get these to you alive, but you will need to keep them that way - there are some good research and blog sites to help with that on the internet. These are stand-alone exotic pets. Do not feed children to them. Quick Facts Scientific Name Bagarius yarrelli Origin South and Southeast Asia Care Level Difficult (grows very large) Temperament Predatory Adult Size Up to 6 feet in the wild Lifespan 15+ years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 8" Care Guide Tank setup: They grow very large, so give them strong filtration, a sand bottom, sturdy decorations and a heavy, tight lid. Feeding: Feed meaty foods like quality carnivore pellets and frozen shrimp or fish. Many learn to take pellets once settled. Tankmates: They will eat any fish that fits in their mouth. Keep them only with large, robust fish. Good to know: Goonch catfish come from fast, rocky rivers and need strong current and plenty of oxygen.

The pineapple pleco is an amazing example of the colorful family of cactus plecos from Brazil. These plecos are tough to find and command a high price. Show size plecos are beautiful and hardy. These plecos will get to a large size but will be good tank mates with any neighbors that can't fit into their mouth. At five inches the deep red and gold fringes are just beginning to show. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pseudorinelepis genibarbis Origin Amazon basin, Brazil and Peru Care Level Moderate (grows large) Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 12–16" Lifespan 15+ years Diet Omnivore (meaty sinking foods) Water Temperature 76–84°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 4" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them caves, driftwood, good current and good filtration. They are most active at night. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets once a day, ideally in the evening when they are most active. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and shrimp. Tankmates: They are peaceful and get along with most fish, including cichlids. Avoid keeping two large plecos in the same tank. Good to know: Pineapple plecos develop red and gold edges on their fins as they grow.

Stone catfish, also called the dwarf anchor catfish for the shape of their body, are small scavengers that will do well with any fish that cannot eat them. These are great nano tank and planted tank additions as they will not eat fancy shrimp and other smaller tank mates. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hara jerdoni Origin India and Bangladesh Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1½" Lifespan 5 years Diet Omnivore (bottom feeder) Water Temperature 64–77°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. ¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a sand or fine gravel bottom, leaf litter and smooth stones. They like cool, clean water with gentle current. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets once a day, ideally in the evening when they are most active. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms. Tankmates: They are tiny and peaceful, so they are safe with shrimp and small community fish. Good to know: Stone catfish are well camouflaged and often sit still on rocks and wood.

The Black phantom guppy has a big black tail with blue iridescence on the small body. Females have a black tail and a tan body. These fish are the Thai style. Each order comes with one male and one female. Quick Facts Scientific Name Poecilia reticulata Origin Northern South America (captive-bred in Thailand) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Sold as a pair (1 male + 1 female) Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and plenty of plants, including some floating plants where babies can hide. Guppies like slightly hard water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Guppies get along with other small, peaceful fish such as platies, mollies, corydoras, small tetras and rasboras. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs and larger fish that could eat them. Breeding: Guppies are livebearers and breed easily. Females give birth to live babies about once a month, and adults will eat the babies, so thick plants give them a place to hide. Good to know: The blue shine on the black tail is easiest to see under bright aquarium lighting.

The exotic blind cave fish were discovered in a completely dark cave in Mexico. Also known as the Mexican tetra, blind cave tetra or blind fish, these fish don't have eyes or pigmentation. This unusual-looking fish is a bit nippy, as it tends to overcompensate, but it generally fits well in a community tank as long as there's good room to swim. These fish are very active as they troll for food and explore their surroundings; they are interesting additions to the fish tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name Astyanax mexicanus (blind cave form) Origin Caves of the Sierra de El Abra, Mexico; aquarium-bred Care Level Easy Temperament Semi-aggressive (may nip fins) Adult Size Up to 3½" Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 68–78°F pH 6.5–8.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Blind cave tetras find their way by sensing water movement, so they do fine in a normal tank. Give them open swimming space, smooth rocks and caves, and avoid sharp decorations. Lighting can be dim. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets or flake once or twice a day. They find food by smell, so sinking foods work well. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They do well with robust, active fish of similar size like larger tetras, barbs, danios and rainbowfish. Avoid slow, long-finned fish, which they may nip. Good to know: Blind cave tetras are born with eyes, which become covered by skin as they grow; they rely on their lateral line to sense their surroundings.

The beautiful cyprichromis cichlid is a perfect example of the dither fish. Dithering fish are schooling fish that, through their schooling movement, signal the coast is clear. This allows the timid hiding creatures in the tank to come out of their shells and caves so they can actually be seen in the aquarium. The blue and yellow colors, sleek body, and peaceful disposition make these beautiful additions to any larger community tank or cichlid tank. Cyprichromis are best in schools of four or more, but these cichlids are hard to come by and are not cheap. Quick Facts Scientific Name Cyprichromis leptosoma "Kitumba" Origin Lake Tanganyika, Africa Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful for a cichlid Adult Size Up to 4" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.8–9.0 Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a fine sand bottom and plenty of open swimming space, with a few rocks along the back. Lake Malawi and Lake Tanganyika cichlids need hard, alkaline water; crushed coral or aragonite sand helps hold the pH up. Feeding: Feed a quality small pellet or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like brine shrimp. Tankmates: They do best with other peaceful Tanganyikans such as cyprichromis, calvus, frontosa (when large enough) and synodontis catfish. Keep them in a group. Good to know: Cyprichromis live in open water in large schools, so they are happiest in a group with plenty of swimming room above the rocks.

The Lemon Jake Peacock Cichlid is a beautiful long-finned blue and yellow cichlid from Lake Malawi. Lemon Jakes, like Yellow Peacocks, do not get color until three inches, and males have more color and longer fins than the females. Of course males always display better with the presence of the other sex. PLEASE NOTE: on peacock cichlids, and most African cichlids, the adult colors do not become present until the fish is a good 3 inches in size. Quick Facts Scientific Name Aulonocara sp. "Lemon Jake" Origin Lake Malawi, Africa (captive-bred) Care Level Easy Temperament Semi-aggressive Adult Size Up to 5–6" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 76–82°F pH 7.8–8.6 Group Size Keep more females than males Shipping Size Approx. 2–4½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a sand bottom, rocks and open swimming space. African cichlids need hard, alkaline water; crushed coral or aragonite sand helps hold the pH up. Feeding: Feed a quality cichlid pellet or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Peacocks are among the calmer African cichlids. Keep them with other peacocks, haps and calm mbuna. Good to know: Peacock cichlids show their adult colors at around three inches, and males are much more colorful than females.

The Paskai Rainbowfish, also called the Red Neon Rainbowfish, are a jewel of the small aquarium. First featured in Amazonas magazine in 2011, these fish were captured and bred and now are available to AquariumFish.com. Like all rainbowfish, these little rainbows are egg layers and will mate in the aquarium. Both males and females have blue eyes and red bodies; males' fins are slightly larger than the females. These are peaceful small schooling fish and should not be kept with large hungry fish with large mouths! Quick Facts Scientific Name Pseudomugil luminatus Origin Western New Guinea, Indonesia Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1¼" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a planted tank with gentle filtration, some floating plants and a lid. They are small, so a sponge over the filter intake keeps them safe. Feeding: Feed crushed flake or micro pellets once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Blue-eyes are small and gentle, so keep them with other small, peaceful fish such as rasboras, small tetras, pygmy corydoras and shrimp. Good to know: Males turn a glowing orange-red with blue eyes as they mature.

The blue panchax, or blue wonder killifish, is found all over Pakistan and in two small hot springs in Singapore. These light blue and white killifish grow to three inches and are very hardy. The blue panchax are sold individually but will school at the upper part of the fish tank. In nature the panchax swims near the surface of the water and eats mosquito larvae. Quick Facts Scientific Name Aplocheilus panchax Origin South and Southeast Asia (Pakistan and India to Indonesia) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful with fish its size; eats very small fish Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 3–4 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods; takes flake) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single, pair or small group Shipping Size Approx. 1–1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Panchax cruise near the surface, so give them plants and floating cover. They are excellent jumpers, so keep a tight-fitting lid on the tank. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or floating pellet once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Panchax do well with peaceful fish too big to fit in their mouth, such as larger tetras, barbs, gouramis, rainbowfish and corydoras. They will eat very small fish like lampeyes and fry. Good to know: Panchax are surface hunters that eat insects in the wild.

The beautiful Daisy's blue eye ricefish are similar to killifish but belong to their own genus, Oryzias , spread throughout Asia from China to Japan. Ricefish are schooling fish that swim near the surface of rice paddies to control the mosquito population. These are great tank mates for any peaceful community tank, goldfish and betta tanks (they do not require a heater), and of course rice paddies. These fish can also handle water temperature down to the 60s. Quick Facts Scientific Name Oryzias woworae Origin Sulawesi, Indonesia Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1¼" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F (tropical; use a heater) pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a planted tank with floating plants, gentle filtration and a lid. Daisy's ricefish are tropical, so keep the water heated to 75–82°F. Feeding: Feed crushed flake or micro pellets once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Daisy's ricefish are a great fit for peaceful community tanks with small rasboras, tetras, pygmy corydoras and shrimp. Avoid large or aggressive fish. Good to know: Daisy's ricefish come from Sulawesi, Indonesia, and were first described in 2010. Males show the brightest blue and red on their fins.

Blue Eye Candy Cane Cardinal Features a striped body with its characteristic blue eyeliner surrounding its eyes. They should be given a dark shelter, since they are active at night and specifically hides under ledges and corals during the day. Therefore, the reef tank has to be decorated with enough rock work and reef crevices. The Blue Eye Cardinal thrives well in lower temperatures, but 72-78 degrees Fahrenheit while ensuring a strong filtration is acceptable. The levels of nitrate, ammonia and nitrite should be kept low for its healthy survival and growth. An American discovered this fish - Hiram Smith in 1912. Scientific Name: Apogon compressus Origin: Indo-Pacific Max Size: 4 inches Required Tank Size: 30+ gallons Shipping Size: 1-3 inches

The polli synodontis, or Poll's synodontis, are considered a dwarf species, though this fish grows to four inches in Lake Tanganyika. Petricola fish are small Synodontis. These fish are tan with black spots. They have white lines. These fish are similar to dwarf petricola but the coloration is olive with black spots. Dwarf Petricola catfish are omnivores, and should be offered both meaty foods and vegetation. This can be in the form of flakes, pellets, and freeze-dried or frozen foods like bloodworms and blackworms. They are peaceful fish and can be kept in most community aquariums. Many can tolerate a wide range of water conditions, including hard water and high pH, and of course all synodontis can be kept in African cichlid aquariums. Quick Facts Scientific Name Synodontis polli Origin Lake Tanganyika, Africa Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 4" Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.5–8.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them caves, rocks or driftwood to hide in, and good filtration. They are most active at night. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets once a day, ideally in the evening. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms. Tankmates: They get along with most fish of similar size, including many cichlids. They may eat very small fish. Good to know: Dwarf synodontis are a great fit for African cichlid tanks, where they clean up food that falls to the bottom.

Blue Banded Coral Shrimp Blue Coral Banded Shrimp, Stenopus tenuirostris , features a striking translucent and blue body with long white antennae and two muscular pinchers. It can also be known as the Boxing Shrimp for its propensity to hit its prey with those large claws. Mostly peaceful towards other species, the Blue Coral Banded Shrimp should not be housed with members of its own species unless they are a mated pair. The Coral Banded Shrimp can be sensitive to water quality so it is recommended you keep your water in pristine shape. They prefer tanks with plenty of live rock hiding places to search for their carnivorous diet. They will often lose their exoskeleton in a process called molting while they are growing. Overall, the Blue Coral Banded Shrimp is a staple in the home aquarium for its unique and beautiful appearance and ability to eat pesky bristle worms and flat worms. Scientific Name: Stenopus tenuirostris Max Size: 3 inches Diet: In the wild, the Banded Coral Shrimp is a scavenger. In the home aquarium, it will accept most flaked and frozen foods. Shipping Size: Approx. 1 to 1 1/2 inches

The Four Eyed Anablep is one of the oddest fish in the Amazon, and only imported from Guyana, so this is a hard-to-find fish. Anableps have four eyes, one pair to see above the water, and another pair to see below. Hence, the Four Eyed Anablep generally swims along the surface to take advantage of both perspectives. These are peaceful fish, eat flake food, and prefer a little salt in the water. Anableps are livebearers and in the wild feed on surface insects and small fish. Quick Facts Scientific Name Anableps anableps Origin Northern South America (Guyana) Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 8–12" Lifespan 10 years Diet Carnivore (insects, meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.5–8.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 5" Care Guide Tank setup: Four-eyed fish live right at the surface and do best in slightly salty (brackish) water. Keep the water level a little lower, with a sandy shore or flat rocks they can rest on, and a tight lid, since they jump. Feeding: Feed floating pellets or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms. Tankmates: They are peaceful but will eat small fish. Keep them with their own kind or other brackish fish like scats and monos. Good to know: Each eye is split in two, so they can see above and below the water at the same time.

Orange Seahorse Lined Seahorse, is considered by many hobbyists to be the most attractive of all the seahorses. These are young and the size is about 2-3 inches. The coloration of these tank raised seahorses range from shades of black, to gray to brown. Their coloration may change in the aquarium, and is highly dependent on the colors of its environment. As they mature and become ready to mate the male lined seahorse dance around, show off his pouch and may have color changes. If the female is interested they will tangle tails and dance as she deposits up to 600 eggs in his pouch. It usually takes about 2 weeks then the male will birth as many 50 to 400 babies. Scientific Name: Hippocampus erectus Origin: Captive bred Max Size: 7 inches Diet: Frozen brine shrimp Shipping Size: Up to 2 1/2 inches

Platys have been bred to produce many different colors and patterns. The marigold wag platy, like the marigold platy, is a bright yellow and orange fish but with a solid black tail that looks like it wags when the fish moves its caudal (tail) fin. Quick Facts Scientific Name Xiphophorus maculatus Origin Southern Mexico and Central America Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 3–4 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 70–80°F pH 7.0–8.2 Breeding Livebearer – breeds easily in the aquarium Shipping Size Approx. 1¼" Care Guide Tank setup: Platies are hardy and easy to keep. Give them a filter, a lid and plenty of plants. Use a heater to keep the water steady in the 70s. They prefer harder, slightly alkaline water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. Platies also need some plant matter, so a vegetable flake is a good choice. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Platies get along with most peaceful community fish, such as other livebearers (mollies, guppies and swordtails), tetras, rasboras and corydoras. Avoid large or aggressive fish that may bully or eat them. Breeding: Platies are livebearers, so a tank with males and females will almost certainly have babies (fry). Adults will eat fry, so add dense plants or use a breeding box if you want to raise them. Keeping more females than males gives the females a break from the males' attention. Good to know: Platies are one of the easiest fish to keep, which makes them a great choice for a first aquarium.

The painted platy is also called the red berlin platy and the red koi platy. The fish features a solid red body with black splotches and spots, like some sneaky swordtail threw some black paint on an unsuspecting red platy. The panda platy has been meticulously bred to resemble the coloration of the Asian panda bear. These are uncommon and a bit more expensive than other platies. These timid fish should be kept in a school of four or more. Platys have been bred to produce many different colors and patterns. The most common color of platy is red, and these fish are bright additions to the fish tank. Larger than the dwarf coral red platy, the red has a brighter orange tone than the deep red of the dwarf platy. One of the more colorful variations, the neon red tail platy has a bit of everything, from a black and blue shiny body to a bright red tail. The calico sunburst platy has more black than the painted platy and less than the tuxedo platy, with much more color. Calico platies feature reds, blues, and yellows with black patterning. Quick Facts Scientific Name Xiphophorus maculatus Origin Southern Mexico and Central America Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 3–4 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 70–80°F pH 7.0–8.2 Breeding Livebearer – breeds easily in the aquarium Shipping Size Approx. 1¼" Care Guide Tank setup: Platies are hardy and easy to keep. Give them a filter, a lid and plenty of plants. Use a heater to keep the water steady in the 70s. They prefer harder, slightly alkaline water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. Platies also need some plant matter, so a vegetable flake is a good choice. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Platies get along with most peaceful community fish, such as other livebearers (mollies, guppies and swordtails), tetras, rasboras and corydoras. Avoid large or aggressive fish that may bully or eat them. Breeding: Platies are livebearers, so a tank with males and females will almost certainly have babies (fry). Adults will eat fry, so add dense plants or use a breeding box if you want to raise them. Keeping more females than males gives the females a break from the males' attention. Good to know: Platies are one of the easiest fish to keep, which makes them a great choice for a first aquarium.

The red tux platy has a solid black body (like a red tuxedo jacket) with a bright red outline on the body and fins. The dalmatian platy has a white body with a painted black pattern. A school of these looks like a bunch of dalmatian puppies. Quick Facts Scientific Name Xiphophorus maculatus Origin Southern Mexico and Central America Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 3–4 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 70–80°F pH 7.0–8.2 Breeding Livebearer – breeds easily in the aquarium Shipping Size Approx. 1¼" Care Guide Tank setup: Platies are hardy and easy to keep. The clown knife fish, also called the clown featherback, is a fine cuisine fish of Thailand, where they grow to two feet. In the aquarium, these fish do well with similar-size species but will eat smaller fish like tetras and rasboras. The clown knife is named for the "harlequin" spots on the body. Quick Facts Scientific Name Chitala ornata Origin Southeast Asia Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful with fish its size Adult Size Up to 2 feet Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 3–4" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them hiding places like large tubes or caves, dim lighting, strong filtration and a tight lid. They are most active at night. Feeding: Feed meaty foods like frozen shrimp and bloodworms, plus sinking carnivore pellets once they learn to take them. Avoid feeder fish, which can carry disease. Tankmates: They will eat any fish that fits in their mouth. Keep them with large, peaceful fish. Good to know: Clown knifefish are shy when young and do best with a hiding spot, like a short length of PVC pipe.

The ocellated puffer is a rare brackish puffer from Malaysia that grows to six inches and is docile enough for a large brackish community tank or as a pet fish. Ocellated puffers have not been bred in captivity and require frozen or live foods. These fish may be conditioned to freshwater - slowly. Quick Facts Scientific Name Leiodon cutcutia Origin South and Southeast Asia Care Level Moderate Temperament Semi-aggressive Adult Size Up to 6" Lifespan 10+ years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods, snails) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: These puffers live in fresh water when young but do best in slightly salty (brackish) water as they mature. Give them rocks, plants and good filtration. Feeding: Puffers need meaty foods and usually won't eat flake. Feed frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp once a day. They also enjoy small snails, which help keep their teeth trimmed. Tankmates: Puffers nip fins and are best kept alone or with their own kind. Good to know: Ocellated puffers have a dark eye-spot on each side and are calmer than many other puffers.

The ruby tetra is a small, bright ruby-red tetra not often seen in the trade. These fish are wild-caught in small streams of Colombia and must be kept in schools of at least six. The ruby tetra needs clean water and will eat flake food. They are great for community tanks, nano tanks and planted aquariums. Quick Facts Scientific Name Axelrodia riesei Origin Upper Meta River, Colombia Care Level Moderate (needs soft, clean water) Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to ¾" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 5.5–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ¼–½" Care Guide Tank setup: These small tetras do best in a planted tank with soft, slightly acidic water, a dark substrate, driftwood, floating plants and gentle filtration. A larger school makes them more confident and colorful. Feeding: Feed small amounts of micro pellets or crushed flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other small, peaceful fish like rasboras, small tetras, pencilfish, pygmy corydoras, otocinclus and dwarf shrimp. Avoid large or boisterous fish that could eat or bully them. Good to know: Small tetras show their best color in a large school in a planted tank with soft lighting.

The purple tetra is not bred and must be caught in Colombia. These bright, peaceful schooling fish are slender and unique, featuring a purple reflective stripe on a light silver body. These fish should be kept in a school of six or more. Since these are wild-caught, size will vary, but they grow quickly. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hyphessobrycon metae Origin Meta River (Orinoco basin), Colombia Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1¼" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 5.5–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ¾" Care Guide Tank setup: These small tetras do best in a planted tank with soft, slightly acidic water, a dark substrate, driftwood, floating plants and gentle filtration. A larger school makes them more confident and colorful. Feeding: Feed small amounts of micro pellets or crushed flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other small, peaceful fish like rasboras, small tetras, pencilfish, pygmy corydoras, otocinclus and dwarf shrimp. Avoid large or boisterous fish that could eat or bully them. Good to know: Small tetras show their best color in a large school in a planted tank with soft lighting.

This tetra looks like a bleeding heart tetra that lost its heart. The body of the rosy tetra is a solid rose color, and the fins are red. These very pretty fish are community mid-level swimmers and should be kept in a school of four or more to keep them happy. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hyphessobrycon rosaceus Origin Amazon basin and the Guianas Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1¾" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a dark substrate, which brings out their color. Keep a lid on the tank, since tetras can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, rasboras, danios, corydoras, dwarf cichlids, gouramis and livebearers. Good to know: Tetras feel safer and show better color in a group. A larger school also spreads out any chasing.

The whip tail catfish, also called the twig catfish, is prolific in the Amazon basin. In muddy flats this peaceful little catfish whips its tail back and forth to propel itself from one water hole to another. Shaped like a twig with subtle broad stripes, the twig catfish utilizes camouflage for survival, since it isn't much of a thinker. Quick Facts Scientific Name Rineloricaria sp. Origin Amazon basin, South America Care Level Easy Temperament Very peaceful Adult Size Up to 5–6" Lifespan 6–10 years Diet Omnivore (algae and sinking foods) Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 3–4" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a sand bottom, driftwood and gentle filtration. Feeding: They graze on algae. Also feed algae wafers and sinking pellets. Tankmates: They are very peaceful and get along with most calm community fish. Good to know: Whiptail catfish blend in with sand and wood and are easy keepers in a calm community tank.

The Red Belly Pacu is an infamous fish among pet store owners. Red Belly Pacus are generally sold at about two inches and returned ten years later at about two feet. This fish is a great pet fish and a companion to fish of similar size, but the pacu will eat smaller fish. The red belly pacu looks like the red belly piranha and is indeed in the same family. The main difference between the piranha and the pacu is the teeth. The pacu has teeth like a cow; the piranha has teeth like - well - a piranha, very sharp. Pacu prefer veggies but will eat anything. One note on transitioning pacus or any metynnis to new places: they tend to break out in ich (small white spots). So temperature should be warm and the tank should not be overcrowded. A little ich medicine on hand is a good idea in general. If they do break out, treat as prescribed and they should be fine in a week. Quick Facts Scientific Name Piaractus brachypomus Origin South America Care Level Easy (grows very large) Temperament Peaceful (may eat small fish) Adult Size Up to 30" Lifespan 15–20+ years Diet Omnivore (pellets, vegetables) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Pacu grow very large and fast. Give them open swimming space, strong filtration and a heavy, tight lid. Feeding: Feed a quality pellet once or twice a day. They also enjoy vegetables and fruit. Tankmates: Pacu are peaceful but very large, so keep them only with other large fish. Good to know: Pacu grow very fast, so check their adult size before buying.

The Marble Hatchet only grows to an inch and it is not quite as hardy as the silver hatchet, but this is a great aquarium fish. These fish stay near the surface of the aquarium and are truly shaped like little hatchets. The body has a black marbled pattern and Hatchetfish can jump, so we recommend a cover on the fish tank. Hatchet fish are peaceful and may be kept with nano tank species. Quick Facts Scientific Name Carnegiella strigata Origin Amazon basin, South America Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1½" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Hatchetfish live at the very surface, so give them floating plants, gentle filtration and a tight-fitting lid, since they are excellent jumpers. Feeding: Feed a quality floating flake once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy small frozen foods like brine shrimp. Tankmates: Hatchetfish are peaceful and get along with small community fish such as tetras, rasboras, corydoras and dwarf cichlids. Avoid fish that swim at the surface and might bully them. Good to know: Hatchetfish feel safest in a group and stay near the surface, so floating plants give them cover.

Leporinus are hardy scavenger fish and will eat most anything fed to them in the aquarium. These fish are rare and, though not strikingly colorful, have an unusual body shape and feeding behavior - similar to a headstander. Leporinus prefer to rest in a hidden area but will be active at feeding time. These fish, at some point, will outgrow small fish such as tetras but are suitable for most mid-size and large aquarium pets. Quick Facts Scientific Name Leporinus friderici Origin Amazon basin, South America Care Level Easy Temperament Semi-aggressive (eats very small fish) Adult Size Up to 12" Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Omnivore (needs plant matter) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 2–3" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants, driftwood and a tight lid, since they can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or pellet with vegetable content once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They can nip at each other and at long-finned fish. Keep them with robust, fast fish of similar size. Good to know: Three-spot leporinus are named for the dark spots along their sides, which can fade as they grow.

Banjo catfish are shaped like a banjo, with prehistoric appearing scales to complete the look. The knock on these peaceful scavengers is that they tend to just sit about the bottom of the fish tank until night, when they troll for treats. As long as you do not expect a spectacular swimming demonstration, these are very nice fish for the aquarium. Though the appearance is odd, banjo catfish are very common in South America. Quick Facts Scientific Name Bunocephalus coracoideus Origin Amazon basin, South America Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 5–6" Lifespan 6–10 years Diet Omnivore (bottom feeder) Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 2–3" Care Guide Tank setup: Banjo catfish like to bury themselves, so give them a soft sand bottom, leaf litter and driftwood. Keep the lighting dim. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets once a day, ideally in the evening when they are most active. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms. Tankmates: They are peaceful and get along with most community fish too large to fit in their mouth. Good to know: Banjo catfish can shed their skin, which is normal, and they often stay buried with just their head showing.

Black line pike cichlids have a cream-colored body and bold black horizontal lines. Pike cichlids are a great bottom dweller for a larger species community tank. These cichlids have beautiful markings and get along with other species of their same size, but they will eat fish they can fit in their mouth. AquariumFish.com imports our wild pike cichlids from Colombia, and they vary in pattern depending upon which area of the Amazon basin they are caught in. Pictured is a full-size adult male. Quick Facts Scientific Name Crenicichla strigata Origin Amazon basin, South America Care Level Moderate Temperament Predatory; eats smaller fish Adult Size Up to 12–14" Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods; takes pellets) Water Temperature 76–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 4" Care Guide Tank setup: Give pike cichlids a sand bottom, caves, driftwood and rocks to hide in, plus a tight lid. Strong filtration is important, since they eat meaty foods. Feeding: Feed meaty foods like frozen shrimp, plus quality sinking pellets once the fish learns to take them. Avoid feeder fish, which can carry disease. Tankmates: Keep pike cichlids with robust fish too large to swallow, such as larger cichlids, plecos and catfish. Pike cichlids can be aggressive toward each other. Good to know: Pike cichlids are ambush predators that hide among rocks and driftwood and strike quickly at food.

The double tail veil bettas have two caudal tails, technically one split double tail. This variation of betta splendens came on the market in the 1990s. The appeal is in the magnificent display the male makes with his back fins when courting a female or challenging another male. To see this display, simply put a face mirror in front of him. There are many names for the particular betta color patterns, but most are variations of blue and/or red colors. Fish pictured here are representative only. If you are looking for a specific coloration, contact customer service or put it in the notes of your order, or simply let our fish catchers pick one of our favorites for you! Quick Facts Scientific Name Betta splendens Origin Thailand (captive-bred) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Males fight each other; peaceful toward most other fish Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 76–82°F (needs a heater) pH 6.5–7.5 Breathes Air Yes – labyrinth fish take air from the surface Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give him a heater (bettas are tropical fish), a gentle filter and live or silk plants. Floating plants or a "betta leaf" near the surface give him a place to rest. Keep a lid on the tank and leave a gap of air under it, since bettas breathe from the surface. Feeding: Feed a few betta pellets or a pinch of flake once or twice a day. Bettas overeat easily, so small meals are best. They also enjoy frozen bloodworms. Tankmates: Never keep two male bettas together. A male can live with small, peaceful fish that don't nip fins, such as corydoras, small rasboras, otocinclus and snails. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs and flashy, long-finned fish like fancy guppies. Good to know: A short look in a mirror (a minute or two) lets him flare and show off his double tail, but long sessions stress him.

There is something about the reflective, shiny scales of the dragon scale betta that just makes this fish look fearsome. Perhaps they actually breathe fire, and we just can't ever see it with all the water? The scales are larger and iridescent and accent the dragon-like appearance of the Siamese fighter fish. There are many names for the particular betta color patterns, but most are variations of blue and/or red colors. Fish pictured here are representative only. If you are looking for a specific coloration, add a note to the order or simply allow us to choose one of our favorites for you! Quick Facts Scientific Name Betta splendens Origin Thailand (captive-bred) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Males fight each other; peaceful toward most other fish Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 76–82°F (needs a heater) pH 6.5–7.5 Breathes Air Yes – labyrinth fish take air from the surface Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give him a heater (bettas are tropical fish), a gentle filter and live or silk plants. Floating plants or a "betta leaf" near the surface give him a place to rest. Keep a lid on the tank and leave a gap of air under it, since bettas breathe from the surface. Feeding: Feed a few betta pellets or a pinch of flake once or twice a day. Bettas overeat easily, so small meals are best. They also enjoy frozen bloodworms. Tankmates: Never keep two male bettas together. A male can live with small, peaceful fish that don't nip fins, such as corydoras, small rasboras, otocinclus and snails. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs and flashy, long-finned fish like fancy guppies. Good to know: Dragon scale bettas have thick, metallic scales that develop as they mature. Clean water keeps the scales and fins looking their best.

Plakat is short for Plakat Thung, which means "fighter fish" in Thai. Plakats were once a specific wild breed, but now this term is used in general for larger round tail bettas. Round tail bettas tend to be more aggressive, and the fighter strain is not only more aggressive but also a bit larger than other Betta splendens variations. Fish pictured here are representative only, though most true plakats are primarily black in color. If you are looking for a specific coloration, add a note to the order or simply allow us to choose one of our favorites for you! Quick Facts Scientific Name Betta splendens Origin Thailand (captive-bred) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Males fight each other; peaceful toward most other fish Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 76–82°F (needs a heater) pH 6.5–7.5 Breathes Air Yes – labyrinth fish take air from the surface Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give him a heater (bettas are tropical fish), a gentle filter and live or silk plants. Plakats are active swimmers and like room to patrol. Keep a lid on the tank and leave a gap of air under it, since bettas breathe from the surface. Feeding: Feed a few betta pellets or a pinch of flake once or twice a day. Bettas overeat easily, so small meals are best. They also enjoy frozen bloodworms. Tankmates: Never keep two male bettas together. Plakats are among the boldest bettas, so they do best alone or with sturdy, peaceful fish like corydoras and snails. Avoid fin-nippers and other labyrinth fish. Good to know: Short-finned plakats are strong, fast swimmers and the closest to the original fighting fish, so they are usually the most aggressive bettas. Keep them on their own or with sturdy, peaceful tankmates.

The orange Venezuelan cory, or red sailfin Venezuelan cory, has an orange dorsal fin and does not grow as large as the similar Brazilian Adolfoi cory. The orange color does not begin to appear until the cory is about one inch in length. These are very pretty corys and make great packs to keep the bottom of the aquarium clean. Quick Facts Scientific Name Corydoras aeneus (Venezuelan color form) Origin Venezuela Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 5–10 years Diet Omnivore (bottom feeder) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and a soft sand or smooth, fine gravel bottom. Plants, driftwood and a few shady spots help them feel secure. Corys are sensitive to salt and some medications (especially copper), so check labels before treating the tank. Feeding: Corys need their own food, not just leftovers. Feed sinking pellets or wafers once or twice a day so food reaches the bottom. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Corys get along with almost any peaceful community fish, such as tetras, rasboras, livebearers, gouramis, angelfish and bettas. Avoid large fish that could swallow them and aggressive bottom dwellers. Good to know: The orange color develops as they grow past about an inch, so young fish may look plain at first.

The red telescope head goldfish, also called the telescope eye goldfish, has a solid bright orange color that accents the extended eyes. These fish will not compete well with fast-moving species, so put food close to them. They may look very pretty, but they are a little slow. The telescope eye feature was created by selective breeding in China at the end of the 16th century, and most of the standard colors today were further refined in Japan. Quick Facts Scientific Name Carassius auratus Origin China Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 8" Lifespan 10–15 years, often longer with good care Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 65–75°F (no heater needed in most homes) pH 7.0–8.0 Shipping Size Approx. 2–4" Care Guide Tank setup: Telescope goldfish produce a lot of waste, so give them plenty of room and a strong filter. Use smooth decorations and live or silk plants, and keep the water current gentle. Feeding: Feed small amounts of a quality sinking pellet or flake once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. Sinking foods are easier for them to find than floating ones. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them only with other slow-swimming fancy goldfish, such as telescopes, black moors, celestials, bubble eyes, lionheads and ranchus. Avoid faster goldfish like comets, shubunkins and even lively ryukins, which will outcompete them for food. Also avoid tropical fish and fin-nippers. Ponds: Telescope goldfish can live in ponds in mild climates, but they are less cold-hardy than comets and shubunkins. Bring them indoors where winters are harsh, and keep them away from fast, aggressive pond fish. Good to know: Their eyesight is poor, so make sure food reaches them, and avoid sharp decorations that can injure their protruding eyes.

Calico Fantail Goldfish are a hardy and popular pond and aquarium species. Fantail goldfish were developed in Europe from the Ryukin Goldfish and have less slope on the back and are faster swimmers. These fish will do well in a pond and aquarium and compete fine for food. Calico Fantails are a bright orange, black, and white mottled color. Unlike cats, Calico colored goldfish are just as common in males and females. (Only female cats are calico). AquariumFish.com generally sells goldfish no smaller than two inches to ensure a safe trip and good adaptation to the fish tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name Carassius auratus Origin China (captive-bred) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 6–8" Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 65–75°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 2–4" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a strong filter and smooth decorations. Goldfish are cool-water fish and do not need a heater. Feeding: Feed a quality goldfish flake or pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp and bloodworms. Tankmates: Keep them with other fancy goldfish. They are also hardy enough for ponds. Good to know: Calico goldfish have a mix of orange, black, white and blue that is different on every fish.

The red cap oranda is a famous and popular color variation of the oranda, and when first introduced to the West, it won many show prizes in the late 1800s. The word "Oranda" is Dutch for Lionhead, but unlike the Lionhead goldfish, the Oranda has a prominent dorsal fin. Like the lionhead goldfish, oranda goldfish were selectively bred to create the bubbly head the Chinese call the "wen" and we usually call the "crown" or "cap". The body of the red cap oranda is bright white, and the wen is bright red. Note: Our stock of Orandas is young and does not have the developed wen seen in the images. The wen develops when they mature. Quick Facts Scientific Name Carassius auratus Origin China Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 8" Lifespan 10–15 years, often longer with good care Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 65–75°F (no heater needed in most homes) pH 7.0–8.0 Shipping Size Approx. 2–4" Care Guide Tank setup: Orandas produce a lot of waste, so give them plenty of room and a strong filter. Evansi Anthias: The Yellowback Reef Dither The Evansi Anthias (Pseudanthias evansi), often called the Yellowback Anthias or Yellowtail Anthias , is a stunning, active marine fish highly prized for its brilliant coloration. This species typically displays a beautiful cerise-pink to lavender body that contrasts sharply with a striking yellow or gold coloration along its back, dorsal fin, and caudal fin (tail) . Males are slightly more vibrant and may develop elongated fin rays. Native to the Indian Ocean , including the Maldives and Sri Lanka, the Evansi Anthias is a planktivore found schooling in large groups along outer reef slopes and drop-offs where currents deliver a constant supply of food. It is a smaller species, reaching a maximum adult length of around 4 to 5 inches (10-12 cm). While peaceful and reef-safe, the Evansi Anthias is considered an intermediate to expert-level fish. Its small mouth and high metabolism demand a strict and frequent feeding regimen, making it susceptible to starvation in tanks where it must compete with faster-feeding fish. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: This is a dedicated Planktivore/Carnivore . In the wild, it feeds constantly on zooplankton. In captivity, it requires multiple small feedings (3 to 5 times) per day . The diet must be varied and planktonic in size, including vitamin-enriched frozen foods such as mysis shrimp, cyclop-eeze, capelin roe, and enriched brine shrimp. Newly introduced specimens often require live foods (copepods, enriched artemia) to initiate feeding. Feeding: Due to its constant feeding requirement, a well-established tank with an abundant supply of live copepods and amphipods (often cultivated in an attached refugium) is highly beneficial. Skip any day's feeding, and this fish risks decline. Reef Compatibility: It is Reef Safe. The Evansi Anthias will not harm corals, clams, or other sessile invertebrates. It is an excellent dither fish, bringing activity to the mid-water column and helping shyer fish feel secure. Temperament: It is Peaceful. It should only be housed with similarly docile tankmates. Aggressive or fast-swimming fish will outcompete the Anthias for food and cause it chronic stress, leading to illness. Avoid housing with triggerfish, large aggressive angels, or puffers. Social Structure: Like most Pseudanthias species, the Evansi Anthias is a protogynous hermaphrodite , living in harems of one male and several females. They do best kept in a small group of 3 to 7 individuals in a large aquarium (100+ gallons) to allow for a proper social hierarchy. If the dominant male dies, the largest female in the group will typically transition to a male. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Pseudanthias evansi Primary Common Name: Evansi Anthias Other Common Names: Yellowback Anthias, Yellowtail Anthias Origin: Indian Ocean (Maldives, Sri Lanka, Andaman Sea) Max Size: 4-5 inches (10-12 cm) Temperament: Peaceful / Social (Schooling/Harem) Diet: Planktivore (Requires 3-5 small feedings daily) Minimum Tank Size: 75 gallons (single), 100+ gallons (harem) Reef Compatibility: Yes (Excellent Reef Fish) Care Level: Intermediate to Expert

Yellow tail spiny eels only grow to six inches and adapt well to the aquarium, but these eels do require live, freeze-dried, or frozen food, preferably worms. Spiny eels are shy and at first may bury themselves up to their head and just peek around until they are comfortable with their tank mates. Only the very smallest aquarium pets such as ornamental shrimp can fit in their mouths, so these are good community tank fish. ****This item does not ship to Texas or Florida**** Quick Facts Scientific Name Macrognathus pancalus Origin South and Southeast Asia Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 6–7" Lifespan 10 years Diet Carnivore (small meaty foods) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 4–6" Care Guide Tank setup: Spiny eels like to burrow, so give them a soft sand bottom, plants and hiding places. The yellow marlboro discus, like the red marlboro, was bred by Jack Wattley and first called the Yellow Panda after the solid yellow body and cream color face. AquariumFish.com discus are bred in Singapore to hold color, handle a wide range of pH, and eat pellet and frozen foods. Of course, discus love live blackworms and brine shrimp as treats. We feed our discus live and frozen worms and Sera discus food. Quick Facts Scientific Name Symphysodon aequifasciatus (captive-bred color variety) Origin Amazon basin (captive-bred in Singapore) Care Level Moderate (needs warm, very clean water) Temperament Peaceful, shy; social Adult Size Up to 6–7" Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 82–88°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1½–4" (by size option) Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a reliable heater, gentle but strong filtration, and a bare bottom or fine sand for easy cleaning. Keep the tank in a quiet spot. Discus need very clean water. Feeding: Feed small meals of quality discus pellets or granules a few times a day, and remove uneaten food within a few minutes, since leftovers quickly foul the water. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. New arrivals may need frozen food for a while before they accept pellets. Tankmates: Discus are calm and shy, so choose gentle tankmates that enjoy the same warm water: cardinal and rummynose tetras, sterbai corydoras and small plecos are popular choices. Avoid fast, boisterous or fin-nipping fish, and anything that competes hard for food. Many keepers avoid angelfish, which can bully discus and share diseases. Living in groups: Discus are social and feel safest in a group. A single discus, or just two, tends to be stressed. When a pair forms to breed, they may claim part of the tank, so a group spreads out the attention. Good to know: Solid yellow and gold discus show best against a dark background and substrate. Discus show stress by darkening their color and hiding. A dark discus in a corner usually means the water quality or tankmates need checking.
