Grade A Panda Butterfly Goldfish command a very high price, ten times more than Grade B fish, and have dramatic solid white and black color and no red. Unfortunately, nearly all Grade A Panda Butterfly Goldfish are sold to the Asian market and are not available to the USA market. What we get is pictured below: a silvery black and off-white butterfly with a small amount of orange. Butterfly goldfish have very wide caudal (tail) fins, like the wings of a butterfly. Quick Facts Scientific Name Carassius auratus Origin China Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 8" Lifespan 10–15 years, often longer with good care Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 65–75°F (no heater needed in most homes) pH 7.0–8.0 Shipping Size Approx. 2–4" Care Guide Tank setup: Butterfly goldfish produce a lot of waste, so give them plenty of room and a strong filter. Use smooth decorations and live or silk plants, and keep the water current gentle. Feeding: Feed small amounts of a quality sinking pellet or flake once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other fancy goldfish of similar size and speed. Avoid fast single-tail goldfish like comets and shubunkins, which will outcompete them for food. Also avoid tropical fish, which need warmer water, and fin-nippers. Ponds: Butterfly goldfish can live in ponds in mild climates, but they are less cold-hardy than comets and shubunkins. Bring them indoors where winters are harsh, and keep them away from fast, aggressive pond fish. Good to know: The wide, delicate tail fins look best from above and can tear in strong currents, so keep the flow gentle.

Blue Star Leopard Wrasse Blue Star Leopard Wrasse, also known as the Vermiculite Wrasse, or Divided Wrasse, has a distinct color pattern. The females or juveniles have a pearly white body with a combination of mottled oranges, yellows, and browns, with light blue spots found throughout the pattern, along with a large blue to black spot on their stomach. The males are brilliant neon green and blue with black outlines in a broken striped pattern down the length of their bodies. Like other Labroids these fishes have the ability to change sex, as the most dominant fish in the group can turn into a fully functioning male. Scientific Name: Macropharyngodon bipartitus Family: Labridae Origin: Africa, Maldives Diet: vitamin enriched frozen mysis shrimp, vitamin enriched frozen brine shrimp, and other meaty foods along with a high quality marine flake and marine pellet food Shipping Size: 1 to 3 inches

There are 15 known species of peacock bass, great predators and game fish of the Amazon River basin. Peacock bass are fast predators and good jumpers. They are suitable tank mates with larger, aggressive fish. They will eat small fish before you even knew they were in the tank. They hunt in packs if you can put a school of four together. The orinocensis peacock bass is also called the orinoco bass for the Amazon river that this fish calls home - or used to, before he landed in our aquariums. The orinocensis peacock bass develops into a deep green and spotted predator and is the second smallest of the peacock bass - Kelberi is the smallest. These fish grow quickly and need a covered tank and eventually a big tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name Cichla orinocensis Origin Orinoco and Amazon basins, South America Care Level Moderate (grows very large) Temperament Predatory Adult Size Up to 2 feet Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 76–84°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Peacock bass grow very large and fast. Give them open swimming space, strong filtration and a heavy, tight lid. Feeding: Feed meaty foods like quality carnivore pellets and frozen shrimp or fish. Many learn to take pellets once settled. Avoid feeder fish, which can carry disease. Tankmates: They will eat any fish that fits in their mouth. Keep them only with large, robust fish. Good to know: Peacock bass are named for the eye-like spot on the tail, similar to a peacock feather.

Bushynose plecos are found all over the Amazon basin and are good tankmates, as they eat algae and scavenge uneaten food and only grow to 5 inches in the fish tank. Though these are plentiful and affordable plecos, they have a very unique appearance. They are also called bristlenose plecos; the antler-like growths at the top of their nose get larger and larger as the fish ages. Quick Facts Scientific Name Ancistrus sp. (super red variety) Origin Aquarium-bred Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful (males guard caves) Adult Size Up to 4–5" Lifespan 10–12 years Diet Herbivore (algae and plant-based foods) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single, pair or group with a cave each Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Bristlenose plecos do well in most community tanks. Give them driftwood to rasp on, caves or hiding spots, and good filtration. They keep glass, rocks and plants clean of algae. Feeding: They graze on algae, but also feed algae wafers. Tankmates: Bristlenose plecos get along with nearly all community fish, plus shrimp and snails. Avoid large aggressive fish that might harass them. Good to know: Males grow larger, bushier "bristles" on the snout than females. Bristlenose plecos stay small and are one of the best algae-eaters for home aquariums.

The green jade shrimp are solid deep green, and while they may blend in from time to time on moss balls and Amazon sword leaves, these are spectacular shrimp to add to your collection against any other background. Like all Neocaridina shrimp, jade shrimp will not tolerate pH above 7.8 and will feed off algae wafers and exotic shrimp pellets. Quick Facts Scientific Name Neocaridina davidi (green jade) Origin East Asia (aquarium-bred, mostly Taiwan) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1–1¼" Lifespan 1–2 years Diet Omnivore (grazes on algae) Water Temperature 65–80°F pH 6.5–8.0 Water Hardness GH 6–12 (moderately hard) Group Size Does best in a group (breeds readily) Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Neocaridina are hardy and ideal for beginners. Use a cycled, planted tank with moss, plants and hiding spots, and a sponge filter or a sponge over the filter intake so shrimp aren't pulled in. Keep the water stable. Feeding: Shrimp graze on algae all day. Feed a small amount of quality shrimp food once a day and remove anything uneaten after a few hours. Tankmates: Keep shrimp alone or with tiny, peaceful fish like small rasboras, ember tetras, otocinclus and pygmy corydoras, plus snails. Most fish will eat baby shrimp, and cichlids (even dwarf cichlids like rams and apistogrammas) and larger fish will eat adults. Different Neocaridina colors will crossbreed and lose their color over time. Good to know: Shrimp are very sensitive to copper and many medications. Never treat a tank with shrimp, and check plant fertilizers and treatments for copper.

The vampire shrimp looks like something that could eat your baby, but these are the gentlest creatures in the aquarium. These shrimp are wild-caught in Nigeria and live in rocks, where they filter out debris from the water for food. The vampire shrimp, or filter shrimp, is the world's largest freshwater filter shrimp and will not harm any other species. The scientific name gabonensis is from Gabon, where the shrimp was discovered. There are plenty in the wild, so please don't fret; we are keeping a fisherman in business and helping sustain a local natural economy. :) Despite their pleasant disposition, these shrimp can handle even aggressive fish tanks if they have a place to hide. Quick Facts Scientific Name Atya gabonensis Origin West Africa (Gabon to Senegal) and northeastern South America Care Level Moderate (needs current and a mature tank) Temperament Very peaceful Adult Size Up to 5–6" Lifespan 3–5+ years Diet Filter feeder (fine powdered foods) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Water Hardness GH 6–15 Group Size Single or small group Shipping Size Approx. 1–2" Care Guide Tank setup: Filter shrimp catch food with fan-like hands, so they need a mature tank with steady current (near a filter outlet) and rocks or driftwood to perch on. If they pick at the bottom instead of fanning, they may be hungry; add powdered food near the current. Feeding: Feed a fine powdered food or crushed flake, released near the current so the shrimp can catch it. Tankmates: They do well in peaceful community tanks with tetras, rasboras, gouramis and corydoras. Avoid fish that pick at invertebrates, like large cichlids, puffers and loaches. Good to know: Filter shrimp molt regularly and may hide for a day or two afterward. Never treat their tank with copper-based medications.

The red nose pinocchio shrimp, or freshwater pinocchio shrimp, is a long, thin scavenger suited for gentle tank mates. Our favorite name, and the one we use around Christmas, is Rudolph the red nose shrimp. Pinocchio shrimp are great algae eaters. In fact, they will go after hair algae in its early stages. Quick Facts Scientific Name Caridina gracilirostris Origin Southeast Asia Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1½" Lifespan 1–2 years Diet Omnivore (grazes on algae) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Water Hardness GH 6–12 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a cycled, planted tank with moss and hiding spots, plus a sponge filter or a sponge over the filter intake. Keep the water clean and stable. Feeding: They graze on algae. Also feed shrimp pellets or algae wafers. Tankmates: They do well with small, peaceful fish and other shrimp. Avoid cichlids and larger fish that will eat them. Good to know: Pinocchio shrimp larvae need brackish water to develop, so they rarely breed in a freshwater tank.

The name says it all in this specialty-bred shrimp from Taiwan. The body is similar in color to the super yellow shrimp, with a bold-colored back. The shrimp is a bit stockier than the sakura yellow shrimp. Quick Facts Scientific Name Neocaridina davidi (gold back yellow) Origin Taiwan (aquarium-bred) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1–1¼" Lifespan 1–2 years Diet Omnivore (grazes on algae) Water Temperature 65–80°F pH 6.5–8.0 Water Hardness GH 6–12 (moderately hard) Group Size Does best in a group (breeds readily) Shipping Size Approx. ½–¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Neocaridina are hardy and ideal for beginners. Use a cycled, planted tank with moss, plants and hiding spots, and a sponge filter or a sponge over the filter intake so shrimp aren't pulled in. Keep the water stable. Feeding: Shrimp graze on algae all day. Feed a small amount of quality shrimp food once a day and remove anything uneaten after a few hours. Tankmates: Keep shrimp alone or with tiny, peaceful fish like small rasboras, ember tetras, otocinclus and pygmy corydoras, plus snails. Most fish will eat baby shrimp, and cichlids (even dwarf cichlids like rams and apistogrammas) and larger fish will eat adults. Different Neocaridina colors will crossbreed and lose their color over time. Good to know: Shrimp are very sensitive to copper and many medications. Never treat a tank with shrimp, and check plant fertilizers and treatments for copper.

The blue and black rili shrimp features a pretty light blue and deep blue-to-black banded pattern. The coloration, however, is very difficult to breed, and the carbon rili, or black and blue rili, are rare in comparison to the blue rili and red rili shrimp. Quick Facts Scientific Name Neocaridina davidi (carbon rili) Origin East Asia (aquarium-bred, mostly Taiwan) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1–1¼" Lifespan 1–2 years Diet Omnivore (grazes on algae) Water Temperature 65–80°F pH 6.5–8.0 Water Hardness GH 6–12 (moderately hard) Group Size Does best in a group (breeds readily) Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Neocaridina are hardy and ideal for beginners. Use a cycled, planted tank with moss, plants and hiding spots, and a sponge filter or a sponge over the filter intake so shrimp aren't pulled in. Keep the water stable. Feeding: Shrimp graze on algae all day. Feed a small amount of quality shrimp food once a day and remove anything uneaten after a few hours. Tankmates: Keep shrimp alone or with tiny, peaceful fish like small rasboras, ember tetras, otocinclus and pygmy corydoras, plus snails. Most fish will eat baby shrimp, and cichlids (even dwarf cichlids like rams and apistogrammas) and larger fish will eat adults. Different Neocaridina colors will crossbreed and lose their color over time. Good to know: Shrimp are very sensitive to copper and many medications. Never treat a tank with shrimp, and check plant fertilizers and treatments for copper.

Italian Val Italian val, also called straight vallisneria, is a hardy val and slightly smaller than the larger jungle val and has long green narrow stems. Each order contains three bunched plants. If anyone out there knows where the common name "Italian" came from we would like to add it here! In aquascaping this plant is usually lace in the back or middle of the aquarium. Scientific Name: Vallisneria spiralis Shipping Size: Approx. 10 inches, THREE plants with one lead weight

Nana Anubias This anubias plant is native to West Africa, grows well partially and fully submersed and is tolerant of low light. Nana anubias are very dark green and have round leaves and are extremely hardy. These plants grow slow but can handle low and high lighting and can be planted in substrate or tied to wood and rocks. Pictured is a SMALL planted Anubias barteri. Scientific Name: ANUBIAS NANA Origin: West Africa Max Size: 12 inches Shipping Size: 2 to 8 inches (2 inches comes in a 2 inch pot)

Burgess' Butterflyfish Burgess' Butterfly-fish is a true beauty in the industry. It originates from the deep waters of the reefs in the Western Pacific. Remaining relatively small, the Burgess' Butterflyfish is predominately black and white in color. There are three black bands that mark these fish. The first black band forms a mask covering the eyes of the fish. The last black band covers a majority of the back of the fish, giving it a unique look. They are relatively hardy fish that will add beauty to the marine aquarium. *Burgess' Butterfly's diet primarily consists of coral polyps, crustaceans, and algae in the wild. In an aquarium, frozen and freeze-dried diets containing algae are good substitutes and can be supplemented with dried algae and vitamin enriched brine and mysis shrimp. Scientific Name: Chaetodon burgess Family: Chaetodontidae Origin: Fiji,Indonesia Max Size: 5 1/2 Shipping Size: 2 to 3 1/2 inches

Yellow Line Sweetlips Yellow Lined Sweetlips also known as the Striped Sweetlips, is a slender sweetlips fish that can grow up to 20 inches. The Yellow Lined Sweetlips are notoriously difficult to keep in home marine aquariums. Therefore it is recommended that only expert or very experienced aquarists attempt to keep the Yellow Lined Sweetlips in their tanks. Further, even small fluctuations of conditions within the tank can make the Yellow Lined Sweetlip unruly and unwilling to feed. Scientific Name: Plectorhinchus Diagrammus Max Size: 20 inches Diet: Requires a meaty diet and to be fed 2-3 times a day. Shipping Size: 2 to 3 inches

Apistogramma Agassizi (Wild) Apistogramma agassizi in the wild come in several color morphs. The most common is gold and red, and these hail from Colombia. These wild apistogrammas are true dwarf cichlids that are gentle and will do well with other peaceful fish. Larger-size fancy shrimp are also fine with these species, but do not introduce small fancy shrimp to the tank once the apistos approach their full size. Quick Facts Scientific Name Apistogramma agassizii Origin Brazil, Colombia and Peru (Amazon basin) Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful (males territorial with each other) Adult Size Males up to 3"; females about 2" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 76–84°F pH 5.0–7.0 Shipping Size Approx. ¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter, dim lighting and lots of plants, driftwood and leaf litter. Add a cave (a coconut shell or small clay pot) for each female. Most apistos prefer soft, slightly acidic water. Feeding: Feed small pellets or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with small, peaceful fish such as tetras, rasboras, pencilfish, otocinclus and corydoras. A calm school of small "dither" fish helps apistos feel safe enough to come out. Keep one male per tank unless it is large and well planted, and avoid large or boisterous fish. Adults may eat small shrimp and baby shrimp. Breeding: Apistos are cave spawners. The female lays her eggs inside a cave and guards the fry, while the male patrols the territory. One male with several females works well in a planted tank. Good to know: Wild agassizii come in several regional color forms. Soft, acidic water brings out the best color in the males.

The scientific name is the same as the fluorescent GloFish tetras. Natural skirts come in two variations: the one featured here, the black skirt tetra, a pretty little fish with wide black bands that in a very imaginative way could resemble a skirt. The second variation is the white skirt tetra, which is rather drab but is the parent fish of the genetically modified GloFish tetra. One white skirt tetra plus one gene of a jellyfish equals one GloFish tetra. (Zebra danios are the parent fish for GloFish danios.) Quick Facts Scientific Name Gymnocorymbus ternetzi Origin Paraguay and Guaporé basins (Brazil, Bolivia, Paraguay); farm-raised Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful (may nip long fins) Adult Size Up to 2¼" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a dark substrate, which brings out their color. Keep a lid on the tank, since tetras can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, rasboras, danios, corydoras, dwarf cichlids, gouramis and livebearers. Good to know: Tetras feel safer and show better color in a group. A larger school also spreads out any chasing.

The beckford pencilfish, also known as the golden pencilfish, is the most prevalent fish of this family in the aquarium trade. These fish are easy to breed and quite hardy. Pencilfish get their common name because they look like small pencils, but it would be quite unpleasant to try to write with one. The body of the beckford pencil is gold with a pencil-carbon-colored black band and red highlights on the fins. Quick Facts Scientific Name Nannostomus beckfordi Origin Northern South America Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ¾–1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a planted tank with floating plants, gentle filtration and a lid, since they can jump. Soft, slightly acidic water brings out their best color. Feeding: Feed crushed flake or micro pellets once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Pencilfish are shy and peaceful, so keep them with other small, gentle fish such as small tetras, rasboras, pygmy corydoras and shrimp. Good to know: At night, pencilfish change to a blotchy "night" pattern, which is normal.

Orange Linckia Starfish: The Expert-Only Icon The Orange Linckia Starfish (Linckia laevigata) is a highly sought-after invertebrate celebrated for its striking, vibrant orange coloration. It is a color morph of the more commonly recognized Blue Linckia Starfish, both of which belong to the same species. While undeniably beautiful and peaceful, the Linckia Sea Star has a reputation in the hobby for being exceptionally challenging to keep long-term due to its highly specialized dietary needs and extreme sensitivity to water quality fluctuations. Native to the Indo-Pacific, these starfish typically have five long, cylindrical arms and glide gracefully across live rock and tank glass. They can grow quite large, with adult specimens reaching up to 12 inches (30 cm) in diameter. Successfully keeping this species requires a very mature and stable aquarium , rich in the microbial life that forms the bulk of its diet. Due to its specialized requirements and often short lifespan in all but the most established systems, the Orange Linckia Starfish is categorized as Expert-Only . Diet & Compatibility: Diet: The Orange Linckia Starfish is an Omnivore/Specialized Scavenger . Its primary diet consists of bacterial films (biofilm) , microscopic organisms, and certain species of sponge and detritus that thrive on the surface of live rock in a mature aquarium. Feeding in Captivity: This is the major challenge for this species. It is rarely successfully spot-fed in a way that sustains it long-term. In most home aquariums, the microbial film it relies on is quickly depleted, leading to slow starvation. Occasional offerings of meaty foods (like clam or scallop) placed directly beneath its body are sometimes accepted but are not a sufficient substitute for its natural diet. Tank Requirements: Success is strongly correlated with tank maturity ( 1+ year old minimum ) and size. A large tank ( 100−150 gallons minimum ) with a high volume of well-cured live rock provides the vast surface area needed to grow enough natural food. Reef Compatibility: It is Reef Safe . It poses no threat to corals, motile invertebrates, or fish. Temperament: It is Peaceful and Solitary . It should be monitored for parasitic snails that sometimes attack sea stars, and should be protected from predatory invertebrates like large shrimp or crabs. Acclimation Sensitivity: The Linckia Starfish is extremely sensitive to changes in salinity, temperature, and pH. A very slow, 2+ hour drip acclimation is mandatory. Never expose the starfish to air as this can trap fatal air bubbles in its internal systems. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Linckia laevigata (Orange Morp) Primary Common Name: Orange Linckia Starfish Other Common Names: Orange Sea Star, Blue Linckia (same species) Origin: Indo-Pacific Max Size: 6−12 inches (15−30 cm) in diameter Temperament: Peaceful Diet: Specialized Scavenger (Bacterial films, micro-organisms) Minimum Tank Size: 100−150 Gallons (min.) Reef Compatibility: Yes Care Level: Difficult (Expert Only)

Gold rams have a regal gold body with blue highlights. Ram is short for the species name “ramirezi”, but it is also reminiscent of their tendency to butt heads like a terrestrial ram. These are beautiful fish whether captive-bred for color, such as German blue rams, or wild, such as Bolivian rams. They are peaceful, hardy and get along with other species. Quick Facts Scientific Name Mikrogeophagus ramirezi (gold variety) Origin Venezuela and Colombia (Orinoco basin); aquarium-bred Care Level Moderate (needs warm, clean, soft water) Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 2–4 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 80–86°F pH 5.0–7.0 Group Size Sold as a group of 4 Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Rams need warm, very clean, soft water. Give them a sand bottom, plants, driftwood, leaf litter and flat stones for spawning. Rams are sensitive to poor water quality. Feeding: Feed small amounts of quality micro pellets or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Rams do well with small, peaceful fish that like warm, soft water, such as tetras, rasboras, hatchetfish, corydoras and discus. They may eat small shrimp. Avoid large or boisterous fish. Good to know: Rams often form pairs and lay eggs on flat stones. Stable, warm water is the key to keeping them healthy.

listings.commonName: WYSIWYG Yellow-Green Goniopora Colony Vibrant LPS - 012
listings.description: Yellow-Green Goniopora Colony: A Vibrant, Flowing LPS Showpiece The Yellow-Green Goniopora Colony is a striking Large Polyp Stony (LPS) coral featuring vibrant yellow-green coloration and long, flower-like polyps that create constant movement throughout the reef aquarium. This established colony offers significantly more visual presence than a small frag, making it an excellent centerpiece or feature coral. Under blue-spectrum reef lighting, the yellow and green coloration becomes especially vivid, while the extended polyps create the flowing appearance Goniopora corals are known for. When fully extended, the colony adds both bright color and dynamic movement to the aquarium. Goniopora corals are photosynthetic but can also benefit from supplemental feeding. Stable reef parameters, moderate lighting, gentle-to-moderate water movement, and access to fine particulate foods can help support healthy polyp extension, growth, and coloration. WYSIWYG: The Yellow-Green Goniopora Colony pictured is the exact coral you will receive. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: Mixotroph. Primarily photosynthetic but can benefit from supplemental feeding. Feeding: Offer fine particulate coral foods, powdered reef foods, or other appropriately sized planktonic foods approximately 1–2 times per week. Reef Compatibility: Reef Safe, but should be provided adequate space from neighboring corals. Temperament: Semi-Aggressive toward nearby corals. Placement: Best positioned where the colony has enough open space for its long polyps to fully extend without contacting neighboring corals. Water Requirements: Maintain stable reef conditions with consistent alkalinity, calcium, and magnesium. Avoid rapid fluctuations in salinity, temperature, or other major parameters. Water Flow: Moderate, preferably indirect. Enough flow should be provided to gently move the polyps without constantly blasting or retracting them. Lighting: Moderate reef lighting is generally appropriate. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Goniopora sp. Primary Common Name: Yellow-Green Goniopora Colony Other Common Names: Yellow-Green Flowerpot Coral, Goniopora Flowerpot Coral, Flowerpot Coral Origin: Indo-Pacific Size: Established Colony Temperament: Semi-Aggressive Diet: Photosynthetic / Planktivorous Feeding: Supplemental fine-particle feeding beneficial Placement: Lower to Middle Rockwork Water Flow: Moderate, Indirect Lighting: Moderate Reef Compatibility: Yes Care Level: Moderate

The least rasbora ( Boraras urophthalmoides ), also commonly known as the exclamation point rasbora, is a tiny, peaceful schooling fish perfect for nano tanks and planted aquariums. Their slender bodies feature a dark horizontal marking ending in a distinct spot near the tail, giving them their “exclamation point” nickname. Least rasboras earn their name by staying small, so they are great for aquariums with small shrimp. Growing to only around 3/4 inch, least rasboras are true micro fish and look their best when kept in a school of at least six. Larger groups will generally be more confident and display more natural schooling behavior. Their peaceful temperament also makes them excellent tank mates for fancy shrimp and other small, gentle species. Quick Facts Scientific Name Boraras urophthalmoides Origin Thailand, Cambodia and Vietnam Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to ¾" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them dense plants, floating plants, a dark substrate and gentle filtration (a sponge filter is ideal, since they are small enough to be pulled into strong intakes). Soft, slightly acidic water brings out their best color. Feeding: Feed crushed flake or micro pellets once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other tiny, peaceful fish such as other micro rasboras, small tetras, pygmy corydoras, otocinclus and dwarf shrimp. Avoid large or boisterous fish, which can eat or stress them. Good to know: Micro rasboras show their best color and natural schooling behavior in larger groups and well-planted tanks.

Neon Red Rasbora The neon red rasbora ( Microrasbora rubescens ), also known as the Burmese red dwarf rasbora or cardinal rasbora, is a small, peaceful freshwater schooling fish known for its warm reddish-orange coloration and slender body. Native to Myanmar, these micro fish are an excellent choice for nano tanks, planted aquariums and peaceful community setups. A well-planted aquarium with gentle filtration and plenty of cover provides an ideal environment. Feed a varied diet of crushed flake, micro pellets, baby brine shrimp, and other appropriately sized frozen or live foods. Quick Facts Scientific Name Microrasbora rubescens Origin Inle Lake region, Myanmar Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 68–77°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ½–¾" Care Guide Tank setup: These fish come from cool, clear, hard-water lakes and ponds in Myanmar. Give them dense plants, gentle filtration and plenty of cover. They do not need very warm water, and stable, slightly alkaline water suits them. Feeding: Feed crushed flake or micro pellets once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other small, peaceful fish that like similar water, such as celestial pearl danios, micro rasboras, small livebearers and dwarf shrimp. Avoid large or boisterous fish. Good to know: They are a little shy at first; plenty of plants and a group of their own kind help them settle in and color up.

The aquarium does not need a large school of these platies to get some great interaction and color. Quick Facts Scientific Name Xiphophorus maculatus Origin Southern Mexico and Central America Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 3–4 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 70–80°F pH 7.0–8.2 Breeding Livebearer – breeds easily in the aquarium Group Size Sold as a school of 4 Shipping Size Approx. 1¼" Care Guide Tank setup: Platies are hardy and easy to keep. Give them a filter, a lid and plenty of plants. Use a heater to keep the water steady in the 70s. They prefer harder, slightly alkaline water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. Platies also need some plant matter, so a vegetable flake is a good choice. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Platies get along with most peaceful community fish, such as other livebearers (mollies, guppies and swordtails), tetras, rasboras and corydoras. Avoid large or aggressive fish that may bully or eat them. Breeding: Platies are livebearers, so a tank with males and females will almost certainly have babies (fry). Adults will eat fry, so add dense plants or use a breeding box if you want to raise them. Keeping more females than males gives the females a break from the males' attention. Good to know: Platies are one of the easiest fish to keep, which makes them a great choice for a first aquarium.

This is not a big tetra, so keeping them in a natural school will keep them calm and active. And who wouldn't want six rubies in their home? Quick Facts Scientific Name Axelrodia riesei Origin Upper Meta River, Colombia Care Level Moderate (needs soft, clean water) Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to ¾" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 5.5–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 6 Shipping Size Approx. ¼–½" Care Guide Tank setup: These small tetras do best in a planted tank with soft, slightly acidic water, a dark substrate, driftwood, floating plants and gentle filtration. A larger school makes them more confident and colorful. Feeding: Feed small amounts of micro pellets or crushed flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other small, peaceful fish like rasboras, small tetras, pencilfish, pygmy corydoras, otocinclus and dwarf shrimp. Avoid large or boisterous fish that could eat or bully them. Good to know: Small tetras show their best color in a large school in a planted tank with soft lighting.

Purple is such an unusual color in the wild, you might as well take advantage of this species and fill the tank with a complete school. Quick Facts Scientific Name Inpaichthys kerri Origin Rio Aripuanã basin, Brazil Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1½" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 6 Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a dark substrate, which brings out their color. Keep a lid on the tank, since tetras can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, rasboras, danios, corydoras, dwarf cichlids, gouramis and livebearers. Good to know: Tetras feel safer and show better color in a group. A larger school also spreads out any chasing.

Naoko's Fairy Wrasse (male) The Naoko's Wrasse is a reef-associated, tropical wrasse and it makes a fantastic aquarium fish. First described by Jack Randall and Dr. Hiroyuki Tanaka in January 2009, this is a semi aggresive wrasse that is both active and hardy. Rarely available but worth the wait. Scientific Name: Cirrhilabrus naokoae Origin: Indian Ocean Max Size: 4 inches Diet: Marine flake food, frozen and live feeders Shipping Size: 2 to 3 inches

Scarlet Wrasse Scarlet Wrasse aka Filamented Flasher Wrasse is a very peaceful, active fish that will bring both color and activity to a fish-only or reef aquarium of 55 gallons or larger. They will not bother any corals or invertebrates making them a perfect fish for the reef aquarium. A single male can be kept with a Group of females that is introduced prior to or at the same time as the male. These wrasses like to jump, so a tight fitting canopy is recommended. Scientific Name: Paracheilinus filamentosus Origin: Indonesia Max Size: 3 inches Diet: Carnivore Shipping Size: 1 to 2 inches

A school of five ricefish with white reflective scales makes a very visible display in the fish tank. Medaka Galaxy Ricefish are standouts in small community fish tanks and planted aquariums. These fish can also handle temperatures into the 60s. From the side, these fish are bright white, and from the top they reflect a silver white. Quick Facts Scientific Name Oryzias latipes (galaxy variety) Origin Japan (aquarium-bred) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1½" Lifespan 2–4 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 64–80°F (handles cooler water; no heater needed in most homes) pH 6.5–8.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Ricefish stay near the surface, so give them plants, floating plants and a lid. They are cool-water fish and do fine at room temperature, and they also do well in outdoor ponds and patio tubs in warm months. Feeding: Feed crushed flake or micro pellets once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Ricefish get along with other small, peaceful fish like white clouds, small rasboras, danios and shrimp. They can share an unheated tank with cool-water species, but avoid large or fast fish (including fancy goldfish) that may eat or outcompete them. Good to know: Medaka have been kept in Japan for centuries and are one of the hardiest small fish in the hobby. Both sexes are colorful; males have slightly larger fins.

The Raccoon Tetra was rarely seen in the aquarium scene until this past year when breeders in Indonesia figured the fish out. We can now get these beautiful rose and gold small tetras on a regular basis. Originally found by Smithsonian ichthyologists Murilo Pastana and William Ohara in the Brazilian Amazonia, they may soon be endangered due to deforestation. Hopefully the natives that make their living from the aquarium trade and some outside forces will have enough pull to protect this species and other species. The scientific name "procyon" is a nod to the Amazon state the fish was discovered in (and that state is named after the star Procyon). The trade calls the fish the Raccoon Tetra due to the raccoonish eye markings. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hyphessobrycon procyon Origin Brazil Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1½" Lifespan 5 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 5.5–7.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: These small tetras do best in a planted tank with soft, slightly acidic water, a dark substrate, driftwood, floating plants and gentle filtration. A larger school makes them more confident and colorful. Feeding: Feed small amounts of micro pellets or crushed flake food once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other small, peaceful fish like rasboras , small tetras , pencilfish , pygmy corydoras , otocinclus and dwarf shrimp . Avoid large or boisterous fish that could eat or bully them. Good to know: Small tetras show their best color in a large school in a planted tank with soft lighting.

Five active breeding Red Platies makes a nice show piece in peaceful community fish tanks. Platys have been bred to produce many different colors and patterns. The most common color of platy is red, and these fish are bright additions to the fish tank. Larger than the dwarf coral red platy, the red has a brighter orange tone than the deep red of the Dwarf Platy. Quick Facts Scientific Name Xiphophorus maculatus Origin Southern Mexico and Central America Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 3–4 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 70–80°F pH 7.0–8.2 Breeding Livebearer – breeds easily in the aquarium Shipping Size Approx. 1¼" Care Guide Tank setup: Platies are hardy and easy to keep. Give them a filter, a lid and plenty of plants. Use a heater to keep the water steady in the 70s. They prefer harder, slightly alkaline water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. Platies also need some plant matter, so a vegetable flake is a good choice. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Platies get along with most peaceful community fish, such as other livebearers (mollies, guppies and swordtails), tetras, rasboras and corydoras. Avoid large or aggressive fish that may bully or eat them. Breeding: Platies are livebearers, so a tank with males and females will almost certainly have babies (fry). Adults will eat fry, so add dense plants or use a breeding box if you want to raise them. Keeping more females than males gives the females a break from the males' attention. Good to know: Platies are one of the easiest fish to keep, which makes them a great choice for a first aquarium.

Originally from Lake Tanganyika, the Brevis Shell Dweller spends its life in and around his chosen shell, so they only need a small area in the aquarium to keep them happy. Male brevis love to share their shell with females but will fight with other males to keep their shell to themselves. Shell dwellers are hardy and great additions to community tanks and peaceful cichlid tanks. These small fish love their shells, so try to keep a few in the aquarium that are lightweight and not too large for them to manipulate but large enough for them to get into. Quick Facts Scientific Name Neolamprologus brevis Origin Lake Tanganyika, Africa Care Level Easy Temperament Territorial around their shells Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 6–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.8–9.0 Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Use a fine sand bottom they can dig in and provide more empty snail shells (escargot shells work well) than there are fish. Lake Malawi and Lake Tanganyika cichlids need hard, alkaline water; crushed coral or aragonite sand helps hold the pH up. Feeding: Feed crushed flake or micro pellets once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep shell dwellers in a species tank or with small, peaceful Tanganyikans like cyprichromis or julidochromis. Larger cichlids will bully or eat them. Good to know: Brevis are unusual in that a male and female often share the same shell.

The hecqui shell dweller is similar in behavior to the brevis shell dweller but grows just about one inch larger. The Hecqui Shell Dweller spends its life in and around his chosen shell, so he only needs a small area in the aquarium to keep himself content. Male hecqui love to share their shell with females but will fight with other males to keep their shell to themselves. Shell dwellers are hardy and great additions to community tanks and peaceful cichlid tanks. These small fish love their shells, so try to keep a few in the aquarium that are lightweight and not too large for them to manipulate but large enough for them to get into. Quick Facts Scientific Name Neolamprologus hecqui Origin Lake Tanganyika, Africa Care Level Easy Temperament Territorial around their shells Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 6–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.8–9.0 Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Use a fine sand bottom they can dig in and provide more empty snail shells (escargot shells work well) than there are fish. Lake Malawi and Lake Tanganyika cichlids need hard, alkaline water; crushed coral or aragonite sand helps hold the pH up. Feeding: Feed crushed flake or micro pellets once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep shell dwellers in a species tank or with small, peaceful Tanganyikans like cyprichromis or julidochromis. Larger cichlids will bully or eat them. Good to know: Shell dwellers are fun to watch as they move shells and dig sand to arrange their territory.

Blue Xenia The Anthelia Waving Hand Coral is also referred to as a Glove Coral. It is a Group of colonial animals with several individual polyps attached to a piece of solid substrate. They are blue, brown, or tan, in color, and their polyps have the distinctive eight-leaved tentacles associated with all of the members of this family. Scientific Name: ANTHELIA SP Family: Xeniidea Origin: Indo Care: medium to strong waterflow and moderate to high light

The blond dwarf frog is a natural color morph of the fully aquatic oddball, the African dwarf frog. These little frogs are not albino and are very hardy, and will eat flake foods and do well in a gentle community fish tank. Since they are fully aquatic, the frogs do not require an above water surface and will eat the same prepared food as their tank mates. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hymenochirus boettgeri Origin Central Africa (captive-bred) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1½" Lifespan 5 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 72–78°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a fully aquatic tank with plants and hiding spots, gentle filtration and a lid. They breathe air, so keep the water shallow enough for them to reach the surface easily. Feeding: Feed sinking frog pellets or frozen bloodworms once a day. They eat slowly, so make sure faster fish don't take all the food. Tankmates: Dwarf frogs are peaceful and do best with other small, gentle fish such as small tetras and rasboras, or with their own kind. Good to know: Dwarf frogs are fully aquatic but breathe air, so you will see them float up to the surface for a breath.

Bitterling are hardy schooling fish found in streams and ponds of Japan and in backyard garden ponds around the World. The bitterling is a small, 2 1/2-inch, flashy schooling fish perfect for small and large ponds. These are very active fish and are not happy in small tropical fish tanks. Like koi, bitterlings can handle different seasons. Quick Facts Scientific Name Rhodeus sp. Origin East Asia Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 50–77°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: These are hardy, cool-water fish that do fine at room temperature without a heater. They also do well in outdoor ponds in warm months. Keep a lid on the tank. Feeding: Feed a quality flake once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. Tankmates: Bitterlings get along with other peaceful, cool-water fish such as white cloud minnows, rosy minnows and small goldfish. Good to know: Bitterlings are famous for laying their eggs inside freshwater mussels.

The body and tentacles of the Sea Apple, or Philippine Sea Apple, can be a vareity of colors, but it always has yellow feet. The oral region is usually blue to violet, hence the common name Violet Sea Apple or Violet Sea Urchin.This Sea Apple could be poisonous when stressed or die.Do not house these cucumbers in an aquarium that contains any fish that may pick on its tentacles. Generally, any fish that is prone to pick on feather dusters, will pick on the tentacles of the Indonesian Sea Apple. These fish include; Butterflyfish, Large Angels, and any species that is listed not safe with invertebrates. Scientific Name: Pseudocolochirus Violaceus Family: Cucumariidae Origin:Indo, Singapore Max Size:8 Care and Diet:When feeding, it will extend its oral tentacles into the current to filter out food. As the food is trapped, it will then draw its entire tentacle into its mouth. In the aquarium, it will need to be fed a diet of phytoplankton - frozen, liquid, or dried - on a daily basis. Approximate Size: 4 to 4 1/2 inches

Spider Sponge Spider Sponge, features white horizontal lines over a striking red body. Its tree-like base is covered by a white web-like polyp colony. It is a peaceful organism that should not be housed with aggressive species of fish or inverts. If threatened, it may release a toxin that can harm other tank mates. The Spider Sponge can reach heights of 8 inches and needs a tank of at least 30 gallons. Like other sponge species, the Spider Sponge should never be exposed to open air. It is relatively difficult to maintain in the home aquarium so it should be reserved for experienced aquarists only. Scientific Name: Trikentrion flabelliforme Origin: Australia Diet: dissolved organic foods containing phytoplanktons and other microfauna

Purple is an odd color for any wild creature, but these endlers are not dyed; they are natural purple. The purple endlers are bred in Sri Lanka and offer a lot of movement and color in any community or nano aquarium. Quick Facts Scientific Name Poecilia wingei Origin Venezuela (captive-bred in Sri Lanka) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1" (males about ¾") Lifespan 2–4 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and plenty of plants. Endlers are small, so a sponge filter or a sponge over the filter intake keeps them safe. Feeding: Feed a quality flake, crushed small, or micro pellets once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Endlers do well with other small, peaceful fish such as small rasboras, corydoras, otocinclus and shrimp. Avoid larger fish that could eat them. Good to know: Male endlers are the colorful ones, and a group of males will spar and show off to each other without doing harm.

The white skirt tetra is the parent fish of the fluorescent GloFish tetras. Natural skirts come in two variations: the one featured here, the white skirt tetra, and the black skirt tetra. One white skirt tetra plus one gene of a jellyfish equals one GloFish tetra. (Zebra danios are the parent fish for GloFish danios.) These are great schooling fish that will grow to about 2 inches and also contrast well with their more colorful cousins. We recommend a few of these with the GloFish tetras. Quick Facts Scientific Name Gymnocorymbus ternetzi (white variety) Origin Aquarium-bred (wild form from Brazil, Bolivia, Paraguay) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful (may nip long fins) Adult Size Up to 2¼" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a dark substrate, which brings out their color. Keep a lid on the tank, since tetras can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, rasboras, danios, corydoras, dwarf cichlids, gouramis and livebearers. Good to know: Tetras feel safer and show better color in a group. A larger school also spreads out any chasing.

Phoenix rasboras, or rasbora merah, are similar to brigittae rasboras but without the black horizontal line on the brigittae. The phoenix rasbora has black dots. In the retail trade these fish are often sold as brigittae and vice versa, but the colors are distinct to each species. Both the common name and scientific name refer to the striking color of the body: merah is Indonesian for red, and phoenix refers to the red flaming bird rising from the ashes. These are small schooling aquarium fish suited to peaceful tanks and planted aquariums. Quick Facts Scientific Name Boraras merah Origin Borneo (Kalimantan), Indonesia Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to ¾" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them dense plants, floating plants, a dark substrate and gentle filtration (a sponge filter is ideal, since they are small enough to be pulled into strong intakes). Soft, slightly acidic water brings out their best color. Feeding: Feed crushed flake or micro pellets once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other tiny, peaceful fish such as other micro rasboras, small tetras, pygmy corydoras, otocinclus and dwarf shrimp. Avoid large or boisterous fish, which can eat or stress them. Good to know: Micro rasboras show their best color and natural schooling behavior in larger groups and well-planted tanks.

These hardy little fish do not come from Europe; the "Euro" is just a play on the scientific name. Micro euro rasboras are often confused with the more expensive brigittae rasbora. In fact, we thought it would be fun to download a common picture of the urophthalmoides from the internet, which actually describes the fish as brigittae. Check the pictures of our brigittae, phoenix and micro euro rasboras to see the actual difference. However, both size and temperament of all three species are the same. Quick Facts Scientific Name Boraras urophthalmoides Origin Thailand, Cambodia and Vietnam Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to ¾" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them dense plants, floating plants, a dark substrate and gentle filtration (a sponge filter is ideal, since they are small enough to be pulled into strong intakes). Soft, slightly acidic water brings out their best color. Feeding: Feed crushed flake or micro pellets once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other tiny, peaceful fish such as other micro rasboras, small tetras, pygmy corydoras, otocinclus and dwarf shrimp. Avoid large or boisterous fish, which can eat or stress them. Good to know: Micro rasboras show their best color and natural schooling behavior in larger groups and well-planted tanks.

The clown rasbora should not be confused with the small dwarf clown rasbora. The true clown rasbora, Rasbora kalochroma , is one of the largest rasboras available to the aquarium trade. These fish grow to three and a half inches. Since the clown rasbora comes from low-pH black water, these are great schooling fish for discus and South American–themed tanks if you do not mind a little Asian diversity. Clown rasboras will not tolerate high-pH tanks, so they are not suitable for African cichlid tanks and water with a pH over 7.5. The clown rasbora is named for its deep red color with clownish harlequin black markings. Quick Facts Scientific Name Rasbora kalochroma Origin Malaysia, Sumatra and Borneo Care Level Moderate (needs soft, acidic water) Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 4" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 5.0–7.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: These are active, fast swimmers, so give them open swimming space, plants along the back and sides, and a tight-fitting lid, since they can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They do well with other active, peaceful to semi-aggressive fish of similar size, such as barbs, larger tetras, danios, rainbowfish, gouramis and corydoras. Their speed can stress slow, long-finned fish. Good to know: They are hardy, active schoolers that look best with open swimming space where the group can move together.

Electric green glow sharks are a gene-spliced version of the albino rainbow shark. Rainbow sharks from Indonesia have deep red fins on a silver body. These sharks are actually catfish and are hardy and easy to keep and peaceful. The rainbow shark grows to about six inches. On the other hand, Green Glo Sharks are a solid fluorescent color and keep this color throughout their lives. In fact, if a Green Glo Shark breeds with another Green Glo Shark, they make baby green glo sharks. Weird science. Quick Facts Scientific Name Epalzeorhynchos frenatum (genetically modified) Origin Farm-raised (genetically modified) Care Level Moderate Temperament Semi-aggressive, territorial (especially toward other sharks) Adult Size Up to 6" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Keep one per tank Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Rainbow sharks patrol a territory, so give one caves, driftwood and plants to break up sight lines, plus a tight lid. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets or wafers and a quality flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy algae wafers and frozen bloodworms. Tankmates: Keep only one rainbow shark per tank, and avoid other bottom-dwelling sharks and territorial fish like red-tailed sharks. They do best with fast, mid- to upper-level swimmers such as danios, barbs, rainbowfish and larger tetras. Good to know: GloFish sharks are rainbow sharks, which are members of the carp family, not true sharks or catfish. They claim a territory near the bottom and chase other bottom dwellers, so give them caves and keep only one per tank. GloFish colors look brightest under a blue or actinic LED light, but they are colorful under normal lighting too.

On the other hand, Blue Glo Sharks are a solid fluorescent blue and keep this color throughout their lives. In fact, if a Blue Glo Shark breeds with another Blue Glo Shark, they make baby blue glo sharks. Weird science. Electric Green Long-Fin GloFish Tetra The green long-fin tetra was created by splicing the genes of hi-fin white skirt tetras and phosphorescent coral. These GloFish are the latest to be patented and licensed for sale in the USA. Quick Facts Scientific Name Gymnocorymbus ternetzi (long-fin, genetically modified) Origin Farm-raised (genetically modified) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a filter, plants and open swimming space. A dark substrate and background make the colors pop. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: GloFish tetras get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, danios, rasboras, corydoras and livebearers. Keep them in a group so they don't nip the fins of slow, long-finned fish like bettas. Good to know: Long flowing fins are easy targets for fin-nippers, so avoid tiger barbs and serpae tetras. GloFish colors look brightest under a blue or actinic LED light, but they are colorful under normal lighting too.
