The Trinidad pleco was the first pleco sold in the trade. Originally from South America, invasive plecos can be found all over Florida. These plecos are cheap and tough to kill. The plecos are so hardy and grow so large that many are sold to the pond trade, though the fish do not tolerate temperatures below 68°F. These fish grow fast and are great scavengers. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hypostomus sp. (common pleco) Origin Northern South America and Trinidad; farm-raised Care Level Easy (but grows very large) Temperament Peaceful (can be territorial as adults) Adult Size Up to 12–18" Lifespan 15–20 years Diet Omnivore (algae and sinking foods) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 6.5–7.8 Group Size Single Shipping Size Small: 1½" · Medium: 2–3" · Large: 4–5"+ Care Guide Tank setup: Give them driftwood and strong filtration. They may uproot or eat soft plants. Feeding: Feed algae wafers and sinking pellets daily. Don't rely on tank algae alone, especially as they grow. Tankmates: They get along with most medium to large fish, including cichlids and goldfish. Avoid keeping two large plecos in the same tank. Good to know: These plecos grow quickly. Never release one into the wild; they are invasive in Florida, Texas and other warm regions.

The freshwater panda garra is part goby, part algae eater. Also called the Burmese banded loach, or panda goby, these fish come from small streams in Myanmar and are infrequently imported to the United States aquarium trade. The panda garra grows to just under four inches and will not bother other fish, though they will eat decorative tiny shrimp. Known as herbivores, panda garras actually consume a bit of everything and will move small pebbles and sand around in their search for food. Garras are not true gobies, but it is the closest family they will ever have. Quick Facts Scientific Name Garra flavatra Origin Rakhine (Arakan) region, Myanmar Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful, active Adult Size Up to 3–3½" Lifespan 4–6 years Diet Omnivore (grazes on algae) Water Temperature 68–82°F pH 6.5–8.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Garras are active and like flowing, well-oxygenated water. Give them smooth rocks, driftwood, some current and a lid, since they can climb and jump. Feeding: Garras graze on algae. Also feed algae wafers, sinking pellets or flake. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish, such as danios, barbs, rasboras, loaches and rainbowfish. Good to know: Garras use a sucker-like mouth to graze algae from rocks and glass.

We import our Juruensis apistos from Peru. Peruvian apistogrammas tend to grow larger and feature more color than apistogrammas from other regions of the Amazon. Quick Facts Scientific Name Apistogramma juruensis Origin Peru and Brazil (Juruá River) Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful (males territorial with each other) Adult Size Males up to 2½"; females smaller Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 76–84°F pH 5.0–6.5 Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter, dim lighting and lots of plants, driftwood and leaf litter. Add a cave (a coconut shell or small clay pot) for each female. Most apistos prefer soft, slightly acidic water. Feeding: Feed small pellets or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with small, peaceful fish such as tetras, rasboras, pencilfish, otocinclus and corydoras. A calm school of small "dither" fish helps apistos feel safe enough to come out. Keep one male per tank unless it is large and well planted, and avoid large or boisterous fish. Adults may eat small shrimp and baby shrimp. Breeding: Apistos are cave spawners. The female lays her eggs inside a cave and guards the fry, while the male patrols the territory. One male with several females works well in a planted tank. Good to know: Juruensis are sensitive to water quality, so keep the water soft, acidic and very clean, and add new fish slowly.

When Albert Günther discovered this cichlid in Costa Rica back in 1867, there must have been a rainbow over the water. These are pretty cichlids, but the color is subtle. The males exhibit yellow, red and green shades, and the females have the same shades but less color. A little color-enhancing food will bring out the red in the rainbow cichlid. One great feature of the rainbow cichlid is its voracious appetite for hair algae (filamentous algae). Quick Facts Scientific Name Archocentrus multispinosus Origin Central America (Honduras to Costa Rica) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful for a cichlid (territorial when breeding) Adult Size Up to 4–5" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore (grazes on algae) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Single or pair Shipping Size Approx. 2½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a sand or gravel bottom, rocks, caves and driftwood to create territories. Anchor decorations well, since they like to dig. Strong filtration is important. Feeding: Feed a quality cichlid pellet or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other robust Central American cichlids of similar size, plus larger catfish and plecos. Give each fish its own territory, and avoid small or timid fish. Good to know: Central American cichlids are hardy and easy to breed. Pairs become very protective of their eggs and fry.

At two inches these are incredible rainbow-reflecting fish; at one inch, not so much. The good news is that these are active schoolers that grow quickly and are incredibly hardy. These schooling fish grow to 3.5 inches and can handle African cichlid and community tanks. This is a very adaptable species. Males have slightly longer fins than females, but both have the same remarkable rainbow reflection. We do not recommend male-only schools, as there will not be as much interplay and the males will not display as well. Quick Facts Scientific Name Phenacogrammus interruptus Origin Congo River basin (DR Congo) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful (shy) Adult Size Up to 3–3½" Lifespan 5–10 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1–2" Care Guide Tank setup: These are larger, active schooling fish, so give them open swimming space, plants or driftwood along the back and a tight-fitting lid, since they jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They do well with other active, similar-size fish such as larger tetras, barbs, rainbowfish, peaceful cichlids, corydoras and plecos. Very small fish may be eaten or bullied. Good to know: Larger tetras are hardy and long-lived, and a big school makes a striking display.

The blue ram is the bred, aquarium-hardy version of the wild ram of Colombia. These rams have blue and gold colors and grow to only two and a half inches. Quick Facts Scientific Name Mikrogeophagus ramirezi (blue variety) Origin Venezuela and Colombia (Orinoco basin); aquarium-bred Care Level Moderate (needs warm, clean, soft water) Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 2–4 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 80–86°F pH 5.0–7.0 Group Size Pair or small group Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Rams need warm, very clean, soft water. Give them a sand bottom, plants, driftwood, leaf litter and flat stones for spawning. Rams are sensitive to poor water quality. Feeding: Feed small amounts of quality micro pellets or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Rams do well with small, peaceful fish that like warm, soft water, such as tetras, rasboras, hatchetfish, corydoras and discus. They may eat small shrimp. Avoid large or boisterous fish. Good to know: Rams often form pairs and lay eggs on flat stones. Stable, warm water is the key to keeping them healthy.

Papa plecos earn their name for their size, which at full maturity can be large, with long, flowing lyre tail filaments. It will take a few years for the catfish to grow that large, but even at full maturity these fish are gentle tank mates. Papa plecos are also known as lyre tail royal plecos and share the same coloration. The difference is that papa plecos all come from Peru and have a long lyre tail. Check Google to see these mature creatures. Pictured is a 2-inch juvenile (who happens to be in detention). Large and jumbo papa plecos have beautiful long stringers off the tail. Quick Facts Scientific Name Panaque bathyphilus (L-090) Origin Ucayali and Amazon rivers, Peru Care Level Moderate (grows large) Temperament Peaceful (territorial with other plecos) Adult Size Up to 12–16" (plus tail filaments) Lifespan 15–20+ years Diet Herbivore (driftwood, algae wafers) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Medium: 2–3" body · Jumbo: 8" body Care Guide Tank setup: Royal-type plecos eat wood, so give them plenty of driftwood, strong filtration and caves. They produce a lot of waste, so good filtration is important. Feeding: Feed algae wafers and sinking pellets, and keep plenty of driftwood in the tank for them to rasp, since wood is part of their diet. Tankmates: They do well with medium to large community fish and cichlids. Keep one per tank unless the tank is very large, since they are territorial with other plecos. Good to know: Royal-type plecos are among the few fish that can actually digest wood. Plan for an adult-size tank before buying.

The male orange variegated guppy has beautiful orange and blue variations along the tail. In the trade, these fancy guppies are also called blue variegated guppies. Females also have some red and blue color, but very little of the variegated pattern. Quick Facts Scientific Name Poecilia reticulata Origin Northern South America (captive-bred) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Sold as a pair (1 male + 1 female) Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and plenty of plants, including some floating plants where babies can hide. Guppies like slightly hard water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Guppies get along with other small, peaceful fish such as platies, mollies, corydoras, small tetras and rasboras. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs and larger fish that could eat them. Breeding: Guppies are livebearers and breed easily. Females give birth to live babies about once a month, and adults will eat the babies, so thick plants give them a place to hide. Good to know: Males carry the bright colors and long tails; females are plainer but needed for breeding.

The Purple Passion Danio is rarely found in the trade and is wild-caught in Thailand. Like most danios, these fish are fast but friendly. A school of danios freely swimming in the aquarium will draw out the timid fish, since this is a sign in nature that the coast is clear. Hence, danios are also called dither fish. Purple Passion or Rose Danio have a solid purple reflective body, with cleaner markings but similar to the turquoise danio. Quick Facts Scientific Name Danio roseus Origin Thailand, Laos and Myanmar Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful, very active Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 68–79°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Danios are fast swimmers, so give them open swimming space, a filter, plants around the edges and a tight-fitting lid, since they jump. Make sure the tank is fully cycled (which takes several weeks) before adding fish. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Danios get along with most peaceful community fish, such as tetras, rasboras, barbs, corydoras and livebearers. Their speed can stress slow, long-finned fish like bettas and fancy guppies, and large predatory fish will eat them. Good to know: A busy school of rose danios acts as "dither fish," signaling to shy tankmates that it is safe to come out. Danios are fast and jump when startled, so keep a lid on the tank.

Sea Salt for Aquariums Weco Sea Salt provides the balanced salt ions needed to provide a healthy environment for salt water and brackish fish. In addition, Weco salt is excellent for dermal medication and also for creating salt water for a brine shrimp hatchery. Each bag comes with one pound of pure sea salt. To medicate use a tablespoon per 10 gallons. To create brackish water conditions use 1/2 pound per ten gallons. Shipping Size: One pound (fits inside any fish order box)

The freshwater aquarium Garra rufa , or foot cleaner goby, or the doctor fish, or just the spa fish, originated in Turkey but is now bred by the thousands in China and exported to the global spa market. These little fish eat the dead skin off feet, so they are ready for a complete pedicure! Out of the spa and in the aquarium, the garra rufa is a very good algae eater, eating both filamentous algae (stringy algae) and flat algae. These fish are active and friendly with just about every species in the aquarium. Garra rufa swim in a school, and we recommend the purchase of at least three to keep each other company. Quick Facts Scientific Name Garra rufa Origin Turkey and the Middle East; farm-raised in Asia Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful, active Adult Size Up to 4–5" Lifespan 4–6 years Diet Omnivore (grazes on algae) Water Temperature 68–82°F pH 6.5–8.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Garras are active and like flowing, well-oxygenated water. Give them smooth rocks, driftwood, some current and a lid, since they can climb and jump. Feeding: Garras graze on algae. Also feed algae wafers, sinking pellets or flake. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish, such as danios, barbs, rasboras, loaches and rainbowfish. Good to know: Garras use a sucker-like mouth to graze algae from rocks and glass.

Skunk Tilefish Goby Tilefish resemble some gobies but are actually from a different family, Malacanthidae . Like most of their goby relatives, tilefish are long and slender with smooth bodies and rounded heads. Tilefish grow larger in general; some species can get close to two feet in length although the most common aquarium species only reach about 4-6 inches. They are found higher in the water column but can quickly retreat into rockwork if threatened. Scientific Name: Hoplolatius marcosi Origin: Indo-Pacific Max Size: 5 inches Diet: Carnivore Shipping Size: 2 to 3 inches

The yellow rabbit snail is carefully selected for a solid chocolate shell and clean yellow body. The shell has some white blotches and an elongated turban shape. Due to these little blotches, no shell is quite the same. Rabbit snails are larger than most freshwater aquarium snails and are effective scavengers. Some aquarium snails prefer cold water, such as Japanese trapdoor snails, but rabbit snails prefer clean water and warmer conditions and are great tankmates for discus and other tropical fish. Quick Facts Scientific Name Tylomelania sp. Origin Sulawesi, Indonesia Care Level Moderate (needs warm water) Temperament Peaceful; may nibble soft plants Adult Size Up to 3–4" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Scavenger (sinking pellets, algae wafers) Water Temperature 76–84°F pH 7.2–8.5 Breeding Livebearer; slowly produces one baby at a time, so it won't overrun the tank Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Rabbit snails come from warm, clean lakes in Sulawesi. Give them a soft sand bottom they can burrow in, warm water (76–84°F) and good water quality. Add calcium if your water is soft. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets and algae wafers daily. Rabbit snails are big eaters and also clean up leftover food. Tankmates: Rabbit snails do well with peaceful fish, shrimp and other snails that like warm water, such as discus and tetras. Avoid puffers, loaches and large cichlids. Good to know: Rabbit snails are slow-moving and gentle, and they wave their long "ear-like" tentacles as they move. Remove snails before using copper or other medications.

The chocolate rabbit snail is carefully selected for a white chocolate shell and a chocolate body. As appealing as these snails may be, they will not taste like chocolate. As far as rabbit snails go, the chocolate snails are about half the size of yellow and orange rabbit snails. Rabbit snails are larger than most freshwater aquarium snails and are effective scavengers. Some aquarium snails prefer cold water, such as Japanese trapdoor snails, but rabbit snails prefer clean water and warmer conditions and are great tankmates for discus and other tropical fish. Quick Facts Scientific Name Tylomelania sp. Origin Sulawesi, Indonesia Care Level Moderate (needs warm water) Temperament Peaceful; may nibble soft plants Adult Size Up to 1½–2" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Scavenger (sinking pellets, algae wafers) Water Temperature 76–84°F pH 7.2–8.5 Breeding Livebearer; slowly produces one baby at a time, so it won't overrun the tank Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Rabbit snails come from warm, clean lakes in Sulawesi. Give them a soft sand bottom they can burrow in, warm water (76–84°F) and good water quality. Add calcium if your water is soft. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets and algae wafers daily. Rabbit snails are big eaters and also clean up leftover food. Tankmates: Rabbit snails do well with peaceful fish, shrimp and other snails that like warm water, such as discus and tetras. Avoid puffers, loaches and large cichlids. Good to know: Rabbit snails are slow-moving and gentle, and they wave their long "ear-like" tentacles as they move. Remove snails before using copper or other medications.

Female halfmoon bettas are a bit larger and more aggressive than show female bettas. The offspring of halfmoon females and halfmoon males will be a mix of variations: standard fins, super delta fins, and halfmoon fins. AquariumFish.com imports the specific female varieties from Thailand. Quick Facts Scientific Name Betta splendens Origin Thailand (captive-bred) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Can live in groups (sororities) with care Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 76–82°F (needs a heater) pH 6.5–7.5 Breathes Air Yes – labyrinth fish take air from the surface Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a filter and lots of plants and hiding places to break up sight lines. Keep a lid on the tank and leave a gap of air under it, since bettas breathe from the surface. Feeding: Feed a few betta pellets or a pinch of flake once or twice a day. Bettas overeat easily, so small meals are best. They also enjoy frozen bloodworms. Tankmates: Females can share a tank with small, peaceful fish like corydoras, rasboras and snails. Never add a male to a sorority tank, and avoid fin-nippers. Good to know: Females color up when relaxed. In a sorority, watch for bullying and remove any female that is constantly chased.

Mustard flame bettas, also called mustard gas bettas, are bred for a full halfmoon fin display with aqua blue and mustard yellow fins. When on display, the male mustard gas looks like a small blue and yellow explosion. A simple picture like the one here does not give the betta true credit. These fish are magnificent show quality and difficult to breed. Quick Facts Scientific Name Betta splendens Origin Thailand (captive-bred) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Males fight each other; peaceful toward most other fish Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 76–82°F (needs a heater) pH 6.5–7.5 Breathes Air Yes – labyrinth fish take air from the surface Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give him a heater (bettas are tropical fish), a gentle filter and live or silk plants. Floating plants or a "betta leaf" near the surface give him a place to rest. Keep a lid on the tank and leave a gap of air under it, since bettas breathe from the surface. Feeding: Feed a few betta pellets or a pinch of flake once or twice a day. Bettas overeat easily, so small meals are best. They also enjoy frozen bloodworms. Tankmates: Never keep two male bettas together. A male can live with small, peaceful fish that don't nip fins, such as corydoras, small rasboras, otocinclus and snails. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs and flashy, long-finned fish like fancy guppies. Good to know: Long, heavy fins tear easily, so keep the filter flow gentle and choose soft plants and smooth decorations. Clean, warm water helps prevent fin rot.

The Koi Betta is a highly sought color variation that comes in roundtail (plakat) and veil tail fins. The koi betta has a variable color pattern that features red, white, and black and is named after the color pattern of the sanke and showa koi found in ponds. No two koi bettas have the same pattern, but all are truly rare. Quick Facts Scientific Name Betta splendens Origin Thailand (captive-bred) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Males fight each other; peaceful toward most other fish Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 76–82°F (needs a heater) pH 6.5–7.5 Breathes Air Yes – labyrinth fish take air from the surface Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give him a heater (bettas are tropical fish), a gentle filter and live or silk plants. Floating plants or a "betta leaf" near the surface give him a place to rest. Keep a lid on the tank and leave a gap of air under it, since bettas breathe from the surface. Feeding: Feed a few betta pellets or a pinch of flake once or twice a day. Bettas overeat easily, so small meals are best. They also enjoy frozen bloodworms. Tankmates: Never keep two male bettas together. A male can live with small, peaceful fish that don't nip fins, such as corydoras, small rasboras, otocinclus and snails. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs and flashy, long-finned fish like fancy guppies. Good to know: Koi and galaxy bettas carry the "marble" gene, so their colors and patterns can shift throughout their lives. No two look alike for long.

The glorious betta macrostoma, also called the Tail Spot Betta, is the largest betta available to the trade. These rare fish are wild-caught in Borneo and grow to four inches. Wild macrostoma bettas can be placed together with other macrostomas and other fish of similar size. These expensive species are jumpers, so please keep the tank covered, or you will lose them. The male is pictured below; the female is similar in size and appearance but without the tail spot. Quick Facts Scientific Name Betta macrostoma Origin Borneo (Brunei and Sarawak) Care Level Difficult (for experienced keepers) Temperament Peaceful; pairs can be kept together Adult Size Up to 4–5" Lifespan Up to 8 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 72–78°F pH 5.0–7.0 (soft water) Breathes Air Yes – labyrinth fish take air from the surface Group Size Sold as a pair (1 male + 1 female) Shipping Size Approx. 3–4" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them soft water, a gentle current, a heater, caves, driftwood and plenty of cover. A tight-fitting lid is essential; they are strong jumpers. Feeding: Feed small amounts once or twice a day. Many will learn to take betta pellets once settled. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Best kept as a pair in a species tank, or with calm fish of similar size that like soft water. Avoid boisterous or nippy fish. Good to know: Macrostoma are mouthbrooders: the male carries the eggs in his mouth. They are strong jumpers, so keep the tank tightly covered.

The Forest Halfbeak gets its name from the small clear forest streams it inhabits in Thailand. This halfbeak is wild-caught and has more color than other half beaks. You should have some brine shrimp and other small live food available since these fish sometimes require transitioning to flake food. The forest halfbeak is a surface dweller in the aquarium and very rare in the trade. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hemirhamphodon pogognathus Origin Thailand and Malaysia Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful (males spar) Adult Size Up to 4" Lifespan 5 years Diet Carnivore (small meaty foods) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Halfbeaks live at the surface, so give them floating plants and a tight-fitting lid, since they jump. They are easily startled, so avoid sudden movements around the tank. Feeding: Offer small floating foods like flake and frozen brine shrimp once or twice a day. New fish may only take frozen foods at first. Tankmates: They get along with peaceful fish that swim lower in the tank, such as rasboras, corydoras and gouramis. Males may spar with each other. Breeding: Halfbeaks are livebearers. Adults will eat the babies, so floating plants give them a place to hide. Good to know: Forest halfbeaks have more color on their fins than most halfbeaks.

The rainbow tetra is rare in the aquarium trade since it is not commercially bred. When these fish are imported from the jungles of Colombia, they sell quick. The rainbow tetra is a small peaceful schooling fish that adapts well to the fish tank environment. The tetra features long fins and a multi-colored body. These peaceful swimmers should be kept in a school of six or more. Quick Facts Scientific Name Nematobrycon lacortei Origin Colombia Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 73–80°F pH 5.5–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ¾–1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a gentle filter. A dark substrate brings out their color. Keep a lid on the tank, since they can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, rasboras, corydoras, small gouramis and livebearers. Good to know: Rainbow tetras have red eyes and long, pointed tail fins, and males show the brightest colors.

Start the pond off right with a small breeding school of mosquito fish to keep all those pesky flying vampires at bay. Quick Facts Scientific Name Gambusia affinis Origin Southeastern USA Care Level Easy Temperament Semi-aggressive (can nip fins) Adult Size Up to 1½–2½" (females larger) Lifespan 1–3 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 50–85°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Sold as a school of 20 Shipping Size Wild-caught mix of sizes Care Guide Tank setup: Mosquito fish are very hardy and do fine at room temperature without a heater. They also do well in outdoor ponds, where they eat mosquito larvae. Keep a lid on the tank. Feeding: Feed a quality flake once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. Outdoors, they also eat insects and mosquito larvae. Tankmates: Mosquito fish can be nippy, so keep them with other hardy, fast fish rather than slow, long-finned fish. Breeding: They are livebearers and breed easily. Adults will eat the babies, so thick plants give them a place to hide. Good to know: Mosquito fish are livebearers and breed quickly in ponds, which is why they are so good at keeping mosquitoes under control.

The gold Inca snail is a variation of the gold mystery snail. These snails are generally larger and are delivered at about the size of a quarter. Gold Inca snails do not eat plants. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pomacea diffusa (sold as P. bridgesii ) Origin South America (Amazon basin); farm-raised Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful; plant-safe Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 1–2 years Diet Scavenger (algae and leftover food) Water Temperature 68–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 (hard water for healthy shells) Breeding Lays pink egg clutches above the waterline; needs a male and female Shipping Size Approx. ½–1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give mystery snails a covered tank with a gap of an inch or two above the water, since females climb out to lay eggs. Keep the water hard and alkaline for healthy shells, and add calcium (cuttlebone or crushed coral) if your water is soft. Feeding: Mystery snails eat algae and leftover food, but give them sinking pellets or algae wafers too so they don't go hungry. Tankmates: Mystery snails do well with peaceful fish, shrimp and other snails. Avoid fish that nip antennae or eat snails, like puffers, loaches, large cichlids and some bettas, and keep them away from assassin snails. Good to know: Remove snails before treating the tank with copper or other medications, which are toxic to invertebrates.

The bumblebee catfish, or dwarf marble catfish, comes from small streams in Colombia and Venezuela. These catfish are hardy and peaceful. They will come out to grab food during the day but prefer to come out at night. In the wild, these little pet fish will live in schools of hundreds. Quick Facts Scientific Name Microglanis poecilus Origin Colombia and Venezuela Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them caves, driftwood and dim lighting. They hide during the day and come out at night. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets once a day, ideally in the evening when they are most active. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms. Tankmates: They are small and peaceful but may eat very small fish at night. Keep them with community fish too large to fit in their mouth. Good to know: Bumblebee catfish hide during the day and come out at night, so a cave or driftwood helps them settle in.

The redhead cichlid, or vieja synspilum, is from Mexico and Central America. These fish are pond-raised in Florida for the aquarium trade. Synspilums are prized for their colors by the Asian aquarium community and are used to hybridize parrot fish and flowerhorns. A male vieja synspilum in breeding display is typically pictured, but as with all Central and South American cichlids, the color is more subtle most of the time. Quick Facts Scientific Name Vieja melanurus (formerly V. synspilum ) Origin Southern Mexico, Guatemala and Belize; pond-raised in Florida Care Level Moderate Temperament Aggressive (territorial) Adult Size Up to 12–14" Lifespan 12–15 years Diet Omnivore (needs plant matter) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Single or pair Shipping Size Medium: approx. 2½" · Large: approx. 3–4" Care Guide Tank setup: These are large, powerful cichlids, so give them a sand bottom, large rocks and driftwood. Anchor decorations well, since they dig and rearrange the tank, and use strong filtration. Feeding: Feed a quality cichlid pellet once a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like shrimp. Avoid feeder fish, which can carry disease. Tankmates: Keep them alone or with other large, robust cichlids and catfish that can hold their own. They will eat any fish small enough to fit in their mouth. Good to know: These cichlids are full of personality and often learn to recognize their owners. They grow large, so check their adult size before buying.

The only reason the gulper catfish is not featured on River Monsters is due to its size. The maximum length of a full grown gulper catfish is 12 inches, but these South American catfish can gulp a fish half the size of their body. So, at the very least, these guys are aquarium monsters. However, gulper catfish are not aggressive to species of similar size or larger and get along well with larger discus, jumbo angelfish, leporinus, and large cichlids. Also called the Torpedo Catfish, the gulper will eat prepared and frozen foods. And kittens. Quick Facts Scientific Name Asterophysus batrachus Origin Amazon and Orinoco basins, South America Care Level Moderate Temperament Predatory (can swallow large prey) Adult Size Up to 10–12" Lifespan 15–20 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 6" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them caves, driftwood and dim lighting. They hide during the day and come out at night. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets once a day, ideally in the evening when they are most active. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms. Tankmates: Gulper catfish can swallow fish half their own size. Keep them only with large, robust fish. Good to know: Gulper catfish have a stretchy stomach that lets them swallow surprisingly large meals.

The rabauti cory is similar to the skunk cory but has a rust-colored body and wider black bands. Also called Rabaut's cory or the rust cory, these are wild-caught in small streams in Colombia. Rabautis like to school in small packs, and females have slightly larger bellies, but otherwise they are difficult to sex. Quick Facts Scientific Name Corydoras rabauti Origin Peru, Brazil and Colombia Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 5–10 years Diet Omnivore (bottom feeder) Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and a soft sand or smooth, fine gravel bottom. Plants, driftwood and a few shady spots help them feel secure. Corys are sensitive to salt and some medications (especially copper), so check labels before treating the tank. Feeding: Corys need their own food, not just leftovers. Feed sinking pellets or wafers once or twice a day so food reaches the bottom. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Corys get along with almost any peaceful community fish, such as tetras, rasboras, livebearers, gouramis, angelfish and bettas. Avoid large fish that could swallow them and aggressive bottom dwellers. Good to know: Corys sometimes dart to the surface to gulp a bit of air. That's normal behavior, not a sign of trouble.

Driftwood Madagascar Driftwood in the aquarium provides a haven for fish and invertebrates, food for certain species such as plecos, and offers natural water conditioning. Most of all driftwood looks nice. Madagascar driftwood sinks but needs several days to soak, just place in the aquarium and eventually the driftwood will fall to the bottom. To speed the process along tie a rock and sink the wood. And of course the pieces are selected to fit within a live fish box. Shipping Size: Approx. 4-6 inches

The L-14 goes by a lot of names, including the golden peacock, goldy, goldie and sunshine. Regardless, this is a rare and beautiful plecostomus from Brazil. The sunshine pleco grows to about 12 inches and lives a long time. Provide wood and room, and this is a hardy fish and a great tank mate for everything from small schooling tetras to large cichlids. Quick Facts Scientific Name Scobinancistrus aureatus (L-014) Origin Rio Xingu, Brazil Care Level Moderate (needs warm, oxygen-rich water) Temperament Peaceful with fish; territorial with other plecos Adult Size Up to 10–12" Lifespan 12–15+ years Diet Omnivore (sinking foods) Water Temperature 78–84°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single, or several with a cave each Shipping Size Approx. 3–4" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them strong current, high oxygen, rocky caves and driftwood. Keep the water warm and very clean, since they produce a lot of waste on a meaty diet. Feeding: Feed meaty sinking foods like carnivore pellets. They also enjoy frozen foods like shrimp and bloodworms. Tankmates: They do well with most community fish and cichlids of similar size. They may eat very small fish or shrimp. Give each pleco its own cave. Good to know: These plecos have strong, toothed mouths and prefer meaty foods; they usually leave plants alone.

The batik snail is one of the prettier nerite snails but difficult to source. These snails are not prolific breeders, and they love algae and also make good scavengers for leftover food. Nerites only grow to a little less than one inch, so several would be needed for effective algae control in an aquarium of ten gallons or more. Quick Facts Scientific Name Neritina sp. Origin East Africa and Indo-Pacific coastal streams (wild-caught) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful; plant-safe Adult Size Up to 1" Lifespan 1–2+ years Diet Algae eater (also eats algae wafers) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.5 (hard water for healthy shells) Breeding Lays small white eggs on hard surfaces, but they won't hatch in freshwater, so nerites won't overrun the tank Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Nerites do well in most established tanks with algae to graze. Keep the water hard and alkaline for healthy shells, and keep a lid on the tank, since nerites sometimes climb out. If one flips onto its back, turn it over, since some can't right themselves. Feeding: Nerites mostly graze on algae. If the tank is very clean, add algae wafers so they don't go hungry. Tankmates: Nerites get along with peaceful fish, shrimp and other snails. Avoid puffers, loaches and large cichlids, which eat snails, and keep them away from assassin snails. Good to know: Remove snails before treating the tank with copper or other medications, which are toxic to invertebrates.

Snow White discus have a completely white body, and a blue hue develops on the fins as the fish matures. The snow white discus can come with some blue at the end of their fins; in that case, the fish is referred to as a white diamond discus. This variation was developed in the 1990s in Thailand. Quick Facts Scientific Name Symphysodon aequifasciatus (captive-bred color variety) Origin Amazon basin (captive-bred in Thailand and Singapore) Care Level Moderate (needs warm, very clean water) Temperament Peaceful, shy; social Adult Size Up to 6–7" Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 82–88°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a reliable heater, gentle but strong filtration, and a bare bottom or fine sand for easy cleaning. Keep the tank in a quiet spot. Discus need very clean water. Feeding: Feed small meals of quality discus pellets or granules a few times a day, and remove uneaten food within a few minutes, since leftovers quickly foul the water. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. New arrivals may need frozen food for a while before they accept pellets. Tankmates: Discus are calm and shy, so choose gentle tankmates that enjoy the same warm water: cardinal and rummynose tetras, sterbai corydoras and small plecos are popular choices. Avoid fast, boisterous or fin-nipping fish, and anything that competes hard for food. Many keepers avoid angelfish, which can bully discus and share diseases. Living in groups: Discus are social and feel safest in a group. A single discus, or just two, tends to be stressed. When a pair forms to breed, they may claim part of the tank, so a group spreads out the attention. Good to know: White discus show every mark, so very clean water and stable conditions keep them looking their best. Discus show stress by darkening their color and hiding. A dark discus in a corner usually means the water quality or tankmates need checking.

The leopard skin discus variation was bred by Jack Wattley in the 1970s and once commanded an incredible price. We have to give Mr. Wattley some homage for all he has done for the discus fish, and in fact he still breeds and sells his fine discus. Our AquariumFish.com discus are bred in Singapore and are reasonably priced (for an expensive variant) and very suitable for the community planted or discus aquarium. Leopard discus are primarily red and feature a spotted and lined color pattern. Keep the tank in a quiet spot. Discus need very clean water. Feeding: Feed small meals of quality discus pellets or granules a few times a day, and remove uneaten food within a few minutes, since leftovers quickly foul the water. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. New arrivals may need frozen food for a while before they accept pellets. Tankmates: Discus are calm and shy, so choose gentle tankmates that enjoy the same warm water: cardinal and rummynose tetras, sterbai corydoras and small plecos are popular choices. Living in groups: Discus are social and feel safest in a group. A single discus, or just two, tends to be stressed. When a pair forms to breed, they may claim part of the tank, so a group spreads out the attention. Good to know: Red discus keep their brightest color with clean water, a varied diet and a color-enhancing discus food.

Diamond blue discus, or blue diamond discus, were developed by Jack Wattley in the United States in the 1960s and became popular in the aquarium trade in the 1980s. Blue diamond discus are solid cobalt blue and often feature red eyes. The blue diamond discus, as opposed to the cobalt blue discus, do not have black markings on the body. Like all our tank-bred discus, AquariumFish.com imports from a terrific breeder in Singapore. Quick Facts Scientific Name Symphysodon aequifasciatus (captive-bred color variety) Origin Amazon basin (captive-bred in Singapore) Care Level Moderate (needs warm, very clean water) Temperament Peaceful, shy; social Adult Size Up to 6–7" Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 82–88°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Small: approx. 2" · Medium: approx. 3" · Large: approx. 4" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a reliable heater, gentle but strong filtration, and a bare bottom or fine sand for easy cleaning. Keep the tank in a quiet spot. Discus need very clean water. Feeding: Feed small meals of quality discus pellets or granules a few times a day, and remove uneaten food within a few minutes, since leftovers quickly foul the water. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. New arrivals may need frozen food for a while before they accept pellets. When a pair forms to breed, they may claim part of the tank, so a group spreads out the attention. Good to know: Blue discus look most vivid under full-spectrum lighting and against a dark background. Discus show stress by darkening their color and hiding. A dark discus in a corner usually means the water quality or tankmates need checking.

The checkerboard discus, a variation of the parent pigeon blood discus, has a distinct red checkerboard pattern on a cream body. The checkerboard variation was developed in Thailand in the 1980s and is slightly harder to create than the turquoise varieties, hence the checkerboard discus are a bit more expensive. These beautiful discus fish come from our exporters' tanks in Singapore. Quick Facts Scientific Name Symphysodon aequifasciatus (captive-bred color variety) Origin Amazon basin (captive-bred in Thailand and Singapore) Care Level Moderate (needs warm, very clean water) Temperament Peaceful, shy; social Adult Size Up to 6–7" Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 82–88°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1½–4" (by size option) Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a reliable heater, gentle but strong filtration, and a bare bottom or fine sand for easy cleaning. Keep the tank in a quiet spot. Discus need very clean water. Feeding: Feed small meals of quality discus pellets or granules a few times a day, and remove uneaten food within a few minutes, since leftovers quickly foul the water. Tankmates: Discus are calm and shy, so choose gentle tankmates that enjoy the same warm water: cardinal and rummynose tetras, sterbai corydoras and small plecos are popular choices.
