Living in groups: Discus are social and feel safest in a group. A single discus, or just two, tends to be stressed. When a pair forms to breed, they may claim part of the tank, so a group spreads out the attention. Good to know: Pigeon blood strains can show small black "peppering" marks depending on lighting, stress and diet. They usually fade in good conditions.

The red frontosa is a variation of the Burundi frontosa bred in Taiwan to bring out a red color on the body of the fish. These frontosas are sometimes called the copper band frontosa, though the banding on the variant is really black. In all other ways, the red frontosa is similar to the six band frontosa. These fish sell about as quickly as they are bred, so it is difficult to import anything more than a small size specification. This week the breeder only had little guys, but they seem to be hardy. Quick Facts Scientific Name Cyphotilapia frontosa (line-bred) Origin Lake Tanganyika, Africa (bred in Taiwan) Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful for its size, but eats small fish Adult Size Up to 10–12" Lifespan 20+ years Diet Carnivore Water Temperature 75–80°F pH 7.8–9.0 Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Frontosa need a sand bottom, a few large, stable rock caves and lots of open water. Keep the lighting moderate. Lake Malawi and Lake Tanganyika cichlids need hard, alkaline water; crushed coral or aragonite sand helps hold the pH up. Feeding: Feed a quality sinking cichlid pellet once a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like shrimp. Avoid feeder fish, which can carry disease. Tankmates: Frontosa do best in a group with other peaceful, large Tanganyikans like calvus and cyprichromis (adult frontosa will eat small fish), plus synodontis catfish. Good to know: Frontosa grow slowly and can live 20 years or more, so they are a long-term commitment.

Also known as a Blue Mpimbwe, the Zaire Blue Frontosa is rare, difficult to breed, and commands a higher price than other frontosas. In part, the demand for blue Zaires is due to the nice blue color accents on the fins and bar body pattern. Like all frontosas, these cichlids are hardy and live more than twenty years. They are a rusty-colored version of their broad-banded cousins. These are splendid cichlids, and males grow a distinctive hump on their head. These fish are appropriate for a large species community or cichlid tank. Since they are difficult to breed and grow slowly like most Tanganyikans, they are a bit more expensive than their Lake Malawi cousins. Some Tanganyikans, like tropheus cichlids, require vegetables, but the frontosa is a big, fat-headed meat eater. The breeders are selling the blue Zaires before they get very big, so right now they are only one inch. Quick Facts Scientific Name Cyphotilapia gibberosa Origin Lake Tanganyika, Africa Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful for its size, but eats small fish Adult Size Up to 12" Lifespan 20+ years Diet Carnivore Water Temperature 75–80°F pH 7.8–9.0 Shipping Size Small: approx. 1½" · Medium: approx. 2" · Large: approx. 5" Care Guide Tank setup: Frontosa need a sand bottom, a few large, stable rock caves and lots of open water. Keep the lighting moderate. Lake Malawi and Lake Tanganyika cichlids need hard, alkaline water; crushed coral or aragonite sand helps hold the pH up. Feeding: Feed a quality sinking cichlid pellet once a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like shrimp. Avoid feeder fish, which can carry disease. Tankmates: Frontosa do best in a group with other peaceful, large Tanganyikans like calvus and cyprichromis (adult frontosa will eat small fish), plus synodontis catfish. Good to know: Frontosa grow slowly and can live 20 years or more, so they are a long-term commitment.

Like the parent rainbow shark, these gentle sharks grow to five to six inches. Albino rainbow sharks are a tank-raised variation of the native rainbow shark. Quick Facts Scientific Name Epalzeorhynchos frenatum (albino variety) Origin Aquarium-bred (wild form from the Mekong basin) Care Level Moderate Temperament Semi-aggressive, territorial (especially toward other sharks) Adult Size Up to 6" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Keep one per tank Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give a rainbow-type shark caves, driftwood and plants to break up sight lines, plus a tight lid, since they jump. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets or wafers and a quality flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy algae wafers and frozen bloodworms. Tankmates: Keep only one rainbow-type shark per tank, and avoid other bottom-dwelling sharks and territorial fish like red-tailed sharks. They do best with fast, mid- to upper-level swimmers such as danios, barbs, rainbowfish and larger tetras. Good to know: Despite the name, these "sharks" are members of the carp family, not true sharks or catfish. They claim a territory near the bottom and chase other bottom dwellers, so give them caves and keep only one per tank.

The flying fox shark is an algae eater but will become a primary scavenger as it grows to its full size. Flying foxes are peaceful and can adjust to aggressive or peaceful fish tanks. We are working with a group of river collectors that are shipping the correct or closest-to-correct species; we may ship you flying fox or a hybrid species, but they will be healthy, good algae eaters. Quick Facts Scientific Name Epalzeorhynchos kalopterus Origin Indonesia (Sumatra, Borneo), Malaysia and Thailand Care Level Easy Temperament Semi-aggressive (territorial with its own kind) Adult Size Up to 6" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore (grazes on algae) Water Temperature 75–79°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Keep one per tank Shipping Size Approx. 1–2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give a flying fox plants, driftwood and smooth rocks to graze, some current and a tight lid. Feeding: They graze on algae, but also feed algae wafers, sinking pellets or flake daily. Tankmates: Keep one flying fox per tank with peaceful to semi-aggressive community fish of similar size, such as barbs, danios, gouramis and larger tetras. Avoid red-tailed and rainbow sharks. Good to know: Flying foxes are often confused with Siamese algae eaters; flying foxes have a gold stripe above the black one and colored fins.

The Siamese algae eater, or siamensis, is a great algae eater and scavenger and will not be aggressive even as it grows to its full five inches. These fish are hard workers and will spend most of the day grooming plants, rocks and glass in their quest for food. We are working with a group of river collectors that are shipping the correct or closest-to-correct species; we may ship you flying fox or a hybrid species, but they will be healthy, good algae eaters. Available in a group Quick Facts Scientific Name Crossocheilus oblongus Origin Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 6" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore (grazes on algae) Water Temperature 75–79°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Siamese algae eaters are active swimmers. Give them plants, driftwood and smooth rocks to graze, some current and a tight lid, since they can jump. Feeding: They graze on algae, but don't rely on algae alone. Feed algae wafers, sinking pellets or flake daily. Adults eat less algae and more prepared food. Tankmates: Siamese algae eaters get along with most peaceful community fish, such as tetras, rasboras, gouramis, barbs, corydoras and rainbowfish. Adults may squabble with each other or with red-tailed and rainbow sharks. Good to know: True Siamese algae eaters are one of the few fish that eat black beard algae. Look for the black stripe running all the way into the tail fin.

Named for the long fins reminiscent of the wings of another Apollo. These sharks, actually catfish, are seldom seen in the trade, since they are not bred and must be wild-caught in fast-moving streams in Thailand. Quick Facts Scientific Name Luciosoma setigerum Origin Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful but very active Adult Size Up to 10" Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore (surface feeder) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 3" Care Guide Tank setup: These are fast, schooling fish that grow large, so give them plenty of open swimming space, strong filtration and a heavy, tight-fitting lid, since they jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or pellet once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other large, peaceful to semi-aggressive fish such as silver dollars, tinfoil barbs, larger gouramis, plecos and peaceful cichlids. They will eat very small fish once they are large. Good to know: These "sharks" are members of the carp family, not true sharks. They grow quickly, so check their adult size before buying.

The white tip shark, oddly also called the black tip shark, is a brackish South American catfish. These fish may be transitioned to complete marine aquariums, but in freshwater tanks they will always need a little salt. Sleek and very similar to actual sharks. Quick Facts Scientific Name Ariopsis seemanni (formerly Arius jordani ) Origin Pacific coast of Central and South America (Mexico to Peru) Care Level Moderate (needs brackish water as it matures) Temperament Peaceful schooler; eats small fish Adult Size Up to 12–14" Lifespan 10+ years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods, pellets) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 7.5–8.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 3" Care Guide Tank setup: Colombian sharks are active schoolers that need lots of swimming space and strong filtration. Juveniles can live in fresh or lightly brackish water, but as they mature (over about 5 inches) they need brackish water, rising to a specific gravity of about 1.010–1.015; many keepers eventually move them to full marine. Keep a lid on the tank. Feeding: Feed sinking carnivore pellets once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like shrimp and bloodworms. Tankmates: Keep them with other brackish fish that are too large to swallow, such as monos, scats and larger archerfish. Their fin spines are venomous, so handle them with care. Good to know: Colombian sharks are catfish with venomous fin spines. They are true brackish fish and do poorly long-term in pure freshwater.

The hi-fin banded shark, also called the high fin banded shark, has its origin in China and grows to nearly three feet, so it is a popular aquarium fish and, due to its size, a popular pond fish. These fish are actually catfish and are very peaceful. The high fin banded shark features a dramatically high dorsal fin. New season, so these are still on the small side. Quick Facts Scientific Name Myxocyprinus asiaticus Origin Yangtze River basin, China (farm-raised) Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 36" or more Lifespan 20+ years Diet Omnivore (scavenger) Water Temperature 55–75°F (coldwater) pH 6.8–7.5 Group Size Single or small group Shipping Size Approx. 2–3" Care Guide Tank setup: Hi-fin banded sharks are coldwater fish that grow to over three feet, so they are best kept in a large outdoor pond. Juveniles can live in a large, cool, well-oxygenated aquarium with smooth gravel and good filtration while they are small. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets and algae wafers daily. In a pond they also graze algae and scavenge. Tankmates: In a pond they get along with koi and goldfish. In an aquarium, keep them with other peaceful coldwater fish. Good to know: Hi-fin banded sharks change dramatically as they grow: juveniles have tall sail-like fins and bold bands, while adults become long-bodied and reddish. They are protected in their native China.

Vampire crabs are semi-aquatic and need a place to get out of the water in the aquarium. These crabs have brightly colored shells and big yellow eyes. The vampire crab is also a great addition to the terrarium or paludarium tank. In the wild, vampire crabs live in the water of large flowers. These crabs are imported from India and have very vivid colors of red, green, or orange. Quick Facts Scientific Name Geosesarma sp. Origin Southeast Asia Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1½" (leg span) Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Omnivore (scavenger) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: These crabs need land as well as water. Use a paludarium or a tank with a large land area and a shallow water section. Keep a tight lid on the tank, since they are escape artists. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets or shrimp food once a day. They also eat vegetables and small bits of fish food. Tankmates: They are best kept in a species-only setup, since they may catch small fish. Good to know: Vampire crabs get their name from their glowing yellow eyes. They hide a lot, so more hiding places mean more confident crabs.

The purple matano crab has a deep, rich purple color, and these crabs are semi-aquatic and need a place to get out of the water in the aquarium. These crabs are brightly colored and also great additions to the terrarium. Native to Indonesia. Quick Facts Scientific Name Syntripsa matannensis Origin Lake Matano, Sulawesi, Indonesia Care Level Moderate Temperament Semi-aggressive Adult Size Up to 3–4" (leg span) Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (scavenger) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.5–8.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them rocks, caves and a place to climb out of the water, plus a tight-fitting lid, since they are escape artists. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets once a day. They also eat frozen foods and leftover food. Tankmates: They may catch slow fish, shrimp and snails. They are best kept in a species-only setup. Good to know: Matano crabs come from Lake Matano, one of the oldest and deepest lakes in Southeast Asia.

The panther crab has a spotted panther color pattern. These crabs are brightly colored and also great additions to the terrarium. Native to Indonesia. Quick Facts Scientific Name Parathelphusa pantherina Origin Lake Matano, Sulawesi, Indonesia Care Level Moderate Temperament Aggressive Adult Size Up to 4–5" (leg span) Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (scavenger) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.5–8.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a tank with plenty of rocks and caves, a tight-fitting lid and a rock or ledge where they can climb out of the water if they choose. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets once a day. They also eat frozen foods and leftover food. Tankmates: Panther crabs will catch fish, shrimp and snails, and they can fight with each other. They are best kept alone. Good to know: Panther crabs come from Lake Matano, one of the oldest and deepest lakes in Southeast Asia.

Freshwater gobies have quite a bit of personality and unusual movement, so they are a great addition to the aquarium. They are bottom dwellers and a bit territorial, but easy to keep and feed. Stiphodons are a group of smaller gobies that go well with smaller-species fish tanks and planted aquariums. The gold spot stiphodon has a bright gold head and gold reflective markings along the body. Quick Facts Scientific Name Stiphodon sp. Origin Indonesian island streams Care Level Moderate (needs clean, oxygen-rich, flowing water) Temperament Peaceful with other fish; males territorial with each other Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Algae eater Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size One male with several females Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: These gobies come from clear, fast-flowing island streams. Give them a mature tank with strong current, high oxygen, smooth rocks covered in algae and biofilm, and a tight lid, since they can climb out. Feeding: These gobies graze on algae off rocks, so they do best in a mature tank. Also feed algae wafers. They may go hungry in a very clean, new tank. Tankmates: They do well with small, peaceful fish that like cool, flowing water, such as danios, rasboras, hillstream loaches and dwarf shrimp. Males may spar with each other. Good to know: Stream gobies cling to rocks with a sucker formed by their pelvic fins. Their larvae drift to the sea to develop, so they rarely breed in aquariums.

The freshwater aquarium lipstick goby is named for the ruby-colored mouth on this nano goby species. Also called the red lips goby, the lipstick goby is wild-caught in small streams and not often seen in the aquarium trade... or beauty contests. These gobies are excellent for nano tanks and planted aquariums; they do not harm fancy shrimp or other invertebrates. Quick Facts Scientific Name Sicyopus jonklaasi Origin Sri Lanka Care Level Moderate (needs clean, oxygen-rich, flowing water) Temperament Peaceful with other fish; males territorial with each other Adult Size Up to 1½" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Carnivore (small meaty foods) Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size One male with several females Shipping Size Approx. 1¼" Care Guide Tank setup: These gobies come from clear, fast-flowing island streams. Give them a mature tank with strong current, high oxygen, smooth rocks covered in algae and biofilm, and a tight lid, since they can climb out. Feeding: These gobies graze on algae off rocks, so they do best in a mature tank. Also feed algae wafers. They may go hungry in a very clean, new tank. Tankmates: They do well with small, peaceful fish that like cool, flowing water, such as danios, rasboras, hillstream loaches and dwarf shrimp. Males may spar with each other. Good to know: Stream gobies cling to rocks with a sucker formed by their pelvic fins. Their larvae drift to the sea to develop, so they rarely breed in aquariums.

The beautiful predator fish called the Jardini Arowana is also referred to as the Black Arowana or Australian Arowana. The fish is similar in shape to the endangered Formosa Arowana or Asian Arowana. Jardini grow to about two feet in the aquarium and three feet in the wild. Aquarists can transition Jardini to floating pellet food, but these monster fish still require some live feeder fish. Please have small feeders available, particularly for the smaller size. Quick Facts Scientific Name Scleropages jardinii Origin Northern Australia and New Guinea Care Level Difficult (grows very large) Temperament Aggressive Adult Size Up to 2 feet Lifespan 15–20 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–86°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 3–8" Care Guide Tank setup: Arowanas are powerful jumpers, so a heavy, tight-fitting lid is a must. Give them open swimming space and strong filtration. Feeding: Feed floating carnivore pellets and frozen foods like shrimp. Tankmates: Jardinis are among the more aggressive arowanas. Keep them alone or only with large, robust fish. Good to know: Jardini arowanas have pink or red spots on each scale that get brighter as they grow.

The pitbull pleco is a variation of the L-187A spotted rubberlip pleco, with a lighter color pattern and polka dots. Otherwise this is the same fat-lipped fish with a much cooler common name. These plecos are similar in behavior too: great scavengers, somewhat shy and good tank mates. Quick Facts Scientific Name Chaetostoma sp. Origin Andean streams of Colombia Care Level Moderate (needs cool, fast, oxygen-rich water) Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 4–5" Lifespan 8–12 years Diet Algae eater (also eats algae wafers) Water Temperature 68–77°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 2–3" Care Guide Tank setup: Rubberlip plecos come from cool, fast mountain streams. Give them a tank with strong current, high oxygen, smooth rocks covered in algae and cooler water (68–77°F). They do poorly in warm, still tanks. Feeding: They graze on algae. Also feed algae wafers. Tankmates: They do well with peaceful fish that like cooler, flowing water, such as danios, white clouds and hillstream loaches. Good to know: Rubberlip plecos hold onto rocks in fast water with their broad sucker mouth.

Royal plecos earn their name for their beautiful gold and green color patterns and the large crown-shaped body pattern. These were some of the first exotic plecos exported to the trade, and so they got first dibs on this grand "common" name (pardon the oxymoron). Variations of the royal pleco include the L-191 pleco, which is the same species but with fewer spots and more lines; hence it is referred to as the broken line pleco. Watermelon royal plecos, also called L-330 gold royals, again the same species, develop rounder heads and shorter tails in the wild, hence the "watermelon" shape. All royal plecos are gentle giants that grow to a stunning show-quality 8 to 16 inches in the aquarium. Royal plecos are hardy scavengers and should be kept with a piece of driftwood for their home base. Quick Facts Scientific Name Panaque cf. nigrolineatus (L-191) Origin Orinoco basin (Colombia and Venezuela) Care Level Moderate (grows large) Temperament Peaceful (territorial with other plecos) Adult Size Up to 12–16" Lifespan 15–20+ years Diet Herbivore (driftwood, algae wafers) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Small: approx. 1½" · Medium: 2–4" · Large: 4–5" · Show: approx. 7–8" Care Guide Tank setup: Royal-type plecos eat wood, so give them plenty of driftwood, strong filtration and caves. They produce a lot of waste, so good filtration is important. Feeding: Feed algae wafers and sinking pellets, and keep plenty of driftwood in the tank for them to rasp, since wood is part of their diet. Tankmates: They do well with medium to large community fish and cichlids. Keep one per tank unless the tank is very large, since they are territorial with other plecos. Good to know: Royal-type plecos are among the few fish that can actually digest wood. Plan for an adult-size tank before buying.

Bushynose plecos are found all over the Amazon basin and are good tankmates, as they eat algae and scavenge uneaten food and only grow to five inches in the fish tank. Though these are plentiful and affordable plecos, they have a very unique appearance. They are also called bristlenose plecos; the antler-like growths at the top of their nose get larger and larger as the fish ages. The long fin bushynose is bred for extended flowing fins on a chocolate body. Quick Facts Scientific Name Ancistrus sp. (long fin variety) Origin Amazon basin (wild form); aquarium-bred Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful (males guard caves) Adult Size Up to 5" Lifespan 10–12 years Diet Herbivore (algae and plant-based foods) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single, pair or group with a cave each Shipping Size Small: 1" · Medium: 2" · Large: 3–4" Care Guide Tank setup: Bristlenose plecos do well in most community tanks. Give them driftwood to rasp on, caves or hiding spots, and good filtration. They keep glass, rocks and plants clean of algae. Feeding: They graze on algae, but also feed algae wafers. Tankmates: Bristlenose plecos get along with nearly all community fish, plus shrimp and snails. Avoid large aggressive fish that might harass them. Good to know: Males grow larger, bushier "bristles" on the snout than females. Bristlenose plecos stay small and are one of the best algae-eaters for home aquariums.

Sailfin plecos are named for their giant dorsal fin. Their pattern is a muted marble or spotted, and the L001 has a spotted one. Sometimes called the gold spotted sailfin pleco, these plecos grow very big and live a long time. Adaptable and hardy, they get along with all other fish but can outgrow a small aquarium. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pterygoplichthys joselimaianus Origin Tocantins River basin, Brazil Care Level Easy (grows large) Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 12–18" Lifespan 15–20 years Diet Omnivore (algae and sinking foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 2–3" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them driftwood, caves and strong filtration, since large plecos produce a lot of waste. Feeding: Feed algae wafers and sinking pellets once a day, ideally in the evening when they are most active. They also enjoy frozen bloodworms. Tankmates: They get along with most fish, including cichlids. Avoid keeping two large plecos in the same tank. Good to know: Sailfin plecos are named for their tall dorsal fin, and their gold spots stay bright as they grow.

Plecostomus are a specialty of AquariumFish.com. These catfish originate in South America, and many colors, sizes and patterns can be found; so many that common names often aren’t enough to identify one pleco from another, so in 1988 a tropical fish magazine in Germany called DATZ assigned “L” numbers to distinguish species. Though not exactly scientific, the system works. We carry a couple of plecos that have not been assigned their L number, but the Germans are a cautious folk, and we are sure they will get around to it in a precise and correct manner. Medium size is 2” to 3”. Most plecos do better with a little driftwood in the tank. The leopard cactus pleco grows quite slowly and must be wild-caught in Brazil. These are beautiful cactus plecos and very good companions in peaceful and aggressive species tanks. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pseudacanthicus leopardus (L-114) Origin Rio Branco (Brazil) and Essequibo (Guyana) Care Level Moderate (grows large) Temperament Peaceful with fish; territorial with other plecos Adult Size Up to 10–12" Lifespan 15–20 years Diet Omnivore (sinking foods) Water Temperature 78–84°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 4" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them strong current, high oxygen, large caves and driftwood, and keep the water warm and very clean. Feeding: Feed meaty sinking foods like carnivore pellets. They also enjoy frozen foods like shrimp and bloodworms. Tankmates: They do well with medium to large community fish and cichlids. They may eat very small fish or shrimp, and they are territorial with other plecos. Good to know: Cactus plecos get more colorful as they mature and can live for decades with good care.

One of the rarest and most interesting plecos in the trade, the blue-eye pleco is uncommon, and as wild populations recover, we will begin to see a few more available to the trade. These are expensive but very hardy catfish. Blue-eye plecos, or blue-eye suttoni, require driftwood and veggies in their diet. Quick Facts Scientific Name Panaque cochliodon (formerly P. suttoni ) Origin Magdalena River basin, Colombia Care Level Moderate (grows large) Temperament Peaceful (territorial with other plecos) Adult Size Up to 12–16" Lifespan 15–20+ years Diet Herbivore (driftwood, algae wafers) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 8" Care Guide Tank setup: Royal-type plecos eat wood, so give them plenty of driftwood, strong filtration and caves. They produce a lot of waste, so good filtration is important. Feeding: Feed algae wafers and sinking pellets, and keep plenty of driftwood in the tank for them to rasp, since wood is part of their diet. Tankmates: They do well with medium to large community fish and cichlids. Keep one per tank unless the tank is very large, since they are territorial with other plecos. Good to know: Royal-type plecos are among the few fish that can actually digest wood. Plan for an adult-size tank before buying.

The finest South American cichlid in color and rarity is the Zebrina Pike Cichlid. This species is rare but hardy and easy to keep. Zebrina pikes need live feeders and do better in lower pH water. These exotic pet fish are aggressive and need their own hiding place, but they are compatible with larger aggressive species. Our Zebrina Pikes were caught on the border of Colombia and Venezuela. Quick Facts Scientific Name Crenicichla zebrina Origin Orinoco basin (Colombia and Venezuela) Care Level Moderate Temperament Aggressive Adult Size Up to 12–15" Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 76–84°F pH 6.0–7.0 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 4" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a sand bottom, caves, driftwood and rocks to hide in, plus a tight lid. Strong filtration is important, since they eat meaty foods. Feeding: Feed meaty foods like quality cichlid pellets and frozen shrimp. Tankmates: Pike cichlids are predators and will eat small fish. Keep them with robust fish of similar size. Good to know: Pike cichlids are ambush hunters that lie in wait near cover before darting out.

The lenticulata pike cichlid is a collector's dream. A rare and beautiful South American cichlid, these unusual pikes feature a freckled face and bright coloration. Also called the Freckle Face Pike, the lenticulata pike cichlid is aggressive and prefers to stay near their own private hiding place. These fish are compatible with larger aggressive species, and will feed on pellets but prefer live feeders. Quick Facts Scientific Name Crenicichla lenticulata Origin Colombia and Venezuela Care Level Moderate Temperament Aggressive Adult Size Up to 12–15" Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 76–84°F pH 6.0–7.0 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 7" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a sand bottom, caves, driftwood and rocks to hide in, plus a tight lid. Strong filtration is important, since they eat meaty foods. Feeding: Feed meaty foods like quality cichlid pellets and frozen shrimp. Tankmates: Pike cichlids are predators and will eat small fish. Keep them with robust fish of similar size. Good to know: Pike cichlids are ambush hunters that lie in wait near cover before darting out.

Ivory snails are hardy and excellent scavengers with a nice, subtle color pattern. Mystery snails will grow to two inches and will not eat plants. These snails can handle a wide range of water and temperature conditions. Be sure to pull out snails and other invertebrates when treating the fish tank for ich and other diseases. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pomacea diffusa (sold as P. bridgesii ) Origin South America (Amazon basin); farm-raised Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful; plant-safe Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 1–2 years Diet Scavenger (algae and leftover food) Water Temperature 68–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 (hard water for healthy shells) Breeding Lays pink egg clutches above the waterline; needs a male and female Shipping Size Approx. ½–¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Give mystery snails a covered tank with a gap of an inch or two above the water, since females climb out to lay eggs. Keep the water hard and alkaline for healthy shells, and add calcium (cuttlebone or crushed coral) if your water is soft. Feeding: Mystery snails eat algae and leftover food, but give them sinking pellets or algae wafers too so they don't go hungry. Tankmates: Mystery snails do well with peaceful fish, shrimp and other snails. Avoid fish that nip antennae or eat snails, like puffers, loaches, large cichlids and some bettas, and keep them away from assassin snails. Good to know: Remove snails before treating the tank with copper or other medications, which are toxic to invertebrates.

Many in the trade confuse the banded severum with the gold severum and the red spotted severum. Though the same species, each of these fish is a different variation. The gold severum is the original severum introduced to aquarium hobbyists a century ago, bred from wild species to get a solid gold color and a hardy disposition. Gold severums have been an aquarium staple for beginners and experts for generations. The green banded severum has a green body with vertical black stripes, often gets red shoulder markings as it matures, and is wild-caught in Colombia and Peru. The red spotted severum, pond-raised in Florida and Taiwan, looks like a gold severum with red dots over the body. The red spotted severum needs a little more care, similar to discus. Quick Facts Scientific Name Heros efasciatus (gold variety) Origin Amazon basin (wild ancestors); aquarium-bred Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Peaceful for a cichlid Adult Size Up to 8" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 76–84°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single, pair or small group Shipping Size Small: approx. 1–2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a sand or fine gravel bottom, driftwood, rocks and sturdy plants. Good filtration is important, since these cichlids grow large and produce a lot of waste. Feeding: Feed a quality cichlid pellet or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They do well with other peaceful South American cichlids of similar size like angelfish, eartheaters and severums, plus larger tetras, silver dollars and plecos. They may eat very small fish. Good to know: These cichlids are known for their personality and often learn to recognize their owners.

Like the common red rili shrimp, these exotic shrimp have a clear middle body. The coloration, however, is very difficult to breed, and the orange rili are rare in comparison to the blue rili and red rili shrimp. The orange rili shrimp have bright orange bands against clear bands along the body. Quick Facts Scientific Name Neocaridina davidi (orange rili) Origin East Asia (aquarium-bred, mostly Taiwan) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1–1¼" Lifespan 1–2 years Diet Omnivore (grazes on algae) Water Temperature 65–80°F pH 6.5–8.0 Water Hardness GH 6–12 (moderately hard) Group Size Does best in a group (breeds readily) Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Neocaridina are hardy and ideal for beginners. Use a cycled, planted tank with moss, plants and hiding spots, and a sponge filter or a sponge over the filter intake so shrimp aren't pulled in. Keep the water stable. Feeding: Shrimp graze on algae all day. Feed a small amount of quality shrimp food once a day and remove anything uneaten after a few hours. Tankmates: Keep shrimp alone or with tiny, peaceful fish like small rasboras, ember tetras, otocinclus and pygmy corydoras, plus snails. Most fish will eat baby shrimp, and cichlids (even dwarf cichlids like rams and apistogrammas) and larger fish will eat adults. Different Neocaridina colors will crossbreed and lose their color over time. Good to know: Shrimp are very sensitive to copper and many medications. Never treat a tank with shrimp, and check plant fertilizers and treatments for copper.

One of the most unusual freshwater schooling fish from Thailand is the giant humphead glass fish. This creature gets 4 inches in size and looks just plain weird. The humphead glass fish lives off of small insects in the wild and prefers live black worms and small frozen foods in the aquarium. Quick Facts Scientific Name Parambassis pulcinella Origin Thailand and Myanmar Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 3–4" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Carnivore (small meaty foods) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 3" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants, hiding places and gentle filtration. They like slightly hard water, and a little aquarium salt is optional. Feeding: Offer small frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp once or twice a day. Some learn to take small pellets once settled. Tankmates: Glassfish are peaceful and get along with other small community fish such as rasboras, danios, livebearers and corydoras. Good to know: Humphead glassfish are named for the tall hump on their back, and they are see-through like other glassfish.

The electric blue cichlid is one of the most popular pet fish from Lake Malawi. These cichlids have a peaceful disposition towards most other African cichlids. However, since they look similar to Peacock cichlids, the males will fight with the Peacock males for breeding territory. The electric blue cichlid is also called the Hap Blue, and a similar species, the Ahli cichlid, is the same in all respects except that it will grow to eight inches. Both species are called Hap Electric Blues. Quick Facts Scientific Name Sciaenochromis fryeri Origin Lake Malawi, Africa Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Semi-aggressive (males territorial) Adult Size Up to 6" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 76–82°F pH 7.8–8.6 Shipping Size Medium: approx. 2" · Large: approx. 3" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a sand bottom, open swimming space in front and rockwork along the back. Lake Malawi and Lake Tanganyika cichlids need hard, alkaline water; crushed coral or aragonite sand helps hold the pH up. Feeding: Feed a quality cichlid pellet or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like brine shrimp. Tankmates: Haps do well with peacocks and other haps of similar size, plus robust catfish like synodontis. Keep one male per similar-looking species, with several females, to limit fighting and crossbreeding. Good to know: Males show the deepest electric blue once they mature and when females are in the tank.

Like the blood red parrot cichlid, the flowerhorn cichlid is a successful hybrid from two or several species, including red terror, synpillum, and citrinellus cichlids. Some flowerhorns are further hybridized to bring out more dramatic colors - such as the blue diamond flowerhorn. This flowerhorn variation is bred and imported from Thailand. Most flowerhorns do not show a bump on their forehead until they are more than three inches in size. The diamond blue flowerhorn has only a slight rise on the forehead, though it does get a bit more pronounced as the fish ages. Quick Facts Scientific Name Amphilophus hybrid Origin Captive-bred hybrid (Thailand) Care Level Moderate Temperament Aggressive Adult Size Up to 10–12" Lifespan 10–12 years Diet Omnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 78–86°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Keep one per tank Shipping Size Approx. 2–6" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them strong filtration, a smooth bottom and only a few sturdy decorations, since they rearrange the tank. Feeding: Feed a quality cichlid pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like shrimp. Tankmates: Flowerhorns are very aggressive and are usually kept alone. Good to know: Flowerhorns are full of personality and often learn to recognize their owners.

Like its smaller cousin, the Zebra Otocinclus is a terrific scavenger and algae grazer in the aquarium. These fish are best with some natural wood in the fish tank, and in the wild these are schooling fish, so they prefer to swim in groups of three or more. Zebra Otocinclus must be wild-caught and are fished from the Rio Tigre river in Peru. Quick Facts Scientific Name Otocinclus cocama Origin Amazon basin, Peru Care Level Moderate (needs a mature tank) Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Algae eater (also eats algae wafers) Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1–2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a mature, planted tank with algae to graze, gentle filtration and stable, clean water. Feeding: Otocinclus graze on soft algae, but don't rely on algae alone. Also feed algae wafers. Tankmates: Otos are very peaceful and get along with almost any small community fish, plus shrimp and snails. Good to know: Zebra otos are a rare striped otocinclus with bold black-and-white bands.

Goldline Knifefish are seldom seen in the aquarium hobby. The Goldline Knifefish, or Yellowline Knifefish, are caught in the Amazon basin near the border of Colombia and Brazil. This makes for a difficult journey to the warehouses of AquariumFish.com! Goldline Knifefish are wild and require some live foods such as black worms or feeder white clouds, but you can transition them to frozen foods. These fish project an electric field to find their prey, but cannot generate enough power to subdue their prey the way the electric eel does (electric eels are technically knife fish). Little is known about the Goldline Knifefish - it is only assumed they grow as big as Black Knifefish. Their temperament is similar, and these fish are compatible with fish that cannot fit in their mouth. Quick Facts Scientific Name Sternopygus macrurus Origin Amazon basin (Colombia and Brazil) Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful (eats fish that fit in its mouth) Adult Size Up to 18" or more Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 10" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them hiding places like large tubes or caves, dim lighting, strong filtration and a tight lid. They are most active at night. Feeding: Feed meaty foods like frozen shrimp and bloodworms, plus sinking carnivore pellets once they learn to take them. Tankmates: They will eat any fish that fits in their mouth. Keep them with large, peaceful fish. Good to know: Knifefish sense their surroundings with a weak electric field, which helps them hunt in the dark.

Flowerhorn (or Flower Horn) collectors look for certain color patterns and a nice-size hump on the forehead of the fish. Hump head variations are bred to display a prominent bulge on the forehead and this is apparent even at three inches. The pearl color is a very special color pattern and not as common as the red dragon pattern. AquariumFish.com imports Pearl Humphead Flowerhorns from a breeder in Thailand. This Pearl Flowerhorn will grow to an amazing pet fish, but Flowerhorns are aggressive! These fish already display their magnificent colors and prominent hump. Quick Facts Scientific Name Amphilophus hybrid Origin Captive-bred hybrid (Thailand) Care Level Moderate Temperament Aggressive Adult Size Up to 12" Lifespan 10–12 years Diet Omnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 78–86°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Keep one per tank Shipping Size Approx. 3–5" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them strong filtration, a smooth bottom and only a few sturdy decorations, since they rearrange the tank. Feeding: Feed a quality cichlid pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like shrimp. Tankmates: Flowerhorns are very aggressive and are usually kept alone. Good to know: Flowerhorns are full of personality and often learn to recognize their owners.

The L-183 starlight pleco is sometimes referred to as the L-181 peppermint pleco. This is not the L-59 peppermint pleco; this one has a darker black body with a pretty cream fringe on the fins when the fish matures. This pleco comes from Brazil and grows to about eight inches. The dark body with the contrasting white spots and light-colored fringe on the dorsal fin make this a beautiful addition to the aquarium. Starlight plecos are omnivores and will scavenge, but it is best to also add some sinking pellets to their diet. Like most plecos, the starlight pleco will be compatible with nearly all species except extremely small shrimp and similar creatures. Pictured is a three-inch pleco. As the fish matures, the white fringe and spots become more pronounced. Google images generally show a fish that is mature and fully colored. Quick Facts Scientific Name Ancistrus sp. (L-183) Origin Rio Negro, Brazil Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful (males guard caves) Adult Size Up to 5–6" Lifespan 10–12 years Diet Herbivore (algae and plant-based foods) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 5.5–7.0 Group Size Single, pair or group with a cave each Shipping Size Approx. 1¼" Care Guide Tank setup: Bristlenose plecos do well in most community tanks. Give them driftwood to rasp on, caves or hiding spots, and good filtration. They keep glass, rocks and plants clean of algae. Feeding: They graze on algae, but also feed algae wafers. Tankmates: Bristlenose plecos get along with nearly all community fish, plus shrimp and snails. Avoid large aggressive fish that might harass them. Good to know: Males grow larger, bushier "bristles" on the snout than females. Bristlenose plecos stay small and are one of the best algae-eaters for home aquariums.

The prehistoric dragon goby looks like something out of the ancient past. These little beasts are actually peaceful and will only consume the smallest of aquatic species, such as fancy shrimp. In the wild these gobies sift through mud for small critters to eat; in the aquarium they readily adapt to scavenging and frozen foods or live blackworms. We import our dragon gobies from Ecuador. Dragon gobies adapt to brackish and freshwater fish tanks, but a little salt is a good idea even in a freshwater aquarium. Also, regarding salt, we put about four ounces in 20 gallons, but these fish are hit or miss. If they do not like your water, they may perish within a week, so don't fall in love with them too quickly, and let customer service know if you have issues. Quick Facts Scientific Name Gobioides sp. (sold as G. broussonnetii ) Origin Coastal Americas (wild-caught; ours from Ecuador) Care Level Moderate (needs brackish water and a soft sand bottom) Temperament Peaceful (but eats very small fish and shrimp) Adult Size Up to 15–20" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore (sifts sand for food) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.5–8.5 Group Size Single or small group Shipping Size Approx. 6" Care Guide Tank setup: Dragon gobies need a soft, fine sand bottom to sift through, caves or pipes to hide in, and brackish water (specific gravity about 1.005–1.010). Keep a tight lid on the tank. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets and algae wafers. They sift food from the sand, so sinking foods work best. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with peaceful brackish fish such as mollies, monos and scats that won't outcompete them for food. They may eat very small fish and shrimp. Good to know: Dragon gobies have poor eyesight and find food by sifting sand. Their fierce-looking teeth are used for scraping, not attacking.

Beau Gregory Damselfish The Beau Gregory Damselfish, or simply the Gregory Damsel, is reef safe but territorial. This damsel needs some rock crevices to claim its own. These colorful fish will only get to about 2 inches in size. It's an odd name - but beau just means pretty, and gregory is a common name used by taxonomists for damselfish. Bet you were hoping for a story. Scientific name: Chrysiptera sp. Diet: variety of meaty foods, herbivore preparations, and flaked foods. Max Size: 2 inches Required tank size: 30+ gallons Shipping Size: Approx. 1 1/2 inches

Yellow Sun Coral The yellow sun coral, or orange sun coral, is a bright addition to the the aquarium and is best placed on lower live rocks. Similar to dendro coral but a little hardier, the sun coral do not rely on the sun - ironically - so these corals do not need much light to thrive. Sun coral should be fed four times a week. We import our coral from Mexico and the lps sun corals also come in blue and green. Scientific Name: Tubastrea aurea Food : micro-plankton or brine shrimp, liquid mystis Care: Water flow medium, moderate to low lighting Shipping Size: 2 to 5 inches

Borbonius Anthias: The Rare Deepwater Showpiece The Borbonius Anthias (Odontanthias borbonius), also widely known as the Blotched Anthias , Checked Swallowtail , or Yellow-spotted Anthias , is one of the most highly prized and sought-after fish in the aquarium hobby. Unlike many other anthias species, which are collected in shallow waters, the Borbonius Anthias originates from deep-water (mesophotic) reefs, often found at depths between 200 and 1,000 feet (60-300m), making it an expensive and difficult specimen to acquire and acclimate. This striking fish displays a unique coloration that can vary, but typically features a beautiful pale pink to reddish-orange body adorned with scattered large, irregular gold or yellow blotches. Its fins, particularly the deep, lyre-shaped caudal (tail) fin, are often highlighted with bright yellow. Like all anthias, it is a protogynous hermaphrodite, with the largest female transitioning to a male in the absence of one. Males may be identified by a slightly larger size and an elongated third dorsal spine. Due to its specialized deep-water origin, this species is sensitive to bright lighting and requires a well-established, stable aquarium of at least 100-125 gallons. It is best maintained in an environment with lower light levels and ample dark caves and overhangs to provide security and mimic its natural habitat. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: The Borbonius Anthias is a Carnivore and plankton feeder with a high metabolism. A consistent feeding regimen of small amounts 3-5 times per day is crucial. The diet must be varied and include highly nutritious, finely chopped, meaty foods like frozen mysis shrimp, copepods, rotifers, and vitamin-enriched brine shrimp. It may be a shy eater when first introduced and should be fed near its hiding spots. Social Structure: While many anthias are kept in harems, the Borbonius Anthias is often found solitarily or in small, loose groups in the wild. In the aquarium, it is often recommended to keep them singly in smaller systems (under 180 gallons) or in a small harem (one male with 2-3 females) in very large systems, as they can be territorial toward conspecifics (members of the same species). Do not keep two males together. Reef Compatibility: It is Completely Reef Safe. This species poses no threat to corals or sessile invertebrates. It is a true plankton feeder and should not bother any members of the clean-up crew. Temperament: It is Peaceful to Semi-Aggressive. It is docile toward most tankmates, but can be easily stressed by overly aggressive or boisterous fish. Tankmates should be peaceful, such as tangs, clownfish, gobies, and other non-competing species. It requires excellent water quality and stable parameters to thrive. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Odontanthias borbonius Primary Common Name: Borbonius Anthias Other Common Names: Blotched Anthias, Checked Swallowtail, Yellow-spotted Anthias Origin: Indo-Pacific (Deepwater Reefs: South Africa, Japan, Réunion) Max Size: 6 inches (15 cm) Temperament: Peaceful / Active (Can be territorial to conspecifics) Diet: Carnivore (Requires frequent small feedings of meaty foods) Minimum Tank Size: 100-125+ Gallons Reef Compatibility: Yes (Safe with all corals and invertebrates)

The classic Asian-bred Hump Head Flowerhorn is prized for the bright colors and big protruding forehead. Flowerhorns are aggressive and, when they are large, usually become the only pet fish in the aquarium. AquariumFish.com imports hump head flowerhorns from a breeder in Thailand. This red hump head flowerhorn already has a well-formed hump and great colors. Quick Facts Scientific Name Amphilophus hybrid Origin Captive-bred hybrid (Thailand) Care Level Moderate Temperament Aggressive Adult Size Up to 12" Lifespan 10–12 years Diet Omnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 78–86°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Keep one per tank Shipping Size Approx. 3–5" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them strong filtration, a smooth bottom and only a few sturdy decorations, since they rearrange the tank. Feeding: Feed a quality cichlid pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like shrimp. Tankmates: Flowerhorns are very aggressive and are usually kept alone. Good to know: Flowerhorns are full of personality and often learn to recognize their owners.

The rosy loach, or Burmese rosy loach, is a suitable small aquarium species, perfect with exotic fish, rasboras and exotic shrimp. These loaches are very small and have a light pink and brown color. Rosy loaches are wild-caught and uncommon in the aquarium hobby. In the wild and in the fish tank, rosy loaches prefer to swim in packs and will adapt to flake food that floats to the bottom. These loaches are ideal for natural planted aquariums, and they love to run around the leaves. Quick Facts Scientific Name Petruichthys brevis Origin Inle Lake region, Myanmar Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1¼" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Carnivore (tiny foods; takes flake) Water Temperature 68–76°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a planted tank with a fine gravel or sand bottom, leaf litter and gentle filtration. Keep the water clean, cool and well oxygenated. Feeding: Feed crushed flake or micro pellets once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other tiny, peaceful fish like rasboras, small danios, white clouds and dwarf shrimp. Good to know: These tiny loaches swim in loose groups in the middle and lower water, unlike most bottom-hugging loaches.

Longfin Black Ice Clownfish Longfin Clownfish have long flowing fins with a rounded, more even outline. This sets them apart from the typical longfin strain that display jagged, stiff fins with uneven edges. The reason for the different look of Sea & Reef's longfin clownfish is due to different genetics Scientific Name : Amphiprion ocellaris Diet: pellets, flake food, frozen Mysis shrimp, and frozen brine shrimp

The uncommon and lovely sultan pleco comes from a small river off the Amazon in Brazil. These fish have a light grey body with large black spots and white fringe on the fins. Like most plecos, they should have a mix of veggies and meats and do best with some natural driftwood in the aquarium. Quick Facts Scientific Name Leporacanthicus joselimai (L-264) Origin Rio Tapajós, Brazil Care Level Moderate (needs warm, oxygen-rich water) Temperament Peaceful with fish; territorial with other plecos Adult Size Up to 8" Lifespan 12–15+ years Diet Omnivore (sinking foods) Water Temperature 78–84°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single, or several with a cave each Shipping Size Approx. 3" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them strong current, high oxygen, rocky caves and driftwood. Keep the water warm and very clean, since they produce a lot of waste on a meaty diet. Feeding: Feed meaty sinking foods like carnivore pellets. They also enjoy frozen foods like shrimp and bloodworms. Tankmates: They do well with most community fish and cichlids of similar size. They may eat very small fish or shrimp. Give each pleco its own cave. Good to know: These plecos have strong, toothed mouths and prefer meaty foods; they usually leave plants alone.

Red Bowerbankii Coral This species is found infrequently in both the wild and the aquarium trade. It is easy to keep in an aquarium, fast growing, and grows best under moderate lighting. The Acan Hillae is often intensely colored with a mosaic of blues, reds, yellows, greens, purples, and oranges - a truly beautiful coral. Its soft tissue often looks almost splattered with color, like a Jackson Pollock painting. Scientific Name: Acanthastrea Hillae Diet: mysis and brine shrimp Approximate Size: 2 inches

It is easy to keep in an aquarium, fast growing, and grows best under moderate lighting. The Acan Hillae is often intensely colored with a mosaic of blues, reds, yellows, greens, purples, and oranges - a truly beautiful coral. Thunder Maroon Clownfish: A Striking & Unique Centerpiece The Thunder Maroon Clownfish (Premnas biaculeatus) is a beautiful and unique designer variant of the Maroon Clownfish. This captive-bred species features a rich, vibrant maroon body with a highly variable white pattern that resembles a thunderclap or a jagged white band across the fish. Like all Maroon Clownfish, it is a bold and territorial species, making it a spectacular centerpiece for a large, semi-aggressive community tank. Its hardiness and striking looks make it a favorite for experienced aquarists. Important Note: The Maroon Clownfish is known for its aggressive and territorial behavior, especially as it matures. It should be introduced to the tank before more docile species and is best kept as a single specimen or a well-established pair. Why the Thunder Maroon Clownfish is a Great Choice: Unique Designer Appearance: Its one-of-a-kind pattern makes it an unforgettable showpiece. Hardy & Resilient: This captive-bred species is known for its resilience and adaptability, making it a great choice for a well-maintained system. Distinct Personality: Its bold and confident nature adds a dynamic presence to the aquarium. Reef-Safe: The Thunder Maroon Clownfish will not harm corals, though it may be territorial with other fish in the tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Premnas biaculeatus Origin: Captive-bred (Designer Variety) Max Size: 6 inches Lifespan: 10 years or more Diet: Omnivore. A varied diet of high-quality frozen foods, marine pellets, and algae. Shipping Size: 1.5-2.5 inches

Black Seahorse -Tank Raised The Black Seahorse, also called the Lined Seahorse, is considered by many hobbyists to be the most attractive of all the seahorses. These are young and the size is about 2-3 inches. The coloration of these tank raised seahorses range from shades of black, to gray to brown, yellow. Their coloration may change in the aquarium, and is highly dependent on the colors of its environment. As they mature and become ready to mate the male lined seahorse dance around, show off his pouch and may have color changes. If the female is interested they will tangle tails and dance as she deposits up to 600 eggs in his pouch. It usually takes about 2 weeks then the male will birth as many 50 to 400 babies. Scientific Name: Hippocampus erectus Origin: Captive bred Max Size: 7 inches Diet: Frozen brine shrimp Shipping Size: Up to 2 1/2 inches

The Buffalo Head Cichlid, also called the Lionhead cichlid or African blockhead, has a distinct fat forehead that earns its common names. These cichlids are wild from the Congo River and rarely make it to the aquarium trade. Buffalo head cichlids grow to just under four inches and will do well in any African cichlid tank. The cichlids prefer a cave to inhabit and protect. Quick Facts Scientific Name Steatocranus casuarius Origin Congo River, Africa Care Level Easy Temperament Territorial Adult Size Up to 4–5" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.5–8.0 Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: West African cichlids prefer soft to neutral water. Use a sand or fine gravel bottom with plants, driftwood and caves or flowerpots for spawning. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with peaceful community fish like tetras, barbs, rasboras, corydoras and plecos. Give each pair its own territory, and expect more defensiveness when breeding. Good to know: Buffalo heads come from fast rapids, so they like good water flow and stay near the bottom, hopping between rocks and caves.

Black balloon mollies feature a solid black body like a little black balloon. All mollies are livebearers, and these fish will naturally breed and bear young in the aquarium. Small fry will be eaten unless there are plenty of plastic or natural plants for them to hide in. Mollies are hardy and can handle beginner freshwater aquariums and advanced brackish fish tanks. Quick Facts Scientific Name Poecilia sphenops (balloon-bodied aquarium strain) Origin Mexico and Central America (wild ancestors); aquarium-bred Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2½–3" Lifespan 3–4 years Diet Omnivore (needs plant matter) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.5–8.5 (hard water) Group Size Keep more females than males Shipping Size Approx. 1¼" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them hard, alkaline water with plants and gentle filtration, since balloon mollies are slower swimmers than other mollies. Aquarium salt is optional; they also do well in brackish tanks. Feeding: Feed small amounts of a quality flake that includes vegetable matter once or twice a day. They also enjoy algae wafers. Avoid overfeeding, since balloon mollies are prone to bloating. Tankmates: Mollies get along with most peaceful community fish that like similar hard water, such as platies, swordtails, guppies, danios, rainbowfish, corydoras and plecos. Avoid fin-nippers and soft-water specialists. Keeping more females than males keeps any one female from being harassed. Good to know: The balloon shape comes from a shortened, curved spine bred into this strain, so they swim more slowly. Feed them where they can reach food easily and don't house them with fast, pushy eaters.

Barteri Anubias This anubias plant is native to West Africa, grows well partially and fully submersed and is tolerant of low light. Barteri anubias are very dark green and have oval leaves and are extremely hardy. Anubias barteri are the most popular anubias in the aquarium hobby. These plants grow slow but can handle low and high lighting and can be planted in substrate or tied to wood and rocks. Pictured is a SMALL planted Anubias barteri. Scientific Name: ANUBIAS Barteris Origin: West Africa Max Size: 12 inches Shipping Size: 2 to 8 inches (2 inches comes in a 2 inch pot)

The African Lungfish can live in mud and lie dormant for 10 years without water - amazing creatures. Lungfish require live food such as feeder goldfish and will grow to nearly three feet. In fact, natives of the Congo will place a mud-encrusted block with a lungfish in their hut for eating on a later occasion. These African exotic fish are truly prehistoric and a favorite of public aquariums. This is the perfect pet fish if ever there was one - and you can eat them. Quick Facts Scientific Name Protopterus annectens Origin West Africa Care Level Moderate (grows very large) Temperament Aggressive Adult Size Up to 3 feet Lifespan 20–40 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 8" Care Guide Tank setup: Lungfish breathe air, so they need easy access to the surface and a tight-fitting lid. Give them a soft bottom, hiding places and strong filtration. Feeding: Feed meaty foods like frozen shrimp, bloodworms and sinking carnivore pellets. Tankmates: Lungfish will eat any fish that fits in their mouth and can be aggressive. They are best kept alone. Good to know: African lungfish can survive dry seasons by burying themselves in mud and breathing air.

The L-333 king tiger pleco, also called the gold tiger pleco, has a color pattern similar to the L-46 zebra pleco, sometimes with the same contrasting black and white pattern and sometimes with a gold background instead of white. Like most plecos, these exotic aquarium fish need some driftwood in the fish tank. Most L-333 king tiger plecos are tank-raised in the trade, but some wild-caught specimens from Brazil are available. AquariumFish.com offers both wild and tank-raised fish, depending upon availability. Our current batch features the more desirable vibrant black and white color pattern. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hypancistrus sp. (L-333) Origin Rio Xingu, Brazil; mostly captive-bred Care Level Moderate (needs clean, warm, oxygen-rich water) Temperament Peaceful (shy; territorial with other plecos) Adult Size Up to 5" Lifespan 10–15+ years Diet Omnivore (meaty sinking foods) Water Temperature 78–86°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single, or several with a cave each Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: These plecos come from warm, fast, clear rivers. Give them a tank with strong current, high oxygen, very clean water, rocky caves (or pleco caves) and a sand or smooth gravel bottom. Feeding: Feed meaty sinking foods like quality carnivore pellets, ideally in the evening when they are most active. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They do well with peaceful fish that like warm water, such as tetras, rasboras, discus and dwarf cichlids. Avoid boisterous tankmates that outcompete them for food, and give each pleco its own cave. Good to know: These plecos are nocturnal and shy; a cave and dim lighting help them feel secure. Many are wild-caught and slow-growing.

The Rainbow Endler is the closest variation of the wild endlers in Venezuela. These petite livebearers are bred in Florida for AquariumFish.com and have a red, blue, white, and black pattern. The color patterns are variable, but each fish is brightly colored and very attractive. Available in a group Quick Facts Scientific Name Poecilia wingei Origin Venezuela (captive-bred in Florida) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1" (males about ¾") Lifespan 2–4 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and plenty of plants. Endlers are small, so a sponge filter or a sponge over the filter intake keeps them safe. Feeding: Feed a quality flake, crushed small, or micro pellets once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Endlers do well with other small, peaceful fish such as small rasboras, corydoras, otocinclus and shrimp. Avoid larger fish that could eat them. Good to know: Each rainbow endler has a slightly different color pattern, so a group gives a lot of variety.

The elegant royal farlowella has the slender body of the farlowella but with majestic dorsal finnage and a larger size. Royal farlowellas are uncommon and are caught in Colombia. Like other twig catfish, these critters tend to stick to the side of the fish tank and swim slowly from time to time in search of scraps. Our royals are tank-raised, about 2 inches, and aquarium tank-ready. Quick Facts Scientific Name Sturisoma aureum Origin Colombia Care Level Moderate Temperament Very peaceful Adult Size Up to 8–10" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore (algae and sinking foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a mature tank with driftwood, plants and gentle current. They need clean, stable water. Feeding: They graze on algae. Also feed algae wafers and sinking pellets. Tankmates: They are very peaceful and slow, so keep them with calm community fish that won't outcompete them for food. Good to know: Royal farlowellas have tall, sail-like fins and long tail streamers that make them a striking centerpiece.

The L-239 pleco is a solid navy blue, very unique for saltwater or freshwater fish. Blue panaques are scavengers but also require veggies, so it is a good idea to add algae veggie wafers a few times a week to the aquarium. The blue panaque is peaceful and only grows to six inches, but it will not tolerate temperatures below 75 degrees. These beautiful exotic aquarium fish tend to break out with ich when stressed, and if that occurs, treat with malachite green. The L-239 pleco is wild-caught in Colombia and varies in size when exported, from 2 inches to 4 inches. And of course these guys like a piece of driftwood. Quick Facts Scientific Name Baryancistrus beggini (L-239) Origin Orinoco basin (Venezuela and Colombia) Care Level Moderate (needs warm, oxygen-rich water) Temperament Peaceful (territorial with other plecos) Adult Size Up to 6" Lifespan 12–15+ years Diet Omnivore (algae and sinking foods) Water Temperature 77–84°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single, or several with a cave each Shipping Size Approx. 2–4" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them strong current, high oxygen, smooth rocks, caves and driftwood. Many come from warm, fast rivers in Brazil, so keep the water clean and warm. Feeding: Feed algae wafers and quality sinking pellets. They also enjoy frozen foods now and then. Tankmates: They do well with most community fish and peaceful cichlids. Give each pleco its own cave to limit territorial squabbles. Good to know: Many of these plecos come from fast-flowing rivers threatened by dam projects, so wild-caught specimens are increasingly rare.

The vampire family of plecos receives their name due to a sharp tooth on the sucker mouth. The L-007 vampire pleco is also called the tooth-nose pleco and the galaxy pleco. The bite causes little more than surprise, but they do bite. Vampire plecos are scavengers and meat eaters. The L-007 galaxy vampire pleco has larger dots than the L-29 and L-240 vampire plecos. These exotic aquarium fish love to hang on driftwood like bats in a cave. Keep the water warm and very clean, since they produce a lot of waste on a meaty diet. Feeding: Feed meaty sinking foods like carnivore pellets.
