The weitzmani tetra, or black darter tetra, is imported from Guyana, home of other uncommon fish such as the four-eyed anableps. Black darter tetras are fast-swimming, beautiful, tiny schooling fish for the aquarium. HOWEVER, these fish need live food, preferably live brine shrimp or chopped worms. The tetra can adapt to frozen small foods but seldom to flake. We highly recommend hatching some brine shrimp when you place your order! Also, these are schooling fish and need three or more companions to survive in the wild or the fish tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name Poecilocharax weitzmani Origin Rio Negro and upper Orinoco (Brazil, Venezuela, Colombia, Peru) Care Level Difficult (needs very soft water) Temperament Peaceful (shy) Adult Size Up to 1" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Carnivore (tiny meaty foods) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 4.5–6.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ½–¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Pencilfish need a mature, densely planted tank with soft, acidic water, floating plants, leaf litter and very gentle filtration. They are shy and do best with other tiny, calm fish. Feeding: Feed crushed flake or micro pellets once or twice a day. They also enjoy small frozen foods like brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other tiny, calm fish like small tetras, rasboras, pygmy corydoras and dwarf shrimp. Avoid fast or boisterous tankmates that outcompete them for food. Good to know: Pencilfish change their pattern between day and night, often showing bars or dots after dark.

The black kuhli loach is similar in structure and behavior to its more common cousin, the banded kuhli loach. However, black kuhli loaches feature a solid charcoal color. Like all kuhli loaches, these exotic Asian oddballs are most active at twilight and at nighttime, both in nature and in the home aquarium. They are easily kept with non-aggressive fish like corydoras, danios, rasboras and tetras. Since they are relatively small, they do well in nano and mid-size tanks and are safe with small cichlids, but larger cichlids and eels might go after them. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pangio oblonga (often sold as P. javanica ) Origin Southeast Asia (Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful (shy, nocturnal) Adult Size Up to 3–3½" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore (sinking foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 5.5–7.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Kuhlis love to burrow, so use a soft sand bottom with plants, leaf litter and hiding spots. Cover filter intakes with a sponge, since they can squeeze into small gaps, and keep a lid on the tank. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets or wafers, ideally in the evening when kuhlis are most active. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Kuhlis do well with peaceful fish like tetras, rasboras, corydoras, danios and dwarf shrimp. Avoid large or aggressive fish that could eat them. Good to know: Kuhlis are shy during the day; a larger group and plenty of cover help them come out more often.

The reticulated butterfly loach, or reticulated hillstream loach, has a broader body than the standard hillstream loach. The most striking feature of this freshwater loach, besides its unusually flat profile, is the fine-line color pattern, called reticulation. Normally hillstream loaches are gathered on rocks of swift-flowing streams in China, and their unusual flat, wide fins are perfectly suited to this environment. Freshwater loaches are hardy and feed on just about anything and are quite the sight hanging on the other side of the aquarium glass. Quick Facts Scientific Name Sewellia lineolata Origin Central Vietnam Care Level Moderate (needs cool, fast, oxygen-rich water) Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Algae eater Water Temperature 68–75°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Hillstream loaches come from fast, clear mountain streams. Give them smooth rocks, strong current, lots of oxygen and cool water. They graze on algae, so a mature tank with algae-covered rocks is ideal. Feeding: Hillstream loaches graze on algae. Also feed algae wafers or sinking pellets. Tankmates: Hillstream loaches do well with peaceful fish that like cool, flowing water, such as white clouds, danios, rasboras and dwarf shrimp. Avoid tropical fish that need warm water. Good to know: Hillstream loaches cling to rocks and glass with their flat, sucker-like bodies, just like they do in fast mountain streams.

Trifasciatus Rainbowfish, or three-banded rainbowfish, are found in small rivers and ponds and billabongs (there is that word again!) around Australia. The Banded Rainbowfish grows to nearly five inches and prefers a planted aquarium. These are active swimmers and also prefer to swim in schools, which is a fantastic feature in a large freshwater aquarium. Colors vary depending upon food, water conditions, and presence of females (males always display their fins and colors better with ladies around). Quick Facts Scientific Name Melanotaenia trifasciata Origin Northern Australia Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 4–5" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Rainbowfish are active swimmers, so leave open swimming space along the front, with plants along the back and sides. Use a filter, a heater and a tight-fitting lid, since they can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with peaceful fish of similar size, such as other rainbowfish, larger tetras, barbs, danios, corydoras and plecos. Good to know: Banded rainbowfish come in several regional color forms, and males show brighter colors with females around.

Strawberry Crab Strawberry Crab, features a unique pink body with varied white spots atop its head. They are found off the coast of Hawaii and are a peaceful, reef safe species. So long as they are housed in a tank with plenty of live rock, algae for it to eat, and with regular water changing they will thrive. The Strawberry Crab eats a diet of algae as well as various carnivorous preparations that can be spot fed every few days. Interestingly, the Strawberry Crab can sometimes be seen carrying the shells of other inverts on its back. Scientific Name: Neoliomera pubescens Origin: Indo Pacific, Hawaii Max Size: 2 inches Diet: Omnivore Shipping size: 1 inch

Tonga Fighting Conch Excellent for keeping substrate clean as well as glass and rock, this snail is a nocturnal feeder and will usually be less visible during daylight hours. Tonga Fighting Conch's are great for keeping your sandbed algae free. Mostly nocturnal, the Tonga Fighting Conch uses it's 'trunk' like a vacuum to remove algae from the rocks. It buries itself in the sand to sleep and will also turn up the sandbed. No supplemental feedings are necessary unless there is not enough algae in the aquarium, then it is recommended to wrap a piece of dried seaweed around a rock and place in the aquarium Scientific Name: Strombus Gibberulus Origin: Tonga Max Size: 2 inches Shipping Size: 3/4 to 1 inch

Red Goniopora Coral Frag Jewel Red Goniopora is often referred to as Flowerpot, Daisy coral, ball coral, or sunflower coral. It is not overly aggressive but space should still be provided between itself and other neighboring corals, its polyps can extend far past its base into the reef aquarium where it can sting other species of corals. Also comes in other colors, clownfish will often be found in association with the flowerpot coral and play in its polyps if no anemone can be found in the tank. Goniopora/flowerpot require addition calcium, strontium and other trace elements to the water. Scientific Name: Goniopora sp. Care : Waterflow strong and lighting Diet: algae and zooxanthellae Shipping Size: 2 inches

Red Tip Hermit Crab: The Reef Clean-Up Specialist The Red Tip Hermit Crab (Clibanarius digueti), also known as the Dwarf Red Tip Hermit Crab or Mexican Red Leg Hermit Crab, is a popular and beneficial addition to the marine and reef aquarium trade. They are highly valued as a core member of any clean-up crew due to their voracious appetite for nuisance algae and detritus. Unlike true crabs, hermit crabs have a soft, vulnerable abdomen which they protect by inhabiting the empty shells of marine snails. As they grow, they must find a larger shell to move into. The Red Tip Hermit Crab is a small species, distinguished by its bright red-tipped legs and often a slight blue or white spotting on its body. This species is considered one of the best choices for both beginner and advanced hobbyists due to its small size, easy care, and non-aggressive nature toward corals and most tank inhabitants. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: This is a very beneficial Omnivore/Herbivore . They are known for their appetite for a wide variety of undesirable substances in the aquarium, including hair algae , cyanobacteria (red slime algae) , detritus, and uneaten fish food. If algae levels are insufficient, supplement their diet with dried seaweed (nori) or quality sinking invertebrate pellets. Shell Requirement: Hermit crabs need a constant supply of empty shells to accommodate their growth. You should always provide at least 3-5 empty shells of various sizes, with a slightly larger opening than the one they currently occupy, to prevent them from attacking and consuming live snails for their shell. Popular choices include empty Turbo or Nerite snail shells. Reef Compatibility: Reef Safe (with minor caution) . They pose no threat to corals. The only potential issue is the possibility of them stealing shells from live snails if not enough empty shells are provided. Temperament: Peaceful . They are non-aggressive toward fish and other invertebrates. They are social and thrive when kept in groups. Quick Facts (Clibanarius digueti) Scientific Name: Clibanarius digueti Primary Common Name: Red Tip Hermit Crab Other Common Names: Dwarf Red Tip Hermit Crab, Mexican Red Leg Hermit Crab, Cortez Red Leg Hermit Crab Origin: Coastal waters of Mexico (Eastern Pacific) Max Size: Up to 1 inch (2.5 cm) Temperament: Peaceful Diet: Omnivore (Algae, detritus, and leftover food) Minimum Tank Size: 10 Gallons Reef Compatibility: Yes (Excellent Clean-up Crew member)

The marigold swordtail is a prize color variation of breeders and is the brightest pattern of all the swordtails. The vibrant yellows and oranges get stronger as the fish gets older, and some color-enhancing flake food helps too. Marigolds are a bit more expensive than the green or pineapple swordtails because they are a little more difficult to breed. If a certain sex ratio is desired, we will do our best to fulfill it. A good ratio is two females to one male, so the females get some rest. Quick Facts Scientific Name Xiphophorus hellerii (marigold) Origin Southern Mexico to Honduras (wild ancestors); aquarium-bred Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful (males may spar) Adult Size Up to 4–5" (not counting the sword) Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 7.0–8.0 (hard water) Group Size Keep more females than males Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Swordtails are active swimmers, so give them plants, open swimming space and a tight-fitting lid, since they are good jumpers. They prefer hard, alkaline water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet with some vegetable content once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Swordtails get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as platies, mollies, larger tetras, danios, rainbowfish, gouramis and corydoras. Keep more females than males, since males chase females and may spar with each other. Avoid fin-nippers and large cichlids. Good to know: Swordtails are livebearers and breed readily. Fry are born free-swimming and will be eaten unless there are dense plants or a breeding box for them to hide in. Only males grow the "sword" on the tail.

The first line of GloFish Tetras, spliced with jellyfish and the White Skirt Tetra (Gymnocorymbus Ternetzi), comes in six fluorescent colors, and AquariumFish.com assortments guarantee at least three colors right to your door! Great schooling fish, GloFish Tetras create a spectacular school of color and movement in the aquarium. Six fish will require a tank of ten gallons or larger to keep their stress level low. GloFish Tetras are good companions in any community fish tank. Each order comes with 3 or 6 assorted color GloFish. Quick Facts Scientific Name Gymnocorymbus ternetzi (genetically modified) Origin Farm-raised (genetically modified) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful (may nip long fins) Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a filter, plants and open swimming space. A dark substrate and background make the colors pop. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: GloFish tetras get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, danios, rasboras, corydoras and livebearers. Keep them in a group so they don't nip the fins of slow, long-finned fish like bettas. Good to know: GloFish colors look brightest under a blue or actinic LED light, but they are colorful under normal lighting too. Mixing colors in one school creates the best display.

The super kuhli loach, also called the giant kuhli loach, is larger than the smaller banded or common kuhli loach. The super kuhli looks similar, with a yellow-orange body and dark brown vertical stripes. Like other loaches, they have barbels around the mouth, which are used to find food in the substrate. The super kuhli is most active at twilight and at nighttime, both in nature and in the home aquarium, remaining hidden or buried in the sand during the day. These are very nocturnal creatures, so often they wait until dark to move throughout the fish tank. We recommend a small school of three to four so at least you have a chance to see a couple of them during the daylight hours. The season just started on this species, so they are shipping on the small side, approx. 2 inches. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pangio myersi Origin Mekong basin (Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful (shy, nocturnal) Adult Size Up to 4" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore (sinking foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 5.5–7.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 2–3" Care Guide Tank setup: Kuhlis love to burrow, so use a soft sand bottom with plants, leaf litter and hiding spots. Cover filter intakes with a sponge, since they can squeeze into small gaps, and keep a lid on the tank. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets or wafers, ideally in the evening when kuhlis are most active. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Kuhlis do well with peaceful fish like tetras, rasboras, corydoras, danios and dwarf shrimp. Avoid large or aggressive fish that could eat them. Good to know: Kuhlis are shy during the day; a larger group and plenty of cover help them come out more often.

The lamprologus ocellatus cichlid is one of the most desired and hard-to-find shell dwellers among enthusiasts. These are tough to find and harder to breed, so they are a bit more expensive than the brevis or hecqui shell dweller cichlids. Like the other shell dwellers, ocellatus love to share their shell with females but will fight with other males to keep their shell to themselves. Shell dwellers are hardy and great additions to community tanks and peaceful cichlid tanks. These small fish love their shells, so try to keep a few in the aquarium that are lightweight and not too large for them to manipulate but large enough for them to get into. Quick Facts Scientific Name Lamprologus ocellatus Origin Lake Tanganyika, Africa Care Level Easy Temperament Territorial around their shells Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 6–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.8–9.0 Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Use a fine sand bottom they can dig in and provide more empty snail shells (escargot shells work well) than there are fish. Lake Malawi and Lake Tanganyika cichlids need hard, alkaline water; crushed coral or aragonite sand helps hold the pH up. Feeding: Feed crushed flake or micro pellets once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep shell dwellers in a species tank or with small, peaceful Tanganyikans like cyprichromis or julidochromis. Larger cichlids will bully or eat them. Good to know: Ocellatus are bold little shell dwellers that will defend their shell against much bigger fish. One male with several females works well.

The brilliant rummynose, or platinum rummynose tetra, is sometimes called the false rummynose, as the fish has the features of the true rummynose tetra but with a platinum-colored body. Discovered by Heiko Bleher, this is a natural variation of the rummynose tetra. These tetras are generally found in the Brazil portion of the Amazon basin. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hemigrammus bleheri (platinum variety) Origin Brazil (Rio Negro region); captive-bred Care Level Moderate (needs soft, clean water) Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a dark substrate, which brings out their color. Keep a lid on the tank, since tetras can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, rasboras, danios, corydoras, dwarf cichlids, gouramis and livebearers. Good to know: Tetras feel safer and show better color in a group. A larger school also spreads out any chasing.

Rarely found in the trade and pricey, the phoenix tetra sports flowing filaments off its fins and displays bright red tails when attracting mates. These fish are best in schools of six or more, peaceful and hardy. Once wild-caught in Brazil, these are no longer exported. BUT we have one breeder that makes these beautiful fish available to the trade, and when we can get a school of them, we grab 'em. Another name for these tetras is the filamentous tetra. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hemigrammus filamentosus Origin Brazil; captive-bred Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a dark substrate, which brings out their color. Keep a lid on the tank, since tetras can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, rasboras, danios, corydoras, dwarf cichlids, gouramis and livebearers. Good to know: Tetras feel safer and show better color in a group. A larger school also spreads out any chasing.

A group of four mystery snails adds a little variety of subtle colors to the fish tank. Mystery snails are hardy and excellent scavengers with a nice, subtle color pattern. These snails grow to two inches, and mystery snails are not plant eaters. These snails can handle a wide range of water and temperature conditions. Be sure to pull out snails and other invertebrates when treating the fish tank for ich and other diseases. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pomacea diffusa (sold as P. bridgesii ) Origin South America (Amazon basin); farm-raised Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful; plant-safe Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 1–2 years Diet Scavenger (algae and leftover food) Water Temperature 68–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 (hard water for healthy shells) Breeding Lays pink egg clutches above the waterline; needs a male and female Group Size Sold as a pack of 4 Shipping Size Approx. ½–¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Give mystery snails a covered tank with a gap of an inch or two above the water, since females climb out to lay eggs. Keep the water hard and alkaline for healthy shells, and add calcium (cuttlebone or crushed coral) if your water is soft. Feeding: Mystery snails eat algae and leftover food, but give them sinking pellets or algae wafers too so they don't go hungry. Tankmates: Mystery snails do well with peaceful fish, shrimp and other snails. Avoid fish that nip antennae or eat snails, like puffers, loaches, large cichlids and some bettas, and keep them away from assassin snails. Good to know: Remove snails before treating the tank with copper or other medications, which are toxic to invertebrates.

The gold ring danio is found in the same rivers of Myanmar (Burma) as the glowlight danio, and is even more rare to the aquarium trade. Also called the blue ring danio, these are active schooling fish and hardy. The scientific name "tinwini" is the name of a friend of the discoverer of the fish. Good to have friends! Tinwini danio will get along with fancy shrimp and most community fish. Quick Facts Scientific Name Danio tinwini Origin Myanmar (Burma) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1¼" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 68–79°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a gentle filter, a heater and plenty of plants, including some floating plants for cover. Keep a lid on the tank. Make sure the tank is fully cycled (which takes several weeks) before adding fish. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other small, gentle fish such as rasboras, small tetras, pygmy corydoras and shrimp. Avoid large or boisterous fish. Good to know: Gold ring danios are small and safe with adult shrimp. They show best in a planted tank.

Black koi may be hard to spot in an outdoor pond but they, at least according to Japanese culture, bring luck to the pond owner. Black koi are solid black and, when large, are like scary sea monsters rising from the deep. True solid black koi are hard to come by and when we do get them, they are about four inches in size. One black koi is a must for every pond. Quick Facts Scientific Name Cyprinus carpio Origin Captive-bred (Asia) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2–3 feet Lifespan 25–35 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 50–80°F pH 7.0–8.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 4" Care Guide Tank setup: Koi grow large and are best kept in an outdoor pond with strong filtration. They are cool-water fish and do not need a heater. Feeding: Feed a quality koi or goldfish pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a few minutes. Feed less when the water is cool. Tankmates: Koi get along with goldfish and other pond fish. Good to know: Black koi (karasu) are said to bring good luck to the pond owner.

Albino cherry barbs have a very nice pink, red, and white color theme, and males and females are just as pretty. Cherry barbs have small little whiskers and are very active schooling fish, suitable for most community tanks and nano tanks. Quick Facts Scientific Name Puntius titteya Origin Sri Lanka Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful, a bit shy Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 4–6 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 73–81°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a filter, a heater and plenty of plants. They feel safest with places to hide and show more color in a planted tank. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other small, peaceful fish such as rasboras, small tetras, corydoras and dwarf shrimp. Avoid large or boisterous fish and fin-nippers. Good to know: Cherry barbs are one of the most peaceful barbs, so they mix well with small community fish and shrimp-safe planted tanks. Males color up most when a few females are around.

Thai Micro Crabs are the World's smallest crabs and fully aquatic and the most peaceful aquatic species that can be introduced into the nano tank or small aquarium. In the wilds of Thailand, micro crabs spend most of their time crawling along floating plant roots. The Thai micro crab is also called the micro spider crab. Tiny hairs cover their body and catch floating debris that becomes their food source. These little guys will never hurt anybody and have no defenses and get along fine with rasboras, snails, and shrimp. Quick Facts Scientific Name Limnopilos naiyanetri Origin Thailand Care Level Moderate Temperament Very peaceful Adult Size Up to ½" Lifespan 1–2 years Diet Scavenger (fine foods) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. ¼–½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a mature, planted tank with rocks and hiding places, and keep a lid on the tank. Feeding: Micro crabs pick tiny bits of food from plants and moss. In a mature tank they find much of their own food; also offer a little crushed flake or powdered food. Tankmates: Micro crabs are tiny and very peaceful. Keep them with shrimp, snails and small, gentle fish that won't eat them. Good to know: These are among the smallest crabs in the hobby. They are fully aquatic and spend most of their time hiding in moss and plant roots.

Blue Spotted Sea Hare, Dolabella sp. , also known as the Wedge Sea Hare, is one of the best algae-eaters in the home aquarium. The Blue Spotted Sea Hare can clean an entire 125 gallon reef tank of all hair algae in about two weeks - they are quite the efficient janitors. They are rather sensitive to pH and salinity changes and can take a little while to fully acclimate to a new tank (they should be drip acclimated). Featuring a dulled grey/brown color with muted blue spots and soft spiky appendages, the Blue Spotted Sea Hare makes for an interesting invert. They are slow moving and well camouflaged within the rocks of a reef tank. The Blue Spotted Sea Hare is reef safe and is a relatively risk-free addition to any tank as it is an incredibly beneficial algae-eater. Scienticic Name: Dolabella Sp Diet:Herbivore Approximate Size :2

There are two species of platy from southern Mexico: platy maculatus and platy variatus. The variatus have higher dorsal fins, jump a bit more, and grow slightly larger than the maculatus. The two species will breed, and several hybrids are available, particularly the assorted hi-fin platies. AquariumFish.com carries the sunset variatus for their striking color and overall friendly disposition. These fish can live in freshwater and brackish water. Quick Facts Scientific Name Xiphophorus variatus Origin Southern Mexico Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 3–4 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 65–77°F (handles cooler water than common platies) pH 7.0–8.2 Breeding Livebearer – breeds easily in the aquarium Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Platies are hardy and easy to keep. Give them a filter, a lid and plenty of plants. They can live without a heater in rooms that stay above about 65°F. They prefer harder, slightly alkaline water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. Platies also need some plant matter, so a vegetable flake is a good choice. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Platies get along with most peaceful community fish, such as other livebearers (mollies, guppies and swordtails), tetras, rasboras and corydoras. Avoid large or aggressive fish that may bully or eat them. Breeding: Platies are livebearers, so a tank with males and females will almost certainly have babies (fry). Adults will eat fry, so add dense plants or use a breeding box if you want to raise them. Keeping more females than males gives the females a break from the males' attention. Good to know: Variatus are keen jumpers, so keep a tight-fitting lid on the tank.

Pencil Wrasse The Pencil Wrasse is commonly referred to as the Smalltail Wrasse or Small Tail Wrasse. The Small Tail Pencil Wrasse has a stunning coloration that can enhance the beauty of any home aquarium. The Small Tail Pencil Wrasse is peaceful and should be put in a tank with aggressive tangs and triggers. Pencil wrasse come in various shades of blue, green, and red and are very active. Scientific Name: Pseudojuloides cerasinus Origin: Indonesia Max Size: 4 inches Diet: B rine shrimp, mysis shrimp and the frozen meaty preparations Shipping Size: Approximate 2 to 3 inches

Splendid Garden Eel The Splendid Garden Eel from Fiji is also called the Orange-barred Garden Eel. Like all garden eels, the Splendid Eel is 100% reef safe. These eels face the current and feed on passing zooplankton. The garden eel will always keep a part of its body inside the burrow even when feeding. In the wild triggerfish are known for digging out garden eels right out of their burrow in pursuit of a meal. Scientific Name: Gorgasia preclara Origin: Fiji Max Size: 16 inches Diet: Floating Zooplankton Shipping Size: Approx. 7 inches ****This item does not ship to Texas or Florida****

The wild Peru discus, sometimes called by the less romantic name brown discus, has a golden yellow body with black stripes and blue edging. For exotic fish, these discus fish are hardy and very adaptable to the aquarium. Our Peru discus are caught on the border of Brazil and Peru, and these fish are excellent community and planted tank species, AND perfect for South American theme aquariums. Quick Facts Scientific Name Symphysodon aequifasciatus (wild brown form) Origin Peru–Brazil border (wild-caught) Care Level Difficult (for experienced keepers) Temperament Peaceful, shy; social Adult Size Up to 7–8" Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Omnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 82–86°F pH 5.0–6.5 (very soft water) Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 5" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a reliable heater, gentle filtration, driftwood and dim lighting. Wild discus need very soft, acidic water and very clean, stable conditions. Feeding: Start with frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp, then slowly add discus granules or pellets. Feed small meals a few times a day and remove anything uneaten within a few minutes. Tankmates: Discus are calm and shy, so choose gentle tankmates that enjoy the same warm water: cardinal and rummynose tetras, sterbai corydoras and small plecos are popular choices. Avoid fast, boisterous or fin-nipping fish, and anything that competes hard for food. Many keepers avoid angelfish, which can bully discus and share diseases. Living in groups: Discus are social and feel safest in a group. A single discus, or just two, tends to be stressed. When a pair forms to breed, they may claim part of the tank, so a group spreads out the attention. Good to know: Wild discus need very soft, acidic water and slow acclimation. Quarantine them before adding to a tank with captive-bred discus.

The South American lungfish lives in the swamps of the Amazon basin and will eventually grow to nearly four feet. At maturity, these creatures no longer use their gills and periodically rise to the top of the tank like a slow-moving whale and suck in air. In smaller sizes, these fish adapt well to most aquariums, but they will eat small critters that can fit into their small mouth. Generally, frozen food is all they need, but when under six inches, small black worms, feeder shrimp, and feeder fry work best. Lungfish are solid black and, when small, like to stay in the leaves of plants when not feeding, so a few floating plants, plastic or natural, will help simulate their natural habitat. When they grow large, they go just about wherever they want. Quick Facts Scientific Name Lepidosiren paradoxa Origin Amazon basin, South America Care Level Moderate (grows very large) Temperament Predatory Adult Size Up to 3–4 feet Lifespan 20+ years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 3" Care Guide Tank setup: Lungfish breathe air, so they need easy access to the surface and a tight-fitting lid. Give them a soft bottom, hiding places and strong filtration. Feeding: Feed meaty foods like frozen shrimp, bloodworms and sinking carnivore pellets. Tankmates: Lungfish will eat any fish that fits in their mouth and can be aggressive. They are best kept alone. Good to know: Adult South American lungfish rely on breathing air and will drown if they can't reach the surface.

One of the rare knifefish occasionally caught in Peru is the Tiger Macana Knifefish, or simply the tiger knifefish. The pattern is a tiger stripe, and the fish has a very elegant, elongated body that will grow to about 16 inches. Knifefish will eat worms, frozen foods, and small live foods and generally eat at night. Sometimes, during the day, these fish will sleep on their sides like some kind of tired farm animal, but they are very active in the evening. These fish will eat very small fish such as small neon tetras, but in general get along with most other species. Quick Facts Scientific Name Gymnotus anguillaris Origin Amazon basin, Peru Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful (eats very small fish) Adult Size Up to 16" Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 8" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them hiding places like large tubes or caves, dim lighting, strong filtration and a tight lid. They are most active at night. Feeding: Feed meaty foods like frozen shrimp and bloodworms, plus sinking carnivore pellets once they learn to take them. Tankmates: They will eat very small fish but get along with most fish too large to swallow. Avoid keeping two knifefish together, since they may fight. Good to know: Knifefish sense their surroundings with a weak electric field, which helps them hunt in the dark.

Arrow Crab: The Bristleworm Hunter The Arrow Crab (Stenorhynchus seticornis), also known as the Yellowline Arrow Crab or Spider Crab , is a popular and instantly recognizable marine invertebrate. It is easily identified by its long, thin, spider-like legs and its distinctively triangular, arrow-shaped carapace (body) that tapers to a long, pointed rostrum (snout). Native to the Western Atlantic, including the Caribbean, this crab is often sought after for its appetite for nuisance pests, particularly bristleworms , which it actively hunts and consumes. Its coloration typically consists of a whitish or tan body covered in fine dark lines, with its long legs sometimes banded with red, yellow, or brown, and its claws tipped with striking blue or violet. The Arrow Crab is a relatively hardy and long-lived addition to a mature saltwater system, but its opportunistic and territorial nature requires careful consideration when selecting tankmates. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: The Arrow Crab is an opportunistic Carnivore / Scavenger. Its natural diet includes small invertebrates, detritus, and worms. Its most desirable function in the aquarium is its effective control of unwanted Bristleworms and small feather duster worms. Feeding: While it will scavenge for leftovers and pests, it should be spot-fed meaty foods several times a week to prevent it from preying on desirable tankmates. Offer pieces of frozen shrimp, squid, clam, or sinking invertebrate pellets. Reef Compatibility: It is generally considered Reef Safe With Caution. It will not consume most corals, but a hungry or large specimen may pick at soft corals, zoanthids, or mushroom polyps while searching for small prey or detritus. Provide ample food and hiding spaces to mitigate this risk. Temperament: It is Semi-Aggressive and highly Territorial, especially towards its own species. Do not house two Arrow Crabs together in tanks under 75 gallons, as they will often fight to the death. It may pose a risk to ornamental shrimp (like Cleaner Shrimp) and small, slow-moving fish, especially at night when it is most active. Aquarium Requirements: Provide plenty of live rock with caves, crevices, and ledges for hiding during the day, as this species is primarily nocturnal. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Stenorhynchus seticornis Primary Common Name: Arrow Crab Other Common Names: Yellowline Arrow Crab, Spider Crab, Decorator Arrow Crab Origin: Western Atlantic (Caribbean, North Carolina to Brazil) Max Size (Leg Span): 6-10 inches (15-25 cm) Temperament: Semi-Aggressive / Territorial ( Predatory toward small inverts/fish ) Diet: Carnivore / Scavenger (Excellent Bristleworm hunter) Minimum Tank Size: 30 Gallons (75+ Gallons for multiple crabs) Reef Compatibility: With Caution (May pick at corals if underfed; predatory toward small shrimp) Care Level: Easy

Chestnut Turbo Snail is an elegant, yet functional, addition to any reef aquarium. Like other snails, Turbo castanae is a powerhouse when it comes to cleaning algae and detritus from your aquarium. The reef safe snail will also feed on the algae covering aquarium glass. Combined with their easy care requirements, the Turbo castanae is ideal for both beginning and advanced reef hobbyists. Scientific name: Turbinidae Sp. Max Size: 1 inch Origin: Caribbean Shipping size: Approx 1/2 to 1 inch

Green Acanthastrea Coral The Acan Echinata Acanthastrea echinata is a colorful large polyp stony (LPS). They are found in some intense oranges to intense green and red combinations. The Echinata Coral is the second most popular and sought after of the Acanthastrea species, following the Acan lord A. lordhowensis . Some descriptive names the A. echinata are known by include Echinata Coral, Starry Cup Coral, Artichoke Coral, Pineapple coral, Rainbow Acanthastrea, Rainbow Acan, and Acan Brain Coral. Be aware that Acanthastrea are voracious nocturnal predators and competitively extrude mesenterial filaments and digest organisms within reach. Great care must be taken in determining the placement and distance between Acan Brain Coral colonies The use of a quality protein skimmer helps maintain water quality and combat the effects of heavy feeding. Scientific Name: Acanthastrea Echinata Care: Moderate Water flow low, moderate lighting Food: meaty foods and zooplankton Shipping Size: 2 to 3 inches

The giant otocinclus looks like the common otocinclus was hit by the Avengers™ Ant Man gamma ray machine. Giant otocinclus come from Peru and grow to 4 inches. These peaceful catfish are scavengers and algae eaters like their smaller cousins, but the giant otocinclus will not tolerate pH over 7.5. These are rare fish prized by Amazon aquarium enthusiasts. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hypoptopoma gulare Origin Amazon basin, Peru Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 4" Lifespan 5–6 years Diet Algae eater (also eats algae wafers) Water Temperature 74–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 2–4" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a mature, planted tank with algae to graze, gentle filtration and stable, clean water. Feeding: Otocinclus graze on soft algae, but don't rely on algae alone. Also feed algae wafers. Tankmates: Otos are very peaceful and get along with almost any small community fish, plus shrimp and snails. Good to know: Giant otos often rest on plant leaves and glass and graze much like their smaller cousins.

The flagtail porthole catfish grows to 5 inches and sports a black and white banded caudal (tail) fin. Similar body to the more common porthole catfish, flagtail cats come from Brazil, grow larger, and display a more distinct pattern. Flagtail porthole cats prefer lower pH and will not tolerate pH over 8.0. These are considered hardy Amazon catfish and will be suitable to most aquariums - except they may eat small creatures that fit in their small mouths! Quick Facts Scientific Name Dianema urostriatum Origin Amazon basin, Brazil Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful (eats very small fish) Adult Size Up to 5" Lifespan 6–10 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 3–4" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a soft sand bottom, driftwood and plants. They are calm fish that like dim lighting. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets once a day, ideally in the evening when they are most active. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms. Tankmates: They are peaceful but will eat very small fish. Keep them with community fish too large to fit in their mouth. Good to know: Flagtail porthole catfish are named for the bold black-and-white stripes on their tail.

The porthole catfish has a black spot on the body in the shape of a porthole on a ship - in fact their long slender body is shaped a bit like a ship. These catfish come from Peru where they are caught in large schools in small streams. Porthole catfish do not tolerate pH over 8.0 but otherwise are hardy and friendly additions to the fish tank. Porthole catfish are not classic schooling fish but definitely prefer to stick together, so consider the addition of a small group of three to keep everyone happy. Quick Facts Scientific Name Dianema longibarbis Origin Amazon basin, Peru Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 3–4" Lifespan 6–10 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 2–3" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a soft sand bottom, driftwood and plants. They are calm fish that like dim lighting. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets once a day, ideally in the evening when they are most active. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms. Tankmates: They are peaceful but will eat very small fish. Keep them with community fish too large to fit in their mouth. Good to know: Porthole catfish often hover in midwater together, which is unusual for catfish.

The paradise fish is one of the original aquarium fish. These fish were first imported from Vietnam to France for display in aquariums in 1869! The person responsible is early aquarium pioneer Pierre Carbonnier. Obviously, these are hardy fish to ship by ocean from Vietnam to France. Paradise fish show red and blue colors, and males have slightly more color than females, but both sexes are beautiful. Color patterns vary by breeder, so the picture is close but may not exactly match the fish we ship. Paradise fish will eat community flake food and are great planted tank and community tank fish, except that they are known to nip at female bettas and eat very small shrimp and fry. Quick Facts Scientific Name Macropodus opercularis Origin East Asia (China, Vietnam, Korea, Taiwan) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Semi-aggressive (males fight) Adult Size Up to 3–4" Lifespan 6–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 61–79°F (often fine without a heater) pH 6.0–8.0 Breathes Air Yes – labyrinth fish take air from the surface Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants and hiding places. They handle cool water, so a heater is optional in most homes. Keep a lid on the tank and leave a gap of air above the water, since gouramis breathe from the surface. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Males fight each other, so keep one male per tank. They do best with sturdy, similar-sized fish and should not be kept with bettas, very small fish or small shrimp. Good to know: Paradise fish handle cool water and can live unheated, which is how they survived the long trip to become one of the first aquarium fish kept in Europe.

Ventralis Nasuta Cichlid The ophthalmotilapia is part of the ventralis cichlid family from Lake Tanganyika. The nasuta grows into a beautiful gold with long ventral fins, a distinguishing characteristic of this rare cichlid family. Quick Facts Scientific Name Ophthalmotilapia nasuta Origin Lake Tanganyika, Africa Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful for a cichlid Adult Size Up to 7" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.8–9.0 Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a fine sand bottom and plenty of open swimming space, with a few rocks along the back. Lake Malawi and Lake Tanganyika cichlids need hard, alkaline water; crushed coral or aragonite sand helps hold the pH up. Feeding: Feed a quality small pellet or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like brine shrimp. Tankmates: They do best with other peaceful Tanganyikans such as cyprichromis, calvus, frontosa (when large enough) and synodontis catfish. Keep them in a group.

Kenyi cichlids are popular in the African cichlid aquarium due to their relatively friendly disposition and the bright colors of the males and females. Females are a colorful blue with a striped pattern, and males are a bright yellow, though the sexes are capable of changing color to the opposite sex for short periods of time. Males may change to avoid a fight with stronger males; females may change to avoid the attentions of males. Quick Facts Scientific Name Maylandia lombardoi Origin Lake Malawi, Africa Care Level Moderate Temperament Aggressive (territorial rock-dweller) Adult Size Up to 4½–5" Lifespan 6–10 years Diet Omnivore (needs plant matter) Water Temperature 76–82°F pH 7.8–8.6 Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Use a sand or crushed-coral bottom and stack plenty of rockwork with caves and hiding spots so each male can claim a territory and others can escape. Lake Malawi and Lake Tanganyika cichlids need hard, alkaline water; crushed coral or aragonite sand helps hold the pH up. Feeding: Mbuna are mostly plant eaters. Feed a vegetable-based flake or pellet once or twice a day, and avoid high-protein foods, which can upset their digestion. Tankmates: Keep mbuna with other mbuna of similar size and temperament, stocked in a group to spread out aggression. Avoid mixing them with peaceful peacocks and haps unless the tank is large, and avoid closely related species that look alike, which can crossbreed. Good to know: Kenyi males become quite aggressive as they mature, so they do best in a crowded mbuna tank with plenty of rockwork.

The diamond head neon tetra is a sparkling color morph of the wild neon tetra. Diamond head neons were discovered in Venezuela, and now these small schooling fish are bred in Singapore for the aquarium trade. The diamond head tetra exhibits a reflective head with the coloration of the standard neon tetra. A small school of diamond heads flashing in the fish tank is quite a sight; we recommend the purchase of six. Quick Facts Scientific Name Paracheirodon innesi (diamond head variety) Origin Aquarium-bred (Singapore) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1¼" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 5.5–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ½–¾" Care Guide Tank setup: These small tetras do best in a planted tank with soft, slightly acidic water, a dark substrate, driftwood, floating plants and gentle filtration. A larger school makes them more confident and colorful. Feeding: Feed small amounts of micro pellets or crushed flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other small, peaceful fish like rasboras, small tetras, pencilfish, pygmy corydoras, otocinclus and dwarf shrimp. Avoid large or boisterous fish that could eat or bully them. Good to know: Small tetras show their best color in a large school in a planted tank with soft lighting.

Cobalt discus are diamond blue discus with one or more black vertical stripes on the body. The stripes can range from just a couple to markings all along the body. Cobalt discus are hardy and from the AquariumFish.com breeder in Singapore to assure these are clean and aquarium-ready fish. Quick Facts Scientific Name Symphysodon aequifasciatus (captive-bred color variety) Origin Amazon basin (captive-bred in Singapore) Care Level Moderate (needs warm, very clean water) Temperament Peaceful, shy; social Adult Size Up to 6–7" Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 82–88°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1½–4" (by size option) Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a reliable heater, gentle but strong filtration, and a bare bottom or fine sand for easy cleaning. Keep the tank in a quiet spot. Discus need very clean water. Feeding: Feed small meals of quality discus pellets or granules a few times a day, and remove uneaten food within a few minutes, since leftovers quickly foul the water. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. New arrivals may need frozen food for a while before they accept pellets. Tankmates: Discus are calm and shy, so choose gentle tankmates that enjoy the same warm water: cardinal and rummynose tetras, sterbai corydoras and small plecos are popular choices. Avoid fast, boisterous or fin-nipping fish, and anything that competes hard for food. Many keepers avoid angelfish, which can bully discus and share diseases. Living in groups: Discus are social and feel safest in a group. A single discus, or just two, tends to be stressed. When a pair forms to breed, they may claim part of the tank, so a group spreads out the attention. Good to know: Blue discus look most vivid under full-spectrum lighting and against a dark background. Discus show stress by darkening their color and hiding. A dark discus in a corner usually means the water quality or tankmates need checking.

The hi-fin neon swordtail sports a tall and colorful dorsal fin (pictured). These swords have the same characteristic gold, orange and black markings as the neon sword, with a sailfin to boot! If a certain sex ratio is desired, we will do our best to fulfill it. A good ratio is two females to one male, so the females get some rest. Quick Facts Scientific Name Xiphophorus hellerii (neon hi-fin) Origin Southern Mexico to Honduras (wild ancestors); aquarium-bred Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful (males may spar) Adult Size Up to 4–5" (not counting the sword) Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 7.0–8.0 (hard water) Group Size Keep more females than males Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Swordtails are active swimmers, so give them plants, open swimming space and a tight-fitting lid, since they are good jumpers. They prefer hard, alkaline water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet with some vegetable content once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Swordtails get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as platies, mollies, larger tetras, danios, rainbowfish, gouramis and corydoras. Keep more females than males, since males chase females and may spar with each other. Avoid fin-nippers and large cichlids. Good to know: Lyretail and hi-fin swordtails have extra-long fins, so keep them away from fin-nippers like tiger barbs. Many lyretail males have an elongated gonopodium and can't breed, so lyretail fry usually come from lyretail females mated with standard-finned males.

The Gold Cobra Guppy is one of the most popular color variations and tends to grow larger than other colors with a bold golden to lemon and black marbled tail. Females also feature some green on the body. Quick Facts Scientific Name Poecilia reticulata Origin Northern South America (captive-bred) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Sold as a pair (1 male + 1 female) Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and plenty of plants, including some floating plants where babies can hide. Guppies like slightly hard water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Guppies get along with other small, peaceful fish such as platies, mollies, corydoras, small tetras and rasboras. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs and larger fish that could eat them. Breeding: Guppies are livebearers and breed easily. Females give birth to live babies about once a month, and adults will eat the babies, so thick plants give them a place to hide. Good to know: Cobra guppies are named for the snakeskin-like pattern on the males' bodies.

The neon swordtail is a hybrid of the green and pineapple swordtail and conveys the brightest colors of both those fish. They prefer hard, alkaline water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet with some vegetable content once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Swordtails get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as platies, mollies, larger tetras, danios, rainbowfish, gouramis and corydoras. Keep more females than males, since males chase females and may spar with each other. Avoid fin-nippers and large cichlids. Good to know: Swordtails are livebearers and breed readily. Fry are born free-swimming and will be eaten unless there are dense plants or a breeding box for them to hide in. Only males grow the "sword" on the tail.

The coveted Black Moscow guppy has an interesting history. The half-black guppy was developed in East Berlin in the late 1960s. Quite a bit of breeding was done behind the Iron Curtain since it was very difficult - impossible actually - to import new varieties. That is one reason that even today many amazing killies, cichlids, guppies, and apistogrammas come from Central European breeders. Russian breeders took the half-black variety and were able to produce a full black male - very striking. These fish are still tough to breed but well worth the effort! Females have a little silver on the body, and not all offspring are full black; most, in fact, are half-black. Each order comes with one male and one female. Quick Facts Scientific Name Poecilia reticulata Origin Northern South America (captive-bred) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Sold as a pair (1 male + 1 female) Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and plenty of plants, including some floating plants where babies can hide. Guppies like slightly hard water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Guppies get along with other small, peaceful fish such as platies, mollies, corydoras, small tetras and rasboras. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs and larger fish that could eat them. Breeding: Guppies are livebearers and breed easily. Females give birth to live babies about once a month, and adults will eat the babies, so thick plants give them a place to hide. Good to know: Moscow guppies are known for their solid, deep body color.

The Dumbo Ear Betta, roundtail variety, is bred to showcase the extended pectoral fins (the "dumbo ears"). The roundtail is bred so that the other fins do not compete with the appearance of the pectoral fins. Roundtail dumbo ears are hardy bettas, but they can't fly. There are many names for the particular betta color patterns, but most are variations of blue and/or red colors. Fish pictured here are representative only. If you are looking for a specific coloration, message us, add to the order notes, or simply allow us to choose one of our favorites for you. When messaging, please note your order number. Quick Facts Scientific Name Betta splendens Origin Thailand (captive-bred) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Males fight each other; peaceful toward most other fish Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 76–82°F (needs a heater) pH 6.5–7.5 Breathes Air Yes – labyrinth fish take air from the surface Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give him a heater (bettas are tropical fish), a gentle filter and live or silk plants. Plakats are active swimmers and like room to patrol. Keep a lid on the tank and leave a gap of air under it, since bettas breathe from the surface. Feeding: Feed a few betta pellets or a pinch of flake once or twice a day. Bettas overeat easily, so small meals are best. They also enjoy frozen bloodworms. Tankmates: Never keep two male bettas together. Plakats are among the boldest bettas, so they do best alone or with sturdy, peaceful fish like corydoras and snails. Avoid fin-nippers and other labyrinth fish. Good to know: The big "dumbo ear" pectoral fins act like paddles, so dumbos swim a little slower. Give them gentle flow and resting spots near the surface.

The rare Lime Green Endler is bred in Sri Lanka, and this beautiful fish is difficult to obtain. Lime green endlers brighten up any small nano tank or planted aquarium. Quick Facts Scientific Name Poecilia wingei Origin Venezuela (captive-bred in Sri Lanka) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1" (males about ¾") Lifespan 2–4 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and plenty of plants. Endlers are small, so a sponge filter or a sponge over the filter intake keeps them safe. Feeding: Feed a quality flake, crushed small, or micro pellets once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Endlers do well with other small, peaceful fish such as small rasboras, corydoras, otocinclus and shrimp. Avoid larger fish that could eat them. Good to know: Male endlers are the colorful ones, and a group of males will spar and show off to each other without doing harm.

Gem Tang: The Crown Jewel of the Reef Aquarium The Gem Tang (Zebrasoma gemmatum) also known as the Gemmatum Tang is one of the most highly sought-after and exquisite species in the marine aquarium hobby. Often referred to as the "holy grail" of tangs , its rare beauty is unparalleled. This magnificent fish has a dark, near-black body that is completely covered in a dense pattern of brilliant white or iridescent blue spots, creating a stunning visual effect reminiscent of a starry night sky. The Gem Tang is an active swimmer and a tireless algae grazer, making it not only a breathtaking centerpiece but also a beneficial member of a reef tank cleanup crew. Despite its high value, it is generally a peaceful and hardy fish that thrives in a well-established, larger aquarium with ample room to swim and plenty of live rock for foraging. Why the Gem Tang is a Great Choice: Unrivaled Beauty: Its mesmerizing spotted pattern makes it a true collector's item and a centerpiece in any tank. Highly Desirable Rarity: Its limited availability makes it a prestige species for serious hobbyists. Natural Algae Control: It constantly grazes on algae, helping to maintain a clean and healthy environment. Peaceful Temperament: It is generally non-aggressive with other fish, making it a great community tank addition. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Zebrasoma gemmatum Origin: Western Indian Ocean (Madagascar, Reunion Island) Max Size: 8 inches Lifespan: 10+ years Diet: Herbivore. Primarily feeds on marine algae and prepared foods. Shipping Size: 2-4 inches EXPERT ONLY - No Refunds

Assasi Triggerfish Also known as the Picasso Triggerfish, has a wacky, painted appearance. It has a tan body with gradient dark bands running through the eye area and by the base of the tail. Also, there are vibrant blue and black stripes on the top of the head, with a yellow stripe from cheek to cheek and highly contrasting yellow eyes. The Assasi Triggerfish needs a varied diet of meaty foods including; squid, krill, clams, small fish and hard shelled shrimp to help wear down their ever growing teeth. Scientific Name: Rhinecanthus assasi Origin: Red Sea Max Size: 11 inches Diet: Carnivore Shipping Size: 2 to 7 inches

The South American leaf fish, or "true" leaf fish, or Amazon Leaf Fish, is an effective camouflage predator in the slow-moving streams of the Brazil Amazon basin. The leaf fish looks JUST like a leaf and will eat fish up to one half inch in size, along with live black worms and brine shrimp. The leaf fish may be transitioned to all frozen food but please don't count on it. These fish are egg layers though it is rare to get these guys (and girls of course) to breed in the aquarium. In the aquarium, Amazon leaf fish tend to hover near the upper zone. The leaf fish can change colors in the wild and in the aquarium to hide in the surroundings. These fish will also mimic the movement of waterlogged leaves and let the current drift them towards their innocent prey. Leaf fish do well in an aquarium provided the tank is low pH; anything higher than 7.4 and they will slowly fade. These fish are amazing in planted tanks! Quick Facts Scientific Name Monocirrhus polyacanthus Origin Amazon basin, Brazil Care Level Difficult Temperament Predatory Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 8 years Diet Carnivore (live and meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.0 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 2½–3" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a planted tank with driftwood, leaf litter and gentle current. They hunt by ambush and stay still for long periods. Feeding: Leaf fish are predators that usually eat only live or frozen foods. Offer frozen foods like bloodworms and shrimp; some never take pellets. Tankmates: They will eat any fish that fits in their mouth. Keep them only with fish too large to swallow. Good to know: Leaf fish can change color to blend in with the leaves and wood around them.

Domino Clownfish The Domino Clownfish is named for just what it looks like - a swimming domino. The Domino Clownfish is a captive variant of the Black Ocellaris Clownfish. Just like the parent Ocellaris Clownfish the Domino Clownfish is hardy and adaptable to community and reef aquariums and will even breed in the fish tank under the right conditions. Scientific Name: Amphiprion percula Origin: captive bred Max Size: 3 inches Diet: Omnivore Shipping Size: 3/4 to 1 1/4 inches

The black panda shrimp, or crystal black panda shrimp, is one of the jewels of the fancy shrimp collectors. These aquarium shrimp are very difficult to breed and will grow into a striking, broad black and white banded species. Breeders do not hold onto these shrimp very long, and so they arrive at our airport on the small side, just one half inch, so make sure you have the right habitat for this little beast. Quick Facts Scientific Name Caridina cf. cantonensis (black panda, crystal black) Origin Taiwan (aquarium-bred) Care Level Moderate to difficult (needs soft, stable water) Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1" Lifespan 1½–2 years Diet Omnivore (grazes on algae) Water Temperature 68–76°F pH 5.8–6.8 Water Hardness GH 4–6, KH 0–1 (soft) Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Caridina bee and Taiwan bee shrimp need soft, slightly acidic water. Use a mature, cycled tank with an active (buffering) shrimp substrate, RO water remineralized for shrimp, moss and plants, and a sponge filter. Feeding: Feed a small amount of quality shrimp food once a day, and remove any uneaten food after a few hours. Tankmates: Caridina are best kept in a shrimp-only tank or with tiny, peaceful fish like otocinclus, plus snails. Avoid cichlids and other fish that will eat shrimp. Different bee and Taiwan bee varieties can crossbreed, but they will not breed with Neocaridina. Good to know: Acclimate slowly (drip for an hour or more). Stable water matters more than perfect numbers, and sudden changes in temperature or hardness are the most common cause of losses.

Orange Toadfish The Orange Toadfish, which also has the silly name Oyster Cracker, is one of the more unique and interesting fish available in the aquarium trade. It is a bottom dwelling predator that seeks out small fish and inverts. For this reason it is best kept in a large aquarium devoid of these small organisms. With such a large mouth and a voracious appetite, the Toadfish can make many small organisms prey. They are hardy and can handle large fluctuations in tank specs. The Toadfish is easy to keep as long as it is kept out of the way of small organisms - if done, it will not bother corals or large fish or inverts. Scientific Name: Opsanus beta Origin: Gulf of Mexico Max Size: 12 inches Diet: Carnivore Shipping Size: 5 to 7 inches

Grey Smooth Hound Shark The Greyhound Shark, or grey smooth hound shark, looks like a dwarf version of the very scary open water grey shark. Growing to about 20 inches these marine sharks still require a large aquarium - at least 300 gallons when they reach maturity. In the wild these sharks can be found from teh near surface to 200 feet. Scientific Name: Mustelus californicus Origin: Gulf of California Max Size: 2 feet Recommended Tank Size: 300 gallon+ Diet: Feed off of crabs, squid, shrimp, clams

Big Eye Catalufa Rarer than the Popeye Soldierfish, The Popeye Catalufa Soldierfish, also known as the Bigeye Soldierfish, features burnt orange to red color with several white highlights. Despite the name "soldier" this oddball aquarium fish is quite peaceful. The dorsal fin has a feathery appearance and the other fins are marked in dark black at the ends. The Bigeye Catalufa is an interesting aquarium species. Juveniles are shy and will hide by day whereas adults are more bold and will swim in the open areas of an aquarium. The Catalufa is gentle to most tankmates but does like to eat small species like ornamental shrimp. Only Bigeye Catalufa Solder should be kept per aquarium. And score one for America, this fish was discovered by American ichthyologist Charles Gilbert in 1891. Scientific Name: Pristigenys serrula Origin: Costa Rica Max Size: 7 inches Diet: feeder shrimp should be used to entice this fish to eat. The diet should vary between live feeder shrimps, freeze-dried shrimps, chopped marine meats. Shipping Size: 3 to 6 inches

The red devil angelfish is the color most people hope to see after they Google koi angelfish. Koi angelfish are mainly black and white with bright orange markings. Often they are depicted as nearly solid bright red through the tricks of lighting and hormones. HOWEVER, the Red Devil variation does indeed have the bright red gene and displays a body covered with red markings. These are seldom seen in the trade, but we hope the breeder becomes more successful with this particular color strain. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pterophyllum scalare Origin Amazon basin, South America (captive-bred) Care Level Easy Temperament Semi-aggressive (territorial when pairing) Adult Size Up to 6" long and 8" tall Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them tall plants or driftwood, a heater and a gentle filter. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Choose peaceful fish too large to swallow, such as larger tetras, corydoras, plecos, rams, gouramis and peaceful barbs. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs, and small fish like neon tetras that adult angels may eat. Breeding: Angelfish pair off and lay eggs on flat surfaces like broad leaves or slate. A breeding pair can become territorial, so give them room and places for other fish to retreat. Good to know: Orange and red color varies with diet, age and mood. A color-enhancing food and a darker background help it show at its best.

The Kamaka rainbowfish was discovered in the Kamaka Lake on the island of Irian Jaya (Indonesia). These beautiful blue and purple hued fish are now bred in Florida where we source some of our rainbows, including the Kamaka. Kamakas are larger, reaching about three and a half inches, and they are a peaceful schooling fish, great for planted and mid-size community tanks. Quick Facts Scientific Name Melanotaenia kamaka Origin Western New Guinea, Indonesia (captive-bred in Florida) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 3½" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Rainbowfish are active swimmers, so leave open swimming space along the front, with plants along the back and sides. Use a filter, a heater and a tight-fitting lid, since they can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with peaceful fish of similar size, such as other rainbowfish, larger tetras, barbs, danios, corydoras and plecos. Good to know: Kamaka rainbows show blue and purple shades that look best under good aquarium lighting.
Red Mushroom Coral These coral display a very nice color tone, with about 12 heads .These corals grow quickly. Scientific Name: Rhodactis sp. Shipping Size: 3 inches

Red Banded Trochus Snail: The Cleanup Workhorse The Red Banded Trochus Snail (Trochus histrio) is a highly valued member of the aquarium clean-up crew, prized by aquarists of all experience levels for its peaceful nature and exceptional algae-grazing capabilities. It belongs to the Trochidae family, giving it a distinctive, pyramid-shaped shell that is typically pale gray and adorned with attractive maroon or purple stripes . Unlike some other common snails, one of the Banded Trochus Snail's most significant advantages is its ability to right itself when it falls or is knocked over by fish or water flow, greatly increasing its survival rate in the home aquarium. It is a tireless herbivore, constantly grazing on live rock, glass, and the substrate. While hardy, the Banded Trochus Snail requires a well-established aquarium with stable water parameters, particularly low nitrate levels . It is also completely intolerant of copper-based medications. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: This snail is a dedicated Herbivore and an essential part of the clean-up crew. It naturally grazes on common nuisance algae, including diatoms, green film algae , and cyanobacteria . It is less effective on tougher, mature hair algae. Feeding: In established tanks with sufficient algae growth, the Banded Trochus Snail may not require supplemental feeding. If the algae is depleted, its diet should be supplemented with dried seaweed (Nori) , algae wafers, or high-quality vegetable flakes to prevent starvation. They are mostly nocturnal and will graze primarily at night. Reef Compatibility: Yes . This snail is 100% reef-safe and poses no threat to corals, motile invertebrates, or other cleanup crew members. Its grazing activity benefits coral health by preventing algae from settling and smothering them. Temperament: Peaceful . They are ideal community tank inhabitants. The only compatibility concerns are predators. Avoid housing them with Pufferfish, Triggerfish, certain aggressive Wrasses , and predatory crustaceans like the Arrow Crab or larger hermit crabs that may try to steal their shell. Reproduction: These snails are known to reproduce sexually in the home aquarium, often releasing clouds of white gametes into the water column, particularly following large water changes or shifts in lighting. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Trochus histrio Primary Common Name: Banded Trochus Snail Other Common Names: Trochus Turbo Snail, Top Shell, Actor Top Origin: Indo-Pacific (Widespread) Max Size: 1 – 1.5 inches (2.5 – 4 cm) Temperament: Peaceful (Sessile Herbivore) Diet: Herbivore (Primarily Diatoms, Film Algae, and Cyanobacteria) Minimum Tank Size: 10 Gallons (20+ for established reef) Reef Compatibility: Yes (Excellent clean-up crew member)

Also known as the Coral cat shark. The eyes are set in front of large spiracles, which are used to move water into the gill chambers when the shark is at rest or feeding. The name comes from the cat-like shape and the color of the eyes.
