Also known as African glass catfish, they come from the Congo River tributaries and grow to about four inches. These fish are great in a community fish tank and will create an undulating, moving school that gravitates to the lower sections of the fish tank. Debauwi catfish are shy and do better in a group than by themselves, but are hardy and will eat community pellet or flake food. Similar in appearance to Asian glass catfish except they have a black line along the middle of the body. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pareutropius debauwi Origin Congo River basin, Africa Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 3–4" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants, driftwood and gentle current, with some open swimming space in the middle of the tank. They feel safest with others of their kind. Feeding: Feed small amounts of a quality flake or micro pellet once or twice a day. They also enjoy small frozen foods like brine shrimp and bloodworms. Tankmates: Ghost glass catfish are peaceful and shy. Keep them with other gentle community fish such as tetras, rasboras and corydoras. Good to know: Debauwi catfish swim together in open water, which is unusual for catfish.

The spotted silver dollar, or green spotted silver dollar, is a larger schooling fish of the streams and rivers of the Brazilian Amazon basin. Though related to the common silver dollar, the spotted silver dollar is a different species. Like silver dollars, spotted silver dollars are one of the hardiest fish in the aquarium trade. Adults have a green hue to the body and black spots. These are peaceful community fish but should not be kept with fish that can fit in their mouths. A school of four makes a nice display. Pictured is an adult silver dollar with full colors. Quick Facts Scientific Name Metynnis lippincottianus Origin Amazon basin, Brazil Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 6" Lifespan 10+ years Diet Herbivore (plant-based foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1–1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Silver dollars are active schooling fish. Give them open swimming space, a tight lid and sturdy or artificial plants, since they eat soft plants. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or pellet with vegetable content once or twice a day. They also enjoy vegetable foods like peas. Tankmates: They are peaceful and get along with other medium to large fish such as larger tetras, plecos, parrots and peaceful cichlids. Good to know: Adults develop a green sheen and dark spots that young fish don't have yet.

The striped silver dollar, or tiger silver dollar, is rare and comes from the Brazilian side of the Amazon Basin. From time to time, bred tiger-striped silver dollars can be found from one breeder in Florida. Though related to the common silver dollar, the striped dollar is a different species. Like silver dollars, striped silver dollars are hardy. The tiger striping becomes more remarkable as the fish ages. A school of four makes a nice display like a pack of little tigers that look like fish and swim. Quick Facts Scientific Name Metynnis fasciatus Origin Amazon basin, Brazil Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 6" Lifespan 10+ years Diet Herbivore (plant-based foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Silver dollars are active schooling fish. Give them open swimming space, a tight lid and sturdy or artificial plants, since they eat soft plants. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or pellet with vegetable content once or twice a day. They also enjoy vegetable foods like peas. Tankmates: They are peaceful and get along with other medium to large fish such as larger tetras, plecos, parrots and peaceful cichlids. Good to know: The tiger stripes get bolder as the fish grows.

Rose Anemone This species has diverse colors some are just Rose Anemone, with the base color usually brown to what ever color the anemone is. The tentacles may or may not have different color. The tentacles may occasionally develop a bubble-like appearance to them. Family: Actiniidae Diet: Should include feedings of fish, mussels, shrimp, or other foods of this type Approximate Size: 2 1/2 to 3 1/2 inches

Red Coco Worm: The Filter-Feeding Showpiece The Red Coco Worm (Protula bispiralis, sometimes marketed as Protula magnifica) is a magnificent marine invertebrate and a captivating addition to a mature reef aquarium. This filter-feeding worm builds a hard, calcareous tube (hence the common name Hard Tube Feather Duster) for protection, often reaching 6 to 8 inches (15-20 cm) in length, with its crown extending up to 5 inches (12 cm) in diameter. The animal is admired for its striking, fan-like spiral crown of radioles, which are typically a vibrant shade of red, pink, or reddish-orange with white markings. When disturbed by a shadow, touch, or a passing fish, the worm rapidly retracts its entire crown into its tube. Unlike its close relatives, the Red Coco Worm does not have an operculum (a trap door) to seal the tube opening. Due to its reliance on constant, high-quality nutrition and pristine water, the Red Coco Worm is best suited for Intermediate to Advanced aquarists who are diligent about routine feedings and water stability. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: This is a dedicated Filter Feeder. It uses its feathery crown to capture fine suspended particles, primarily phytoplankton, zooplankton, and very fine organic particulate matter (marine snow) from the water column. Feeding: Regular supplemental feeding is essential for long-term survival. The worm cannot sustain itself solely on natural plankton in a typical aquarium. Feed the tank with high-quality liquid phytoplankton, rotifers, oyster eggs, or other commercially prepared liquid coral foods once or twice daily. Do not dispense food directly onto the crown, as this causes retraction; instead, pour it into an area with moderate flow. Reef Compatibility: It is Reef Safe. The Coco Worm is peaceful and poses no threat to corals or other invertebrates. It requires ample calcium and alkalinity to build its hard tube, making a stable reef environment ideal. Temperament: It is Peaceful. The primary compatibility concern is not the worm itself but its susceptibility to predation. Avoid all fish known to nip at sedentary invertebrates, including Angelfish, Butterflyfish, Triggerfish, Pufferfish, and certain large, aggressive Wrasses. Large predatory shrimp and crabs should also be avoided. Placement: Place the tube in a shaded area or crevice, preferably near the bottom, with gentle to moderate water flow to ensure food delivery without damaging the delicate crown. It is highly sensitive to poor water quality and copper-based medications. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Protula bispiralis (often sold as Protula magnifica) Primary Common Name: Red Coco Worm Other Common Names: Magnificent Tubeworm, Hard Tube Feather Duster, Red Fanworm Origin: Indo-Pacific Max Size: Tube up to 8 inches (20 cm), Crown up to 5 inches (12 cm) Temperament: Peaceful (Sensitive filter feeder) Diet: Filter Feeder (Requires regular phytoplankton/plankton supplements) Minimum Tank Size: 55 Gallons (Requires stable, mature water) Reef Compatibility: Yes (Excellent)

Gold Banded Coral Shrimp Gold Coral Banded Shrimp, Stenopus tenuirostris , features a striking translucent and gold body with long white antennae and two muscular pinchers. It can also be known as the Boxing Shrimp for its propensity to hit its prey with those large claws. Mostly peaceful towards other species, the Gold Coral Banded Shrimp should not be housed with members of its own species unless they are a mated pair. The Coral Banded Shrimp can be sensitive to water quality so it is recommended you keep your water in pristine shape. They prefer tanks with plenty of live rock hiding places to search for their carnivorous diet. They will often lose their exoskeleton in a process called molting while they are growing. Overall, the Blue Coral Banded Shrimp is a staple in the home aquarium for its unique and beautiful appearance and ability to eat pesky bristle worms and flat worms. Scientific Name: Stenopus tenuirostris Max Size: 3 inches Diet: In the wild, the Banded Coral Shrimp is a scavenger. In the home aquarium, it will accept most flaked and frozen foods. Shipping Size: Approx. 1 to 1 1/2inches

Also known as Starry, steallate is a m edium-sized fish which grows up to 13 inches in length. Its body is oval shaped, spherical and relatively elongated. The skin is not covered with scales but is prickly. The fish has no pelvic fin and no lateral line. The dorsal fin and the anal fin are small, symmetric, and located at the rear end of the body. The head is large with a short snout that has two pairs of nostrils, and the mouth is terminal with four strong teeth. Scientific Name: Arothron stellatus Origin: Indonesia, Solomon Islands,BAIL Lifespan: 10-15 years Max Size: 13 inches Diet: Snails and clams Shipping Size: 7-8 inches

listings.commonName: Red Tail Black Neon Variatus Platy
listings.description: There are two species of platy from southern Mexico: platy maculatus and platy variatus. The variatus have higher dorsal fins, jump a bit more, and grow slightly larger than the maculatus. The two species will breed, and several hybrids are available, particularly the assorted hi-fin platies. AquariumFish.com carries just a few of these select variations for their striking color and great fins. The picture of the neon red tail variatus says it all. These fish can live in freshwater and brackish water. Quick Facts Scientific Name Xiphophorus variatus Origin Southern Mexico Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 3–4 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 65–77°F (handles cooler water than common platies) pH 7.0–8.2 Breeding Livebearer – breeds easily in the aquarium Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Platies are hardy and easy to keep. Give them a filter, a lid and plenty of plants. They can live without a heater in rooms that stay above about 65°F. They prefer harder, slightly alkaline water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. Platies also need some plant matter, so a vegetable flake is a good choice. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Platies get along with most peaceful community fish, such as other livebearers (mollies, guppies and swordtails), tetras, rasboras and corydoras. Avoid large or aggressive fish that may bully or eat them. Breeding: Platies are livebearers, so a tank with males and females will almost certainly have babies (fry). Adults will eat fry, so add dense plants or use a breeding box if you want to raise them. Keeping more females than males gives the females a break from the males' attention. Good to know: Variatus are keen jumpers, so keep a tight-fitting lid on the tank.

The most popular platy around is probably the red mickey mouse. The small black spots on the tail truly look like the hats from Disney's Mickey Mouse Club. These fish are the closest living relatives to Justin Timberlake and Britney Spears that we carry. Quick Facts Scientific Name Xiphophorus maculatus Origin Southern Mexico and Central America Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 3–4 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 70–80°F pH 7.0–8.2 Breeding Livebearer – breeds easily in the aquarium Care Guide Tank setup: Platies are hardy and easy to keep. Give them a filter, a lid and plenty of plants. Use a heater to keep the water steady in the 70s. They prefer harder, slightly alkaline water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. Platies also need some plant matter, so a vegetable flake is a good choice. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Platies get along with most peaceful community fish, such as other livebearers (mollies, guppies and swordtails), tetras, rasboras and corydoras. Avoid large or aggressive fish that may bully or eat them. Breeding: Platies are livebearers, so a tank with males and females will almost certainly have babies (fry). Adults will eat fry, so add dense plants or use a breeding box if you want to raise them. Keeping more females than males gives the females a break from the males' attention. Good to know: Platies are one of the easiest fish to keep, which makes them a great choice for a first aquarium.

Ricefish are similar to killifish but belong to their own genus, Oryzias , spread throughout Asia from China to Japan. Ricefish are schooling fish that swim near the surface of rice paddies to control the mosquito population. The pink medaka ricefish is bred to display a bold solid white and pinkish body so they can be seen in the rice fields – and of course in aquariums and ponds! Ricefish are sold individually but do best in a school of six or more. These are hardy fish that can handle temperatures down to the high 50s. Quick Facts Scientific Name Oryzias latipes (pink/white variety) Origin Japan (aquarium-bred) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1½" Lifespan 2–4 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 64–80°F (handles cooler water; no heater needed in most homes) pH 6.5–8.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Ricefish stay near the surface, so give them plants, floating plants and a lid. They are cool-water fish and do fine at room temperature, and they also do well in outdoor ponds and patio tubs in warm months. Feeding: Feed crushed flake or micro pellets once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Ricefish get along with other small, peaceful fish like white clouds, small rasboras, danios and shrimp. They can share an unheated tank with cool-water species, but avoid large or fast fish (including fancy goldfish) that may eat or outcompete them. Good to know: Medaka have been kept in Japan for centuries and are one of the hardiest small fish in the hobby. Both sexes are colorful; males have slightly larger fins.

Full moon male bettas are bred to display a nearly circular array of fins when the betta is showing off. Spectacular. Sure to attract the pickiest female and scare off stronger males. Full moon bettas come in several colors, so if you want a particular color, please note it in the comment area of the order, and we will match as closely as we can. There are many names for the particular betta color patterns, but most are variations of blue and/or red colors. Fish pictured here are representative only. If you are looking for a specific coloration, please note it on your order, or simply allow us to choose one of our favorites for you! Quick Facts Scientific Name Betta splendens Origin Thailand (captive-bred) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Males fight each other; peaceful toward most other fish Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 76–82°F (needs a heater) pH 6.5–7.5 Breathes Air Yes – labyrinth fish take air from the surface Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give him a heater (bettas are tropical fish), a gentle filter and live or silk plants. Floating plants or a "betta leaf" near the surface give him a place to rest. Keep a lid on the tank and leave a gap of air under it, since bettas breathe from the surface. Feeding: Feed a few betta pellets or a pinch of flake once or twice a day. Bettas overeat easily, so small meals are best. They also enjoy frozen bloodworms. Tankmates: Never keep two male bettas together. A male can live with small, peaceful fish that don't nip fins, such as corydoras, small rasboras, otocinclus and snails. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs and flashy, long-finned fish like fancy guppies. Good to know: Long, heavy fins tear easily, so keep the filter flow gentle and choose soft plants and smooth decorations. Clean, warm water helps prevent fin rot.

The Copella arnoldi , or splashing tetra, is a pretty, slender schooling fish from northern South America. Splashing tetras get their name from their breeding behavior. The male and female jump out of the water and land together on low leaves. They then breed and fertilize the eggs and jump back into the stream. These tetras are great community fish, but there should be a cover on the fish tank in case a couple of them get in the mood. These tetras are fast swimmers and range over the whole aquarium. Males get a bright, fringed, large dorsal fin. Quick Facts Scientific Name Copella arnoldi Origin The Guianas and lower Amazon (Guyana, Suriname, French Guiana, Brazil) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2–3" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1–1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a dark substrate, which brings out their color. Keep a lid on the tank, since tetras can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, rasboras, danios, corydoras, dwarf cichlids, gouramis and livebearers. Good to know: Tetras feel safer and show better color in a group. A larger school also spreads out any chasing.

The sexy red lips snail doesn't look like anything special from the top, but through the glass the snail has ruby-red lips, which can be seen kissing the tank all over. Like all nerite snails, the red lips snail does not overrun the fish tank, and the aquarium snails only grow to about one inch at full maturity. Nerites do well in most water conditions except for pH below 7.0. These attractive snails do not get bigger than an inch, and we recommend several for algae control in larger tanks. Quick Facts Scientific Name Neritina sp. Origin East Africa and Indo-Pacific coastal streams (wild-caught) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful; plant-safe Adult Size Up to 1" Lifespan 1–2+ years Diet Algae eater (also eats algae wafers) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.5 (hard water for healthy shells) Breeding Lays small white eggs on hard surfaces, but they won't hatch in freshwater, so nerites won't overrun the tank Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Nerites do well in most established tanks with algae to graze. Keep the water hard and alkaline for healthy shells, and keep a lid on the tank, since nerites sometimes climb out. If one flips onto its back, turn it over, since some can't right themselves. Feeding: Nerites mostly graze on algae. If the tank is very clean, add algae wafers so they don't go hungry. Tankmates: Nerites get along with peaceful fish, shrimp and other snails. Avoid puffers, loaches and large cichlids, which eat snails, and keep them away from assassin snails. Good to know: Remove snails before treating the tank with copper or other medications, which are toxic to invertebrates.

The classic blue-eye gertrudae is a beautiful small schooling rainbowfish suitable for planted aquariums and most community fish tanks. As with most rainbow fish, the male gertrudae have larger fins and more color than the female, but both sexes are attractive. We ship these as close as possible to a 50:50 mix of males and females. We recommend a school of six or more, but a pair would do well in a peaceful community tank. The ARU II is a variation bred for higher color (and a little higher price). Quick Facts Scientific Name Pseudomugil gertrudae Origin Northern Australia and New Guinea Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1¼" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ½–¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a planted tank with gentle filtration, some floating plants and a lid. They are small, so a sponge over the filter intake keeps them safe. Feeding: Feed crushed flake or micro pellets once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Blue-eyes are small and gentle, so keep them with other small, peaceful fish such as rasboras, small tetras, pygmy corydoras and shrimp. Good to know: Males have spotted, sail-like fins they flare at each other to show off. Their bright blue eyes stand out in a planted tank.

The L-47 mango pleco is a rare pleco from Brazil that features a broad mango-yellow outer band along the edges of the fins. Also called magnum plecos, these fish are not often caught and have not been bred in captivity. Mango plecos do need some driftwood and will eat algae pellets and scavenge. Quick Facts Scientific Name Baryancistrus chrysolomus (L-047) Origin Rio Xingu, Brazil Care Level Moderate (needs warm, oxygen-rich water) Temperament Peaceful (territorial with other plecos) Adult Size Up to 8–10" Lifespan 12–15+ years Diet Omnivore (algae and sinking foods) Water Temperature 78–84°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single, or several with a cave each Shipping Size Approx. 4" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them strong current, high oxygen, smooth rocks, caves and driftwood. Many come from warm, fast rivers in Brazil, so keep the water clean and warm. Feeding: Feed algae wafers and quality sinking pellets. They also enjoy frozen foods now and then. Tankmates: They do well with most community fish and peaceful cichlids. Give each pleco its own cave to limit territorial squabbles. Good to know: Many of these plecos come from fast-flowing rivers threatened by dam projects, so wild-caught specimens are increasingly rare.

Two breeders are responsible for this special color variation of the wild blue ram, one in Taiwan and one in the Czech Republic. We select from either one when they become available, which is not very often. The black ram, or black German ram, has the same behavior and care requirements as the German blue ram and is a peaceful aquarium fish. Though the body is dark, the fins display iridescent colors. These very difficult-to-breed fish are the most expensive ram on the market, but a great addition to any peaceful fish tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name Mikrogeophagus ramirezi (black variety) Origin Wild ancestors from Venezuela and Colombia; bred in Taiwan and the Czech Republic Care Level Moderate (needs warm, clean, soft water) Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 2–4 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 80–86°F pH 5.0–7.0 Group Size Pair or small group Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Rams need warm, very clean, soft water. Give them a sand bottom, plants, driftwood, leaf litter and flat stones for spawning. Rams are sensitive to poor water quality. Feeding: Feed small amounts of quality micro pellets or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Rams do well with small, peaceful fish that like warm, soft water, such as tetras, rasboras, hatchetfish, corydoras and discus. They may eat small shrimp. Avoid large or boisterous fish. Good to know: Rams often form pairs and lay eggs on flat stones. Stable, warm water is the key to keeping them healthy.

The albino paradise fish was one of the first color morphs bred for the aquarium trade. These fish are bright white, with red and blue highlights, a carryover from the parent blue paradise fish. Quick Facts Scientific Name Macropodus opercularis (albino variety) Origin East Asia (China, Vietnam, Korea, Taiwan) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Semi-aggressive (males fight) Adult Size Up to 3–4" Lifespan 6–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 61–79°F (often fine without a heater) pH 6.0–8.0 Breathes Air Yes – labyrinth fish take air from the surface Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants and hiding places. They handle cool water, so a heater is optional in most homes. Keep a lid on the tank and leave a gap of air above the water, since gouramis breathe from the surface. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Males fight each other, so keep one male per tank. They do best with sturdy, similar-sized fish and should not be kept with bettas, very small fish or small shrimp. Good to know: Albino paradise fish have the same tough, cool-water nature as the classic paradise fish, just in white with red and blue highlights.

The color variation of the dumbo ear guppy from Sri Lanka is a cross between the dragon and red cobra guppy. Large front ventral fins are what give this fish its name - like Dumbo the Elephant these fins make this fancy guppy look like it could fly! Please be advised, colors may vary. This week, for instance, we have higher end golden dumbo ear! Quick Facts Scientific Name Poecilia reticulata Origin Northern South America (captive-bred in Sri Lanka) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and plenty of plants. Guppies like slightly hard water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Male guppies get along with other small, peaceful fish such as platies, mollies, corydoras, small tetras and rasboras. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs, which go after their long tails, and larger fish that could eat them. Good to know: Dumbo ear guppies are named for their oversized, ear-like pectoral fins.

Live Bamboo The bamboo plant with its long classic stem and curly leaf is a classic accessory to goldfish and betta bowls and small nano tanks. The bamboo with survive for months if some if it is submerged but the leafy end is exposed to air. We sell these one a piece, as opposed to the common 10 pack found on online plant stores. Scientific Name: Draceana sanderiana Origin: India Max Size: 15 inches Shipping Size: 12 inches

Most original variations of guppies came from Thailand, but the Sakura black originated in Singapore and the breeders are reluctant to part with their females. Crossbreeding with any black variation female should produce a few of this amazing color, however. The fancy sakura black guppy features a solid black body and contrasting, brightly colored cobra tail and dorsal sailfin. Quick Facts Scientific Name Poecilia reticulata Origin Northern South America (captive-bred in Singapore) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Sold as a pair (1 male + 1 female) Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and plenty of plants, including some floating plants where babies can hide. Guppies like slightly hard water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Guppies get along with other small, peaceful fish such as platies, mollies, corydoras, small tetras and rasboras. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs and larger fish that could eat them. Breeding: Guppies are livebearers and breed easily. Females give birth to live babies about once a month, and adults will eat the babies, so thick plants give them a place to hide. Good to know: The solid black body makes the bright tail colors stand out even more.

Bubble Coral It is commonly called "Bubble Coral" due to its bubbly appearance. The "Bubbles" are grape-sized which increase their surface area according to the amount of light available: they are larger during the day, but smaller during the night, when tentacles reach out to capture food. This species requires low light and a gentle water flow. Scientific Name: Plerogyra sinuosa

SOFT Green Star Polyps Coral These coral usually come in brown, tan, green, connected by a rubbery colored mat. When placed together, large colonies can create a dense carpet across rock and substrate. Growth is likely in home aquariums. The Star Polyp requires tanks with moderate lighting but may develop more intense colors under intense lighting, moderate water flow, and mid to high placement. Please keep them some distance away from other corals to prevent their tentacles from harming other corals at night. They feed photo-synthetically and require no supplemental feedings.

Flashy and fast, danios add a lot of schooling action to any aquarium, and they get along with everyone. The gold long fin danio has angelic gold fins, so they make a fabulous-looking school in the aquarium. These fish are very hardy and can even survive and thrive in warm water ponds. Gold long-fin danios are bred from their parent gold danio from the Ganges region in Eastern India. Quick Facts Scientific Name Danio rerio (gold long-fin variety) Origin India, Bangladesh and Nepal (Ganges region) (captive-bred) Care Level Very easy, great for beginners Temperament Peaceful, very active Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 64–77°F (often fine without a heater) pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Danios are fast swimmers, so give them open swimming space, a filter, plants around the edges and a tight-fitting lid, since they jump. Make sure the tank is fully cycled (which takes several weeks) before adding fish. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Danios get along with most peaceful community fish, such as tetras, rasboras, barbs, corydoras and livebearers. Their speed can stress slow, long-finned fish like bettas and fancy guppies, and large predatory fish will eat them. Good to know: Long fins make these danios a little slower than regular zebras, so avoid fin-nipping tankmates like tiger barbs.

Flashy and fast, danios add a lot of schooling action to any aquarium, and they get along with everyone. The gold danio has a bright gold body with less marking than the parent zebra danio. These fish are very hardy and can even survive and thrive in warm water ponds. Gold zebra danios are bred from their parent zebra danio from the Ganges region in Eastern India. These fish create fast-moving bright schools and are particularly suited to darker aquariums and small ponds (in warmer climates, of course; danios are tropical fish). Quick Facts Scientific Name Danio rerio (gold variety) Origin India, Bangladesh and Nepal (Ganges region) (captive-bred) Care Level Very easy, great for beginners Temperament Peaceful, very active Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 64–77°F (often fine without a heater) pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Danios are fast swimmers, so give them open swimming space, a filter, plants around the edges and a tight-fitting lid, since they jump. Make sure the tank is fully cycled (which takes several weeks) before adding fish. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Danios get along with most peaceful community fish, such as tetras, rasboras, barbs, corydoras and livebearers. Their speed can stress slow, long-finned fish like bettas and fancy guppies, and large predatory fish will eat them. Good to know: Gold danios show up beautifully against dark substrate and backgrounds. Danios are fast and jump when startled, so keep a lid on the tank.

The slender tetra, or green line lizard tetra, comes from the Amazon basin in Brazil and is rare in the fish trade. No one has successfully bred this unique species, which is a shame. These expensive little schooling fish are caught along small streams around the border of Colombia and Brazil. The tetra grows to nearly four inches and is peaceful but fast. Slender tetras will eat flake food, but it is advisable to have some frozen brine shrimp on hand, since these are all wild-caught. This rare aquarium fish is long like a lizard and has a thin reflective green line along the middle of the body. Quick Facts Scientific Name Iguanodectes spilurus Origin Amazon and Orinoco basins Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful but active Adult Size Up to 2½–4" Lifespan 5–10 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: These are larger, active schooling fish, so give them open swimming space, plants or driftwood along the back and a tight-fitting lid, since they jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They do well with other active, similar-size fish such as larger tetras, barbs, rainbowfish, peaceful cichlids, corydoras and plecos. Very small fish may be eaten or bullied. Good to know: Larger tetras are hardy and long-lived, and a big school makes a striking display.

Orange Spotted Rabbitfish: The Venomous Algae Specialist The Orange Spotted Rabbitfish (Siganus guttatus), also known as the Goldlined Spinefoot or Yellow Blotch Rabbitfish , is a large, highly sought-after species for its vibrant coloration and exceptional algae-eating capabilities. This fish is characterized by a sleek, compressed body that is typically a pearly white or light blue-grey, covered in numerous striking orange to yellow spots . A distinctive large yellow or orange blotch often appears near the base of the caudal fin (tail). Native to the Indo-West Pacific, the Orange Spotted Rabbitfish is a peaceful herbivore that can reach a significant adult size of 10 to 15 inches (25-38 cm) in captivity. Due to its potential size and active nature, a large marine aquarium of at least 120 gallons is required to provide adequate swimming space and stable water quality. Like all rabbitfish, the Orange Spotted Rabbitfish possesses venomous spines on its dorsal, anal, and pelvic fins. While generally non-aggressive, these spines can be quickly raised when the fish feels threatened, demanding extreme caution during all tank maintenance and handling. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: This fish is a dedicated Herbivore (Algae Eater). Its diet is absolutely critical and must consist primarily of various algae. In the aquarium, it should be fed large amounts of dried seaweed (Nori) attached to a clip, multiple times per week. The diet should be supplemented with high-quality vegetable-based flake or pellet foods containing Spirulina. A well-established tank with plenty of live rock for grazing is essential. Algae Control: Rabbitfish are one of the few species known to aggressively graze on nuisance algae, including hair algae and bubble algae , making them an invaluable part of the clean-up crew. Reef Compatibility: It is Reef Safe With Caution . When well-fed on marine algae, it generally leaves corals alone. However, if underfed, it may begin to nip at or consume the polyps of some Large Polyp Stony (LPS) and soft corals . Monitor closely when first introduced to a reef system. Temperament: It is Peaceful toward most other tankmates, including tangs, wrasses, and angels. Its venomous spines allow it to coexist even with larger, more aggressive fish. It should not be housed with other rabbitfish (including Foxfaces, which are a related species), as they will often fight, though a well-established mated pair can sometimes be kept in a very large tank (180+ gallons). Venomous Spines: The venom is delivered through grooves in the spines and causes extreme pain but is rarely life-threatening to healthy humans. If stung, immediately soak the affected area in the hottest water you can tolerate (not scalding) for 30-90 minutes, as heat breaks down the protein-based venom. Seek medical attention immediately. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Siganus guttatus Primary Common Name: Orange Spotted Rabbitfish Other Common Names: Yellow Blotch Rabbitfish, Goldlined Spinefoot, Gold Saddle Rabbitfish Origin: Indo-West Pacific (Widespread) Max Size: 10-15 inches (25-38 cm) Temperament: Peaceful ( Venomous Spines ) Diet: Herbivore (Requires continuous grazing/algae sheets) Minimum Tank Size: 120+ Gallons Reef Compatibility: With Caution (May nip LPS/Soft corals if underfed) Care Level: Moderate

Purple Tube Anemone The Tube Anemone Cerianthus membranaceus , also known as the Tube Dwelling Anemone, has some very interesting traits. Purple Base Green Bubble Anemone: The Hardy Clownfish Host The Purple Base Green Bubble Anemone (Entacmaea quadricolor), often abbreviated as BTA, is one of the most popular and commonly recommended sea anemones in the marine hobby. This name refers to a specific color morph of the anemone, which features green, bulbous-tipped tentacles and a distinctly purple, red, or maroon foot/column used for attachment. Native to the Indo-Pacific, this anemone is prized for its hardiness and its reliability as a host for many species of clownfish, including the Ocellaris, Percula, and Maroon Clownfish. It is an excellent choice for intermediate keepers looking for an anemone that is generally easier to care for than other host species. The Purple Base Green BTA can grow to a substantial size, reaching 12 inches (30 cm) or more in diameter. It requires a stable, mature aquarium of at least 30 gallons (though 50+ gallons is recommended to accommodate its size and movement). Diet & Compatibility: Diet: This anemone is a Photosynthetic Carnivore. It is largely sustained by the symbiotic algae (zooxanthellae) within its tissues, which require strong lighting. It must be supplemented with meaty food. Feeding: Feed 2–3 times per week by target-feeding small pieces of raw marine shrimp, clam, squid, or chopped fish. Supplemental feeding is crucial for its health and to maintain its vibrant color and characteristic "bubble" tips. Lighting & Flow: Requires Moderate to High Intensity Lighting and Moderate Water Flow. Insufficient lighting is the primary reason an anemone will wander the tank in search of a better spot. Placement: The BTA is a "crevice-dweller" and will attach its foot deep within the live rock structure. It will move until it finds a location with ideal light and flow. All powerheads and filter intakes MUST be guarded to prevent fatal injury from being sucked in. Reef Compatibility: Reef Safe With Caution. The anemone has a potent, aggressive sting and is mobile. It will sting and damage any coral or sessile invertebrate (like clams) that it comes into contact with. Provide ample clear space (at least 6-12 inches) between the anemone and all corals. Propagation: Happy, mature BTAs are famous for their ability to reproduce asexually by splitting (fission). Quick Facts Scientific Name: Entacmaea quadricolor Primary Common Name: Purple Base Green Bubble Anemone Other Common Names: Bubble Tip Anemone (BTA), Rose Bubble Tip Anemone (RBTA), Bulb-Tentacle Anemone Origin: Indo-Pacific (Widespread) Max Size: 12+ inches (30+ cm) Temperament: Semi-Aggressive (Stinging and Motile) Diet: Photosynthetic Carnivore (Requires strong light and target feeding) Care Level: Moderate (Requires stable, mature tank) Minimum Tank Size: 30–50+ Gallons Reef Compatibility: With Caution (Will sting corals and sessile inverts)

Sebae Anemone: The Leather and Corkscrew Host The Sebae Anemone (Heteractis crispa), also known as the Leather Anemone or Corkscrew Anemone , is a popular but challenging large sea anemone found across the Indo-Pacific. It is characterized by its long, flowing tentacles (typically 1.5 to 2.5 inches) that often have a noticeable blue, purple, or blue-green color on the tips, contrasting with a white, beige, or brown main body. This species is highly mobile when initially placed in an aquarium or if water conditions become unstable, and it can move to find its preferred spot. Once settled, it will typically anchor its foot (pedal disc) in a crevice of live rock, often near the sandy substrate. It is a large anemone, capable of reaching an impressive diameter of 12 to 30 inches (30-76 cm) in captivity, which necessitates a spacious and well-established aquarium. The Sebae Anemone is a host species for several types of clownfish, including the Ocellaris and Percula Clownfish . Due to its size and stinging nematocysts, it requires a minimum tank size of 55 gallons , with 100+ gallons highly recommended for its long-term health and stability. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: The Sebae Anemone is both Photosynthetic and Carnivore . It gains most of its energy from the symbiotic zooxanthellae algae in its tissues, which requires Moderate to High lighting . Supplemental feeding is essential for long-term health and should consist of meaty foods like chopped shrimp, clam, krill, or silversides placed gently near its mouth once or twice per week. Lighting/Flow: It requires High Lighting (150-250 PAR is often recommended) and Moderate Flow. The flow should be non-direct but sufficient to keep detritus off its tentacles and provide gas exchange. The anemone will move to find its preferred light and flow zone. Reef Compatibility: It is Reef Safe With Caution . While it will not typically harm corals through predation, its powerful nematocysts (stinging cells) can seriously damage or kill corals and other sessile invertebrates (like other anemones) it comes into contact with. It also possesses a predatory temperament and may consume small, slow-moving fish or ornamental invertebrates like shrimp and crabs that wander into its tentacles. Temperament: It is Semi-Aggressive / Predatory (Stinging) . It is one of the more difficult anemones to keep, requiring a stable and mature aquarium (ideally running for 6+ months). When handling, always wear protective gloves, as its sting can cause skin irritation or allergic reactions in humans. Symbiotic Host: It hosts numerous species of clownfish, including Ocellaris ( A.ocellaris ) and Percula ( A.percula ). The clownfish will clean the anemone and provide nutrients, benefiting the anemone's growth and survival. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Heteractis crispa Primary Common Name: Sebae Anemone Other Common Names: Leather Anemone, Corkscrew Anemone Origin: Indo-Pacific Max Size: 12 - 30 inches (30 - 76 cm) diameter Temperament: Semi-Aggressive / Predatory ( Potent Sting ) Diet: Photosynthetic / Carnivore (Requires supplemental meaty food) Minimum Tank Size: 55+ Gallons (100+ Gallons Recommended) Reef Compatibility: With Caution (Will sting corals and eat small fish/inverts)

Long Tentacle Green Anemone: The Elegant Sand Dweller The Long Tentacle Green Anemone (Macrodactyla doreensis), often called the Corkscrew Anemone , Sand Anemone, or Red Base Anemone, is a popular and relatively hardy species known for its long, slender, and often wavy tentacles. This anemone typically features an oral disc with visible striping and a column base that is frequently a vibrant red or orange (the "Red Base" moniker), though its tentacles come in shades of green, tan, white, or purple. Hailing from the shallow lagoons and sandy flats of the Indo-Pacific, this anemone buries its foot deep into the substrate, leaving only the oral disc and tentacles exposed. It can grow to a substantial size, reaching a diameter of 12 to 20 inches (30-50 cm), requiring a minimum tank size of 50 gallons to accommodate its size and territorial needs. The Long Tentacle Green Anemone is considered a good choice for intermediate keepers who can provide stable water conditions, strong lighting, and the crucial deep sand bed it needs to thrive and anchor itself properly. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: This anemone is a Photosynthetic Carnivore. It derives most of its energy from symbiotic algae (zooxanthellae) and requires moderate to high lighting. However, supplemental feeding is essential for long-term health and growth. Feeding: Feed 2-3 times per week with meaty foods, such as pieces of raw marine shrimp, clam, fish flesh, or anemone-specific pellets. The food item should be placed directly onto the oral disc. Substrate & Placement: A deep sand bed (at least 4–6 inches) is mandatory, as this species prefers to bury its foot for stability and protection. Without a proper substrate, it will wander. It is vital to keep all powerheads guarded or far away from its wandering path, as being sucked in is often fatal. Reef Compatibility: Reef Safe With Caution. This anemone will not actively target corals, but its venomous, sweeping tentacles will sting and kill any stationary coral or sessile invertebrate (like clams) they touch during movement or full expansion. It must be given a large, open area on the sand. Symbiosis: The Long Tentacle Anemone hosts several species of clownfish, including the Clarkii, Saddleback, and Pink Skunk clownfish ( Amphiprion perideraion ). The presence of a host clownfish can improve the anemone's long-term health. Handling Warning: Like all anemones, it possesses stinging nematocysts. Always use gloves during maintenance, and never expose the anemone to air during transfer, as this can cause internal damage. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Macrodactyla doreensis Primary Common Name: Long Tentacle Green Anemone Other Common Names: Corkscrew Anemone, Sand Anemone, Red Base Anemone Origin: Indo-Pacific Max Size: 12–20 inches (30–50 cm) Temperament: Semi-Aggressive / Stinging (Motile) Diet: Photosynthetic Carnivore (Requires strong light and target feeding) Care Level: Moderate Minimum Tank Size: 50+ Gallons Reef Compatibility: With Caution (Stings nearby corals)

Open Trachy may be a folded or figure-eight shape and comes in colors like red,green, tan.Tracy Brain coral fluoresce brightly under lighting they do best in a well established reef tank aquarium. Food: on micro-plankton or food designed for filter feeding invertebrates . APPROXIMATE SIZE:SM 2 INCHES TO 3, MD 3INCHES TO 4 INCHES,LG 4TO 6

Lobophyllia Red Brain Brain coral is a large polyp stony(LPS) often referred to as a lobed colored ,carpet, flat, or open brain coral meat coral. Lobophyllia has fleshy polyp that hide its calcareous skeleton. It is found in a variety of textures and color forms theirs smooth, while others are pimply and look like carpet.Lobo are semi-aggressive and it will sting other corals with its extended sweeper tentacles during the night, try to provide plenty of space between it and other neighboring corals. They are easy to maintain and making it an candidate for the beginner's. Requires moderate to strong lighting combined with a moderate water movement within the aquarium, addition calcium, strontium and other trace elements to the water. APPROXIMATE SIZE:SM 2INCHES TO 3,MD3 INCHES TO 4 INCHES

Purple Rhodactis Mushroom Purple Rhodactis is also known as the Tonga Blue Mushroom. Less commonly, it is referred to as a Hairy or Small Elephant Ear Mushroom. It usually is a violet to blue color, often with margins and highlights of green. It may have a red mouth, has papillae that form cauliflower-like patterns, and can grow up to 3 inches in diameter. Rhodactis Mushroom Coral is semi aggressive in nature as compared to other marine aquarium invertebrates. It is recommended to keep the Rhodactis Mushroom Coral away from other corals just to avoid the aggressive behavior in the aquarium. It needs low water flow and low illumination for its growth and development. Scientific Name: Rhodactis inchoata Fmaily: Discosomatidae Origin: Tonga ,Fiji Food :symbiotic algae zooxanthellae hosted within its body provide the majority of its nutritional requirements through photosynthesis. It may also eat plankton and small invertebrates. Care: Water flow low and low to moderate lighting Approximate Size : sm 2'' to 3 inches, md 3'' to 4inches

Bullfrog tadpoles look nice and friendly at two inches, but these guys will grow from little mosquito eaters to big fly catchers in no time. Perfect for pest control in the pond; in the aquarium, they will become frogs and run away. Quick Facts Scientific Name Lithobates catesbeianus Origin North America Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful as tadpoles Adult Size Tadpoles up to 6"; adult frogs 6–8" Lifespan Tadpole stage 1–3 years; adult frogs 7–10 years Diet Herbivore (algae and plant matter) Water Temperature 50–80°F pH 6.5–8.0 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Bullfrog tadpoles are best suited to outdoor ponds with plants and algae. Once they grow legs and turn into frogs, they need a way to climb out of the water, and adult bullfrogs often leave the pond. Feeding: Tadpoles graze on algae and plant matter. Also feed algae wafers or a sinking pellet. Tankmates: Tadpoles are peaceful, but adult bullfrogs will eat anything that fits in their mouth, including fish. Good to know: Bullfrog tadpoles can take one to three years to turn into frogs.

The snowball shrimp is a bright white variation, perfect for green planted tanks with a dark base. These shrimp require the same care as other Neocaridina exotic species. Please remember never to add medications to water with shrimp present. Quick Facts Scientific Name Neocaridina davidi (snowball) Origin East Asia (aquarium-bred, mostly Taiwan) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1–1¼" Lifespan 1–2 years Diet Omnivore (grazes on algae) Water Temperature 65–80°F pH 6.5–8.0 Water Hardness GH 6–12 (moderately hard) Group Size Does best in a group (breeds readily) Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Neocaridina are hardy and ideal for beginners. Use a cycled, planted tank with moss, plants and hiding spots, and a sponge filter or a sponge over the filter intake so shrimp aren't pulled in. Keep the water stable. Feeding: Shrimp graze on algae all day. Feed a small amount of quality shrimp food once a day and remove anything uneaten after a few hours. Tankmates: Keep shrimp alone or with tiny, peaceful fish like small rasboras, ember tetras, otocinclus and pygmy corydoras, plus snails. Most fish will eat baby shrimp, and cichlids (even dwarf cichlids like rams and apistogrammas) and larger fish will eat adults. Different Neocaridina colors will crossbreed and lose their color over time. Good to know: Shrimp are very sensitive to copper and many medications. Never treat a tank with shrimp, and check plant fertilizers and treatments for copper.

The long fin tiger oscar, or veil oscar, takes a lot of sorting and breeding to get to our warehouse, so these are a bit more expensive than the classic tiger oscar. The long, flowing fins that get even more pronounced as this fish gets bigger are what that extra money is for! Long fin tiger oscars will eat just about anything, including small fish, but get along with most fish their own size until they get to breeding size; some can get a bit mean at that time. Quick Facts Scientific Name Astronotus ocellatus (long fin tiger variety) Origin Amazon basin, South America; aquarium-bred Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Semi-aggressive; eats smaller fish Adult Size Up to 12–14" Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods; takes pellets) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single or pair Shipping Size Approx. 2½" Care Guide Tank setup: Use a sand bottom, a few large rocks or driftwood, strong filtration and a tight lid, since they can jump. Oscars often rearrange decorations and uproot plants. Feeding: Feed a quality cichlid pellet once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like shrimp. Avoid feeder goldfish, which can carry disease. Tankmates: Oscars can live with other large, peaceful-to-semi-aggressive fish like silver dollars, large plecos, severums and other oscars. They will eat any fish that fits in their mouth. Good to know: Oscars are known as "water puppies" for their personality and often learn to recognize their owners and beg for food.

The Nemo Koi Betta is an even rarer color variant of the rare koi betta, bred to show primarily red and orange colors. The nemo pattern is named for the famous and fictional Disney star. In fact, this show betta color pattern is similar to the classic saltwater clownfish. The pictured betta is 3 inches, fully matured with full color; the betta we ship will get there, but it is 2 inches. Quick Facts Scientific Name Betta splendens Origin Thailand (captive-bred) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Males fight each other; peaceful toward most other fish Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 76–82°F (needs a heater) pH 6.5–7.5 Breathes Air Yes – labyrinth fish take air from the surface Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give him a heater (bettas are tropical fish), a gentle filter and live or silk plants. Plakats are active swimmers and like room to patrol. Keep a lid on the tank and leave a gap of air under it, since bettas breathe from the surface. Feeding: Feed a few betta pellets or a pinch of flake once or twice a day. Bettas overeat easily, so small meals are best. They also enjoy frozen bloodworms. Tankmates: Never keep two male bettas together. Plakats are among the boldest bettas, so they do best alone or with sturdy, peaceful fish like corydoras and snails. Avoid fin-nippers and other labyrinth fish. Good to know: Koi and galaxy bettas carry the "marble" gene, so their colors and patterns can shift throughout their lives. No two look alike for long. Short plakat fins make them sturdy, active swimmers.

listings.commonName: Yasha hase Goby and Red Pistol Shrimp (Pair)
listings.description: Yasha goby fish is a distinctive variety of goby fish known for its fantastic behavior and appearance. It is not very common in the aquarium hobby but is immensely popular among goby enthusiasts. It is a tropical marine fish centered mainly in the Western Pacific Ocean, where it is found inhabiting the outer reef slopes in the depth of 15 to 40 meters. Males are generally smaller than females. Their symbiotic shrimp is almost half the size of them.

The long flowing fins of the tiger barb, along with the natural active disposition of the aquarium species, make this fish very suited to most community tanks that need some beauty and motion. The long fin tiger barbs will breed in captivity, and most offspring will feature the long-fin gene. Barbs are mid-size schooling fish. Tiger barbs are slightly more aggressive than tetras, and larger barbs can handle mid-size African cichlid tanks. Quick Facts Scientific Name Puntigrus tetrazona (long-fin variety) Origin Indonesia (Sumatra, Borneo) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Semi-aggressive (fin-nipper) Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 5–7 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group (helps prevent fin-nipping) Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a filter, a heater and plenty of open swimming space. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Pick fast, sturdy tankmates such as other barbs, danios, loaches, corydoras and larger tetras. Avoid slow, long-finned fish like bettas, angelfish, gouramis and guppies. Good to know: Keep them in a group so they nip each other's fins less, and give them plenty of open swimming space.

Black Nubian hi-fin swordtails have solid black bodies with black and clear fins, and an extra-high dorsal fin. This bred variation is called hi-fin or sailfin. With the clear and black color of the tail, these fish really do look like they are dragging swords. Black Nubian hi-fin swordtails look great against green plants and reflect light with an iridescent sheen. We recommend the purchase of at least one pair, male and female. Pairs will tend to stay together as they swim about the tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name Xiphophorus hellerii (black hi-fin) Origin Southern Mexico to Honduras (wild ancestors); aquarium-bred Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful (males may spar) Adult Size Up to 4–5" (not counting the sword) Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 7.0–8.0 (hard water) Group Size Keep more females than males Shipping Size Approx. 1½–2" Care Guide Tank setup: Swordtails are active swimmers, so give them plants, open swimming space and a tight-fitting lid, since they are good jumpers. They prefer hard, alkaline water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet with some vegetable content once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Swordtails get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as platies, mollies, larger tetras, danios, rainbowfish, gouramis and corydoras. Keep more females than males, since males chase females and may spar with each other. Avoid fin-nippers and large cichlids. Good to know: Lyretail and hi-fin swordtails have extra-long fins, so keep them away from fin-nippers like tiger barbs. Many lyretail males have an elongated gonopodium and can't breed, so lyretail fry usually come from lyretail females mated with standard-finned males.

The sumo loach is named for the broad, colorful band around the body that mimics the belt around a martial artist's waist. And these guys will push each other around to control their own part of the tank, but they are gentle to all other creatures. Since sumo loaches only grow to two inches, large fish such as African cichlids would not be appropriate tank mates. Generally any community species should get along with the sumo loach. These small martial artists stay on the bottom of the fish tank and scavenge for most of their food. Since the loaches are caught in small streams in Burma, they need good aeration in the water; any airstone will work. Quick Facts Scientific Name Schistura balteata Origin Myanmar (Burma) and Thailand Care Level Moderate (needs clean, oxygen-rich water) Temperament Peaceful with other fish; territorial with its own kind Adult Size Up to 2–2½" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore (bottom feeder) Water Temperature 68–77°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single, or a group with plenty of hiding spots Shipping Size Approx. 1½–2" Care Guide Tank setup: These loaches come from clear, flowing streams. Give them a tank with a sand or smooth gravel bottom, rocks and caves to claim, some current and good oxygen. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as danios, rasboras, barbs and tetras. Give each loach its own hiding spot to limit squabbles. Good to know: These loaches are active and curious, and they often perch on rocks to watch the tank.

Also called the convict juli or simply regani cichlid, these striped, slender cichlids belong to a family of small Tanganyikan rock dwellers. The Regani get to 5 inches and are hardy but will not do well in low pH (nothing below 7). The juli regani was discovered by Charles Regan in 1902 at the British Museum of Natural History. Charles was also the same ichthyologist that first classified the popular betta fish, along with 50 other species we find in the aquarium hobby, all without leaving his London office. Quick Facts Scientific Name Julidochromis regani Origin Lake Tanganyika, Africa Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Territorial Adult Size Up to 4–5" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.8–9.0 Shipping Size Approx. 1¼" Care Guide Tank setup: Use a sand bottom with rockwork, caves and crevices for spawning sites. Lake Malawi and Lake Tanganyika cichlids need hard, alkaline water; crushed coral or aragonite sand helps hold the pH up. Feeding: Feed a quality cichlid pellet or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like brine shrimp. Tankmates: Tanganyikan cichlids do best with other Tanganyikans of similar size, such as julidochromis, neolamprologus and synodontis catfish. Give each pair its own territory. Good to know: Julies are rock dwellers that swim upside down and sideways along rock faces. Give them stacked rocks with lots of crevices.

This unique, brilliant rasbora displays red on the tail along with reflective red and gold lateral lines. Bora rasboras, also called red tail rasboras, are active schooling fish and are hardy, handle a wide temperature range and eat flake foods. Rasboras look best in small planted aquariums, and they get along with fancy shrimp and other gentle tank mates, along with tougher species such as angelfish. Quick Facts Scientific Name Rasbora borapetensis Origin Thailand, Cambodia, Laos and Malaysia Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a dark substrate. Soft, slightly acidic water and gentle filtration bring out their best color. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as tetras, other rasboras, danios, corydoras, gouramis and dwarf shrimp. Avoid large predatory fish that could eat them. Good to know: In a well-planted tank a school of rasboras swims together in the middle of the tank, and their colors deepen as they settle in.

These exotic goldfish feature eyes that look right up at you, giving these guys quite a bit of character. A small school of celestial eye goldfish can be quite unnerving. We import celestial eyes from Canton, where the Chinese have been breeding odd variations for generations. Quick Facts Scientific Name Carassius auratus Origin China Care Level Moderate (needs a gentle setup) Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 6" Lifespan 10–15 years, often longer with good care Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 65–75°F (no heater needed in most homes) pH 7.0–8.0 Shipping Size Approx. 2–4" Care Guide Tank setup: Celestial eye goldfish produce a lot of waste, so give them plenty of room and a strong filter. Use smooth decorations and live or silk plants, and keep the water current gentle. Feeding: Feed small amounts of a quality sinking pellet or flake once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. Sinking foods are easier for them to find than floating ones. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them only with other slow-swimming fancy goldfish, such as telescopes, black moors, celestials, bubble eyes, lionheads and ranchus. Avoid faster goldfish like comets, shubunkins and even lively ryukins, which will outcompete them for food. Also avoid tropical fish and fin-nippers. Ponds: Celestial eye goldfish can live in ponds in mild climates, but they are less cold-hardy than comets and shubunkins. Bring them indoors where winters are harsh, and keep them away from fast, aggressive pond fish. Good to know: Their upturned eyes make it hard to see food below them, so feed slow-sinking foods. Like lionheads and ranchus, celestials have no dorsal fin, which makes them slow swimmers.

Stars and Stripes Puffer Stars and Stripes Puffer is referred to as the Whitespotted Pufferfish, or Hispid Pufferfish. It is named appropriately because of its unusual markings of stripes over the top of the body and the spots on its underside making a very attractive and striking pattern. It also features a beak-like mouth that has teeth in both upper jaw as well as lower jaw, is fused into two plates. Like all other puffers, it can also inflate its body with water or air to intimidate predators. Since the Stars and Stripes Puffer may eat invertebrates found in a reef tank, it is not well suited to the reef aquarium. It feeds on a variety of foods including algae, coral, sponges, starfish, mollusks, anemones, urchins and other invertebrates. The Stars and Stripes Puffer is nocturnal hunter just like other puffers, and would nip at slow-moving fish and long-finned fish, but is not aggressive with others in its own family. It is not at all reef safe species and should not be kept in a reef tank. Scientific Name: Arothron hispidus Origin: Indonesia, Fiji Food: krill, raw table shrimp, squid, clam and mussel. It is also a good idea to occasionally supplement with some type of herbivore diet. Shipping Size: 2 to 4 inches

Leporinus fasciatus, or striped leporinus, are great community fish for fish their own size. As they grow, they may consume their very small tank mates like neon tetras. The striped leporinus is a hardy scavenger fish and will eat most anything fed to them. These fish are rare and, though not strikingly colorful, have an unusual body shape and feeding behavior - similar to a headstander. Leporinus prefer to rest in a hidden area but will be active at feeding time. These fish, at some point, will outgrow small fish such as tetras but are suitable for most mid-size and large aquarium pets. Quick Facts Scientific Name Leporinus fasciatus Origin Amazon basin, South America Care Level Easy Temperament Semi-aggressive (eats very small fish) Adult Size Up to 12" Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Omnivore (needs plant matter) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 2–6" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants, driftwood and a tight lid, since they can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or pellet with vegetable content once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They can nip at each other and at long-finned fish. Keep them with robust, fast fish of similar size. Good to know: Leporinus are related to headstanders and often feed with their heads tilted down.

Long nose corydoras, such as the cory septentrionalis (saying the name makes you smarter), have longer snouts, which can give them a kind of puppy dog appearance, and they "sniff" their way about the tank floor. The septentrionalis is one of the more rare cory and as such costs a bit more. Behavior and care are similar to the leopard spot cories like cory julii and cory agassizi. Quick Facts Scientific Name Corydoras septentrionalis Origin Venezuela Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 5–10 years Diet Omnivore (bottom feeder) Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 6.0–7.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and a soft sand or smooth, fine gravel bottom. Plants, driftwood and a few shady spots help them feel secure. Corys are sensitive to salt and some medications (especially copper), so check labels before treating the tank. Feeding: Corys need their own food, not just leftovers. Feed sinking pellets or wafers once or twice a day so food reaches the bottom. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Corys get along with almost any peaceful community fish, such as tetras, rasboras, livebearers, gouramis, angelfish and bettas. Avoid large fish that could swallow them and aggressive bottom dwellers. Good to know: Corys sift through the substrate with their sensitive barbels, so soft sand or smooth, fine gravel keeps those barbels healthy.

The Hognose brochis, or more elegantly named cory multiradiatus, is the largest of the aquarium cory and is caught in the wilds of Ecuador. Hognose brochis look like giant emerald green cory and are about three inches in size. Despite the size, these are gentle giants and scavenge and root around just like little corydoras. The name multiradiatus comes from the 18 rays on the wide dorsal fin. Quick Facts Scientific Name Corydoras multiradiatus (formerly Brochis multiradiatus ) Origin Ecuador and Peru Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 4" Lifespan 5–10 years Diet Omnivore (bottom feeder) Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 3" Care Guide Tank setup: These larger corys need a wide, open sandy bottom, a heater, good filtration and some plants or driftwood for cover. Corys are sensitive to salt and some medications (especially copper), so check labels before treating the tank. Feeding: Corys need their own food, not just leftovers. Feed sinking pellets or wafers once or twice a day so food reaches the bottom. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish, including larger tetras, gouramis, angelfish and other corys. Avoid fish big enough to swallow them. Good to know: Hognose brochis are the largest corys. They need bigger sinking foods than small corys, but are just as peaceful.

Concolor Cory Venezuela Also called the Venezuelan Cory, the concolor cory is rare and has a distinct color pattern. The body is a solid slate with red patches, but the fins and tail have bronze and green colors. These cute little scavengers grow to just under two inches. Like all corys, these dwarf catfish are peaceful and playful aquatic pets. Corydoras prefer to swim in packs of three or more, but will do fine alone. Quick Facts Scientific Name Corydoras concolor Origin Venezuela Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 5–10 years Diet Omnivore (bottom feeder) Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1–2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and a soft sand or smooth, fine gravel bottom. Plants, driftwood and a few shady spots help them feel secure. Corys are sensitive to salt and some medications (especially copper), so check labels before treating the tank. Feeding: Corys need their own food, not just leftovers. Feed sinking pellets or wafers once or twice a day so food reaches the bottom. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Corys get along with almost any peaceful community fish, such as tetras, rasboras, livebearers, gouramis, angelfish and bettas. Avoid large fish that could swallow them and aggressive bottom dwellers. Good to know: Corys sift through the substrate with their sensitive barbels, so soft sand or smooth, fine gravel keeps those barbels healthy.

The eques cory, also called the orange saddle cory, is caught in Colombia and has soft orange markings on the body. This is a pretty little cory and not often available. Hardy and a good scavenger in the tank or a small Venezuelan stream. Quick Facts Scientific Name Corydoras eques Origin Colombia and Brazil Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 5–10 years Diet Omnivore (bottom feeder) Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 6.0–7.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and a soft sand or smooth, fine gravel bottom. Plants, driftwood and a few shady spots help them feel secure. Corys are sensitive to salt and some medications (especially copper), so check labels before treating the tank. Feeding: Corys need their own food, not just leftovers. Feed sinking pellets or wafers once or twice a day so food reaches the bottom. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Corys get along with almost any peaceful community fish, such as tetras, rasboras, livebearers, gouramis, angelfish and bettas. Avoid large fish that could swallow them and aggressive bottom dwellers. Good to know: Corys sift through the substrate with their sensitive barbels, so soft sand or smooth, fine gravel keeps those barbels healthy.

Gold clown barbs are small, wild-caught fish from Malaysia. These little jewels are not often caught and only grow to one inch. The pattern of the gold clown barb is distinct and makes a very pretty school in a small community tank or planted tank. These fish will eat flake food; it is unknown if they breed in the aquarium. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pethia gelius Origin South Asia (wild-caught) Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful, a bit shy Adult Size About 1" Lifespan 4–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 68–77°F pH 6.0–7.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a filter, a heater and plenty of plants. They feel safest with places to hide and show more color in a planted tank. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other small, peaceful fish such as rasboras, small tetras, corydoras and dwarf shrimp. Avoid large or boisterous fish and fin-nippers. Good to know: Their tiny size makes them a great fit for planted tanks, but keep them away from larger, boisterous fish.

The spottail curimata, or redline curimatopsis tetra, is a rare find from Brazil. These small, tetra-like fish belong to a family called the Curimatidae, and the evelinae is one of the smaller, more colorful species. A rare and exotic aquarium species, this fish adapts well to the fish tank, grows to only about an inch and a half and eats flake foods. These are truly for the small-fish aficionado. Quick Facts Scientific Name Curimatopsis evelinae Origin Amazon basin, Brazil Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1½" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 5.5–7.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1¼" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a dark substrate, which brings out their color. Keep a lid on the tank, since tetras can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, rasboras, danios, corydoras, dwarf cichlids, gouramis and livebearers. Good to know: Tetras feel safer and show better color in a group. A larger school also spreads out any chasing.

Pennywort Brazilian pennywort is a pretty round leaf stem plant from the Amazon tropics. Scientific Name: HYDROCOTYLE LEUCOCEPHALA Shipping Size: 5 plants bunched with lead weight, approx. 7 inches tall

The worm line pleco is found under different common names and L numbers; we use the one our exporter prefers. This pretty little pleco comes from the border of Brazil and Colombia and only grows to 5 inches, so it is a perfect aquarium catfish. Worm line plecos are not algae eaters; they are mainly meaty scavengers, so cichlid pellets and similar food will keep them happy, and a little driftwood to hide in will complete their home. Quick Facts Scientific Name Peckoltia braueri (L-121) Origin Rio Negro and upper Orinoco (Brazil, Colombia, Venezuela) Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Peaceful (territorial with other plecos) Adult Size Up to 4–5" Lifespan 10–12+ years Diet Omnivore (sinking foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single, or several with a cave each Shipping Size Approx. 3" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them caves, driftwood and good filtration with some current. A sand or smooth gravel bottom suits them best. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets or wafers, ideally in the evening when they are most active. They also enjoy frozen bloodworms. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish. Give each pleco its own cave to limit territorial squabbles. Good to know: These plecos are most active at night; dim lighting and caves help them feel secure.

Seachem Flourish Plant Food This plant fertilizer has natural minerals and other nutrients for all the basic needs of aquarium plants. Formulated to increase growth rate and promote glossy leaves. Comprehensive supplement for the planted aquarium Provides micro elements, trace elements and other nutrients Does not contain significant levels of nitrogen or phosphorus Each bottle contains 250 ml (9 oz) of plant loving nutrients

The Burmese archer fish, also called the clouded archer fish after the attractive cloud-shaped spots on the body, is a pretty archer wild-caught in Burma. Like the banded archer fish, the Burmese archer fish is peaceful and easy to care for though it will eat very small fish. The dorsal and anal fin are more rounded than the banded archer. In the fish tank, archer fish continue to periodically spit, so don't be surprised to be hit by water from time to time. These fish can tolerate brackish and freshwater conditions. Quick Facts Scientific Name Toxotes blythii Origin Myanmar Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful (eats very small fish) Adult Size Up to 6" Lifespan 10 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Archerfish hunt at the surface, so leave space between the water and the lid. They do best in slightly salty (brackish) water. Keep a lid on the tank. Feeding: Feed floating pellets or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms. Tankmates: They are peaceful but will eat very small fish. Keep them with other brackish fish like scats and monos. Good to know: Archerfish can shoot a jet of water to knock insects off leaves above the water.

Also known as the Dragon Moray Eel, Hawaiian Dragon Moray Eel, and the Dragonface Moray Eel, is a menacing moray eel species found in the Pacific Ocean. Their bodies are mosaics of red, yellow, black, orange, and white markings all over their entire body. Their faces are the most intimidating feature of this specimen. They have incredibly large mouths and sharp teeth coupled with what appears like horns atop its head. Truly a living dragon in the aquarium. Dragon Moray Eels require specific tank conditions to thrive. They can reach up to 24 inches must be kept in a large tank of over 150 gallons that have a tightly secured lid to prevent potential escapes. The tank must also have rock work cavities large enough to accommodate the entire length of the eel inside. They are coral safe, but must not be placed with small inverts or fish that can easily fit into their mouths, as those fish will quickly become prey and should only be kept with large tank mates. Sometimes in the early weeks of their introduction to the tank, the Dragon Moray may not eat at all, this is normal. Because of their poor eyesight, you should never attempt to hand feed the Dragon Moray as they may bite. ****This item does not ship to Texas or Florida**** Scientific Name: Enchelycore pardalis Origin: Japan, Pacific Ocean Max Size: 36 inches Diet: Carnivore Shipping Size: 12 inches
