General Starfish: The Striking, but Predatory, Centerpiece The General Starfish (Protoreaster linckii) is a visually stunning marine invertebrate often sought after for its vibrant colors and imposing size. Also widely recognized as the African Red Knob Starfish or Red Knob Sea Star , this species features a thick, robust body, typically a pale gray or tan color, adorned with numerous bright red or orange tubercles (knobs) that are often connected by a striking, grid-like pattern of red stripes. This is a major species in the aquarium trade, both in terms of popularity and physical size, easily reaching 10 to 12 inches (25-30 cm) in diameter. While hardy, the General Starfish is a carnivorous predator and is not suitable for a mixed reef aquarium. It is best kept in large Fish-Only (F/O) or FOWLR (Fish Only With Live Rock) systems where its tank mates are safe from predation. Diet & Compatibility: Profile: The General Starfish is a Carnivore / Omnivore. As it grows, it relies heavily on meaty foods to sustain its large body mass. Feeding Habit: It must be target fed regularly (once or twice a week is standard) with substantial pieces of food. Use items like chopped clam, squid, mussel, or fresh shrimp, placing the food directly on the substrate near the starfish's underside to ensure consumption. Aquarium Environment: Due to its potential size, a minimum tank size of 75-100 gallons is strongly recommended. It demands a highly stable environment and is extremely sensitive to fluctuations in salinity, pH, and water quality. High nitrates are poorly tolerated. Reef Compatibility: NOT Reef Safe. This starfish is a known predator of sessile (non-moving) invertebrates. It will consume soft corals, sponges, clams, tubeworms, and even other smaller starfish if it can reach them. Handling Caution: Drip acclimation (1.5-2 hours) is essential to avoid osmotic shock. NEVER expose the starfish to open air during transfer, as this can trap air bubbles inside its water vascular system, which is fatal. Tank Mates: Only house the General Starfish with large, non-aggressive fish. Exclude all known star-predators like Harlequin Shrimp and some Pufferfish or Triggerfish species. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Protoreaster linckii Primary Common Name: General Starfish Other Common Names: African Red Knob Starfish, Red Knob Sea Star, Red-knobbed Starfish Origin: Indian Ocean (Coast of Africa, Indo-Pacific) Max Size: 10–12 inches (25–30 cm) Temperament: Semi-Aggressive (Predatory) Diet: Carnivore (Requires target feeding) Minimum Tank Size: 75+ Gallons Reef Compatibility: NOT Reef Safe

Green Pavona Pavona are commonly referred to as Cactus Corals as several of their growth forms resemble cacti. They are a fast growing SPS Coral and can quickly form a large colony from a single frag. They are considered one of the easiest SPS corals to care for. These corals form thin plates as branches that are covered with polyps giving it a fuzzy appearance. Its color varies from shades of light and dark brown to green with cream or white margins. They have a fluorescent glow that can be seen beneath the polyps, giving these corals an interesting look. Scientific Name: Pavona Decussatus Origin: Indo, Fiji and Tonga Diet: Micro-plankton or brine shrimp when the tentacles are visible Care: Strong water flow and moderate high lighting Shipping Size: 2 to 6 inches

Wellsi Red Blastomussa Coral Blastomussa is a LPS ,have much lager visible mouths so corals like this are lot easiest to see, very peaceful coral and can be found in many different colors like blue, red, brown and green. It's body contains the symbiotic algae zooxanthellae from which it receives the majority of its nutritional requirements through photosynthesis. It does not require additional food to maintain its health in the reef aquarium, it will feed on micro-plankton or foods designed for filter feeding invertebrates. Shipping size: 2 to 5 inches

Candy Stripe Coral Please ask for a color you're looking for. As this picture is a reference. The Candy Cane Coral (LPS) gets it's common name from the alternating stripes on it's polyps. This candy cane coral has a striped pattern on top of the polyp with usually a solid colored interior part of the polyp. There are a few different color variations including brown, green and cream colors, purple, usually with alternating white stripes. Candy cane corals fluoresce magnificently under blue moon lights, making it look like something from outer space when viewing the tank at night when the aquarium lights are off. Scientific Name: Caulastrea Furcata Diet: brine shrimp or micro-plankton. Approximate Size: 2 to 5 inches

Acan Echinata The Acan Echinata Acanthastrea echinata is a colorful large polyp stony (LPS). They are found in some intense oranges to intense green and red combinations. The Echinata Coral is the second most popular and sought after of the Acanthastrea species, following the Acan lord A. lordhowensis . Some descriptive names the A. echinata are known by include Echinata Coral, Starry Cup Coral, Artichoke Coral, Pineapple coral, Rainbow Acanthastrea, Rainbow Acan, and Acan Brain Coral.Be aware that Acanthastrea are voracious nocturnal predators and competitively extrude mesenterial filaments and digest organisms within reach. Great care must be taken in determining the placement and distance between Acan Brain Coral colonies. Feed minced meaty foods and zooplankton for best growth and frag recovery time. The use of a quality protein skimmer helps maintain water quality and combat the effects of heavy feeding. Scientific Name: Acanthastrea echinata Family: Mussidea Approximate Size: sm 2 to 3 inches, md 3 to 4 inches,lg 4 to 6 inches Care: Moderate water flow low, moderate lighting

Green Torch Coral Frag Often referred to as Trumpet Coral or Pom-Pom Coral. Provide plenty of room between the Euphyllia Torch Coral and other sessile animals, since at night its sweeper tentacles can extend up to several inches from its base and sting other coral species. Scientific Name: Euphyllia glabrescens Diet: micro-plankton or brine shrimp.

listings.commonName: Super Red L-144 Bushynose Pleco Long-fin
listings.description: A magnificent variation of the already stunning super red bushynose! Like the super red bushynose, this exotic captive-bred aquarium fish will display a solid bright orange to red color (spirulina wafers will really help bring out the red), and they will grow exceptionally long fins. They are shipped small, so have good-quality pleco wafers ready, and do not stock them with large, aggressive tank fish. Pictured are young long fins without any color enhancement, still a nice pretty rust color. Quick Facts Scientific Name Ancistrus sp. (super red long fin variety) Origin Aquarium-bred (local breeder) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful (males guard caves) Adult Size Up to 4–5" Lifespan 10–12 years Diet Herbivore (algae and plant-based foods) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single, pair or group with a cave each Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Bristlenose plecos do well in most community tanks. Give them driftwood to rasp on, caves or hiding spots, and good filtration. They keep glass, rocks and plants clean of algae. Feeding: They graze on algae, but also feed algae wafers. Tankmates: Bristlenose plecos get along with nearly all community fish, plus shrimp and snails. Avoid large aggressive fish that might harass them. Good to know: Males grow larger, bushier "bristles" on the snout than females. Bristlenose plecos stay small and are one of the best algae-eaters for home aquariums.

Torch Coral This coral also known as Euphyllia glabrescens, is often referred to as Trumpet Coral or Pom-Pom Coral. It has long and flowing polyps with single rounded tips which are visible throughout the day and night, hiding its branching skeletal base most of the time. Its sweeper tentacles can extend up to several inches from its base and sting other coral species.Can also be frag and sell per heads. Approximate Purchase Size: 2 inches to 3 inches Scientific Name: Euphyllia Glabrescens Diet: It will also benefit from additional food fed weekly in the form of micro-plankton or brine shrimp.

Goniopora Green Flowerpot Coral Is often referred to as Flowerpot, Daisy coral, ball coral, or sunflower coral. It is not overly aggressive but space should still be provided between itself and other neighboring corals, its polyps can extend far past its base into the reef aquarium where it can sting other species of corals. Also comes in other colors, clownfish will often be found in association with the flowerpot coral and play in its polyps if no anemone can be found in the tank. Goniopora flowerpot require addition calcium, strontium and other trace elements to the water. Scientific Name: Goniopora stokesi Diet: micro-plankton or brine shrimp. Care: Water flow medium, moderate lighting Shipping Size: 2 to 7 inches

Pink Stylophora Coral is a small polyp stony (SPS) .It is a beautiful pink in color, and is able to adapt to many different lighting and water flow regimes in the aquarium. The Stylophora genus is one of the better known, and well studied groups of corals. The Club Finger Coral S. pistillata, also known as the Cat's Paw Coral, forms attractive branching colonies. They are wide spread in nature, fast growing, and can adapt to many conditions. The branches are flat and thick, with round blunt tips. The polyps are small, yet visible and extend at night in the wild, but both day and night in a captive reef. The colors they come in are cream, pink, blue, and greens. Scientific Name : Stylophora spp. Food: Micro-plankton or foods designed for filter feeding invertebrates in the evening when its polyps are expanded. Care: water flow strong and Moderate to High lighting Approximate Size : Sm 2" to 3"; Md 3" to 4"; Large: 4" to 5 inches

Tricolor Acropora Acropora are one of the primary reef builders in world oceans and they are highly sought after by reef tank hobbyists for their remarkable growth rates and intense colors. Fragging acroporas can also multiply your tank and sales. There are literally tons of different species of acropora (pronounced ah-crop-orah or ak-roh-pohr-ah). You can find them in many different colors like blue, green, purple, brown, yellow, pink, spotting colors. Requires high lighting, high variable and turbulent water flow, stable water temperature 75-82f (24-28c), high level of calcium and strontium and other trace elements to the water. Family: Acroporidae Diet: Feeding micro-plankton or food designed for filter feeding. Approximate Size: 2 to 3 inches ORIGN : TONGA

Only the male guppy of this variation features the unique lyre tail, but to produce young with lyre tails, these guppies need to be mated with the proper females. Quick Facts Scientific Name Poecilia reticulata Origin Northern South America (captive-bred) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Sold as a pair (1 male + 1 female) Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and plenty of plants, including some floating plants where babies can hide. Guppies like slightly hard water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Guppies get along with other small, peaceful fish such as platies, mollies, corydoras, small tetras and rasboras. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs and larger fish that could eat them. Breeding: Guppies are livebearers and breed easily. Females give birth to live babies about once a month, and adults will eat the babies, so thick plants give them a place to hide. Good to know: Lyretail guppies have long points on the top and bottom of the tail, shaped like a lyre.

Neon Orange Lobsters are bred for a vivid, bright, solid orange body. As they grow, they shed their shells. Soft-shelled (naked) crayfish are totally vulnerable until their shells re-harden and need a place to hide. Neon red lobsters, like all decapods, grow by eating lots of food and sucking in lots of water. This action eventually cracks their shells open, then they wriggle out of their former armor and hide while their new larger exoskeleton hardens. Neon orange lobsters cannot be kept with small shrimp or small schooling fish and will act like bullies to defend their home. Quick Facts Scientific Name Procambarus clarkii Origin Captive-bred (Florida) Care Level Easy Temperament Semi-aggressive Adult Size Up to 5–6" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (scavenger) Water Temperature 65–80°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 2–3" Care Guide Tank setup: Crayfish need plenty of hiding places like caves or pipes and a tight-fitting lid, since they climb out. Avoid copper-based medications. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets once a day. They also eat vegetables and leftover food. Tankmates: Crayfish will catch and eat slow fish, shrimp and snails. They are best kept alone. Molting: Crayfish shed their shell to grow. Leave the old shell in the tank; they eat it to regain calcium. Good to know: These "lobsters" are actually a color form of the red swamp crayfish.

The lemon cory is a rare little catfish from Peru featuring a light yellow body and small black spots. These fish are shy and prefer to travel with a few others of their kind; we recommend a school of three or more. Quick Facts Scientific Name Corydoras sychri Origin Peru Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1½" Lifespan 5–10 years Diet Omnivore (bottom feeder) Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 6.0–7.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and a soft sand or smooth, fine gravel bottom. Plants, driftwood and a few shady spots help them feel secure. Corys are sensitive to salt and some medications (especially copper), so check labels before treating the tank. Feeding: Corys need their own food, not just leftovers. Feed sinking pellets or wafers once or twice a day so food reaches the bottom. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Corys get along with almost any peaceful community fish, such as tetras, rasboras, livebearers, gouramis, angelfish and bettas. Avoid large fish that could swallow them and aggressive bottom dwellers. Good to know: Lemon corys are shy and come out more in a group with plenty of plant cover.

The polar blue parrot fish, also known as the polar blue convict cichlid, is a beautiful new hybrid that is finding fast approval among cichlid enthusiasts. The parent convict cichlid is one of the easiest and hardiest fish in the hobby, and the polar blue variation is just as hardy. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hybrid ( Amatitlania nigrofasciata / convict cichlid cross) Origin Aquarium-bred (Florida) Care Level Easy Temperament Semi-aggressive (territorial, especially when breeding) Adult Size Up to 6" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Single or pair Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a sand or gravel bottom, rocks, caves and driftwood to create territories. Anchor decorations well, since they like to dig. Strong filtration is important. Feeding: Feed a quality cichlid pellet or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other robust Central American cichlids of similar size, plus larger catfish and plecos. Give each fish its own territory, and avoid small or timid fish. Good to know: Central American cichlids are hardy and easy to breed. Pairs become very protective of their eggs and fry.

The checkerboard loach is named after the checkerboard pattern along its long, narrow body. Also called the checkerboard sand loach, this active and very friendly pet fish likes to dig in the substrate and look for food. Though the fish grows to nearly four inches, this loach will get along with nearly every member of a community fish tank. The narrow head looks a bit like a horse's, and if a couple of these are in the tank together, they tend to pal around. Hardy but not good for temperatures higher than 80 degrees, the checkerboard sand loach will eat prepared and frozen foods. Quick Facts Scientific Name Nemacheilus masyai Origin Southeast Asia (Thailand and Malaysia) Care Level Moderate (needs clean, oxygen-rich water) Temperament Peaceful with other fish; territorial with its own kind Adult Size Up to 3–4" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore (bottom feeder) Water Temperature 68–77°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single, or a group with plenty of hiding spots Shipping Size Approx. 1½–2" Care Guide Tank setup: These loaches come from clear, flowing streams. Give them a tank with a sand or smooth gravel bottom, rocks and caves to claim, some current and good oxygen. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as danios, rasboras, barbs and tetras. Give each loach its own hiding spot to limit squabbles. Good to know: These loaches are active and curious, and they often perch on rocks to watch the tank.

The King Kong variety of Parrot Cichlids is a morph of three different hybrids and gets larger than the "standard" parrot cichlid. The purple color of the King Kong parrot is a reddish purple and they will hold their color as they age. For parrot cichlid enthusiasts, this is a very desirable pet fish. Parrot fish will get along with fish their same size, but will eat smaller neighbors. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hybrid cichlid Origin Captive-bred hybrid (Thailand) Care Level Easy Temperament Semi-aggressive (eats smaller fish) Adult Size Up to 10–12" Lifespan 10–12 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 76–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 3" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them caves, rocks or driftwood, a smooth bottom and good filtration. Feeding: Feed a quality floating cichlid pellet once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: King Kong parrots get along with fish their own size but will eat smaller neighbors. Keep them with robust fish such as other parrots, larger cichlids and plecos. Good to know: King Kong parrots grow larger than regular parrot cichlids and keep their color as they age.

The jewel cichlid is an aptly named bright red and reflective spotted African cichlid. These aquarium cichlids are egg layers that readily breed in the fish tank. Jewel cichlids are territorial and aggressive, so keep them with other African species of similar size. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hemichromis lifalili Origin Congo River basin, Africa Care Level Easy Temperament Aggressive (especially when breeding) Adult Size Up to 4–5" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Shipping Size Approx. 1½–2" Care Guide Tank setup: West African cichlids prefer soft to neutral water. Use a sand or fine gravel bottom with plants, driftwood and caves or flowerpots for spawning. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with peaceful community fish like tetras, barbs, rasboras, corydoras and plecos. Give each pair its own territory, and expect more defensiveness when breeding. Good to know: Jewel cichlids are very protective parents and can be fierce while guarding fry. Keep them as a pair or with sturdy fish.

The vulpinus tetra is the bigger, scarier cousin of the payara vampire tetra. This species of saber-tooth tetra gets twice the weight of Hydrolycus payara and even bigger fangs. In all other respects, the vulpinus has the same temperament and requirements as the payara. Quick Facts Scientific Name Rhaphiodon vulpinus Origin Amazon, Orinoco and Paraná basins Care Level Difficult Temperament Predatory; eats smaller fish Adult Size Up to 30" Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Carnivore (eats smaller fish) Water Temperature 76–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Usually kept singly Shipping Size Small: approx. 3" · Medium: approx. 4" · Large: approx. 6" Care Guide Tank setup: These are large, fast predators that need powerful filtration, strong current, high oxygen and a heavy, tight lid. They are skittish, so avoid sudden movements and bright lights. Feeding: Young fish may need meaty foods at first, and many can be trained to take frozen foods and pellets. Avoid feeder goldfish, which can carry disease. Tankmates: Keep them only with large, robust fish too big to swallow, such as large catfish, arowanas and big cichlids. Good to know: These fish have long, saber-like teeth and are popular with monster-fish keepers, but they grow very large and need experienced care.

The gold angelfish is free of black colors and has gold edges on the fins and body. Gold angelfish, like most angelfish, are hardy and easy to care for. This particular variation tends not to be overbred and will do well in most community fish tanks. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pterophyllum scalare Origin Amazon basin, South America (captive-bred) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Semi-aggressive (territorial when pairing) Adult Size Up to 6" long and 8" tall Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Shipping Size Approx. 1½–4" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them tall plants or driftwood, a heater and a gentle filter. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Choose peaceful fish too large to swallow, such as larger tetras, corydoras, plecos, rams, gouramis and peaceful barbs. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs, and small fish like neon tetras that adult angels may eat. Breeding: Angelfish pair off and lay eggs on flat surfaces like broad leaves or slate. A breeding pair can become territorial, so give them room and places for other fish to retreat. Good to know: Adult angelfish will eat any fish small enough to fit in their mouths, including neon tetras, so choose tankmates that are too big to swallow.

Spotted raphael catfish have a rough hide and white-spotted black body. The raphael catfish are part of a family of talking catfish from Peru. Talking catfish make grunting noises when stressed, and if you want to hear it, just catch one in a net. Please remember that stress is harmful and should be minimized for any creature! Raphael catfish are caught in small, slow streams feeding tributaries of the Amazon. These fish are gentle pet fish that scavenge at night and will not harm other fish. However, catfish will accidentally swallow small tankmates. Quick Facts Scientific Name Agamyxis pectinifrons Origin Amazon basin, Peru Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 5–6" Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 3" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them caves, driftwood and a soft bottom. They hide during the day and come out at night. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets once a day, ideally in the evening when they are most active. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms. Tankmates: They are peaceful and armored, so they get along with most fish, including many cichlids. They may eat very small fish. Good to know: Raphael catfish are armored with bony plates and spines, so use a container rather than a net when moving them.

Striped raphael catfish have a rough hide and white lines along the length of the dark body. The raphael catfish are part of a family of talking catfish from Peru. Talking catfish make grunting noises when stressed, and if you want to hear it, just catch one in a net. Please remember that stress is harmful and should be minimized for any creature! Raphael catfish are caught in small, slow streams feeding tributaries of the Amazon. These fish are gentle pet fish that scavenge at night and will not harm other fish. However, catfish will accidentally swallow small tankmates. The lined pattern is a little more common than the spotted pattern. Quick Facts Scientific Name Platydoras armatulus Origin Amazon basin, Peru Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 6" Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them caves, driftwood and a soft bottom. They hide during the day and come out at night. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets once a day, ideally in the evening when they are most active. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms. Tankmates: They are peaceful and armored, so they get along with most fish, including many cichlids. They may eat very small fish. Good to know: Raphael catfish are armored with bony plates and spines, so use a container rather than a net when moving them.

Guppy feeders are small and inexpensive fish to feed smaller predator fish or to grow out to become colorful little aquarium livebearers. Each pack comes with about 40 fish, give or take 5%. These feeder guppies are hardy but do require an airstone and clean water. In general, feeder fish can tolerate temperatures from the 60s to the low 80s. Quick Facts Scientific Name Poecilia reticulata Origin Northern South America (captive-bred) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1½" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 60–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Sold as a pack of 40 Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and plenty of plants, including some floating plants where babies can hide. Guppies like slightly hard water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Guppies get along with other small, peaceful fish such as platies, mollies, corydoras, small tetras and rasboras. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs and larger fish that could eat them. Breeding: Guppies are livebearers and breed easily. Females give birth to live babies about once a month, and adults will eat the babies, so thick plants give them a place to hide. Good to know: Feeder guppies are hardy, and extras can be grown out as colorful pets.

Flashy and fast, leopard danios add a lot of schooling action to any aquarium, and they get along with everyone. The leopard danio boasts instantly recognizable little spots all over the body, like a little wild leopard cat. A favorite for beginners, Danio rerio comes in several bred variations, and the leopard pattern is one of the most popular. Quick Facts Scientific Name Danio rerio (leopard variety) Origin India, Bangladesh and Nepal (Ganges region) (captive-bred) Care Level Very easy, great for beginners Temperament Peaceful, very active Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 64–77°F (often fine without a heater) pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Danios are fast swimmers, so give them open swimming space, a filter, plants around the edges and a tight-fitting lid, since they jump. Make sure the tank is fully cycled (which takes several weeks) before adding fish. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Danios get along with most peaceful community fish, such as tetras, rasboras, barbs, corydoras and livebearers. Their speed can stress slow, long-finned fish like bettas and fancy guppies, and large predatory fish will eat them. Good to know: Leopard danios are a spotted form of the zebra danio, once thought to be a separate species ("Danio frankei"). Danios are fast and jump when startled, so keep a lid on the tank.

The Koi Betta is a highly sought color variation that comes in roundtail (plakat) and veil tail fins. The koi betta has a variable color pattern that features red, white, and black and is named after the color pattern of the sanke and showa koi found in ponds. No two koi bettas have the same pattern, but all koi bettas are truly rare. The roundtail shape is prized by not very nice Thai who prefer this body type for betta fighting; the body tends to be stronger and the tail is harder to grab. Quick Facts Scientific Name Betta splendens Origin Thailand (captive-bred) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Males fight each other; peaceful toward most other fish Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 76–82°F (needs a heater) pH 6.5–7.5 Breathes Air Yes – labyrinth fish take air from the surface Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give him a heater (bettas are tropical fish), a gentle filter and live or silk plants. Plakats are active swimmers and like room to patrol. Keep a lid on the tank and leave a gap of air under it, since bettas breathe from the surface. Feeding: Feed a few betta pellets or a pinch of flake once or twice a day. Bettas overeat easily, so small meals are best. They also enjoy frozen bloodworms. Tankmates: Never keep two male bettas together. Plakats are among the boldest bettas, so they do best alone or with sturdy, peaceful fish like corydoras and snails. Avoid fin-nippers and other labyrinth fish. Good to know: Koi and galaxy bettas carry the "marble" gene, so their colors and patterns can shift throughout their lives. No two look alike for long. Short plakat fins make them sturdy, active swimmers.

Here is another Tanganyikan that is so rare that we have to say the full name; apparently only common fish get common names. Though territorial, the fish are not large and do well with other African cichlids. These cichlids are maternal mouthbrooders, and the moms have distinct large mouths, for sifting sand as well as rearing young. Quick Facts Scientific Name Enantiopus kilesa Origin Lake Tanganyika, Africa Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful for a cichlid Adult Size Up to 4–5" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.8–9.0 Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a fine sand bottom and plenty of open swimming space, with a few rocks along the back. Lake Malawi and Lake Tanganyika cichlids need hard, alkaline water; crushed coral or aragonite sand helps hold the pH up. Feeding: Feed a quality small pellet or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like brine shrimp. Tankmates: They do best with other peaceful Tanganyikans such as cyprichromis, calvus, frontosa (when large enough) and synodontis catfish. Keep them in a group. Good to know: Kilesa are sand sifters that need a wide, open sandy bottom and calm tankmates. Males dig spawning pits in the sand.

The red gold honey dwarf gourami features the gold of the honey dwarf gourami and the red of the fire red dwarf gourami, and only grows to 1 1/2 to 2 inches. This species is bred in Florida for color and temperament, and the red gold dwarf gourami is a terrific addition to peaceful community aquariums and planted tanks. Click here for school of 4 and save Quick Facts Scientific Name Trichogaster chuna Origin India and Bangladesh (bred in Florida) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 4–6 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Breathes Air Yes – labyrinth fish take air from the surface Shipping Size Approx. 1–1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and plenty of plants, including some floating plants for cover. Keep a lid on the tank and leave a gap of air above the water, since gouramis breathe from the surface. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with small, peaceful fish such as rasboras, small tetras, corydoras and otocinclus. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs and larger, boisterous fish. Good to know: Honey gouramis are among the most peaceful gouramis, which makes them a great first gourami for a community tank.

One of the rarest and most color-textured peacock cichlids is the aulonocara hueseri, or the midnight peacock cichlid. Like all peacock cichlids, the beauty of this fish becomes more pronounced as it ages; too bad I cannot say that for the author. The night peacock cichlid will begin to show the rare black dorsal fin and blue and yellow body at 3 inches. Quick Facts Scientific Name Aulonocara hueseri Origin Lake Malawi, Africa Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Semi-aggressive (males territorial) Adult Size Up to 4–5" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 76–82°F pH 7.8–8.6 Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a sand bottom, open swimming space in front and rockwork along the back. Lake Malawi and Lake Tanganyika cichlids need hard, alkaline water; crushed coral or aragonite sand helps hold the pH up. Feeding: Feed a quality cichlid pellet or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like brine shrimp. Tankmates: Haps do well with peacocks and other haps of similar size, plus robust catfish like synodontis. Keep one male per similar-looking species, with several females, to limit fighting and crossbreeding. Good to know: Males take a year or more to show full adult color, and color best when females are present.

The bloodfin tetra, often confused with the glass bloodfin tetra, has a solid bluish-silver body with bright red fins. A group of these fish makes a very pretty school in the fish tank. The bloodfin tetra is a peaceful, very active and hardy species. Long-lived for a small fish and active most of the day. Quick Facts Scientific Name Aphyocharax anisitsi Origin Paraná basin (Argentina, Paraguay, Brazil) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 64–82°F (tolerates cooler water) pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a dark substrate, which brings out their color. Keep a lid on the tank, since tetras can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, rasboras, danios, corydoras, dwarf cichlids, gouramis and livebearers. Good to know: Tetras feel safer and show better color in a group. A larger school also spreads out any chasing.

The long fin white skirt tetra is the parent fish of the fluorescent long fin GloFish tetras. Natural skirts come in two variations: the one featured here, the white skirt tetra, and the black skirt tetra. One white skirt tetra plus one gene of a jellyfish equals one GloFish tetra. (Zebra danios are the parent fish for GloFish danios.) These are great schooling fish that will grow to about 2 inches and also contrast well with their more colorful cousins. We recommend a few of these with the GloFish tetras. The long fin, or hi-fin, variation of the white skirt tetra is bred to display a high dorsal fin and long, flowing white anal and caudal fins. Quick Facts Scientific Name Gymnocorymbus ternetzi (white long fin variety) Origin Aquarium-bred Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful (may nip long fins) Adult Size Up to 2¼" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a dark substrate, which brings out their color. Keep a lid on the tank, since tetras can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, rasboras, danios, corydoras, dwarf cichlids, gouramis and livebearers. Good to know: Tetras feel safer and show better color in a group. A larger school also spreads out any chasing.

Cory melanistius is a lesser-known leopard-spotted cory from Peru and Colombia. These little catfish are similar to Cory julii: they like to school, they do not grow very large, and they are very friendly. Quick Facts Scientific Name Corydoras melanistius Origin South America Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 5–10 years Diet Omnivore (bottom feeder) Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and a soft sand or smooth, fine gravel bottom. Plants, driftwood and a few shady spots help them feel secure. Corys are sensitive to salt and some medications (especially copper), so check labels before treating the tank. Feeding: Corys need their own food, not just leftovers. Feed sinking pellets or wafers once or twice a day so food reaches the bottom. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Corys get along with almost any peaceful community fish, such as tetras, rasboras, livebearers, gouramis, angelfish and bettas. Avoid large fish that could swallow them and aggressive bottom dwellers. Good to know: Corys sift through the substrate with their sensitive barbels, so soft sand or smooth, fine gravel keeps those barbels healthy.

The black tiger dario is a rare small freshwater species from ponds in Burma (Myanmar) where they feed on tiny pond crustaceans and insects. Because of that, some frozen food should be used to transition these beautiful little fish to pellet and flake foods. The black tiger dario are perfect for planted aquariums and nano tanks. Males have very deep, rich colors and show more when in the presence of females. We try to ship an even number of both, as these fish tend to do better in small groups. Quick Facts Scientific Name Dario sp. Origin Myanmar Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful (males spar with each other) Adult Size Up to 1" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Carnivore (tiny meaty foods) Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group with plenty of hiding spots Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a planted tank with caves, leaf litter and gentle filtration. They are shy and like plenty of hiding places. Feeding: Badis are shy eaters that prefer small frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Some will learn to take small pellets once settled. Feed small amounts once or twice a day. Tankmates: Keep them with small, calm fish such as rasboras, pygmy corydoras and shrimp. Avoid fast, pushy fish that would outcompete them for food. Good to know: Males show their deepest colors when females are around.

The Galaxy Betta presents an explosion of bright colors without any pattern but chaos. These variations are highly prized by Thai breeders to add color to their breeding stock and are a bit pricier than "standard" show bettas. There are many names for the particular betta color patterns, but most are variations of blue and/or red colors. Fish pictured here are representative only. If you are looking for a specific coloration, please note it on your order, or simply allow us to choose one of our favorites for you! Quick Facts Scientific Name Betta splendens Origin Thailand (captive-bred) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Males fight each other; peaceful toward most other fish Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 76–82°F (needs a heater) pH 6.5–7.5 Breathes Air Yes – labyrinth fish take air from the surface Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give him a heater (bettas are tropical fish), a gentle filter and live or silk plants. Floating plants or a "betta leaf" near the surface give him a place to rest. Keep a lid on the tank and leave a gap of air under it, since bettas breathe from the surface. Feeding: Feed a few betta pellets or a pinch of flake once or twice a day. Bettas overeat easily, so small meals are best. They also enjoy frozen bloodworms. Tankmates: Never keep two male bettas together. A male can live with small, peaceful fish that don't nip fins, such as corydoras, small rasboras, otocinclus and snails. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs and flashy, long-finned fish like fancy guppies. Good to know: Koi and galaxy bettas carry the "marble" gene, so their colors and patterns can shift throughout their lives. No two look alike for long.

The green lizard loach is part of the hillstream loach family and goes by several common names, including gecko loach and Tweedie's hillstream loach (after the discoverer). Green lizard loaches come from Indonesia and are wild-caught and not often available for us hobbyists. The freshwater loach is hardy, peaceful and adapts well to most aquariums. However, these are mountain loaches and will not tolerate water temperatures above 80 degrees. These loaches can even be kept in indoor aquariums without heaters. Quick Facts Scientific Name Homalopteroides tweediei Origin Malaysia and Indonesia Care Level Moderate (needs cool, fast, oxygen-rich water) Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Algae eater Water Temperature 68–75°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Hillstream loaches come from fast, clear mountain streams. Give them smooth rocks, strong current, lots of oxygen and cool water. They graze on algae, so a mature tank with algae-covered rocks is ideal. Feeding: Hillstream loaches graze on algae. Also feed algae wafers or sinking pellets. Tankmates: Hillstream loaches do well with peaceful fish that like cool, flowing water, such as white clouds, danios, rasboras and dwarf shrimp. Avoid tropical fish that need warm water. Good to know: Hillstream loaches cling to rocks and glass with their flat, sucker-like bodies, just like they do in fast mountain streams.

Breeders work with several variations to bring out a platy that has all the colors of the rainbow: blues, reds, yellows, and black. The rainbow platy is diversity at its finest, and these platies are as hardy and adaptable as any of the other straighter variations. Quick Facts Scientific Name Xiphophorus maculatus Origin Southern Mexico and Central America Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 3–4 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 70–80°F pH 7.0–8.2 Breeding Livebearer – breeds easily in the aquarium Care Guide Tank setup: Platies are hardy and easy to keep. Give them a filter, a lid and plenty of plants. Use a heater to keep the water steady in the 70s. They prefer harder, slightly alkaline water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. Platies also need some plant matter, so a vegetable flake is a good choice. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Platies get along with most peaceful community fish, such as other livebearers (mollies, guppies and swordtails), tetras, rasboras and corydoras. Avoid large or aggressive fish that may bully or eat them. Breeding: Platies are livebearers, so a tank with males and females will almost certainly have babies (fry). Adults will eat fry, so add dense plants or use a breeding box if you want to raise them. Keeping more females than males gives the females a break from the males' attention. Good to know: Platies are one of the easiest fish to keep, which makes them a great choice for a first aquarium.

The starry night eel is a completely freshwater eel with a spotted pattern like the stars in the sky. These eels are caught in slow-moving streams that feed Lake Tanganyika in the Congo delta. Starry night eels are peaceful and will eat frozen foods, but they are known to eat very small tankmates if they fit in their mouth. These eels are not nippers and get along well with cichlids, rainbowfish, sailfin molly, and other fish of similar size. Quick Facts Scientific Name Mastacembelus frenatus Origin Lake Tanganyika and Congo basin, Africa Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful (eats very small fish) Adult Size Up to 14" Lifespan 10 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.5–8.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 4–5" Care Guide Tank setup: Spiny eels like to burrow, so give them a soft sand bottom, plants and hiding places. They are expert escape artists, so a tight-fitting lid is a must. Feeding: Feed frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp once a day. Some learn to take sinking pellets. Tankmates: They are peaceful but will eat very small fish. Keep them with community fish too large to fit in their mouth. Good to know: Starry night eels are true freshwater spiny eels, not real eels, and they like to burrow with just their head poking out.

The albino threadfin geophagus is a bit more dramatic than your typical albino cichlid morph. These exotic cichlids are bred in Taiwan and display the classic long fins of the parent threadfin heckelii, in vivid pink tones. Quick Facts Scientific Name Acarichthys heckelii (albino variety) Origin Amazon basin (wild ancestors); bred in Taiwan Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful (territorial when breeding) Adult Size Up to 8" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore (sifts sand for food) Water Temperature 77–84°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Eartheaters sift sand through their gills, so use a fine sand bottom (no sharp gravel). Give them open sand areas, driftwood and some rocks. Good filtration and clean water are important. Feeding: Feed a quality sinking pellet or granule once or twice a day. Sinking foods let them feed naturally by sifting the sand. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Eartheaters do well with other peaceful South American fish of similar size, such as angelfish, severums, festivums, larger tetras, hatchetfish and plecos. Avoid aggressive cichlids that would bully them. Good to know: Many eartheaters are mouthbrooders. Watch for parents taking eggs or fry into their mouths for protection.

The pom pom crab is a rare find in the high mountains of Taiwan and seldom exported to the USA. These small crabs are fully aquatic, but they will still try to escape the aquarium so there needs to be a good cover or several inches of glass so they cannot climb out. Pom pom crabs use their "pom pom" filaments to catch detritus for feeding and are quite a little spectacle when they do feed. Sinking pellets and scavenging should keep these guys happy. Quick Facts Scientific Name Ptychognathus barbatus Origin Taiwan Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1½" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Scavenger (sinking pellets, leftover food) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a mature, planted tank with rocks and hiding places, and keep a lid on the tank. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets or shrimp food once a day. They also scavenge leftover food. Tankmates: They are peaceful and do well with shrimp, snails and small peaceful fish. Good to know: Pom pom crabs are named for the fuzzy tufts on their claws, which they use to catch tiny bits of food.

listings.commonName: King Kong Shrimp Black Grade S
listings.description: The black king kong shrimp is one of the highly sought-after varieties of aquarium fancy shrimp, and when first introduced was considered the most prized, the "King Kong" of hybrids. The parent variety is most likely the bee shrimp, and these shrimp have the same requirements as the bee shrimp. Quick Facts Scientific Name Caridina cf. cantonensis (black king kong, Taiwan bee) Origin Taiwan (aquarium-bred) Care Level Moderate to difficult (needs soft, stable water) Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1" Lifespan 1½–2 years Diet Omnivore (grazes on algae) Water Temperature 68–76°F pH 5.8–6.8 Water Hardness GH 4–6, KH 0–1 (soft) Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Caridina bee and Taiwan bee shrimp need soft, slightly acidic water. Use a mature, cycled tank with an active (buffering) shrimp substrate, RO water remineralized for shrimp, moss and plants, and a sponge filter. Feeding: Feed a small amount of quality shrimp food once a day, and remove any uneaten food after a few hours. Tankmates: Caridina are best kept in a shrimp-only tank or with tiny, peaceful fish like otocinclus, plus snails. Avoid cichlids and other fish that will eat shrimp. Different bee and Taiwan bee varieties can crossbreed, but they will not breed with Neocaridina. Good to know: Acclimate slowly (drip for an hour or more). Stable water matters more than perfect numbers, and sudden changes in temperature or hardness are the most common cause of losses.

Magnolia Leaves Indian almond leaves, tea leaves, and magnolia leaves have some extraordinary conditioning properties for the freshwater aquarium. Placement of a couple of these leaves in an aquarium will slowly lower the Ph and soften the water as each Magnolia leaf biodegrades. As the leaves degrade, tannins and flavonoids are released which have healing properties against fish disease. The introduction of natural dried leaves will slowly move tap based aquarium water to the conditions of water found in South America and Southeast Asia biotopes. Fish that y benefit from magnolia leaves and Indian almond leaves include bettas, rasboras, platies, angelfish, discus, corys, and many many more. Each order of AquariumFishSale magnolia leaves comes with ten cleaned and dried large leaves, and can be dropped right into a box of delivered live fish. Pack Size: 10 large Leaves

The polka dot butterfly loach, or hillstream loach, comes from the island of Borneo and is also called the Borneo sucker. The most striking feature of this freshwater loach, besides its unusual UFO profile, is the fine spotted pattern. Freshwater loaches are hardy and feed on just about anything and are quite the sight hanging on the other side of the aquarium glass eating algae (FYI, they are great aquarium algae eaters). Hillstream loaches do not tolerate acidic low-pH water or high temperatures, so no discus tanks. Otherwise, these are outstanding community fish and can even be kept with fancy shrimp. Quick Facts Scientific Name Gastromyzon punctulatus Origin Sarawak, Borneo (Malaysia) Care Level Moderate (needs cool, fast, oxygen-rich water) Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2–2½" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Algae eater Water Temperature 68–75°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Hillstream loaches come from fast, clear mountain streams. Give them smooth rocks, strong current, lots of oxygen and cool water. They graze on algae, so a mature tank with algae-covered rocks is ideal. Feeding: Hillstream loaches graze on algae. Also feed algae wafers or sinking pellets. Tankmates: Hillstream loaches do well with peaceful fish that like cool, flowing water, such as white clouds, danios, rasboras and dwarf shrimp. Avoid tropical fish that need warm water. Good to know: Hillstream loaches cling to rocks and glass with their flat, sucker-like bodies, just like they do in fast mountain streams.

Cyphastrea Orange Coral Frag If there is one coral you do not want to put in strong light or even moderate light to begin with it is a Cyphastrea because it takes a long time for them to adjust to high intensity light. We recommend lighting intensity under 100 PAR to start and if you want to move them into higher light conditions, do so very slowly. There are not a Lot of benefits to giving this coral an over-abundance of light and it introduces substantial risk of overexposure. When in doubt, go with dimmer light and if you want to try and acclimate them to a brighter area of the tank do so slowly, and be prepared to move it back to shadier areas at the first signs of trouble for example if it starts to bleach or the polyps remain tightly closed. Approximate size : 1 inch FOOD:zooxanthellae

Montipora Coral, Plating is a small polyp stony (SPS) coral often referred to as a Vase Coral. Montipora Corals come in a vast variety of forms and colors. M. capricornis is shaped like a vase; M. digitata is generally a branching species; M. stellata has rough, irregular, upright plates. Other species are encrusting. This form of Montipora is plating and will add diversity to your reef aquarium. SCIENTIFIC NAME:Montipora capricornis APPROX SIZE:MD

Cristata Torch Coral Similar to its close relative the FROGSPAWN CORAL Euphyllia divisa . However its tentacles look nothing like the Frogspawn, but rather more like shorter versions of the TORCH CORAL Euphyllia glabrescens tentacles. A close look will quickly help you to easily identify this coral. The Grape coral does not have branching polyps and each tentacle is perfectly straight with one contrasting tip. Family: Euphyllia cristata Shipping Size: Small Frag

Cristata Euphyllia Euphyllia cristata, commonly called grape coral, is a species of hard coral in the family Euphylliidae. The grape coral is widespread throughout the tropical waters of the Indo-West Pacific area with a large presence in Indonesia. Scientific Name: Euphyllia cristata Origin: Indo-West Pacific

The platinum white arowana is a very, very rare color morph of the South American silver arowana. Only one in 10,000 wild arowanas display this solid white color. However, with good breeding practices these rare fish are now available to the trade via Indonesia. (IF YOU SEE albino silver arowana sold on the internet, most likely they will have black eyes and actually be the platinum arowana.) Like the silver arowana, these fish are predators and will be a truly exceptional addition to the aquarium. Quick Facts Scientific Name Osteoglossum bicirrhosum (platinum) Origin South America (captive-bred in Indonesia) Care Level Difficult (grows very large) Temperament Predatory Adult Size Up to 3 feet Lifespan 15–20 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–86°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 6–7" Care Guide Tank setup: Arowanas are powerful jumpers, so a heavy, tight-fitting lid is a must. Give them open swimming space and strong filtration. Feeding: Feed floating carnivore pellets and frozen foods like shrimp. Avoid feeder fish, which can carry disease. Tankmates: Arowanas will eat any fish that fits in their mouth. Keep them only with large, robust fish such as large catfish, big cichlids and stingrays. Good to know: Arowanas swim near the surface and use the barbels on their chin to sense food.

The devil thorn snail is a conical-shaped, peaceful snail that grows to three inches. Devil thorn snails are named for the long, horn-shaped shell, similar in shape to trumpet snails but a much deeper color. Like nerite snails, devil thorn snails must breed in saltwater, so they will not lay eggs and take over the aquarium. These snails will be fine in any size tank with any but the largest, most aggressive species. ALSO, like nerite snails, devil thorn snails, also called lava snails, will not do well in high pH; a pH of 8 or higher will kill them. Quick Facts Scientific Name Faunus ater Origin Indo-Pacific (Philippines and Indonesia; wild-caught) Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful; plant-safe Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 2–4 years Diet Algae eater (also eats algae wafers) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 6.5–7.8 Breeding Larvae need brackish water, so it won't breed in freshwater Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give devil thorn snails a mature tank with a sand bottom they can burrow in and plenty of algae and biofilm to graze. Keep the water stable and avoid sudden pH swings. Feeding: They graze on algae and leftover food. Also feed algae wafers or sinking pellets. Tankmates: They do well with peaceful fish, shrimp and other snails. Avoid puffers, loaches and assassin snails. Good to know: Devil thorn snails often bury themselves in the sand during the day and come out to graze at night.

The bronze cory, or green cory aeneus, is the wild parent cory of many variations found in the Amazon, including the red and green laser cory. Cory aeneus have a greenish bronze color and like to swim in small packs. These dwarf catfish are good scavengers and so-so algae eaters. Quick Facts Scientific Name Corydoras aeneus Origin South America (widespread) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 5–10 years Diet Omnivore (bottom feeder) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–8.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and a soft sand or smooth, fine gravel bottom. Plants, driftwood and a few shady spots help them feel secure. Corys are sensitive to salt and some medications (especially copper), so check labels before treating the tank. Feeding: Corys need their own food, not just leftovers. Feed sinking pellets or wafers once or twice a day so food reaches the bottom. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Corys get along with almost any peaceful community fish, such as tetras, rasboras, livebearers, gouramis, angelfish and bettas. Avoid large fish that could swallow them and aggressive bottom dwellers. Good to know: Corys sift through the substrate with their sensitive barbels, so soft sand or smooth, fine gravel keeps those barbels healthy.

In the aquatic trade the word tuxedo refers to a black color on the middle of the body, like a tuxedo. Though pretentious fashion is not what the red tuxedo swordtail is best known for, one can envision a tux on the fish. The body color ranges from orange to red with the black pattern, and the red can be brought out further with spirulina and other color-enhancing foods. Quick Facts Scientific Name Xiphophorus hellerii (red tuxedo) Origin Southern Mexico to Honduras (wild ancestors); aquarium-bred Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful (males may spar) Adult Size Up to 4–5" (not counting the sword) Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 7.0–8.0 (hard water) Group Size Keep more females than males Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Swordtails are active swimmers, so give them plants, open swimming space and a tight-fitting lid, since they are good jumpers. They prefer hard, alkaline water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet with some vegetable content once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Swordtails get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as platies, mollies, larger tetras, danios, rainbowfish, gouramis and corydoras. Keep more females than males, since males chase females and may spar with each other. Avoid fin-nippers and large cichlids. Good to know: Swordtails are livebearers and breed readily. Fry are born free-swimming and will be eaten unless there are dense plants or a breeding box for them to hide in. Only males grow the "sword" on the tail.

Shaped like a medieval castle in Japan, the pagoda snail is a gold-brown scavenger and algae eater not known to breed and take over fish tanks. These snails are wild-caught in rivers of Thailand and only available a few times a year. The pagoda snail grows very slowly to a maximum size of two inches and adapts well to any freshwater aquarium. Pagoda shells often have short spikes like the overhangs of pagoda roofs. Quick Facts Scientific Name Brotia armata Origin Thailand and Myanmar (wild-caught) Care Level Moderate (needs clean, well-oxygenated water) Temperament Peaceful; plant-safe Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 2–5 years Diet Algae eater (also eats algae wafers) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 7.0–8.0 Breeding Livebearer; rarely breeds in aquariums Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Pagoda snails come from clear, flowing streams. Give them a mature tank with good current, high oxygen, smooth rocks covered in biofilm and very clean water. They do best in established tanks with plenty of natural algae. Feeding: They graze on algae. Also feed algae wafers or sinking pellets, since pagoda snails can go hungry in tanks that are too clean. Tankmates: They do well with peaceful fish, shrimp and other snails. Avoid puffers, loaches and assassin snails. Good to know: Pagoda snails are wild-caught and can take time to settle in. Check that they are alive by watching for movement; a closed trapdoor usually means they are resting.

In the aquarium trade, most star sapphire cichlids are bred by domestic breeders and sold to AquariumFish.com and other aquarium retailers. Wild star sapphire cichlids are rare. Actually, bred star sapphire cichlids are rare. This cichlid is known for small white reflections like the gem of a sapphire, and the body is a deep blue. The star sapphire cichlid has a disposition similar to peacock cichlids and can be kept in a community African cichlid tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name Placidochromis phenochilus "Tanzania" Origin Lake Malawi, Africa Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Semi-aggressive (males territorial) Adult Size Up to 7" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 76–82°F pH 7.8–8.6 Shipping Size Small: approx. 1½" · Medium: approx. 2" · Large: approx. 3–4" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a sand bottom, open swimming space in front and rockwork along the back. Lake Malawi and Lake Tanganyika cichlids need hard, alkaline water; crushed coral or aragonite sand helps hold the pH up. Feeding: Feed a quality cichlid pellet or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like brine shrimp. Tankmates: Haps do well with peacocks and other haps of similar size, plus robust catfish like synodontis. Keep one male per similar-looking species, with several females, to limit fighting and crossbreeding. Good to know: Males take a year or more to show full adult color, and color best when females are present.

The spilonotus cichlid is one of the most colorful African species, with bold blue and yellow throughout the body. Even the females look good! These aquarium fish are very hardy and do fine in a community African cichlid tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name Protomelas spilonotus Origin Lake Malawi, Africa Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Semi-aggressive (males territorial) Adult Size Up to 7" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 76–82°F pH 7.8–8.6 Shipping Size Approx. 2–3" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a sand bottom, open swimming space in front and rockwork along the back. Lake Malawi and Lake Tanganyika cichlids need hard, alkaline water; crushed coral or aragonite sand helps hold the pH up. Feeding: Feed a quality cichlid pellet or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like brine shrimp. Tankmates: Haps do well with peacocks and other haps of similar size, plus robust catfish like synodontis. Keep one male per similar-looking species, with several females, to limit fighting and crossbreeding. Good to know: Males take a year or more to show full adult color, and color best when females are present.

Tinfoil barbs are all over the aquarium trade and may be the hardiest, biggest schooling fish there is in the freshwater aquarium hobby. Tinfoil barbs will eat just about anything and get along with all fish of similar size, even large, aggressive cichlids. These aquarium pets will grow with two-inch cichlids until you have a tank of monsters. Quick Facts Scientific Name Barbonymus schwanenfeldii Origin Southeast Asia Care Level Easy (but grows very large) Temperament Peaceful, but eats small fish Adult Size Up to 12–14" Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Small: approx. 1½" · Medium: approx. 2–3" Care Guide Tank setup: Tinfoil barbs start small but can reach a foot long, so give them strong filtration and a tight lid. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets or large flakes once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. Tinfoils eat a lot of plant matter and will also eat live aquarium plants. Tankmates: Keep them with other large fish such as big cichlids, plecos, silver dollars and other tinfoils. Any fish small enough to swallow will be eaten. Good to know: Tinfoil barbs grow fast and will eat any fish small enough to fit in their mouths, so check their adult size before buying.

The snakeskin discus is a more recent bred variation of the beautiful family of ornamental discus fish. The snakeskin pattern is noted for the fine striations of color throughout the body. The discus are bred in Singapore and tolerate hard water and higher pH, but not higher than 7.6! Snakeskin patterns are a bit more difficult to breed, so they demand a higher price, but all the patterns are pretty :) Quick Facts Scientific Name Symphysodon aequifasciatus (captive-bred color variety) Origin Amazon basin (captive-bred in Singapore) Care Level Moderate (needs warm, very clean water) Temperament Peaceful, shy; social Adult Size Up to 6–7" Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 82–88°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1½–4" (by size option) Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a reliable heater, gentle but strong filtration, and a bare bottom or fine sand for easy cleaning. Keep the tank in a quiet spot. Discus need very clean water. Feeding: Feed small meals of quality discus pellets or granules a few times a day, and remove uneaten food within a few minutes, since leftovers quickly foul the water. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. New arrivals may need frozen food for a while before they accept pellets. Tankmates: Discus are calm and shy, so choose gentle tankmates that enjoy the same warm water: cardinal and rummynose tetras, sterbai corydoras and small plecos are popular choices. Avoid fast, boisterous or fin-nipping fish, and anything that competes hard for food. Many keepers avoid angelfish, which can bully discus and share diseases. Living in groups: Discus are social and feel safest in a group. A single discus, or just two, tends to be stressed. When a pair forms to breed, they may claim part of the tank, so a group spreads out the attention. Good to know: The fine snakeskin striations become more detailed as the fish grows. Discus show stress by darkening their color and hiding. A dark discus in a corner usually means the water quality or tankmates need checking.

The Asian leaf fish, Nandus nandus , is an obvious ambush predator. Not as good a mimic of a dead leaf as the South American leaf fish, but the Asian leaf fish is hardier and more adaptable to frozen foods. Leaf fish prefer small critters like ghost shrimp and feeder guppies. Peaceful to similar-size fish, these fish are only dangerous to tank mates that fit in their mouth and think they are a leaf. Quick Facts Scientific Name Nandus nandus Origin South and Southeast Asia Care Level Moderate Temperament Predatory Adult Size Up to 6" Lifespan 8 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a planted tank with driftwood, leaf litter and gentle current. They hunt by ambush and stay still for long periods. Feeding: Asian leaf fish adapt to frozen foods more easily than other leaf fish. Offer frozen foods like bloodworms and shrimp once a day. Tankmates: They will eat any fish that fits in their mouth. Keep them only with fish too large to swallow. Good to know: Leaf fish drift slowly toward their prey like a fallen leaf, then strike very quickly.

The Ranchu goldfish was created through selective breeding in Japan and is named "ranchu," or "hooded," for the pebbly head. The ranchu goldfish is considered the top of its class by Japanese breeders. The black ranchu displays the hooded features in a unique fashion. Quick Facts Scientific Name Carassius auratus Origin Japan Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 6" Lifespan 10–15 years, often longer with good care Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 65–75°F (no heater needed in most homes) pH 7.0–8.0 Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Ranchus produce a lot of waste, so give them plenty of room and a strong filter. Use smooth decorations and live or silk plants, and keep the water current gentle. Feeding: Feed small amounts of a quality sinking pellet or flake once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. Sinking foods are easier for them to find than floating ones. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them only with other slow-swimming fancy goldfish, such as telescopes, black moors, celestials, bubble eyes, lionheads and ranchus. Avoid faster goldfish like comets, shubunkins and even lively ryukins, which will outcompete them for food. Also avoid tropical fish and fin-nippers. Ponds: Ranchus can live in ponds in mild climates, but they are less cold-hardy than comets and shubunkins. Bring them indoors where winters are harsh, and keep them away from fast, aggressive pond fish. Good to know: With no dorsal fin, they are slow, wobbly swimmers. Keep the water very clean, since the wen (head growth) can trap debris.

Rotala macranda There are several varieties of rotala macandra, the most suitable aquarium plant is the yellow variety sold here (and pictured). Macranda originate from Vietnam but most available for aquariums are grown in Florida. Scientific Name: ROTALA macandra Shipping Size: Bunched five plants with lead weight approx. five inches tall

The Longfin Blue Danio is a type of Zebra Danio, or danio rerio, bred in India to display more of the blue gene in the aquarium. This community schooling fish has a lined and spotted blue body and does well in groups of six or more. These aquarium fish are hardy and great for beginners or for advanced aquarists with planted fish tanks. Quick Facts Scientific Name Danio rerio (blue long-fin variety) Origin India, Bangladesh and Nepal (Ganges region) (captive-bred) Care Level Very easy, great for beginners Temperament Peaceful, very active Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 64–77°F (often fine without a heater) pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Care Guide Tank setup: Danios are fast swimmers, so give them open swimming space, a filter, plants around the edges and a tight-fitting lid, since they jump. Make sure the tank is fully cycled (which takes several weeks) before adding fish. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Danios get along with most peaceful community fish, such as tetras, rasboras, barbs, corydoras and livebearers. Their speed can stress slow, long-finned fish like bettas and fancy guppies, and large predatory fish will eat them. Good to know: Long fins make these danios a little slower than regular zebras, so avoid fin-nipping tankmates like tiger barbs.

JBJ 4 LED Refugium Light Description The JBJ Refugium Light features four high intensity LEDs providing evenly distributed light to macro algae for optimum bioactivity. The unique magnetic fastener allows placement anywhere.

JBJ Internal Glass Thermometer Description The JBJ glass thermometer comes with a rating of 30 to 110 degrees and a green safety zone on the indicator for easy reference. Each thermometer comes with a suction cup. The glass thermometers are for use with freshwater and saltwater aquariums.

The yellow tux guppy, or yellow tuxedo guppy, features a black "tuxedo" body with a bright yellow tail. This variety is a bit harder to breed and is a standout in small community fish tanks. The yellow appears brighter due to the black of the body. Quick Facts Scientific Name Poecilia reticulata Origin Northern South America (captive-bred) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Sold as a pair (1 male + 1 female) Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and plenty of plants, including some floating plants where babies can hide. Guppies like slightly hard water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Guppies get along with other small, peaceful fish such as platies, mollies, corydoras, small tetras and rasboras. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs and larger fish that could eat them. Breeding: Guppies are livebearers and breed easily. Females give birth to live babies about once a month, and adults will eat the babies, so thick plants give them a place to hide. Good to know: Tuxedo guppies have a dark back half that looks like a tuxedo jacket.

Hikari Algae Wafers Slow sinking Hikari Algae Wafers are the perfect food for hard to please plecostomus and other algae eaters. The high grade Hikari formulation will not foul the aquarium and provides essential vegetable nutrition to bottom dwelling herbivore and omnivore aquarium fish. Each package contains 100 tablets and approximately 3 ounces of high quality aquarium fish food. Shipping Size: 2.89 oz

The red calico swordtail, also called the red painted swordtail, has black spots on a red body. Originally bred in Florida in the 1970s, this variation is popular all over the world. Quick Facts Scientific Name Xiphophorus hellerii (red calico) Origin Southern Mexico to Honduras (wild ancestors); aquarium-bred Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful (males may spar) Adult Size Up to 4–5" (not counting the sword) Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 7.0–8.0 (hard water) Group Size Keep more females than males Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Swordtails are active swimmers, so give them plants, open swimming space and a tight-fitting lid, since they are good jumpers. They prefer hard, alkaline water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet with some vegetable content once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Swordtails get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as platies, mollies, larger tetras, danios, rainbowfish, gouramis and corydoras. Keep more females than males, since males chase females and may spar with each other. Avoid fin-nippers and large cichlids. Good to know: Swordtails are livebearers and breed readily. Fry are born free-swimming and will be eaten unless there are dense plants or a breeding box for them to hide in. Only males grow the "sword" on the tail.

Red head angelfish are probably more aptly called orange head angelfish, though with spirulina-enhanced flakes and the right water conditions, these fish can get red in color. The orange is very bright and vivid against the cream body of this color variation developed in Indonesia. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pterophyllum scalare Origin Amazon basin (bred in Indonesia) Care Level Easy Temperament Semi-aggressive (territorial when pairing) Adult Size Up to 6" long and 8" tall Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Shipping Size Approx. 1½–4" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them tall plants or driftwood, a heater and a gentle filter. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Choose peaceful fish too large to swallow, such as larger tetras, corydoras, plecos, rams, gouramis and peaceful barbs. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs, and small fish like neon tetras that adult angels may eat. Breeding: Angelfish pair off and lay eggs on flat surfaces like broad leaves or slate. A breeding pair can become territorial, so give them room and places for other fish to retreat. Good to know: Orange and red color varies with diet, age and mood. A color-enhancing food and a darker background help it show at its best.

Full Black Angelfish with long flowing veil fins is one of the most beautiful fish in a planted aquarium, or any freshwater aquarium for that matter. Like most angelfish (except true altums), these community fish will eat flake food and are hardy, and at maturity and with the proper mate, will breed in the aquarium (or with an improper mate, for that matter). The black veil angelfish on sale at AquariumFish.com are bred in Indonesia for the aquarium hobby. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pterophyllum scalare (veil-fin variety) Origin Amazon basin (bred in Indonesia) Care Level Easy Temperament Semi-aggressive (territorial when pairing) Adult Size Up to 6" long, with extra-long fins Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them tall plants or driftwood, a heater and a gentle filter. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Choose peaceful fish too large to swallow, such as larger tetras, corydoras, plecos, rams, gouramis and peaceful barbs. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs, and small fish like neon tetras that adult angels may eat. Breeding: Angelfish pair off and lay eggs on flat surfaces like broad leaves or slate. A breeding pair can become territorial, so give them room and places for other fish to retreat. Good to know: Long veil fins are easy targets for fin-nippers and can get infected in dirty water, so keep the water clean and skip nippy tankmates.

The male Cockatoo or Apistogramma Cacatuoides dwarf cichlid is truly magnificent when he grows to his full two-inch size, but the red bred variation is something else entirely. Females are a bit drabber but still have nice yellow and red coloration. AquariumFish.com pairs these items because the male is happier with a female around and displays his colors better. Each order comes with one male and one female. Quick Facts Scientific Name Apistogramma cacatuoides (double orange variety) Origin Amazon basin (bred in Indonesia) Care Level Easy, a good first apisto Temperament Peaceful (males territorial with each other) Adult Size Males up to 3"; females about 2" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 75–84°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a pair (1 male + 1 female) Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter, dim lighting and lots of plants, driftwood and leaf litter. Add a cave (a coconut shell or small clay pot) for each female. Most apistos prefer soft, slightly acidic water. Feeding: Feed small pellets or flake once or twice a day.
