They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with small, peaceful fish such as tetras, rasboras, pencilfish, otocinclus and corydoras. A calm school of small "dither" fish helps apistos feel safe enough to come out. Keep one male per tank unless it is large and well planted, and avoid large or boisterous fish. Adults may eat small shrimp and baby shrimp. Breeding: Apistos are cave spawners. The female lays her eggs inside a cave and guards the fry, while the male patrols the territory. One male with several females works well in a planted tank. Good to know: Tank-bred double orange cockatoos are hardy and adaptable. Males show their tallest fins and brightest orange when a female is present.

If the exotic South American Red Tail Catfish is not tough enough for you, Asia has its own version. The Asian red tail catfish is found more often on dinner plates and aquariums in Southeast Asia for a reason. The Asian red tail catfish grows to four feet and is among the most aggressive aquarium fish in the World. These fish will eat everything and are as tough as flowerhorns and butterkoferi but get much, much bigger. AquariumFishSale offers the fish at about three inches and the bright red tail will begin to show at six inches. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hemibagrus wyckioides Origin Mekong River basin, Thailand Care Level Difficult (grows very large) Temperament Aggressive Adult Size Up to 3–4 feet Lifespan 15–20+ years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 3" Care Guide Tank setup: They grow very large, so give them strong filtration, a sand bottom, sturdy decorations and a heavy, tight lid. Feeding: Feed meaty foods like quality carnivore pellets and frozen shrimp or fish. Many learn to take pellets once settled. Avoid feeder fish, which can carry disease. Tankmates: They will eat any fish that fits in their mouth. Keep them only with large, robust fish. Good to know: The red tail starts to show at around six inches and gets brighter as the fish grows.

The male guppy of this variation features the unique lyre tail, but to produce young with lyre tails, these guppies need to be mated with the proper green females. The green lyretail guppy features color highlights of red and blue on a green base. Each order comes with a male and a female lyre guppy. Quick Facts Scientific Name Poecilia reticulata Origin Northern South America (captive-bred) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Sold as a pair (1 male + 1 female) Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and plenty of plants, including some floating plants where babies can hide. Guppies like slightly hard water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Guppies get along with other small, peaceful fish such as platies, mollies, corydoras, small tetras and rasboras. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs and larger fish that could eat them. Breeding: Guppies are livebearers and breed easily. Females give birth to live babies about once a month, and adults will eat the babies, so thick plants give them a place to hide. Good to know: Lyretail guppies have long points on the top and bottom of the tail, shaped like a lyre.

The dojo loach is also called the weather loach because it tends to get more active when bad weather approaches. In fact, this aquarium fish has been used for centuries to predict coming storms. Dojo loaches need clean water and room to swim. Dojo loaches are friendly, tolerate colder water temperatures and will eat most foods. *A few states will not allow gold or regular dojos: New York, Illinois, Michigan, Minnesota and Alabama. Quick Facts Scientific Name Misgurnus anguillicaudatus Origin East Asia (China, Japan, Korea); farm-raised Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 6–10" Lifespan 7–10 years Diet Omnivore (bottom feeder) Water Temperature 50–77°F (coldwater) pH 6.5–8.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 4" Care Guide Tank setup: These are coldwater loaches that need no heater in most homes. Give them a soft sand bottom for burrowing, smooth rocks, plants and a tight-fitting lid, since they are skilled escape artists. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets or wafers once or twice a day. They scavenge leftover food from the bottom and also enjoy frozen bloodworms. Tankmates: They do well with other peaceful coldwater fish like goldfish, white clouds and other loaches. Avoid tropical fish that need warm water. Good to know: Dojo loaches are sometimes called weather loaches because they become restless when air pressure changes before a storm.

Dwarf Sagittaria The dwarf sagittaria plant does not take special care but needs moderate lighting and a substrate that will allow purchase for its small starting roots. Ideally these plants will tank hold and propogate, they can form a very pretty four inch high blanket of green in the fish tank. Worst case, the dwarf sag forms a nice spot of green in the fish tank for a couple months. Sagittaria plants are found throughout the USA East Coast and South America and some varieties grow three feet, but the dwarf sag is particularly suited to aquariums. Scientific Name: Sagittaria subulata Shipping Size: Approx. 3 to 4 inches, three plants with one lead weight

Purple Waffle The purple waffle is named for the waffling deep purple leaves. These aquatic plants are outstanding in the fish tank but if fully submerged will fade over time. They thrive partially submerged in a terrarium or paludarium, or a shelf in the fish tank. The color is a deep purple and the plant grows slow and requires moderate to strong light. Originally from Vietnam, this species is cultivated in Florida. Scientific Name: Hemigraphis exotica Shipping Size: Six inches, grows to eight inches, bunched with lead weight.

The albino clown knifefish, or knife fish (both are proper), is a truly phantasmic sight in an aquarium. Ghosts of any kind are a rare sight, but with the purchase of this fish, you can see one every day! Bred in Thailand for the aquarium trade, these fish are seldom exported to the USA. Outside of their unusual appearance, albino knifefish are the same as the parent clown knife. Quick Facts Scientific Name Chitala ornata (albino) Origin Southeast Asia (captive-bred in Thailand) Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful with fish its size Adult Size Up to 2 feet Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 4" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them hiding places like large tubes or caves, dim lighting, strong filtration and a tight lid. They are most active at night. Feeding: Feed meaty foods like frozen shrimp and bloodworms, plus sinking carnivore pellets once they learn to take them. Avoid feeder fish, which can carry disease. Tankmates: They will eat any fish that fits in their mouth. Keep them with large, peaceful fish. Good to know: Clown knifefish are shy when young and do best with a hiding spot, like a short length of PVC pipe.

The galaxy platy comes from a breeder in Thailand and displays spots (stars of the galaxy) on a blue or blue and red body. The galaxy platy will leave platy lovers starstruck, and like most platies, this variety is hardy and will eat community flake or pellet fish food. Quick Facts Scientific Name Xiphophorus maculatus Origin Southern Mexico and Central America Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 3–4 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 70–80°F pH 7.0–8.2 Breeding Livebearer – breeds easily in the aquarium Care Guide Tank setup: Platies are hardy and easy to keep. Give them a filter, a lid and plenty of plants. Use a heater to keep the water steady in the 70s. They prefer harder, slightly alkaline water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. Platies also need some plant matter, so a vegetable flake is a good choice. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Platies get along with most peaceful community fish, such as other livebearers (mollies, guppies and swordtails), tetras, rasboras and corydoras. Avoid large or aggressive fish that may bully or eat them. Breeding: Platies are livebearers, so a tank with males and females will almost certainly have babies (fry). Adults will eat fry, so add dense plants or use a breeding box if you want to raise them. Keeping more females than males gives the females a break from the males' attention. Good to know: Platies are one of the easiest fish to keep, which makes them a great choice for a first aquarium.

Gold angel veil rams have long, flowing deep yellow fins and a gold balloon body. Gold veil rams, or gold balloon hi-fin rams, are peaceful and hardy in a community fish tank. Though they may eat small fancy aquarium shrimp, these aquatic species are good tankmates to most other small species. Quick Facts Scientific Name Mikrogeophagus ramirezi (gold balloon veil variety) Origin Venezuela and Colombia (Orinoco basin); aquarium-bred Care Level Moderate (needs warm, clean, soft water) Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 2–4 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 80–86°F pH 5.0–7.0 Group Size Pair or small group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Rams need warm, very clean, soft water. Give them a sand bottom, plants, driftwood, leaf litter and flat stones for spawning. Rams are sensitive to poor water quality. Feeding: Feed small amounts of quality micro pellets or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Rams do well with small, peaceful fish that like warm, soft water, such as tetras, rasboras, hatchetfish, corydoras and discus. They may eat small shrimp. Avoid large or boisterous fish. Good to know: Rams often form pairs and lay eggs on flat stones. Stable, warm water is the key to keeping them healthy.

The black widow frontosa is a variation of the Burundi frontosa bred in Taiwan to bring out a mapping black pattern roughly like a spider web. These frontosa are difficult to breed and command a higher price, but they are beautiful fish. Quick Facts Scientific Name Cyphotilapia frontosa (line-bred) Origin Lake Tanganyika, Africa (bred in Taiwan) Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful for its size, but eats small fish Adult Size Up to 12–14" Lifespan 20+ years Diet Carnivore Water Temperature 75–80°F pH 7.8–9.0 Shipping Size Approx. 1–2" Care Guide Tank setup: Frontosa need a sand bottom, a few large, stable rock caves and lots of open water. Keep the lighting moderate. Lake Malawi and Lake Tanganyika cichlids need hard, alkaline water; crushed coral or aragonite sand helps hold the pH up. Feeding: Feed a quality sinking cichlid pellet once a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like shrimp. Avoid feeder fish, which can carry disease. Tankmates: Frontosa do best in a group with other peaceful, large Tanganyikans like calvus and cyprichromis (adult frontosa will eat small fish), plus synodontis catfish. Good to know: Frontosa grow slowly and can live 20 years or more, so they are a long-term commitment.

The red comet platy is named for the black streaks along the top and bottom of the caudal (tail) fin. These bright red schooling livebearers do well in most community aquariums and nano tanks, and will even breed right in the aquarium. Quick Facts Scientific Name Xiphophorus maculatus Origin Southern Mexico and Central America Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 3–4 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 70–80°F pH 7.0–8.2 Breeding Livebearer – breeds easily in the aquarium Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Platies are hardy and easy to keep. Give them a filter, a lid and plenty of plants. Use a heater to keep the water steady in the 70s. They prefer harder, slightly alkaline water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. Platies also need some plant matter, so a vegetable flake is a good choice. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Platies get along with most peaceful community fish, such as other livebearers (mollies, guppies and swordtails), tetras, rasboras and corydoras. Avoid large or aggressive fish that may bully or eat them. Breeding: Platies are livebearers, so a tank with males and females will almost certainly have babies (fry). Adults will eat fry, so add dense plants or use a breeding box if you want to raise them. Keeping more females than males gives the females a break from the males' attention. Good to know: Platies are one of the easiest fish to keep, which makes them a great choice for a first aquarium.

Ogon indicates any solid color. The platinum ogon is prized for the solid silver-white body that can be seen across even the murkiest pond water. Quick Facts Scientific Name Cyprinus carpio Origin Captive-bred (Asia) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2–3 feet Lifespan 25–35 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 50–80°F pH 7.0–8.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 6" Care Guide Tank setup: Koi grow large and are best kept in an outdoor pond with strong filtration. They are cool-water fish and do not need a heater. Feeding: Feed a quality koi or goldfish pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a few minutes. Feed less when the water is cool. Tankmates: Koi get along with goldfish and other pond fish. Good to know: Platinum ogons are one of the brightest koi and stand out in any pond.

The deep red of the bloody Mary shrimp is named for the drink, which is named for the unfortunate monarch Queen Mary I. These exotic aquarium shrimp have a deeper color than the sakura-grade fire red and cherry red shrimp. Terrific in small fish tanks and planted tanks, be wary of keeping these exotic pets with small rams and apistogrammas. Quick Facts Scientific Name Neocaridina davidi (bloody mary) Origin East Asia (aquarium-bred, mostly Taiwan) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1" Lifespan 1–2 years Diet Omnivore (grazes on algae) Water Temperature 65–80°F pH 6.5–8.0 Water Hardness GH 6–12 (moderately hard) Group Size Does best in a group (breeds readily) Shipping Size Approx. ⅓–½" Care Guide Tank setup: Neocaridina are hardy and ideal for beginners. Use a cycled, planted tank with moss, plants and hiding spots, and a sponge filter or a sponge over the filter intake so shrimp aren't pulled in. Keep the water stable. Feeding: Shrimp graze on algae all day. Feed a small amount of quality shrimp food once a day and remove anything uneaten after a few hours. Tankmates: Keep shrimp alone or with tiny, peaceful fish like small rasboras, ember tetras, otocinclus and pygmy corydoras, plus snails. Most fish will eat baby shrimp, and cichlids (even dwarf cichlids like rams and apistogrammas) and larger fish will eat adults. Different Neocaridina colors will crossbreed and lose their color over time. Good to know: Shrimp are very sensitive to copper and many medications. Never treat a tank with shrimp, and check plant fertilizers and treatments for copper.

The crimson loach, named for the partial ruby-red body, is also called the jasper loach after the original English discoverer. These loaches were known long before the English found and named them in southern India, but at least they were legitimately "discovered" for the aquarium hobby by Mr. Jasper. The loaches get along well with any fish that cannot eat them and will find most food that falls to the bottom of the fish tank. Crimson loaches will fight each other for territory in the fish tank, but once they have their own areas, things should settle down. The crimson loach is part of the Schistura genus, and all these loaches do well with even small rasboras. Quick Facts Scientific Name Schistura sp. Origin Southern India Care Level Moderate (needs clean, oxygen-rich water) Temperament Peaceful with other fish; territorial with its own kind Adult Size Up to 3–4" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore (bottom feeder) Water Temperature 68–77°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single, or a group with plenty of hiding spots Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: These loaches come from clear, flowing streams. Give them a tank with a sand or smooth gravel bottom, rocks and caves to claim, some current and good oxygen. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as danios, rasboras, barbs and tetras. Give each loach its own hiding spot to limit squabbles. Good to know: These loaches are active and curious, and they often perch on rocks to watch the tank.

The white cheek moray eel will tolerate freshwater but does best with a low salt, brackish environment. Moray eels feed on small live feeders and frozen food and are hardy and friendly companions to creatures that do not fit into their mouth. The white cheek moray only grows to about a foot, so it is suited to most aquariums. Our morays come from brackish waters in the Philippines. Quick Facts Scientific Name Echidna rhodochilus Origin Philippines Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful with fish its size Adult Size Up to 12–13" Lifespan 10+ years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.5–8.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 8–10" Care Guide Tank setup: White cheek morays do best in slightly salty (brackish) water. Give them rocks or pipes to hide in and a tight-fitting lid, since eels are escape artists. Feeding: Feed meaty foods like frozen shrimp or fish a few pieces at a time. Many learn to take food from feeding tongs. Tankmates: They are peaceful with fish too large to swallow. Keep them with other brackish fish like scats and monos. Good to know: Morays open and close their mouth constantly to breathe, which is normal and not a sign of aggression.

Another big catfish from Asia is the iridescent shark, or panga catfish. The iridescent nod comes from the reflective silver body of the fish, which can give the illusion that it glows - it doesn't. It does grow and will reach 12 inches in the aquarium and is known to get to 3 feet in the wild. The panga cat, because of the name, is confused with the wild panga catfish from India that can get to ten feet and is a major food source around the World. Sorry if you are hungry; the iridescent shark won't grow that big. These fish prefer to school in the wild, and we recommend at least three if your tank can handle these fast swimmers. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pangasianodon hypophthalmus Origin Mekong River basin, Southeast Asia Care Level Moderate (grows very large) Temperament Peaceful (eats small fish) Adult Size Up to 12–15" in aquariums; larger in the wild Lifespan 10–20 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Iridescent sharks are fast, skittish swimmers. Give them open swimming space, strong filtration and a tight lid, and avoid sudden movements around the tank. Feeding: Feed a quality pellet or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like shrimp. Tankmates: They are peaceful but will eat small fish. Keep them with other large, peaceful fish. Good to know: Iridescent sharks are catfish, not sharks. They grow fast and can startle easily, so a calm spot for the tank helps.

Hikari Fancy Guppy Food Hikari guppy food features small slow sinking pellets formulated with high proteins and vitamins for the demanding life of the aquarium livebearer - including platies, swordtail, mollies, and of course the fancy guppy. Each package is .77 ounces and the pellets are designed to float momentarily, allowing shy top dwellers to get their chance at the food. Hikari guppy food will enhance breeding and brighten the colors of fancy guppies and other livebearers including mollies, platies, endlers, and swordtails.

Tiger Lotus Plant The aquarium tiger lotus is a dwarf version of the pond lotus plant. The safest way to buy a tiger lotus bulb is to skip the purchase of a bulb and go right to the plant, because they do not always sprout even from the best aquatic nursery. The tiger lotus plant has stems and leaves and varies from just a couple inches to about six inches and, though never a large plant, they grow quickly and make a pretty effect when the leaves make it to the surface of the aquarium. These plants can be potted or simply put right into the substrate. We ship our bulb plants without pot (bare root). If you get a bulb and is does not sprout within two weeks, it's a dud and let us know, we will refund you. Most of the time they work. Scientific Name: NYMPHAEA LOTUS Shipping Size : One small plant with leaves

The hi-fin lyretail variety of the marigold swordtail stands out for color and shape. The long, flowing tail and dorsal with the remarkable marigold color is a collector's prize. Lyretails are bred into the species, and many offspring will have the same stunning attribute. Quick Facts Scientific Name Xiphophorus hellerii (marigold hi-fin lyretail) Origin Southern Mexico to Honduras (wild ancestors); aquarium-bred Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful (males may spar) Adult Size Up to 4–5" (not counting the sword) Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 7.0–8.0 (hard water) Group Size Keep more females than males Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Swordtails are active swimmers, so give them plants, open swimming space and a tight-fitting lid, since they are good jumpers. They prefer hard, alkaline water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet with some vegetable content once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Swordtails get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as platies, mollies, larger tetras, danios, rainbowfish, gouramis and corydoras. Keep more females than males, since males chase females and may spar with each other. Avoid fin-nippers and large cichlids. Good to know: Lyretail and hi-fin swordtails have extra-long fins, so keep them away from fin-nippers like tiger barbs. Many lyretail males have an elongated gonopodium and can't breed, so lyretail fry usually come from lyretail females mated with standard-finned males.

Zebra Afra Cichlid The zebra afra cichlid, or dogtooth cichlid, may be the most colorful of the dwarf cichlids from Lake Malawi. They are pricey but very hardy. The females are a bit smaller without as much color, but the males have a yellow top with a black and blue body. These fish will only grow to about three inches in the aquarium and will breed if happy with the right territory and the right mate. These are small fish but will hold their own against larger mbuna to defend their space. The common name dogtooth comes from the little teeth these fish have to chew veggies in the wild. Cynotilapia species need veggies in prepared pellet food or fresh. Quick Facts Scientific Name Cynotilapia afra "Jalo Reef" Origin Lake Malawi, Africa Care Level Moderate Temperament Aggressive (territorial rock-dweller) Adult Size Up to 3–4" Lifespan 6–10 years Diet Omnivore (needs plant matter) Water Temperature 76–82°F pH 7.8–8.6 Shipping Size Approx. 2½" Care Guide Tank setup: Use a sand or crushed-coral bottom and stack plenty of rockwork with caves and hiding spots so each male can claim a territory and others can escape. Lake Malawi and Lake Tanganyika cichlids need hard, alkaline water; crushed coral or aragonite sand helps hold the pH up. Feeding: Mbuna are mostly plant eaters. Feed a vegetable-based flake or pellet once or twice a day, and avoid high-protein foods, which can upset their digestion. Tankmates: Keep mbuna with other mbuna of similar size and temperament, stocked in a group to spread out aggression. Avoid mixing them with peaceful peacocks and haps unless the tank is large, and avoid closely related species that look alike, which can crossbreed. Good to know: Mbuna stay calmer when the tank is slightly crowded and well decorated, which keeps any one fish from dominating.

The white wizard trapdoor snail, similar to but bigger than the Japanese trapdoor snail, is a soft white color. These aquatic snails grow to 2 inches. The name comes from the ability to predict poor water conditions: the snail will snap its door shut until water conditions improve. So this wizard will help the aquarist maintain the fish tank as best he can. And the wizard white snail does NOT eat plants. Quick Facts Scientific Name Filopaludina martensi Origin Southeast Asia (Thailand and nearby) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful; plant-safe Adult Size Up to 1½–2" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Scavenger (algae and leftover food) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.5 Breeding Livebearer; produces small numbers of live young Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a mature tank with some algae and detritus to graze and stable, warm water. Keep the water hard enough for healthy shells. Feeding: They graze on algae and leftover food and filter food from the water. In a clean aquarium, add algae wafers or sinking pellets. Tankmates: They do well with peaceful community fish, shrimp and other snails. Avoid puffers, loaches and assassin snails. Good to know: The "trapdoor" (operculum) lets them seal their shell when disturbed or when conditions are poor. Remove snails before using copper or other medications.

The golden shark is up there with tinfoil barbs and pacus as a schooling fish that gets enormous. Also called the cigar barb, these beautiful fast swimmers are colorful and very hardy but will outgrow a medium fish tank within a year. Golden sharks will eat flake and pellets and will grow from the shipping size of about three inches to two feet. In fact, these fish are a delicacy in Thailand, but what you do with a two-foot fish is your business. If you want a schooling fish and want to have a big fish tank, these are the ones. Quick Facts Scientific Name Leptobarbus hoevenii Origin Southeast Asia (Thailand, Malaysia, Sumatra, Borneo) Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful but very active Adult Size Up to 24" Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 3" Care Guide Tank setup: These are fast, schooling fish that grow large, so give them plenty of open swimming space, strong filtration and a heavy, tight-fitting lid, since they jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or pellet once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other large, peaceful to semi-aggressive fish such as silver dollars, tinfoil barbs, larger gouramis, plecos and peaceful cichlids. They will eat very small fish once they are large. Good to know: These "sharks" are members of the carp family, not true sharks. They grow quickly, so check their adult size before buying.

The pineapple wag swordtail displays the same bright colors as the parent pineapple sword, but the tail is solid black instead of red. The color contrast brings out the reds and yellows of the body. Our pineapple wag swords are bred in Florida and tolerate a wide range of water conditions. Quick Facts Scientific Name Xiphophorus hellerii (pineapple wag) Origin Southern Mexico to Honduras (wild ancestors); aquarium-bred Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful (males may spar) Adult Size Up to 4–5" (not counting the sword) Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 7.0–8.0 (hard water) Group Size Keep more females than males Care Guide Tank setup: Swordtails are active swimmers, so give them plants, open swimming space and a tight-fitting lid, since they are good jumpers. They prefer hard, alkaline water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet with some vegetable content once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Swordtails get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as platies, mollies, larger tetras, danios, rainbowfish, gouramis and corydoras. Keep more females than males, since males chase females and may spar with each other. Avoid fin-nippers and large cichlids. Good to know: Swordtails are livebearers and breed readily. Fry are born free-swimming and will be eaten unless there are dense plants or a breeding box for them to hide in. Only males grow the "sword" on the tail.

Floating Salvinia - Portion Salvinia is a pretty small floating leaf plant. These plants under the right conditions will propogate on top of the fish bowl and look nice from the top of from below. Each order comes in a two inch portion. These are great floating plants for small fish tanks and even betta bowls. Scientific Name: Salvinia natans Origin: Florida farm Shipping Size: 2 inch dish
Wendtii Green Our potted versions are all ready to place within the substrate already rooted in fish safe and clean rockwool and a 2 inch plastic pot. Scientific Name: CRYPTOCORYNE WENDTII

The long fin pearl danio, also called the long fin turquoise danio, is bred in Thailand to display longer, colorful flowing fins. The body size and color are the same as the parent fish. A school of these fish looks like red and blue flowing wind in the fish tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name Danio albolineatus (long-fin variety) Origin Myanmar, Thailand and Sumatra (captive-bred in Thailand) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful, very active Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 68–79°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Danios are fast swimmers, so give them open swimming space, a filter, plants around the edges and a tight-fitting lid, since they jump. Make sure the tank is fully cycled (which takes several weeks) before adding fish. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Danios get along with most peaceful community fish, such as tetras, rasboras, barbs, corydoras and livebearers. Their speed can stress slow, long-finned fish like bettas and fancy guppies, and large predatory fish will eat them. Good to know: Long fins make these danios a little slower than regular zebras, so avoid fin-nipping tankmates like tiger barbs.

Moonrise pink glo tetra is the gene-spliced, bright pink colored skirt tetra. The pink color was the first to be patented and offers a classic soft accent to the aquarium. Pictured are pink and green glo tetras for those looking to create a 1980s preppy theme. Quick Facts Scientific Name Gymnocorymbus ternetzi (genetically modified) Origin Farm-raised (genetically modified) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful (may nip long fins) Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a filter, plants and open swimming space. A dark substrate and background make the colors pop. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: GloFish tetras get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, danios, rasboras, corydoras and livebearers. Keep them in a group so they don't nip the fins of slow, long-finned fish like bettas. Good to know: GloFish colors look brightest under a blue or actinic LED light, but they are colorful under normal lighting too. Mixing colors in one school creates the best display.

Carniverous Pitcher Plant The carniverous pitcher plant eats bugs. The pitcher plant has modified leaves that create a pitfall. When an insect is attracted to the carniverous plant by the plant nectar, it crawls into the leave and never comes out. At the bottom of the leave pit is digestive fluids that turn the bug into liquid for the plant digestion. This species of pitcher plant is a bog plant perfect for a terrarium. Scientific Name: Sarracenia sp. Shipping Size: Approx. three inch to four inch leaves in a two inch pot

Venus Flytrap The carnivorous venus flytrap, or fly trap, has leaves that attract then spring close around insects. Once the insect gets trapped, the leaves emit digestive fluids and consume the poor critter. Let's hope its a mosquito. Venus flytraps are found in wetlands of the Southeast United States and are perfect for a terrarium. In fact they develop a very attractive white flower. Scientific Name: Dionaea muscipula Shipping Size: Approx. 2-3 inch stems in a 2 inch pot

This newest glo barb was gene-spliced with tiger barbs and phosphorescent coral. They display a bright orange fluorescent color and show the same remarkable quick movements as the parent tiger barb. Though these fish do not actually glow in the dark, they are truly fluorescent and will keep that bright color throughout their lifespan. Quick Facts Scientific Name Puntigrus tetrazona (genetically modified) Origin Bred in the USA from tiger barbs Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Semi-aggressive (fin-nipper) Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 5–7 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group (helps prevent fin-nipping) Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a filter, a heater and plenty of open swimming space. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Pick fast, sturdy tankmates such as other barbs, danios, loaches, corydoras and larger tetras. Avoid slow, long-finned fish like bettas, angelfish, gouramis and guppies. Good to know: GloFish colors look brightest under a blue or actinic LED light. They have the same care needs and temperament as regular tiger barbs.

The Long Fin Zebra Danio is a veil fin variation of the zebra danio. The fins grow longer and more distinctive as the fish grows to its maximum size. These schooling fish are hardy, eat flake food, and get along with everyone. Quick Facts Scientific Name Danio rerio (long-fin variety) Origin India, Bangladesh and Nepal (Ganges region) (captive-bred) Care Level Very easy, great for beginners Temperament Peaceful, very active Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 64–77°F (often fine without a heater) pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Danios are fast swimmers, so give them open swimming space, a filter, plants around the edges and a tight-fitting lid, since they jump. Make sure the tank is fully cycled (which takes several weeks) before adding fish. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Danios get along with most peaceful community fish, such as tetras, rasboras, barbs, corydoras and livebearers. Their speed can stress slow, long-finned fish like bettas and fancy guppies, and large predatory fish will eat them. Good to know: Long fins make these danios a little slower than regular zebras, so avoid fin-nipping tankmates like tiger barbs.

The red onion snail, or onion nerite snail, is a scavenger and algae eater and, like all nerites, plant-safe. The pattern is a red body with small line patterns around the shell. Nerite snails do not overrun the fish tank and only grow to about one inch at full maturity. In fact, to breed, nerite snails need salt water. Nerites do well in most water conditions except for pH below 7.0. These attractive snails do not get bigger than an inch, and we recommend several for algae control in larger tanks. Quick Facts Scientific Name Neritina sp. Origin East Africa and Indo-Pacific coastal streams (wild-caught) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful; plant-safe Adult Size Up to 1" Lifespan 1–2+ years Diet Algae eater (also eats algae wafers) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.5 (hard water for healthy shells) Breeding Lays small white eggs on hard surfaces, but they won't hatch in freshwater, so nerites won't overrun the tank Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Nerites do well in most established tanks with algae to graze. Keep the water hard and alkaline for healthy shells, and keep a lid on the tank, since nerites sometimes climb out. If one flips onto its back, turn it over, since some can't right themselves. Feeding: Nerites mostly graze on algae. If the tank is very clean, add algae wafers so they don't go hungry. Tankmates: Nerites get along with peaceful fish, shrimp and other snails. Avoid puffers, loaches and large cichlids, which eat snails, and keep them away from assassin snails. Good to know: Remove snails before treating the tank with copper or other medications, which are toxic to invertebrates.

Willow Moss Willow moss is just a bit more, well, willowy than java moss, and both make beautiful live ground cover. Mosses are a welcome home to smaller aquatic critters such as fry, fancy shrimp, and freshwater crabs. We ship one half-full standard betta cup portion with each order, enough to cover the bottom of a typical betta tank. We recommend the addition of willow or java moss to any fancy shrimp tank. Scientific Name: Fontinalis antipryetion Shipping Size: One two inch cup Approx. 4 oz

Ricefish are similar to killifish but belong to their own genus, Oryzias , spread throughout Asia from China to Japan. The orange speckled ricefish, or "youkihi" ricefish, is bred in Japan to display pretty orange coloring. Ricefish are common in Japan, but the ricefish offered in the aquatic trade are bred to show superior coloration. The orange ricefish is rare. Both sexes are colorful; males have slightly larger fins. Ricefish are sold individually but do best in a school of six or more. Quick Facts Scientific Name Oryzias latipes (youkihi variety) Origin Japan (aquarium-bred) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1½" Lifespan 2–4 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 64–80°F (handles cooler water; no heater needed in most homes) pH 6.5–8.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Ricefish stay near the surface, so give them plants, floating plants and a lid. They are cool-water fish and do fine at room temperature, and they also do well in outdoor ponds and patio tubs in warm months. Feeding: Feed crushed flake or micro pellets once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Ricefish get along with other small, peaceful fish like white clouds, small rasboras, danios and shrimp. They can share an unheated tank with cool-water species, but avoid large or fast fish (including fancy goldfish) that may eat or outcompete them. Good to know: Medaka have been kept in Japan for centuries and are one of the hardiest small fish in the hobby. Both sexes are colorful; males have slightly larger fins.

The blue wag platy and the red wag platy are two of the most popular color variations of the friendly platy fish. The wag refers to the black tail on the solid blue body. We recommend purchasing a small school of males and females to get the most play and interaction with the pet fish. Quick Facts Scientific Name Xiphophorus maculatus Origin Southern Mexico and Central America Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 3–4 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 70–80°F pH 7.0–8.2 Breeding Livebearer – breeds easily in the aquarium Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Platies are hardy and easy to keep. Give them a filter, a lid and plenty of plants. Use a heater to keep the water steady in the 70s. They prefer harder, slightly alkaline water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. Platies also need some plant matter, so a vegetable flake is a good choice. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Platies get along with most peaceful community fish, such as other livebearers (mollies, guppies and swordtails), tetras, rasboras and corydoras. Avoid large or aggressive fish that may bully or eat them. Breeding: Platies are livebearers, so a tank with males and females will almost certainly have babies (fry). Adults will eat fry, so add dense plants or use a breeding box if you want to raise them. Keeping more females than males gives the females a break from the males' attention. Good to know: Platies are one of the easiest fish to keep, which makes them a great choice for a first aquarium.

Variatus feeders are small but a little larger than feeder guppies, and are inexpensive fish to feed smaller predator fish or to grow out to become colorful little aquarium livebearers. The variatus is a cousin of the platy species, and it is difficult to tell them apart. Each pack comes with about 50 fish, give or take 5%. These feeders are hardy but do require an airstone and clean water. In general, feeder fish can tolerate temperatures from the 60s to the low 80s. Quick Facts Scientific Name Xiphophorus variatus Origin Mexico (captive-bred) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 2–4 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 60–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Sold as a pack of 50 Shipping Size Approx. ½–¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a filter, a heater and plenty of plants. They like slightly hard, alkaline water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also like some plant matter, such as a vegetable flake. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as guppies, platies, mollies, tetras and corydoras. Breeding: They are livebearers and breed easily. Adults will eat the babies, so thick plants give them a place to hide. Good to know: Variatus platies are hardy and colorful as adults, so extras can be grown out as pets.

Instant Ocean Hydrometer Hydrometers measure the salinity in a marine aquarium via specific gravity, The optimum salinity level is a specific gravity reading between 1.02 and 1.026 for nearly all saltwater aquariums. The Instant Ocean Hydrometer is the industry standard for affordable and accurate salinity measuring devices. The hydrometer is completely accurate when measuring saltwater between 68 and 85 degrees Fahrenheit. The Instant Ocean Hydrometer is ready to use, just open the pack, dunk the Hydrometer in the water (you do not even have to get your hands wet) and take a reading. The scale is even color coded - fun! If you don't have one you need one - it will slip right into an order of live saltwater fish and coral. These are a necessity for brackish fish tanks too.

Brine Shrimp Eggs As San Francisco Bay Brand says right on the package - "Hatch your very own live fish food!". Aquarium fish - tropical freshwater or marine fish - go crazy for live brine shrimp and these critters are a great source of natural proteins and lipids and will promote color in most species. Plus, it's fun to hatch sea monkeys. To hatch shrimp use a couple tablespoons of kosher or marine salt to one quart of water, keep it aerated with an air stone, and let the sea monkey games begin. Brine shrimp eggs are quite stable and have a shelf life of three years without impairment of the hatching process. Shipping Size: Net weight of eggs 6 grams

Hikari Jumbo Carnisticks for Large Carnivores One bag of Hikari Carnistick food contains the same calorie content as 1,100 feeder goldfish! And think of all the little lives you would save. Jumbo Carnisticks by Hikari are large floating food sticks high in protein and, obviously, calories. The attractant level is high so even the most finicky arowana, arapaima, and piranhas will go for it. We recommend Jumbo Sticks for arowanas greater than 8 inches and cichlids greater than six inches. Shipping Size: 6.37 oz

Hikari Seaweed Extreme Seaweed Extreme is ideal for marine herbivores like tangs (surgeonfish) and rabbitfish and lots of other species. The formulation contains 67% seaweed - more than any other brand - and 33% binders and kindness. Seaweed pellets are designed to sink for easy grazing. These pellets are full of nutrition and it does not take much to keep your pet fish happy. So please do not overfeed. Shipping Size: 3.52 oz.

Hikari Micro Pellets Hikari formulated this food to appeal and benefit most freshwater tropical fish. The pellet size is optimum for all small to mid-size aquarium fish. The ingredients include algaes and fish sourced proteins, krill, and brewers yeast (a favorite ingredient for beerfish). Community fish food should be fed two to three times per day, and no more than the fish will consume in five minutes. These small packets of pellets fit right into any order of live tropical fish:) Shipping Size: 1.58 oz.

Hikari Goldfish Food Gold The "Gold" grade of Hikari Goldfish Food offers the finest selection of ingredients to promote color and proper body formation in fancy goldfish. The pellets are suitable for goldfish bowls, aquariums, and ponds. Goldfish, like koi, are top grazers and these pellets will float for a short period of time. As an added bonus Hikari includes polyphenol to support the immune system. Shipping Size: 3.5 oz.

Hikari Bio-Gold Discus Food Live black worms are tough to find and frozen foods are not always in the freezer for this fish so sublime. Few fancy tropical fish are a picky as a discus but Hikari cracked the code. Discus Bio-Gold promotes color and body conformity and growth, and most importantly, discus will actually eat it! We know, we tested it and feed our own discus with this food - as we do with all the foods we sell. Discus do not like the upper zone of the aquarium so the pellets are formulated to sink, with lots of attractant so the discus will sense they are about the tank. The main ingredients are krill and crushed silkworm. Nothing is too good for discus fish. Shipping Size: 2.82 oz.

Hikari Shrimp Food It is unfortunate that Hikari named this food "Hikari Shrimp Cuisine" because so many fish eat these little creatures that it sounds like it is packed with them. Nothing can be further from the truth. Hikari Shrimp Cuisine is the ultimate nutrition for the most expensive per pound pet fish in the World - the aquarium fancy shrimp. These small micro sinking wafers will appeal and benefit the wide range of fancy bred shrimp available to the trade today - and will also please their tankmates such as the panda loach and pygmy cory. Amano shrimp, crystal red shrimp, super blue (sakura) will all benefit from shrimp cuisine - and of course a small package will go a long way. Shipping Size: 0.32 oz.

Tetra Tetracolor Community Tropical Fakes When Dr. Ulrich Baensch created the first tropical fish food - called Tetramin - in 1958 he did not know that this one small innovation would spawn the massive aquarium hobby we have today. How many of us would keep fish if we have to catch live bugs under rocks and shorelines? Tetra continued to advance the hobby with Tetracolor, perhaps the finest community flake food. Flake food is ideal for community tanks as it floats and spreads about the fish tank allowing a chance for aggressive and shy tank mates to grab some grub. Tetracolor will enhance the natural color of tropical fish and the complete formulation provides nutrition from the top grazers to the bottom scavengers. Shipping Size: 2.2 oz.

Hikari Cichlid Staple - small pellets Hakari Cichlid Staple provides just what the name implies, a staple formulation for all aquarium cichlids. Fish and shrimp meal provides protein for the meat lovers and alfalfa, seaweed, and kale offer veggies for the vegans in the family. This growth enhancing recipe is designed to minimize color fading as the cichlid ages. Shipping Size: 2.01 oz.

Hikari Food Sticks For top-feeding predators has attractants so no transition time between live and prepared foods should be required. In fact the formula will provide a balanced diet without the need for live food. Cichlids, arowana, peacock bass are perfect candidates for these predator food sticks. The food is prepared in a manner which allows the pellets to float and locks in the nutrient value of the ingredients. Shipping Size: 2.01 oz.

The espei rasbora, also called the pork chop rasbora, is a hardy cousin of the harlequin rasbora. These are a separate species and have a more distinct pork chop shaped black mark on the body than the harlequin rasbora. The fish are caught in smaller streams in Thailand. Pork chop rasboras eat flake food and prefer to school in groups of five or more. Espei/pork chop rasboras are a wild-caught species, so size varies based on whatever the fishermen caught that week and exported. A German ichthyologist Hermann Meinken discovered the species in 1967 and named it after a popular hobbyist and fish importer named Heinrich Espe. So it pays to make fish friends. Quick Facts Scientific Name Trigonostigma espei Origin Thailand and Cambodia Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1¼" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ½–¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a dark substrate. Soft, slightly acidic water and gentle filtration bring out their best color. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as tetras, other rasboras, danios, corydoras, gouramis and dwarf shrimp. Avoid large predatory fish that could eat them. Good to know: In a well-planted tank a school of rasboras swims together in the middle of the tank, and their colors deepen as they settle in.

The rare "ish" manacapuru red shoulder angelfish comes from a very small area of Venezuela and Brazil and features orange to red shoulders on a silver stripe body. These angelfish will adapt more easily than altum angelfish and will accept pellet, flake food, frozen and live food. Manacapuru are the same species as the common wild silver angelfish, just with a few added genes. pH should not be above 7.5, and these fish will look amazing among live plants. Look for the red shoulder to begin appearing as the fish ages to about three inches. Pictured is a juvenile medium angelfish; a full adult male ready to mate will feature the brighter orange shoulder, but expect something more subtle the first year (unless it's a full-grown male ready to mate, of course). Quick Facts Scientific Name Pterophyllum scalare (wild form) Origin Brazil (Manacapuru, Amazon basin) Care Level Moderate Temperament Semi-aggressive (territorial when pairing) Adult Size Up to 6" long and 8–10" tall Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 78–84°F pH 5.5–7.0 Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, gentle filtration, driftwood and tall plants. Wild-type angels do best in soft, slightly acidic water. Feeding: Feed small amounts once or twice a day. Many wild angels learn to take flake and pellets once settled. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Choose calm fish that like soft, warm water and are too large to swallow, such as larger tetras, corydoras and peaceful dwarf cichlids. Avoid fin-nippers and boisterous fish. Breeding: Angelfish pair off and lay eggs on flat surfaces like broad leaves or slate. A breeding pair can become territorial, so give them room and places for other fish to retreat. Good to know: Wild-type angelfish are more sensitive than tank-bred angels. Acclimate them slowly and keep the water soft, warm and very clean.

The hastatus cory is a rare pygmy cory from Brazil. The regular pygmy pygmaeus cory is often misidentified as the more expensive hastatus. A true hastatus has a clear body with only a black dot on the tail. The black dot on close examination is in the shape of a spear, hence the name. "Hastatus" is Latin for "with a spear". Quick Facts Scientific Name Corydoras hastatus Origin Brazil, Bolivia and Paraguay Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1" Lifespan 3–4 years Diet Omnivore (bottom feeder) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ⅓–½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a gentle, sponge-type filter, a heater, fine sand and plenty of plants. Corys are sensitive to salt and some medications (especially copper), so check labels before treating the tank. Feeding: Feed tiny sinking pellets or crushed flake once or twice a day. Make sure the food reaches them before faster fish eat it all. Tankmates: Keep them with other tiny, gentle fish such as small rasboras, ember tetras, shrimp and bettas. Anything big enough to swallow them will. Good to know: Hastatus spend much of their time swimming in midwater schools. Look for the spear-shaped spot on the tail to tell them apart.

The red chromide cichlid, sometimes called the orange chromide, is wild-caught from India and is remarkable in that this species can tolerate brackish water, fresh water, salt water, and high pH water. The chromide fish grows to only three inches and will feed on frozen food and cichlid pellets. The red and orange chromide are the same species, just a slight color variation. The green chromide is Etroplus suratensis, a separate species but similar on all accounts but color. Quick Facts Scientific Name Etroplus maculatus Origin Southern India and Sri Lanka Care Level Easy Temperament Semi-aggressive (territorial when breeding) Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.5–8.5 Group Size Pair Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants, rocks and hiding spots. They like hard water and do well with a little aquarium salt. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They can be territorial when breeding. Keep them with other hardy fish that like slightly salty water, such as mollies and scats. Good to know: Chromides are one of the few cichlids from Asia, and pairs take good care of their eggs and young.

Glowlight Pygmy Barbs bring a pretty and fast-moving highlight to nano fish tanks and planted aquariums. Pygmy Barbs grow to a maximum of 3/4 inch and are suitable tankmates for any nano species, including Panda Loaches, Pygmy Cory, and Fancy Shrimp. These little nano fish need to be in a school to avoid stress, so AquariumFish recommends the purchase of at least five - they do not take up much room! Quick Facts Scientific Name Horadandia atukorali Origin Sri Lanka and southern India Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to ¾" Lifespan 3–4 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a planted tank with gentle filtration. They are tiny, so a sponge over the filter intake keeps them safe. Keep a lid on the tank. Feeding: Feed crushed flake or micro pellets once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: They are tiny and gentle, so keep them with other small, peaceful fish and shrimp. Good to know: Glowlight pygmy barbs have a bright, glowing stripe that shows best against dark plants.

The Asians created GloFish® by splicing the genes of zebra danios and hi-fin white skirt tetras and tiger barbs with phosphorescent corals and jellyfish. The fish were patented and licensed for sale in the USA several years ago once the FDA determined them to be safe for the environment. Though these fish do not actually glow in the dark, they are truly fluorescent and will keep that bright color throughout their lifespan. When they breed, even the babies feature the same fluorescence. Spooky. The purple glo barb is the newest invention added to the family. Quick Facts Scientific Name Puntigrus tetrazona (genetically modified) Origin Bred in the USA from tiger barbs Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Semi-aggressive (fin-nipper) Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 5–7 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group (helps prevent fin-nipping) Shipping Size Approx. 1¼" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a filter, a heater and plenty of open swimming space. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Pick fast, sturdy tankmates such as other barbs, danios, loaches, corydoras and larger tetras. Avoid slow, long-finned fish like bettas, angelfish, gouramis and guppies. Good to know: GloFish colors look brightest under a blue or actinic LED light. They have the same care needs and temperament as regular tiger barbs.

Rhomboid Golden Fairy Wrasse Also commonly referred as the Rhomboid Wrasse, Golden- tail Fairy Wrasse, Diamond-tail Fairy Wrasse. The Rhomboid Golden Fairy Wrasse should be kept in a tank with plenty of rock work to provide ample hiding spaces if needed, with a thick sand bed and a tight lid to prevent escapes. Scientific Name: Cirrhilabrus rhomboidalis Origin: Marshall Islands Max Size: 4 inches Diet: Carnivore Shipping Size: 1 to 3 inches

The platinum white halfmoon betta is a spectacular show as well as a gentle pet. Bettas are solitary creatures, so these fish are quite comfortable with a fish bowl all their own. The Thai betta breeders that AquariumFish.com uses take quite a bit of time and work to breed flawless white variations. The price is well worth it. Quick Facts Scientific Name Betta splendens Origin Thailand (captive-bred) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Males fight each other; peaceful toward most other fish Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 76–82°F (needs a heater) pH 6.5–7.5 Breathes Air Yes – labyrinth fish take air from the surface Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give him a heater (bettas are tropical fish), a gentle filter and live or silk plants. Floating plants or a "betta leaf" near the surface give him a place to rest. Keep a lid on the tank and leave a gap of air under it, since bettas breathe from the surface. Feeding: Feed a few betta pellets or a pinch of flake once or twice a day. Bettas overeat easily, so small meals are best. They also enjoy frozen bloodworms. Tankmates: Never keep two male bettas together. A male can live with small, peaceful fish that don't nip fins, such as corydoras, small rasboras, otocinclus and snails. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs and flashy, long-finned fish like fancy guppies. Good to know: Long, heavy fins tear easily, so keep the filter flow gentle and choose soft plants and smooth decorations. Clean, warm water helps prevent fin rot.

Synodontis albolineatus, or mustard cat, has broad white lines on a chocolate body, and on the edges the white turns to a mustard color. Albo lineatus in fact is Latin for "white lines". In the wild, these African catfish from Cameroon only grow to four inches, about the same in the fish tank. Synodontis albolineatus are hardy scavengers and will eat a bit of everything that falls to the bottom of the tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name Synodontis albolineatus Origin Cameroon Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 4" Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 74–80°F pH 6.5–8.0 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them caves, rocks or driftwood to hide in, and good filtration. They are most active at night. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets once a day, ideally in the evening. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms. Tankmates: They get along with most fish of similar size, including many cichlids. They may eat very small fish. Good to know: Synodontis catfish often swim upside down under leaves and driftwood, which is normal behavior.

The male red empress gets an astonishing rainbow pattern; the female is also pretty, with reflective bluish scales, and is slightly smaller. These cichlids behave like peacock cichlids: relatively peaceful except when breeding. The red empress is popular because of the colors and size; these African cichlids only grow to five inches. The color of the red empress cichlid improves as it ages and is most vibrant during breeding time. Less mature fish have just a hint of the future color pattern. Quick Facts Scientific Name Protomelas taeniolatus Origin Lake Malawi, Africa Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Semi-aggressive (males territorial) Adult Size Up to 5–6" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 76–82°F pH 7.8–8.6 Shipping Size Medium: approx. 2" · Large: approx. 3" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a sand bottom, open swimming space in front and rockwork along the back. Lake Malawi and Lake Tanganyika cichlids need hard, alkaline water; crushed coral or aragonite sand helps hold the pH up. Feeding: Feed a quality cichlid pellet or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like brine shrimp. Tankmates: Haps do well with peacocks and other haps of similar size, plus robust catfish like synodontis. Keep one male per similar-looking species, with several females, to limit fighting and crossbreeding. Good to know: Males take a year or more to show full adult color, and color best when females are present.

The tropheus moorii ilangi, or firecracker tropheus, is called the "king of the tropheus" because this species may be the rarest and prettiest of all Lake Tanganyikan species. The Ilangi come from a small bay of Lake Tanganyika and are difficult-to-breed mouthbrooders. In the wild, these colorful fish live in colonies of about 20 adults. All tropheus cichlids are herbivores and need veggies but will eat frozen foods from time to time. This fish is territorial but peaceful enough to keep with a community cichlid tank. Slow to grow but hardy. Quick Facts Scientific Name Tropheus sp. "Ilangi" Origin Lake Tanganyika, Africa Care Level Moderate to difficult Temperament Aggressive with their own kind; keep in large groups Adult Size Up to 6" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Herbivore (plant-based foods) Water Temperature 76–80°F pH 8.0–9.0 Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Use a sand bottom and plenty of rockwork that grows algae for grazing. Strong filtration and very clean water are essential. Lake Malawi and Lake Tanganyika cichlids need hard, alkaline water; crushed coral or aragonite sand helps hold the pH up. Feeding: Tropheus are strict plant eaters. Feed a vegetable-based flake or pellet in small amounts, and avoid rich, meaty foods, which can make them very sick. Tankmates: Keep Tropheus in a group of a single variety, with one or a few males. Avoid mixing different Tropheus varieties, which will crossbreed and fight. Peaceful Tanganyikans like cyprichromis or synodontis can share the tank. Good to know: Add Tropheus all at once as a group; adding single fish later often leads to fighting.

The Asian floating frog comes from Indonesia, where they are a common sight floating among the rice paddies and feeding on insects. The Asian floating frog is hardy and prefers live insects like crickets and worms, but the aquatic frog will eat frozen and freeze dried treats. These amphibians are not fully aquatic. The floating frog likes to get out and sunbathe as well as search for food, so they need a floating leaf or rock they can get out on. Otherwise, he just likes to float along the surface of the water. If there are several frogs in the area, they usually join hands and float together. Quick Facts Scientific Name Occidozyga lima Origin Indonesia Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 5 years Diet Carnivore (insects, meaty foods) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Floating frogs need both water and a place to climb out. Give them shallow water, floating plants or leaves to rest on, and a tight lid, since they can jump. Feeding: Feed small insects like crickets, or frozen foods like bloodworms. They also take freeze-dried foods. Tankmates: They are peaceful but will eat anything that fits in their mouth. Keep them with their own kind or with fish too large to swallow. Good to know: Floating frogs spend much of their time drifting at the surface with just their eyes above the water.

The long fin green cory is a bred variation of the wild emerald green cory. These aquarium catfish only grow to half the size of the wild Brochis splendens, but they feature a long dorsal fin (sailfin). Like all cory, the long fin cory is hardy, a great scavenger, and prefers to run around in packs. Quick Facts Scientific Name Corydoras splendens (long-fin variety) Origin Captive-bred in Taiwan Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2–3" Lifespan 5–10 years Diet Omnivore (bottom feeder) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and a soft sand or smooth, fine gravel bottom. Plants, driftwood and a few shady spots help them feel secure. Corys are sensitive to salt and some medications (especially copper), so check labels before treating the tank. Feeding: Corys need their own food, not just leftovers. Feed sinking pellets or wafers once or twice a day so food reaches the bottom. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Corys get along with almost any peaceful community fish, such as tetras, rasboras, livebearers, gouramis, angelfish and bettas. Avoid large fish that could swallow them and aggressive bottom dwellers. Good to know: The tall sailfin is a target for fin-nippers, so keep them with gentle tankmates.

The wild chocolate ghost knife comes from Colombia and grows to 24 inches. Very similar to the black ghost knife, these fish have not been bred in captivity. Chocolate ghosts do need some live feeders available - brine shrimp or live black worms would do. The local natives believe the black ghost knife fish holds the spirits of dead ancestors. Perhaps the chocolate ghost knife holds the spirits of eaten M&Ms. Quick Facts Scientific Name Apteronotus leptorhynchus Origin Colombia Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful with fish its size Adult Size Up to 20" Lifespan 15 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 4" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them hiding places like large tubes or caves, dim lighting, strong filtration and a tight lid. They are most active at night. Feeding: Feed frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp once a day, ideally in the evening. Some learn to take sinking pellets. Tankmates: They will eat any fish that fits in their mouth. Keep them with large, peaceful fish. Good to know: Ghost knifefish find their way in the dark using a weak electric field.

Tetra TetraMarine Saltwater Flakes When Dr. Ulrich Baensch created the first tropical fish food - called Tetramin - in 1958 he did not know that this one small innovation would spawn the massive aquarium hobby we have today. How many of us would keep fish if we have to catch live bugs under rocks and shorelines? Tetra continued to advance the hobby with Tetracolor, perhaps the finest community flake food. Flake food is ideal for community tanks as it floats and spreads about the fish tank allowing a chance for aggressive and shy tank mates to grab some grub. TetraMarine Saltwater Flakes is an ideal community food for saltwater aquariums. The formulation is balanced so that just about everything in the fish tank will get something from these high quality fish flakes. In addition the fish food flakes will not cloud the water! Shipping Size: 5.65 oz and 1.84 oz

A unique variation of the crowntail betta bred in Thailand, the patriot crowntail betta displays red, white, and blue on the already bold crowntail body and fins. Only males are available; the breeders will not part with their females. But that's okay, the males are much prettier. Quick Facts Scientific Name Betta splendens Origin Thailand (captive-bred) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Males fight each other; peaceful toward most other fish Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 76–82°F (needs a heater) pH 6.5–7.5 Breathes Air Yes – labyrinth fish take air from the surface Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give him a heater (bettas are tropical fish), a gentle filter and live or silk plants. Floating plants or a "betta leaf" near the surface give him a place to rest. Keep a lid on the tank and leave a gap of air under it, since bettas breathe from the surface. Feeding: Feed a few betta pellets or a pinch of flake once or twice a day. Bettas overeat easily, so small meals are best. They also enjoy frozen bloodworms. Tankmates: Never keep two male bettas together. A male can live with small, peaceful fish that don't nip fins, such as corydoras, small rasboras, otocinclus and snails. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs and flashy, long-finned fish like fancy guppies. Good to know: Crowntail fin rays can split or curl in poor water, so keep the water clean and warm. A short look in a mirror (a minute or two) lets him flare, but long sessions stress him.

The multifasciatus shell dweller, or multi shell dweller, actively defends his little territory around his shell, which doesn't need to be big since these little Tanganyikan cichlids only grow to two inches. The multi shell dweller cichlid is prized for the attractive light blue and brown stripe pattern on the body and his pugnacious attitude. All shell dwellers are hardy and great additions to community tanks and peaceful cichlid tanks. These small fish love their shells, so try to keep a few in the aquarium that are lightweight and not too large for them to manipulate but large enough for them to get into. Quick Facts Scientific Name Neolamprologus multifasciatus Origin Lake Tanganyika, Africa Care Level Easy Temperament Territorial around their shells Adult Size Up to 1½–2" Lifespan 6–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.8–9.0 Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Use a fine sand bottom they can dig in and provide more empty snail shells (escargot shells work well) than there are fish. Lake Malawi and Lake Tanganyika cichlids need hard, alkaline water; crushed coral or aragonite sand helps hold the pH up. Feeding: Feed crushed flake or micro pellets once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep shell dwellers in a species tank or with small, peaceful Tanganyikans like cyprichromis or julidochromis. Larger cichlids will bully or eat them. Good to know: Multis are the smallest shell dwellers and live in colonies, digging into the sand around their shells.

The bandit cichlid is caught in Colombia and named for the broad black vertical lines that look a bit like a bandit mask. This South American cichlid is a cave spawner and will breed in the aquarium under the right conditions. The bandit cichlid requires a cave and some driftwood to get in the mood. It is a peaceful tankmate for medium-size community cichlid tanks. Quick Facts Scientific Name Guianacara geayi Origin Guiana Shield (French Guiana, Suriname and northern Brazil) Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Peaceful for a cichlid Adult Size Up to 4–5" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 76–84°F pH 5.5–7.0 Group Size Single, pair or small group Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a sand or fine gravel bottom, driftwood, rocks and sturdy plants. Good filtration is important, since these cichlids grow large and produce a lot of waste. Feeding: Feed a quality cichlid pellet or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They do well with other peaceful South American cichlids of similar size like angelfish, eartheaters and severums, plus larger tetras, silver dollars and plecos. They may eat very small fish. Good to know: These cichlids are known for their personality and often learn to recognize their owners.

The Giant Betta is a splendens variation bred in Thailand to get twice the size of regular Betta splendens. These beautiful monsters have dramatic colors and twice the fierce attitude of the smaller fighters. Since Giant Bettas are already expensive, we focus on the more colorful selections. The Giant Bettas should have an adequate size bowl, about a half gallon or more, since they need more space. This week's giant bettas are a solid purple to blue color. There are many names for the particular betta color patterns, but most are variations of blue and/or red colors. Fish pictured here are representative only. If you are looking for a specific coloration, please note it on your order, or simply allow us to choose one of our favorites for you! Quick Facts Scientific Name Betta splendens Origin Thailand (captive-bred) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Males fight each other; peaceful toward most other fish Adult Size Up to 5" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 76–82°F (needs a heater) pH 6.5–7.5 Breathes Air Yes – labyrinth fish take air from the surface Shipping Size Approx. 3" Care Guide Tank setup: Give him a heater (bettas are tropical fish), a gentle filter and live or silk plants. Plakats are active swimmers and like room to patrol. Keep a lid on the tank and leave a gap of air under it, since bettas breathe from the surface. Feeding: Feed a few betta pellets or a pinch of flake once or twice a day. Bettas overeat easily, so small meals are best. They also enjoy frozen bloodworms. Tankmates: Never keep two male bettas together. Plakats are among the boldest bettas, so they do best alone or with sturdy, peaceful fish like corydoras and snails. Avoid fin-nippers and other labyrinth fish. Good to know: Giant bettas grow up to twice the size of regular bettas. They are just as territorial as other males.

The harlequin molly is named after the classic colors of the harlequin clowns. Fortunately, unlike certain clowns, these fish are peaceful and friendly. We do our best to pair these if you order two. The lyre tail is named for that ancient curved string instrument from Greece, even though this species originates in Central America. Quick Facts Scientific Name Poecilia sphenops (aquarium-bred hybrids) Origin Mexico and Central America (wild ancestors); aquarium-bred Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 3–4" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (needs plant matter) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.5–8.5 (hard water) Group Size Keep more females than males Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Mollies like hard, alkaline water. Give them plants, open swimming space and good filtration, since they are active and produce a fair amount of waste. Aquarium salt is optional; they also do well in brackish tanks. Feeding: Mollies graze on algae, so feed a quality flake that includes vegetable matter once or twice a day. They also enjoy algae wafers and frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Mollies get along with most peaceful community fish that like similar hard water, such as platies, swordtails, guppies, danios, rainbowfish, corydoras and plecos. Avoid fin-nippers and soft-water specialists. Keeping more females than males keeps any one female from being harassed. Good to know: Mollies are livebearers that breed readily. Fry are born free-swimming and will be eaten unless there are dense plants or a breeding box for them to hide in.

The crystal black shrimp is the black and white cousin of the crystal red shrimp. Crystal shrimp have a white background, as opposed to rili shrimp, which have a clear background. The white color makes for a stronger contrast, but crystal shrimp are a little more difficult to breed than rili shrimp, so the price is a bit higher. Quick Facts Scientific Name Caridina cf. cantonensis (crystal black) Origin Taiwan (aquarium-bred) Care Level Moderate to difficult (needs soft, stable water) Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1" Lifespan 1½–2 years Diet Omnivore (grazes on algae) Water Temperature 68–76°F pH 5.8–6.8 Water Hardness GH 4–6, KH 0–1 (soft) Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Caridina bee and Taiwan bee shrimp need soft, slightly acidic water. Use a mature, cycled tank with an active (buffering) shrimp substrate, RO water remineralized for shrimp, moss and plants, and a sponge filter. Feeding: Feed a small amount of quality shrimp food once a day, and remove any uneaten food after a few hours. Tankmates: Caridina are best kept in a shrimp-only tank or with tiny, peaceful fish like otocinclus, plus snails. Avoid cichlids and other fish that will eat shrimp. Different bee and Taiwan bee varieties can crossbreed, but they will not breed with Neocaridina. Good to know: Acclimate slowly (drip for an hour or more). Stable water matters more than perfect numbers, and sudden changes in temperature or hardness are the most common cause of losses.

Percula Clownfish: The Iconic Reef Tank Inhabitant The Percula Clownfish (Amphiprion percula) is perhaps the most iconic and beloved species in the marine aquarium hobby. Its classic and vibrant appearance features a brilliant orange body with three distinct white stripes , each outlined in a thin black line. Known for its charming and peaceful personality, this fish is an excellent choice for beginner and experienced hobbyists alike. It is famously known for its symbiotic relationship with various anemone species, where it will happily host and defend its home. Why the Percula Clownfish is a Great Choice: Iconic Appearance: Its classic orange, white, and black pattern makes it an instantly recognizable and attractive inhabitant. Highly Hardy: This species is incredibly resilient and easy to care for, making it a perfect first fish for a new tank. Peaceful Temperament: It is a great community fish that can coexist with a variety of other species without issues. Reef-Safe: The Percula Clownfish is completely safe to keep with all types of corals and invertebrates. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Amphiprion percula Origin: Western Pacific Ocean and Great Barrier Reef Max Size: 4 inches Lifespan: 6-10 years Diet: Omnivore. A varied diet of high-quality flakes, pellets, and frozen foods. Shipping Size: .75-3 inches
