Wyoming White Clownfish: A Dazzling Designer Clownfish The Wyoming White Clownfish is a stunning designer variety of the Ocellaris Clownfish (Amphiprion ocellaris) that stands out with its incredible hardiness and pure, all-white body. This specific captive-bred variant is highly sought after for its lack of traditional orange coloration, making it a unique and eye-catching inhabitant in any marine aquarium . Its charming and peaceful personality makes it an excellent choice for beginner and experienced hobbyists alike. Why the Wyoming White Clownfish is a Great Choice: Unique Appearance: Its one-of-a-kind, solid white body is a stunning and attractive deviation from the standard clownfish. Highly Hardy: As a captive-bred fish, it is incredibly resilient and easy to care for, making it a perfect first fish. Peaceful Temperament: It is a great community fish that can coexist with a variety of other species without issues. Reef-Safe: The Wyoming White Clownfish is completely safe to keep with all types of corals and invertebrates. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Amphiprion ocellaris (Designer Variant) Origin: Captive-Bred Max Size: 3 inches Lifespan: 6-10 years Diet: Omnivore. A varied diet of high-quality flakes, pellets, and frozen foods. Shipping Size: 1-2 inches

The L-006 Leopard Spotted Pleco is a rare pleco and seldom found since the expansion of the hydroelectric power program in Brazil. Since the colors are a bit muted, this pleco is not as popular as the gold nugget pleco which often inhabits the same areas. Quick Facts Scientific Name Peckoltia vermiculata Origin Lower Amazon basin, Brazil Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 4–5" Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore (algae and sinking foods) Water Temperature 77–84°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single, or several with a cave each Shipping Size Approx. 3" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them caves, driftwood and good filtration. They are most active at night. Feeding: Feed algae wafers and sinking pellets once a day, ideally in the evening when they are most active. They also enjoy frozen bloodworms. Tankmates: They are peaceful and get along with most community fish. Males may squabble over caves, so give each one its own hiding spot. Good to know: Leopard plecos stay small and spend the day tucked into caves and driftwood.

The green laser corydoras are found in still or slow-moving clear waters in Peru. The green color band is even rarer than the orange and red laser cory. In a school or singly, the bright reflective band stands out in the aquarium. The color of the reflective band is closer to gold than green on a greenish body, though from time to time we get stronger green band colors. Quick Facts Scientific Name Corydoras aeneus group (wild color form) Origin Peru and Brazil Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 5–10 years Diet Omnivore (bottom feeder) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and a soft sand or smooth, fine gravel bottom. Plants, driftwood and a few shady spots help them feel secure. Corys are sensitive to salt and some medications (especially copper), so check labels before treating the tank. Feeding: Corys need their own food, not just leftovers. Feed sinking pellets or wafers once or twice a day so food reaches the bottom. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Corys get along with almost any peaceful community fish, such as tetras, rasboras, livebearers, gouramis, angelfish and bettas. Avoid large fish that could swallow them and aggressive bottom dwellers. Good to know: The reflective "laser" stripe shows best under good lighting against a darker substrate.

The silver darter tetra, or banded darter tetra, is much hardier and more aquarium-safe than the weitzmani tetra, or black darter tetra. Silver darter tetras are caught in Colombia and roam in large schools in the shallow areas of streams. The darter moves along the aquarium like a goby, and these fish are sometimes called goby tetras. A small school of these fish makes quite a sight roaming along the bottom of the tank. Silver darter tetras will scavenge and eat flake and small pellet food. Quick Facts Scientific Name Characidium cf. fasciatum Origin South America (wild-caught; species varies by region) Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1½–2" Lifespan 4–6 years Diet Omnivore (bottom feeder) Water Temperature 68–78°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Darter tetras live on the bottom of clear, flowing streams. Give them a sand or smooth gravel bottom, rocks and some current from the filter. Keep a lid on the tank. Feeding: Feed sinking micro pellets or crushed flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They do well with peaceful community fish like tetras, rasboras, danios and corydoras. Give them room on the bottom away from territorial bottom dwellers. Good to know: Darter tetras perch on rocks and dart along the bottom like gobies, which is fun to watch in a group.

The Ice Blue Cichlid comes from a small area of southern Lake Malawi. Fortunately, breeders keep this fish available to the aquarium hobby; the colors are a unique light blue and yellow to red. Ice Blue Cichlids are hardy and moderately aggressive, similar to peacock cichlids in size and temperament. We also like the ice blue cichlid because the scientific name is not credited to a famous ichthyologist or zoologist, but a humble aquarium hobbyist from Germany named Alfons Greshake. NOTE: These fish vary in color. The body is a consistent blue as they mature, but fin highlights vary from yellow to red. Pictured here is the yellow variation. Quick Facts Scientific Name Maylandia greshakei Origin Lake Malawi, Africa Care Level Moderate Temperament Aggressive (territorial rock-dweller) Adult Size Up to 5" Lifespan 6–10 years Diet Omnivore (needs plant matter) Water Temperature 76–82°F pH 7.8–8.6 Shipping Size Medium: approx. 2" · Large: approx. 3" Care Guide Tank setup: Use a sand or crushed-coral bottom and stack plenty of rockwork with caves and hiding spots so each male can claim a territory and others can escape. Lake Malawi and Lake Tanganyika cichlids need hard, alkaline water; crushed coral or aragonite sand helps hold the pH up. Feeding: Mbuna are mostly plant eaters. Feed a vegetable-based flake or pellet once or twice a day, and avoid high-protein foods, which can upset their digestion. Tankmates: Keep mbuna with other mbuna of similar size and temperament, stocked in a group to spread out aggression. Avoid mixing them with peaceful peacocks and haps unless the tank is large, and avoid closely related species that look alike, which can crossbreed. Good to know: Mbuna stay calmer when the tank is slightly crowded and well decorated, which keeps any one fish from dominating.

The purple mystery snail is a natural hue found among wild mystery snails, and now enough have been bred to offer this color. Mystery snails are hardy, and this aquarium snail grows to two inches over time, is plant-safe and is an excellent scavenger. These snails can handle a wide range of water and temperature conditions, though they cannot tolerate temperatures below 60 degrees. Be sure to pull out snails and other invertebrates when treating the fish tank for ich and other diseases. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pomacea diffusa (sold as P. bridgesii ) Origin South America (Amazon basin); farm-raised Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful; plant-safe Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 1–2 years Diet Scavenger (algae and leftover food) Water Temperature 68–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 (hard water for healthy shells) Breeding Lays pink egg clutches above the waterline; needs a male and female Shipping Size Approx. ½–¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Give mystery snails a covered tank with a gap of an inch or two above the water, since females climb out to lay eggs. Keep the water hard and alkaline for healthy shells, and add calcium (cuttlebone or crushed coral) if your water is soft. Feeding: Mystery snails eat algae and leftover food, but give them sinking pellets or algae wafers too so they don't go hungry. Tankmates: Mystery snails do well with peaceful fish, shrimp and other snails. Avoid fish that nip antennae or eat snails, like puffers, loaches, large cichlids and some bettas, and keep them away from assassin snails. Good to know: Remove snails before treating the tank with copper or other medications, which are toxic to invertebrates.

The freshwater red devil crab is gathered in large colonies in the swampy regions of Indonesia. Red devil crabs are effective scavengers and not fully aquatic. In the aquarium, the red devil will require a place to get out of the water. The red devil crab is also suited for a terrarium or paludarium. Red devils will leave fish alone and spend much of their time around rocks and other areas where food might accumulate. Quick Facts Scientific Name Geosesarma hagen Origin Indonesia Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" (leg span) Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Omnivore (scavenger) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: These crabs need land as well as water. Use a paludarium or a tank with a large land area and a shallow water section. Keep a tight lid on the tank, since they are escape artists. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets or shrimp food once a day. They also eat vegetables and small bits of fish food. Tankmates: Red devil crabs are best kept in a species-only setup, since they may catch small fish or be bothered by larger ones. Good to know: Red devil crabs are bright red with yellow-orange eyes and spend much of their time on land.

Glo Danios were the very first species introduced to the aquarium hobby. New colors were developed and patented. Now there are five colors in the Glo Danio family. Our assortments will have at least three colors, and all colors will school together. Quick Facts Scientific Name Danio rerio (genetically modified) Origin Farm-raised (genetically modified) Care Level Very easy, great for beginners Temperament Peaceful, very active Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 64–77°F (often fine without a heater) pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Danios are fast swimmers, so give them open swimming space and a tight-fitting lid, since they jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Danios get along with most peaceful community fish, such as tetras, rasboras, barbs and corydoras. Their speed can stress slow, long-finned fish like bettas. Good to know: GloFish colors look brightest under a blue or actinic LED light, but they are colorful under normal lighting too. Danios are fast jumpers, so keep a lid on the tank.

Seachem Prime Water Conditioner Prime is considered the finest solution to make tap water aquarium safe and aquarium water safer. In existing fish tank water, just a small amount of Prime detoxifies ammonia, nitrites, and nitrates. For new water a small addition of Prime removes all the chlorine and chloramine to make the water safe for fish. Complete and concentrated conditioner for both fresh and saltwater Removes chlorine, chloramine Detoxiﬁes ammonia, nitrite, and nitrate 5X more concentrated than competing products Each bottle is 250 mL and treats up to 2,500 gallons! Shipping Size: 250 ml/ 8.5 fl oz

Fire Fish Cichlid The Dragon's Blood Peacock Cichlid, or Fire Fish, is a bright pinkish red, mild African cichlid of the Aulonocara family. The black eyes appear larger than regular peacocks and give it a distinctive "dragon" look. These exotic cichlids are bred in Taiwan to create bright pink and red color throughout the body and should not be confused with the lower-priced Strawberry Peacock Cichlid, often sold as Dragon's Blood for a cheap price. This fancy cichlid responds to spirulina and other color enhancers, and without this, some of the color fades. Quick Facts Scientific Name Aulonocara sp. (line-bred) Origin Lake Malawi, Africa (bred in Taiwan) Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Semi-aggressive (males territorial) Adult Size Up to 5" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 76–82°F pH 7.8–8.6 Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a sand bottom, open swimming space in front and rockwork along the back. Lake Malawi and Lake Tanganyika cichlids need hard, alkaline water; crushed coral or aragonite sand helps hold the pH up. Feeding: Feed a quality cichlid pellet or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like brine shrimp. Tankmates: Haps do well with peacocks and other haps of similar size, plus robust catfish like synodontis. Keep one male per similar-looking species, with several females, to limit fighting and crossbreeding. Good to know: Fire fish peacocks keep their best pink-red color with a color-enhancing food.

listings.commonName: Red Hi Fin Lyre Tail Swordtail
listings.description: The hi-fin lyre red swordtail sports a tall and colorful dorsal fin with a curved, long lyre tail. Orange to red in color, these fish are vibrant additions to the fish tank and are active members of the community fish tank. One male to one or two females is a good ratio; two males might wear out a single female. Quick Facts Scientific Name Xiphophorus hellerii (red hi-fin lyretail) Origin Southern Mexico to Honduras (wild ancestors); aquarium-bred Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful (males may spar) Adult Size Up to 4–5" (not counting the sword) Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 7.0–8.0 (hard water) Group Size Keep more females than males Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Swordtails are active swimmers, so give them plants, open swimming space and a tight-fitting lid, since they are good jumpers. They prefer hard, alkaline water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet with some vegetable content once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Swordtails get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as platies, mollies, larger tetras, danios, rainbowfish, gouramis and corydoras. Keep more females than males, since males chase females and may spar with each other. Avoid fin-nippers and large cichlids. Good to know: Lyretail and hi-fin swordtails have extra-long fins, so keep them away from fin-nippers like tiger barbs. Many lyretail males have an elongated gonopodium and can't breed, so lyretail fry usually come from lyretail females mated with standard-finned males.

The horseface loach has a remarkable head that looks just like a horse's head. Horseface loaches are active swimmers and love to dig in aquarium sand and gravel. These hardy aquarium loaches are wild-caught in Southeast Asia and seldom available to the trade. Quick Facts Scientific Name Acantopsis dialuzona Origin Southeast Asia (Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia) Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 8–10" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore (sifts sand for food) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 2½" Care Guide Tank setup: Horseface loaches bury themselves in the bottom, so a soft, fine sand bottom is a must. Give them plants, driftwood and good filtration. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets once or twice a day, ideally in the evening. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They do well with peaceful community fish like tetras, rasboras, gouramis and corydoras. Avoid aggressive bottom dwellers. Good to know: Horseface loaches often bury themselves with only their eyes showing; this is normal behavior.

The gold zebra loach, or Burmese loach, has a playful disposition in the fish tank and will swim through the bottom region of the tank in search of food and action. The color of the gold zebra loach gets deeper and deeper in contrast as the fish grows. These are hardy and colorful aquarium loaches. Quick Facts Scientific Name Botia histrionica Origin Myanmar (Burma) Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Peaceful to semi-aggressive (squabbles with its own kind) Adult Size Up to 3–4" Lifespan 8–15 years Diet Omnivore (bottom feeder; eats snails) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Botia loaches are active bottom dwellers. Give a group plenty of caves, driftwood and rockwork to claim, a soft sand or smooth gravel bottom and good filtration. Keep a lid on the tank. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets or wafers once or twice a day so food reaches the bottom. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Botia loaches also eat pest snails. Tankmates: They do well with most community fish of similar size, such as barbs, danios, rasboras, gouramis and larger tetras. They will eat snails and may eat small shrimp. Good to know: Botia loaches "click" when they feed or squabble, and they sometimes rest on their sides, which is normal behavior.

The freshwater tiger goby, also called the micro tiger goby, is a small (one and a half inch) goby that is a peaceful community fish and is seldom available to the aquarium hobby. Micro tiger gobies can change their colors and will get along with most fish of similar size. Quick Facts Scientific Name Schismatogobius ampluvinculus Origin Southeast Asian island streams Care Level Moderate (needs clean, oxygen-rich, flowing water) Temperament Peaceful with other fish; males territorial with each other Adult Size Up to 1½" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Carnivore (small meaty foods) Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size One male with several females Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: These gobies come from clear, fast-flowing island streams. Give them a mature tank with strong current, high oxygen, smooth rocks covered in algae and biofilm, and a tight lid, since they can climb out. Feeding: These gobies graze on algae off rocks, so they do best in a mature tank. Also feed algae wafers. They may go hungry in a very clean, new tank. Tankmates: They do well with small, peaceful fish that like cool, flowing water, such as danios, rasboras, hillstream loaches and dwarf shrimp. Males may spar with each other. Good to know: Stream gobies cling to rocks with a sucker formed by their pelvic fins. Their larvae drift to the sea to develop, so they rarely breed in aquariums.

The freshwater glass goby from Indonesia requires clean water and some meaty food, like scavenged flake food or live or frozen brine shrimp. These small gobies grow to one inch and are safe for nano to medium aquarium community fish. Quick Facts Scientific Name Gobiopterus chuno Origin South and Southeast Asia (coastal fresh and brackish waters) Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Carnivore (small meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.5–8.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ¾" Care Guide Tank setup: These small gobies do best with plenty of caves and hiding spots (small shells and rocks work well) and hard, alkaline water. Many do best with a little marine salt in the water (brackish, specific gravity about 1.002–1.008). Feeding: Feed small amounts once or twice a day. They prefer small frozen foods like brine shrimp and bloodworms, and some will not eat flake reliably. Tankmates: Keep them in a species tank or with other small, peaceful brackish fish such as mollies, glassfish and small livebearers. Avoid larger fish that could eat them. Good to know: These tiny gobies are full of personality and often perch on rocks or glass to watch their surroundings.

Crinum Natans Crinum natans is a larger member of the crinum onion family and will grow extensive leaves. Very similar to Crinum calimistratum, when well established the narrow wavy deep green leaves of the crinum onion will grow several feet and look stunning in the fish tank. Scientific Name: CRINUM NATANS Origin: Florida Farm Shipping Size : Approx. 6 inches

Crypto lutea Originally from Sri Lanka, we gather our crypto from a Florida nursery that grows these plants specifically for the aquarium hobby. Crypto lutea are low light plants that grow to about eight inches and will root in common aquarium gravel. Scientific Name: CRYPTOCORYNE LUTEA Shipping Size: Bare root on plant approx. 6 inches

Fiji Bicolor Foxface: The Peaceful & Stunning Reef Grazer The Fiji Bicolor Foxface (Siganus uspi), also known as the Bicolor Foxface Rabbitfish , is a beautiful and highly beneficial species that adds a splash of vibrant color and a gentle presence to any marine aquarium . This quirky fish has a truly distinct appearance, with a vibrant yellow on the front half of its body and a solid black on the rear half, which provides a striking contrast. The Fiji Bicolor Foxface is a very peaceful and timid species that is completely reef-safe and will not harm corals, clams, or other invertebrates. It is a fantastic algae grazer, helping to keep unwanted growths in check. A key point for aquarists to remember is that it has venomous dorsal spines, so care should be taken when handling it. Why the Fiji Bicolor Foxface is a Great Choice: Natural Algae Control: It constantly grazes on algae, helping to maintain a clean and healthy environment. Stunning Appearance: Its one-of-a-kind two-tone pattern makes it a true showpiece. Completely Reef-Safe: It will not harm corals, clams, or most other invertebrates. Peaceful Temperament: It is a non-aggressive species that coexists well with other peaceful fish. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Siganus uspi Origin: Fiji Max Size: 8 inches Lifespan: 10+ years Diet: Herbivore. Primarily feeds on marine algae and prepared foods. Shipping Size: 2-3 inches

Hygro Willow Hygrophila willow, or hygro willow, is named for the willowy leaves that sway with the water motion. the willow plant is hardy and required medium light. Hygo plants are shipped five stems to an order with a lead weight for easier planting. An order of hygo easily fits into a fish order box. Scientific Name: HYGROPHILA angustifolia Shipping Size: Approx. 6 inches, bunched with lead weight

The Humpback Dragon Puffer from Thailand is a full freshwater puffer fish. These puffers swim in slow-moving ponds and streams and use their camouflage to catch their prey. Except for snails, no camouflage required for those critters. Dragon Puffers will tolerate other tankmates of similar size and will eat any snails they can get their beak on. The puffer fish also feeds on frozen meaty foods. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pao palembangensis Origin Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia Care Level Moderate Temperament Aggressive Adult Size Up to 8" Lifespan 10+ years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods, snails) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 4" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants, rocks and hiding places, and good filtration, since puffers are messy eaters. Feeding: Puffers need meaty foods and usually won't eat flake. Feed frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp once a day. They also enjoy small snails, which help keep their teeth trimmed. Tankmates: Dragon puffers are ambush predators that may bite other fish. Keep them alone or only with large, robust fish of similar size. Good to know: Dragon puffers spend much of their time sitting still and blending in, then lunge at food.

The Red Phoenix tropheus moorii, or Red Bishop Moorii, begins to show color at one inch and is a solid bright red moorii with the same distinct face and body profile of the tropheus family. Like other tropheus, the red phoenix moorii prefers to school in groups of six or more but will adapt to just a couple of friends in the fish tank. Red phoenix is a highly bred and rare color variation of the native Tanganyikan tropheus cichlids. This fish is territorial but peaceful enough to keep with a community cichlid tank. Slow to grow but hardy, keep the water clean and make sure it has flake or pellet food that contains veggies. Quick Facts Scientific Name Tropheus moorii (red line-bred form) Origin Lake Tanganyika, Africa Care Level Moderate to difficult Temperament Aggressive with their own kind; keep in large groups Adult Size Up to 5" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Herbivore (plant-based foods) Water Temperature 76–80°F pH 8.0–9.0 Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Use a sand bottom and plenty of rockwork that grows algae for grazing. Strong filtration and very clean water are essential. Lake Malawi and Lake Tanganyika cichlids need hard, alkaline water; crushed coral or aragonite sand helps hold the pH up. Feeding: Tropheus are strict plant eaters. Feed a vegetable-based flake or pellet in small amounts, and avoid rich, meaty foods, which can make them very sick. Tankmates: Keep Tropheus in a group of a single variety, with one or a few males. Avoid mixing different Tropheus varieties, which will crossbreed and fight. Peaceful Tanganyikans like cyprichromis or synodontis can share the tank. Good to know: Add Tropheus all at once as a group; adding single fish later often leads to fighting.

Few tetras are truly yellow, so lemon tetras are favored for their bright yellow highlights, and these fish are best kept in schools of six or more. The lemon tetra is hardy and peaceful but does not do well on its own. In nature lemon tetras use their black and yellow highlights to confuse predators when in flight. These are great pet fish for community tanks, nano tanks and planted aquariums. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hyphessobrycon pulchripinnis Origin Tocantins basin, Brazil Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a dark substrate, which brings out their color. Keep a lid on the tank, since tetras can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, rasboras, danios, corydoras, dwarf cichlids, gouramis and livebearers. Good to know: Tetras feel safer and show better color in a group. A larger school also spreads out any chasing.

Bleeding Heart Tetra This fish has a characteristic red spot on the chest resembling a heart. This is a peaceful, relatively large tetra, making them excellent display fish. Like most tetras, they are best kept in schools or at least in pairs; they have kind hearts and lose color when lonely. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hyphessobrycon erythrostigma Origin Upper Amazon (Peru, Colombia, Brazil) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1¼" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a dark substrate, which brings out their color. Keep a lid on the tank, since tetras can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, rasboras, danios, corydoras, dwarf cichlids, gouramis and livebearers. Good to know: Tetras feel safer and show better color in a group. A larger school also spreads out any chasing.

The parent of the long-fin serpae tetra, with the same color but shorter fins, the serpae tetra is more peaceful (and less expensive) than the long-fin variety. The serpae tetra is often called the red minor tetra in the fish trade, but less and less often. Looks like that will be one of those common names that will go by the wayside. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hyphessobrycon eques Origin Amazon and Paraguay basins (Brazil, Paraguay, Argentina) Care Level Easy Temperament Semi-aggressive (known fin-nipper) Adult Size Up to 1¾" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a dark substrate, which brings out their color. Keep a lid on the tank, since tetras can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, rasboras, danios, corydoras, dwarf cichlids, gouramis and livebearers. Good to know: Tetras feel safer and show better color in a group. A larger school also spreads out any chasing.

Fire-red and reflective blue stripes along the length of this fish helped make the cardinal tetra the most popular aquarium fish in Europe. An entire industry in Brazil is involved in catching and sustaining this species, employing thousands who would otherwise work in deforestation industries. Therefore, cardinal tetras are one of the many tropical fish that help save the rainforest. So, keeping aquariums helps the planet. Cardinals are the most popular fish in the aquarium trade in Europe and second to GloFish in the USA. These fish will not tolerate pH over 7.4 and need good, clean water, just like the Amazon. Quick Facts Scientific Name Paracheirodon axelrodi Origin Rio Negro and Orinoco basins (Brazil, Colombia, Venezuela) Care Level Moderate (needs soft, clean water) Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1½" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 76–84°F pH 5.0–7.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Medium: approx. ¾–1" · Large: approx. 1¼–1½" Care Guide Tank setup: These small tetras do best in a planted tank with soft, slightly acidic water, a dark substrate, driftwood, floating plants and gentle filtration. A larger school makes them more confident and colorful. Feeding: Feed small amounts of micro pellets or crushed flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other small, peaceful fish like rasboras, small tetras, pencilfish, pygmy corydoras, otocinclus and dwarf shrimp. Avoid large or boisterous fish that could eat or bully them. Good to know: Small tetras show their best color in a large school in a planted tank with soft lighting.

The third most popular aquarium fish in the USA market, the neon tetra is affordable, sturdy and so friendly the fish will school with other species. Should be kept in groups of six or more. Similar to cardinal tetras, they do not grow quite as large and have a horizontal red bar that extends only halfway along the body. The bright red and blue reflective colors look wonderful as they school around in community and planted tanks. Green neon tetras are a fragile fish to import, which makes them a rarity in the trade. Green neons display a bright reflective green and create one of the most beautiful schools in nature and the aquarium. These fish do not live in alkaline hard water; they die in it. Due to their small size, they should not be mixed with larger discus, unless the intent is to provide them with an exotic treat. These fish are all wild-caught, and size will vary. The scientific name "herbertaxelrodi" is named after one of the few people to ever get rich in the aquarium trade, the famed Herbert Axelrod. Black neons have a distinct, bright yellow-green reflective line that stands out on a deep black body. These fish are upper-level schooling fish and swim just below hatchetfish. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hyphessobrycon herbertaxelrodi Origin Paraguay basin (Rio Taquari), Brazil Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1½" Lifespan 4–6 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ¾–1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a dark substrate, which brings out their color. Keep a lid on the tank, since tetras can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, rasboras, danios, corydoras, dwarf cichlids, gouramis and livebearers. Good to know: Tetras feel safer and show better color in a group. A larger school also spreads out any chasing.

As the name implies, the diamond tetra is a very flashy fish, but it takes nearly six months to develop the diamond reflective scales for which this fish is known. These tetras are great community fish and grow to a nice two and a half inches. Diamond tetras are difficult to breed and grow slowly, but the diamond scale pattern is worth the wait. With the right lighting, these fish will be the "jewel" of the aquarium. Normally we ship these tetras at one inch in size, when the diamond scales are just beginning to develop. Red eye monks tend to school in the lower levels of the tank and need to be kept in groups, or they can get a bit aggressive. The larger these fish get, the bolder the blue body and red fins become, and fortunately these tetras live for seven years. Called the red blue Colombian tetra or simply the Colombian tetra, this fish is wild-caught in Colombia. However, the tetra breeds easily, and most in the trade are imported from a fish farm in Singapore. The fish have only been around since the 1990s, but they are very adaptive to community tanks if kept in groups of five or more. Loners get unhappy and nippy. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hyphessobrycon columbianus Origin Northern Colombia (Caribbean slope) Care Level Easy Temperament Semi-aggressive (may nip fins if kept in small groups) Adult Size Up to 2½–3" Lifespan 5–10 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: These are larger, active schooling fish, so give them open swimming space, plants or driftwood along the back and a tight-fitting lid, since they jump. Tankmates: They do well with other active, similar-size fish such as larger tetras, barbs, rainbowfish, peaceful cichlids, corydoras and plecos. Very small fish may be eaten or bullied. Good to know: Larger tetras are hardy and long-lived, and a big school makes a striking display.

Orange is not a common color among tetras, but this one has orange all over. Generally captive-bred in Florida, though originally from Brazil. Purple, black and blue distinctive fins create a visual treat for this mid-level schooling fish. Purple emperor tetras do not like to be chased and are prone to disease if stressed, so do not keep these with semi-aggressive community fish. The purple emperor tetra is also called the black emperor tetra in the aquarium trade, but that is confusing, since there is another emperor tetra called the blue-eye black emperor that has a darker body and blue eyes, and no purple. These guys are purple. The rummynose name is a bit anthropomorphic, but mature adults do have bright red noses like drunken old sailors. Rummynose tetras look great in a school with their sharp black and white caudal fins and tend to school in the mid-levels of the tank. The males and females get the red noses, and the red becomes more prominent as the fish ages, just like a heavy drinker. AquariumFish.com imports wild and bred rummynose tetras, depending on the season. These tetras can be found in most countries within the Amazon basin. They are perfect mates for most African and South American cichlids and should be kept in schools of at least four. These fish come in various sizes, as they are wild-caught in the Congo River tributaries. The glass bloodfin tetra is similar to the bloodfin tetra but provides bolder red coloration that is even more striking when viewed in a school of these clear-bodied fish. These are great fish in the aquarium. The glass bloodfin tetra is a peaceful, very active species with bright red fins on a clear, somewhat silver body. Long-lived for a small fish and active most of the day. The glowlight tetra, or glolite tetra, has a bright, primarily gold stripe along the body, which flashes reflective light as it swims throughout the fish tank. These fish tend to swim separately, then bunch when threatened, so it makes for lively action. Glowlight tetras have been in the aquarium trade for decades and are truly classics. Males and females look the same. The front and rear reflective spots create a spectacle when these fish move around in a school, and we recommend a group of eight for a midsize fish tank. The tetra is hardy, peaceful and easy to keep in any size aquarium. The fish has silver tips, but silvertip tetras also have beautiful gold and red on the fins and body. These fish are peaceful but very active, so they are a nice addition to the aquarium. Just like the name, this "honey" of a fish has the coloration of a bumblebee. The bumblebee cichlid can handle aggressive cichlids like buttikoferi and zebras. It's a very active fish and seems to enjoy navigating the whole tank. Both males and females show the bold yellow and black pattern. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pseudotropheus crabro Origin Lake Malawi, Africa Care Level Moderate Temperament Aggressive (territorial rock-dweller) Adult Size Up to 5–6" Lifespan 6–10 years Diet Omnivore (needs plant matter) Water Temperature 76–82°F pH 7.8–8.6 Shipping Size Small: approx. 1" · Medium: approx. 2" · Jumbo: approx. 5" Care Guide Tank setup: Use a sand or crushed-coral bottom and stack plenty of rockwork with caves and hiding spots so each male can claim a territory and others can escape. Lake Malawi and Lake Tanganyika cichlids need hard, alkaline water; crushed coral or aragonite sand helps hold the pH up. Feeding: Mbuna are mostly plant eaters. Feed a vegetable-based flake or pellet once or twice a day, and avoid high-protein foods, which can upset their digestion. Tankmates: Keep mbuna with other mbuna of similar size and temperament, stocked in a group to spread out aggression. Avoid mixing them with peaceful peacocks and haps unless the tank is large, and avoid closely related species that look alike, which can crossbreed. Good to know: Bumblebee cichlids can change color, turning dark brown or black when stressed or showing dominance.

Once this fish gets to ten inches, it should be given its own tank or eaten. This is a very aggressive fish and can handle other aggressive species such as red devils and zebras, but keep a lookout for bullying when they get bigger. In Africa, this is a prized fish for eating, but in the USA, this is a prized aggressive pet fish. Quick Facts Scientific Name Heterotilapia buttikoferi Origin Liberia, Sierra Leone and Guinea-Bissau (West African rivers) Care Level Moderate Temperament Very aggressive Adult Size Up to 12–14" Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Omnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.5–8.0 Shipping Size Approx. 1¼" Care Guide Tank setup: Use a sand bottom, sturdy rockwork or driftwood and strong filtration, since big cichlids are messy eaters. Anchor decorations well, as they like to dig. Feeding: Feed a quality cichlid pellet once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like shrimp. Avoid feeder fish, which can carry disease. Tankmates: Keep them only with other large, robust cichlids and catfish that can hold their own. They will eat any fish small enough to fit in their mouth. Good to know: Buttikoferi grow fast and become very aggressive as adults, so many keepers end up housing them alone or with equally large, tough fish.

One of the most popular mbunas due to its solid cobalt blue color, it gets along with other zebra cichlids and haplochromis cichlids but is aggressive towards mild-mannered cichlids. Cobalt cichlids are good species for the aquarium, since this pet fish only grows to 3 1/2 inches. Just as in the wild, these cichlids prefer rocky areas to inhabit and breed. Cobalt Blue, or Cobalt Zebra Cichlids, are mouthbrooders and easy to breed. A strange-looking fish with the scary nickname Malawi Eye-biter, or the purple eye biter, they are no worse than any other cichlid when it comes to biting eyes. Haplochromis compressiceps, or more properly Nimbochromis compressiceps, are longer and slimmer than other cichlids, so they add variety to a cichlid tank. The males develop a deep purple shade to the body at four inches. Quick Facts Scientific Name Dimidiochromis compressiceps Origin Lake Malawi, Africa Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Semi-aggressive (males territorial) Adult Size Up to 10" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 76–82°F pH 7.8–8.6 Shipping Size Medium: approx. 2" · Large: approx. 3" · Jumbo: approx. 5" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a sand bottom, open swimming space in front and rockwork along the back. Lake Malawi and Lake Tanganyika cichlids need hard, alkaline water; crushed coral or aragonite sand helps hold the pH up. Feeding: Feed a quality cichlid pellet or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like brine shrimp. Tankmates: Haps do well with peacocks and other haps of similar size, plus robust catfish like synodontis. Keep one male per similar-looking species, with several females, to limit fighting and crossbreeding. Good to know: Compressiceps are ambush predators of small fish, so keep them with tankmates too big to swallow.

Demasoni are beautiful and curious fish, continuously exploring the nooks around the aquarium. They only get to 4", so they are a good fit with other mid-size and smaller cichlids. Slow growers and a bit more difficult to breed, they are priced accordingly. Demasoni are distinguished by the bold reflective blue vertical stripes along the entire body of the fish. Small samples of these can be found at PetSmart for as low as $9.00 for a 1/2-inch fish, but we believe superior breeding and better size will improve the aquatic experience. Hence, a bigger fish at a bigger price. The hump, more dominant on the males, will begin to develop at three inches. Solid blue with some black, it is relatively friendly to other cichlids. Even at two inches, these cichlids have beautiful color and are peaceful additions to a community cichlid tank. Keep one male per similar-looking species, with several females, to limit fighting and crossbreeding. The male kribensis gets a bright purplish red belly, so they can be easily distinguished from females. Kribensis, or simply kribs, are some of the smallest African cichlids, growing to only three inches, easy to breed, and they go well with other cichlids, barbs, and angelfish. Nano aquarium species, like crystal red shrimp and chili rasboras, are not appropriate for any cichlid, even dwarf (little fishies) like our kribs. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with peaceful community fish like tetras, barbs, rasboras, corydoras and plecos. Give each pair its own territory, and expect more defensiveness when breeding. Good to know: Kribs are cave spawners. A pair will claim a cave and guard their fry, and can become pushy while breeding.

These are really big, very cool cichlids from Madagascar. At two to three inches, they show the distinctive solid black body with a starry night pattern. You can teach these fish to feed out of your hand, but they are similar to Oscars: mean to fish smaller than themselves. The polleni cichlid is the only tropical fish from Madagascar available to the aquarium trade. Quick Facts Scientific Name Paratilapia polleni Origin Madagascar Care Level Moderate Temperament Aggressive; eats smaller fish Adult Size Up to 10" Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Omnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.5–8.0 Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Use a sand bottom, sturdy rockwork or driftwood and strong filtration, since big cichlids are messy eaters. Anchor decorations well, as they like to dig. Feeding: Feed a quality cichlid pellet once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like shrimp. Avoid feeder fish, which can carry disease. Tankmates: Keep them only with other large, robust cichlids and catfish that can hold their own. They will eat any fish small enough to fit in their mouth. Good to know: Polleni are personable "pet" fish that learn to recognize their owners, but they will eat any fish small enough to swallow.

The snow white zebra mbuna is a bit more peaceful than other mbunas and can get along with peacock cichlids. The solid white body brings great contrast to a cichlid community tank. In a community cichlid tank, the white body brings a great color contrast to the red zebras and cobalt blues, not to mention a red, white, and blue patriotic flair. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pseudotropheus socolofi (albino) Origin Lake Malawi, Africa Care Level Moderate Temperament Semi-aggressive (calmer than most mbuna) Adult Size Up to 4–5" Lifespan 6–10 years Diet Omnivore (needs plant matter) Water Temperature 76–82°F pH 7.8–8.6 Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Use a sand or crushed-coral bottom and stack plenty of rockwork with caves and hiding spots so each male can claim a territory and others can escape. Lake Malawi and Lake Tanganyika cichlids need hard, alkaline water; crushed coral or aragonite sand helps hold the pH up. Feeding: Mbuna are mostly plant eaters. Feed a vegetable-based flake or pellet once or twice a day, and avoid high-protein foods, which can upset their digestion. Tankmates: Keep mbuna with other mbuna of similar size and temperament, stocked in a group to spread out aggression. Avoid mixing them with peaceful peacocks and haps unless the tank is large, and avoid closely related species that look alike, which can crossbreed. Good to know: Mbuna stay calmer when the tank is slightly crowded and well decorated, which keeps any one fish from dominating.

The red zebra is a solid red mbuna cichlid found in Lake Malawi. The red zebra cichlid is quite active and will be aggressive with other species, so zebra cichlids should not be kept with peaceful species such as kribensis cichlids. In a community cichlid tank, the red zebra offers a great color contrast to yellow labs, snow white, and cobalt blue cichlids. This popular cichlid has the colors of a giraffe with a blue face, grows to ten inches, and gets along with mbunas and peacocks. The color pattern is similar to the Haplochromis livingstoni, but the livingstoni males do not get the blue accents at maturity. Female venustus cichlids have the same gold and brown mottled pattern but do not grow quite as large and do not exhibit the blue markings. The brichardi cichlid is a great example of Lake Tanganyika dwarf cichlids. Also called the Fairy Cichlid, the brichardi are one of the few schooling cichlids in the wild. Brichardi cichlids are easy to breed and very hardy, a great starter small cichlid but very territorial. These pretty little cichlids get their nickname "fairy cichlid" for their wing-like fins and lyre tails, not their behavior. Quick Facts Scientific Name Neolamprologus brichardi Origin Lake Tanganyika, Africa Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Territorial Adult Size Up to 4" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.8–9.0 Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Use a sand bottom with rockwork, caves and crevices for spawning sites. The tropheus duboisi is a solid black cichlid with small white spots. As the fish matures, duboisi get broad colorful bands around the body. This African cichlid is territorial but can be kept with a large group of other tropheus. Slow to grow but hardy, keep the water clean and make sure it has flake food that contains veggies. Quick Facts Scientific Name Tropheus duboisi Origin Lake Tanganyika, Africa Care Level Moderate to difficult Temperament Aggressive with their own kind; keep in large groups Adult Size Up to 4–5" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Herbivore (plant-based foods) Water Temperature 76–80°F pH 8.0–9.0 Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Use a sand bottom and plenty of rockwork that grows algae for grazing. Strong filtration and very clean water are essential. Lake Malawi and Lake Tanganyika cichlids need hard, alkaline water; crushed coral or aragonite sand helps hold the pH up. Feeding: Tropheus are strict plant eaters. Feed a vegetable-based flake or pellet in small amounts, and avoid rich, meaty foods, which can make them very sick. Tankmates: Keep Tropheus in a group of a single variety, with one or a few males. Avoid mixing different Tropheus varieties, which will crossbreed and fight. Peaceful Tanganyikans like cyprichromis or synodontis can share the tank. Good to know: Young duboisi are black with white polka dots; the spots fade into a bright yellow or white band as they mature.

The red band tropheus moorii, or tropheus moorii bemba, will begin showing color at two inches, though shipping size is normally between one and two inches, so please be patient. This fish is territorial but peaceful enough to keep with a community cichlid tank. Slow to grow but hardy, keep the water clean and make sure it has flake food that contains veggies. These sell as fast as our Taiwan breeder breeds them, so we generally can only get small sizes. The yellow band moorii, also called the Kaiser II Cichlid or the Tropheus Moorii Ikola, is a schooling cichlid in the wild, and a few of these mature species in the aquarium is a marvelous sight. At only two inches, the yellow band becomes distinct, so don't worry when you receive the fish at one to one and a half inches and the band is not visible. Slow to grow but hardy, keep the water clean and make sure it has flake food that contains veggies. Tropheus cichlids appreciate lettuce treats from time to time. Quick Facts Scientific Name Tropheus moorii "Ikola" Origin Lake Tanganyika, Africa Care Level Moderate to difficult Temperament Aggressive with their own kind; keep in large groups Adult Size Up to 5" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Herbivore (plant-based foods) Water Temperature 76–80°F pH 8.0–9.0 Shipping Size Approx. 1–1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Use a sand bottom and plenty of rockwork that grows algae for grazing. Strong filtration and very clean water are essential. Lake Malawi and Lake Tanganyika cichlids need hard, alkaline water; crushed coral or aragonite sand helps hold the pH up. Feeding: Tropheus are strict plant eaters. Feed a vegetable-based flake or pellet in small amounts, and avoid rich, meaty foods, which can make them very sick. Tankmates: Keep Tropheus in a group of a single variety, with one or a few males. Avoid mixing different Tropheus varieties, which will crossbreed and fight. Peaceful Tanganyikans like cyprichromis or synodontis can share the tank. Good to know: Add Tropheus all at once as a group; adding single fish later often leads to fighting.

Quick Facts Scientific Name Apistogramma borellii Origin Paraguay, Argentina and Brazil (Paraná basin) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful (males territorial with each other) Adult Size Males up to 2½"; females smaller Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 70–79°F (handles cooler water than most apistos) pH 6.0–7.5 Shipping Size Approx. ¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter, dim lighting and lots of plants, driftwood and leaf litter. Add a cave (a coconut shell or small clay pot) for each female. Most apistos prefer soft, slightly acidic water. Feeding: Feed small pellets or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with small, peaceful fish such as tetras, rasboras, pencilfish, otocinclus and corydoras. A calm school of small "dither" fish helps apistos feel safe enough to come out. Keep one male per tank unless it is large and well planted, and avoid large or boisterous fish. Ram is short for the species name “ramirezi”, but it is also reminiscent of their tendency to butt heads like a terrestrial ram. Wild-caught rams' appearance depends upon the region of the Amazon. Colombian rams are very similar to the bred German rams, though slightly smaller. Wild rams are interesting, since they will feature variations in behavior and appearance that only nature can account for. Quick Facts Scientific Name Mikrogeophagus ramirezi (wild) Origin Colombia (wild-caught) Care Level Moderate (needs warm, clean, soft water) Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 2–4 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 80–86°F pH 5.0–7.0 Group Size Pair or small group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Rams need warm, very clean, soft water. Give them a sand bottom, plants, driftwood, leaf litter and flat stones for spawning. Rams are sensitive to poor water quality. Feeding: Feed small amounts of quality micro pellets or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Rams do well with small, peaceful fish that like warm, soft water, such as tetras, rasboras, hatchetfish, corydoras and discus. They may eat small shrimp. Avoid large or boisterous fish. Good to know: Rams often form pairs and lay eggs on flat stones. Stable, warm water is the key to keeping them healthy.

Quick Facts Scientific Name Geophagus surinamensis Origin The Guianas; similar fish exported from Venezuela and Colombia Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful (territorial when breeding) Adult Size Up to 8–10" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore (sifts sand for food) Water Temperature 77–84°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1½–2½" Care Guide Tank setup: Eartheaters sift sand through their gills, so use a fine sand bottom (no sharp gravel). AquariumFish.com imports as many as we can to provide a broad selection for our aquarists. Convict cichlids are so easy to breed they are never caught in the wild. AquariumFish.com sources convicts from a pond breeder in Florida. These species will get aggressive as they grow but adapt well to other large species in the tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name Amatitlania nigrofasciata Origin Central America (Guatemala to Panama); pond-raised in Florida Care Level Easy Temperament Semi-aggressive (territorial, especially when breeding) Adult Size Up to 5–6" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Single or pair Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a sand or gravel bottom, rocks, caves and driftwood to create territories. Anchor decorations well, since they like to dig. Strong filtration is important. Feeding: Feed a quality cichlid pellet or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other robust Central American cichlids of similar size, plus larger catfish and plecos. Give each fish its own territory, and avoid small or timid fish. Good to know: Central American cichlids are hardy and easy to breed. Pairs become very protective of their eggs and fry.

The festivus cichlid, also called simply festivum, comes from Venezuela. Another name for the cichlid is the flag cichlid. These fish were first kept in aquariums by Germans back in 1908. Despite the long history, these fish are wild-caught and not often seen in the aquarium trade, though they were once common. The peaceful behavior, unique body structure and bold angular line across the body make the cichlid a great addition to the fish tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name Mesonauta festivus Origin Amazon and Paraguay basins (Brazil, Bolivia, Peru, Paraguay) Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Peaceful for a cichlid Adult Size Up to 6" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 76–84°F pH 5.5–7.0 Group Size Single, pair or small group Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a sand or fine gravel bottom, driftwood, rocks and sturdy plants. Good filtration is important, since these cichlids grow large and produce a lot of waste. Feeding: Feed a quality cichlid pellet or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They do well with other peaceful South American cichlids of similar size like angelfish, eartheaters and severums, plus larger tetras, silver dollars and plecos. They may eat very small fish. Good to know: These cichlids are known for their personality and often learn to recognize their owners.

The firemouth cichlid is one of the hardiest and classic South American cichlids available. These fish have red markings around the gills and mouth, which they can display to ward off predators or display against each other in territory disputes. Nevertheless, the firemouth is peaceful and may be kept with other species of similar size. The wild blue acaras are quite a colorful fish and inhabit small streams of the Amazon basin. These fish prefer lower pH and plants but are tolerant of higher-pH water. Blue acaras are small, non-aggressive cichlids, but they will eat fancy shrimp. This is a hardy species that makes an excellent choice for the beginning cichlid keeper. They are moderately easy to care for as long as the water quality is maintained and they are provided a quality diet. They are ready feeders, and if bred they become excellent parents. They spawn easily and take very good care of their fry. The electric blue acara was first bred in Asia and entered the trade about 2008. These fish have a solid, reflective cobalt blue body and the same behavior as the wild blue acara. These are good community fish but will eat very small species such as fancy shrimp. Quick Facts Scientific Name Andinoacara pulcher (electric blue) Origin Captive-bred (Asia) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful (for a cichlid) Adult Size Up to 6" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single or pair Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a sand bottom, plants, driftwood and flat stones for spawning. The wolf cichlid, or dovii cichlid, is so called for the arched back of the species that is reminiscent of a wolf. These are active Central American cichlids and will be suitable with species of their own size. When these fish mature they truly look magnificent (mature fish pictured). These fish are prized large predators and can grow up to two feet. Our wolf cichlids are pond-raised and, when caught for shipping, can vary in size from just under two inches to three inches. Quick Facts Scientific Name Parachromis dovii Origin Central America (Honduras to Costa Rica); pond-raised Care Level Moderate Temperament Very aggressive; eats smaller fish Adult Size Up to 20–24" Lifespan 12–15 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods; takes pellets) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Single or pair Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: These are large, powerful cichlids, so give them a sand bottom, large rocks and driftwood. Anchor decorations well, since they dig and rearrange the tank, and use strong filtration. Feeding: Feed a quality cichlid pellet once a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like shrimp. Avoid feeder fish, which can carry disease. Tankmates: Keep them alone or with other large, robust cichlids and catfish that can hold their own. They will eat any fish small enough to fit in their mouth. Good to know: These cichlids are full of personality and often learn to recognize their owners. They grow large, so check their adult size before buying.

The jaguar cichlid, or "simply" the managuensis, is a beautiful jade and black South American species that is not as common as other species, in part due to its origin in Central America. Most South American species come from the Amazon basin, so there are fewer collectors in this region of the world. The jaguar cichlid is a predator, as the name implies, and makes a great single pet fish, but these cichlids are also good tank mates with similar-size species. Originally bred for fighting, these tough fish make nice pets. But they aren't nice. Like the blood red parrot cichlid, the flowerhorn cichlid is a successful hybrid from two or several species, including red terror, synpillum, and citrinellus cichlids. Malaysian breeders were the first to successfully export these to the United States. Today there are more strains than can be mentioned in this short description, but the red dragon flowerhorn is a hardy and affordable creature. When these fish get big, they get mean, really mean, so expect to provide them with their own aquarium down the road. Quick Facts Scientific Name Amphilophus hybrid Origin Captive-bred hybrid (Malaysia) Care Level Moderate Temperament Aggressive Adult Size Up to 10–12" Lifespan 10–12 years Diet Omnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 78–86°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Keep one per tank Shipping Size Approx. 1–3" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them strong filtration, a smooth bottom and only a few sturdy decorations, since they rearrange the tank. Feeding: Feed a quality cichlid pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like shrimp. Tankmates: Flowerhorns are very aggressive and are usually kept alone. Good to know: Flowerhorns are full of personality and often learn to recognize their owners.

Despite the name, angelfish can be quite territorial, particularly when they pair up to breed in the aquarium. At that time, these fish do not act like angels. Gold Marble Angelfish are hardy and easy to care for. Each order comes with four angelfish, which are generally marble, silver, gold, and gold marble. Fish pictured here are representative only. If you are looking for a specific coloration, add a note to the order or simply allow us to choose one of our favorites for you! Quick Facts Scientific Name Pterophyllum scalare Origin Amazon basin, South America (captive-bred) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Semi-aggressive (territorial when pairing) Adult Size Up to 6" long and 8" tall Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 4 Shipping Size Approx. 1½–4" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them tall plants or driftwood, a heater and a gentle filter. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Choose peaceful fish too large to swallow, such as larger tetras, corydoras, plecos, rams, gouramis and peaceful barbs. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs, and small fish like neon tetras that adult angels may eat. Breeding: Angelfish pair off and lay eggs on flat surfaces like broad leaves or slate. A breeding pair can become territorial, so give them room and places for other fish to retreat. Good to know: In a group, two angelfish often pair off and claim part of the tank. If a pair forms and starts chasing the others, add more hiding places or rehome the extras.

The blue zebra angelfish has been bred to display a blue tinge to the body of a regular zebra angelfish. The blue is unremarkable when the fish is under three inches, but becomes more obvious as the fish grows and the blue highlights dominate. Angelfish are a hardy, popular species found in rivers all throughout South America, primarily the Amazon River and its tributaries. This family of aquarium fish all have the tall, wing-size fins giving the fish their namesake. Full black angels are bred to show a smoky to solid dark black body and fins, which makes a remarkable contrast in a planted aquarium. Our black angelfish are captive-bred in the USA and in Taiwan. These popular species are bred from a similar pattern found in rivers all throughout the Amazon River basin. From the more mottled pattern of the wild silver angelfish, breeders in Taiwan were able to isolate the blue gene along with the unique marble and spotted "leopard" pattern. One striking feature of the leopard angelfish is that the blue gene becomes apparent at the jumbo size, but do not expect any hint of blue at smaller sizes. If you "google" the picture of a blue leopard, often you will get the picture to the right, a pattern very similar to blue pinoy. Our Indo breeders are notorious for sending either pattern for the leopard, and we never know until they get in. If you are dead set on one or the other pattern, let us know when you order in the comment section or ask prior to ordering! Angelfish are a very popular species found in rivers all throughout the Amazon River basin. They are unique in appearance, very thin with long dorsal and ventral fins that can grow more than 6 inches long and 8 inches tall. Freshwater angels come in a variety of colors and patterns and get along with many other species, though it's best to keep them with fish too large for them to eat. Koi Angelfish have a marble pattern with an orange to red-orange head, named after the pond koi fish with a similar color pattern. Australian rainbows are larger, three-inch schooling fish and have an iridescent pattern. We recommend good swimming space and a school of four or more. The aquarium should be at least 20 gallons for any larger rainbow. The larger rainbows from AquariumFish.com come from a pond breeder in Florida and tend to have better size and coloration than Asian-bred rainbows. Quick Facts Scientific Name Melanotaenia fluviatilis Origin Southeastern Australia (pond-raised in Florida) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 3½" Lifespan 5–6 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 68–79°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1½–3" Care Guide Tank setup: Rainbowfish are active swimmers, so leave open swimming space along the front, with plants along the back and sides. Use a filter, a heater if your room runs cool, and a tight-fitting lid, since they can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with peaceful fish of similar size, such as other rainbowfish, larger tetras, barbs, danios, corydoras and plecos. Good to know: Rainbowfish color up as they mature and settle in, and males show their brightest colors when displaying to each other.

The boesemani rainbow was first discovered, at least from the aquarium trade's point of view, by the Dutch ichthyologist Dr. Marinus Boeseman 50 years ago. Boeseman was a heroic aquarist who joined the resistance against the Nazis while publishing his doctoral thesis - on cherry bitterlings. He was caught and imprisoned. Fortunately, the Nazis did not get a chance to execute the great aquarist and after the war he went on to discover and name the most popular rainbow in our Hobby. These fish should at least be purchased as a pair of two to lower their stress level in the tank. Females have nice color, but not as much as the males. Large rainbows are good with all but the smallest aquarium species, such as fancy shrimp. Quick Facts Scientific Name Melanotaenia boesemani Origin Western New Guinea, Indonesia Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 4" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1½–2" Care Guide Tank setup: Rainbowfish are active swimmers, so leave open swimming space along the front, with plants along the back and sides. Use a filter, a heater and a tight-fitting lid, since they can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with peaceful fish of similar size, such as other rainbowfish, larger tetras, barbs, danios, corydoras and plecos. Good to know: Boesemani are half blue and half orange, and their colors get stronger as they grow.

As with most rainbow fish, the male blue eye tenellus rainbow fish have larger fins and more color than the female, but both sexes are attractive. The tenellus is a great example of a small schooling rainbow. In the wild these fish are found in the "billabongs" of Australia (a word for a seasonal pond that only Australians could come up with). We ship these as close as possible to a 50:50 mix of males and females. We recommend a school of six or more, but a pair would do well in a peaceful community tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pseudomugil tenellus Origin Northern Australia and southern New Guinea Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1½" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a planted tank with gentle filtration, some floating plants and a lid. They are small, so a sponge over the filter intake keeps them safe. Feeding: Feed crushed flake or micro pellets once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Blue-eyes are small and gentle, so keep them with other small, peaceful fish such as rasboras, small tetras, pygmy corydoras and shrimp. Good to know: Male tenellus have long, spotted fins they flare to show off to females.

Celebese rainbows come from the Indonesian island once known as Celebese, which for political correctness is now the Island of Sulawesi. Common in small streams around the island, these little rainbows can handle light brackish water as well as salt water, so they can be transitioned to a brackish fish tank. Please don't try this with any other rainbowfish. Male Celebese rainbows throw out their fins to display in front of the slightly smaller female. We recommend keeping both sexes in the fish tank and try to keep an even ratio of males and females when shipping. Quick Facts Scientific Name Marosatherina ladigesi Origin Sulawesi, Indonesia Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 2–4 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Keep males and females together Shipping Size Approx. 1–2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants, open swimming space and a lid. They like hard, alkaline water and also handle slightly salty (brackish) water. Feeding: Feed crushed flake or micro pellets once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with other peaceful fish of similar size, such as rainbowfish, danios, livebearers and corydoras. Good to know: Male Celebes rainbows have long, black-edged yellow fin rays that they flare when displaying.

The emerald rainbowfish, or wanamensis rainbowfish, is another example of a splendid species that might soon only exist due to the aquarium hobby. In native Papua New Guinea, tilapia were introduced as a food source, and since then the emerald rainbow population decreased rapidly. Fortunately, a very effective breeding program in Florida allows these amazing green rainbows to be sustained for the aquarium hobby. Wanamensis rainbowfish are large, growing up to four inches. These rainbowfish are not common and a bit pricier than their rainbow cousins. Tankmates: They get along with peaceful fish of similar size, such as other rainbowfish, larger tetras, barbs, danios, corydoras and plecos. The forktail rainbowfish, also known as the furcata rainbow, is prized for the bright yellow fringe all along the fins when the fish reaches maturity. Caudal (tail) fins have a fork shape, hence the name forktail. These rainbowfish are part of the pseudomugil family, which in general are small schooling rainbowfish perfect for peaceful community fish tanks, nano aquariums, and planted tanks. These rainbowfish will not harm fancy shrimp either! New season coming in small. Most rainbowfish are a group of small, colorful fish found in the rivers and lakes of Australia and New Guinea. A few rainbowfish can be found in other parts of the World and one of these is the colorful, sleek Madagascar Rainbow from France - just kidding - from Madagascar. Males have red in the tail and females do not, but both sexes have a nice color pattern and the same size and shape. The wrong scientific name, Bedotia geayi , is often applied to this species but actually refers to a similar but nearly extinct species in Madagascar. The neon dwarf rainbowfish, or praecox rainbow, loves to school and the colors on these fish get bolder and bolder as the fish age. These fish are easy to care for in the aquarium and are a great addition to nano tanks, planted aquariums and community aquariums. Neon dwarf rainbows are best in schools of six or more, and these fish are active swimmers. Quick Facts Scientific Name Melanotaenia praecox Origin Western New Guinea, Indonesia Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Rainbowfish are active swimmers, so leave open swimming space along the front, with plants along the back and sides. Tankmates: They get along with peaceful fish of similar size, such as other rainbowfish, larger tetras, barbs, danios, corydoras and plecos. Good to know: Neon dwarf rainbows have a shiny blue body and red fins (yellow-orange in females) that sparkle under good lighting.

The red rainbowfish is one of the larger rainbows, growing to about four inches, and the males become deep, deep red while the females are a solid copper color. These are schooling fish and we recommend at least a pair - one male and one female - to keep the pet fish happy. WE CANNOT SELL MALE ONLY. This leaves a tank of females, which feature a nice solid copper color - but no one ever asks for females and our warehouse would soon be overwhelmed with one sex. Unhappily, these fish are threatened in Indonesia since overpopulation of another species - humans - has overwhelmed their native habitat. The good news is that red rainbows are successfully bred in Asia and Florida and common in the aquarium trade. Red rainbowfish are often called Red Irian Rainbow and Red Millennium Rainbowfish. The millennium rainbow is a premium species bred in Florida to provide a hardier and more colorful fish for the aquarium trade and that is the species we sell. Good to know: Males show their brightest colors when females are around, so a mix of both looks best.

Also called the spotted blue eye rainbowfish, Signifer is Latin for signal and this refers to the offset fins of the male signifer. These fins expand and compress when males are sparring. The signifer rainbowfish is abundant in Australia and swims in schools in shallow waters, so these fish will tend to school at the upper level of the aquarium. We recommend a school of six or more to establish natural conditions for this aquarium-hardy species. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pseudomugil signifer Origin Eastern Australia Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a planted tank with gentle filtration, some floating plants and a lid. The Turquoise Rainbowfish is also known as the Lake Kutubu Rainbowfish and grows to a beautiful blue schooling fish. Like many Indonesian tropical fish, the native habitat of these fish is either being destroyed or converted to fish farms due to overpopulation. Fortunately, these fish are bred in Asia and Florida and have proven to be quite hardy in the aquarium environment. So, once again, the aquarium trade comes to the rescue of a beautiful species. Tankmates: They get along with peaceful fish of similar size, such as other rainbowfish, larger tetras, barbs, danios, corydoras and plecos. Good to know: Turquoise rainbows get bluer as they mature, and males develop a taller back.

The Threadfin Rainbowfish, also called the Featherfin Rainbowfish, are well known and cherished for the long flowing fins of the male. These are community schooling fish and best kept in a small school of six or more. AquariumFish.com will deliver in an even number of males and females. Males will display their pretty fins better in the presence of other tankmates. Females are easy to distinguish from the males; they do not have the long dorsal and anal fins. Quick Facts Scientific Name Iriatherina werneri Origin New Guinea and northern Australia Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 2–4 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ¾–1¼" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a planted tank with gentle filtration, some floating plants and a lid. They are small, so a sponge over the filter intake keeps them safe. Feeding: Feed crushed flake or micro pellets once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Threadfins are gentle and slow, so keep them with small, peaceful fish. Avoid fin-nippers, which go after their long fin threads. Good to know: Males grow long, thread-like fins that they spread out to show off to females.

The yellow rainbowfish is one of the larger and rarer rainbowfish of New Guinea and similar in size and behavior to the emerald and red rainbowfish. Discovered by that great fish adventurer Dr. Axelrod, males are much more colorful than the females but will only display their full color in the presence of a female, so we recommend the purchase of a pair. We cannot sell groups of males only; this leaves our warehouse full of females. They are colorful, but just not as colorful as the males. Tankmates: They get along with peaceful fish of similar size, such as other rainbowfish, larger tetras, barbs, danios, corydoras and plecos.
