Give them a soft bottom, caves and driftwood. They breathe air, so leave a gap above the water. Feeding: Feed sinking carnivore pellets once a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and shrimp. Tankmates: They will eat any fish that fits in their mouth. Keep them with fish too large to swallow. Breathes air: Bichirs take gulps of air from the surface, which is normal behavior. Good to know: Bichirs have small eyes and rely mostly on smell to find food.

Like all puffer fish, Fahaka puffers from West Africa have beaks to break apart their food. If threatened, they can blow up to three times their normal size. Fahaka puffers are fine in freshwater and brackish water aquariums. Fahaka puffers make terrific pet fish and prefer a diet of live foods, including snails and crayfish. Quick Facts Scientific Name Tetraodon lineatus Origin Nile and West African rivers Care Level Moderate (grows large) Temperament Aggressive Adult Size Up to 14–16" Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods, snails) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 1¼–2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants, rocks and hiding places, and good filtration, since puffers are messy eaters. Feeding: Puffers need meaty foods and usually won't eat flake. Feed frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp once a day. They also enjoy small snails, which help keep their teeth trimmed. Tankmates: Fahaka puffers are aggressive and are best kept alone. Good to know: Fahaka puffers are full of personality and often learn to recognize their owners.

The miurus puffer from Senegal is seldom seen in the trade, prefers live foods, and will make a terrific pet fish, but a terrible roommate. These puffers can be kept in a larger species tank, but keep them well fed or the miurus puffer will take bites out of the neighbors. As an ambush predator, in the wild or in the aquarium, the miurus puffer will dig itself in the silty or sandy floor and jump out to capture live victims. Miurus puffers can adapt to complete freshwater aquariums. Quick Facts Scientific Name Tetraodon miurus Origin Congo River basin, Africa Care Level Moderate Temperament Aggressive Adult Size Up to 6" Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods, snails) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 3" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a soft sand bottom they can bury into, some rocks and good filtration, since puffers are messy eaters. Feeding: Puffers need meaty foods and usually won't eat flake. Feed frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp once a day. They also enjoy small snails, which help keep their teeth trimmed. Tankmates: Miurus puffers are ambush hunters that bite. They are best kept alone. Good to know: Miurus puffers bury themselves in sand with only their eyes showing, then strike at passing food.

The holy grail of pet puffers, the MBU puffer. Like all puffers, they have beaks to break apart their food. If threatened, they can blow up to three times their normal size. When they get big, it takes a master aquarist to keep these fish compatible with other tank mates. Most people keep these as single pets. Snails, frozen and live feeders, and crayfish are all foods consumed by the MBU. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pao mbu Origin Congo River basin and Lake Tanganyika, Africa Care Level Expert only (grows very large) Temperament Aggressive Adult Size Up to 2 feet Lifespan 15–20 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods, snails) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 3½–4" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants, rocks and hiding places, and good filtration, since puffers are messy eaters. Feeding: Puffers need meaty foods and usually won't eat flake. Feed frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp once a day. They also enjoy small snails, which help keep their teeth trimmed. Tankmates: Mbu puffers grow very large and are best kept alone. Good to know: Mbu puffers are the largest freshwater puffers and often become very tame, recognizing their owners.

The reed fish, also called the rope fish, are in the African bichir family but truly look and behave like benign eels. These gentle, long fish have lungs that enable them to tolerate all kinds of water conditions and they can live in brackish or salt water. Good luck breeding them; the males and females are identical and no one has ever done it. Reedfish move more at night and will not harm anything that can't fit in their very small mouths. Quick Facts Scientific Name Erpetoichthys calabaricus Origin West Africa Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 14–16" Lifespan 10–20 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 10" Care Guide Tank setup: Bichirs are expert escape artists, so a tight-fitting lid is a must. Give them a soft bottom, caves and driftwood. They breathe air, so leave a gap above the water. Feeding: Feed frozen foods like bloodworms and shrimp, plus sinking carnivore pellets once they learn to take them. Tankmates: Ropefish are gentle but will eat very small fish. Keep them with peaceful fish too large to fit in their mouth. Breathes air: Bichirs take gulps of air from the surface, which is normal behavior. Good to know: Ropefish are expert escape artists and can slip through tiny gaps, so cover every opening in the lid.

The African butterfly fish is a specialized surface insect hunter and can actually glide a couple feet, so a tank cover is required. Freshwater butterfly fish are suitable with other species of similar size; these fish will eat small tank mates that fit in their mouth. Butterfly fish also have a single lung along with the gills that allows them to spend their entire life near the water surface. Freshwater butterfly fish are one of the most ancient species available in the trade. Feed them flies and crickets along with floating foods and they will be happy. They look like the freshwater version of the saltwater lion fish. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pantodon buchholzi Origin West and Central Africa Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful (eats small fish) Adult Size Up to 5" Lifespan 5–7 years Diet Carnivore (insects, meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–86°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 3" Care Guide Tank setup: Butterflyfish live right at the surface and can jump and glide, so a tight-fitting lid is a must. Give them floating plants and calm water. Feeding: Feed floating foods like flake, floating pellets or freeze-dried insects. They also enjoy small live insects like crickets. Tankmates: They will eat small fish at the surface. Keep them with calm, mid-size fish that stay lower in the tank. Good to know: African butterflyfish have large, wing-like fins and can glide short distances out of the water.

The elephant nose evolved to locate prey through a low voltage electric field. This takes a lot of brain power, so in one aspect these fish have a higher brain mass to body weight than humans or dolphins. There has never been a report that anyone has successfully applied for their assistance with homework. However, most agree that they are a fascinating feature in the tank. They do need live and/or frozen foods, not known as flake or pellet eaters. We feed frozen blood worms to our elephants. Quick Facts Scientific Name Gnathonemus petersii Origin West and Central Africa Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful (territorial with its own kind) Adult Size Up to 9" Lifespan 6–10 years Diet Carnivore (small meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 5" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a soft sand bottom, caves or tubes to hide in, dim lighting and a tight lid. They are most active in the evening. Feeding: Feed small frozen foods like bloodworms once or twice a day, ideally in the evening. Some learn to take small sinking pellets. Tankmates: Elephant noses are peaceful with other fish but may squabble with their own kind. Keep them with calm fish that won't outcompete them for food. Good to know: Elephant noses use their long "trunk" to probe the sand for worms, and they sense food with a weak electric field.

Dolphin fish look like dolphins but belong to the mormyrid family that also includes baby whales and elephant nose. These fish go well with an African theme aquarium and they are hardy and a bit aggressive. It is usually best to have live feeders on hand as these fish come wild from Nigeria and sometimes need to be transitioned to prepared foods. Like other mormyrids, the dolphin fish prefers a hiding place. When adapted to the aquarium, it is a bit unsettling when one approaches the glass like Flipper asking for a treat. Quick Facts Scientific Name Mormyrus longirostris Origin Central and East Africa Care Level Moderate Temperament Semi-aggressive Adult Size Up to 2 feet Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Carnivore (small meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a soft sand bottom, caves or tubes to hide in, dim lighting and a tight lid. They are most active in the evening. Feeding: Feed small frozen foods like bloodworms once or twice a day, ideally in the evening. Some learn to take small sinking pellets. Tankmates: Dolphin fish can be territorial. Keep them with robust fish of similar size, and only one per tank. Good to know: Dolphin fish use a weak electric field to find food and communicate.

The Baby Whale is an intelligent Mormyrid that is an interesting fish to keep, and it has quite a good personality. These fish are active, but they will need a cave or some type of hiding spot to seek cover in the aquarium. The "baby whale" is a carnivore, and it should be fed a diet of live and frozen foods such as ghost shrimp, blood worms and black worms. These fish will get aggressive as they get larger, so they are not suitable with small timid schooling fish. Quick Facts Scientific Name Brienomyrus brachyistius Origin West Africa Care Level Moderate Temperament Semi-aggressive (more so as adults) Adult Size Up to 6–8" Lifespan 10 years Diet Carnivore (small meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 2–3" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a soft sand bottom, caves or tubes to hide in, dim lighting and a tight lid. They are most active in the evening. Feeding: Feed small frozen foods like bloodworms once or twice a day, ideally in the evening. Some learn to take small sinking pellets. Tankmates: Baby whales get more territorial as they grow. Keep them with robust fish of similar size, and avoid small, timid fish. Good to know: Baby whales use a weak electric field to find food and communicate.

African mudskippers spend much of their lives out of water; these guys love to sunbathe and require a surface area - rock or driftwood will do. The mudskipper will climb out of the water and enjoy the lamp. In the wilds, these aquarium pets are caught on river banks of brackish waters, so it is a good idea to add a little aquarium salt to the water. Typically, a tank with mudskippers, toads, and other amphibians has only a few inches of water. These "amphibians" are beautiful species for terrariums and will jump quite far to catch live crickets. African mudskippers will eat small fish and they will eat Indian dwarf mudskippers; however, larger fish and amphibians will live in peace and harmony. Quick Facts Scientific Name Periophthalmus barbarus Origin West Africa Care Level Difficult Temperament Territorial Adult Size Up to 6" Lifespan 5–10 years Diet Carnivore (insects, meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–85°F pH 7.5–8.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 3" Care Guide Tank setup: Mudskippers spend much of their time out of the water. Give them a tank with a large land area of mud, sand or rocks, a few inches of slightly salty (brackish) water, warm, humid air and a tight lid. Feeding: Feed small insects like crickets, or frozen foods like bloodworms and shrimp. Many learn to take sinking pellets on land. Tankmates: Mudskippers are territorial with each other and will eat small fish. Give each one its own space. Good to know: Mudskippers breathe through their skin and mouth when out of the water, so the air above the tank must stay warm and humid.

A group of frogs is called an army, and you can get your own army of four - maybe a bit undisciplined but still an army. Each order comes with four medium dwarf African frogs. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hymenochirus boettgeri Origin Central Africa (captive-bred) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1½" Lifespan 5 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 72–78°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Sold as a group of 4 Shipping Size Approx. ¾–1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a fully aquatic tank with plants and hiding spots, gentle filtration and a lid. They breathe air, so keep the water shallow enough for them to reach the surface easily. Feeding: Feed sinking frog pellets or frozen bloodworms once a day. They eat slowly, so make sure faster fish don't take all the food. Tankmates: Dwarf frogs are peaceful and do best with other small, gentle fish such as small tetras and rasboras, or with their own kind. Good to know: African dwarf frogs are fully aquatic but breathe air, so you will see them float up to the surface for a breath.

Leopard ctenopomas, or African leaf fish, feature the most "colorful" pattern within the leaf fish family. Leaf fish disguise themselves as leaves and jump on their prey, so "colorful" in this case is relative. These leaf fish are yellow with brown leopard spots. Small ctenopomas will eat live black worms, frozen treats, and sometimes flake food. Larger ctenopomas will eat small fish, so choose tank mates appropriately. Quick Facts Scientific Name Ctenopoma acutirostre Origin Congo River basin, Africa Care Level Easy Temperament Predatory (eats small fish) Adult Size Up to 6–8" Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 1½–2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a planted tank with driftwood, leaf litter and gentle current. They hunt by ambush and stay still for long periods. Feeding: Leopard leaf fish adapt to frozen foods and some take pellets. Offer frozen foods like bloodworms and shrimp once a day. Tankmates: They will eat small fish but are peaceful with fish too large to swallow. Good to know: Leopard ctenopomas are labyrinth fish and can breathe some air from the surface.

African leaf fish are part of the ctenopoma family and are true ambush predators mimicking the color and shape of surrounding leaves. Unsuspecting small prey are snatched with a small movement when too near (or near enough from the leaf fish point of view). These fish do not get large and will only eat the smallest of species; otherwise, they are appropriate for a community tank, planted tank, and a mid-size cichlid tank. Leaf fish will eat frozen food, but be sure to have access to brine shrimp or live black worms in case some transition is required. Leaf fish are wild-caught in Nigeria. Quick Facts Scientific Name Polycentropsis abbreviata Origin West Africa (Nigeria) Care Level Moderate Temperament Predatory (eats very small fish) Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 5–7 years Diet Carnivore (small meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a planted tank with driftwood, leaf litter and gentle current. They hunt by ambush and stay still for long periods. Feeding: African leaf fish adapt to frozen foods. Offer frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp once a day. Tankmates: They only eat very small fish, so they are fine with community fish too large to swallow. Good to know: Leaf fish drift slowly toward their prey like a fallen leaf, then strike very quickly.

The odoe pike is a smaller Nigerian river predator and a good fit for a larger species aggressive fish tank. Like most predators, the odoe pike are active swimmers and good jumpers, so keep a cover on the fish tank. In the wilds of Africa, this fish is also a game fish for sport fishing. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hepsetus odoe Origin West and Central Africa Care Level Moderate Temperament Predatory Adult Size Up to 10–12" Lifespan 7–10 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 10" Care Guide Tank setup: Gars are fast, long-bodied predators. Give them open swimming space, strong filtration and a heavy, tight lid. Feeding: Feed meaty foods like frozen shrimp and fish, plus floating carnivore pellets once they learn to take them. Avoid feeder fish, which can carry disease. Tankmates: They will eat any fish that fits in their mouth. Keep them only with large, robust fish. Good to know: African pike build floating bubble nests for their eggs, which is unusual for a predator.

The Vittatus Tigerfish is second to the top of the food chain in West Africa. This is a monster fish related to the piranha but a lot bigger. In this case second place means a big deal since these fish are eaten by Goliath tigerfish in the wild. With that exception, all other species are its prey. Tigerfish need live food such as feeder guppies and feeder goldfish and they are fast. This predator fish can jump, so some type of screen or cover is needed. Also, the tigerfish is a solitary predator in the aquarium; two cannot be kept together unless the aquarium is enormous. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hydrocynus vittatus Origin Africa Care Level Expert only (grows very large) Temperament Predatory Adult Size Up to 2–3 feet Lifespan 15–20 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 3" Care Guide Tank setup: Gars are fast, long-bodied predators. Give them open swimming space, strong filtration and a heavy, tight lid. Feeding: Feed meaty foods like frozen fish and shrimp. Some can be trained to take carnivore pellets. Avoid feeding only feeder goldfish, which can carry disease. Tankmates: They will eat any fish that fits in their mouth. Keep them only with large, robust fish. Good to know: Tigerfish are fast, powerful swimmers related to piranhas and tetras.

The Goliath tigerfish is the top of the food chain in West Africa, and has a larger body and longer teeth than the smaller Vittatus tigerfish. These fish are caught in the smaller rivers of the Niger River basin and rarely appear in the trade, though the fish is often featured on TV shows such as "River Monsters". Tigerfish require live feeder fish, which is part of their appeal. The diet should not just consist of feeder goldfish but mixed with other species and some can be adapted to frozen foods. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hydrocynus goliath Origin Congo River basin, Africa Care Level Expert only (grows very large) Temperament Predatory Adult Size Up to 3 feet or more Lifespan 15–20 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 4" Care Guide Tank setup: Gars are fast, long-bodied predators. Give them open swimming space, strong filtration and a heavy, tight lid. Feeding: Feed meaty foods like frozen fish and shrimp. Some can be trained to take carnivore pellets. Avoid feeding only feeder goldfish, which can carry disease. Tankmates: They will eat any fish that fits in their mouth. Keep them only with large, robust fish. Good to know: Goliath tigerfish have long, sharp teeth that show even when the mouth is closed.

Electric Catfish from Nigeria grow to 20 inches and can produce a shock of 200 volts to disable prey. The charge from a two-inch Electric Catfish feels like touching an exposed Christmas tree light. Most of the guys at AquariumFish.com can attest to this. Electric catfish are catfish and will eat live, frozen, and sinking pellets. Electric catfish are classified as nocturnal, and during the day these fish usually just sleep around. At night, these guys are pretty active. ****This item does not ship to Texas or Florida**** Quick Facts Scientific Name Malapterurus electricus Origin West and Central Africa Care Level Moderate Temperament Aggressive (can shock) Adult Size Up to 2 feet Lifespan 10–20 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 6" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them caves, driftwood, dim lighting and strong filtration, plus a tight lid. Use a net or tools rather than your hands, since they can deliver a shock. Feeding: Feed sinking carnivore pellets or frozen foods like shrimp, ideally in the evening. Tankmates: Electric catfish will shock and eat other fish. Keep them alone. Good to know: Electric catfish can produce a shock strong enough to stun their prey, so always use tools when working in their tank.

Angelicus, like most synodontis species, will readily eat flakes, pellets, catfish wafers, frozen and live foods like brine shrimp. The synodontis angelicus is rare and offers a beautiful black and white pattern. The angelicus botia is also called the angel squeaker or polka dot squeaker and comes from the Congo basin of Cameroon. These aquarium catfish are difficult to source due to the remote origins, so they command a high price. Quick Facts Scientific Name Synodontis angelicus Origin Congo River basin, Africa Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 8" Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them caves, rocks or driftwood to hide in, and good filtration. They are most active at night. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets once a day, ideally in the evening. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms. Tankmates: They get along with most fish of similar size, including many cichlids. They may eat very small fish. Good to know: Young angelicus have the boldest polka dots, which become more spread out as the fish grows.

These exotic fish are from the rivers and lakes of Africa. They are wide catfish and have a pale coloration with black spots. As a digger, the Synodontis Eupterus Catfish will appreciate a fine sandy bottom with large roots and crevices for hiding places in a big tank. It is sensitive to nitrates, so good water conditions are necessary. It prefers a current in the aquarium. It can be kept as a schooling fish or in a tank with other Synodontis species. The Synodontis Eupterus Catfish may also be maintained with most African Cichlids of similar size. Quick Facts Scientific Name Synodontis eupterus Origin Central and West Africa Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 8–9" Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 1¼" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them caves, rocks or driftwood to hide in, and good filtration. They are most active at night. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets once a day, ideally in the evening. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms. Tankmates: They get along with most fish of similar size, including many cichlids. They may eat very small fish. Good to know: Featherfin synodontis grow a tall, feathery back fin as they mature.

There is no common name for the synodontis multipunctatus, so one has to learn to say it. These African catfish are slow growers and very difficult to breed, but they are among the most colorful in the fish tank. The multipunctatus has a greenish-hued body with a leopard pattern and white fringed fins. Since these fish only grow to three inches, they are perfect for most aquariums. Originally flown in from Lake Tanganyika in the Great Rift Valley of Africa, today these catfish are normally bred by specialists in the USA. These catfish should not be confused with the Synodontis decorus, a much larger and common species that grows to 10 inches but looks similar when young. Quick Facts Scientific Name Synodontis multipunctatus Origin Lake Tanganyika, Africa Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 4–5" Lifespan 10–12 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.5–8.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them caves, rocks or driftwood to hide in, and good filtration. They are most active at night. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets once a day, ideally in the evening. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms. Tankmates: They get along with most fish of similar size, including many cichlids. They may eat very small fish. Good to know: In the wild, multipunctatus lay their eggs among mouthbrooding cichlids, which then raise the catfish babies.

Upside Down fish for sale ready to add to your aquarium. Upside Down catfish have been popular since the days of ancient Egypt! Nearly all African catfish fall into the Synodontis family. AFS carries a few others, such as electric catfish and glass catfish found in other sections. Synodontis are upside down catfish, with long barbed dorsal fins and some striking patterns. They are easy to care for, eat just about anything, and get along with nearly all fish, including small tetras. They squeak as a form of communicating. Quick Facts Scientific Name Synodontis nigriventris Origin Congo River basin, Africa Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 4" Lifespan 10 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them caves, rocks or driftwood to hide in, and good filtration. Tankmates: They get along with most fish of similar size, including many cichlids. They may eat very small fish. Good to know: Upside down catfish really do spend most of their time swimming belly-up under leaves and wood.

This is a great looking freshwater fish in the Synodontis family. We can ship the Synodontis Schoutendeni fish live and fresh. This fish has interesting patterns and is easy to care for. They eat almost anything and are friendly with other fish, even small tetras. Quick Facts Scientific Name Synodontis schoutedeni Origin Congo River basin, Africa Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 6–7" Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them caves, rocks or driftwood to hide in, and good filtration. They are most active at night. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets once a day, ideally in the evening. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms. Tankmates: They get along with most fish of similar size, including many cichlids. They may eat very small fish. Petricola fish are small Synodontis. These fish are tan with black spots. They have white-lined black fins and white whiskers. Synodontis catfish need water that is oxygenated and has a relatively strong current. Provide hiding places situated in areas of heavy current for shelter. Dwarf Petricola catfish are omnivores, and should be offered both meaty foods and vegetation. This can be in the form of flakes, pellets, and freeze-dried or frozen foods like bloodworms and blackworms. They are peaceful fish and can be kept in most community aquariums. Many can tolerate a wide range of water conditions, including hard water and high pH, and can even be kept in some African cichlid aquariums. Quick Facts Scientific Name Synodontis petricola Origin Lake Tanganyika, Africa Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 4" Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.5–8.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. ¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them caves, rocks or driftwood to hide in, and good filtration. They are most active at night. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets once a day, ideally in the evening. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms. Tankmates: They get along with most fish of similar size, including many cichlids. They may eat very small fish. Good to know: Dwarf petricolas are a great fit for African cichlid tanks, where they clean up food that falls to the bottom.

The rare and very hard-to-find Synodontis Decorus Catfish from West Africa are stunning fish and one of the rare catfishes that don't have scales; their skin is smooth with a long top fin that extends and hangs like an antenna from the fishes back. Surprisingly they are great for African Cichlid tanks and they are well suited for the pH of Malawi and Tanganyikan tanks. Feeding: In their native habitat they live on invertebrates, small fishes and crustaceans. In the aquarium they will take a wide range of foods bearing in mind that it might be better to feed at night to make sure that they get their fair share in a community tank. They will accept live food, frozen food, catfish tablets, pellets, and a good quality flake food. DO NOT feed worms to synodontis! Quick Facts Scientific Name Synodontis decorus Origin Congo River basin, Africa Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 8–10" Lifespan 15 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.5–8.0 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them caves, rocks or driftwood to hide in, and good filtration. They are most active at night. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets once a day, ideally in the evening. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms. Tankmates: They get along with most fish of similar size, including many cichlids. They may eat very small fish. Good to know: Decorus catfish grow a long thread from the top of their back fin as they mature.

The blue turquoise discus was the second color-bred variation of the wild discus developed by Schmidt-Focke of Germany (the first was the red turquoise discus). Blue turquoise are primarily blue with some red and with black vertical stripes on the body and are our most popular variety. AquariumFish.com blue turquoise discus are bred in Singapore to tolerate a wide pH range (but not above 7.6) and feed on frozen and pellet foods! Quick Facts Scientific Name Symphysodon aequifasciatus (captive-bred color variety) Origin Amazon basin (captive-bred in Singapore) Care Level Moderate (needs warm, very clean water) Temperament Peaceful, shy; social Adult Size Up to 6–7" Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 82–88°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1½–4" (by size option) Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a reliable heater, gentle but strong filtration, and a bare bottom or fine sand for easy cleaning. Keep the tank in a quiet spot. Discus need very clean water. Feeding: Feed small meals of quality discus pellets or granules a few times a day, and remove uneaten food within a few minutes, since leftovers quickly foul the water. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. New arrivals may need frozen food for a while before they accept pellets. Tankmates: Discus are calm and shy, so choose gentle tankmates that enjoy the same warm water: cardinal and rummynose tetras, sterbai corydoras and small plecos are popular choices. Avoid fast, boisterous or fin-nipping fish, and anything that competes hard for food. Many keepers avoid angelfish, which can bully discus and share diseases. Living in groups: Discus are social and feel safest in a group. A single discus, or just two, tends to be stressed. When a pair forms to breed, they may claim part of the tank, so a group spreads out the attention. Good to know: Blue discus look most vivid under full-spectrum lighting and against a dark background. Discus show stress by darkening their color and hiding. A dark discus in a corner usually means the water quality or tankmates need checking.

The red turquoise discus, sometimes called the tiger turquoise discus, was the first color-bred variation of the wild discus, developed by Schmidt-Focke of Germany. This color discus tends to be hardier and easier to replicate than the other color variations available to the aquarium trade. Red turquoise are primarily red with some blue and with black vertical stripes on the body. Our red turquoise discus are bred in Singapore to tolerate a wide pH range and feed on frozen, flake, and pellet foods. Tankmates: Discus are calm and shy, so choose gentle tankmates that enjoy the same warm water: cardinal and rummynose tetras, sterbai corydoras and small plecos are popular choices. Dr. Pellegrin discovered this subspecies in the western Amazon basin of Brazil in a region called Tefé, hence this discus is referred to as the green discus or Tefé green discus. The green discus features a light olive green body with wide black vertical bands. Most Tefé discus develop small red spots on their body as they age, considered a desirable feature by wild discus enthusiasts. The larger and older this discus gets, the more color and red spots it displays. Kind of like people. Quick Facts Scientific Name Symphysodon tarzoo (green discus) Origin Brazil, Lake Tefé region (wild-caught) Care Level Difficult (for experienced keepers) Temperament Peaceful, shy; social Adult Size Up to 7–8" Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Omnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 82–86°F pH 5.0–6.5 (very soft water) Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 3" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a reliable heater, gentle filtration, driftwood and dim lighting. Wild discus need very soft, acidic water and very clean, stable conditions. Feeding: Start with frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp, then slowly add discus granules or pellets. Feed small meals a few times a day and remove anything uneaten within a few minutes. Tankmates: Discus are calm and shy, so choose gentle tankmates that enjoy the same warm water: cardinal and rummynose tetras, sterbai corydoras and small plecos are popular choices. Avoid fast, boisterous or fin-nipping fish, and anything that competes hard for food. Many keepers avoid angelfish, which can bully discus and share diseases. Living in groups: Discus are social and feel safest in a group. A single discus, or just two, tends to be stressed. When a pair forms to breed, they may claim part of the tank, so a group spreads out the attention. Good to know: Tefé greens develop more red spotting as they mature. Like all wild discus, they need soft, acidic water and slow acclimation.

Fire eels are the most sought-after eel for larger fish tanks. These eels have personality, size, and color. Unfortunately they will eat small fish. They require live and frozen food but may be trained to feed on sinking pellets. Fire eels are so named for the bright red line that goes along the whole length of their body. ****This item does not ship to Texas or Florida**** Quick Facts Scientific Name Mastacembelus erythrotaenia Origin Southeast Asia Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful with fish its size Adult Size Up to 2–3 feet Lifespan 15–20 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 3–20" Care Guide Tank setup: Spiny eels like to burrow, so give them a soft sand bottom, plants and hiding places. Tankmates: They are peaceful with fish too large to swallow, but will eat small fish. Good to know: Fire eels often become pets that recognize their owners and come out at feeding time.

These gentle creatures are great inhabitants of small and large fish aquariums. They require live and frozen food, and will eat very small creatures such as fancy crystal red shrimp, but are safe for platies and tetras. These gentle creatures are great inhabitants of large fish aquariums. They require live and frozen food, and will hunt smaller fish and crustaceans. Tire track eels get to almost 20 inches and like to bury themselves in substrate with just their head showing during daylight hours. The name "Tire track" is from the black pattern on the body. The striped peacock eel is hardier than the standard peacock eel. These gentle creatures are great inhabitants of medium and large fish aquariums. They require live and frozen food, and will hunt smaller fish and crustaceans, but they only grow to about ten inches and have small mouths, so only half-inch or smaller fish would be prey. A popular fish for many freshwater aquarium hobbyists, the clown loach is peaceful and gets along well with many fish tank mates. The clown loach is amazing to watch and care for. Quick Facts Scientific Name Chromobotia macracanthus Origin Borneo and Sumatra, Indonesia Care Level Moderate (grows large; prone to ich) Temperament Peaceful, playful Adult Size Up to 8–12" Lifespan 15–20+ years Diet Omnivore (bottom feeder; eats snails) Water Temperature 77–86°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1–4" (by size option) Care Guide Tank setup: Clown loaches grow slowly but eventually reach 8–12 inches. The kuhli loach has an eel- or snake-like appearance with a yellow body and dark brown vertical stripes. Anglerfish (Frogfish) The Anglerfish, or frogfish, is known for its remarkable ability to blend into its surroundings, this fish is the ultimate ambush predator. The Anglerfish is a master of camouflage, spending most of its life motionless on the substrate. Its defining feature is a modified first dorsal spine, the illicium, which acts as a "fishing rod." At the tip is the fleshy lure, or esca, which the fish wiggles to mimic a small worm, shrimp, or fish. When an unsuspecting meal is attracted close enough, the Anglerfish executes one of the fastest strikes known in the animal kingdom, inhaling its prey whole. Species in this genus vary in size; most popular aquarium types (like the Warty Angler or Striated Angler) grow to 6 to 8 inches (15-20 cm), but larger species like the Giant Angler (A. commerson) can reach over 15 inches (38 cm). Due to their predatory nature and low activity level, they are best suited for a dedicated, species-only aquarium with ample live rock or structure for perching, with a minimum size of 20 to 50 gallons, depending on the expected adult size. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: The Anglerfish is a dedicated Carnivore. The primary challenge for the aquarist is transitioning the fish from its natural diet of live prey to non-living, frozen foods. They must be trained to accept meaty items offered via feeding tongs, as they will not chase food through the water column. Weaning to Frozen: Start with gut-loaded live marine shrimp or small, marine-acclimated feeder fish. Gradually introduce frozen meaty foods (e.g., large chunks of squid, clam, shrimp, or fish flesh) by waving them in front of the Angler with tongs to simulate the lure's movement. Feeding Frequency: Anglerfish have a slow metabolism and require infrequent feeding. Adults should be fed only once or twice per week with a substantial meal. Overfeeding is a common cause of health issues and can cause the fish to fast for long periods. Reef Compatibility: With Extreme Caution. While Anglerfish generally ignore corals and sessile inverts, they are a significant danger to nearly all ornamental invertebrates (shrimp, crabs, snails) and any fish small enough to fit in their massive mouth, which can be up to their own body size. They are best housed with very large, fast-moving, non-aggressive fish, or alone. Handling Caution: Anglerfish are non-venomous but will inflate their bodies with air if netted and removed from the water, which can be fatal. Always transfer an Anglerfish using a submerged plastic container to avoid air ingestion. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Antennarius sp. (General Anglerfish/Frogfish) Primary Common Name: Anglerfish Other Common Names: Frogfish, Warty Angler, Painted Angler, Striated Angler Origin: Indo-Pacific (Widespread in tropical and subtropical waters) Max Size: Varies greatly; typically 6–15 inches (15–38 cm) Temperament: Aggressive / Predatory (Sessile Ambush Hunter) Diet: Carnivore (Must be trained onto frozen meaty foods) Minimum Tank Size: 20–50 Gallons (depending on adult size) Reef Compatibility: With Caution (Will eat all small fish and inverts)

Tail Spot Blenny: The Shy & Beneficial Algae Eater The Tail Spot Blenny (Ecsenius stigmatura) is a delightful and highly beneficial species that is a must-have for any marine aquarium . This small blenny gets its name from the prominent black spot at the base of its tail, which contrasts beautifully with its tan or light blue body and dark eyes. Known for its endearing and curious personality, the Tail Spot Blenny spends its day tirelessly perching on live rock and grazing on nuisance algae. It’s a peaceful and non-aggressive species that makes a fantastic addition to a community reef tank, acting as a natural part of the cleanup crew. Why the Tail Spot Blenny is a Great Choice: Natural Algae Control: Its constant grazing helps keep your live rock and glass free of nuisance algae. Unique Personality: The blenny's comical expressions and perching behavior make it a fascinating and entertaining fish to watch. Peaceful Temperament: It's a non-aggressive species that coexists well with other peaceful tank mates. Reef-Safe: The Tail Spot Blenny is completely safe to keep with all types of corals and invertebrates. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Ecsenius stigmatura Origin: Indo-Pacific Reefs Max Size: 2.5 inches Lifespan: 2-4 years Diet: Herbivore. Primarily feeds on marine algae and prepared foods like Spirulina flakes and nori. Shipping Size: 1-2 inches

Platys are common aquarium fish found in North and Central America. They are a staple for community tanks and will get along with other non-aggressive species. Live birth of fish is almost guaranteed in a tank containing mixed sexes, similar to guppies. Platys have been bred to produce many different colors and patterns. AquariumFish.com will do its best to match your color requests. Groups of platies are shipped approximately half males and half females. Quick Facts Scientific Name Xiphophorus maculatus Origin Southern Mexico and Central America Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 3–4 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 70–80°F pH 7.0–8.2 Breeding Livebearer – breeds easily in the aquarium Group Size Sold as a lot of 6 Care Guide Tank setup: Platies are hardy and easy to keep. Give them a filter, a lid and plenty of plants. Use a heater to keep the water steady in the 70s. They prefer harder, slightly alkaline water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. Platies also need some plant matter, so a vegetable flake is a good choice. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Platies get along with most peaceful community fish, such as other livebearers (mollies, guppies and swordtails), tetras, rasboras and corydoras. Avoid large or aggressive fish that may bully or eat them. Breeding: Platies are livebearers, so a tank with males and females will almost certainly have babies (fry). Adults will eat fry, so add dense plants or use a breeding box if you want to raise them. Keeping more females than males gives the females a break from the males' attention. Good to know: Platies are one of the easiest fish to keep, which makes them a great choice for a first aquarium.

They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Platies get along with most peaceful community fish, such as other livebearers (mollies, guppies and swordtails), tetras, rasboras and corydoras. Avoid large or aggressive fish that may bully or eat them. Breeding: Platies are livebearers, so a tank with males and females will almost certainly have babies (fry). Adults will eat fry, so add dense plants or use a breeding box if you want to raise them. Keeping more females than males gives the females a break from the males' attention. Good to know: This premium color variety is calmer and shows its best color in a group.

The bleeding heart platy, also called the tiger ruby platy, has a light cream body and orange stripes that come together at the chest, hence the name "bleeding heart." These platies are difficult color variations to breed and command a higher price. Bleeding heart platies are mild-mannered fish (after all, they do wear a bleeding heart on their body) and feel less stress in a group of four or more. Falco Hawkfish The dwarf falco hawkfish typically rests at the bottom of massive corals in the reef area. It usually occurs singly but may be in pairs and feeds on fish larvae, small crustaceans and other invertebrates on the seabed. Like many fish, this species can change sex. If a harem becomes too large, one of the females may become a male and take on part of the harem as a dominant male. What makes this species unusual is that the new male may revert to the female sex if challenged by a more powerful male. A male can become a female and successfully breed, laying fertile eggs. Scientific Name: Cirrhitichthys falco Origin: Indo - Pacific Lifespan: 2-4 years Max Size: 3 inches Food: live, flake, frozen Shipping Size: 1 to 2 inches

Red Banded Hawkfish Also known as a Blood Red or Redbar Hawkfish, these hardy fish can be a little aggressive with smaller tank mates. Scientific Name: Cirrhitops fasciatus Origin: Christmas Island Max Size: 5 inches Diet: Carnivore Shipping Size: 1 to 3 inches

Aluminum Plant The Aluminum Plant gets its name from the aluminum color finish on the leaves. These fish are true semi-aquatic plants and suited for a paludarium or terrarium. However if the aluminum plant is completely submerged in a fish tank it will look fine for several weeks before the inevitable demise. Aluminum plants are native to Vietnam where they grow in bogs and swamps and grow to 12 inches. Each order of Aluminum plants come in a bunch of 5 with a lead weight so they can be fully immersed if desired. These pseudo aquarium plants come about six inches tall with large leaves and fit easily with a box of fish. Scientific Name: PILEA CADIEREI Shipping Size: Five plants with lead weight, six inches tall.

Anacharis Anacharis is a staple live veggie source for aquarium fish. These aquarium plants will arrive as bunched with five separate plants and a lead weight so they can be easily placed. The anacharis plant was the first aquarium plant and remains a staple today, though this is not the hardiest plant. Once these plants take however they grow quickly and can handle cold and warm water. Anacharis will not tolerate water temperatures above 75 degrees for long, but can handle temperatures all the way down to 50 degrees - perfect for goldfish and koi. Scientific Name: EGERIA DENSA Origin: Florida farm Shipping Size: Approx. 7 inches

Baby Tears Baby tears will flourish in the aquarium under good lighting and water conditions, though even without ideal conditions the plants should last a few months and offer a nice sanctuary for smaller community fish and crustaceans. These are desirable to add some balance to the aquarium and greenery to the foreground. Each order comes with a small bnch of five plants with a lead weight or a small bush in a 2 inch pot, depending on which looks best. Hornwort will either grow exceptionally well or will begin to fall apart within a few weeks after introduction to the aquarium. If these plants begin to fall apart simply remove them so they don't make too much of a mess and try a different plant. If they take good luck they are fast growers. Each order comes with a bunch of 5 plants and a lead weight though these plants do not need to be rooted. Scientific Name: CERTOPHYLLUM DEMERSUM Shipping Size: Approx. 8 inches, five plants per order bunched w lead weight

Scientific Name: HYGROPHILA PINNATIFIDA Shipping Size: Approx. 6 inches

In the aquarium these are hardy and pretty plants with red and green leaves. Each order come with five plants bunched with a lead weight. These plants fit into an order of fish easily:) Scientific Name: LUDWIGIA repens Shipping Size: Approx. 8 inches, five stems and a lead weight

Amazon Sword Plant The most basic most popular sword plant in the aquarium hobby is the Amazon Sword. The sword family echinodorus grows all over the Western Hemisphere. Swords are actually marsh plants that will grow emersed and submersed. The Amazon sword in found throughout shallow waterways and marshes in South America. Amazon Swords require some fertilizer, a few hours of direct light, and can grow in common aquarium gravel. Swords are hardy and can handle temperatures from 70 to 80 degrees but will not handle Ph above 7.5. Maximum size of the Amazon Sword is 20 inches. Scientific Name: ECHINODORUS amazonicus Food: Good lighting and iron fertilizer Shipping Size: Medium approx. 7 inches, Large approx. 12 inches

Native to streams and shallows in Brazil, the plant has the same temperament as Amazon sword, hardy but requires good lighting and some CO2 to really grow. Even so, the red melon sword is one of the few aquarium plants that tolerate high Ph and low levels of light. Under these conditions it will look pretty, it just wont grow. Scientific Name: ECHINODORUS BARTHII Shipping Size: 6 to 12 inches
Sword Plant. Scientific Name: ECHINODORUS MARTII

In the wild, swordtails are found throughout Central America. The males have long extensions on the caudal fin that look like swords. This is absent in females, but they tend to grow slightly larger. They are closely related to the livebearing platy and do well in community tanks. Like guppies and platies, they will breed readily in an aquarium. When we make assorted bunches, we try to pack an even number of males and females, though the ratio may vary. Lot of 4 Quick Facts Scientific Name Xiphophorus hellerii (assorted colors) Origin Southern Mexico to Honduras (wild ancestors); aquarium-bred Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful (males may spar) Adult Size Up to 4–5" (not counting the sword) Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 7.0–8.0 (hard water) Group Size Sold as a lot of 4 Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Swordtails are active swimmers, so give them plants, open swimming space and a tight-fitting lid, since they are good jumpers. They prefer hard, alkaline water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet with some vegetable content once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Swordtails get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as platies, mollies, larger tetras, danios, rainbowfish, gouramis and corydoras. Keep more females than males, since males chase females and may spar with each other. Avoid fin-nippers and large cichlids. Good to know: Swordtails are livebearers and breed readily. Fry are born free-swimming and will be eaten unless there are dense plants or a breeding box for them to hide in. Only males grow the "sword" on the tail.

The red red-eye lyre swordtail is a product of an intense breeding program in Asia, and these are the brightest, largest swordtails available. Red-eye lyre swordtails are show quality and require a little salt in the aquarium (one tablespoon to 20 gallons) and can even be kept in brackish conditions. Unlike other swordtails, these fish are difficult to breed, as the females and males both have long veil fins that get in the way of the process. In fact, if not for the gonopodium, it would be difficult to distinguish males from females. Quick Facts Scientific Name Xiphophorus hellerii (red red-eye lyretail) Origin Southern Mexico to Honduras (wild ancestors); bred in Asia Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful (males may spar) Adult Size Up to 5" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 7.0–8.0 (hard water) Group Size Keep more females than males Shipping Size Approx. 3" Care Guide Tank setup: Swordtails are active swimmers, so give them plants, open swimming space and a tight-fitting lid, since they are good jumpers. They prefer hard, alkaline water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet with some vegetable content once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Swordtails get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as platies, mollies, larger tetras, danios, rainbowfish, gouramis and corydoras. Keep more females than males, since males chase females and may spar with each other. Avoid fin-nippers and large cichlids. Good to know: Lyretail and hi-fin swordtails have extra-long fins, so keep them away from fin-nippers like tiger barbs. Many lyretail males have an elongated gonopodium and can't breed, so lyretail fry usually come from lyretail females mated with standard-finned males.

Red red-eye swordtails do not have the long veil fins of the lyre sword, but they share the remarkable bright solid red body and deep red eyes. Like most swords, these swords prefer water with a touch of aquarium salt in the system. In a planted tank or any tank with some contrasting dark background, the bright red bodies and bright red eyes stand out. Quick Facts Scientific Name Xiphophorus hellerii (blood red, red-eye) Origin Southern Mexico to Honduras (wild ancestors); aquarium-bred Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful (males may spar) Adult Size Up to 4–5" (not counting the sword) Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 7.0–8.0 (hard water) Group Size Keep more females than males Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Swordtails are active swimmers, so give them plants, open swimming space and a tight-fitting lid, since they are good jumpers. They prefer hard, alkaline water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet with some vegetable content once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Swordtails get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as platies, mollies, larger tetras, danios, rainbowfish, gouramis and corydoras. Fry are born free-swimming and will be eaten unless there are dense plants or a breeding box for them to hide in. Only males grow the "sword" on the tail.

Unlike the deep red body of the velvet red swordtail, the red and red wag swordtails have a little orange in the red color of the body. If you need to have a specific sex, please request it in the note section when placing the order. The sanke swordtail, also called the sanshoku swordtail or tri-color swordtail, is bred to display the red, black and white color pattern of the famous sanke show pattern of Japanese pond koi. Coloration patterns vary, but all breeders keep the three primary colors, and we think all our breeders do a nice job with the sanshoku swordtail. When two or more swordtails are ordered, we try to keep an even mix of males and females. The color pattern is difficult to breed, so these fish are slightly more expensive than the green swords and red wag swords. Albino Aeneus Cory The albino cory is a color morph of Corydoras aeneus. Cory catfish are found in still or slow-moving clear waters in South America. All species are non-aggressive and can be housed with any species that is not large enough to eat them. Most corydoras are small, with the exception of a few that can reach 4 inches in adulthood. They come in a wide variety of patterns and spend their time schooling on the bottom of the tank, using their barbels to search for food in the gravel or sand. Quick Facts Scientific Name Corydoras aeneus (albino variety) Origin Captive-bred Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 5–10 years Diet Omnivore (bottom feeder) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–8.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Medium: approx. 1" · Large: approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and a soft sand or smooth, fine gravel bottom. Plants, driftwood and a few shady spots help them feel secure. Corys are sensitive to salt and some medications (especially copper), so check labels before treating the tank. Feeding: Corys need their own food, not just leftovers. Feed sinking pellets or wafers once or twice a day so food reaches the bottom. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Corys get along with almost any peaceful community fish, such as tetras, rasboras, livebearers, gouramis, angelfish and bettas. Avoid large fish that could swallow them and aggressive bottom dwellers. Good to know: Albino corys are among the hardiest corys and stand out against dark sand. Corys sometimes dart to the surface to gulp a bit of air. That's normal behavior, not a sign of trouble.

These fish come from the Amazon basin of Colombia and get greener as they mature. The body is light silver with black spots like the South American leopard but with the disposition of a kitten. (Just a quick note on julii and false julii cory: the breeders and collectors do not distinguish between the two, and the differences are minor, so AquariumFish.com does not distinguish either.) If you really, really need to know, ask customer service, and we will take a look at this week's cory julii. Pygmy Cory are cute, tiny algae eaters that are friendly to everyone. These fish are very small and should be kept in small schools. These fish are a must for any nano tank and planted aquarium and a great addition to a peaceful community fish tank. These fish are large enough to keep with bettas too. Quick Facts Scientific Name Corydoras pygmaeus Origin Brazil, Peru and Colombia Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1" Lifespan 3–4 years Diet Omnivore (bottom feeder) Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a gentle, sponge-type filter, a heater, fine sand and plenty of plants. Make sure the food reaches them before faster fish eat it all. Tankmates: Keep them with other tiny, gentle fish such as small rasboras, ember tetras, shrimp and bettas. Anything big enough to swallow them will. Good to know: Unlike most corys, pygmy corys often swim in little schools in the middle of the tank, not just along the bottom.

Female guppies may not display all the color of the males, but they do determine most of the features of the offspring. We pick a random selection of 6 guppies; all will be pretty, but if you wish to have a selection heavier in one color, just ask. Quick Facts Scientific Name Poecilia reticulata Origin Northern South America (captive-bred) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Sold as a school of 6 Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and plenty of plants, including some floating plants where babies can hide. Guppies like slightly hard water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Guppies get along with other small, peaceful fish such as platies, mollies, corydoras, small tetras and rasboras. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs and larger fish that could eat them. Breeding: Guppies are livebearers and breed easily. Females give birth to live babies about once a month, and adults will eat the babies, so thick plants give them a place to hide. Good to know: Female guppies are larger and plainer than males, but many fancy varieties show some color in the tail.

Plakat is short for Plakat Thung, which means "fighter fish" in Thai. Plakats were once a specific wild breed, but now this term is used in general for larger round tail bettas. Round tail bettas tend to be more aggressive, and the fighter strain is not only more aggressive but also a bit larger than other Betta splendens variations. The most "true fighter" strain is black, but round tail plakat bettas come in all colors. Quick Facts Scientific Name Betta splendens Origin Thailand (captive-bred) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Males fight each other; peaceful toward most other fish Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 76–82°F (needs a heater) pH 6.5–7.5 Breathes Air Yes – labyrinth fish take air from the surface Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give him a heater (bettas are tropical fish), a gentle filter and live or silk plants. Plakats are active swimmers and like room to patrol. Keep a lid on the tank and leave a gap of air under it, since bettas breathe from the surface. Feeding: Feed a few betta pellets or a pinch of flake once or twice a day. Bettas overeat easily, so small meals are best. They also enjoy frozen bloodworms. Tankmates: Never keep two male bettas together. Plakats are among the boldest bettas, so they do best alone or with sturdy, peaceful fish like corydoras and snails. Avoid fin-nippers and other labyrinth fish. Good to know: Short-finned plakats are strong, fast swimmers and the closest to the original fighting fish, so they are usually the most aggressive bettas. Keep them on their own or with sturdy, peaceful tankmates.

The checkered barb, or checker barb, gets its name from the checkerboard pattern on the body. These hardy barbs are great for beginners and will reach two inches. They are a great schooling fish, and large males have slightly more black and red color on the fins. Checker barbs originally came from lakes in Sumatra, Indonesia, but are now bred all over Asia for the aquarium hobby. Some were released in South America during a breeding program and are now found in some of the smaller streams in Colombia. Checkered barbs will not tolerate high pH near 8, but otherwise they are hard to disappoint. Quick Facts Scientific Name Oliotius oligolepis Origin Indonesia (Sumatra) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 5–6 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 6.0–7.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a well-planted tank with a filter, a heater and some dim, sheltered areas. They do best in soft, slightly acidic water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other peaceful fish such as rasboras, tetras, gouramis and corydoras. Avoid large or boisterous fish that can outcompete them. Good to know: Checker barbs prefer neutral to slightly acidic water. A planted tank with a darker substrate shows off the checkerboard pattern.

AGA Water Sealant Description All Glass Aquarium offers a fish safe quick dry and clear sealant for glass aquariums for those rare leaks. AGA Sealant is made from high strength silicon specific for aquarium repair. 1 oz ready to use package.

Doc Wellfish's Cleaning Pad Description Aquarium Pharmaceuticals, Inc (API) created this indestructible cleaning pad to wipe down the inside of a glass aquarium so you can keep an eye on all those tank creatures. Fish safe and easy to rinse.

Doc Wellfish's Cleaning Pad - Acrylic Aquariums Aquarium Pharmaceuticals, Inc (API) created this indestructible cleaning pad to wipe down the inside of a acrylic aquarium so you can keep an eye on all those tank creatures. Fish safe and easy to rinse and will not scratch the viewing surface of acrylic fish tanks.

Aquarium Gravel Cleaner Aquarium gravel cleaners are essential to proper aquarium maintenance. Aquatop Gravel cleaners remove waste from the bottom of the tank through siphon action. Siphoning is an effective way to also remove dirty water for partial water changes. The siphon activates with a few shakes - nearly automatic. The Large 24 inch Gravel Cleaner includes a six foot flexible water removal tube and a fish and gravel filter. The size is perfect for 25 gallon aquariums and up. The small aquarium gravel cleaner has a twelve inch tube good for 5 gallon aquariums and up.

JBJ Sintered Airstone Only from AquariumFishSale, JBJ offers extra wide (for extra bubbles) airstones in two sizes to enhance conditions for any size aquarium. JBJ porous sintered air stones create small air bubbles for even distribution and good airflow within the fish tank. Air is essential for plant and fish health. These are the highest grade airstones on the market. JBJ Airstones connect with any air pump and standard airline tubing. Size: Small 3 inches, Medium 4 inches, Large 6 inches

JBJ Low Noise Air Pump The JBJ low noise Air Pump includes an airline, check valve, airstone, and a quite air pump. The 1500 model enhances air quantity in any size tank and provides all the air required in aquariums up to 30 gallons.
1/4 Inch Clear Airline Tubing Soft clear universal airline tubing is fish safe, flexible, and kink resistant. You can't ever have enough airline tubing. Length: 25 ft

Bio-sponge Filter Small Our round 2 inch high by 4.75 inch wide sponge filter complete with weighted base and tube to hold the airline will help keep ammonia down in aquariums up to 40 gallons. This is a great for small to mid-size aquariums. Used with an external air pump and connected with airline tubing, sponge filters provide the simplest means of biofiltration for an aquarium. Just keep rinsing every few weeks.

Bio-sponge Filter Large Our round 6 inch sponge filter is suitable for medium to large aquariums. Used with an external air pump and connected with airline tubing, sponge filters provide the simplest means of biofiltration for an aquarium. Just keep rinsing every few weeks and keep on fish keep'n.

Aquarium Algae Killer Ponds and Aquarium Pharmaceuticals, Inc offers Algaefix. AlgaeFix is a broad treatment algaecide that kills and controls most types of algae in the fish tank. Complete instructions come with the bottle, and always remove aquarium invertebrates when treating, but safe for fish and plants. Each bottle is 8 fluid ounces.

Aquarium pH Buffer 7.0 Aquarium Pharmaceuticals, Inc offers Proper pH 7.0, designed to stabilize the fish tank at about 7.0 while removing harmful chlorines and metals. pH 7.0 also adds aloe vera and electrolytes to enhance fish health. Excellent addition for new tanks and water changes. Bottle contains 250 gms of fast acting and dissolving powder.

API pH Down Aquarium Pharmaceuticals, Inc offers pH Down to prevent high pH alkaline water harmful to many exotic tropical fish, including tetras, rasboras, gouramis, South American cichlids, exotic shrimp, and many other species. Fast acting and easy to use, drops pH to safe levels. Bottle contains 1.25 ounces.

API pH Up Aquarium Pharmaceuticals, Inc offers pH Up to prevent low pH water harmful to many exotic tropical fish and marine species. African fish including morymids and cichlids do not thrive in acidic conditions. Also, some tap water is simply too acidic for many fish. Bottle contains 1.25 ounces.

API General Fungus Cure Aquarium Pharmaceuticals, Inc offers General Fungus Cure. General Fungus Cure treats a broad spectrum of fish fungus infections. Often fungus is a secondary infection to injuries and the fish may not heal on its own. Fungus usually appears as cottony patches. General Fungus Cure will treat mouth fungus, eye fungus, fin and tail rot, and boy slime. Each Package Contains 10 packets of treatment powder.

Hikari Prazipro Hikari and Aquarium Solutions offers a stronger solution to control parasites in aquariums and ponds. Prazipro is the go to product for quick cure but is stronger than some other "general" formulations. Prazipro is effective for freshwater aquarium parasites and saltwater aquarium parasites and it will not hurt biological filtration. Each Bottle contains 4 ounces.

Seachem Marine Buffer Seachem Marine Buffer safely raises marine water pH to 8.3. Even if overapplied it will not raise the pH above 8.3 and will continue to buffer the water and maintain an ideal pH condition. Contains carbonates, calcium, magnesium, potassium, salts. API Master Test Kit The API Master Test Kit for Freshwater Aquariums includes more than 800 tests. If one test type runs out smaller refills can be ordered.
