API Master Test Kit for Saltwater Aquariums The API Master Test Kit for Saltwater Aquariums includes more than 800 tests. If one test type runs out smaller refills can be ordered. Tests include pH, ammonia, nitrite, and nitrate levels. The kits comes in a water proof pack and contains the test ingredients, glass tubes, directions, and color charts.

The mini rabbit snail from Indonesia features the same little bunny-like antennae as the larger golden rabbit snail but only grows to 1 1/2 inches. Mini rabbit snails tolerate higher temperatures and higher pH and do not do well under 75°F. Great scavengers for smaller aquariums. Quick Facts Scientific Name Tylomelania sp. Origin Sulawesi, Indonesia Care Level Moderate (needs warm water) Temperament Peaceful; may nibble soft plants Adult Size Up to 1½–2" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Scavenger (sinking pellets, algae wafers) Water Temperature 76–84°F pH 7.2–8.5 Breeding Livebearer; slowly produces one baby at a time, so it won't overrun the tank Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Rabbit snails come from warm, clean lakes in Sulawesi. Give them a soft sand bottom they can burrow in, warm water (76–84°F) and good water quality. Add calcium if your water is soft. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets and algae wafers daily. Rabbit snails are big eaters and also clean up leftover food. Tankmates: Rabbit snails do well with peaceful fish, shrimp and other snails that like warm water, such as discus and tetras. Avoid puffers, loaches and large cichlids. Good to know: Rabbit snails are slow-moving and gentle, and they wave their long "ear-like" tentacles as they move. Remove snails before using copper or other medications.

Male and female clown killifish look similar; males have a bit more color, but they are both quite small. A small group of these small fish is the best way to view them. Quick Facts Scientific Name Epiplatys annulatus Origin Sierra Leone, Guinea and Liberia, West Africa Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1¼" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Carnivore (tiny meaty foods) Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 6.0–7.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Clown killifish live at the very surface, so use a planted tank with floating plants, a gentle filter (a sponge filter is ideal) and a tight lid. Keep the water warm, soft and clean. Feeding: Feed tiny foods like crushed flake or micro pellets in small amounts a few times a day. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep clown killifish in a species tank or with other tiny, peaceful fish like small rasboras, pygmy corydoras and shrimp. Larger fish will outcompete them or eat them. Good to know: Males show the bright, striped tail fin that gives the fish its name; females are plainer.

The gardneri killifish is a brightly colored gem from West Africa. These peaceful fish are great additions to a community tank or planted aquarium. Females are not as colorful as the males but still display some nice polka dots. Gardneri killifish are egg layers and will breed under the right conditions. Quick Facts Scientific Name Fundulopanchax gardneri Origin Nigeria and Cameroon, West Africa Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful (males may spar with each other) Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods; takes flake) Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 6.0–7.0 Group Size Pair, or one male with several females Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Use a planted tank with soft, slightly acidic water, a dark substrate, gentle filtration and floating plants. Killifish are expert jumpers, so a tight-fitting lid is a must. Feeding: Feed small amounts of a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Killifish do well with small, peaceful fish like tetras, rasboras, corydoras and other killifish of similar size. Avoid fin-nippers and large fish. Keep one male per tank unless the tank is large, since males may spar. Good to know: Killifish are egg-layers that spawn readily in plants or spawning mops, and their eggs can be hatched separately.

The gold dream panchax, also called the gold wonder killifish or gold wonder panchax, grows quickly to just over three inches, features a bright gold pattern, and tends to school at the surface of the aquarium. These fish are hardy and eat flake food. Like all killifish they are good jumpers, so keep the aquarium covered. If you do not have a cover, a screen for the first couple of days usually trains the fish to stop jumping. Both males and females are colorful, and the gold dream panchax are sold individually. Quick Facts Scientific Name Aplocheilus lineatus (golden variety) Origin India and Sri Lanka Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful with fish its size; eats very small fish Adult Size Up to 4" Lifespan 3–4 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods; takes flake) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single, pair or small group Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Panchax cruise near the surface, so give them plants and floating cover. They are excellent jumpers, so keep a tight-fitting lid on the tank. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or floating pellet once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Panchax do well with peaceful fish too big to fit in their mouth, such as larger tetras, barbs, gouramis, rainbowfish and corydoras. They will eat very small fish like lampeyes and fry. Good to know: Panchax are surface hunters that eat insects in the wild.

Lampeye killis have large reflective eyes and look awesome in a school under the right lighting. AquariumFish.com recommends a school of at least six. Norman's lampeyes are the most popular of the lampeye killis because they also have a nice blue reflective body and are quite hardy. These are perfect fish for nano and planted aquariums and make great community fish. Quick Facts Scientific Name Poropanchax normani Origin West Africa (Senegal to Cameroon) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1½" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a planted tank with gentle filtration, floating plants and a dark background, which shows off their glowing eyes. Keep a lid on the tank. Feeding: Feed crushed flake or micro pellets once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Lampeyes get along with other tiny, peaceful fish such as small rasboras, tetras, pygmy corydoras and shrimp. Avoid large or boisterous fish that may eat or stress them. Good to know: Their glowing eyes show best in a group under soft lighting with a dark background.

Great algae eaters - particularly filamentous algae, or hair algae. Males actually display the American flag on the side of their body. These are one of the few truly North American species available to the trade and native to Florida. Male and female flagfish are great algae eaters and colorful, and these fish are sold individually. If more than one is purchased, we try to ship you an even ratio of males and females. Quick Facts Scientific Name Jordanella floridae Origin Florida, USA Care Level Easy Temperament Semi-aggressive (males are territorial) Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (needs plant matter) Water Temperature 68–79°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plenty of plants and some algae to graze. They are hardy and do fine at room temperature in most homes. Feeding: Feed a quality flake that includes vegetable matter once or twice a day. They also graze on algae, including hair algae. Tankmates: Flagfish can be a little nippy and territorial, so keep them with other hardy, active fish rather than slow, long-finned fish. Good to know: Flagfish are named for the male's red-and-blue pattern, which looks a bit like the American flag.

The Black Moor got its name from the Japanese, who refined this breed and traded with… well… black Moors from Northern Africa. These fish were also referred to as black dragons, but are now only referred to as the Black Moor. This goldfish is nearly the same fish as a solid black telescope goldfish, but with slightly less protruding eyes, so this fish is a bit hardier and has a bit better eyesight than telescope-eye and celestial-eye goldfish. Black Moors are pretty fish in the aquarium or pond and do not get quite as big as some of the other fancy goldfish. Quick Facts Scientific Name Carassius auratus Origin China (refined in Japan) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 6" Lifespan 10–15 years, often longer with good care Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 65–75°F (no heater needed in most homes) pH 7.0–8.0 Shipping Size Medium: approx. 2" · Large: approx. 3" Care Guide Tank setup: Black Moors produce a lot of waste, so give them plenty of room and a strong filter. Use smooth decorations, rounded rocks and live or silk plants, because sharp edges can injure their protruding eyes. Feeding: Feed small amounts of a quality sinking pellet or flake once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. Sinking foods are easier for them to find than floating ones. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other slow-swimming fancy goldfish, such as telescopes, orandas, ryukins and ranchus. Avoid fast single-tail goldfish like comets and shubunkins, which will outcompete them for food. Also avoid tropical fish, which need warmer water, and fin-nippers. Ponds: Black Moors do well in ponds in mild climates. Shallow ponds with very cold winters aren't a good fit, and they're best kept away from fast, aggressive pond fish. Good to know: Some Black Moors slowly turn bronze or orange as they age, especially in warmer water. This is normal and not a sign of illness.

The Red Fantail Goldfish is one of the hardiest and most prolific goldfish in the trade. Fantail Goldfish were developed in Europe from the Ryukin goldfish and have less slope on the back and are faster swimmers. These fish will do well in a pond and aquarium and compete fine for food. Red fantails are a solid bright orange color. AquariumFish.com generally sells goldfish no smaller than two inches to ensure a safe trip and good adaptation to the fish tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name Carassius auratus Origin Captive-bred (Asia) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 6–8" Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 65–75°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 2–4" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a strong filter and smooth decorations. Goldfish are cool-water fish and do not need a heater. Feeding: Feed a quality goldfish flake or pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp and bloodworms. Tankmates: Keep them with other fancy goldfish. They are also hardy enough for ponds. Good to know: Fantails have a split, double tail that fans out as they swim.

Ryukin Goldfish have similar bodies to Oranda Goldfish, but do not display the distinctive head patch. AquariumFish.com will do its best to accommodate color requests. Quick Facts Scientific Name Carassius auratus Origin Japan (developed from Chinese fantails) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful, active Adult Size Up to 8" Lifespan 10–15 years, often longer with good care Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 65–75°F (no heater needed in most homes) pH 7.0–8.0 Care Guide Tank setup: Ryukins produce a lot of waste, so give them plenty of room and a strong filter. Feeding: Feed small amounts of a quality sinking pellet or flake once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other fancy goldfish of similar size and speed. Avoid fast single-tail goldfish like comets and shubunkins, which will outcompete them for food. Also avoid tropical fish, which need warmer water, and fin-nippers. Ponds: Ryukins can live in ponds in mild climates, but they are less cold-hardy than comets and shubunkins. Bring them indoors where winters are harsh, and keep them away from fast, aggressive pond fish. Good to know: Ryukins are livelier than most fancy goldfish, so they can outcompete very slow types like telescopes and bubble eyes at feeding time.

The calico telescope head goldfish, also called the telescope eye goldfish, has a mottled orange, black and white body with very extended eyes. These fish will not compete well with fast-moving species, so put food close to them. They may look very pretty, but they are a little slow. The telescope eye feature was created by selective breeding in China at the end of the 16th century, and most of the standard colors today were further refined in Japan. Quick Facts Scientific Name Carassius auratus Origin China Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 8" Lifespan 10–15 years, often longer with good care Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 65–75°F (no heater needed in most homes) pH 7.0–8.0 Shipping Size Medium: approx. 2" · Large: approx. 3–4" Care Guide Tank setup: Telescope goldfish produce a lot of waste, so give them plenty of room and a strong filter. Use smooth decorations and live or silk plants, and keep the water current gentle. Feeding: Feed small amounts of a quality sinking pellet or flake once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. Sinking foods are easier for them to find than floating ones. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them only with other slow-swimming fancy goldfish, such as telescopes, black moors, celestials, bubble eyes, lionheads and ranchus. Avoid faster goldfish like comets, shubunkins and even lively ryukins, which will outcompete them for food. Also avoid tropical fish and fin-nippers. Ponds: Telescope goldfish can live in ponds in mild climates, but they are less cold-hardy than comets and shubunkins. Bring them indoors where winters are harsh, and keep them away from fast, aggressive pond fish. Good to know: Their eyesight is poor, so make sure food reaches them, and avoid sharp decorations that can injure their protruding eyes.

These distinctive pond fish have long tails and elongated bodies, perfect for viewing from above in the pond environment. The Red and White Comet goldfish are very hardy. Quick Facts Scientific Name Carassius auratus Origin USA (developed from Chinese goldfish) Care Level Very easy, extremely hardy Temperament Peaceful, very active Adult Size Up to 10" or more in ponds Lifespan 10–15 years; 20+ years in ponds Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 50–75°F (tolerates cold winters in ponds) pH 7.0–8.0 Shipping Size Small: approx. 2" · Large: approx. 4" Care Guide Tank setup: Comets are fast, active swimmers that grow big and produce a lot of waste. They do very well in outdoor ponds; indoors, use a strong filter. Feeding: Feed small amounts of a quality sinking pellet or flake once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other single-tail goldfish like comets and shubunkins, or with koi in a pond. Avoid slow fancy goldfish, which can't compete for food, and tropical fish, which need warmer water. Ponds: This is where they shine. They handle cold winters as long as part of the pond stays deep enough not to freeze solid. Stop feeding when the water drops below about 50°F. Good to know: Comets grow quickly and are well suited to ponds.

The shubunkin goldfish is a variation of the sarassa comet and is now bred in the USA primarily for ponds. Shubunkin goldfish are red, white, and black in color and need a lot of swimming room. These goldfish look great viewed from the side in a large aquarium or from above in an outdoor pond. Quick Facts Scientific Name Carassius auratus Origin Japan (now bred in the USA) Care Level Very easy, extremely hardy Temperament Peaceful, very active Adult Size Up to 10" or more in ponds Lifespan 10–15 years; 20+ years in ponds Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 50–75°F (tolerates cold winters in ponds) pH 7.0–8.0 Shipping Size Medium: approx. 3–4" · Large: approx. 5–6" Care Guide Tank setup: Shubunkins are fast, active swimmers that grow big and produce a lot of waste. They do very well in outdoor ponds; indoors, use a strong filter. Feeding: Feed small amounts of a quality sinking pellet or flake once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other single-tail goldfish like comets and shubunkins, or with koi in a pond. Avoid slow fancy goldfish, which can't compete for food, and tropical fish, which need warmer water. Ponds: This is where they shine. They handle cold winters as long as part of the pond stays deep enough not to freeze solid. Stop feeding when the water drops below about 50°F. Good to know: Shubunkins grow quickly and are well suited to ponds.

The word "Oranda" is Dutch for Lionhead, but unlike the Lionhead goldfish, the Oranda has a prominent dorsal fin. Like the lionhead goldfish, oranda goldfish were selectively bred to create the bubbly head the Chinese call the "wen" and we usually call the "crown" or "cap". Quick Facts Scientific Name Carassius auratus Origin China Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 8" Lifespan 10–15 years, often longer with good care Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 65–75°F (no heater needed in most homes) pH 7.0–8.0 Shipping Size Approx. 2–4" Care Guide Tank setup: Orandas produce a lot of waste, so give them plenty of room and a strong filter. Feeding: Feed small amounts of a quality sinking pellet or flake once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other fancy goldfish of similar size and speed. Avoid fast single-tail goldfish like comets and shubunkins, which will outcompete them for food. Also avoid tropical fish, which need warmer water, and fin-nippers. Ponds: Orandas can live in ponds in mild climates, but they are less cold-hardy than comets and shubunkins. Bring them indoors where winters are harsh, and keep them away from fast, aggressive pond fish. Good to know: The wen (crown) keeps growing for the first couple of years and can trap debris, so clean water is the key to a healthy, full wen.

Koi are hardy carp originally bred for color in Japan six hundred years ago. Today many color variations adorn indoor and outdoor ponds and aquariums. We will try to match as closely as possible to special color requests from available stock. Our koi quality specification is Select Grade A. Quick Facts Scientific Name Cyprinus carpio Origin Captive-bred (Asia) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2–3 feet Lifespan 25–35 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 50–80°F pH 7.0–8.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 3–4" Care Guide Tank setup: Koi grow large and are best kept in an outdoor pond with strong filtration. They are cool-water fish and do not need a heater. Feeding: Feed a quality koi or goldfish pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a few minutes. Feed less when the water is cool. Tankmates: Koi get along with goldfish and other pond fish. Good to know: Koi recognize the person who feeds them and can become very tame.

Koi are hardy carp originally bred for color in Japan six hundred years ago. Today many color variations adorn indoor and outdoor ponds and aquariums. We will try to match as closely as possible to special color requests from available stock. Our quality is called select grade A. Quick Facts Scientific Name Cyprinus carpio Origin Captive-bred (Asia) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2–3 feet Lifespan 25–35 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 50–80°F pH 7.0–8.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 6–7" Care Guide Tank setup: Koi grow large and are best kept in an outdoor pond with strong filtration. They are cool-water fish and do not need a heater. Feeding: Feed a quality koi or goldfish pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a few minutes. Feed less when the water is cool. Tankmates: Koi get along with goldfish and other pond fish. Good to know: Koi recognize the person who feeds them and can become very tame.

Butterfly koi do not have the specific color patterns of the show koi, but they have their own unique bright patterns. These hybrid koi feature long, flowing fins, which give the koi their name. Due to their flowing body shape, many pond owners prefer the butterfly hybrid koi over traditional show koi. The quality specification is Select. Butterfly koi are not graded via A, AA, AAA like show koi, as their patterns are less distinguishable. Quick Facts Scientific Name Cyprinus carpio Origin Captive-bred (Asia) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2–3 feet Lifespan 25–35 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 50–80°F pH 7.0–8.5 Group Size Sold as a lot of 4 Shipping Size Approx. 5" Care Guide Tank setup: Koi grow large and are best kept in an outdoor pond with strong filtration. They are cool-water fish and do not need a heater. Feeding: Feed a quality koi or goldfish pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a few minutes. Feed less when the water is cool. Tankmates: Koi get along with goldfish and other pond fish. Good to know: Each lot is an assortment, so colors and patterns will vary.

Ogon indicates solid color and yamabuki means gold or yellow. So the yamabuki koi is a bright, solid gold koi, a must for any pond. Quick Facts Scientific Name Cyprinus carpio Origin Captive-bred (Asia) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2–3 feet Lifespan 25–35 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 50–80°F pH 7.0–8.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 4–7" Care Guide Tank setup: Koi grow large and are best kept in an outdoor pond with strong filtration. They are cool-water fish and do not need a heater. Feeding: Feed a quality koi or goldfish pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a few minutes. Feed less when the water is cool. Tankmates: Koi get along with goldfish and other pond fish. Good to know: Koi recognize the person who feeds them and can become very tame.

The fancy guppies we carry are larger than one would find in a national chain store. Males and females come in matching color patterns. We will pick our nicest that particular week and send. Quick Facts Scientific Name Poecilia reticulata Origin Northern South America (captive-bred) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Sold as a pair (1 male + 1 female) Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and plenty of plants, including some floating plants where babies can hide. These livebearers also make a good contrast to GloFish . Quick Facts Scientific Name Poecilia sphenops (aquarium-bred hybrids) Origin Mexico and Central America (wild ancestors); aquarium-bred Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 3–4" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (needs plant matter) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.5–8.5 (hard water) Group Size Keep more females than males Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Mollies like hard, alkaline water. Give them plants, open swimming space and good filtration, since they are active and produce a fair amount of waste. Aquarium salt is optional; they also do well in brackish tanks. Feeding: Mollies graze on algae, so feed a quality flake that includes vegetable matter once or twice a day. They also enjoy algae wafers and frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Mollies get along with most peaceful community fish that like similar hard water, such as platies, swordtails, guppies, danios, rainbowfish, corydoras and plecos. Avoid fin-nippers and soft-water specialists. Keeping more females than males keeps any one female from being harassed. Good to know: Mollies are livebearers that breed readily. Fry are born free-swimming and will be eaten unless there are dense plants or a breeding box for them to hide in.

The blue speckled ricefish is bred in Japan to display subtle blue spots and blue highlights on the fins. Common ricefish are used throughout Asia to control mosquitoes in rice fields, but the variants are quite beautiful and very hardy in the fish tank. Ricefish are similar to killifish but belong to their own genus, Oryzias . Like other ricefish, both sexes are colorful; males have slightly larger fins. Ricefish are sold individually but do best in a school of six or more. Quick Facts Scientific Name Oryzias latipes (blue speckled variety) Origin Japan (aquarium-bred) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1½" Lifespan 2–4 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 64–80°F (handles cooler water; no heater needed in most homes) pH 6.5–8.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Ricefish stay near the surface, so give them plants, floating plants and a lid. They are cool-water fish and do fine at room temperature, and they also do well in outdoor ponds and patio tubs in warm months. Feeding: Feed crushed flake or micro pellets once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Ricefish get along with other small, peaceful fish like white clouds, small rasboras, danios and shrimp. They can share an unheated tank with cool-water species, but avoid large or fast fish (including fancy goldfish) that may eat or outcompete them. Good to know: Medaka have been kept in Japan for centuries and are one of the hardiest small fish in the hobby. Both sexes are colorful; males have slightly larger fins.

Cory reticulatus, or the reticulated cory, exhibits a delicate network pattern throughout the body. Wild-caught in the Brazil Amazon tributaries, these are a great and very hardy addition to the aquarium. Like all cory, this little catfish can get along by himself but prefers to swim around with a couple of friends. Quick Facts Scientific Name Corydoras reticulatus Origin Brazil and Peru Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 5–10 years Diet Omnivore (bottom feeder) Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 6.0–7.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and a soft sand or smooth, fine gravel bottom. Plants, driftwood and a few shady spots help them feel secure. Corys are sensitive to salt and some medications (especially copper), so check labels before treating the tank. Feeding: Corys need their own food, not just leftovers. Feed sinking pellets or wafers once or twice a day so food reaches the bottom. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Corys get along with almost any peaceful community fish, such as tetras, rasboras, livebearers, gouramis, angelfish and bettas. Avoid large fish that could swallow them and aggressive bottom dwellers. Good to know: Corys sift through the substrate with their sensitive barbels, so soft sand or smooth, fine gravel keeps those barbels healthy.

One of the oddest and rarest members of the farlowella catfish family is the Chameleon Whiptail Catfish. The chameleon whiptail has a triangular flat head with two beady eyes on top and a long broadly striped body. These exotic catfish live in leafy and sandy substrates and scavenge small insects, vegetable matter, and, well, behave like a catfish. So, in the aquarium, a sandy area is required to keep these fish alive. Other than that, the chameleon whiptail will feed on most aquarium food. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pseudohemiodon apithanos Origin Colombia Care Level Moderate Temperament Very peaceful Adult Size Up to 8" Lifespan 8 years Diet Omnivore (sifts sand for food) Water Temperature 74–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 6" Care Guide Tank setup: A soft sand bottom is a must, since they bury themselves and sift sand for food. Add driftwood, leaf litter and gentle filtration. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets or wafers once a day so food reaches the bottom. They also enjoy frozen bloodworms. Tankmates: They are very peaceful and get along with most calm community fish. Good to know: Chameleon whiptails can lighten or darken their color to match the sand around them.

listings.commonName: Reptomin Turtle, Newt and Frog Food
listings.description: Reptomin 3 in 1 Amphibian Food Another industry standard from the Tetra people, Reptomin is the staple for aquatic turtles. Reptomin 3 in 1 contains one section of the staple Reptomin mini sticks for a complete diet and one section each for baby krill and baby shrimp for treats. Reptomin 3 in 1 is perfect for most amphibians in the aquarium including turtles, tadpoles, frogs, and newts. Maybe mudskippers, we haven't tried it on them. Shipping Size: 3.7 oz

The Acei cichlid, or yellow tail violet cichlid, is valued for its unique color pattern. The Acei cichlid has bright yellow fins and a violet blue body. The acei is a mbuna cichlid from Lake Malawi. In the wild, these fish scrape algae from rocks near shorelines, and in the aquarium these fish do need some veggies in the diet. The famed ichthyologist Dr. Charles Regan discovered the Acei cichlid in 1922, and the fish has been popular for cichlid tanks for nearly half a century. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pseudotropheus acei Origin Lake Malawi, Africa Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful for a mbuna Adult Size Up to 6" Lifespan 6–10 years Diet Omnivore (needs plant matter) Water Temperature 76–82°F pH 7.8–8.6 Shipping Size Approx. 2–5" (by size option) Care Guide Tank setup: Use a sand or crushed-coral bottom and stack plenty of rockwork with caves and hiding spots so each male can claim a territory and others can escape. Lake Malawi and Lake Tanganyika cichlids need hard, alkaline water; crushed coral or aragonite sand helps hold the pH up. Feeding: Mbuna are mostly plant eaters. Feed a vegetable-based flake or pellet once or twice a day, and avoid high-protein foods, which can upset their digestion. Tankmates: Keep mbuna with other mbuna of similar size and temperament, stocked in a group to spread out aggression. Avoid mixing them with peaceful peacocks and haps unless the tank is large, and avoid closely related species that look alike, which can crossbreed. Good to know: Acei are one of the calmest mbuna and often school together, so they suit mixed Malawi tanks well.

Gold sailfin mollies have a bright orange to gold body with reflective scales and red eyes. These are large livebearers but passive in the community tank. In a planted aquarium or with a dark background, these fish almost glow. Quick Facts Scientific Name Poecilia latipinna / P. velifera (aquarium-bred) Origin Southeastern U.S. and Mexico (wild ancestors); aquarium-bred Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Peaceful (males can chase females and rival males) Adult Size Up to 4–5" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (needs plant matter) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.5–8.5 (hard water) Group Size Keep more females than males Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give sailfins hard, alkaline water with plants, open swimming space and good filtration. Aquarium salt is optional; they also do well in brackish tanks. Feeding: Mollies graze on algae, so feed a quality flake that includes vegetable matter once or twice a day. They also enjoy algae wafers and frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Mollies get along with most peaceful community fish that like similar hard water, such as platies, swordtails, guppies, danios, rainbowfish, corydoras and plecos. Avoid fin-nippers and soft-water specialists. Keeping more females than males keeps any one female from being harassed. Good to know: Male sailfins raise their tall dorsal fin to show off to females and rival males. Their sails grow fuller as they mature, so juveniles may not show a full sail yet.

These are popular fish due to their Dalmatian puppy coloration, though the lyre tail version is a bit more popular, maybe because of the puppy tail. Quick Facts Scientific Name Poecilia sphenops (aquarium-bred hybrids) Origin Mexico and Central America (wild ancestors); aquarium-bred Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 3–4" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (needs plant matter) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.5–8.5 (hard water) Group Size Keep more females than males Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Mollies like hard, alkaline water. Give them plants, open swimming space and good filtration, since they are active and produce a fair amount of waste. Aquarium salt is optional; they also do well in brackish tanks. Feeding: Mollies graze on algae, so feed a quality flake that includes vegetable matter once or twice a day. They also enjoy algae wafers and frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Mollies get along with most peaceful community fish that like similar hard water, such as platies, swordtails, guppies, danios, rainbowfish, corydoras and plecos. Avoid fin-nippers and soft-water specialists. Keeping more females than males keeps any one female from being harassed. Good to know: Mollies are livebearers that breed readily. Fry are born free-swimming and will be eaten unless there are dense plants or a breeding box for them to hide in.

The harlequin molly is named after the classic colors of the harlequin clowns. Fortunately, unlike certain clowns, these fish are peaceful and friendly. We do our best to pair these if you order two. The crowntail betta, or rooster tail betta, is a popular betta variation and really looks amazing when displaying against another male (just let him see his reflection in a mirror). The fins look like the crown of a rooster. Male bettas cannot be kept with other bettas, but they get along fine with most other aquarium species. There are many names for the particular betta color patterns, but most are variations of blue and/or red colors. Fish pictured here are representative only. If you are looking for a specific coloration, add a note to the order or simply allow us to choose one of our favorites for you! Quick Facts Scientific Name Betta splendens Origin Thailand (captive-bred) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Males fight each other; peaceful toward most other fish Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 76–82°F (needs a heater) pH 6.5–7.5 Breathes Air Yes – labyrinth fish take air from the surface Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give him a heater (bettas are tropical fish), a gentle filter and live or silk plants. Floating plants or a "betta leaf" near the surface give him a place to rest. Keep a lid on the tank and leave a gap of air under it, since bettas breathe from the surface. Feeding: Feed a few betta pellets or a pinch of flake once or twice a day. Bettas overeat easily, so small meals are best. They also enjoy frozen bloodworms. Tankmates: Never keep two male bettas together. A male can live with small, peaceful fish that don't nip fins, such as corydoras, small rasboras, otocinclus and snails. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs and flashy, long-finned fish like fancy guppies. Good to know: Crowntail fin rays can split or curl in poor water, so keep the water clean and warm. A short look in a mirror (a minute or two) lets him flare, but long sessions stress him.

The super delta betta (the word "delta" is Latin for the letter "D" and stands for the shape of the tail) is also called the super veil tail betta. This betta variation is one grade above the standard show betta and one grade below halfmoon bettas. However, the body of the super delta betta tends to grow a bit larger than the half moon bettas, and the fish has great color and very long fins. The caudal fin (tail fin) extends between 120 and 160 degrees but does not quite come together with the dorsal fin and anal fin. There are many names for the particular betta color patterns, but most are variations of blue and/or red colors. Fish pictured here are representative only. If you are looking for a specific coloration, add a note to the order or simply allow us to choose one of our favorites for you! These Halfmoon Bettas are the prettiest freshwater fish you can put in your aquarium. This type of Betta features a variety of bright colors and a tail in the shape of a half moon. Though all show bettas come from the same species, breeders develop each variation for specific characteristics. A show betta will have some spacing between all its fins, a veil betta will have slightly larger fins and very little spacing, and a half moon betta will have closure when his fins are fully displayed, creating the "half moon" effect. There are many names for the particular betta color patterns, but most are variations of blue and/or red colors. Fish pictured here are representative only. If you are looking for a specific coloration, contact customer service or note it within the order, or simply allow us to choose one of our favorites for you! The halfmoon rosetail betta, or halfmoon rose petal betta, is an amazing variation of betta splendens. These fish come in a variety of color patterns, but all have fins so large that they fold over on themselves. The folding of the fins gives the fish its name, since the folds resemble the petals of a flower. There are many names for the particular betta color patterns, but most are variations of blue and/or red colors. Fish pictured here are representative only. If you are looking for a specific coloration, please note it on your order, or simply allow us to choose one of our favorites for you! The Halfmoon Butterfly Betta is a beautiful blue color variety of the magnificent Halfmoon Butterfly Betta. The Halfmoon Butterfly Betta boasts a breathtaking color pattern in which the body coloration radiates partially into the fins. The fin coloration then progresses to a delicate clear/white coloration. The crisp margin between the solid body color and white creates a distinct "banding" effect, forming a rough oval or "bull's-eye" pattern. This two-tone "Butterfly" color pattern imparts a striking, yet ephemeral quality to the standard Halfmoon Betta. There are many names for the particular betta color patterns, but most are variations of blue and/or red colors. Fish pictured here are representative only. If you are looking for a specific coloration, contact a livestock department representative or simply allow us to choose one of our favorites for you! Show bettas are the standard bettas found in any pet store. However, we import a larger bred quality from Thailand and hope you will see the difference. Male bettas should never be kept together, but they can be placed in a community tank with other species. There are many names for the particular betta color patterns, but most are variations of blue and/or red colors. Fish pictured here are representative only. If you are looking for a specific coloration, add a note to the order or simply allow us to choose one of our favorites for you! Quick Facts Scientific Name Betta splendens Origin Thailand (captive-bred) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Males fight each other; peaceful toward most other fish Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 76–82°F (needs a heater) pH 6.5–7.5 Breathes Air Yes – labyrinth fish take air from the surface Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give him a heater (bettas are tropical fish), a gentle filter and live or silk plants. Feeding: Feed a few betta pellets or a pinch of flake once or twice a day. Bettas overeat easily, so small meals are best. They also enjoy frozen bloodworms. Tankmates: Never keep two male bettas together. A male can live with small, peaceful fish that don't nip fins, such as corydoras, small rasboras, otocinclus and snails. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs and flashy, long-finned fish like fancy guppies. Good to know: Bettas are labyrinth fish and breathe air at the surface, so leave a gap under the lid. Despite their reputation, they live longer and show better color in a heated, filtered tank than in a bowl.

Female bettas are sociable and may be kept in most aquariums, and multiple female bettas can share the same tank. Breeding bettas is a tricky subject and imperils the safety of the female, so please study the subject before attempting this feat. Female bettas are hardy and colorful but do not have the long fins of the male Betta splendens. Quick Facts Scientific Name Betta splendens Origin Thailand (captive-bred) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Can live in groups (sororities) with care Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 76–82°F (needs a heater) pH 6.5–7.5 Breathes Air Yes – labyrinth fish take air from the surface Shipping Size Approx. 1¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a filter and lots of plants and hiding places to break up sight lines. Keep a lid on the tank and leave a gap of air under it, since bettas breathe from the surface. Feeding: Feed a few betta pellets or a pinch of flake once or twice a day. Bettas overeat easily, so small meals are best. They also enjoy frozen bloodworms. Tankmates: Females can share a tank with small, peaceful fish like corydoras, rasboras and snails. Never add a male to a sorority tank, and avoid fin-nippers. Good to know: Females color up when relaxed. In a sorority, watch for bullying and remove any female that is constantly chased.

Just as the name implies, chocolate gourami have a pleasant chocolate color (but probably not a pleasant chocolate taste) and are terrific pet fish in nano and planted tanks. These fish may be kept with other nano tank species, including fancy shrimp, and will eat flake food. However, chocolate gourami are not tolerant of hard, high-pH water, so try to keep it at 7.0 or below. Quick Facts Scientific Name Sphaerichthys osphromenoides Origin Malaysia and Indonesia (peat swamps) Care Level Difficult (for experienced keepers) Temperament Peaceful, shy Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 4–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 4.0–6.5 (very soft water) Breathes Air Yes – labyrinth fish take air from the surface Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: These are blackwater fish: they need very soft, acidic water, dim lighting, a gentle filter and lots of plants and leaf litter. Peat or Indian almond leaves help tint and soften the water. Keep a lid on the tank and leave a gap of air above the water, since gouramis breathe from the surface and warm, humid air protects their labyrinth organ. Change small amounts of water often rather than large amounts at once. Feeding: Feed small amounts once or twice a day. Many will learn to take fine flake or micro pellets once settled. They also enjoy small frozen foods like brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them only with tiny, gentle fish that like the same soft, acidic water, such as small rasboras and pygmy corydoras. Avoid anything boisterous or larger. Good to know: Chocolate gouramis are sensitive to sudden changes, so change small amounts of water often and keep conditions stable.

Blue Gourami are hardy fish, and like all labyrinth species, they can breathe surface air as well as water-borne oxygen through their gills. The Blue Gourami from AquariumFish.com are pond-raised in Florida for larger size and color and handle a wide range of pH and temperature. Also called the Three-Spot Gourami, Blue Gourami are similar to Opaline Gourami but have a bluish body with three dark spots on the side of the body. Quick Facts Scientific Name Trichopodus trichopterus (color variety) Origin Southeast Asia (pond-raised in Florida) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Semi-aggressive (males can be territorial) Adult Size Up to 6" Lifespan 4–6+ years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 6.0–8.0 Breathes Air Yes – labyrinth fish take air from the surface Shipping Size Medium: approx. 1½–2" · Large: approx. 2–3" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a filter and plenty of plants and hiding spots to break up sight lines between males. Keep a lid on the tank and leave a gap of air above the water, since gouramis breathe from the surface. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Pair them with sturdy, similar-sized fish such as larger tetras, barbs, rainbowfish, loaches and peaceful cichlids. Avoid small fish, slow long-finned fish and bettas. Good to know: Males can bully smaller or slower fish, so give them room and plenty of plants, and keep one male per tank unless the tank is large.

Both male and female Gold Gourami have solid gold bodies with a faint black leopard pattern. Gold Gourami from AquariumFish.com are bred in Florida ponds and have stronger color and larger bodies than the Asian-bred species. Gold Gourami are peaceful and easy pet fish. The samurai gourami, also called Vaillant's chocolate gourami after biologist Leon Vaillant (from way back in 1888), is a gem of the planted aquarium. In nature, this species prefers low pH and low light and will not adapt well to hard water with high pH. The samurai gourami is peaceful, and a small school of these will provide a lot of interesting interaction as the males compete for the females. This is one of the few species in nature where the females are the more colorful gender. The bright red pattern of the female looks a bit like the polished decorative armor of an ancient Japanese warrior. We recommend the purchase of at least a pair of these beautiful fish. The female will display her colors with a male present, and both will be much happier pet fish. Avoid anything boisterous or larger. Good to know: Unusually, the female is the more colorful sex, with bright red bands. Males are mouthbrooders and carry the eggs in their mouths.

Similar to the Blue Gourami, the Opaline Gourami has a bluish body and a black snakeskin pattern. Very hardy and very beautiful, these fish are suitable for any community tank, and larger sizes can handle cichlid tanks. The pearl gourami can breathe air through a labyrinth organ similar to a lung, as well as oxygen through its gills. These fish have a beautiful multicolored body with pearly white spotting. Pearl gourami have beautiful pearl color on a spotted pattern when they grow to two inches or more. Pictured is a two-inch sample. Larger ones have much more color. Quick Facts Scientific Name Trichopodus leerii Origin Southeast Asia (Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 4–5" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 77–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Breathes Air Yes – labyrinth fish take air from the surface Shipping Size Medium: approx. 1½" · Large: approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and plenty of plants, with some open space for swimming. Keep a lid on the tank and leave a gap of air above the water, since gouramis breathe from the surface. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as tetras, rasboras, corydoras and peaceful barbs. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs. Good to know: Mature males develop a bright orange-red throat and chest, especially when they are ready to breed.

The Licorice Gourami is a beautiful species but requires low-pH water (under 7.0 would be fine) and is only one inch in size. This fish can be kept with other fish that can tolerate low pH and cannot be in the same aquarium as larger, aggressive fish. These gourami are wild-caught in ponds in Indonesia, and many come in and out of the trade as new ponds are discovered and old ponds are paved over. Unfortunately. But they are active breeders, and there are many in the wild. The colors vary on these small creatures, depending on the pond in which they are caught. Quick Facts Scientific Name Parosphromenus sp.
