They also enjoy small frozen foods like brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them only with tiny, gentle fish that like the same soft, acidic water, such as small rasboras and pygmy corydoras. Avoid anything boisterous or larger. Good to know: Wild-caught licorice gouramis may ignore flake at first. Offer small frozen foods like brine shrimp until they settle in.

The pink kissing gourami has large lips, which it uses to spar with other fish for food and territory. When the gourami uses the mouth in such a fashion, it appears to kiss. Males and females look the same, so everyone is kissing everyone in a school of these pretty fish. The kissing gourami will grow to eight inches in the aquarium, so eventually the fish will need room. These are hardy pet fish and eat both veggies and meats, so a community pellet or flake food should suffice. Quick Facts Scientific Name Helostoma temminckii Origin Southeast Asia Care Level Easy Temperament Semi-aggressive (spars with its lips) Adult Size Up to 8" (larger in the wild) Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 6.5–8.0 Breathes Air Yes – labyrinth fish take air from the surface Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Kissing gouramis grow to about 8" in aquariums, so give them strong filtration and sturdy or artificial plants. Keep a lid on the tank and leave a gap of air above the water, since gouramis breathe from the surface. Feeding: Feed a quality pellet or flake with plenty of vegetable content once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods now and then. Tankmates: Keep them with other medium to large, sturdy fish such as larger barbs, rainbowfish, plecos and peaceful cichlids. Small or timid fish may be bullied. Good to know: The "kissing" is actually sparring between rivals. They also graze algae with those lips, so they appreciate vegetables and may munch soft plants.

The gold tiger datnoid, also called the Siamese tiger fish, is a predator from Southeast Asia. We import these fish from Vietnam and Indonesia. Indonesian datnoids have more stripes, but both have the same gold coloration and body shape. Even though datnoids are predators and will eat small fish, they are not aggressive to similar size fish in the fish tank. Gold tiger datnoids are wild-caught and not as common as the silver datnoid. Small datnoids will eat cut earth worms, live black worms, ghost shrimp, and can be transitioned to frozen. Medium datnoids can also eat feeder white clouds and feeder guppies. Quick Facts Scientific Name Datnioides microlepis Origin Southeast Asia Care Level Moderate Temperament Predatory Adult Size Up to 10–14" Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 1–3" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them driftwood, roots and hiding places, plus good filtration. They do well in fresh or slightly salty (brackish) water. Feeding: Feed meaty foods like quality cichlid pellets and frozen shrimp. Tankmates: Datnoids eat small fish but are not aggressive toward fish their size. Keep them with large, peaceful fish. Good to know: Datnoids can change their color from bright to dark depending on mood.

The rare broad band datnoid, usually called the Irian Jaya Datnoid, has broader bands and much brighter markings than the gold or silver common datnoids. The species was discovered by an American air force pilot named Stuart Campbell, who got to add his part to biology history. Another name for the fish is the New Guinea Tiger Perch and it is found in only one river system on New Guinea. Be prepared to feed live black worms or live brine shrimp, and you should be able to transition the fish to frozen over time. Many brackish fish can be slowly transitioned to entirely fresh or entirely salt water. Aquarium Fish Sale brackish fish are maintained in LIGHT brackish conditions, the same conditions which our live bearers are kept, so most can be transitioned to all fresh water. However, a pinch of salt never hurt anybody. Quick Facts Scientific Name Datnioides campbelli Origin New Guinea Care Level Moderate Temperament Predatory Adult Size Up to 12–14" Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 3" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them driftwood, roots and hiding places, plus good filtration. They do well in fresh or slightly salty (brackish) water. Feeding: Feed meaty foods like quality cichlid pellets and frozen shrimp. Tankmates: Datnoids eat small fish but are not aggressive toward fish their size. Keep them with large, peaceful fish. Good to know: Datnoids can change their color from bright to dark depending on mood.

Pipefish are unusual looking ambush predators, and share many characteristics with the seahorse. Their long skinny body looks like sticks in the pond, and these fish will float near their prey and whip their mouth to the right or left and grab it. The dorichthys pipefish is a rare freshwater fish and looks great in a planted aquarium. Freshwater pipefish can also do well in a brackish aquarium. This species will do well in small tanks as well as large, and is peaceful with other fish that cannot fit into their long narrow jaws. Quick Facts Scientific Name Microphis brachyurus Origin Indo-Pacific Care Level Difficult Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 6–8" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Carnivore (small meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 4–6" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a planted tank with gentle current and plenty of places to hide. They do well in fresh or slightly salty (brackish) water. Feeding: Pipefish eat small meaty foods like frozen brine shrimp and bloodworms. Feed small amounts once or twice a day, and make sure they get enough. Tankmates: Pipefish are slow eaters. Keep them with calm, small fish that won't outcompete them for food. Good to know: Pipefish are close cousins of seahorses, and the males carry the eggs.

Mono argentus can be slowly transitioned to entirely salt water but will always need some salt in the water in a primarily freshwater fish tank. The argentus earns its name for the gold fringe (argentus is Latin for gold) around the fins. These are great schooling fish that do well with other fish and will eat prepared foods such as flake. Quick Facts Scientific Name Monodactylus argenteus Origin Indo-Pacific Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 8–10" Lifespan 10 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.5–8.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Monos are fast, active swimmers that do best in brackish or full saltwater as adults. Give them open swimming space and strong filtration. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or pellet once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like brine shrimp. Tankmates: Monos are peaceful with fish their size and do best with other brackish fish like scats and archerfish. Good to know: Monos have a bright silver body with yellow fins and swim together in a tight group.

Many brackish fish can be slowly transitioned to entirely fresh or entirely salt water. Aquarium Fish Sale brackish fish are maintained in LIGHT brackish conditions, the same conditions which our live bearers are kept, so most can be transitioned to all fresh water. However, a pinch of salt never hurt anybody. Wild-caught, the size of these guys can vary greatly, from one inch to three inches. Quick Facts Scientific Name Monodactylus sebae Origin West Africa Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 8" Lifespan 10 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.5–8.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Monos are fast, active swimmers that do best in brackish or full saltwater as adults. Give them open swimming space and strong filtration. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or pellet once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like brine shrimp. Tankmates: Monos are peaceful with fish their size and do best with other brackish fish like scats and archerfish. Good to know: Sebae monos are much taller than they are long and look a bit like freshwater angelfish.

The red scat, also called the ruby scat, are wild-caught and will vary in size and color, but always have some bright red markings somewhere. Like many brackish fish, scats can be transitioned to entirely salt water, but not the other way around. Red scats are hardy and will eat prepared and live foods. Quick Facts Scientific Name Scatophagus argus Origin Indo-Pacific Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 8–10" Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore (needs plant matter) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.5–8.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1–3" Care Guide Tank setup: Scats are active swimmers that grow larger over time. They do best in slightly salty (brackish) water as adults. Give them open swimming space and strong filtration. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or pellet once or twice a day. They also enjoy vegetable foods and frozen foods like brine shrimp. Tankmates: Scats are peaceful and do best with other fish that like brackish water, such as monos and other scats. Good to know: Scats are big eaters of plant matter and will eat soft aquarium plants.

Silver sailfin mollies, also called platinum sailfin mollies, brighten up the aquarium with solid white reflective dorsal fins. These fish are solid white and look great among green plants and dark gravel. Quick Facts Scientific Name Poecilia latipinna / P. velifera (aquarium-bred) Origin Southeastern U.S. and Mexico (wild ancestors); aquarium-bred Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Peaceful (males can chase females and rival males) Adult Size Up to 4–5" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (needs plant matter) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.5–8.5 (hard water) Group Size Keep more females than males Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give sailfins hard, alkaline water with plants, open swimming space and good filtration. Aquarium salt is optional; they also do well in brackish tanks. Feeding: Mollies graze on algae, so feed a quality flake that includes vegetable matter once or twice a day. They also enjoy algae wafers and frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Mollies get along with most peaceful community fish that like similar hard water, such as platies, swordtails, guppies, danios, rainbowfish, corydoras and plecos. Avoid fin-nippers and soft-water specialists. Keeping more females than males keeps any one female from being harassed. Good to know: Male sailfins raise their tall dorsal fin to show off to females and rival males. Their sails grow fuller as they mature, so juveniles may not show a full sail yet.

The green scat comes in various amounts of green on the body depending on where the fish is caught. All scats are wild-caught, and the red and green scats are the same species; they just come from different sides of the tracks (of the Indian Ocean). All the scats are pretty, but will get a bland dark color when stressed. Scats will eat prepared foods but also like treats like live black worms. Quick Facts Scientific Name Scatophagus argus Origin Indo-Pacific Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 8–10" Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore (needs plant matter) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.5–8.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1½–4" Care Guide Tank setup: Scats are active swimmers that grow larger over time. They do best in slightly salty (brackish) water as adults. Give them open swimming space and strong filtration. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or pellet once or twice a day. They also enjoy vegetable foods and frozen foods like brine shrimp. Tankmates: Scats are peaceful and do best with other fish that like brackish water, such as monos and other scats. Good to know: Scats are big eaters of plant matter and will eat soft aquarium plants.

The silver scat is a separate species from the green and red scats, which are actually the same species from different parts of the Ocean. The silver scat has a black lined pattern on a silver body, and if desired, these fish can be transitioned to a marine aquarium, though they are not reef compatible. The silver scat is a schooling fish but will do fine on its own. Quick Facts Scientific Name Selenotoca multifasciata Origin Southeast Asia and Australia Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 6–8" Lifespan 10 years Diet Omnivore (needs plant matter) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.5–8.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Scats are active swimmers that grow larger over time. They do best in slightly salty (brackish) water as adults. Give them open swimming space and strong filtration. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or pellet once or twice a day. They also enjoy vegetable foods and frozen foods like brine shrimp. Tankmates: Scats are peaceful and do best with other fish that like brackish water, such as monos and other scats. Good to know: Silver scats are calmer than spotted scats and can live in fresh, brackish or salt water as adults.

Indian pea puffers, also called dwarf Indian puffers, do well in brackish and 100% freshwater aquariums. Pea puffers are caught in the wild and are seasonal - summer is when they start growing again so they are a bit more difficult to find and small during the summer months. These aquarium puffers are terrific baby snail eaters and do fine in planted aquariums and nano tanks. Oddly, these fish seem to handle themselves even among larger species without getting eaten. They are known to nip at the fins of their neighbors, but their mouths are so small it is generally not more than a nuisance. Quick Facts Scientific Name Carinotetraodon travancoricus Origin Southwestern India Care Level Moderate Temperament Semi-aggressive (nips fins) Adult Size Up to 1" Lifespan 4–5 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods, snails) Water Temperature 74–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. ¼–½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a planted tank with lots of plants and hiding places to break up sight lines, and good filtration, since puffers are messy eaters. Feeding: Puffers need meaty foods and usually won't eat flake. Feed frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp once a day. They also enjoy small snails, which help keep their teeth trimmed. Tankmates: Pea puffers can nip fins and are best kept with their own kind, or with fast, tough fish like otocinclus. Shrimp and snails may be eaten. Good to know: Pea puffers are the smallest puffers in the hobby and are true freshwater fish. They are curious and often watch their owners.

Figure eight puffers have a bright figure eight pattern on their body. These fish are good companions to other fish their own size but will need at least a light level of salt in the water. The figure 8 puffer is collected in brackish waters around Indonesia and is quite common in the wild. Though originating in brackish water, figure 8 puffers can handle freshwater. Quick Facts Scientific Name Dichotomyctere ocellatus Origin Southeast Asia Care Level Moderate Temperament Semi-aggressive Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 10 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods, snails) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 1–2" Care Guide Tank setup: Figure 8 puffers do best in slightly salty (brackish) water but can handle fresh water. Give them rocks, plants and good filtration. Feeding: Puffers need meaty foods and usually won't eat flake. Feed frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp once a day. They also enjoy small snails, which help keep their teeth trimmed. Tankmates: Puffers nip fins and are best kept alone or with their own kind. Good to know: Figure 8 puffers are named for the yellow figure-eight pattern on their back.

Tetraodon nigroviridis , or the spotted puffer, leopard puffer as it’s also called, is a unique fish. Its back has saturated green color that contrasts beautifully against its white abdomen. The green spotted puffer, like most puffers, has some personality – at least it recognizes its owner and becomes very active. As long as there is some salt present in the water these are very easy pet fish to keep. The puffer will eat snails and can be a bit nippy. Quick Facts Scientific Name Dichotomyctere nigroviridis Origin Southeast Asia Care Level Moderate Temperament Aggressive (nips fins) Adult Size Up to 6" Lifespan 10 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods, snails) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.5–8.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: These puffers live in fresh water when young but do best in slightly salty (brackish) water as they mature. Give them rocks, plants and good filtration. Feeding: Puffers need meaty foods and usually won't eat flake. Feed frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp once a day. They also enjoy small snails, which help keep their teeth trimmed. Tankmates: Puffers nip fins and are best kept alone or with their own kind. Good to know: Green spotted puffers are full of personality and often recognize their owners.

The fugu puffer, or saddle puffer, is best known as the sushi puffer - but only professionals should prepare this toxic species. These puffers need some salt in the water to thrive and have beautiful orange on green coloration. Wild-caught and very seasonal, we do not often offer this species. Quick Facts Scientific Name Takifugu ocellatus Origin Coastal East and Southeast Asia Care Level Difficult Temperament Aggressive Adult Size Up to 6" Lifespan 10 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods, snails) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 7.5–8.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 3–4" Care Guide Tank setup: These puffers live in fresh water when young but do best in slightly salty (brackish) water as they mature. Give them rocks, plants and good filtration. Feeding: Puffers need meaty foods and usually won't eat flake. Feed frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp once a day. They also enjoy small snails, which help keep their teeth trimmed. Tankmates: Puffers nip fins and are best kept alone or with their own kind. Good to know: Fugu puffers have bright orange saddle markings on a green back.

The banded archer fish is named for bow and arrow hunters. In the wilds of the Indonesian jungles, archer fish will swim near the surface of slow-moving water. When a small insect is near, whether in flight or napping on a tree leaf, the archer fish will shoot a stream of drops to dislodge the insect so that it falls to the water surface. Then the archer fish eats it. In the fish tank, they continue to spit, so don't be surprised to be hit by water from time to time. Frozen food works well, though sometimes these fish will adapt to flake. Always bugs. Quick Facts Scientific Name Toxotes jaculatrix Origin Southeast Asia and northern Australia Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful (eats very small fish) Adult Size Up to 6–10" Lifespan 10 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Archerfish hunt at the surface, so leave space between the water and the lid. They do best in slightly salty (brackish) water. Keep a lid on the tank. Feeding: Feed floating pellets or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms. Tankmates: They are peaceful but will eat very small fish. Keep them with other brackish fish like scats and monos. Good to know: Archerfish can shoot a jet of water to knock insects off leaves above the water.

Also known as an Albino Wrestling Half-Beak, it is a schooling fish that is very entertaining to watch. Male fish of this species have very colorful fins and a black lobe on the lower jaw. Females have less color in the fins and have a red or uncolored lobe. Half-beaks, along with four-eye anableps, are the aquarium's most unusual livebearers. The best environment for a half-beak fish is a community aquarium with plants, rocks, caves, and driftwood. A small school should be kept with other peaceful fish of similar size. Half-beaks tend to swim near the top of the aquarium. Quick Facts Scientific Name Dermogenys pusilla Origin Southeast Asia Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful (males spar) Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Halfbeaks live at the surface, so give them floating plants and a tight-fitting lid, since they jump. They are easily startled, so avoid sudden movements around the tank. Feeding: Feed a quality floating flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy small frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with peaceful fish that swim lower in the tank, such as rasboras, corydoras and gouramis. Males may spar with each other. Breeding: Halfbeaks are livebearers. Adults will eat the babies, so floating plants give them a place to hide. Good to know: Halfbeaks have a long lower jaw that helps them catch insects at the surface.

The celebese half beak is a very strange livebearing fish from Indonesia. Like all half beaks, these fish swim at the surface of the aquarium and are territorial, so they cannot be kept with smaller platinum half beaks or hatchet fish. Other than that, these fish are good additions to a community tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name Nomorhamphus liemi Origin Sulawesi, Indonesia Care Level Moderate Temperament Semi-aggressive (males spar) Adult Size Up to 3–4" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Halfbeaks live at the surface, so give them floating plants and a tight-fitting lid, since they jump. They are easily startled, so avoid sudden movements around the tank. Feeding: Feed floating foods like flake and frozen bloodworms once or twice a day. Tankmates: They get along with peaceful fish that swim lower in the tank, such as rasboras, corydoras and gouramis. Males may spar with each other. Breeding: Halfbeaks are livebearers. Adults will eat the babies, so floating plants give them a place to hide. Good to know: Celebes halfbeaks have a short beak and colorful red-and-black fins on the males.

Badis badis are excellent planted tank, community tank, and nano tank pets. The badis comes from the wild in Indonesia and are very hardy and only grow to a little less than two inches. The badis fish develop a rainbow color pattern and will be peaceful tank mates with other small community fish. Quick Facts Scientific Name Badis badis Origin India, Bangladesh and Myanmar Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful (males are territorial) Adult Size Up to 2–3" Lifespan 4–6 years Diet Carnivore (small meaty foods) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single, pair or small group Shipping Size Approx. ¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a planted tank with caves, leaf litter and gentle filtration. They are shy and like plenty of hiding places. Feeding: Badis are shy eaters that prefer small frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Some will learn to take small pellets once settled. Feed small amounts once or twice a day. Tankmates: Keep them with small, calm fish such as rasboras, pygmy corydoras and shrimp. Avoid fast, pushy fish that would outcompete them for food. Good to know: Badis can change color depending on their mood, from pale to deep red and blue.

Male neon blue dwarf gourami feature a reflective blue and black body with bright red and blue fins. We ship only colorful male dwarf gouramis, whether neon blue, standard dwarf, powder blue, or red flame. Female dwarf gouramis are sold separately at a lower price. Females are a solid tan color and will breed with any of the previously mentioned males; with their plain color, they cannot afford to be picky. Neon blue dwarf gouramis are tolerant of a wide range of temperature and water conditions. Quick Facts Scientific Name Trichogaster lalius Origin India and Bangladesh Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful (males can be territorial) Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 4–6 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Breathes Air Yes – labyrinth fish take air from the surface Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and plenty of plants, including floating plants. Keep a lid on the tank and leave a gap of air above the water, since gouramis breathe from the surface. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with small, peaceful fish such as rasboras, small tetras, corydoras and otocinclus. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs and other male dwarf gouramis. Good to know: Males can squabble with each other, so keep one male per tank, or several only in a heavily planted tank with lots of hiding places.

The scarlet gem badis, or simply the scarlet gem, is a bright red striped nano fish that needs a peaceful fish tank. Scarlet gems come from India and are actually micro predators. These nano fish feed on very small insects in the wild but will eat prepared flake food in the aquarium. Though not schooling fish, these fish are small and more sociable in a small group of three or four. Quick Facts Scientific Name Dario dario Origin India Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful (males spar with each other) Adult Size Up to ¾" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Carnivore (tiny meaty foods) Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group with plenty of hiding spots Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a planted tank with caves, leaf litter and gentle filtration. They are shy and like plenty of hiding places. Feeding: Badis are shy eaters that prefer small frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Some will learn to take small pellets once settled. Feed small amounts once or twice a day. Tankmates: Keep them with small, calm fish such as rasboras, pygmy corydoras and shrimp. Avoid fast, pushy fish that would outcompete them for food. Good to know: Males are bright red with blue fins; females are plain silver.

The needle nose gar, or needlenose gar, from Indonesia is an outstanding predator and does not outgrow the fish tank. These predator fish have long snouts and small teeth and feed on feeder guppies, ghost shrimp, black worms, and other live foods. Not to be confused with the giant longnose gar, the needle nose gar is perfectly suitable to any mid-size and large aquarium. Needle nose gars may be kept with other larger species and mid-size fish, and they are not aggressive to each other. Quick Facts Scientific Name Xenentodon cancila Origin South and Southeast Asia Care Level Moderate Temperament Predatory Adult Size Up to 10–12" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 6" Care Guide Tank setup: Needlenose gars swim near the surface and are easily startled, so give them open swimming space, floating plants and a tight-fitting lid. Feeding: Feed meaty foods like frozen shrimp and fish, plus floating carnivore pellets once they learn to take them. Tankmates: They will eat any fish that fits in their mouth. Keep them only with large, robust fish. Good to know: Needlenose gars are actually halfbeak relatives, not true gars, and they can jump when startled.

Dwarf female gourami are plain tan-colored creatures that breed with any of the male Colisa lalia dwarf gourami varieties. It is a good idea to keep a few females with a school of males. The male dwarf gourami will display their colors more boldly for the females. Who wouldn't? The internet provides abundant information on breeding gourami. Quick Facts Scientific Name Trichogaster lalius Origin India and Bangladesh Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 4–6 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Breathes Air Yes – labyrinth fish take air from the surface Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and plenty of plants, including floating plants. Keep a lid on the tank and leave a gap of air above the water, since gouramis breathe from the surface. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with small, peaceful fish such as rasboras, small tetras, corydoras and otocinclus. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs and other male dwarf gouramis. Good to know: Keeping more females than males spreads out his attention. Males build bubble nests at the surface when they are ready to breed.

The red flame dwarf gourami is also called the cinnamon dwarf gourami. Male red flame dwarf gourami feature a solid bright red body with blue fins. When you order the flame dwarf gourami, we ship only the colorful males, whether neon blue, standard dwarf, powder blue, or red flame. Female dwarf gouramis are sold separately at a lower price. Females are a solid tan color and will breed with any of the previously mentioned males; with their plain color, they cannot afford to be picky. Quick Facts Scientific Name Trichogaster lalius Origin India and Bangladesh Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful (males can be territorial) Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 4–6 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Breathes Air Yes – labyrinth fish take air from the surface Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and plenty of plants, including floating plants. Keep a lid on the tank and leave a gap of air above the water, since gouramis breathe from the surface. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with small, peaceful fish such as rasboras, small tetras, corydoras and otocinclus. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs and other male dwarf gouramis. Good to know: Males can squabble with each other, so keep one male per tank, or several only in a heavily planted tank with lots of hiding places.

Honey dwarf gourami range in color from a deep honey yellow to yellow and red. These gourami are small, hardy, and peaceful. Like most small aquatic species, small dwarf gourami are less stressed when kept in a school. These smaller gourami take nearly a year to develop their rich colors, and only hints of color appear when first placed in the aquarium. Quick Facts Scientific Name Trichogaster chuna Origin India and Bangladesh Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 4–6 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Breathes Air Yes – labyrinth fish take air from the surface Shipping Size Approx. 1–1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and plenty of plants, including some floating plants for cover. Keep a lid on the tank and leave a gap of air above the water, since gouramis breathe from the surface. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with small, peaceful fish such as rasboras, small tetras, corydoras and otocinclus. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs and larger, boisterous fish. Good to know: Honey gouramis are among the most peaceful gouramis, which makes them a great first gourami for a community tank.

Nothobranchius guentheri is an exotic killifish from Zanzibar. In the wild these fish control mosquito populations in swampy areas. Before the dry season, guentheri killifish lay eggs in the mud, and when the swamps dry and the parents die, the eggs live on until the next wet period. In the aquarium the active male will display his colors year-round for the female without any fear of getting dry. Guentheri are hardy and adapt well to prepared flake and pellet aquarium food. Each order comes with one male and one female. Quick Facts Scientific Name Nothobranchius guentheri Origin Zanzibar and coastal Tanzania, East Africa Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful (males may spar with each other) Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 1–2 years (annual killifish) Diet Carnivore (meaty foods; takes flake) Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Sold as a pair (1 male + 1 female) Shipping Size Approx. 1¼" male; female under 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them soft to medium water, plants, gentle filtration and a dark substrate. Killifish are expert jumpers, so a tight-fitting lid is a must. Feeding: Feed small amounts of a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They are best kept in a species tank or with other peaceful killifish. Avoid fin-nippers and large fish. Keep one male per tank unless the tank is large, since males may spar. Good to know: In the wild these fish live in seasonal pools. Their eggs survive the dry season buried in mud, and many breeders incubate them in damp peat for several weeks before hatching.

Metallic patterns are prized for the deep, reflective solid colors on the tailfin of the males. AquariumFishSale imports the blue metallic guppy from Thailand, where the breeders are known for producing the classic large-tail, small-body pattern of show guppies. Quick Facts Scientific Name Poecilia reticulata Origin Northern South America (captive-bred in Thailand) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Sold as a pair (1 male + 1 female) Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and plenty of plants, including some floating plants where babies can hide. Guppies like slightly hard water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Guppies get along with other small, peaceful fish such as platies, mollies, corydoras, small tetras and rasboras. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs and larger fish that could eat them. Breeding: Guppies are livebearers and breed easily. Females give birth to live babies about once a month, and adults will eat the babies, so thick plants give them a place to hide. Good to know: Metallic guppies have a shiny, reflective sheen that changes with the light.

Tetra Pond Stocks Tetra created the first prepared food for pond fish in Germany back in 1972. Since that time Tetra became the benchmark for pond nutrition. The food stock formulation allows complete digestion of the nutrients to keep the koi and goldfish healthy and the water clear. Since pond fish lack teeth, Tetra Pond Stocks break apart easily for complete digestion. Koi and goldfish should not be fed during extremely high temperatures or when they are dormant during the cold winter (when water temperature falls below 40 degrees). Otherwise eat up! Shipping Size: 3.54 oz.

API pH Test Kit The API pH Test Kit uses drops for much more accuracy (and tests!) than strip tests. The test is quick and easy and measures pH between 6.0 and 7.6. If that doesn't cover you then you are going to need API pH up or pH down:) Each kit comes with color scale, drops, instructions, and beaker. 250 tests with each kit!

API KH Test Kit The API KH Test Kit uses drops for much more accuracy (and tests!) than strip tests. Carbonate hardness measures the fish tank ability to moderate pH fluctuations. Also some fish require harder or softer water. The KH test kit comes with enough solution for more than 100 tests and each kit comes with color scale, drops, instructions, and beaker. API KH Test Kits for carbonate hardness work with saltwater and freshwater aquarium water.

API Ammonia Test Kit The API Ammonia Test Kit for NH3 and NH4 provides enough solution for 130 tests. Solution is a far more accurate measure than colored test strips and is nearly as fast and easy. Each kit comes with color scale, drops, instructions, and beaker. Periodic ammonia checks are a must to prevent rapid fish loss - the crashing tank phenomena. API Ammonia Kits for carbonate hardness work with saltwater and freshwater aquarium water.

Rarer than the Ossa Knifefish, the Elephant Nose Knifefish is wild caught in a small area of the Peruvian Amazon basin. Elephant nose knifefish have a long snout used to grab and eat small worms and similar food and will feed on frozen blood worms. Ideally, a source of live black worms would be safer to feed the fish from time to time. These knifefish have a white line on top of a black body and grow to nearly 18 inches. Quick Facts Scientific Name Sternarchorhynchus oxyrhynchus Origin Amazon basin, Peru Care Level Difficult Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 18" Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Carnivore (small meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.0 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 8" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them hiding places like large tubes or caves, dim lighting, strong filtration and a tight lid. They are most active at night. Feeding: Feed small frozen foods like bloodworms once or twice a day, ideally in the evening. They use their long snout to pick food from the bottom. Tankmates: They are peaceful but can be outcompeted for food. Keep them with calm fish too large to fit in their mouth. Good to know: Like other knifefish, they find food in the dark with a weak electric field.

The Teugelsi Bichir, like other African bichirs, has a lung and gill so they can survive for short periods out of the water. The Teugelsi bichir is a newly discovered species found in the Cross River in Cameroon in 2004. These bichirs have a pretty crosshatch pattern and grow to 30 inches in the wild - probably about 24 inches in the aquarium. Quick Facts Scientific Name Polypterus teugelsi Origin Cross River, Cameroon Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful with fish its size Adult Size Up to 2 feet Lifespan 15+ years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 3" Care Guide Tank setup: Bichirs are expert escape artists, so a tight-fitting lid is a must. Give them a soft bottom, caves and driftwood. They breathe air, so leave a gap above the water. Feeding: Feed sinking carnivore pellets once a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and shrimp. Tankmates: They will eat any fish that fits in their mouth. Keep them with fish too large to swallow. Breathes air: Bichirs take gulps of air from the surface, which is normal behavior. Good to know: Teugelsi bichirs have a bold spotted and banded pattern that makes them one of the most striking bichirs.

Japonica shrimp, or amano shrimp, are great algae eaters and terrific in community tanks. These shrimp are among the most popular at AquariumFish.com; they grow to about 2 inches and develop a light blue color. The great planted tank pioneer Takashi Amano brought these shrimp to the aquarium hobby, and eventually the shrimp acquired his name for their own. Amano shrimp are wild-caught in the highlands of Taiwan. Fortunately, we also have a breeder in Taiwan to supplement our inventory during monsoon season. Quick Facts Scientific Name Caridina multidentata Origin Japan and Taiwan (wild-caught and farm-raised) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Omnivore (excellent algae eater) Water Temperature 65–80°F pH 6.5–7.8 Water Hardness GH 6–12 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ½–1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a cycled, planted tank with moss, driftwood and hiding spots. Cover filter intakes with a sponge and keep a lid on the tank, since amanos can climb out. Feeding: Amanos eat algae and leftover food. If algae runs low, feed algae wafers or shrimp pellets. Tankmates: Amanos do well with most peaceful community fish, plus other shrimp and snails. Avoid cichlids, goldfish, loaches and other fish large enough to eat them. Good to know: Amano shrimp breed in captivity, but their larvae need brackish water to develop, so they will not overpopulate a freshwater tank.

In shrimp language, grade S is better than grade B or even grade A: a more distinct color pattern, and it will develop to a better size. Our shrimp are S grade. Do not keep fancy shrimp with cichlids of any kind; to those fish they just look like food, no matter what the color. Don't worry about the short life span; shrimp breed fast. Some of the chain stores' quality on this shrimp is so bad they can only refer to it as red and white shrimp. Quick Facts Scientific Name Caridina cf. cantonensis (crystal red) Origin Taiwan (aquarium-bred) Care Level Moderate to difficult (needs soft, stable water) Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1" Lifespan 1½–2 years Diet Omnivore (grazes on algae) Water Temperature 68–76°F pH 5.8–6.8 Water Hardness GH 4–6, KH 0–1 (soft) Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Caridina bee and Taiwan bee shrimp need soft, slightly acidic water. Use a mature, cycled tank with an active (buffering) shrimp substrate, RO water remineralized for shrimp, moss and plants, and a sponge filter. Feeding: Feed a small amount of quality shrimp food once a day, and remove any uneaten food after a few hours. Tankmates: Caridina are best kept in a shrimp-only tank or with tiny, peaceful fish like otocinclus, plus snails. Avoid cichlids and other fish that will eat shrimp. Different bee and Taiwan bee varieties can crossbreed, but they will not breed with Neocaridina. Good to know: Acclimate slowly (drip for an hour or more). Stable water matters more than perfect numbers, and sudden changes in temperature or hardness are the most common cause of losses.

The blue velvet shrimp, or super blue shrimp, is a solid aqua blue and bred in Taiwan to create this amazing color. Like most exotic shrimp, blue velvet shrimp enjoy hanging on moss balls that collect detritus from the water. Neocaridina are active swimmers and breeders and beautiful in planted aquariums and nano tanks. Just ensure that the tank filter system is safe (will not suck them up) and the water is free of malachite green, copper and other medications. Quick Facts Scientific Name Neocaridina davidi (blue velvet) Origin East Asia (aquarium-bred, mostly Taiwan) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1–1¼" Lifespan 1–2 years Diet Omnivore (grazes on algae) Water Temperature 65–80°F pH 6.5–8.0 Water Hardness GH 6–12 (moderately hard) Group Size Does best in a group (breeds readily) Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Neocaridina are hardy and ideal for beginners. Use a cycled, planted tank with moss, plants and hiding spots, and a sponge filter or a sponge over the filter intake so shrimp aren't pulled in. Keep the water stable. Feeding: Shrimp graze on algae all day. Feed a small amount of quality shrimp food once a day and remove anything uneaten after a few hours. Tankmates: Keep shrimp alone or with tiny, peaceful fish like small rasboras, ember tetras, otocinclus and pygmy corydoras, plus snails. Most fish will eat baby shrimp, and cichlids (even dwarf cichlids like rams and apistogrammas) and larger fish will eat adults. Different Neocaridina colors will crossbreed and lose their color over time. Good to know: Shrimp are very sensitive to copper and many medications. Never treat a tank with shrimp, and check plant fertilizers and treatments for copper.

The super red shrimp, or red sakura shrimp , is solid deep red and a fantastic addition to the planted aquarium. These exotic shrimp require the same care as other Neocaridina exotic species. Sakura-grade red shrimp are "super red"; less than sakura grade are "cherry red". Please remember never to add medications to water with shrimp present. And also, exotic aquarium fish do not tolerate high-pH water. The arulius barb is caught in the Kaveri River in Southeast India and makes it into the aquarium trade from time to time. These active, colorful barbs grow to four inches and, if in a school, will not nip at other fish. These are best kept in a school of five or six. Similar in disposition to tiger barbs (though they get bigger!), arulius will eat prepared flake or pellet foods and get along with most other mildly aggressive community fish. Arulius barbs do best in clean, low-pH water (anything near 8 will kill them off). Quick Facts Scientific Name Dawkinsia arulius Origin Southern India Care Level Moderate Temperament Semi-aggressive Adult Size Up to 4–5" Lifespan 6–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 6.0–7.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: These barbs grow large and swim fast, so give them lots of open space, strong filtration and a tight-fitting lid, since they can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with similar-sized, active fish such as rainbowfish, larger barbs, larger tetras, loaches and peaceful cichlids. Very small fish may be eaten or stressed. Good to know: Arulius barbs behave best in a school. Males grow long, trailing dorsal fins as they mature.

The bulu point tropheus moorii, or cherry spot tropheus, displays large cherry red blotches on a black body. Compatible with other Lake Tanganyika cichlids, tropheus moorii are slow to grow, hardy, and require clean water and food that contains veggies. This distinct-pattern fish was discovered, of course, near Bulu Point, Lake Tanganyika, but today we import our specially bred fish from our breeder in Taiwan. Quick Facts Scientific Name Tropheus moorii "Bulu Point" Origin Lake Tanganyika, Africa (bred in Taiwan) Care Level Moderate to difficult Temperament Aggressive with their own kind; keep in large groups Adult Size Up to 5" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Herbivore (plant-based foods) Water Temperature 76–80°F pH 8.0–9.0 Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Use a sand bottom and plenty of rockwork that grows algae for grazing. Strong filtration and very clean water are essential. Lake Malawi and Lake Tanganyika cichlids need hard, alkaline water; crushed coral or aragonite sand helps hold the pH up. Feeding: Tropheus are strict plant eaters. Feed a vegetable-based flake or pellet in small amounts, and avoid rich, meaty foods, which can make them very sick. Tankmates: Keep Tropheus in a group of a single variety, with one or a few males. Avoid mixing different Tropheus varieties, which will crossbreed and fight. Peaceful Tanganyikans like cyprichromis or synodontis can share the tank. Good to know: Add Tropheus all at once as a group; adding single fish later often leads to fighting.

The Thomasi cichlid, or African butterfly cichlid, is one of the smallest cichlids found in Africa. Thomasi cichlids have a temperament similar to South American rams and should not be kept in a typical African cichlid tank. These dwarf cichlids are excellent additions to planted and community fish tanks. One interesting thing these fish do in the small streams of Liberia: when threatened, they burrow as deep as a foot into the mud and can stay there for as long as an hour. Thomasi dwarf cichlids adapt to flake and pellet food and handle low pH water conditions. Quick Facts Scientific Name Anomalochromis thomasi Origin Liberia, Sierra Leone and Guinea (streams) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful (territorial when breeding) Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: West African cichlids prefer soft to neutral water. Use a sand or fine gravel bottom with plants, driftwood and caves or flowerpots for spawning. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with peaceful community fish like tetras, barbs, rasboras, corydoras and plecos. Give each pair its own territory, and expect more defensiveness when breeding. Good to know: Thomasi are peaceful dwarf cichlids for planted community tanks, not for rift-lake cichlid tanks.

Chubby plecos come from rocky streams in Brazil and earn their name. Even their scales are fat and wide. The Chubby Pleco may change color in the aquarium; this species can alternate between gold and black colors. In fact, Golden Chubby Plecos cost about ten times more than the chocolate ones! Our Chubby Plecos will most likely remain a solid chocolate color, so they won't make you rich, but they WILL make you happy. Quick Facts Scientific Name Parancistrus aurantiacus Origin Rio Xingu basin, Brazil Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 7–9" Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore (algae and sinking foods) Water Temperature 77–84°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single, or several with a cave each Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Chubby plecos come from fast, rocky rivers. Give them smooth rocks, caves, driftwood, good current and high oxygen. Feeding: Feed algae wafers and sinking pellets once a day, ideally in the evening when they are most active. They also enjoy frozen bloodworms. Tankmates: They are peaceful and get along with most community fish. Males may squabble over caves, so give each one its own hiding spot. Good to know: Chubby plecos can shift between gold and dark chocolate colors depending on mood and surroundings.

The Dorado Catfish, or the Goliath Gilded Cat, is one of the largest known catfish in the World. This catfish also holds the record for the longest freshwater fish migration - from the spawning areas in the foothills of Peru to the deep waters of the Amazon, 7000 miles. Though the Dorado catfish will grow to six feet in the wild, these wild catfish seldom top three feet in the aquarium. At the juvenile stage, the Dorado sports very long whiskers and tail filaments and make a very pretty addition to the fish tank. Remember these start very small and will require frozen blood worms and maybe some live feeder guppies. Quick Facts Scientific Name Brachyplatystoma rousseauxii Origin Amazon basin, Peru Care Level Difficult (grows very large) Temperament Predatory Adult Size Up to 3 feet in aquariums; larger in the wild Lifespan 15+ years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 2" body plus tail Care Guide Tank setup: Shovelnose catfish grow large and are strong swimmers. Give them open swimming space, a sand bottom, strong filtration and a heavy, tight lid. Feeding: Feed meaty foods like quality carnivore pellets and frozen shrimp or fish. Many learn to take pellets once settled. Tankmates: They will eat any fish that fits in their mouth. Keep them only with large, robust fish. Good to know: Young dorados have very long whiskers and tail streamers that shorten as they grow.

Giant Hairgrass Giant hairgrass is a terrific background hardy tall plant. The leafs are narrow, spiky, and dark green. Scientific Name: ELEOCHARIS MONTEVIDENSIS Shipping Size: 2 inch potted, approx. ten inch tall large clump

The black Venezuelan cory is a rare treat. When first imported to Germany in the 1990s, these were thought to be a variation of the cory aeneus species, but these are correctly the corydoras schultzei. The other thing the Germans got wrong was the origin: the black Venezuelan cory comes from Peru. These mid-size, peaceful cory are coal black with rust to red fins. Like all cory, they are best kept with one or more tank mates since they are social catfish. Expensive, but hardy and very effective scavengers. Quick Facts Scientific Name Corydoras schultzei (black form) Origin Peru Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 5–10 years Diet Omnivore (bottom feeder) Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and a soft sand or smooth, fine gravel bottom. Plants, driftwood and a few shady spots help them feel secure. Corys are sensitive to salt and some medications (especially copper), so check labels before treating the tank. Feeding: Corys need their own food, not just leftovers. Feed sinking pellets or wafers once or twice a day so food reaches the bottom. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Corys get along with almost any peaceful community fish, such as tetras, rasboras, livebearers, gouramis, angelfish and bettas. Avoid large fish that could swallow them and aggressive bottom dwellers. Good to know: Corys sift through the substrate with their sensitive barbels, so soft sand or smooth, fine gravel keeps those barbels healthy.

Green Mandarin Goby The Green Mandarin Goby is one of the most colorful creatures on the planer. Most beginner saltwater aquarium owners will buy one and kill one. These gobies need special care - live food and clean water. Primarily a bottom-dweller, the Mandarin Goby will "hunt" across the substrate and rock for live food to graze on. It is slower and more methodical than most reef fish, and cannot compete with more active or aggressive tank mates for food. Scientific Name: Synchiropus splendidus Origin: Philippines Lifespan: 4 years Max Size: 4 inches Food: Live, flake, frozen Shipping Size: 1 to 3 inches

The mandarin orange shrimp, also known as the pumpkin shrimp or orange sakura shrimp, is a higher-grade solid orange shrimp from the orange bee shrimp family. The orange variation is bright and remains strong throughout its adult life. Neocaridina are prolific breeders when they are happy. Exotic shrimp are happy with plants, moss balls and some pellet food supplements. Please do not ever medicate a fish tank with exotic shrimp present. Quick Facts Scientific Name Neocaridina davidi (orange sakura) Origin Taiwan (aquarium-bred) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1–1¼" Lifespan 1–2 years Diet Omnivore (grazes on algae) Water Temperature 65–80°F pH 6.5–8.0 Water Hardness GH 6–12 (moderately hard) Group Size Does best in a group (breeds readily) Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Neocaridina are hardy and ideal for beginners. Use a cycled, planted tank with moss, plants and hiding spots, and a sponge filter or a sponge over the filter intake so shrimp aren't pulled in. Keep the water stable. Feeding: Shrimp graze on algae all day. Feed a small amount of quality shrimp food once a day and remove anything uneaten after a few hours. Tankmates: Keep shrimp alone or with tiny, peaceful fish like small rasboras, ember tetras, otocinclus and pygmy corydoras, plus snails. Most fish will eat baby shrimp, and cichlids (even dwarf cichlids like rams and apistogrammas) and larger fish will eat adults. Different Neocaridina colors will crossbreed and lose their color over time. Good to know: Shrimp are very sensitive to copper and many medications. Never treat a tank with shrimp, and check plant fertilizers and treatments for copper.

Cherry shrimp are a variation of the red sakura shrimp, or "super red shrimp". In general they are a lighter "cherry" red than the deeper color of the sakura grade, but the same species. Though less pricey, many aquarists enjoy the bright red and subtle color variations of cherry shrimp. These exotic shrimp will breed with other Neocaridina varieties in the aquarium. The offspring colors will be unpredictable. Cherry shrimp are delicate scavengers and are attractive inhabitants of planted tanks and small aquariums. Cichlids and aggressive larger fish will eat them, but otocinclus, most tetras, small loaches, rasboras and snails all make good tank mates. Bumblebee shrimp look like little aquatic bees as they shuttle around the tank with their black-striped little bodies. These are great aquarium species for small tanks, but be aware that dwarf cichlids will eat these expensive critters. The bumblebee shrimp is similar to crystal black and black rili shrimp but does not have the distinct black and white and clear pattern; they are a bit more muted. Flower shrimp, also called bamboo shrimp, wood shrimp and Singapore shrimp, are hardy and popular filter shrimp, feeding off detritus floating in the tank water. These exotic shrimp have a beautiful segmented orange color pattern on the body (hence the common name bamboo). Flower shrimp are peaceful and grow large enough to keep with most community species, except of course aggressive cichlids and predator species. Flower shrimp are wild-caught in Singapore. In the aquarium, flower shrimp will find a location to settle and filter food from flowing water. They may look big, but they are gentle and will not harm smaller tankmates. Quick Facts Scientific Name Atyopsis moluccensis Origin Southeast Asia Care Level Moderate (needs current and a mature tank) Temperament Very peaceful Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 2–5 years Diet Filter feeder (fine powdered foods) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Water Hardness GH 6–15 Group Size Single or small group Shipping Size Approx. 1½–2½" (wild-caught, varies) Care Guide Tank setup: Filter shrimp catch food with fan-like hands, so they need a mature tank with steady current (near a filter outlet) and rocks or driftwood to perch on. If they pick at the bottom instead of fanning, they may be hungry; add powdered food near the current. Feeding: Feed a fine powdered food or crushed flake, released near the current so the shrimp can catch it. Tankmates: They do well in peaceful community tanks with tetras, rasboras, gouramis and corydoras. Avoid fish that pick at invertebrates, like large cichlids, puffers and loaches. Good to know: Filter shrimp molt regularly and may hide for a day or two afterward. Never treat their tank with copper-based medications.

Neon Red Lobsters live in a suit of armor. Their color is so bright that they can look like a neon light. As they grow, they shed their shells. Soft-shelled (naked) crayfish are totally vulnerable until their shells re-harden and need a place to hide. Neon red lobsters, like all decapods, grow by eating lots of food and sucking in lots of water. This action eventually cracks their shells open, then they wriggle out of their former armor and hide while their new larger exoskeleton hardens. Neon red lobsters cannot be kept with small shrimp or small schooling fish and will act like bullies to defend their home. Quick Facts Scientific Name Procambarus clarkii Origin Captive-bred (Florida) Care Level Easy Temperament Semi-aggressive Adult Size Up to 5–6" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (scavenger) Water Temperature 65–80°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 2–3" Care Guide Tank setup: Crayfish need plenty of hiding places like caves or pipes and a tight-fitting lid, since they climb out. Avoid copper-based medications. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets once a day. They also eat vegetables and leftover food. Tankmates: Crayfish will catch and eat slow fish, shrimp and snails. They are best kept alone. Molting: Crayfish shed their shell to grow. Leave the old shell in the tank; they eat it to regain calcium. Good to know: These "lobsters" are actually a color form of the red swamp crayfish.

The Cobalt Hammers lobster was bred by a Mr. Hammer in Florida to get a cobalt blue body on a lobster that will not outgrow the fish tank and feature a less aggressive nature than other cherax species. He succeeded. Similar in color to the dwarf blue lobster, the Hammers Cobalt will grow to a larger size and actually gets more blue as it ages. Quick Facts Scientific Name Procambarus sp. Origin Captive-bred (Florida) Care Level Easy Temperament Semi-aggressive Adult Size Up to 4–5" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (scavenger) Water Temperature 65–80°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 3" Care Guide Tank setup: Crayfish need plenty of hiding places like caves or pipes and a tight-fitting lid, since they climb out. Avoid copper-based medications. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets once a day. They also eat vegetables and leftover food. Tankmates: Crayfish will catch and eat slow fish, shrimp and snails. They are best kept alone. Molting: Crayfish shed their shell to grow. Leave the old shell in the tank; they eat it to regain calcium. Good to know: Hammers cobalt crayfish get bluer as they get older.

The freshwater fiddler crab is aquatic but requires a place to get out of the water from time to time. Male fiddler crabs constantly wave their large claw to attract a mate. When he is the only crab in the tank, this is a sad and lonely sight. Fiddler crabs will leave fish alone and spend much of their time around rocks and other areas where food might accumulate. Quick Facts Scientific Name Uca pugnax Origin Florida, USA Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Omnivore (scavenger) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.5–8.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Fiddler crabs need land as well as water. Give them a tank with a sandy beach or rocks to climb out on, and slightly salty (brackish) water. Keep a tight lid on the tank. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets or shrimp food once a day. They also eat vegetables and small bits of fish food. Tankmates: Fiddler crabs leave most fish alone, but they do best in a brackish setup with their own kind. Good to know: Male fiddler crabs wave their one large claw to attract mates and warn off rivals.

Freshwater flounder are small, maximum two-inch flat fish found in the Peace River and other areas of Florida where they have been wild caught for home aquariums for generations. These little guys stick to the sides of the tank and will swim occasionally. They add a little dimension to the fish tank, even if that dimension is only one dimensional. Quick Facts Scientific Name Achirus lineatus Origin Florida, USA Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2–3" Lifespan 5 years Diet Carnivore (small meaty foods) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. ½–1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a soft sand bottom they can bury into and calm water. They do well in fresh or slightly salty (brackish) water. Feeding: Feed small frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp once a day. Make sure food reaches the bottom where they can find it. Tankmates: They are peaceful and small, so keep them with gentle fish that won't outcompete them for food. Good to know: Flounder lie flat on their side and have both eyes on one side of the head.

The assassin snail is small but deadly. Assassin snails are so named because they feed on other snails. Not all snails are welcome additions to the fish tank, and even desirable snails sometimes get a little carried away with their "romance", so these snails are perfect additions for the aquarist who needs to control a snail problem. Fight fire with fire. Assassin snails are hardy, totally safe for fish, seem to just take care of themselves and do not overrun the fish tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name Anentome helena Origin Southeast Asia (Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful with fish; eats other snails Adult Size Up to ¾–1" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Carnivore (eats snails and meaty foods) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Breeding Slow breeder; lays single eggs on hard surfaces Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Assassin snails like a sand bottom they can burrow in. Add them to a tank with pest snails and they will hunt them down over time. If you have no pest snails, feed meaty foods so they don't starve. Feeding: Assassin snails eat other snails, plus sinking pellets and other meaty foods. Tankmates: Assassin snails are safe with fish and adult shrimp, but they will eat other snails, including small nerites, mystery snails and rabbit snails. Keep them away from snails you want to keep. Good to know: Assassin snails won't wipe out pest snails overnight, but over a few weeks they keep pest-snail populations under control.

The trapdoor snail, or Japanese trapdoor snail, is a hardy species and popular in freshwater aquariums and ponds. These snails are good scavengers that can live through a wide range of temperatures, including northern winters. Quick Facts Scientific Name Cipangopaludina japonica (sold as Viviparus malleatus ) Origin East Asia (Japan, China, Korea); farm-raised Care Level Easy, good for beginners and ponds Temperament Peaceful; plant-safe Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Scavenger (algae and leftover food) Water Temperature 40–82°F (survives pond winters) pH 7.0–8.5 Breeding Livebearer; produces small numbers of live young Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Japanese trapdoor snails are hardy coldwater snails that do well in aquariums and outdoor ponds year-round. Give them a mature tank or pond with some algae and detritus to graze, and keep the water hard enough for healthy shells. Feeding: They graze on algae and leftover food and filter food from the water. In a clean aquarium, add algae wafers or sinking pellets. Tankmates: They do well with goldfish, koi and other peaceful fish in ponds and aquariums. Avoid puffers and snail-eating loaches. Good to know: Japanese trapdoor snails are invasive in parts of the U.S., and some states restrict them. Never release snails into the wild, and check local rules before adding them to an outdoor pond that connects to natural waters.

The true golden rabbit snail, or gold rabbit snail, is carefully selected for a solid chocolate shell and clean gold body. Lesser grades are sold as yellow rabbit snails, but who wants a lesser rabbit? These snails are larger than most freshwater aquatic species and are effective scavengers. Quick Facts Scientific Name Tylomelania sp. Origin Sulawesi, Indonesia Care Level Moderate (needs warm water) Temperament Peaceful; may nibble soft plants Adult Size Up to 3–4" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Scavenger (sinking pellets, algae wafers) Water Temperature 76–84°F pH 7.2–8.5 Breeding Livebearer; slowly produces one baby at a time, so it won't overrun the tank Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Rabbit snails come from warm, clean lakes in Sulawesi. Give them a soft sand bottom they can burrow in, warm water (76–84°F) and good water quality. Add calcium if your water is soft. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets and algae wafers daily. Rabbit snails are big eaters and also clean up leftover food. Tankmates: Rabbit snails do well with peaceful fish, shrimp and other snails that like warm water, such as discus and tetras. Avoid puffers, loaches and large cichlids. Good to know: Rabbit snails are slow-moving and gentle, and they wave their long "ear-like" tentacles as they move. Remove snails before using copper or other medications.

The tiger blood snail, or tiger nerite snail, has a distinct wavy pattern on the shell and loves algae. These snails do not harm plants or overrun the aquarium. Nerites only grow to a little less than one inch, so several would be needed for effective algae control in an aquarium of ten gallons or more. Quick Facts Scientific Name Neritina sp. Origin East Africa and Indo-Pacific coastal streams (wild-caught) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful; plant-safe Adult Size Up to 1" Lifespan 1–2+ years Diet Algae eater (also eats algae wafers) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.5 (hard water for healthy shells) Breeding Lays small white eggs on hard surfaces, but they won't hatch in freshwater, so nerites won't overrun the tank Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Nerites do well in most established tanks with algae to graze. Keep the water hard and alkaline for healthy shells, and keep a lid on the tank, since nerites sometimes climb out. If one flips onto its back, turn it over, since some can't right themselves. Feeding: Nerites mostly graze on algae. If the tank is very clean, add algae wafers so they don't go hungry. Tankmates: Nerites get along with peaceful fish, shrimp and other snails. Avoid puffers, loaches and large cichlids, which eat snails, and keep them away from assassin snails. Good to know: Remove snails before treating the tank with copper or other medications, which are toxic to invertebrates.

The racing olive snail, or olive nerite snail, is a scavenger and algae eater and, like all nerites, plant-safe. Nerite snails do not overrun the fish tank and only grow to about one inch at full maturity. Nerites do well in most water conditions except for pH below 7.0. Quick Facts Scientific Name Neritina sp. Mystery snails are hardy and excellent scavengers with a nice, subtle color pattern. Golden mystery snails handle a wide range of water and temperature conditions. Mystery snails are not plant eaters. Be sure to pull out snails and other invertebrates when treating the fish tank for ich and other diseases. All mystery snails from AquariumFish.com come from a breeder in Florida and are free of parasites and disease. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pomacea diffusa (sold as P. bridgesii ) Origin South America (Amazon basin); farm-raised Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful; plant-safe Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 1–2 years Diet Scavenger (algae and leftover food) Water Temperature 68–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 (hard water for healthy shells) Breeding Lays pink egg clutches above the waterline; needs a male and female Shipping Size Approx. ½–¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Give mystery snails a covered tank with a gap of an inch or two above the water, since females climb out to lay eggs. Keep the water hard and alkaline for healthy shells, and add calcium (cuttlebone or crushed coral) if your water is soft. Feeding: Mystery snails eat algae and leftover food, but give them sinking pellets or algae wafers too so they don't go hungry. Tankmates: Mystery snails do well with peaceful fish, shrimp and other snails. Avoid fish that nip antennae or eat snails, like puffers, loaches, large cichlids and some bettas, and keep them away from assassin snails. Good to know: Remove snails before treating the tank with copper or other medications, which are toxic to invertebrates.

The Siberian spiny loach, also called the Siberian tiger loach, is caught in the wild in southern China and Taiwan. Not only is this loach adaptable, thriving on both sides of the Taiwan Strait, but the Siberian spiny loach is also personable and active. This loach does well in the aquarium and will thrive if kept in small groups of three or more. Water temperature needs to be under 80 degrees, however, and the Siberian spiny loach can tolerate temperatures into the high 60s. The loaches will pair up when they reach the adult stage; females are larger, about 4 inches, and males about 3 inches. Like most loaches in the fish tank, they will swim along the bottom and middle zones of the aquarium and feed on food that sank to the bottom. Quick Facts Scientific Name Cobitis sinensis Origin Southern China and Taiwan Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 3–4" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore (bottom feeder) Water Temperature 60–78°F pH 6.5–8.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 2–3" Care Guide Tank setup: These are coldwater loaches that need no heater in most homes. Give them a soft sand bottom for burrowing, smooth rocks, plants and a tight-fitting lid, since they are skilled escape artists. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets or wafers once or twice a day. They scavenge leftover food from the bottom and also enjoy frozen bloodworms. Tankmates: They do well with other peaceful coldwater fish like goldfish, white clouds and other loaches. Avoid tropical fish that need warm water. Good to know: Dojo loaches are sometimes called weather loaches because they become restless when air pressure changes before a storm.

Created by splicing the genes of zebra danios and hi-fin white skirt tetras and tiger barbs with phosphorescent corals and jellyfish, the fish were patented and licensed for sale in the USA several years ago once the FDA determined them to be safe for the environment. Though these fish do not actually glow in the dark, they are truly fluorescent and will keep that bright color throughout their lifespan. When two green glo tetras breed, they actually make green glo babies. Quick Facts Scientific Name Gymnocorymbus ternetzi (genetically modified) Origin Farm-raised (genetically modified) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful (may nip long fins) Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a filter, plants and open swimming space. A dark substrate and background make the colors pop. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: GloFish tetras get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, danios, rasboras, corydoras and livebearers. Keep them in a group so they don't nip the fins of slow, long-finned fish like bettas. Good to know: GloFish colors look brightest under a blue or actinic LED light, but they are colorful under normal lighting too. Mixing colors in one school creates the best display.

A dark substrate and background make the colors pop. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: GloFish tetras get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, danios, rasboras, corydoras and livebearers. Keep them in a group so they don't nip the fins of slow, long-finned fish like bettas. Good to know: GloFish colors look brightest under a blue or actinic LED light, but they are colorful under normal lighting too. Mixing colors in one school creates the best display.

The Asians created GloFish® by splicing the genes of zebra danios and hi-fin white skirt tetras and tiger barbs with phosphorescent corals and jellyfish. The fish were patented and licensed for sale in the USA several years ago once the FDA determined them to be safe for the environment. Though these fish do not actually glow in the dark, they are truly fluorescent and will keep that bright color throughout their lifespan. Quick Facts Scientific Name Danio rerio (genetically modified) Origin Farm-raised (genetically modified) Care Level Very easy, great for beginners Temperament Peaceful, very active Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 64–77°F (often fine without a heater) pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Danios are fast swimmers, so give them open swimming space, a filter, plants around the edges and a tight-fitting lid, since they jump. Make sure the tank is fully cycled (which takes several weeks) before adding fish. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Danios get along with most peaceful community fish, such as tetras, rasboras, barbs, corydoras and livebearers. Their speed can stress slow, long-finned fish like bettas and fancy guppies, and large predatory fish will eat them. Good to know: GloFish colors look brightest under a blue or actinic LED light. Care is the same as for any zebra danio. Danios are fast and jump when startled, so keep a lid on the tank.
