The freshwater bumblebee goby has quite a bit of personality and unusual movement, so it is a great addition to the aquarium. Bumblebee gobies are bottom dwellers and a bit territorial, but easy to keep and feed. Some freshwater gobies, such as the bumblebee and dragon goby, do better with a little salt in the water. Fine for brackish or freshwater tanks. The bumblebee goby looks like a little yellow and black bumblebee and only grows to an inch. Available in a group Quick Facts Scientific Name Brachygobius doriae Origin Malaysia and Indonesia (Borneo, Sumatra) Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful with other fish; territorial with its own kind Adult Size Up to 1–1½" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Carnivore (small meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.5–8.5 Group Size Does best in a group, with plenty of hiding spots Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: These small gobies do best with plenty of caves and hiding spots (small shells and rocks work well) and hard, alkaline water. Many do best with a little marine salt in the water (brackish, specific gravity about 1.002–1.008). Feeding: Feed small amounts once or twice a day. They prefer small frozen foods like brine shrimp and bloodworms, and some will not eat flake reliably. Tankmates: Keep them in a species tank or with other small, peaceful brackish fish such as mollies, glassfish and small livebearers. Avoid larger fish that could eat them. Good to know: These tiny gobies are full of personality and often perch on rocks or glass to watch their surroundings.

Freshwater gobies have quite a bit of personality and unusual movement, so they are a great addition to the aquarium. They are bottom dwellers and a bit territorial, but easy to keep and feed. Stiphodons are a group of smaller gobies that go well with smaller-species fish tanks and planted aquariums. The neon blue stiphodon has a bright, reflective blue horizontal stripe along the body. Quick Facts Scientific Name Stiphodon atropurpureus / S. semoni Origin Indo-Pacific island streams (Indonesia, Philippines, Taiwan) Care Level Moderate (needs clean, oxygen-rich, flowing water) Temperament Peaceful with other fish; males territorial with each other Adult Size Up to 1½–2" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Algae eater Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size One male with several females Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: These gobies come from clear, fast-flowing island streams. Give them a mature tank with strong current, high oxygen, smooth rocks covered in algae and biofilm, and a tight lid, since they can climb out. Feeding: These gobies graze on algae off rocks, so they do best in a mature tank. Also feed algae wafers. They may go hungry in a very clean, new tank. Tankmates: They do well with small, peaceful fish that like cool, flowing water, such as danios, rasboras, hillstream loaches and dwarf shrimp. Males may spar with each other. Good to know: Stream gobies cling to rocks with a sucker formed by their pelvic fins. Their larvae drift to the sea to develop, so they rarely breed in aquariums.

The freshwater aquarium fan dance goby, also known as the knight goby, generally grows to only three inches. The fan dance goby is peaceful and hardy. The nickname "fan dance" comes from the way the fish fans out and displays its fins. For a kids' tank, maybe we should just stick with the other name, knight goby; it's cooler-sounding anyway. Quick Facts Scientific Name Stigmatogobius sadanundio Origin South and Southeast Asia (coastal fresh and brackish waters) Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful with other fish; territorial with its own kind Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.5–8.5 Group Size Does best in a group, with plenty of hiding spots Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: These small gobies do best with plenty of caves and hiding spots (small shells and rocks work well) and hard, alkaline water. Many do best with a little marine salt in the water (brackish, specific gravity about 1.002–1.008). Feeding: Feed small amounts once or twice a day. They prefer small frozen foods like brine shrimp and bloodworms, and some will not eat flake reliably. Tankmates: Keep them in a species tank or with other small, peaceful brackish fish such as mollies, glassfish and small livebearers. Avoid larger fish that could eat them. Good to know: These tiny gobies are full of personality and often perch on rocks or glass to watch their surroundings.

Freshwater aquarium peacock gudgeon gobies are commonly called peacock gudgeons. The peacock goby is a colorful bottom dweller from Papua New Guinea, and males and females both have pleasant red and yellow colors. The peacock goby is hardy and readily available in the aquarium trade, as these freshwater gobies are imported from Asia and pond-raised in Florida. Quick Facts Scientific Name Tateurndina ocellicauda Origin Papua New Guinea; farm-raised Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2½–3" Lifespan 4–6 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.5–7.8 Group Size Pair or small group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a planted tank with caves, driftwood and gentle filtration. They are cave spawners, so small caves or pipes encourage breeding. Feeding: Feed micro pellets or a quality flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with small, peaceful community fish such as tetras, rasboras, rainbowfish and corydoras. They may eat baby shrimp. Good to know: Gudgeons are cave spawners; the male guards the eggs until they hatch.

The freshwater empire goby, or empire gudgeon goby, has dramatic rainbow colors and is wild-caught, and therefore not often seen in the trade. Pictured is an adult male displaying his colors to a female. Females are not as colorful as the males, but the males don't display their color without the female. We recommend the purchase of a pair, one male and one female. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hypseleotris compressa Origin Northern and eastern Australia and southern New Guinea Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 3–4" Lifespan 4–6 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.5–7.8 Group Size Pair or small group Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a planted tank with caves, driftwood and gentle filtration. Good to know: Gudgeons are cave spawners; the male guards the eggs until they hatch.

The freshwater purple spot goby is a bottom dweller and a bit territorial, but easy to keep and feed. The purple spot goby has light reflective purple along the body; males display a bit more color than females. Bushynose plecos are found all over the Amazon basin and are good tankmates, as they eat algae and scavenge uneaten food and only grow to five inches in the fish tank. Though these are plentiful and affordable plecos, they have a very unique appearance. They are also called bristlenose plecos for the antler-like growths at the top of their nose, which get larger and larger as the fish ages. Quick Facts Scientific Name Ancistrus sp. Origin Amazon basin (wild form); aquarium-bred Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful (males guard caves) Adult Size Up to 5" Lifespan 10–12 years Diet Herbivore (algae and plant-based foods) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single, pair or group with a cave each Shipping Size Small: 1" · Medium: 2–3" · Large: 3–4" Care Guide Tank setup: Bristlenose plecos do well in most community tanks. Give them driftwood to rasp on, caves or hiding spots, and good filtration. They keep glass, rocks and plants clean of algae. Feeding: They graze on algae, but also feed algae wafers. Tankmates: Bristlenose plecos get along with nearly all community fish, plus shrimp and snails. Avoid large aggressive fish that might harass them. Good to know: Males grow larger, bushier "bristles" on the snout than females. Bristlenose plecos stay small and are one of the best algae-eaters for home aquariums.

Bushynose plecos, also called bristlenose plecos, grow fascinating small branches at the end of their nose, which get larger and larger as they grow to their full body length of 5 inches. At that point, the branching can extend to more than an inch. Males feature more branches than females. The bred albino bushynose plecos will not grow quite as large as their wild brown counterparts, but these aquarium catfish feature the same unique branching in eye-popping pink. The off-white body and flowing fins of the L-144 long fin albino bushynose pleco are a beautiful contrast to the darker, muted colors usually associated with bottom dwellers. These catfish are bred for this pattern and are not available in the wild. These fish only grow to 4 inches and will do well with other species except aggressive predators. Plecostomus are a specialty of AquariumFish.com. These catfish originate in South America, and many colors, sizes and patterns can be found; so many that common names often aren’t enough to identify one pleco from another, so in 1988 a tropical fish magazine in Germany called DATZ assigned “L” numbers to distinguish species. Though not exactly scientific, the system works. We carry a couple of plecos that have not been assigned their L number, but the Germans are a cautious folk, and we are sure they will get around to it in a precise and correct manner. Medium size is 2” to 3”. Most plecos do better with a little driftwood in the tank. In full disclosure, even the fishmongers have trouble telling the clown pleco from the candy stripe pleco (candy stripe plecos should have narrower orange bands). Often one is sent instead of the other, but both plecos are gentle, attractive scavengers that go well in planted aquariums and community aquariums. These fish live a long time and do not outgrow even a small aquarium tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name Peckoltia vittata (L-015 / L-135) Origin Amazon basin, Brazil Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Peaceful (territorial with other plecos) Adult Size Up to 4" Lifespan 10–12+ years Diet Omnivore (sinking foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single, or several with a cave each Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them caves, driftwood and good filtration with some current. A sand or smooth gravel bottom suits them best. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets or wafers, ideally in the evening when they are most active. They also enjoy frozen bloodworms. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish. Give each pleco its own cave to limit territorial squabbles. Good to know: These plecos are most active at night; dim lighting and caves help them feel secure.

Plecostomus are a specialty of AquariumFish.com. Though not exactly scientific, the system works. We carry a couple of plecos that have not been assigned their L number, but the Germans are a cautious folk, and we are sure they will get around to it in a precise and correct manner. Medium size is 2” to 3”. Most plecos do better with a little driftwood in the tank. The clown pleco has an orange stripe pattern to earn the name. These little catfish are not scary clowns; the species is compatible with pretty much all other fish in the aquarium, except those that can eat them. One advantage of the clown pleco is that it will not outgrow even a small aquarium. Quick Facts Scientific Name Panaqolus maccus (L-104) Origin Orinoco basin (Venezuela and Colombia) Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Peaceful (territorial with other plecos) Adult Size Up to 3½–4" Lifespan 10–12+ years Diet Herbivore (driftwood, algae wafers) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single, or several with a cave each Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: These small plecos rasp and digest wood, so driftwood is essential, not just decoration. Give them caves, driftwood and good filtration, since wood-eaters produce a lot of waste. Feeding: Feed algae wafers and sinking pellets, and always keep driftwood in the tank, since they rasp on it as part of their diet. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish. Keep only one per cave, since plecos can be territorial with each other. Good to know: Wood-eating plecos produce fine "wood dust" waste, which is normal.

Butterfly plecos have a flatter profile and wide ventral fins with bright colors, like butterfly wings. These plecos require veggies like algae wafers and scavenge. The color pattern is broad, distinct lines. A sand or smooth gravel bottom suits them best. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets or wafers, ideally in the evening when they are most active. They also enjoy frozen bloodworms. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish. Give each pleco its own cave to limit territorial squabbles. The green phantom pleco is found in a separate region and developed a greenish-yellow body, as opposed to the blue body of the related blue phantom pleco. Another reason to thank the Germans for the invention of the L numbers. These fish are good scavengers and good tank mates. They do need veggies if not present in the prepared foods, though community prepared foods have a veggie component, or should (check the ingredients!). Also, these plecos are more comfortable with some driftwood to hang onto. Quick Facts Scientific Name Baryancistrus demantoides (L-200) Origin Orinoco basin, Venezuela Care Level Moderate (needs warm, oxygen-rich water) Temperament Peaceful (territorial with other plecos) Adult Size Up to 6–8" Lifespan 12–15+ years Diet Omnivore (algae and sinking foods) Water Temperature 78–84°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single, or several with a cave each Shipping Size Medium: approx. 3" · Large: approx. 5" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them strong current, high oxygen, smooth rocks, caves and driftwood. Many come from warm, fast rivers in Brazil, so keep the water clean and warm. Feeding: Feed algae wafers and quality sinking pellets. They also enjoy frozen foods now and then. Tankmates: They do well with most community fish and peaceful cichlids. Give each pleco its own cave to limit territorial squabbles. Good to know: Many of these plecos come from fast-flowing rivers threatened by dam projects, so wild-caught specimens are increasingly rare.

The L-128 blue phantom pleco is truly blue; not saltwater-fish blue, but genuinely freshwater-fish subtle blue. These fish are related to the L-200 green phantom pleco but are found in different regions and have a distinct color pattern. These exotic species do need some type of veggies in their diet if algae is not present; a little slice of cucumber would do. Like most plecos, driftwood helps them acclimate to the fish tank. Tiger plecos are not ferocious, but they do have a tiger pattern. These plecos are similar in pattern to butterfly plecos but with a higher body profile. Tiger plecos are scavengers, hardy, and do most of their scavenging at night, just like real tigers. Except they don't eat people, or fish. Based on where the fish is caught, the color pattern may vary from straight vertical broad lines to an almost marble pattern. Quick Facts Scientific Name Peckoltia sp. (L-069) Origin Venezuela Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Peaceful (territorial with other plecos) Adult Size Up to 5–6" Lifespan 10–12+ years Diet Omnivore (sinking foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single, or several with a cave each Shipping Size Approx. 3" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them caves, driftwood and good filtration with some current. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish. Give each pleco its own cave to limit territorial squabbles. Also known as the imperial king tiger pleco, the gypsy king pleco has very thin, deep black lines and a grey to white body. These fish have a pattern contrast that is almost as strong as the L-46 true zebra pleco, but with lots more lines. The gypsy king pleco requires very clean water and driftwood. They are omnivorous, but it is a good idea to treat them with cucumber or good-quality algae wafers. These plecos come from the Brazilian Amazon basin and are rarely seen. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hypancistrus sp. (L-066) Origin Rio Xingu, Brazil Care Level Moderate (needs clean, warm, oxygen-rich water) Temperament Peaceful (shy; territorial with other plecos) Adult Size Up to 5–6" Lifespan 10–15+ years Diet Omnivore (meaty sinking foods) Water Temperature 78–86°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single, or several with a cave each Shipping Size Approx. 4" Care Guide Tank setup: These plecos come from warm, fast, clear rivers. Give them a tank with strong current, high oxygen, very clean water, rocky caves (or pleco caves) and a sand or smooth gravel bottom. Feeding: Feed meaty sinking foods like quality carnivore pellets, ideally in the evening when they are most active. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They do well with peaceful fish that like warm water, such as tetras, rasboras, discus and dwarf cichlids. Avoid boisterous tankmates that outcompete them for food, and give each pleco its own cave. Good to know: These plecos are nocturnal and shy; a cave and dim lighting help them feel secure. Many are wild-caught and slow-growing.

The L-201 inspector pleco is also known as the L-102 inspector pleco, or the snowball pleco. Sometimes these plecos are confused by collectors in the wild with the L-48 and vice versa, but the inspector plecos have darker bodies and larger spots and do not grow quite as large as the L-48 mustard spot plecos. The snowball pleco has a deep black body and bold white, sometimes yellowish, large dots on the body. They are great scavengers and only grow to five inches, so these are great additions to most freshwater fish tanks. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hypancistrus inspector / H. contradens (L-102 / L-201) Origin Rio Negro and Casiquiare (Venezuela, Brazil) Care Level Moderate (needs clean, warm, oxygen-rich water) Temperament Peaceful (shy; territorial with other plecos) Adult Size Up to 5–6" Lifespan 10–15+ years Diet Omnivore (meaty sinking foods) Water Temperature 78–86°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single, or several with a cave each Shipping Size Approx. 3" Care Guide Tank setup: These plecos come from warm, fast, clear rivers. Give them a tank with strong current, high oxygen, very clean water, rocky caves (or pleco caves) and a sand or smooth gravel bottom. Feeding: Feed meaty sinking foods like quality carnivore pellets, ideally in the evening when they are most active. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They do well with peaceful fish that like warm water, such as tetras, rasboras, discus and dwarf cichlids. Avoid boisterous tankmates that outcompete them for food, and give each pleco its own cave. Good to know: These plecos are nocturnal and shy; a cave and dim lighting help them feel secure. Many are wild-caught and slow-growing.

The ranger pleco is a wild-caught species from Peru. These plecos only grow to about one and a half inches and look like they were hit by a shrink machine. Caution, though: the fishermen do not discriminate when they catch these small catfish. Often several babies of other exotic Peruvian plecos, including the grand ranger, are caught and shipped with these fish. We do our best to separate them, but be prepared to have a surprise after a year or two. L number unassigned Quick Facts Scientific Name Undescribed loricariid (no L-number) Origin Peru (wild-caught) Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Peaceful (territorial with other plecos) Adult Size Up to 1½" Lifespan 10–12+ years Diet Omnivore (sinking foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single, or several with a cave each Shipping Size Approx. ½–¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them caves, driftwood and good filtration with some current. A sand or smooth gravel bottom suits them best. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets or wafers, ideally in the evening when they are most active. They also enjoy frozen bloodworms. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish. Give each pleco its own cave to limit territorial squabbles. Good to know: These plecos are most active at night; dim lighting and caves help them feel secure.

The L-46 zebra pleco was once very common in the aquarium trade, but after much of its native habitat was affected by dams in Brazil, export of wild L-46 plecos from Brazil was banned. The black and white contrast is what makes this pleco so remarkable. The L-46 zebra pleco is nocturnal and will try to hide during the day. AquariumFish.com sells legal captive-bred specimens. These are generally small and grow slowly. These fish require absolutely clean water, so please know what you are doing before you make a purchase. People have been known to buy one, put it in the aquarium and never see it again. Lost in the filter? The true Rio de Para pleco is rare and may be the most exceptionally colored pleco on the market. It is also called the L-75 leopard pleco, and when they are caught by our Colombian exporter, it is a treat. These plecos are bright yellow and gold with a leopard spot pattern on the dorsal fin and broad lines and spots all over the body. Typically caught at three inches, many come in at five and six inches. All are gentle scavengers and very hardy. At two to three inches the pattern is not as exciting as it will be when they get to four to five inches, but the pattern is still there. Quick Facts Scientific Name Peckoltia sabaji (L-075) Origin Amazon, Orinoco and Essequibo basins (Brazil, Venezuela, Guyana) Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Peaceful (territorial with other plecos) Adult Size Up to 6–7" Lifespan 10–12+ years Diet Omnivore (sinking foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single, or several with a cave each Shipping Size Medium: approx. 2" · X-Large: 7–8" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them caves, driftwood and good filtration with some current. A sand or smooth gravel bottom suits them best. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets or wafers, ideally in the evening when they are most active. They also enjoy frozen bloodworms. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish. Give each pleco its own cave to limit territorial squabbles. Good to know: These plecos are most active at night; dim lighting and caves help them feel secure.

Royal plecos earn their name for their beautiful gold and green color patterns and the large crown-shaped body pattern. These were some of the first exotic plecos exported to the trade, and so they got first dibs on this grand "common" name (pardon the oxymoron). Variations of the royal pleco include the L-191 pleco, which is the same species but with fewer spots and more lines; hence it is referred to as the broken line pleco. Watermelon royal plecos, also called L-330 gold royals, again the same species, develop rounder heads and shorter tails in the wild, hence the "watermelon" shape. All royal plecos are gentle giants that grow to a stunning show-quality 12 to 16 inches in the aquarium. Royal plecos are hardy scavengers and should be kept with a piece of driftwood for their home base. Quick Facts Scientific Name Panaque nigrolineatus (L-190) Origin Orinoco basin (Colombia and Venezuela) Care Level Moderate (grows large) Temperament Peaceful (territorial with other plecos) Adult Size Up to 12–16" Lifespan 15–20+ years Diet Herbivore (driftwood, algae wafers) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 3" Care Guide Tank setup: Royal-type plecos eat wood, so give them plenty of driftwood, strong filtration and caves. They produce a lot of waste, so good filtration is important. Feeding: Feed algae wafers and sinking pellets, and keep plenty of driftwood in the tank for them to rasp, since wood is part of their diet. Tankmates: They do well with medium to large community fish and cichlids. Keep one per tank unless the tank is very large, since they are territorial with other plecos. Good to know: Royal-type plecos are among the few fish that can actually digest wood. Plan for an adult-size tank before buying.

The monk goby lives in freshwater as an adult, but its larvae drift to brackish and salt water. It was originally discovered and classified in southern Japan by the great ichthyologist Shigeho Tanaka in 1909. Unfortunately this goby is so rare in the aquarium trade that a lot more is written about Dr. Tanaka (who lived 96 years, proof that ichthyology extends your life) than about the monk goby. Also called the grazing goby, these gobies eat lots of algae and will eat film algae on glass and rocks in the aquarium. Since these fish need veggies, we suggest dropping a couple of algae wafers in the tank each week. Quick Facts Scientific Name Sicyopterus japonicus Origin Japan and Taiwan Care Level Moderate (needs clean, oxygen-rich, flowing water) Temperament Peaceful with other fish; males territorial with each other Adult Size Up to 5" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Algae eater Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size One male with several females Shipping Size Approx. 4" Care Guide Tank setup: These gobies come from clear, fast-flowing island streams. Give them a mature tank with strong current, high oxygen, smooth rocks covered in algae and biofilm, and a tight lid, since they can climb out. Feeding: These gobies graze on algae off rocks, so they do best in a mature tank. Also feed algae wafers. They may go hungry in a very clean, new tank. Tankmates: They do well with small, peaceful fish that like cool, flowing water, such as danios, rasboras, hillstream loaches and dwarf shrimp. Males may spar with each other. Good to know: Stream gobies cling to rocks with a sucker formed by their pelvic fins. Their larvae drift to the sea to develop, so they rarely breed in aquariums.

The leopard frog pleco is collected in the middle Amazon basin. These are rare aquarium fish and at first sight look like a false zebra pleco, but their dorsal fins truly have magnificent coloration, and the pattern is much more distinct. The color pattern is rich and clear, and the lines are broader. Look for bright yellow to cream, depending on where the fish was caught. This fish is a collector's dream. Quick Facts Scientific Name Peckoltia compta (L-134) Origin Rio Tapajós, Brazil Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Peaceful (territorial with other plecos) Adult Size Up to 4" Lifespan 10–12+ years Diet Omnivore (sinking foods) Water Temperature 78–84°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single, or several with a cave each Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them caves, driftwood and good filtration with some current. A sand or smooth gravel bottom suits them best. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets or wafers, ideally in the evening when they are most active. They also enjoy frozen bloodworms. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish. Give each pleco its own cave to limit territorial squabbles. Good to know: These plecos are most active at night; dim lighting and caves help them feel secure.

The L-129 false zebra pleco, compared to the L-127 false zebra pleco, has a more distinct color pattern and is an even better substitute for the sensitive and overpriced L-46 Brazilian zebra pleco. Both these fish are collected in the Orinoco basin, and the color pattern determines which L number they are assigned. Many are wild-caught and slow-growing.

Plecostomus are a specialty of AquariumFish.com. These catfish originate in South America, and many colors, sizes and patterns can be found; so many that common names often aren’t enough to identify one pleco from another, so in 1988 a tropical fish magazine in Germany called DATZ assigned “L” numbers to distinguish species. Though not exactly scientific, the system works. We carry a couple of plecos that have not been assigned their L number, but the Germans are a cautious folk, and we are sure they will get around to it in a precise and correct manner. Medium size is 2” to 3”. Most plecos do better with a little driftwood in the tank. The L-127 false zebra pleco is a good alternative to the L-46 true zebra pleco, since these fish are one-tenth the price and still feature a very attractive color pattern. Our L-127 plecos are wild-caught under sustainable practices in Colombia. The pattern on the L-127 pleco is slightly more mottled than the similar L-129 pleco. (L-127) Origin Orinoco basin (Colombia, Venezuela) Care Level Moderate (needs clean, warm, oxygen-rich water) Temperament Peaceful (shy; territorial with other plecos) Adult Size Up to 5–6" Lifespan 10–15+ years Diet Omnivore (meaty sinking foods) Water Temperature 78–86°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single, or several with a cave each Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: These plecos come from warm, fast, clear rivers. Avoid boisterous tankmates that outcompete them for food, and give each pleco its own cave. Good to know: These plecos are nocturnal and shy; a cave and dim lighting help them feel secure. Many are wild-caught and slow-growing.

South American exporters love this pleco and export quite a few to Europe and Asia. The pleco is expensive, however, and not as popular in America. Perhaps the bright fringe colors on the dorsal fin are just too small for American tastes, but the fish truly has subtle beauty. These catfish grow large but do not outgrow a medium-size aquarium and fit right in a large tank. These plecos are hardy scavengers that like to hang on driftwood. Quick Facts Scientific Name Leporacanthicus triactis (L-091) Origin Orinoco basin, Venezuela Care Level Moderate (needs warm, oxygen-rich water) Temperament Peaceful with fish; territorial with other plecos Adult Size Up to 8–10" Lifespan 12–15+ years Diet Omnivore (sinking foods) Water Temperature 78–84°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single, or several with a cave each Shipping Size Medium: 2–3" · Large: 6–7" (pattern shows at about 3") Care Guide Tank setup: Give them strong current, high oxygen, rocky caves and driftwood. Keep the water warm and very clean, since they produce a lot of waste on a meaty diet. Feeding: Feed meaty sinking foods like carnivore pellets. They also enjoy frozen foods like shrimp and bloodworms. Tankmates: They do well with most community fish and cichlids of similar size. They may eat very small fish or shrimp. Give each pleco its own cave. Good to know: These plecos have strong, toothed mouths and prefer meaty foods; they usually leave plants alone.

The megaclown pleco from the Orinoco basin in Venezuela is very similar to the gold zebra pleco of Brazil. These plecos have a pattern like the L-46 zebra pleco, with gold lines instead of bright white lines. Megaclown plecos are a superior grade to the common clown pleco, so maybe that is where the common name originated. Many are wild-caught and slow-growing.

The L-160 is a rare pleco, seldom found since the expansion of the hydroelectric power program in Brazil. These plecos are hardy omnivores and should be kept with a piece of driftwood. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pseudacanthicus sp. (L-160) Origin Brazil Care Level Moderate (grows large) Temperament Peaceful with fish; territorial with other plecos Adult Size Up to 10–12" Lifespan 15–20 years Diet Omnivore (sinking foods) Water Temperature 78–84°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Medium: approx. 3" · Show: approx. 10" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them strong current, high oxygen, large caves and driftwood, and keep the water warm and very clean. Feeding: Feed meaty sinking foods like carnivore pellets. They also enjoy frozen foods like shrimp and bloodworms. Tankmates: They do well with medium to large community fish and cichlids. They may eat very small fish or shrimp, and they are territorial with other plecos. Good to know: Cactus plecos get more colorful as they mature and can live for decades with good care.

The rhino plecostomus, sometimes called the alligator pleco, does not need an L number. Only this pleco has such a distinct little horn above each nostril and a massive dorsal fin. Solid chocolate and covered with ridges, this pleco looks prehistoric. These plecos are very hardy and suitable for aggressive and community tanks but will disturb plants. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pterygoplichthys scrophus Origin Upper Amazon (Peru, Brazil) Care Level Easy (but grows very large) Temperament Peaceful (can be territorial as adults) Adult Size Up to 12–16" Lifespan 15–20 years Diet Omnivore (algae and sinking foods) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 6.5–7.8 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 3½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them driftwood and strong filtration. They may uproot or eat soft plants. Feeding: Feed algae wafers and sinking pellets daily. Don't rely on tank algae alone, especially as they grow. Tankmates: They get along with most medium to large fish, including cichlids and goldfish. Avoid keeping two large plecos in the same tank. Good to know: These plecos grow quickly. Never release one into the wild; they are invasive in Florida, Texas and other warm regions.

The L-83 marble sailfin pleco has a muted marble and spotted pattern and a large dorsal fin. These plecos grow big and may outgrow the fish tank and can disturb planted tanks, but they are hardy and peaceful scavengers. They may uproot or eat soft plants. Feeding: Feed algae wafers and sinking pellets daily. Don't rely on tank algae alone, especially as they grow. Tankmates: They get along with most medium to large fish, including cichlids and goldfish. Avoid keeping two large plecos in the same tank. Good to know: These plecos grow quickly. Never release one into the wild; they are invasive in Florida, Texas and other warm regions.

Sailfin plecos are named for their giant dorsal fin. Their pattern is a muted marble or spotted, and the L-83 has a marble pattern. These plecos grow very big and live a long time. Adaptable and hardy, they get along with all other fish but can outgrow a small aquarium. Because these fish grow large and have a big dorsal fin, the albino variation is striking. These catfish originate in South America, and many colors, sizes and patterns can be found; so many that common names often aren’t enough to identify one pleco from another, so in 1988 a tropical fish magazine in Germany called DATZ assigned “L” numbers to distinguish species. Though not exactly scientific, the system works. We carry a couple of plecos that have not been assigned their L number, but the Germans are a cautious folk, and we are sure they will get around to it in a precise and correct manner. Medium size is 2” to 3”. Most plecos do better with a little driftwood in the tank. The red lizard pleco is a great catfish for nano tanks and will not even disturb larger fancy shrimp. The rust-red color stands out against green plants. The pleco only grows to 3 inches. Quick Facts Scientific Name Rineloricaria sp. (L-010A) Origin Peru (wild form); mostly captive-bred Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 4–5" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore (sinking foods) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 1–2" Care Guide Tank setup: Whiptail and lizard plecos prefer a sand bottom, plants and driftwood with gentle to moderate current. They are peaceful and suit planted community tanks. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets and algae wafers, ideally in the evening. They also enjoy frozen bloodworms. Tankmates: They get along with peaceful community fish, plus shrimp and snails. Avoid fin-nippers and aggressive bottom dwellers. Good to know: Whiptail males guard eggs laid on flat surfaces and develop bristles on their heads when breeding.

The rubberlip pleco is often seen cleaning the side of the aquarium with its broad mouth, which features oversized lips. Rubberlip plecos are voracious algae eaters and are compatible with all freshwater species. These plecos only grow to four inches in the aquarium, maybe six inches in the wild. Quick Facts Scientific Name Chaetostoma sp. (L-146) Origin Andean streams of Colombia Care Level Moderate (needs cool, fast, oxygen-rich water) Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 4–6" Lifespan 8–12 years Diet Algae eater (also eats algae wafers) Water Temperature 68–77°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Rubberlip plecos come from cool, fast mountain streams. Give them a tank with strong current, high oxygen, smooth rocks covered in algae and cooler water (68–77°F). They do poorly in warm, still tanks. Feeding: They graze on algae. Also feed algae wafers. Tankmates: They do well with peaceful fish that like cooler, flowing water, such as danios, white clouds and hillstream loaches. Good to know: Rubberlip plecos hold onto rocks in fast water with their broad sucker mouth.

The spotted rubberlip is a close cousin of the rubberlip pleco and may be crossbred, but in the wild these plecos are generally found in separate groups. Spotted rubberlip plecos have the same body shape as the common rubberlip but feature a light spotted pattern and are often called albino rubberlips by the fishermen, though they are not true albinos. These plecos are similar in behavior too: great scavengers, somewhat shy and good tank mates. Quick Facts Scientific Name Chaetostoma sp. (L-187A) Origin Andean streams of Colombia Care Level Moderate (needs cool, fast, oxygen-rich water) Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 4–5" Lifespan 8–12 years Diet Algae eater (also eats algae wafers) Water Temperature 68–77°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Rubberlip plecos come from cool, fast mountain streams. Give them a tank with strong current, high oxygen, smooth rocks covered in algae and cooler water (68–77°F). They do poorly in warm, still tanks. Feeding: They graze on algae. Also feed algae wafers. Tankmates: They do well with peaceful fish that like cooler, flowing water, such as danios, white clouds and hillstream loaches. Good to know: Rubberlip plecos hold onto rocks in fast water with their broad sucker mouth.

The L-257 tigrinnis pleco is tough to find and a bit pricey, but the markings are so unique and this fish is so long-lived that the fish is worth the price. These fish only grow to six inches and do better with driftwood and a hiding place. These plecos are scavengers and meat eaters. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pseudolithoxus tigris (L-257) Origin Orinoco and Casiquiare basins (Venezuela, Colombia) Care Level Moderate (needs warm, oxygen-rich water) Temperament Peaceful with fish; territorial with other plecos Adult Size Up to 5–6" Lifespan 12–15+ years Diet Omnivore (sinking foods) Water Temperature 78–84°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single, or several with a cave each Shipping Size Approx. 3" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them strong current, high oxygen, rocky caves and driftwood. Keep the water warm and very clean, since they produce a lot of waste on a meaty diet. Feeding: Feed meaty sinking foods like carnivore pellets. They also enjoy frozen foods like shrimp and bloodworms. Tankmates: They do well with most community fish and cichlids of similar size. They may eat very small fish or shrimp. Give each pleco its own cave. Good to know: These plecos have strong, toothed mouths and prefer meaty foods; they usually leave plants alone.

This South American Oddball is a hardy, large, schooling fish with a beautiful pink tail. It is perfect for large tanks. These wild South American fish are a schooling fish that many feel belong to the tetra family, and though expensive, the pink tail chalceus does live long and will be gentle with other pet fish, except small species. These fish are predators and will eat small neons and similar species. These are great fish to add to larger species tanks and cichlid tanks. Quick Facts Scientific Name Chalceus macrolepidotus Origin Amazon basin, South America Care Level Easy Temperament Semi-aggressive (eats small fish) Adult Size Up to 10" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 5" Care Guide Tank setup: Chalceus are fast, active swimmers and strong jumpers. Give them open swimming space, good filtration and a tight-fitting lid. Feeding: Feed a quality pellet or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like shrimp and bloodworms. Tankmates: They are peaceful with fish their size but will eat small fish like neon tetras. Keep them with larger fish and cichlids. Good to know: Pink tail chalceus have large, shiny scales and a bright pink tail that stands out in a group.

The Red Hook Metynnis, or simply the redhook or redhook silver dollar, is a member of the silver dollar family with a bright red anal fin - the red hook. Redhooks are schooling fish collected from the Amazon basin region of Colombia. These are hardy and adaptable fish that create a beautiful sight with other larger fish in the tank. Redhooks eat flakes and pellets. Quick Facts Scientific Name Myloplus rubripinnis Origin Amazon basin, South America Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 8" Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Herbivore (plant-based foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 3–4" Care Guide Tank setup: Silver dollars are active schooling fish. Give them open swimming space, a tight lid and sturdy or artificial plants, since they eat soft plants. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or pellet with vegetable content once or twice a day. They also enjoy vegetable foods like peas. Tankmates: They are peaceful and get along with other medium to large fish such as larger tetras, plecos, parrots and peaceful cichlids. Good to know: The red "hook" on the bottom fin is brightest on mature males.

Freshwater barracudas are small freshwater predators collected in the Amazon basin of Colombia. Also called the red tail barracuda, these monster fish only grow to eight inches, so they are quite suitable predators for the aquarium. Red tail barracudas have no relation to the salt water version other than they are sleek, fast, and have teeth. A source of ghost shrimp, small feeder guppies, small goldfish or similar food will sustain these guys. The color on the tail varies from yellow to red, depending upon the region from which it is caught. Quick Facts Scientific Name Acestrorhynchus falcatus Origin Amazon and Orinoco basins, South America Care Level Moderate Temperament Predatory Adult Size Up to 8–10" Lifespan 10–12 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 6" Care Guide Tank setup: Gars are fast, long-bodied predators. Give them open swimming space, strong filtration and a heavy, tight lid. Feeding: Feed meaty foods like frozen shrimp and fish, plus floating carnivore pellets once they learn to take them. Tankmates: They will eat any fish that fits in their mouth. Keep them only with large, robust fish. Good to know: Freshwater barracudas are fast, sleek hunters with sharp teeth, and their tail color ranges from yellow to red.

AquariumFish.com offers one of the scariest-looking fish from the Amazon, also called the vampire tetra for the way they wait, hanging vampire-like, for their prey, or the payara, for something we are trying to figure out (if you know, please let us know). Saber-tooth tetras are strong predators and will grow to 20 inches. These predator tetras require live food such as feeder guppies and ghost shrimp. Even at the smaller three-inch size, the sharp teeth are visible. Small feeder white clouds or small feeder guppies are best for small payara, larger fish can handle larger feeders, and these fish may adapt to frozen food, but not always. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hydrolycus scomberoides Origin Amazon basin (Peru, Brazil) Care Level Difficult Temperament Predatory; eats smaller fish Adult Size Up to 18–20" Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Carnivore (eats smaller fish) Water Temperature 76–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Usually kept singly Shipping Size Small: approx. 2" · Medium: approx. 3" · Large: approx. 6" Care Guide Tank setup: These are large, fast predators that need powerful filtration, strong current, high oxygen and a heavy, tight lid. They are skittish, so avoid sudden movements and bright lights. Feeding: Young fish may need meaty foods at first, and many can be trained to take frozen foods and pellets. Avoid feeder goldfish, which can carry disease. Tankmates: Keep them only with large, robust fish too big to swallow, such as large catfish, arowanas and big cichlids. Good to know: These fish have long, saber-like teeth and are popular with monster-fish keepers, but they grow very large and need experienced care.

The bucktooth tetra, or simply exodon, should be kept in a small school with larger aggressive species. In the wild this fish likes to school around the teeth of larger piranhas and pick at the meat in their teeth. The bucktooth tetra, or exodon tetra, will eat smaller, less aggressive fish. These are one of the few tetras with visible teeth. Quick Facts Scientific Name Exodon paradoxus Origin Amazon and Tocantins basins (Brazil, Guyana) Care Level Moderate (species tank only) Temperament Very aggressive (scale-eater; attacks other fish) Adult Size Up to 5–6" Lifespan 5–10 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1½–2" Care Guide Tank setup: These are larger, active schooling fish, so give them open swimming space, plants or driftwood along the back and a tight-fitting lid, since they jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They do well with other active, similar-size fish such as larger tetras, barbs, rainbowfish, peaceful cichlids, corydoras and plecos. Very small fish may be eaten or bullied. Good to know: Larger tetras are hardy and long-lived, and a big school makes a striking display.

AquariumFish offers the most peaceful puffer on the planet. Also called the bumblebee puffer, the Amazon pufferfish handles brackish and totally fresh water, and gets along with nearly everybody. Small snails may disagree with the previous statement since bumblebee puffers eat them. These puffers are seasonal and right now they are coming in at only one inch and feeding on live and frozen blood worms or black worms. Quick Facts Scientific Name Colomesus asellus Origin Amazon basin, South America Care Level Moderate Temperament Semi-aggressive (may nip) Adult Size Up to 3–4" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods, snails) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Amazon puffers are active swimmers and true freshwater fish. Give them plants, open swimming space and good filtration, since puffers are messy eaters. Feeding: Puffers need meaty foods and usually won't eat flake. Feed frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp once a day. They also enjoy small snails, which help keep their teeth trimmed. Tankmates: Amazon puffers are among the calmest puffers and do well in a group of their own kind, or with fast fish that won't get nipped. Snails and shrimp will be eaten. Good to know: Amazon puffers are always on the move and often swim together like a small school.

The spotted headstander hovers upside down midway in the water looking for food on the floor of the tank. Headstanders are common in small streams and ponds of the Amazon basin. When food is spotted, the headstander bobs down for a bite. Such an obvious way to look for food; it is surprising few fish demonstrate this feeding habit! Headstander fish are gentle, require clean water, and frozen or live black worms and sinking pellets. In the wild these are schooling fish and do best in small groups. Water temperature should be about 80 degrees. Headstanders are common in small streams and ponds of the Amazon basin. Quick Facts Scientific Name Chilodus punctatus Origin Amazon basin, South America Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 3–4" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants, driftwood and a tight lid, since they can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or pellet with vegetable content once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Spotted headstanders are gentle and get along with peaceful community fish such as tetras, pencilfish and corydoras. Good to know: Spotted headstanders hang head-down in the water, then bob down to pick at food.

Aquarium Fish Sale offers this nicely patterned and rare knifefish once every few months. Do not get alarmed when the banded knifefish is seen unmoving on the bottom of the tank. These knifefish tend to sleep on their sides like cows in a pasture during the day. But come evening, these are very active in the aquarium and make a beautiful sight with their zebra-striped, elongated body. Like other knife fish, the banded knifefish, or zebra knifefish, uses electrolocation to hunt for prey along the bed of the aquarium. Wild knife fish prefer live black worms but will accept frozen. Only fish small enough to fit in their mouth pose a problem. Quick Facts Scientific Name Gymnotus carapo Origin South America Care Level Easy Temperament Semi-aggressive (eats small fish) Adult Size Up to 18–24" Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 8" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them hiding places like large tubes or caves, dim lighting, strong filtration and a tight lid. They are most active at night. Feeding: Feed meaty foods like frozen shrimp and bloodworms, plus sinking carnivore pellets once they learn to take them. Tankmates: Banded knifefish will eat small fish and may fight with other knifefish. Keep them with robust fish too large to swallow. Good to know: Knifefish sense their surroundings with a weak electric field, which helps them hunt in the dark.

AquariumFish offers this unusually shaped long-snouted knife fish – and do not get alarmed when it is seen unmoving on the bottom of the tank. They tend to sleep on their sides. The trumpet knife, or ossa knife, is wild-caught in Peru and prefers live black worms and similar treats, and feeds primarily at night. These knife fish live a long time, are docile, and have a very nice, fine marble pattern. Quick Facts Scientific Name Rhamphichthys rostratus Origin Amazon basin, South America Care Level Difficult Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2 feet or more Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Carnivore (small meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 8–10" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a soft sand bottom they can burrow into, plants, dim lighting and a tight lid. They are most active at night. Feeding: Feed small frozen foods like bloodworms in the evening. They use their long snout to pick food from the sand. Tankmates: They are peaceful and gentle. Keep them with calm fish that won't outcompete them for food. Good to know: Trumpet knifefish often rest on their side on the bottom, which is normal.

Aquarium Fish Sale offers the only knife fish that is tank raised for the trade. Fortunately, the black ghost knife is also the most popular knife fish for aquariums. In the wild, native fishermen once believed that the spirits of dead fish reside in the Black Ghost, hence the name. These fish grow very slowly and generally eat at night. Frozen foods or live small worms are preferred. Quick Facts Scientific Name Apteronotus albifrons Origin Amazon basin, South America Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful (eats very small fish) Adult Size Up to 18–20" Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 3–8" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them hiding places like large tubes or caves, dim lighting, strong filtration and a tight lid. They are most active at night. Feeding: Feed frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp once a day, ideally in the evening. Many learn to take sinking pellets. Tankmates: They are peaceful but will eat very small fish. Keep them with calm fish too large to fit in their mouth, and only one knifefish per tank. Good to know: Knifefish sense their surroundings with a weak electric field, which helps them hunt in the dark.

The Transparent knifefish, or simply the Glass knifefish, loves live black worms, but the species will adapt to frozen foods. In the fish tank, these are marvelous creatures with unique movement. Knifefish are fragile to ship, and please transition slowly to the aquarium; they are sensitive to sudden pH and temperature changes. Please ensure the aquarium is at least 30 gallons. These fish are more active at night, but will use their electrolocation powers to scavenge for food during the day. Quick Facts Scientific Name Eigenmannia virescens Origin South America Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 8–12" Lifespan 10–12 years Diet Carnivore (small meaty foods) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 3–4" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants, driftwood and tubes or caves to hide in, plus dim lighting. They are most active at night. Feeding: Feed frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp once a day. Some learn to take sinking pellets. Tankmates: They are shy and peaceful, so keep them with calm community fish too large to fit in their mouth. Good to know: Glass knifefish are see-through and do well in a small group, where they hover together.

The ruby red pencilfish, or coral red pencilfish, ranks up there with the rare espei pencilfish as one of the holy grails among pencilfish enthusiasts. Common pencilfish are generally grouped with tetras, since they share similar size and schooling characteristics. Ruby reds display a deep, deep red color and are only found in a few protected tributaries of the Peruvian Amazon basin. Quick Facts Scientific Name Nannostomus mortenthaleri Origin Peruvian Amazon (Nanay River region) Care Level Moderate to difficult (needs soft, acidic water) Temperament Peaceful (shy) Adult Size Up to 1" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Carnivore (tiny meaty foods) Water Temperature 74–82°F pH 5.0–6.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Pencilfish need a mature, densely planted tank with soft, acidic water, floating plants, leaf litter and very gentle filtration. They are shy and do best with other tiny, calm fish. Feeding: Feed crushed flake or micro pellets once or twice a day. They also enjoy small frozen foods like brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other tiny, calm fish like small tetras, rasboras, pygmy corydoras and dwarf shrimp. Avoid fast or boisterous tankmates that outcompete them for food. Good to know: Pencilfish change their pattern between day and night, often showing bars or dots after dark.

The unifasciatus pencilfish is also known as the hockeystick and the zipper pencil fish. Oh - it is also called the rocket pencilfish since half the time his head is pointing up like he is ready to take off. Of course, the other half of the time his head is pointed down like he is going for a crash landing. In a school, these fish hover at alternating 45 degrees, creating the famous zipper pattern. We recommend the purchase of at least six to see this visual effect! Quick Facts Scientific Name Nannostomus unifasciatus Origin Colombia and the Amazon basin Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 5–6 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a planted tank with floating plants, gentle filtration and a lid, since they can jump. Soft, slightly acidic water brings out their best color. Feeding: Feed crushed flake or micro pellets once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Pencilfish are shy and peaceful, so keep them with other small, gentle fish such as small tetras, rasboras, pygmy corydoras and shrimp. Good to know: Rocket pencilfish swim at an angle, and a group tilted in different directions creates their famous "zipper" look.

The silver arowana is a classic predator of the Amazon and a classic pet fish in the aquatic trade. Silver arowanas are fine with other fish their same size, but over the years these monster fish will grow to three feet. In the wild, these fish can jump in the air to catch small birds, so the aquarium will need a top cover. The arowana can be converted to feed on floating pellet food, but have a source of feeder fish as well. Small arowana often have a yolk sac, which will disappear within a few days. At that point they will need small live food or meaty flake food. Quick Facts Scientific Name Osteoglossum bicirrhosum Origin Amazon basin, South America Care Level Difficult (grows very large) Temperament Predatory Adult Size Up to 3 feet Lifespan 15–20 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–86°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 2–12" Care Guide Tank setup: Arowanas are powerful jumpers, so a heavy, tight-fitting lid is a must. Give them open swimming space and strong filtration. Feeding: Feed floating carnivore pellets and frozen foods like shrimp. Tankmates: Arowanas will eat any fish that fits in their mouth. Keep them only with large, robust fish such as large catfish, big cichlids and stingrays. Good to know: Arowanas swim near the surface and use the barbels on their chin to sense food.

Aquarium Fish Sale offers this rare blue (also called black – same fish) jumping predator in a 4-inch to 12-inch size, depending on what the fishermen were lucky to get, ready to feed on small goldfish and guppies. Blue arowana swim with the silver arowana in the Amazon tributaries but are an entirely different species with a longer body and more color. These rare fish have an elegance rarely seen in predator species. Colors are subtle blue, black, and yellow highlights on a dark silver body. Quick Facts Scientific Name Osteoglossum ferreirai Origin Rio Negro basin, South America Care Level Difficult (grows very large) Temperament Predatory Adult Size Up to 2–3 feet Lifespan 15–20 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–86°F pH 6.0–7.0 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 5–15" Care Guide Tank setup: Arowanas are powerful jumpers, so a heavy, tight-fitting lid is a must. Give them open swimming space and strong filtration. Feeding: Feed floating carnivore pellets and frozen foods like shrimp. Avoid feeder fish, which can carry disease. Tankmates: Arowanas will eat any fish that fits in their mouth. Keep them only with large, robust fish such as large catfish, big cichlids and stingrays. Good to know: Arowanas swim near the surface and use the barbels on their chin to sense food.

The Hoplo Catfish are found throughout the Amazon River basin region and are often caught in large schools by the native collectors. In the fish tank, these catfish prefer to stake out their own territory in a rocky or wooded area. The hoplo catfish is a good tankmate with similar size fish and will eat small tankmates, so don't keep this pet fish with fish he can fit in his mouth. Quick Facts Scientific Name Megalechis thoracata Origin Amazon basin, South America Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful (eats very small fish) Adult Size Up to 6" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Hoplos are hardy. Give them a soft bottom, plants and a lid, since they gulp air at the surface. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms. Tankmates: They are peaceful and get along with most medium-sized community fish and cichlids. Good to know: Hoplos are very hardy and can gulp air from the surface, so they handle many conditions well.

Aquarium Fish Sale offers the top dog in the catfish family. No catfish has such a strong pattern (outside of the L46 True Zebra Pleco). These fish are hardy but difficult to find and command a bit of a high price. They are quick growers and very good companions in a large fish tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name Merodontotus tigrinus Origin Amazon basin, Peru and Brazil Care Level Moderate Temperament Predatory Adult Size Up to 2 feet Lifespan 15–20 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 3–6" (plus tail streamer) Care Guide Tank setup: Shovelnose catfish grow large and are strong swimmers. Give them open swimming space, a sand bottom, strong filtration and a heavy, tight lid. Feeding: Feed meaty foods like quality carnivore pellets and frozen shrimp or fish. Many learn to take pellets once settled. Avoid feeder fish, which can carry disease. Tankmates: They will eat any fish that fits in their mouth. Keep them only with large, robust fish. Good to know: True tigrinis catfish have bold zebra stripes that make them one of the most prized catfish in the hobby.

The false tigrinis catfish, or gold zebra catfish, is found in the wilds of the Peru Amazon basin. Though gold zebra is a prettier name, the catfish is commonly referred to as the False Tigrinis since the catfish is almost identical to the very expensive True tigrinis catfish. The difference in the species is the color pattern. The striping is muted in the False tigrinis. No one has been able to breed this in captivity and it is difficult to determine the sex of the species. Very small feeder, live worms, and other live feeders may be required initially, but this is a catfish and they will scavenge other foods and leftovers once adapted to the fish tank. By the way, the streamer off the tail is amazingly long. Quick Facts Scientific Name Brachyplatystoma juruense Origin Amazon basin, Peru Care Level Moderate Temperament Predatory Adult Size Up to 2 feet Lifespan 15–20 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 3–5" (plus tail streamer) Care Guide Tank setup: Shovelnose catfish grow large and are strong swimmers. Give them open swimming space, a sand bottom, strong filtration and a heavy, tight lid. Feeding: Feed meaty foods like quality carnivore pellets and frozen shrimp or fish. Many learn to take pellets once settled. Tankmates: They will eat any fish that fits in their mouth. Keep them only with large, robust fish. Good to know: Young false tigrinis have a very long tail streamer that shortens as they grow.

AquariumFish offers the unusual turushuki catfish, also called the blue sawtooth cat, or the ripsaw catfish for the serrated edges on its lateral lines. These remarkable fish, with their odd sawtooth edges, come in shades of blue and black. Though slow growers, these catfish should be kept with fish their own size and will grow very large over time. Quick Facts Scientific Name Oxydoras niger Origin Amazon basin, South America Care Level Easy (grows very large) Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2–3 feet Lifespan 15–20 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 4–5" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them caves, driftwood and a soft bottom. They hide during the day and come out at night. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets once a day, ideally in the evening when they are most active. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms. Tankmates: Ripsaw catfish are peaceful but grow very large and will swallow small fish. Keep them with large fish. Good to know: Ripsaw catfish are gentle giants and sift the bottom for food rather than hunting fish.

The marble gar is an ambush predator relying on the spotted and striped pattern to blend into the background as he (or she) slowly maneuvers near the victim before he (or she) strikes. Using small teeth, the gar grabs the victim and chews it a bit before swallowing. If this sounds alluring, then this is the fish for you. Marble gars are great aquarium predators; these fish are not monsters. The marble or spotted gar grows to "only" ten inches, unlike the Florida gar which quickly outgrows any fish tank. Also, marble gars get along with other species that cannot fit in his mouth. Some hobbyists adapted these predators to cichlid pellets, but please do not rely on that and have live feeders ready. Quick Facts Scientific Name Boulengerella maculata Origin Amazon basin, South America Care Level Moderate Temperament Predatory Adult Size Up to 10–14" Lifespan 10 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 4–7" Care Guide Tank setup: Gars are fast, long-bodied predators. Give them open swimming space, strong filtration and a heavy, tight lid. Feeding: Feed meaty foods like frozen shrimp and fish, plus floating carnivore pellets once they learn to take them. Tankmates: They will eat any fish that fits in their mouth. Keep them only with large, robust fish. Good to know: Marbled gars are pike characins, not true gars, and they stay much smaller than real gars.

Aquarium Fish Sale offers what was once a rare item in the trade, but thanks to captive breeding, hujeta gars, or black spot gars, have come down in price. They are good with larger South American species, but these gars will eat fish small enough to fit in their mouth. Black spot gars can adapt to frozen foods, but one step at a time - we recommend small live feeders to start. Ambush predators, the gar will float near the target before his (or her - they are difficult to sex) sudden attack. Quick Facts Scientific Name Ctenolucius hujeta Origin Colombia and Venezuela Care Level Moderate Temperament Predatory Adult Size Up to 10–12" Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 3" Care Guide Tank setup: Gars are fast, long-bodied predators. Give them open swimming space, strong filtration and a heavy, tight lid. Feeding: Feed meaty foods like frozen shrimp and fish, plus floating carnivore pellets once they learn to take them. Tankmates: They will eat any fish that fits in their mouth. Keep them only with large, robust fish. Good to know: Black spot gars are not true gars but pike characins, which stay much smaller than real gars.

The Red Tail Catfish has been featured on River Monsters as a true monster predator of South America. The catfish features a beautiful red tail and a chocolate body with a white belly. The fish grows slowly to about four feet in the wild, about three feet in the aquarium. These fish should be kept with other fish of similar size. The red tail catfish will become the favorite pet in the aquarium, since he will eventually get big enough to eat all the other pets. Quick Facts Scientific Name Phractocephalus hemioliopterus Origin Amazon and Orinoco basins, South America Care Level Difficult (grows very large) Temperament Predatory Adult Size Up to 3–4 feet Lifespan 20+ years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 2–4" Care Guide Tank setup: They grow very large, so give them strong filtration, a sand bottom, sturdy decorations and a heavy, tight lid. Feeding: Feed meaty foods like quality carnivore pellets and frozen shrimp or fish. Many learn to take pellets once settled. Avoid feeder fish, which can carry disease. Tankmates: They will eat any fish that fits in their mouth. Keep them only with large, robust fish. Good to know: Red tail catfish keep their bold red tail and white belly as adults and often learn to beg for food.

Electric Eels are a dangerous fish and we will not knowingly sell this to anyone with children. These eels, actually the largest knifefish in the World that happens to be shaped like an eel, at maximum size will emit 800 Volts. Our largest specimens are sold only to public aquariums. Please, please take these fish seriously and ignore the internet nonsense that says these cannot kill a human; they can. However, they are an amazing and unique pet and hardy. Kindly do your research on how you will conduct water changes and general maintenance without getting shocked prior to purchasing this animal. Electric eels feed on small live feeder fish. AquariumFish.com will not sell these eels to anyone under the age of 21. If the eels are more than 2 feet, you would need to be an aquarist associated with an aquarium store or public aquarium. (Available only to Public Aquariums or Similar) ****This item does not ship to Texas or Florida**** Quick Facts Scientific Name Electrophorus electricus Origin Amazon basin, South America Care Level Expert only (dangerous) Temperament Predatory Adult Size Up to 6 feet Lifespan 15–20+ years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 76–84°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 12" Care Guide Tank setup: Electric eels need strong filtration, a heavy, locked lid and open access to the surface, since they breathe air. Never put your hands in the tank, and use insulated tools for maintenance. Feeding: Feed meaty foods like frozen fish and shrimp using long feeding tongs. Some learn to take carnivore pellets. Tankmates: Electric eels can stun and eat other fish. Keep them alone. Good to know: Electric eels can produce a shock strong enough to injure a person. They are not true eels but are related to knifefish.

The colorful Red Tail Prochilodus, also called the Flag Tail Prochilodus, are amazing jumpers, so keep a good cover. In fact they are probably the best jumpers in the AquariumFish.com freshwater warehouse. There is a Silver Prochilodus, but these cheaper variations have little color and are seldom imported for the aquarium trade. Prochilodus are herbivores, so they require prepared food with some veggies. Oddly, they are mean herbivores - they will eat small prey even if they don't like the flavor. These fish do well with other species of similar size - or at least two inches. But please keep a cover on the tank at all times. Prochilodus are jumpers! Quick Facts Scientific Name Semaprochilodus taeniurus Origin Amazon basin, South America Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful with fish its size Adult Size Up to 8–12" Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Herbivore (plant-based foods) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 6" Care Guide Tank setup: Prochilodus are strong jumpers, so a tight-fitting lid is a must. Give them open swimming space, some driftwood and good filtration. Feeding: Feed a vegetable-based flake or pellet once or twice a day. They also graze on algae. Tankmates: They get along with most fish of similar size. Avoid very small fish. Good to know: Prochilodus are named for their flag-like striped tail and are among the best jumpers in the hobby.

AquariumFish offers the largest freshwater fish of the Western Hemisphere. The largest freshwater fish in the World is the Beluga sturgeon, not adaptable to the aquarium. Back to the arapaima: these monster fish are built like torpedoes and never stop feeding and looking for food. They grow massive, so have a game plan in mind down the road, but you can enjoy this magnificent beast for a few years until then. Public aquariums love this monster fish. Predator fish and most fish do not grow to the tank size, they aren’t muffins. These fish are endangered in the wild and we bring pond raised specimens from Peru under CITES preservation permits. A source for ghost shrimp, small feeder guppies, or similar foods must be secured before bringing this fish into the aquarium. They also eat flake and pellet food, but need a good mix. ****This item does not ship to Texas or Florida**** Quick Facts Scientific Name Arapaima gigas Origin Amazon basin, Peru (pond-raised) Care Level Difficult (grows very large) Temperament Predatory Adult Size Up to 6–8 feet Lifespan 20+ years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–84°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 5" Care Guide Tank setup: Arapaima are powerful jumpers and breathe air from the surface, so they need open water at the top and a heavy, tight-fitting lid. Give them strong filtration and lots of swimming space. Feeding: Feed meaty foods like frozen shrimp and fish, plus floating carnivore pellets once they learn to take them. Tankmates: Arapaima will eat any fish that fits in their mouth. Keep them only with very large, robust fish. Good to know: Arapaima must breathe air from the surface every few minutes, so never block their access to the top.

There are 15 known species of peacock bass, great predators and game fish of the Amazon River basin. Peacock bass are fast predators and good jumpers. They are suitable tank mates with larger, aggressive fish. They will eat small fish before you even knew they were in the tank. They hunt in packs if you can put a school of four together. Ocellaris grow fast and quite large and grow best with live feeder fish, but can adapt to cichlid pellets. Quick Facts Scientific Name Cichla ocellaris Origin Amazon basin, South America Care Level Moderate (grows very large) Temperament Predatory Adult Size Up to 2–3 feet Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 76–84°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 2½–3" Care Guide Tank setup: Peacock bass grow very large and fast. Give them open swimming space, strong filtration and a heavy, tight lid. Feeding: Feed meaty foods like quality carnivore pellets and frozen shrimp or fish. Many learn to take pellets once settled. Tankmates: They will eat any fish that fits in their mouth. Keep them only with large, robust fish. Good to know: Peacock bass are named for the eye-like spot on the tail, similar to a peacock feather.

The cigar fish gets the name for its perfect cigar shape and size when it reaches maturity. Cigar fish are the largest member of the pencil fish family and must be caught in the wild, so they are somewhat rare. Please note: when the statement "caught in the wild" applies to South American species, these fish are caught under rigorous protective laws. In fact, the aquatic trade is one of the few industries that ensure the conservation of the Amazon forest. Cigar fish are clever swimmers and will go through all sorts of antics to find food. Buy one and you will see what we mean! All pencil fish do well in schools, but larger cigar fish can adapt to a solo life in the aquarium. Quick Facts Scientific Name Anostomus anostomus Origin Amazon and Orinoco basins, South America Care Level Easy Temperament Semi-aggressive (may nip) Adult Size Up to 5–6" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants, driftwood and a tight lid, since they can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or pellet with vegetable content once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They can nip at each other and at long-finned fish. Keep them with robust, fast fish of similar size. Good to know: Cigar fish often swim head-down while picking at algae and food on rocks and wood.

Leopoldi Angelfish, also called the teardrop and dwarf Leopold's angelfish, are truly wild angels with vibrant black striping and a tough wild nature that one does not see in captive-bred angelfish. The Leopoldi Angelfish will grow larger than common bred Silver Angelfish and often develop red or light green spots on the body. Unlike the Altum Angelfish, wild Leopoldi are well suited to the aquarium environment and eat flake foods. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pterophyllum leopoldi Origin Amazon basin (Brazil, Peru, Colombia) Care Level Moderate Temperament Semi-aggressive (territorial when pairing) Adult Size Up to 4–5" (the smallest angelfish species) Lifespan 10 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 78–84°F pH 5.5–7.0 Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, gentle filtration, driftwood and tall plants. Wild-type angels do best in soft, slightly acidic water. Feeding: Feed small amounts once or twice a day. Many wild angels learn to take flake and pellets once settled. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Choose calm fish that like soft, warm water and are too large to swallow, such as larger tetras, corydoras and peaceful dwarf cichlids. Avoid fin-nippers and boisterous fish. Breeding: Angelfish pair off and lay eggs on flat surfaces like broad leaves or slate. A breeding pair can become territorial, so give them room and places for other fish to retreat. Good to know: Leopoldi are the smallest angelfish species and one of the hardiest wild angels, but they still appreciate soft, warm water.

AquariumFish.com offers a beautiful variation of the wild angelfish. These are not true altum angels of Colombia, Scalare altum, as they do not get the massive elongated dorsal fins, but they are much hardier and adaptable to the aquarium. Also called the red spotted angelfish, this wild variety comes from Peru and will get red markings on the fins and rust spots on the body. Like the true Altum, these angelfish have a pointed snout and long dorsal fins. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pterophyllum scalare (wild form) Origin Peru (wild-caught) Care Level Moderate Temperament Semi-aggressive (territorial when pairing) Adult Size Up to 6" long and 8–10" tall Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 78–84°F pH 5.5–7.0 Shipping Size Medium: approx. 2" · Large: approx. 3" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, gentle filtration, driftwood and tall plants. Wild-type angels do best in soft, slightly acidic water. Feeding: Feed small amounts once or twice a day. Many wild angels learn to take flake and pellets once settled. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Choose calm fish that like soft, warm water and are too large to swallow, such as larger tetras, corydoras and peaceful dwarf cichlids. Avoid fin-nippers and boisterous fish. Breeding: Angelfish pair off and lay eggs on flat surfaces like broad leaves or slate. A breeding pair can become territorial, so give them room and places for other fish to retreat. Good to know: Wild-type angelfish are more sensitive than tank-bred angels. Acclimate them slowly and keep the water soft, warm and very clean.

AquariumFish.com loves Altums and offers this "holy grail" fish to experts and people trying to become expert hobbyists. These are truly wild fish and need expert care to get them acclimated, so please do research. One interesting note on these fish: China loves altums too! While visiting our exporters in Bogota this fall, our warehouse manager watched an export of 4,000 altums go out to China. Apparently, raising altums is the next big thing for hobbyists in that country. Please research, and ensure you have low-pH water (no higher than 6.5 and preferably lower) and live brine shrimp, worms, small feeder guppies, or similar foods. Also, these fish prefer temps around 80 degrees.
