Quick Facts Scientific Name Pterophyllum altum Origin Colombia and Venezuela (Orinoco basin) Care Level Difficult (for experienced keepers) Temperament Peaceful for an angelfish, but shy Adult Size Up to 7" long and 15" tall Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 80–86°F pH 4.5–6.5 (very soft water) Shipping Size Approx. 2" (tip of head to start of tail) Care Guide Tank setup: Altums need very soft and acidic water, warm temperatures, gentle flow, driftwood and tall plants. Keep the water exceptionally clean. Feeding: Start with frozen foods like brine shrimp, then slowly add flake or pellets, which some altums eventually accept. Tankmates: Keep them with other altums or very calm, soft-water fish like larger tetras and corydoras. Avoid anything boisterous, which will stress these shy fish. Breeding: Angelfish pair off and lay eggs on flat surfaces like broad leaves or slate. A breeding pair can become territorial, so give them room and places for other fish to retreat. Good to know: Altums are wild-caught and the most demanding angelfish. They need very soft, acidic, warm water and calm tankmates, and may only take frozen foods at first.

The Japanese Blue Swordtail Guppies are sold only as males since we cannot get the Thai breeders to ship us females. However, mate this impressive variety with diamond or blue delta female guppies and a few offspring will feature the distinctive swordtail. In a couple of years, maybe AquariumFishSale can buy the females from you. Swordtail guppies do not get as large as some of the other varieties. These exotic aquarium fish stay closer to endler size. Quick Facts Scientific Name Poecilia reticulata Origin Northern South America (captive-bred) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1¼" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and plenty of plants. Guppies like slightly hard water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Male guppies get along with other small, peaceful fish such as platies, mollies, corydoras, small tetras and rasboras. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs, which go after their long tails, and larger fish that could eat them. Good to know: Swordtail guppies have a pointed extension on the tail, like a small sword.

The Yuanbao parrot cichlid, or Yuan Bao Parrot Cichlid, has dramatic speckled and barred patterns and a unique round shape - like a Yuan Bao Chinese coin. The red parrot and flowerhorn cross can be aggressive, but that is also part of their appeal. These are beautiful fish to add to a larger aggressive fish tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hybrid cichlid Origin Captive-bred hybrid (Thailand) Care Level Easy Temperament Semi-aggressive Adult Size Up to 8" Lifespan 10 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 76–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 3–4" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them caves, rocks or driftwood, a smooth bottom and good filtration. Feeding: Feed a quality floating cichlid pellet once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Yuanbao parrots can be pushy. Keep them with robust fish of similar size, such as other parrots, larger cichlids and plecos. Good to know: Yuanbao parrots are named for their round shape, which looks like an old Chinese gold coin.

The CW-045 cory is sometimes called the False Armatus Cory since it has a similar appearance to the armatus cory of Peru. However, these are different species and are caught in a difficult area to get to near the Colombia–Brazil border. To distinguish rarer cory, the trade began using CW numbers similar to the L numbers for plecos. This rare cory is generally just called the CW-045 cory. Both the CW and L numbers are not part of zoology. CW is a fiction like the L numbers for plecos; both were invented by the hobby community and are not a true part of zoology. DATZ, a German magazine, came up with the L numbers for plecos so we can figure out who is who. The hobby site CorydorasWorld invented the CW system for corys. It works, because no one else has come up with a more common name for Cory CW-045, and we all know what cory it is. Cory CW-045 is a big cory, getting to three inches, and is charcoal with a red sash on the head. Quick Facts Scientific Name Corydoras sp. CW045 Origin Colombia–Brazil border region Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 5–10 years Diet Omnivore (bottom feeder) Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 6.0–7.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and a soft sand or smooth, fine gravel bottom. Plants, driftwood and a few shady spots help them feel secure. Corys are sensitive to salt and some medications (especially copper), so check labels before treating the tank. Feeding: Corys need their own food, not just leftovers. Feed sinking pellets or wafers once or twice a day so food reaches the bottom. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Corys get along with almost any peaceful community fish, such as tetras, rasboras, livebearers, gouramis, angelfish and bettas. Avoid large fish that could swallow them and aggressive bottom dwellers. Good to know: Corys sift through the substrate with their sensitive barbels, so soft sand or smooth, fine gravel keeps those barbels healthy.

Blue glaze shrimp are an exotic variation of the Caridina species bred in Taiwan for bright blue and sparkling patterns. Each shrimp features small dark blue dots on a varying blue pattern on the body (see picture). These shrimp are a step up from the blue velvet and are difficult to breed in a consistent color pattern. You might find this out if these breed in your crustacean clubhouse. Moss, plants and small pieces of driftwood make excellent hangouts for these scavengers. We suggest shrimp pellets to ensure they get a complete diet. They don't need much, so don't overfeed! Also, do not use medication or raise the water temperature over 78 degrees. Blue glaze shrimp can tolerate a little salt in the water. Quick Facts Scientific Name Caridina cf. cantonensis (blue glaze) Origin Taiwan (aquarium-bred) Care Level Moderate to difficult (needs soft, stable water) Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1" Lifespan 1½–2 years Diet Omnivore (grazes on algae) Water Temperature 68–76°F pH 5.8–6.8 Water Hardness GH 4–6, KH 0–1 (soft) Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Caridina bee and Taiwan bee shrimp need soft, slightly acidic water. Use a mature, cycled tank with an active (buffering) shrimp substrate, RO water remineralized for shrimp, moss and plants, and a sponge filter. Feeding: Feed a small amount of quality shrimp food once a day, and remove any uneaten food after a few hours. Tankmates: Caridina are best kept in a shrimp-only tank or with tiny, peaceful fish like otocinclus, plus snails. Avoid cichlids and other fish that will eat shrimp. Different bee and Taiwan bee varieties can crossbreed, but they will not breed with Neocaridina. Good to know: Acclimate slowly (drip for an hour or more). Stable water matters more than perfect numbers, and sudden changes in temperature or hardness are the most common cause of losses.

The tretocephalus cichlid is sometimes referred to as the five banded or five barred cichlid. Breeders use this common name to distinguish the neolamprologus five bar from the six bar neolamprologus sexfasciatus. However, the tretocephalus has a different color pattern as well. These Tanganyikan cichlids are prized for the bright white and blue pattern and their very active behavior in the fish tank. Tretocephalus is territorial but will tolerate other Tanganyikan cichlids such as julidochromis and lamprologus species. In the wild, the African cichlid feeds on small snails and clams, so they are great for snail population control. Not so great with desirable aquarium snails. Quick Facts Scientific Name Neolamprologus tretocephalus Origin Lake Tanganyika, Africa Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Territorial Adult Size Up to 5" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.8–9.0 Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Use a sand bottom with rockwork, caves and crevices for spawning sites. Lake Malawi and Lake Tanganyika cichlids need hard, alkaline water; crushed coral or aragonite sand helps hold the pH up. Feeding: Feed a quality cichlid pellet or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like brine shrimp. Tankmates: Tanganyikan cichlids do best with other Tanganyikans of similar size, such as julidochromis, neolamprologus and synodontis catfish. Give each pair its own territory. Good to know: Tretocephalus eat snails, so they are great for pest control but will also eat any snails you want to keep.

The solid blue-hued Blue Moscow Guppy was developed after the black moscow guppy by Sri Lanka breeders who kept with the "moscow" naming theme. This fancy guppy will stand out in a peaceful community fish tank. Though the guppies will breed in the aquarium environment, not all the offspring will feature the true blue-hued body of the true blue moscow guppy, but the next generation will all be pretty. Quick Facts Scientific Name Poecilia reticulata Origin Northern South America (captive-bred in Sri Lanka) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Sold as a pair (1 male + 1 female) Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and plenty of plants, including some floating plants where babies can hide. Guppies like slightly hard water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Guppies get along with other small, peaceful fish such as platies, mollies, corydoras, small tetras and rasboras. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs and larger fish that could eat them. Breeding: Guppies are livebearers and breed easily. Females give birth to live babies about once a month, and adults will eat the babies, so thick plants give them a place to hide. Good to know: Moscow guppies are known for their solid, deep body color.

The Sunburst Orange Glo Shark is a gene-spliced albino rainbow shark and some kind of secret jellyfish in Asia. Rainbow sharks from Indonesia have deep red fins on a silver body. Those natural sharks are actually catfish and are hardy and easy to keep and peaceful. The rainbow shark grows to about six inches. On the other hand, Glo Sharks are a solid fluorescent color and keep this color throughout their lives. In fact, if a Sunburst Glo Shark breeds with another Orange Glo Shark, they make baby orange glo sharks. Weird science. Quick Facts Scientific Name Epalzeorhynchos frenatum (genetically modified) Origin Farm-raised (genetically modified) Care Level Moderate Temperament Semi-aggressive, territorial (especially toward other sharks) Adult Size Up to 6" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Keep one per tank Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Rainbow sharks patrol a territory, so give one caves, driftwood and plants to break up sight lines, plus a tight lid. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets or wafers and a quality flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy algae wafers and frozen bloodworms. Tankmates: Keep only one rainbow shark per tank, and avoid other bottom-dwelling sharks and territorial fish like red-tailed sharks. They do best with fast, mid- to upper-level swimmers such as danios, barbs, rainbowfish and larger tetras. Good to know: GloFish sharks are rainbow sharks, which are members of the carp family, not true sharks or catfish. They claim a territory near the bottom and chase other bottom dwellers, so give them caves and keep only one per tank. GloFish colors look brightest under a blue or actinic LED light, but they are colorful under normal lighting too.

The lemon color body and deep blue eyes of the Lemon Blue Eye Pleco make this a very personable pleco. He seems to be just a bit more aware than your average brown eye fish. Difficult to breed, these fish are a little more expensive than the albino variation. Quick Facts Scientific Name Ancistrus sp. "Lemon Blue Eye" Origin Captive-bred (wild form from South America) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 4–5" Lifespan 10+ years Diet Herbivore (algae wafers) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single, or several with a cave each Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them caves, driftwood and good filtration. They are most active at night. Feeding: Feed algae wafers and sinking pellets once a day, ideally in the evening when they are most active. They also enjoy frozen bloodworms. Tankmates: They are peaceful and get along with most community fish. Males may squabble over caves, so give each one its own hiding spot. Good to know: Male bushynose plecos grow soft bristles on their snout as they mature. They are great algae grazers.

The Centipede Knifefish earns the name by creating the illusion of small walking centipede feet as the long anal fin undulates. This wild knifefish from the Amazon basin also earns another name - the leaf knifefish - due to its habit of finding leaves to lie beside until night, when it awakens and begins the hunt for small insects. Centipede knifefish will adapt to frozen brine and other foods but it is best to have a supply of live brine or live black worms to help with the transition. Suitable for most community aquariums without very small micro species (shrimp, micro rasboras), an addition of a centipede knifefish will create quite the stir. AND these knifefish only grow to nine inches, so they are never a threat to mid-size tetras and barbs. Quick Facts Scientific Name Steatogenys duidae Origin Amazon basin, Brazil Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 9" Lifespan 10 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.0 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 5–7" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants, driftwood and tubes or caves to hide in, plus dim lighting. They are most active at night. Feeding: Feed frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp once a day. Some learn to take sinking pellets. Tankmates: They are shy and peaceful, so keep them with calm community fish too large to fit in their mouth. Good to know: Like other knifefish, they swim by rippling one long fin along their belly and can move backward easily.

Pacman frogs are famous for their giant Pacman Arcade mouth - in fact grown adults may be fed pinkie mice (but no more than once every couple of weeks). Normally these not-so-adorable pets will thrive on mealworms and crickets. This is a terrestrial species - the frog only needs to soak in water every couple of days. In fact, these frogs are such bad swimmers that they will drown in a deep bowl, so just provide a deep dish. Native to the Amazon basin, the pacman frog lives in leaf litter on the bottom of the rainforest floor and eats anything that can fit in its giant mouth. In the home, a small aquarium and soft litter three to four inches deep will suffice. Coconut litter (clean - no fertilizer enhanced) from the local garden store is perfect litter. ALSO, Pacman Frogs bite anything - including your finger - and it hurts! Quick Facts Scientific Name Ceratophrys cranwelli Origin South America (captive-bred) Care Level Easy Temperament Aggressive (bites) Adult Size Females up to 6"; males up to 3" Lifespan 10 years Diet Carnivore (insects) Water Temperature 75–85°F pH Not applicable (land frog) Group Size Keep one per enclosure Shipping Size Approx. 1½–2" Care Guide Tank setup: Pacman frogs live on land, not in the water. Give them a covered tank with soft, damp substrate like coconut fiber they can burrow into, plus a shallow water dish. Keep the enclosure warm. Feeding: Feed insects like crickets or mealworms. Remove uneaten insects so they don't bother the frog. Tankmates: Pacman frogs will eat anything that fits in their mouth, including other frogs. Keep them alone. Good to know: Pacman frogs spend most of their time buried with just their eyes showing, waiting for food to come by.

Rosette Sword Plant Rosette Sword aquarium plant is natural to the Amazon river basin where it grows along the shallows and reaches about 8 inches. Since the rosette sword has a modest size this is a nice "mid base" plant in the fish tank. Rosette Swords require some fertilizer, a few hours of direct light, and they do not require injected CO2 and they will grow in aquarium gravel. Scientific Name: ECHINODORUS parviflorus Food: Good lighting and iron fertilizer Shipping Size: Medium approx. 4 inches, Large approx. 6 inches

Marine Krill Flavored Pellets NewVision features krill soaked omnivorous food pellets. The krill will attract even the most finicky eaters and the ingredients inside will ensure a complete diet. Formulated for omnivores and carnivores, all your marine fish will get a treat out of this complete fish fish. Shipping Size: 2.8 oz

API Fin and Body Cure Aquarium Pharmaceuticals, Inc offers General Bactieria Cure. General Bacteria Cure treats external AND internal bacteria infections. Typical aquarium fish disease treated include eye cloud, gill disease, open sores, fin and tail rot, and hemorrhagic septicemia. Each Package Contains 10 packets of treatment powder.

Yes, the Hell Boy Betta, or hellboy betta, is named after the featured star of the Hell Boy movies. The betta varies in color patterns but always has a predominant deep red plakat (fancy round tail) body. Some hellboy bettas are red and white, some have some blue, and some are nearly all deep red. This is a great fish for those that like fantasy and sci-fi :) Fish pictured here are representative only, and the picture shows a mature hell boy betta in full display. Most hell boy plakats are primarily blood red in color. Quick Facts Scientific Name Betta splendens Origin Thailand (captive-bred) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Males fight each other; peaceful toward most other fish Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 76–82°F (needs a heater) pH 6.5–7.5 Breathes Air Yes – labyrinth fish take air from the surface Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give him a heater (bettas are tropical fish), a gentle filter and live or silk plants. Plakats are active swimmers and like room to patrol. Keep a lid on the tank and leave a gap of air under it, since bettas breathe from the surface. Feeding: Feed a few betta pellets or a pinch of flake once or twice a day. Bettas overeat easily, so small meals are best. They also enjoy frozen bloodworms. Tankmates: Never keep two male bettas together. Plakats are among the boldest bettas, so they do best alone or with sturdy, peaceful fish like corydoras and snails. Avoid fin-nippers and other labyrinth fish. Good to know: Short-finned plakats are strong, fast swimmers and the closest to the original fighting fish, so they are usually the most aggressive bettas. Keep them on their own or with sturdy, peaceful tankmates.

The pink tail shark, also called Hoven's carp or the Asian golden shark, is a very large and active schooling barb and will actually grow to nearly three feet in the wild. Similar in appearance to the pink tail chalceus, these peaceful omnivores will eat flake and pellet food and are very suitable for large aggressive and community aquariums. In the fish tank assume these guys will get to about 20 inches in about three years, so plan accordingly! The fins are all pink and the body is gold and silver. The pink tail chalceus from South America is a very different fish, but they are often confused in the trade, since both species are called "pink tail sharks". Quick Facts Scientific Name Leptobarbus hoevenii Origin Borneo and Southeast Asia Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful but very active Adult Size Up to 24–36" Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Small: 3" · Medium: 5–7" Care Guide Tank setup: These are fast, schooling fish that grow large, so give them plenty of open swimming space, strong filtration and a heavy, tight-fitting lid, since they jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or pellet once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other large, peaceful to semi-aggressive fish such as silver dollars, tinfoil barbs, larger gouramis, plecos and peaceful cichlids. They will eat very small fish once they are large. Good to know: These "sharks" are members of the carp family, not true sharks. They grow quickly, so check their adult size before buying.

The skunk loach is shaped like a slug, as opposed to the more slender kubotai and yo-yo loaches. Also in the botia family, these loaches only grow to 2 inches and like to pal around and chase each other in the fish tank. The skunk loach, also called the mouse loach for its size and shape, is a bottom dweller and effective scavenger, but it is a good idea to drop in some sinking pellets a couple of times each week. In the wild, skunk loaches inhabit rocky crevices along smaller rivers of Cambodia and Thailand. Quick Facts Scientific Name Yasuhikotakia morleti Origin Mekong and Chao Phraya basins (Thailand, Laos, Cambodia) Care Level Moderate Temperament Semi-aggressive (territorial; can harass tankmates) Adult Size Up to 3–4" Lifespan 8–15 years Diet Omnivore (bottom feeder; eats snails) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them many caves, rocks and driftwood so each loach can claim its own spot, a soft sand or smooth gravel bottom and good filtration. Keep a lid on the tank. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets or wafers once or twice a day so food reaches the bottom. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. They also eat pest snails. Tankmates: Keep them with robust, fast fish of similar or larger size, such as barbs, danios, rainbowfish and semi-aggressive cichlids. Avoid slow, long-finned fish and other bottom dwellers that can't hold their own. They eat snails and shrimp. Good to know: These loaches are bold and territorial; adding them last to an established tank with plenty of caves helps keep the peace.

Pandurini Dwarf Cichlid The pandurini dwarf cichlid is called the apisto panda and the apisto panduro, and is a small, colorful and peaceful community fish from Peru. Apistogramma pandurini live in black (low pH) water similar to wild discus, and these dwarf cichlids do not tolerate pH above 7.5. Other than that, the apisto panda is quite hardy, and aquarium hobbyists successfully breed the species. These are show-quality males. Quick Facts Scientific Name Apistogramma panduro Origin Peru (wild-caught) Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful (males territorial with each other) Adult Size Males up to 3"; females about 2" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 5.0–6.5 Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter, dim lighting and lots of plants, driftwood and leaf litter. Add a cave (a coconut shell or small clay pot) for each female. Most apistos prefer soft, slightly acidic water. Feeding: Feed small pellets or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with small, peaceful fish such as tetras, rasboras, pencilfish, otocinclus and corydoras. A calm school of small "dither" fish helps apistos feel safe enough to come out. Keep one male per tank unless it is large and well planted, and avoid large or boisterous fish. Adults may eat small shrimp and baby shrimp. Breeding: Apistos are cave spawners. The female lays her eggs inside a cave and guards the fry, while the male patrols the territory. One male with several females works well in a planted tank. Good to know: Panduro (pandurini) are true blackwater fish. Peat, leaf litter and very soft water bring out the striking red tail in the males.

The giant bumblebee catfish is also called the Jelly Cat, but we think the first name fits better. These catfish from Venezuela are a great addition to an aquarium because they are actually quite peaceful. Jelly cats eat frozen foods and sinking pellets and only grow to around eight inches. The fish gets along with anything it can't fit in its mouth - and it is not the type to chase for its food. In the wild, jelly cats lie in slow-moving streams and use their color pattern and camouflage to allow the current to bring small prey to their mouths. In the fish tank, they will lie around all day like sleeping old cats. At night they prowl around for anything they can eat that doesn't give them much of a chase. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pseudopimelodus bufonius Origin Venezuela and Brazil Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful (eats fish that fit in its mouth) Adult Size Up to 8–12" Lifespan 15+ years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 7" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them caves, driftwood and dim lighting. They hide during the day and come out at night. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets once a day, ideally in the evening when they are most active. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms. Tankmates: They will eat small fish at night. Keep them with fish too large to fit in their mouth. Good to know: Bumblebee catfish have huge mouths for their size, so choose tankmates carefully.

Christmas Moss Like Java moss, Christmas moss creates a thick green ground cover and a haven for shrimp and fry. The tips of the plant will go up and look like tiny Christmas trees. Scientific Name: VESICULARIA montagnei Shipping Size: One two inch cup: Approx 2.5 oz

Creeping Jenny The creeping jenny has small green and golden leaves on a short stemmed plant. Each creepy order comes with a small bunch containing five plants with a lead weight or a small bush in a 2 inch pot, depending on which one is available from the grower. Scientific Name: Lloydiella sp. Shipping Size: Approx. four inch bush

The prambanan snail, sometimes referred to by its scientific name, Thiara winteri , is a rare decorative snail from Indonesia. The cone-shaped snails are chocolate and bronze with some small spikes. The prambanan snail will not eat plants or harm other aquarium crustaceans, like fancy aquarium shrimp. Great scavengers, these snails can grow to three inches. Quick Facts Scientific Name Thiara winteri Origin Indonesia (Java) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful; plant-safe Adult Size Up to 2–3" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Scavenger (algae and sinking foods) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Breeding Livebearer; breeds slowly Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a mature tank with a sand or fine gravel bottom and some algae and detritus to graze. Keep the water hard enough for healthy shells. Feeding: They graze on algae and leftover food. Also feed algae wafers or sinking pellets. Tankmates: They do well with peaceful fish, shrimp and other snails. Avoid puffers, loaches and assassin snails. Good to know: Remove snails before treating the tank with copper or other medications, which are toxic to invertebrates.

The uncommon black emperor tetra is captive-bred in Indonesia but was first found as a naturally occurring variation in the Orinoco River basin in Venezuela. The deep colors and bright blue eyes create a phantasmic scene in the aquarium. These community fish will grow to two inches over time, and their fins grow longer as they age. Quick Facts Scientific Name Nematobrycon palmeri (black variety) Origin Colombia (wild form); captive-bred Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a dark substrate, which brings out their color. Keep a lid on the tank, since tetras can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, rasboras, danios, corydoras, dwarf cichlids, gouramis and livebearers. Good to know: Tetras feel safer and show better color in a group. A larger school also spreads out any chasing.

Coral platies are smaller than your average livebearer and do well in small and mid-size community aquariums. The diminutive coral wag platy has a cute black tail on a bright red body. Quick Facts Scientific Name Xiphophorus maculatus Origin Southern Mexico and Central America Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful, a bit timid Adult Size Up to 1" Lifespan 3–4 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 70–80°F pH 7.0–8.2 Breeding Livebearer – breeds easily in the aquarium Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Platies are hardy and easy to keep. Give them a filter, a lid and plenty of plants. Use a heater to keep the water steady in the 70s. They prefer harder, slightly alkaline water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. Platies also need some plant matter, so a vegetable flake is a good choice. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Platies get along with most peaceful community fish, such as other livebearers (mollies, guppies and swordtails), tetras, rasboras and corydoras. Avoid large or aggressive fish that may bully or eat them. Breeding: Platies are livebearers, so a tank with males and females will almost certainly have babies (fry). Adults will eat fry, so add dense plants or use a breeding box if you want to raise them. Keeping more females than males gives the females a break from the males' attention. Good to know: Dwarf platies are small and easily intimidated, so keep them with other small, gentle fish.

The green tiger botia loach is a bit more aggressive than other aquarium botias. These slender loaches will eat snails and small shrimp and push away fish to get to food. Very attractive and wild-caught in Borneo, the loach is a great addition to cichlid tanks and medium-aggressive tanks, but not nano aquariums. Quick Facts Scientific Name Syncrossus hymenophysa Origin Malaysia, Indonesia (Borneo, Sumatra) and Thailand Care Level Moderate Temperament Semi-aggressive (territorial; can harass tankmates) Adult Size Up to 8–10" Lifespan 8–15 years Diet Omnivore (bottom feeder; eats snails) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them many caves, rocks and driftwood so each loach can claim its own spot, a soft sand or smooth gravel bottom and good filtration. Keep a lid on the tank. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets or wafers once or twice a day so food reaches the bottom. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. They also eat pest snails. Tankmates: Keep them with robust, fast fish of similar or larger size, such as barbs, danios, rainbowfish and semi-aggressive cichlids. Avoid slow, long-finned fish and other bottom dwellers that can't hold their own. They eat snails and shrimp. Good to know: These loaches are bold and territorial; adding them last to an established tank with plenty of caves helps keep the peace.

Lately, the female koi bettas have been getting as much attention as their longer-fin partners. Female bettas, unlike males, can be placed together. In fact, a group of female bettas is called a sorority. Not sure which one; Kappa Kappa Gamma probably. The female koi betta is as appealing as the male, not just for its more gentle disposition, but this variation also offers vivid koi colors. These colorful bettas make a pretty harem. Buy four! Quick Facts Scientific Name Betta splendens Origin Thailand (captive-bred) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Can live in groups (sororities) with care Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 76–82°F (needs a heater) pH 6.5–7.5 Breathes Air Yes – labyrinth fish take air from the surface Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a filter and lots of plants and hiding places to break up sight lines. Keep a lid on the tank and leave a gap of air under it, since bettas breathe from the surface. Feeding: Feed a few betta pellets or a pinch of flake once or twice a day. Bettas overeat easily, so small meals are best. They also enjoy frozen bloodworms. Tankmates: Females can share a tank with small, peaceful fish like corydoras, rasboras and snails. Never add a male to a sorority tank, and avoid fin-nippers. Good to know: Females color up when relaxed. In a sorority, watch for bullying and remove any female that is constantly chased.

The snakeskin barb is one of the more desirable barbs of the puntius family, with its unique "snakeskin" body markings. These are schooling fish and should be kept in a group of at least four to keep their stress low. Good filtration for all puntius barbs is a requirement. Otherwise, the fish is hardy, eats flake and small pellet food, and is a good asset to any community fish tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name Desmopuntius rhomboocellatus Origin Borneo (Indonesia) Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 5–6 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 5.5–7.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a well-planted tank with a filter, a heater and some dim, sheltered areas. They do best in soft, slightly acidic water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other peaceful fish such as rasboras, tetras, gouramis and corydoras. Avoid large or boisterous fish that can outcompete them. Good to know: Snakeskin barbs show their best markings in soft, slightly acidic water with plants and dim areas to explore.

The pineapple guppy is a vibrant multicolor cobra variant. The color pattern is difficult to breed, so these guppies are not seen as often as other color variants. Our pineapple guppies are bred in Singapore and each order comes with one male and one female. Quick Facts Scientific Name Poecilia reticulata Origin Northern South America (captive-bred in Singapore) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Sold as a pair (1 male + 1 female) Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and plenty of plants, including some floating plants where babies can hide. Guppies like slightly hard water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Guppies get along with other small, peaceful fish such as platies, mollies, corydoras, small tetras and rasboras. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs and larger fish that could eat them. Breeding: Guppies are livebearers and breed easily. Females give birth to live babies about once a month, and adults will eat the babies, so thick plants give them a place to hide. Good to know: Pineapple guppies show yellow, orange and green tones that look a bit like the fruit.

The flavescent peacock cichlid (flavescent means to turn yellow) is a natural color pattern found on rocky shorelines of the Usisya Bay of Lake Malawi. Just a bit harder to breed than some other color morphs, flavescent peacock cichlids will begin with a bluish striped pattern at two inches and then begin the blue and yellow color transition at three inches. Like other peacock cichlids, USISYA flavescent peacocks are territorial and hardy and will do well in any African cichlid tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name Aulonocara stuartgranti "Usisya" Origin Lake Malawi, Africa Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Semi-aggressive (males territorial) Adult Size Up to 5" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 76–82°F pH 7.8–8.6 Shipping Size Approx. ¾–4" (by size option) Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a sand bottom, open swimming space in front and rockwork along the back. Lake Malawi and Lake Tanganyika cichlids need hard, alkaline water; crushed coral or aragonite sand helps hold the pH up. Feeding: Feed a quality cichlid pellet or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like brine shrimp. Tankmates: Haps do well with peacocks and other haps of similar size, plus robust catfish like synodontis. Keep one male per similar-looking species, with several females, to limit fighting and crossbreeding. Good to know: Males take a year or more to show full adult color, and color best when females are present.

The giant talking catfish known as the irwini catfish grows to two feet and is caught in the Brazilian Amazon. Like the Red Tail Catfish, irwini keep their vibrant color pattern through their adulthood and look like a giant raphael catfish. Irwini catfish are scavengers but will eat fish that fit into their mouths. These exotic catfish do not take bites out of other fish and are suitable for a large species aquarium. Quick Facts Scientific Name Megalodoras uranoscopus Origin Amazon basin, Brazil Care Level Easy (grows very large) Temperament Peaceful (eats fish that fit in its mouth) Adult Size Up to 2 feet Lifespan 15–20 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 6" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them caves, driftwood and a soft bottom. They hide during the day and come out at night. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets once a day, ideally in the evening when they are most active. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms. Tankmates: They are peaceful and armored, so they get along with most fish, including many cichlids. They may eat very small fish. Good to know: Irwini are armored "talking" catfish that make grunting sounds and keep their bold pattern into adulthood.

When the Iron Curtain fell over Eastern Europe in the Cold War, aquarium hobbyists in communist countries were left to their own devices and became adept breeders. Many natural genes of wild fish were isolated. Today, beautiful variations from that (hopefully) bygone era are found in the hobby. The Bulgarian gene promotes inky black fins on a cream or koi body. Seal Point angelfish have a cream body along with the distinct solid dark fins. Note: Bulgarian Seal Point Angels may vary in appearance, typically distinguished by wide dark markings on the dorsal fin. Their body coloration can range from solid silver to silver with stripes. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pterophyllum scalare Origin Amazon basin, South America (captive-bred) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Semi-aggressive (territorial when pairing) Adult Size Up to 6" long and 8" tall Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them tall plants or driftwood, a heater and a gentle filter. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Choose peaceful fish too large to swallow, such as larger tetras, corydoras, plecos, rams, gouramis and peaceful barbs. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs, and small fish like neon tetras that adult angels may eat. Breeding: Angelfish pair off and lay eggs on flat surfaces like broad leaves or slate. A breeding pair can become territorial, so give them room and places for other fish to retreat. Good to know: Adult angelfish will eat any fish small enough to fit in their mouths, including neon tetras, so choose tankmates that are too big to swallow.

The Pinoy Paraiba Angelfish is a domestic-bred jewel of the aquarium trade. Wild blue genes crossed with established genes of the smoky pinoy angels created these magnificent variants of the angelfish family. Fins are generally veil, and some small bronze patching and blue patching occur as the angel ages. These are hard fish to find, and we try to carry them whenever our breeder makes them available. Almost solid black, the blue highlights become more pronounced as the fish ages. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pterophyllum scalare Origin Amazon basin, South America (captive-bred) Care Level Easy Temperament Semi-aggressive (territorial when pairing) Adult Size Up to 6" long and 8" tall Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Shipping Size Approx. 3" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them tall plants or driftwood, a heater and a gentle filter. A breeding pair can become territorial, so give them room and places for other fish to retreat. Good to know: The blue color develops with age and is often hard to see until the fish reach about 3", so young fish may look mostly silver or black.

The Clown Angelfish will not joke around any more than a zebra angelfish, but their pattern is reminiscent of the black harlequin pattern of a clown suit. Hence the name. Clown angelfish are hardy, but the pattern, a cross of full black and zebra, is difficult to obtain, so this freshwater angelfish can be a bit pricey. Black Lace Angelfish have light and dark black striations along the body, and fins with lacy ends. Like high-end lingerie, these lacy fish are worth the price. Generally, the pattern remains the same as the fish ages; no blues or orange patches develop. The zebra angelfish features a true polka dot and striped black and silver pattern just like the African zebra, except the body is silver, not white, or is the body of the African zebra black with white stripes? Zebra angelfish remain true to their silver and black pattern, while blue zebras get a more visible blue sheen as they age, but their pattern is really like a silver angelfish, not an African zebra. Not all catfish look pretty when they grow, but the Achara Catfish will keep its leopard pattern throughout its life. Achara Catfish, or Sailfin Pim, are caught in the Amazon basin on the Peru side, usually about three to four inches. These are peaceful catfish that will grow to 24 inches, and like most catfish they will swallow most edibles that fit in their mouth, including slow-moving small fish. These fish have been bred with Tiger Shovelnose to create a tank-hardy catfish that looks more like a classic Tiger shovelnose, but the Achara referenced here are the real McCoy. Quick Facts Scientific Name Leiarius marmoratus Origin Amazon basin, Peru Care Level Moderate (grows very large) Temperament Peaceful (eats fish that fit in its mouth) Adult Size Up to 2 feet Lifespan 15–20 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 3" Care Guide Tank setup: Shovelnose catfish grow large and are strong swimmers. Give them open swimming space, a sand bottom, strong filtration and a heavy, tight lid. Feeding: Feed meaty foods like quality carnivore pellets and frozen shrimp or fish. Many learn to take pellets once settled. Avoid feeder fish, which can carry disease. Tankmates: They will eat any fish that fits in their mouth. Keep them only with large, robust fish. Good to know: Achara catfish keep their leopard pattern and tall sail-like dorsal fin as adults.

We have to say "true" parrot cichlid because this is the real thing, not the hybridized version found all over the pet trade that shares the same name. These parrot cichlids come from Colombia in the wild and have no relation to the common parrot cichlid other than they both have distinguishing large "bird-like" eyes. The true parrot cichlid has a turquoise body with olive and black markings and vivid red eyes. Colors get bolder as the fish gets older. The mouth is also unique; the true parrot cichlid looks like it has a constant frown. True parrot cichlids (unlike the red devil hybrids) are more peaceful than most other large South American cichlids. They do swallow small fish, though, so choose wisely. Also, parrot cichlids are hardy as long as the pH is below 7.8, and they adapt well to pellet food. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hoplarchus psittacus Origin Rio Negro and Orinoco basins (Colombia, Venezuela, Brazil) Care Level Moderate (needs soft, acidic water) Temperament Peaceful for a cichlid Adult Size Up to 10–12" Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 76–84°F pH 5.0–7.0 Group Size Single, pair or small group Shipping Size Approx. 4" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a sand or fine gravel bottom, driftwood, rocks and sturdy plants. Good filtration is important, since these cichlids grow large and produce a lot of waste. Feeding: Feed a quality cichlid pellet or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They do well with other peaceful South American cichlids of similar size like angelfish, eartheaters and severums, plus larger tetras, silver dollars and plecos. They may eat very small fish. Good to know: These cichlids are known for their personality and often learn to recognize their owners.

Mermaid The aquarium mermaid is a small bushy plant that grows to about ten inches and features green and pinkish fern like leaves. If kept in a tank not set up for live plants with CO2 and the rest, the plant will still look nice for a time but if the light and water aren't just right it will start to shed leaves. Scientific Name: Proserpinaca palustris Shipping Size: Approx. 8 inches, five stems and a lead weight

The three lined pencil fish, or trilineatus pencil, has three horizontal lines on a copper and red body. These are small schooling fish from small rivers of the Amazon and only grow to an inch. Very gentle fish, they are also hardy and will eat flake food. However, these are wild Amazon fish and will not tolerate pH higher than about 7.6. Quick Facts Scientific Name Nannostomus trifasciatus Origin Amazon basin, South America Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a planted tank with floating plants, gentle filtration and a lid, since they can jump. Soft, slightly acidic water brings out their best color. Feeding: Feed crushed flake or micro pellets once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Pencilfish are shy and peaceful, so keep them with other small, gentle fish such as small tetras, rasboras, pygmy corydoras and shrimp. Good to know: Three-lined pencilfish have bright red spots on their fins that stand out against their black and gold stripes.

The veil fin, or long fin cherry barb, is bred to develop longer flowing fins. Long fin cherry barbs are just as hardy as the parent standard fin cherry barb, and males are bright red while the females are closer to a copper color. Our Florida breeder takes special care developing these for the aquarium hobby, and they are normally shipped in a good medium to large size. Quick Facts Scientific Name Puntius titteya Origin Sri Lanka (bred in Florida) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful, a bit shy Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 4–6 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 73–81°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a filter, a heater and plenty of plants. They feel safest with places to hide and show more color in a planted tank. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other small, peaceful fish such as rasboras, small tetras, corydoras and dwarf shrimp. Avoid large or boisterous fish and fin-nippers. Good to know: The long fins are best kept away from fin-nippers like tiger barbs, so pair them with other gentle fish.

The Guinean Bichir, from the African country of Guinea, is not often available. When we can get them from that more remote area of Africa, we don't have them for long! Guinean bichirs, also called the Ansorgii Bichir, have short dorsal fins similar to a stegosaurus dinosaur with a black and cream marble body. These African bichirs are larger than most and grow to 30 inches. In the aquarium, like other bichir, the ansorgii bichir will eat frozen and pellet food. These exotic fish are compatible with most species that won't fit in their mouth. Quick Facts Scientific Name Polypterus ansorgii Origin Guinea and Guinea-Bissau, West Africa Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful with fish its size Adult Size Up to 2½ feet Lifespan 15+ years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 4–5" Care Guide Tank setup: Bichirs are expert escape artists, so a tight-fitting lid is a must. Give them a soft bottom, caves and driftwood. They breathe air, so leave a gap above the water. Feeding: Feed sinking carnivore pellets once a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and shrimp. Tankmates: They will eat any fish that fits in their mouth. Keep them with fish too large to swallow. Breathes air: Bichirs take gulps of air from the surface, which is normal behavior. Good to know: Ansorgii bichirs are among the largest and rarest bichirs in the hobby.

The Blue Hook Metynnis, or simply blue hook, is a rare member of the silver dollar family. Wild-caught in Colombia, these fish are peaceful vegetarians and grow to 7 inches without eating the smaller neons schooling around them. These fish will also eat flake and pellet food, so they are a bit omnivorous. Quick Facts Scientific Name Myloplus schomburgkii Origin Colombia and the Amazon basin Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 7" Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Herbivore (plant-based foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 4" Care Guide Tank setup: Silver dollars are active schooling fish. Give them open swimming space, a tight lid and sturdy or artificial plants, since they eat soft plants. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or pellet with vegetable content once or twice a day. They also enjoy vegetable foods like peas. Tankmates: They are peaceful and get along with other medium to large fish such as larger tetras, plecos, parrots and peaceful cichlids. Good to know: Blue hooks are named for the blue sheen and hooked fin on mature males.

The variatus and platy are different species but are closely related and can breed with each other. Variatus tend to have larger fins, are more avid jumpers, and get a little larger. The red tux hi fin variatus is a remarkable livebearer with long, flowing fins and reflective red and black scales. Quick Facts Scientific Name Xiphophorus variatus Origin Southern Mexico Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 3–4 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 65–77°F (handles cooler water than common platies) pH 7.0–8.2 Breeding Livebearer – breeds easily in the aquarium Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Platies are hardy and easy to keep. Give them a filter, a lid and plenty of plants. They can live without a heater in rooms that stay above about 65°F. They prefer harder, slightly alkaline water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. Platies also need some plant matter, so a vegetable flake is a good choice. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Platies get along with most peaceful community fish, such as other livebearers (mollies, guppies and swordtails), tetras, rasboras and corydoras. Avoid large or aggressive fish that may bully or eat them. Breeding: Platies are livebearers, so a tank with males and females will almost certainly have babies (fry). Adults will eat fry, so add dense plants or use a breeding box if you want to raise them. Keeping more females than males gives the females a break from the males' attention. Good to know: Variatus are keen jumpers, so keep a tight-fitting lid on the tank. Their long fins can attract fin-nippers, so skip tiger barbs and other nippy fish.

Vagabond Butterflyfish: The Elegant & Patterned Centerpiece The Vagabond Butterflyfish (Chaetodon vagabundus) is a beautiful and unique fish that makes an excellent addition to a large fish-only marine aquarium . This butterflyfish is easily recognized by its elegant coloration: a yellowish-white body with a striking V-shaped pattern of dark vertical and horizontal lines. It has a distinctive black eye-band and a prominent black spot on its tail. It is an active and graceful swimmer that requires plenty of open space. While generally peaceful, it can be territorial towards other butterflyfish. It is not considered reef-safe , as it is known to nip at corals and various other invertebrates. Why the Vagabond Butterflyfish is a Great Choice: Stunning Appearance: Its high-contrast coloration and intricate pattern make it a true showpiece. Adds Energy to the Tank: It adds a lot of energy and graceful movement to a spacious aquarium. Impressive Size: It grows to a large size, making it a commanding and impressive fish. Hardy & Resilient: It is known to be a very durable and adaptable species. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Chaetodon vagabundus Origin: Indo-Pacific Reefs Max Size: 8 inches Lifespan: 10+ years Diet: Omnivore. Feeds on a varied diet of butterflyfish formulas and frozen foods. Shipping Size: 2-4 inches

Tobacco Basslet The tobacco basslet is a small but onery saltwater fish known for its tobacco color and pugnacious style. The basslet is native to the Tropical Western Atlantic and Caribbean regions. The fish was discovered and named by famous ichthyologist (back when everyone was just called a zoologist) Georges Cuvier - who loved his cigars. The tobacco basslet is typically found over sandy or rocky bottom areas near reefs and drop-offs. It adapts to any substrate in the aquarium. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: The Tobacco Basslet is an opportunistic predator. In the wild, its diet consists mainly of small crustaceans and smaller fish. In captivity, it readily accepts a varied diet of meaty frozen foods, including mysis shrimp, finely chopped squid, enriched brine shrimp, and marine fish flesh. They are generally easy to feed and will often take high-quality marine pellets and flake foods as well. Feeding: Due to their higher metabolism, feed them 1-2 times daily, offering only what they can consume quickly. Reef Compatibility: It is Reef Safe With Caution . While the Tobacco Basslet will leave corals alone, its predatory nature means it will readily consume small, ornamental invertebrates (shrimp and small crabs) and any fish small enough to fit into its mouth, including tiny gobies, blennies, and some damselfish. It is best suited for a Fish Only With Live Rock (FOWLR) system. Temperament: It is Semi-Aggressive / Territorial . They are generally peaceful toward larger, robust fish but can be aggressive toward smaller, more docile tankmates, especially those that swim near the bottom. If keeping more than one Tobacco Basslet, the tank must be very large (125+ gallons), and all individuals should be introduced simultaneously to mitigate dominance issues. Tank Requirements: A minimum tank size of 70 gallons is recommended for a single adult to provide adequate swimming room and plenty of live rock for hiding places and territorial establishment. They are known jumpers, so a secure lid is essential. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Serranus tabacarius Primary Common Name: Tobacco Basslet Other Common Names: Tobacco Fish, Tobacco Bass, Tobaccofish Origin: Tropical Western Atlantic, Caribbean, Bermuda Max Size: 7-8.5 inches (18-22 cm) Temperament: Semi-Aggressive / Predatory Diet: Carnivore (Meaty frozen foods, pellets) Minimum Tank Size: 70+ Gallons Reef Compatibility: With Caution (Will eat small shrimp and fish) Unique Feature: Synchronous Hermaphrodite (possesses both sexes)

Chalk Basslet The chalk basslet is reef safe, peaceful, and a good fish for the beginning hobbyist. This little basslet is shy and needs places to hide. Scientific Name: Serranus tortugarum Origin: Caribbean Max Size: 3 inches Diet: Carnivore Shipping Size: 1 to 2 inches

Red Spotted Pseudochromis Red Spotted Dottyback originates from the reefs of the Indian Ocean, and is a beautiful addition to any saltwater aquarium. Its pale body and fins are adorned with beautiful red spots, which create a lined pattern. This pseudochromis should be housed with moderately aggressive fish larger than itself. Although it is an excellent reef fish, it may eat small ornamental shrimp. Scientific Name : Pseudochromis sp Max Size: 4 inches Family : Pseudochromidae Origin: Indian Ocean Diet: frozen marine fish, squid, mysis shrimp, vitamin-enriched brine shrimp, and frozen carnivore preparations. Shipping Size: Approx. 1 inch

Big Eye Squirrelfish Also known as a Black Bar Soldierfish, the bigeye squirrelfish is nocturnal. During the daytime it will hide in caves and avoid the light. Make sure it has some nice hiding places to help avoid the daylight. The man who named and discovered this fish in 1829 was one of the most famous zoologists of the time, Frenchman Georges Cuvier. We see the name "cuvier" quite a bit in our hobby. Scientific Classification: Myripristis sp Origin: Sri Lanka Max Size: 8 inches Required Tank Size: 70+ gallons Diet: feeder shrimp, freeze dried shrimp, and chopped marine meats Shipping Size: 2 to 4 inches

The neon red stiphodon is wild-caught in small streams and ponds in Sumatra and occasionally exported to the aquarium trade. Freshwater gobies have quite a bit of personality and unusual movement, so they are a great addition to the aquarium. They are bottom dwellers and a bit territorial, but easy to keep and feed. Red stiphodon gobies only grow to two inches and will eat small pellet food and flake food as well as small frozen foods. Quick Facts Scientific Name Stiphodon rutilaureus Origin Indo-Pacific island streams Care Level Moderate (needs clean, oxygen-rich, flowing water) Temperament Peaceful with other fish; males territorial with each other Adult Size Up to 1½–2" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Algae eater Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size One male with several females Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: These gobies come from clear, fast-flowing island streams. Give them a mature tank with strong current, high oxygen, smooth rocks covered in algae and biofilm, and a tight lid, since they can climb out. Feeding: These gobies graze on algae off rocks, so they do best in a mature tank. Also feed algae wafers. They may go hungry in a very clean, new tank. Tankmates: They do well with small, peaceful fish that like cool, flowing water, such as danios, rasboras, hillstream loaches and dwarf shrimp. Males may spar with each other. Good to know: Stream gobies cling to rocks with a sucker formed by their pelvic fins. Their larvae drift to the sea to develop, so they rarely breed in aquariums.

Seachem Denitrate Denitrate removes nitrates and nitrites from saltwater aquarium water and freshwater aquarium water. Simply add the denitrifying stones to the filter media and let them do their work. Each bottle contains 250 ml, enough to treat 25 gallons.

API pH Adjuster Kit API pH Adjustment Kit contains instructions and ingredient for 250 tests and both pH Up and pH Down solutions to keep your aquarium balanced. Simple and easy, measures pH ranges from 6.0 to 7.6. Use the included solutions when out of target range. Bottle contains: 250 tests and pH Up and pH Down Solution

The coral blue sailfin variatus is a breathtaking livebearer. Not large, but with a very long red dorsal fin on a blue body, these fish will be a showcase in the aquarium. Variatus platy, or simply variatus, are a livebearing species from southern Mexico. A different species from the common platy, variatus get slightly larger and have higher dorsal fins. The species are close enough that they will crossbreed. The aquarium trade inevitably developed lovely variations of the variatus . Our blue hi-fin variatus is one of the loveliest. Quick Facts Scientific Name Xiphophorus variatus Origin Southern Mexico Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 3–4 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 65–77°F (handles cooler water than common platies) pH 7.0–8.2 Breeding Livebearer – breeds easily in the aquarium Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Platies are hardy and easy to keep. Give them a filter, a lid and plenty of plants. They can live without a heater in rooms that stay above about 65°F. They prefer harder, slightly alkaline water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. Platies also need some plant matter, so a vegetable flake is a good choice. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Platies get along with most peaceful community fish, such as other livebearers (mollies, guppies and swordtails), tetras, rasboras and corydoras. Avoid large or aggressive fish that may bully or eat them. Breeding: Platies are livebearers, so a tank with males and females will almost certainly have babies (fry). Adults will eat fry, so add dense plants or use a breeding box if you want to raise them. Keeping more females than males gives the females a break from the males' attention. Good to know: Variatus are keen jumpers, so keep a tight-fitting lid on the tank. Their long fins can attract fin-nippers, so skip tiger barbs and other nippy fish.

Temple Plant The aquarium temple plant come bunched and leaded for easy adaption to the fish tank. Temple plant is a large leave deep green plant that required light and room to grow. Scientific Name: Hygrophila corymbosa Shipping Size: Approx. 6 inches, potted and ready

Calico Bubble Eye goldfish will never be found in the wild. Bred in China for show, not speed, the calico bubble eye goldfish, like the blue bubble eye goldfish, have distinctive fluid-filled sacs beneath the eyes. If a sac should rupture, it will grow back, but please keep sharp objects and aggressive fish away from these poor creatures. Bubble eye goldfish are not good swimmers and should be kept with slower-moving fish to make sure they get their food. Quick Facts Scientific Name Carassius auratus Origin China Care Level Moderate (needs a gentle setup) Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 6" Lifespan 10–12 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 65–75°F (no heater needed in most homes) pH 7.0–8.0 Shipping Size Medium: approx. 2" · Large: approx. 3–4" Care Guide Tank setup: Bubble eye goldfish produce a lot of waste, so give them plenty of room and a strong filter. Use smooth decorations and live or silk plants, and keep the water current gentle. Feeding: Feed small amounts of a quality sinking pellet or flake once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. Sinking foods are easier for them to find than floating ones. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them only with other slow-swimming fancy goldfish, such as telescopes, black moors, celestials, bubble eyes, lionheads and ranchus. Avoid faster goldfish like comets, shubunkins and even lively ryukins, which will outcompete them for food. Also avoid tropical fish and fin-nippers. Ponds: Bubble eye goldfish can live in ponds in mild climates, but they are less cold-hardy than comets and shubunkins. Bring them indoors where winters are harsh, and keep them away from fast, aggressive pond fish. Good to know: Cover filter intakes with a sponge so the delicate eye sacs can't be pulled in or damaged.

Aspidoras Pygmy Cory Rarely caught in the upper streams of Brazil, the aspidoras C125 catfish is also called the false cory and the sixray cory. These little cory-like dwarf catfish behave like cory but are a bit more fussy, and they love algae! These pygmy cory do not tolerate high pH, so please keep the tank below 7.8. Otherwise, the aspidoras tolerates an aquarium environment quite well. Quick Facts Scientific Name Aspidoras pauciradiatus Origin Brazil Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1½" Lifespan 4–6 years Diet Omnivore (bottom feeder) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and a soft sand or smooth, fine gravel bottom. Plants, driftwood and a few shady spots help them feel secure. Corys are sensitive to salt and some medications (especially copper), so check labels before treating the tank. Feeding: Corys need their own food, not just leftovers. Feed sinking pellets or wafers once or twice a day so food reaches the bottom. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Corys get along with almost any peaceful community fish, such as tetras, rasboras, livebearers, gouramis, angelfish and bettas. Avoid large fish that could swallow them and aggressive bottom dwellers. Good to know: Aspidoras graze on algae and biofilm more than most corys, so a mature, planted tank suits them best.

The Mota Catfish, or vulture catfish, is wild-caught in Venezuela around the Orinoco River basin and sports a light silver body with a black leopard pattern and long whiskers. Considered "monster fish," these exotic catfish only grow to 16 inches and are actually good tank mates in a large aggressive aquarium. Mota catfish will eat small livebearers, frozen food and pellet food. NOTE: Our current giant Mota was born with only one eye! So we offer this at a big discount. Otherwise healthy! Feeding: Feed meaty foods like quality carnivore pellets and frozen shrimp or fish. Many learn to take pellets once settled. Tankmates: They will eat any fish that fits in their mouth. Keep them only with large, robust fish. Good to know: Vulture catfish are fast, active swimmers and big eaters, so they do best with fish too big to fit in their mouth.

The endlicheri bichir, or saddle bichir, is one of the less common bichirs available from Cameroon. Like all other bichirs, the saddle bichir will eat frozen food and any live fish that fit in its mouth, but they are not nippers and get along with larger community fish. Interesting fact: Bichirs have small eyes and rely on smell to hunt in the wild. The saddle bichir has several broad bands on the body that sort of look like saddles, hence the name. Quick Facts Scientific Name Polypterus endlicheri Origin West and Central Africa Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful with fish its size Adult Size Up to 2 feet Lifespan 15+ years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 3" Care Guide Tank setup: Bichirs are expert escape artists, so a tight-fitting lid is a must. Give them a soft bottom, caves and driftwood. They breathe air, so leave a gap above the water. Feeding: Feed sinking carnivore pellets once a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and shrimp. Tankmates: They will eat any fish that fits in their mouth. Keep them with fish too large to swallow. Breathes air: Bichirs take gulps of air from the surface, which is normal behavior. Good to know: Bichirs have small eyes and rely mostly on smell to find food.

The red firecracker tropheus moorii, or tropheus chipimbi, will begin showing color at two inches, though shipping size is normally just around an inch, so please be patient. This fish is territorial but peaceful enough to keep with a community cichlid tank. Slow to grow but hardy, keep the water clean and make sure it has flake food that contains veggies. Quick Facts Scientific Name Tropheus moorii "Chipimbi" Origin Lake Tanganyika, Africa Care Level Moderate to difficult Temperament Aggressive with their own kind; keep in large groups Adult Size Up to 5" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Herbivore (plant-based foods) Water Temperature 76–80°F pH 8.0–9.0 Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Use a sand bottom and plenty of rockwork that grows algae for grazing. Strong filtration and very clean water are essential. Lake Malawi and Lake Tanganyika cichlids need hard, alkaline water; crushed coral or aragonite sand helps hold the pH up. Feeding: Tropheus are strict plant eaters. Feed a vegetable-based flake or pellet in small amounts, and avoid rich, meaty foods, which can make them very sick. Tankmates: Keep Tropheus in a group of a single variety, with one or a few males. Avoid mixing different Tropheus varieties, which will crossbreed and fight. Peaceful Tanganyikans like cyprichromis or synodontis can share the tank. Good to know: Add Tropheus all at once as a group; adding single fish later often leads to fighting.

A stunning multicolored fish native to America, the rainbow shiner is becoming a popular aquarium fish and does not require a heater, since the shiner fish can tolerate colder temperatures. Rainbow shiners do well in ponds and aquariums where the temperature does not get above 80 degrees. Hardy schooling fish, rainbow shiners will eat flake and pellet food. Note: Since we carry juvenile fish, their adult colors will take some time to develop. Quick Facts Scientific Name Notropis chrosomus (see note) Origin Southeastern United States (Alabama, Georgia, Tennessee) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful but very active Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 3–4 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 55–75°F (cool water; no heater needed) pH 6.5–7.8 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Rainbow shiners are active, cool-water stream fish. Give them a sand or gravel bottom, smooth rocks, some current and strong aeration. Keep the water below about 75°F and keep a lid on the tank. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other peaceful, cool-water fish of similar size, such as other native minnows and darters, white clouds or danios. The red point Honduran is a new species to the aquarium hobby. These cichlids are a more colorful member of the Amatitlania group of cichlids, which also includes convict cichlids. Red points have gold and red and, unlike convict cichlids, they are peaceful and actually skittish. Not a true schooling fish, a group of Honduran red points will stick together like glue in the fish tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name Amatitlania sp. "Honduran Red Point" Origin Rio Danli, Honduras Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful for a cichlid (territorial when breeding) Adult Size Up to 4–5" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Single or pair Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a sand or gravel bottom, rocks, caves and driftwood to create territories. Anchor decorations well, since they like to dig. Strong filtration is important. Feeding: Feed a quality cichlid pellet or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other robust Central American cichlids of similar size, plus larger catfish and plecos. Give each fish its own territory, and avoid small or timid fish. Good to know: Central American cichlids are hardy and easy to breed. Pairs become very protective of their eggs and fry.

Golden-Headed Sleeper Goby: The Reef Tank Sand Sifter The Golden-Headed Sleeper Goby (Valenciennea strigata) is one of the most popular and beneficial fish for a marine aquarium with a deep sand bed. It is known by several other common names, including Blueband Goby , Blue Cheek Goby , and Yellow-headed Sleeper Goby . This striking fish is easily identified by its bright golden-yellow head that contrasts with a pearly white to pale-grey body, featuring a distinct blue-streak or band running from the mouth to the gill plate. Native to the sandy lagoons and reef slopes of the Indo-Pacific, this goby is prized for its sand-sifting behavior. It constantly takes large mouthfuls of sand, sifts through it for tiny food items (small invertebrates, microfauna, and detritus), and expels the cleaned sand through its gills. This activity keeps the substrate clean and well-oxygenated , helping to prevent detritus buildup and nuisance algae. The Golden-Headed Sleeper Goby can reach a maximum size of about 6 to 7 inches (15-18 cm) and requires a minimum aquarium size of 30 to 55 gallons with a well-established, deep sand bed (at least 2-4 inches). It is a known jumper, so a tight-fitting lid is essential . Diet & Compatibility: Diet: This goby is a Carnivore whose primary natural diet consists of small benthic invertebrates (copepods, amphipods, etc.) and other microfauna that it sifts from the sand. In the home aquarium, its greatest challenge is starvation , as it can quickly deplete the food source in the sand bed. It must be fed frequently (3-4 times daily) with sinking meaty foods like frozen mysis shrimp, enriched brine shrimp, finely chopped seafood, and high-quality sinking pellets . Soaking food to allow it to sink and land on the sand is highly recommended. A mature tank with a refugium that produces microfauna is ideal. Reef Compatibility: It is considered Reef Safe and poses no threat to corals or most motile invertebrates. However, its constant sand-sifting behavior can be problematic. It will create small mounds and valleys in the sand bed and may cover low-lying corals, clams, or other sessile invertebrates with expelled sand , potentially leading to their decline. Temperament: It is a Peaceful community fish. It is often found in the wild as a mated pair and can be kept in pairs in captivity, but only one individual or a confirmed pair should be kept per tank, as they can be aggressive toward conspecifics or other sand-sifting gobies (e.g., other $$Valenciennea$$ species). Burrowing: This species is a burrow dweller and will dig under live rock or décor to create a protected refuge. It is critical to ensure that all rockwork is securely stabilized and cannot collapse when the sand underneath is removed. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Valenciennea strigata Primary Common Name: Golden-Headed Sleeper Goby Other Common Names: Blueband Goby, Blue Cheek Goby, Yellow-headed Sleeper Goby Origin: Indo-Pacific (East Africa to Tuamoto Islands) Max Size: 6-7 inches (15-18 cm) Temperament: Peaceful / Sand Sifter Diet: Carnivore (Feeds on microfauna; requires frequent supplemental feeding) Minimum Tank Size: 30-55 Gallons (Requires deep sand bed) Reef Compatibility: Yes, but with Caution (May bury sessile invertebrates)

Creeping Charlie Creeping Charlie is also known as aquatic moneywort. These are not names you would normally invite into your house but this rangy but this rangy fast growing plant does quite well in most aquariums even without CO2. Also called mint charlie, the green leaves and vines can be trimmed to any length. Scientific Name: Clinopodium brownei Shipping Size: Approx, 6 inch bunch of five plants w lead weight

The rhino horn goby, sometimes called the freshwater clown goby, has a distinct extension on the dorsal fin, which gives the fish its name. Rhino horn gobies are dwarf bottom dwellers that have similar behavior to wild cory catfish. The rhino horn goby is caught in the wild regions of Sri Lanka in freshwater AND brackish water, so these aquarium fish can handle either condition. Quick Facts Scientific Name Redigobius balteatus Origin Sri Lanka and the Indo-Pacific Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful with other fish; territorial with its own kind Adult Size Up to 1½" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Carnivore (small meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.5–8.5 Group Size Does best in a group, with plenty of hiding spots Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: These small gobies do best with plenty of caves and hiding spots (small shells and rocks work well) and hard, alkaline water. Many do best with a little marine salt in the water (brackish, specific gravity about 1.002–1.008). Feeding: Feed small amounts once or twice a day. They prefer small frozen foods like brine shrimp and bloodworms, and some will not eat flake reliably. Tankmates: Keep them in a species tank or with other small, peaceful brackish fish such as mollies, glassfish and small livebearers. Avoid larger fish that could eat them. Good to know: These tiny gobies are full of personality and often perch on rocks or glass to watch their surroundings.
