From Lake Tanganyika, the threadfin furcifer feeds on plankton and algae, and in the aquarium will need some veggies in their flakes and pellets. Quick Facts Scientific Name Cyathopharynx furcifer Origin Lake Tanganyika, Africa Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful for a cichlid Adult Size Up to 8" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.8–9.0 Shipping Size Medium: approx. 1½" · Large: approx. 3" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a fine sand bottom and plenty of open swimming space, with a few rocks along the back. Lake Malawi and Lake Tanganyika cichlids need hard, alkaline water; crushed coral or aragonite sand helps hold the pH up. Feeding: Feed a quality small pellet or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like brine shrimp. Tankmates: They do best with other peaceful Tanganyikans such as cyprichromis, calvus, frontosa (when large enough) and synodontis catfish. Keep them in a group. Good to know: Featherfins like open sand areas, where males build sand "bowers" to court females.

The candy cane tetra, or HY511 tetra, looks like a cross between the red phantom tetra and bleeding heart tetra. These Venezuelan tetras feature a pink body with white-tipped fins and make a terrific-looking school. Now captive-bred, these tetras were once rare and hard to find in the hobby. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hyphessobrycon sp. "HY511" Origin Aquarium-bred (exact wild origin uncertain) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a dark substrate, which brings out their color. Keep a lid on the tank, since tetras can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, rasboras, danios, corydoras, dwarf cichlids, gouramis and livebearers. Good to know: Tetras feel safer and show better color in a group. A larger school also spreads out any chasing.

Parrot's Feather The parrot feather has bright small leaves off of a long stem that will grow our of the aquarium. Technically these are pond plants and while the rooting takes place under water, most of the leaves grow above the water line. The plants will arrive as bunched with five separate plants and a lead weight. Scientific Name: Myriophyllum aquaticum Origin: Florida farm Shipping Size: Approx. 7 inches

JBJ Air Curtain This flexible rod provides thousands of micro bubbles every hour and provides a beautiful air curtain display as an added benefit. No need for suction cups, the flexible air curtain has weights built in to keep it in place. Size: 30 inches (suitable for 10 gallons and up)

Teardrop Butterflyfish: The Vibrant & Eye-Catching Centerpiece The Teardrop Butterflyfish (Chaetodon unimaculatus) is a beautiful and highly sought-after fish that makes an excellent addition to a large fish-only marine aquarium . This butterflyfish is easily recognized by its vibrant coloration: a bright yellow body with a large, prominent black "teardrop" shaped spot below the dorsal fin. It also has a distinct black eye-band. It is an active and graceful swimmer that requires plenty of open space. While generally peaceful, it can be territorial towards other butterflyfish. It is not considered reef-safe , as it is a specialized corallivore in the wild and will actively eat stony corals in an aquarium. Why the Teardrop Butterflyfish is a Great Choice: Stunning Appearance: Its vibrant coloration and unique "teardrop" pattern make it a true showpiece. Adds Energy to the Tank: It adds a lot of energy and graceful movement to a spacious aquarium. Impressive Size: It grows to a large size, making it a commanding and impressive fish. Hardy & Resilient: It is known to be a very durable and adaptable species. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Chaetodon unimaculatus Origin: Indo-Pacific Reefs, Hawaii Max Size: 8 inches Lifespan: 10+ years Diet: Corallivore. It will accept meaty frozen foods but will primarily feed on corals. Shipping Size: 2-4 inches

Scooter Blenny: The Benthic Bottom-Crawler The **Scooter Blenny** (Synchiropus ocellatus), also known as the Ocellated Dragonet, is a unique and captivating bottom-dwelling fish, widely sought after for its intricate coloration and quirky "scooting" movement across the substrate. Its body features a stunning, mottled pattern of **tan, brown, black, and white** blotches, which act as excellent camouflage in the sand and rubble zones it inhabits. Though often called a "blenny" in the aquarium trade, this fish is actually a member of the **Dragonet family** (*Callionymidae*). Like its cousin, the Mandarin Dragonet, the male Scooter Blenny possesses an elegant, sail-like dorsal fin that it often flares during territorial or courtship displays. The **Scooter Blenny** is **completely reef safe** and incredibly peaceful, posing no threat to corals or invertebrates. It spends its days meticulously hunting and grazing, making it an excellent fish for observing benthic behavior. Critical Care Requirement: The Scooter Blenny is a highly specialized eater, relying almost exclusively on **live copepods** and other micro-invertebrates found on live rock and in the sandbed. Success hinges on a **well-established, mature aquarium** (at least 6 months old) with a robust, continuous natural food source. While some **captive-bred** individuals may be trained to accept frozen foods (like mysis or cyclops), a dedicated **refugium** for cultivating copepods is strongly recommended to ensure long-term health, as they will quickly starve if outcompeted by faster fish. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Synchiropus ocellatus Common Names: Scooter Blenny, Ocellated Dragonet, Scooter Dragonet Origin: Indo-Pacific Max Size: 3 inches Temperament: Peaceful (Difficult to feed; avoid aggressive tank mates) Diet: Carnivore. Requires constant supply of live copepods, supplemented by frozen foods. Minimum Tank Size: 30 Gallons (must be mature/established) Reef Safe: Yes, excellent for coral systems.

Even six assorted bunched live plant order fits right in the same box as the fish order and offers a surprise grab bag of different sizes and colors of available aquarium plants. This is a great way to sample new plants and jump start a planted aquarium. Weights are affixed to each bunch of plants for easy placement. Shipping Size: (6) each of various species stemmed plants, AND EACH OF THE SPECIES COMES IN A BUNCH OF 5, SO REALLY 30 PLANTS.

Yasha goby fish is a distinctive variety of goby fish known for its fantastic behavior and appearance. It is not very common in the aquarium hobby but is immensely popular among goby enthusiasts. It is a tropical marine fish centered mainly in the Western Pacific Ocean, where it is found inhabiting the outer reef slopes in the depth of 15 to 40 meters. Males are generally smaller than females. Their symbiotic shrimp is almost half the size of them.

A more exotic version of the blood red parrot fish, as if that wasn't exotic enough, is the solid white Platinum Parrot. This extraordinary hybrid offers the unique characteristics of the classic parrot and contrasts well in an aquarium with plants and darker substrate. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hybrid cichlid Origin Captive-bred hybrid (Thailand) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful to semi-aggressive Adult Size Up to 8" Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 76–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them caves, rocks or driftwood, a smooth bottom and good filtration. Feeding: Feed a quality floating cichlid pellet once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Parrot cichlids are usually peaceful for cichlids. Keep them with other fish of similar size, such as other parrots, silver dollars, larger tetras, plecos and peaceful cichlids. Good to know: Platinum parrots look best against dark gravel and green plants, which make their white color stand out.

Spotted Hawkfish: A Unique & Hardy Perching Fish The Spotted Hawkfish (Cirrhitichthys oxycephalus) is a fascinating and active species that adds a touch of unique character to any marine aquarium . Its distinct appearance features a white or pale body with intricate red or brown spots and a "tassled" dorsal fin. This fish is known for its unique behavior of "perching" on live rock and coral branches, patiently waiting for its next meal. The Spotted Hawkfish is a hardy and resilient species, making it an excellent choice for a fish-only with live rock (FOWLR) tank or a large community tank with other semi-aggressive species. Why the Spotted Hawkfish is a Great Choice: Unique Perching Behavior: Its habit of perching on rocks and coral branches creates a dynamic and interesting display. Highly Hardy: This species is incredibly resilient and easy to care for, making it a great choice for intermediate hobbyists. Natural Predator: It will actively hunt and eat small pest invertebrates. Reef-Safe (with caution): While generally safe with corals, it may pose a threat to small invertebrates like snails, crabs, and shrimp. Important Note: The Spotted Hawkfish can be semi-aggressive and territorial, especially towards smaller, more passive fish. It is a carnivorous predator and should not be kept with ornamental shrimp or small crabs. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Cirrhitichthys oxycephalus Origin: Indo-Pacific Reefs Max Size: 4 inches Lifespan: 5 years or more Diet: Carnivore. A varied diet of high-quality frozen foods like shrimp and krill. Shipping Size: 1.5-2.5 inches

Longnose Hawkfish: The Checkered Perching Predator The Longnose Hawkfish (Oxycirrhites typus) is one of the most popular and instantly recognizable members of the Hawkfish family (Cirrhitidae). Distinguished by its striking, bright red and white checkered or crosshatch pattern and its uniquely elongated, pointed snout, this fish adds a distinct look and personality to any marine aquarium. Native to the vast Indo-Pacific region, from the Red Sea to Hawaii, the Longnose Hawkfish is an ambush predator that lacks a swim bladder. Due to this, it does not actively swim in the water column but instead uses its thick, unbranched lower pectoral rays to "perch" on rock ledges, corals, and gorgonians, where it patiently waits to swoop down on small prey. It is an inquisitive and hardy fish, but its predatory nature requires careful tankmate selection. This species is moderately sized, reaching a maximum length of about 5 inches (13 cm), and requires a minimum aquarium size of 30 gallons, though 50+ gallons is preferred to provide ample perching and hiding opportunities. Like all hawkfish, it is a known jumper, so a tight-fitting lid is absolutely essential to prevent escape. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: The Longnose Hawkfish is a dedicated Carnivore and a micropredator in the wild. Its diet should consist of a variety of small, meaty marine foods, including frozen mysis shrimp, finely chopped squid or fish flesh, and vitamin-enriched brine shrimp. Due to its long, thin snout, food items should be appropriately small. It is a voracious eater and will quickly learn to accept food directly from the water column. Feeding: Feed once or twice daily. Some specimens may require live foods (like copepods or small ghost shrimp) to encourage initial feeding, but they usually transition easily to frozen foods. Reef Compatibility: It is Reef Safe With Caution. The Longnose Hawkfish will not consume corals or large, sessile invertebrates, but it will systematically hunt and eat all ornamental shrimp, small crabs, and snails that can fit into its mouth. It can also irritate, but rarely harm, corals by habitually perching on them. Temperament: It is Semi-Aggressive / Predatory. It is generally peaceful toward most fish tankmates that are significantly larger, but it should not be housed with small, docile fish (like tiny gobies or dartfish) that it may view as prey. It is strongly territorial toward other hawkfish and should generally be kept singly unless a proven, male-female pair is acquired and the tank is large. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Oxycirrhites typus Primary Common Name: Longnose Hawkfish Other Common Names: Checked Swallowtail, Yellow-spotted Anthias, Blotched Anthias Origin: Indo-Pacific (Widespread) Max Size: 5 inches (13 cm) Temperament: Semi-Aggressive / Predatory Diet: Carnivore (Meaty Foods) Minimum Tank Size: 30-50+ Gallons (Requires a tight-fitting lid) Reef Compatibility: With Caution (Will eat ornamental shrimp and crabs)

Golden Puffer Golden puffers have a great personality The family of Puffers is a distinct family marked by their ability to ingest water into the ventral portion of their body causing them to blow up for protection. These fish also have incredibly strong plated mouth structures that are used to bite and crush even the toughest shells. Almost all puffers are slow swimming fishes with powerful jaws made up of fused teeth feeding on a variety of slow moving and often hard animals. Also have a poison in their skin, tissues and organs. The poison is an alkaloid nerve poison. They will do well in a fish-only aquarium. Keep only one per tank. Puffers have bodies that are very rounded and often tapered at the mouth and caudal (tail) fin regions. Color varies, but many species have light spots and or spines. Feeds mainly on mollusks (hard, powerful teeth enable them to break through mollusk shells); also fed on other invertebrates including sponges and coral. Scientific Name : Arothro Meleagris Shipping Size : 7-8 inches Max Size: 15 inches

The pygmy hatchetfish, found in Colombia and Peru, has small, delicate features and indeed is the smallest hatchetfish. These fish are mild-mannered and eat flake food. Fine for all community tanks but will not do well with aggressive species. These are great schooling fish for the upper region of the aquarium and will even tolerate small nano tanks - and large peaceful tanks. Quick Facts Scientific Name Carnegiella myersi Origin Colombia and Peru Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Hatchetfish live at the very surface, so give them floating plants, gentle filtration and a tight-fitting lid, since they are excellent jumpers. Feeding: Feed a quality floating flake once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy small frozen foods like brine shrimp. Tankmates: Hatchetfish are peaceful and get along with small community fish such as tetras, rasboras, corydoras and dwarf cichlids. Avoid fish that swim at the surface and might bully them. Good to know: Pygmy hatchetfish are the smallest hatchetfish and stay near the surface, so floating plants give them cover.

Chocolate cichlids, also called emerald cichlids for the small amount of green on the otherwise chocolate body, come from Central America, so they are not as common in the trade as other cichlids. The chocolate cichlid is gentle, gets along with other South American cichlids and grows to about the same size as an oscar. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hypselecara temporalis Origin Amazon basin (Brazil, Peru, Colombia) Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Peaceful for a cichlid Adult Size Up to 10–12" Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 76–84°F pH 5.5–7.0 Group Size Single, pair or small group Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a sand or fine gravel bottom, driftwood, rocks and sturdy plants. Good filtration is important, since these cichlids grow large and produce a lot of waste. Feeding: Feed a quality cichlid pellet or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They do well with other peaceful South American cichlids of similar size like angelfish, eartheaters and severums, plus larger tetras, silver dollars and plecos. They may eat very small fish. Good to know: These cichlids are known for their personality and often learn to recognize their owners.

Pygmy Angelfish: A Perfect Dwarf Angelfish for Nano Reefs The Pygmy Angelfish (Centropyge argi), also known as the Cherub Angelfish , is a beautiful and exceptionally small species that makes an excellent addition to nano and small marine aquariums. It is highly sought after for its vibrant coloration: a brilliant blue body with an unmistakable orange-yellow face and chest. Known for its hardiness and active personality, the Pygmy Angelfish is a great choice for both beginner and experienced hobbyists. It is a constant forager, exploring rockwork and adding a lively presence to your tank without overwhelming a small space. Why the Pygmy Angelfish is a Great Choice: Ideal for Smaller Tanks: Its compact size makes it one of the few angelfish suitable for nano reef aquariums. Vibrant Color: Its stunning, two-toned coloration makes it a highly visible and attractive inhabitant. Exceptional Hardiness: This species is incredibly resilient and easy to care for, making it a perfect first angelfish. Generally Reef-Safe: While its behavior should be monitored, this species is a great candidate for many reef tanks and is less prone to nipping corals than larger angelfish. Important Note: Like most dwarf angelfish, this species can be territorial, especially towards other dwarf angelfish. It is best to introduce it into a tank with a well-established aquascape to give it a place to hide and claim as its own. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Centropyge argi Origin: Western Atlantic Ocean and Caribbean Max Size: 3 inches Lifespan: 5 years or more Diet: Omnivore. A varied diet of high-quality flakes, pellets, and frozen foods. Shipping Size: 1-2 inches

Painted Sweetlips Also known as slate sweetlips, Diagramma pictum, is a species of marine fish in the family Haemulidae. It is widespread throughout the tropical waters of the Indo-West Pacific region, Red Sea included. This species reaches a length of 100 cm, but common size is 55 cm.

California Stingray The California Stingray, or Haller's Round Ray, is a species of round ray, family Urotrygonidae, found in the coastal waters of the eastern Pacific Ocean. It is a small, common ray that feeds mostly on benthic invertebrates. On the beaches of southern California. In nature, round stingrays strongly segregate by age and sex, with the females staying in water deeper than 14 m and males and juveniles in shallower habitat. The juveniles feed on polychaete worms and small benthic crabs until they are 14 cm across. As they mature, their diet shifts towards bivalve mollusc. Round stingrays are daytime foragers that are most active in the warm temperatures of summer and fall. Using their pectoral disc and mouths, they dig large pits to uncover buried prey. The digging of these pits plays an ecologically important role, as they also uncover prey for smaller fish. Scientific name: Urobatis halleri Origin: California Max size: 10 inches Diet: Ghost shrimp, meaty pieces like squid Shipping Size: Small 3 to 5 inches Medium 5 to 6 inches Large 7 to 10 inches

Whitley Boxfish The Whitley Boxfish may be the prettiest boxfish, but it is pretty deadly. ONLY for those willing to risk their whole fish tank because these fish cannot be stressed lest they release their protective toxin. Scientific Name: Ostracion whitleyi Origin: Indo-Pacific Size: Approx 2 inches

Yellow Seahorse Yellow seahorse, also known as the common seahorse and sea pony, are about as non aggressive as they come. They do best in tanks with other shy, docile fish. They can be harmed by some corals and stinging anemones and need live brine shrimp as a food source in the aquarium. The yellow seahorse comes in shades of grey, yellow, and rusty red. In the wild these fish live in slow running estuaries but to protect the species the seahorse are tank raised for the aquarium trade. Scientific Name: Hippocampus kuda Origin: Persia Max Size: 6 inches Diet: frozen mysis shrimp, amphipods, other small crustaceans found in live rock Shipping Size: 3 inches

The zebra snail, or zebra nerite snail, is a scavenger and algae eater and, like all nerites, plant-safe. Nerite snails do not overrun the fish tank and only grow to about one inch at full maturity. Nerites do well in most water conditions except for pH below 7.0. These attractive snails do not get bigger than an inch, and we recommend several for algae control in larger tanks. Quick Facts Scientific Name Neritina natalensis Origin East Africa (wild-caught) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful; plant-safe Adult Size Up to 1" Lifespan 1–2+ years Diet Algae eater (also eats algae wafers) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.5 (hard water for healthy shells) Breeding Lays small white eggs on hard surfaces, but they won't hatch in freshwater, so nerites won't overrun the tank Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Nerites do well in most established tanks with algae to graze. Keep the water hard and alkaline for healthy shells, and keep a lid on the tank, since nerites sometimes climb out. If one flips onto its back, turn it over, since some can't right themselves. Feeding: Nerites mostly graze on algae. If the tank is very clean, add algae wafers so they don't go hungry. Tankmates: Nerites get along with peaceful fish, shrimp and other snails. Avoid puffers, loaches and large cichlids, which eat snails, and keep them away from assassin snails. Good to know: Remove snails before treating the tank with copper or other medications, which are toxic to invertebrates.

The thorny tricolor snail, also called the horned nerite snail, is a small algae eater that only grows to 1/2 inch. These aquarium snails are popular for small tanks, however, as they are attractive and eat quite a bit of scum algae (algae on the glass walls). These are terrific snails for little tanks but will get lost in large fish tanks. This class of freshwater snail is plant-safe and can handle fresh and light brackish water conditions. Quick Facts Scientific Name Clithon diadema Origin Indo-Pacific (Philippines and Indonesia; wild-caught) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful; plant-safe Adult Size Up to ½–¾" Lifespan 1–2+ years Diet Algae eater (also eats algae wafers) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.5 Breeding Lays small white eggs that won't hatch in freshwater Shipping Size Approx. ¼–½" Care Guide Tank setup: Keep the water hard and alkaline for healthy shells, and keep a lid on the tank, since nerites sometimes climb out. Feeding: They graze on algae. In a very clean tank, add algae wafers so they don't go hungry. Tankmates: They are ideal tankmates for shrimp and small peaceful fish. Avoid puffers, loaches and assassin snails. Good to know: Their small "horns" are part of the shell. Remove snails before treating the tank with copper or other medications.

The thorny sunshine snail, also called a horned nerite snail, or simply the sun snail, is an aggressive (if you can use that word for a snail) algae eater. These snails are the same size as the nerite family, with similar care requirements. Sun snails are more difficult to breed and so command a slightly higher price than the nerite snail. These are SMALL snails and great for small tanks, but they will get lost in larger tanks. Clithon snails are plant-safe and can handle fresh and light brackish water conditions. Quick Facts Scientific Name Clithon sp. (sold as C. subgranosa ) Origin Indo-Pacific (Philippines and Indonesia; wild-caught) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful; plant-safe Adult Size Up to ¾" Lifespan 1–2+ years Diet Algae eater (also eats algae wafers) Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.5 Breeding Lays small white eggs that won't hatch in freshwater Shipping Size Approx. ¼–½" Care Guide Tank setup: Keep the water hard and alkaline for healthy shells, and keep a lid on the tank, since nerites sometimes climb out. Feeding: They graze on algae. In a very clean tank, add algae wafers so they don't go hungry. Tankmates: They are ideal tankmates for shrimp and small peaceful fish. Avoid puffers, loaches and assassin snails. Good to know: Their small "horns" are part of the shell. Remove snails before treating the tank with copper or other medications.

The orange rabbit snail is carefully selected for a solid chocolate shell and clean orange body. Lesser grades are sold as yellow rabbit snails, but who wants a lesser rabbit? However, the yellow rabbit is not a bad snail; it just has defects on the shell. These snails are larger than most freshwater aquatic species and are effective scavengers. Quick Facts Scientific Name Tylomelania sp. Origin Sulawesi, Indonesia Care Level Moderate (needs warm water) Temperament Peaceful; may nibble soft plants Adult Size Up to 3–4" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Scavenger (sinking pellets, algae wafers) Water Temperature 76–84°F pH 7.2–8.5 Breeding Livebearer; slowly produces one baby at a time, so it won't overrun the tank Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Rabbit snails come from warm, clean lakes in Sulawesi. Give them a soft sand bottom they can burrow in, warm water (76–84°F) and good water quality. Add calcium if your water is soft. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets and algae wafers daily. Rabbit snails are big eaters and also clean up leftover food. Tankmates: Rabbit snails do well with peaceful fish, shrimp and other snails that like warm water, such as discus and tetras. Avoid puffers, loaches and large cichlids. Good to know: Rabbit snails are slow-moving and gentle, and they wave their long "ear-like" tentacles as they move. Remove snails before using copper or other medications.

The Chinese algae eater is an adequate algae eater until this fish reaches a size of about three inches, when it becomes a scavenger. Also, Chinese algae eaters become aggressive, so these fish will work well as scavengers in a larger fish tank but may not be suitable for small fish tanks. Most Chinese algae eaters come from streams in Thailand, not China. Quick Facts Scientific Name Gyrinocheilus aymonieri Origin Thailand, Laos, Cambodia and Vietnam Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful when young; territorial and aggressive as adults Adult Size Up to 10–11" Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore (grazes on algae) Water Temperature 74–80°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single (adults fight with each other) Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them driftwood, rocks, caves and good current. Keep a lid on the tank. Feeding: Young fish graze on algae, but adults eat less algae and more prepared food. Feed algae wafers and sinking pellets daily. Well-fed adults are less likely to bother other fish. Tankmates: Chinese algae eaters do best with fast, robust fish like larger barbs, danios and semi-aggressive cichlids. Avoid slow, flat-sided fish like angelfish, discus and goldfish, which adults may latch onto and harm. Good to know: Chinese algae eaters are not from China; most come from Thailand and nearby countries. Their algae-eating slows as they grow.

The gold algae eater is a color morph of the Chinese algae eater and is bred in Thailand for the aquarium market. This fish will not grow quite as large as the standard Chinese algae eater, and gold algae eaters are less aggressive and better algae eaters. Quick Facts Scientific Name Gyrinocheilus aymonieri (gold variety) Origin Aquarium-bred (Thailand) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful when young; territorial and aggressive as adults Adult Size Up to 8–10" Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore (grazes on algae) Water Temperature 74–80°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single (adults fight with each other) Shipping Size Approx. 1–2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them driftwood, rocks, caves and good current. Keep a lid on the tank. Feeding: Young fish graze on algae, but adults eat less algae and more prepared food. Feed algae wafers and sinking pellets daily. Well-fed adults are less likely to bother other fish. Tankmates: Chinese algae eaters do best with fast, robust fish like larger barbs, danios and semi-aggressive cichlids. Avoid slow, flat-sided fish like angelfish, discus and goldfish, which adults may latch onto and harm. Good to know: Chinese algae eaters are not from China; most come from Thailand and nearby countries. Their algae-eating slows as they grow.

The white blizzard lobster is a magnificent pet with a solid white body. In the aquarium, at the least they are a brat, and at worst a serial killer. These lobsters will attack sleeping small prey, so white blizzards are only suitable with tolerant larger species. Technically in the same order as shrimp, they cannot be kept with fancy aquarium shrimp. Snails are okay. Quick Facts Scientific Name Procambarus clarkii Origin Captive-bred (Florida) Care Level Easy Temperament Aggressive Adult Size Up to 5–6" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (scavenger) Water Temperature 65–80°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 3" Care Guide Tank setup: Crayfish need plenty of hiding places like caves or pipes and a tight-fitting lid, since they climb out. Avoid copper-based medications. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets once a day. They also eat vegetables and leftover food. Tankmates: Crayfish will catch and eat slow fish, shrimp and snails. They are best kept alone. Molting: Crayfish shed their shell to grow. Leave the old shell in the tank; they eat it to regain calcium. Good to know: These "lobsters" are actually a color form of the red swamp crayfish.

The barred bichir, armored bichir, or banded bichir is an elongated fish found in the Congo River, specifically in the upper and middle portions. This species is one of the more commonly available to the aquarium hobbyist. All bichirs look like prehistoric dragons with just a little variance in size and color pattern. They generally live a long time, get along with any fish that cannot fit into their mouth, and so make an excellent addition to a large fish tank. They are easy to take care of and feed. The dilemma in purchasing odd large fish is that they are usually available in smaller sizes and need to grow with the tank. Best to match them with appropriate sizes of other species, for instance, match a five-inch bichir to medium-size cichlids, and a foot-long bichir to larger fish. Medium size is 4 to 6”, large size is 12” or more. Quick Facts Scientific Name Polypterus delhezi Origin Congo River basin, Africa Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful with fish its size Adult Size Up to 14–16" Lifespan 15+ years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 3" Care Guide Tank setup: Bichirs are expert escape artists, so a tight-fitting lid is a must. Give them a soft bottom, caves and driftwood. They breathe air, so leave a gap above the water. Feeding: Feed sinking carnivore pellets once a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and shrimp. Tankmates: They will eat any fish that fits in their mouth. Keep them with fish too large to swallow. Breathes air: Bichirs take gulps of air from the surface, which is normal behavior. Good to know: Delhezi bichirs have bold dark bands that stay crisp as they grow.

Also known as a duckbill sleeper, or upside-down sleeper, it is a species of sleeper goby that are native to brackish and freshwater coastal habitats. Quick Facts Scientific Name Butis butis Origin Coastal Indian Ocean and western Pacific Care Level Moderate Temperament Predatory (eats small fish) Adult Size Up to 5–6" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.5–8.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 2–3½" Care Guide Tank setup: Crazy fish do best in slightly salty (brackish) water. Give them plants, roots or driftwood to cling to, and a lid. Feeding: Feed meaty foods like frozen bloodworms and shrimp once a day. Some learn to take sinking pellets. Tankmates: They will eat small fish. Keep them with other brackish fish too large to swallow. Good to know: Crazy fish often hang upside down or sideways along roots and plants, which is how they got their name.

Male Cherry Barbs become a nice light cherry red color, while the females are a tan color. Therefore, the males command a slightly higher price than females. Unlike some fish species, male cherry barbs do not require the presence of females to promote their colors. Quick Facts Scientific Name Puntius titteya Origin Sri Lanka Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful, a bit shy Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 4–6 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 73–81°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a filter, a heater and plenty of plants. They feel safest with places to hide and show more color in a planted tank. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other small, peaceful fish such as rasboras, small tetras, corydoras and dwarf shrimp. Avoid large or boisterous fish and fin-nippers. Good to know: Cherry barbs are one of the most peaceful barbs, so they mix well with small community fish and shrimp-safe planted tanks. Males color up most when a few females are around.

The Asians created GloFish® by splicing the genes of Zebra Danios and Hi-Fin White Skirt Tetras and Tiger Barbs with phosphorescent corals and jellyfish. The fish were patented and licensed for sale in the USA several years ago once the FDA determined them to be safe for the environment. Though these fish do not actually glow in the dark, they are truly fluorescent and will keep that bright color throughout their lifespan. When they breed, even the babies feature the same fluorescence. Spooky. Quick Facts Scientific Name Puntigrus tetrazona (genetically modified) Origin Bred in the USA from tiger barbs Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Semi-aggressive (fin-nipper) Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 5–7 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group (helps prevent fin-nipping) Shipping Size Approx. 1¼" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a filter, a heater and plenty of open swimming space. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Pick fast, sturdy tankmates such as other barbs, danios, loaches, corydoras and larger tetras. Avoid slow, long-finned fish like bettas, angelfish, gouramis and guppies. Good to know: GloFish colors look brightest under a blue or actinic LED light. They have the same care needs and temperament as regular tiger barbs.

The Asians created GloFish® by splicing the genes of zebra danios and hi-fin white skirt tetras and tiger barbs with phosphorescent corals and jellyfish. The fish were patented and licensed for sale in the USA several years ago once the FDA determined them to be safe for the environment. Though these fish do not actually glow in the dark, they are truly fluorescent and will keep that bright color throughout their lifespan. Cosmic Blue GloFish Danios are hardy, and their color never fades. Quick Facts Scientific Name Danio rerio (genetically modified) Origin Farm-raised (genetically modified) Care Level Very easy, great for beginners Temperament Peaceful, very active Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 64–77°F (often fine without a heater) pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Danios are fast swimmers, so give them open swimming space, a filter, plants around the edges and a tight-fitting lid, since they jump. Make sure the tank is fully cycled (which takes several weeks) before adding fish. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Danios get along with most peaceful community fish, such as tetras, rasboras, barbs, corydoras and livebearers. Their speed can stress slow, long-finned fish like bettas and fancy guppies, and large predatory fish will eat them. Good to know: GloFish colors look brightest under a blue or actinic LED light. Care is the same as for any zebra danio. Danios are fast and jump when startled, so keep a lid on the tank.

The Galactic Purple Glo Shark is a gene-spliced albino rainbow shark. Rainbow sharks from Indonesia have deep red fins on a silver body. These sharks are actually catfish and are hardy and easy to keep and peaceful. The rainbow shark grows to about six inches. On the other hand, Purple Glo Sharks are a solid purple and keep this color throughout their lives. In fact, if a Purple Glo Shark breeds with another Purple Glo Shark, they make baby purple glo sharks. Weird science. Quick Facts Scientific Name Epalzeorhynchos frenatum (genetically modified) Origin Farm-raised (genetically modified) Care Level Moderate Temperament Semi-aggressive, territorial (especially toward other sharks) Adult Size Up to 6" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Keep one per tank Shipping Size Approx. 3" Care Guide Tank setup: Rainbow sharks patrol a territory, so give one caves, driftwood and plants to break up sight lines, plus a tight lid. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets or wafers and a quality flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy algae wafers and frozen bloodworms. Tankmates: Keep only one rainbow shark per tank, and avoid other bottom-dwelling sharks and territorial fish like red-tailed sharks. They do best with fast, mid- to upper-level swimmers such as danios, barbs, rainbowfish and larger tetras. Good to know: GloFish sharks are rainbow sharks, which are members of the carp family, not true sharks or catfish. They claim a territory near the bottom and chase other bottom dwellers, so give them caves and keep only one per tank. GloFish colors look brightest under a blue or actinic LED light, but they are colorful under normal lighting too.

Celestial danios, or galaxy danios, are small, beautiful aquarium pets. Also called galaxy rasboras, these small aquarium fish have a starry night pattern on the body. Celestials are some of the most popular small schooling fish in the aquarium trade, extremely popular for planted and nano tanks. These rasboras (technically danios) look best in small planted aquariums, and they get along with fancy shrimp and other gentle tank mates. Quick Facts Scientific Name Danio margaritatus Origin Myanmar (Shan Plateau) Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 72–78°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: These fish come from cool, clear, hard-water lakes and ponds in Myanmar. Give them dense plants, gentle filtration and plenty of cover. They do not need very warm water, and stable, slightly alkaline water suits them. Feeding: Feed crushed flake or micro pellets once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other small, peaceful fish that like similar water, such as celestial pearl danios, micro rasboras, small livebearers and dwarf shrimp. Avoid large or boisterous fish. Good to know: They are a little shy at first; plenty of plants and a group of their own kind help them settle in and color up.

The purple harlequin rasbora, also known as the black harlequin rasbora, is a rare color variant of the harlequin rasbora. The color really depends on the light reflecting off the body, which displays a purple hue and a black surface. Though these fish do occur in the wilds of Borneo and elsewhere, with color shades varying from purple to black, the purple harlequin in the fish trade is captive-bred. The purple hue on the body of the rasbora gets richer as the fish ages. This species gets along with nearly every species and grows large enough to keep in a larger community fish tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name Trigonostigma heteromorpha (purple variety) Origin Southeast Asia (captive-bred) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1¼" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a dark substrate. Soft, slightly acidic water and gentle filtration bring out their best color. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as tetras, other rasboras, danios, corydoras, gouramis and dwarf shrimp. Avoid large predatory fish that could eat them. Good to know: In a well-planted tank a school of rasboras swims together in the middle of the tank, and their colors deepen as they settle in.

Glowlight Danios, sometimes called the Glolight Danio, are one of the original nano tank species featuring remarkable coloration, particularly in a planted aquarium. These small danios are schooling fish, and we recommend a school of four or more. The Glowlight Danio will get along with fancy shrimp and other gentle tank mates. These fish were once called Danio Choprae after collector Dr. Chopra who discovered them in the mountain rivers of Myanmar (Burma at the time). Glowlight Danios are stunning schooling fish and stand out with darker backgrounds and plants. Quick Facts Scientific Name Danio choprae Origin Myanmar Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1¼" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 68–79°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ¾–1" Care Guide Tank setup: Danios are fast swimmers, so give them open swimming space, plants around the edges and a tight-fitting lid, since they jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish, such as other danios, rasboras, tetras, barbs, corydoras and livebearers. Good to know: Glowlight danios have bright orange and blue-green bars that look their best in a planted tank.

White cloud minnows are popular and hardy schooling fish found throughout the global aquatic community. Unfortunately, these fish may be extinct in the wild. Like many Asian species, white clouds are kept in existence by our hobby alone. The fish was discovered on White Cloud Mountain in China during a scouting trip by a Boy Scout named Tan, hence the scientific name Tanichthys . White clouds are hardy, handle a wide range of temperatures and eat flake food. Quick Facts Scientific Name Tanichthys albonubes Origin Southern China and northern Vietnam (aquarium-bred) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1½" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 64–75°F (no heater needed in most homes) pH 6.5–8.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants and gentle filtration. These are cool-water fish that do fine at room temperature, and they also do well in outdoor ponds and patio tubs in warm months. Keep a lid on the tank. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with other small, peaceful fish like ricefish, danios, small rasboras, and dwarf shrimp, and can share an unheated tank with other cool-water species. Avoid large fish (including goldfish) that may eat them. Good to know: White clouds have been kept in aquariums since the 1930s and are one of the hardiest small fish in the hobby. Males show the brightest color when they display to each other.

Gold white cloud minnows, also called albino white clouds, are hardy, easy to breed and make a tight school in the aquarium. Gold white clouds are bred to produce a pink and gold body. Quick Facts Scientific Name Tanichthys albonubes (gold variety) Origin Southern China and northern Vietnam (aquarium-bred) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1½" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 64–75°F (no heater needed in most homes) pH 6.5–8.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants and gentle filtration. These are cool-water fish that do fine at room temperature, and they also do well in outdoor ponds and patio tubs in warm months. Keep a lid on the tank. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Avoid large fish (including goldfish) that may eat them. Good to know: White clouds have been kept in aquariums since the 1930s and are one of the hardiest small fish in the hobby. Males show the brightest color when they display to each other.

The elegant long fin white cloud is a feat of selective breeding and as the fish ages the fins become longer and longer. As hardy as the parent white cloud and the gold white cloud variation, the long fin white cloud is just a bit more expensive. Quick Facts Scientific Name Tanichthys albonubes (long fin variety) Origin Southern China and northern Vietnam (aquarium-bred) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1½" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 64–75°F (no heater needed in most homes) pH 6.5–8.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants and gentle filtration. These are cool-water fish that do fine at room temperature, and they also do well in outdoor ponds and patio tubs in warm months. Keep a lid on the tank. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with other small, peaceful fish like ricefish, danios, small rasboras, and dwarf shrimp, and can share an unheated tank with other cool-water species. Ghost shrimp, or Florida glass shrimp, are trapped in Florida growing ponds and sold either as interesting small scavengers for the aquarium or as live feeders for saltwater and freshwater predator fish. At AquariumFish.com we package these shrimp at an amount and a price so the hobbyist can decide their fate. These shrimp are peaceful to other fish, but it is NOT advisable to place them with fancy colored Asian shrimp. Each order comes with a bag of twenty live ghost shrimp. Quick Facts Scientific Name Palaemonetes paludosus Origin Southeastern United States (Florida ponds) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful with fish; may eat baby shrimp and fry Adult Size Up to 1½" Lifespan About 1 year Diet Omnivore (scavenger) Water Temperature 65–80°F pH 7.0–8.0 Water Hardness GH 6–15 Group Size Sold as a pack of 20 Shipping Size Approx. ½–1" Care Guide Tank setup: Ghost shrimp are hardy. Give them a cycled tank with plants and hiding spots, and cover filter intakes with a sponge. Feeding: Feed small sinking pellets, flake or algae wafers once a day. They also scavenge leftover food. Tankmates: Ghost shrimp do well with peaceful community fish. They may eat baby shrimp and fry, so don't keep them with fancy shrimp you want to breed. Good to know: Ghost shrimp are nearly transparent, so you can see their food moving through their body as they eat.

As the sulphur head peacock cichlid matures, the blazing band of color on the head and dorsal becomes more vibrant. The body gets a darker blue. The blaze can be yellow or white. Quick Facts Scientific Name Aulonocara maylandi Origin Lake Malawi, Africa Care Level Easy Temperament Semi-aggressive Adult Size Up to 4–5" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 76–82°F pH 7.8–8.6 Group Size Keep more females than males Shipping Size Approx. 2–4" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a sand bottom, rocks and open swimming space. African cichlids need hard, alkaline water; crushed coral or aragonite sand helps hold the pH up. Feeding: Feed a quality cichlid pellet or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Peacocks are among the calmer African cichlids. Keep them with other peacocks, haps and calm mbuna. Good to know: Peacock cichlids show their adult colors at around three inches, and males are much more colorful than females.

Zebra Lace Angelfish have longer fins than the silver angelfish and a dot and dash pattern on the body. Zebra Lace Angels are hardy and grow to about eight inches in the aquarium. The jumbo size often has the blue color gene present on the dorsal fin. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pterophyllum scalare Origin Amazon basin, South America (captive-bred) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Semi-aggressive (territorial when pairing) Adult Size Up to 6" long and 8" tall Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Shipping Size Medium: approx. 1½" · Large: approx. 2" · Jumbo: approx. 4" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them tall plants or driftwood, a heater and a gentle filter. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Choose peaceful fish too large to swallow, such as larger tetras, corydoras, plecos, rams, gouramis and peaceful barbs. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs, and small fish like neon tetras that adult angels may eat. Breeding: Angelfish pair off and lay eggs on flat surfaces like broad leaves or slate. A breeding pair can become territorial, so give them room and places for other fish to retreat. Good to know: Adult angelfish will eat any fish small enough to fit in their mouths, including neon tetras, so choose tankmates that are too big to swallow.

Male powder blue dwarf gourami feature a solid reflective light blue body with blue fins. We ship only colorful male dwarf gouramis, whether neon blue, standard dwarf, powder blue, or red flame. Female dwarf gouramis are sold separately at a lower price. Females are a solid tan color and will breed with any of the previously mentioned males; with their plain color, they cannot afford to be picky. Powder blue dwarf gourami are hardy and very peaceful members of any community tank or planted aquarium. Quick Facts Scientific Name Trichogaster lalius Origin India and Bangladesh Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful (males can be territorial) Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 4–6 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Breathes Air Yes – labyrinth fish take air from the surface Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and plenty of plants, including floating plants. Keep a lid on the tank and leave a gap of air above the water, since gouramis breathe from the surface. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with small, peaceful fish such as rasboras, small tetras, corydoras and otocinclus. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs and other male dwarf gouramis. Good to know: Males can squabble with each other, so keep one male per tank, or several only in a heavily planted tank with lots of hiding places.

Male dwarf gourami feature a blue body with red vertical stripes and blue fins. Female dwarf gourami are sold separately at a lower price. Females are a solid tan color. Dwarf gourami are peaceful and easy to take care of and are suitable for nearly every type of freshwater aquarium. Quick Facts Scientific Name Trichogaster lalius Origin India and Bangladesh Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful (males can be territorial) Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 4–6 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Breathes Air Yes – labyrinth fish take air from the surface Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and plenty of plants, including floating plants. Keep a lid on the tank and leave a gap of air above the water, since gouramis breathe from the surface. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with small, peaceful fish such as rasboras, small tetras, corydoras and otocinclus. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs and other male dwarf gouramis. Good to know: Males can squabble with each other, so keep one male per tank, or several only in a heavily planted tank with lots of hiding places.

The giant gourami looks like an ugly gentle giant when it gains its massive size, but looks are deceiving. Giant gourami have a lot of personality and are a favorite single fish pet. The giant gourami is an ideal pet for large species fish tanks where everyone is tough enough to respect each other. The fish comes from Indonesia, where it is more popular for taste than personality. In fact, the giant gourami is an important source of food for the natives of that region. So, if he gets too rough for the fish tank.... These fish are easy to care for and eat just about anything. Be prepared to have them for a long, long time. Quick Facts Scientific Name Osphronemus goramy Origin Southeast Asia Care Level Easy (but grows very large) Temperament Peaceful when young; territorial as adults Adult Size Up to 24" Lifespan 15–20+ years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 6.5–8.0 Breathes Air Yes – labyrinth fish take air from the surface Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Giant gouramis start small but can reach two feet, so they need very strong filtration. Keep a lid on the tank and leave a gap of air above the water, since gouramis breathe from the surface. Feeding: Feed a quality pellet or flake with plenty of vegetable content once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods now and then. Tankmates: Young giant gouramis are peaceful, but adults need equally large, robust tankmates such as large catfish, oscars or arowanas. Anything small will be eaten. Good to know: Giant gouramis grow fast and learn to recognize their owners, which is why they are kept as single "pet fish."

Sparkling gourami, also called dwarf sparkling gourami and pygmy sparkling gourami, adapt to almost all freshwater aquarium conditions and eat flake food. Gourami are not generally schooling fish, but a group of these bright little gems makes a colorful display in the small aquatic setting. The sparkling gourami will only grow to one inch and may be kept with peaceful tank mates, including exotic freshwater shrimp. Quick Facts Scientific Name Trichopsis pumila Origin Southeast Asia Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1½" Lifespan 4–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Breathes Air Yes – labyrinth fish take air from the surface Shipping Size Approx. ¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and plenty of plants, including some floating plants for cover. Keep a lid on the tank and leave a gap of air above the water, since gouramis breathe from the surface. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with small, peaceful fish such as rasboras, small tetras, corydoras and otocinclus. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs and larger, boisterous fish. Good to know: Sparkling gouramis are also called pygmy croaking gouramis because males make soft croaking sounds when they display to each other.

The flowing fins, particularly on the males, earn the fish its name. The curvature of the dorsal fins is reminiscent of a robed emperor. These fish need to be kept in a school to keep them happy. Simply giving them homework will not do the trick. Quick Facts Scientific Name Nematobrycon palmeri Origin Pacific slope of Colombia (San Juan and Atrato rivers) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a dark substrate, which brings out their color. Keep a lid on the tank, since tetras can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, rasboras, danios, corydoras, dwarf cichlids, gouramis and livebearers. Good to know: Tetras feel safer and show better color in a group. A larger school also spreads out any chasing.

The long-fin serpae tetra has the same bold red and black colors as the parent serpae tetra, but these aquarium fish have been bred to develop long, flowing fins. Usually harmless, these fish tend to chase around smaller peaceful fish. The long-fin serpae tetra is also called the long-fin red minor. Good to know: Tetras feel safer and show better color in a group. A larger school also spreads out any chasing.

One cannot tell from a picture of a single fish, but the penguin is the first thing that comes to mind when a school of these fish is observed. The half-black tail and the shaky movements of this tetra earn the name. Quick Facts Scientific Name Thayeria boehlkei Origin Amazon basin (Peru, Brazil) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a dark substrate, which brings out their color. Keep a lid on the tank, since tetras can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, rasboras, danios, corydoras, dwarf cichlids, gouramis and livebearers. Good to know: Tetras feel safer and show better color in a group. A larger school also spreads out any chasing.

The blue king tetra, or simply the blue tetra, is prolific in the Amazon basin and very hardy for a wild-caught fish. These tetras grow to nearly two inches and feature a pale blue body with black and white caudal (tail) fins. The color of the fins does not stand out until the fish is about one year of age. Asian imports are cheaper, but these fish tend to be washed out in color. Blue tetras from AquariumFish.com are imported from the Amazon basin through Belém, Brazil. Quick Facts Scientific Name Boehlkea fredcochui Origin Upper Amazon (Peru, Colombia) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful but active Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 5–10 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1¼" Care Guide Tank setup: These are larger, active schooling fish, so give them open swimming space, plants or driftwood along the back and a tight-fitting lid, since they jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They do well with other active, similar-size fish such as larger tetras, barbs, rainbowfish, peaceful cichlids, corydoras and plecos. Very small fish may be eaten or bullied. Good to know: Larger tetras are hardy and long-lived, and a big school makes a striking display.

The green fire tetra is popular for its unique green color, unusual for freshwater fish. Just to complete the picture, the green fire tetra has bright red shading along with the green body. Once wild-caught in Brazil, most green fire tetras are imported from a fish farm in Asia. The bred fish do hold their color and tend to be very stable and hardy in most aquarium conditions. Quick Facts Scientific Name Aphyocharax rathbuni Origin Paraguay and Paraná basins (Paraguay, Brazil) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1¾" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a dark substrate, which brings out their color. Keep a lid on the tank, since tetras can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, rasboras, danios, corydoras, dwarf cichlids, gouramis and livebearers. Good to know: Tetras feel safer and show better color in a group. A larger school also spreads out any chasing.

The ember tetra was once more commonly called the amandae tetra, before the fish was successfully bred in Singapore. The amandae tetra was discovered by the famous fish finder Heiko Bleher back in 1987, and he named the tetra after his mom, Amanda. These bright red little fish make a pretty school and stand out in a planted tank with driftwood. Ember tetras are hardy and peaceful and may be kept with small species such as fancy exotic shrimp. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hyphessobrycon amandae Origin Araguaia River basin, Brazil Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to ¾" Lifespan 2–4 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 5.5–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: These small tetras do best in a planted tank with soft, slightly acidic water, a dark substrate, driftwood, floating plants and gentle filtration. A larger school makes them more confident and colorful. Feeding: Feed small amounts of micro pellets or crushed flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other small, peaceful fish like rasboras, small tetras, pencilfish, pygmy corydoras, otocinclus and dwarf shrimp. Avoid large or boisterous fish that could eat or bully them. Good to know: Small tetras show their best color in a large school in a planted tank with soft lighting.

The gold tetra, also called the brass tetra or the golden tetra, is often found in the trade as an imported tank-raised species. Unfortunately, the bred tetras simply do not have color. We import wild gold tetras from Brazil, where they tend to have the most color. Size can vary within one school of fish, since they are wild-caught, but these fish will hold their magnificent 24-karat color. Actually, the color shade varies depending upon where they are caught; hence sometimes they are gold, sometimes brass. These are peaceful fish that will not even harm nano tank species but are fast enough to be kept with small and mid-size cichlids. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hemigrammus rodwayi Origin Guyana, Suriname, French Guiana and Brazil Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a dark substrate, which brings out their color. Keep a lid on the tank, since tetras can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, rasboras, danios, corydoras, dwarf cichlids, gouramis and livebearers. Good to know: Tetras feel safer and show better color in a group. A larger school also spreads out any chasing.

AquariumFish.com imports red phantom tetras from Colombia, where they seem to have the most vibrant red. Males have solid red dorsal fins that are a tad higher than the females', and the females have white- and black-tipped dorsal fins. Red phantom tetras swim in schools of six or more and generally move around the mid-level of the aquarium. Keep a lid on the tank, since tetras can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, rasboras, danios, corydoras, dwarf cichlids, gouramis and livebearers. Good to know: Tetras feel safer and show better color in a group. A larger school also spreads out any chasing.

The black phantom tetra displays large dorsal fins for such a small fish, and a small school of these "large"-finned tetras makes a very nice display. Keep a lid on the tank, since tetras can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes.
