Compatibility: While peaceful as a juvenile, this fish will consume any crustacean, mollusk, worm, or fish small enough to fit in its large mouth as it grows, making it **NOT Reef Safe**. It is also easily intimidated by overly aggressive tank mates. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Plectorhinchus chaetodonoides Common Names: Harlequin Sweetlips, Clown Sweetlips, Harlequin Sweetlips Origin: Indo-Pacific Max Size: Up to 28 inches Temperament: Semi-Aggressive (as an adult predator) Diet: Carnivore (Difficult to feed; requires live/meaty foods) Minimum Tank Size: 500+ Gallons (Expert Only)

The Filamentosa Barb is also called the Mascara Barb or Black Spot Barb, but the true Mascara Barb is a slightly different species called Daw. assimilis. Similar in appearance and behavior, the Mascara Barb is a bit less common and has more color along the lateral line of the body, and male mascara barbs do not sport as long a dorsal fin. The male Filamentosa Barb gets a lacy, long, colorful dorsal fin (hence Filamentosa) and color highlights on the body that look like makeup (hence it is sometimes called the Mascara Barb). These barbs are rare and wild from India and seldom seen in the trade, one reason they are a bit pricey. The good news is that these fish are hardy and adapt well to aquariums. Quick Facts Scientific Name Dawkinsia filamentosa Origin Southwestern India Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful, very active Adult Size Up to 5" Lifespan 6–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 70–77°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: These barbs grow large and swim fast, so give them lots of open space, strong filtration and a tight-fitting lid, since they can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with similar-sized, active fish such as rainbowfish, larger barbs, larger tetras, loaches and peaceful cichlids. Very small fish may be eaten or stressed. Good to know: Males grow the long, threadlike dorsal fin as they mature, so young fish may not show it yet.

Similar to the filamentosa barbs, the teardrop barb is even rarer and larger. Also called the Rohani Barb, these fish are seldom seen in the aquarium trade. Larger barbs are hardy schooling fish that require room to swim; they are not suited to aquariums under 20 gallons. Quick Facts Scientific Name Dawkinsia rohani Origin Southern India Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful, active Adult Size Up to 4" Lifespan 6–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1–2" Care Guide Tank setup: These barbs grow large and swim fast, so give them lots of open space, strong filtration and a tight-fitting lid, since they can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with similar-sized, active fish such as rainbowfish, larger barbs, larger tetras, loaches and peaceful cichlids. Very small fish may be eaten or stressed. Good to know: Teardrop barbs are rare in the trade. Like their filamentosa cousins, they need clean water and plenty of swimming room.

In the wilds of the Amazon River basin, the actual wild oscar is black with some white, hence the name zebra oscar. These oscars are less common than the tank-raised tiger and red oscars. Wild oscars are active and hardy and share the same characteristics as the aquarium-bred varieties. When larger, wild oscars get a bold red dot on the tail. Quick Facts Scientific Name Astronotus ocellatus (wild type) Origin Amazon basin, South America Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Semi-aggressive; eats smaller fish Adult Size Up to 12–14" Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods; takes pellets) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single or pair Shipping Size Small: 1½" · Medium: approx. 2" · Large: 4" Care Guide Tank setup: Use a sand bottom, a few large rocks or driftwood, strong filtration and a tight lid, since they can jump. Oscars often rearrange decorations and uproot plants. Feeding: Feed a quality cichlid pellet once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like shrimp. Avoid feeder goldfish, which can carry disease. Tankmates: Oscars can live with other large, peaceful-to-semi-aggressive fish like silver dollars, large plecos, severums and other oscars. They will eat any fish that fits in their mouth. Good to know: Oscars are known as "water puppies" for their personality and often learn to recognize their owners and beg for food.

It took a few years after the tiger oscar, but the yellow pigment was finally bred into this beautiful cichlid, and though these fish are a bit pricier than the other colors, the sight is worth the money. Lemon oscars will retain their lemon color throughout their life span. Quick Facts Scientific Name Astronotus ocellatus (lemon variety) Origin Amazon basin, South America; aquarium-bred Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Semi-aggressive; eats smaller fish Adult Size Up to 12–14" Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods; takes pellets) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single or pair Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Use a sand bottom, a few large rocks or driftwood, strong filtration and a tight lid, since they can jump. Oscars often rearrange decorations and uproot plants. Feeding: Feed a quality cichlid pellet once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like shrimp. Avoid feeder goldfish, which can carry disease. Tankmates: Oscars can live with other large, peaceful-to-semi-aggressive fish like silver dollars, large plecos, severums and other oscars. They will eat any fish that fits in their mouth. Good to know: Oscars are known as "water puppies" for their personality and often learn to recognize their owners and beg for food.

Fuzzy Dwarf Lionfish: The Small, Personal Predator The Fuzzy Dwarf Lionfish (Dendrochirus brachypterus) is one of the most popular and manageable lionfish species available to marine hobbyists. Its common name comes from the small, fleshy, fuzzy-looking appendages on its head and fins, which aid in camouflage. Also known as the Shortfin Lionfish or Dwarf Lionfish , this species typically displays a striking mottled pattern of red, black, and white, with color variations ranging from dark brown to rare yellows. Native to the Indo-Pacific, the Fuzzy Dwarf Lionfish is a smaller, more sedentary predator, reaching a maximum size of 6 to 7 inches (15–18 cm). Its smaller adult size makes it suitable for smaller predator systems than its larger Pterois cousins, requiring a minimum aquarium size of 50 gallons or more. Like all lionfish, it is a cryptic, nocturnal hunter that prefers dim lighting and plenty of rockwork, caves, and overhangs where it can perch, often upside-down, waiting for prey. The Fuzzy Dwarf Lionfish is known for developing a surprising personality, quickly recognizing and responding to its owner, making it a true "pet" fish—but its venomous spines necessitate extreme caution. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: This fish is a dedicated Carnivore , primarily feeding on small crustaceans and fish in the wild. Initial feeding often requires live saltwater ghost shrimp or similar prey to stimulate a feeding response. It should be gradually weaned onto a captive diet of varied frozen, meaty foods, such as silversides , krill, raw shrimp, and squid. Use a feeding stick or tongs to target feed. Feeding: Due to a low metabolism, the Dwarf Lionfish only needs to be fed a large meal 2–3 times per week. **Never feed freshwater feeder fish** (like guppies or goldfish), as this leads to fatal nutritional deficiencies. Reef Compatibility: It is Reef Safe With Caution . While it will not bother corals, it will systematically hunt and consume ornamental shrimp, crabs, and any fish small enough to fit into its mouth. Temperament: It is Semi-Aggressive / Predatory . It is generally peaceful toward tankmates that are too large to be considered food (over half its body length). Do not house with aggressive fish (e.g., certain large triggers, large puffers) that may nip at its delicate fins. Venomous Spines: The sting is painful, often likened to a severe bee sting. If stung, the standard treatment is to soak the affected area in the hottest water you can tolerate (not scalding) for 30–90 minutes to break down the protein-based venom. Seek medical attention immediately. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Dendrochirus brachypterus Primary Common Name: Fuzzy Dwarf Lionfish Other Common Names: Shortfin Lionfish, Dwarf Lionfish, Shortfin Turkeyfish Origin: Indo-Pacific (Widespread) Max Size: 6-7 inches (15-18 cm) Temperament: Semi-Aggressive / Predatory ( Venomous ) Diet: Carnivore (Must be converted to frozen meaty foods) Minimum Tank Size: 50+ Gallons Reef Compatibility: With Caution (Eats all small invertebrates and fish)

Banded Pipefish: The Graceful Reef-Dweller The Banded Pipefish , Doryrhamphus dactyliophorus (often listed under the synonym Dunckerocampus dactyliophorus), is a stunning and graceful fish highly sought after by advanced marine aquarists. Distinguished by its long, slender body and striking color pattern, it is a fascinating member of the Syngnathidae family, which also includes seahorses. This species features a body banded with alternating red/black and white/yellow rings , culminating in a beautiful, oval or 'flag-like' tail fin that is typically red with a white margin and central spot . The Banded Pipefish is a "flagtail" or "reef" pipefish, making it a stronger swimmer than many of its pipefish and seahorse relatives. In the wild, it is often found in caves and under rocky overhangs on reef slopes throughout the Indo-Pacific, where it exhibits a unique behavior: cleaning parasites from larger fish. Due to its specialized feeding habits, the Banded Pipefish is considered an Expert-Only species. They require a stable, mature aquarium and a constant supply of live micro-fauna to thrive. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: This fish is a dedicated Carnivore with an extremely small, tubular mouth. Its diet must consist primarily of live foods , such as live copepods (like Tisbe, Tigriopus, or Apocyclops), enriched live baby brine shrimp, and rotifers. They are constant, slow feeders and will starve if they must compete with faster fish for food. Feeding: It is crucial to maintain a massive, constantly reproducing population of live copepods in the display tank and/or a connected refugium. While captive-bred specimens are sometimes trained to accept small frozen foods (like Cyclop-Eeze or tiny mysis shrimp), this must be supplemented with live fare. Reef Compatibility: It is Reef Safe With Caution. They pose no threat to corals but can be harmed by invertebrates with stinging tentacles, such as anemones or large corals like brain corals. They are generally safe with ornamental shrimp and snails but should be protected from larger, predatory inverts (like certain crabs). Temperament: It is Peaceful. The Banded Pipefish is highly social and should ideally be kept as a mated pair or in small groups. They should only be housed with very small, equally peaceful, and slow-moving tankmates, such as firefish, mandarins, seahorses, and non-aggressive gobies. Breeding: The Banded Pipefish is a pouch-brooder, meaning the female deposits her eggs into a specialized pouch on the male's underside, where he carries them until they hatch. Captive breeding is possible and preferred for increased hardiness. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Doryrhamphus dactyliophorus Primary Common Name: Banded Pipefish Other Common Names: Ringed Pipefish, Flagtail Pipefish, Red Banded Pipefish Origin: Indo-Pacific (Red Sea to Samoa, north to Japan, south to Australia) Max Size: Up to 7.5 inches (19 cm) Temperament: Peaceful (Best kept in pairs) Diet: Carnivore (Relies on a constant supply of live copepods ) Minimum Tank Size: 50+ Gallons (Highly stable, mature system recommended) Reef Compatibility: With Caution (Avoid stinging corals/anemones) Aquarist Level: Expert Only

Yellow Foxface Rabbitfish: The Algae Grazer with Venomous Spines The Yellow Foxface Rabbitfish (Siganus vulpinus), commonly referred to simply as the Foxface Lo or Foxface Rabbitfish , is a strikingly beautiful and highly beneficial marine fish. Recognizable by its elongated, fox-like snout and electric yellow body, it features a distinctive pattern of black and white markings covering its face and chest. The face marking often makes it look like it's wearing a black mask. Native to the coral-rich lagoons and seaward reefs of the Western Pacific (from Indonesia to the Great Barrier Reef), the Foxface is a popular choice for reef and FOWLR aquariums due to its peaceful temperament and prolific appetite for nuisance algae. This species is an active swimmer, growing to a maximum size of around 8 to 9 inches (20-23 cm). A minimum tank size of 100 to 125 gallons is recommended to provide ample swimming room and grazing territory. A notable feature of all Rabbitfish is the presence of 13 sharp, venomous dorsal spines (and spines on the anal and pelvic fins). While they are peaceful and use these spines only defensively, the sting is highly painful. Extreme caution must be exercised during handling or tank maintenance. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: The Foxface is primarily a Herbivore and a dedicated algae grazer. Its diet must be rich in plant matter to remain healthy and prevent head and lateral line erosion (HLLE). Provide plenty of quality marine algae, such as Nori sheets clipped to the tank glass, spirulina flakes, and herbivore pellets. Although it will accept meaty foods like mysis or brine shrimp, these should only be offered as an occasional supplement. Algae Control: This species is highly valued for its ability to consume certain types of nuisance algae, including hair algae and even some Bryopsis strains. Reef Compatibility: It is considered Reef Safe With Caution . While the Foxface generally ignores small fish and invertebrates, if underfed, it may begin to nip at the fleshy polyps of certain LPS (Large Polyp Stony) or soft corals like Xenia or Montipora. Keeping it well-fed on greens is the best way to mitigate this risk. Temperament: Peaceful with most tankmates, even semi-aggressive fish like Triggerfish or Groupers, as its venomous spines deter potential predators. It is generally intolerant of other Rabbitfish (conspecifics) and should be kept singly or as a bonded pair, requiring close monitoring if another Rabbitfish is introduced. Stress Behavior: When stressed or sleeping, the Foxface will rapidly change its coloration to a dark, mottled pattern of browns and blacks for camouflage. This is a natural response and not a sign of illness. Venomous Spines: If stung, immediately immerse the affected area in the hottest water you can tolerate (not scalding) for 30-90 minutes, as heat breaks down the protein-based venom. Seek medical attention immediately. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Siganus vulpinus Primary Common Name: Yellow Foxface Rabbitfish Other Common Names: Foxface Lo, Foxface, Common Foxface Origin: Western Pacific (Indo-Pacific, Great Barrier Reef) Max Size: 8-9 inches (20-23 cm) Temperament: Peaceful ( Venomous Spines ) Diet: Herbivore (Primarily algae/Nori) Minimum Tank Size: 100-125 Gallons Reef Compatibility: With Caution (May nip corals if underfed)

The Silver Hatchetfish is the only hatchet fish bred in captivity, and this is the hardiest of the hatchetfish family. Silver hatchets school at the top of the aquarium and eat flake food. These fish can jump, so we recommend a cover on the fish tank. Hatchet fish are peaceful and may be kept with nano tank species. Quick Facts Scientific Name Gasteropelecus sternicla Origin South America Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Hatchetfish live at the very surface, so give them floating plants, gentle filtration and a tight-fitting lid, since they are excellent jumpers. Feeding: Feed a quality floating flake once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy small frozen foods like brine shrimp. Tankmates: Hatchetfish are peaceful and get along with small community fish such as tetras, rasboras, corydoras and dwarf cichlids. Avoid fish that swim at the surface and might bully them. Good to know: Hatchetfish feel safest in a group and stay near the surface, so floating plants give them cover.

Hawaiian Cleaner Wrasse The Bicolor Cleaner Wrasse is also known as cleaner Wrasses, Bicolored Cleanerfish, Two-color Cleaner Wrasse, Two-color Cleanerfish, Two-colored Cleaner Wrasse, Two-colored Cleanerfish, Cleanerfish and Yellow Diesel Wrasse. This fish has been the focus of many research studies and are most commonly sold. The Bicolor Cleaner Wrasse forms a great symbiotic relationship with other reef fish by cleaning them of their unwanted parasites. They are the peaceful attractive fish with a most intriguing "dance" that they perform to solicit other fishes to allow them to remove parasites and other debris from those fishes body, fins, and mouths. Scientific Name: Labroides bicolor Origin: Bali Lifespan: 4 years Max Size: 2.5 inches Shipping Size: Approx. 2 inches Food: Live, Frozen and Flake

Gold Rim Tang: A Striking & Bold Algae Grazer The Gold Rim Tang (Acanthurus nigricans), also known as the White Cheek Tang, is a captivating and highly beneficial species that adds a touch of elegant beauty to any large marine aquarium . Its stunning appearance features a dark, almost black body with a distinct white "cheek" patch below its eye and a vibrant yellow caudal fin . This fish is known for its graceful swimming behavior and its constant grazing on algae, making it a valuable member of any cleanup crew. It is an excellent choice for a community reef tank, where it will leave corals and invertebrates completely unharmed while helping to keep nuisance algae in check. Why the Gold Rim Tang is a Great Choice: Elegant Appearance: Its beautiful coloration and graceful swimming create a captivating display. Natural Algae Control: It constantly grazes on algae, a valuable service for any tank. Active Behavior: It adds constant, peaceful movement to the water column. Reef-Safe: The God Rim Tang is completely safe to keep with all types of corals and invertebrates. Important Note: The Gold Rim Tang can be territorial and semi-aggressive, especially towards other tangs and fish of similar body shapes. It's best to introduce it to a large tank with ample swimming space and live rock for hiding. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Acanthurus nigricans Origin: Indo-Pacific Reefs Max Size: 8.5 inches Lifespan: 10 years or more Diet: Herbivore. Primarily feeds on marine algae. A varied diet of dried seaweed (nori) is essential. Shipping Size: 2-6 inches

Naso Tang: The Majestic & Graceful Unicornfish The Naso Tang (Naso lituratus), also known as the Orange Spined Unicornfish, is a majestic and highly sought-after species that adds a touch of elegance to any very large marine aquarium . This magnificent tang has a striking appearance, featuring a dark body with a vibrant yellow-orange mask over its eyes and an equally bright orange "scalpel" at the base of its tail. As it matures, it develops a long, graceful, lyre-shaped tail. The Naso Tang is a non-stop swimmer, gliding gracefully through the water column, and is a tireless algae grazer, making it a valuable part of the cleanup crew. Its generally peaceful nature and stunning visual presence make it a fantastic centerpiece for a well-established, spacious reef tank. Why the Naso Tang is a Great Choice: Graceful & Majestic: Its large size and elegant swimming style make it a captivating centerpiece. Striking Coloration: The vibrant orange facial stripe and tail spurs provide a beautiful contrast against its dark body. Natural Algae Control: It constantly grazes on algae, helping to maintain a clean and healthy environment. Peaceful Temperament: It is generally non-aggressive with other fish, making it a great community tank addition. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Naso lituratus Origin: Indo-Pacific Reefs Max Size: 18 inches Lifespan: 10+ years Diet: Herbivore. Primarily feeds on marine algae and prepared foods. Shipping Size: 3-5 inches

Blonde Naso Tang: The Elegant & Peaceful Algae Grazer The Blonde Naso Tang (Naso elegans) also called the Orangespine Unicornfish , or Gold Naso Tang is an exceptionally graceful and beautiful fish, making it a highly sought-after addition for any spacious marine aquarium . This tang is easily identified by its unique coloration: a beautiful gray or brownish body, a striking bright yellow dorsal fin, and a prominent black stripe that runs from its eye to the tip of its nose. It is generally peaceful with other fish but can be territorial towards similar-looking species or other tangs, so it's often best to introduce it to the tank last. As a herbivore, it is a fantastic algae-eater , making it a valuable and hardworking member of any clean-up crew. It is completely reef-safe and will not harm corals or invertebrates. Why the Blonde Naso Tang is a Great Choice: Stunning Appearance: Its distinctive coloration and graceful swimming make it a true showpiece. Excellent Algae Control: It tirelessly grazes on nuisance algae, helping to keep the tank clean and healthy. Generally Peaceful: It coexists well with other fish, making it a great community tank addition. Active Swimmer: It adds a lot of energy and elegant movement to a very large aquarium. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Naso elegans Origin: Indo-Pacific Reefs Max Size: 18 inches Lifespan: 10+ years Diet: Herbivore. Primarily feeds on marine algae. Shipping Size: 3-5 inches

Desjardini Sailfin Tang: The Graceful Giant of the Reef The Desjardini Sailfin Tang (Zebrasoma desjardinii), also known as the Red Sea Sailfin Tang , is a large and elegant species that brings a commanding presence to any marine aquarium . Its defining feature is its stunning, sail-like dorsal fin, which it can raise to display its intricate network of white, blue, and yellow lines against a dark brown body. This pattern intensifies and changes as the fish matures, creating a mesmerizing visual display. The Desjardini Sailfin Tang is a tireless algae grazer, making it an excellent addition to a cleanup crew in a well-established, spacious reef tank. Despite its size, it is generally peaceful and coexists well with other fish, provided it has ample space to swim and plenty of live rock for foraging. Why the Desjardini Sailfin Tang is a Great Choice: Commanding Presence: Its large size and majestic "sailfin" make it a true centerpiece in a large tank. Intricate Coloration: The beautiful and detailed pattern on its body provides a striking visual display. Natural Algae Control: It constantly grazes on algae, helping to maintain a clean and healthy environment. Peaceful Temperament: It is generally non-aggressive with other fish, making it a great community tank addition. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Zebrasoma desjardinii Origin: Indo-Pacific Reefs Max Size: 16 inches Lifespan: 10+ years Diet: Herbivore. Primarily feeds on marine algae and prepared foods. Shipping Size: 3-5 inches

Perlmutt means "mother of pearl" in German, and the word adequately describes the beautiful body color of the Perlmutt cichlid. Fins are yellow with blue highlights. The Perlmutt cichlid offers a nice size contrast in a community cichlid tank, since the fish only grows to three inches. Perlmutt cichlids are hardy and omnivorous. This pet fish needs a rocky area to make itself feel at home. Quick Facts Scientific Name Labidochromis sp. "Perlmutt" Origin Lake Malawi, Africa Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful for a mbuna Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 6–10 years Diet Omnivore (needs plant matter) Water Temperature 76–82°F pH 7.8–8.6 Shipping Size Approx. 1½–2" Care Guide Tank setup: Use a sand or crushed-coral bottom and stack plenty of rockwork with caves and hiding spots so each male can claim a territory and others can escape. Lake Malawi and Lake Tanganyika cichlids need hard, alkaline water; crushed coral or aragonite sand helps hold the pH up. Feeding: Mbuna are mostly plant eaters. Feed a vegetable-based flake or pellet once or twice a day, and avoid high-protein foods, which can upset their digestion. Tankmates: Keep mbuna with other mbuna of similar size and temperament, stocked in a group to spread out aggression. Avoid mixing them with peaceful peacocks and haps unless the tank is large, and avoid closely related species that look alike, which can crossbreed. Good to know: Mbuna stay calmer when the tank is slightly crowded and well decorated, which keeps any one fish from dominating.

Williamsi blue lips cichlids, also called williamsi north cichlids, are mouthbrooders from Lake Malawi with big blue lips. Females do not have as much yellow in the body but also feature the big lips. Coloration varies for these cichlids, but in general, males are yellow with blue highlights, and females are brown with yellow highlights. Quick Facts Scientific Name Placidochromis sp. "Williamsi North" Origin Lake Malawi, Africa Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Semi-aggressive (males territorial) Adult Size Up to 7" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 76–82°F pH 7.8–8.6 Shipping Size Approx. 4" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a sand bottom, open swimming space in front and rockwork along the back. Lake Malawi and Lake Tanganyika cichlids need hard, alkaline water; crushed coral or aragonite sand helps hold the pH up. Feeding: Feed a quality cichlid pellet or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like brine shrimp. Tankmates: Haps do well with peacocks and other haps of similar size, plus robust catfish like synodontis. Keep one male per similar-looking species, with several females, to limit fighting and crossbreeding. Good to know: Males take a year or more to show full adult color, and color best when females are present.

The nyererei cichlid has a name that is difficult to spell but an appearance that is easy to look at. Nyererei cichlids originate in Lake Victoria and range in colors from yellow to red. These fish are moderately aggressive and omnivores and adapt easily to a cichlid fish tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pundamilia nyererei Origin Lake Victoria, Africa Care Level Moderate Temperament Semi-aggressive Adult Size Up to 4–5" Lifespan 8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 76–82°F pH 7.5–8.5 Group Size Keep more females than males Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them rocks and caves, open swimming space and good filtration. Lake Victoria cichlids like hard, alkaline water. Feeding: Feed a quality cichlid pellet or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other Lake Victoria or calm African cichlids of similar size. Plenty of rockwork helps spread out aggression. Good to know: Male nyererei are brightly colored in red, yellow and blue, while females are a plain silvery brown.

The obliquidens zebra cichlid from Lake Victoria has zebra stripes on a red and yellow body, an extremely colorful schooling cichlid. Obliquidens are carnivorous and moderately aggressive but adapt well to aquariums and cichlid pellet food. Quick Facts Scientific Name Astatotilapia latifasciata Origin Lake Victoria basin, Africa Care Level Easy Temperament Semi-aggressive Adult Size Up to 5" Lifespan 8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.5–8.5 Shipping Size Approx. 3" Care Guide Tank setup: Use a sand bottom with rockwork and caves. Lake Victoria cichlids do well in moderately hard, slightly alkaline water. Feeding: Feed a quality cichlid pellet or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other Victorian or robust Malawi cichlids of similar size, with plenty of rockwork to break up territories. Good to know: Many Lake Victoria cichlids are rare or extinct in the wild, so aquarium populations are important.

The winemilleri is also called the striped tail geophagus for the bright red markings on the tail, which also mark the bright ventral fins. Eartheaters are a group of species, most belonging to the genus Geophagus , that share physical characteristics (when you see an eartheater, you know it’s an eartheater) and behavioral characteristics: they eat earth and spit it out. Winemilleri are fished in the Brazil portion of the Amazon basin. At two inches the color begins to show on the fins. Currently the breeder has limited stock, and the fish are coming in quite small. Quick Facts Scientific Name Geophagus winemilleri Origin Upper Orinoco and Rio Negro basins (Venezuela, Colombia, Brazil) Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful (territorial when breeding) Adult Size Up to 8" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore (sifts sand for food) Water Temperature 77–84°F pH 5.0–7.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 5" Care Guide Tank setup: Eartheaters sift sand through their gills, so use a fine sand bottom (no sharp gravel). Give them open sand areas, driftwood and some rocks. Good filtration and clean water are important. Feeding: Feed a quality sinking pellet or granule once or twice a day. Sinking foods let them feed naturally by sifting the sand. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Eartheaters do well with other peaceful South American fish of similar size, such as angelfish, severums, festivums, larger tetras, hatchetfish and plecos. Avoid aggressive cichlids that would bully them. Good to know: Many eartheaters are mouthbrooders. Watch for parents taking eggs or fry into their mouths for protection.

Our wild apistogramma come from small streams in the Colombia basin of the Amazon and can belong to one or more of 15 species in that region. All apistogrammas are peaceful and get along well with community fish, but they may eat small fancy shrimp. So this item is basically a grab bag right from Colombia. Many of the apistos cannot even be identified until they have matured, but all are terrific fish. Each order comes with four assorted apistogramma. Quick Facts Scientific Name Apistogramma spp. Origin Colombia (wild-caught) Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful (males territorial with each other) Adult Size Up to 2–3", depending on species Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 76–84°F pH 5.0–7.0 Group Size Sold as a lot of 4 Shipping Size Approx. ¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter, dim lighting and lots of plants, driftwood and leaf litter. Add a cave (a coconut shell or small clay pot) for each female. Most apistos prefer soft, slightly acidic water. Feeding: Feed small pellets or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with small, peaceful fish such as tetras, rasboras, pencilfish, otocinclus and corydoras. A calm school of small "dither" fish helps apistos feel safe enough to come out. Keep one male per tank unless it is large and well planted, and avoid large or boisterous fish. Adults may eat small shrimp and baby shrimp. Breeding: Apistos are cave spawners. The female lays her eggs inside a cave and guards the fry, while the male patrols the territory. One male with several females works well in a planted tank. Good to know: Wild-caught assortments can include several species that are hard to tell apart until they mature, so each fish is a bit of a surprise as it grows.

The L-155 Adonis Pleco (Acanthicus adonis), also commonly known as the Polka Dot Lyretail Pleco or Adonis Catfish, is wild-caught in Peru. AquariumFish.com imports what the fishermen catch, so size can vary from a body size of 3 to 6 inches. The size does not include the long, streaming tail fin, which is the hallmark of Adonis Plecos. Quick Facts Scientific Name Acanthicus adonis Origin Peru and Brazil Care Level Moderate (grows very large) Temperament Peaceful when young; territorial as adults Adult Size Up to 2–3 feet Lifespan 15–20+ years Diet Omnivore (meaty sinking foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 1–6" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them sturdy caves, heavy driftwood, strong filtration and good current. They are most active at night. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets once a day, ideally in the evening when they are most active. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and shrimp. Tankmates: Young adonis plecos are peaceful, but adults become territorial and can bully other bottom dwellers. Keep them with large, robust fish. Good to know: Young adonis plecos are black with white polka dots, and the spots fade to gray as they grow.

The Blue Heckel Discus is a true wild subspecies of the Blue Discus found in the Brazilian Amazon basin. Blue Heckels were discovered by Dr. Johann Heckel in 1884 when he was examining wild-caught species from the Johann Natterer expedition (the guy who discovered discus in 1835). The Blue Heckel discus is a Blue Discus with a solid black vertical bar across the face that covers the eye. Blue Heckel Discus are hardy and will even breed in the aquarium. This discus variation must be in every proper discus tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name Symphysodon discus (Heckel discus) Origin Brazil, Rio Negro (wild-caught) Care Level Difficult (for experienced keepers) Temperament Peaceful, shy; social Adult Size Up to 7–8" Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Omnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 82–86°F pH 5.0–6.5 (very soft water) Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 5" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a reliable heater, gentle filtration, driftwood and dim lighting. Wild discus need very soft, acidic water and very clean, stable conditions. Feeding: Start with frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp, then slowly add discus granules or pellets. Feed small meals a few times a day and remove anything uneaten within a few minutes. Tankmates: Discus are calm and shy, so choose gentle tankmates that enjoy the same warm water: cardinal and rummynose tetras, sterbai corydoras and small plecos are popular choices. Avoid fast, boisterous or fin-nipping fish, and anything that competes hard for food. Many keepers avoid angelfish, which can bully discus and share diseases. Living in groups: Discus are social and feel safest in a group. A single discus, or just two, tends to be stressed. When a pair forms to breed, they may claim part of the tank, so a group spreads out the attention. Good to know: Heckels come from very soft blackwater and are the most demanding discus. Acclimate slowly and keep the water soft, acidic and stable.

Oren's Tilefish: A Graceful & Unique Aquarium Fish The Oren's Tilefish (Hoplolatilus oreni) is a graceful and sought-after species that adds a touch of subtle elegance to any marine aquarium . Its stunning appearance features an elongated, sleek body with a pale, pearlescent blue or white sheen and a distinctive vibrant orange stripe running horizontally from its head to its tail. This fish is known for its peaceful temperament and unique behavior of building intricate burrows in a deep sand bed. It's a fantastic choice for a community reef tank, where it will add an active yet non-aggressive presence to the water column. Why Oren's Tilefish is a Great Choice: Unique Appearance: Its elongated body and striking orange stripe make it a memorable and beautiful fish. Peaceful Temperament: It is a non-aggressive species that coexists well with other peaceful tank mates. Active Behavior: It adds constant, graceful movement to the water column. Reef-Safe: Oren's Tilefish is completely safe to keep with all types of corals and invertebrates. Unique Behavior: Its burrow-building habit in a deep sand bed adds an interesting dynamic to the tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Hoplolatilus oreni Origin: Red Sea Max Size: 5 inches Lifespan: 5 years or more Diet: Carnivore. Primarily a planktivore, it requires a varied diet of high-quality frozen foods like mysis shrimp and enriched brine shrimp. Shipping Size: 2-3 inches *No Refunds

Well, we had the blue lips Williamsi, and now we also have the white lips mdoka from Lake Malawi. The white lips mdoka likes to sift sand for snacks, so he is a bit more at home with some part of the aquarium with a sandy bottom. These fish are navy blue with bright white lips and grow to about seven inches. Omnivores, but they do require meat; flake or pellet food is fine. Quick Facts Scientific Name Placidochromis phenochilus "Mdoka" Origin Lake Malawi, Africa Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Semi-aggressive (males territorial) Adult Size Up to 7" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 76–82°F pH 7.8–8.6 Shipping Size Approx. 3" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a sand bottom, open swimming space in front and rockwork along the back. Lake Malawi and Lake Tanganyika cichlids need hard, alkaline water; crushed coral or aragonite sand helps hold the pH up. Feeding: Feed a quality cichlid pellet or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like brine shrimp. Tankmates: Haps do well with peacocks and other haps of similar size, plus robust catfish like synodontis. Keep one male per similar-looking species, with several females, to limit fighting and crossbreeding. Good to know: Mdoka sift sand for food, so a sandy bottom keeps them busy and happy.

The Black Bar Endler has a bold vertical black bar on the body, which makes the reds and greens more vivid. These are remarkable endlers and will breed with any female endler. Currently we only ship male black bar endlers. Quick Facts Scientific Name Poecilia wingei Origin Venezuela (captive-bred in Sri Lanka) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1" (males about ¾") Lifespan 2–4 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and plenty of plants. Endlers are small, so a sponge filter or a sponge over the filter intake keeps them safe. Feeding: Feed a quality flake, crushed small, or micro pellets once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Endlers do well with other small, peaceful fish such as small rasboras, corydoras, otocinclus and shrimp. Avoid larger fish that could eat them. Good to know: Black bar endlers are named for the bold black bar on each male's side.

listings.commonName: King Kong Shrimp Red Grade S
listings.description: The red king kong shrimp is a bright red version of the black king kong shrimp and just as difficult to breed. S quality is an extremely high grade. The parent variety is most likely the bee shrimp, and these shrimp have the same requirements as the bee shrimp. Quick Facts Scientific Name Caridina cf. cantonensis (red king kong, Taiwan bee) Origin Taiwan (aquarium-bred) Care Level Moderate to difficult (needs soft, stable water) Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1" Lifespan 1½–2 years Diet Omnivore (grazes on algae) Water Temperature 68–76°F pH 5.8–6.8 Water Hardness GH 4–6, KH 0–1 (soft) Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Caridina bee and Taiwan bee shrimp need soft, slightly acidic water. Use a mature, cycled tank with an active (buffering) shrimp substrate, RO water remineralized for shrimp, moss and plants, and a sponge filter. Feeding: Feed a small amount of quality shrimp food once a day, and remove any uneaten food after a few hours. Tankmates: Caridina are best kept in a shrimp-only tank or with tiny, peaceful fish like otocinclus, plus snails. Avoid cichlids and other fish that will eat shrimp. Different bee and Taiwan bee varieties can crossbreed, but they will not breed with Neocaridina. Good to know: Acclimate slowly (drip for an hour or more). Stable water matters more than perfect numbers, and sudden changes in temperature or hardness are the most common cause of losses.

Zoanthids Have a color in mind? They are formed as individual polyps, or are attached by a fleshy stolon or from small pieces of sediment, sand and rock.Colony Polyps have the ability to sting other polyps or corals. While the sting is not strong, be sure to provide sufficient space between them and other corals because of its semi-aggressive temperament and potential to crowd out neighbors. Comes in many colors ,best to have in tanks is in the middle to top. Family: Zoanthidea Care: Medium water flow, lighting moderate Food: Micro-plankton,baby brine shrimp Shipping size: 1-1/2 to 2 inches

The Blue Discus from Colombia features blues, greens, and browns on the body. Wild discus are hardy and much more active than the very bred colored discus. It was from these small variations in color that are demonstrated in the wild Blue Discus that all the domestic colored discus originate. Quick Facts Scientific Name Symphysodon haraldi (blue discus) Origin Colombia (wild-caught) Care Level Difficult (for experienced keepers) Temperament Peaceful, shy; social Adult Size Up to 7–8" Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Omnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 82–86°F pH 5.0–6.5 (very soft water) Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 4" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a reliable heater, gentle filtration, driftwood and dim lighting. Wild discus need very soft, acidic water and very clean, stable conditions. Feeding: Start with frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp, then slowly add discus granules or pellets. Feed small meals a few times a day and remove anything uneaten within a few minutes. Tankmates: Discus are calm and shy, so choose gentle tankmates that enjoy the same warm water: cardinal and rummynose tetras, sterbai corydoras and small plecos are popular choices. Avoid fast, boisterous or fin-nipping fish, and anything that competes hard for food. Many keepers avoid angelfish, which can bully discus and share diseases. Living in groups: Discus are social and feel safest in a group. A single discus, or just two, tends to be stressed. When a pair forms to breed, they may claim part of the tank, so a group spreads out the attention. Good to know: Wild discus need very soft, acidic water and slow acclimation. Quarantine them before adding to a tank with captive-bred discus.

The golden mbuna cichlid, or auratus cichlid, is a classic African mbuna family cichlid from Lake Malawi. These cichlids were among the first introduced to the aquarium trade and are easy to breed in an aquarium. The cichlid gets along with most other Africans and has a unique gold, brown, and yellow color pattern. Quick Facts Scientific Name Melanochromis auratus Origin Lake Malawi, Africa Care Level Moderate Temperament Aggressive (territorial rock-dweller) Adult Size Up to 4" Lifespan 6–10 years Diet Omnivore (needs plant matter) Water Temperature 76–82°F pH 7.8–8.6 Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Use a sand or crushed-coral bottom and stack plenty of rockwork with caves and hiding spots so each male can claim a territory and others can escape. Lake Malawi and Lake Tanganyika cichlids need hard, alkaline water; crushed coral or aragonite sand helps hold the pH up. Feeding: Mbuna are mostly plant eaters. Feed a vegetable-based flake or pellet once or twice a day, and avoid high-protein foods, which can upset their digestion. Tankmates: Keep mbuna with other mbuna of similar size and temperament, stocked in a group to spread out aggression. Avoid mixing them with peaceful peacocks and haps unless the tank is large, and avoid closely related species that look alike, which can crossbreed. Good to know: Auratus are one of the more aggressive mbuna. Males turn dark brown and black as they mature, while females stay gold.

The gold wag swordtail is a majestic livebearer with a long black sword and tail on a bright gold body. Quick Facts Scientific Name Xiphophorus hellerii (gold wag) Origin Southern Mexico to Honduras (wild ancestors); aquarium-bred Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful (males may spar) Adult Size Up to 4–5" (not counting the sword) Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 7.0–8.0 (hard water) Group Size Keep more females than males Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Swordtails are active swimmers, so give them plants, open swimming space and a tight-fitting lid, since they are good jumpers. They prefer hard, alkaline water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet with some vegetable content once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Swordtails get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as platies, mollies, larger tetras, danios, rainbowfish, gouramis and corydoras. Keep more females than males, since males chase females and may spar with each other. Avoid fin-nippers and large cichlids. Good to know: Swordtails are livebearers and breed readily. Fry are born free-swimming and will be eaten unless there are dense plants or a breeding box for them to hide in. Only males grow the "sword" on the tail.

The black galaxy shrimp grade A to S are a high-quality grade (higher than "pinto" et al.). Not nearly as expensive as grade SSS or grade SS, which sell for $100s, but we have a tough time telling the difference. Galaxy shrimp feature spots and stripes and very, very bold color contrasts. Quick Facts Scientific Name Caridina cf. cantonensis (black galaxy pinto, Taiwan bee) Origin Taiwan (aquarium-bred) Care Level Moderate to difficult (needs soft, stable water) Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1" Lifespan 1½–2 years Diet Omnivore (grazes on algae) Water Temperature 68–76°F pH 5.8–6.8 Water Hardness GH 4–6, KH 0–1 (soft) Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Caridina bee and Taiwan bee shrimp need soft, slightly acidic water. Use a mature, cycled tank with an active (buffering) shrimp substrate, RO water remineralized for shrimp, moss and plants, and a sponge filter. Feeding: Feed a small amount of quality shrimp food once a day, and remove any uneaten food after a few hours. Tankmates: Caridina are best kept in a shrimp-only tank or with tiny, peaceful fish like otocinclus, plus snails. Avoid cichlids and other fish that will eat shrimp. Different bee and Taiwan bee varieties can crossbreed, but they will not breed with Neocaridina. Good to know: Acclimate slowly (drip for an hour or more). Stable water matters more than perfect numbers, and sudden changes in temperature or hardness are the most common cause of losses.

TM style Shrimp Food The TM Group breeds some of the finest caridina shrimp ever exported from Taiwan. Their exclusive TM style shrimp food will promote shell strength, activity and color. Just add one pellet twice a week to the shrimp aquarium and watch them all gather in seconds. TM style shrimp food contains cyanobacteria, chlorella, spirulina, and amino acids. Each container is 40 grams.

Ocellaris Clownfish: The Classic Reef Tank Resident The Ocellaris Clownfish (Amphiprion ocellaris), also known as the False Percula Clownfish, is a cornerstone of the marine aquarium hobby. Its classic and vibrant appearance features a brilliant orange body with three distinct white stripes , each outlined in a thin black line. Known for its charming and peaceful personality, this fish is an excellent choice for beginner and experienced hobbyists alike. It is famously known for its symbiotic relationship with various anemone species, where it will happily host and defend its home. Why the Ocellaris Clownfish is a Great Choice: Iconic Appearance: Its classic orange, white, and black pattern makes it an instantly recognizable and attractive inhabitant. Highly Hardy: This species is incredibly resilient and easy to care for, making it a perfect first fish for a new tank. Peaceful Temperament: It is a great community fish that can coexist with a variety of other species without issues. Reef-Safe: The Ocellaris Clownfish is completely safe to keep with all types of corals and invertebrates. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Amphiprion ocellaris Origin: Indo-Pacific Ocean Max Size: 3 inches Lifespan: 6-10 years Diet: Omnivore. A varied diet of high-quality flakes, pellets, and frozen foods. Shipping Size: 1-1.5 inches

Pignose puffers are mean and will eat any small fish and frozen meaty foods - but supply snails and crayfish from time to time so they can keep their teeth in shape. Also called the arrowhead puffer, these are freshwater puffers and live a long time in the wild Mekong River. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pao suvattii Origin Mekong River basin, Thailand and Laos Care Level Moderate Temperament Aggressive Adult Size Up to 6" Lifespan 10+ years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods, snails) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 4" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants, rocks and hiding places, and good filtration, since puffers are messy eaters. Feeding: Puffers need meaty foods and usually won't eat flake. Feed frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp once a day. They also enjoy small snails, which help keep their teeth trimmed. Tankmates: Pignose puffers will eat any small fish and bite others. Keep them alone. Good to know: Pignose puffers bury themselves in sand and wait to ambush food, often with just their eyes showing.

Butterfly koi do not have the specific color patterns of the show koi sought by enthusiasts. Instead, they display their own random color patterns unique to this long-fin hybrid. The long, flowing fins are remarkable when viewed from above. Quick Facts Scientific Name Cyprinus carpio Origin Captive-bred (Asia) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2–3 feet Lifespan 25–35 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 50–80°F pH 7.0–8.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 3–4" Care Guide Tank setup: Koi grow large and are best kept in an outdoor pond with strong filtration. They are cool-water fish and do not need a heater. Feeding: Feed a quality koi or goldfish pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a few minutes. Feed less when the water is cool. Tankmates: Koi get along with goldfish and other pond fish. Good to know: Butterfly koi have long, flowing fins and are a cross between koi and Asian long-finned carp.

The zipper pencilfish is also known as the diptail pencil fish and hockey stick pencil. Oh - it is also called the rocket pencilfish. Each name fits. Half the time the zipper pencil is pointing up like he is ready to take off like a rocket. Of course, the other half of the time his head is pointed down like he is going for a crash landing. In a school, these fish hover at alternating 45 degrees, creating the famous zipper pattern. We recommend the purchase of at least six to see this visual effect! Quick Facts Scientific Name Nannostomus unifasciatus Origin Colombia and the Amazon basin Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 5–6 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a planted tank with floating plants, gentle filtration and a lid, since they can jump. Soft, slightly acidic water brings out their best color. Feeding: Feed crushed flake or micro pellets once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Pencilfish are shy and peaceful, so keep them with other small, gentle fish such as small tetras, rasboras, pygmy corydoras and shrimp. Good to know: Zipper pencilfish swim at an angle, and a group tilted in different directions creates their famous "zipper" look.
Weco Wonder Plants - Freshwater Pro Series Anacharis - realistic and keeps its color long term under all aquarium lighting and water conditions.

Unlike most other pike cichlids, the regani pike cichlids are great community fish and safe for plants. With the exception of nano species like fancy shrimp, regani pike cichlids will leave small fish alone. Caught in small streams in Brazil, the species is also unique because it likes to travel in packs. Regani pike cichlids only grow to four inches and eat flake foods, frozen foods and cichlid pellets. Quick Facts Scientific Name Crenicichla regani Origin Amazon basin, Brazil Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful for a pike cichlid; may eat shrimp and fry Adult Size Up to 4–5" Lifespan 6–8 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods; takes flake and pellets) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 3" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a sand bottom, plants, caves and driftwood. Soft, slightly acidic water and gentle current suit them best. Feeding: Feed quality flake and small pellets. They also enjoy small frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They do well with peaceful South American fish of similar or larger size, such as tetras, pencilfish, corydoras and other peaceful cichlids. They may eat shrimp and fry. Good to know: Dwarf pike cichlids are colorful and active, and pairs will spawn in caves.

The extreme red king kong shrimp, or for the shrimp aficionado the EXRKK shrimp, has a deep solid red body and a bold white-tipped tail. Obviously a difficult-to-breed Caridina species, they cost a little more. Quick Facts Scientific Name Caridina cf. cantonensis (extreme red king kong, Taiwan bee) Origin Taiwan (aquarium-bred) Care Level Moderate to difficult (needs soft, stable water) Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1" Lifespan 1½–2 years Diet Omnivore (grazes on algae) Water Temperature 68–76°F pH 5.8–6.8 Water Hardness GH 4–6, KH 0–1 (soft) Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Caridina bee and Taiwan bee shrimp need soft, slightly acidic water. Use a mature, cycled tank with an active (buffering) shrimp substrate, RO water remineralized for shrimp, moss and plants, and a sponge filter. Feeding: Feed a small amount of quality shrimp food once a day, and remove any uneaten food after a few hours. Tankmates: Caridina are best kept in a shrimp-only tank or with tiny, peaceful fish like otocinclus, plus snails. Avoid cichlids and other fish that will eat shrimp. Different bee and Taiwan bee varieties can crossbreed, but they will not breed with Neocaridina. Good to know: Acclimate slowly (drip for an hour or more). Stable water matters more than perfect numbers, and sudden changes in temperature or hardness are the most common cause of losses.

A highly refined version of the beautiful crystal red shrimp, the pure red line shrimp (PRL shrimp for the pros out there) has a bold white body and deep red line, just like the picture. Like all Caridina, these shrimp tolerate temperatures down to the 60s but will not tolerate temperatures of 80 and above. Also, Caridina shrimp need clean, soft water. Spoiling them is worth it. We recommend TMC or Hikari shrimp food for all our shrimp. Quick Facts Scientific Name Caridina cf. cantonensis (pure red line, crystal red) Origin Taiwan (aquarium-bred) Care Level Moderate to difficult (needs soft, stable water) Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1" Lifespan 1½–2 years Diet Omnivore (grazes on algae) Water Temperature 68–76°F pH 5.8–6.8 Water Hardness GH 4–6, KH 0–1 (soft) Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Caridina bee and Taiwan bee shrimp need soft, slightly acidic water. Use a mature, cycled tank with an active (buffering) shrimp substrate, RO water remineralized for shrimp, moss and plants, and a sponge filter. Feeding: Feed a small amount of quality shrimp food once a day, and remove any uneaten food after a few hours. Tankmates: Caridina are best kept in a shrimp-only tank or with tiny, peaceful fish like otocinclus, plus snails. Avoid cichlids and other fish that will eat shrimp. Different bee and Taiwan bee varieties can crossbreed, but they will not breed with Neocaridina. Good to know: Acclimate slowly (drip for an hour or more). Stable water matters more than perfect numbers, and sudden changes in temperature or hardness are the most common cause of losses.

listings.commonName: New Life Spectrum Marine Fish Food
listings.description: Saltwater Aquarium Fish Food New Life Spectrum Marine Fish is a complete color enhancing diet without harmful soybean and hormone additives. Primarily krill, squid, and marine veggies, these sinking pellets will be gobbled up! As with most foods, feed twice daily, no more than can be consumed within two minutes. (and made in the USA!) Shipping Size: 80 gms/ 2.8 oz

Cory loxozonus are pretty patterned schooling cory. These little guys are also called the dirty bandit cory and the slant-bar cory. The dirty bandit name comes from the pattern that is a combination of the bandit cory and a skunk cory, with small leopard spots like a julii cory. The slant-bar name comes from the definition of its Latin name: loxo zonus just means oblique band (which means slant-bar). Quick Facts Scientific Name Corydoras loxozonus Origin Colombia Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 5–10 years Diet Omnivore (bottom feeder) Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 6.0–7.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and a soft sand or smooth, fine gravel bottom. Plants, driftwood and a few shady spots help them feel secure. Corys are sensitive to salt and some medications (especially copper), so check labels before treating the tank. Feeding: Corys need their own food, not just leftovers. Feed sinking pellets or wafers once or twice a day so food reaches the bottom. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Corys get along with almost any peaceful community fish, such as tetras, rasboras, livebearers, gouramis, angelfish and bettas. Avoid large fish that could swallow them and aggressive bottom dwellers. Good to know: Corys sift through the substrate with their sensitive barbels, so soft sand or smooth, fine gravel keeps those barbels healthy.

The Geophagus Braziliansis cichlid is also called Pearl Cichlid. First discovered in northern Brazil, these fish are hardy and most commonly sold by pond breeders in Florida. Eartheaters are a group of species, most belonging to the genus Geophagus , that share physical characteristics (when you see an eartheater, you know it’s an eartheater) and behavioral characteristics: they eat earth and spit it out. They live a long time, and most are peaceful and elegant. Quick Facts Scientific Name Geophagus brasiliensis Origin Coastal eastern and southern Brazil and Uruguay Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful (territorial when breeding) Adult Size Up to 6–8" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore (sifts sand for food) Water Temperature 68–82°F pH 6.5–8.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 2–5" Care Guide Tank setup: Eartheaters sift sand through their gills, so use a fine sand bottom (no sharp gravel). Give them open sand areas, driftwood and some rocks. Good filtration and clean water are important. Feeding: Feed a quality sinking pellet or granule once or twice a day. Sinking foods let them feed naturally by sifting the sand. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Eartheaters do well with other peaceful South American fish of similar size, such as angelfish, severums, festivums, larger tetras, hatchetfish and plecos. Avoid aggressive cichlids that would bully them. Good to know: Many eartheaters are mouthbrooders. Watch for parents taking eggs or fry into their mouths for protection.

Long Fin Albino cherry barbs are the long fin version of the already bold pink albino cherry barb. Bred in Florida for the aquarium trade, these schooling wonders are hardy and adaptable. They are great for community fish tanks and planted aquariums. Quick Facts Scientific Name Puntius titteya Origin Sri Lanka (bred in Florida) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful, a bit shy Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 4–6 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 73–81°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a filter, a heater and plenty of plants. They feel safest with places to hide and show more color in a planted tank. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other small, peaceful fish such as rasboras, small tetras, corydoras and dwarf shrimp. Avoid large or boisterous fish and fin-nippers. Good to know: The long fins are best kept away from fin-nippers like tiger barbs, so pair them with other gentle fish.

Red rili shrimp are active, pretty little shrimp with clear bodies and bold red bands. These shrimp are from the hardy Neocaridina family and will be a delight in the shrimp tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name Neocaridina davidi (red rili) Origin East Asia (aquarium-bred, mostly Taiwan) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1–1¼" Lifespan 1–2 years Diet Omnivore (grazes on algae) Water Temperature 65–80°F pH 6.5–8.0 Water Hardness GH 6–12 (moderately hard) Group Size Does best in a group (breeds readily) Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Neocaridina are hardy and ideal for beginners. Use a cycled, planted tank with moss, plants and hiding spots, and a sponge filter or a sponge over the filter intake so shrimp aren't pulled in. Keep the water stable. Feeding: Shrimp graze on algae all day. Feed a small amount of quality shrimp food once a day and remove anything uneaten after a few hours. Tankmates: Keep shrimp alone or with tiny, peaceful fish like small rasboras, ember tetras, otocinclus and pygmy corydoras, plus snails. Most fish will eat baby shrimp, and cichlids (even dwarf cichlids like rams and apistogrammas) and larger fish will eat adults. Different Neocaridina colors will crossbreed and lose their color over time. Good to know: Shrimp are very sensitive to copper and many medications. Never treat a tank with shrimp, and check plant fertilizers and treatments for copper.

The Hyphessobrycon amapaensis , also known as the redline tetra, boasts vibrant red and shimmering silver-white stripes, making it a stunning addition to your freshwater aquarium. This South American beauty is a wonderful choice for aquarists looking to add a touch of brilliance to their underwater paradise. Redline tetras thrive in softer, slightly acidic water, similar to the conditions found in their native Amazon habitats. They prefer a low pH and clean, well-maintained water conditions. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hyphessobrycon amapaensis Origin Amapá, Brazil Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1¾" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 5.5–7.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a dark substrate, which brings out their color. Keep a lid on the tank, since tetras can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, rasboras, danios, corydoras, dwarf cichlids, gouramis and livebearers. Good to know: Tetras feel safer and show better color in a group. A larger school also spreads out any chasing.

The royal clown knife fish is a rare and wild-caught fish from Thailand. Featuring a distinct spotted pattern, these fish are great with larger community fish but require a space to hide (a short PVC pipe will do). These fish grow to three feet over time and adapt well to the aquarium. Have frozen foods ready. Quick Facts Scientific Name Chitala blanci Origin Mekong River basin, Thailand and Laos Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful with fish its size Adult Size Up to 3 feet Lifespan 15–20 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 7" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them hiding places like large tubes or caves, dim lighting, strong filtration and a tight lid. They are most active at night. Feeding: Feed meaty foods like frozen shrimp and bloodworms, plus sinking carnivore pellets once they learn to take them. Avoid feeder fish, which can carry disease. Tankmates: They will eat any fish that fits in their mouth. Keep them with large, peaceful fish. Good to know: Royal clown knives are shy when young and do best with a hiding spot, like a short length of PVC pipe.

Extra Large Fantail Goldfish Beautiful, big, and ready for the pond or large aquarium. With massive flowing fins and bright, varied body markings, these domestic-bred fish are hardy in any weather. Shipping size: approximately 4 to 5 inches. Fish pictured here are representative only. If you are looking for a specific coloration, add a note to the order or simply allow us to choose one of our favorites for you! Each order comes with 4 big fish. Quick Facts Scientific Name Carassius auratus Origin China Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 8" Lifespan 10–15 years, often longer with good care Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 65–75°F (no heater needed in most homes) pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Sold as a lot of 4 Shipping Size Approx. 4–5" Care Guide Tank setup: Fantails produce a lot of waste, so give them plenty of room and a strong filter. Feeding: Feed small amounts of a quality sinking pellet or flake once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other fancy goldfish of similar size and speed. Avoid fast single-tail goldfish like comets and shubunkins, which will outcompete them for food. Also avoid tropical fish, which need warmer water, and fin-nippers. Ponds: Fantails can live in ponds in mild climates, but they are less cold-hardy than comets and shubunkins. Bring them indoors where winters are harsh, and keep them away from fast, aggressive pond fish. Good to know: Fantails are among the hardiest fancy goldfish, which makes them a great first goldfish and a good fit for ponds in mild climates.

Rummynose rasboras have a solid bluish body, but only the males feature a deep red face, hence the rummynose designation. Though females don't have the bright red colors, you can't breed without 'em. Not as available for export as the males, AquariumFish.com does offer the females from time to time. Quick Facts Scientific Name Sawbwa resplendens Origin Inle Lake, Myanmar Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1½" Lifespan 4–6 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 68–77°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: These fish come from cool, clear, hard-water lakes and ponds in Myanmar. Give them dense plants, gentle filtration and plenty of cover. They do not need very warm water, and stable, slightly alkaline water suits them. Feeding: Feed crushed flake or micro pellets once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other small, peaceful fish that like similar water, such as celestial pearl danios, micro rasboras, small livebearers and dwarf shrimp. Avoid large or boisterous fish. Good to know: They are a little shy at first; plenty of plants and a group of their own kind help them settle in and color up.

The bivittatum killifish, or two-stripe killi, was discovered in a small stream in Cameroon in the late 1800s and went right into the aquarium trade. Today these beautiful killis are bred in Indonesia. The male grows to two inches and has most of the color, but the smaller female is a great swimmer. Each order comes with one male and one female. Quick Facts Scientific Name Aphyosemion bivittatum Origin Cameroon and Nigeria, West Africa Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful (males may spar with each other) Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods; takes flake) Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 6.0–7.0 Group Size Sold as a pair (1 male + 1 female) Shipping Size Medium: approx. 1¼" male; female smaller Care Guide Tank setup: Use a planted tank with soft, slightly acidic water, a dark substrate, gentle filtration and floating plants. Killifish are expert jumpers, so a tight-fitting lid is a must. Feeding: Feed small amounts of a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Killifish do well with small, peaceful fish like tetras, rasboras, corydoras and other killifish of similar size. Avoid fin-nippers and large fish. Keep one male per tank unless the tank is large, since males may spar. Good to know: Killifish are egg-layers that spawn readily in plants or spawning mops, and their eggs can be hatched separately.

The red galaxy shrimp grade A to S are a high-quality grade (higher than "pinto" et al.). Not nearly as expensive as grade SSS or grade SS, which sell for $100s, but we have a tough time telling the difference. Galaxy shrimp feature spots and stripes and very, very bold color contrasts. (Pictured is our current mix of red and black galaxy shrimp.) Quick Facts Scientific Name Caridina cf. cantonensis (red galaxy pinto, Taiwan bee) Origin Taiwan (aquarium-bred) Care Level Moderate to difficult (needs soft, stable water) Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1" Lifespan 1½–2 years Diet Omnivore (grazes on algae) Water Temperature 68–76°F pH 5.8–6.8 Water Hardness GH 4–6, KH 0–1 (soft) Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Caridina bee and Taiwan bee shrimp need soft, slightly acidic water. Use a mature, cycled tank with an active (buffering) shrimp substrate, RO water remineralized for shrimp, moss and plants, and a sponge filter. Feeding: Feed a small amount of quality shrimp food once a day, and remove any uneaten food after a few hours. Tankmates: Caridina are best kept in a shrimp-only tank or with tiny, peaceful fish like otocinclus, plus snails. Avoid cichlids and other fish that will eat shrimp. Different bee and Taiwan bee varieties can crossbreed, but they will not breed with Neocaridina. Good to know: Acclimate slowly (drip for an hour or more). Stable water matters more than perfect numbers, and sudden changes in temperature or hardness are the most common cause of losses.

Pearl Weed Pearl Weed is known for easy trimming and shaping into a desired pattern. This small leaf deep green bushy plant is hardy and needs moderate light. Our pearl weed comes in a ready to plant pot. Scientific Name: Hemianthus micranthemoides Shipping Size: Approx. 3 inches tall, potted

Ammania gracilis This popular aquarium plant does not come with an easy common name, but it sure is pretty. Featuring long slender leaves on a red, purple, and green colors, this bunched bushy plant makes a nice addition to the fish tank. Ammania needs lots of light and a little liquid fertilizer. Scientific Name: Ammania gracilis Shipping Size: Approx 5 inches, bunched, several plants to a bunch.

Tetra Algae Wafers Tetra PlecoWafers provides a complete diet for algae eaters. The aquarium fish food also contains stabilized vitamins for optimum health. These wafers are great for all herbivores in the tank, including tropheus, plecos, and corys. All in a resealable pouch. Shipping Size: 5.29 oz

Pencil Urchin Pencil urchins are not reef safe because they will eat a variety of corals including soft, LPS, and SPS. Even if they are provided a Lot of algae to eat, they will still consume most corals that they come in contact with. These urchins will need at least a 30 gallon aquarium with plenty of live rock for hiding and grazing. They do not tolerate high levels of copper, and they do not thrive in tanks with high nitrate levels in it. They are peaceful and fun to watch, but you are taking a risk if you add them to a tank with corals in it. Scientific Name: Eucidaris tribuloides Famliy: Origin: Caribbean and Fiji Shipping Size: 1 1/2 to 2 inches Food:Algae, Sponges, meaty foods ,shrimp

These distinctive pond fish thrive well in the pond and in the aquarium (at room temperature, not tropical temperature). Goldfish were bred to be viewed from above in the pond, similar to koi, but they still look great in a goldfish bowl. Quick Facts Scientific Name Carassius auratus Origin USA (developed from Chinese goldfish) Care Level Very easy, extremely hardy Temperament Peaceful, very active Adult Size Up to 10" or more in ponds Lifespan 10–15 years; 20+ years in ponds Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 50–75°F (tolerates cold winters in ponds) pH 7.0–8.0 Shipping Size Small: approx. 2" · Large: approx. 4" Care Guide Tank setup: Comets are fast, active swimmers that grow big and produce a lot of waste. They do very well in outdoor ponds; indoors, use a strong filter. Feeding: Feed small amounts of a quality sinking pellet or flake once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other single-tail goldfish like comets and shubunkins, or with koi in a pond. Avoid slow fancy goldfish, which can't compete for food, and tropical fish, which need warmer water. Ponds: This is where they shine. They handle cold winters as long as part of the pond stays deep enough not to freeze solid. Stop feeding when the water drops below about 50°F. Good to know: Comets grow quickly and are well suited to ponds.

Famed aquarist and adventurer Heiko Bleher discovered the species in a remote area of Indonesia. The bleheri is not often found in the fish trade, though the Indonesia breeders figured them out. The problem is that the color doesn't appear until the fish is two inches; prior, it is just silver. Breeders usually don't hang on to fish for too long, so the first few in the trade just looked silver. BUT in a few months these fish became a rainbow wonder. So please be patient! They will look like the picture. And they should become popular. Quick Facts Scientific Name Chilatherina bleheri Origin Western New Guinea, Indonesia Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 4" Lifespan 5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Rainbowfish are active swimmers, so leave open swimming space along the front, with plants along the back and sides. Use a filter, a heater and a tight-fitting lid, since they can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with peaceful fish of similar size, such as other rainbowfish, larger tetras, barbs, danios, corydoras and plecos. Good to know: Young bleheri are silver and take a few months to show their full color, so be patient.

Aquazen 10 Gallon Complete Aquarium Description The Aquazen 10 Gallon Aquarium fits on any desktop and most aquarium stands and comes with all the features needed to maintain a small fish community. The three stage cleanable biofilter requires minimum maintenance. The LED lighting will last for years and is suitable to grow plants. The open rimless design provides beauty and life to any room. A heater or airstone, if required. purchased separately. Features High clarity flat glass panels Fish and plant health promoting LED lighting. Removable, easy rinse filter cartridge. Universal placement internal filter rated for 10 gallons with a rated speed of 76 GPH (gallons per hour). Dimensions: 19 inches wide x 10 inches wide x 11 inches high Glass Thickness: 8 mm (High Clarity High Strength) Capacity: 10 gal Complete with all components including lighting and filter

The similis cory, or smudge pot cory for its coal-colored areas, is a wild Brazil cory. These little catfish prefer to swim in groups of three or four, and often hang out on large leaves and similar surfaces in the aquarium. Quick Facts Scientific Name Corydoras similis Origin Brazil Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 5–10 years Diet Omnivore (bottom feeder) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1–1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and a soft sand or smooth, fine gravel bottom. Plants, driftwood and a few shady spots help them feel secure. Corys are sensitive to salt and some medications (especially copper), so check labels before treating the tank. Feeding: Corys need their own food, not just leftovers. Feed sinking pellets or wafers once or twice a day so food reaches the bottom. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Corys get along with almost any peaceful community fish, such as tetras, rasboras, livebearers, gouramis, angelfish and bettas. Avoid large fish that could swallow them and aggressive bottom dwellers. Good to know: Corys sometimes dart to the surface to gulp a bit of air. That's normal behavior, not a sign of trouble.

Omega One Brine Shrimp Omega One Freeze Dried Brine Shrimp offers the convenience of wholesome brine shrimp without the troubles of frozen or live brine shrimp. Keep dry and this item can be stored indefinitely. Brine shrimp are a good discus food and food for most other freshwater and saltwater species. Shipping Size: 19 gm

API Vacation Fish Feeder The API Vacation Pyramid Fish Feeder provides low level nutrition in a calcium base. Fish will pick at the pyramid until it is consumed in about 14 days. If you return from your vacation beforehand just take what's left and toss. The calcium base dissolves over a two week period and acts as a buffer to keep aquarium water in healthy parameters. Each "pyramid" feeds up to 10 inches of fish (so if you have a school of 10 zebra danios there you go) for up to fourteen days. If you have a very large tank with lots of expensive fish and you will be away for two or more weeks, then these vacation blocks are not what you need. You'll need someone to visit the tank and lightly feed the fish every couple days until our return. Shipping Size: One 1.2 oz pyramid

This colorful purple and green aquatic plant is a USA home grown favorite. The cardinal plant is moderately hardy and can handle tropical aquarium temperatures. Native to the Carolinas, we ship these in from a nursery in Florida. Each order comes with one cute little purple plant. Scientific Name: Lobelia cardinalis Shipping Size: Approx. 6 inches single colorful stemmed plant

Plant Weights Heavy plant weights are used to hold down plants in the aquarium. One lead weight can wrap around about 5 stemmed plants and sink the base to the substrate.
