Without lead weights or pots for some type of restriction most plants will float to the surface until they are naturally rooted. Each bag comes with 10 reusable weights.

CO2 Tablets JBJ CO2 Tablets slowly release CO2 to live aquarium plants for the course of the day. For very lightly planted tanks these may not be necessary, but for medium planted tanks these are perfect sources of CO2 without the bother of a CO2 canister and diffuser system! When is use don't panic when you see these dissolve in just a couple hours....they are not designed to dissolve over a 24 hour period, but to deliver 24 hours worth of plant growing CO2 into the aquarium environment. Each package comes with 100 tablets.

listings.commonName: Smart Automatic Water Top Off System
listings.description: Automatic Top Off System JBJ Advanced Automatic Water Top Off System will sense when water is low and automatically top off the tank to a preset level. Everything is included except the reservior which is usually just a one gallon bottle or small bucket. This is great for people who tend to travel or just want the next cool device for the fish tank. Each Nano ATO Top-off system comes with the sensor, pump, tubing, power supply, and accessories to put it all together - which is simple. Great for tanks up to 100 gallons. You might need something bigger for larger tanks.

Aquarium Light Timer ZooMed is best known for reptile products but the top brass there are avid aquarium hobbyists. So the company does come out with some fine aquarium products, like this very simple Aquasun Aquarium Timer. This is a carefree way to keep your aquatic pets on a regular cycle and, if applicable, ensure aquatic fauna (plants) get all the light they need. And all the sleep they need too.

The glowlight rasbora, or hengeli rasbora, has the same bright central markings and shape as the harlequin rasbora. However, the glowlight rasbora has a see-through body and yellow fins. These are not as common as harlequin rasboras but are very, very hardy and peaceful. A schooling fish, these should be purchased as four or more. Quick Facts Scientific Name Trigonostigma hengeli Origin Sumatra and Borneo, Indonesia Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1¼" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a dark substrate. Soft, slightly acidic water and gentle filtration bring out their best color. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as tetras, other rasboras, danios, corydoras, gouramis and dwarf shrimp. Avoid large predatory fish that could eat them. Good to know: In a well-planted tank a school of rasboras swims together in the middle of the tank, and their colors deepen as they settle in.
3" tall, 2 1/4" wide. Includes lid.

The zulu haplochromis of Lake Malawi in Africa features a bright blue head and a red and purple body with black vertical stripes. These fish are not as common in the trade but go well with peacock and mbuna cichlids. Zulu cichlids grow to nearly seven inches and do fine with good-quality cichlid pellets. Quick Facts Scientific Name Haplochromis "boadzulu" Origin Lake Malawi, Africa Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Semi-aggressive (males territorial) Adult Size Up to 7" Lifespan 8–10 years Diet Omnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 76–82°F pH 7.8–8.6 Shipping Size Medium: approx. 2" · Large: approx. 3" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a sand bottom, open swimming space in front and rockwork along the back. Lake Malawi and Lake Tanganyika cichlids need hard, alkaline water; crushed coral or aragonite sand helps hold the pH up. Feeding: Feed a quality cichlid pellet or flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like brine shrimp. Tankmates: Haps do well with peacocks and other haps of similar size, plus robust catfish like synodontis. Keep one male per similar-looking species, with several females, to limit fighting and crossbreeding. Good to know: Males take a year or more to show full adult color, and color best when females are present.

The rare Kyburzi Rainbow Tetra is a mesmerizing addition to the freshwater aquarium world, boasting bright, iridescent colors that shimmer as they swim. Native to Colombia's rivers, these active swimmers dazzle aquarists with their vibrant hues and playful demeanor. Best kept in schools of six or more, they flourish in well-planted tanks, where they can engage in their natural schooling and darting behaviors. Males typically showcase more intense coloration, especially during spawning seasons, while females are slightly more subdued. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hyphessobrycon sp. "Kyburzi" Origin Colombia Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2–3" Lifespan 5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a gentle filter. A dark substrate brings out their color. Keep a lid on the tank, since they can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, rasboras, corydoras, small gouramis and livebearers. Good to know: Males show the brightest rainbow colors, especially when they are settled in a planted tank.

Red Rivulus Killifish The Red Rivulus Killifish, often recognized for its striking red hue, is a captivating addition to any freshwater aquarium. While the juveniles may not exhibit the vibrant colors of their adult counterparts, with proper care, they will mature into the radiant red beauties they are known for. These fish are best kept in groups, as they thrive in a community setting. Scientific Name: Rivulus rubrolineatus Origin: South America,coastal regions from Venezuela to Brazil Lifespan: Up to 3 years Max Size: 2 to 3 inches Food: Flake, live, frozen Shipping Size: Juveniles, approx. 1 inch

Giant Hatchetfish The Giant Hatchetfish, also known as the Greater Silver Hatchetfish, is a unique marine fish recognized for its distinct hatchet-like shape. This species is found in every ocean except the North Pacific, primarily residing in the mesopelagic zone of tropical and subtropical waters. While the term "giant" is relative, this fish is the largest among marine hatchetfishes, often exceeding 110 millimeters (4.3 inches) in standard length. Ideal for advanced aquarists familiar with deep-sea species care. Scientific Name: Argyropelecus gigas Origin: Found in every ocean except the North Pacific Max Size: 3.5 inches Food: Typically small marine organisms Shipping Size: 2-3 inch

Neon Gold Twinbar Platy Immersed in vivid gold hues, the Neon Gold Twinbar Platy illuminates your aquarium with its effervescent presence. The twinbars on the tail fin accentuate its lively demeanor, making this variant a radiant addition to any community tank. The playful shimmer of gold combined with the distinctive twin bars brings a unique aesthetic charm, enlivening the underwater landscape. Scientific Name: Xiphophorus maculatus Origin: Central America Lifespan: 3-4 years Max Size: 2 1/2 inches Food: Flake, Live, Frozen Shipping Size: Approx. 1 inch

Lacey Java Fern Lacey Java Ferns are excellent additions to wooded aquariums, nano tanks, and a diverse range of planted tanks. They thrive with minimal care, making them a suitable choice for both novice and experienced aquarists. The unique lacey texture of the leaves creates an attractive underwater scenery and provides shelter for smaller aquatic inhabitants. Scientific Name - Microsorum pteropus 'Windelov' Shipping Size - 3-5 Inches

The Pigeon Blood (or Pigeon) Discus was developed in Germany in the 1970s by using the genetic stock of wild discus with red markings discovered by Heiko Bleher. The Pigeon Blood Discus subsequently became the parent to all other Red Discus, including Super-Reds, Red Marlboro, and Checkerboard. Quick Facts Scientific Name Symphysodon aequifasciatus (captive-bred color variety) Origin Amazon basin (captive-bred in Singapore) Care Level Moderate (needs warm, very clean water) Temperament Peaceful, shy; social Adult Size Up to 6–7" Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 82–88°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1½–4" (by size option) Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a reliable heater, gentle but strong filtration, and a bare bottom or fine sand for easy cleaning. Keep the tank in a quiet spot. Discus need very clean water. Feeding: Feed small meals of quality discus pellets or granules a few times a day, and remove uneaten food within a few minutes, since leftovers quickly foul the water. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. New arrivals may need frozen food for a while before they accept pellets. Tankmates: Discus are calm and shy, so choose gentle tankmates that enjoy the same warm water: cardinal and rummynose tetras, sterbai corydoras and small plecos are popular choices. Avoid fast, boisterous or fin-nipping fish, and anything that competes hard for food. Many keepers avoid angelfish, which can bully discus and share diseases. Living in groups: Discus are social and feel safest in a group. A single discus, or just two, tends to be stressed. When a pair forms to breed, they may claim part of the tank, so a group spreads out the attention. Good to know: Pigeon blood strains can show small black "peppering" marks depending on lighting, stress and diet. They usually fade in good conditions.

After just a few years, the breeders worked their Disney magic and created the Avatar Betta, complete with dark blue and black markings. These beautiful variations are large and awesome. Also, they are tough to breed, so they are a bit pricey. Quick Facts Scientific Name Betta splendens Origin Thailand (captive-bred) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Males fight each other; peaceful toward most other fish Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 76–82°F (needs a heater) pH 6.5–7.5 Breathes Air Yes – labyrinth fish take air from the surface Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give him a heater (bettas are tropical fish), a gentle filter and live or silk plants. Plakats are active swimmers and like room to patrol. Keep a lid on the tank and leave a gap of air under it, since bettas breathe from the surface. Feeding: Feed a few betta pellets or a pinch of flake once or twice a day. Bettas overeat easily, so small meals are best. They also enjoy frozen bloodworms. Tankmates: Never keep two male bettas together. Plakats are among the boldest bettas, so they do best alone or with sturdy, peaceful fish like corydoras and snails. Avoid fin-nippers and other labyrinth fish. Good to know: Short-finned plakats are strong, fast swimmers and the closest to the original fighting fish, so they are usually the most aggressive bettas. Keep them on their own or with sturdy, peaceful tankmates.

The Four Line Pictus Catfish has the same amazing whiskers and sleek body line as its cousin the spotted pictus catfish. The main difference between these two species is the marking - four line pictus catfish feature horizontal lines and dark spots along its light silver body. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pimelodus blochii Origin Colombia Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful (eats small fish) Adult Size Up to 6" Lifespan 8+ years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 2–3" Care Guide Tank setup: Pictus are active swimmers. Give them open swimming space, some hiding places, a soft bottom and good filtration. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms. Tankmates: They are peaceful but will eat small fish like neon tetras. Keep them with fish too large to fit in their mouth. Good to know: Pictus catfish have sharp spines in their fins, so use a container rather than a net when moving them.

The green dwarf farlowella is an olive-colored, skinny catfish that only grows to three inches. A great fish for small aquariums or big planted tanks if you want the challenge of finding the guy. These are wild caught fish from Colombia and need water temps above 74 degrees. Quick Facts Scientific Name Acestridium dichromum Origin Colombia Care Level Moderate Temperament Very peaceful Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 5 years Diet Algae eater (also eats algae wafers) Water Temperature 74–82°F pH 6.0–7.0 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a mature tank with driftwood, plants and gentle current. They need clean, stable water. Feeding: They graze on algae. Also feed algae wafers and sinking pellets. Tankmates: They are very peaceful and slow, so keep them with calm community fish that won't outcompete them for food. Good to know: These thin catfish blend in perfectly with plant stems, so you may have to look closely to spot them.

The L-002 Tiger Pleco only grows to 5 inches. The pattern varies from black stripes to reddish chocolate stripes. Tiger Plecos are scavengers, hardy, and do most of their scavenging at night, just like real tigers. Except they don't eat people, or fish. They might accidentally eat small fancy shrimp if they accidentally catch them. Quick Facts Scientific Name Panaqolus sp. L-002 Origin Tocantins River basin, Brazil Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 4–5" Lifespan 10+ years Diet Herbivore (driftwood, algae wafers) Water Temperature 76–84°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single, or several with a cave each Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plenty of driftwood, caves and good filtration. They are most active at night. Feeding: Feed algae wafers and sinking pellets, and keep driftwood in the tank, since they rasp on it as part of their diet. Tankmates: They are peaceful and get along with most community fish. Males may squabble over caves, so give each one its own hiding spot. Good to know: Tiger plecos stay small and keep their bold stripes as adults, which makes them a favorite for community tanks.

Only once a year are these catfish caught and exported from Colombia. The Colombian Dolphin Catfish is closely related to the marmoratus hammerhead catfish from Brazil and Peru. There are slight differences in the color pattern and dorsal fin. With its sleek appearance, this catfish is truly a standout in any aquatic setting. They are naturally found in soft-bottomed habitats, blending seamlessly with the substrate due to their unique coloration. In terms of temperament, they are relatively peaceful and thrive best when housed with other non-aggressive species of similar size. *This particular fish is a rare gem, and AFS offers it only once per year, making it a unique addition for the discerning aquarist. Quick Facts Scientific Name Ageneiosus magoi Origin Colombia Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful with fish its size Adult Size Up to 10" Lifespan 10+ years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 6" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a soft sand bottom, some open swimming space, driftwood and good filtration, plus a tight lid. Feeding: Feed meaty foods like quality carnivore pellets and frozen shrimp or fish. Many learn to take pellets once settled. Avoid feeder fish, which can carry disease. Tankmates: They are relatively peaceful but will eat small fish. Keep them with calm fish of similar size. Good to know: Dolphin catfish are sleek, active swimmers rather than bottom-sitters, so they cruise the open water more than most catfish.

A very rare color, the Barbie pink lobster is a new varietal bred in Taiwan and extremely hard to find. The pink freshwater lobster is less aggressive than the white and neon red and is suitable for most freshwater aquariums. Quick Facts Scientific Name Procambarus clarkii Origin Taiwan (captive-bred) Care Level Easy Temperament Semi-aggressive Adult Size Up to 4–5" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (scavenger) Water Temperature 65–80°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Single Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Crayfish need plenty of hiding places like caves or pipes and a tight-fitting lid, since they climb out. Avoid copper-based medications. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets once a day. They also eat vegetables and leftover food. Tankmates: Crayfish will catch and eat slow fish, shrimp and snails. They are best kept alone. Molting: Crayfish shed their shell to grow. Leave the old shell in the tank; they eat it to regain calcium. Good to know: These "lobsters" are actually a color form of the red swamp crayfish.

The extreme blue bolt shrimp has a blue body with soft white cloudy highlights. These are true Caridina, so they require clean water and cannot tolerate temperatures above 78 degrees. The high-grade extreme blue bolt shrimp will be a great complement to any very small aquarium. Quick Facts Scientific Name Caridina cf. cantonensis (blue bolt, Taiwan bee) Origin Taiwan (aquarium-bred) Care Level Moderate to difficult (needs soft, stable water) Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to ¾–1" Lifespan 1½–2 years Diet Omnivore (grazes on algae) Water Temperature 68–76°F pH 5.8–6.8 Water Hardness GH 4–6, KH 0–1 (soft) Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Caridina bee and Taiwan bee shrimp need soft, slightly acidic water. Use a mature, cycled tank with an active (buffering) shrimp substrate, RO water remineralized for shrimp, moss and plants, and a sponge filter. Feeding: Feed a small amount of quality shrimp food once a day, and remove any uneaten food after a few hours. Tankmates: Caridina are best kept in a shrimp-only tank or with tiny, peaceful fish like otocinclus, plus snails. Avoid cichlids and other fish that will eat shrimp. Different bee and Taiwan bee varieties can crossbreed, but they will not breed with Neocaridina. Good to know: Acclimate slowly (drip for an hour or more). Stable water matters more than perfect numbers, and sudden changes in temperature or hardness are the most common cause of losses.

Rusty Pygmy Angelfish: The Miniature Gem The Rusty Pygmy Angelfish (Centropyge ferrugata), also known simply as the Rusty Angelfish or Ferrugata Angelfish , is a hardy and attractive dwarf angelfish highly valued in the marine aquarium hobby. This species is named for its primary coloration: a deep rusty-orange or amber body color accented with numerous irregularly shaped black spots that decrease in size toward the ventral area. Its striking appearance is completed by brilliant sapphire-blue margins on both the dorsal and anal fins. As a small member of the Pomacanthidae family, the Rusty Angelfish typically reaches a maximum size of only 4 inches (10 cm) , making it suitable for smaller marine systems. Native to the Western Pacific (from Japan to the Philippines), this fish is a continuous grazer that requires a mature system with ample live rock for hiding, grazing on microalgae, and establishing territory. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: The Rusty Angelfish is an Omnivore. Its diet must be balanced between meaty foods and vegetable matter. It should be offered a varied diet consisting of marine algae (like Spirulina), high-quality angelfish preparations, and meaty frozen foods such as mysis shrimp, brine shrimp, and chopped krill. Frequent feeding (2-3 times per day) is essential to minimize the likelihood of it nipping at corals. Minimum Tank Size: A minimum of 50–70 gallons is recommended to provide sufficient live rock for grazing and enough space to establish a territory, reducing aggression. Reef Compatibility: It is rated Reef Safe With Caution. Like many dwarf angels, this species is prone to occasionally nip at the mantles of Tridacna clams and the polyps of certain corals, particularly stony corals (LPS/SPS) and soft corals. It is best suited for a fish-only-with-live-rock (FOWLR) tank or a mixed reef where the hobbyist is prepared for potential nipping. Temperament: It is Semi-Aggressive / Territorial. While peaceful toward larger, dissimilar-looking fish, it is highly territorial toward other dwarf angelfish species, especially those with similar coloration (e.g., Coral Beauties or Potter's Angels). It must be kept as the sole Centropyge angelfish unless housed in a very large aquarium (350+ gallons) with different species introduced simultaneously. It is best kept singly. Social Behavior: This is a hermaphroditic species, capable of changing sex from female to male. A single fish is recommended, but pairs or harems can be kept in a large system if introduced at the same time. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Centropyge ferrugata Primary Common Name: Rusty Pygmy Angelfish Other Common Names: Rusty Angelfish, Ferrugata Angelfish, Dwarf Rusty Angel Origin: Western Pacific (Japan, Philippines, Indonesia) Max Size: 4 inches (10 cm) Temperament: Semi-Aggressive / Territorial Care Level: Moderate Diet: Omnivore (Requires a balanced diet of meaty and algae-based foods) Minimum Tank Size: 50–70 Gallons Reef Compatibility: With Caution (Prone to nipping corals and clam mantles)

Multibarred Angelfish: Expert-Level Care The Multibarred Angelfish (Paracentropyge multifasciata), also known as the Many-Banded Angelfish or Barred Angelfish , is a strikingly patterned but demanding dwarf angelfish species. It is characterized by its white or pale yellow body crossed with 8 to 9 bold, vertical black bands, a yellow snout and belly, and usually a blue eyespot (ocellus) on the dorsal fin of juveniles. This species originates from the steep outer reef slopes of the Indo-Pacific, typically inhabiting deep caves and crevices between 60 to over 200 feet. Because of its deepwater origin and specialized dietary needs—particularly its reliance on sponges—the Multibar Angel is generally only recommended for advanced or expert aquarists with very stable, mature reef systems. In the aquarium, the Multibar Angel is shy and secretive initially, requiring abundant hiding places to feel secure. While generally peaceful towards most tankmates, it requires careful monitoring in a reef environment due to its diet. Diet & Compatibility: Care Level: Expert / Advanced . This fish is sensitive to stress and water quality fluctuations and can be notoriously difficult to acclimate and feed, especially if wild-caught. Captive-bred specimens are strongly preferred as they are pre-conditioned to prepared foods. Diet: The Multibar Angel is an Omnivore that feeds heavily on sponges, algae, and small benthic organisms in the wild. Its aquarium diet must be diverse and include high-quality marine algae, spirulina, and various meaty frozen foods (mysis shrimp, enriched brine shrimp). Angelfish formulas containing sponge material are highly beneficial for long-term health. Feeding: Feed 2–3 times daily. Using a feeding clip or smearing food on rocks (like Masstick) encourages its natural grazing behavior and may help finicky eaters. Minimum Tank Size: A minimum of 70–90 gallons is required. The tank must be well-established (6+ months old) with plenty of live rock to support grazing. Reef Compatibility: It is rated Reef Safe With Caution. It may occasionally nip at clam mantles (Tridacnid clams), sponges, and the polyps of certain Large Polyp Stony (LPS) corals and soft corals. A well-fed Multibar Angel is less likely to engage in destructive nipping. Temperament: It is Semi-Aggressive / Territorial. It is peaceful to most large, non-aggressive fish but will become territorial toward other dwarf angelfish, particularly those in the same genus. It is best kept as the sole dwarf angelfish in the tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Paracentropyge multifasciata Primary Common Name: Multibarred Angelfish Other Common Names: Many-Banded Angelfish, Barred Angelfish Origin: Indo-Pacific (Deepwater slopes) Max Size: 4.5-5 inches (11-12 cm) Temperament: Semi-Aggressive / Territorial (Shy) Diet: Omnivore (Requires sponge and algae content) Minimum Tank Size: 70-90+ Gallons Reef Compatibility: With Caution (May nip at LPS/clams)

Xanthurus Cream Angelfish: The Indian Ocean Beauty The Xanthurus Cream Angelfish (Apolemichthys xanthurus), also frequently sold as the Indian Yellowtail Angelfish or Cream Angelfish, is a highly regarded and relatively hardy choice among the medium-sized marine angelfishes. It is native to the Western Indian Ocean, with populations around Mauritius, the Maldives, Sri Lanka, and the eastern coast of India. Its striking coloration matures from a juvenile pattern of dark bars into a beautiful adult presentation: a cream or pale gold body covered in a delicate, dark, lattice-like pattern on the scales. The Xanthurus Cream Angelfish adapts well to aquarium life, making it a good choice for intermediate aquarists with large fish-only or fish-only-with-live-rock (FOWLR) systems. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: This is an Omnivore with a natural diet consisting of algae, sponges, and small crustaceans. In the aquarium, a diverse diet is crucial for health and to curb potential nipping behavior. Offer high-quality marine flakes and pellets, Spirulina-enriched foods, frozen preparations for herbivores (like seaweed and algae sheets), and meaty foods (mysis shrimp, enriched brine shrimp, chopped squid). Aquarium Environment: A minimum tank size of 125 gallons is recommended to provide ample swimming space and territory. Provide plenty of live rock structures with caves and crevices for grazing and hiding, as the fish can be shy when first introduced. Reef Compatibility: It is generally considered Reef Safe With Caution . This species is prone to nipping at the mantles of large clams (Tridacna spp.) and may sample certain stony (LPS/SPS) and soft corals. The likelihood of nipping often decreases with consistent and abundant feeding of appropriate foods. Temperament: It is Semi-Aggressive and generally peaceful toward most tankmates, but it will be territorial toward other angelfish, especially those of the same genus (Apolemichthys). It should be kept singly and is best housed with other active or semi-aggressive fish, such as tangs, large wrasses, and puffers. Avoid keeping with smaller, very placid fish. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Apolemichthys xanthurus Primary Common Name: Xanthurus Cream Angelfish Other Common Names: Indian Yellowtail Angelfish, Cream Angelfish, Yellowtail Black Angelfish Origin: Western Indian Ocean (Maldives, Sri Lanka, India) Max Size: Up to 7-8 inches (18-20 cm) Temperament: Semi-Aggressive / Territorial Diet: Omnivore (Requires a mixed diet of sponges, algae, and meaty foods) Minimum Tank Size: 125 Gallons Reef Compatibility: With Caution (May nip clams, soft corals, and LPS)

Blue Reef Chromis (Chromis cyanea): The Electric Blue Schooler The Blue Reef Chromis (Chromis cyanea) is one of the most popular and visually striking damselfish species in the marine aquarium hobby. It is highly valued for its intense electric blue coloration and its active, schooling behavior, which brings life and movement to the mid-water column of the reef tank. The Blue Reef Chromis features a brilliant, saturated electric blue body with an elongated, deeply forked tail. Mature males often develop dark or black margins on the dorsal and caudal fins. Unlike the related Blue/Green Chromis (C. viridis), C. cyanea maintains a deeper, more fluorescent blue color, making it an excellent addition to showcase vibrant reef lighting. This species is a planktivore and is naturally found in large, active schools over coral reefs. To replicate their natural social structure and minimize territorial aggression, they are best kept in odd-numbered groups of three or more, though groups of five or more are ideal for long-term success. Care & Compatibility: Diet: The Blue Reef Chromis is an Omnivore/Planktivore and feeds constantly in the wild. They require a varied diet, primarily consisting of high-quality marine flake food, pellet food, and small meaty frozen foods like Mysis shrimp, Artemia (Brine shrimp), and finely chopped seafood. Frequent, small feedings (3-4 times daily) are crucial due to their high metabolism. Temperament: Generally Peaceful, especially when housed in a school. However, if kept singly or in pairs, they can become territorial or aggressive toward smaller, less aggressive tankmates. Keeping them in an appropriately sized group diffuses aggression among themselves. Reef Compatibility: Excellent (Reef Safe). They pose no threat to corals (SPS, LPS, or Soft Corals), ornamental shrimp, or other invertebrates. They actively swim in the water column and rarely disturb the substrate. Tank Requirements: While a single specimen can live in a 30-gallon tank, a school requires 75 gallons or more to provide adequate swimming space and minimize territorial stress among the group. They require strong, turbulent water flow to simulate their natural reef environment. Acclimation & Health: They are relatively hardy once settled, but they are planktivores that rely on constant food intake. They should be observed closely during acclimation and quarantine to ensure they are eating immediately. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Chromis cyanea Primary Common Name: Blue Reef Chromis Other Common Names: Blue Chromis, Deep Blue Damsel Origin: Western Atlantic Ocean (Caribbean, Florida, Bahamas) Maximum Size: 3.5 – 4 inches (8-10 cm) Temperament: Peaceful (Best kept in schools) Diet: Omnivore/Planktivore Minimum Tank Size: 75 Gallons (For a school of 5+) Reef Compatibility: Excellent (Reef Safe) Care Level: Easy to Moderate

The Garden Eel is 100% reef safe. A garden eel's diet is comprised of floating zooplankton brought to it by the water's current, which needs to be duplicated with the appropriate marine food. The garden eel will always keep a part of its body inside the burrow even when feeding. If it cannot reach the food while also maintaining a "foot" in its burrow it will just simply let it pass by uneaten. For this reason the spotted garden eel is even compatible with the smallest of ornamental shrimps and you simply won't have to worry about the eel eating its neighbors. You will however have to worry about the eel's neighbors eating the eels due to their small size and docile nature. In the wild triggerfish are known for digging out garden eels right out of their burrow in pursuit of a meal (Shedd Aquarium 2011). For this reason avoid any aggressive fish-eating specimens as tank mates for your garden eels. Big active fishes will spook the eels and force them to spend much of their time inside their burrows or with only their heads sticking out. This will prevent them from eating properly and cause them undue stress. This eel is cool seen in the tank half in the sand half out. Scientific Name: Heterocongrinae Origin: Ind onesia Max Size : 14 inches Diet: Floating zooplankton Shipping Size: Approx. 5 inches

Green Wolf Eel: The Cave-Dwelling Blenny The Green Wolf Eel (Congrogadus subducens) is a unique and captivating marine fish often sold under the misleading name "eel" due to its elongated, snake-like body and reclusive behavior. It is actually a member of the family Congrogadidae (Eel Blennies) and is a popular choice for large, predatory marine aquariums. Native to the Indo-Pacific region, this species is known for its highly variable coloration, ranging from bright olive green to marbled shades of brown, often with iridescent blue or white spots near the head. They are primarily nocturnal ambush predators, spending their day hiding among rocks, caves, or thick coral branches, with only their head exposed. Despite its intimidating appearance, the Green Wolf Eel is shy and generally peaceful towards tankmates that are too large to be considered prey. It typically reaches an adult size of 16 to 18 inches (40-45 cm) in the home aquarium and requires a secure environment that accommodates its need for substantial hiding spots. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: This fish is a dedicated Carnivore, feeding primarily on small invertebrates and fish in the wild. In captivity, it must be offered meaty foods, including frozen items like krill, silversides, chopped market shrimp, and squid. It can be slow to recognize non-living food and may need to be offered food via tongs until acclimated. Feeding: Feed adults every 2-3 days, ensuring they receive enough to maintain their robust body condition. A hungry wolf eel may become more bold and aggressive toward smaller tankmates. Reef Compatibility: It is Not Reef Safe. While they will typically leave corals alone, they will consume nearly all ornamental invertebrates (shrimp, crabs, snails) and any small fish that fit into their mouth. They are best kept in a large Fish Only With Live Rock (FOWLR) system. Temperament: It is Semi-Aggressive / Predatory. It should only be housed with large, robust, and fast-moving tankmates that are too large to be swallowed. Good tankmates include large angelfish, puffers, and morays. They should not be kept with other Congrogadus species unless in a very large tank or if a mated pair is established. Housing Requirements: Provide a deep sand bed and ample rockwork to create multiple, tight-fitting caves. These fish will rearrange substrate to make their preferred home. A tight-fitting lid is essential as they are known to escape. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Congrogadus subducens Primary Common Name: Green Wolf Eel Other Common Names: Wolf Blenny, Green Wolf Blenny, False Eel, Marine Eel Origin: Indo-Pacific (Widespread) Max Size: 16-18 inches (40-45 cm) Temperament: Semi-Aggressive / Predatory Diet: Carnivore (Meaty frozen foods) Minimum Tank Size: 75+ Gallons Reef Compatibility: No (Will eat invertebrates and small fish)

Tessalata Eel: The Giant of the Reef The Tessalata Eel (Gymnothorax favagineus), also widely known as the Honeycomb Moray or Laced Moray , is one of the largest and most dramatically patterned moray eels available to hobbyists. It is easily identified by its striking, high-contrast coloration: a white or creamy yellow body overlaid with dark brown to black blotches that form a distinct honeycomb or tessellated pattern . This impressive fish is a magnificent, though highly demanding, addition to a very large marine aquarium. Native to the Indo-Pacific region, from the Red Sea to the Great Barrier Reef, the Tessalata Eel is a true giant, capable of reaching lengths of 5 to 6 feet (150–180 cm) in captivity, and up to 10 feet in the wild. Due to its size, immense bioload, and powerful build, a minimum aquarium size of 180 gallons is required, with larger systems (300+ gallons) highly recommended for long-term adult care. The Tessalata Eel is a powerful, nocturnal predator that requires a tightly sealed aquarium, as all morays are notorious escape artists. Extreme caution should always be exercised when performing tank maintenance, as its bite is powerful and can lead to serious bacterial infection. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: This eel is a dedicated Carnivore and an ambush predator . It feeds primarily on fish and cephalopods (like octopus) at night. In captivity, it must be fed a varied diet of meaty frozen foods, such as silversides , krill, pieces of raw fish, squid, and shrimp. It should be fed via tongs or a feeding stick to reduce the risk of biting the owner's hand. Feeding: To prevent digestive issues and limit bioload, large morays should be fed one substantial meal only every 3–4 days . Overfeeding can cause health problems and aggressive behavior. Reef Compatibility: It is Reef Safe With Caution . While the eel will generally ignore corals, its large size and powerful movements can easily knock over rockwork and coral colonies. **It is NOT Invert Safe**, and will consume virtually all ornamental shrimp, crabs, and smaller fish. Temperament: It is Aggressive / Predatory . This species should only be housed in a Fish Only With Live Rock (FOWLR) system with very large, robust, and equally aggressive tankmates (e.g., large groupers, triggerfish, or large angels) that are too big to be swallowed. It is generally solitary and should not be kept with other morays unless in a massive aquarium. Housing Requirements: The aquarium must be scaped with large, stable, and well-anchored rockwork to provide multiple secure caves and crevices where the eel can hide its entire body. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Gymnothorax favagineus Primary Common Name: Tessalata Eel Other Common Names: Honeycomb Moray, Laced Moray, Leopard Eel Origin: Indo-Pacific (Red Sea to Great Barrier Reef) Max Size: 5–10 feet (150–300 cm) Temperament: Aggressive / Predatory ( Requires Caution ) Diet: Carnivore (Meaty frozen foods) Minimum Tank Size: 180+ Gallons (Larger is strongly preferred) Reef Compatibility: With Caution (Will consume small fish and invertebrates)

Aurora Goby The Aurora Goby (Amblyeleotris aurora), also known as the Pinkbar Goby , features a pearly-white body marked with broad, vertical bright pink or orange-red bars and a distinctive yellow tail. Aurora was the Greek goddess of sunrise, which is the namesake of this sunrise colored fish. Stunning Appearance: Its vibrant pink stripes and yellow tail make it a colorful and beautiful feature. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Amblyeleotris aurora Origin: Indo-Pacific Reefs, Africa Max Size: 4.5 inches Lifespan: 5+ years Diet: Carnivore. Requires a varied diet of meaty frozen foods, such as mysis shrimp, brine shrimp, and pellet foods. Shipping Size: 1.5-3 inches

This blenny is known for its beautiful light blue or greenish coloration and its calm, non-aggressive demeanor. The Forktail Blenny possesses a fascinating defense mechanism: a set of venomous fangs that it uses to deter predators. Because of this, it is rarely bothered by larger fish, making it a confident and lively inhabitant. It's a fantastic choice for a community reef tank due to its peaceful nature and hardiness. Why the Forktail Blenny is a Great Choice: Elegant Appearance: Its streamlined body and graceful forked tail provide a unique aesthetic to any tank. Peaceful Temperament: It is a non-aggressive species that coexists well with other peaceful tank mates. Hardy & Resilient: This species is known for its resilience and adaptability, making it an excellent choice for a variety of tank conditions. Reef-Safe: The Canary Blenny is completely safe to keep with all types of corals and invertebrates. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Meiacanthus oualanensis Origin: Western Pacific Reefs Max Size: 4.5 inches Lifespan: 3-5 years Diet: Omnivore. It feeds on small invertebrates and prepared foods like mysis shrimp, brine shrimp, and high-quality pellets. Shipping Size: 1.5-2.5 inches

Clown Citron Goby The Citron Clown Goby, or as Wikki calls it the Lemon Coralgoby, is hardy and small. The Lemon Coralgoby is a good addition to a beginner small tank and small saltwater aquariums. The Citron Goby is a loner and will fight with other Citron Goby, but otherwise these guys are peaceful tankmates. Clown gobies are called clowns because their odd shy darting behavior, and coral gobies because they tend to crawl along coral branches. Scientific Name: Gobiodon citrinus Max Size: 2 inches Diet: brine shrimp, frozen mysis shrimp, table shrimp, and frozen food preparations for carnivores. Require Tank Size: 10+ gallon

Black Clown Goby The Black Clown Goby will grow to less than two inches so these fish cannot be kept with large species. Other than that, they are mild, hardy, and if kept happy and in groups they will even spawn in the aquarium. Great beginner fish and very affordable. Scientific Name: Gobiodon strangulatus Diet: a variety of brine shrimp, frozen mysis shrimp, table shrimp, and frozen food preparations for carnivores. Max Size: 2 inches Require tank size: 10+ gallons Shipping Size: Approx. 1 1/2 inches

Engineer Goby: The Master Architect of the Substrate The Engineer Goby (Pholidichthys leucotaenia), also widely known as the Convict Goby or Convict Blenny , is one of the most intriguing and unique marine fish available to hobbyists. Despite its common names, this species is neither a true goby nor a blenny; it belongs to its own distinct family, Pholidichthyidae. Juveniles feature striking black-and-white horizontal stripes reminiscent of a convict's uniform or a coral cat shark, while adults undergo a dramatic visual transformation into a pattern of dark, vertical bars and marbling on an elongated, eel-like body. Native to the Central Indo-Pacific, from the Philippines to the Solomon Islands, the Engineer Goby is famous for its tireless burrowing behavior. In the wild and in home aquariums, it creates extensive network tunnels beneath rockwork and sand. Individuals can reach an impressive maximum length of 10 to 12 inches (25-30 cm). Because of their constant digging and adult size, a minimum aquarium size of 55 gallons is required, along with a deep sand bed and rockwork secured directly to the bottom glass to prevent structural collapses. The Engineer Goby is an exceptionally peaceful and hardy species that adds tremendous character to a marine setup. While completely harmless to corals and fish, its endless engineering projects mean aquarists must ensure all rock formations are completely stable. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: This species is a dedicated Carnivore . In captivity, it readily accepts a wide variety of frozen meaty foods such as mysis shrimp , chopped brine shrimp, krill, finely chopped squid, and high-quality carnivore pellets or flakes. Juveniles are active feeders in the water column, while secretive adults often wait near their burrow entrances for food to drift past. Feeding: Feed 1-2 times daily. Target feeding near their primary burrow entrance using a pipette or feeding tongs can ensure timid or shy individuals receive sufficient nutrition. Reef Compatibility: It is Reef Safe with minor caveats. The Engineer Goby will never nip at or consume hard or soft corals. However, its digging can undermine rock bases, potentially tipping corals over or smothering low-lying species (like brain corals or acans) in sand dust clouds. Temperament: It is Peaceful . They are non-aggressive toward other fish species and can easily be kept individually, in pairs, or in small groups (provided there is ample sand bed space and hiding spots for each individual). Substrate & Safety: Always place your live rock directly on the bottom glass panel before adding sand. If rockwork rests on top of the substrate, the Engineer Goby's tunneling will cause the structure to shift, collapse, or crack the glass. A fine-to-medium sand bed of at least 2 to 3 inches is essential for their natural digging behavior. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Pholidichthys leucotaenia Primary Common Name: Engineer Goby Other Common Names: Convict Goby, Convict Blenny, Pacific Eel Goby Origin: Indo-Pacific (Philippines, Indonesia, Solomon Islands) Max Size: 10-12 inches (25-30 cm) Temperament: Peaceful Diet: Carnivore (Frozen meaty foods, mysis, marine pelleted diets) Minimum Tank Size: 55+ Gallons Reef Compatibility: Reef Safe (With caution for rockwork stability)

Firefish Goby: An Elegant & Peaceful Reef Dweller The Firefish Goby (Nemateleotris magnifica), also known as the Firefish Dartfish, is a captivating and popular species that adds a touch of graceful elegance to any marine aquarium . Its stunning appearance features a slender body that is a pale yellow or white at the head and transitions to a brilliant fiery red or orange towards its tail. This fish is known for its graceful, hovering movements in the water column and its peaceful, shy temperament. It is an excellent choice for a reef aquarium, where it will leave corals and invertebrates completely unharmed. Why the Firefish Goby is a Great Choice: Stunning Coloration: Its vibrant red-to-orange tail creates a beautiful, eye-catching display. Peaceful & Shy: It is a non-aggressive species that coexists well with other peaceful tank mates. Unique Behavior: It hovers elegantly in the water column, adding graceful movement to the tank. Reef-Safe: The Firefish Goby is completely safe to keep with all types of corals and invertebrates. Important Note: The Firefish Goby is a known jumper, especially when startled. A secure, tight-fitting lid is essential to prevent it from escaping the tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Nemateleotris magnifica Origin: Indo-Pacific Reefs Max Size: 3 inches Lifespan: 5 years or more Diet: Omnivore. A varied diet of high-quality frozen foods like brine shrimp and mysis shrimp, as well as flake foods. Shipping Size: 1-2 inches

Forktail Blenny The Forktail Blenny is also known as the Lyretail Fang Blenny or Yellowtail Fang Blenny. The Forktail Blenny has a caudal fin that resembles a fork, with two long exterior spines and five much shorter middle spines. The body is a pale blue that runs like watercolor into a bluish-yellow at the tail. Males are generally larger than females and experience a succession of color changes when breeding. Scientific Name: Meiacanthus atrodorsalis Origin: Pacific Ocean Lifespan: 4 years Max Size : 5 inches Diet: zooplankton,algae Shipping Size: 1 1/4 to 3 inches

Pearly Yellowhead Jawfish: The Charismatic Burrow-Builder The Yellowhead Jawfish (Opistognathus aurifrons) is a fascinating and highly sought-after species known for its unique behavior and vibrant coloration. With a brilliant yellow head and a pearly blue body, this fish is a true centerpiece for any marine aquarium. The Yellowhead Jawfish is renowned for its charming habit of building a burrow in the sand bed, which it meticulously maintains and defends. It spends its day hovering vertically just above the entrance, darting down headfirst into its home when startled. This peaceful and captivating fish is an excellent choice for a community reef tank, provided it has a deep sand bed with plenty of rubble to construct its burrow. Why the Yellowhead Jawfish is a Great Choice: Unique Personality: Its burrow-building behavior and hovering stance make it one of the most entertaining fish to watch. Striking Appearance: The bright yellow head provides a beautiful splash of color to the tank. Peaceful Temperament: It's a non-aggressive species that coexists well with other peaceful tank mates. Reef-Safe: The Yellowhead Jawfish is completely safe to keep with all types of corals and invertebrates. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Opistognathus aurifrons Origin: Western Atlantic Ocean Max Size: 4 inches Lifespan: 5 years or more Diet: Carnivore. It feeds on small invertebrates in the water column and will readily accept high-quality prepared foods like mysis shrimp and brine shrimp. Shipping Size: 1.5-2.5 inches

Neon Blue Goby The saltwater Blue Stripe Goby, or Neon Blue Goby, only grows to two inches but these fish are tough and handle a wide range of water conditions. Very colorful and suitable for beginners and experts. These fish will adapt to nano tanks and reef tanks. The Neon Blue Goby are cleaner fish and happily remove parasites from larger species. Scientific Name: Elacatinus oceanops Origin: Captive bred Max Size: 2 inches Diet: Carnivore Shipping Size: 1 to 1 1/2 inches

Red Scooter Blenny: The Charismatic Stargazer The Red Scooter Blenny (Synchiropus stellatus), more accurately a type of dragonet (Stargazer Dragonet), is a captivating and popular species known for its unique "scooting" motion and vibrant coloration. With a body covered in a beautiful mosaic of red, orange, and white patterns, this fish adds an intricate and dynamic presence to any marine aquarium. The Red Scooter Blenny spends its day tirelessly searching for food, "scooting" along the live rock and substrate. It is a peaceful and non-aggressive species, but it is recommended for experienced aquarists only due to its highly specialized diet. Like other dragonets, it requires a constant supply of live copepods and other tiny invertebrates, making a mature and well-established tank essential for its survival. Why the Red Scooter Blenny is a Great Choice (for the right tank): Exquisite Coloration: Its intricate red and orange patterns provide a stunning visual contrast. Unique Behavior: Its distinctive "scooting" and foraging habits add a fascinating element to the reef floor. Peaceful Temperament: It's a non-aggressive species that poses no threat to other fish, corals, or invertebrates. Reef-Safe: It is completely safe to keep with all types of corals and invertebrates. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Synchiropus stellatus Origin: Western Indo-Pacific Reefs Max Size: 3 inches Lifespan: 5 years or more Diet: Carnivore. Requires a constant supply of live copepods and other tiny invertebrates. Shipping Size: 1-2 inches

Railway Sleeper Goby The Railway Sleeper Goby is also known as a Sleeper Railway Glider Goby. This timid saltwater goby is a great addition to a reef aquarium. They have very bright parallel lines like railroad tracks and they are lazy and docile and help maintain the sand bed. Scientific Name: Valenciennea helsdingeni Origin: Indonesia Max Size: 6 inches Diet: Carnivore Shipping Size: 1 1/2 to 3 inches

Rainfordi Goby The Rainfordi Goby is also called the Old Glory Goby due to the Southern Flag cross stripes on the body. The fish grow to three inches and are very hardy. Named after Australia's most famous wine maker, we are sure why. E.H. Rainford. Scientific name: Koumansetta rainfordi Origin: Australia Max Size: 2 1/2 inches Diet: Frozen meaty foods Shipping Size: 1 to 2 inches

Randall's Goby Randall's Goby or Orange Stripe Prawn Goby , is one of the most desirable gobies in the aquatic trade due to its adaptability, hardiness, and beauty. It is a peaceful fish, but may occasionally quarrel with conspecifics if kept together, or if the tank is too small . At a full size of only three inches Randall's Goby is suitable for nano tanks and larger rock and reef tanks. It is possible for the Orange Stripe Prawn Goby to spawn successfully in an aquarium. They may also form a symbiotic relationship with any pistol shrimp. Scientific Name: Amblyeleotris randalli Origin: Cebu Max Size: 4 1/2 inches Diet: mysis shrimp, vitamin-enriched brine shrimp, and chopped table shrimp. It needs to be fed at least twice per day. Approximate Size: 1 to 2 inches

Red Lip Blenny The saltwater Red Lip Blenny is a lso known as the Lipstick Blenny, and Devilfish, has a grayish brown elongated body and an extended mouth with its namesake red lips. The Red Lip Blenny exhibits the characteristic continuous dorsal fin, blunt head, and specialized teeth found in the blenny family. They will often find a favorite spot in the tank and spend most of their time in that "home". In their time spent outside of their home, they will explore the nooks and crannies created by nicely constructed live rock work. The Red Lip Blenny is a prolific jumper so it should only be housed in a tank with tightly sealed lid to prevent potential escape. Scientific Name: Ophloblennius atlanticus Origin: Caribbean Max Size: 5 inches Diet: Omnivore Shipping Size: 1 to 2 1/2 inches

Red Dragonet Blenny: The Jeweled Gem of the Reef The Red Dragonet (Synchiropus sycorax), also known as the Ruby Red Mandarin , is a highly sought-after and exquisite species that adds a vibrant splash of color and a gentle presence to any marine aquarium . This magnificent dragonet has a brilliant red-orange body adorned with striking electric blue dots that shimmer under aquarium lighting. Its unique appearance and shy, peaceful demeanor make it a prized addition. Unlike other fish that swim constantly, the Red Dragonet Blenny "walks" along the rockwork and substrate, constantly hunting for food. It is completely reef-safe and will not harm corals, clams, or other invertebrates. It's crucial to note that this species has a highly specialized diet and requires a well-established, mature tank with a thriving population of live copepods to survive. Why the Red Dragonet Blenny is a Great Choice: Stunning Appearance: Its vibrant red body and electric blue dots make it a true showpiece. Completely Reef-Safe: It will not harm corals, clams, or most other invertebrates. Peaceful Temperament: It is a non-aggressive species that coexists well with other peaceful fish. Unique Behavior: Its habit of "walking" on the substrate adds a unique and interesting dynamic to the tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Synchiropus sycorax Origin: Western Pacific Reefs Max Size: 2-3 inches Lifespan: 5-7 years Diet: Carnivore. Primarily feeds on live copepods and other microfauna. Shipping Size: 1.5-2.5 inches

Scissortail Goby: The Elegant & Graceful Dartfish The Scissortail Goby (Ptereleotris evides), also known as the Darterfish, is a striking and peaceful species that adds a beautiful, dynamic presence to any marine aquarium . Its unique appearance features a streamlined body with a pearly white or light blue front half that transitions to a solid black back half, ending in a deeply forked "scissortail" . This graceful fish spends its time hovering in the water column, darting into rockwork when startled. The Scissortail Goby is a non-aggressive species and is a perfect choice for a community reef tank with other peaceful tank mates. Its tranquil nature and elegant swimming style make it a captivating addition for hobbyists of all experience levels. Why the Scissortail Goby is a Great Choice: Striking Coloration: Its two-toned body and unique tail provide a beautiful visual contrast. Peaceful Temperament: It is a non-aggressive species that coexists well with other peaceful tank mates. Graceful Movement: It hovers and darts with a unique, elegant swimming style. Reef-Safe: The Scissortail Goby is completely safe to keep with all types of corals and invertebrates. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Ptereleotris evides Origin: Indo-Pacific Reefs Max Size: 5.5 inches Lifespan: 3-5 years Diet: Carnivore. It feeds on small invertebrates in the water column and will readily accept high-quality prepared foods. Shipping Size: 2-3 inches

Steinitz Goby In the wild the Steinitz Goby is a "prawn goby". Prawn gobies like with prawns and use their burrows to hide. In exchange prawn goby alert the prawns to approaching predators. In the aquarium these gobies get along with other fish and will require some tunnels or rocks to hide, and a two inch deep substrate of sand. Scientific name: Amblyeleotris steinitzi Origin: Red Sea Max Size: 5 inches Diet: Frozen meaty foods Shipping Size: Approx. 2 inches

Tangaroa Goby The Tangaroa Goby is another prawn goby and if kept with gunman shrimp will demonstrate the symbiotic behavior. The fish do well in nano and reef tanks and only grow to two inches. Tangaroa Gobies need some sandy areas to burrow and a few rocks to explore and hide in. Scientific name: Origin: Indonesia Max Size : 2 inches Diet: Scavenger, meaty foods Shipping Size : Approx. 1 inch

Blueface Tilefish: The Bluehead Flasher The Blueface Tilefish (Hoplolatilus starcki) is a beautiful and highly active marine fish prized for its striking coloration: a vibrant cobalt blue head that contrasts sharply with a pale yellow or yellowish-white body and tail. It is also known as the Stark's Tilefish, Bluehead Tilefish, or Purplehead Tilefish. Native to the deep reef slopes and rubble areas of the Indo-Pacific, this species is a fast and constant swimmer, spending its days hovering mid-water to ambush zooplankton. Its key behavior is its ability to quickly dart, head-first, into a burrow it excavates in the sand or under rubble when threatened. This burrow serves as a crucial overnight shelter and a safe haven when stressed. The Blueface Tilefish is considered a moderate-care fish due to its shy nature, sensitivity to stress (especially during transport and acclimation), and the need for frequent feeding. Because they are notorious for jumping when startled, a tight-fitting aquarium lid is absolutely essential for their successful, long-term care. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: This fish is a dedicated Carnivore that feeds primarily on zooplankton from the water column. In the aquarium, their diet must consist of small, meaty foods like frozen Mysis shrimp, enriched Brine shrimp, and finely chopped crustacean flesh. Feeding: Due to their fast metabolism and need to compete in the water column, they require frequent feeding, ideally 2 to 3 times per day, especially when newly introduced to the tank. They will rarely, if ever, feed from the substrate. Reef Compatibility: It is generally considered Reef Safe. It will not harm corals. However, like many carnivores, it may occasionally prey upon very small ornamental shrimp or tiny crabs, though this is less frequent than with more aggressive predators. Temperament: It is a Peaceful fish. It should only be housed with other peaceful to semi-aggressive fish (like smaller tangs, wrasses, and anthias) that will not harass it or outcompete it for food. Avoid large, aggressive predators that will cause undue stress. They can be kept singly, in mated pairs, or in small groups in very large, established aquariums. Tank Requirements: Requires a minimum 50-75 gallon tank with a secure lid. The substrate must be a deep sand bed (at least 3 inches) with scattered rubble or stable rockwork to allow the fish to construct and maintain a secure burrow. They thrive with moderate to high water quality and plenty of open swimming space. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Hoplolatilus starcki Primary Common Name: Blueface Tilefish Other Common Names: Stark's Tilefish, Bluehead Tilefish, Purplehead Tilefish, Blue Jaw Tilefish Origin: Indo-Pacific (Western and South Pacific) Max Size: Up to 6 inches (15 cm) Temperament: Peaceful (Active, but shy) Diet: Carnivore (Zooplankton feeder) Minimum Tank Size: 50-75 Gallons Reef Compatibility: Yes (With caution regarding tiny inverts)

Purple Tile Goby: The Vivid Deepwater Glider The Purple Tile Goby (Hoplolatilus purpureus) is one of the most stunningly colored fish available to the marine hobbyist. Despite its common name, it is important to note that it is technically a Tilefish from the family Malacanthidae, not a true Goby (family Gobiidae), although it shares the elongated body shape and burrowing behavior. It is also known as the Purple Tilefish , Purple Sand Tilefish , or Deepwater Tilefish . This fish is celebrated for its intense, solid lilac-purple to violet body color , often highlighted by a touch of red or crimson on the tail lobes. It is a sleek, fast swimmer that spends much of its time hovering gracefully in the water column a few inches above the substrate, giving it the appearance of "gliding." Native to the deeper rubble and sand slopes of the Indo-Pacific, the Purple Tile Goby is a relatively delicate species, making it best suited for intermediate to expert aquarists . It reaches a maximum size of about 5 to 6 inches (13-15 cm) and requires a minimum tank size of 50 gallons to provide ample swimming room and a deep substrate for shelter. A tight-fitting lid is absolutely essential , as Tilefish are renowned for being excellent jumpers, especially when startled. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: The Purple Tile Goby is a Carnivore that feeds primarily on zooplankton in the wild. It is accustomed to capturing food from the water column, so it will rarely feed from the bottom. It requires multiple small feedings per day (2-3 times) of high-quality, enriched frozen meaty foods such as mysis shrimp , enriched brine shrimp, cyclops, and finely chopped marine seafood. It can be challenging to acclimate and may require live foods initially (like enriched copepods or black worms) to entice a feeding response. Acclimation: This species is highly sensitive to stress, particularly during shipping and initial introduction. It benefits from a dimly lit tank and the presence of dither fish (other small, peaceful, and active fish) to help it feel secure and encourage it to swim in the open. Burrowing: Tilefish will excavate a burrow in the sand or under rockwork, which they use as a retreat. The substrate should be a mix of sand and rubble to allow for proper construction. Ensure all rockwork is placed securely on the aquarium glass before adding the substrate to prevent collapses. Reef Compatibility: It is considered Reef Safe and will not bother corals. Caution is advised with very small ornamental shrimp or tiny invertebrates, but for the most part, it is a non-destructive community fish. Temperament: The Purple Tile Goby is Peaceful but Timid . It should only be kept with other peaceful tankmates such as small wrasses, anthias, firefish, and cardinalfish. It will become stressed and hide if housed with aggressive or boisterous fish. It is best kept singly or as a confirmed pair in larger systems. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Hoplolatilus purpureus Primary Common Name: Purple Tile Goby Other Common Names: Purple Tilefish, Purple Sand Tilefish, Deepwater Tilefish Origin: Indo-Pacific Max Size: 5-6 inches (13-15 cm) Temperament: Peaceful / Timid ( Excellent Jumper ) Diet: Carnivore (Requires multiple feedings of suspended meaty foods) Minimum Tank Size: 50+ Gallons (Requires deep, stable substrate) Reef Compatibility: Yes (Generally safe with corals and large inverts)

Pink Spotted Watchman Goby: The Reef's Natural Sentry The Pink Spotted Watchman Goby (Cryptocentrus cinctus), also known by its beautiful color morph, Also known as the Yellow Watchman Goby , is a popular and beneficial species that serves as a living sentry in any marine aquarium . Its unique appearance features a bright yellow or grayish body with a series of vibrant iridescent blue or pink spots. This goby is renowned for its charming habit of perching at the entrance of its burrow, often created in a symbiotic relationship with a pistol shrimp . The goby acts as a "watchman," alerting its nearly-blind shrimp partner to danger. This peaceful and captivating fish is an excellent choice for a community reef tank, provided it has a deep sand bed and plenty of rock rubble to maintain its home. Why the Pink Spotted Watchman Goby is a Great Choice: Natural Sand-Sifter: While perching, it also sifts through sand, helping to keep the substrate clean and aerated. Unique Appearance: Its bright yellow color and iridescent spots provide a beautiful splash of color. Beneficial Symbiosis: Can form a captivating partnership with a pistol shrimp, adding an element of natural behavior to your tank. Peaceful Temperament: It's a non-aggressive species that coexists well with other peaceful tank mates. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Cryptocentrus cinctus Origin: Indo-Pacific Reefs Max Size: 4 inches Lifespan: 3-5 years Diet: Carnivore. It feeds on small invertebrates found in the sand, supplemented by high-quality frozen foods. Shipping Size: 1.5-2.5 inches

Blue Spot Watchman Goby Blue-spot Watchman Goby grow a bit larger the Pink Watchman Goby but have similar markings - obviously blue instead of pink. Watchman gobies will form a symbiotic relationship with prawn in the wild and in the aquarium, often sharing their sand burrows. In fact the name "watchman" comes from this behavior. Watchman gobies stand as look outs for predators while shrimp to the digging. Scientific Name: Cryptocentrus pavoninoides Max Size: 5 1/2 inches Diet: mysis shrimp, brine shrimp, and table shrimp Required Tank Size: 30+ gallons Shipping Size: 1 to 3 inches

The tail of the pineapple Mickey Mouse swordtail displays the black-eared Mickey Mouse hat. It's an odd phenomenon in platies and swordtails and a fun spectacle in the aquarium. These fish are terrific swimmers, but not so good at song and dance. Quick Facts Scientific Name Xiphophorus hellerii (pineapple Mickey Mouse) Origin Southern Mexico to Honduras (wild ancestors); aquarium-bred Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful (males may spar) Adult Size Up to 4–5" (not counting the sword) Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 7.0–8.0 (hard water) Group Size Keep more females than males Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Swordtails are active swimmers, so give them plants, open swimming space and a tight-fitting lid, since they are good jumpers. They prefer hard, alkaline water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet with some vegetable content once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Swordtails get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as platies, mollies, larger tetras, danios, rainbowfish, gouramis and corydoras. Keep more females than males, since males chase females and may spar with each other. Avoid fin-nippers and large cichlids. Good to know: Swordtails are livebearers and breed readily. Fry are born free-swimming and will be eaten unless there are dense plants or a breeding box for them to hide in. Only males grow the "sword" on the tail.

The chili oscar is the newest and very popular variation of the oscar family. Also known as the fire red oscar or the blood red oscar (though the color is closer to fire red), these pet fish are bred in Thailand. The fish features a solid bright red color with small cream highlights; these are in demand and expensive. Like all oscars, chili oscars are hardy and omnivorous and will eat flake and pellet foods. Quick Facts Scientific Name Astronotus ocellatus (red chili variety) Origin Amazon basin, South America; bred in Thailand Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Semi-aggressive; eats smaller fish Adult Size Up to 12–14" Lifespan 10–15 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods; takes pellets) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single or pair Shipping Size Approx. 2–3" Care Guide Tank setup: Use a sand bottom, a few large rocks or driftwood, strong filtration and a tight lid, since they can jump. Oscars often rearrange decorations and uproot plants. Feeding: Feed a quality cichlid pellet once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like shrimp. Avoid feeder goldfish, which can carry disease. Tankmates: Oscars can live with other large, peaceful-to-semi-aggressive fish like silver dollars, large plecos, severums and other oscars. They will eat any fish that fits in their mouth. Good to know: Oscars are known as "water puppies" for their personality and often learn to recognize their owners and beg for food.

The blackberry silver dollar, or blueberry silver dollar, is definitely the most costly and prettiest variety of the silver dollar family. Bred in Indonesia, this hybrid features a dark blue body with splashes of yellow. Just like the parent common silver dollar, the blackberry silver dollar is omnivorous and will eat just about anything. Quick Facts Scientific Name Myloplus schomburgkii (blackberry variety) Origin Amazon basin, South America (captive-bred in Indonesia) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 6" Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore (needs plant matter) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Silver dollars are active schooling fish. Give them open swimming space, a tight lid and sturdy or artificial plants, since they eat soft plants. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or pellet with vegetable content once or twice a day. They also enjoy vegetable foods like peas. Tankmates: They are peaceful and get along with other medium to large fish such as larger tetras, plecos, parrots and peaceful cichlids. Good to know: Silver dollars are a calm schooling fish that look best in a group with open swimming space.

Betta coccina, also known as the scarlet betta and red wine betta, is a true wild species unrelated to the common betta splendens. Betta coccina may be kept in small schools as long as there is enough space for pairs and competitive males to have their own area. Native to Malaysia, these bettas require lower pH water, below 7, and will eat betta pellets and flakes. Quick Facts Scientific Name Betta coccina Origin Malaysia and Sumatra (peat swamps) Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful, shy; males territorial Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 4.5–6.5 (very soft water) Breathes Air Yes – labyrinth fish take air from the surface Shipping Size Approx. 1½–2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them soft, acidic water, dim lighting, a gentle filter, a heater, and plenty of plants and leaf litter. Keep a lid on the tank and leave a gap of air under it, since bettas breathe from the surface. Feeding: Feed small amounts once or twice a day. Many will learn to take betta pellets once settled. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with tiny, calm fish that like the same soft, acidic water, such as small rasboras and pygmy corydoras, or in a species tank. Males can be territorial with each other. Good to know: Coccina come from soft, tea-colored peat swamp water. Indian almond leaves, dim light and a tight lid help them settle; they are good jumpers.

Sera Flora Nature Veggies Food Sera Flora Nature flake food is formulated for all herbivorous (vegetarian) fish. A few examples include small plecos, tropheus and demasoni cichlids. Brine Shrimp Hatching Kit Sera offers a complete hatching kit including the brine shrimp eggs, salt, airline tubing, pipe extractor and brine shrimp separator. YOU WILL NEED A SMALL AIRPUMP. Santa Claus Guppies come with Christmas reds and Santa Claus beard whites on the body. To make the picture complete, the fins, even the dumbo ear ventral fins, are large and colorful. Unlike the gift-giving Santa Claus, these fish will stay with you through all four seasons. Breeders do not like to part with females. If you want to try to breed these yourselves, you might try crossing with pink flamingo, blond tux, or red delta females. Quick Facts Scientific Name Poecilia reticulata Origin Northern South America (captive-bred) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and plenty of plants. Guppies like slightly hard water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Male guppies get along with other small, peaceful fish such as platies, mollies, corydoras, small tetras and rasboras. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs, which go after their long tails, and larger fish that could eat them. Good to know: Male guppies are the colorful ones and get along well with each other in an all-male tank.

Oranda Goldfish Show Quality Orandas take five years to fully develop. Our jumbo orandas, selected from the Thailand breeder to be worthy of keeping to full size, have four-inch bodies and massive wens. Quick Facts Scientific Name Carassius auratus Origin China Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 8" Lifespan 10–15 years, often longer with good care Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 65–75°F (no heater needed in most homes) pH 7.0–8.0 Shipping Size Approx. 5" (including tail) Care Guide Tank setup: Orandas produce a lot of waste, so give them plenty of room and a strong filter. Feeding: Feed small amounts of a quality sinking pellet or flake once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other fancy goldfish of similar size and speed. Avoid fast single-tail goldfish like comets and shubunkins, which will outcompete them for food. Also avoid tropical fish, which need warmer water, and fin-nippers. Ponds: Orandas can live in ponds in mild climates, but they are less cold-hardy than comets and shubunkins. Bring them indoors where winters are harsh, and keep them away from fast, aggressive pond fish. Good to know: The wen (crown) keeps growing for the first couple of years and can trap debris, so clean water is the key to a healthy, full wen.

The most recent variation developed in our ever-evolving hobby is the Snow White Pleco. Quick Facts Scientific Name Ancistrus sp. L-144 "Snow White" Origin Captive-bred (wild form from South America) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 4–5" Lifespan 10+ years Diet Herbivore (algae wafers) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single, or several with a cave each Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them caves, driftwood and good filtration. They are most active at night. Feeding: Feed algae wafers and sinking pellets once a day, ideally in the evening when they are most active. They also enjoy frozen bloodworms. Tankmates: They are peaceful and get along with most community fish. Males may squabble over caves, so give each one its own hiding spot. Good to know: Male bushynose plecos grow soft bristles on their snout as they mature, while females stay smoother-faced. They are great algae grazers.

"stardust" Food: Moderate light moderate fertilizer Shipping Size: Medium approx. 7 inches, Large approx. 12 inches
