The red tail hemiodus is a swift, slender, beautiful schooling fish from streams of Venezuela. Hemiodus are in a class of their own, and it is surprising they are hard to find in aquarium stores. These are perfect larger schoolers for cichlid tanks and larger community aquariums. Hemiodus are omnivores, so they need both veggies and meat in their pellet or flake food (so any good-quality community food). These fish are wild-caught in Venezuela and will not tolerate higher pH, so please keep pH below 7.5. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hemiodus gracilis Origin Amazon and Orinoco basins (Venezuela, Colombia, Brazil, Peru) Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful schooler Adult Size Up to 6" Lifespan 6–8 years Diet Omnivore (needs plant matter) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 4" Care Guide Tank setup: Hemiodus are fast, active schoolers, so give them plenty of open swimming space, some current and a tight-fitting lid, since they jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet with some vegetable content once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Hemiodus do well with larger peaceful to semi-aggressive fish such as larger tetras, silver dollars, geophagus, severums and peaceful South American cichlids. Good to know: Hemiodus are not cichlids; they are fast, schooling characins that make a good "dither fish" for cichlid tanks.

The ninja catfish, in the Tatia woodcat family, is also called Tatia musaica since it is so rare that often just the scientific name is used. Ninja cats are black and white, small, and nocturnal. Very peaceful and omnivorous, they feed at night and will leave other fish alone. Ninja catfish only grow to about two inches and do better with clean, well-filtered water and some driftwood to make their home. Quick Facts Scientific Name Tatia musaica Origin Venezuela Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them caves, driftwood and a soft bottom. They hide during the day and come out at night. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets once a day, ideally in the evening when they are most active. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms. Tankmates: They are very peaceful and leave other fish alone, though they may eat very small fry at night. Good to know: Ninja catfish spend the day tucked into driftwood and come out to feed after the lights go off.

The "cabeza de pelo" dwarf banjo catfish are hard to find as they come from only a small area of Colombia, so they are not often exported. Similar in appearance but more active than full size banjo cats, the dwarf banjo only grows to 2 inches. If you have several in the aquarium, you will see these fish sleep on top of one another for protection. Very peaceful and very adaptable to nano and mid-size aquariums. Quick Facts Scientific Name Bunocephalus sp. "cabeza de pelo" Origin Colombia Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 5–6 years Diet Omnivore (bottom feeder) Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Banjo catfish like to bury themselves, so give them a soft sand bottom, leaf litter and driftwood. Keep the lighting dim. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets once a day, ideally in the evening when they are most active. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms. Tankmates: They are small and very peaceful, so they are safe with small community fish and shrimp. Good to know: Dwarf banjos are more active than their larger cousins, and a group will often rest piled on top of each other.

Madagascar Lace Bulb with Plant Already with good plant growth, these unique plants with their lacy leaves will grow quickly in the aquarium. Scientific Name: APONOGETON MADAGASCARIENSIS Shipping Size: One bulb w medium plant growth

The Colombian cigar fish grows slightly smaller than the Peruvian cigar fish ( Anostomus anostomus ) and gets a reddish nose as opposed to reddish fins. Very adaptable to prepared foods and safe in community, planted and species tanks. Quick Facts Scientific Name Anostomus ternetzi Origin Colombia Care Level Easy Temperament Semi-aggressive (may nip) Adult Size Up to 4" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants, driftwood and a tight lid, since they can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or pellet with vegetable content once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They can nip at each other and at long-finned fish. Keep them with robust, fast fish of similar size. Good to know: Like their headstander cousins, cigar fish swim with their heads tilted down as they pick food from rocks and wood.

Medaka galaxy ricefish are standouts in small community fish tanks and planted aquariums. These fish can also handle temperatures into the 60s. From the side these fish are bright white, and from the top they reflect a silver white. Quick Facts Scientific Name Oryzias latipes (galaxy variety) Origin Japan (aquarium-bred) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1½" Lifespan 2–4 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 64–80°F (handles cooler water; no heater needed in most homes) pH 6.5–8.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. ¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Ricefish stay near the surface, so give them plants, floating plants and a lid. They are cool-water fish and do fine at room temperature, and they also do well in outdoor ponds and patio tubs in warm months. Feeding: Feed crushed flake or micro pellets once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Ricefish get along with other small, peaceful fish like white clouds, small rasboras, danios and shrimp. They can share an unheated tank with cool-water species, but avoid large or fast fish (including fancy goldfish) that may eat or outcompete them. Good to know: Medaka have been kept in Japan for centuries and are one of the hardiest small fish in the hobby. Both sexes are colorful; males have slightly larger fins.

African Blue Tang The African Blue Tang (Paracanthurus hepatus), perhaps better known as the Blue Tang , or, if we must, Dory , is one of the most popular and recognizable marine aquarium fish in the world. This vibrant surgeonfish is admired for its striking, deep blue body, black palette-shaped markings, and yellow tail. A healthy African Blue Tang is a fast, active swimmer, making it a spectacular focal point for a large marine display tank. The African Blue Tang is generally peaceful towards most tankmates but can be territorial toward other tangs, particularly those of similar shape or color. Like all surgeonfish, it possesses a sharp, scalpel-like spine near its tail, which is used for defense and territorial disputes. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: As a surgeonfish, this fish is primarily an Herbivore that grazes continuously on algae in the wild. A captive diet must be rich in vegetable matter, including dried seaweed (nori) and high-quality vegetable flakes or pellets. While they will accept meaty foods like brine shrimp, these should be offered sparingly as supplements only. Feeding: Offer dried marine seaweed (nori) attached to a clip in the aquarium multiple times per week. The majority of their diet should be plant-based to support digestive health and boost their immune system against common diseases. Reef Compatibility: It is considered Reef Safe. The African Blue Tang is an excellent addition to a reef tank, where its constant grazing helps control nuisance algae growth without harming corals. Caution should be exercised with very small or delicate sessile invertebrates, but overall they are a great reef resident. Temperament: It is Semi-Aggressive / Active. While peaceful towards other fish species, it can be aggressive toward its own kind or other blue-colored tangs. If housing a group, it is best to introduce a few small juveniles simultaneously into a very large tank to help distribute aggression. Special Care: This species is highly susceptible to Marine Ich and other parasitic infections, especially when stressed. Maintaining pristine water quality, a stable temperature, and a diet rich in vitamins (such as soaking food in a vitamin supplement like Selcon) is critical for long-term health. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Paracanthurus hepatus Primary Common Name: African Blue Tang Other Common Names: Blue Tang, Palette Surgeonfish, Dory Origin: Indo-Pacific (Widespread) Max Size: 10-12 inches (25-30 cm) Temperament: Semi-Aggressive / Active Diet: Herbivore (Primarily algae and seaweed) Minimum Tank Size: 180+ Gallons Reef Compatibility: Reef Safe (Excellent for algae control)

Chevron Tang The Chevron Tang is a native of Hawaii, as demonstrated by the scientific name. The pretty orange color changes shades as the fish matures in the aquarium, but even at the full 10 inches in size, the Chevron Tang is pretty. The fish is very peaceful and makes a good companion to most marine aquariums. Scientific Name: Ctenochaetus hawaiiensis Origin: Hawaii Max Size: 10 inches Diet: Herbivore Shipping Size: 2 to 3 inches

Convict Tang: The Peaceful & Hardworking Algae Grazer The Convict Tang (Acanthurus triostegus), also known as the Convict Surgeonfish, is a popular and very beneficial addition to a marine aquarium . This tang is easily identified by its unique pattern: a light gray or white body with five to six prominent black vertical stripes that give it a "convict" look. While many tangs are known for their aggression, the Convict Tang is generally peaceful with other species, making it an excellent community tank resident. As a herbivore, it is a fantastic algae-eater and is a valuable part of any clean-up crew. It is completely reef-safe and will not harm corals or invertebrates. Why the Convict Tang is a Great Choice: Unique Appearance: Its distinctive striped pattern makes it a standout fish. Excellent Algae Control: As a herbivore, it helps keep nuisance algae in check. Completely Reef-Safe: It will not harm corals, clams, or other invertebrates. Generally Peaceful: It coexists well with other fish, making it a great community tank addition. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Acanthurus triostegus Origin: Indo-Pacific Reefs Max Size: 10 inches Lifespan: 10+ years Diet: Herbivore. Primarily feeds on marine algae. Shipping Size: 2-4 inches

Yellow Eye Kole Tang Also called the Yellow-eye Tang and Yellow-eye Surgeon. The marine species grows to only 7 inches and these lively fish are suitable for most marine aquariums larger than 30 gallons. Scientific Name: Ctenochaetus strigosus Origin: Pacific, Hawaii Max Size: 7 inches Diet: Herbivore Shipping Size: 2 to 3 inches

Lavender Tang: The Hardy & Hardworking Algae Grazer The Lavender Tang (Acanthurus nigrofuscus), also known as the Brown Tang or Dusky Surgeonfish , is a popular and very beneficial addition to a marine aquarium . This tang is easily identified by its unique coloration: a beautiful purplish-brown body with distinct black spots behind its eye and at the base of its dorsal fin. It is an active and graceful swimmer that requires plenty of open space to roam. While it is generally peaceful with most other species, it can be territorial towards other tangs, so it's often best to introduce it to the tank last. As a herbivore, it is a fantastic algae-eater , making it a valuable and hardworking member of any clean-up crew. It is completely reef-safe and will not harm corals or invertebrates. Why the Lavender Tang is a Great Choice: Hardy & Durable: This is a very robust species that is easy to care for and a great choice for beginners. Excellent Algae Control: It tirelessly grazes on nuisance algae, helping to keep the tank clean and healthy. Completely Reef-Safe: It will not harm corals, clams, or other invertebrates. Adds Energy to the Tank: It adds a lot of energy and graceful movement to a spacious aquarium. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Acanthurus nigrofuscus Origin: Indo-Pacific Reefs Max Size: 8 inches Lifespan: 10+ years Diet: Herbivore. Primarily feeds on marine algae. Shipping Size: 2-4 inches

Mustard Tang: The Unique & Hardworking Algae Grazer The Mustard Tang (Acanthurus guttatus), also known as the Spotted Tang, is a popular and very beneficial addition to a marine aquarium . This tang is easily identified by its unique coloration: a beautiful brownish-gray body covered in numerous white spots, with a striking yellow or orange patch behind its eye. It is an active and graceful swimmer that requires plenty of open space to roam. While it is generally peaceful with most other species, it can be territorial towards other tangs, so it's often best to introduce it to the tank last. As a herbivore, it is a fantastic algae-eater , making it a valuable and hardworking member of any clean-up crew. It is completely reef-safe and will not harm corals or invertebrates. Why the Mustard Tang is a Great Choice: Unique Appearance: Its distinctive coloration and markings make it a true showpiece. Excellent Algae Control: It tirelessly grazes on nuisance algae, helping to keep the tank clean and healthy. Completely Reef-Safe: It will not harm corals, clams, or other invertebrates. Adds Energy to the Tank: It adds a lot of energy and movement to a spacious aquarium. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Acanthurus guttatus Origin: Indo-Pacific Reefs Max Size: 8 inches Lifespan: 10+ years Diet: Herbivore. Primarily feeds on marine algae. Shipping Size: 2-4 inches

Orange Shoulder Tang: The Transforming Algae Grazer The Orange Shoulder Tang (Acanthurus olivaceus), also known as the Orange Spot Tang , is a very popular and beneficial addition to a marine aquarium . This tang is unique for its dramatic transformation from juvenile to adult. Juveniles are a beautiful bright yellow, while adults develop a brownish or grayish body with a prominent orange patch behind the pectoral fin. It is a peaceful fish but can be territorial towards other tangs, so it's often best to introduce it to the tank last. As a herbivore, it is a fantastic algae-eater , making it a valuable and hardworking member of any clean-up crew. It is completely reef-safe and will not harm corals or invertebrates. Why the Orange Shoulder Tang is a Great Choice: Stunning Appearance: Its unique coloration, especially the juvenile phase, makes it a true showpiece. Excellent Algae Control: It tirelessly grazes on nuisance algae, helping to keep the tank clean and healthy. Completely Reef-Safe: It will not harm corals, clams, or other invertebrates. Active Swimmer: It adds a lot of energy and graceful movement to a spacious aquarium. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Acanthurus olivaceus Origin: Indo-Pacific Reefs Max Size: 12 inches Lifespan: 10+ years Diet: Herbivore. Primarily feeds on marine algae. Shipping Size: 2-4 inches

Yellow Tang Also known as the Yellow Hawaiian Tang or Yellow Surgeonfish is one of the most popular and hardy saltwater aquarium fish. Solid yellow, these fish seem to be a must in any community and reef tank. Scientific name: Zebrasoma flavescens Origin: Indonesia Lifespan: 10 Years Max size: 8 inches Shipping Size: 1 to 3 inches

Bursa Triggerfish: The Aggressive Bottom Forager The Bursa Triggerfish (Rhinecanthus verrucosus), also widely known as the Blackbelly Triggerfish or Blackpatch Triggerfish, is a captivating and hardy species. It is a highly territorial fish distinguished by the large, dark spot on its lower flank and is best suited for experienced keepers in fish-only or FOWLR (Fish-Only With Live Rock) systems. This species is visually appealing, displaying a striking pattern of lines and colors, and grows up to 9-12 inches in length. The Bursa Triggerfish is a powerful and active swimmer, requiring a minimum aquarium size of 125 gallons or more to provide adequate room for movement and territory establishment. The tank should feature securely placed rockwork and ample caves. Due to its powerful nature, this fish will rearrange light décor and substrate, and it is known to make a loud "grunting" sound when alarmed. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: This trigger is a voracious carnivore and bottom-forager. It requires a varied diet of meaty frozen foods, including squid, krill, shrimp, and clams. Teeth Care: It is essential to regularly provide hard-shelled, meaty foods (such as whole clams or mussels in the shell) to naturally file down its constantly growing beak and prevent overgrowth, which can cause feeding issues. Reef Compatibility: The Rhinecanthus genus is notoriously Not Reef Safe . The Bursa Triggerfish will use its powerful jaws to crush and consume most ornamental invertebrates (shrimp, crabs, snails) and will likely pick at and destroy corals. Temperament: It is **Aggressive** and highly territorial. It should be housed with other large, assertive, and robust fish that can defend themselves. Unlike some other triggers, this species exhibits little sexual dimorphism. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Rhinecanthus verrucosus Primary Common Name: Bursa Triggerfish Other Common Names: Blackbelly Triggerfish, Blackpatch Triggerfish Origin: Indo-Pacific Max Size: 9-12 inches (23-30 cm) Temperament: Aggressive (Highly Territorial) Diet: Carnivore/Omnivore (Must include hard-shelled food) Minimum Tank Size: 125+ Gallons Reef Compatibility: Not Reef Safe

Undulatus Triggerfish Bright orange and green markings make the Undulatus Trigger a great pet or addition to an aggressive tank. This fish will eat a reef tank and small fish. The Undulatus Trigger grows to about one foot and is a very hardy fish. Scientific Name: Balistapus undulatus Origin: Fiji, Indonedia Max Size: 12 inches Diet: Carnivore Shipping Size: 1 to 3 inches

Blue Flasher Wrasse The Blue Flasher Wrasse is more red than blue but these wrasses will flash their caudal fins as they are quite active swimmers. The Blue Flasher Wrasse is only three inches and goes very well in small aquariums, reef tanks, and peaceful community aquariums. The reef safe Blue Flasher Wrasse enjoys swimming in the open water of the marine aquarium which will embolden shy species to come out into the open, another benefit of these little saltwater fish. Scientific Name: Paracheilinus cyaneus Max Size: 3 inches Diet: Since they feed on zooplankton and rarely pick at organisms on live rock, they will not thrive in the reef tank if they are fed infrequently. Require Tank Size: 55+ gallons Shipping Size: 2 to 2-1/2 inches

China Wrasse The China wrasse is also known as a Black-Backed Wrasse has an elongated girthy body. It has a shade of black on the top half of the body and white on the lower half. The China Wrasse requires a well-established tank with plenty of live rock and thick sandy substrate. It will pick at many unwanted organisms in the tank but will also eat larger invertebrates. Difficult to feed in the home aquarium. Scientific Name: Anampses neoguinaicus Origin: Fiji Max Size: 9 inches Diet: Carnivore Require tank size: 120+ gallons Shipping Size: 3 to 4 inches

Harlequin Tuskfish: A Stunning & Hardy Reef Fish The Harlequin Tuskfish (Choerodon fasciatus) is a truly stunning and highly sought-after species that adds a touch of bold, vibrant color to any marine aquarium . Its brilliant appearance features a bright orange body with distinct blue horizontal stripes , a brilliant blue dorsal fin, and a face of intricate blue and white markings. The most unique feature of this fish is its prominent, protruding teeth, or "tusks." This species is known for its hardiness, intelligence, and active swimming behavior. It's an excellent choice for a fish-only with live rock (FOWLR) or large community tank with other semi-aggressive species. Why the Harlequin Tuskfish is a Great Choice: Exceptional Coloration: Its multi-colored pattern and unique features make it a true showstopper. Highly Hardy: This species is incredibly resilient and easy to care for, making it a perfect choice for intermediate hobbyists. Engaging Behavior: Its active nature and intelligence make it a rewarding fish to watch. Reef-Safe (with caution): While generally safe with corals, it may pose a threat to small invertebrates like snails, crabs, and shrimp. Important Note: The Harlequin Tuskfish can be territorial and aggressive, especially towards smaller, passive fish. It is a carnivorous predator that will eat small crustaceans. It is best to introduce it to the tank after establishing other, larger fish. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Choerodon fasciatus Origin: Western Pacific Ocean and Great Barrier Reef Max Size: 10 inches Lifespan: 10+ years Diet: Carnivore. A varied diet of high-quality frozen foods like shrimp, clams, and squid. Shipping Size: 2-4 inches

Lineatus Fairy Wrasse The Lineatus Wrasse is also called the Purple-lined Wrasse and the Lavender Wrasse. The Lineatus Wrasse is expensive and will jump, so please keep in a covered tank. Lineatus are peaceful saltwater aquarium fish and need some rocks for hiding and open space for gliding. Males can be aggressive to females unless the female wrasse is established in the marine tank first. Scientific Name: Cirrhilabrus lineatus Origin: Australia Max Size: 5 inches Diet: Carnivore, marine pellets and flakes and frozen foods Shipping Size: 2 to 3 inches

Paddlefin Wrasse The Paddlefin Wrasse is named not only for its native environment, the Sea of Cortez, but also for its bold rainbow coloring. Like all the Thalassoma wrasses, the Cortez Rainbow Wrasse has more than one color phase and for this fish there are two. In their natural environment the these fish are most abundant as juveniles and initial phase females with a striped rainbow pattern. A few terminal phase males, like the one pictured above, will be mixed in. In either phase they are beautiful and a joy to watch. It should reside in a 75 gallon or larger aquarium with larger, aggressive tank mates, and plenty of rocks for hiding. It will become territorial and harass any new additions to the community, therefore, it should be the last fish added to the community. It may be kept with a mate if the aquarium is 125 gallons or larger. It may eat mantis shrimp and bristleworms. It does not eat corals or live plants. Scientific Name: Thalassoma lucasanum Max Size: 7 inches Origin: Central America Food: Vitamin enriched frozen mysis shrimp, vitamin enriched frozen brine shrimp and other meaty food along with high quality marine pellet food. Shipping Size: Approx. SM 1 TO 3 INCHES,MD 3 TO 4 INCHES,LG 4 TO 6INCHES (Picture is a Adult Paddlefin Wrasse)

Red Coris Wrasse: The Colorful, Sand-Burrowing Carnivore The Red Coris Wrasse (Coris gaimard), also known as the Clown Wrasse , Yellowtail Coris , or African Coris , is a large, highly active, and brilliantly colored species that undergoes one of the most dramatic color changes in the marine hobby. While captivating, this fish is only suitable for very large, mature, fish-only-with-live-rock (FOWLR) systems due to its size and predatory, burrowing nature. The Juvenile phase is stunningly attractive: a brilliant orange to red body with three to five black-edged white saddle markings along the back. This coloration is often why hobbyists purchase the fish, unaware of its immense adult size. As the fish matures into an Adult (Terminal Male), the appearance changes completely to a mottled blue-green body covered in small, bright blue spots, a greenish-orange head with intricate green stripes, and a contrasting bright yellow caudal fin (tail). They are capable of reaching a maximum size of up to 16 inches (40 cm) in the wild, though typically closer to 12 inches (30 cm) in a home aquarium. The Red Coris Wrasse is a tireless bottom-dweller, constantly sifting and turning over substrate and small pieces of rock in its quest for food. This digging behavior makes a fine, deep sand bed (4+ inches) an absolute requirement, both for hunting and to provide a safe place to bury itself completely when frightened or at night for sleeping. Diet & Compatibility: Diet: This is a dedicated Carnivore. Its natural diet consists almost entirely of hard-shelled benthic invertebrates, including mollusks (snails, clams), crabs, hermit crabs, and sea urchins. In the aquarium, it must be fed a variety of high-quality, vitamin-enriched, meaty frozen foods, such as Mysis shrimp, frozen silversides, krill, and chopped marine seafood. Juveniles should be fed several times daily due to their high metabolism. Reef Compatibility: Not Reef Safe. While they generally ignore corals, their natural foraging behavior involves flipping and moving rocks and stirring the sand, which will dislodge unmounted corals and perpetually dust them with substrate. Crucially, they will systematically hunt and consume nearly all ornamental invertebrates, including all snails, hermit crabs, shrimp, and even clam mantles. Temperament: Semi-Aggressive / Boisterous. They are active swimmers and generally non-aggressive toward large, robust tankmates, but they can be aggressive toward smaller, more passive fish. They are best housed with other large, aggressive fish like Tangs, Triggerfish, Groupers, and large Angelfish. They should be kept singly, or occasionally as a pair/harem if added simultaneously to a very large system. Tank Requirements: Due to their large adult size and high activity level, a 125-150 gallon tank is the minimum size. A secure, tight-fitting lid is mandatory as this species is a known jumper. The sand bed should be fine to medium grain (not crushed coral) and at least 4 inches deep to prevent injury when burrowing. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Coris gaimard Primary Common Name: Red Coris Wrasse Other Common Names: Clown Wrasse, Yellowtail Coris, African Coris, Gaimard Rainbow-Wrasse Origin: Indo-Pacific (Widespread, including Hawaii) Max Size: Up to 16 inches (40 cm) Temperament: Semi-Aggressive / Boisterous ( Highly Predatory ) Diet: Carnivore (Crustaceans, Mollusks, Inverts) Minimum Tank Size: 125-150+ Gallons Reef Compatibility: Not Reef Safe (Predatory toward inverts; highly destructive digging behavior)

Shrimp Net TM Style, our Taiwanese shrimp breeders, created a specialized net to safely handle shrimp in the aquarium. Each net is hand for shrimp keeping, two inches wide and without any folds or edges to trap and injure the pet, these nets are a must for shrimp enthusiasts. Shipping Size: Approx. 2 inches

Double yeee haw! The electric blue Texas cichlid has all the hardiness of the parent Texas cichlid but with even more colorful attitude. Bright reflective blue spots throughout the body make this one fancy fish. Quick Facts Scientific Name Herichthys cyanoguttatus (electric blue variety) Origin Southern Texas and northeastern Mexico (wild ancestors); aquarium-bred Care Level Moderate Temperament Aggressive (territorial) Adult Size Up to 10–12" Lifespan 10–13 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Single or pair Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: These are large, powerful cichlids, so give them a sand bottom, large rocks and driftwood. Anchor decorations well, since they dig and rearrange the tank, and use strong filtration. Feeding: Feed a quality cichlid pellet once a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like shrimp. Avoid feeder fish, which can carry disease. Tankmates: Keep them alone or with other large, robust cichlids and catfish that can hold their own. They will eat any fish small enough to fit in their mouth. Good to know: These cichlids are full of personality and often learn to recognize their owners. They grow large, so check their adult size before buying.

The sunburst mickey mouse platy is one cheerful addition to the fish tank. Bright yellow and orange, with the classic black mickey mouse ears on the tail, this fish makes a happy tank mate. Quick Facts Scientific Name Xiphophorus maculatus Origin Southern Mexico and Central America Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 3–4 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 70–80°F pH 7.0–8.2 Breeding Livebearer – breeds easily in the aquarium Care Guide Tank setup: Platies are hardy and easy to keep. Give them a filter, a lid and plenty of plants. Use a heater to keep the water steady in the 70s. They prefer harder, slightly alkaline water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. Platies also need some plant matter, so a vegetable flake is a good choice. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Platies get along with most peaceful community fish, such as other livebearers (mollies, guppies and swordtails), tetras, rasboras and corydoras. Avoid large or aggressive fish that may bully or eat them. Breeding: Platies are livebearers, so a tank with males and females will almost certainly have babies (fry). Adults will eat fry, so add dense plants or use a breeding box if you want to raise them. Keeping more females than males gives the females a break from the males' attention. Good to know: Platies are one of the easiest fish to keep, which makes them a great choice for a first aquarium.

The Black Phantasm Pleco, with an equally fantastic scientific name, is seldom seen in the aquarium hobby. These black plecos with some chocolate marbling sport a high-profile body and big dorsal fin. Hardy and adaptable to most aquariums. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hypancistrus sp. L-501 Origin Rio Tapajós basin, Brazil Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 4–5" Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore (meaty sinking foods) Water Temperature 78–84°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Single, or several with a cave each Shipping Size Approx. 3–5" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them caves, driftwood, good current and good filtration. They are most active at night. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets once a day, ideally in the evening when they are most active. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and shrimp. Tankmates: They are peaceful and get along with most community fish. Males may squabble over caves, so give each one its own hiding spot. Good to know: Unlike many plecos, black phantasms eat mostly meaty foods rather than algae, and they leave plants alone.

The female guppy genes are the most dominant when looking for inherited traits in offspring. Since the males are constantly trying to mate with the females, it is always a good idea to have more females than males in the fish tank. We offer a grab bag selection of female guppies for a low price to keep the balance in this battle of the sexes. Do not be surprised to receive pregnant guppies; see the BLOG. Males and females are sorted by type and separated by the breeders and we keep them separated at the warehouse. However, many females are pregnant prior to separating, and females can have several broods before the "occurrence" runs its course. Quick Facts Scientific Name Poecilia reticulata Origin Northern South America (captive-bred) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Keep more females than males Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and plenty of plants, including some floating plants where babies can hide. Guppies like slightly hard water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Guppies get along with other small, peaceful fish such as platies, mollies, corydoras, small tetras and rasboras. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs and larger fish that could eat them. Breeding: Guppies are livebearers and breed easily. Females give birth to live babies about once a month, and adults will eat the babies, so thick plants give them a place to hide. Good to know: Female guppies are larger and plainer than males, but many fancy varieties show some color in the tail.

The male guppy displays all the color, the female does all the work. We offer a grab bag selection of fancy colored male guppies to enhance the color in your aquarium. But don't expect them to do much of the heavy lifting. Quick Facts Scientific Name Poecilia reticulata Origin Northern South America (captive-bred) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and plenty of plants. Guppies like slightly hard water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Male guppies get along with other small, peaceful fish such as platies, mollies, corydoras, small tetras and rasboras. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs, which go after their long tails, and larger fish that could eat them. Good to know: Each order is a grab-bag mix of fancy male guppies, so colors will vary.

Aquazen 4 Gallon Complete Aquarium Description The Aquazen 4 Gallon Aquarium fits anywhere and comes complete with efficient LED lights and an internal filter. Though only 4 gallons, this system is capable of providing a healthy environment for dwarf cichlids, shrimp, tetras, rasboras, and all kinds of small aquatic species. The LED lighting system will sustain plants and allow for great visibliy. Features High clarity flat glass panels. Fish and plant health promoting LED lighting. Removable, easy rinse filter cartridge. Universal placement internal filter rated for 10 gallons with a rated speed of 76 GPH (gallons per hour).

Some fish like the elephant nose and butterfly look just like their name, and so does the new hybrid ALIEN betta. Thai breeders hybridized the wild betta coccina with the domestic betta splendens to create the remarkable alien betta. With green-blue hues and a Martian man face, these guys look like they belong on a spaceship, but they survive best in a small aquarium. Quick Facts Scientific Name Betta splendens × wild Betta species (hybrid) Origin Thailand (captive-bred) Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Males fight each other; peaceful toward most other fish Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 76–82°F (needs a heater) pH 6.5–7.5 Breathes Air Yes – labyrinth fish take air from the surface Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Give him a heater (bettas are tropical fish), a gentle filter and live or silk plants. Floating plants or a "betta leaf" near the surface give him a place to rest. Keep a lid on the tank and leave a gap of air under it, since bettas breathe from the surface. Feeding: Feed a few betta pellets or a pinch of flake once or twice a day. Bettas overeat easily, so small meals are best. They also enjoy frozen bloodworms. Tankmates: Never keep two male bettas together. A male can live with small, peaceful fish that don't nip fins, such as corydoras, small rasboras, otocinclus and snails. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs and flashy, long-finned fish like fancy guppies. Good to know: Alien bettas are hybrids with wild betta species, so they are tough and active. Like other male bettas, keep only one per tank.

The African dwarf frog will live its entire life underwater. However, they are lung breathers and need access to the surface. These little amphibians will eat flake foods and do well in a gentle community fish tank. In nature, they are found in the jungles of Cameroon and Nigeria. All in the aquarium trade are tank raised. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hymenochirus boettgeri Origin Central Africa (captive-bred) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1½" Lifespan 5 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 72–78°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Single or group Shipping Size Approx. ¾–1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a fully aquatic tank with plants and hiding spots, gentle filtration and a lid. They breathe air, so keep the water shallow enough for them to reach the surface easily. Feeding: Feed sinking frog pellets or frozen bloodworms once a day. They eat slowly, so make sure faster fish don't take all the food. Tankmates: Dwarf frogs are peaceful and do best with other small, gentle fish such as small tetras and rasboras, or with their own kind. Good to know: African dwarf frogs are fully aquatic but breathe air, so you will see them float up to the surface for a breath.

AFS packers pick three pretty females and three handsome males in this fancy guppy order. These brightly colored guppies will be quite active as they compete for each other's friendship. Quick Facts Scientific Name Poecilia reticulata Origin Northern South America (captive-bred) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Sold as 3 pairs (3 males + 3 females) Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and plenty of plants, including some floating plants where babies can hide. Guppies like slightly hard water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Guppies get along with other small, peaceful fish such as platies, mollies, corydoras, small tetras and rasboras. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs and larger fish that could eat them. Breeding: Guppies are livebearers and breed easily. Females give birth to live babies about once a month, and adults will eat the babies, so thick plants give them a place to hide. Good to know: Each order is a mix of fancy guppy varieties, so colors will vary.

The agassizi cory is a wild-caught corydoras, usually from Brazil streams, sometimes Colombia. These cory have a distinct leopard pattern that is less "lined" than the cory julii. Quick Facts Scientific Name Corydoras agassizii Origin Brazil and Peru Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 5–10 years Diet Omnivore (bottom feeder) Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 6.0–7.0 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and a soft sand or smooth, fine gravel bottom. Plants, driftwood and a few shady spots help them feel secure. Corys are sensitive to salt and some medications (especially copper), so check labels before treating the tank. Feeding: Corys need their own food, not just leftovers. Feed sinking pellets or wafers once or twice a day so food reaches the bottom. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Corys get along with almost any peaceful community fish, such as tetras, rasboras, livebearers, gouramis, angelfish and bettas. Avoid large fish that could swallow them and aggressive bottom dwellers. Good to know: Corys sift through the substrate with their sensitive barbels, so soft sand or smooth, fine gravel keeps those barbels healthy.

Like many peaceful schooling fish, black neon tetras do not do well on their own. A small group of six will stay in a pretty school as it moves about the aquarium. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hyphessobrycon herbertaxelrodi Origin Paraguay basin (Rio Taquari), Brazil Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1½" Lifespan 4–6 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 6 Shipping Size Approx. ¾–1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a dark substrate, which brings out their color. Keep a lid on the tank, since tetras can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, rasboras, danios, corydoras, dwarf cichlids, gouramis and livebearers. Good to know: Tetras feel safer and show better color in a group. A larger school also spreads out any chasing.

Though not the most colorful of the tropical tetras, black phantoms feature quite a bit of action. Males will constantly display their high fins for the females while pushing around competing mates. This interaction is quite interesting to observe if you have a small school in the tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hyphessobrycon megalopterus Origin Guaporé and Paraguay basins (Brazil, Bolivia) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1¾" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a dark substrate, which brings out their color. Keep a lid on the tank, since tetras can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, rasboras, danios, corydoras, dwarf cichlids, gouramis and livebearers. Good to know: Tetras feel safer and show better color in a group. A larger school also spreads out any chasing.

Add a splash of vibrant gold to your aquarium with the Golden Swordtail! Renowned for its striking color and active nature, this fish is a dynamic addition to any freshwater setup. Ideal for beginners and seasoned aquarists alike, Golden Swordtails are resilient and harmonize well in community tanks. Quick Facts Scientific Name Xiphophorus hellerii Origin Central America (captive-bred) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 3–4" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.3 Group Size Keep more females than males Shipping Size Approx. 2" Care Guide Tank setup: Swordtails are active swimmers, so give them plants, open swimming space and a tight-fitting lid, since they are good jumpers. They prefer hard, alkaline water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Swordtails get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as platies, mollies, larger tetras, danios, rainbowfish and corydoras. Keep more females than males, since males chase females and may spar with each other. Breeding: Swordtails are livebearers and breed easily. Adults will eat the babies, so thick plants give them a place to hide. Good to know: Only males grow the long "sword" on the bottom of the tail.

A group of 4 medium Boesemani ready to grow old and beautiful in the fish tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name Melanotaenia boesemani Origin Western New Guinea, Indonesia Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 4" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Sold as a school of 4 Shipping Size Approx. 1½–2" Care Guide Tank setup: Rainbowfish are active swimmers, so leave open swimming space along the front, with plants along the back and sides. Use a filter, a heater and a tight-fitting lid, since they can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with peaceful fish of similar size, such as other rainbowfish, larger tetras, barbs, danios, corydoras and plecos. Good to know: Boesemani are half blue and half orange, and their colors get stronger as they grow.

Similar to bleeding heart tetras, with a sweeter nickname, this will be a very fancy school. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hyphessobrycon sp. "HY511" Origin Aquarium-bred (exact wild origin uncertain) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 6 Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a dark substrate, which brings out their color. Keep a lid on the tank, since tetras can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, rasboras, danios, corydoras, dwarf cichlids, gouramis and livebearers. Good to know: Tetras feel safer and show better color in a group. A larger school also spreads out any chasing.

Male and female clown killifish look similar; males have a bit more color, but they are both quite small. A small group of these small fish is the best way to view them. Quick Facts Scientific Name Epiplatys annulatus Origin Sierra Leone, Guinea and Liberia, West Africa Care Level Moderate Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1¼" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Carnivore (tiny meaty foods) Water Temperature 72–79°F pH 6.0–7.0 Group Size Sold as a school of 4 Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Clown killifish live at the very surface, so use a planted tank with floating plants, a gentle filter (a sponge filter is ideal) and a tight lid. Keep the water warm, soft and clean. Feeding: Feed tiny foods like crushed flake or micro pellets in small amounts a few times a day. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep clown killifish in a species tank or with other tiny, peaceful fish like small rasboras, pygmy corydoras and shrimp. Larger fish will outcompete them or eat them. Good to know: Males show the bright, striped tail fin that gives the fish its name; females are plainer.

A nice mix of these red males and pinkish brown females will be a perfect addition to a peaceful community fish tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name Puntius titteya Origin Sri Lanka Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful, a bit shy Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 4–6 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 73–81°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 6 Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a filter, a heater and plenty of plants. They feel safest with places to hide and show more color in a planted tank. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other small, peaceful fish such as rasboras, small tetras, corydoras and dwarf shrimp. Avoid large or boisterous fish and fin-nippers. Good to know: Cherry barbs are one of the most peaceful barbs, so they mix well with small community fish and shrimp-safe planted tanks. Males color up most when a few females are around.

A small school of the incredibly tough Congo tetra will be at home in a peaceful community tank and a nice, colorful African cichlid tank, oh, and a planted aquarium. These are shipped medium size. Quick Facts Scientific Name Phenacogrammus interruptus Origin Congo River basin (DR Congo) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful (shy) Adult Size Up to 3–3½" Lifespan 5–10 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 5 Shipping Size Approx. 1–2" Care Guide Tank setup: These are larger, active schooling fish, so give them open swimming space, plants or driftwood along the back and a tight-fitting lid, since they jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They do well with other active, similar-size fish such as larger tetras, barbs, rainbowfish, peaceful cichlids, corydoras and plecos. Very small fish may be eaten or bullied. Good to know: Larger tetras are hardy and long-lived, and a big school makes a striking display.

A group of fish might be called a school, but the Dalmatian colors of these fish are just like a Dalmatian puppy's, so we had to call this little group of black and white pets a pack. Quick Facts Scientific Name Poecilia sphenops (aquarium-bred hybrids) Origin Mexico and Central America (wild ancestors); aquarium-bred Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 3–4" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (needs plant matter) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 7.5–8.5 (hard water) Group Size Sold as a pack of 4 Care Guide Tank setup: Mollies like hard, alkaline water. Give them plants, open swimming space and good filtration, since they are active and produce a fair amount of waste. Aquarium salt is optional; they also do well in brackish tanks. Feeding: Mollies graze on algae, so feed a quality flake that includes vegetable matter once or twice a day. They also enjoy algae wafers and frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Mollies get along with most peaceful community fish that like similar hard water, such as platies, swordtails, guppies, danios, rainbowfish, corydoras and plecos. Avoid fin-nippers and soft-water specialists. Keeping more females than males keeps any one female from being harassed. Good to know: Mollies are livebearers that breed readily. Fry are born free-swimming and will be eaten unless there are dense plants or a breeding box for them to hide in.

The long reflective lines of glowlight tetras (or glolites) are made to be seen in a group. Also, these skittish tetras are best kept in groups of at least five or six. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hemigrammus erythrozonus Origin Essequibo River, Guyana Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1½" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 5 Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a dark substrate, which brings out their color. Keep a lid on the tank, since tetras can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, rasboras, danios, corydoras, dwarf cichlids, gouramis and livebearers. Good to know: Tetras feel safer and show better color in a group. A larger school also spreads out any chasing.

At maturity this wild species is smaller than the classic neon tetra and really should be kept in a school of six or more. Quick Facts Scientific Name Paracheirodon simulans Origin Rio Negro and upper Orinoco (Brazil, Colombia, Venezuela) Care Level Moderate to difficult (needs very soft, acidic water) Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to ¾" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 76–84°F pH 4.5–6.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 6 Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: These small tetras do best in a planted tank with soft, slightly acidic water, a dark substrate, driftwood, floating plants and gentle filtration. A larger school makes them more confident and colorful. Feeding: Feed small amounts of micro pellets or crushed flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other small, peaceful fish like rasboras, small tetras, pencilfish, pygmy corydoras, otocinclus and dwarf shrimp. Avoid large or boisterous fish that could eat or bully them. Good to know: Small tetras show their best color in a large school in a planted tank with soft lighting.

Reds and blues are some of the prettiest and easiest-to-spot colors in an aquarium. That is just one of the reasons these fish are so popular. Quick Facts Scientific Name Paracheirodon innesi Origin Upper Amazon (Peru, Colombia, Brazil); mostly farm-raised Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1¼" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 5.5–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 6 Shipping Size Approx. ½–1" Care Guide Tank setup: These small tetras do best in a planted tank with soft, slightly acidic water, a dark substrate, driftwood, floating plants and gentle filtration. A larger school makes them more confident and colorful. Feeding: Feed small amounts of micro pellets or crushed flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other small, peaceful fish like rasboras, small tetras, pencilfish, pygmy corydoras, otocinclus and dwarf shrimp. Avoid large or boisterous fish that could eat or bully them. Good to know: Small tetras show their best color in a large school in a planted tank with soft lighting.

Active and affordable, why not keep a small group together? 3 Paleatus or Salt and Pepper Cory will be quite content. Quick Facts Scientific Name Corydoras paleatus Origin Southern Brazil, Uruguay and Argentina Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 5–10 years Diet Omnivore (bottom feeder) Water Temperature 64–77°F (handles cooler water) pH 6.0–8.0 Group Size Sold as a group of 3 Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and a soft sand or smooth, fine gravel bottom. Plants, driftwood and a few shady spots help them feel secure. Corys are sensitive to salt and some medications (especially copper), so check labels before treating the tank. Feeding: Corys need their own food, not just leftovers. Feed sinking pellets or wafers once or twice a day so food reaches the bottom. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Corys get along with almost any peaceful community fish, such as tetras, rasboras, livebearers, gouramis, angelfish and bettas. Avoid large fish that could swallow them and aggressive bottom dwellers. Good to know: Paleatus come from cooler southern rivers, so they suit unheated or cooler tanks better than most corys.

listings.commonName: Red Gold Honey Dwarf Gourami (School of 4)
listings.description: Males and females constantly interact in this group of aquarium fish, so a small school of 4 makes for a little more action with this species. Quick Facts Scientific Name Trichogaster chuna Origin India and Bangladesh (bred in Florida) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 4–6 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Breathes Air Yes – labyrinth fish take air from the surface Group Size Sold as a school of 4 Shipping Size Approx. 1–1½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and plenty of plants, including some floating plants for cover. Keep a lid on the tank and leave a gap of air above the water, since gouramis breathe from the surface. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with small, peaceful fish such as rasboras, small tetras, corydoras and otocinclus. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs and larger, boisterous fish. Good to know: Honey gouramis are among the most peaceful gouramis, which makes them a great first gourami for a community tank.

Twelve of these 1½- to 2-inch hardy goldfish would be a great starter school for a pond, or a great giveaway for your own backyard circus… or even for Persian New Year. Quick Facts Scientific Name Carassius auratus Origin USA (developed from Chinese goldfish) Care Level Very easy, extremely hardy Temperament Peaceful, very active Adult Size Up to 10" or more in ponds Lifespan 10–15 years; 20+ years in ponds Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 50–75°F (tolerates cold winters in ponds) pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Sold as a group of 12 Shipping Size Approx. 1½–2" Care Guide Tank setup: Comets are fast, active swimmers that grow big and produce a lot of waste. They do very well in outdoor ponds; indoors, use a strong filter. Feeding: Feed small amounts of a quality sinking pellet or flake once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other single-tail goldfish like comets and shubunkins, or with koi in a pond. Avoid slow fancy goldfish, which can't compete for food, and tropical fish, which need warmer water. Ponds: This is where they shine. They handle cold winters as long as part of the pond stays deep enough not to freeze solid. Stop feeding when the water drops below about 50°F. Good to know: Comets grow quickly and are well suited to ponds.

The red minor, or serpae tetra, never swims alone in the wild and shouldn't have to in the aquarium. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hyphessobrycon eques Origin Amazon and Paraguay basins (Brazil, Paraguay, Argentina) Care Level Easy Temperament Semi-aggressive (known fin-nipper) Adult Size Up to 1¾" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 6 Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a dark substrate, which brings out their color. Keep a lid on the tank, since tetras can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, rasboras, danios, corydoras, dwarf cichlids, gouramis and livebearers. Good to know: Tetras feel safer and show better color in a group. A larger school also spreads out any chasing.

One of the few very small examples of the Gourami family, Sparkling Gourami only get to 1.5 inches at full maturity. A small pack of these is a very suitable addition to a nano aquarium or any planted fish tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name Trichopsis pumila Origin Southeast Asia Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1½" Lifespan 4–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Breathes Air Yes – labyrinth fish take air from the surface Group Size Sold as a group of 4 Shipping Size Approx. ¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and plenty of plants, including some floating plants for cover. Keep a lid on the tank and leave a gap of air above the water, since gouramis breathe from the surface. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with small, peaceful fish such as rasboras, small tetras, corydoras and otocinclus. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs and larger, boisterous fish. Good to know: Sparkling gouramis are also called pygmy croaking gouramis because males make soft croaking sounds when they display to each other.

One of the most popular fish in the hobby due to their adaptability and hardiness, a school (or "pride," if they were real tiger cats) of 6 Tiger Barbs will complement any size aquarium with almost any but the largest tank mates. Quick Facts Scientific Name Puntigrus tetrazona Origin Indonesia (Sumatra, Borneo) Care Level Easy, good for beginners Temperament Semi-aggressive (fin-nipper) Adult Size Up to 3" Lifespan 5–7 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a group of 6 Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a filter, a heater and plenty of open swimming space. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Pick fast, sturdy tankmates such as other barbs, danios, loaches, corydoras and larger tetras. Avoid slow, long-finned fish like bettas, angelfish, gouramis and guppies. Good to know: Tiger barbs nip fins mostly when kept in small numbers. Keeping them in a group keeps the chasing within the school.

It should be a crime, or at least a misdemeanor, to put one yo-yo all by himself in a fish tank. This species lives to chase each other about the fish tank and generally just pal around. Quick Facts Scientific Name Botia almorhae (often sold as B. lohachata ) Origin Northern India, Nepal and Pakistan Care Level Easy to moderate Temperament Peaceful to semi-aggressive (squabbles with its own kind) Adult Size Up to 4–5" Lifespan 8–15 years Diet Omnivore (bottom feeder; eats snails) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a group of 3 Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Botia loaches are active bottom dwellers. Give a group plenty of caves, driftwood and rockwork to claim, a soft sand or smooth gravel bottom and good filtration. Keep a lid on the tank. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets or wafers once or twice a day so food reaches the bottom. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Botia loaches also eat pest snails. Tankmates: They do well with most community fish of similar size, such as barbs, danios, rasboras, gouramis and larger tetras. They will eat snails and may eat small shrimp. Good to know: Botia loaches "click" when they feed or squabble, and they sometimes rest on their sides, which is normal behavior.

The Zebra Danio is a prolific breeder and just downright playful. Any school of these fish will add quite a bit of fun and action to any fish tank. Of course, some will get eaten by larger predatory fish, so please place them with the appropriate neighbors. Quick Facts Scientific Name Danio rerio Origin India, Bangladesh and Nepal (Ganges region) Care Level Very easy, great for beginners Temperament Peaceful, very active Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 64–77°F (often fine without a heater) pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 8 Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Danios are fast swimmers, so give them open swimming space, a filter, plants around the edges and a tight-fitting lid, since they jump. Make sure the tank is fully cycled (which takes several weeks) before adding fish. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Danios get along with most peaceful community fish, such as tetras, rasboras, barbs, corydoras and livebearers. Their speed can stress slow, long-finned fish like bettas and fancy guppies, and large predatory fish will eat them. Good to know: Zebra danios are one of the hardiest aquarium fish and among the few that handle cooler, unheated tanks. Danios are fast and jump when startled, so keep a lid on the tank.

Since only the fins of this pretty schooler have the bright lemon colors, a group of six will provide all the yellows the aquarium needs. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hyphessobrycon pulchripinnis Origin Tocantins basin, Brazil Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 5–8 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 6 Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them plants along the back and sides, open swimming space in front and a dark substrate, which brings out their color. Keep a lid on the tank, since tetras can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with most peaceful community fish of similar size, such as other tetras, rasboras, danios, corydoras, dwarf cichlids, gouramis and livebearers. Good to know: Tetras feel safer and show better color in a group. A larger school also spreads out any chasing.

The prized red cap kohaku guppy has the red and white colors of the kohaku koi fish, with the addition of the long, flowing fins of a highly bred fancy guppy. One male and one female of this variety will ensure beautiful, vivid red and white offspring. Quick Facts Scientific Name Poecilia reticulata Origin Northern South America (captive-bred in Thailand) Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 2" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Sold as a pair (1 male + 1 female) Shipping Size Approx. 1¼" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a heater, a gentle filter and plenty of plants, including some floating plants where babies can hide. Guppies like slightly hard water. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: Guppies get along with other small, peaceful fish such as platies, mollies, corydoras, small tetras and rasboras. Avoid fin-nippers like tiger barbs and larger fish that could eat them. Breeding: Guppies are livebearers and breed easily. Females give birth to live babies about once a month, and adults will eat the babies, so thick plants give them a place to hide. Good to know: To keep the red and white kohaku pattern in the babies, breed them only with other kohaku guppies.

The green lamp-eyes of this rasbora are very apparent when it's swimming in a group. German zoologist Georg Dunker discovered these in a stream in Malaysia. We are certain he would wish you to buy as large a school as possible. Soft, slightly acidic water and gentle filtration bring out their best color. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Avoid large predatory fish that could eat them. Good to know: In a well-planted tank a school of rasboras swims together in the middle of the tank, and their colors deepen as they settle in.

Technically a loach is a fish, and any group of fish is a school, but a "school of loaches" just doesn't have as good a ring. Quick Facts Scientific Name Yasuhikotakia morleti Origin Mekong and Chao Phraya basins (Thailand, Laos, Cambodia) Care Level Moderate Temperament Semi-aggressive (territorial; can harass tankmates) Adult Size Up to 3–4" Lifespan 8–15 years Diet Omnivore (bottom feeder; eats snails) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Sold as a group of 3 Care Guide Tank setup: Give them many caves, rocks and driftwood so each loach can claim its own spot, a soft sand or smooth gravel bottom and good filtration. Keep a lid on the tank. Feeding: Feed sinking pellets or wafers once or twice a day so food reaches the bottom. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. They also eat pest snails. Tankmates: Keep them with robust, fast fish of similar or larger size, such as barbs, danios, rainbowfish and semi-aggressive cichlids. Avoid slow, long-finned fish and other bottom dwellers that can't hold their own. They eat snails and shrimp. Good to know: These loaches are bold and territorial; adding them last to an established tank with plenty of caves helps keep the peace.

Paskai or Blue Eye Luminous Rainbowfish are small but hardy and a school of 5 will adapt well to small and mid-size fish tanks. Quick Facts Scientific Name Pseudomugil luminatus Origin Western New Guinea, Indonesia Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to 1¼" Lifespan 2–3 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 75–82°F pH 6.5–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 5 Shipping Size Approx. ¾" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a planted tank with gentle filtration, some floating plants and a lid. They are small, so a sponge over the filter intake keeps them safe. Feeding: Feed crushed flake or micro pellets once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Blue-eyes are small and gentle, so keep them with other small, peaceful fish such as rasboras, small tetras, pygmy corydoras and shrimp. Good to know: Males turn a glowing orange-red with blue eyes as they mature.

These bright red schooling fish are healthier in small schools. Smaller schooling fish like the ember tetra, also called the amandae tetra, live longer in a school than out of one. Quick Facts Scientific Name Hyphessobrycon amandae Origin Araguaia River basin, Brazil Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful Adult Size Up to ¾" Lifespan 2–4 years Diet Omnivore (tiny foods) Water Temperature 72–80°F pH 5.5–7.5 Group Size Sold as a school of 6 Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: These small tetras do best in a planted tank with soft, slightly acidic water, a dark substrate, driftwood, floating plants and gentle filtration. A larger school makes them more confident and colorful. Feeding: Feed small amounts of micro pellets or crushed flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other small, peaceful fish like rasboras, small tetras, pencilfish, pygmy corydoras, otocinclus and dwarf shrimp. Avoid large or boisterous fish that could eat or bully them. Good to know: Small tetras show their best color in a large school in a planted tank with soft lighting.

If harlequins are old and alone, they tend to get nippy with other peaceful fish. Keeping them in a school will keep them peaceful and happy. Pea puffers are not schoolers and just one or two will be fine in a fish tank, but watching four swim about looking for little snails is much more fun than watching one. Quick Facts Scientific Name Carinotetraodon travancoricus Origin Southwestern India Care Level Moderate Temperament Semi-aggressive (nips fins) Adult Size Up to 1" Lifespan 4–5 years Diet Carnivore (meaty foods, snails) Water Temperature 74–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Sold as a group of 4 Shipping Size Approx. ½" Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a planted tank with lots of plants and hiding places to break up sight lines, and good filtration, since puffers are messy eaters. Feeding: Puffers need meaty foods and usually won't eat flake. Feed frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp once a day. They also enjoy small snails, which help keep their teeth trimmed. Tankmates: Pea puffers nip fins and are best kept with their own kind, or with fast, tough fish like otocinclus. Shrimp and snails may be eaten. Good to know: Pea puffers are the smallest puffers in the hobby and are true freshwater fish. They are curious and often watch their owners.

Every nano tank needs a pride of tigers to stalk the tank for small food flakes. Give them dense plants, gentle filtration and plenty of cover. They do not need very warm water, and stable, slightly alkaline water suits them. Feeding: Feed crushed flake or micro pellets once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. They also enjoy frozen brine shrimp. Tankmates: Keep them with other small, peaceful fish that like similar water, such as celestial pearl danios, micro rasboras, small livebearers and dwarf shrimp. Avoid large or boisterous fish. Good to know: They are a little shy at first; plenty of plants and a group of their own kind help them settle in and color up.

The best view of these diminutive killifish is in a group, where their reflective eyes look like lights continuously turning on and off. These dwarf Praecox Rainbowfish are stress-free and more likely to swim about in the middle of the tank when they can swim with friends. Tankmates: They get along with peaceful fish of similar size, such as other rainbowfish, larger tetras, barbs, danios, corydoras and plecos. Good to know: Neon dwarf rainbows have a shiny blue body and red fins (yellow-orange in females) that sparkle under good lighting.

An unusual livebearer and a top dwelling species, four Half Beaks will make for some lively interaction at the top level of the fish tank. Quick Facts Scientific Name Dermogenys pusilla Origin Southeast Asia Care Level Easy Temperament Peaceful (males spar) Adult Size Up to 2½" Lifespan 3–5 years Diet Omnivore Water Temperature 72–82°F pH 7.0–8.0 Group Size Sold as a group of 4 Shipping Size Approx. 1" Care Guide Tank setup: Halfbeaks live at the surface, so give them floating plants and a tight-fitting lid, since they jump. They are easily startled, so avoid sudden movements around the tank. Feeding: Feed a quality floating flake once or twice a day. They also enjoy small frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. Tankmates: They get along with peaceful fish that swim lower in the tank, such as rasboras, corydoras and gouramis. Males may spar with each other. Breeding: Halfbeaks are livebearers. Adults will eat the babies, so floating plants give them a place to hide. Good to know: Halfbeaks have a long lower jaw that helps them catch insects at the surface.

The Parkisoni Rainbowfish was discovered in 1978 in Papua New Guinea (Indonesia) and has since become a somewhat uncommon member of our aquarium hobby. Bred in Florida, these rainbowfish are hardy as long as the water is kept warm and pH is mid 7.5 area. Omnivorous, parkisoni rainbows do require some veggies and meats, so a good community flake food (Sera for example) should keep them healthy. These are larger rainbowfish and grow to about 4 1/2 inches. Use a filter, a heater and a tight-fitting lid, since they can jump. Feeding: Feed a quality flake or small pellet once or twice a day, only as much as they eat in a couple of minutes. Limnophila hippuridoides This pinkish green and feathery stem plant created a flowing sensation and makes a nice harbor for fry. Scientific Name: Limnophila hiipuridoides Shipping Size: Approx. 8 inches, five stems and a lead weight

The red marlboro discus was bred by Jack Wattley and first called the Red Panda after the solid red body and cream color face. AquariumFish.com discus are bred in Singapore to handle a wide range of pH and eat pellet and frozen foods, and hold their color! Of course, discus love live blackworms and brine shrimp as treats. Always keep some frozen food available for new discus, as some take some time to feed on pellets. We feed our discus live and frozen worms. Quick Facts Scientific Name Symphysodon aequifasciatus (captive-bred color variety) Origin Amazon basin (captive-bred in Singapore) Care Level Moderate (needs warm, very clean water) Temperament Peaceful, shy; social Adult Size Up to 6–7" Lifespan 10+ years Diet Omnivore (meaty foods) Water Temperature 82–88°F pH 6.0–7.5 Group Size Does best in a group Shipping Size Approx. 1½–4" (by size option) Care Guide Tank setup: Give them a reliable heater, gentle but strong filtration, and a bare bottom or fine sand for easy cleaning. Keep the tank in a quiet spot. Discus need very clean water. Feeding: Feed small meals of quality discus pellets or granules a few times a day, and remove uneaten food within a few minutes, since leftovers quickly foul the water. They also enjoy frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp. New arrivals may need frozen food for a while before they accept pellets. Tankmates: Discus are calm and shy, so choose gentle tankmates that enjoy the same warm water: cardinal and rummynose tetras, sterbai corydoras and small plecos are popular choices. Avoid fast, boisterous or fin-nipping fish, and anything that competes hard for food. Many keepers avoid angelfish, which can bully discus and share diseases. Living in groups: Discus are social and feel safest in a group. A single discus, or just two, tends to be stressed. When a pair forms to breed, they may claim part of the tank, so a group spreads out the attention. Good to know: Red discus keep their brightest color with clean water, a varied diet and a color-enhancing discus food.

Bartlett's Anthias The Bartlett's Anthias (Pseudanthias bartlettorum) has a sleek body that is a brilliant shade of purple or pink, with a strikingly contrasting yellow dorsal fin and tail. It is a very active, open-water swimmer that prefers to be kept in a group, which creates a breathtaking visual display as they swim together. The Bartlett's Anthias is completely reef-safe and will not harm corals or invertebrates, making it a fantastic addition to a community tank. Due to its high metabolism, it requires a well-established tank and frequent, small feedings throughout the day. Ichthyologist John Randall officially described the fish in 1981 and named the fish after Nathan Bartlett, who was the first to photograph Bartlett's anthias. Why the Bartlett's Anthias is a Great Choice: Schooling Behavior: Keeping a group of these fish provides a dynamic and engaging visual display. Stunning Coloration: Its brilliant purple body and vibrant yellow fins make it a true showpiece. Completely Reef-Safe: It will not harm corals, clams, or most other invertebrates. Peaceful Temperament: It is a non-aggressive species that coexists well with other peaceful fish. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Pseudanthias bartlettorum Origin: Indo-Pacific Reefs Max Size: 3.5 inches Lifespan: 5-7 years Diet: Carnivore. Primarily feeds on meaty foods such as shrimp, krill, and prepared foods. Shipping Size: 2-3 inches

Blue Spotted Rabbitfish The Blue Spotted Rabbitfish is actually a yellow fish but the species gets more and more blue spots as it ages. Rabbitfish are reef safe but will grow to one foot in size. Also, caution is required when handling rabbitfish due to their venomous dorsal fin. It is a very peaceful species except when housed with other rabbitfish. The Blue Spotted Rabbitfish may be housed with more aggressive fish and can be kept in pairs. Its predators will tend to leave it alone because of its venomous dorsal spines which it can raise when disturbed. Care must be taken when handling this fish to avoid the possibility of being stung by its venomous spines. Scientific Name: Siganus corallinus Max Size: 8 inches Diet: fresh vegetables and algae. This fish also has a tendency to nip at soft corals. Required Tank Size: 120+ gallons Shipping Size: 2 to 3 inches

Banggai Cardinalfish The Banggai Cardinal is a graceful oddly finned small saltwater aquarium fish. Great for community tanks and reef safe, banggais have a peaceful temperment. An odd characteristic of the Banggai Cardinalfish is that it is a mouth-brooder, with the male carrying the eggs and young in its mouth, a fascinating behavior to observe. It is an excellent choice for a reef aquarium, where it will leave corals and invertebrates completely unharmed. The name Banggai comes from the Banggai Islands in Indonesia where it was discovered. Why the Banggai Cardinalfish is a Great Choice: Elegant Appearance: Its unique body shape and striking pattern make it a captivating inhabitant. Peaceful & Shy: It is a non-aggressive species that coexists well with other peaceful tank mates. Unique Breeding Behavior: The fascinating process of male mouth brooding is a unique and rewarding sight for hobbyists. Reef-Safe: The Banggai Cardinalfish is completely safe to keep with all types of corals and invertebrates. Quick Facts Scientific Name: Pterapogon kauderni Origin: Banggai Islands, Indonesia Max Size: 3 inches Lifespan: 5 years or more Diet: Carnivore. A varied diet of high-quality frozen foods like brine shrimp and mysis shrimp. Shipping Size: 1-2 inches
