listings.description: * For the safety of our animals, we now ship live fish exclusively via UPS Next Day Air. If your order contains this item, you will only see UPS Next Day Air as a shipping option during checkout * We are proud to offer an extremely rare albino color morph or this exquisite tetra, and its incredible yellow and blue coloration are much more striking than the usual “all-pink” albino! The Albino Emperor Tetra ( Nematobrycon palmeri ) is a very attractive shoaling fish for the community aquarium. Unlike many albino color morphs, this tetra is not just the usual pink color. As it matures, both male and female specimens show canary yellow and iridescent blue coloration in addition to the characteristic “pink eye” that is typically displayed by albino specimens display. In addition, adult males have dramatically elongated dorsal and caudal fins, including an extended middle caudal ray that creates a “trident” tail. Females are generally smaller and thicker in size. The Albino Emperor Tetra typically breeds in pairs and must be kept in shoals of at least 6 to 10 fish. While juveniles will school in the typical manner of young tetras, adults are more likely to shoal and stake off their own small territories. Mature males will posture and compete for females, but this aggression is not a problem in aquariums with ample space and plenty of décor. The Albino Emperor Tetra typically occupies the top and middle level of the water column, although it can often be seen swimming and feeding in the middle and bottom levels as well. It is safe to keep with other peaceful, small fish. Though it has a relatively robust, larger body than many smaller tetras, it has a very small mouth. Adult dwarf shrimp are possibly safe tankmates as well, but adult Albino Emperor Tetras may eat small dwarf shrimp and their fry. Larger, peaceful invertebrates can also make good tankmates. Since they are tank-raised, Albino Emperor Tetras are fairly adaptable, but their natural habitat contains soft, acidic water rich in tannins and leaf litter. While not a picky eater, the Albino Emperor Tetra will thrive and remain very colorful on a varied diet of meaty foods. High-quality flake food, pellets, and frozen or freeze-dried foods will all be readily accepted. listings.description: ⚠️ Important Legal Note: All aquatic invertebrates are prohibited to possess in any form or sell in the state of Maine . Please check your local regulations before purchasing. We are unable to ship livestock from this listing to Maine. If you reside in Maine and try to checkout with this in your cart you will be unable to checkout and receive an error message until it is removed from the cart. * For the safety of our animals, we now ship Sulawesi Snails exclusively via UPS Next Day Air. If your order contains this item, you will only see UPS Next Day Air as a shipping option during checkout * This exceptional snail is one of the celebrated Rabbit Snail species, and it is a wonderful aquarium inhabitant with proper care! Sulawesi Rabbit Snails ( Tylomelania sp .) are some of the most fascinating snails in the aquarium hobby, and the White Spotted Towuti Snail is no exception. Also known as Elephant Snails, their natural habitat is in Indonesia and they are only rarely seen in the United States. The "Rabbit" name likely comes from their rabbit-like faces and drooping antennae that resemble a rabbit's ears. However, the resemblance to an elephant is also clear with their wrinkled, rubbery-looking skin and their long "snouts" (which is functionally more like the snail's foot). Needless to say, these snails are certainly unique in appearance in several aspects! Our White Spotted Rabbit Sulawesi Snails possess black bodies adorned with white spots. Their shells are long and spiral-shaped and taper toward a point at the end, which makes the shell resemble unicorn's horn in shape. Like Gold/Yellow Rabbit Snails, these shells are usually brown with white coloration at the tip of the shell. These snails seem curious by nature, and each snail uses its elongated, muscular "foot" to pull and “hop” itself around on the glass and aquarium decor. This is a very striking snail and is sure to impress viewers, almost all of which will have never seen one before. Giant Sulawesi Snails are some of the largest freshwater snails in the world, growing as large as 4 inches as adults. Since they can grow so large, they need room to move, so it's a good idea to avoid dense vegetation or overcrowding in your aquarium. They are decent algae-eaters, but they also feed on leftover food and any kind of fish food. While most aquatic plants are safe from these snails, they have been known to munch on more delicate or thin-leaved plants. There are reports of successful breeding of these snails in the aquarium, but they generally reproduce much too slowly for overpopulation to be a concern. Wild-caught adult specimens may have some shell damage, but they will readily spawn in the home aquarium. Their fry will have a pristine shell and will provide years of viewing with good care! What We Like About These Snails: Black with white-spotted body coloration Interesting movement and curious nature Completely peaceful Grow to a large and impressive size RECOMMENDED TANK PARAMETERS: Temperature : 76° - 84° F (24.4° - 29° C) pH : 7.5 - 8.5 KH : 2 - 15 dKH Minimum tank size : 10 gallons per snail CARE GUIDELINES: Diet : They eat algae and decaying plant matter, and they have also been known to munch on more delicate plants. They can mostly subsist on leftover fish/invertebrate flakes or pellets, but their diets should be occasionally supplemented with algae wafers and/or blanched vegetables such as zucchini, kale, spinach, or cucumber. Warning! Avoid any food product, medication, or plant fertilizer that contains Copper of any form. Copper is toxic to invertebrates. Many commercial fish foods, medications, and plant fertilizers contain copper or more commonly copper sulfate. Always look at the ingredient list for any product going into the aquarium to ensure they are copper free. Social behavior : Peaceful and solitary; will not engage with tankmates. Filtration & Water Movement Use gentle to moderate filtration that provides biological filtration and oxygenation without creating excessive current. Sponge filters and adjustable-flow filters are suitable choices. Aquatic Plants & Shelter Dense plant growth, floating vegetation, and fine-leaved plants provide security for adults and hiding places for newborn fry. Leave open areas for swimming and feeding. Substrate & Lighting Fine gravel or sand works well, particularly when combined with planted areas. Moderate lighting supports plant growth while shaded areas help the fish feel secure. Aquarium Maturity & Stability Introduce Four-Spot Merry Widows only to fully cycled aquariums. Consistent maintenance and gradual changes in water conditions are especially important when keeping uncommon livebearers. Group Size & Social Structure Maintain a small group rather than a single fish. When keeping both sexes, a female-heavy ratio helps distribute male courtship attention and supports more natural social behavior. Aquatic Arts Tip Ask about the breeder's water parameters when acquiring Four-Spot Merry Widows. Because this species is rarely available and typically maintained through small captive-breeding programs, matching the conditions in which the fish were raised can be more valuable than chasing a narrowly defined set of numbers. Make any necessary adjustments gradually.

Species Overview The Blue Tail Goodeid ( Ataeniobius toweri ), also known as the Blue-Tailed Goodeid, is an uncommon Mexican freshwater fish best known for the beautiful blue coloration that develops in the tails of mature males. Unlike many ornamental livebearers, this species has a more understated appearance, with much of its appeal coming from the contrast between its natural body coloration, blue tail, and fascinating social behavior. Native to the freshwater systems of San Luis Potosí, Mexico , the Blue Tail Goodeid belongs to the family Goodeidae, a group of livebearing fishes with a reproductive biology quite different from familiar guppies, platies, and mollies. Female goodeids nourish developing young through specialized structures called trophotaeniae , and give birth to relatively large, well-developed fry. This makes them particularly interesting for aquarists who enjoy observing natural behavior and working with less commonly maintained species. Blue Tail Goodeids are active, social fish that can display territorial and competitive behavior, especially among mature males. They are best suited to aquariums with plenty of swimming room, planted retreats, and hardscape that breaks up direct lines of sight. Their compatibility with other fish should be evaluated carefully rather than assuming they will behave like peaceful community livebearers. For aquarists interested in something beyond the usual aquarium species, the Blue Tail Goodeid offers an opportunity to maintain a distinctive Mexican livebearer with genuine conservation significance. Several Mexican goodeids have experienced serious declines due to habitat degradation and other environmental pressures, making responsible captive maintenance and breeding especially valuable. What We Love About This Fish Beautiful blue tail coloration develops in mature males, creating a striking contrast with their more naturally colored bodies. USA Bred and Locally Bred options support captive breeding efforts for this uncommon Mexican livebearer. Fascinating social and breeding behavior , including male displays and the unique reproductive biology that distinguishes goodeids from guppies and other familiar livebearers. Conservation significance makes the Blue Tail Goodeid especially rewarding for aquarists interested in maintaining and breeding less commonly available freshwater species. Quick Care Guide Care Level: Moderate Temperament: Semi-Aggressive; Social with Its Own Species Adult Size: Males approximately 2.8 inches (7 cm); females up to 3.9 inches (10 cm) Diet: Omnivore (Quality Flakes, Pellets, Algae-Based Foods, Frozen Foods, and Live Foods) Minimum Tank Size: 30 Gallons – Provides horizontal swimming space, planted shelter, and room for a breeding group. Swimming Zone: Middle to Lower Social Behavior: Social Livebearer, Not a Schooling Fish Group Size: Best maintained in a group with multiple females per male, adequate swimming space, and plenty of visual barriers Origin: Mexico (San Luis Potosí) Source: USA Bred / Locally Bred Scientific Name: Ataeniobius toweri Approximate Purchase Size: Varies by Age and Available Stock Important Care Consideration: Unlike many tropical livebearers, Blue Tail Goodeids appreciate cooler, well-oxygenated freshwater and should not automatically be maintained at the higher temperatures commonly used for guppies and mollies. Their social interactions can also be more assertive, making aquarium size, group composition, and visual barriers especially important. Recommended Water Parameters & Aquarium Requirements Temperature: 68–77°F (20–25°C) pH: 7.0–8.0 GH: Moderately Hard to Hard KH: Sufficient to Maintain Stable, Neutral to Slightly Alkaline Water Ammonia: 0 ppm Nitrite: 0 ppm Nitrate: Ideally Below 20 ppm Recommended Minimum Tank Size: 30 Gallons for a Small Group Understanding Their Water Requirements Temperature: Blue Tail Goodeids ( Ataeniobius toweri ) are unusual among Mexican goodeids because their natural habitats include warm, spring-fed waterways. They tolerate a relatively broad temperature range, but moderate aquarium temperatures are preferable for routine maintenance. Extended exposure to excessive warmth should be avoided, particularly when oxygen levels are insufficient. Water Hardness and pH: Neutral to slightly alkaline, mineral-rich freshwater is appropriate for this species. Maintaining consistent water chemistry is more important than making frequent adjustments to reach an exact hardness or pH reading. Filtration and Oxygenation: Blue Tail Goodeids benefit from clean, oxygen-rich water. Good surface agitation and effective biological filtration are important, but strong directional currents are unnecessary. Their natural habitats include quiet waters and areas with moderate flow. Aquarium Size and Layout: A 30-gallon aquarium provides a practical starting point for a small group. A longer footprint is especially useful because these active fish benefit from horizontal swimming room. Include planted areas and natural structures while preserving open swimming space. Water Quality and Maintenance: Blue Tail Goodeids benefit from substantial, regular water changes and a mature filtration system. Ammonia and nitrite should remain undetectable, while nitrate should be kept low through appropriate stocking, feeding, and maintenance. Seasonal Considerations: Experienced breeders sometimes provide a cooler seasonal period to support natural reproductive cycles. This is a husbandry option rather than a requirement for newly acquired fish, and temperature changes should always be gradual.

The Peugeot Tetra ( Hyphessobrycon peugeoti ) is a distinctive South American freshwater fish prized for its developing red coloration, dark tail marking, and elegant finnage. Mature males can display especially rich coloration and an elongated, filament-like dorsal fin, while younger fish may appear more subdued. Native to Brazil's Rio Juruena drainage, this relatively uncommon tetra offers something different from the more familiar species found in community aquariums. Peaceful and social, Peugeot Tetras are best maintained in groups in mature, planted aquariums with open swimming space and sheltered areas. Their small size makes them attractive for thoughtfully stocked community setups, while their developing coloration and interactions among group members give aquarists plenty to observe. Aquatic Arts offers these Peugeot Tetras as Tank-Bred specimens. Distinctive Coloration: Peugeot Tetras ( Hyphessobrycon peugeoti ) develop subtle reddish tones and contrasting dark markings as they mature. Younger fish may display more subdued coloration. Elegant Male Finnage: Mature males can develop an elongated dorsal fin that adds visual interest during natural displays and interactions. Interesting Group Behavior: These peaceful, social tetras are best maintained in groups, where aquarists can observe their swimming behavior and occasional displays between males. Tank-Bred: Aquatic Arts offers Tank-Bred Peugeot Tetras, providing an opportunity to keep a less commonly encountered South American tetra. Quick Care Guide Common Name: Peugeot Tetra Scientific Name: Hyphessobrycon peugeoti Care Level: Moderate — Best maintained in an established aquarium with stable water conditions. Temperament: Generally Peaceful Adult Size: Approximately 1.5 inches (4 cm), including the tail fin; estimated Purchase Size: 2–3 cm (approximately 0.8–1.2 inches), including the tail fin Minimum Tank Size: 20 Gallons Long — Aquatic Arts recommendation for adequate group swimming space. Recommended Group Size: 8–10 or More Diet: Omnivore — Appropriately sized pellets, crushed flakes, and small live or frozen foods. Swimming Zone: Primarily Midwater, with access to planted cover Water Flow: Gentle to Moderate Aquarium Setup: Planted aquarium with sheltered areas and open swimming space. Sourcing: Tank-Bred Important Care Consideration: Maintain Peugeot Tetras in a suitable group with stable water conditions and appropriately sized foods. At the offered size of 2–3 cm, some individuals may still be developing their adult coloration and finnage. Recommended Water Parameters & Aquarium Requirements Peugeot Tetras ( Hyphessobrycon peugeoti ) thrive in established aquariums with consistent water conditions, reliable filtration, and room to swim as a group. A planted aquarium with a balance of open space and sheltered areas provides an excellent setup. Temperature: 72–79°F (22–26°C) — Maintain consistent temperatures to support healthy activity and reduce stress. pH: 6.0–7.5 — Slightly acidic to neutral water is recommended. Avoid sudden changes in water chemistry. General Hardness (GH): 2–10 dGH — Soft to moderately hard water is preferred. Carbonate Hardness (KH): 1–6 dKH — Maintain stable water chemistry rather than frequently adjusting hardness. Minimum Tank Size: 20 Gallons Long — The longer footprint provides more horizontal swimming space for a group. Water Flow: Gentle to Moderate — Provide good circulation with calmer areas where fish can retreat from the current. Lighting: Moderate with Shaded Areas — Live plants and floating cover can provide shelter without requiring a dimly lit aquarium. Filtration: Established biological filtration — A properly sized filter helps maintain consistent water quality. Water Quality: Ammonia 0 ppm, Nitrite 0 ppm, and Nitrate ideally below 20 ppm — Regular maintenance helps prevent harmful waste accumulation. Aquatic Arts Recommendation: Introduce Peugeot Tetras to a fully cycled aquarium and acclimate them carefully to the existing water conditions. Avoid making sudden adjustments to pH or hardness in an attempt to reach an exact number. Consistency is especially important when settling a new group into its aquarium.

listings.commonName: Bred by Aquatic Arts™ Mix & Match Neocaridina Shrimp – Choose 2
listings.description: Species Overview Create your own combination of colorful freshwater shrimp with our Bred by Aquatic Arts™ Mix & Match Neocaridina Shrimp – Choose 2 . Select two 5-packs from our collection of Neocaridina varieties, all bred and raised right here at Aquatic Arts. This customizable offering is an excellent way to begin two separate shrimp colonies, add to existing colonies, or enjoy two different colors in the same aquarium. Whether you prefer the contrast of red and blue, the warmth of orange and yellow, or another combination entirely, the choice is yours. Different Neocaridina color varieties can generally live together peacefully, but they may also interbreed. Their offspring can develop unpredictable coloration, including more subdued or wild-type appearances over subsequent generations. If maintaining the distinct colors of your chosen varieties is important, we recommend keeping them in separate aquariums. Each order includes two 5-packs of your choice, for a total of 10 Bred by Aquatic Arts™ Neocaridina shrimp. Aquatic Arts Tip: Decide whether your goal is a colorful display or maintaining separate breeding lines before selecting your varieties. Both approaches can be rewarding, but they have different implications for future generations. What We Love About This Mix & Match Pack Two Colors, Your Choice: Build your own combination from our selection of Bred by Aquatic Arts™ Neocaridina shrimp. Two Ways to Enjoy Them: Start separate color colonies or create a colorful display aquarium without the expectation of maintaining distinct breeding lines. Bred by Aquatic Arts™: Every shrimp in this offering is bred and raised in our facilities, where we oversee its care and development. Natural Grazers: Neocaridina shrimp spend their days exploring plants, moss, and hardscape while feeding on biofilm and soft algae. Perfect for Planted Aquariums: Their peaceful nature, small size, and constant activity make them engaging additions to established freshwater aquascapes. Aquatic Arts Tip: If you're adding these shrimp to an existing colony, select varieties with your long-term breeding goals in mind. Adding a different color line may change the appearance of future offspring. Quick Care Guide Care Category Recommendation Scientific Name Neocaridina spp. (variety dependent) Common Name Neocaridina Dwarf Shrimp Origin Bred by Aquatic Arts™ Adult Size Approximately 1–1.5 inches Purchase Size Juvenile to young adult; approximately ⅙–¾ inch, depending on variety Temperament Peaceful Care Level Beginner-friendly in established aquariums Minimum Aquarium Size 5 gallons; 10+ gallons recommended for developing colonies Temperature 64–78°F (18–26°C) pH 6.8–7.5 GH 6–15 dGH KH 0–10 dKH TDS 180–400 ppm Diet Omnivorous grazer Breeding Freshwater, direct development Plant Safe Yes Shrimp Safe Yes, with compatible dwarf shrimp Neocaridina shrimp are adaptable, but they do best in mature aquariums with stable water chemistry. Appropriate mineral content supports healthy molting, while established plants, moss, and hardscape provide the biofilm they graze on throughout the day. Aquatic Arts Tip: A 5-gallon aquarium can house a small group, but a 10-gallon or larger aquarium generally offers greater stability and room for a growing colony. Choose your aquarium size based on your long-term goals, not just the number of shrimp arriving. Water Parameters & Requirements Neocaridina shrimp are adaptable to a range of freshwater conditions, but stability is essential to their long-term health. Rather than continually adjusting water chemistry to reach specific numbers, focus on maintaining consistent parameters within the recommended ranges outlined in the Quick Care Guide. Mineral Balance & Molting: Calcium and magnesium are important for normal physiological function and successful molting. Maintaining appropriate general hardness (GH) and carbonate hardness (KH) helps support a stable environment. Sudden changes in mineral content can stress shrimp, particularly during and after molting. Aquarium Maturity: A fully cycled aquarium is essential, but an established aquarium with developed biofilm is even better. Biofilm provides a continuous natural food source, particularly for young shrimp, while mature biological filtration helps maintain water quality. Filtration & Water Movement: Sponge filters are excellent for shrimp aquariums because they provide biological filtration, gentle circulation, and grazing surfaces. If using a hang-on-back or canister filter, protect the intake with a fine sponge to prevent shrimplets from being drawn into the filtration system. Water Changes & Acclimation: Regular, modest water changes help maintain water quality without causing abrupt shifts in temperature or mineral content. When introducing new shrimp, acclimate them carefully to differences between their shipping water and aquarium water. Water Quality & Maintenance: Ammonia and nitrite must remain at zero, and nitrate should be kept low. Avoid overfeeding, remove decaying food, and monitor the aquarium for sudden changes in water chemistry. Always verify that fertilizers, medications, and other aquarium treatments are safe for freshwater shrimp. For aquarists establishing two separate color colonies, maintaining similar, stable conditions in both aquariums will make ongoing care easier and help each group settle into its new environment. Aquatic Arts Tip: Don't chase exact water parameter readings. When your shrimp are healthy, molting normally, and actively grazing, avoid unnecessary adjustments that could destabilize an established aquarium. If problems develop, test the water and identify the cause before making corrections.

listings.description: Species Overview Why choose just one Neocaridina color when you can pick two? Our Bred by Aquatic Arts™ Mix & Match Neocaridina Shrimp Combo Box – Choose 2 lets you select two 5-packs from our available Aquatic Arts-bred varieties and build a combination that's entirely your choice. Each combo also includes an Aquatic Arts Botanical Combo Pack, Shrimp Sample Food Pack, and a portion of live aquarium moss . These are some of the same additions we use and recommend for shrimp aquariums. The moss provides shelter and grazing areas, botanicals add natural surfaces for biofilm, and the food samples give you several feeding options to try. You can choose contrasting colors for a display aquarium, add to colonies you already have, or keep your two selections in separate aquariums if you're interested in maintaining their individual color lines. What's Included First Shrimp Selection: One 5-pack of Bred by Aquatic Arts™ Neocaridina shrimp. Second Shrimp Selection: Another 5-pack from the available color varieties. Aquatic Arts Botanical Combo Pack: Natural aquarium botanicals. Aquatic Arts Shrimp Sample Food Pack: A selection of prepared shrimp foods. Aquatic Arts Live Moss Portion: Live aquarium moss for shelter and grazing. Total: 10 Neocaridina shrimp, plus the Botanical Combo Pack, Shrimp Sample Food Pack, and live moss. Different Neocaridina colors can live together peacefully, but they can also interbreed. If maintaining a particular color strain is important to you, we recommend keeping those varieties separately. Aquatic Arts Tip: Think about whether you want a colorful display or two separate breeding colonies before making your selections. Both are good reasons to choose this combo, but they'll give you different results if your shrimp reproduce. What We Love About This Mix & Match Combo Two Colors, Your Choice: Select two of your favorite Bred by Aquatic Arts™ Neocaridina varieties rather than receiving a randomly chosen assortment. Bred by Aquatic Arts™: The shrimp are bred and raised in our own facilities, where we oversee their care from young shrimp through shipping. More Than Just Shrimp: The included Botanical Combo Pack, food samples, and live moss are useful additions whether you're starting a shrimp aquarium or adding to an established one. Two Ways to Enjoy Them: Keep your selections together for a colorful display or in separate aquariums to maintain their individual breeding lines. Aquatic Arts Tip: If you're adding to an existing Neocaridina colony, consider whether you want to introduce another color line. The adult shrimp will retain their own coloration, but mixed breeding can change the appearance of future generations. Quick Care Guide Care Category Recommendation Scientific Name Neocaridina davidi Common Name Neocaridina Dwarf Shrimp Origin Bred by Aquatic Arts™ Adult Size Approximately 1–1.5 inches Purchase Size Juvenile to young adult; size varies by color variety Temperament Peaceful Care Level Beginner-friendly in established aquariums Minimum Aquarium Size 5 gallons; 10+ gallons recommended for colonies Temperature 64–78°F (18–26°C) pH 6.8–7.5 GH 6–15 dGH KH 0–10 dKH Diet Omnivorous grazer Breeding Freshwater, direct development Plant Safe Yes Shrimp Safe Yes, with compatible shrimp species Aquatic Arts Tip: A 5-gallon aquarium can accommodate a small group, but we prefer 10 gallons or larger when there's room for a colony to grow. The extra water volume makes maintenance and water stability easier. Water Parameters & Requirements Neocaridina are fairly adaptable shrimp, but we pay particular attention to water stability, mineral content, and filtration when raising them at Aquatic Arts. Mineral Balance & Molting: Calcium and magnesium are important for normal molting and exoskeleton development. Check GH and KH before making changes to your water. If you're using reverse osmosis water, it generally needs to be remineralized for Neocaridina. Aquarium Maturity: A fully cycled aquarium is essential. An aquarium that's been running long enough to develop biofilm on plants, moss, and hardscape is even better, particularly for younger shrimp. Filtration & Water Movement: Sponge filters work very well for Neocaridina. They provide biological filtration, gentle circulation, and a surface shrimp can graze. Other filters can work too, but protect their intakes with a fine sponge. Water Changes & Acclimation: Regular water changes help maintain water quality, but avoid sudden changes in temperature or mineral content. Use replacement water reasonably close to the aquarium's existing conditions and follow the acclimation instructions included with your shipment. Water Quality & Maintenance: Ammonia and nitrite should remain undetectable, and nitrate should be kept low. Remove uneaten food before it deteriorates, and check that any aquarium medications or treatments are safe for shrimp. Aquatic Arts Tip: Don't make adjustments simply because a test result isn't exactly in the middle of a recommended range. If your water is suitable and your shrimp are doing well, consistency is usually better than constant correction.

listings.commonName: Thai Onion Plant (Crinum thaianum), Plant with Bulb
listings.description: This rare plant will grow to an impressive size and flower beautifully under optimal conditions! The Thai Onion Plant ( Crinum thaianum ) is a unique bulb plant that can be grown emersed or submersed. It can grow quite tall and will produce a large white flower under good conditions. This plant grows in a rosette formation and is generally resilient as long as it is not moved often. Care for the Thai Onion Plant is not difficult as long as a few key needs are met. Its bulb base should not be completely buried in the substrate or it can rot. It requires moderate to high light. It does not require CO2 supplementation, though it will certainly benefit from such supplementation and is more likely to flower under such conditions. The Thai Onion Plant develops a strong root structure, so it will benefit from nutrient-rich substrate. It is best planted in the middle or background of the aquarium. In addition to its attractive appearance, Thai Onion Plant provides a valuable refuge for aquarium animals, especially dwarf shrimp, nano fish, and fry. Thai Onion Plant can easily flourish and grow to become a major centerpiece of the planted aquarium! Like most plants, Thai Onion Plant will benefit from supplementation such as Seachem Flourish, Flourish Excel, Nitrogen and other plant supplements. However, supplementation is not absolutely required for this plant to grow and stay healthy in a nutrient-rich aquarium. No aquarium plant distributor/nursery/wholesaler/retailer can or will guarantee their plants to be 100% snail free. We can not guarantee our plants will be snail free. What We Like About This Plant: Grows to an impressive size Beatiful long, green leaves Truly aquatic and undemanding Fairly uncommon in the aquarium hobby Care Guidelines: Temperature: 68° - 82.4° F (20° - 28° C) pH: 6.0 – 9.0 Lighting: Moderate to High Origin: Indigenous to Thailand, cultivated in US nurseries Aquarium placement: Middle and Background, but bulb should not be fully buried in substrate Care: Easy to Moderate All Aquatic Arts brand plants and animals come with a 100% live arrival guarantee, plus free email support!

The Blue Zebra Angelfish ( Pterophyllum scalare ), is an incredible variant that naturally displays blue coloration over the classic "zebra" striping that is characteristic of the wild coloration. Juveniles often do not display much of the blue/turquoise coloration, but will develop it generously as they grow and approach maturity. This shoaling cichlid is relatively peaceful compared to other members of the cichlid family. It also has a very thin, tall body unlike most other cichlids. The Blue Zebra Angelfish is indigenous to several river systems in Northern South America, but virtually all specimens in the aquarium hobby have been tank-raised for generations. The Blue Zebra Angelfish will thrive in a heavily planted aquarium with driftwood and/or rock formations and gentle water flow. It is not overly reclusive, but this fish strongly prefers the cover of plants and, due to its body shape, is not likely to seek refuge in rock caves and similar structures. The Blue Zebra Angelfish is generally compatible with other peaceful fish as long as it has plenty of space. Territoriality is typically at its peak during spawning. Dwarf shrimp and other small, delicate invertebrates should not be kept with the Blue Zebra Angelfish, but more durable, larger shrimp and snails could possibly make good tankmates in a large enough aquarium. If spawning is desired, tankmates of other species should be kept to a minimum or avoided altogether unless the aquarium is very spacious. Feeding is simple for the unfussy Blue Zebra Angelfish. The Congo Tetra ( Phenacogrammus interruptus ) is a very attractive schooling fish for the planted community aquarium. It has an overall silver body, but develops intense, iridescent blue, green, gold, and even pink coloration as it matures. Males also develop very elegant fin extensions with maturity. The Congo Tetra grows to a larger size than many other well-known tetra species, but it is still very peaceful and is a wonderful fish for larger setups. A school of adults is quite a sight to see! Since it is tank-bred, the Congo Tetra is fairly adaptable, but its natural habitat contains soft, acidic water rich in tannins and leaf litter. This fish should be kept in schools of at least 6-8 specimens and will display its best coloration in a group that includes males and females. The Gold Racer Nerite Snail ( Vittina waigiensis ) is an extraordinarily beautiful freshwater nerite species that is native to the Philippines. It is among the rarest snail species in the aquarium world, so it is very seldom available. The Gold Racer Nerite Snail has a highly variable shell appearance, but its many possible patterns are all among the most attractive of any ornamental freshwater or marine snail. It can live for upwards of 4 years, so it is relatively long-lived among its relatives. It requires brackish or marine water for its fry to survive, so it will not proliferate in a freshwater aquarium and it is not known to have been bred commercially. Most of the nerite snails we offer have very similar care requirements and characteristics, and the Gold Racer Nerite Snail is no exception. It inhabits fresh and brackish water areas and cannot reproduce in freshwater. This snail is a very effective algae eater and will thrive in a mature aquarium that has plenty of algae and biofilm growth. Some nerite snails are initially finicky about eating dry foods, but most will come to accept them, especially with foods that are high in spirulina or other plant content. Fresh vegetables are typically accepted as well. Nerite snails are hardy in a mature, stable, well-maintained aquarium, but they are not as hardy as some other snail species in subpar setups. It is important to remember that scavengers such as snails do not consume as much oxygen as most fish, but they still contribute to the bioload of the aquarium and they should not be overstocked long-term. It should also be noted that, while this snail can live in a wide variety of pH levels, it will live for much longer in alkaline water of over 7.0 pH. If it is kept in acidic water, it is more prone to experience shell erosion. Calcium supplementation (especially when using R/O water) is highly recommended for maintaining the quality of this snail’s magnificent shell. The L401 Royal King Alenquer Pleco ( Hypancistrus sp. ), also known as the Rio Curuá Pleco, is a very rare and recently identified member of the Loricariidae family of South American suckermouth catfishes. Its entire body is covered in black and white/yellow “maze-like” stripes, making it a very striking fish for the planted or nano aquarium. In the past, it was considered to possibly be a significantly different geographic variant of the L333 King Tiger Pleco, but it has since been determined to be its own distinct species. Like many plecos, the Royal King Alenquer Pleco has generally been a wild-caught species, but we are proud to be among the first stores to offer superior tank-raised juveniles at a MUCH lower cost than wild-caught specimens (and much lower than many other stores’ tank-raised specimens)! A generally peaceful and hardy species, the Royal King Alenquer Pleco is an excellent, undemanding candidate for most aquariums. Unlike the widely-seen Common Pleco ( Hypostomus plecostomus ) and Trinidad Pleco ( Hypostomus punctatus), which easily reach a monstrous size of 18 to 20+ inches (45 to 51+ cm), the Royal King Alenquer Pleco grows to a size of only 3.9 inches (10 cm). This smaller size makes for a much more manageable (and less messy) pleco that can thrive permanently in a well-maintained aquarium as small as 30 gallons. Male plecos may be somewhat territorial with other males of their species, but disputes can usually be diffused by providing ample territory and hiding places for each fish. All other fish tankmates will be generally ignored, although it is possible that juvenile and subadult dwarf shrimp will fall prey to the Royal King Alenquer Pleco. However, ornamental snails will not be bothered and large Amano, Green Lace, Flower, and Vampire Shrimp are generally unthreatened by the Royal King Alenquer Pleco. Please note that this fish requires a significantly warmer temperature than some other fish and invertebrates, especially subtropical species. Some shrimp will not thrive in these high temperatures. The Royal King Alenquer Pleco is primarily nocturnal, but will often become active during daytime hours once established in an aquarium with plenty of driftwood, rockwork, and other hiding places. It is not known to eat wood heavily like some plecos ( Panaque sp., etc.), but it may benefit from some supplementary wood (or bio-film on driftwood). The Royal King Alenquer Pleco will not bother most plants and it is not an effective algae eater. Feed the Royal King Alenquer Pleco a diet heavy in both meaty and vegetable matter, including high-quality vegetable flakes, sinking algae wafers and pellets. Like most Hypancistrus species, the Royal King Alenquer Pleco is omnivorous, but but it leans heavily on the carnivorous side. It will also appreciate being fed some fresh vegetables such as shelled peas, spinach, zucchini and cucumber. Meaty foods such as bloodworms are definitely necessary for this species, especially in comparison to some other “pleco” species. This species also requires a very clean, well-maintained aquarium with moderate to high water flow in order to thrive. The L401 Royal King Alenquer Pleco is a reclusive species, but it will typically be increasingly outgoing in a heavily planted and decorated aquarium with peaceful tankmates. The El Niño Fern ( Bolbitis heteroclita ), also known as Asian Water Fern or Bolbitis Broadleaf, is a beautiful and undemanding but uncommon plant for the freshwater aquarium. Its long, flowing, green leaves are very elegant and delicate in appearance. Unlike many plants, the El Niño Fern attaches itself to and propagates on aquarium décor. El Niño Fern is relatively rare because it is very slow growing. It only requires low to moderate lighting and nutrient rich soil, although its growth rate can be increased through CO 2 injection/supplementation. It reproduces through rhizome division and the production of offshoots, and it thrives in areas with strong water currents. El Niño Fern should not be planted with its rhizome (roots) buried in the substrate because it will rot and recede. Instead, it can be attached to rocks, driftwood, and other decorations in the aquarium, or it can be planted on top of the substrate as long as the roots are not completely buried. Due to its delicate leaves, it should never be housed with large crayfish, medium to large cichlids, goldfish, or any other animals that are prone to picking at plants. CO 2 supplementation is beneficial, but not necessary for this plant. Like most plants, El Niño Fern will benefit from supplementation such as Seachem Flourish, Flourish Excel, Nitrogen and other plant supplements. Our El Niño Ferns are well-established portions and are ideal for the low-light or low-tech aquarium. This plant is very hardy and resilient! The Orange Fin Stiphodon Goby ( Stiphodon maculidorsalis ) is a lesser known freshwater dwarf goby that is native to Indonesia. It is distinctive for the bright orange dorsal fins that both males and most females display. Females are not as colorful, but are still very attractively marked with black and cream-colored stripes. This fascinating, peaceful fish is an algae and biofilm grazer that is an excellent candidate for the mature nano aquarium. An aquarium with heavy water flow (10 to 15 times turnover per hour) and very clean, clear water is required for the Orange Fin Stiphodon Goby. This fish is native to shallow, clear, fast-flowing waters and it is sensitive to declines in water quality, so regular aquarium maintenance is a must. The Orange Fin Stiphodon Goby is a biofilm and algae grazer in nature. It is known to usually accept frozen meaty foods, but such foods should only be fed occasionally. This fish will also sometimes accept high-quality dry foods that are rich in plant matter, but it is absolutely essential that biofilm and algae are naturally available in the aquarium to ensure its long-term health or else it may slowly starve. As long as it is kept in a well-maintained, mature aquarium with good biofilm and algae growth as well as high water flow, the Orange Fin Stiphodon Goby is a hardy and entertaining fish. It will not bother aquarium plants. In fact, Anubias species are an excellent plant to keep with this goby because Anubias can foster significant biofilm/algae growth in an aquarium with moderate to high lighting. Most small rasboras, tetras, hillstream loaches, and other small, peaceful fish are good tankmates for the Orange Fin Stiphodon Goby. Due to its small size and diet, the it can also be kept with dwarf shrimp, although it might eat a few of their fry. Dwarf shrimp are particularly good tankmates in larger aquariums where they can find areas of lower water flow. Peaceful bottom-dwelling fish are also a possibility, but care must be taken to make sure that the passive Orange Fin Stiphodon Goby is not outcompeted for food. Female Orange Fin Stiphodon Gobies will often congregate together, even with other goby species such as the Blue or Gold Neon Dwarf Goby. Males seem to be able to differentiate between females of different species during courtship behavior. There are reported cases of the Orange Fin Stiphodon Goby spawning in the aquarium, but it is very difficult (if not currently impossible) to raise the fry due to their complex larval stages. In nature, adults spawn and their fry hatch in freshwater, then they are immediately swept downstream to marine ocean waters where they feed and develop. As the fry mature, they swim great distances back to full freshwater streams, often on completely different islands than where they originated. At this point, the fry have become young adults and will soon be sexually mature and exhibit adult coloration. Many Stiphodon gobies have the ability to climb glass, so an aquarium lid and/or rim are necessary to prevent escape. Our young adult specimens are in excellent health, but many of the males are not yet showing their full mature coloration. This color will be most vivid when the fish are kept in a group. The Super Red Bristlenose Pleco ( Ancistrus sp . “Super Red”), also known as the Bushynose or Bushymouth Pleco, is a member of the Loricariidae family of South American suckermouth catfishes. While many suckermouth catfish species have yet to be bred on any major scale in aquariums, the Super Red Bristlenose Pleco is being propogated by a few commercial breeders. Its facial area becomes adorned with many bristle-like appendages beginning in sub-adulthood. Both sexes grow the appendages, but the growth and length is much more pronounced in males. This "super red" variant has a yellowish appearance as a juvenile, but both males and females develop very deep red-orange coloration as they mature. A generally peaceful and hardy species, the Super Red Bristlenose Pleco is an excellent, undemanding candidate for most aquariums. Unlike the widely-seen Common Pleco ( Hypostomus plecostomus ) and Trinidad Pleco ( Hypostomus punctatus ), which easily reach a monstrous size of 18 to 20+ inches (45 to 51+ cm), the Super Red Bristlenose Pleco grows to a size of only 4 to 5.9 inches (10 to 15 cm). This smaller size makes for a much more manageable (and less messy) pleco that can thrive permanently in a well-maintained aquarium as small as 30 to 40 gallons. Male plecos may be somewhat territorial with other males of their species, but disputes can usually be diffused by providing ample territory and hiding places for each fish. All other tankmates will be generally ignored, although it is possible that small shrimp fry might fall prey to the Super Red Bristlenose Pleco. However, some large-scale shrimp suppliers breed Super Red Bristlenose Plecos in the same pools they use for shrimp breeding. The Super Red Bristlenose Pleco is primarily nocturnal, but will often become active during daytime hours once established in an aquarium with plenty of driftwood, rockwork, and other hiding places. It is not known to eat wood heavily like some plecos ( Panaque sp., etc.), but it may benefit from some supplementary wood (or bio-film on driftwood). The Super Red Bristlenose Pleco will not bother most plants, but it will eat plenty of algae in the aquarium, especially as a juvenile. Feed the Super Red Bristlenose Pleco a diet heavy in vegetable matter, including high-quality vegetable flakes, sinking algae wafers and pellets. It will also appreciate being fed some fresh vegetables such as shelled peas, spinach, zucchini and cucumber. Occasional meaty foods such as bloodworms are also beneficial when fed sparingly. This fish eats constantly, so too much meat/animal protein in its diet can be unhealthy for the fish as well as the level of waste it produces in the aquarium. The Short Nose Algae Shrimp ( Caridina longirostris ) is an unusual freshwater species that is native to Taiwan, Japan, Philippines, Indonesia, and Malaysia. It is among the best algae-eating species of freshwater shrimp, so it is a very valuable maintenance animal. It will eat most types of algae, and it will even reportedly eat the dreaded BBA (Black Beard/Brush Algae)! The Short Nose Algae Shrimp is mostly clear and similar in appearance to the Pinokio Shrimp ( Caridina gracilirostris ), but it has a shorter rostrum (nose). Like the Pinokio Shrimp, it has several highlights of red and gold coloration. The Short Nose Algae Shrimp, like most shrimp, lives in large colonies and spends most of its time foraging for food. As stated above, it is a voracious eater of algae in the aquarium and is not only a very active, outgoing species, but it is also very useful as a solution to fighting algae issues. It aggressively feeds on most varieties of algae and, in appropriate numbers, will often eradicate even the most persistent algae growth on plants and other aquarium decorations. It is also very effective in eating decaying plant matter, such as shed leaves and needles of aquarium plants. However, it does not bother or damage ornamental plants. Care for the Short Nose Algae Shrimp is fairly simple and straightforward. It does not require the more acidic pH of its "bee-type" Caridina cantonensis cousins. It inhabits waterways that fluctuate widely in temperature and pH according to rainfall, so it will thrive in a variety of water parameters as long as it has very clean water. The Short Nose Algae Shrimp has reportedly been bred and reared successfully in the aquarium, but not on a wide commercial scale. This is likely due to its plentiful and widespread distrubution in the wild as well as the lack of known color morphs achievable through selective breeding. The bulk of its diet is biofilm, algae, and decaying plant matter so it will work diligently to clean up detritus in any aquarium. It feeds constantly and displays constant activity. In a less mature aquarium, it should be fed high quality flake and mini pellet dry foods with high algae/spirulina/plant content. This hardy, low-maintenance plant is a unique and beautiful addition to the aquarium or paludarium! Dwarf Aquarium Lily ( Nymphaea stellata ) is a very distinctive and colorful bulb plant that is native to India. It is known for its triangular leaves and the green, red, and pink coloration that they develop as the plant grows. It typically grows to a size of less than 5 inches (12.7 cm), so it is an excellent plant for the aquarium foreground or even the midground of smaller aquariums. It will sometimes flower when kept in shallow enough water or emersed conditions, so it is a terrific plant for paludariums as well. Care for Dwarf Aquarium Lily is very easy. Its bulb base must not be completely buried in the substrate or it will rot. In fact, burying just 1/4 of the bulb in the substrate should be sufficient. Also, this warm water plant will sometimes quickly deteriorate if the temperature is too low. Finally, it will periodically go through dormant periods where it will shed its leaves for a few weeks, but then grow new leaves. With quality care, the Dwarf Aquarium Lily will grow at a moderate rate. It propagates through shoots, and once new growth has roots of its own, it can be cut and replanted. This sword plant hybrid is one of the most spectacularly red plants that can be the centerpiece fauna of even large aquariums! This plant will benefit from CO2 supplementation, but it does not require it. While it will thrive in high lighting, it is also very durable and can do very well under moderate lighting. It requires nutrient-rich substrate for its extensive root structure. It produces very large leaves, so it must be planted with care to not cast too much shade on other plants as it grows. It is certainly only suitable for background placement in smaller aquariums, but it can also be placed in the middle ground of larger aquariums. The Red Rubin Sword reproduces through rhizome division as well as by the production of side shoots, which can be removed and replanted. It is very intolerant of copper, so please keep this in mind if you use tap water in your aquarium. The L397 Alenquer Tiger Pleco ( Panaqolus sp. ) is an exceptionally colorful and rare loricariid (suckermouth catfish) species that has been successfully tank-bred commercially in just the last few years. Its bright orange and black striping are very distinguishable and among the most striking colorations of the hundreds of known plecos. Like many plecos, the L397 Alenquer Tiger Pleco has generally been a wild-caught species, but we are proud to offer tank-raised juveniles of this beautiful fish at a fraction of the price of other stores! A generally peaceful and hardy species, the L397 Alenquer Tiger Pleco is an excellent, undemanding candidate for most aquariums. Unlike the widely-seen Common Pleco ( Hypostomus plecostomus ) and Trinidad Pleco ( Hypostomus punctatus ), which easily reach a monstrous size of 18 to 20+ inches (45 to 51+ cm), the L397 Alenquer Tiger Pleco grows to a maximum size of only around 5 inches (12.7 cm). This smaller size makes for a much more manageable (and less messy) pleco that can thrive permanently in a well-maintained aquarium as small as 30 to 40 gallons. Male plecos may be somewhat territorial with other males of their species, but disputes can usually be diffused by providing ample territory and hiding places for each fish. All other tankmates will be generally ignored, although it is possible that small shrimp fry might fall prey to the omnivorous L397 Alenquer Tiger Pleco. The L397 Alenquer Tiger Pleco is primarily nocturnal, but will often become active during daytime hours once established in an aquarium with plenty of driftwood, rockwork, and other hiding places. Like its larger cousins of the Panaque genus, the L397 Alenquer Tiger Pleco is a "wood eating" pleco whose sucker mouth contains teeth that rasp biofilm from driftwood. It is ideal to have multiple driftwood pieces upon which this fish can graze, and at least some wood must be present at all times. The L397 Alenquer Tiger is not a particularly efficient algae eater, but its rasping habits may result in damage to ornamental plants, particularly in smaller tanks. It is possible that it would not do noticeable damage to more durable plants in a fairly large tank with plenty of driftwood. It will also appreciate being fed some fresh vegetables such as shelled peas, spinach, zucchini, and cucumber, or dry and frozen foods that are very rich in vegetable matter. The addition of GlasGarten Bacter AE will aid greatly in biofilm growth for this fish's diet. What We Like About This Fish: An extremely beautiful, very peaceful, and hardy addition to almost any aquarium. At a maximum size of 5 inches, this is a very practical and manageable fish. Superb tank-bred juvenile specimens The L397 Alenquer Tiger Pleco is an aquarium fish with a unique appearance as well as plenty of personality. (we try our absolute best to send a true males and females, but due to the nature of Apistogrammas we can't fully guarantee the genders) What We Love About This Fish: • Beautiful Redfin Details : Vibrant red edging on dorsal and tail fins. • Peaceful Dwarf Cichlid Personality : Ideal for smaller aquariums with compatible tankmates. • Dynamic Behavior : Active and curious, often displaying intricate courtship and social interactions. • Versatile Aquascaping Compatibility : Complements heavily planted or natural aquariums. Natural Habitat: Native to the calm, slow-moving waters of South America, specifically in the Paraguay River Basin, these cichlids inhabit areas with dense vegetation, leaf litter, and plenty of hiding spots. The water is typically soft and slightly acidic, with subdued lighting created by overhanging plants. Aquascaping: • Plants : Best suited to tanks with plants such as Amazon Swords , Cryptocorynes , Java Ferns , and floating plants for shade. • Hardscape : Include driftwood, leaf litter, and small caves or shelters like coconut huts for breeding or hiding. • Botanicals : Indian Almond Leaves or alder cones can help replicate their natural habitat, releasing beneficial tannins and creating a slightly acidic environment. Botanical Combo Packs have an assortment of plants leaves that work well with breeding dwarf cichlids. Diet and Feeding: Redfin Three-Striped Dwarf Cichlids thrive on a varied diet. Offer a combination of high-quality foods such as: Live or frozen foods like brine shrimp, daphnia , or bloodworms. High-quality pellet or flake foods designed for cichlids. Occasional treats of blanched vegetables like zucchini or spinach to add variety. Tank Mates and Compatibility: These peaceful dwarf cichlids do well in community tanks with similarly sized, non-aggressive species. Suitable tankmates include: Small schooling fish like neon tetras or pencilfish . Corydoras catfish or small plecos. Avoid larger or aggressive tankmates, as well as other cichlid species in smaller setups. Not Shrimp Safe: Not recommended for tanks with small shrimp or shrimp fry, as they may see them as food. However, they can cohabitate with adult shrimp in large, heavily planted tanks. Breeding: Breeding Redfin Three-Striped Dwarf Cichlids is relatively straightforward in a well-planned setup: Provide soft, slightly acidic water (pH 6.0-7.0). Offer small structures like Ceramic Dwarf Cichlid Breeding Huts , caves, or coconut shells for the female to lay eggs. These structures mimic their natural hiding spots and create a secure environment for spawning. Males display vivid coloration during courtship to attract females. After spawning, the female typically guards the eggs while the male protects the surrounding territory. Fry can be fed freshly hatched brine shrimp or powdered fry food once they become free-swimming. Recommended Tank Parameters: • Temperature : 75° - 82°F (24° - 28°C) • pH : 6.0 - 7.5 • KH : 1 - 6 • Minimum Tank Size : 20 gallons Care Guidelines: • Diet : Feed a varied diet of live, frozen, and prepared foods to maintain health and coloration. • Social Behavior : Best kept in pairs or harems (1 male, multiple females). Males can be territorial with other males in smaller tanks. • Origin : Tank-bred by professional breeders, ensuring adaptability to home aquariums. • Average Adult Size : 2.5 - 3 inches (6.5 - 7.5 cm) • Average Purchase Size : 1.5 - 2 inches (4 - 5 cm) Live Arrival Guarantee: We guarantee live arrival for all our fish. listings.description: This slow-growing plant forms into bushy patches that provide perfect hiding places for fish and shrimp, as well as their fry. Loma Fern/Round Pellia/Süsswassertang Liverwort ( Lomariopsis cf. lineata ), is an uncommon fern gametophyte that, until a few years ago, was considered to be a liverwort or moss. The German terms “Süsswassertang” and “Sübwassertang” translate to “freshwater seaweed.” This is a great plant to keep in any freshwater aquarium due to its low lighting requirements. It is a slow-growing plant that is capable of living in somewhat coldwater tanks as well as tropical tanks. It grows into bushy patches that are always a favorite hiding place for shrimp and fish fry. We definitely foresee this plant becoming much more popular in the hobby in the near future. It is easy to attach to and begin propagating on rocks, driftwood, or aquarium substrate. With care, it can even grow along the walls of the aquarium. The plant is grown outdoors and may contain a few pest snails or terrestrial bugs (the bugs will not survive or reproduce underwater). There are some reports that this extremely slow-growing plant does not respond well to some plant fertilizers, so supplement with caution! No aquarium plant distributor/nursery/wholesaler/retailer can or will guarantee their plants to be 100% snail free. We can not guarantee our plants will be snail free. We offer two portions of Loma Fern which can be selected directly under the "Select a Portion" option at the top of this page: 1/2 Cup- This is a smaller portion of Loma Fern, which is enough to start two to three patches that will grow out quickly. The moss ships as a loose portion/bunch in a plastic container. 1 Cup - This is a large portion of Loma Fern, which is enough to start 4 to 6 patches that will grow out quickly. It is also shipped as a loose portion/bunch in a plastic container. listings.description: Lloydiella is a very hardy stem plant that has bright green leaves and is perfect for low-tech setups! Creeping Jenny AKA Lloydiella ( Lysimachia nummularia ) is a very hardy, attractive stem plant with bright green leaves. It can thrive in low-tech setups as long as it has moderate to (preferably) high lighting. As it matures, it can grow to an impressive height that is very suitable for the background of the aquarium. While Creeping Jenny naturally grows emersed, it is very adaptable to long-term submersed conditions. In addition to being an excellent aquarium plant, it is also ideal for paludariums and terrariums. Lloydiella is an easy plant to maintain. It does not require CO 2 supplementation, though it will certainly benefit from it. It will look its best under moderate to high lighting and will be sturdiest under high lighting. Due to the thin texture of its leaves, Lloydiella is not suitable for aquariums with destructive animals such as crayfish, large cichlids, or goldfish. Like most plants, Lloydiella will benefit from supplementation such as Seachem Flourish, Flourish Excel, nitrogen, and other plant supplements. It actually requires a relatively high level of nutrients and will begin to yellow if it is undernourished. However, it is a rather resilient plant and its high nutrient consumption will contribute greatly to limiting algae growth. listings.commonName: Japanese Dwarf Pennywort (Hydrocotyle tripartita var. “Japan”) Tissue Culture
listings.description: Japanese Dwarf Pennywort is an incredible bright green, hardy carpeting plant that is excellent for almost any planted aquarium! Japanese Dwarf Pennywort ( Hydrocotyle tripartita var. “Japan”) is a very popular foreground and middle ground plant for the serious freshwater planted aquarium. With proper care, this hardy, fast-growing plant can flourish and form a dense carpet in aquariums with high lighting, and it can grow into a bush-like formation in lower lighting. Its lily pad-like leaves are very elegant and delicate in appearance. This variety of Japanese Dwarf Pennywort can thrive in low to high lighting. It tends to grow densely and horizontally in high lighting, and it grows much more slowly, loosely, and horizontally in lower lighting. Its trimmings can be replanted to increase the size of the mat. If used for carpeting the aquarium, it should be trimmed weekly to promote horizontal growth. It does not require substrate, but does seem to absorb some of its nutrients through its roots when planted in substrate or attached to another surface. It will also sometimes even grow over rocks and mats. It will also benefit from CO 2 supplementation, but this is not required. In fact, it will require much more frequent trimming when CO 2 supplementation due to the dramatically increased, denser growth rate that such supplementation will promote. This listing is for the tissue culture form of Japanese Dwarf Pennywort. Tissue cultures are superior to traditional forms of aquarium plants in many ways. They are produced in a completely sterile environment which eliminates the possibility of them carrying pest snails or algae spores. They have a shelf life of several months if properly maintained and they are housed in a nutrient gel until introduced to the aquarium. To introduce a tissue culture plant to the aquarium, simply rinse off as much nutrient gel as possible, then plant as usual. The nutrient gel will not harm your aquarium. Like most plants, Japanese Dwarf Pennywort will benefit from supplementation such as Seachem Flourish, Flourish Excel, Flourish Nitrogen, Flourish Iron, and other plant supplements. This listing is for the tissue culture form of Japanese Dwarf Pennywort. Tissue cultures are superior to traditional forms of aquarium plants in many ways. We were mistakenly sent a few very nice specimens of this fish by a supplier, so we want to find them good homes and are offering them at a price that is much lower than usual for medium-sized (3+ inch) specimens. Goldfish are incompatible with nearly all other plants and animals that we regularly carry.*** The Blue Oranda Goldfish ( Carassius auratus auratus ) is a beautiful blue-gray color variant of the classic oranda group of fancy goldfish. Like other orandas, it displays a double tail and the distinctive, fleshy “wen” hood on its entire head. In addition to its blue-gray color, it sometimes also has patches of shining gold (not orange) on its body, although this gold coloration often disappears or recedes as the fish reaches maturity. A generally peaceful and hardy species, the Blue Oranda Goldfish is an excellent, undemanding candidate for coldwater, goldfish-centric aquariums. Though it is very hardy, it requires a spacious tank with very clean water, powerful filtration, and frequent water changes. Debris can collect in the fleshy wen hood of orandas, sometimes causing disease, so it is especially important to maintain extra clean water for such goldfish varieties. This fish is not particularly fussy about pH or hardness as long as its aquarium is well-maintained and stable. Like all goldfish, orandas are not schooling fish per se, but they are very social and appreciate the company of other goldfish. The Blue Oranda Goldfish constantly searches for food at all levels of the aquarium. It will uproot and pick at plants, so it is not a good candidate for the heavily planted aquarium. Any plants kept with it must be relatively rigid and able to withstand the oranda’s constant grazing. The Blue Oranda Goldfish will also pick at anything else that it might consider potential food, so it should not be kept with most invertebrates. In fact, there are very few non-goldfish species that make good tankmates for goldfish due to the feeding habits and exceptionally high waste production of all goldfish. Feeding is very simple for the omnivorous Blue Oranda Goldfish. However, protein content should only make up about one-third of its diet. It should be fed a varied diet of high-quality dry foods that are specifically designed for goldfish, and it will also appreciate some fresh vegetable matter. Care must be taken not to overfeed goldfish since they will eat any and all food that is present, even to the point of internal injury. listings.commonName: Pingu Guppy (Poecilia reticulata var. “Pingu”), Males and Females, Tank-Bred!
listings.description: Species Overview The Pingu Guppy is a beautiful selectively bred guppy variety that combines shimmering metallic blue coloration with bright yellow finnage to create one of the most eye-catching color combinations available in the freshwater aquarium hobby. The contrast between the iridescent blue shoulder, silver-white body, and vibrant yellow tail gives this strain a clean, elegant appearance that immediately stands out in planted aquariums and community displays. Unlike heavily patterned guppy strains that rely on intricate markings, the beauty of the Pingu Guppy comes from its simplicity and contrast. As these fish move through the aquarium, light reflects from the metallic blue scales while the bright yellow finnage creates flashes of color among the plants and hardscape. Mature males display the most intense coloration, while females exhibit a more subtle appearance and are essential for hobbyists interested in breeding projects. One of the most exciting aspects of this strain is the availability of both regular and ribbon-fin forms. Regular Pingu Guppies display the classic guppy profile and finnage that hobbyists have enjoyed for generations. Ribbon Pingu Guppies develop elongated fin rays that create a more flowing and dramatic appearance, adding an entirely different visual dimension to the fish. Whether selecting regular fish, ribbon fish, or breeding pairs, hobbyists can choose the option that best fits their aquarium goals. Like most guppy varieties, Pingu Guppies are peaceful, active, and highly adaptable community fish. Their constant movement brings life and energy to the aquarium while their distinctive coloration provides a focal point among plants, driftwood, and hardscape. Whether maintained as a showcase fish, part of a larger guppy colony, or within a selective breeding project, the Pingu Guppy offers an outstanding combination of beauty, personality, and ease of care. listings.description: * For the safety of our animals, we now ship live fish exclusively via UPS Next Day Air. If your order contains this item, you will only see UPS Next Day Air as a shipping option during checkout * Overview The L066 King Tiger Pleco (Hypancistrus seideli) is a striking and highly sought-after species from Brazil’s Rio Xingu , famous for its black-and-white striping and elegant, compact form. Unlike most plecos that graze primarily on algae, this species thrives on a protein-based diet and prefers shaded, fast-flowing habitats. A perfect fit for aquarists who enjoy natural river-style aquascapes, this peaceful bottom dweller brings authentic South American character to any aquarium setup. What We Love About This Fish: • Distinctive Patterning: Beautiful black and white banding that varies from fish to fish. • Compact Size: Averages 6 – 8 cm at purchase, making it well-suited to most community tanks. • Peaceful & Reserved: Non-aggressive, ideal for planted aquariums. • True River Behavior: Nocturnal by nature and enjoys resting in caves or under driftwood. Natural Habitat: The L066 King Tiger Pleco originates from the Rio Xingu , a clear and powerful tributary of the Amazon River in northern Brazil. The Xingu’s underwater landscape is a mosaic of rocky outcrops, driftwood branches, and sandy channels , with strong water flow and high oxygen levels. During the wet season , the river floods the forest edge, carrying leaf litter and wood debris that enrich the water with tannins. In the dry season , the current intensifies, and the plecos shelter among rocks and driftwood, where they feed on meaty particles and biofilm. In the aquarium, they remain nocturnal or crepuscular , resting during daylight hours. Providing ample hiding spots —such as caves, tunnels, and driftwood—helps them feel secure and encourages natural behavior. Aquascaping: • Plants: Hardy species such as Anubias , Java Fern , and Amazon Sword that attach easily to rock or wood. • Hardscape: Combine smooth river stones, driftwood, and slate caves to create shaded areas and natural boundaries. • Botanicals: Include Indian Almond Leaves , Casuarina Pods , or Catappa Bark from the Aquatic Arts Botanical Combo Pack to simulate blackwater conditions, add tannins, and promote beneficial biofilm. Diet and Feeding: The L066 King Tiger Pleco is a carnivorous species that benefits from a high-protein diet with minimal plant matter. Feed a combination of: Sinking carnivore pellets or wafers designed for bottom dwellers. Frozen or live foods such as bloodworms, brine shrimp, and blackworms. Occasional blanched vegetables like spinach or peas for dietary variety. Feed primarily after lights-out to align with their natural nocturnal feeding rhythm. While they may nibble on biofilm, they will not clean your tank —regular aquarium maintenance remains essential. Tank Mates and Compatibility: A peaceful species that thrives alongside tetras, rasboras, dwarf cichlids, Corydoras, and shrimp . Avoid large, aggressive, or highly territorial bottom dwellers. When keeping more than one pleco, ensure the tank includes multiple caves and shaded areas to define territory and prevent stress. Shrimp Compatibility: This species is compatible with most freshwater shrimp . Adult shrimp are typically ignored, though tiny fry may be disturbed while the pleco forages. Providing dense plant cover, moss, or leaf litter ensures shrimp colonies remain safe and active. Breeding: Breeding occurs in tight-fitting caves or tubes , where males guard the eggs until hatching. Maintain stable, warm, oxygen-rich water and offer a high-protein diet to promote spawning behavior. Fry feed on biofilm and fine foods like crushed pellets or baby brine shrimp after becoming free-swimming. Recommended Tank Parameters: • Temperature: 78° - 84° F (25° - 29° C) • pH: 6.5 - 7.5 • KH: 2 - 8 dKH • Minimum Tank Size: 30 gallons Care Guidelines: • Diet: Carnivorous; prefers protein-rich foods with occasional vegetable matter. • Social Behavior: Peaceful bottom-dweller; mildly territorial toward similar species. • Activity Level: Primarily nocturnal; prefers dim lighting and shaded cover. • Origin: Wild-caught from the Rio Xingu, Brazil. • Average Adult Size: 10 – 12 cm (4 – 5 inches) • Average Purchase Size: 6 – 8 cm (2.5 – 3 inches) Live Arrival Guarantee: All Aquatic Arts brand animals are covered by our 100% Live Arrival Guarantee , plus free email support from our aquatics experts.

The Lightning Bolt Nerite Snail ( Neritina sp.) is a very rare nerite species that is native to the Philippines and is known for its highly variable zigzag pattern of gold and black coloration. It can live for upwards of 4 years, so it is relatively long-lived among its relatives. Though it inhabits freshwater habitats as an adult, its fry require brackish or marine water to survive, so it will not proliferate in a freshwater aquarium and it is not known to have been bred commercially or otherwise. Most of the nerite snails we offer have very similar care requirements and characteristics, and the Lightning Bolt Nerite Snail is no exception. It inhabits fresh and brackish water areas and cannot reproduce in freshwater. This snail is a very effective algae eater and will thrive in a mature aquarium that has plenty of algae and biofilm growth. Some nerite snails are initially finicky about eating dry foods, but most will come to accept them, especially with foods that are high in spirulina or other plant content. Fresh vegetables are typically accepted as well. Nerite snails are hardy in a mature, stable, well-maintained aquarium, but they are not as hardy as some other snail species in subpar setups. It is important to remember that scavengers such as snails do not consume as much oxygen as most fish, but they still contribute to the bioload of the aquarium and they should not be overstocked long-term. It should also be noted that, while this snail can live in a wide variety of pH levels, it will live for much longer in alkaline water of over 7.0 pH. listings.commonName: Orange Venezuelan Cory Catfish (Corydoras aeneus "Venezuela"), Tank-Bred
listings.description: Species Overview The Orange Venezuelan Cory Catfish ( Corydoras aeneus "Venezuela") is one of the most striking and sought-after Corydoras available to freshwater aquarists. Combining the peaceful personality that has made Bronze Corys a longtime favorite with brilliant orange to copper body coloration and an iridescent blue-green saddle across the back, this beautiful South American catfish brings constant activity and vibrant color to the bottom of the aquarium. At Aquatic Arts, we offer both our classic Tank-Bred Regular Fin Orange Venezuelan Corys and our beautiful Locally Bred Longfin variety. The longfin form features elegantly extended dorsal, pectoral, and caudal fins that flow gracefully as the fish glide across the substrate, while the regular-fin variety closely resembles the natural body shape found in wild populations. Both variants share the same peaceful temperament, hardiness, and fascinating social behavior that make this species one of the best Corydoras for community aquariums. Unlike many bottom-dwelling fish that spend most of their time hiding, Orange Venezuelan Cory Catfish remain active throughout the day. They constantly patrol the aquarium floor in coordinated groups, sifting through sand with their sensitive barbels in search of tiny food particles while occasionally darting to the surface for a quick gulp of atmospheric air—a completely normal behavior unique to Corydoras catfish. Whether you're building your first peaceful community aquarium or adding another beautiful Corydoras species to an established collection, Orange Venezuelan Cory Catfish provide endless activity, gentle personalities, and stunning coloration that continues to improve as they mature in a healthy planted aquarium. What We Love About This Fish Brilliant orange body highlighted by an iridescent blue-green saddle Available in both classic regular-fin and elegant locally bred longfin varieties Constantly active during daylight hours Peaceful community fish that thrives in groups Excellent choice for planted aquariums and nature-inspired aquascapes Hardy, beginner-friendly, and rewarding for experienced hobbyists alike Fun to watch as they forage together across the aquarium floor Quick Care Guide Care Level: Easy Temperament: Peaceful Adult Size: 2.5–3 Inches Diet: Omnivore (Sinking Pellets, Frozen Foods, Live Foods, Repashy) Minimum Tank Size: 20 Gallons Swimming Zone: Bottom Group Size: 6 or More (They are highly social schooling catfish that become more confident, active, and display more natural behaviors when maintained in groups.) Schooling: Yes — Orange Venezuelan Cory Catfish naturally live in groups and rely on companionship for security. Keeping them in schools encourages synchronized foraging, reduces stress, and brings out their most engaging behavior. The Blue Gardner's Killifish ( Fundulopanchax gardneri ) is an extremely colorful, peaceful fish whose small size makes it absolutely perfect for the nano or planted aquarium. Native to stagnant swamps and slow-moving waterways in Nigeria, this colorful fish is excellent for aquariums with very low water flow or, under the correct strict maintenance schedule, no water flow at all. The Blue Gardner's Killifish occupies the top level of the water column almost exclusively. It is not afraid to jump, so it must be kept in an aquarium with either a lid/hood/canopy or at least a significantly lowered water level. It will not eat or bother ornamental plants and it will appreciate the cover, especially with floating plants. The Blue Gardner's Killifish is possibly compatible with other peaceful fish and invertebrate species that thrive in low water flow, but only if those species will not outcompete the Blue Gardner's Killifish for food and are too large to be considered prey for the killifish. Also, other fish species will eat most of the fry of the killifish when spawning occurs, so other tankmate species are not recommended if breeding is desired. While many killifish are kept in pairs, this is not absolutely necessary for the Blue Gardner's Killifish, and some aquarists report the best luck when keeping multiple females per male. The Blue Gardner's Killifish is not a particularly picky eater, though it requires a varied diet of mostly meaty foods supplemented with some algae and microfauna. It is primarily a micropredator and it feeds at the top of the water. It may initially ignore floating dry foods, but will typically accept them. Appropriately sized frozen foods such as Tubifex , Daphnia , and Artemia will usually be accepted, and bloodworms can also be used as long as they are a manageable size. Live foods are the excellent for the Blue Gardner's Killifish, and it will gladly accept fruit flies and live specimens of the aforementioned frozen foods. Narrowleaf Vallisneria should be planted with its crown above the substrate. It will establish strong roots and is unlikely to be uprooted by bottom-dwelling fish.
