Plant Profile Alternanthera Lilacina is a stunning, color-rich variant of the popular Alternanthera reineckii species native to Central and South America. Famous for its striking reddish-purple stems and deep purple-to-ruby leaf undersides, this variety features distinctly narrower and longer leaves than standard AR varieties. When grown under strong lighting and optimal nutrient levels, new leaf shoots produce brilliant pink and red hues that offer an incredible change of pace from traditional green aquascapes, making it an ideal midground or background focal point. *Form Notice: Photos display this plant in both its emersed (above-water) and submerged forms. Depending on nursery availability and seasonality, you may receive this plant in either form. Learn more about what to expect by reading our guide on Emersed vs. Submerged-Grown Aquatic Plants . Key Features & Benefits Striking magenta, purple, and deep ruby leaf undersides deliver rich color contrast in midground and background zones. Narrower, elongated foliage provides a distinct structural silhouette compared to broader Alternanthera varieties. Dense leaves give cover and shelter for dwarf shrimp and timid fish species. Care & Planting Instructions Remove lead weight and cotton wrap (or foam) surrounding the base, then strip the lower inch of foliage so bare stems anchor cleanly into soil without rotting. Use fine-tip pinsettes to push individual stems 1 to 2 inches into soil, spacing them so light reaches lower growth. Provide medium-to-high lighting. Pressurized CO2 injection is highly recommended to yield maximum ruby-purple coloration and prevent stunted leaf growth. See our guide to growing red aquarium plants . Maintain stable water parameters and avoid sudden environmental shifts to prevent leaf melt or stem rotting. Trim stem tops with straight scissors once they reach the desired height to keep growth compact, and replant the trimmings into the substrate to propagate. Read our trimming & propagation guide for details. Quick Facts Listed information should be treated as general guidelines only. Team Buce Plant encourages you to do thorough research to ensure healthy growth! As new growth adapts, the plant will shed its olive-green emersed foliage and sprout soft, deep magenta-purple underwater leaves. Once new shoots develop, trim away old lower growth to encourage dense branching.

With broad leaves and sturdy vertical stems, it’s the kind of resilient species that shrugs at most freshwater conditions. It grows just as happily fully submerged as it does emersed in paludariums and terrariums. *Form Notice: Photos display this plant in both its emersed (above-water) and submerged forms. Depending on nursery availability and seasonality, you may receive this plant in either form. Learn more about what to expect by reading our guide on Emersed vs. Submerged-Grown Aquatic Plants . Key Features & Benefits Fast-growing green stem plant that absorbs excess nutrients to help keep water clear and deter nuisance algae. Highly versatile growth habit makes it equally suitable for submerged aquariums or emersed paludarium setups. Care & Planting Instructions Remove lead weight and cotton wrap (or foam) surrounding the base, then strip the lower inch of foliage so bare stems anchor cleanly into soil without rotting. Use fine-tip pinsettes to push individual stems 1 to 2 inches into substrate, spacing them slightly apart so light reaches lower foliage. Provide moderate-to-high lighting for steady growth, though pressurized CO2 injection will accelerate development and leaf size. Maintain stable water parameters and cooler water temperatures when possible, though the plant adapts easily to tropical aquarium conditions. Trim stem tops with straight scissors once they reach the water surface to encourage new lateral side branches. Read our trimming & propagation guide for details. Oval, slightly reflexed leaves show off an intricate, lattice-like mosaic of brick-red, copper, and orange marbling over a golden-green base, giving it a leaf pattern unlike almost anything else in the hobby. Because it's tough to find commercially, experienced hobbyists chase it down specifically to build an unforgettable centerpiece or midground Dutch street, planting it in dense, well-lit groups where that lattice detail really gets to shine. *Form Notice: Photos display this plant in both its emersed (above-water) and submerged forms. Depending on nursery availability and seasonality, you may receive this plant in either form. Learn more about what to expect by reading our guide on Emersed vs. Submerged-Grown Aquatic Plants . Key Features & Benefits Lattice-like leaf pattern in brick-red, copper, and golden orange. Rare African species with standout leaf architecture for midground zones. Compact growth, ideal for high-contrast focal points and Dutch-style streets. Care & Planting Instructions Remove lead weight (or pot) and cotton wrap (or foam) surrounding the roots, then strip lower foliage so bare stems anchor cleanly into soil without rotting. * Ludwigia stems can be fragile, so handle with care during preparation. Pressurized CO2 injection and regular liquid nutrient dosing, especially iron and micronutrients, are strongly recommended to prevent leaf decay and bring out intense red vein marbling. See our guide to growing red aquarium plants . Maintain stable water parameters and avoid sudden environmental shifts to prevent leaf melt or stem rotting. Trim main stem tops with straight scissors once stems reach the desired height, and replant trimmings directly into substrate to propagate and expand your bush. What makes Java Fern Petite different from regular Java Fern? Java Fern Petite produces much smaller, more compact fronds than standard Java Fern. This dwarf growth habit makes it significantly easier to integrate into small desktop nano tanks, foreground rock crevices, or detailed hardscape features without overwhelming the scale of the layout. 2. Why are there small black spots and tiny leaves growing under my Java Fern Petite leaves? Do not panic; your plant is not diseased! Java Fern reproduces naturally through adventitious plantlets. Small dark bumps (sporangia) form along the undersides of mature leaves, sprouting tiny brown roots and mini green fronds. Once these baby plantlets develop 3–4 leaves, you can gently pop them off the mother leaf and glue them elsewhere in your aquarium. 3. Can I plant Java Fern Petite into substrate? No. Java Fern Petite is an epiphyte that absorbs nutrients directly from the water column through its foliage and fine root network. If you bury its horizontal rhizome beneath aquarium soil, sand, or gravel, the stem will suffocate, rot, and die. Always attach it to rocks or driftwood using aquarium-safe glue or thread. 4. Will fish like cichlids or goldfish eat Java Fern Petite? Generally, no. Java Fern leaves are thick, fibrous, and contain bitter-tasting compounds that deter most plant-eating fish. While aggressive diggers might knock it off hardscape if not glued securely, they rarely consume the foliage.

Plant Profile Helanthium quadricostatus (formerly categorized as Echinodorus quadricostatus), commonly known as the Dwarf Sword, is a fast-growing species native to South America that brings a bright, fresh look to the lower sections of an aquascape. Reaching about 6 inches tall, its thin, light-green foliage forms low rosettes and spreads quickly by sending runner shoots across the substrate. When planted in small clusters, it fills in over time to create a dense, grassy carpet or a bushy midground hedge in smaller setups. It is easygoing, adapts easily to different water conditions, and makes a reliable choice for filling in empty ground space without needing complicated care. Tissue culture cups ensure your aquascape gets a super clean starting point. Lab-grown and fully sterile, it arrives without pests, snails, duckweed, or any unwanted algae. It’s the go-to option for anyone who wants peace of mind when adding fresh greenery to a carefully maintained setup. Key Features & Notes Light-green rosette foliage spreads via runner chains to quickly cover foreground and midground spaces. Fast-growing and hardy plant that fills in gaps easily without demanding complex care regimens. Care & Planting Instructions Prep the plant by carefully removing the plantlets from the cup and rinsing away all sterile nutrient gel under lukewarm, dechlorinated water before mounting. Plant individual clumps deeply into your aquarium soil, making sure the central crown rests just above the substrate line to prevent rot. All Echinodorus and Helanthium species are heavy root feeders; placing root tabs near the base supports steady growth and vibrant leaf color. Provide low to moderate lighting; while CO2 injection isn't strictly required, supplemental CO2 and decent light will encourage faster runner production and denser carpet growth. Maintain stable water parameters to prevent leaf shedding during the initial transition period. Trim spreading runner shoots with sharp aquascaping scissors to control its footprint or replant plantlets elsewhere. Quick Facts Listed information should be treated as general guidelines only. Plant Profile Alternanthera reineckii ' Rosaefolia ', commonly known as Scarlet Temple or AR Rosaefolia, is a classic, highly favored red stem plant originating from South America. Celebrated for its bold, intense magenta-to-scarlet red leaves and distinct white vein-like patterns running along its foliage, this species is a staple focal point in Dutch-style aquascapes and nature aquariums. Densely leafed stem structure creates reliable protective cover and shelter for sensitive dwarf shrimp and shy fish species. Care & Planting Instructions Remove lead weight and cotton wrap (or foam) surrounding the base, then strip the lower inch of foliage so bare stems anchor cleanly into soil without rotting. Use fine-tip pinsettes to push individual stems 1 to 2 inches into substrate, spacing them slightly apart so light reaches lower growth. Provide medium-to-high lighting. Regular dosing of liquid fertilizers like UNS Plant Food and pressurized CO2 injection are highly recommended to yield maximum scarlet coloration and prevent stunted growth. See our guide to growing red aquarium plants . Maintain stable water parameters and avoid sudden environmental shifts to prevent leaf melt or stem rotting. Trim stem tops with straight scissors once they reach the desired height to encourage branching and replant the trimmings directly into the substrate to propagate. Plant Profile Alternanthera Reineckii Rosaefolia Mini, aka AR Rosaefolia Mini, is a compact dwarf cultivar of the popular South American stem plant. Famous for its intense ruby-red, magenta, and deep pink foliage accented by subtle lighter vein patterns along its leaves, this mini variant offers all the high-voltage color of classic AR Rosaefolia in a much more manageable, low-growing form. Reaching a height of 4 to 8 inches, its compact habit makes it a premier choice for foreground carpets, colorful midground borders, and high-contrast Dutch-style plant streets in nano tanks and large aquascapes alike. *Form Notice: Photos display this plant in both its emersed (above-water) and submerged forms. Depending on nursery availability and seasonality, you may receive this plant in either form. Learn more about what to expect by reading our guide on Emersed vs. Submerged-Grown Aquatic Plants . Key Features & Benefits Compact growth, ideal for high-contrast focal points and Dutch-style. Easily pruned into dense, colorful hedges and structured plant streets. Dense, broad-leafed structure shelters shy fish and dwarf shrimp. Care & Planting Instructions Remove lead weight (or pot) and cotton wrap (or foam) surrounding the roots, then strip lower foliage so bare stems anchor cleanly into soil without rotting. Use fine-tip pinsettes to push stems 1–2 inches into soil, spacing them apart for light penetration. Provide medium-to-high lighting. Regular dosing of liquid fertilizers like UNS Plant Food (2–3 times per week) alongside pressurized CO2 injection will prevent leaf dulling and maintain vibrant red coloration. See our guide to growing red aquarium plants . Maintain stable water parameters and avoid sudden environmental shifts to prevent leaf melt or stem rotting. Trim main stem tops with sharp straight scissors once stems reach the desired height, and replant trimmings directly into substrate to propagate and expand your carpet or hedge. Plant Profile Bacopa Salzmannii Purple (aka Bacopa Purple) is a sought-after aquatic stem plant native to the tropical Americas and Southeastern United States. Most Bacopa species stay green, but this one doesn't get the memo! Instead, it produces purple and magenta foliage when grown under optimal aquarium conditions. Featuring rounded, succulent-like leaves set along sturdy vertical stems, it doesn't demand perfect conditions to hold its color (unlike a lot of high-color stem plants), making it a solid pick for beginners. It works well as a midground or foreground focal point, adding dark-purple contrast against greener neighbors in a planted aquascape. *Form Notice: Photos display this plant in both its emersed (above-water) and submerged forms. Depending on nursery availability and seasonality, you may receive this plant in either form. Learn more about what to expect by reading our guide on Emersed vs. Submerged-Grown Aquatic Plants . Key Features & Benefits Deep purple, violet, and magenta leaves deliver uncommon color. Vertical stems and rounded leaves form structured midground terraces through routine pruning and replanting. Hardiness and adaptability make it a rewarding purple choice for both high-tech and modest planted tanks. Use fine-tip pinsettes to push individual stems 1 to 2 inches into substrate, spacing them slightly apart so light reaches lower growth. Provide medium-to-high lighting and consistent liquid or root fertilization; adding pressurized CO2 injection and iron supplementation maximizes its deep purple pigmentation. Maintain stable water parameters and clean water conditions to support fast root attachment and steady growth. Under high-tech aquarium conditions with intense lighting, soft acidic water, and pressurized CO2, it fully commits to the bit, shifting from olive-pink into an intense, saturated crimson-red to deep wine color. Reaching 10+ inches tall, Red Cabomba makes a striking midground centerpiece or a lush, feathery background hedge in high-tech nature aquariums and Dutch-style layouts, no fire extinguisher required. When grown emersed, this plant can produce beautiful purple flowers. *Form Notice: Photos display this plant in both its emersed (above-water) and submerged forms. While its appearance resembles that of a traditional stem plant, it naturally grows in compact, short bushes that create a lush, spreading bush effect in the midground of your aquarium. When grown submerged and kept under proper conditions, its foliage develops a rich reddish-brown to deep pink coloration with a distinct light central vein. *Form Notice: Photos display this plant in both its emersed (above-water) and submerged forms. Slender foliage turns a deep reddish-brown and pink under strong lighting, offering warm color depth and distinct leaf texture. Produces vibrant purple flowers when cultivated in an emersed terrarium or paludarium setups. While CO2 injection is optional, it is strongly recommended to achieve rich reddish-brown coloration and compact growth. See our guide to growing red aquarium plants . Plant Profile Ludwigia Brevipes, commonly known as Long Eames, is a delicate and fast-growing aquatic stem plant native to the coastal boggy wetlands of the Southeastern United States. Bearing a striking resemblance to Ludwigia arcuata , this charming species features long, narrow, needle-like leaves that branch densely along sturdy central stems. Depending on light intensity and nutrient dosing, its foliage transitions from a soft yellow-green to fiery orange and glowing copper-red, especially at the shoot tips. Key Features & Benefits Slender, needle-like foliage displays a vibrant color gradient from soft green to warm orange and copper-red. Fast-growing stem habit easily forms dense, feathery bushes when routinely trimmed. Hardy and adaptable species native to North America, suitable for both submerged aquariums and emersed setups. Care & Planting Instructions Remove lead weight (or pot) and cotton wrap (or foam) surrounding the roots, then strip lower foliage so bare stems anchor cleanly into soil without rotting. * Ludwigia stems and leaves are fragile, so handle stems with care during preparation. Use fine-tip pinsettes to insert individual stems 1 to 2 inches deep into aquarium soil. Provide medium-to-high lighting and clean water conditions; while adaptable without CO2, supplying pressurized CO2 injection and regular liquid fertilization rich in iron yields the deepest orange-red tones. See our guide to growing red aquarium plants . Maintain soft, slightly acidic water parameters and avoid sudden parameter swings to prevent stem melting or leaf shedding. To propagate, trim main stem tops or side shoots with sharp straight shears and replant trimmings directly into substrate. Read our trimming & propagation guide for details. Plant Profile Ludwigia Inclinata 'Twister', also known as Ludwigia Twister or Curly Ludwigia, is a unique stem plant with for its long, slender leaves that grow in a distinctive spiral formation. Its leaves are typically light green, with reddish tips developing near the water's surface under stronger lighting. When grown emersed, this species can also produce small yellow flowers. With its unusual leaf shape and tall growth, Ludwigia Twister makes an excellent addition to the midground or background of an aquarium. It grows quickly under high lighting and CO2 injection, making regular trimming necessary to maintain its shape. Its distinctive appearance adds texture and movement to planted aquariums, especially when used alongside plants with broader leaves. Key Features & Benefits Unique Spiral Leaves: Long, narrow leaves twist as they grow, giving this Ludwigia its distinctive appearance. Color Variation: Light green leaves can develop reddish tips as they reach the water's surface and receive stronger light. Fast-Growing Stem Plant: Quickly fills out the midground or background with its tall, upright growth. See our guide to prepping aquarium plants . Plant stems individually into a quality aquarium substrate, leaving enough space between them for light to reach the lower leaves. Provide high lighting and CO2 injection to encourage healthy, vigorous growth. Maintain stable water parameters and avoid drastic changes to prevent plant melt and rotting. Under medium to high lighting and clean water conditions, it forms tight, feathery green shoots that bring extraordinary visual texture and soft movement to aquascapes. Fast-growing and easily branches when trimmed to build thick, rolling midground bushes. Versatile and decorative species that provides excellent contrast against broad-leaved or red aquatic plants. Use fine-tip pinsettes to insert individual stems 1 inch apart into aquarium soil. Maintain soft, slightly acidic water parameters and avoid sudden parameter shifts to prevent stem melting or leaf shedding. Plant Profile Java Fern Kiat is a rare hybrid variety that combines genetic traits from both Bolbitis and classic Java Fern . Featuring broader, highly textured leaf blades that merge the tough structure of Microsorum with the deep, lush aesthetic of Bolbitis, it reaches 5 to 10 inches in height for a standout midground or background accent. This bulletproof hybrid epiphyte thrives in low to moderate lighting, forgives parameter swings, and is unbothered by curious fish looking for a snack. Key Features & Notes Unique hybrid combination of Bolbitis and Java Fern delivers broad, beautifully textured fronds that elevate midground layouts. Exceptional hardiness lets it thrive in non-CO2 tanks and low-light environments. Care & Planting Instructions Prep the plant by removing it from the pot and clearing all rockwool from the roots . Java Fern Kiat is an epiphytic fern that should be attached to rocks or driftwood with aquarium-safe glue or thread; never bury the horizontal rhizome in substrate, as it will rot and melt. Avoid making drastic changes to your water parameters or lighting because unstable conditions are the primary cause of leaf melt in new specimens. While this plant is hardy and low-maintenance in standard setups, gentle water movement and regular liquid fertilizing will yield much faster growth and broader fronds. Master long-term care and troubleshoot common leaf issues by checking out our Java Fern Care Guide . Final size and foliage pattern depend entirely on your specific aquarium conditions; please note that photos are a representation, and individual plants may vary. What makes Java Fern Kiat different from standard Java Fern? Java Fern Kiat is a unique hybrid cross between Bolbitis heteroclita and Microsorum pteropus. This cross results in broader, robust leaves with a richer, slightly ruffled texture that combines the elegance of Bolbitis with the bulletproof durability of Java Fern. 2. Why are there small black spots and tiny leaves growing under my Java Fern Kiat leaves? Do not panic; your plant is not diseased! Java Fern reproduces naturally through adventitious plantlets. Small dark bumps (sporangia) form along the undersides of mature leaves, sprouting tiny brown roots and mini green fronds. Once these baby plantlets develop 3–4 leaves, you can gently pop them off the mother leaf and glue them elsewhere in your aquarium. 3. Can I plant Java Fern Kiat into substrate? No. Java Fern Kiat is an epiphyte that absorbs nutrients directly from the water column through its foliage and fine root network. If you bury its horizontal rhizome beneath aquarium soil, sand, or gravel, the stem will suffocate, rot, and die. Always attach it to rocks or driftwood using aquarium-safe glue or thread. 4. Will fish like cichlids or goldfish eat Java Fern Kiat? Generally, no. Java Fern leaves are thick, fibrous, and contain bitter-tasting compounds that deter most plant-eating fish. While aggressive diggers might knock it off hardscape if not glued securely, they rarely consume the foliage.

Plant Profile Rotala Macrandra Red, aka Giant Red Rotala, is widely considered one of the most vividly colored and stunning aquatic stem plants in the aquascaping hobby. Native to the warm, soft-water river systems of India, this species features delicate, wavy-edged leaves that grow in opposing pairs along supple stems. Under high-tech aquarium conditions, its foliage displays an exceptionally rich, saturated blood-red to deep magenta coloration. Known for its rapid growth rate of up to 4 inches per week in ideal environments, Rotala Macrandra Red makes a breathtaking focal centerpiece or structured Dutch-style street when contrasted against bright lime-green background plants. *Form Notice: Photos display this plant in both its emersed (above-water) and submerged forms. Depending on nursery availability and seasonality, you may receive this plant in either form. Learn more about what to expect by reading our guide on Emersed vs. Submerged-Grown Aquatic Plants . Key Features & Benefits Displays exceptionally intense, saturated blood-red and magenta foliage for unrivaled visual impact. Delicate wavy-edged leaves add soft texture and high-contrast color depth to midground and background zones. Classic high-tech aquascaping species ideal for creating striking centerpiece accents and Dutch-style plant streets. Care & Planting Instructions Remove lead weight (or pot) and cotton wrap (or foam) surrounding the roots, then strip lower foliage so bare stems anchor cleanly into soil without rotting. * Rotala macrandra stems and leaves are extraordinarily thin and delicate, so handle with extreme care during preparation. Use fine-tip pinsettes to push individual stems 1 to 2 inches into substrate, spacing them slightly apart so light reaches lower foliage and prevents leggy decay. Provide high-intensity lighting and quality aquarium soil; mandatory pressurized CO2 injection alongside elevated phosphates (1.5–2.0 ppm) and lean nitrates (<10 ppm) are essential to prevent leaf stunting and maintain vivid red pigmentation. See our guide to growing red aquarium plants . Maintain stable water parameters and avoid sudden environmental shifts to prevent leaf melt or stem rotting. Trim main stem tops with sharp straight scissors once stems reach the desired height, and replant trimmings directly into substrate to propagate and expand coverage. Read our trimming & propagation guide for details. Quick Facts Listed information should be treated as general guidelines only. Team Buce Plant encourages you to do thorough research to ensure healthy growth! Attribute Specification Scientific Name Rotala macrandra Common Name(s) Rotala Macrandra Red, Giant Red Rotala, Red Rotala Macrandra Family Lythraceae Plant Type / Taxonomy Stem Plant Care Difficulty Difficult / Advanced Light Requirement High (High intensity required to prevent lower leaf loss) CO2 Requirement Required (High CO2 essential for healthy leaf formation) Placement / Usage Midground / Background Centerpiece & Dutch Street Height / Size 4–12”+ Growth Rate Fast (Up to 4” per week under ideal conditions) Water Parameters pH 6.5–7.5 Propagation Method Cuttings (Cut stem and replant tops) Origin Asia (India) Frequently Asked Questions 1. Why are the lower leaves falling off my stem plants? Lower leaf loss (leggy stems) usually occurs when lighting cannot reach the bottom of the plant due to overcrowding or shading from larger plants. Spacing individual stems slightly apart during initial planting and maintaining strong light penetration will keep lower leaves healthy. 2. How do I bring out the bright red color in Rotala Macrandra Red? Achieving deep blood-red coloration on Rotala Macrandra Red requires high-intensity lighting, high levels of injected CO2, soft water, and balanced fertilization. Maintaining elevated phosphate levels (1.5–2.0 ppm) while limiting nitrates (<10 ppm) encourages maximum color saturation and prevents stunted leaf tips. 3. How do I transition Rotala Macrandra Red from emersed to submerged growth? When transitioning from emersed to submerged growth, plant bare stems securely into rich substrate under strong lighting and high CO2 while keeping water parameters stable. As new growth adapts, the plant will shed its stiffer emersed leaves and sprout soft, wavy-edged red underwater foliage. Once new shoots take root, trim away old lower growth to encourage dense branching.

Plant Profile Vallisneria Spiralis 'Leopard', commonly known as Leopard Tape Grass or Leopard Eel Grass, is a striking and robust background rosette plant. While classic Vallisneria spiralis has been a favorite in freshwater aquariums since the mid-19th century across Asia, Africa, and Southern Europe, the 'Leopard' variant is distinguished by its broader, thicker, ribbon-like leaves adorned with dark horizontal leopard spots and subtle tiger striping. Under moderate-to-high lighting and consistent nutrient dosing, especially iron, the leaves can display vibrant orange, copper, and reddish highlights. Growing tall and swaying gracefully in filter currents, Vallisneria Spiralis Leopard is ideal for creating dense, natural aquatic backdrops in medium to large aquariums. Key Features & Benefits Ribbon-like leaves with leopard spots and tiger stripes for unique texture. Orange, copper, and red highlights under high light and iron dosing. Fast-growing background rosette that spreads via runners to form lush forests. Care & Planting Instructions Remove lead weight and cotton wrap surrounding the root crown, taking care not to crush or damage the roots. Use fine-tip pinsettes to anchor the roots securely into substrate, ensuring the root crown remains slightly elevated above the soil line to prevent crown rot. Provide moderate-to-high lighting and consistent substrate fertilization; supplemental iron dosing enhances its signature leopard patterning and orange-red foliage tones. See our guide to growing red aquarium plants . Maintain stable water parameters and avoid sudden environmental shifts to prevent leaf melting. Prune oversized leaves near the crown with sharp aquatic scissors, and trim or separate lateral runners to manage spreading across the aquarium floor. Quick Facts Listed information should be treated as general guidelines only. Team Buce Plant encourages you to do thorough research to ensure healthy growth! Attribute Specification Scientific Name Vallisneria spiralis 'Leopard' Common Name(s) Vallisneria Spiralis Leopard, Leopard Tape Grass, Leopard Eel Grass Family Hydrocharitaceae Plant Type / Taxonomy Rosette / Runner Plant Care Difficulty Moderate Light Requirement Moderate to High CO2 Requirement Recommended (Optional for standard growth) Placement / Usage Background / Side Wall Backdrop Height / Size 8–12”+ (Can grow taller in high-tech setups) Growth Rate Fast Water Parameters pH 6.0–7.5 Propagation Method Runners (Separate lateral plantlets along runners) Origin Cultivar / Asia, Africa, Southern Europe Frequently Asked Questions 1. How do I plant Vallisneria Spiralis Leopard so it doesn't rot? When planting Vallisneria, it is critical not to bury the central root crown below the substrate line. Push the roots firmly into the substrate, then gently pull the plant upward until the base of the leaves where they meet the crown is fully exposed above the soil surface. 2. How do I bring out the leopard spots and red coloration on Vallisneria Leopard? While Vallisneria Leopard will stay greenish-brown under basic lighting, providing high light intensity, pressurized CO2, and regular micronutrient dosing, especially liquid iron, will significantly intensify the leaf spot contrast and bring out rich orange and red leaf highlights. 3. Can I trim the leaves of Vallisneria if they grow too tall for my aquarium? Yes, you can trim individual leaves to the desired height using sharp aquatic scissors. However, because cut Vallisneria leaf tips can occasionally fray or melt back, the cleanest way to prune the plant long-term is to clip entire older leaves at the root crown or separate and remove lateral runners.

Plant Profile Lobelia Cardinalis Red, commonly known as the Red Cardinal Plant, is an aquatic stem species native to marshlands, riverbanks, and waterways across North America. In submerged aquarium conditions, it produces sturdy vertical stems lined with rounded, light-to-medium green leaves. As the plant grows taller toward the water surface or under higher light levels, the undersides and margins of the foliage develop purple and deep red coloration. Reaching a height of up to 12 inches, its columnar growth makes it a popular choice for structured midground rows, Dutch-style streets, and background placements. Growing well in basic setups without required CO2, it serves as a beginner-friendly and low-tech plant option for aquascapers adding structure to a planted tank. Key Features & Benefits Columnar stem provides structured vertical lines and Dutch-style plant street layouts. Submerged foliage transitions from bright green to purple and red undertones under moderate to high light. Hardy North American marsh species that adapts well to a range of low-tech and high-tech aquarium setups. Care & Planting Instructions Gently remove the plant from its lead bunch wrap or potted container, carefully inspecting the lower stem bases under room-temperature water. Use fine-tip pinsettes to insert individual stems 1 inch apart into your aquarium soil to allow light to reach lower leaves. Provide medium to high lighting; while CO2 injection is not required, supplying pressurized CO2 and regular liquid iron supplementation helps intensify the red and purple leaf hues. See our guide to growing red aquarium plants . Maintain stable water parameters to avoid leaf melting or stem deterioration during the transition period. To propagate, trim main stem tops or side shoots with sharp straight shears and replant the cuttings directly into your aquarium soil. Read our trimming & propagation guide for details. How do I prep bunched Lobelia Cardinalis Red before planting? Remove the lead weight, rubber band, or foam wrapping surrounding the lower stems under room-temperature water. How do I bring out the red and purple colors on Lobelia Cardinalis Red? While submerged leaves remain green under basic lighting, providing moderate to high light intensity, pressurized CO2, and regular iron supplementation will encourage deep red and purple undertones on the foliage. 3. How is Lobelia Cardinalis Red used in Dutch-style aquascapes? Because Lobelia Cardinalis Red grows in structured, upright columns, aquascapers frequently plant stems at stepped heights in a diagonal row, creating a clean "Dutch plant street" that provides depth across the aquarium floor.

Plant Profile Pogostemon Sampsonii is a unique and attention-grabbing aquatic stem plant native to the tropical waterways of Thailand. Featuring narrow, spiky leaves that radiate outwards from rigid central stems in symmetrical whorls, it presents a distinct starburst texture that stands out in any aquascape layout. When grown in dense groups, it creates an eye-catching background or midground bush with fine visual depth. Moderate to fast-growing under high-tech aquarium conditions, Pogostemon Sampsonii responds exceptionally well to routine pruning, branching aggressively to form thick, lush hedges. Key Features & Benefits Pointed, spiky foliage creates an attention-grabbing starburst texture in background and midground zones. Fast-branching stem habit easily forms dense, bushy hedges when routinely trimmed. Versatile stem species that provides excellent contrast against broad-leaved green and red aquatic plants. Care & Planting Instructions Remove lead weight and cotton wrap (or foam) surrounding the base, then strip the lower inch of foliage so bare stems anchor cleanly into soil without rotting. Use fine-tip pinsettes to insert individual stems 1 to 2 inches deep into aquarium soil. Provide medium-to-high lighting and pressurized CO2 injection; consistent liquid fertilization with essential macro and micro nutrients yields robust stem growth and prevents lower leaf loss. Maintain stable water parameters and avoid sudden parameter swings to prevent leaf melting or stem rot. To propagate, simply trim main stems with sharp straight shears and replant the trimmings directly into the substrate; two new shoots will sprout from the cut site on the original stem. Read our trimming & propagation guide for details. Quick Facts Listed information should be treated as general guidelines only. Team Buce Plant encourages you to do thorough research to ensure healthy growth! Attribute Specification Scientific Name Pogostemon sampsonii Common Name(s) Pogostemon Sampsonii Family Lamiaceae Plant Type / Taxonomy Stem Plant Care Difficulty Medium Light Requirement Medium to High CO2 Requirement Recommended (Promotes dense whorls and faster branching) Placement / Usage Midground / Background Bushing Height / Size 4–10”+ Growth Rate Moderate to Fast Water Parameters pH 6.0–7.5 Propagation Method Cuttings (Trim stems anywhere along the internode and replant) Origin Thailand Frequently Asked Questions 1. How do I transition Pogostemon Sampsonii from emersed to submerged growth? When transitioning from emersed to submerged growth, plant bare stems securely into rich substrate under medium-to-high lighting and keep water parameters stable. As new growth adapts, the plant will shed its broader land leaves and sprout slender, greenish-yellow underwater foliage. Once new shoots develop, trim away old lower growth to encourage dense branching. 2. How do I get Pogostemon Sampsonii to grow into a thick, bushy hedge? Routine topping is key. When you trim the main stem, two or more new lateral shoots will branch out right below the cut site, effectively doubling stem density and forming a dense foliage bush over time. 3. Does Pogostemon Sampsonii require CO2 injection? While Pogostemon Sampsonii can survive in moderate-light, low-tech setups, pressurized CO2 injection along with nutrient-rich aquasoil yields significantly tighter leaf whorls, richer green coloration, and much faster branching after pruning.

listings.commonName: Pogostemon Helferi 'Downoi' Aquatic Farmer Tissue Culture
listings.description: Plant Profile Pogostemon Helferi, also known as Downoi (Thai for "Little Star"), is an iconic and uniquely textured aquatic plant native to the sunlit, calcium-rich riverbeds and wetlands of Thailand. Instantly recognizable by its rosette-forming growth habit and crinkled, wavy-edged foliage, this species resembles a sea anemone or miniature palm tree underwater. Growing to a compact height of just 2 to 3 inches, Downoi serves as an extraordinary accent for foreground carpets, midground transitions, or focal points around hardscape bases in both small nano tanks and large display aquascapes. Tissue Culture cups ensure your aquascape gets a super clean starting point. Lab‑grown and fully sterile, it arrives without pests, snails, duckweed, or any unwanted algae. It’s the go‑to option for anyone who wants peace of mind when adding fresh greenery to a carefully maintained setup. Key Features & Benefits Unique crinkled, wavy-edged rosette foliage provides an eye-catching, starburst texture unlike any other foreground plant. Compact, low-growing habit forms dense, bushy green clusters perfect for foreground carpets and midground accents. Care & Planting Instructions Thoroughly wash away the nutrient gel from the roots with your fingers before parting it out into manageable portions. Use fine-tip pinsettes to plant small clusters 1 inch apart into aquarium soil. Provide medium-to-high lighting and clean water conditions; while adaptable without CO2, supplying pressurized CO2 injection promotes substantially thicker foliage and faster side-shoot development. Maintain stable water parameters and avoid sudden parameter swings to prevent leaf melt. Propagate as the plant matures by carefully cutting developed side shoots along with their root structures and replanting them into substrate. Read our trimming & propagation guide for details. Quick Facts Listed information should be treated as general guidelines only. Team Buce Plant encourages you to do thorough research to ensure healthy growth! Attribute Specification Scientific Name Pogostemon helferi Common Name(s) Downoi, Pogostemon Helferi, Little Star Family Lamiaceae Plant Type / Taxonomy Rosette / Stem Plant Care Difficulty Medium Light Requirement Medium to High CO2 Requirement Recommended (Promotes dense rosettes and vigorous side shoots) Placement / Usage Foreground Carpet / Midground Accent Height / Size 2–3” (Cup portion size: 2–3”) Growth Rate Moderate Water Parameters pH 6.0–7.5 Propagation Method Side Shoots (Cut mature side shoots with roots and replant) Origin Thailand Frequently Asked Questions 1. Why are the leaves on my Downoi melting or turning yellow? Downoi can be sensitive to sudden parameter shifts or insufficient lighting. Ensuring stable water conditions, adequate light penetration, and a nutrient-rich substrate supplying micronutrients like iron will prevent leaf melt and keep rosettes crisp and green. 2. Can I grow Pogostemon Helferi 'Downoi' without CO2 injection? Yes, Downoi can be grown in low-tech setups provided moderate-to-high lighting and a rich aquasoil are available. However, adding pressurized CO2 yields much tighter rosettes, brighter coloration, and faster side-shoot propagation. 3. How do I prepare Pogostemon Helferi 'Downoi' Tissue Culture before planting? Carefully remove the gel from the roots by washing the plant in a bowl of room-temperature water or gently rinsing it under a tap. Once the gel is removed, separate the cluster into smaller clumps or individual rosettes and plant them into substrate using fine pinsettes.

Plant Profile Potamogeton gayi, commonly known as Pondweed, is a delicate stem plant native to the river basins of southern South America. It features thin, translucent, ribbon-like leaves that flow effortlessly in filter currents, creating a soft, natural texture in the water column. Depending on light intensity, its foliage ranges from olive green to warm coppery-orange and reddish-brown. It spreads continuously by sending subterranean runner stolons through the substrate alongside vertical stem shoots. Fast-growing and highly adaptable, it fills out midground or background zones quickly and provides a fine-textured contrast against broad-leaved species. Key Features & Notes Thin ribbon leaves shift from olive green to coppery brown under decent lighting. Hardy and adaptable species that handles a wide range of water hardness and low-tech parameters. Care & Planting Instructions Prep the plant by removing it from the pot and clearing all rockwool from the roots. Plant individual stems into your aquarium soil using fine-tipped tweezers, spacing stems slightly apart to allow light penetration to lower leaves. Provide moderate to high lighting; higher light levels encourage richer coppery-brown leaf coloration. Supplemental CO2 injection speeds up growth density, though it grows reliably in low-tech setups without pressurized CO2. Prune vertical stems frequently with sharp aquascaping scissors to control bushiness and prevent overshading neighboring plants. Propagate easily by taking stem tip cuttings or trimming lateral runner shoots and replanting them into the substrate. Quick Facts Listed information should be treated as general guidelines only. Team Buce Plant encourages you to do thorough research to ensure healthy growth! Attribute Specification Scientific Name Potamogeton gayi Common Name(s) Pondweed, Gay's Pondweed Family Potamogetonaceae Plant Type / Taxonomy Stem / Stoloniferous plant Care Difficulty Easy Light Requirement Moderate to High CO2 Requirement Low to Medium (Grows well in low-tech setups; CO2 increases density) Placement / Usage Midground / Background Height / Size 5–12 inches Growth Rate Fast Water Parameters pH 6.0–8.0 Propagation Method Stem cuttings and runner division Origin Southern South America Frequently Asked Questions 1. How do I get Potamogeton gayi to show coppery-red colors? Providing moderate-to-high light intensity directly over the stems, along with balanced micronutrient dosing, encourages the thin leaf blades to transition from green to warm orange and coppery-brown tones. 2. How fast does Potamogeton gayi spread in the tank? It is a fast grower that sends underground runner stolons out in all directions while growing vertical stems. Regular pruning keeps it from overtaking neighboring slow-growing species. 3. Can Potamogeton gayi grow in low-tech aquariums without CO2? Yes, it is very hardy and adapts well to low-tech tanks without pressurized CO2. It will grow steadily in standard aquarium lighting, though growth will be more compact with CO2 injection.

Common Name: Staurogyne sp Bihar Staurogyne Sp. Bihar is a relatively rare find within the worldwide aquarium hobby, especially with its limited availability in European counties. This aquatic plant was originally identified as a Hygrophila species, but upon seeing its flowering abilities, it was reidentified as a Staurogyne species. When grown submerged, t his aquatic plant is said to resemble the popular favorite, Hygrophila Pinnatifida. It boasts beautiful color varieties from deep green to reddish brown. If you enjoy lush aquatic vegetation and want something different than your average Hygrophila species this would be an excellent addition to your planted tank. Family Name: Acanthaceae Origin: India Height: 2-6” pH: 6-7.5 Care: Medium Light: Medium to High Co2: Recommended Propagation: Cut new growth along with roots Growth rate: Moderate

Plant Profile Staurogyne sp. Porto Velho is a distinctive, creeping foreground and midground aquatic plant native to South America. Known for its narrow, lanceolate leaves and low-growing, carpeting habit, this species develops lush olive-green foliage that often displays a subtle grayish-purple to silvery-pink sheen under strong lighting. Slightly more demanding than the popular Staurogyne repens , Staurogyne sp. Porto Velho is highly favored by experienced aquascapers for creating dense, carpeted lawns, terraced slopes, or transitional ground cover in high-tech aquariums, paludariums, and vivariums. *Form Notice: Photos display this plant in both its emersed (above-water) and submerged forms. Depending on nursery availability and seasonality, you may receive this plant in either form. Learn more about what to expect by reading our guide on Emersed vs. Submerged-Grown Aquatic Plants . Key Features & Benefits Creeping habit forms dense foreground lawns and midground slopes. Leaves show a grayish-purple sheen under high-intensity light and tuned fertilization. Thrives submerged in planted tanks or emersed in paludariums and terrariums. Care & Planting Instructions Prep the plant by removing it from the pot and clearing all rockwool from the roots. Use fine-tip pinsettes to plant individual stem cuttings 1 to 2 inches into substrate, spacing them 1 inch apart to encourage horizontal runner development. Provide medium-to-high lighting; pressurized CO2 injection is highly recommended to encourage low, creeping growth and bring out its subtle purplish highlights. See our guide to growing red aquarium plants . Maintain stable water parameters (acidic to neutral pH 5.0–7.0 preferred) and avoid sudden parameter swings to prevent leaf melt. Trim vertical stems tops with curved scissors to force lateral shoot spreading, and replant trimmings with roots to propagate. Read our trimming & propagation guide for details. Quick Facts Listed information should be treated as general guidelines only. Team Buce Plant encourages you to do thorough research to ensure healthy growth! Porto Velho Family Acanthaceae Plant Type / Taxonomy Carpeting Stem Plant Care Difficulty Medium / Advanced Light Requirement Medium to High CO2 Requirement Recommended (Essential for low, spreading carpet) Placement / Usage Foreground Carpet / Midground Transition Height / Size 2–6” Growth Rate Moderate Water Parameters pH 5.0–7.0 Propagation Method Cuttings (Cut vertical shoots and replant) Origin South America (Brazil) Frequently Asked Questions 1. How does Staurogyne sp. Porto Velho differ from Staurogyne Repens? Staurogyne sp. Porto Velho features narrower, more elongated leaves and grows in a lower, more creeping horizontal carpet compared to Staurogyne repens , which has broader oval leaves and grows slightly taller and bushier. Porto Velho also develops a unique purplish sheen under strong light. 2. How do I keep Staurogyne sp. Porto Velho growing low as a carpet? To encourage low, horizontal carpeting rather than tall vertical growth, provide high light intensity, pressurized CO2, and routinely trim off any shoots that reach upward. Trimming forces the plant to send out side shoots along the substrate. 3. How do I transition Staurogyne sp. Porto Velho from emersed to submerged growth? When transitioning from emersed to submerged growth, plant individual stem clusters securely into nutrient-rich soil under strong lighting and pressurized CO2 while maintaining stable water parameters. As new growth adapts, the plant will shed its stiffer emersed foliage and sprout soft, narrow underwater leaves with a purplish tint. Once new runners develop, trim away old lower growth to maintain a tight carpet.

Plant Profile Tonina Fluviatilis is a rare, highly sought-after aquatic stem plant native to the tropical wetlands and rivers of Central and South America, prized for whorls of bright green, starburst foliage that radiate along sturdy vertical stems like miniature underwater palm trees. It's a collector's species for experienced hobbyists running high-tech setups, demanding soft, acidic water, rich aquasoil, high lighting, and pressurized CO2. Positioned as a midground or background centerpiece in Dutch-style aquascapes, its crisp green tone makes an extraordinary visual accent. Key Features & Benefits Distinctive starburst palm-like foliage adds unique texture and decorative character to high-tech aquascapes. Rare collector stem species highly prized for Dutch-style layouts and detailed midground plant streets. Care & Planting Instructions Remove lead weight and remove cotton wrap (or foam) surrounding the base, then strip the lower inch of foliage so bare stems anchor cleanly into soil without rotting. Use fine-tip pinsettes to plant small stem clusters 1 inch apart into aquarium soil substrate. Provide high-intensity lighting and pressurized CO2 injection; maintain soft water conditions and consistent dosing of iron and micronutrients (ensuring nitrate and phosphate levels never drop to zero). Maintain stable water parameters and avoid sudden parameter swings to prevent stem melting or rotting. To propagate, trim offshoots about 2 inches in length and replant them directly into substrate, which prevents aerial root growth and maintains clean stem aesthetics. Quick Facts Listed information should be treated as general guidelines only. Team Buce Plant encourages you to do thorough research to ensure healthy growth! Attribute Specification Scientific Name Tonina fluviatilis Common Name(s) Tonina Fluviatilis, Tonina Family Eriocaulaceae Plant Type / Taxonomy Stem Plant Care Difficulty Advanced / Expert Light Requirement High CO2 Requirement Required (Essential in soft acidic water) Placement / Usage Midground / Background Centerpiece & Dutch Streets Height / Size 1–4”+ Growth Rate Slow to Moderate Water Parameters pH 5.0–6.8 (Soft acidic water required) Propagation Method Cuttings (Cut offshoots approx. 2” long and replant) Origin Central & South America, West Indies, Mexico Frequently Asked Questions 1. Why is Tonina Fluviatilis considered a difficult plant? Tonina Fluviatilis requires very specific water chemistry to thrive, including soft acidic water, nutrient-rich soil substrate, high light intensity, and consistent pressurized CO2 injection along with steady iron and micronutrient dosing. 2. How do I propagate Tonina Fluviatilis without causing aerial roots? To propagate Tonina Fluviatilis, snip lateral offshoots or main stem tops once they reach a healthy length. Keep your cuttings no longer than 2 inches in length when replanting into substrate; longer stem cuttings tend to sprout unsightly aerial roots along the sides instead of growing clean, upright starburst stems. 3. Why is my Tonina Fluviatilis melting or turning yellow after planting? Tonina Fluviatilis is extremely sensitive to hard water (high GH/KH) and sudden parameter swings. It requires soft, acidic water (pH 5.0–6.8) and a nutrient-rich aquasoil substrate. If introduced to a high-pH or hard-water tank, stems can melt quickly. Ensure stable soft-water parameters, strong lighting, and rich iron dosing to help the plant establish.

listings.commonName: Rotala Rotundifolia PLATINUM Aquatic Farmer Tissue Culture
listings.description: Common Name: Rotala Rotundifolia Rotala Rotundifolia Platinum is an extremely rare variant of the well known and favorite Rotala stem plant. This all-white aquatic plant is a rare mutation that occurs in the generally green or red variants of Rotala Rotundifolia. Propagation is like any other aquatic stem plant, simply cut anywhere along the stem and replace it. This plant grows relatively fast so frequent pruning is recommended to keep it growing thick and prevent the bottom leaves from getting starved off of lighting. Notes: Rotala has fragile leaves! Be sure to handle with care. Final coloration is ultimately dependent upon the conditions this plant is kept in. This is a live plant meaning size, shape and color may vary. Do not make drastic changes to the aquarium. Unstable parameters will result in melt and rotting of the aquarium plant. Tissue culture plants are grown in vitro from a state of the art laboratory specialized in propagating aquatic plants. They provide the best option for those who want to ensure that absolutely zero unwanted pests are introduced into the aquarium. Remove tissue culture gel before planting. Simply wash the gel away or soak the plant in water and squeeze the gel off with your fingers. For instructions on how to properly plant tissue culture aquarium plants, click here . CO2 injection and quality aquarium soil will yield better growth. Please research appropriately to ensure your plant thrives. Family Name: Lythraceae Origin: Southeast Asia Height: 4-8” pH: 6.5-7.5 Care: Easy Light: High Co2: 20-30ppm Propagation: Cuttings Growth Rate: Fast

listings.commonName: Lilaeopsis Brasilensis Aquatic Farmer Tissue Culture
listings.description: Plant Profile Common Name: Micro Sword, Lilaeopsis Brasiliensis Lilaeopsis brasiliensis, also known as Micro Sword, is a go‑to pick for aquascapers wanting to recreate a realistic, classic grass lawn look underwater. With its short stems and pale green, blade‑like leaves, this aquarium carpeting plant sends out a web of runners that knit together across the foreground, turning your tank into a neat little yard. It’s a super versatile plant that brings a fresh, tidy texture to any layout, making it a long‑time favorite in both traditional and nature‑style scapes. Tissue Culture cups ensure your aquascape gets a super clean starting point. Lab‑grown and fully sterile, it arrives without pests, snails, duckweed, or any unwanted algae. It’s the go‑to option for anyone who wants peace of mind when adding fresh greenery to a carefully maintained setup. Key Features & Benefits Short, pale green, blade-like foliage forms a realistic, turf-style lawn. Subterranean runners interlock across an open substrate to form a tight, dense mat. Resilient species capable of tolerating mild salinity in low-brackish aquariums. Care & Planting Instructions Thoroughly wash away the nutrient gel from the roots with your fingers before parting it out into manageable portions and planting. Plant the tissue culture in small clumps spaced roughly 1.5 to 2 inches apart to give the runners room to spread and fuse into a seamless carpet. Use a dry start method or Wabi Kusa setup to give its root system plenty of time to firmly anchor into the substrate before you flood the tank. Provide medium to high lighting and ensure it receives direct light without shading from taller neighboring plants to maintain a compact, low profile. Provide nutrient-rich aquarium soil and supplement with pressurized CO2 to drastically accelerate its runner expansion and carpet density. Maintain stable aquarium parameters and avoid drastic shifts in water quality to prevent your new grass from melting. Master the basics by learning how to properly grow aquarium carpet plants to ensure your new layout fills in quickly, evenly, and stays free of algae. Quick Facts Listed information should be treated as general guidelines only. Team Buce Plant encourages you to do thorough research to ensure healthy growth! Attribute Specification Scientific Name Lilaeopsis brasiliensis Common Name(s) Micro Sword, Lilaeopsis Brasiliensis Family Apiaceae Plant Type / Taxonomy Rosette / Carpeting Foreground Care Difficulty Medium Light Requirement Medium to High CO2 Requirement Recommended (Speeds up runner formation) Placement / Usage Foreground Carpet Height / Size 1-2 inches Growth Rate Medium Water Parameters pH 6.0 – 7.5 | Temperature 68°F – 80°F (20°C – 27°C) Propagation Method Separate runners or split dense clumps Origin Southeastern South America Frequently Asked Questions 1. How do I plant Micro Sword tissue culture? Use fine tweezers to plant them about 1.5 inches apart into substrate. 2. Does Micro Sword require CO2 to form a lawn? While Micro Sword can grow without CO2, it spreads relatively slowly in low-tech tanks. Adding pressurized CO2 paired with strong lighting and nutrient-dense soil drastically increases the speed and density of its subterranean runners. 3. Why is my Micro Sword growing tall instead of spreading out? When Micro Sword receives insufficient light, its blades reach upward toward the water surface to capture light energy. Increasing light intensity will force new leaves to stay short and encourage the plant to send out horizontal runners along the substrate.

Plant Profile If you want to fast-track your way to a stunning green floor without the tedious wait, this pre-attached Christmas Moss on Stainless Steel is ready to lay down some serious groundwork. We have grown this iconic, tree-like favorite directly onto a 3" x 3" metal pad, giving you a lush, instant carpet that behaves perfectly and stays exactly where you put it. Plant Profile Echinodorus 'Reni' is a dwarf red sword cultivar known for being one of the most compact red species in the Echinodorus family. Reaching between 6 and 15 inches tall, it fits comfortably into midground zones or compact background layouts where larger sword varieties might quickly outgrow their space. Under moderate to high lighting, its foliage undergoes a dramatic color transformation, producing vibrant young leaves in shades of deep wine red and reddish-brown that mature into rich olive green with distinct dark reddish veins. Naturally hardy and undemanding, it offers aquascapers a striking contrast of deep red coloration without requiring high-maintenance care, securing its place as an accessible favorite among aquarium plants for beginners. Key Features & Notes Compact growth habit allows it to fit seamlessly into midground or smaller background zones. Striking foliage transitions from deep wine red and reddish-bronze on new growth to rich olive green as it matures. A hardy and adaptable species that delivers bold color contrast without requiring complex care regimens. Care & Planting Instructions Prep the plant by removing it from the pot and clearing all rockwool from the roots. Plant the roots deeply into your aquarium soil, keeping the crown of the plant resting just above the substrate line to prevent rot. All Echinodorus are heavy root feeders that rely on rich substrate nutrition; placing root tabs near the base supports steady, healthy leaf development. Provide moderate to high lighting; while CO2 injection isn't strictly required, good lighting will enhance its reddish-brown colors. See our guide to growing red aquarium plants. See our guide to growing red aquarium plants . Maintain stable water parameters to prevent leaf shedding during the initial transition period. Final size and coloration depend entirely on your specific aquarium conditions; please note that photos are a representation, and individual plants may vary. Considered one of the smallest Buce varieties in the planted tank hobby, its petite size makes it especially useful for nano aquascapes and detailed foreground work. Like other epiphytes, it can grow submerged or emersed and prefers to attach its rhizome to driftwood or rock rather than be buried in substrate. Over time, its thin rhizomes slowly spread into compact, shimmering clusters that add plenty of color and detail without taking up much room. Key Features & Notes Under stable conditions and proper lighting, the tiny leaves develop a spectrum of metallic colors that catch the light beautifully. Its exceptionally small leaf profile makes it the perfect tool for creating a sense of massive scale in nano aquascapes. This is one of the most durable species in the hobby and thrives in shaded areas . It is an ideal choice for planted tanks where other plants might struggle. Care & Planting Instructions Prep the plant by removing it from the pot and clearing all rockwool from the roots . Bucephalandra is an epiphytic plant that should be attached to rocks or driftwood using aquarium-safe glue or thread; never bury the horizontal rhizome in substrate, as this will cause the plant to rot and melt. Avoid making drastic changes to your water parameters or lighting because unstable conditions are the primary cause of leaf melt in new specimens. While this plant is hardy and low-maintenance in standard low-light aquarium plant setups, CO2 injection and regular liquid fertilizing will yield much faster growth and richer iridescence. It is an exquisite choice for the midground or background of freshwater aquascapes, where its impressive 6-inch leaves add dramatic texture and architectural depth within a planted tank. The foliage is notably sturdier to the touch than common species, featuring deep green curves that mimic the appearance of premium Bucephalandra Belindae. While care is similar to other Bornean epiphytes, its rarity makes it best suited for aquarists experienced with slow-growing Araceae species. Plant Profile If you appreciate the bulletproof reliability of classic Anubias Barteri but want a rarer, heavily textured centerpiece, Anubias Gabon (also known as Congo Anubias) is an exceptional addition to planted tanks. This distinct cultivar stands out with rounded leaf blades that taper to a sharp point, crossed by prominent, raised veins that create a deeply ribbed surface. Reaching 4 to 10 inches tall as it matures, this hardy epiphyte attaches its rhizome directly to driftwood or rockwork rather than taking root in substrate, creating a lush midground focal point or background anchor in low-tech aquariums, terrariums, and paludariums. Tissue culture cups ensure your aquascape gets a super clean starting point. Lab-grown and fully sterile, it arrives without pests, snails, duckweed, or any unwanted algae. It’s the go-to option for anyone who wants peace of mind when adding fresh greenery to a carefully maintained setup. Key Features & Benefits Prominent, raised leaf venation creates dramatic tactile texture that stands apart from smooth-leafed Anubias varieties. Adaptable mature height transitions smoothly from a dense midground cluster into a bold background accent. Thick, durable foliage resists grazing from herbivorous fish, snails, and active dwarf shrimp. Care & Planting Instructions Prep the plant by carefully removing the plantlets from the cup and rinsing away all sterile nutrient gel under lukewarm, dechlorinated water. Gently divide into smaller clumps and attach to hardscape using a tiny dot of aquarium-safe glue gel or cotton thread, keeping the horizontal rhizome above the substrate. Maintain stable water parameters during the first few weeks to help the young lab-grown foliage transition smoothly to submerged life. Avoid intense direct light and ensure gentle water circulation to keep slow-growing leaves free of spot algae. CO₂ is optional, though mild injection helps young tissue culture plantlets establish faster and build thicker leaves. Quick Facts Listed information should be treated as general guidelines only. Anubias Gabon has flatter, pointed oval leaves defined by sharp, raised veins running visibly across the leaf blade. 2. How do I attach small tissue culture Anubias Gabon plantlets without damaging them? Rinse off every trace of agar gel first, as leftover gel can cause mold or rot. Use a toothpick to apply a pinpoint drop of cyanoacrylate glue gel onto driftwood or stone, then gently press the base of the young rhizome onto the glue. 3. Do tissue culture Anubias plants need CO₂ to survive? No, Anubias Gabon will adapt and grow in low-tech tanks without CO₂. However, because tissue culture plantlets start small with delicate emersed leaves, gentle CO₂ injection speeds up their transition to submerged life and reduces initial melt.

Plant Profile Selaginella kraussiana, commonly known as African Club Moss or Krauss' Spikemoss, is a terrestrial plant that carpets the floor in dense mats of bright emerald, branching foliage that creeps steadily across damp substrate and knits between low hardscape roots. Its fine, feathery texture softens jagged dark lava rock edges and fills shaded pockets beneath sprawling driftwood where coarser leaves look out of scale. Positioned away from direct heat and harsh light, it spreads reliably to establish a rich living floor alongside other humidity-loving plants in emersed setups. Key Features & Notes Fine-textured creeping foliage weaves a dense, bright green carpet over damp substrate. Durable root network anchors securely and holds up well under active enclosure animals. Spreads readily as a ground layer across humid terrarium and paludarium floors. Care & Planting Instructions Prep the plant by removing it from the pot and gently clearing all packing media from the roots. Spread the rooted runners across a few inches of loose, nutrient-rich tropical substrate so the rootlets have ample depth to dig in and establish. Provide low to medium indirect light; direct rays will quickly scorch the tips, while overly dark corners will cause thin, patchy spreading. Maintain humidity above 70% and keep the soil evenly moist, but ensure good bottom drainage because stagnant, waterlogged soil causes the foliage to turn yellow. Trim back overgrown runners with clean shears to direct growth away from slower-growing neighbors. Final size and carpet density depend entirely on your specific setup conditions; please note that photos are a representation, and individual plants may vary. Selaginella kraussiana are terrestrial plants, and being submerged will result in the death of the plants. Quick Facts Listed information should be treated as general guidelines only. Team Buce Plant encourages you to do thorough research to ensure healthy growth! Yellowing leaves generally indicate overwatering or poor drainage. Ensure excess moisture drains away from the substrate so the root system is not sitting in stagnant mud. 3. How do you propagate Selaginella kraussiana? Clip a healthy section of branching stem with visible rootlets and press it directly onto damp soil or sphagnum moss; it will take root on its own within days under high humidity.

Common Name: Spike Moss Selaginella Wallichi is another species of Selaginella that is similar to African Club Moss but grows much larger in size and in a different style. This particular species grows sporadically and will spread throughout the entire enclosure if left to grow without pruning. Like other terrarium plants, Selaginella Wallichi shouldn't be completely submerged but does love staying moist with good levels of humidity. Soil thickness should be a few inches as Spike Moss will root fairly deep once it takes off. As long as it is kept out of direct lighting and the previous conditions are provided, it is typically forgiving and easy to care for. Spike moss is durable and great for livestock that tends to get rowdy in their enclosures! Notes: This is not an aquarium plant. Submerging it completely will result in the death of this plant. Plant Profile Hemigraphis repanda 'Green', commonly known as Green Dragon's Tongue, is a tropical perennial shrub sporting slender, ribbon-like leaves with deeply crinkled margins and a clean, grass-green coloration. Just like its purple sibling, this green form is a frequent victim of big-box store trickery, masquerading in submerged aquarium tanks where it stubbornly holds its breath for a month before staging a catastrophic underwater melt. Keep it in a warm, humid terrarium where it actually belongs, and its rippled, grassy foliage will reward you with steady growth and occasionally tiny white blossoms. Key Features & Notes Slender, crinkled bright green leaves create a fine-textured, grass-like appearance on the floor. Strictly terrestrial perennial that will turn to mush if you try to plant it underwater. Clean, light-colored foliage stands out nicely against dark hardscape and shadowy corners. Care & Planting Instructions Prep the plant by removing it from the pot and clearing all rockwool from the roots . Tuck the root cluster gently into an airy, moisture-retentive tropical soil blend with plenty of bark and perlite, avoiding dense mixes that stay soggy. Provide medium to bright indirect light; good lighting keeps the rippled foliage compact and encourage small white flowers, but harsh direct rays will scorch the narrow leaf tips. Maintain humidity above 70% while ensuring the substrate drains freely, as sitting in standing, stagnant water will lead to stem melt. Pinch back the growing tips just above a leaf node to keep the stems compact and prevent them from looking stretched or leggy. Final size and leaf density depend entirely on your specific setup conditions; please note that photos are a representation, and individual plants may vary. Hemigraphis repanda Green are terrestrial plants, and being submerged will result in the death of the plants. Quick Facts Listed information should be treated as general guidelines only. listings.description: Plant Profile Selaginella erythropus 'Ruby Red', commonly known as Red Spikemoss or Ruby Red Clubmoss, is a low-growing tropical lycophyte recognized for its distinct two-tone foliage: the upper surfaces of its feathery fronds display a deep forest green, while the stems and leaf undersides are flushed in a rich, ruby-red hue. Because it cannot handle full submersion, it belongs in high-humidity setups where its bicolored fronds break up solid mats of green moss and pop against rugged driftwood branches along the enclosure floor or upper paludarium ledges. Key Features & Notes Two-tone fronds pair deep forest-green upper surfaces with distinct ruby-red undersides and stems. Slow, compact spreading habit creates a colorful understory carpet that stays between 3 and 6 inches tall. Feathery foliage breaks up monochromatic green plantings in enclosed, high-humidity tanks. Care & Planting Instructions Prep the plant by removing it from the pot and clearing all rockwool from the roots. Tuck the root cluster gently into an airy, moisture-retentive tropical substrate blend of bark, sphagnum moss, and perlite across foreground or midground pockets. Provide low to moderate indirect lighting; harsh direct light will fade the deep red tones and burn the delicate fronds. Maintain humidity above 75% at all times, as dry air will quickly cause the feathery frond tips to wither, curl, and crisp. Trim older or browning outer foliage close to the stem base with clean shears to maintain a clean clumping habit. Selaginella erythropus are terrestrial plants, and being submerged will result in the death of the plants. Quick Facts Listed information should be treated as general guidelines only. Team Buce Plant encourages you to do thorough research to ensure healthy growth! Plant Profile Selaginella siamensis Hieron is a compact tropical lycophyte native to the shaded forest floors of Thailand and neighboring regions of Southeast Asia, characterized by small, feathery, glossy leaves that arrange into neat, spreading rosettes. Grown strictly above the waterline, its rich emerald green tone contrasts cleanly against light-colored driftwood and pale stones, serving as a dependable living base along shaded terrarium foreground zones or moist terrestrial ledges in a paludarium. Unlike rambling spikemosses that send wild runners, this species maintains a tight clumping form that stays low and composed as it fills in. Key Features & Notes Glossy, feathery foliage grows in distinct rosette clusters that stay low to the substrate. Native understory habit makes it well suited for shaded lower zones with steady indirect lighting. Clumping growth rate fills out floor beds cleanly without aggressive rambling over hardscape. Care & Planting Instructions Prep the plant by removing it from the pot and clearing all rockwool from the roots. Tuck the root cluster gently into an airy, moisture-retentive tropical substrate blend of bark, sphagnum moss, and perlite across foreground or midground soil pockets. Provide low to moderate indirect light; avoid harsh direct lighting that can scorch delicate leaf tips and fade the green color. Maintain humidity above 75% while ensuring the soil drains freely, as soggy or waterlogged substrate will cause yellowing leaves and crown melt. Prune older outer foliage close to the base with clean shears to maintain tidy clumps and encourage fresh growth. Selaginella siamensis are terrestrial plants, and being submerged will result in the death of the plants. Quick Facts Listed information should be treated as general guidelines only. Plant Profile Selaginella Indonesia, commonly known as Blue Spikemoss or Spring Blue Spikemoss, is a trailing lycophyte featuring delicate scale-like foliage with a distinct blue-green iridescence. A reliable pick for emersed setups, its cool metallic hue stands out cleanly against dark soil, damp lava rock, and deep green mosses across the floor or along the moist shoreline of a paludarium. Although often compared to true mosses or miniature ferns, it is a primitive creeping plant that stays low, rarely topping 3 inches in height while it spreads. Key Features & Notes Delicate scale foliage displays an iridescent blue-green sheen under indirect lighting. Forms a soft groundcover alongside other humidity-loving plants in terrariums or vivariums Prefers high ambient humidity and damp, well-aerated soil to avoid stem dieback. Care & Planting Instructions Prep the plant by removing it from the pot and clearing all rockwool from the roots. Press trailing stem portions gently onto a moist, well-draining tropical substrate mix of bark, sphagnum moss, and perlite across the foreground floor. Provide low to medium indirect light; direct light exposure can scorch the fronds and dry out the tips. Maintain humidity above 75% while ensuring the soil remains aerated and damp; yellowing leaves typically indicate waterlogged, anaerobic soil. Trim wandering stem tips with sharp shears to control spread and encourage denser branching across the ground. Selaginella Indonesia are terrestrial plants, and being submerged will result in the death of the plants. Quick Facts Listed information should be treated as general guidelines only. Team Buce Plant encourages you to do thorough research to ensure healthy growth! Attribute Specification Scientific Name Selaginella sp. 'Indonesia' Common Name(s) Blue Spikemoss, Peacock Spikemoss, Spring Blue Spikemoss Family Selaginellaceae Plant Type Creeping Lycophyte / Spikemoss Care Difficulty Easy Light Requirement Low to Medium (Indirect / Partial Shade) Submersion Suitability Emersed Only (Not for full submersion) Placement / Usage Foreground Carpet, Terrarium Floor, Paludarium Shoreline Height / Size 2"–3" (5–7.5 cm) Growth Rate Moderate to Fast Humidity Requirement High (> 75% RH) Propagation Method Stem Cuttings / Division Origin Southeast Asia (Indonesia) Frequently Asked Questions 1. Can Selaginella Indonesia survive in a closed terrarium? Yes. It thrives in enclosed glass containers where high humidity keeps its fine trailing stems from drying out and crisping. 2. Why are the stems on my Selaginella turning yellow or browning? Yellowing foliage usually points to waterlogged, soggy substrate, while dry brown tips typically indicate intense direct lighting or low ambient humidity. 3. How do you propagate Selaginella Indonesia? Snip a trailing stem cutting with visible root nodes and press it flat against moist sphagnum moss or damp tropical substrate under high humidity until it roots.

Tab K Potassium Potassium Deficiency: Distinct pinholes forming in older foliage or yellowing leaf borders. Promotes photosynthesis; ideal for restoring osmotic balance and plant tissue strength. Tab Fe Iron Iron Deficiency: New leaves lack color, turn white, or red aquatic plants lose rich coloration. Enhances color development; resolves new leaf chlorosis and boosts red plant vibrancy. Tab St. Long Organic Fertilizer Blend Calcium Deficiency: Abnormal, twisted, or stunted new growth tissue. Solid / No CO2 Tab Substrate Carbon & Organic Nutrients Carbon Shortage: Sluggish growth rates in low-tech aquariums without gas injection.
