If a plant consistently produces only green growth, removing fully green shoots can help prevent them from overtaking the more variegated growth. 3. Can Anubias barteri 'King' be used in a paludarium or terrarium? Yes. It can be grown emersed in a humid environment, making it suitable for paludariums and other high-humidity setups.

Plant Profile Helanthium Tenellum Micro is a compact, grass-like carpeting plant with fine green blades that bring a clean, natural look to the foreground of an aquarium. This miniature form stays significantly smaller than standard Helanthium Tenellum , making it especially well-suited for nano aquariums and smaller-scale aquascapes. It spreads through runners and, when provided with a nutrient-rich substrate, can gradually form a dense carpet across the foreground. Tissue Culture cups ensure your aquascape gets a super clean starting point. Lab‑grown and fully sterile, it arrives without pests, snails, and algae. It’s the go‑to option for anyone who wants peace of mind when adding fresh greenery to a carefully maintained setup. Key Features & Benefits Produces short, blade-like leaves suitable for nano aquarium foregrounds. Spreads via underground runners to form a dense carpet. Root-heavy feeder that draws nutrients primarily from the substrate. Care & Planting Instructions Thoroughly wash away the nutrient gel from the roots with your fingers before parting it out into manageable portions and planting. Use a dry start method or Wabi Kusa setup to give its root system plenty of time to firmly anchor into the substrate before you flood the tank. Plant in high-quality, nutrient-dense aquarium soil or use root tabs, as this species relies heavily on root feeding. Maintain stable aquarium parameters and avoid drastic shifts in water quality to prevent your new grass from melting. Provide medium to high lighting and inject pressurized CO2 to maximize its growth speed and encourage tight, horizontal expansion. Master the basics by learning how to properly grow aquarium carpet plants to ensure your new layout fills in quickly, evenly, and stays free of algae. The 'Micro' variant stays much smaller (1–2 inches tall) than standard Helanthium Tenellum (2–3+ inches tall), making it far better suited for precise nano aquascapes where maintaining a tiny visual scale is essential. 2. Does Helanthium Tenellum Micro require aquarium soil? Yes. If planted in inert gravel or sand, root tabs should be added nearby to supply the iron and nutrients required for healthy growth. 3. How do I plant and propagate Helanthium Tenellum Micro tissue culture? Use fine tweezers to plant them 1 inch apart. As the plant establishes, it will naturally send subterranean runners into open areas of substrate.

Plant Profile Rotala Macrandra Green is a classic green cultivar of one of aquascaping's most beloved stem plants. It's known for its soft, wavy leaves and fast growth, with lush light-green coloration that can develop delicate pink to orange tips under high lighting and regular nutrient dosing. This stem plant works well as a background or midground plant, where its fast vertical growth can be trimmed into dense, textured bushes. Green Rotala is considered a demanding plant and performs best in high-tech aquariums with strong lighting and pressurized CO2. Tissue culture aquarium plants are grown in a controlled laboratory environment and arrive free of algae, pests, and other unwanted organisms, making them a convenient option for establishing a clean planted aquarium. Key Features & Benefits Delicate leaves give the plant a soft, textured appearance. Can develop pink to orange tones on newer growth when conditions are well suited to the plant. Responds well to regular trimming, allowing you to shape and maintain a dense group of stems. Tissue culture format provides a clean starting point without algae or common aquarium pests. Individual portions can be planted separately to spread the cup across a larger area of the aquarium. Care & Planting Instructions Remove the plant from the cup and gently wash away all nutrient gel with clean water. Separate the tissue culture into several smaller portions rather than planting the entire clump together. Plant individual portions into nutrient-rich aquarium substrate, spacing them slightly apart so light can reach the lower growth. Rotala Macrandra Green requires high-intensity lighting and pressurized CO2 for healthy growth and leaf development. Maintain stable water parameters and avoid sudden environmental changes to help prevent leaf loss or stunted growth. To encourage pink and orange coloration on the leaf tips, maintain phosphate around 1.5–2.0 ppm with nitrate around 10 ppm or less. Some leaf loss may occur as the plant adjusts to aquarium conditions. New submerged growth should develop as it acclimates. Once established, trim the taller stems to encourage branching and replant healthy cuttings to propagate. Maintain stable water parameters and avoid sudden environmental shifts to prevent leaf melt or stem stunting. Trim stem tops with straight scissors once they reach the water surface to encourage dense side branching, and replant trimmings directly into substrate to propagate. Read our trimming & propagation guide for details. Quick Facts Listed information should be treated as general guidelines only. listings.commonName: UNS Stem Plant Holding System 120 - Triple Decker
listings.description: The UNS Stem Plant Holding System 120 - Triple Decker is a high-capacity solution for growing, organizing, and maintaining large collections of aquatic plants. Featuring three stacked, shallow all-in-one tanks supported by a durable aluminum stand, this system maximizes growing space while keeping plants easily accessible. Each tank features independent filtration, adjustable water flow, and height-adjustable plant trays to accommodate different stem plant sizes. A centralized plumbing system simplifies maintenance by allowing water changes across all three tanks simultaneously, while optional inline CO2 integration supports healthy plant growth. Whether you're maintaining a personal plant collection or simply searching for a functional display, the UNS Triple Decker provides an efficient, organized setup for growing and displaying aquatic plants. Key Features Durable Aluminum Cabinet – Built to last with a sleek, modern design. Streamlined Water Changes Interconnected plumbing allows for simultaneous water changes on all three tanks. Drain and return pipes neatly clamp to the side of the stand. Pre-installed hose barbs connect to standard hoses and drainage lines for a hassle-free experience. Independent Filtration & Plumbing – Each tank operates with its own separate filtration system for optimal water quality. Includes an acrylic baffle tray for filter floss, making waste removal quick and easy. Two Flow Options for Maximum Efficiency: 1. Standard Flow Water flows through filter floss into the back chamber before being returned to the same tank. Adjustable flow direction via top duckbill nozzle or bottom spray bar. Right ball valve allows precise control of flow between the two outflow nozzles. The spray bar helps push debris into the filtration chamber, ensuring a cleaner tank. 2. Flush Option Uses the same pump but reverses the water flow via a three-way ball valve. The left spray bar directs debris into the bulkhead drain on the right for quick cleaning. Simplified Plumbing System – The 3-way valve prevents over-complication and protects the pump from potential damage. CO2 Integration – Easily add an in-line CO2 diffuser into the soft tubing for optimal CO2 dispersion. Adjustable Plant Trays – Included trays are height-adjustable for flexible plant arrangement. Pump Compatibility – Pumps NOT included; recommended model: Sicce Syncra 5.0 per tank. Plant Profile Isoetes Lacustris, commonly known as Lake Quillwort, is an aquatic plant with a grass-like appearance. Rather than growing from traditional stems, it produces a cluster of stiff, dark green, needle-like leaves from a compact base. Its simple, upright growth makes it an interesting choice for natural-style aquascapes, particularly setups designed around cooler water conditions. Key Features & Benefits Grass-Like Appearance: Produces narrow, upright leaves that resemble small tufts of grass or rushes. Compact Rosette Growth: Leaves emerge from a central base, creating a dense, rounded cluster. Dark Green Coloration: Features firm, dark green leaves that provide a natural contrast against lighter plants and hardscape. Unique Plant Structure: Belongs to a group of spore-producing plants. Natural Habitat: Native to cool, clear, nutrient-poor lakes and streams, where it typically grows rooted in gravelly or sandy substrates. Care & Planting Instructions Remove lead weight and cotton wrap (or foam) surrounding the base, then strip lower foliage so bare stems anchor cleanly into soil without rotting. Use fine-tip pinsettes to push individual stems 1 to 2 inches into substrate, spacing them slightly apart so light reaches lower leaves. Moderate to high lighting is recommended to support healthy growth and maintain strong, upright leaf development. Provide consistent lighting without excessive intensity or sudden changes in photoperiod. CO2 supplementation may encourage healthier growth, but it is not necessarily required. Consistent CO2 levels and stable water conditions are more important than frequent fluctuations. Prefers cool water between 41–68°F. It is naturally adapted to cold-water lakes and may struggle in the warmer temperatures commonly found in tropical aquariums. Avoid prolonged exposure to high temperatures. Naturally grows in soft, slightly acidic water with low nutrient availability. Stable water conditions are important, and it generally does best without excessive nutrient buildup. Prefers sandy or fine gravel substrates similar to those found in its natural lake habitats. A nutrient-rich substrate is not essential, as Isoetes lacustris is adapted to nutrient-poor environments. A suitable substrate should allow its roots to anchor securely. Best suited for the midground or background, where its tall, upright leaves can add natural texture and vertical interest. Plant individually or in small groups to create a grass-like appearance without overcrowding surrounding plants. Quick Facts Listed information should be treated as general guidelines only. Team Buce Plant encourages you to do thorough research to ensure healthy growth! Attribute Specification Scientific Name Isoetes lacustris Common Name(s) Lake Quillwort Family Isoetaceae Plant Type / Taxonomy Rosette Care Difficulty Advanced Light Requirement Moderate to High CO2 Requirement Not required Placement / Usage Foreground / Midground Height / Size 4-10”+ Growth Rate Very Slow Water Parameters pH 5.3–7.0 | Temp 41–68°F Propagation Method Spores Origin Northern Europe, Greenland, and Western Siberia Frequently Asked Questions 1. Can Isoetes Lacustris grow in a tropical aquarium? Isoetes lacustris naturally grows in cool-water environments. Most tropical aquariums operate above its preferred temperature range, making them less suitable for long-term growth. 2. Is Isoetes Lacustris a true aquatic plant? Yes, it is a fully submerged aquatic plant that naturally grows underwater in lakes and streams. 3. Does Isoetes Lacustris produce flowers? No, it is a non-flowering plant that reproduces through spores produced in structures near the base of its leaves.

listings.commonName: Java Fern Trident on Coco Fiber Mat
listings.description: Plant Profile Java Fern Trident ( Microsorum pteropus 'Trident') is a popular aquarium fern known for its narrow green leaves that branch into distinctive, multi-pronged tips. Its finely divided leaf shape creates a delicate, textured appearance that adds depth and natural detail to aquarium layouts. With its compact growth and hardy nature, Java Fern Trident is a great way to add texture and greenery to aquarium hardscape, making it a versatile addition to midground layouts. This Java Fern comes with its rhizomes attached to a coco fiber mat, making it easy to incorporate into an aquascape. The mat can be conveniently tied, glued, or wedged into driftwood and rocks to create a natural-looking planted hardscape. Key Features & Notes Distinctive Leaf Shape: Narrow, branching leaves give Java Fern Trident a more delicate, finely textured appearance than traditional Java Fern varieties. Easy Hardscape Placement: The pre-attached coco fiber mat makes it simple to add greenery to driftwood, rocks, and other aquarium surfaces. Natural-Looking Coverage: Multiple plants growing across the mat create a fuller, more established look without having to position individual rhizomes. Beginner-Friendly: Its hardy nature and ability to adapt to a range of aquarium conditions make it a forgiving choice for planted tanks Care & Planting Instructions Prep the plant by rinsing the coco fiber mat gently in clean freshwater to clear any loose debris before placing it directly into your aquarium. Java Fern Trident on Coco Fiber Mat is a pre-bound epiphytic fern that can be rested directly on top of substrate or hardscape ; never bury the horizontal rhizome beneath sand or soil, as it will rot and melt. Avoid making drastic changes to your water parameters or lighting because unstable conditions are the primary cause of leaf melt in new specimens. While this plant is hardy and low-maintenance in standard setups, gentle water movement and regular liquid fertilizing will yield much faster growth and broader fronds. Master long-term care and troubleshoot common leaf issues by checking out our Java Fern Care Guide . Can I leave Java Fern Trident attached to the coco fiber mat when adding it to my aquarium? Yes! Java Fern Trident comes pre-attached to the coco fiber mat and does not need to be removed before adding it to your aquarium. Simply place the mat directly in your aquarium wherever you'd like to add greenery. No tying, gluing, or separating the plants is necessary. 2. Why does my Java Fern Trident have black spots underneath its leaves? Small black or brown spots on the undersides of mature Java Fern Trident leaves are usually sori, which are natural reproductive structures that produce spores. These are normal and not a sign of disease or poor plant health. 3. Can I bury the coco fiber mat into substrate? You can rest the mat flat on top of your substrate, but you must ensure the horizontal green rhizomes remain uncovered and exposed to the water column. Plant Profile Add a natural, cascading accent to your aquarium with a Weeping Moss Dome. Covered in Weeping Moss, this compact dome features the moss's signature downward-growing strands, creating a soft, waterfall-like appearance. Its rounded shape and trailing green growth make it an easy way to add texture and dimension to an aquascape without having to attach moss to hardscape yourself. Place it among rocks and driftwood, use it as a standalone accent, or incorporate it into a larger planted layout. Key Features & Benefits Cascading Growth: Weeping Moss develops distinctive, downward-hanging strands that create a natural waterfall effect. Ready-to-Use Design: Pre-attached to a weighted dome for easy placement without additional glue or thread. Natural Shelter: Dense moss growth provides small fish and shrimp with places to explore, forage, and seek cover. Versatile Accent: Adds depth and greenery to nano tanks, planted aquariums, and hardscape-focused layouts. Care & Planting Instructions Place the dome directly onto your aquarium substrate or nestle it between rocks and driftwood to create a natural-looking accent. Provide low to medium lighting. Excessively strong lighting can encourage algae growth within the dense moss. Maintain stable water parameters and good water circulation to help keep the moss healthy. Avoid sudden changes in water conditions. Trim the moss occasionally with sharp aquascaping scissors to maintain its shape and prevent excessive growth. Removing loose debris during water changes will also help keep the inner growth healthy. CO2 injection is not required, but supplemental CO2 can encourage faster growth and denser moss coverage. Propagate Weeping Moss by separating small portions from the dome and attaching them to other surfaces using aquarium-safe superglue or thread. How do I keep my Weeping Moss Dome from turning brown or yellow? Weeping Moss prefers clean, moving water and cooler temperatures (under 78°F). Browning usually occurs when organic debris gets trapped inside the dense fronds or when water temperatures run too high. Gently siphoning debris out during water changes will keep the inner growth green and healthy. 2. Can I remove Weeping Moss from the dome and attach it to driftwood or rocks? Yes! You can carefully separate small portions of Weeping Moss from the dome and attach them to driftwood, rocks, or other hardscape using aquarium-safe gel superglue or dark cotton thread. This allows you to spread the moss throughout your aquascape. 3. How do I stop moss trimmings from spreading everywhere during maintenance? Always turn off your filter pumps and powerheads before trimming moss. Use sharp curved shears to make clean cuts, and immediately scoop or siphon out floating cuttings so they don't take root in unwanted areas of your aquarium.

Plant Profile Mini Bolbitis is a delightful dwarf fern species celebrated as one of the most intricate low-light plants available for detailed aquascaping. Featuring delicate, parsley-like miniature fronds that stay remarkably compact at just 2 to 4 inches tall, it provides a finely textured, miniature forest look that scales perfectly in nano tanks. Virtually bulletproof and capable of growing both submerged and emersed in high-humidity setups, it anchors naturally to wood or stone crevices while shrugging off low lighting and curious fish. We fern-ly believe this is hands-down one of the best aquarium plants for beginners! Key Features & Notes Tough, fibrous foliage easily withstands curious nipping from herbivorous fish like cichlids, goldfish, and large snails. Miniature, finely lobed fronds offer exceptional detail and texture, making it an outstanding focal choice for nano tanks or hardscape nooks. Exceptional hardiness lets it thrive in non-CO2 tanks and low-light environments. Care & Planting Instructions Prep the plant by removing it from the pot and clearing all rockwool from the roots . Mini Bolbitis is an epiphytic fern that should be attached to rocks or driftwood with aquarium-safe glue or thread; never bury the horizontal rhizome in substrate, as it will rot and melt. Bolbitis prefers to be placed in areas of an aquarium that experience higher flow rates. Avoid making drastic changes to your water parameters or lighting because unstable conditions are the primary cause of leaf melt in new specimens. While this plant is hardy and low-maintenance in standard setups, gentle water movement and regular liquid fertilizing will yield much faster growth and broader fronds. Final size and foliage pattern depend entirely on your specific aquarium conditions; please note that photos are a representation, and individual plants may vary. Why are the new leaves on my Mini Bolbitis translucent or brown? Translucent or brownish foliage is common when Mini Bolbitis adapts to a new tank or transitions from emersed farm growth to submerged conditions. Do not remove the plant; as long as the horizontal rhizome remains firm and green, it will shed old leaves and sprout fully adapted underwater fronds. 2. Can Mini Bolbitis be grown out of water in a terrarium or paludarium? Absolutely! Mini Bolbitis is an exceptional candidate for humid terrariums, paludariums, and misted Wabi Kusa displays. When grown emersed in high humidity (above 70–80%), it develops tight, compact foliage and grows slightly faster than it does fully submerged underwater. 3. Can I plant Mini Bolbitis into substrate? No. Mini Bolbitis is an epiphyte that absorbs nutrients directly from the water column through its foliage and root network. If you bury its horizontal rhizome beneath aquarium soil, sand, or gravel, the stem will suffocate, rot, and die. Always attach it to rocks or driftwood using aquarium-safe glue or thread.

Plant Profile Echinodorus Fancy Twist lives up to its name with a fun, colorful plot twist as it adapts to your tank. When grown emersed, its leaves stay a modest, simple green, but once submerged under decent light and given proper care, new growth transitions into stunning shades of deep blood red. Because it grows as a large, sweeping rosette species, it fills out a planted tank background with serious visual impact without requiring high-tech maintenance. It is an undemanding, beginner-friendly staple for larger displays where you want bold red tones without the fussy maintenance usually required by high-color stem plants. Key Features & Notes Broad leaves shift from bright green to deep red under adequate aquarium lighting. Broad rosette structure offers dense background coverage and focal point placement. Hardy species that grows reliably without pressurized CO2 injection or high-intensity light. Care & Planting Instructions Prep the plant by removing it from the pot and clearing all rockwool from the roots. Plant the roots deeply into your aquarium soil, keeping the crown of the plant resting just above the substrate line to prevent rot. All Echinodorus are heavy root feeders that rely on rich substrate nutrition; placing root tabs near the base supports steady, healthy leaf development. Supplemental CO2 injection accelerates growth and encourages denser, fuller foliage, though the plant will still grow steadily in low-tech setups. Maintain stable water parameters to prevent leaf shedding during the initial transition period. Final size and coloration depend entirely on your specific aquarium conditions; please note that photos are a representation, and individual plants may vary. Why are the leaves on my new Echinodorus melting or turning yellow? Sword plants are often grown emersed and shed their old emersed leaves when submerged to adapt to underwater growth. Keep water parameters stable and supply root tabs near the base to support new leaves.

Plant Profile Give your aquascape a sharper silhouette with Anubias Short and Sharp. The naming department might have been having a bit of fun, considering there isn't actually anything particularly "short" about it. Reaching up to 8 inches tall, this aquarium plant has long, lance-shaped leaves with subtly rippled edges, adding texture among rounded foliage and smooth stones. It's a great pick for a midground or background accent in planted aquariums, terrariums, and paludariums. Key Features & Benefits Sleek, lance-shaped leaves with distinct wavy edges provide a sharp, dynamic texture. Thick foliage resists grazing from cichlids, herbivorous fish, snails, and active dwarf shrimp. Resilient nature handles a wide range of water parameters in low-tech setups with ease. Care & Planting Instructions Prep the plant by removing it from the pot and clearing all rockwool from the roots. Attach to hardscape using aquarium‑safe glue or thread; keep the rhizome above substrate to prevent rot. Maintain stable conditions to support smooth acclimation and reduce leaf loss. Avoid intense light and ensure good water flow to prevent spot algae on slow‑growing leaves. CO₂ is optional but improves growth and leaf density. Learn more about planting these species by reading our guide on How to Plant Epiphyte Aquatic Plants. Master long-term care and propagation with the article All About Anubias Aquarium Plants. How is Anubias Short and Sharp different from standard Anubias Nana? While standard Anubias Nana has rounded, spoon-shaped leaves, Anubias Short and Sharp produces narrow, lance-shaped blades that taper into distinct pointed tips with subtly wavy edges, giving it a much sleeker, more architectural profile. 2. Can I trim the pointed leaf tips if Anubias Short and Sharp grows too tall? Avoid trimming individual leaf blades, as cut edges will turn brown and attract algae. Instead, snip the tallest petioles cleanly at the base of the horizontal rhizome using sharp shears to encourage fresh, lower-growing foliage. 3. How do I stop spot algae from forming on Anubias Short and Sharp's leaves? Because its leaves grow slowly and stay on the plant for months, direct high-PAR light will quickly coat them in green spot algae. Position it in partial shade beneath taller stem plants or floating plants and keep steady circulation moving through the canopy.

Plant Profile If you're dreaming of a lush green lawn in your aquarium without committing to the relentless trimming of traditional carpet plants, Crypt parva is the ultimate mini power plant. Native to the central highlands of Sri Lanka, this tiny titan holds the crown as the smallest species in the entire Cryptocoryne genus, showing off slender, blade-like leaves that cap out at just a few inches tall. As with all crypts, it can be sensitive to sudden parameter shifts and strongly objects to being relocated once planted. Give it a permanent spot in your foreground, however, and its tiny, glossy rosettes will slowly form a dense, bulletproof carpet that holds up effortlessly under almost any light level. Key Features & Benefits Miniature grass-like leaves create a clean, low-profile carpet across foreground and midground zones. Can be grown emersed in high-humidity setups where it will periodically produce unique flowering spathes. Remarkably durable once rooted, offering a bulletproof alternative to demanding, fast-growing carpet plants. Care & Planting Instructions Prep the plant by removing it from the pot and clearing all rockwool from the roots . Use fine-tip pinsettes to push roots deep into quality aquarium soil, as Crypt species are heavy root feeders. Insert root tab fertilizers if using an inert substrate like sand or gravel. Inject pressurized CO2 for faster growth, though not required for long-term health. Choose a permanent spot from day one; moving an established plant will likely trigger leaf loss. Crypt species can be grown emersed in high-humidity setups or submerged in aquariums. Propagate by splitting the rhizome or replanting new growth shoots. Don't discard the plant if leaves dissolve early on; see our guide to managing Cryptocoryne melt to help your plant recover smoothly. Why are my Cryptocoryne Parva leaves melting away? Transplanting Crypts into new water parameters often triggers a temporary reaction where old leaves dissolve. As long as the root system remains undisturbed in healthy soil, fresh foliage will sprout shortly. Check out our guide on Cryptocoryne melt for step-by-step recovery tips. 2. Can I move my Cryptocoryne to a new spot in the tank later? It is best to leave your Crypt permanently in its original spot. Uprooting an established plant damages its fine root hairs and almost always causes another cycle of leaf melt. 3. Do I need root tabs if I already use liquid fertilizers for my Cryptocoryne? Yes. Because Cryptocoryne plants absorb the vast majority of their nutrients through their roots rather than their leaves, providing nutrient-rich aquasoil or root tabs inside sand or gravel is far more effective than relying on water column liquid fertilizers alone.

Plant Profile Hygrophila pinnatifida is a unique aquatic stem species native to India that brings distinct texture and rich coloration to aquascapes. Staying around 5 to 8 inches in height under standard conditions, its pinnate, fern-like leaves range from olive green to warm bronze, fiery red, and deep purple depending on light intensity and nutrient availability. What makes it especially versatile is its ability to grow either rooted in substrate or attached directly to hardscape, where its lateral runners send out roots that grip tightly to rocks and driftwood. It is an excellent choice for hobbyists looking for a multi-use accent plant that bridges the gap between hardscape features and taller background plants. Key Features & Notes Adapts to both substrate and epiphytic growth on hardscape, sending out horizontal runners to form a spreading layer. Moderate-to-high lighting and rich fertilization encourage compact growth and bring out deep red and purple pigmentation. Care & Planting Instructions Prep the plant by removing it from the pot or lead wrap and clearing all rockwool from the roots . Plant stems deeply into aquarium soil or attach them directly onto rocks and driftwood using thread or aquarium glue until adventitious roots anchor securely. Monitor potassium levels carefully and supplement liquid fertilizer as needed to prevent small pinholes from developing in older foliage. Under high lighting, the stems generally stay shorter and more compact while sending out lateral shoots, which can be cut and replanted or simply left alone to grow. Cutting the stems horizontally can work as well, but in our experience, new growth tends to take longer. Final size and coloration depend entirely on your specific aquarium conditions; please note that photos are a representation, and individual plants may vary. Ensure adequate light reaches the base by thinning out dense upper growth, and supply consistent water-column dosing with adequate potassium to protect lower foliage health.

Plant Profile Dwarf Hairgrass is a long‑standing staple in the aquascaping world, thanks to its reliability and versatility in shaping a natural, field-like foreground. With its fine, needle‑thin foliage and tidy growth pattern, it forms a cohesive carpet that spreads by sending out a steady network of runners beneath the substrate, making it great for filling tight gaps around hardscape or creating scattered clusters where shrimp and nano fish love to forage. Highly adaptable, it thrives fully submerged but also performs beautifully in emersed setups like dry starts or Wabi‑Kusa, giving you plenty of flexibility in how you use it. Need Dwarf Hair Grass but this listing is out of stock? Check out these other popular variants : Dwarf Hair Grass - Eleocharis Belem Dwarf Hair Grass - Eleocharis Pusillis Key Features & Benefits Recreate a classic, realistic grass lawn aesthetic using its fine, needle-thin blades. Versatile species that adapts beautifully to both submerged aquariums and emersed setups. Care & Planting Instructions Separate larger mats into small, bite-sized portions and plant them roughly an inch apart, burying them about halfway into your substrate. Maintain low to high lighting parameters, though higher light will drastically encourage a shorter, thicker carpet. Choose to inject pressurized CO2 to accelerate its growth speed and achieve a dense, wall-to-wall foreground. Propagate the plant effortlessly by cutting mature new growth along with the roots and moving them to bare spots. Plant Profile Bucephalandra ‘Green Wavy’ on Driftwood is a beginner-friendly, low-tech epiphyte that arrives pre-mounted to a natural piece of driftwood so you can drop it straight into your tank without dealing with glue, thread, or rockwool prep! Known for its bright green leaves with ruffled margins and a subtle sheen under quality LEDs, this variety naturally branches out into a dense, bushy clump over time. Staying around 2 to 4 inches tall, it works great as an instant foreground or midground accent that softens hardscape transitions. Key Features & Notes Arrives pre-attached to natural driftwood, giving you a drop-in hardscape accent with zero glue or thread prep required. This is one of the most durable species in the hobby and thrives in shaded areas . It is an ideal choice for planted tanks where other plants might struggle. Textured wood and ruffled foliage collect natural biofilm, making it an active grazing spot for dwarf shrimp and snails. Care & Planting Instructions Give the wood and foliage a quick rinse in dechlorinated water before setting the piece directly onto your substrate or wedging it into existing hardscape. Bucephalandra is an epiphytic plant that should remain attached to rocks or driftwood ; avoid pushing the driftwood so deep into aquarium soil or gravel that the horizontal rhizome gets buried, as this will cause rot. Avoid making drastic changes to your water parameters or lighting because unstable conditions are the primary cause of leaf melt in new specimens. While this plant is hardy and low-maintenance in standard low-light setups, supplemental CO2 injection and regular liquid fertilizers will yield faster branching and denser leaf growth. You can lightly nestle the bottom of the driftwood into aquarium soil or gravel to stabilize it, as long as the attached Bucephalandra rhizome sits completely exposed above the substrate line. Burying the rhizome under the substrate blocks water flow and causes rot.

Plant Profile We have taken the absolute most legendary and bulletproof plant in the hobby and pre-attached a lush layer of it directly onto a clean 4-inch piece of natural driftwood. Famous for its thin, deep green fronds and near-indestructible nature, Java Moss is a favorite among absolute beginners and expert breeders alike. It easily handles low lighting and an incredibly wide range of tank conditions, transforming a plain piece of wood into an ancient-looking, weathered riverbed feature the moment it drops into your tank. Key Features & Benefits Pre-wrapped on 4-inch wood base for an instant midground accent, no tying or floating parts. Interlocking fronds trap organic particles for shrimp foraging and fry shelter. Moss softens wood edges for an authentic, mature ecosystem look. Care & Planting Instructions Place the 4-inch driftwood stick directly onto your substrate, or wedge it securely into your rockwork to add immediate vertical dimension to your layout. Give the moss an occasional light haircut with sharp aquascaping shears to keep its shape neat, compact, and perfectly balanced. Plant Profile Aquascapers looking to introduce sharp, dramatic foliage to planted tanks will find their match in Anubias Congensis. Diverging from the broad, circular foliage of Anubias Barteri or Anubias Nana , this West African aquatic epiphyte produces sleek, slender, lanceolate leaves with pointed tips. Reaching a height of 6 to 8 inches, its upright growth habit makes it an exceptional midground anchor or background accent for medium and large aquariums. Key Features & Benefits Thrives submerged in aquariums or emersed in humid terrariums and paludariums. Upright growth serves as a versatile midground anchor or compact background filler for medium to large tanks. Thick foliage resists grazing from curious cichlids, snails, and active dwarf shrimp. Care & Planting Instructions Prep the plant by removing it from the pot and clearing all rockwool from the roots. Attach to hardscape using aquarium‑safe glue or thread; keep the rhizome above substrate to prevent rot. Maintain stable conditions to support smooth acclimation and reduce leaf loss. Avoid intense light and ensure good water flow to prevent spot algae on slow‑growing leaves. CO₂ is optional but improves growth and leaf density. Product Overview Ultum Nature Systems Controsoil Brown is a volcanic ash-based aquarium soil from Japan designed to support healthy planted tanks. Selecting the right substrate is foundational not only for aquatic plants to flourish, but also for maintaining optimal water parameters for sensitive livestock like dwarf shrimp and tropical fish. While other substrates might leach excessive ammonia (NH3) and trigger the dreaded "new tank syndrome", resulting in cloudy water and aggressive initial algae spikes, Controsoil keeps initial ammonia release minimal while buffering alkaline water to a slightly acidic pH below 7.0. This natural parameter control simplifies early tank maintenance and creates a stable aquatic ecosystem right out of the bag without daily water changes as the tank establishes itself. Offered in Extra Fine (~1mm), Fine (~3mm), and Normal (~5mm) granule sizes, it provides the ideal foundation for anchoring delicate foreground carpeting species or building a high-impact aquascape for heavy root-feeding plants. Key Features & Benefits Natural soil and volcanic ash composition absorbs impurities and maintains water clarity from initial setup. Natural parameter control buffers alkaline water below 7.0 pH and lowers total hardness for soft-water species. Controlled low ammonia release prevents initial algae blooms while simplifying early aquarium establishment. Durable granule structure resists breakdown over time to prevent compaction and encourage deep root growth. Usage & Application Guidelines Do not rinse this aquarium soil before placing it into your tank. Distribute the granules to achieve a depth of two to three inches sloping toward the back glass to support root systems and build visual perspective. Fill the aquarium gently by pouring water over a plate or plastic wrap to keep the substrate layer undisturbed. Do I need to rinse this aquarium substrate before adding it to my tank? No, you should never rinse aquarium soil before adding it to your setup. How much substrate do I need for my aquarium size? To calculate the required volume in liters, multiply the length of your aquarium by the width and desired substrate depth in inches, then divide the total by 60. For example, a standard tank measuring 24 inches long by 12 inches wide with a 2-inch bed requires approximately 9.6 liters of soil. 3. How does this substrate affect my water parameters? Yes, combining aquarium soil with decorative aquarium sand is a popular technique for high-contrast aquascaping layouts. You can place soil in the rear or planting zones for root growth and cosmetic sand in the foreground or pathway areas for visual contrast.

Plant Profile Common Name: Glosso, Glossostigma Elatinoides Glossostigma elatinoides, affectionately known as Glosso to hobbyists, is an absolute classic from New Zealand that helped define the iconic look of aquarium carpets. Its small, round, bright‑green leaves create a gorgeous contrast against darker substrates and instantly brighten up a layout. Give it the right balance of light and nutrients, and Glosso will reward you by stitching itself into a pristine, low‑growing sheet of green that hugs the bottom of your tank like a tiny velvet blanket living its best life. Key Features & Benefits Form a dense, classic carpet of small, round, vibrant green leaves. An energetic grower that quickly blankets bare substrate areas when provided with optimal conditions. Care & Planting Instructions Provide high lighting and steady CO2 injection to encourage tight, low horizontal growth and prevent the stalks from reaching upward. Keep an eye out for thin, vertically stretched stalks, which are a clear sign your plant is reaching out for more light. Check your nutrients if leaves look thin or yellow, as these are classic signs of a lack of CO2 or a nutritional deficiency. Trim regularly once the plant takes off under proper conditions, as it can grow quickly and will need haircuts to stay neat. Plant Profile Java Fern is a classic epiphytic species widely celebrated as one of the most popular picks for low-light aquarium plants. If you have ever felt personally victimized by delicate stem plants that melt into green mush the moment you turn off your grow lights, Java Fern is here to restore your confidence. Virtually bulletproof and exceptionally adaptable, it tolerates extreme ranges in water hardness, temperature, and lighting that would send other species into survival shock. It is hands-down one of the best aquarium plants for beginners, featuring broad, leathery green fronds that anchor onto hardscape and look even better as they mature into lush background displays. Key Features & Notes Tough, fibrous foliage easily withstands curious nipping from herbivorous fish like cichlids, goldfish, and large snails. Broad vertical fronds create a natural, leafy backdrop that masks equipment while providing territory cover for timid fish. Exceptional hardiness lets it thrive in non-CO2 tanks and low-light environments. Care & Planting Instructions Prep the plant by removing it from the pot and clearing all rockwool from the roots . Java Fern is an epiphytic fern that should be attached to rocks or driftwood with aquarium-safe glue or thread; never bury the horizontal rhizome in substrate, as it will rot and melt. Avoid making drastic changes to your water parameters or lighting because unstable conditions are the primary cause of leaf melt in new specimens. While this plant is hardy and low-maintenance in standard setups, gentle water movement and regular liquid fertilizing will yield much faster growth and broader fronds. Master long-term care and troubleshoot common leaf issues by checking out our Java Fern Care Guide . Final size and foliage pattern depend entirely on your specific aquarium conditions; please note that photos are a representation, and individual plants may vary. Why are there small black spots and tiny leaves growing under my Java Fern leaves? Do not panic; your plant is not diseased! Java Fern reproduces naturally through adventitious plantlets. Small dark bumps (sporangia) form along the undersides of mature leaves, sprouting tiny brown roots and mini green fronds. Once these baby plantlets develop 3–4 leaves, you can gently pop them off the mother leaf and glue them elsewhere in your aquarium. 2. Can I plant Java Fern into substrate? No. Java Fern is an epiphyte that absorbs nutrients directly from the water column through its foliage and fine root network. If you bury its horizontal rhizome beneath aquarium soil, sand, or gravel, the stem will suffocate, rot, and die. Always attach it to rocks or driftwood using aquarium-safe glue or thread. 3. Why is Java Fern considered one of the best low light aquarium plants for beginners? Java Fern is exceptionally resilient because it does not require specialized substrate, grows reliably under basic LED lighting, and tolerates a massive range of water conditions without needing pressurized CO2 injection. 4. Will fish like cichlids or goldfish eat Java Fern? Generally, no. Java Fern leaves are thick, fibrous, and contain bitter-tasting compounds that deter most plant-eating fish. While aggressive diggers might knock it off hardscape if not glued securely, they rarely consume the foliage.

Plant Profile Give Cryptocoryne wendtii 'Brown' a permanent spot in your substrate, and its dark foliage will reward you with a lush, self-sustaining clump that contrasts beautifully against lighter hardscape and green aquatic plants. Native to the mineral-rich streams of Sri Lanka, this iconic classic sports deep bronze-to-chocolate leaves with textured, slightly dimpled, wavy margins, an earthy focal point that breaks up the monotonous sea of green without adding strict maintenance to your routine. Like all crypts, though, it can be sensitive to sudden parameter shifts and strongly objects to being moved once planted, so choose its home wisely from the start. Key Features & Benefits Deep bronze and chocolate foliage with wavy margins adds rich earthy contrast. Can be grown emersed in high-humidity setups, periodically producing flowering spathes. Versatile and tolerant of hard water, great for community tanks and cichlid setups alike. Care & Planting Instructions Prep the plant by removing it from the pot and clearing all rockwool from the roots . Use fine-tip pinsettes to push roots deep into quality aquarium soil, as Crypt species are heavy root feeders. Insert root tab fertilizers if using an inert substrate like sand or gravel. Inject pressurized CO2 for faster growth, though not required for long-term health. Choose a permanent spot from day one; moving an established plant will likely trigger leaf loss. Crypt species can be grown emersed in high-humidity setups or submerged in aquariums. Propagate by splitting the rhizome or replanting new growth shoots. Don't discard the plant if leaves dissolve early on; see our guide to managing Cryptocoryne melt to help your plant recover smoothly. Because Cryptocoryne plants absorb the vast majority of their nutrients through their roots rather than their leaves, providing nutrient-rich aquasoil or root tabs inside sand or gravel is far more effective than relying on water column liquid fertilizers alone.

No. It thrives in low to moderate lighting without CO2 injection. Plant Profile If smooth, pristine foliage feels a little too routine for your aquascape, Anubias Barteri 'Wrinkle Leaf' is here to bring some serious character! True to its name, this uncommon epiphyte takes the classic, dependable round leaves of standard Barteri and gives them a bold, ruffled upgrade. Spanning up to 3 inches long on 4 to 6-inch stems, its broad, crinkled leaves create an immediate pop of tactile depth that makes smooth rocks and plain driftwood look downright boring by comparison. It grows slowly under low light, tolerates wide water parameters, and thrives submerged in aquariums or emersed in humid terrariums. Key Features & Benefits Distinctly ruffled, crinkled leaf margins offer an eye-catching, textured look that instantly breaks up monotonous aquariums. Broad, large leaf blades provide fantastic midground structure and soft background coverage. Built like a tank! Thick foliage naturally resists nibbling from curious fish, snails, and active dwarf shrimp. Care & Planting Instructions Prep the plant by removing it from the pot and clearing all rockwool from the roots. Attach to hardscape using aquarium‑safe glue or thread; keep the rhizome above substrate to prevent rot. Maintain stable conditions to support smooth acclimation and reduce leaf loss. Avoid intense light and ensure good water flow to prevent spot algae on slow‑growing leaves. CO₂ is optional but improves growth and leaf density. Learn more about planting these species by reading our guide on How to Plant Epiphyte Aquatic Plants. Master long-term care and propagation with the article All About Anubias Aquarium Plants. Its tough leaves are also resistant to plant-eating fish like cichlids or goldfish.

Resting atop tall, graceful stems similar to classic Anubias Barteri , its broad, coin-shaped leaves bring a playful geometry and rich green texture that instantly softens heavy rockwork and dark driftwood. Thriving across a wide range of water parameters with minimal effort, this epiphyte makes a standout foreground or midground accent that pays major visual dividends. Key Features & Benefits Circular leaf shape offers a geometric contrast against pointed or lanceolate aquatic plants. Tall stem structure provides impressive verticality, making it an ideal midground anchor or soft background centerpiece. Hardiness ensures it adapts to low-tech setups, varying water conditions, and active tank mates. Anubias Round Golden Coin generally reaches up to 8 inches in overall height, with individual circular leaves spanning 2 to 3.5 inches across, making it an excellent midground anchor for tanks 20 gallons and larger. 3. Its thick, tough leaves resist the persistent picking and substrate-digging behavior typical of African and South American cichlids.

Plant Profile Bolbitis serves as the larger-leaf counterpart to Mini Bolbitis , producing broad, elegant fronds with a rich, lacy texture. Native to humid riverbanks across Southeast Asia, this slow-growing epiphyte stays compact at 2 to 4 inches, making it a versatile, beginner-friendly midground accent for planted aquariums, terrariums, and paludariums alike. It attaches to driftwood or stones to deliver sophisticated, high-end texture without any high-tech maintenance drama. Key Features & Notes Tough, fibrous foliage easily withstands curious nipping from herbivorous fish like cichlids, goldfish, and large snails. Broad, lacy leaf structure provides vibrant, bushy midground coverage compared to smaller-leaf variants. Exceptional hardiness lets it thrive in non-CO2 tanks and low-light environments. Care & Planting Instructions Prep the plant by removing it from the pot and clearing all rockwool from the roots . Bolbitis is an epiphytic fern that should be attached to rocks or driftwood with aquarium-safe glue or thread; never bury the horizontal rhizome in substrate, as it will rot and melt. Position this plant in areas with moderate to high water circulation, as Bolbitis species thrive when water currents pass gently through their fronds. Avoid making drastic changes to your water parameters or lighting because unstable conditions are the primary cause of leaf melt in new specimens. While this plant is hardy and low-maintenance in standard setups, gentle water movement and regular liquid fertilizing will yield much faster growth and broader fronds. Final size and foliage pattern depend entirely on your specific aquarium conditions; please note that photos are a representation, and individual plants may vary. Can Bolbitis be grown in terrariums or paludariums? Yes! Bolbitis transitions into emersed growth effortlessly. Given high ambient humidity (80%+), it’s an absolute rockstar for humid terrariums, vivariums, and paludarium land sections mounted on wet stone or moss walls. 4. Will fish like cichlids or goldfish eat Bolbitis? Generally, no. Bolbitis fronds are thick, fibrous, and bitter-tasting, making them naturally unappealing to herbivorous fish. While boisterous diggers might knock unglued plants around, they rarely eat the foliage.

Plant Profile The Hadi Red Pearl Sword is a cultivated Amazon Sword variety known for its distinct foliage patterns and sturdy structure. This plant features broad, spade-shaped green leaves marked with red spots and streaks running throughout the leaf blade. Growing to a height of 4 to 9 inches, its rosette form serves as a central focal point in midground or background zones in planted tanks. Because it adapts to low lighting conditions and grows without mandatory CO2 injection, it is a beginner-friendly and low-tech plant choice for medium or larger tanks. Key Features & Benefits Broad green leaves marked with dark red spots add color contrast to midground and background zones. Hardy rosette growth structure provides reliable architectural presence in planted aquarium layouts. Adaptable species that grows submerged in aquariums or emersed in humid terrarium setups. Care & Planting Instructions Prep the plant by removing it from the pot and clearing all rockwool from the roots. Plant the roots deeply into your aquarium soil, keeping the crown of the plant resting just above the substrate line to prevent rot. All Echinodorus are heavy root feeders that rely on rich substrate nutrition; placing root tabs near the base supports steady, healthy leaf development. Provide low to moderate lighting; while it tolerates basic low-tech conditions, supplying moderate light and liquid iron supplements helps highlight the red spots on new foliage. See our guide to growing red aquarium plants . Maintain stable water parameters to prevent leaf shedding during the initial transition period. To propagate, separate developed daughter plantlets that form along runner stems or at the base once they produce independent roots, then replant them directly into your aquarium soil. Read our trimming & propagation guide for details. Quick Facts Listed information should be treated as general guidelines only. Team Buce Plant encourages you to do thorough research to ensure healthy growth! Yes, the Hadi Red Pearl Sword grows submerged in aquariums as well as emersed in humid terrarium setups. When grown emersed, leaves may grow slightly stiffer and produce taller stems above the water line.

Plant Profile Java Moss is moss-tly famous for being the undisputed heavyweight moss of the aquarium hobby, and it has earned its reputation for a good reason. This legendary staple has earned its residency in the hobby because it can survive almost any water parameter or temperature swing you throw its way. Its deep green, thin, interlocking fronds grow in a wild, free-form pattern that is excellent for softening hard landscape lines or creating a natural, aged look on wood and rocks. Key Features & Benefits Draping or placing this moss near hardscape elements gives driftwood and stones a mature, weathered look that mimics wild riverbeds. Chaotic, interlocking network of fine fronds creates a safe foraging ground for shrimp and fry. Loose portions can be tied, glued, or tucked into hardscape crevices. Care & Planting Instructions Place the moss directly onto your substrate, or secure it to your hardscape using dark thread or dabs of aquarium-safe superglue gel. Maintain a stable aquarium environment and avoid sudden, drastic changes to your water parameters to keep your moss looking vibrant and healthy. Give the moss an occasional light haircut with sharp aquascaping shears to keep its shape neat, compact, and perfectly balanced. Propagate your patch in seconds by cutting or pulling a small clump apart and anchoring it to a new surface in your tank. Add CO2 injection if you want to accelerate growth and unlock the most intense, eye-popping green coloration possible. Quick Facts Listed information should be treated as general guidelines only. How do I stop moss trimmings from spreading everywhere during maintenance? Always turn off your filter pumps and powerheads before trimming moss. Plant Profile Micranthemum ‘Monte Carlo’ is the ultimate aquatic carpeting plant to give your aquarium that lush, velvety rolling-hill look you’ve been dreaming of. With its tiny, round leaves and bright green color, it pops beautifully against neutral substrates. If you’ve ever struggled to grow notoriously finicky Dwarf Baby Tears (HC) , Monte Carlo is the friendlier, more forgiving alternative you’ve been looking for. It spreads out into a thick, uniform mat, giving you maximum aquascaping rewards without the heartbreak. Tissue Culture cups ensure your aquascape gets a super clean starting point. Lab‑grown and fully sterile, it arrives without pests, snails, duckweed, or any unwanted algae. It’s the go‑to option for anyone who wants peace of mind when adding fresh greenery to a carefully maintained setup. Key Features & Benefits Forms a tight, velvety foreground lawn with small, bright green leaves that add an incredible sense of scale and depth to your aquascape. Far easier to cultivate than Dwarf Baby Tears, making it an accessible carpet option for hobbyists of all experience levels. Care & Planting Instructions Thoroughly wash away the nutrient gel from the roots with your fingers before parting it out into manageable portions and planting. Use a dry start method or Wabi Kusa setup to give its root system plenty of time to firmly anchor into the substrate before you flood the tank. Maintain stable aquarium parameters and avoid drastic shifts in water quality to prevent your new grass from melting. Provide medium to high lighting and inject pressurized CO2 to supercharge its density and growth rate, keeping it low and compact. Master the basics by learning how to properly grow aquarium carpet plants to ensure your new layout fills in quickly. Quick Facts Listed information should be treated as general guidelines only. Team Buce Plant encourages you to do thorough research to ensure healthy growth! Planting small clumps deeply into fine soil or letting the tank grow emersed using the Dry Start Method will anchor the roots securely before flooding.

listings.description: Plant Profile Formally known as Hemianthus callitrichoides (or simply HC), Dwarf Baby Tears is pretty much the poster child of aquatic carpeting plants. As one of the tiniest live plants available in the hobby, it’s the go‑to choice for creating those jaw‑dropping, bright green fields you see in classic Iwagumi layouts. This ultra-compact carpeting plant relies on its tiny leaves to create an incredible sense of scale, making even modest tanks look like massive, captivating rolling landscapes. While it requires high-tech care to reach its full potential, nothing rivals the breathtaking, velvety carpet of a thriving HC lawn. Tissue Culture cups ensure your aquascape gets a super clean starting point. Lab‑grown and fully sterile, it arrives without pests, snails, duckweed, or any unwanted algae. It’s the go‑to option for anyone who wants peace of mind when adding fresh greenery to a carefully maintained setup. Key Features & Benefits Forms the tightest, most compact green carpet possible. Creates the iconic, professional Iwagumi aesthetic with vast fields of green. Care & Planting Instructions Thoroughly wash away the nutrient gel from the roots with your fingers before parting it out into manageable portions and planting. Use a dry start method or Wabi Kusa setup to give its tiny root system plenty of time to firmly anchor into the substrate before you flood the tank. Inject pressurized CO2 and stick to a reliable fertilization schedule. While some hobbyists have found success using liquid carbon like Excel in small tanks, real CO2 is highly recommended to maintain a nice foreground. Maintain stable aquarium parameters and avoid drastic shifts in water quality to prevent your new grass from melting. Master the basics by learning how to properly grow aquarium carpet plants to ensure your new layout fills in quickly. Quick Facts Listed information should be treated as general guidelines only. Team Buce Plant encourages you to do thorough research to ensure healthy growth! How do I plant Dwarf Baby Tears tissue culture? Use fine-tip pinsettes to push each portion deep into fine aquasoil at a 45-degree angle. Leave only a few leaves showing above the surface so they don't float. 2. Can I grow Dwarf Baby Tears without pressurized CO2? No. Dwarf Baby Tears has very high metabolic demands and an extremely delicate root system. Without pressurized CO2 injection and strong lighting, the stems will weaken, stop spreading, and slowly melt away. 3. Why is my newly planted Dwarf Baby Tears floating up? Because the roots are microscopic, water currents and livestock can easily pull them out of the soil. Planting tiny portions deeply into fine aquasoil or growing them emersed using the Dry Start Method for 4–6 weeks will anchor the root system securely before you flood the tank.

Plant Profile Ludwigia Arcuata, aka Needle Leaf Ludwigia, is proof that high-end texture doesn't have to come with high-maintenance drama. This easy-going stem plant features delicate, needle-thin leaves growing in pairs that shift from soft olive-green to deep bronze and rich reds depending on your light and dosing. Keep up with frequent prunings, and it will happily branch out into a dense, bushy filler that adds incredible fine texture and movement to your midground or background. *Form Notice: Photos display this plant in both its emersed (above-water) and submerged forms. Depending on nursery availability and seasonality, you may receive this plant in either form. Learn more about what to expect by reading our guide on Emersed vs. Submerged-Grown Aquatic Plants . Key Features & Benefits Thin, needle-like foliage provides a unique fine texture contrast against broader-leaved aquarium plants. Leaf hues shift into fiery orange and deep red tones under high-intensity lighting paired with iron and micronutrient supplementation. Care & Planting Instructions Remove lead weight and cotton wrap (or foam) surrounding the base, then strip the lower inch of foliage so bare stems anchor cleanly into soil without rotting. * Ludwigia stems can be fragile, so handle with care during preparation. Use fine-tip pinsettes to push stems 1–2 inches into soil, spacing them apart for light penetration. Provide medium-to-high lighting. While CO2 injection is not strictly required, it yields much thicker stems and richer coloration. See our guide to growing red aquarium plants . Maintain stable water parameters and avoid sudden environmental shifts to prevent leaf melt or rotting in fragile stems. Trim stem tops with straight scissors once they reach the surface to encourage lower stems to branch into dense bushes. Read our trimming & propagation guide for details. Spacing individual stems slightly apart during initial planting and maintaining strong light penetration will keep lower leaves healthy. 2. How do I get my Needle Leaf Ludwigia to turn bright red or orange? Providing high light intensity along with regular dosing of iron and liquid fertilizers (like UNS Plant Food) triggers Ludwigia Arcuata to produce rich anthocyanin pigments, turning its needle-like leaves vivid orange or red. 3. How do I transition Ludwigia Arcuata from emersed to submerged growth? When grown emersed, Ludwigia Arcuata produces rounder, thicker green leaves. When transitioning to submerged growth, plant bare stems securely into rich substrate under medium-to-high lighting and maintain stable water parameters. As the plant adapts underwater, it will shed its land foliage and sprout delicate, needle-thin orange and red leaves.

Plant Profile Pogostemon Helferi, also known as Downoi (Thai for "Little Star"), is an iconic and uniquely textured aquatic plant native to the sunlit, calcium-rich riverbeds and wetlands of Thailand. Instantly recognizable by its rosette-forming growth habit and crinkled, wavy-edged foliage, this species resembles a sea anemone or miniature palm tree underwater. Growing to a compact height of just 2 to 3 inches, Downoi serves as an extraordinary accent for foreground carpets, midground transitions, or focal points around hardscape bases in both small nano tanks and large display aquascapes. Tissue Culture cups ensure your aquascape gets a super clean starting point. Lab‑grown and fully sterile, it arrives without pests, snails, duckweed, or any unwanted algae. It’s the go‑to option for anyone who wants peace of mind when adding fresh greenery to a carefully maintained setup. Key Features & Benefits Unique crinkled, wavy-edged rosette foliage provides an eye-catching, starburst texture unlike any other foreground plant. Compact, low-growing habit forms dense, bushy green clusters perfect for foreground carpets and midground accents. Care & Planting Instructions Thoroughly wash away the nutrient gel from the roots with your fingers before parting it out into manageable portions. Use fine-tip pinsettes to plant small clusters 1 inch apart into aquarium soil. Provide medium-to-high lighting and clean water conditions; while adaptable without CO2, supplying pressurized CO2 injection promotes substantially thicker foliage and faster side-shoot development. Maintain stable water parameters and avoid sudden parameter swings to prevent leaf melt. Propagate as the plant matures by carefully cutting developed side shoots along with their root structures and replanting them into substrate. Read our trimming & propagation guide for details. listings.description: Plant Profile Homalomena sp. Sekadau South is a rare rheophytic aquatic plant native to the shaded streams of Borneo, belonging to the Araceae family alongside Bucephalandra and Anubias . Staying under 6 inches in height, this uncommon collector plant features deep green, glossy leaves with visible venation that bring a distinct tropical rainforest aesthetic to the midground zones of a planted tank. Similar to its Bucephalandra cousins, it develops a creeping rhizome that can be anchored directly onto rocks and driftwood or placed loosely in substrate without burying the rhizome. Because it naturally thrives in shaded forest waters, it is a slow grower that performs best under low to moderate lighting where algae growth on the foliage can be kept in check. Tissue culture cups ensure your aquascape gets a super clean starting point. Lab-grown and fully sterile, it arrives without pests, snails, duckweed, or any unwanted algae. It’s the go-to option for anyone who wants peace of mind when adding fresh greenery to a carefully maintained setup. Key Features & Notes Broad, textured Araceae foliage introduces a rare and unique visual accent to hardscape structures. Rheophytic growth habit allows the plant to anchor directly onto rocks and driftwood via its creeping rhizome. Care & Planting Instructions Prep the plant by carefully removing the plantlets from the cup and rinsing away all sterile nutrient gel under lukewarm, dechlorinated water before mounting. Attach the rhizome directly onto rocks or driftwood using aquarium glue or thread, ensuring the main rhizome remains uncovered to avoid rot. Avoid excessive high-intensity lighting to prevent green spot algae from forming on the slow-growing leaves. Supplemental CO2 injection encourages faster growth and stronger root attachment, though it can be adapted to low-tech setups with stable parameters. Maintain consistent water parameters to prevent leaf melting during the initial acclimatization period. Final size and coloration depend entirely on your specific aquarium conditions; please note that photos are a representation, and individual plants may vary. Plant Profile Lagenandra Meeboldii 'Red' brings the classic Crypt look with a color palette that doesn't play by Crypt rules. It develops broad, oval-shaped leaves that showcase a blend of dusty green, olive, rich red-violet, and bright purple-pink, often all on the same leaf. Fresh new foliage unfolds in a soft pastel pink before maturing into deep reddish-brown tones. Native to the shady streams and damp riverbanks of Southwestern India, this eye-catching member of the Araceae family shares close ties with both Bucephalandra and Cryptocoryne. Reaching 5 or more inches in height with a wide-spreading habit, Lagenandra Meeboldii 'Red' makes an unforgettable, low-maintenance centerpiece for midground zones in both high- and low-tech aquariums. Tissue Culture cups ensure your aquascape gets a super clean starting point. Lab‑grown and fully sterile, it arrives without pests, snails, duckweed, or any unwanted algae. It’s the go‑to option for anyone who wants peace of mind when adding fresh greenery to a carefully maintained setup. Key Features & Benefits Broad oval foliage displays a mix of bronze, olive green, pink, and red-violet tones. Hardy rhizome growth habit provides structural focal points in midground areas. Care & Planting Instructions Thoroughly wash away the nutrient gel from the roots with your fingers before parting it out into manageable portions. Plant the roots into your aquarium soil, ensuring the central horizontal rhizome remains resting slightly above the substrate line to prevent rot. As a heavy root feeder, Lagenandra Meeboldii 'Red' responds well to root nutrition; placing root tabs near the root base in your aquarium soil supports steady growth and leaf development. Provide low to medium lighting; while CO2 is not required, supplying moderate light and regular liquid iron supplements helps highlight the red-violet tones on mature leaves. See our guide to growing red aquarium plants . Maintain stable water parameters to avoid leaf melting during the initial transition period. To propagate, use a sharp blade to cut the thick rhizome into smaller sections (ensuring each piece has several leaves and roots attached) and replant them into your aquarium soil. Read our trimming & propagation guide for details. Quick Facts Listed information should be treated as general guidelines only. Plant Profile Common Name: Bucephalandra Giant Motleyana Buce ‘Giant Motleyana’ is a robust aquarium plant featuring elongated, dark olive leaves that often display a striking bluish shine. This variety is prized for its substantial leaf size and deep color palette, which can range from rich reds to dark forest greens under optimal conditions. Highly versatile, it can be grown submerged or emersed, usually attached to hardscape such as driftwood or rocks rather than being buried in traditional aquarium substrate. Giant Motleyana is a great pick for the midground of freshwater aquascapes, where its slow-growing rhizomes create a dense, architectural colony that adds significant depth to a planted tank. Key Features & Notes Under quality aquarium LED lighting, the mature olive foliage of Giant Motleyana develops a distinct metallic blue sheen that stands out against green plants. Unlike the miniature variants, this species provides a bolder texture, making it an excellent anchor for the base of driftwood or large stone formations. This is one of the most durable species in the hobby and thrives in shaded areas . It is an ideal choice for aquascapes where other plants might struggle. It is perfectly at home fully submerged in an aquarium or emersed in high-humidity terrariums, vivariums, and paludariums. Care Tips & Preparation Bucephalandra is an epiphytic plant that should be attached to rocks or driftwood . Never bury the rhizome in substrate, as this will cause the plant to rot and melt. Carefully remove the plant from its pot and clear away all rockwool from the roots. For a deep dive on prepping potted plants, click here . Avoid making drastic changes to your water parameters or lighting. Unstable conditions are the primary cause of leaf melt in new specimens. While this plant is hardy and low-maintenance, CO2 injection will yield much faster growth. We recommend researching your specific water chemistry to ensure your plant thrives. Final size and coloration depend entirely on your specific aquarium conditions. Please note that photos are a representation, and individual plants may vary. Please research appropriately to ensure your plant thrives. Additional Information Listed information should be treated as general guidelines only. Team Buce Plant encourages you to do thorough research to ensure healthy growth! Plant Profile Aridarum Narrow is an uncommon aquarium plant in the family Araceae, native to the torrential stream banks and rocky waterfalls of Borneo. It features slender, strap-like green foliage with a tough, waxy cuticle designed to withstand crashing river currents, clustering tightly along a stout creeping rhizome to create a clean, linear silhouette that adds a wild, riverbed texture when wedged into hardscape crevices. Whether you are cultivating it submerged in a high-energy aquascape or emersed along a damp riparium splash zone, make sure the rhizome stays completely exposed to open water and ambient flow, because burying it in aquarium soil is a fast track to rot. Key Features & Notes Narrow strap-like foliage features a tough, waxy texture adapted to high-flow river rapids and waterfall cascades. Exceptional shade tolerance allows steady growth in low-light aquarium setups and low-tech community tanks. Care & Planting Instructions Prep the plant by removing it from the pot and clearing all rockwool from the roots . Aridarum is an epiphytic plant that should be attached to rocks or driftwood using aquarium-safe glue or thread; never bury the horizontal rhizome in substrate, as it will rot and melt. Avoid making drastic changes to your water parameters or lighting because unstable conditions are the primary cause of leaf melt in new specimens. While this plant is hardy and low-maintenance in standard setups, moderate water movement and regular liquid fertilizing will yield much faster growth and broader fronds. Final size and foliage pattern depend entirely on your specific aquarium conditions; please note that photos are a representation, and individual plants may vary. Quick Facts Listed information should be treated as general guidelines only. Team Buce Plant encourages you to do thorough research to ensure healthy growth! Aridarum Narrow develops distinctly slender, smooth-margined, strap-shaped foliage, whereas Aridarum Sabertooth features broader leaves characterized by pronounced serrated or tooth-like undulating margins along the blade edges. 2. Does Aridarum Narrow require pressurized CO2 injection to thrive? No. Aridarum Narrow grows steadily under low to moderate lighting in non-CO2 aquarium setups. While pressurized CO2 and supplemental liquid micro-nutrients encourage denser leaf production and faster growth, they are not mandatory for long-term health. 3. Why are the leaves on my new Aridarum Narrow melting? Melt typically occurs when the plant is introduced to an unstable tank or experiences sharp fluctuations in water chemistry, temperature, or lighting. If the creeping rhizome remains firm and green, leave it secured to your hardscape while it acclimates and sprouts fresh submerged leaves.

Plant Profile Anubias Barteri Broad Leaf is an easy-care, beginner-friendly aquarium plant with wide, dark-green leaves that add height and coverage to midground and background zones. Taking the classic profile of standard Anubias Barteri and scaling it up, this cultivar produces wide, oval dark-green leaves nearly twice the size of its parent species! Growing up to 16 inches tall, it suits medium and large tanks with low to moderate light. Attach it to rock or driftwood and keep the rhizome above the substrate to prevent rot. Key Features & Benefits Massive leaves bring dramatic scale, making medium and large aquariums feel lush and mature. Broad foliage creates natural shaded pockets, providing shelter to shy fish or shrimp. Thrives in low-tech submerged aquariums or humid emersed setups like terrariums and paludariums. Care & Planting Instructions Prep the plant by removing it from the pot and clearing all rockwool from the roots. Attach to hardscape using aquarium‑safe glue or thread; keep the rhizome above substrate to prevent rot. Maintain stable conditions to support smooth acclimation and reduce leaf loss. Avoid intense light and ensure good water flow to prevent spot algae on slow‑growing leaves. CO₂ is optional but improves growth speed and leaf density. Learn more about planting these species by reading our guide on How to Plant Epiphyte Aquatic Plants. Master long-term care and propagation with the article All About Anubias Aquarium Plants. Use this to your advantage by tucking shade-loving Bucephalandra, Cryptocoryne, or Anubias Nana Petite beneath its leaves while carpeting stems get open light elsewhere. 3. How do I stop green spot algae from covering the wide leaf surfaces? Wide, horizontal leaves act like solar panels under high light and quickly collect green spot algae if phosphate levels drop. Keep the plant out of direct high-PAR beams, maintain steady flow across the canopy, and wipe older leaves gently with a soft sponge during water changes.

Common Name: Horemanii Red Sword Echinodorus Horemanii Red is a spectacular variety of sword plant that can add some beautiful colors to your aquarium. New leaves tend to be completely red like the stem while older leaves turn greener while still retaining red outlines. Like most swords, they should be planted directly into the substrate. When using inert substrates such as sand or gravel, it is important to supplement the plants with root tabs as Echinodorus are heavy root feeders. The plant can be grown both emersed and submerged and often times, new leaves can grow to the top above the water line. Overall, this plant is easy and undemanding and very suitable for larger tanks. Notes: Echinodorus is a very hardy species of aquatic plants. Most Echinodorus require nutrient-dense soil to thrive as they are heavy root feeders. Echinodorus grow fairly large and are more suitable for larger planted aquariums. Do not make drastic changes to the aquarium. Unstable parameters will result in melt and rotting of the aquarium plant. Please be sure to remove this plant from its pot. Common Name: Cardinal Plant, Lobelia Cardinalis The Cardinal Plant (Lobelia cardinalis) is a versatile North American species that thrives in aquariums, paludariums, and terrariums, whether grown submerged or emersed. This unique plant works beautifully as a foreground or midground accent in your freshwater aquarium, and with the right care, it can even make a striking background feature when allowed to grow taller. In nature, it can be found growing along streams, rivers, and waterways. With sufficient height, it can even serve well in the background. Its submerged form showcases vibrant green foliage, occasionally tinged with red-purple on the leaf undersides, though this hue is more commonly observed in its emersed form. Notably, the Cardinal Plant is renowned for its striking red flowers that bloom from its emersed growth. To thrive, the Cardinal Plant requires moderate to high levels of lighting. Regular trimming of its tops allows for mat expansion, while proper care encourages the development of lush side shoot leaves. The addition of fertilizers can be advantageous in maintaining optimal coloration and overall plant health. Plant Profile Low-growing, spade-shaped green leaves form dense, bushy carpet mats that make Staurogyne Repens one of the most popular foreground and midground plants for aquascaping. Reaching a low-profile height of 1 to 3 inches, its stiff, branching stems stay close to the substrate, making it ideal for filling gaps around hardscape bases, creating foreground lawns, or trimming into clean midground hedges. While adaptable in standard conditions, providing moderate to high lighting along with pressurized CO2 keeps growth compact and prevents stems from stretching vertically. Key Features & Benefits Low-growing leaves branch horizontally to form dense foreground carpets and midground hedges. Popular aquascaping species valued for filling gaps around rocks and driftwood bases. Adapts smoothly to fully submerged aquariums or emersed growth in humid terrariums. Care & Planting Instructions Prep the plant by removing it from the pot and clearing all rockwool from the roots. Use fine-tip pinsettes to plant individual stems or small portions 0.5 to 1 inch apart into your aquarium soil to encourage horizontal branching across the substrate. Provide medium to high lighting and pressurized CO2 injection; consistent liquid fertilization rich in macro and micro nutrients supports thick leaf development and prevents leaf yellowing. Maintain stable water parameters to avoid leaf shedding or stem melt during the initial transition period. To propagate, trim vertical stem tops with sharp straight shears and replant the cuttings directly into your aquarium soil to extend your carpet coverage. As the vibrant, chartreuse sibling of classic Anubias Nana , this compact aquatic epiphyte proves you don't need a high-tech light setup to strike gold.
