Plant Profile Rotala Indica is a classic aquatic stem plant native to the rice paddies, wetlands, and slow-moving waterways of Southeast Asia and India. Historically prized by aquascapers for its clean architectural look, this species is characterized by thick, vertical stems lined with small, rounded, cup-like leaves that grow horizontally in opposite pairs. While its lower foliage maintains a vibrant, light-green color, the growing tips shift into soft pink, orange, and bright reddish tones under high-intensity lighting and fertilization. When planted in dense groupings toward the background or midground of a planted tank, routine pruning turns Rotala Indica into a dazzling, thick geometric hedge. *Form Notice: Photos display this plant in both its emersed (above-water) and submerged forms. Depending on nursery availability and seasonality, you may receive this plant in either form. Learn more about what to expect by reading our guide on Emersed vs. Submerged-Grown Aquatic Plants . Key Features & Benefits Sturdy vertical stems with rounded horizontal leaves provide clean structural symmetry and unique architectural texture. Growing leaf tips transition from light green into soft pink and reddish tones when provided with high lighting and iron supplementation. Care & Planting Instructions Remove lead weight and cotton wrap (or foam) surrounding the base, then strip the lower inch of foliage so bare stems anchor cleanly into soil without rotting. * Rotala leaves can be fragile, so handle stems with care during preparation. Use fine-tip pinsettes to push individual stems 1 to 2 inches into soil, spacing them about half an inch apart in the background or midground so light reaches lower foliage. Provide medium-to-high lighting. Adding pressurized CO2 and liquid iron fertilizers accelerates growth and triggers vibrant pinkish-red leaf tips. See our guide to growing red aquarium plants . Maintain stable water parameters and avoid sudden environmental shifts to prevent leaf melt or stem rotting. Trim stem tops with straight scissors once they reach the water surface to encourage new lateral shoots and create a dense, bushy hedge. Read our trimming & propagation guide for details. As new growth adapts, the plant will shed its rounded land leaves and sprout soft, colorful underwater foliage. Once new shoots develop, trim away old lower growth to encourage dense, bushy branching.

Species Profile Fire Red Cherry Shrimp ( Neocaridina davidi ) are a selectively bred, high-grade color morph that leaves ordinary wild-type translucency behind in favor of dense, opaque crimson shells. Unlike lower-grade cherries with patchy coloration, true Fire Reds carry uniform red coverage extending through their carapace, abdomen, and walking legs. They are classic planted tank favorites for good reason: their bold scarlet hue pops vividly against bright green carpeting plants, mosses, and dark hardscape. Beyond their looks, they are diligent biofilm pickers and algae grazers that safely scour delicate foliage and foreground runners without uprooting plants or damaging healthy leaves. Hardy and adaptable to standard tap water, they are easy to keep and breed, making them a staple for nano scapes and peaceful community layouts alike. **Note: All livestock orders will come carefully packaged with solid wall Styrofoam insulation and shipped via 1-day shipping only. No extra insulation needs to be added to your cart for your livestock. Key Features & Notes Dense, opaque red coverage extending through the carapace and legs contrasts sharply with green mosses and dark hardscape. Active, plant-safe scavenger that continuously grazes soft algae and biofilm without disrupting carpet runners. Hardy Neocaridina strain that adapts easily to standard tap water parameters and readily breeds in established setups. Care Specifications Maintain clean, well-filtered water with stable GH and KH levels to ensure problem-free molting cycles. Keep water parameters strictly free of copper-based medications or heavy metals. Supplement their diet with plant-based shrimp pellets, spirulina, and blanched vegetables to ensure proper minerals for molting when natural algae is low. Their semi-translucent bodies feature broken reddish-brown dashed lines and a pale dorsal stripe, making them subtle enough to blend into wood and stone without distracting from your hardscape. They are active scavengers that leave healthy live plants and carpets undisturbed, though their fearless feeding habits mean they will readily sprint off with whole sinking pellets right out from under your fish. **Note: All livestock orders will come carefully packaged with solid wall Styrofoam insulation and shipped via 1-day shipping only. Species Profile The Black Pinto is a freshwater shrimp known in the hobby as a "Taitibee," which is a “mischling” or crossbreed. Their lineage begins by crossing a Tiger Shrimp with a Taiwan Bee to produce a "Tibee." Breeders then cross that Tibee back to a Taiwan Bee to stabilize the Pinto pattern. This specific breeding results in three distinct visual patterns: Zebra (vertical stripes), Spotted Head (white dots on the cephalothorax), and Fancy (which includes the Cloud or Skunk patterns). Thus, they are a striking addition to any shrimp tank due to their bold color and unique markings. Because they are the product of intensive selective breeding, Black Pinto Shrimp are more sensitive to water fluctuations than standard freshwater shrimp. While they can be kept in smaller setups, it is best practice to use a shrimp aquarium of at least 25 gallons. A larger volume of water is easier to keep chemically stable, which is vital for their survival. They serve as an excellent "indicator species" for the overall health of your ecosystem. **Note: All livestock orders will come carefully packaged with solid wall Styrofoam insulation and shipped via 1-day shipping only. No additional insulation is needed for your livestock. Key Features & Notes Tank-raised Taitibee specimens exhibiting deep black and stark white Zebra or Spotted Head patterns. Hardy, beginner-friendly Neocaridina variety adapts smoothly to a wide range of water parameters. Highly prized choice as peaceful dwarf shrimp for aquariums looking for top-tier hybrid genetics and visual impact. Care Specifications Maintain stable, soft, acidic water chemistry using an active buffering substrate to support sensitive Caridina health. Keep water parameters strictly free of copper-based medications or heavy metals. Supplement their diet with plant-based shrimp pellets, spirulina, and blanched vegetables to ensure proper minerals for molting when natural algae is low. Plant Profile Despite its name, Anubias Minima grows 6–10 inches tall, bringing slender, wavy-edged leaves to the midground or background of an aquarium. Its upright shape offers a textural contrast to broad-leaf Anubias varieties, especially when nestled among driftwood branches or rock crevices. It thrives under low light without requiring CO₂ injection and transitions easily between submerged aquariums and humid emersed setups such as paludariums or terrariums. Key Features & Benefits Slender, lance-shaped foliage with ruffled, wavy margins provides dynamic textural contrast against smooth stones and broad leaves. Upright growth acts as a sleek midground accent without overpowering nano tanks or large layouts. Thick, leathery leaves deter plant-nibbling cichlids, goldfish, snails, and active dwarf shrimp. Care & Planting Instructions Prep the plant by removing it from the pot and clearing all rockwool from the roots. Attach to hardscape using aquarium‑safe glue or thread; keep the rhizome above substrate to prevent rot. Maintain stable conditions to support smooth acclimation and reduce leaf loss. Avoid intense light and ensure good water flow to prevent spot algae on slow‑growing leaves. CO₂ is optional but improves growth and leaf density. Plant Profile Ammania Gracilis is a large aquatic stem plant native to the tropical riverbanks and wetlands of West Africa. Known for its opposing, wavy-edged leaves that arch out from sturdy central stems, this species brings warm, sunset-hued color contrast to planted tanks. Depending on light levels and nutrient availability, its foliage shifts from pale olive-green to pink, salmon, and deep copper-red. Reaching 5 to 8+ inches in height, Ammania Gracilis works well as a midground centerpiece or background accent alongside bright green plants. *Form Notice: Photos display this plant in both its emersed (above-water) and submerged forms. Depending on nursery availability and seasonality, you may receive this plant in either form. Learn more about what to expect by reading our guide on Emersed vs. Submerged-Grown Aquatic Plants . Key Features & Benefits Elegantly arching, wavy-edged leaves display a vibrant blend of blushing pink, salmon, and deep copper-red. Versatile in submerged aquariums, open-top paludariums, and bog gardens, blooms purple flowers emersed. Care & Planting Instructions Remove lead weight (or pot) and cotton wrap (or foam) surrounding the roots, then strip lower foliage so bare stems anchor cleanly into soil without rotting. Use fine-tip pinsettes to push individual stems 1 to 2 inches into substrate, spacing them slightly apart so high light reaches lower leaves and prevents leaf shedding. Provide high-intensity lighting. Pressurized CO2 injection (25–30 ppm) alongside elevated phosphates, rich micronutrients/iron, and lean nitrates will yield the most vibrant pink and red leaf coloration. See our guide to growing red aquarium plants . Maintain stable water parameters and avoid sudden environmental shifts to prevent leaf melt or stem rotting. Trim main stem tops with straight scissors once stems reach the desired height, and replant trimmings directly into substrate to propagate and expand coverage. Read our trimming & propagation guide for details. Quick Facts Listed information should be treated as general guidelines only. Once new shoots take root, trim away old lower growth to encourage dense branching.

Plant Profile Micranthemum Umbrosum, or Giant Baby Tears, is a bright green aquatic stem plant native to the ponds, ditches, and damp soils of the southeastern United States and Central America that's basically Pearl Weed's bigger, bolder cousin. Tiny, perfectly round leaves grow in opposing pairs along delicate, creeping stems, and while it gets compared to Pearl Weed a lot, the rounder, larger leaves are what earned it the "Giant" in its name. Highly adaptable, it can be pruned frequently under strong light to form a lush foreground carpet, or left untrimmed to create soft, bushy midground and background accent mounds. *Form Notice: Photos display this plant in both its emersed (above-water) and submerged forms. Depending on nursery availability and seasonality, you may receive this plant in either form. Learn more about what to expect by reading our guide on Emersed vs. Submerged-Grown Aquatic Plants . Key Features & Benefits Round, bright-green leaves add fine texture and color contrast to foreground and midground zones. Trains into a low foreground carpet with pruning, or grows tall as a bushy background stem. Beginner-friendly alternative to more demanding foreground carpet plants. Care & Planting Instructions Remove lead weight (or pot) and cotton wrap (or foam) surrounding the roots, then strip lower foliage so bare stems anchor cleanly into soil without rotting. Use fine-tip pinsettes to plant small stem bundles 1 inch apart into substrate, ensuring other taller foliage does not shade them out. Provide moderate-to-high lighting and clean water conditions; while adaptable without CO2, supplying pressurized CO2 (6–14 ppm) and strong lighting yields much denser, horizontal creeping growth. Maintain stable water parameters and avoid sudden environmental shifts to prevent leaf melt or stem rotting. Trim stem tops with curved scissors to shape into desired mounds or carpets, and replant trimmings directly into substrate to propagate and expand coverage. Plant Profile The Banana Plant is a charmingly distinct floating plant with rounded, heart-shaped leaves anchored by a cluster of swollen green tubers that look just like a tiny bunch of bananas. What makes these aquarium floaters so versatile is their dual nature: you can leave them to float freely on the water surface or gently rest them on your substrate to anchor as midground accents. Left to float, their long stems quickly shoot upward to form a canopy of miniature lily pads across the top of your tank, occasionally even blossoming with delicate white flowers. That makes them a fantastic, resilient choice for community aquariums, low-tech scapes, and paludariums where their vibrant green tubers pop dramatically against dark substrate. Key Features & Benefits Banana-shaped tuber clusters create an eye-catching focal point near the substrate or floating at the surface. Fast-growing lily pad canopy provides a soothing overhead shade layer that helps keep nuisance algae in check. Absorbs excess nitrates and biological waste to support a healthy water column. Care & Planting Instructions Rest the banana tubers directly on top of your substrate, ensuring you do not bury them more than 1/4 an inch deep to prevent tuber rot. If left to float freely on the surface, the plant will naturally grow white roots that reach downward toward the substrate to anchor itself. Keep water movement calm and gentle, as heavy turbulence or rapid filter currents can disrupt leaf growth and stem stability. Prune surface leaves occasionally with sharp aquascaping scissors to prevent the floating lily pads from completely blocking light to plants below. Propagate new plants by letting trimmed leaves float on the water surface until tiny roots and brand-new tubers begin to sprout. How do I properly plant my Banana Plant into the substrate without killing the tubers? Never fully bury the green "banana" tubers under your soil or gravel, as burying them completely will cause them to rot. Simply set the plant on top of the substrate or press the tubers no deeper than a quarter-inch into the top layer. The plant will naturally send down long, white anchoring roots into the substrate on its own. 2. Can I propagate new Banana Plants from leaf trimmings? Yes, propagating Banana Plants is surprisingly easy. When you trim off long stems or surface leaves to keep the canopy under control, allow those cut leaves to float freely on the water surface. Over time, adventitious roots and miniature green tubers will sprout directly from the leaf base, giving you brand-new plants. 3. Why is my Banana Plant sending up long stems with pads to the surface? This is a natural growth habit of Nymphoides aquatica as it seeks light. It sends pad-like leaves straight up to the surface to capture carbon dioxide and light, acting just like a miniature lily pad. If you prefer a shorter, bushier look near the substrate, simply trim those long surface-bound stems at the base.

Plant Profile Dwarf Sagittaria (Sagittaria subulata) brings that fresh‑cut‑lawn energy straight into your tank. This hobby‑favorite foreground plant adds subtle depth to your layout, but it’s versatile enough to stretch into the midground or even background of your aquascape when it’s feeling extra ambitious. Its bright green, wide blades mimic those dreamy riverbank vibes while doubling as a cozy hideout for shrimp and nano fish. It grows happily emersed or submersed, and once it matures, it can even reach the surface and pop out tiny white flowers. Key Features & Benefits Wide green blades function as a low-tech foreground carpet or midground accent. Hardy species that adapts to hard water conditions where softer plants might fail. Provides foraging ground, shelter, and security for baby fish, dwarf shrimp, and nano inhabitants. Care & Planting Instructions Plant into your substrate and let it readily send out runners to produce a thick, effortless carpet on its own. Maintain moderate to high lighting, keeping in mind that higher light keeps growth compact, while lower light encourages it to grow taller toward the surface. Supplement with iron and root fertilizers if you notice the leaves turning a sickly yellow, as this species is a heavy root-feeder. Plant Profile If your background layout needs a sense of tranquil flow and dramatic texture, Cryptocoryne balansae creates a stunning canopy that commands attention. Hailing from the fast-flowing, limestone-rich rivers of Southern Thailand, this impressive species has long been a favorite for its towering height and distinctive, heavily puckered (bullated) leaf texture. Its long, ribbon-like leaves stream elegantly in the water current, creating a dynamic backdrop that contrasts beautifully against rigid hardscape materials. As with all crypt plants, this species can be sensitive to changes in water parameters and strongly objects to being relocated once planted. Give it a permanent home at the rear of your tank, however, and its extensive root system will lock in to support healthy, long-lasting foliage that fish love to explore. Key Features & Benefits Tall, bullate ribbon-like foliage delivers dynamic movement and a commanding texture to your background layout. Adapts to emersed high-humidity paludarium displays where mature plants can bloom. Native riverine history makes it tolerant of hard water, providing hideouts for larger community fish. Care & Planting Instructions Prep the plant by removing it from the pot and clearing all rockwool from the roots . Use fine-tip pinsettes to push roots deep into quality aquarium soil, as Crypt species are heavy root feeders. Insert root tab fertilizers if using an inert substrate like sand or gravel. Provide a calcium supplement to prevent new foliage from growing twisted or deformed because this species originates from high-limestone environments. Provide moderate to high lighting to achieve the attractive puckering effect on the leaves and bring out potential bronze tints. Inject pressurized CO2 for faster growth, though not required for long-term health. Choose a permanent spot from day one; moving an established plant will likely trigger leaf loss. Cryptocoryne species can be grown emersed in high-humidity setups or submerged in aquariums. Propagate by splitting the rhizome or replanting new growth shoots. Don't discard the plant if leaves dissolve early on; see our guide to managing Cryptocoryne melt to help your plant recover smoothly. Reaching 10 to 24 inches tall, its foliage shifts from bright emerald green to rich olive and bronze tones under moderate lighting. As with all crypt plants, it can be sensitive to sudden parameter shifts and strongly objects to being relocated once planted. Plant Profile Echinodorus 'Rose' is a cultivated sword plant popular in freshwater aquascaping. Native to tropical regions of the Western Hemisphere through its parent lineage, this hybrid is characterized by wide, oblong leaves with wavy edges and visible leaf veins. Newly emerging leaves display pink and bronze colors before maturing to bright green and dark olive-green as they age. Its substantial footprint allows it to function as a bold midground centerpiece in larger aquariums or a sweeping background accent in medium layouts. Because it thrives in low to moderate lighting without requiring CO2, it is a beginner-friendly and low-tech plant choice for adding color to a planted tank. Key Features & Benefits Foliage shifts color from pink and bronze on new leaves to dark green on mature growth. Broad leaf structure provides coverage and structural focal points in midground and background areas. Hardy rosette growth adapts to a range of water conditions and low-tech tank setups. Care & Planting Instructions Prep the plant by removing it from the pot and clearing all rockwool from the roots. Plant the roots into your aquarium soil, ensuring the central crown remains positioned just above the substrate line to avoid root rot. All Echinodorus are heavy root feeders that rely on rich substrate nutrition; placing root tabs near the base supports steady, healthy leaf development. Provide low to moderate lighting; while CO2 is not required, supplying moderate light and liquid iron supplements helps highlight the pink and bronze tones on young leaves. See our guide to growing red aquarium plants . Maintain stable water parameters to prevent leaf shedding during the initial transition period. To propagate submerged plants, allow runner shoots to develop off the main plant, then separate rooted plantlets and replant them directly into your aquarium soil. Plant Profile Unlike massive background swords that threaten to breach the waterline, Echinodorus xinguensis , commonly known as the Xingu Sword or Dwarf Amazon Sword, brings classic sword plant structure down to a manageable scale. Native to South America, this uncommon species maxes out around 12 inches tall, making it a versatile midground centerpiece or foreground accent in medium-to-large aquariums. Its bright green leaves look like a bold, lush grass with distinct structural depth. Naturally hardy and forgiving, it offers a refreshing alternative to standard foreground species without demanding complex high-tech equipment. Key Features & Notes Compact scale allows flexible placement in midground and foreground zones. Hardy species that adapt smoothly across a wide range of water parameters without mandatory CO2. Care & Planting Instructions Prep the plant by removing it from the pot and clearing all rockwool from the roots. Plant individual crowns into your aquarium soil, making sure the root crown rests just above the substrate line to prevent rot. All Echinodorus are heavy root feeders that rely on rich substrate nutrition; placing root tabs near the base supports steady growth and vibrant leaf color. Plant Profile Echinodorus bleheri, aka the classic Amazon Sword, is one of the most popular and recognizable species in the freshwater aquarium hobby. It has vibrant, bright-to-deep green lanceolate foliage that arches outward in a full, symmetrical rosette. Each leaf features strong parallel venation and subtle, rippled margins, creating an architectural fan of greenery that anchors the background of planted tanks. First popularized in the mid-20th century under old trade names like Echinodorus paniculatus, it helped shape early aquascaping and remains a timeless staple across community aquariums worldwide. Thanks to its historical roots, timeless aesthetic, and forgiving nature under low-tech setups, it remains a quintessential favorite among aquarium plants for beginners. Key Features & Notes Classic lanceolate green foliage with prominent veins creates a lush backdrop. Growth habit offers extensive coverage to fill open space in medium-to-large tanks. An adaptable species that thrives across a wide range of water parameters without mandatory CO2. Care & Planting Instructions Prep the plant by removing it from the pot and clearing all rockwool from the roots. Plant the roots deeply into your aquarium soil, keeping the central crown resting just above the substrate line to prevent rot. All Echinodorus are heavy root feeders that rely on rich substrate nutrition; placing root tabs near the base supports steady, healthy leaf development. CO2 injection is optional, but it will encourage faster leaf production and denser foliage. Maintain stable water parameters to prevent leaf shedding during the initial transition period. Sword plants propagate through side shoots off of their leaves, which can be trimmed and replanted into the substrate. To control the size of your sword plant, you can remove the side shoots and older leaves. Final size and leaf shape depend on whether the plant is grown fully submerged or emersed; please note that individual plants may vary based on tank conditions. Why are the leaves on my new Echinodorus melting or turning yellow? Sword plants are often grown emersed and shed their old emersed leaves when submerged to adapt to underwater growth. Keep water parameters stable and supply root tabs near the base to support new leaves.

Unlike its massive Amazon Sword cousins, this species stays manageable in size, making it easier to place in midground groupings or serve as part of a layered planted tank background in smaller aquariums. As a hardy and forgiving grower, it stands as a wonderful option among aquarium plants for beginners who want the classic sword plant aesthetic without overwhelming their tank space. Key Features & Notes Hammered leaf texture and strong venation create an eye-catching visual focal point against smoother aquatic flora. Plant the roots deeply into your aquarium soil, keeping the central crown resting just above the substrate line to prevent rot. Plant Profile The Red Rubin Sword ( Echinodorus 'Red Rubin' ) is a popular hybridization that stands out with large, oval leaves that feature slightly wavy edges, prominent golden leaf veins, and an incredible color palette ranging from warm gold and olive-green to deep purple and fiery red. Reaching an impressive height of 10 to 24 inches, it rapidly becomes a majestic backdrop or centerpiece in medium to large aquariums. Extremely hardy and easy to care for, the Red Rubin Sword is a fantastic, adaptable choice for aquascapers looking to create sweeping contrast behind smaller green stem plants and ground covers in a planted tank. Key Features & Benefits Broad, wavy foliage displays a rich mix of gold, red, purple, and deep green hues with distinct golden leaf veins. Hardy, fast-growing background plant that provides magnificent visual structure in larger display tanks. Adaptable and low-maintenance species that thrives under a wide variety of lighting and water conditions. Care & Planting Instructions Prep the plant by removing it from the pot and clearing all rockwool from the roots. Plant the roots deeply into your aquarium soil, keeping the crown of the plant resting just above the substrate surface to prevent rot. All Echinodorus are heavy root feeders that rely on rich substrate nutrition; placing root tabs near the base supports steady, healthy leaf development. Provide moderate lighting; while CO2 injection isn't strictly required, regular liquid iron supplementation and good lighting will enhance its deep ruby-red and purple colors. Avoid using copper-based medications in tanks containing Echinodorus species, as sword plants are particularly sensitive to copper. To propagate, look for adventitious daughter plantlets forming along flowering runners or side shoots; once they sprout small roots, snip them off and plant them directly into your aquarium soil. Echinodorus species are heavy root feeders that draw the vast majority of their nutrients through their extensive root system rather than the water column. Supplementing your aquarium soil with root tabs every few months ensures strong root anchorages and bright, vibrant red foliage.

Plant Profile Rotala Macrandra Mini Pink is a dramatic, high-demand stem plant known for its compact size and striking deep pink-to-red foliage. Highly favored for midground and background placement in high-tech aquascapes, its delicate leaves provide an exceptional visual contrast alongside green aquatic plants. When provided with strong lighting, soft acidic water, and pressurized CO2, Rotala Macrandra Mini Pink grows rapidly into a vibrant, bushy focal point. *Form Notice: Photos display this plant in both its emersed (above-water) and submerged forms. Depending on nursery availability and seasonality, you may receive this plant in either form. Learn more about what to expect by reading our guide on Emersed vs. Submerged-Grown Aquatic Plants . Key Features & Benefits Delivers intense magenta and bright red coloration. Fast-growing stems form dense, bushy midground clusters when provided with optimal light and nutrient levels. Care & Planting Instructions Remove lead weight and cotton wrap (or foam) surrounding the base, then strip the lower inch of foliage so bare stems anchor cleanly into soil without rotting. * Rotala has fragile leaves, so handle stems with care during preparation. Use fine-tip pinsettes to push individual stems 1 to 2 inches into soil, spacing them apart so light reaches lower foliage and prevents leaf loss. Provide high-intensity lighting and pressurized CO2 (15–25 ppm) in soft, acidic water (pH 5.0–7.0). Maintain low nitrates with high phosphates and iron dosing to trigger brilliant red color and prevent pale or white-spotted leaves. See our guide to growing red aquarium plants . Maintain stable water parameters and avoid sudden environmental shifts to prevent leaf melt or rotting. Trim the leafy, robust top half with straight scissors once stems reach the surface and replant into the substrate to encourage dense branching. Read our trimming & propagation guide for details. As new growth adapts, the plant will shed its rounded green land leaves and sprout delicate, deep pink-red underwater foliage. Once new shoots develop, trim away old lower growth to encourage dense, bushy branching.

Plant Profile Ludwigia Inclinata is a high-tech aquatic stem plant native to the tropical wetlands and river margins of Central and South America. Prized for its dramatic coloration and unique wavy leaf texture, its submerged foliage displays a stunning mix of vivid gold, warm orange, and fiery red hues along supple central stems. Fast-growing and voluminous, it easily reaches 6 to 20 inches in height. Best suited for experienced aquascapers, Ludwigia Inclinata requires high-intensity lighting, pressurized CO2, soft acidic water, and rich micronutrient dosing (especially iron) to maintain its vivid red and gold tones. Positioned in the midground or background of larger aquariums, its colorful, branching growth forms a showstopping centerpiece. *Form Notice: Photos display this plant in both its emersed (above-water) and submerged forms. Depending on nursery availability and seasonality, you may receive this plant in either form. Learn more about what to expect by reading our guide on Emersed vs. Submerged-Grown Aquatic Plants . Key Features & Benefits Dramatic foliage displays a vibrant spectrum of gold, orange, and ruby-red with wavy-edged leaves. Fast-growing stem species that branches readily after pruning to create thick, high-contrast midground or background bushes. High-tech collector plant that adds exceptional visual depth and color pop alongside lush green aquatic species. Care & Planting Instructions Remove lead weight and cotton wrap (or foam) surrounding the base, then strip the lower inch of foliage so bare stems anchor cleanly into soil without rotting. * Ludwigia stems and leaves are fragile, so handle stems with care during preparation. Use fine-tip pinsettes to insert individual stems 1 to 2 inches deep into nutrient-rich aquarium soil. Provide high-intensity lighting and pressurized CO2 injection; consistent liquid fertilization rich in iron and essential micronutrients brings out the deepest red and gold hues. See our guide to growing red aquarium plants . Maintain stable water parameters and soft, slightly acidic conditions to prevent stem melting or leaf shedding. To propagate, trim main stem tops with sharp straight shears and replant trimmings directly into substrate. Read our trimming & propagation guide for details. Plant Profile Ludwigia Natans Super Red is an easy-to-keep, fast-growing midground and background stem plant known for its intense bright red coloration and small, round, pointed leaves. Highly favored for adding movement and dimension to aquascapes, this species adds immediate visual depth and contrast. When provided with high lighting and nutrient-rich water, Super Red Ludwigia rapidly branches into dense, bushy clusters that look especially attractive when planted in groups of 10 to 12 stems. *Form Notice: Photos display this plant in both its emersed (above-water) and submerged forms. Depending on nursery availability and seasonality, you may receive this plant in either form. Learn more about what to expect by reading our guide on Emersed vs. Submerged-Grown Aquatic Plants . Key Features & Benefits Leaf color shifts from olive green under low light to fire-engine red under high-intensity LED lighting and elevated iron levels. Beginner-friendly care with striking visual contrast in both high-tech and low-tech setups. Care & Planting Instructions Remove lead weight and cotton wrap (or foam) surrounding the base, then strip the lower inch of foliage so bare stems anchor cleanly into soil without rotting. * Ludwigia can be very fragile. Be sure to handle this aquarium plant with care. Use fine-tip pinsettes to push stems 1–2 inches into soil, spacing them apart for light penetration. Provide medium-to-high light. Adding pressurized CO2 accelerates growth, yields thicker stems, and maximizes red pigmentation. See our guide to growing red aquarium plants . Maintain stable water parameters and avoid drastic environmental changes to prevent leaf melt or rotting in fragile stems. Trim stem tops with straight scissors once they reach the surface to promote branching. Read our trimming & propagation guide for details. Unlike most Ludwigia that stick to growing leaves in opposite pairs, this rebel sprouts alternating oval leaves that shift through a whole sunset palette of gold, orange, pink, and red depending on your tank setup. Plant a dense bunch of 10 to 12 stems together in your midground or foreground, and you’ll instantly get a vibrant, head-turning focal point with minimal effort. *Form Notice: Photos display this plant in both its emersed (above-water) and submerged forms. While CO2 injection is not strictly required, it yields richer red coloration. See our guide to growing red aquarium plants . Plant Profile Diamond Ludwigia is a stem plant that takes its name as a personal challenge to be the most eye-catching thing in your tank. Even in a lower-tech setup, it shows up with olive-to-golden leaf tops and ruby-red undersides, adding depth to the midground without breaking a sweat. Give it high-intensity lighting, pressurized CO2, and iron supplementation, though, and it goes all in, turning into a deep, saturated purplish-red centerpiece that refuses to share the spotlight. Cluster 10 to 12 stems together, and you get a centerpiece that makes every green plant nearby look like it's just there for contrast. *Form Notice: Photos display this plant in both its emersed (above-water) and submerged forms. Depending on nursery availability and seasonality, you may receive this plant in either form. Learn more about what to expect by reading our guide on Emersed vs. Submerged-Grown Aquatic Plants . Produces delicate yellow flowers when cultivated in emersed setups or paludariums. Use fine-tip pinsettes to push stems 1–2 inches into soil, spacing them apart for light penetration. Provide high-intensity lighting. Pressurized CO2 injection and regular liquid iron dosing are highly recommended to yield optimal growth and bring out its brilliant ruby and purplish-red tones. See our guide to growing red aquarium plants . Maintain stable water parameters and avoid sudden environmental shifts to prevent leaf melt or stem rotting. Trim main stem tops with straight scissors once stems reach the desired height, and replant trimmings directly into substrate to propagate and expand your bush. Plant Profile Ludwigia Sedioides, commonly known as the Mosaic Plant, is a truly one-of-a-kind floating aquatic plant native to Central and South America. Living up to its name, its diamond‑shaped green leaves radiate from a central stem in a perfect mandala rosette that drifts across the surface like living tilework. The plant even has a day‑night routine: rosettes open wide during the day and fold slightly at night, as if it’s clocking out. In warm water with high light, it produces charming yellow, buttercup‑like flowers that elevate open‑top aquariums, ponds, and container water gardens with a little extra flourish. A large tank is needed to accommodate the 3-5” width of mosaic plants, especially because they will cut off light to anything underneath them. *Form Notice: Photos display this plant in both its emersed (above-water) and submerged forms. Depending on nursery availability and seasonality, you may receive this plant in either form. Learn more about what to expect by reading our guide on Emersed vs. Submerged-Grown Aquatic Plants . Key Features & Benefits Floating rosettes form geometric, mandala‑like patterns. Color‑shifting foliage produces bright buttercup‑yellow flowers in warm conditions. Day–night leaf movement opens during peak light and folds slightly at night. Care & Planting Instructions Remove lead weight and cotton wrap (or foam) surrounding the base, taking care not to snap the long main stem connected to the floating rosette. * Ludwigia Sedioides stems are fragile, so handle with care during preparation. Anchor the rooted lower stem 1 to 2 inches into aquarium soil using fine-tip pinsettes, allowing the rosette stem to reach vertically so leaves rest flat on the water surface. Provide high-intensity lighting and warm water temperatures; strong lighting is required for compact mandala formatting, vibrant red leaf edges, and flowering. Keep water movement calm at the surface so the floating rosettes stay upright and avoid being pushed under filter outlets. Trim elongated lower stems with straight scissors or harvest side shoots once rosettes fill the surface area to ensure lower submerged plants still receive adequate light. Read our trimming & propagation guide for details. Quick Facts Listed information should be treated as general guidelines only. listings.commonName: Christmas Moss and Java Fern on Driftwood
listings.description: Plant Profile This plug-and-play aquarium plant decor is moss-definitely the easiest way to upgrade your tank! We have pre-attached a lush, velvety coat of classic Christmas Moss and a hardy, broad-leafed Java Fern directly onto a beautiful piece of natural driftwood. Because both of these low-light legends are famously bulletproof and practically care for themselves, you get to drop a mature, established piece straight into your tank. It provides a fantastic, highly textured sanctuary where shy fish and dwarf shrimp can safely forage. Key Features & Benefits Pre-attached to natural wood to bypass the planting stage and anchor an instant two-in-one focal point. Combines feathery, tree-like moss fronds with bold Java Fern leaves for maximum visual contrast and depth. Natural driftwood releases beneficial tannins that help soften water and create a natural tropical habitat. Care & Planting Instructions Position the driftwood piece directly onto your substrate or nestle it securely into your hardscape layout, keeping the thick green Java Fern rhizome completely exposed to the water column to prevent rot. Maintain a stable aquarium environment and avoid sudden, drastic changes to your water parameters to keep both plants looking vibrant and healthy. Give the moss an occasional light haircut with sharp aquascaping shears to keep its shape neat, compact, and perfectly balanced. Propagate by cutting the Java Fern rhizome or snipping off small clumps of thriving moss to attach elsewhere in your tank. Position the plant in partial shade under taller stem plants or hardscape overhangs, ensure moderate water circulation, and avoid photoperiods longer than 8 hours. 3. Can Anubias Barteri survive in cichlid or goldfish aquariums? Yes. Anubias Barteri is one of the top recommended live plants for African cichlid, South American cichlid, and goldfish tanks. Its thick, fibrous leaves and bitter taste naturally discourage herbivorous fish from tearing or eating the foliage, and mounting the rhizome directly to heavy rocks prevents fish from uprooting it.

Use sharp curved shears to make clean cuts, and immediately scoop or siphon out floating cuttings so they don't take root in unwanted areas of your aquarium.

Plant Profile Bacopa Amplexicaulis, known in the aquarium hobby as Lemon Bacopa or Carolina Bacopa, is a hardy aquatic stem plant native to the ponds, marshes, and riverbanks of the Southeastern United States. Named for the pleasant citrus aroma released when its leaves or stems are crushed or pruned, this perennial species features thick, fleshy oval leaves set in opposing pairs along vertical stems. Under moderate lighting, it displays a bright lime-green coloration, but when grown under high light or low phosphate levels, its foliage blushes with attractive bronze, copper, and soft pink highlights. Perfect for beginners, Lemon Bacopa thrives submerged in aquariums or emersed in paludariums, where it produces tiny, vibrant purple and blue flowers above the water surface. *Form Notice: Photos display this plant in both its emersed (above-water) and submerged forms. Depending on nursery availability and seasonality, you may receive this plant in either form. Learn more about what to expect by reading our guide on Emersed vs. Submerged-Grown Aquatic Plants . Key Features & Benefits Thick, oval foliage emits a lemon scent when trimmed or crushed. Beginner-friendly, thrives in low-tech setups without requiring CO2 injection. Foliage blushes bronze, copper, and pink under high-intensity lighting or low phosphate. Care & Planting Instructions Remove lead weight (or pot) and cotton wrap (or foam) surrounding the roots, then strip lower foliage so bare stems anchor cleanly into soil without rotting. * Bacopa stems and leaves can be crisp, so handle with care during preparation. Use fine-tip pinsettes to push individual stems 1 to 2 inches into substrate, spacing them slightly apart so light reaches lower growth. Provide moderate-to-high lighting and clean water conditions; regular fertilization with liquid products like UNS Plant Food encourages thick stems and vibrant color transitions. See our guide to growing colorful aquarium plants . Maintain stable water parameters and avoid sudden environmental shifts to prevent leaf melt or stem rotting. Trim main stem tops with straight scissors once stems reach the desired height, and replant trimmings directly into substrate to easily propagate and expand coverage. Read our trimming & propagation guide for details. Quick Facts Listed information should be treated as general guidelines only. Team Buce Plant encourages you to do thorough research to ensure healthy growth! As new growth adapts, the plant will shed its stiffer land foliage and sprout soft, brightly colored underwater leaves. Once new shoots take root, trim away old lower growth to encourage dense branching.

Plant Profile Bacopa Monnieri, or Moneywort, is a classic, hardy aquatic stem plant favored for its upright stalks paired with light green, rounded leaves. A staple in the planted tank hobby and historically valued in the Ayurvedic tradition of India, Moneywort brings a cheerful, structured accent to the midground and background of any layout. When grown emersed or above the waterline, it even sprouts small, delicate pink and white flowers. Key Features & Benefits Hardy stem plant adapts easily to low-tech setups without requiring CO2. Upright growth creates clean vertical lines and light green contrast in midground or background zones. Do you like variegated plants? Check out Bacopa Monnieri Variegatus . Care & Planting Instructions Remove lead weight and cotton wrap (or foam) surrounding the base, then strip the lower inch of foliage so bare stems anchor cleanly into soil without rotting. * Bacopa leaves can be fragile, so handle stems with care during planting. Use fine-tip pinsettes to push individual stems 1 to 2 inches into substrate, spacing them apart so light reaches lower foliage and prevents stem rot. Provide moderate-to-high lighting for steady growth, as lower leaves will rot if shaded out or kept under insufficient light. Maintain stable water parameters and supply quality aquarium soil or liquid fertilizers to support healthy root formation. Trim stem tops with straight scissors once they reach the water surface to encourage new lateral side branches. Read our trimming & propagation guide for details. Plant Profile Echinodorus 'Ozelot Green' is a classic, colorful hybrid sword plant created by crossing Echinodorus 'Leopard' and Echinodorus barthii. Known for its compact rosette habit and broad leaf shape, it produces bright lime to olive green leaves speckled with dark reddish-brown spots that stand out on new growth. Maxing out around 18 inches tall, it provides lush coverage across the background of medium setups or serves as a solid midground centerpiece in larger tanks. It isn't picky about water parameters, making it an easygoing choice for aquascapers looking for bold pattern contrast without high-maintenance demands. Key Features & Notes Broad, bright green leaves decorated with dark reddish-brown spotted markings. Compact rosette structure provides full, dense coverage for midground or background zones. Hardy hybrid variety that adapts easily across a wide range of low-tech and high-tech tank conditions. Care & Planting Instructions Prep the plant by removing it from the pot and clearing all rockwool from the roots. Plant the roots deeply into your aquarium soil, keeping the central crown resting just above the substrate line to prevent rot. All Echinodorus are heavy root feeders that rely on rich substrate nutrition; placing root tabs near the base supports steady, healthy leaf development. Supplemental CO2 injection accelerates growth and encourages denser, fuller foliage, though the plant will still grow steadily in low-tech setups. Maintain stable water parameters to prevent leaf shedding during the initial transition period. Sword plants propagate through side shoots off of their leaves, which can be trimmed and replanted into the substrate. To control the size of your sword plant, you can remove the side shoots and older leaves. Quick Facts Listed information should be treated as general guidelines only. Plant Profile Christmas Moss on Driftwood is a classic live freshwater aquarium moss pre-attached to a natural driftwood log, offering an instant hardscape accent for planted aquariums. This popular aquatic moss features distinct triangular, fir-like fronds that overlap into dense, deep-green foliage. This setup eliminates the need for plant glue or thread, allowing aquascapers to easily establish a mature, woodland-style centerpiece. Key Features & Benefits Pre-attached moss on natural driftwood creates an instant, organic midground centerpiece with zero adhesives required. Triangular evergreen frond structure combines with natural wood grain to create a mature, aged forest aesthetic. Dense moss canopy provides shade, shelter, and continuous biofilm grazing for freshwater dwarf shrimp and fry. Care & Planting Instructions Place the driftwood piece directly onto your substrate or position it within your hardscape layout wherever you need a natural green focal point. Maintain a stable aquarium environment and avoid sudden water parameter swings to keep your live moss vibrant and healthy. Give the moss fronds an occasional light haircut with sharp aquascaping shears to maintain a compact, bushy shape. Propagate by snipping excess growth or pulling small clumps apart and securing them to new hardscape surfaces throughout your tank. Optionally supply CO2 injection and low-to-medium LED lighting to accelerate growth rate and enhance foliage density. Quick Facts Listed information should be treated as general guidelines only. Plant Profile Low-growing, spade-shaped green leaves form dense, bushy carpet mats that make Staurogyne Repens one of the most popular foreground and midground plants for aquascaping. Reaching a low-profile height of 1 to 3 inches, its stiff, branching stems stay close to the substrate, making it ideal for filling gaps around hardscape bases, creating foreground lawns, or trimming into clean midground hedges. While adaptable in standard conditions, providing moderate to high lighting along with pressurized CO2 keeps growth compact and prevents stems from stretching vertically. Tissue Culture cups ensure your aquascape gets a super clean starting point. Lab‑grown and fully sterile, it arrives without pests, snails, duckweed, or any unwanted algae. It’s the go‑to option for anyone who wants peace of mind when adding fresh greenery to a carefully maintained setup. Key Features & Benefits Low-growing leaves branch horizontally to form dense foreground carpets and midground hedges. Popular aquascaping species valued for filling gaps around rocks and driftwood bases. Adapts smoothly to fully submerged aquariums or emersed growth in humid terrariums. Care & Planting Instructions Thoroughly wash away the nutrient gel from the roots with your fingers before parting it out into manageable portions. Use fine-tip pinsettes to plant individual stems or small portions 0.5 to 1 inch apart into your aquarium soil to encourage horizontal branching across the substrate. Provide medium to high lighting and pressurized CO2 injection; consistent liquid fertilization rich in macro and micro nutrients supports thick leaf development and prevents leaf yellowing. Maintain stable water parameters to avoid leaf shedding or stem melt during the initial transition period. To propagate, trim vertical stem tops with sharp straight shears and replant the cuttings directly into your aquarium soil to extend your carpet coverage. Why is my Staurogyne Repens growing tall instead of forming a carpet? Staurogyne Repens stretches vertically toward the surface when light levels are too low or when stems are planted too closely together. Use sharp aquascaping shears to trim the stem tops down to 1–2 inches from the substrate. Regular top trimming prompts the lower leaf nodes to sprout multiple lateral shoots, building a tight, bushy bush along the foreground.

listings.description: Plant Profile Micro Sword is an excellent foreground plant for beginners trying their hand at growing a carpeting plant for the very first time. When planted densely in groups toward the front of an aquarium, it creates a gorgeous, wild, grass-like effect that brings a highly natural impression to your layout. Over time, it will fill in to form a lush, flowing carpet that sways beautifully in the current. Thanks to its dense growth profile, this plant is incredibly versatile, working just as well as a compact midground accent or even a background filler in smaller nano aquariums. Tissue Culture cups ensure your aquascape gets a super clean starting point. Lab‑grown and fully sterile, it arrives without pests, snails, duckweed, or any unwanted algae. It’s the go‑to option for anyone who wants peace of mind when adding fresh greenery to a carefully maintained setup. Key Features & Benefits A beginner-friendly species that is highly forgiving for first-time carpet growers. Create a wild, flowing, grass-like lawn effect that adds movement and texture to your foreground. Care & Planting Instructions To get that iconic, tight, short-statured grass lawn look, simply pair it with high lighting and a steady supply of CO2. Give this plant room to spread naturally, as it grows by sending out runners horizontally throughout the substrate. Keep the growth short and compact by maintaining high light and CO2 parameters, creating a manicured underwater lawn of green. Propagate simply like other foreground plants by cutting out portions from the horizontal shoots and replanting the clumps that you cut out. Master the prep and planting process by checking out a beginner's guide to tissue culture plants to prevent your delicate new plantlets from melting or floating away. Quick Facts Listed information should be treated as general guidelines only. Team Buce Plant encourages you to do thorough research to ensure healthy growth! How do I plant Micro Sword tissue culture? Rinse away the nutrient gel under cool water, divide the mat into small portions containing 4–6 blades each, and use pinsettes to insert each clump deep into fine aquasoil spaced 1 inch apart. 2. Why is my Micro Sword growing tall instead of staying low? Micro Sword stretches its leaf blades upward in lower lighting setups as it reaches for light. Increasing your light intensity and supplying pressurized CO2 forces the plant to produce shorter, thicker blades and spread horizontally via runners. 3. How long does it take for Micro Sword to form a dense carpet? With medium-to-high light, pressurized CO2, and nutrient-rich soil, runner spreading typically begins within 2–3 weeks, filling in a unified lawn in about 6 to 10 weeks.

Plant Profile Distinguished by its satiny texture and distinct mottled foliage, Piptospatha Ridleyi features broad green leaves covered in a random array of contrasting spots that form a striking, natural camouflage pattern. At a mature height of 4 to 8 inches, this rare plant easily steals the show in the midground. It's ideal for filling that tricky middle gap in your tank, blending smaller foreground plants seamlessly into taller background greenery. Like its close relatives Bucephalandra and Homalomena, it is a flowering species that thrives attached to porous stone or wood rather than buried in substrate, expanding via thick creeping rhizomes in both submerged aquariums and humid paludariums. Tissue culture cups ensure your aquascape gets a super clean starting point. Lab-grown and fully sterile, it arrives without pests, snails, duckweed, or any unwanted algae. It’s the go-to option for anyone who wants peace of mind when adding fresh greenery to a carefully maintained setup. Key Features & Notes The unique foliage displays random variegated spots in various shades of green, giving it a distinctive camouflage pattern. Like Bucephalandra and Anubias, it is a flowering Aroid that thrives in areas with strong, consistent water flow. Care & Planting Instructions Prep the plant by carefully removing the plantlets from the cup and rinsing away all sterile nutrient gel under lukewarm, dechlorinated water before mounting. Piptospatha is an epiphytic plant that should be attached to rocks or driftwood using aquarium-safe glue or thread; never bury the horizontal rhizome in substrate, as this will cause the plant to rot and melt. Avoid making drastic changes to your water parameters or lighting because unstable conditions are the primary cause of leaf melt in new specimens. While this plant is hardy and low-maintenance in standard low-light aquarium plant setups, CO2 injection and regular liquid fertilizing will yield much faster growth and a smoother tissue culture transition. Why is my tissue culture Piptospatha melting after planting? Tissue culture plants undergo an acclimation phase when transitioning to underwater conditions. Maintain stable water parameters, good circulation, and moderate light; as long as the rhizome stays firm, new submerged leaves will emerge. 3. Can tissue culture Piptospatha be planted in substrate? Yes, you can push the roots into substrate or gravel to help anchor the plantlet. However, you must keep the central horizontal rhizome completely exposed above the substrate line, as burying the rhizome starves it of circulation and causes rot.

listings.description: Plant Profile Cardamine lyrata, also known as Japanese Cress or Chinese Ivy, is an expressive East Asian marsh plant that brings a charming, vine‑like texture to aquascapes. Its light‑green, clover‑like leaves trail along fine, creeping stems, giving tanks a soft, whimsical touch. Highly adaptable, it can form lush midground bushes, creep into a low foreground carpet under high light and CO₂, or float at the surface to create a cozy canopy for fish fry and dwarf shrimp. It's a plant that’s basically happy anywhere you let it grow! Tissue culture cups ensure your aquascape gets a super clean starting point. Lab-grown and fully sterile, it arrives without pests, snails, duckweed, or any unwanted algae. It’s the go-to option for anyone who wants peace of mind when adding fresh greenery to a carefully maintained setup. Key Features & Benefits Clover-like foliage trails and adds visual texture. Dense growth shelters fish fry, shrimp, and shy tank inhabitants. Natural nutrient sponge that helps keep water clarity high. Care & Planting Instructions Prep the plant by carefully removing the plantlets from the cup and rinsing away all sterile nutrient gel under lukewarm, dechlorinated water before mounting. Use fine-tip pinsettes to push individual stem clumps 1 to 2 inches into substrate, or allow stem clusters to float freely along the water surface. Provide medium-to-high lighting and cooler water temperatures when possible (68–75°F preferred); adding pressurized CO2 encourages lower, creeping horizontal growth. Maintain stable water parameters and avoid drastic environmental shifts to prevent leaf melt or rotting in delicate stems. Trim stem shoots with straight scissors anywhere along the stem or pull apart dense clumps to propagate and maintain compact growth. Read our trimming & propagation guide for details. Yes! Cardamine Lyrata thrives when left floating along the water surface. Its trailing stems form a tangled green matrix that provides exceptional shade, absorbs nutrients heavily from the water column, and gives baby fry and shrimp a safe place to hide. 3. How do I transition Cardamine Lyrata from emersed to submerged growth? When transitioning from emersed to submerged growth, plant bare stems securely into substrate under medium-to-high lighting and keep water parameters stable. As new growth adapts, the plant will shed its firmer land leaves and sprout delicate, ivy-like submerged foliage. Once new shoots develop, trim away old lower growth to encourage branching.

Plant Profile If you're looking to create the natural look of a grassy hedge without the maintenance of demanding carpeting species, Cryptocoryne lucens is a foolproof freshwater aquarium plant for low-tech setups. Native to Sri Lanka, this dependable favorite sports narrow, bright emerald-green leaves set against rich brown stems that form lush, reed-like thickets when planted in groups. As with all crypt plants, this species can be sensitive to sudden parameter shifts and strongly objects to being relocated once planted. Given a permanent home in your substrate, however, its rosettes mature into a dense, long-lasting accent that adds rich natural texture to your planted tank. Tissue Culture cups ensure your aquascape gets a super clean starting point. Lab‑grown and fully sterile, it arrives without pests, snails, duckweed, or any unwanted algae. It’s the go‑to option for anyone who wants peace of mind when adding fresh greenery to a carefully maintained setup. Key Features & Benefits Slender emerald-green foliage creates a natural, grassy reed effect in foreground and midground zones. Hardy and adaptable, making it an excellent low-maintenance choice for low-tech aquarium setups. Care & Planting Instructions Thoroughly wash away the nutrient gel from the roots with your fingers before parting it out into manageable portions. Use fine-tip pinsettes to push roots deep into quality aquarium soil, as Cryptocoryne species are heavy root feeders. Insert root tab fertilizers if using an inert substrate like sand or gravel to supply essential subterranean nutrients. Inject pressurized CO2 for faster growth and fuller foliage density, though not required for long-term health. Choose a permanent spot from day one; moving an established plant will likely trigger leaf loss. Cryptocoryne species can be grown emersed in high-humidity setups or submerged in aquariums. Propagate by splitting subterranean runners or replanting offshoot plantlets. Don't discard the plant if leaves dissolve early on; see our guide to managing Cryptocoryne melt to help your plant recover smoothly. Quick Facts Listed information should be treated as general guidelines only. Team Buce Plant encourages you to do thorough research to ensure healthy growth! How is Cryptocoryne Lucens used in foreground aquascaping? Because Cryptocoryne Lucens produces narrow, upright foliage, planting several tissue culture portions closely together creates a lush, reed-like meadow effect in low-tech aquariums without needing delicate carpeting plants like Eleocharis or Glossostigma. 2. Does Cryptocoryne Lucens grow faster than Cryptocoryne Parva? Yes. While both feature narrow green foliage, Cryptocoryne Lucens grows noticeably faster and taller than Cryptocoryne Parva, making it easier to establish quickly in midground and foreground spaces. 3. How do I help my Cryptocoryne Lucens recover if it melts after planting? Crypt melt is a standard reaction when shifting water parameters cause old leaves to dissolve so the plant can grow new foliage adapted to your aquarium. Trim away decaying tissue, maintain stable water conditions, and do not disturb the subterranean roots. For complete recovery steps, check out our guide to managing Cryptocoryne melt . Crypt Lucens is a less common type of crypt that can serve as an ideal foreground or midground plant. The slender leaves are bright green with brown stems and when grown in large groups can resemble tall reeds of thick grass. Like other crypts, this plant is recommended for beginners due to its ease in keeping and low care requirements. If grown in good aquarium substrate such as Controsoil, the plant can feed through the roots and grow quickly without the need for high light, CO2 or fertilizer dosing. Crypts can be grown emersed or submerged. Propagate by splitting the rhizome or cutting off new growth and replanting Notes: Tissue culture plants are grown in vitro from a state of the art laboratory specialized in propagating aquatic plants. They provide the best option for those who want to ensure that absolutely zero unwanted pests are introduced into the aquarium. Remove tissue culture gel before planting. Simply wash the gel away or soak the plant in water and squeeze the gel off with your fingers. Cryptocoryne prefer not to be moved once planted. If possible, do not move them! Do not make drastic changes to the aquarium. Unstable parameters will result in melt and rotting of the aquarium plant. For instructions on how to properly plant tissue culture aquarium plants, click here . CO2 injection and quality aquarium soil will yield better growth. Plant Profile If you're looking for a clever way to bridge your foreground and midground with warm, earthy color, Cryptocoryne 'Mioya' is a versatile favorite. Hailing from the shaded riverbanks of Sri Lanka's Mi Oya, this variety is celebrated for its slender, gracefully ruffled leaves that shift seamlessly from bright emerald green to deep copper-brown tones. As with all crypts, it can be sensitive to sudden parameter shifts and strongly objects to being moved once planted. Tissue Culture cups ensure your aquascape gets a super clean starting point. Key Features & Benefits Slender, ruffled leaves transition from bright emerald to rich copper-brown, delivering striking color contrast. Can be grown emersed in high-humidity setups where it will periodically produce unique flowering spathes. Care & Planting Instructions Thoroughly wash away the nutrient gel from the roots with your fingers before parting it out into manageable portions. Use fine-tip pinsettes to push roots deep into quality aquarium soil, as Crypt species are heavy root feeders. In the wild, it's found growing along the bedrocks of streams and rivers in Thailand and other Southeast Asian countries, where its slender leaves are naturally adapted to withstand moving water. That same hardiness carries over into the aquarium, making it a distinctive textural addition for hobbyists looking to break away from the usual broad-leafed crypt look. Plant Profile Hydrocotyle Japan (Hydrocotyle Tripartita) brings a unique, whimsical texture to your tank with its distinct, clover-like leaves. Made famous by legendary aquascapers like Takashi Amano, this fast-growing favorite is incredibly versatile and can be used in the foreground, midground, or background depending on your vision. Left to its own devices, it will happily grow into wild, compact bushes of vibrant green. It is an exceptionally undemanding and energetic grower, meaning it will gladly take over the entire tank if you don't keep its enthusiastic growth in check! Tissue Culture cups ensure your aquascape gets a super clean starting point. Lab‑grown and fully sterile, it arrives without pests, snails, duckweed, or any unwanted algae. It’s the go‑to option for anyone who wants peace of mind when adding fresh greenery to a carefully maintained setup. Key Features & Benefits Clover-like green foliage that adds a playful, natural texture. Fill in your aquascape rapidly thanks to its fast growth rate, making it an excellent option for quickly blanketing bare spots. Care & Planting Instructions Thoroughly wash away the nutrient gel from the roots with your fingers before parting it out into manageable portions. Maintain high lighting and inject pressurized CO2 while frequently trimming new growth to force the plant to stay low and create a tight carpeting effect over your foreground. Keep a pair of trimming scissors handy, as it grows quickly and requires regular pruning to prevent it from out-competing and overgrowing your other tank inhabitants. Propagate whenever you want by simply cutting the stems anywhere along the shoot and replanting them, or by pulling apart dense clumps and splitting the roots. Trim new shoots anywhere along the stem to encourage the plant to branch out even thicker and more compact. Master the basics by learning how to properly grow aquarium carpet plants to ensure your new layout fills in quickly, evenly, and stays free of algae. While typically grown in substrate, Hydrocotyle Japan is extremely versatile and can be tucked into hardscape crevices or attached to driftwood with aquarium glue, where its cascading clover-like runners create a beautiful hanging effect.

Plant Profile Rotala H'ra is a sought-after aquatic stem plant hailing from the Gia Lai province in the central highlands of Vietnam. A distinct geographic variant of Rotala rotundifolia , it's known for profuse, narrow, pointed foliage and a growth habit with a mind of its own: instead of growing politely upright like most stem plants, it overhangs, arches, and branches horizontally, doing its own thing. Under high-intensity lighting, pressurized CO2, and tuned fertilization, its foliage transforms into a breathtaking palette of fiery orange, salmon, and deep ruby-red, making it a stellar pick for sweeping midground bushes or dramatic background slopes. *Form Notice: Photos display this plant in both its emersed (above-water) and submerged forms. Depending on nursery availability and seasonality, you may receive this plant in either form. Learn more about what to expect by reading our guide on Emersed vs. Submerged-Grown Aquatic Plants . Key Features & Benefits Thin, pointed leaves develop vivid salmon, fiery orange, and intense red tones under high-tech aquarium conditions. Unique cascading and arching growth habit naturally forms lush, overhanging bushes. Care & Planting Instructions Remove lead weight and cotton wrap (or foam) surrounding the base, then strip the lower inch of foliage so bare stems anchor cleanly into soil without rotting. * Rotala has fragile leaves, so handle stems with care during preparation. Use fine-tip pinsettes to push individual stems 1 to 2 inches into soil, spacing them about half an inch apart to ensure light reaches lower foliage. Provide high-intensity lighting and pressurized CO2 (20–30 ppm); combining strong light with regular iron dosing yields the deepest fiery red and orange coloration. See our guide to growing red aquarium plants . Maintain stable water parameters and avoid sudden parameter swings to prevent stem melting or rotting. Trim stem tops or side shoots with curved scissors once they reach the desired height, and replant trimmings directly into substrate to propagate and expand coverage. Read our trimming & propagation guide for details. Quick Facts Listed information should be treated as general guidelines only. Achieving deep orange and red hues on Rotala H'ra requires high light intensity, mandatory pressurized CO2 injection (20–30 ppm), low-to-moderate water column nitrates, and regular micronutrient dosing with liquid iron. Under low light, the foliage will remain predominantly green. 3. How do I transition Rotala H'Ra from emersed to submerged growth? When transitioning from emersed to submerged growth, plant bare stems securely into rich substrate under medium-to-high lighting and keep water parameters stable. As new growth adapts, the plant will shed its thicker land leaves and sprout colorful, delicate underwater foliage. Once new shoots develop, trim away old lower growth to encourage branching.

Plant Profile Common Name: Bucephalandra Goliath Buce ‘Goliath’ is a newer, rare, large aquarium plant featuring slender leaves that resemble a cross between Anubias and Skeleton King foliage. True to its name, this variant is one of the larger members of the Bucephalandra family, often developing a thick rhizome that rises like a palm tree as it matures. Highly versatile, it can be grown submerged or emersed, usually attached to hardscape such as driftwood or rocks rather than being buried in traditional aquarium substrate. This is an exquisite choice for the midground or background of freshwater aquascapes, where its massive stature creates a commanding presence within a planted tank. Key Features & Notes It is prized for its substantial size and vertical growth habit, making it one of the few Bucephalandra species capable of serving as a true background focal point. As the plant ages, the rhizome thickens significantly, giving the colony a unique, prehistoric appearance that mimics miniature trees. Despite its size, it remains a slow-growing, hardy species that thrives in shaded areas . It is an ideal choice for aquascapes where other large plants might struggle. It is perfectly at home fully submerged in an aquarium or emersed in high-humidity paludariums and ripariums where its large leaves can truly shine. Care Tips & Preparation Bucephalandra is an epiphytic plant that should be attached to rocks or driftwood . Never bury the rhizome in substrate, as this will cause the plant to rot and melt. Carefully remove the plant from its pot and clear away all rockwool from the roots. For a deep dive on prepping potted plants, click here . Avoid making drastic changes to your water parameters or lighting. Unstable conditions are the primary cause of leaf melt in new specimens. While this plant is hardy and low-maintenance, CO2 injection will yield much faster growth. We recommend researching your specific water chemistry to ensure your plant thrives. Final size and coloration depend entirely on your specific aquarium conditions. Please note that photos are a representation, and individual plants may vary. Plant Profile Homalomena Insignis is a rare rheophytic aroid featuring thick, waxy foliage that displays a striking wash of coral-pink, iridescent purple, and deep forest-green tones. In its native torrential stream beds, it anchors tightly to smooth river stones using thick gripping roots to survive powerful flash floods, meaning it transitions easily between submerged currents and humid open air. Attached to hardscape or planted into substrate, it works cleanly as a midground accent in planted tanks, adding bold jewel color to layouts. Key Features & Notes Thick, waxy foliage exhibits rare coral-pink, iridescent purple, and dark green colorations. Dual-growth habit adapts seamlessly to fully submerged aquascapes, closed terrariums, and paludariums. Tough creeping rhizome anchors securely to driftwood and stone without invasive runner growth. Care & Planting Instructions Prep the plant by removing it from the pot and clearing all rockwool from the roots . Secure the plant onto driftwood or porous rock using thread or plant glue, or press the roots into substrate while keeping the main rhizome exposed above the soil line. Provide low to medium indirect lighting; injecting CO2 in an aquarium setup encourages richer purple coloration and faster root anchoring. Maintain humidity above 75% for emersed setups, or ensure clean, well-circulated water when growing fully submerged. Trim older or melting transition leaves near the rhizome base with sharp aquascaping scissors to stimulate fresh growth. Note that you will receive one healthy plant measuring 4 to 8 inches tall with 3 to 8 established leaves. Final size and iridescent coloration depend entirely on your specific setup conditions; please note that photos are a representation, and individual plants may vary. Plant Profile Cryptocoryne 'Silver Queen' has a way of making a foreground feel intentional, like every leaf was placed just so. This rare crown jewel comes from the specialized river basins of Borneo, and it's easy to see why collectors seek it out: it has pointed oval leaves with a gentle silver wavy margin and dark green foliage dotted with delicate pink or bronze spotting. It's a touch more demanding when submerged than standard crypts, preferring slightly alkaline water (pH above 7.0) to really take off, but the payoff in color makes every bit of extra care worthwhile. Key Features & Benefits Foliage adorned with an elegant wavy margin and silver sheen creates a unique look. Adapts to emersed high-humidity paludarium displays where mature plants can bloom. A collector's plant that introduces dark, sophisticated contrast to foreground and midground zones. Care & Planting Instructions Prep the plant by removing it from the pot and clearing all rockwool from the roots . Use fine-tip pinsettes to push roots deep into quality aquarium soil, as Crypt species are heavy root feeders. Insert root tab fertilizers if using an inert substrate like sand or gravel to supply essential subterranean nutrients. Maintain a neutral-to-slightly-alkaline pH (7.0+) and provide moderate to high lighting with pressurized CO2 to encourage faster, healthier submersed foliage. Choose a permanent spot from day one; moving an established plant will likely trigger leaf loss. Cryptocoryne species can be grown emersed in high-humidity setups or submerged in aquariums. Propagate by splitting the rhizome or replanting new growth shoots. Don't discard the plant if leaves dissolve early on; see our guide to managing Cryptocoryne melt to help your plant recover smoothly. Crypt melt is a standard reaction when shifting water conditions cause old leaves to dissolve so the plant can rebuild foliage adapted to your aquarium. Do I need root tabs if I already use liquid fertilizers for my Cryptocoryne? Yes. Because Cryptocoryne plants absorb the vast majority of their nutrients through their roots rather than their leaves, providing nutrient-rich aquasoil or root tabs inside sand or gravel is far more effective than relying on water column liquid fertilizers alone.

Plant Profile Ammania Senegalensis, aka Copper Leaf Ammania, is an aquatic stem plant native to the tropical wetlands and riverbanks of Western and Central Africa, and it did not choose that nickname lightly. Wavy-edged, oval leaves spiral around robust stems in a base mix of olive-green, gold, and orange, but crank up the light and dial in specialized nutrients, and it oxidizes into a deep copper-red. At a compact 3 to 5 inches tall, it's ready to anchor a midground focal point or background hedge with color other plants just can't match. *Form Notice: Photos display this plant in both its emersed (above-water) and submerged forms. Depending on nursery availability and seasonality, you may receive this plant in either form. Learn more about what to expect by reading our guide on Emersed vs. Submerged-Grown Aquatic Plants . Key Features & Benefits Foliage spans a sunset spectrum from olive-green to orange, gold, and deep copper-red. Rare African stem species adds unique texture and bold focal color to midground and background zones. Beginner-friendly red stem plant displays vibrant color without advanced care. Care & Planting Instructions Remove lead weight (or pot) and cotton wrap (or foam) surrounding the roots, then strip lower foliage so bare stems anchor cleanly into soil without rotting. Use fine-tip pinsettes to push individual stems 1 to 2 inches into substrate, spacing them so light reaches lower leaves. Provide moderate-to-high lighting and consistent nutrient dosing; while CO2 is not mandatory, adding pressurized CO2 and regular liquid iron dosing dramatically speeds up growth, stem robustness, and intensifies deep copper-red pigmentation. See our guide to growing red aquarium plants . Maintain stable water parameters and avoid sudden environmental shifts to prevent leaf melt or stem rotting. Trim main stem tops with straight scissors once stems reach the desired height, and replant trimmings directly into substrate to propagate and expand coverage. Read our trimming & propagation guide for details. Quick Facts Listed information should be treated as general guidelines only. Plant Profile Rotala Bonsai is a rare and sought-after dwarf stem plant native to the tropical regions of Asia. Characterized by its thick, rigid, perfectly upright central stems lined with rounded, fleshy leaves, this species grows at a much slower and more controlled pace than traditional Rotala varieties. Under moderate conditions, it maintains a clean, architectural lime-green appearance, but when exposed to high-intensity lighting, pressurized CO2, and nutrient dosing, its crown tips blush with rich orange, salmon, and deep reddish hues. *Form Notice: Photos display this plant in both its emersed (above-water) and submerged forms. Depending on nursery availability and seasonality, you may receive this plant in either form. Learn more about what to expect by reading our guide on Emersed vs. Submerged-Grown Aquatic Plants . Displays vibrant reddish-orange crown highlights under high-intensity lighting and high-tech parameters. Use fine-tip pinsettes to plant small stem clusters 1 inch apart into aquarium soil. Provide medium-to-high lighting and pressurized CO2 injection; consistent fertilization with a specialized liquid macro and micro formula yields robust stem growth and vibrant reddish-orange tips. See our guide to growing red aquarium plants . Maintain stable water parameters and avoid sudden parameter swings to prevent stem melting or rotting. Trim main stem tops with sharp straight scissors once they reach the desired height, and replant trimmings directly into substrate to propagate and expand coverage.
