Yellow Spotted Rabbit Aquarium Snails Yellow Spotted Rabbit snails resemble Malaysian trumpet snails in shape but rabbit snails are much larger in size. The shape and color of rabbit snails are slightly different as well. They are equally as valuable for your aquarium as Malaysian trumpet snails making them a great alternative. Snails will be equal to or larger than 1/4 of an inch. Main Benefits: Snails help keep a shrimp tank from re-cycling by provided adequate bio-load By burrowing into the substrates, these snails help keep turn the substrate which prevents gas build up. Snails eat left over food to prevent ammonia spikes Hardy so they can adjust to most water parameters When Receiving Snails: Place the snails in a corner of the tank and make a mental note where they were place Watch the snails over 7 days, if they do not move remove them from the aquarium Give the snails a smell and if they stink, then they are dead If they do not smell, add them back to the aquarium and give it another 3 days It is common for snails to burrow into the substrate and disappear from sight More Information: Also know as the elephant snails, rabbit snails are very peaceful in nature. They have a great temperament to them and they enjoy exploring the aquarium. They are never aggressive to other inhabitants. Rabbit snails tend to be active throughout the day and night. They do not favor one time or the other to be active. Care Parameters: TDS between 200 and 400 GH between 6 and 15 KH between 4 and 8 PH around 7.2 to 7.8 These parameters are what we keep them at, they can adjust to other parameters as well. Try to stay on the harder side rather than softer water.

Onion Nerite Snails | 3 Pack The onion nerite snail, also called the red onion nerite snail, has a round shell with brown and cream bands with black spots that could resemble onion rings. These nerite snails love to graze on algae in both freshwater and slightly salty tanks. They stay fairly small and won’t reproduce in a regular aquarium. Onion snails are steady cleaners and with unique shell pattern that make them a popular pick for planted and nano aquarium setups. Background and Key Benefits Nerite snails or Neritina sp. are freshwater snails related to the mollusk family. They will clean algae from glass, substrate, and décor. They are also so popular in our hobby because they do not reproduce in freshwater. In the wild these snails return to brackish water to breed and the baby snails require brackish water for early stages of growth. Therefore, Nerite snails will not overpopulate in an aquarium. Along with serving practical purposes in the aquarium, the snails have beautiful shells and they are fun to watch. If you look at your glass closely after adding them, you will see the tiny track marks these snails make as they graze on algae! We keep these snails on pool filtered sand and in bare bottom tanks with a Matten filters. We also use LED lighting to provide enough natural algae growth for them to feed. Please note: During shipping, snails sometimes go into a hibernation-like state and may not become fully active for up to a week once acclimated to your aquarium. Nitrite Test Kit | Fritz Fritz Liquid Test Kits Easy to Read Instructions Essential for a Healthy Tank Accurate in both Fresh and Saltwater Nitrite is produced continually during the ammonia cycle by nitrifying bacteria in the biological filter. While not as immediately toxic as ammonia, any accumulation of nitrite should still be addressed as soon as possible. The nitrite level will eventually be broken down to non-toxic nitrate. Regular testing for nitrite is recommended - chronic exposure to even low levels of nitrite can cause brown blood disease in fish, which can cause suffocation and death. Dosage / Instructions To remove childproof safety cap, push down while turning. Fill a clean test tube with 5 ml of water to be tested (to the line on the tube). Add 5 drops from Nitrite Test Solution, holding dropper bottle upside down in a completely vertical position to ensure uniformity of drops added to the water sample. Cap the test tube and gently shake several times to mix solution. Attention! Always use the cap. Avoid skin contact as this may affect the test results. Wait five minutes for the color to develop. Read the test results by matching the color of the solution against those on the Nitrite Test Color Chart.

Frequently Asked Questions: Here are some common questions a hobbyist might ask about Japan Blue Guppies, along with answers: 1. What tank size is best for Japan Blue Guppies? A tank size of at least 10 gallons is recommended for a small group of guppies. This provides enough swimming space and helps maintain stable water parameters. If you plan to breed them or keep a larger group, a bigger tank is ideal to accommodate their activity and offspring. 2. What should I feed a Blue Mosaic Guppy? Guppies are omnivorous and thrive on a varied diet. High-quality flake food should form the base of their diet, supplemented with live or frozen foods like brine shrimp, daphnia, and bloodworms. Vegetables such as blanched spinach or zucchini can also be added for variety. 3. How do I differentiate males from females? Males are smaller and more colorful, with elongated and patterned caudal fins. Females are larger, have rounder bodies, and their fins are less vibrant. Observing these traits makes it easy to identify their gender. 4. Can Japan Blue Guppies live with other fish? Yes, they are peaceful and do well in community tanks with other non-aggressive fish of similar size, such as tetras, rasboras, and small catfish. Avoid keeping them with fin-nippers or large predatory fish. 5. How often do Blue Mosaic Guppies reproduce? Guppies are prolific breeders, and females can give birth to fry every 4–6 weeks. If you want to manage the population, consider keeping only one gender or introducing fish like shrimp that might consume some of the fry. 6. Are Japan Blue Guppies good for beginners? Yes, they are hardy and adaptable, making them an excellent choice for new aquarists. Their care requirements are straightforward, and their active, colorful behavior is very rewarding for beginners. 7. What can I do to highlight their colors? A dark substrate and background can help enhance their blue coloration. Providing a balanced diet with color-enhancing foods, such as those rich in carotenoids, can also bring out their natural vibrancy.

Grading Cherry Shrimp The grading of cherry shrimp is as follows: Cherry shrimp in general refers to the lowest grade of Red Neocaridina aquarium shrimp. Regular cherry shrimp are generally pretty clear. Sakura cherry shrimp are a more intense red color. While still possessing clear patches, Sakura shrimp are more solid in color than regular cherry shrimp. Fire red shrimp is the next grade and refers to shrimp that are completely red. Fire Red shrimp are the second to highest grade. Painted fire red shrimp are completely solid in color and have no transparent patches. Painted fire red shrimp usually have red legs as well. Pack of 3 Batik Nerite Snails The batik nerite snail has eye-catching black and gold patterns that make it a perfect choice for nano and planted aquariums. Background and Key Benefits Nerite snails or Neritina sp. are freshwater snails related to the mollusk family. They will clean algae from glass, substrate, and décor. They are also so popular in our hobby because they do not reproduce in freshwater. In the wild these snails return to brackish water to breed and the baby snails require brackish water for early stages of growth. Therefore, Nerite snails will not overpopulate in an aquarium. We also supplement their diet with a mix of Northfin Veggie, Community, and Bug Pro. Frequently Asked Questions: What size tank does the Kohaku Guppy need? Kohaku Guppies are small fish, and they do well in tanks that are at least 10 gallons. A larger tank provides more space for swimming and can help maintain stable water conditions. If you have a group of guppies, a larger tank will also prevent overcrowding. Can Kohaku Guppies live with other fish? Yes, Kohaku Guppies are peaceful and get along well with most community tank fish, such as tetras, mollies, and platies. However, avoid keeping them with very large or aggressive fish that might stress them out. They are best kept with other calm fish that are similar in size. How do I care for Kohaku Guppies? Kohaku Guppies are relatively easy to care for. They need a well-maintained tank with stable water conditions, regular feeding (such as high-quality flake or pellet food), and occasional water changes. They also benefit from some plant cover in the tank, as it provides hiding places and helps reduce stress. How do I breed Kohaku Guppies? Kohaku Guppies are livebearers, meaning they give birth to live young instead of laying eggs. To breed them, you'll need both a male and a female guppy. Female guppies can give birth to several batches of fry from a single mating. If you're not ready for baby guppies, it's important to separate the males and females to avoid overpopulation. How can I tell the difference between male and female Kohaku Guppies? Male Kohaku Guppies are typically smaller and more colorful, with the striking red and white pattern that makes them stand out. They also have a small, modified fin called a gonopodium used for mating. Female Kohaku Guppies are larger, less colorful, and have a rounder body shape due to carrying eggs. What do Kohaku Guppies eat? Kohaku Guppies are omnivores and will eat a variety of foods, including high-quality flakes, pellets, and live or frozen foods like brine shrimp and daphnia. It's important to provide a balanced diet to keep them healthy and vibrant. Feed them small amounts a few times a day, ensuring they don't overeat.

listings.commonName: All in One Aquarium Plant Fertilizer | Shrimple
listings.description: All in One Aquatic Plant Fertilizer | Shrimple Specifically formulated for freshwater aquariums, our all-in-one fertilizer is the perfect solution for thriving planted aquariums. Utilizing our all-in-one fertilizer is imperative in delivering crucial nutrients such as nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium to sustain the optimal growth and vitality of your aquatic plants. Our beginner-friendly formula ensures optimal plant growth, while the convenient dispenser allows for effortless dosing. The bottle holds 500ml (16.09oz) of liquid and will treat up to 2,500 gallons. Please note: In aquarium setups containing invertebrates, we recommend using our Shrimply Fertilizer due to its copper-free composition and trace quantities of nitrates (NO3). Acknowledging the susceptibility of shrimp to copper and the potential toxicity of NO3. Directions: We suggest dosing 1-2 times per week depending on the needs of your aquarium. 1 Pump (2ml) per 10 gallons adds 5ppm NO3, 0.5ppm PO4, 5ppm K and .3ppm Fe. If you notice algae outbreaks cut dose frequency to once a week and wait for algae to disappear then gradually work your way back up. listings.commonName: Shrimply Fertilizer for Sensitive Livestock | Shrimple by Flip Aquatics
listings.description: Aquarium Plant Fertilizer | Copper Free Formula Shrimply Fertilizer is meticulously crafted to be the solution for planted aquariums housing shrimp and other delicate invertebrates. Unlike conventional all-in-one fertilizers, Shrimply Fertilizer is copper free with trace amounts of nitrates (NO3), recognizing the sensitivity of shrimp to copper and NO3 toxicity. By omitting copper and reducing NO3 levels, we ensure that both your invertebrates and your plants can thrive without the risk of serious ailments. Our beginner-friendly formula ensures optimal plant growth, while the convenient dispenser allows for effortless dosing. The bottle holds 500ml (16.09oz) of liquid and will treat up to 2,500 gallons. Disclaimer: Trace amounts of copper are essential for many aquatic species. These trace amounts can be obtained through regular feeding of aquatic food. Nitrates are essential for plan growth and are present in balanced aquariums. NO3 levels should ideally remain at or below 20ppm for optimal invertebrate health. Directions: We suggest dosing 2 times per week for most shrimp focused tanks. 1 Pump (2ml) per 10 gallons adds 1ppm NO3, 0.1ppm PO4, 3ppm K and .25ppm Fe. If you notice algae outbreaks cut dose frequency to once a week and wait for algae to disappear then gradually work your way back up. listings.commonName: Shrimple - Shrimply GH by Flip Aquatics
listings.description: GH Remineralizer | Shrimple Shrimply GH is meticulously designed to maintain optimal GH (General Hardness) levels in freshwater aquariums, particularly benefiting shrimp and other invertebrates. With an ideal range of 4 to 16 dGH (70 to 280 ppm), it is important to determine the needs of your aquatic pets. GH Levels directly impact vital processes like fish muscle and bone development, shrimp molting, snail shell formation and the growth of aquatic plants. Regular monitoring and supplementation will help foster the well-being of your aquatic pets while promoting thriving biological processes essential for a balanced aquarium. Dosing: 1 Pump (2ml) per 10 gallons adds 1dGH For caridina shrimp needing a soft water setup (pH below 7), we find a GH of 4 to 6 dGH to be ideal. For Neocaridina shrimp, we recommend a 2:1 ratio of GH to KH to maintain a pH above 7, with the ideal GH level being 10-16 dGH. Analysis: Magnesium (Mg) 2.9%, Calcium (Ca) 9.3%

listings.commonName: Shrimply KH | Shrimple by Flip Aquatics
listings.description: Shrimply KH | Carbonate Hardness Specifically formulated for freshwater aquariums, Shrimply KH (Carbonate Hardness) is crucial for stabilizing pH levels in aquariums where a pH above 7 is ideal. Without adequate KH, pH can fluctuate quickly causing stress on the animals and premature molting in shrimp. Maintaining a KH between 4 to 8 dKH (70 to 140ppm) is ideal for most freshwater aquariums. Regular monitoring and supplementation will help maintain stability, promoting a consistent environment for your aquatic pets. Dosing: 1 Pump (2ml) per 10 gallons adds 1dKH For neocaridina shrimp, we recommend a 2:1 ratio of GH to KH to maintain a pH above 7, with the ideal KH level being between 4 to 8 dKH. Shrimply KH should not be used if the ideal pH for your aquatic pets is below 7.

listings.description: Shell Envy Mineral Food Shell Envy is a specially formulated mineral-based supplement designed to promote a robust and healthy carapace in shrimp. The carapace plays a crucial role in protecting their vital organs and maintaining their appearance. As shrimp grow, they molt, shedding their old carapace to reveal a softer, new layer that needs time to harden. Providing a mineral-based supplement like Shell Envy ensures that shrimp receive the necessary nutrients to harden their new shell effectively and beautifully. It's important to avoid overfeeding, as excessive mineral intake can lead to molting problems. Made from 100% natural and organic ingredients, Shell Envy features a high mineral content blend of kale, mulberry, nettle, dandelion, moringa, spinach, spirulina, chlorella, bee pollen, kelp, alfalfa, wheatgrass, black walnut, and other beneficial components that shrimp love. It also includes essential nutrients and minerals such as beta-glucan, calcium carbonate, montmorillonite, amino acids, trace minerals, chitin, yeast, and probiotics. This pellet food is designed to be easy to break apart, allowing precise control over feeding amounts. It sinks quickly, and shrimp will eagerly break it apart and distribute it throughout the tank. If leftover food is found after 3-4 hours, it indicates overfeeding, so reduce the pellet size or feeding frequency. Shell Envy is also enjoyed by snails, crayfish, and crabs, making it a versatile choice for your freshwater aquarium. For best results, we recommend feeding Shell Envy based on the guide below. Alkalinity Test Kit | Fritz Fritz Liquid Test Kits Easy to Read Instructions Essential for a Healthy Tank Accurate in both Fresh and Saltwater Carbonate hardness, or alkalinity (KH), is the measure of both carbonates and bicarbonates present in the water. The KH value of your water is important to know, as the carbonate hardness plays a significant role in the water’s pH and the water’s buffering capacity to keep that pH stable. KH naturally falls over time with the introduction of CO2 and other acids, and nitrification. Reverse osmosis water should be buffered with carbonates before use to raise and maintain KH. Some municipal tap water can have variable KH levels throughout the year and should be checked regularly. In saltwater tanks, KH can be tested to monitor the proper ionic balance when dosing. Dosage / Instructions To remove childproof safety cap, push down while turning. Fill a clean test tube with 5 ml of water to be tested (to the line on the tube). Holding KH Reagent Solution dropper bottle upside down in a completely vertical position add one drop at a time. Cap the test tube and gently shake between drops. Ensure you count the drops as they are added. The test is complete when the water in the test tube, after having been gently shaken, turns from blue to yellow. If you have difficulty discerning the color after the first drop of test solution is added, remove the cap from the test tube and while holding it over a white background, look down through the tube. The KH value is determined by the number of drops of reagent that must be added to turn the water in the test tube yellow. See conversion chart to determine KH. Corrective actions: To increase the KH of your water, add Fritz pH Higher. For a more significant KH increase for African cichlid systems, add Fritz Rift Lake Cichlid Buffer as needed. Fritz recommends a minimum of 4 dKH (80 ppm) for nitrification when using FritzZyme 7 or FritzZyme Turbo Start 700 bacteria. To decrease the KH of your water, add Fritz pH Lower, or perform partial water changes.

Fishless Fuel | Fritz Establishing a healthy biological filter is essential to every aquatic system. Fritz Fishless Fuel eliminates the guesswork of dry ammonium chloride powders and other ammonia sources such as fish food or other organic materials. When using Fritz Fishless Fuel, there is also no need to put any livestock in potential danger to start a system. As a pure liquid ammonia source, easily feed your nitrifying bacteria to establish a robust, healthy biological filter. The convenient dropper bottle makes dosing simple. The Fritz Fishless Fuel formula contains 40 mg/mL TAN (total ammonia nitrogen.) DO NOT USE FISHLESS FUEL IN ANY SYSTEM CONTAINING LIVESTOCK. DO NOT ADD ANY ANIMALS TO A SYSTEM THAT HAS MEASURABLE AMMONIA OR NITRITE. Directions & Dosage To bring aquarium to 2 ppm ammonia: Add 4 drops per One U.S. Gallon (3.78 L) or 1 tsp (5 ml) per 25 U.S. Gallons (94.6 L) DO NOT USE WHEN LIVESTOCK IS PRESENT. Fritz Fishless Fuel Ammonia Solution is to be used when performing a fishless cycle. Add required amount of Fritz Fishless Fuel liquid ammonia solution to reach desired ammonia level (Fritz recommends 2-4 ppm). After adding ammonia add FritzZyme Nitrifying Bacteria and test daily. Once ammonia and nitrite levels are reading zero, livestock can be safely added. Continue to monitor ammonia and nitrite on a regular basis. Use along with nitrifying bacteria (FritzZyme or TurboStart) as a food source No equipment restrictions necessary Odor variations are normal; some lots may not have a discernable ammonia odor Contraindications: DO NOT add Ammonium Chloride to an aquarium with livestock present Overdosed? Perform small water changes if needed to dilute Test aquarium water with an ammonia test kit with a range up to at least 4 ppm NOTE: Be careful not to use too much ammonium chloride. Raising ammonia levels above 5.0ppm may actually slow the cycle time.

Blue Steel Shrimp thrive in well-maintained tanks with stable water parameters and make great companions for peaceful fish and other shrimp species. Blue Steel Shrimp are natural algae eaters, helping to keep your aquarium clean and balanced. Silver Kuhli Loach The Silver Kuhli Loach is a super entertaining fish that adds both beauty and intrigue to your freshwater aquarium. The Silver Kuhli Loach has a sleek, eel-like body and shimmers silver tones. The Silver Kuhli Loach is known for its peaceful nature and is a social species that thrives in groups. The Silver Kuhli Loach is often seen burrowing in the substrate or exploring crevices. They are most active during twilight hours, making them a unique addition to your tank's dynamic. Beyond their striking appearance and entertaining nature, Silver Kuhli Loaches are excellent at helping to keep the substrate clean, as they sift through the sand in search of food. They are compatible with a wide range of peaceful tank mates, making them a versatile choice for community aquariums. With proper care and a well-maintained environment, these loaches can live for several years, providing endless fascination as they display their natural behaviors in your aquatic setup. What are Silver Kuhli Loaches like? The Silver Kuhli Loach is a real night owl. They are active mainly at night and can peacefully co-exist with most other fish. During the night, they will look for food that sunk to the bottom of the aquarium. On top of that, their natural curiosity will drive them to explore any crevices and caves that might be around in their habitat. The ideal conditions for the Silver Kuhli Despite the fact that SIlver Kuhli Loaches are scavengers, they still require a relatively clean, well-oxygenated tank. Silver Kuhli Loaches prefer a soft substrate, as it makes searching for food more manageable, so sand or fine gravel would be best. The water should be soft, slightly acidic and at a temperature of 73 – 86 °F, as these are tropical fish. You should also make sure that there is moderate lighting in their habitat. Golden Kuhli Loach The Golden Kuhli Loach, also known as the Pangio dorae, is a unique and friendly fish. With its slender, eel-like body and warm golden color, this loach stands out at the bottom of the tank. Golden Kuhli Loaches are peaceful and get along well with other fish, making them great for community tanks. They love to hide and explore, so providing caves, driftwood, and plants makes them feel at home. These loaches are active at night and prefer a soft, sandy substrate where they can burrow and search for food. As scavengers, Golden Kuhli Loaches help keep the tank clean by eating leftover food. They thrive on a balanced diet of sinking pellets, algae wafers, and treats like frozen or live foods. Our Tank Parameters: Ph: 7-7.8 Gh: 5-7 Kh: 2-4 TDS: 100-150 Temp: 72-80 Tank Recommendations: Rock: Smooth rock (round in shape) Leaves: I ndian Almond or Guava Cones: Alder , Giant Alde r, Cyprus or Casuarina Plants: Java Ferns , Anubias , Sagittaria , Cryptocorene Please Note: All fish shipments have a 100% Live Arrival Guarantee when shipping with Overnight (1 Day) option. All other options void our Live Arrival Guarantee for fish. Frequently Asked Questions 1. How big do Golden Kuhli Loaches get? Golden Kuhli Loaches grow to about 3 to 4 inches in length, making them a good fit for a variety of tank sizes. 2. What tank size is best for Golden Kuhli Loaches? A minimum tank size of 20 gallons is recommended for Golden Kuhli Loaches. Since they enjoy hiding spots and exploring the bottom, a larger tank gives them plenty of room to feel secure. 3. Are Golden Kuhli Loaches peaceful fish? Yes, Golden Kuhli Loaches are very peaceful fish. They do well in community tanks and get along with other non-aggressive species. Because they are shy, they benefit from tank mates that won’t disturb them. 4. What should I feed Golden Kuhli Loaches? Golden Kuhli Loaches are omnivores and thrive on a varied diet. Sinking pellets, algae wafers, and live or frozen foods like bloodworms and brine shrimp are all excellent choices. They’ll also scavenge for leftover food, helping keep the tank clean. 5. Do Golden Kuhli Loaches need a specific type of substrate? Yes, they prefer a soft, sandy substrate where they can burrow safely. Rough or sharp gravel can harm their delicate bodies, so sand or fine gravel is ideal. 6. Do Golden Kuhli Loaches need to be kept in groups? Yes, Golden Kuhli Loaches are social and feel more comfortable in small groups. Keeping at least three to six together encourages them to be more active and reduces their shyness.

listings.description: Amazon Frogbit - Floating Aquarium Plant Amazon Frogbit ( Limnobium laevigatum ) is a floating plant that is equally suitable for both open aquariums and aquariums with a cover. Amazon Frogbit has large bright green leaves and long finely branched roots, the Frogbit not only provides excellent protection for young fish but is also an eye-catcher in any aquarium. Many well-known ornamental fish such as barbs, tetras, and egg-laying toothcarps love Frogbit as an ideal spawning substrate. Here the eggs can develop in peace, and the young fry are protected from predators. Is Amazon Frogbit Beginner Friendly? As far as floating plants go, Amazon Frogbit is an excellent plant for both beginner and more experienced aquarists. Frogbit's main requirement is sufficient light to grow optimally, which generally isn't difficult to achieve with floating plants. What is Frogbit and How Fast does Frogbit Grow? Amazon Frogbit is quite fast-growing. As a result, Frogbit consumes excess nutrients and prevents excessive algae development. Furthermore, the shade provided by the large leaves of the Amazon Frogbit contributes considerably to keeping algae in the aquarium in check. Although Frogbit reproduces quite rapidly through the numerous offshoots that appear, excess specimens of Frogbit can be easily removed. Amazon Frogbit Water Parameters Frogbit is very tolerant of water temperature and grows well in the range of 62 to even 95°F. Soft to medium-hard water is favorable. Good growth is supported by intensive lighting and high humidity. When the water level is low, Amazon Frogbit develops particularly well, because the roots are able to reach the substrate. Under favorable conditions, Frogbit multiplies quite quickly and form a dense floating plant cover, the extent of which can be regulated very easily by collecting excess plants. *All Plants may contain snails or snail eggs. We keep them in all of our tanks for the benefits they provide.*

Rainbow Goby (Stiphodon ornatus) The Rainbow Goby (Stiphodon ornatus), also called the Rainbow Stiphodon Goby or Rainbow Goby Fish, is a small and colorful fish that's perfect for any freshwater aquarium. Males are known for their bright colors, showing off shades of blue, orange, and red. They are peaceful fish that get along well with shrimp and other calm fish, making them a great choice for community tanks. Rainbow Gobies are known for eating algae, which helps keep the tank clean. They do best in tanks with moving water and a sandy or rocky bottom, similar to the streams they come from. They only grow to about 2-3 inches, so they can live in smaller tanks as long as the water is clean and well-filtered. Please Note: All fish shipments have a 100% Live Arrival Guarantee when shipping with Overnight (1 Day) option. All other options void our Live Arrival Guarantee for fish. What size tank do Rainbow Gobies need? Rainbow Gobies are small fish, growing to about 2-3 inches, so they can live in tanks as small as 10 gallons. However, they thrive best in tanks with at least 20 gallons of water, especially when kept in groups or with other species​. What should I feed my Rainbow Goby? Rainbow Gobies are primarily algae eaters. They love grazing on biofilm and algae in the tank, but you should also provide them with supplemental food like algae wafers, blanched vegetables, and occasionally high-quality sinking pellets​. We supplement their diet with a mix of fresh vegetables and Northfin Veggie, Community, Bug Pro, and Northfin Kelp Wafers to ensure a balanced and nutritious diet. We also feed our Gobys prepared algae wafers and let them graze on natural algae and bio-film. This can be supplemented by using Bacter AE. Can Rainbow Gobies live with shrimp and other fish? Yes! Rainbow Gobies are peaceful fish and are shrimp-safe, meaning they can coexist with adult shrimp without harming them. They also do well in community tanks with other non-aggressive fish​. What water conditions do Rainbow Gobies need? Rainbow Gobies need clean, well-filtered water with stable conditions. They prefer slightly alkaline water with a pH of 7.0 to 8.0 and a temperature range of 72-82°F. Since they come from fast-flowing streams, they also do well in tanks with moderate water flow​. Do Rainbow Gobies need a specific type of substrate? Yes, they prefer tanks with smooth sand or small pebbles that mimic their natural riverbed habitat. This type of substrate allows them to graze on algae and biofilm, their primary food source​. How many Rainbow Gobies should I keep together? You can keep a single Rainbow Goby, but they are more active and social in groups. It's recommended to keep at least 3-4 together if space allows. Males can be territorial, so providing enough space and hiding spots is essential​. Do Rainbow Gobies breed in home aquariums? Breeding Rainbow Gobies in home aquariums is rare. In the wild, they lay eggs in streams, and their larvae are swept into the ocean before returning to freshwater as juveniles. Replicating this process in a tank environment is quite challenging​. Our Tank Parameters for Rainbow Gobies To ensure your Rainbow Goby (Stiphodon ornatus) thrives, we maintain specific water parameters that mimic their natural environment. Here’s a breakdown of the ideal conditions we use in our tanks: pH: 7.0 to 8.0 – Rainbow Gobies prefer slightly alkaline water, which supports their health and well-being. GH (General Hardness): 4 to 10 – This range offers the right balance of minerals like calcium and magnesium, keeping their bones and overall health in check. KH (Carbonate Hardness): 2 to 6 – Adequate KH helps stabilize the pH levels, preventing drastic fluctuations that could stress the fish. TDS (Total Dissolved Solids): 100 to 150 – A lower TDS keeps the water clean and close to the conditions these fish experience in nature. Temperature: 70 to 74°F – Maintaining this cool, moderate temperature range helps the Rainbow Goby remain comfortable and active. By keeping your tank within these parameters, you can create an ideal habitat that allows Rainbow Gobies to thrive.

Cochu's Blue Tetra is a peaceful species that thrives in groups of six or more, where they feel secure and display their best colors. Their hardy nature makes them a great option for both new and experienced aquarists. Cochu's Blue Tetras prefer a well-planted tank with open swimming areas, creating a setup that benefits both the fish and the aquarist. A minimum tank size of 20 gallons is recommended for Cochu’s Blue Tetras. Since they are active swimmers and do best in groups, having a larger space allows them to move around freely and display their natural schooling behavior. 3. Are Cochu’s Blue Tetras aggressive? No, Cochu’s Blue Tetras are generally peaceful fish. They do well in community tanks with other non-aggressive species of similar size. Yes, Cochu's Blue Tetras can be kept with other peaceful fish of similar size. They get along well with other tetras, small rasboras, peaceful barbs, and bottom-dwellers like Corydoras catfish. Just avoid larger, aggressive fish that may see them as food.

Sunray Guppy The Sunray Guppy, a freshwater fish, features a vibrant golden-yellow body with flowing fins. Like other guppies, Sunray Guppies are hardy and adaptable, making them an excellent choice for both beginner and experienced aquarists. Pygmy Cory Catfish | Dwarf Corydoras Pygmy Corydoras are the perfect nano cory for small tanks. These tiny cory catfish belong to the genus Corydoras, a group of peaceful, bottom-dwelling catfish. Most only grow to about ¾ of an inch, which makes them ideal for aquariums as small as 5 gallons. As a nano species, they are perfect for nano tanks and other small aquatic setups. Like all corydoras, they enjoy being in groups of 5 or more, but their small size makes them easier to keep in smaller tanks compared to other species. In the wild, pygmy corydoras inhabit tropical inland waters of South America, especially in the Madeira River basin and regions of western Brazil. Corydoras are a widely distributed group of catfish found throughout South America. While pygmy corys sometimes get a bad reputation for being hard to keep, that’s usually due to poor import practices. Thanks to our quarantine process, we consider Pygmy Corydoras beginner-friendly and a great choice for new hobbyists. Pygmy Cory Size Pygmy corydoras are considered a dwarf species of cory. They grow to about 40% the size of most other corydoras, with adults reaching around ¾ of an inch. Males tend to stay even smaller than females. The body shape of the pygmy cory catfish is distinctive, featuring a flat belly and a streamlined form that runs from the snout to the tail. Their coloration is typically silver-gray with a prominent black line that extends from the snout all the way to the tail, making them easy to distinguish from other corydoras species . The only other cory species that’s similar in size is the Corydoras habrosus , which you can check out here. Breeding Pygmy Corydoras We’ve had pygmy corys breed naturally in our aquariums, especially when using Java Moss or spawning mops. Key points for breeding pygmy corydoras include: The female lays fertilized eggs; unfertilized eggs should be removed promptly to prevent fungal growth. Stable water parameters are essential for successful breeding. After hatching, fry should be fed microscopic foods like infusoria to support growth. Frequent water changes help maintain high water quality for healthy fry development. As fry grow, they begin swimming freely in the water column. Some hobbyists use marbles instead of substrate to protect eggs from being eaten. Pygmy corydoras are a great choice for a beginner-friendly breeding project. Feeding Pygmy Corydoras At Flip Aquatics, we feed our pygmy cories, which are specialized bottom feeders and bottom dwellers, a variety of foods suited to their feeding behavior. Pygmy cories and other cories spend most of their time at the bottom of the tank, foraging for food on the substrate. Our food list includes: Frozen Foods (small size like baby brine shrimp, daphnia, cyclops, and bloodworms as an occasional treat) NorthFin Foods (Community Flake and Nano Bits) Canned green beans (unsalted, finely crushed to suit the small mouths of pygmy cories) Pygmy cories and other cories benefit from a varied diet that includes vegetable rich flake or pellets and frozen foods such as baby brine shrimp, bloodworms, and shrimp to support their health and natural bottom-feeding habits. Live Arrival Guarantee All fish orders are covered by our 100% Live Arrival Guarantee . Shop worry-free knowing your fish will arrive healthy or we'll make it right. We quarantine our fish for two or more weeks before shipping to ensure they are healthy and free from diseases, giving you peace of mind when adding pygmy corydoras to your aquarium. Our Water Parameters pH: 7.2 - 7.5 GH: 4 - 6 KH: 2 - 4 TDS: 100 - 150 Temperature: 70 - 74°F Tank Setup Suggestions Size: 5 gallons or more (a nano tank or small home aquarium is ideal for pygmies, as long as there is enough swimming space and plenty of places to hide) Substrate: Sand or smooth substrate Additives: Indian Almond Leaves or Alder Cones When setting up an aquarium for pygmies, it's important to create a peaceful environment with lots of plants and hiding spots. This helps pygmies and other nano species feel secure and allows them to thrive. A well-planted aquarium not only provides cover for pygmies to hide but also encourages natural swimming behavior and reduces stress. Compatible tank mates for pygmies include other nano species, peaceful community fish, dwarf shrimp , snails, tetras (such as neon tetras), celestial pearl danios, and other fish of similar size and temperament. These combinations work well in a nano tank or home aquarium, creating a harmonious community setup. Frequently Asked Questions How many Pygmy Corydoras can I keep in a 10-gallon tank? You can comfortably keep 10 pygmy corydoras in a 10-gallon tank. If you're an experienced hobbyist, it's possible to keep up to 20, as long as you maintain healthy water quality with nitrate levels below 40 ppm. Adding live plants can help with nutrient control and overall tank balance. Do Pygmy Corydoras eat algae? Pygmy corydoras don't eat enough algae to be considered good algae cleaners. However, they are excellent scavengers. They sift through the substrate for leftover food and debris, which can help reduce waste that might otherwise lead to algae growth. Are Pygmy Corydoras nocturnal? Pygmy corydoras are not fully nocturnal, but they will scavenge during both the day and night. They often school during the day, especially when kept with other similar schooling fish like otocinclus. You can often find them resting on sand or perched on plant leaves. How long do Pygmy Corydoras live? With proper care, pygmy corydoras can live 3 to 5 years. Keeping stable water parameters is key to their long-term health. We recommend a balanced diet of frozen foods along with veggie-based flakes or small pellets.

listings.description: Pea Puffer for Sale | Freshwater Dwarf Puffer Pea Puffers (scientific name: Carinotetraodon travancoricus) are truly a rewarding addition to your home aquarium, especially for those who appreciate curious and interactive fish. Despite them being a fairly small fish, Pea Puffers are generally highly inquisitive, and owners can watch their lively interactions, territorial displays, and keen awareness of their surroundings. Their bold black patterns on a yellow-gold body make them easy to spot, but it’s their lively behavior in such a small fish that really makes them desired by so many aquarium enthusiasts. It’s important to note that our Pea Puffers for sale require a diet of live food or frozen foods to thrive, so prospective owners should be prepared to meet these specific food requirements before purchasing. During our 2 weeks quarantine period, we do our best to convert them from live foods to frozen foods to make feeding easier for their new owners. Why Buy Our Pea Puffers? Quarantined for 2 weeks to ensure health and easy transition Fed both live and frozen foods during quarantine Covered by our 100% Live Arrival Guarantee Shipped quickly and carefully with support if any issues happen Regularly updated with fresh arrivals so you always get the healthiest pea puffers Tank Setup | Water Parameters Tank Size: 5 gallons for one, 10+ gallons for groups Water Temperature: 70–74°F pH: 7.2–7.5 GH: 4–8 KH: 2–4 TDS: 80–120 Temperament: Semi-aggressive Lifespan: Up to 5 years Pea puffer fish do best in a planted tank with low water flow. They like hiding spots and ample space to explore. These help reduce aggression and make them feel at home. In the wild, they are found in low flow rivers, so their tank should mimic these natural conditions. We use a sponge filter to reduce flow without impacting the water quality. It is important to note that they are highly sensitive to elevated nitrate levels so adequate filtration is needed. Their diet in the wild consists primarily of small invertebrates, so offering similar foods in captivity is important. Pea Puffer Food As carnivorous fish, our pea puffers thrive on a varied diet rich in protein, with a strong emphasis on live foods to support their health and natural behaviors. Observing their eating behavior is crucial to ensure they are receiving proper nutrition and to ensure reduced aggression. Our main live food offerings include: Daphnia culture : Feeding live daphnia is especially beneficial as it is high in fiber, promoting a healthy digestive system and helping to prevent bloating. Scud culture: These small crustaceans provide essential nutrients and encourage natural hunting behaviors. Bladder snails : Besides serving as a nutritious food source, bladder snails assist in keeping the puffers’ beak-like teeth properly trimmed. In addition to live foods, frozen options such as bloodworms, baby brine shrimp, and frozen daphnia are excellent supplements. However, it is important to avoid overfeeding bloodworms to prevent digestive issues. Many hobbyists also use newly hatched brine shrimp as a live food source. Pea Puffer Tank Environment Creating a natural environment is very important for the health and happiness of pea puffers in your home aquarium. This fascinating species does best in a well-planted tank that looks like their natural home. Adding different aquatic plants like Java moss, Anubias , and Cryptocoryne gives them places to hide and helps keep the water clean. Driftwood, rocks, and caves make the tank more interesting and give your puffers lots of spots to explore and call their own. To mitigate aggression and territorial behavior, it’s important to give them plenty of space and use plants and decorations to block their view of each other (specifically in male heavy groups). Changing the tank layout or adding new objects sometimes can encourage them to explore and stay active, which helps lower stress. Feeding them a variety of foods like live or frozen daphnia, frozen bloodworms, and small snails also keeps their minds busy and stomachs full. Experienced fish keepers often suggest keeping a small group of pea puffers together in a tank just for them. This way, you can watch their unique behaviors without worrying about fights with other fish or shrimp. With the right mix of plants, hiding places, and a good diet, your aquarium will be a lively home that brings out the best in these amazing puffers. Frequently Ask Questions Are Pea Puffers Aggressive? Yes, they can be aggressive, especially toward other puffers or fish with long fins. It’s best to keep them alone or in carefully monitored species only groups. Can Pea Puffers have Tank Mates? They do better in species only tanks in groups or with fast, peaceful fish. They are not considered good options for community tanks. They are known for fin nipping slow or long-finned fish, so you have to choose their tank mates carefully. Do Pea Puffers need Brine Shrimp? Pea puffers are carnivores. They like live or frozen foods, specifically daphnia, scuds and bladder snails. While brine shrimp is a great option, there are plenty of other alternatives. How Many Pea Puffers Can I Keep Together? Pea puffers are social fish and do best in groups , but you need plenty of space and plants to give them hiding spots. A 10-gallon tank can hold about 5 pea puffers if it has lots of plants. How Long Do Pea Puffers Live? With good care, freshwater pea puffers can live 4 to 5 years in your aquarium.

Cherry Red Barb Cherry Barbs, also known as cherry red barbs, are small, peaceful fish that make a great addition to your aquarium. They grow up to 2 inches long and have a bright red color, especially the males. These fish come from Sri Lanka and are perfect for community tanks. Key Features: Size: Up to 2 inches (5 cm) Temperament: Peaceful and friendly Lifespan: 5 to 7 years Diet: Omnivorous; enjoys flakes, live, and freeze-dried foods Ideal Water Temperature: 72–80°F (22–27°C) pH Range: 6.0–8.0 Care Tips: Tank Setup: Cherry barbs thrive in tanks with plenty of plants and places to hide. A darker tank bottom and background can help show off their bright red colors. Adding natural items like driftwood can make them feel more at home. Social Needs: They are happiest in groups of at least six. Keeping more females than males can help the males show their best colors. Tank Mates: Cherry barbs get along well with other peaceful fish like tetras, danios, and cory catfish. They usually swim in the middle to bottom parts of the tank. Feeding: These fish are not picky eaters. They enjoy a mix of dry, frozen, and live foods. Because they have small mouths, it's best to give them small-sized foods like nano pellets, daphnia, and spirulina flakes. Foods with natural red ingredients, like krill flakes and baby brine shrimp, can help keep their colors bright. Breeding: Cherry barbs are easy to breed. They lay eggs on plants and the tank bottom. To protect the eggs, provide lots of plants or a special breeding setup. Once the eggs are laid, it's a good idea to move the adult fish to another tank so they don't eat the eggs. Neon Tetras Neon Tetras are one of the most popular schooling fish in the aquarium hobby, and for good reason. Their bright blue and red colors add movement to a tank, especially in planted aquariums or setups with darker substrate! Neon Tetras are peaceful, active fish that do best in groups. We recommend keeping neon tetras in a school of at least 5 or more, but the bigger the group, the better they usually look and feel. When kept together, they are more comfortable and show more natural schooling behavior. When it comes to neon tetra care and tank requirements, they do best in a stable aquarium with clean water, peaceful tank mates, and plenty of places to feel secure. Plants, driftwood, leaf litter, and rock work can all help create a more natural setup for them. Neon Tetras are generally great community fish, but we don't typically recommend keeping them with shrimp as they might eat baby shrimp and can sometimes bother smaller or more timid shrimp. They're better suited with other peaceful fish that enjoy similar water conditions. Banana Plant The aquatic banana plant, Nymphoides Aquatica , is a captivating plant that brings both beauty and functionality to any freshwater aquarium. Named for its banana-like tubers that rest at the base, the aquatic banana plant is not only a conversation piece but also highly practical. The aquatic banana plant has vibrant green, lily pad-shaped leaves that grow toward the surface, providing gentle cover and shade for fish, while its roots help anchor this plant securely in substrate. The aquatic banana plant thrives in low to moderate lighting, making this plant a versatile choice for beginners and experienced aquarists alike. As a hardy species, the aquatic banana plant adapts well to various tank conditions and is relatively low-maintenance. The aquatic banana plant plays a key role in maintaining water quality by absorbing excess nutrients, helping to keep your tank clean and balanced. Scientific Name: Nymphoides Aquatica Common Names: Banana Plant How to an Aquatic Banana Plant The aquatic banana plant should be placed on top of the substrate, rather than planted. It is not good for the tubers to be buried in substrate. Once settled into an aquarium, the aquatic banana plant will begin to grow roots that make their way into the substrate securing the plant in its place. Caring for the Banana Plant Care Level : Easy Light : Medium CO2 : Not Necessary Fertilizer or Shrimp Safe Fertilizer Propagation: Leaves that are trimmed and left floating on the water's surface will start to grow roots. Note: Please do additional research on your plant to ensure its health. *All Plants may contain snails or snail eggs. We keep them in all of our tanks for the benefits they provide.*

Cholla Wood | Teddy Bear Wood Teddy Bear Cholla wood is identical to regular cholla wood although it is much thicker. The wood is quite rare as it takes more time for the cholla plants to reach the size needed to harvest such thick wood. Cholla wood is the skeleton of a cholla plant after it dies. The cholla wood is made up of a ton of holes and is hollow through the center which provides a natural cover for shrimp to hide. A big benefit of cholla wood is the fact that it grows biofilm which is a main food source for shrimp. It also releases tannins into the water, similarly to Indian Almond leaves and other natural products. Cholla wood is a softwood and will eventually break down in the aquarium. This can take many months and up to 2 years depending on size and thickness. When added directly to an aquarium it will float and usually takes 24-48 hours to sink. To sink cholla wood immediately, it can be boiled for 2-5 minutes. Cool the wood before adding it directly to the aquarium. listings.description: Stone Loach "Thuttinjet" | Nemacheilus sp. The Thuttinjet Stone Loach (Nemacheilus stigmofasciatus) is rare and was only recently introduced to the hobby. Even with that, it’s been easy for us to keep and it accepts most foods. This loach is marked by a thin black line that runs down its side like a dotted roadway. It has a mottled pattern similar to a Yo-Yo Loach, with small “Y” and “O” shapes. The face is rounded, a bit like a Siamese Algae Eater. Since receiving them, we’ve found they’re active and social. For this reason, we recommend keeping a small group of three or more so they have company. As with most loaches, a bit of flow in the tank helps them feel more natural, although it isn’t necessary. What do Stone Loaches Eat Nemacheilus stigmofasciatus has been surprisingly easy to feed. We mainly use NorthFin Kelp Flakes, a mix of small pellets (we grind 3–4 NorthFin pellet types), and frozen foods like cyclops and daphnia. Based on their appetite, the Thuttinjet Stone Loach should accept most foods, but keep their small mouths in mind. Best Parameters for Nemacheilus species We’ve kept them in semi-hard water with TDS about 180, GH 6–8, KH 2–4, and pH around 7.2–7.8. A setup with soft sand or smooth gravel, good oxygen, and a few hiding spots works well. Although, we keep them in a bare bottom aquarium with a sponge or matten filter with no issues. With that, these rare loaches settle in quickly and show off their unique pattern. Our Tank Parameters: Ph: 7.2 to 7.6 Gh: 4 to 8 Kh: 2 to 4 Temp: 70 to 74

Rosy Loaches | Nemacheilus sp. Rosy Loaches (Petruichthys sp. “Rosy”) are tiny, active fish that reach only 1–1.25 inches. They show bright red to orange hues on a slim, classic loach body and can look a bit like Cherry Barbs in color and shape. In our experience, they’re peaceful but bold. The Rosy Loach thrives for us in large species only tanks of 50 or more. If you’re planning to keep this loach, aim for groups of at least four; singles or pairs can become withdrawn since they’re so social. Rosy Loach Diet We feed Rosy Loaches NorthFin Flake Foods, especially Kelp Flake, and small pellets. We grind 3 to 4 different NorthFin pellet types into tiny pieces to fit their very small mouths. As a treat, we offer frozen cyclops and daphnia. Small meals once or twice a day work great. Water Parameters for Rosy Loaches We keep Rosy Loaches in a pH 7.2–7.6, GH 4–8, KH 2–4, and 70–74°F. They’ve been very hardy for us and adjust well to slightly harder water. We mix tap with RO water then add Shrimpy GH+ to dial things in. Our final TDS is around 180. Keeping their aquarium clean with steady parameters is the most essential step to ensure Rosy Loaches thrive. Our Tank Parameters: Ph: 7.2 to 7.6 Gh: 4 to 8 Kh: 2 to 4 Temp: 70 to 74

Green Swordtail Fish The Green Swordtail (Xiphophorus helleri) is a peaceful livebearer from the rivers and streams of Mexico and Central America. Adults reach about 5 to 6 inches. Males grow a long “sword” on the lower tail fin. They’re active swimmers and do best in larger tanks with open space to to swim. We recommend keeping Green Swordtails in groups, with two females to each males to reduce stress. Swordtails are livebearers so they will readily breed with little effort. They can also be kept successfully in male only tanks without issue. They’re great community fish for planted aquariums while plant will also add cover for babies if you plan to breed them. Note that they may eat very small shrimp or their own fry, so choose decor and tankmates with that in mind.

Rabauti Cory Catfish | Rust Cory The Rust Cory Catfish (Corydoras rabauti) is a small, peaceful scavenger from the Amazon basin. It is found in parts of Brazil, Peru, and possibly Colombia. Adults reach about 2 to 2.5 inches. As they mature, they show a mix of colors: rusty orange, soft violet, and a hint of metallic green. Similar to other Corydoras species, Rabauti Cories spend most of their time on the bottom, calmly searching for leftover food. Rabauti Corydoras prefer to be kept in groups of six or more, this could include other cory species if in a community aquarium. They’re great for community tanks and usually do fine with freshwater shrimp, though they may eat tiny shrimp fry. Use soft sand or smooth gravel to protect their barbels and belly. Our Tank Parameters Ph: 7.2 to 7.6 Gh: 4 to 8 Kh: 2 to 4 TDS: 160 to 180 Temp: 70 to 74°F

Corydoras adolfoi | Adolfo's Cory Adolfo’s Cory (Corydoras adolfoi) is a rare cory from Peru and Brazil. As it matures, it develops a bright yellow-orange head patch with a clean black mask. It stays small and peaceful, so it fits well in planted community aquariums. Keep them in groups of six or more so they feel safe and show natural behavior. Good tankmates include dwarf cichlids, angelfish, larger shrimp, and other calm fish. They spend most of their time on the bottom scavenging, so use soft sand or smooth gravel to protect their barbels and belly. They may eat baby shrimp. Our Tank Parameters Ph: 7.2 to 7.6 Gh: 4 to 8 Kh: 2 to 4 TDS: 160 to 180 Temp: 70 to 74°F

This fish gets its “sunset” name from its golden-orange body and yellow fin edges that resemble a sunset. The Sunset Thicklip Gourami is generally peaceful. Adult males may show some territorial behavior toward other male gouramis, but they usually coexist in a roomy, planted tank. They rarely show aggression toward other tankmates, which makes them a good fit for community aquariums. They prefer slow-moving water, so a sponge filter or matten filter works well. Our Tank Parameters Ph: 7.2 to 7.6 Gh: 4 to 8 Kh: 2 to 4 TDS: 160 to 180 Temp: 70 to 74°F

Gudgeon Empire Fish The Empire Gudgeon (Hypseleotris compressa) is a peaceful fish from Australia, south-central New Guinea, and parts of Indonesia. It grows to about 4–5 inches. Empire gudgeon fish are best kept in small groups of three or more in a planted tank with rocks, driftwood, and hiding spots. Normans Lamp Eye Killifish The Norman’s Lampeye Killifish is small, peaceful, and great for beginners due to their easy care. It swims near the surface, so a tight lid is a must to avoid jumping. If they feel safe, they will display their best color in a planted aquarium with floating plants and a dark background. To ensure they feel safe, it is best to keep the lampeye killifish in groups of 6 or more. Breeding Lampeye Killifish Norman’s Lampeye are easy to breed egg scatterers. They spawn near the surface in floating plants or a yarn spawning mop, laying a few sticky eggs each day. For best results, move the mop or the Lampeye killifish so the eggs and fry aren’t eaten. Eggs usually hatch in about 10 to 14 days. Fry can easily feed off biofilm or naturally occurring infusoria until they are ready to eat live baby daphnia. Methylene Blue | Aquarium Treatment Methylene Blue is a commonly used aquarium treatment that helps protect fish, fish eggs, reduce fungal growth, and support fish during stressful situations. It’s often used in breeding setups, quarantine tanks, and hospital tanks where extra support is needed. This treatment is especially popular with breeders, as it can help prevent fungus on fish eggs and improve hatch rates when used correctly. Methylene Blue can also be used in quarantine or hospital tanks to help reduce stress and support fish recovery. It is not recommended for use in established display tanks , as it can stain silicone, decorations, and negatively impact beneficial bacteria. Common Uses for Methylene Blue Helps prevent fungus on fish eggs Used in breeding setups to improve hatch rates Supports fish in quarantine or hospital tanks Useful during transport or stress recovery Treats external fungal issues when used properly Dosing Instructions Standard Treatment: Use 10 drops per gallon or 1 teaspoon per 10 gallons to achieve approximately 3 ppm Methylene Blue. During Treatment: Remove chemical filtration such as carbon while treating. After treatment is complete, replace carbon if needed to help remove the medication. Dip Use: Methylene Blue can also be used as a short dip. Mix 5 teaspoons per 3 gallons of water. Dip fish for no more than 10 seconds, then return them to clean, conditioned water. Methylene Blue is best used in quarantine, hospital, or breeding setups and is not recommended for display tanks due to staining and its effect on beneficial bacteria.

Calcium Liquid Test Kit | Fritz Aquatics Calcium plays a crucial role in aquariums, and it should remain in proper balance with alkalinity (KH) When the balance is off, it can lead to poor growth and tissue necrosis. Calcium uptake in aquariums can change over time, so regular testing is recommended to ensure proper dosing. These Fritz Calcium Test Kits measure calcium levels in both freshwater and saltwater aquariums . Each kit includes the necessary testing solutions, a test tube, and instructions with a color chart to help you read your results. While calcium is more closely monitored in saltwater systems, freshwater aquariums also benefit from routine calcium testing. Aquarium plants require calcium for healthy leaf growth, and invertebrates such as shrimp and snails rely on adequate calcium levels to maintain shell strength and support proper molting. Recommended calcium levels: Tropical community fish: 75+ ppm African cichlids: 120+ ppm Marine aquariums: 300–400 ppm Reef aquariums: 400–450 ppm Directions & Dosage Fill the test tube with 5 ml of aquarium water (to the line on the tube). Add 10 drops of Calcium Test Solution #1, holding the bottle completely vertical for consistent drop size. Cap the test tube and gently shake to mix. Always use the cap and avoid skin contact, as this may affect test results. Vigorously shake Calcium Test Solution #2 for at least 10 seconds. Add Solution #2 drop by drop, gently shaking between drops and counting each one. Stop when the solution changes from pink to blue. As the endpoint approaches, the color may briefly turn purple; after purple forms, only 1–2 additional drops should be needed. Calculate calcium level by multiplying the number of drops by 20. Use the chart provided to confirm results. To lower calcium levels, perform partial water changes using water with lower calcium content.

What should I feed my Bonivesta Guppies? Bonivesta Guppies are omnivores and do best on a varied diet. Offer a high-quality flake food or micro pellets, along with live or frozen foods like brine shrimp, daphnia, or bloodworms to help support their color and overall health. Do Bonivesta Guppies breed easily? Yes, Bonivesta Guppies are livebearers and breed readily in aquariums. If males and females are kept together, it’s common to see fry appear pretty quickly. Can I keep Bonivesta Guppies with other guppy varieties? Yes, Bonivesta Guppies can be kept with other guppy varieties. Just keep in mind that if you want to maintain specific traits, it’s best to keep them separate to avoid crossbreeding.

Albino Pygmy Cory Catfish You've probably heard of the Pygmy Cory, but have you ever seen an Albino Pygmy Cory ?! These tiny little catfish bring all the personality and activity of a traditional Pygmy Cory with a unique bright albino coloration that really stands out in planted aquariums and nano community tanks! Albino Pygmy Corys stay super small, usually around 3/4 of an inch, making them a great choice for smaller aquariums and peaceful community setups! You’ll see them sifting through the substrate, exploring plants, resting on leaves, and even swimming together in the middle of the water column. Like all corydoras, they do best in groups , so we recommend keeping at least 6 or more together. These little catfish do best in a mature aquariums with stable water parameters, sand or smooth substrate to not hurt their bellies, and plenty of plants, driftwood, and hiding spots. They’re peaceful, active, and make great tank mates for shrimp, snails, tetras, rasboras, Celestial Pearl Danios, and other small community fish! Albino Pygmy Corys are excellent scavengers, but they shouldn’t be expected to live on leftovers alone. Feed a varied diet of quality nano foods , small sinking foods, and frozen foods like baby brine shrimp, daphnia, or cyclops to keep them healthy and active. Pygmy Cory Size Pygmy corydoras are considered a dwarf species of cory. They grow to about 40% the size of most other corydoras, with adults reaching around ¾ of an inch. Males tend to stay even smaller than females. The body shape of the pygmy cory catfish is distinctive, featuring a flat belly and a streamlined form that runs from the snout to the tail. Their coloration is typically silver-gray with a prominent black line that extends from the snout all the way to the tail, making them easy to distinguish from other corydoras species . The only other cory species that’s similar in size is the Corydoras habrosus , which you can check out here. Breeding Pygmy Corydoras We’ve had pygmy corys breed naturally in our aquariums, especially when using Java Moss or spawning mops. Key points for breeding pygmy corydoras include: The female lays fertilized eggs; unfertilized eggs should be removed promptly to prevent fungal growth. Stable water parameters are essential for successful breeding. After hatching, fry should be fed microscopic foods like infusoria to support growth. Frequent water changes help maintain high water quality for healthy fry development. As fry grow, they begin swimming freely in the water column. Some hobbyists use marbles instead of substrate to protect eggs from being eaten. Pygmy corydoras are a great choice for a beginner-friendly breeding project. Feeding Pygmy Corydoras At Flip Aquatics, we feed our pygmy cories, which are specialized bottom feeders and bottom dwellers, a variety of foods suited to their feeding behavior. Pygmy cories and other cories spend most of their time at the bottom of the tank, foraging for food on the substrate. Our food list includes: Frozen Foods (small size like baby brine shrimp, daphnia, cyclops, and bloodworms as an occasional treat) NorthFin Foods (Community Flake and Nano Bits) Canned green beans (unsalted, finely crushed to suit the small mouths of pygmy cories) Pygmy cories and other cories benefit from a varied diet that includes vegetable rich flake or pellets and frozen foods such as baby brine shrimp, bloodworms, and shrimp to support their health and natural bottom-feeding habits. Our Water Parameters pH: 7.2 - 7.5 GH: 4 - 6 KH: 2 - 4 TDS: 100 - 150 Temperature: 70 - 74°F Tank Setup Suggestions Size: 5 gallons or more (a nano tank or small home aquarium is ideal for pygmies, as long as there is enough swimming space and plenty of places to hide) Substrate: Sand or smooth substrate Additives: Indian Almond Leaves or Alder Cones When setting up an aquarium for pygmies, it's important to create a peaceful environment with lots of plants and hiding spots. This helps pygmies and other nano species feel secure and allows them to thrive. A well-planted aquarium not only provides cover for pygmies to hide but also encourages natural swimming behavior and reduces stress. Compatible tank mates for pygmies include other nano species, peaceful community fish, dwarf shrimp , snails, tetras (such as neon tetras), celestial pearl danios, and other fish of similar size and temperament. These combinations work well in a nano tank or home aquarium, creating a harmonious community setup. Frequently Asked Questions How many Pygmy Corydoras can I keep in a 10-gallon tank? You can comfortably keep 10 pygmy corydoras in a 10-gallon tank. If you're an experienced hobbyist, it's possible to keep up to 20, as long as you maintain healthy water quality with nitrate levels below 40 ppm. Adding live plants can help with nutrient control and overall tank balance. Do Pygmy Corydoras eat algae? Pygmy corydoras don't eat enough algae to be considered good algae cleaners. However, they are excellent scavengers. They sift through the substrate for leftover food and debris, which can help reduce waste that might otherwise lead to algae growth. Are Pygmy Corydoras nocturnal? Pygmy corydoras are not fully nocturnal, but they will scavenge during both the day and night. They often school during the day, especially when kept with other similar schooling fish like otocinclus. You can often find them resting on sand or perched on plant leaves. How long do Pygmy Corydoras live? With proper care, pygmy corydoras can live 3 to 5 years. Keeping stable water parameters is key to their long-term health. We recommend a balanced diet of frozen foods along with veggie-based flakes or small pellets.

listings.commonName: MicroBacter Start XLF - Live Nitrifying Bacteria
listings.description: MicroBacter Start XLF Starting a new tank? Had a filter crash? Cleaned a little too hard? MicroBacter Start XLF is one of those products that is great to have around just in case. This is a super concentrated live nitrifying bacteria that helps get your biological filtration going and helps bring ammonia and nitrite down fast. It is made for cycling new freshwater aquariums, but it is also really helpful after medications, major cleanings, overcrowding, or anything else that may have messed with the good bacteria in your filter. It is 15x strength, so a little goes a long way. Brightwell says most tanks can cycle in around 5-7 days when used as directed , but always test your water before adding more fish. Zero ammonia and nitrite is the goal! Shake well before using, make sure your water is properly dechlorinated, and dose in an area with good flow. It is normal for it to smell a little earthy, have some clumps, or make your water cloudy for a bit. That is just the live bacteria doing their thing. Why We Like It: Professional 15x strength live nitrifying bacteria Helps cycle new freshwater aquariums in about 5-7 days Quickly helps reduce ammonia and nitrite Useful after medications, deep cleanings, overcrowding, or filter crashes Can be overdosed during aquarium emergencies when used as directed Great choice for tanks with heavier fish loads

RainboCode | Brightwell Rainbowfish are such cool fish, but they do come from waters with their own specific mix of minerals and trace elements. This formula is made to help replace those little elements that can get used up over time or pulled out by things like carbon and chemical filtration. It is designed for rainbowfish, and other fish from Australia and New Guinea. The added trace and minor elements support normal metabolic and neurological functions while also helping provide what fish use to maintain their natural coloration. The best part is that it does all of that without significantly raising your GH or KH, so you are not completely changing your water parameters just by adding it! Why We Like It: Made specifically for rainbowfish Replaces trace and minor elements used up in the aquarium Helps support normal metabolism and neurological function Provides elements used in natural fish pigmentation and coloration Helpful after using activated carbon, resins, or other chemical filtration Made with purified water and ultra-high purity ingredients

Razor Freshwater System Cleaner| Brightwell Got rocks, driftwood, or glass that are looking a little rough? Razor Freshwater is made to help loosen that buildup so it is way easier to scrub, scrape, or siphon out during water changes! It works on the stuff that builds up on your hardscape, decorations, and tank walls, while also helping your filter grab fine floating debris like leftover food and detritus. It is not an overnight miracle product, but with regular use it can help get your tank looking cleaner and clearer without having to go crazy scrubbing everything. It is safe for freshwater fish and live plants when used as directed, but not recommended to use in tanks with shrimp, crabs, crayfish, or other crustaceans. Key Features of Razor Freshwater Helps loosen buildup on rocks, driftwood, decor, and glass Makes tank cleaning and gravel vacuuming easier Helps clump up fine debris so your filter can catch it Helps keep particles from settling back onto your hardscape Safe for fish and plants when used as directed Great for tanks that are looking a little crusty Use every 3 days until you get the look you want, then weekly for maintenance A Few Things to Know: Remove activated carbon while using it since carbon can make it less effective You may need to rinse mechanical filter media more often while dosing This works slowly, so give it a little time and keep up with normal maintenance

Calcium Sweet + Savory | KatsAquatics Sweet + savory, because your shrimp, snails, turtles, and bottom dwellers deserve better than boring calcium food! Calcium Sweet + Savory is a whole food blend made with collard greens, mango, banana, black soldier fly larvae, egg, blue spirulina, and a touch of garlic! It is packed with 30% bioavailable calcium to support healthy shells, smooth molts, growth, and breeding, while still being something your animals will actually want to eat. The little bit of natural fruit flavor makes this a great option for picky eaters, while the leafy greens, protein, and fiber help round out the formula. It holds together well in the tank and breaks down cleanly, so you can feed without turning your water into a mess. Whether you are raising mystery snails, breeding shrimp, feeding bottom dwellers, or supporting shell health in aquatic turtles, this is an easy, tasty way to add extra calcium and nutrition to their routine. Key Features: 30% bioavailable calcium for shells, molts, growth, and breeding Made with real collard greens, mango, banana, black soldier fly larvae, and egg Great for shrimp, snails, turtles, and bottom dwellers Natural fruit flavor helps encourage picky eaters to feed Blue spirulina adds extra micronutrients Garlic helps support appetite Holds its shape and degrades cleanly in the aquarium What animals eat them? Neocaridina/Caridina shrimp All aquatic snails (mystery/ramshorn/rabbit/all!) Plecos and other bottom feeders Any fish that loves to steal bottom feeder food!

Snello Gel Food | KatsAquatics This isn't just snail food, Snello Gel Food is a super premium, whole food gel mix made for snails, shrimp, plecos, corys, turtles, and other hungry little bottom dwellers! Created by the biologist behind KatsAquatics , this formula is packed with real collard greens, kale, zucchini, black soldier fly larvae, banana, egg, spirulina, vitamins, and more. No wheat, soy, fillers, or weird junk your animals do not need. One 4 oz bag makes over 400 little hearts of gel food, so it goes a long way! Just mix the powder with water, gently heat it up, pour it into molds or a container, and let it set. Once it is ready, you have a soft, sliceable gel food your tank can snack on daily. Snails love it, shrimp pick at it, plecos and corys clean it up, and turtles go absolutely crazy for it! Neocaridina shrimp & Caridina shrimp Aquatic snails (mystery/ramshorn/rabbit/all!) Plecos and other bottom feeders Any fish that loves to steal bottom feeder food!

listings.commonName: Hatchling Fuel | Fry Food for Newly Hatched Fish
listings.description: Hatchling Fuel | KatsAquatics Your fry need more than crushed up flakes!! Hatchling Fuel is a super fine fry food made with real Arctic copepods, krill roe, and micro algae to give tiny fish a strong start from day one! The 50-200 micron particle size is perfect for newly hatched fry and can be fed through their first 4 weeks of life. With 50% protein and 15% fat, it is made to support fast growth, healthy development, and all that tiny fish energy. This is a great everyday food for freshwater and marine fry, including livebearers, cichlids, tetras, rainbowfish, and more. Just feed small amounts 1-3 times per day, only what they can finish in about 5 minutes, and remove any extra food to help keep water quality in check. Key Features: Made with real Arctic copepods, krill roe, and micro algae 50-200 micron particle size for newly hatched fry Great for hatching through the first 4 weeks 50% protein and 15% fat to support fast growth Includes squid meal, yeast, vitamins, minerals, and antioxidants Great for freshwater and marine fry Made by a biologist with trusted US suppliers

Kelp & Wood Pleco Pops | KatsAquatics We are big believers that if a food is made for herbivores… greens should probably come first, ya know? Kelp & Wood Pleco Pops are made with real ingredients your plecos and grazing fish will actually recognize, like alfalfa, kelp, moringa, spirulina, and natural oak wood. Not just a bunch of filler shaped like a wafer and called “pleco food" Now yes, there is wheat in these. Before anyone panics, it is there for a reason. Wafers need something to help them stay together underwater, and a little natural starch does the job. It is not the star of the show though, the greens, wood, and grazing-friendly ingredients are! These are handmade in Brooklyn, New York and slowly dehydrated at low temperatures instead of being cranked out by a giant machine. That means they are not all perfectly round, perfectly smooth, or perfectly identical… but your fish don't care! The rougher texture actually gives them something to graze on, which is kind of the whole point They may not be the cheapest or prettiest pleco wafers out there, but they are made with ingredients we would feel good feeding our own fish every day. Key Features: Real greens come first, including alfalfa, kelp, moringa, and spirulina Includes natural oak wood for grazing fish Great for plecos and other veggie-loving bottom dwellers Handmade in Brooklyn, New York Slowly dehydrated at low temperatures Rough texture encourages natural grazing behavior Holds together well underwater Made with only enough wheat to help the wafer stay together

listings.commonName: Defension F | Freshwater Slime Coat Protector
listings.description: Defension-F | Brightwell Whether you're moving your fish, doing a big water change, or netting somebody who absolutely does not want to be caught Defension F is a freshwater slime coat protector made to help fish handle those stressful moments a little better! It adds a protective coating that helps support and restore the fish’s natural slime coat after shipping, bagging, handling, acclimation, or minor abrasions. It is also helpful when setting up a new tank or doing maintenance, especially when fish are already feeling a little stressed The best part? It is copper free and safe to use in shrimp tanks , planted tanks, and aquariums with sensitive invertebrates. No aloe vera, no cellulose-based fillers, and no ingredients that are known to break down and cause extra water-quality issues. Use Defension F when adding new fish, during transport, after netting, or anytime your fish could use a little extra support! Key Features: Made in the USA Supports and helps restore the natural slime coat Helps reduce stress from shipping, bagging, netting, and acclimation Supports recovery after minor scrapes and handling stress Helps reduce the harmful effects of ammonia during stressful situations Copper-free and safe for shrimp, invertebrates, and live plants Great for new fish, water changes, tank maintenance, and transport

Red BOA Caridina Red BOA Caridina shrimp are a high grade pinto shrimp pattern with distinct cheek spots and full back cape. True BOAs will show a cape that runs cleanly across the entire back line along with visible cheek spots, giving them that bold look. Each shrimp will vary slightly in pattern, which is part of what makes BOAs so fun! Our Red BOA Caridina are carefully selected, and the BOAs produced from this line can throw a range of beautiful offspring! No matter what these shrimp produce, you'll have amazing colors and patterns! Please note that red coloration is not guaranteed and often does not fully develop until adulthood. Juvies may appear lighter or less defined, with color and pattern improving as they mature Tank Parameters pH: 5.5-6.7 GH: 3-6 KH: 0-1 TDS: 90-120 Temp: 68 to 72°F Tank Equipment Filter: Matten Filter Active Substrate: Brightwell Rio Escuro or Cafe Soil , Fluval Shrimp Stratum Water: RO/DI Water remineralized with Shrimple GH

Blue Calceo Shrimp | Blue Dragon Shrimp The Blue Calceo Shrimp , also known as the Blue Dragon Shrimp , is a highly sought after, rare Caridina hybrid originally bred in Germany that has incredible color! Their deep blue coloration makes them a standout in almost any aquascape, while their active grazing helps clean up biofilm, algae, and leftover food throughout the aquarium. Blue Dragon Calceo Shrimp thrive in stable, soft, slightly acidic water with plenty of mosses, plants, and hiding places. Like other Caridina shrimp, they do best in established aquariums with consistent water parameters. Their peaceful nature makes them an excellent choice for shrimp only tanks or community aquariums with other small, nonaggressive species. Blue Calceo Shrimp readily accept high quality shrimp foods, algae based wafers, and occasional blanched vegetables. Whether you’re looking to start your first Caridina colony or add a unique blue shrimp to your collection, the Blue Calceo Shrimp is a rewarding species to keep! Peach Steel Shrimp Peach Steel Caridina Shrimp are a unique, selectively bred freshwater shrimp. They’re c losely related to Blue Steel Shrimp and Peach Bolt Shrimp lines , they often display a beautiful milky overcoat with warm peachy/orange tones that give each shrimp its own distinct look. The Peach Steel Caridina Shrimp we offer come from the same trusted local breeder who supplies a lot of our high end Caridina shrimp, and we’ve been consistently impressed with the quality and coloration they produce! Like other high grade Caridina shrimp , they thrive in stable, well established aquariums with soft, slightly acidic water and consistent water parameters. Peach Steel Shrimp are constantly grazing throughout the aquarium, feeding on biofilm, algae, and leftover food. While they won’t replace regular tank maintenance, they do help clean up natural surfaces as they explore! Their peaceful nature makes them a great addition to shrimp colonies and community tanks with other small, non-aggressive species, bringing both color and activity to a well-established aquarium.
