Remarks: Satanoperca mapiritensis , also known as the fine spotted eartheater, is a glittering, beautiful member of its genus. It is known for the iridescent blue spots covering its face that sparkle when the fish turns in the light. While S. mapiritensis is very similar in appearance to others in its genus, it can be identified by how clustered the spots are on the operculum, the white spots on the top of the head, and the pale orange lips present on adult fish. They are a slow growing species, typically taking two years to reach maturity, but the resulting elegant, peaceful fish makes them worth the wait. S. mapiritensis was first described by Venezuelan ichthyologist Agustín Antonio Fernández-Yépes in 1950. Having collected the type specimens from the Rio Mapirito, he named them after the location. It is now known that the species can be found throughout the Río Orinoco basin, not just in this one tributary. Throughout the years, there was a lot of debate over the validity of the species and where it should be placed taxonomically, having originally been placed in the Geophagus genus like others that are now placed in their own genus of Satanoperca . For a time, S. mapiritensis had been argued to be synonymous with S. jurupari and then S. leucosticta . A final analysis by Brazilian Environmental Sciences student Renata Ota in 2013 would solidify S. mapiritensis is its own valid species based on previously mentioned morphological differences. The natural habitat of S. mapiritensis is similar to that of other Satanoperca , typically inhabiting clear, white-water channels and floodplains with a soft mud or sand substrate dotted with leaf litter and fallen branches. Parameters here, like with most South American species, are very soft, warm, and acidic with little pollutants. Being omnivorous eartheaters, S. mapiritensis spend most of their day scooping up mouthfuls of substrate to sift out any morsels of food such as worms and fallen plant matter. When keeping S. mapiritensis in the home aquarium, they will have the best chance at thriving if their native habitat is replicated to the best of one’s ability. Having a soft, fine substrate is required to prevent choking and damage to the mouth and gills as they engage in their earth eating feeding style. As they do not tolerate poor water quality, large, frequent water changes are also recommended to maintain the health of your S. mapiritensis . Like others in its genus, S. mapiritensis is typically docile with territorial aggression only ever seeming to crop up when spawning. Overly aggressive species should be avoided as tankmates as they will overly stress this mellow eartheater. Instead, peaceful species such as tetras will be excellent tankmates so long as they are not small enough to fit in the mouths of S. mapiritensis . While they are peaceful to other fish, some have noted that S. mapiritensis are far less tolerant of conspecifics compared to others in their genus so more space should be provided if keeping multiple pairs. Supplying multiple breaks in line of sight with décor such as live plants, driftwood, and rocks can further help reduce aggression. When looking to breed S. mapiritensis , it is best to start out with a group of six or more juveniles. This is because sexing even adults is very difficult due to males and females having little to no visual differences making determining the sex of young fish is near impossible. Getting six will statistically ensure you will get at least one pair as the fish grow. Keeping pristine water quality while feeding a diverse, high-quality diet with plenty of protein and vegetable matter will help your S. mapiritensis become conditioned for spawning once they are of breeding age. When this species is ready to spawn is usually when you will see the only clear sexual dimorphism with females getting a more rounded abdomen. Spawning takes place on a flat surface the pair have cleaned with the female taking the eggs into her mouth once they are fertilized. The female will then mouthbrood the eggs until the fry hatch and are free swimming. Interestingly, at this point the male will join the female in taking the fry into their mouths when danger is present or when transporting the fry to different locations. Both parents will guard the fry until they are large enough to fend for themselves.

Remarks: While discus are a well known and beloved fish within the hobby, few know that there is more than one species of discus. Most presume that all discus are Symphysodon aequifasciata when there are actually three different recognized species. The red eye discus is a variant of one of the other two species, currently known under the scientific name of Symphysodon tarzoo. The identifying feature of S. tarzoo is the beautiful array of red spots present on the anal fin and body, a pattern that is absent in the other two members of the genus. Another unique aspect of the species is that they are only known to naturally be found upriver from the Purus arch between Manaus and Rio Bauana. An introduced population also exists within the Rio Nanay that fishermen often collect from. Discus are often referred to as the king of aquarium fish. This nickname arose from the sheer beauty of these fish along with their reputation for being difficult to care for making those who keep them successfully revered within the hobby. It being difficult to keep discus was an opinion developed when majority of specimens available were wild caught. With most now being captive bred and even line bred to produce many different color variants such as turquoise and pigeon blood, they are much more hardy. That being said, discus still require very clean, soft, acidic water with little to no nitrates and warm temperatures. These peaceful cichlids tend to be timid, especially when it comes to feeding, so they shouldn't be kept with overly boisterous or aggressive fish. Typically their mouths are very small, but once they reach adulthood they are capable of swallowing very tiny fish so this should also be considered when choosing tankmates. If attempting to breed discus, lots of vertical surfaces should be provided for them to lay their eggs on and it should be noted they can become territorial when spawning. Once the fry hatch and are free-swimming, both parents show an incredible form of parental care in which they feed their fry by allowing them to eat their slime coat. This behavior is an amazing sight and makes breeding discus very enjoyable.

Remarks : One of the most colorful variants of the species, Cyprichromis leptosoma “Yellow Head” are a must have for Tanganyikan collectors. When in breeding dress, males have an electric blue body, a sunshine yellow head and caudal fin, and a dorsal and anal fin that are pitch black. When not displaying, they tend to be more of a silver color like the females. Cyprichromis leptosoma are a mild-mannered cichlid from Lake Tanganyika that exhibit shoaling behaviors higher in the water column. This makes them excellent tankmates for shell- or cave-dwelling cichlids, which rarely venture higher into open water. They act as a relaxing agent for other species as well, much like tetras do with dwarf cichlids - if the Cyprichromis are swimming in the open, it must be "safe." Cyprichromis are long and slender and may be considered the "sardines of Lake Tanganyika." They occur all over the lake and have a wide variety of color patterns. They are maternal mouthbrooders and in the wild, females will spawn all at once with the dominant males in the area. Spawns are typically 5-20 fry as their mouths are small. As these are social fish, we recommend keeping these fish in groups of 6 or more, 10 or more being better. Their high activity also makes us recommend not keeping them in tanks that are not at least 4ft long. Due to the sensitive nature of these fish, DOA claims will only be honored if the fish are in their sealed bags. No exceptions will be made for losses that occur after opening the bags.

Remarks: Clown labs ( Labidochromis chisumulae ) are a rare, close relative of the classic yellow lab ( Labidochromis caeruleus ) endemic to the rocky reefs around Chizumulu Island in Lake Malawi. Despite their close relation, they do have a number of differences with the most apparent being their coloration. Juvenile and female clown labs are cream or platinum white while mature males stand out with a brilliant sky-blue hue accented by a jet-black dorsal fin, mask, and vertical stripes. This coloration is very similar to male Labidochromis sp. 'Chisumulae Mbweca' with the key visual difference between the two species being that male clown labs possess a black band on their backs just below the dorsal fin that is absent in Labidochromis sp. 'Chisumulae Mbweca.' Basic care for clown labs is very similar to that of other Labidochromis species in that they require hard, alkaline conditions in order to thrive and benefit from having plenty of rockwork and a sandy substrate. Where they mainly begin to differ is their diet. Unlike other labs that are mainly herbivorous, clown labs have a primarily carnivorous diet naturally consisting of insects and small crustaceans in the wild. Within captivity, they are not very picky and will take to almost any foods provided. To keep your clown labs healthy and encourage them to show their best colors, provide a varied, high protein diet with the occasional treat of a vegetable-based food such as spirulina flake for added vitamins and fiber. A great benefit of clown labs not having a strict, herbivorous diet is that they can be kept with peacocks and haps without fear of bloat. Making them even more compatible is that they also have a surprisingly mellow disposition for an mbuna cichlid. Just be certain that your clown labs are not kept with other cichlids that are overly aggressive or large enough to swallow them as males of this species rarely exceed 3 inches in length with females being even smaller. It also is not recommended to keep them with other Labidochromis to prevent hybridization and aggression between conspecifics. A 55 gallon aquarium or larger is recommended if keeping clown labs in a Lake Malawi community tank. However, if you are wanting to just keep a small breeding group of 3 or 4, a 40 gallon will be sufficient. Multiple male clown labs can be kept together so long as there is at least one cave and 2-3 females per male to reduce aggression. It is often recommended to keep more than one male as the competition will encourage the more dominant male to display stronger colors. As they are peaceful for an mbuna, do not require large groups unlike many other Labidochromis , form pairs readily, and are very prolific, clown labs make a great breeding project to both beginner and seasoned keepers alike. Simply providing proper care and having the right ratio of males to females (2-3 females per male) can result in spawns. Spawning can take place on just about any horizontal surface within the aquarium with the female taking the eggs into her mouth as like with all mbuna, clown labs are a mouthbrooding species. The female will hold the eggs for approximately 25 days after which she will release the free-swimming fry. To avoid predation, it is recommended to remove the fry at this point to raise away from the parents.

Remarks: The common name of ramshorn snail is used within the hobby for a number of different species of small snail with a flattened, spiral-shaped shell. The species we are offering were imported as Indoplanorbis exustus . More specifically, they are the red variant that display a red foot and a tan shell providing a splash of color that stands out amongst green plants. They are voracious algae-eaters, reproduce readily, are very hardy, and are completely peaceful. These aspects make ramshorn snails excellent additions to almost any aquarium as clean up crew, a low-maintenance food source for snail eaters, or just as an adorable addition to watch crawl all around the tank. Ramshorn snails, like other small, prolific snails commonly seen in the hobby, often get a bad rap of being “pest snails.” Many will see them as a detriment to their aquascapes as they wrongfully believe ramshorn snails will eat their plants and reproduce uncontrollably. In reality, these scavengers actually are feeding on decaying plant matter, only going for living tissue when starving. Their numbers are also something that can be controlled and even come in handy as an indicator of conditions within your aquarium. To produce eggs and grow their population, ramshorn snails need an abundance of food. As they are opportunistic omnivores, this food source can be excess fish food, decaying plant matter, or even a dead fish or invertebrate. Therefore, if you see an explosion in your ramshorn snail population, this can be a sign for you that you are feeding too much or something has died and is decaying within your aquarium. While it is possible to control ramshorn snail populations easily by reducing their access to food, adding predators such as loaches, or physically removing them with traps, this isn’t so easy once they have been introduced to the wild. Indoplanorbis exustus are native throughout India and Southeast Asia, but due to introduction from human activity, invasive population can be found in Africa and North America. They may only have an average lifespan of about 4 months, but being hermaphroditic and prolific breeders allows these snails to take over an area and outcompete native snail populations quickly. To prevent any further damage to the environment, please be careful to not allow any of these snails or their eggs to be let out into the wild. Sterilize any containers they have been in and do not dispose of aquatic plants or substrate outdoors.

Remarks: Tropheus sp. 'Kipili' are an uncommon, not yet officially described species of Tropheus found between Korongwe Bay and Sangamwisha Bay along the Tanzanian shoreline of Lake Tanganyika. They are often incorrectly marketed under the name of Tropheus brichardi ‘Kipili,’ however they have not been officially recognized to be a locality of Tropheus brichardi . In fact, Tropheus sp. 'Kipili' differ so much from the species that most believe it to be a unique species on its own. An interesting aspect of Tropheus sp. 'Kipili' is that juvenile fish often display more color than the adults. When young, they are a vibrant, sunshine yellow with black or dark brown vertical bars giving them a bumblebee-like pattern. As these fish mature, the vertical bars get thicker and thicker until the fish appears to be predominantly black or dark brown with yellow stripes. This change in Tropheus sp. 'Kipili' as they mature is fascinating to watch and makes raising a group of juveniles a very exciting venture. Tropheus are obligate herbivores, and even small amounts of protein can induce bloating conditions. They form social hierarchies and should be kept in large groups, about 10 or more, to spread out any aggression. Tropheus tend to be more peaceful toward non-conspecific species so they can do well in a large Tanganyikan community tank.

Remarks: The midnight demasoni ( Chindongo sp. "Elongatus Mozambique") is known from the Mozambique coast of Lake Malawi. They bear a heavy resemblance to the more well known demasoni cichlid ( Chindongo demasoni ) with it being thought that they might be a locality of C. demasoni . Like their close relative, the midnight demasoni was originally placed in the Pseudotropheus genus, but was later classified within the Chidongo genus following an examination of their teeth and skull structure. They also share the same feisty disposition, small size, algae-based diet, and stunning blue and black coloration seen in both males and females. With such an aggressive and territorial demeanor, these mbuna can hold their own against other mbuna with the same attitude. Avoid placing them with more peaceful species as the midnight mbuna can quickly overwhelm and injure them. Their aggression can be lessened by ensuring they are given plenty of space and rockwork to break up territories. Having at least 2-3 females per male will also help reduce violent behavior. Aside from their feisty nature, midnight demasoni can be a great mbuna species for beginner and experienced keepers alike as they are very hardy and prolific spawners. Also accounting for their elegant coloration and active behavior, it is easy to see why they have found their way into the tanks of many African cichlid enthusiasts.

Remarks: The red flamingo guppy (Poecilia reticulata) is an excellent choice for those looking for a vibrant flash of red. Juvenile and female red flamingo guppies are typically a muted gold or tan color with subtle hints of reds and yellows in their fins. Some adult females will have fully red tails making even females of this guppy strain very colorful. Adult males stand out with neon red coloration starting in the tail and extending up half of the length of the fish. This color is also present in the dorsal fin and on occasion, can go all the way to the head of the adult males. A perfect starter fish! Guppies ( Poecilia reticulata ) are peaceful community fish that reproduce with ease. They are livebearers, meaning the females release live fry rather than laying eggs. It is recommended to keep more females than males, as males can easily harass females with relentless attempts to reproduce, leading to stress in the females. For most strains, males are very colorful while the females remain a gray or silver color. However, there are some exceptions to this rule so sexing these fish is best done by looking at the anal fin. The females will have short, rounded triangle shaped anal fins with a black spot on the body directly above it, these are her female reproductive organs. Males will have long, thin, pointed anal fins that form his male reproductive organs called the gonopodium.

The marble queen sword ( Echinodorus cordifolius "Marble Queen") is a beautifully unique variety of aquatic plant. While it has the standard spade-shaped leaves of a typical sword plant, it stands out with an elegant, mottled, white or light green pattern on a vibrant green base. Like most other swords, the marble queen sword grows impressively large making it an excellent choice for a background or centerpiece plant. While sword plants are usually very hardy and tolerate a variety of conditions, the marble queen sword can be slightly more demanding. Avoid moving the plant too much and provide it with medium to high light as well as fertilizer at the roots utilizing root tabs and/or an aquatic plant substrate. CO2 injection will also be appreciated. Providing proper lighting and fertilization will help ensure your marble queen sword shows the best coloration and consistent growth. You will receive a medium sized potted plant 2-4" tall. If you are only ordering plants, you are eligible for a shipping rate of $19.99. Please include a note or email requesting a partial shipping refund when you order. *Plants may contain snails and/or snail eggs. ***** Please read our SHIPPING AND HANDLING FAQ before ordering. It contains important information about order fulfillment time, shipping speed, etc. *****

Remarks: The costae tetra ( Moenkhausia costae ), also commonly known as the black line tetra, is an uncommon gem of a South American tetra within the hobby. They have elegant, silver, partially see-through bodies and a unique, slanted, black stripe starting at the base of the anal fin and ascending up to the tip of the upper caudal (tail) fin. When costae tetras turn in the light, they shine with an iridescent blue-green sheen making their appearance all the more eye-catching. Like with most tetras, costae tetras are highly social and live in massive schools in their native, Brazilian habitats within the Rio Sao Francisco and Rio Itapicuru. This social behavior carries over into the home aquarium where this species is known for being one of the tightest schooling tetras within the hobby. To ensure your costae tetras do not become stressed and skittish, keep them in groups of at least 6-8. The larger the school, the more interesting social behaviors, such as courting, you will see. You can further encourage your costae tetras to be bolder by not placing them overly aggressive or predatory species large enough to swallow them. While these active schoolers can be nippy toward tankmates with long fins, similar to barbs, this behavior is lessened when kept in large enough groups. They will be too preoccupied with their own kind to mess with other species in the tank. Costae tetras, especially when captive bred, tend be rather hardy and adaptable in a variety of ways. They are omnivorous and not picky in the slightest, so they will often take to almost any food offered. Feeding them a variety of foods is encouraged to make sure they do not have any deficiencies. Water parameters are another aspect that costae tetras are often lenient about. They are able to tolerate moderate pH and water hardness, however they will do best and show the best coloration when kept in soft, acidic water. Such conditions mimic their natural habitat and further doing so by providing botanicals such as driftwood and plenty of live plants will make your costae tetras feel more at home. If cared for properly, these social, active, and elegant tetras make an excellent addition to almost any peaceful, soft water community aquarium.

Remarks: The mascara barb ( Dawkinsia assimilis ) is a large, colorful, and highly active species coveted by many fishkeepers. Juvenile fish are silver or tan in color with a blue-green iridescent sheen and a large black blotch on the flanks just above the anal fin. Near the tip of each point of the caudal (tail) fin, there is also a red spot followed by a black spot. As the fish matures, both males and females will begin to develop a black spot right behind the eye, a line of red spots along the lateral line, a bright orange or gold top half, a pearly white bottom half, and a flash of vibrant red on the dorsal fin and the top of the head. While both sexes are very similar, mature males can be identified by having especially bright colors, filaments on the edges of the dorsal fin, and tubercules on the head when spawning. The known native range of the mascara barb is only within the southwestern Indian states of Karnataka and Kerala making them endemic to those areas. Despite having such a restricted range, they can be found in a variety of habitats from muddy banks with sluggish currents to clear rapids that rush over a rocky substrate. What is shared amongst this assortment of habitats is that the waters are soft, mildly acidic, free of pollutants, and well-oxygenated even in areas with slow flow. Within the home aquarium, mascara barbs will tolerate some deviation when it comes to the pH and hardness to the point they can do just fine in moderate conditions. However, what they will not tolerate is poor water quality or low oxygen levels. Provide plenty of filtration as well as oxygenation through the use of filters and aerators while performing frequent water changes to keep these barbs healthy. Feeding your mascara barbs is very simple as they are not picky. Being voracious omnivores, they will typically take almost any food offered. It should be noted, though, that mascara barbs have very small mouths compared to the rest of their bodies. To accommodate this, feed smaller foods such as bloodworms, brine shrimp, small flakes, and small pellets. Feeding a variety of foods will not only improve the coloration of your barbs, but will also help prevent deficiencies in their diet. Mascara barbs are generally peaceful but can become nippy and might stress out more timid species with their active behavior. Since they are a very social species that naturally lives in massive schools, nipping behaviors and general stress will become far worse if they are not kept in large enough groups. To avoid this, have no less than 6 mascara barbs with 8-10 or more being ideal. Not only will larger groups be less likely to harass tankmates, but having plenty of these barbs will also encourage fascinating behaviors such as sparring and courting as well as better coloration from males. So long as these needs are met, mascara barbs can be enjoyed in a community setting or in a species only tank.

Remarks : These koi plakat bettas ( Betta splendens ) stand out with incredible color, no two look alike! An interesting aspect of this strain is their colors and patterns can change as the fish ages. Each fish is approximately 1-2" in length. This listing has WYSIWYG (what you see is what you get) options where you can see exactly which fish you will be receiving by selecting the corresponding option. For example, if you select "Male 3" you will be shown the photo of that specific betta. We also offer a cheaper "We Pick" option where we will select a betta for you. Betta splendens , also known as Siamese fighting fish or domestic betta fish, have been line bred by humans for over 1000 years making them one of the oldest domesticated fish in the hobby. This line breeding has led to many different tail types, colors, and morphologies. When bettas where first introduced into the hobby they were bred and raised for fighting for onlookers to gamble on resulting in an already aggressive fish becoming even more aggressive but also very hardy compared to their wild counterparts. Male bettas are especially territorial and in general should never be kept in the same aquarium. Females should only be housed together with extreme caution and in very large aquariums with lots of hiding spots. They have gotten a reputation as "puddle fish" due to their labyrinth organ allowing them to survive in low oxygen environments such as puddles resulting in many keeping them in incorrect conditions. In the wild, while the bodies of water bettas are typically found in are small pools or shallow swamps or floodplains, this water is constantly being refreshed either through the groundwater, rain, or flooding of larger nearby bodies of water. These conditions are not the same as the unheated, unfiltered, tiny bowls or vases many have mistakenly believed are enough for a betta. While some may survive in these conditions and they can be okay short term, a betta will only truly thrive if kept in a tank that is at least five gallons, has a heater to keep the water between 78 F and 84 F, soft decor, and an established filter. *** Please do not attempt to house these male bettas together.

Remarks: The silver flying fox ( Crossocheilus reticulatus ) is a peaceful, active river fish from Southeast Asia. It is prized for its algae-grazing abilities and striking silver coloration with a dark, reticulated (net-like) pattern and a large black spot at the base of the tail. Unlike the more commonly imported Siamese algae eater ( Crossocheilus oblongus ) that seeks out more protein as it ages, C. reticulatus tends to get a more voracious appetite for algae as it grows. In the wild, the silver flying fox is known to inhabit areas of the Mekong and Chao Phraya basins with rocky bottoms and rapid, clear currents. Their stream-lined bodies and sucker-like mouths have evolved to aid them in withstanding the fast flow as they graze upon algae and biofilm. Being used to such conditions, the silver flying fox requires heavy oxygenation within the home aquarium which can be achieved via filters, wavemakers, and aerators. Silver flying foxes heavily graze on algae, however they should not be expected to only subsist on it as this can lead to deficiencies. Be sure to supplement their diet with foods heavy in plant-matter such as fresh vegetables, spirulina flakes, and sinking herbivore/algae wafers. Supplemental feeding is especially important if wanting to keep moss in the same tank as your silver flying fox as they are likely to nibble on it if not given other food sources. Due to their passive nature, avoid housing silver flying foxes with aggressive bottom-dwelling fish. Unlike their more territorial relatives, many have found this species to do best when kept in groups of five or more. If given proper amounts of space and hiding spots, housing multiple silver flying foxes together can encourage them to be bolder and display more natural behaviors such as sparring. Captive breeding is extremely uncommon when it comes to the silver flying fox with its natural reproductive queues not being well known. Most specimens in the aquarium trade are wild-collected or produced commercially using hormone induction. For hobbyists looking for an active algae grazer that remains relatively peaceful, Crossocheilus reticulatus is an excellent choice, especially in well-oxygenated community aquariums with plenty of swimming room.

Remarks: The Neolamprologus brevis "Ikola Sunspot" we are currently offering were bred from wild parents here at the farm hence being labelled as "F1." Their wild genetics make for incredibly healthy genes perfect for breeding projects. Neolamprologus brevis "Ikola Sunspot" is a stunning locality of Neolamprologus brevis from the Ikola region along the Tanzanian shoreline. This beautiful locality is prized for the vibrant, sunshine-yellow belly present in breeding age females. This coloration is also occasionally present in dominant males, but is far more muted making them one of the easiest to sex variants. Neolamprologus brevis is one of the smallest lamprologines known to the hobby, rarely growing beyond 2” in length. What these shell-dwellers lack in size, they make up for in their feisty personalities and striking appearance. N. brevis will fearlessly defend their shells against intruders much larger than them, sometimes even nipping the hands of keepers that get too close! This amusing level of bravado combined with the electric blue markings that seem to glow on their tan or silver bodies makes N. brevis a must have for many Tanganyikan cichlid enthusiasts. In the wild, N. brevis populations can be found throughout Lake Tanganyika to which they are endemic. Each locality can differ in both color and pattern, but their habitat type choice remains the same. Being a shell-dwelling species that form monogamous pairs instead of harems, N. brevis are found in open sand where empty snail shells are scattered about with each pair controlling a territory approximately 6” in diameter centered around their chosen shell. They hover outside their shell feeding upon any passing plankton that they snatch out of the water column. A unique trait of N. brevis is that they have a far greater number of gill-rakers compared to other shell-dwellers which gives cause to their robust, frog-like heads that house them. It is suspected that having so many gill-rakers aids this species in feeding upon even the smallest of zooplankton within the lake. Within the home aquarium, it is best to attempt to replicate the natural habitat of N. brevis to allow them to thrive. They require warm, hard, alkaline water parameters, a sandy substrate, and at least one shell per pair. Their monogamous nature allows N. brevis to be comfortable if kept as a single pair with a 10-gallon aquarium being sufficient enough space. If keeping multiple pairs together as a colony or if keeping them in a Tanganyikan community, 20 gallons or more will be needed. While N. brevis are very protective of their shells, they are otherwise peaceful cichlids and thus can be kept with many other Tanganyikan species so long as enough space is provided and tankmates aren’t large enough to swallow them. Feeding N. brevis is both an entertaining and straight forward task. Being true micropredators and planktivores, they will take most small, meaty foods provided. High protein crushed flakes and small pellets, baby brine shrimp, moina/daphnia, small bloodworms, and tubifex are all great options they should take to readily. Since N. brevis usually are not very picky, you can occasionally provide them with a crushed veggie flake as a treat to aid in digestion, but majority of their diet should be high protein. Like with most shell-dwelling species, a lot of the enjoyment most find in keeping N. brevis is being able to witness their breeding and fry-rearing habits. Of course, to begin breeding your own, you will need males and females. Since it can be difficult or near impossible to sex young N. brevis , it is best to start with a group of at least 5-6 young juveniles and allow them to pair off naturally. As they mature, you can begin to spot the handful of differences between males and females. Males will get extensions on their ventral fins, have a more pointed dorsal fin, grow larger, and will have more vibrant blue markings. Females remain smaller, rounder, have smaller fins, and will get a yellow hue to their bellies. How vibrant this yellow color is depends on the locality of your N. brevis with some having very subtle yellow color while others are more intense. When ready to spawn, a pair will select a shell to breed in and use as a hiding spot when threatened. A unique behavior N. brevis display is that both males and females will hide in the same shell, something not seen in other cichlid species. While this species does not tend to bury their shells like many other shell-dwellers, they instead show off surprising strength and resourcefulness when their selected shell is not in ideal placement. By biting onto and manipulating the shell or simply ramming into it, these bulldog-like cichlids are able to move the shell around or even flip it over if needed despite the shell usually being at least twice their size. Once a shell is selected and in prime condition, the female will lay her eggs deep inside the shell with the male then fertilizing them. Both the male and female will guard the eggs and fry until they are free-swimming after which the male typically moves on to another female if one is available. The female will continue to care for the fry until they begin to leave the shell about 1-2 weeks after becoming free-swimming. So long as the fry have other hiding spots to retreat to and the tank is large enough, they typically can be safely left in the same tank as the parents to continue to grow.

listings.description: Remarks: Melanotaenia maccullochi "Stark River" is one of the many localities of the widespread and colorful Macculloch's rainbowfish. They shine with metallic blue and gold iridescence accented by red finnage in males. M. maccullochi "Stark River" are often incorrectly called "Starche Creek" with Professor Peter J. Unmack, a leading expert on Australian freshwater fishes, confirming Stark River to be the correct location. Macculloch's rainbowfish ( Melanotaenia maccullochi ) is a smaller Melanotaenia species that exhibits many horizontal stripes throughout the body. They are found throughout southern New Guinea and the northeastern peninsula of Australia. The variants may be subspecies or entirely new species. Some variants, such as the Skull Creek variant ( M. sahulensis ), have already been identified as a separate species. These fish are omnivorous and should be fed a quality flake food with supplemental proteins such as baby brine shrimp. They require clean water but tolerate a wide variety of water parameters. By providing frequent water changes, you will be rewarded with nearly continuous spawning attempts. Melanotaenia species deposit eggs in weedy areas (often mimicked by a yarn mop) and the eggs hatch 7-10 days later. Eggs can be harvested for hatching in separate tanks to avoid predation. Most Rainbows show their best colors at sunrise, when the males display their bright fins for potential mates. Having more females than males will allow for proper color displays and avoid any unwanted aggression towards lone females.

Remarks: The Rio Tocantins severum ( Heros efasciatus "Rio Tocantins") is a locality of H. efasciatus from the Rio Tocantins in Brazil. While juvenile and stressed fish are mostly a muted gray or silver, healthy, settled adults shine with vibrant blue-green iridescence. Some will also develop red eyes and a complementary yellow or orange hue in their fins. With such beautiful coloration and an attractive speckled pattern, it is no wonder Rio Tocantins severums are highly prized within the hobby. The best way to ensure the Rio Tocantins severum thrives in captivity is to replicate their natural habitat. In the wild, they thrive where the water is soft, acidic, and heavily tannin-stained with plenty of sunken roots and wood for them to hide and forage amongst. Wood and botanicals such as Indian almond leaves can be used in the aquarium to add some tannins that will boost the health of the Rio Tocantins severum and encourage them to show their best coloration. A sandy substrate is heavily recommended as severums enjoy digging which can be a very interesting behavior to observe and act as a source of enrichment. Being opportunistic omnivores, Rio Tocantins severums are not very picky and will take most foods offered. They will benefit from having a varied diet high in both protein and vegetable matter. Like other severums, they have a mostly peaceful disposition outside of territorial disputes among conspecifics, spawning, and predating upon anything small enough to fit in their mouths. To reduce the risk of fighting when keeping multiple severums together, keep them either as a single fish, a male and female pair, or a group of 5 or more. Providing plenty of space as well as décor to break their lines of sight will further help in reducing aggression. Live plants should be used with caution or not at all as severums are very likely to eat them. Severums grow to respectable sizes but not enough to be tank busters and do a good job of defending themselves so they can make a great choice for a South American community tank with other larger cichlids. With their peaceful demeanor, endearing personalities, and vibrant colors, it is easy to see why severums have become such a beloved staple within the hobby.

Remarks: The rainbow humphead cichlid ( Gymnogeophagus lipokarenos ) is a smaller eartheater very rarely seen within the hobby. Such rarity is driven not by lack of interest as many collectors seek them out for their beautiful coloration and impressive nuchal humps present on mature males. Juvenile rainbow humphead cichlids are mostly muted tan in color, but mature fish shine with a rainbow of red, yellow, orange, blue, and green hues giving rise to their common name. Such coloration is most vibrant in dominant males while females and lesser dominant males are more muted. As mentioned previously, the rarity of the rainbow humphead cichlid in home aquariums is not due to a lack of demand, but rather a lack of availability. In the wild, this species is known to only occur in the Río Uruguay and the Río Negro within Brazil and Argentina. Combine the limited native range with the fact many other similar looking species of Gymnogeophagus can also be found in these areas, and the result is that true Gymnogeophagus lipokarenos are almost never exported. Captive breeding has proven to be fairly challenging as well since this species requires conditions to be just right to induce spawning. Rainbow humphead cichlids are not very picky eaters, remain a manageable size, and are very docile even toward smaller fish and conspecifics, but it is not a good choice for those unfamiliar with Gymnogeophagus . This is due to their requirement of having pristine water conditions and an annual cooling period that they would undergo within their natural habitats. Frequent water changes alongside soft, acidic water parameters are a must if one wants to avoid illness. While they will tolerate warmer temperatures for short periods, the health of rainbow humphead cichlids will gradually decline over time if they are not given an annual period of lower temperatures between 57-65 °F for at least a month or so. Make sure the temperature change is done gradually over the course of at least a few days to a few weeks to avoid temperature shock. Not only does this cool period improve the health of your rainbow humphead cichlids, but it is also required to induce spawning. If looking to undertake the challenge of breeding, you can increase your chances of successful spawns if this cool period is induced during what would be the winter months in South America, June-August. When ready to spawn, a pair will select a smooth surface such as a stone that they clean before attaching their eggs. Both the male and female will guard the eggs until they hatch, upon which the female will take the newborn fry into her mouth. Only the female will continue to care for the fry until they are large enough to fend for themselves. Like all eartheaters, rainbow humphead cichlids require a sandy substrate due to their earth-eating habits. They sift mouthfuls of sand through their gills, pulling out bits of food to eat. Gravel presents a very high probability of choking or refusing to eat. Also like their close relatives, these fish do best in groups of 4 or more but can also do well in single male and female pairs. Due to their smaller size, adult can be kept in an aquarium as small as 40 gallons if kept as a single, breeding pair, but 75 gallons or more is recommended if they are to be kept with other fish. Whether undertaking the challenge of breeding this species or looking to keep a cool-water community tank, rainbow humphead cichlids are a joy to keep.

Remarks : The red Nhamunda Heckel discus ( Symphysodon discus ) is a unique variant of the Heckel discus found within the Rio Nhamunda. Unlike other variants of Heckel discus that tend to have a blue base, this one has a warm, reddish-orange base with blue stripes. Such intense, unique coloration stands out beautifully against green plants Heckel discus are one of the most colorful, challenging to keep, and oldest known wild discus species. They display vibrant yellows, oranges, greens, and blues that vary in amount and pattern depending on the exact locality they are sourced from. Typically Heckel discus are identified by the particularly wide and dark band that runs down the center of their body that is particularly round even for a discus. Care should be taken in regards to water parameters as these discus are wild and much less tolerant of incorrect water parameters. For the best chance at being successful, keep them in very soft, acidic, warm water and perform frequent water changes. Discus are often referred to as the king of aquarium fish. This nickname arose from the sheer beauty of these fish along with their reputation for being difficult to care for making those who keep them successfully revered within the hobby. It being difficult to keep discus was an opinion developed when majority of specimens available were wild caught. With most now being captive bred and even line bred to produce many different color variants such as turquoise and pigeon blood, they are much more hardy. That being said, discus still require very clean, soft, acidic water with little to no nitrates and warm temperatures. These peaceful cichlids tend to be timid, especially when it comes to feeding, so they shouldn't be kept with overly boisterous or aggressive fish. Typically their mouths are very small, but once they reach adulthood they are capable of swallowing very tiny fish so this should also be considered when choosing tankmates. If attempting to breed discus, lots of vertical surfaces should be provided for them to lay their eggs on and it should be noted they can become territorial when spawning. Once the fry hatch and are free-swimming, both parents show an incredible form of parental care in which they feed their fry by allowing them to eat their slime coat. This behavior is an amazing sight and makes breeding discus very enjoyable.

Remarks : The strawberry peacock ( Aulonocara sp.) is a neon pink and red variation of the ever popular albino dragon blood peacock. Unlike typical male albino dragon bloods that are usually bright white or light blue with orange faces, the males of the strawberry line have their electric pink and red coloration throughout their whole body. Some may also develop iridescent blue or white scales on the face and along their back. Like most Aulonocara species, coloration in dominant males will be brighter when in the presence of females and competing males. Females and subdominant males tend to be orange while juveniles are cream. The strawberry peacock, like all variations of the dragon blood peacock, is a man-made hybrid, but its exact origins are unknown. Due to their mixed genetics, they show a remarkable variation in color and pattern with most changing as they age. Please note that males under 4" may not show much color, but they typically develop a tremendous amount once they settle into their permanent tank. Like with most hybrid fish, this man-made strain tends to be particularly aggressive and territorial even for a peacock cichlid. This disposition allows them to hold their own against other, more aggressive cichlids, but also makes them a poor choice for more timid species such as Lethrinops sp..

Remarks : The Marajo oscar is a locality of Astronotus ocellatus rarely seen available in the hobby. As their common name denotes, they are found near Marajo Island where the mouth of the Amazon River connects to the Atlantic. With their collection location being so close to the ocean, some suspect they may tolerate mildly brackish conditions, but this has not been confirmed. Oscar collectors covet the Marajo oscar as it is said they show some of the most red coloration seen in wild oscars upon maturity. These oscars are wild caught out of Brazil, so they are going to be much less tolerant of water parameters and pollutants compared to those that are captive bred. The trade off for this is that they will have much healthier genetics comparatively and a known collection point. Oscars have been a mainstay in the fish keeping hobby for many years and are typically very recognizable to even those outside of the hobby. Many are wowed by their bright coloration, impressive size, and entertaining personalities. They have a long lifespan and can be quite personable with their owners, even eating from their hands after some training exercises! Oscars come in a variety of patterns, including tiger, albino, lemon, red, and many more so there are quite a few options to choose from. All of these traits combined with the hardiness shown in captive bred fish have made oscars the favorite of many keepers. Despite their popularity, oscars are not the greatest fish for beginners. Oscars are what many consider to be tank-busters, regularly growing to 12"+ in size and requiring a large amount of swimming space. They can be notoriously territorial upon maturity despite seeming rather docile when young, so there are very few if any options for tank-mates. Oscars are known to swallow any fish that fits in their mouth and ramming and biting those too big to swallow that enter their territory. Being solitary animals outside of spawning, adult oscars usually do best when kept alone. While some can be kept in a very large tank with similarly sized and tempered fish, one should always have a plan in place in case the oscar becomes too aggressive. Spawning pairs will usually work together to protect fry but can turn on each other when not raising young, so plans should also be in place in case they need to be separated temporarily such as with tank dividers. When keeping oscars, it tends to be the case that the fish decides on how the tank is decorated rather than the keeper. This is because oscars will dig and rearrange decor to their liking no matter how many times the keeper flattens the substrate and moves decor back into place. While some find this frustrating, others are amused by the stubbornness oscars display in regards to how their home is set up. Plants are also not safe as oscars will tend to eat them or simply dig them up constantly. Some can get away with hardy plants such as Anubias, but even these plants can sometimes get destroyed. If one wants a particular piece of decor to remain in a certain spot, it is best to glue it in place otherwise they will be at the mercy of their oscar. Oscars are primarily carnivores, feeding on fish, insects, crustaceans, and anything else that can fit in their mouths. However, wild fish will occasionally feed on fruits and nuts that fall in the water as well as graze on aquatic vegetation. In captivity, they should be fed a varied diet high in protein with the occasional vegetable or algae based food. Feeder goldfish are highly advised against as they provide poor nutritional value and can pass diseases on to the oscar. If not provided a proper diet, they will be much more susceptible to diseases such as hole-in-the-head. Some have reported adding a vitamin C supplement to their foods also helps prevent this disease. Oscars have a formidable appetite and will usually beg for food from their owner once they learn to recognize them. With how much they eat along with being particularly messy eaters, oscars can foul their water very quickly. As they do not tolerate poor water quality, this means large, frequent water changes are a must. High levels of pollutants such as ammonia and nitrates along with high bacterial counts can also contribute to oscars contracting hole-in-the-head disease. This disease can be treated through the use of medications such as metronidazole and by improving their diet and water quality. If cared for properly, this disease will likely not become an issue for those keeping oscars.

Remarks: Bucephalandra sp. Giant Velvet, as the name implies, is a larger growing version of Bucephalandra sp. Velvet making it perfect for aquascapes that have more space to fill. Just like normal velvet buce, young leaves start out brown or maroon in color then mature into a dark green hue with a velvet-like texture. Bucephalandra are similar to Anubias in that they are epiphytic meaning that they grow on structures such as wood, rocks, or decor rather than into the soil. They should be attached to structures like this in the aquarium because if their main stem called the rhizome is buried in the substrate, it likely will rot away and the plant will die. You can attach it by gently wedging the rhizome into the structure you want it to grow on or by using nontoxic thread, fishing line, or aquarium plant glues. When using the glue, be sure to use as little as possible and to not cover the rhizome in the glue as it will suffocate it and cause the buce to rot. Another aspect Bucephalandra have in common with Anubias is that they typically are not very fussy plants and can do well in a wide range of parameters granted they are stable and do not have extreme fluctuations. They also can do well in low to medium light so a high end aquarium plant light is not needed, however if one is used the plant will grow much faster. Growth can further be boosted through the use of CO2 injection but it is not necessary. One thing that does set Bucephalandra apart from Anubias is that it does prefer soft to moderate hardness compared the medium to high hardness. This makes buce a great choice for softwater tanks. Remarks: This eartheater was previously known to fishkeepers as Geophagus sp. “Aripuana” since its first introduction to the hobby around 2009. It wouldn’t be until a few years later in early 2015 that it would receive a proper scientific name of Geophagus mirabilis . Mirabilis means “extraordinary,” “marvelous,” or “admirable” in Latin, making it a very fitting name for this fish that wows just about anyone with its vibrant coloration. Juvenile fish are a muted tan or silver color with the occasional iridescent blue scale, going through an incredible “glow-up” as they mature. Adult G. mirabilis practically glow they are covered in so many iridescent blue spots and lines complemented by red, orange, yellow, and pink hues around the face and fins. In fact, the sheer amount of patterning adults of this species has on the face in particular is used alongside the 2-6 black spots arranged horizontally along the middle of the body to distinguish this species from others. The original, temporary name for G. mirabilis , Geophagus sp. “Aripuana,” comes from its original collection point and only known natural habitat, the Rio Aripuanã in southern Brazil. The Dardanelos/ Andorinhas Falls act as a natural barrier keeping G. mirabilis populations upstream and separating it from other members of its genus as it is currently the only known Geophagus species found above the falls. Such a restricted range has led to this species rarely being imported and thus usually only seen in the collections of eartheater collectors. As breeding them is like that of most other Geophagus , a breeding project is very viable and something we encourage anyone looking to keep this stunning eartheater attempt. Like all eartheaters, Geophagus mirabilis require a sandy substrate due to their earth-eating habits. They sift mouthfuls of sand through their gills, pulling out bits of food to eat. Gravel presents a very high probability of choking or refusing to eat. Also like their close relatives, these fish do best in groups of 4 or more but can also do well in single male and female pairs. Due to their somewhat large size, adult Geophagus mirabilis should be kept in an aquarium that is at least 75 gallons if kept as a single, breeding pair, but 100 gallons or more is needed if they are to be kept with other fish. When spawning, they can become territorial as they are protective parents and they have a good chance of swallowing tank mates that can fit in their mouths. These behaviors should be taken into consideration when planning a tank for these wonderful fish.

Remarks: The orca woodcat is possibly one of the most desirable woodcat species available to hobbyists. While most species of woodcat are mostly a muted tan or silver color, the orca woodcat stands out with a stark white belly and a midnight black top separated by a wavey border. Such coloration gives credence to how they ended up being named after the famous black and white cetacean. Their elegant coloration is not the only reason the orca woodcat is so coveted. It also makes a great community tank member with its peaceful disposition and the fact it does not require a very large aquarium due to its small size. While the orca woodcat is very unique, it does have at least one lookalike, Centromochlus musaicus , the ninja woodcat. Both species sport black and white coloration making them often confused for one another, but there are ways to tell them apart. First is to find out where the fish came from. The orca woodcat is found only within the lower rio Nhamundá in Brazil while the ninja woodcat is from the upper and middle rio Orinoco in Venezuela. If you do not know where the fish in question is from, you can take a look at its pattern. The orca woodcat differs from the ninja woodcat in that the ninja woodcat does not have a white spot/blotch underneath the dorsal fin. The ninja woodcat also has far more black coloration while the orca woodcat has more even color distribution. While using coloration is not always a 100% accurate way to identify similar species, it can give you a good guess. Like with all woodcats, the orca woodcat is a shy, nocturnal specie whose large eyes allow it to have excellent night vision. In the wild, it spends daylight hour hiding in crevices of wood or amongst leaf litter, but cruises the surface at night looking for fallen insects to feed on. You can expect similar behavior from the orca woodcat in the home aquarium with them usually only coming out of hiding when there is food or the lights go out. Do not fret over them remaining completely still all day long as this is normal behavior. To encourage your woodcats to come out of hiding and feel safe, provide plenty of hiding spots with plants, leaf litter, and driftwood. Keep lighting to a minimum as well. Only housing them with other peaceful species that are not overly boisterous will also aid in their comfort. Since the orca woodcat naturally inhabits areas of warm, low flow, soft, and acidic waters, replicating these conditions will help keep them healthy and happy long-term. Being insectivores, they will appreciate a diet of frozen-thawed foods such as bloodworms and brine shrimp, live foods like tubifex and blackworms, and prepared foods such as gels and sinking pellets high in insect protein. Use caution feeding foods with animal meat such as beef heart as this can cause the orca woodcat digestive issues if not limited to only being an occasional treat. If fed during the day, they will usually only go for sinking foods. However, at night you can sometimes have them feed on floating foods such as flakes. The orca woodcat, along with other closely related species, has been the subject of great scrutiny on what genus it should be placed in. Ever since its first scientific description in the 1970s, it has been moved back and forth between the Tatia genus and the Centromochlus genus. The most recent update occurred in 2020 with a study placing it in the Centromochlus genus so we shall refer to it as such for the time being.

Remarks: Despite having been known to science since 1892, little is recorded about Spatuloricaria evansii aside from its geographic range and morphology. The holotype for this species of whiptail was originally collected from Mato Grosso state in Brazil by geologist John William Evans after which it was named. It’s now known that the native range of S. evansii extends beyond this collection point and encompasses the Paraguay and Beni river basins that stretch across Argentina, Bolivia, and Brazil. The build of S. evansii is typical of most rapids-dwelling Loricariids with a flat, elongated body that helps it withstand the fast currents. A natural, mottled, tan, gray, and brown pattern is also a useful adaptation as it allows them to naturally blend in with the rocks they hide amongst. Like many whiptails in their range, S. evansii also have wide, gray bands that run up the length of their body that vary in visibility and hue based on the fish’s mood. When mature, males can be told apart from females by their thicker but shorter cheek and pectoral fin spines, more narrow head shape when viewed from above, and the extension on the top of the caudal (tail) fin being far longer and thread-like. As they are a rapids-dwelling species, S. evansii require pristine water and high levels of dissolved oxygen to thrive. While they can reach nearly a foot in length, most aquarium specimens top out around 8”. This still puts them on the larger side for a whiptail and thus need to have plenty of swimming space. S. evansii can be a great choice if you are looking for an omnivorous whiptail that won't be too much competition for species like Otocinclus catfish as they tend to not care much for algae. Instead, they should be provided a varied diet consisting of both meaty and vegetable-based foods. If all their needs are met, these whiptails can be a rare and interesting addition to your South American community tank.

Remarks: The L027d thunder royal pleco is a locality of Panaque armbrusteri known from the Rio Tapajos in Brazil. Young fish start out with the classic royal pleco pattern of gold/yellow and brown/black stripes on their body, but have spots instead of stripes on their fins. As they mature, these spots gradually grow and fuse together to match the rest of their striped pattern. With how large and well armored L027d thunder royal plecos are, they can make a great addition to a tank containing larger and more aggressive fish so long as they share the same preferred water parameters consisting of somewhat soft, acidic conditions with little pollutants. However, it should be kept in mind L027d thunder royal plecos can be territorial toward conspecifics so if housing them with other loricariids, plenty of space and hiding spots should be provided. Other fish being swallowed is not something that needs to be worried about as these fish are almost completely non-predatory. Like other Panaque species, L027d thunder royal plecos supplement their nutrition by rasping wood to consume the microorganisms and algae that live on and below its surface. To ensure proper digestion and nutrition as well as make them feel at home, L027d thunder royal plecos must always have access to wood to graze on. They also appreciate vegetables such as zucchini or cucumbers as well as algae wafers. These fish graze almost 24/7 so that means they also produce a lot of waste. To avoid buildup of pollutants, frequent water changes should be performed. Like with any Loricariid lots of oxygenation is also appreciated which can be achieved through the use of wavemakers, heavy filtration, and aerators. If all their needs are attended to, L027d thunder royal plecos can be a fantastic choice for those looking for a large, robust pleco.

Remarks: The L027b platinum royal pleco is a locality of Panaque armbrusteri also known as the Xingu royal pleco due to it being found within the Rio Xingu. Adult fish tend to be darker colored, more cream and black than brown and gold/green, with thinner tail stripes compared to others of the species. Some fish have a notably pale base color that is such a light cream it is almost white giving credence to their other common name of the platinum royal pleco. We have noticed some of our current stock of L027b platinum royal plecos have an orange hue to their fins adding more beauty to an already incredible fish. With how large and well armored L027b platinum royal plecos are, they can make a great addition to a tank containing larger and more aggressive fish so long as they share the same preferred water parameters consisting of somewhat soft, acidic conditions with little pollutants. However, it should be kept in mind L027b platinum royal plecos can be territorial toward conspecifics so if housing them with other loricariids, plenty of space and hiding spots should be provided. To avoid buildup of pollutants, frequent water changes should be performed. Like with any Loricariid lots of oxygenation is also appreciated which can be achieved through the use of wavemakers, heavy filtration, and aerators. If all their needs are attended to, L027b platinum royal plecos can be a fantastic choice for those looking for a large, robust pleco.

Young leaves start out brown or maroon in color then mature into a dark green hue with a velvet-like texture making it quite the unique addition to any aquascape. Bucephalandra are similar to Anubias in that they are epiphytic meaning that they grow on structures such as wood, rocks, or decor rather than into the soil. They should be attached to structures like this in the aquarium because if their main stem called the rhizome is buried in the substrate, it likely will rot away and the plant will die. When using the glue, be sure to use as little as possible and to not cover the rhizome in the glue as it will suffocate it and cause the buce to rot. They also can do well in low to medium light so a high end aquarium plant light is not needed, however if one is used the plant will grow much faster. One thing that does set Bucephalandra apart from Anubias is that it does prefer soft to moderate hardness compared the medium to high hardness. This makes buce a great choice for softwater tanks.
