Remarks: The red jewel cichlid ( Rubricatochromis paynei ) is a species of jewel cichlid that rarely makes an appearance within the hobby. Exporting wild fish has proven very difficult as its native range of Sierra Leone and Liberia has had a number of socio-political tensions and conflicts. Not only has export proven challenging, but things are made more complicated with many other species of jewel cichlid being incorrectly labeled as R . paynei . This mislabeling is primarily due to how difficult it is to visually differentiate the red jewel cichlid from other species within the genus. The breeders we imported that have produced the fish we currently sell were imported as R . paynei and we believe them to be such. They match the description of having a somewhat small mouth for their genus along with a black spot on the gill plate and a slightly larger black spot in the middle of the body. However, due to aforementioned trouble with acquiring genuine R . paynei , we think it is right to be transparent that there is always the potential that they are a similar species or hybrids. If there are any developments that cause us to believe they are not pure R . paynei , adjustments will be made. Young red jewel cichlids start out a muted tan color with a light scattering of iridescent blue spots. As they grow, these spots increase in number until the entire fish is covered in these dazzling markings. Usually, the base color beneath these shimmering spots is a grayish-tan, but when red jewel cichlids have fry, court mates, and spawn, they develop a vibrant red and orange color. This drastic change is why we recommend keeping this species in spawning pairs to see the best coloration. Red jewel cichlids continue the trend of the genus being hardy and adaptable fish. They are not picky about what they are fed, happily eating almost any foods offered. Slightly soft and moderately acidic to neutral pH is preferred, but we have found them to tolerate and even breed in hard, alkaline Florida water. These colorful cichlids are not only hardy, they stay a fairly modest size too and show a more mellow personality compared other jewel cichlids. A tank as small as 20 gallons can be suitable for a pair of red jewel cichlids with a few dither fish like African tetras. If you plan to keep multiple pairs, a slightly larger tank will be needed. We have found that so long as each pair is given their own spawning site, such as an overturned flower pot, three separate pairs can live comfortably in a 40 gallon. Breeding R . paynei is very easy and straightforward like with most jewel cichlids. We could actually argue they might be even easier due to their more laid-back disposition, massive clutch sizes, and how good of parents they have proven to be. While red jewel cichlids usually aren’t overly aggressive even when they are caring for fry, they will viciously defend their young if something proves to be an actual threat. When a keeper attempts to remove fry, this species will try to fight them off by biting the keeper’s hand for the entire duration of fry collection. It should be noted that while the parents are not a threat to their own fry, the young fish can actually be a threat to each other. They grow very quickly with larger/older juveniles easily out-competing the smaller/younger fish for resources or even attacking them. To prevent losses, remove older broods when a pair has a new set of fry and keep fry in groups that are of the same size as they grow.

listings.commonName: L333 Black and White Pleco (Hypancistrus seideli ‘L333’)
listings.description: Remarks: The L333 black and white pleco ( Hypancistrus seideli ‘L333’) is one of the many localities of Hypancistrus seideli displaying a striking black and white pattern. They can be found in the Rio Xingu in Brazil and display some of the most bold patterning amongst the different varieties of L333. Recently in 2025, a taxonomic study was conducted on the L333 black and white pleco along with a number of other similar looking Hypancistrus . This study determined that the plecos under the L-numbers L333, L66, L236, L399 and L400 were all just different variations/localities of the same highly variable new species. This new species name was deemed Hypancistrus seideli . They were named after professional aquarist, Ingo Seidel, who has been a great influence within the hobby and the scientific realm in regards to Loricariids . He especially made an impact in regards to Hypancistrus species so it is very fitting that he get these amazing little catfish named in honor of him. You can read more on this study by clicking HERE . The L333 black and white pleco is a typical Hypancistrus in regards to their care in captivity. They come from rocky areas of pristine, heavily oxygenated, warm, soft, and acidic water and will gradually decline in health in the home aquarium if these conditions are not replicated. Using a high quality filter with a high flow rate along with a heater and frequent water changes will help keep these plecos happy and healthy. Like all known Hypancistrus , the L333 black and white pleco is a carnivore so they must be fed a varied diet high in protein. Protein rich gel foods like Repashy, bloodworms, and sinking wafers are good choices to feed to meet their dietary needs. To reduce territorial fights and help the L333 black and white pleco feel comfortable in the aquarium, plenty of snug, rocky caves should be provided for them to hide in. These caves are also where these fish will spawn if all other conditions are just right. They can be a very exciting breeding project as they are such a unique and beautiful catfish. An important thing to note, however, is that it is not wise to house the L333 black and white pleco with other similar Hypancistrus as they can hybridize with it being near impossible to tell pure fish from hybrids. We encourage anyone who sets out to keep these fish make an effort to ensure captive populations remain pure to preserve this species in light of dam construction in Brazil destroying their natural habitat.

Remarks: The orange flash cockatoo apisto is a beloved, selectively bred variety of Apistogramma cacatuoides . Adult males and some females develop a tangerine orange anal, dorsal, and caudal (tail) fin that stands out in almost any aquarium. Unlike the more commonly available triple red variety, they do not have black markings in these fins. Apistogramma cacatuoides is one of the most popular Apistogramma species. Wild populations have subtle blue and yellow colors with a few orange spots on the caudal fin, but captive strains have been selected for the orange spots, resulting in the triple red and many other varieties. Males are larger and have more color, as well as longer and more elaborate fins. Females will turn bright yellow with black fins when in breeding dress. Apistogramma cacatuoides is a larger species of Apistogramma and will work well as a pair in a 20 gallon tank. A sandy substrate is necessary due to their earth-eating habits. The tank should be furnished with several caves or nooks to protect and spawn in. Cichlid caves, overturned flower pots, and leaf litter work well. Breeding is achieved by feeding live baby brine shrimp to an adult pair and providing a proper tank setup. Fry are guarded by one or both parents for several weeks. Dither fish such as small tetras and livebearers can be used to provide parents with targets to chase.

Remarks: Ancistrus damasceni are one of the many species of Loricariid commonly referred to as bushynose plecos. Their coloration changes based on mood, ranging from an orange-tinged tan to chocolate brown with spots and striations varying in levels of visibility. While they are common in their native range encompassing the Upper Parnaíba River basin in Brazil, they are uncommon within the hobby with little recorded about their care. It is presumed their care is typical of that of most Ancistrus with them proving to be fairly hardy and undemanding. While bushynose plecos are generally on the smaller side for a pleco, A. damasceni are especially small and almost never exceed 3” in length making them a great choice for smaller aquariums. The terms “bushynose” or “bristlenose” often used in reference to Loricariids belonging to the Ancistrus genus is derived from the long and elaborate tentacles that develop on the faces of males. The bigger the "beard" as some call it, the more dominant the male. Females will occasionally develop bristles as well along the edges of their face making it difficult to differentiate young males from females. These bristles are tempting for nippy and aggressive fish so this combined with bushynose plecos not having much armor compared to other species is why they should not be housed with nippy or aggressive fish. The pleco itself can pose a danger in the case of fish trying to swallow them as they have spines on their fins that they will flare out if being attacked to prevent the fish from eating them. This can result in the fish choking and the loss of both it and the pleco if the pleco remains stuck in the mouth of the fish. Bushynose plecos do not grow very large and are mostly peaceful so they can fit in well in smaller aquariums. Typically, the only aggression shown tends to be among males fighting over spawning caves. They can be kept with shrimp if the population has been given plenty of time to grow and begin reproducing regularly as the bushynose pleco will prey on them occasionally. While they are omnivores, they prefer to have a diet consisting mostly of vegetable matter and will voraciously feed on algae. Their appetite for algae does not diminish as they grow like in the case of common plecos making them an excellent addition to the cleanup crew in a tank. Typically, plants will not be eaten unless the pleco is starving or the plant is already dying. Breeding bushynose plecos can be very easy so long as all their needs are attended to and spawning sites are provided. Bushynose plecos are cave spawners where males will choose a small cave where he will chase females into to spawn. Once the female has laid eggs, it will be left up to the male to guard the cave and keep the eggs clean as the female leaves. They fan the eggs with their fins to keep fresh water flowing over them to help prevent them from fungusing and ensuring they get plenty of oxygen. Once the eggs hatch, the male will keep the fry inside the cave until they have absorbed their yolk sack and have become free swimming. This high level of parental care is fascinating to watch and is also why it is usually best to leave the eggs with the father to care for rather than removing them.

Remarks: The ruby green hap ( Haplochromis sp. 'Ruby Green') is one of the many colorful, undescribed haps typically referred to as Victorian cichlids. They are on the smaller side with males being able to grow to 5.5,” but usually not exceeding 4” in the home aquarium. Females stay slightly smaller. Like with most haps, juveniles and females are mostly gray and light tan in color with dominant males proving to be the true show stoppers. When fully mature and in optimal conditions, male ruby green haps show their namesake in the form of an iridescent, blue-green body topped with a ruby red blaze and matching tail fin. They also will show bold black stripes on the face and body as well as some orange and yellow accents. Despite being considered a Victorian cichlid, the ruby green hap actually is not known to inhabit Lake Victoria. Instead, it can be found in a few, smaller northern satellite lakes such as Lake Kyoga. They inhabit a surprisingly broad variety of habitats from sluggish, turbid expanses to clear, flowing waterways. Unfortunately, at least some ruby green hap populations like those in Lake Nawampasa are at risk due to pollution and eutrophication. Due to the lack of an evaluation by the IUCN and the potential for the ruby green hap to get wiped out before it can be formally described, it has been placed on the CARES list under the name of Haplochromis sp. 'ruby.' Hopefully through captive breeding programs, farms and hobbyists can help keep this beautiful species around. Being adapted for a variety of habitats has made the ruby green hap fairly hardy within the home aquarium, simply needing moderately hard and alkaline conditions alongside consistent water changes to thrive. They are primarily herbivorous, but will take a majority of foods offered and benefit from variety making feeding both fun and easy. Victorian haps have a reputation for being particularly aggressive and territorial and while this is true for the ruby green hap, it is to a much lesser extent. So much so that it is not recommended to keep them with other Victorian haps due to both the risk of hybridization as well as the ruby green hap being outcompeted or even attacked. Instead, they can be kept in a species only breeding group with at least two females to every one male to see their best colors. If you are not looking to breed ruby green haps, you can keep a male or two with a group of all male peacocks and Malawi haps so long as the species chosen are on the smaller and more mellow side. If one considers their vibrant colors, hardy nature, smaller size, and more relaxed personality when compared to other Victorian cichlids, it is easy to see why ruby green haps make a great fish for experienced and beginner keepers alike.

listings.commonName: L011/L035 Red Fin Thresher Pleco (Aphanotorulus emarginatus)
listings.description: Remarks: The red fin thresher pleco ( Aphanotorulus emarginatus ) has become a fish of many names ever since its first classification in 1840. Scientists have reclassified it into multiple different genera throughout the years with the most recent update occurring in 2016 placing it in the Aphanotorulus genus. Amongst hobbyists, it has been known by a handful of different L-numbers depending on collection point with some overlapping; L011, L035, L108, L116, and L131. The fish we currently have were imported under the L-numbers L011 and L035 with their collection point being reported as the Rio Pará. Plecos that accumulate so many L-numbers and have such debate around their classification tend to be ones that are very widespread in their native range. The red fin thresher pleco is subject to this phenomenon with it having populations throughout the Amazon. Arguments are still being had over whether the different populations that tend to have slight variation in color are the same species or not. As mentioned, there is some difference between collection points, but in general, red fin thresher plecos are tan in color with an orange or red tinge to the outer edge of the caudal (tail) fin. This flash of color alongside its leopard spot pattern makes this pleco a must have for Loricariid lovers. The native range of the red fin thresher pleco is broad and varied, but all these habitats are similar in regards to water parameters with conditions being warm, soft, acidic, and heavily oxygenated even in areas of low flow. Replicating these conditions within the home aquarium will keep this species healthy, happy, and looking their best. Many large Loricariids tend to be territorial around other plecos, but the red fin thresher pleco is an exception. They are very peaceful and some have successfully kept them with plecos only a third of their size. On the subject of their size, red fin thresher plecos can get to an impressive 16” long. Such a big species that is also surprisingly active will need an aquarium no smaller than 150 gallons so it has plenty of swimming space and water volume to handle its waste output. Feeding the red fin thresher pleco is very simple and straightforward. They are an herbivore leaning omnivore that will take almost any food offered, but do not seem interested in algae. Since red fin thresher plecos do not appear to rasp on wood, it is not required. While they do not need the presence of wood, this species, like most catfish, will need plenty of hiding spots which can come in the form of rock caves, pvc pipes, and larger flower pots. To handle their waste output and keep oxygen levels high, it is recommended to over filter the aquarium and add wave makers and/or bubblers as needed. With such a relaxed demeanor, elegant pattern, and hardy nature, the red fin thresher pleco can make a great addition to almost any larger South American tank.

Remarks: When the L260 queen arabesque pleco ( Hypancistrus sp. (L260)) was first introduced to the hobby in the late 1990s, it quickly became a well-known and regularly imported favorite amongst aquarists. Many have been drawn to their elegant, midnight black bodies covered in thin, white striations and spots. Their hardiness, small size, and less territorial nature when compared to others in their genus has only added to their desirability. Despite this multi-decade popularity in the hobby, like with many Brazilian Hypancistrus , science has not yet given them a full, official scientific name. While the L260 queen arabesque pleco has a very unique appearance, it does still bear some resemblance to a few closely related species. It can be told apart from both Hypancistrus sp. (L411) and Hypancistrus sp. (L066) by having a smaller size, far thinner white stripes/striations, and also sometimes having small spots which are absent in L411 and L066. Knowing collection location is also helpful when making sure a fish is truly L260 since it is endemic to the lower Rio Tapajós within the Brazilian state of Pará. Care for the L260 queen arabesque pleco does not differ much from most other Hypancistrus . They come from rocky areas of pristine, heavily oxygenated, warm, soft, and acidic water and will gradually decline in health in the home aquarium if these conditions are not replicated. Using a high-quality filter with a high flow rate along with a heater and frequent water changes will help keep these plecos happy and healthy. While the L260 queen arabesque pleco is an omnivore, like all known Hypancistrus , they mostly eat meaty foods with them gradually leaning more and more carnivorous as they age. So, to keep them well fed, they must be fed a varied diet high in protein. Protein rich gel foods like Repashy, bloodworms, and sinking wafers are good choices to feed to meet their dietary needs. It should be noted L260 queen arabesque plecos are particularly shy eaters so overly boisterous tankmates that will aggressively compete with them for food should be avoided. Most smaller Hypancistrus species do best in at least small groups, however they can become territorial especially during breeding. While the L260 queen arabesque pleco is known to be on the more peaceful side, males still might become aggressive over caves. To reduce territorial fights and help the L260 queen arabesque pleco feel comfortable in the aquarium, plenty of snug, rocky caves should be provided for them to hide in. These caves are also where these fish will spawn if all other conditions are just right. They can be a very exciting breeding project as they are such a unique and beautiful catfish whose wild populations unfortunately are threatened by habitat destruction. An important thing to note, however, is that it is not wise to house the L260 queen arabesque pleco with other similar Hypancistrus as they can hybridize with it being near impossible to tell pure fish from hybrids.

Remarks : The pearl cichlid comes from a wide variety of habitats in Brazil and Uruguay with some populations even residing in estuaries where they have developed a tolerance for mildly brackish conditions. A common feature among these habitats is a sandy substrate that is necessary in the aquarium due to their earth-eating habits. While they are earth-eaters, this species will also snatch food out of the water column and will possibly eat any tank-mates that are small enough to fit in their mouths. Their common name comes from the iridescent scales that cover majority of the body upon maturity. Males typically grow larger than females and very dominant individuals will develop a nuchal hump.

Remarks: The L004 angelicus pleco ( Hypancistrus sp. (L004)) is one of the beautiful Hypancistrus displaying an elegant black/dark gray body covered in white spots. These spots are larger in younger fish, growing more numerous and shrinking in size as they age producing a night sky appearance. They are frequently referred to as Peckoltia angelicus within the hobby but this is not a valid scientific name. For a time, plecos with L-numbers L004, L005, L028, and L073 were all thought to be separate species. Now, they are recognized as being the same species with the different L-numbers just representing different populations. L004 and L005 are from the Rio Tocantins near Cametá with L004 just being the juvenile form of L005. L028 are known from the Rio Guamá near Ourém and L073 are known from the Rio Do Pará in the Portel municipality. Care for the L004 angelicus pleco does not differ from most other Hypancistrus . They come from rocky areas of pristine, heavily oxygenated, warm, soft, and acidic water and will gradually decline in health in the home aquarium if these conditions are not replicated. Using a high-quality filter with a high flow rate along with a heater and frequent water changes will help keep these plecos happy and healthy. While the L004 angelicus pleco is an omnivore, like all known Hypancistrus , they mostly eat meaty foods with them gradually leaning more and more carnivorous as they age. So, to keep them well fed, they must be fed a varied diet high in protein. Protein rich gel foods like Repashy, bloodworms, and sinking wafers are good choices to feed to meet their dietary needs. Most smaller Hypancistrus species do best in at least small groups, however they can become territorial especially during breeding. To reduce territorial fights and help the L004 angelicus pleco feel comfortable in the aquarium, plenty of snug, rocky caves should be provided for them to hide in. These caves are also where these fish will spawn if all other conditions are just right. They can be a very exciting breeding project as they are such a unique and beautiful catfish. An important thing to note, however, is that it is not wise to house the L004 angelicus pleco with other similar Hypancistrus as they can hybridize with it being near impossible to tell pure fish from hybrids.

Remarks: One of the most coveted North American native fish within the hobby is the Everglades pygmy sunfish ( Elassoma evergladei ). These shy micropredators have gained popularity for the spectacular coloration of breeding males. When spawning or sparring, dominant male pygmy sunfish turn jet black making their iridescent blue spots across their body and fins seem to glow from the contrast. Juvenile, female, and subdominant males are less flashy with mottled greenish-brown hues and less vibrant spots. Stressed or frightened fish will become even lighter and duller in color, turning tan or cream. As their name indicates, the Everglades pygmy sunfish was originally associated with the Everglades in south Florida. Modern surveys have found their range, however, is far broader. Everglades pygmy sunfish can be found from the Cape Fear River in North Carolina, to Mobile Bay in Alabama, and down to the Everglades in South Florida. The habitats they call home consist of shallow, tannin-stained, vegetation rich, sluggish, pollutant-free, muddy-bottomed waterways and pools. While most in their genus can also be found in blackwater, the Everglades pygmy sunfish is the only one that seems to only occur in it. Such habitats naturally fluctuate in both depth and temperature as the seasons change, some almost completely drying out during parts of the year. Such fluctuation has made pygmy sunfish fairly adaptable in regards to hardness, pH, and temperature, but they still are sensitive to pollutants so frequent water-changes and a mature aquarium are needed. To see their best coloration and have them thrive long-term, we recommend keeping them in slightly acidic, tannin-stained, moderately hard, and room temperature parameters. Considering their tolerance of water parameters, the difficulty in keeping the Everglades pygmy sunfish lies mostly in how picky they are. These micropredators almost never take to dry/prepared foods with most requiring tiny, live foods like moina/daphnia or baby brine shrimp when first introduced to a tank. Sometimes they can be weaned on tiny frozen foods by slowly mixing it into live food feedings, gradually increasing the ratio of frozen to live over time. The same method can be used for trying to train them to take prepared foods, but this is almost never successful. Some, especially wild-caught fish, may never even accept frozen foods. Due to this, we only recommend keeping pygmy sunfish if you are able to provide them small, live foods at least once or twice a day to keep up with their picky appetite and fast metabolism. Everglades pygmy sunfish are true nano fish. While dominant males are capable of growing to 1.3” in length, most never exceed 0.9”. Such small size combined with their very shy personalities can make finding tankmates that won’t eat or stress them out challenging. Pygmy sunfish are best kept in a species only set up with plenty of hiding spots to break up male territories if keeping multiple. A single pair can be kept in a tank as small as 5 gallons, but 10 gallons or more is needed for multiple pairs or keeping them in a community. If you do not want to do a species only tank, the best options for tankmates are small, schooling species that stay toward the middle or top of the tank such as very small tetras and rasboras. Least killifish ( Heterandria formosa ) are an excellent choice if sticking to North American natives. Within the Elassoma genus, there are currently seven recognized species. However, many argue that the different, considerably isolated populations of Elassoma evergladei should be split further based upon genetic and morphological differences amongst them. To preserve the genetics of each population, serious fishkeepers place great importance on tracking collection points and not mixing them. The Everglades pygmy sunfish we currently carry were collected from the Green Swamp in west-central Florida.

Remarks: The rose-spotted pleco (Hypostomus roseopunctatus) stands out as a truly unique member of its genus. Like many Hypostomus they have an impressive sailfin and a well-armored, robust body. Their coloration commands attention with a dark brown to jet black base covered in spots that appear white or pink usually depending on lighting. This pinkish hue that gives the rose-spotted pleco its name also occasionally extends to the body and especially the belly. In the wild, the rose-spotted pleco is known to be found in the Río de la Plata system in Argentina and Brazil, specifically the Uruguay River (Río Uruguai) basin. It often gets incorrectly referred to with the L-number of L-331, but this number actually belongs to similar, undescribed species from the Rio Cuiaba. This undescribed species has more numerous and more closely spaced spots compared to the rose-spotted pleco. In the aquarium, the rose-spotted pleco can be a great choice for an algae-eater to live alongside large, South American cichlids. They have a voracious appetite and can make quick work of many different species of algae but still need to have their diets supplemented with wood, fresh vegetables, and high-quality pellets. This appetite coincides with a high metabolism so frequent water changes are necessary to manage their high waste output. It also should be noted they will eat soft plants so they should only be kept with ones with tough leaves such as Anubias . These plecos can be rather territorial and boisterous so it is best not to house them with other loricariids unless they are in a very large system. This behavior, however makes them very good at handling cichlids with similar demeanors so they pair well with cichlids such as Salvin's cichlids and large severums.

Remarks: The black racer nerite snail ( Neritina pulligera ), also known as the military helmet nerite, is a very unique species. Unlike its more common relatives, it lacks a pattern and instead is entirely jet black or very dark olive. Another unique aspect of the black racer nerite is its very flat shape when compared to other nerites. This flat shape combined with their exceptionally strong grip makes it especially difficult for fish to get enough of a hold on it to flip the black racer nerite over for an attack. B-grade snails have imperfections on their shells such as small chips or scratches but none that are a threat to the snail's health. They most likely will eventually heal and look like any other snail. Nerite snails are excellent algae grazers and they do not reproduce in freshwater due to their larvae requiring brackish conditions, meaning you won't be overrun with tiny snails seemingly crawling out of the substrate. They will deposit eggs on many surfaces, however, and these can be scraped off or left to naturally decay. They seem to appreciate brown algae (diatoms) most. Any tanks housing these snails should have a tight-fitting lid as they can crawl up the glass and escape. Luckily, these snails can close up their shells when out of water to slow the rate at which they dry out. Some have reported finding snails 24 hours or longer after escape that perk back up when placed back in the water.

Remarks: One of the most coveted members of the Peckoltia genus is a pleco known as the L015 candy stripe pleco ( Peckoltia vittata ). With bold black stripes on their pinkish-orange bodies, they show some of the best color of any Peckoltia available in the hobby. The intensity of this coloration depends on genetics, environment, and the current mood of the fish. Not only is the medium-sized pleco beautiful, they have been noted to not be as territorial as their relatives. In fact, they are actually social and like being kept in groups of five or more provided there is enough space and a cave for every fish. While the L015 candy stripe pleco is uncommon in the fishkeeping hobby, they are a common sight in their expansive native range. In the wild, they can be found throughout the middle and lower Amazon River basin in rivers and streams with very warm, soft, acidic, and well oxygenated conditions. In these habitats, the L015 candy stripe pleco hides in rocky caves and feeds on tiny crustaceans, insect larvae, decaying plants, and biofilm. For the L015 candy stripe pleco to thrive in the home aquarium, these conditions should be replicated along with ensuring the water remains very clean through proper filtration and frequent water changes. This along with supplemental aerators will also help with keeping oxygen levels high. A varied diet high in protein will further ensure the L015 candy stripe pleco remains healthy as while they are omnivores, they have a heavy carnivorous leaning. Gel foods, sinking tablets, fresh vegetables, and frozen thawed foods such as blood worms and mysis shrimp are all good choices. The L015 candy stripe pleco is peaceful for the most part with aggression only ever occurring between males when fighting over territory. If keeping multiple males in the same tank, ensure the tank is big enough to accommodate every fish and has plenty of caves for them to choose from. If conditions are right and females are present, these caves are also where the L015 candy stripe pleco will spawn and care for its fry until they have hatched and absorbed their yolk. With their decent size and peaceful nature, these plecos can be excellent tankmates for many South American fish. Just ensure these tankmates are not overly territorial or large enough to swallow the L015 candy stripe pleco.

listings.commonName: Blue Dragon Dumbo Ear Guppy (Poecilia reticulata)
listings.description: Remarks: The blue dragon dumbo ear guppy ( Poecilia reticulata ) shines both in color and finnage. Both males and females have a bicolor body that is silver in the front and black or dark gray in the back as well as the signature dark-colored pectoral fins referred to as "Dumbo ears." While females will sometimes show a bit of blue in their fins, like with all guppies, the males are where you find the most color. Mature male blue dragon dumbo ear guppies practically glow with iridescent blue scales both in their fins and along their backs. Such color placement makes them a great choice for a fish to be viewed from both the side in a typical aquarium and from above in a pond. A perfect starter fish! Guppies ( Poecilia reticulata ) are peaceful community fish that reproduce with ease. They are livebearers, meaning the females release live fry rather than laying eggs. It is recommended to keep more females than males, as males can easily harass females with relentless attempts to reproduce, leading to stress in the females. For most strains, males are very colorful while the females remain a gray or silver color. However, there are some exceptions to this rule so sexing these fish is best done by looking at the anal fin. The females will have short, rounded triangle shaped anal fins with a black spot on the body directly above it, these are her female reproductive organs. Males will have long, thin, pointed anal fins that form his male reproductive organs called the gonopodium.

Remarks : If you love the look of the classic silver angelfish but want a wild side of fresh genes then these Amazon angelfish ( Pterophyllum scalare ) are for you! Captive-bred lines of angelfish have been selected for specific traits for decades and while this has produced adaptable, colorful fish, it comes with the downside of a reduced gene pool that can be very prone to genetic defects. The Amazon angelfish we offer are from wild-caught stock so while they are a bit less tolerant of incorrect parameters, they have fresh, healthy genetics perfect for a breeding project. Similar to the traditional silver angelfish, Amazon angelfish have metallic silver or white bodies with black vertical stripes. When they turn in the light, their scales shine with an iridescent blue sheen. In some individuals, this blue color is nicely contrasted by blood red eyes for some added color on an otherwise monochrome fish. Angelfish are easy-going cichlids that do well in almost any community tank. Captive bred specimens can tolerate a wide range of pH values and are typically peaceful enough to be kept with most tetras and other peaceful South American cichlids. Due to their long ventral fins, we do not recommend keeping them with very nippy fish such as tiger barbs or zebra danios. Breeding Angelfish can often be achieved by giving them a vertical, flat surface to spawn on, such as a leaf of an Amazon Sword or a piece of slate leaning against the wall. Fry will be cared for until a few weeks after they are free swimming, though you can remove the fry or eggs and hatch them artificially if you wish. It is usually best to isolate breeding pairs in their own tank when spawning as they can become territorial.

Remarks : The zebra compressiceps ( Altolamprologus compressiceps ‘Zebra’) is an elegantly colored strain with a pearly white body and black barring. White speckles are also present on the fins and throughout the body. If the fish is young, stressed, or frightened, their barring can dull to more of a gray hue and their bodies can turn brown, but their bold colors return upon maturity and/or once they are in good condition. Compressiceps are best maintained as a single pair, but can be maintained in groups if in large enough aquaria. It's not particularly territorial and can make a good addition to a community of Tanganyikan species, but shouldn’t be kept alongside anything small enough to be considered food. It is not recommended as a companion for Tropheus or any others species requiring a low protein diet. They grow very slowly with some taking years to reach maturity. In the wild, compressiceps are ambush predators that wait in crevices between rocks until prey comes by. Once it does, their mouth juts out to nearly the size of the tallest part of their body in one fast motion, engulfing their prey. These crevices are also where these fish spawn with both parents guarding the eggs and fry.

You will receive the exact fish in the video. Remarks : Green terrors ( Andinoacara rivulatus ) have shining blue-green bodies with orange or white trim on the edges of their fins. The orange and white trims give them another common name, the gold or white saum. There is still some debate about the differences and whether they represent two distinct species or one species with variation. A pair can be managed in a 90 gallon tank but a larger system will be needed if one plans to keep more than one. These large cichlids can do well in large community tanks with other large and aggressive Central and South American species, though aggression will worsen if pairs form.

Remarks: The Isonga tropheus ( Tropheus sp. 'Crescentic' Mkuyu) is an uncommon species with a considerable amount of confusion in the hobby regarding its true identity and native range. This is due to importers incorrectly labelling it under names such as T ropheus brichardi 'Isonga'. Fish imported under this name are actually Tropheus sp. 'Crescentic' collected from the Mkuyu area with the species' iconic crescent-shaped caudal fin (tail) being the main giveaway as Tropheus brichardi have a more straight fin. Despite carrying the trade name of "Isonga," the species is not found there with their actual home of Mkuyu being 160 km north of Isonga. While there is plenty of confusion regarding the name and origin of the Isonga tropheus, this isn't the case when it comes to why they are coveted by cichlid enthusiasts. Upon maturity, both males and females take on a charcoal hue accented by a sky blue eye and a vibrant patch of sunshine yellow around the pectoral fins that sometimes extends into the gills. With the only visual difference between males and females being that females are slightly smaller, the Isonga tropheus is an excellent choice for an eye-catching breeding project. Tropheus are obligate herbivores, and even small amounts of protein can induce bloating conditions. They form social hierarchies and should be kept in large groups, about 10 or more, to spread out any aggression. Tropheus tend to be more peaceful toward non-conspecific species so they can do well in a large Tanganyikan community tank.

Remarks: The true flying fox ( Epalzeorhynchos kalopterum ) is a fish that has been coveted as a colorful addition to an aquarium’s clean up crew. While most “algae-eaters” tend to remain only silver or gray in color, the true flying fox breaks that trend. When mature individuals aren’t stressed, they sport a warm orange color overlaid with a black stripe along the top of the body and another running through each eye. Their double pair of barbels and red and black fins edged with white are used to identify true flying foxes as they otherwise can often be confused for other similar species. While the true flying fox is heralded as an excellent solution to nuisance algae in a manageable size, this mostly only holds true for when they are young. Since most of their time in the hobby has been with them not getting the best care, many have not kept this species alive long enough to see how they change as they age. These fish can live up to and possibly even longer than 15 years and while most max out around 4-5 inches, some can grow as large as 7 inches long. Such a large size paired with their active swimming style means these fish need more space than most realize with a tank no smaller than 40 gallons being appropriate for a single flying fox. As they age, the color on the flying fox intensifies, but not their appetite for algae. Over time, their overall appetite slows down and they begin to prefer a more omnivorous diet. To meet their dietary needs, be sure to feed your flying fox a variety of foods with both vegetable matter and insect proteins. Most are not picky and usually take to almost any food offered. Be careful of housing them with my shy bottom dwellers as the flying fox might bully them away from food. True flying foxes have been known to occur in streams and rivers with fast-flowing currents in Thailand, Singapore, Malaysia, and Indonesia. Unfortunately, due to human development preventing their natural migrations during rainy seasons when these streams and rivers flood, wild populations have begun to dwindle. Due to this, it is suspected most flying foxes in the hobby are farm-raised. While being farm-raised often has fish become hardier, this species still is intolerant of water that is polluted or low in oxygen. To keep the flying fox healthy in your aquarium, provide them with plenty of filtration, water changes, and aeration. If given a wavemaker to simulate heavy currents, it can be an interesting to watch them swim through it almost effortlessly. For the most part, flying foxes are peaceful fish so long as their tankmates don’t look like them. They live in groups but have a very intense pecking order that can extend to conspecifics if they are present. To prevent unneeded stress and potential injuries, only keep one flying fox if they are going to be in a smaller aquarium with tankmates that do not look like them. If wanting to keep as a group, be sure to have them in a large aquarium with plenty of hiding spots and in a group of at least 8 or more. Any less and the school may fixate on the weakest member, bullying them to the point of injury or even death. If the right precautions are taken, you are likely to witness interesting natural behaviors between members of the school as they assert and maintain their place in the pecking order.

Remarks: The Venezuelan striped pike ( Crenicichla sp. ‘Venezuela’) is one of the many undescribed species of pike cichlid within the hobby. They are often confused for Lugubria strigata , but that species is found in Brazil. Instead, the Venezuelan striped pike is found around the Colombia/Venezuela border within the Rio Orinoco basin. The confusion between the two species typically is in regards to the appearance juvenile fish. Both display thin black stripes along the top of the head and back, speckles on the face, and a large horizontal band that starts at the gill plate and ends in a black spot in the caudal fin. Adult Venezuelan striped pikes are far more colorful with a red and green hue that is more saturated along the edges of the fins. Pike cichlids are known to be large, predatory, and territorial fish. Their impressive size and aggressive demeanor allow them to command large areas of territory both in the wild and in the home aquarium. The Venezuelan striped pike is known to be a particularly large and territorial species as most adult individuals will attack other pikes and even other groups of fish that are similar in shape such as chalceus. Some are a bit more mellow and juveniles can be kept together, but it is best to plan for these fish to have high levels of aggression once they reach adulthood. They do best when kept with large, robust, and tall bodied cichlids such as severums and uaru, or as a species only tank. Providing ample space as well as structure in the form of décor along with ensuring they are well fed on a high protein diet will help keep the pike’s aggression down. If cared for properly, the Venezuelan striped pike can be a great addition to a large South American cichlid community tank or can be appreciated in a tank of its own.

Remarks: The green Kambo petrochromis ( Petrochromis sp. "Green Kambo") is a Tanganyikan cichlid that has proven to be shrouded in mystery. Little to no public record about it is available. The exact collection point, specific species, and more are all uncertain, leaving much to assumption. There is no commonly known collection point that goes by the name of “Kambo.” However, brief geographical research has found there is a medical center and primary school to the south-east of the lake that go by that name. Based on proximity, it can be assumed it was originally collected from or near Chituta Bay until more data is made available. Many traits of the green Kambo petrochromis, such as its wide down-turned mouth, yellow fins, olive-green body, and gray vertical bands, all point toward it being a locality of Petrochromis macrognathus , but this has yet to be officially confirmed. Like others in the macrognathus group, this species is a very large and sensitive Petrochromis and, therefore, is not suitable for beginners. Like all that belong to their genus, green Kambo petrochromis are similar to Tropheus in that their natural diet is mostly composed of algae, and they are sensitive to protein, too much of which can cause bloat. Their large, protruding lips are indicative of this diet as they aid them in scraping rocks and other surfaces for algae. Another similarity Petrochromis have with Tropheus is that they are best kept in a species-only tank with at least 12–15 individuals in a ratio of about 5–6 females for every male. These large numbers are needed because while they feel the most comfortable and confident in groups, Petrochromis species are still extremely territorial and have a vicious pecking order. If there are not enough fish to spread out the aggression, the smallest and/or least dominant fish will be picked off until there is only one left. These cichlids also do not tolerate poor water quality or incorrect parameters. Therefore, to keep these fish in large numbers with lots of territory space and pristine water, the absolute minimum tank size would be a 180-gallon tank. 200 gallons or more is ideal, however. All these aspects make Petrochromis a fairly difficult species to keep long-term, but their fascinating behaviors, beautiful colors, and rarity make it worth it for the advanced keeper.

listings.commonName: Red Fin Longola Petrochromis (Petrochromis sp. 'Red Fin Longola')
listings.description: Remarks: One of the most strikingly colored Petrochromis in the hobby is the red fin Longola petrochromis ( Petrochromis sp. 'Red Fin Longola'). Mature males stand out with a deep blue body accented by blood-red fins and yellow egg-spots on the anal fin. When sparring or spawning, their blue coloration can become so intense it drowns out their vertical gray bars. Juveniles and female red fin Longola petrochromis are mostly gray, but occasionally adult females can have a yellow/gold body, a tinge of red in the fins, and even a false egg-spot or two on the anal fin. This particular locality of Petrochromis has gone by a few names over the years, such as Petrochromis sp. 'longnose red longola' and Petrochromis sp. 'dolichorhynchus.' There has also been plenty of debate on whether it is a locality of P. macrognathus or P. polyodon with most just placing it in the “longnose” group as a placeholder. Future genetic analysis should hopefully shed light on where it belongs taxonomically. For now, we at least know it hails from the southwest end of Lake Tanganyika near the Longola coastline and has enough color to make it a must-have for cichlid keepers. It should be noted that this species is a very large and sensitive Petrochromis so they are not a beginner species. Instead, they should be reserved for experienced keepers who already have experience with smaller, more easily kept species such as Petrochromis trewevasae . Like all that belong to their genus, red fin Longola petrochromis are similar to Tropheus in that their natural diet is mostly composed of algae, and they are sensitive to protein, too much of which can cause bloat. Their large, protruding lips are indicative of this diet as they aid them in scraping rocks and other surfaces for algae. Another similarity they have with Tropheus is that they are best kept in a species-only tank with at least 12–15 individuals in a ratio of about 5–6 females for every male. These large numbers are needed because while they feel the most comfortable and confident in groups, Petrochromis species are still extremely territorial and have a vicious pecking order. If there are not enough fish to spread out the aggression, the smallest or at least less dominant fish will be picked off until there is only one left. These cichlids also do not tolerate poor water quality or incorrect parameters. Therefore, to keep these fish in large numbers with lots of territory space and pristine water, the absolute minimum tank size would be a 180-gallon tank. 200 gallons or more is ideal, however. All these aspects make Petrochromis a fairly difficult species to keep long-term, but their fascinating behaviors, beautiful colors, and rarity make it worth it for the advanced keeper.

Remarks: Xenotilapia flavipinnis 'Cape Kabogo' is a must-have locality for Tanganyikan cichlid enthusiasts. While young fish are mostly tan or silver, both adult males and females shine with vibrant gold and iridescent blue hues. This color is most concentrated in the fins and around the lips, but can also be present in the form of horizontal stripes along the body. Spawning and sparring males will often display the most intense coloration. Since males and females differ very little in appearance, it can be difficult to determine the sex of Xenotilapia flavipinnis 'Cape Kabogo.' Those familiar with the practice can use “venting” to identify males and females, but it is particularly challenging with Xenotilapia due to their anatomy. Because of this, if you are looking to breed this species, it is best to start with a group of at least six juveniles and allow them to pair off naturally. Young Xenotilapia flavipinnis 'Cape Kabogo' will shoal together; however, once pairs form, they will separate and begin to display heavily territorial behavior. At this point, it is typically recommended to separate pairs if housing them in a smaller system. While Xenotilapia are omnivores, they lean more toward being carnivores, so they feed mostly on meaty foods such as tiny crustaceans and worms. They naturally feed by scooping up mouthfuls of sand to sift through, similar to the feeding style of South American eartheaters. So, just like an eartheater, soft sand is a must to encourage natural feeding and avoid injury to their mouths and gills. In the aquarium, Xenotilapia are not the easiest Tanganyikan to care for. They do not tolerate poor water quality at all, are very skittish, and require a lot more space than one would expect such a small species would require. This is because males command large territories as they build multiple spawning pits that can span 2 feet in diameter. A 50 gallon tank should be considered the minimum for a single pair. If you want to keep multiple pairs of adult Xenotilapia , a 75 gallon or larger is needed. While Xenotilapia can be belligerent to their own kind, they usually ignore other species that do not dwell on the bottom like they do. This makes them excellent tank mates for Cyprichromis species, though their interesting behaviors and eye-catching colors also make them a great choice for a species-only tank. Due to the sensitive nature of these fish, DOA claims will only be honored if the fish are in their sealed bags. No exceptions will be made for losses that occur after opening the bags.

Remarks: Callochromis melanostigma are fascinating medium-sized Tanganyikan cichlids found in the southern end of the lake. They have a unique shape with their large eyes and tall dorsal fin that seems to end abruptly above where the ventral fins are located. The rounded front of the dorsal fin along with the small, darker colored spikes atop it gives an almost buzzsaw appearance. While females and juveniles are mostly gray, mature males display metallic gold colors on their bodies and fins that seem to shimmer in the light occasionally with a green sheen. Their dorsal fins also contain 4-5 black spots and their anal fins display yellow egg spots. The eyes of males can range anywhere from gold to orange. All these aspects come together to form a truly stunning fish for which pictures cannot do it justice. In the wild, Callochromis melanostigma can be found in shallow, sandy areas that sometimes will have patches of aquatic vegetation such as Vallisneria spiralis . They will use the sparse rock piles also found in these areas as shelter when young or when predators are present, otherwise they patrol the sandy expanses. Males build crater-nests in the open sand to attract mates which is a very fascinating behavior to witness within the aquarium. Spawning occurs in the crater, where females take the eggs into their mouths and mouthbrood for several weeks. To facilitate this behavior in captivity and allow for spawning, a large, open, sandy space is needed that is free of obstructions such as rocks or décor. Not providing enough territory space can result in heightened aggression toward both their own kind and other species. Sand is necessary, as they spend a considerable amount of time sifting it through their gills to feed. Being mostly carnivorous, foods high in protein such as bloodworms should be a staple, but foods containing vegetable matter and algae should also be offered to aid in digestion. Males will act aggressively towards each other, and sexing is difficult when young. Starting with a group of five or more individuals will ensure the best chances at having one male and several females. Extra males will seek refuge in rocky caves. When given enough space, Callochromis melanostigma are not terribly aggressive for a Tanganyikan species, but this can change when they are spawning. They are fairly confident for their size and can defend themselves rather well so they can usually hold their own against more aggressive species such as Neolamprologus tretocephalus . All of these factors combined with their stunning looks makes the Callochromis melanostigma a great choice for many Tanganyikan aquariums.

Remarks: Aspidoras poecilus are related to Corydoras , but differ in several ways. They have smaller eyes, longer bodies, and seem to be a bit more active in terms of swimming activity. Watching their shimmering gold bodies glide back and forth across the sand searching for food, and occasionally doing laps around a face of glass really draws one to this species. Unfortunately their beautiful gold sheen does not show up well in photos but is truly a sight to see in person. They are not very common in the hobby as they are found in Brazil, where exporting can be a challenge. While Aspidoras poecilus are small, they shouldn't be kept in tanks smaller than 20 gallons as they do not tolerate high levels of pollutants, need to be kept in large groups to feel safe, and are very active. Corydoradinae are small, peaceful catfish that are active shoalers and will stay near conspecifics, making for a lovely sight. They feed by searching through sand with their barbels, making such a substrate necessary for their long-term health . Gravel substrates tend to be abrasive and damage the barbels, leading to infections and an inability to find food. While these friendly catfish are willing to swim with other species of Corydoradinae different from their own, this does not provide the same social need as being kept with members of their own species. Because of this, it is highly recommended to keep at least six of each species of Corydoradinae present in the aquarium and only mix species if one has the space to keep at least six of each. Corydoradinae are often looked at as "scavengers," but they should be treated in a similar fashion as the rest of your fish. They are omnivores and require a mixed diet. Sinking prepared foods are readily accepted, as are frozen and live foods such as brine shrimp, blackworms, and bloodworms.

Remarks : Cyprichromis leptosoma are a mild-mannered cichlid from Lake Tanganyika that exhibit shoaling behaviors higher in the water column. This makes them excellent tankmates for shell- or cave-dwelling cichlids, which rarely venture higher into open water. They act as a relaxing agent for other species as well, much like tetras do with dwarf cichlids - if the Cyprichromis are swimming in the open, it must be "safe." Cyprichromis are long and slender and may be considered the "sardines of Lake Tanganyika." They occur all over the lake and have a wide variety of color patterns. They are maternal mouthbrooders and in the wild, females will spawn all at once with the dominant males in the area. Spawns are typically 5-20 fry as their mouths are small. As these are social fish, we recommend keeping these fish in groups of 6 or more, 10 or more being better. Their high activity also makes us recommend not keeping them in tanks that are not at least 4ft long. Due to the sensitive nature of these fish, DOA claims will only be honored if the fish are in their sealed bags. No exceptions will be made for losses that occur after opening the bags. Remarks: The Ornate Brochis is endemic to the lower Rio Tapajo River basin in Brazil. They are slightly more tolerant of slightly higher pH values compared to other Corydoradinae and can grow to a rather decent size. Their bodies are typically dark gray with 2-3 horizontal black stripes along their bodies and the anterior half of their dorsal fin is black. They look very similar to Brochis britoi and Hoplisoma pavanelli with the main difference setting the ornate Brochis apart is the dark mask over its eyes. Ornate Brochis were previously classified as Corydoras ornatus , but were reclassified as Brochis ornatus upon publication of a phylogenomic analysis in 2024 that reclassified many species in the Corydoradinae subfamily. Corydoradinae are small, peaceful catfish that are active shoalers and will stay near conspecifics, making for a lovely sight. They feed by searching through sand with their barbels, making such a substrate necessary for their long-term health . Gravel substrates tend to be abrasive and damage the barbels, leading to infections and an inability to find food. While these friendly catfish are willing to swim with other species of Corydoradinae different from their own, this does not provide the same social need as being kept with members of their own species. Because of this, it is highly recommended to keep at least six of each species of Corydoradinae present in the aquarium and only mix species if one has the space to keep at least six of each. Corydoradinae are often looked at as "scavengers," but they should be treated in a similar fashion as the rest of your fish. They are omnivores and require a mixed diet. Sinking prepared foods are readily accepted, as are frozen and live foods such as brine shrimp, blackworms, and bloodworms.

The dorsal, tail, and anal fins can also display an orange-red coloration. Being large and territorial, care should be taken to provide ample space and appropriate tanks mates, such as similarly sized cichlids, for this species. Remarks: Apistogramma uaupesi is an absolutely stunning dwarf cichlid from the blackwater habitats of the Rio Negro and Rio Orinoco. Their elongated bodies are topped with one of the tallest sail-like dorsal fins seen among apistos that the males flash at females during courtship. Along with this impressive dorsal fin is a caudal fin shaped like a double-pointed spade that usually will be yellow, orange, or red in mature males that contrasts beautifully with their electric blue bodies. Females, in turn, are much more muted in color with smaller finnage. This impressive appearance has made Apistogramma uaupesi a highly desirable species in the aquarium hobby though it is rarely imported and has proven to be a rather sensitive species. This makes it a species that is not suited for those that are not already well versed in the care of apistos. For those ready to take on the challenge, Apistogramma uaupesi does best when kept in a tank with highly acidic, very soft, warm, and clean water with plenty of botanicals and a soft sand substrate. Frequent water changes are a must to keep nitrates as low as possible and prevent infections. Caves in the form of cichlid caves, overturned flower pots, and leaf litter should also be provided as they are rather timid and will become very stressed if they feel exposed. Meet all of these needs and there will be a much better chance your apistos will not only display better coloration and live longer, but have a chance at possibly spawning for you. Being a more small, peaceful and timid species of dwarf cichlid, a single pair can be kept in a 10 gallon aquarium or a 20 gallon for a small group provided they are given plenty of hiding spots. Like most apistos, feeding lots of tiny live foods such as freshly hatched baby brine shrimp can help encourage spawning. Fry are guarded by one or both parents for several weeks. Dither fish such as small tetras and livebearers can be used to provide parents with targets to chase.

Remarks: Cyathopharynx foai "Kachese" are one of the stunning featherfin cichlids found within Lake Tanganyika. These fish are known for their long, elegant ventral fins usually tipped with white or yellow in mature males. Juvenile and female fish are silver in color with mature males also being silver most of the time. However, when displaying to a female or sparring with a rival, they take on a beautiful blue and yellow hue with black accents. They show this coloration the most in the morning when they are most active. It may take some time to see this fantastic coloration as Cyathopharynx foai "Kachese" can take a while to reach maturity with most of their color not appearing until they are at least 4 inches in length. Once one sees a mature fish, it will be clear it is well worth the wait. Unlike some of their more boisterous relatives, Cyathopharynx foai "Kachese" are a bit more mellow for a featherfin. They can get aggressive and territorial during spawning, but it is not to the severity of other featherfins. This makes them a good choice to house alongside Altolamprologus and adult sardine cichlids such as Cyprichromis, but a poor choice for more aggressive species such as other featherfins. Aside from the aggression issue, Cyathopharynx foai "Kachese” should not be kept with other featherfins as they can hybridize which damages the genetics of captive populations. Cyathopharynx foai "Kachese” appreciate having both plentiful rock piles and large areas of open space with a soft sand substrate in the aquarium. The rocks provide a place to hide as well as breaks in lines of sight to reduce aggression amongst males. The sand is for space for the males to dig pits in where they will court and spawn with females. Needing ample of both types of habitat means these fish need quite a bit of space. 90 gallons should be considered the minimum for a breeding group, but if wanting to keep these cichlids in a community setting, a larger tank will be needed. A large volume of water alongside plenty of water changes and heavy filtration will also help keep the Cyathopharynx foai "Kachese” healthy as they are sensitive to water quality. Their health further depends on a well-curated diet heavy in vegetable and algae matter as they are primarily herbivores. Protein rich foods such as brine shrimp can be offered occasionally, but this should be rare to avoid bloat. If cared for properly, those keeping the rare Cyathopharynx foai "Kachese” will be rewarded with a truly stunning fish.

Remarks: The Cribroheros bussingi is a rare Central American cichlid, therefore not much is known about them. It is known that they are an omnivorous sand-sifter that have yellow pelvic fins used to communicate with their fry when spawning. They share these characteristics with their close relative, Cribroheros alfari . Due to this close relation, these fish should not be housed with other species of Cribroheros to avoid hybridization. They are best kept on a sandy substrate as single pairs with similarly sized Central American cichlids. These fish are rather difficult to sex but it is reported that spawning females will sometimes have a dark spot on their dorsal fin. Females also tend to be smaller than males. Both males and females can have yellow fins, a red seam along their dorsal fins, and blue spots underneath their eyes. Remarks: The Cribroheros longimanus is a medium-sized cichlid from Central America. They are sand-sifting omnivores so they should be kept on a sandy substrate. Like many others within their genus, these fish are fairly peaceful with other species but very territorial among their own kind. Due to this behavior, they should be kept alone in pairs or with other species of similarly sized Central American cichlids, but not with other species of Cribroheros as to avoid hybridization. This cichlid has earned the nickname of the ‘Red Breast Cichlid’ due to its bright red belly present on both males and females. Remarks: Neolamprologus leleupi , also known as lemon cichlids, are a classic and ever popular species of Tanganyikan cichlid. Their manageable size, bright yellow color, and fascinating personalities make them a great choice for both beginner and expert keepers alike. While Neolamprologus leleupi are typically bright yellow, their color can actually vary depending on social status and catch location. Some have noted that raising them in bright lighting can help them develop the strongest yellow color upon maturity. Sexing can be difficult, and impossible when young, so groups should be purchased if the intention is to breed them. The Neolamprologus leleupi is a rock dwelling species that can be found in the wild guarding their fry in small crevices from any would be predators. This fierce parentage continues to be shown within captive fish as while they are typically non-aggressive toward non-conspecifics, any that dare to come near the spawning cave of a pair will be swiftly dealt with using their surprisingly sharp fangs. When not spawning, they get along well with most similarly sized Tanganyikan cichlids like Julidochromis , Altolamprologus , and other Neolamprologus . However, care should be taken when housing Neolamprologus leleupi with smaller shell-dwellers as some have seen them become aggressive and bully the shellies away from their shells to eat their fry. Feeding the Neolamprologus leleupi is fairly easy as these mostly carnivorous fish aren't very picky at all. They will eat just about any food offered that can fit in their mouths. While they are carnivores, they do benefit from having a bit of algae and vegetable matter in their diets so herbivore pellets and spirulina flakes should be offered occasionally. Many have noted feeding foods with added marigold, paprika, and astaxanthin can help increase the amount of color in these brightly colored fish if fed regularly. As for water quality, Neolamprologus leleupi aren't quite as sensitive as other Tanganyikans, but will still benefit from frequent water changes and will need to have hard, alkaline water to thrive. If cared for properly, they can be a great pop of color that might be just what your tank needs.

Remarks : The Taiwan reef hap is a fairly peaceful cichlid compared to the majority from Lake Malawi. They also are one of the most colorful with their bright yellow bodies, rich red ventral and anal fins, sapphire blue heads and backs, and a white edge along the top of their dorsal fins. This coloration is absolutely incredible in person as pictures alone do not do these fish justice with showing their beautiful rainbow colors. It should be noted that they can take some time to mature and show their colors as is typical of their genus which includes tangerine tigers and red empress. This means one needs to be patient when it comes to seeing the full potential of these fish, but it is well worth the wait. In the wild, Taiwan reef haps actually have algae make up a large part of their diet as they graze on the many rocks in their natural habitat. However, they are still omnivores so in captivity, their diet should be varied but with a lower protein content. Similar to other mostly herbivorous species, feeding a diet too high in protein can cause the fish to develop bloat. Another thing to keep in mind to be successful with this colorful species is they don't tolerate poor water quality. If water quality starts to decline, they will usually be the first to show symptoms. This can actually be a good thing as the Taiwan reef hap showing bright colors and looking healthy will let you know that water quality is most likely good. If water changes are kept up and plenty of filtration is used, their sensitivity should not be too much of a worry and rather a helpful indictor. To make the Taiwan reef hap an even better cichlid, they are very prolific and will usually ignore their fry once they are free swimming making them a very easy to breed species. With how amazing the males look, especially in the presence of females, they make it worth it to have the duller females around in a breeding group. However, if you do not want to have them in a species only tank, they do well with similarly sized peacocks and haps. Taiwan reef haps tend to be fairly mellow but can defend themselves if they need to so they can be a perfect addition to an all male peacock/hap show tank.
