Remarks: Common plecos quickly outgrow most aquaria and care should be taken to only house them in appropriately sized tanks. While commonly sold as a fish to clean up algae, they actually make it worse due to their high waste output. The larger they get, the more protein they require in their diet. If this is not provided, common plecos can begin attacking tankmates, attempting to eat their eyes and slime coat. They are known to quickly invade local waterways and like all pet fish, should not be released into ponds or streams. Due to how large this species gets, them causing more algae growth than they clean up due to waste, and their frequent release into waterways upon outgrowing a tank causing extreme environmental damage, we no longer carry this species. Remarks: Albino bushynose are the albino variant of the typical bushynose pleco ( Ancistrus sp.) and possibly the second most common within the hobby. This interesting mutation showed up early on back when these classic catfish were first being selectively bred in captivity. They are typically yellow or cream in color with a red eye. You may see some patterning on their bodies left over from their ancestry, but it usually is only a slightly different shade from the rest of their body. Bushynose, or bristlenose plecos, belong to the genus Ancistrus but their exact species is unknown. The common bushynose plecos you see available today are likely line-bred from A. cirrhosus , but there is a chance hybridization with other Ancistrus species occurred at some point. Their common name is derived from the long and elaborate tentacles that develop on the faces of males. The bigger the "beard" as some call it, the more dominant the male. Females will occasionally develop bristles as well along the edges of their face making it difficult to differentiate young males from females. These bristles are tempting for nippy and aggressive fish so this combined with bushynose plecos not having much armor compared to other species is why they should not be housed with nippy or aggressive fish. The pleco itself can pose a danger in the case of fish trying to swallow them as they have spines on their fins that they will flare out if being attacked to prevent the fish from eating them. This can result in the fish choking and the loss of both it and the pleco if the pleco remains stuck in the mouth of the fish. Bushynose plecos do not grow very large and are mostly peaceful so they can fit in well in smaller aquariums. Typically, the only aggression shown tends to be among males fighting over spawning caves. They can be kept with shrimp if the population has been given plenty of time to grow and begin reproducing regularly as the bushynose pleco will prey on them occasionally. While they are omnivores, they prefer to have a diet consisting mostly of vegetable matter and will voraciously feed on algae. Their appetite for algae does not diminish as they grow like in the case of common plecos making them an excellent addition to the cleanup crew in a tank. Typically, plants will not be eaten unless the pleco is starving or the plant is already dying. Bushynose plecos come in a variety of color forms that have been selectively bred for such as green, blue eye lemon, albino, super red, calico, and even a long-finned variant. They do best when kept in soft, acidic water free of pollutants but are not as picky about this compared to other species. Due to how long this pleco has been bred in captivity, they have become extremely hardy and very prolific making them an excellent choice for both beginner and experienced aquarists alike. Breeding bushynose plecos can be very easy so long as all their needs are attended to and spawning sites are provided. Bushynose plecos are cave spawners where males will choose a small cave where he will chase females into to spawn. Once the female has laid eggs, it will be left up to the male to guard the cave and keep the eggs clean as the female leaves. They fan the eggs with their fins to keep fresh water flowing over them to help prevent them from fungusing and ensuring they get plenty of oxygen. Once the eggs hatch, the male will keep the fry inside the cave until they have absorbed their yolk sack and have become free swimming. This high level of parental care is fascinating to watch and is also why it is usually best to leave the eggs with the father to care for rather than removing them.

Remarks: Out of all Loricariids within the hobby, the L046 zebra pleco is one of if not the most desirable species among hobbyists. Few catfish can compare to their striking white bodies and fins covered in black zebra stripes making for some incredible contrast. Their small size also adds to their desirability as it makes it much easier to house them compared to other rare but large plecos. Despite their popularity, the L046 zebra pleco is fairly uncommon in the hobby as it is critically endangered in the wild due to construction of dams and tends to breed rather infrequently in captivity. However, more efforts have thankfully been being made, including here at Imperial Tropicals where we have had a breeding colony for a number of years, to increase their numbers among the captive population. The L046 zebra pleco is a typical Hypancistrus in regards to their care in captivity. They come from rocky areas of pristine, heavily oxygenated, warm, soft, and acidic water. It has been noted that they are surprisingly tolerant of a somewhat broader range of parameters in regards to hardness and pH compared to other sensitive plecos. However, they are unforgiving when it comes to water quality, oxygen levels, and temperature. If any of these are not kept at acceptable levels, the L046 zebra pleco will decline in health and eventually die. Using a high quality filter with a high flow rate along with a heater and frequent water changes will help keep these plecos happy and healthy. Like all known Hypancistrus , the L046 zebra pleco is a carnivore so they must be fed a varied diet high in protein. Protein rich gel foods like Repashy, bloodworms, and sinking wafers are good choices to feed to meet their dietary needs. A unique and important thing to note about the L046 zebra pleco is that they are social fish. If kept in groups less than at least 5-6 fish, it will cause them to become very stressed resulting in the fish hiding even more and even stop eating in some cases. Notably, these small plecos are rather shy even when it comes to eating so they should not be kept with any fish that are overly boisterous, aggressive, or large enough to fit them in their mouths such as large cichlids. While they can be kept in a peaceful community set up with fish that prefer the same parameters, L046 zebra plecos are best kept alone, otherwise careful attention should be paid to ensure they are getting enough to eat and are not getting bullied. While the L046 zebra pleco is a gregarious species, some territorial aggression can pop up among males when they are spawning. To reduce territorial fights and help the L046 zebra pleco feel comfortable in the aquarium, plenty of snug, rocky caves should be provided for them to hide in. These caves are also where these fish will spawn if all other conditions are just right. Males will guard the caves they spawn in, keeping the fry inside until they are able to swim out on their own safely. L046 zebra pleco fry can be fed baby brine shrimp, carnivore Repashy foods, and high protein wafers similar to adults. They can be a very exciting breeding project as they are such a unique and beautiful catfish that requires diligent efforts in regards to breeding to keep them present within the hobby. We encourage any who look to keep this amazing species do so with the intent to breed them.

Vegetables such as cucumbers or zucchini are appreciated as well, and should be offered as a supplement 1-3 times per week. The small size of this species makes them suitable for small tanks, as long as there is at least one piece of driftwood present. Remarks: The L129 Colombian zebra pleco ( Hypancistrus debilittera ) is a smaller species of Hypancistrus and a good introduction to the genus as they have proven to be fairly hardy compared to their relatives. As their common name entails, they are native to Colombia, specifically the Rio Bita and the Rio Meta. They are a very nice looking species with their dark brown or black bodies covered in off-white or yellow stripes. As is typical of their genus, L129 Colombian zebra plecos are mostly carnivorous and like to live in groups. However, they do sometimes quarrel over territory so lots of caves and space should be provided. If this is done and they are kept in the right parameters, you will mostly likely be rewarded with regular spawns as they are very willing to breed in the aquarium.

Remarks : Panaque nigrolineatus , commonly known as the L190 royal pleco, is often seen as the standard royal pleco. Like many of their close relatives, they have a large, robust build and coloration that holds a natural elegance. They can be anywhere from dark brown to olive green with black or dark gray stripes running from their nose to their tail. Also having red eyes to accent it all, L190 royal plecos make for a truly impressive Loricariid . With how large and well armored royal plecos are, they can make a great addition to a tank containing larger and more aggressive fish so long as they share the same preferred water parameters consisting of somewhat soft, acidic conditions with little pollutants. However, it should be kept in mind royal plecos can be territorial toward conspecifics so if housing them with other loricariids, plenty of space and hiding spots should be provided. Other fish being swallowed is not something that needs to be worried about as these fish are almost completely non-predatory. Like other Panaque species, L190 royal plecos supplement their nutrition by rasping wood to consume the microorganisms and algae that live on and below its surface. To ensure proper digestion and nutrition as well as make them feel at home, royal plecos must always have access to wood to graze on. They also appreciate vegetables such as zucchini or cucumbers as well as algae wafers. These fish graze almost 24/7 so that means they also produce a lot of waste. To avoid build up of pollutants, frequent water changes should be performed. Like with any Loricariid lots of oxygenation is also appreciated which can be achieved through the use of wavemakers, heavy filtration, and aerators. If all their needs are attended to, royal plecos can be a fantastic choice for those looking for a large, robust pleco.

Remarks: L200 green phantom plecos are great choices for moderately sized tanks looking for a pleco with a lot of color. They are olive-green with lime green spots that grow more dense on the head. It should be noted, they will lose this nice color if stressed or kept in incorrect parameters. While most typically top out at 6" in length in captivity, wild specimens can get get as large as 8" from nose to tail. Most Loricariids prefer cooler water, but this species is an exception as it actually does better in warmer water. This makes it a great choice for a tank containing other South American species that like things a bit warmer such as angelfish. As they are extremely similar looking, the L200 green phantom pleco, Hemiancistrus subviridis , is commonly mistaken for Baryancistrus demantoides . To make things even more confusing, both are commonly imported under the same L-number. There are a few different ways to tell them apart, however. The easier to see difference is that B. demantoides has a larger dorsal fin that is connected to its adipose fin via a fleshy membrane, while in H. subviridis, these fins are separated and its dorsal fin is smaller. Another difference is that the mouth of B. demantoides is rounded while H. subviridis has a more rectangle shaped mouth.

Remarks : The L201 Orinoco snowball angel pleco is a very beautiful, small, and popular species of Hypancistrus from the Rio Orinoco. Their black bodies covered in white spots stand out in just about any aquarium, but looks best when kept in a tank with a dark background. Captive bred specimens are fairly hardy but they still require soft, acidic water to remain at peak health. Being mostly carnivorous, these little plecos also require a meaty diet but appreciate the occasional vegetable or spirulina pellet to round out their diet. As the L201 Orinoco snowball angel pleco is a fairly small and docile species with an eye-catching pattern, they can be a great addition to a smaller, peaceful, South American community tank.

Remarks: The L240 vampire pleco is a large Loricariid native to fast-flowing sections of a number of rivers in South America. It's common name comes from the interesting and unique dentition it has consisting of two large, sharp teeth that look like fangs, a feature in unique to their genus. It is presumed these teeth aid this pleco in feeding on invertebrates such as snails as it is a carnivorous species. These teeth are also used for defense and in territorial disputes making them rather violent affairs. Its other common name, the galaxy pleco, and the second half of its scientific name, galaxias , are derived from its beautiful pattern. The L240 vampire pleco has a black body and fins with bright white spots making it look like the night sky. Due to its territorial nature, sensitivity to poor water quality, and size, this species is best kept in large tanks of at least 90 gallons and as the only Loricariid. Having lots of hiding spots in the tank will also encourage it to come out more during the day. If kept in the right conditions, these incredible plecos make a fascinating talking point to keep in a large South American community tank.

Remarks : Longfin chocolate bushynose have the classic dark brown or black color and sometimes also display tan patches across their bodies and fins. What sets them apart are their flowing, elegant fins that get longer with age. To prevent their long fins from getting damaged, it is even more important that longfin chocolate bushynose are not to be kept with nippy or aggressive fish. Bushynose, or bristlenose plecos, belong to the genus Ancistrus but their exact species is unknown. The common bushynose plecos you see available today are likely line-bred from A. cirrhosus , but there is a chance hybridization with other Ancistrus species occurred at some point. Their common name is derived from the long and elaborate tentacles that develop on the faces of males. The bigger the "beard" as some call it, the more dominant the male. Females will occasionally develop bristles as well along the edges of their face making it difficult to differentiate young males from females. These bristles are tempting for nippy and aggressive fish so this combined with bushynose plecos not having much armor compared to other species is why they should not be housed with nippy or aggressive fish. The pleco itself can pose a danger in the case of fish trying to swallow them as they have spines on their fins that they will flare out if being attacked to prevent the fish from eating them. This can result in the fish choking and the loss of both it and the pleco if the pleco remains stuck in the mouth of the fish. Bushynose plecos do not grow very large and are mostly peaceful so they can fit in well in smaller aquariums. Typically, the only aggression shown tends to be among males fighting over spawning caves. They can be kept with shrimp if the population has been given plenty of time to grow and begin reproducing regularly as the bushynose pleco will prey on them occasionally. While they are omnivores, they prefer to have a diet consisting mostly of vegetable matter and will voraciously feed on algae. Their appetite for algae does not diminish as they grow like in the case of common plecos making them an excellent addition to the cleanup crew in a tank. Typically, plants will not be eaten unless the pleco is starving or the plant is already dying. Bushynose plecos come in a variety of color forms that have been selectively bred for such as green, blue eye lemon, albino, super red, calico, and even a long-finned variant. They do best when kept in soft, acidic water free of pollutants but are not as picky about this compared to other species. Due to how long this pleco has been bred in captivity, they have become extremely hardy and very prolific making them an excellent choice for both beginner and experienced aquarists alike. Breeding bushynose plecos can be very easy so long as all their needs are attended to and spawning sites are provided. Bushynose plecos are cave spawners where males will choose a small cave where he will chase females into to spawn. Once the female has laid eggs, it will be left up to the male to guard the cave and keep the eggs clean as the female leaves. They fan the eggs with their fins to keep fresh water flowing over them to help prevent them from fungusing and ensuring they get plenty of oxygen. Once the eggs hatch, the male will keep the fry inside the cave until they have absorbed their yolk sack and have become free swimming. This high level of parental care is fascinating to watch and is also why it is usually best to leave the eggs with the father to care for rather than removing them.

Remarks: The golden sailfin pleco ( Hypostomus luteus ) is one of if not the most coveted and colorful member of the Hypostomus genus. They go through an incredibly fascinating color-changing process as they mature with each stage being referred to as “phases.” Phase 1 is the juvenile phase where they are entirely dark gray or black and are covered in yellow spots. Phase 2, the sub-adult stage, is when the golden sailfin pleco’s iconic gold color begins to fade in, usually starting at the tail and working forward into the body. Phase 3 is when their species name of luteus , Latin for “yellow,” is best represented as the adult pleco has turned completely golden yellow. While most golden sailfin plecos follow this process, it should be noted that some never reach full gold coloration and a few may even revert back to earlier phases. It currently is not yet known whether this is due to sex, dominance, aging, or environmental factors. In the wild, the golden sailfin pleco can be found in a handful of waterways in northern Argentina and southern Brazil. However, it is most known to occur in the Rio Uruguai (Uruguay River). Water parameters in these rivers and tributaries are soft, acidic, well-oxygenated, and very cool when compared to more northern South American habitats. While Hypostomus is one of the hardier genera of Loricariid , almost all golden sailfin plecos in the hobby are wild caught so they are less tolerant of incorrect parameters. To have the best success with this species, we highly encourage replicating their natural habitat, performing weekly water changes, and providing plenty of filtration and aeration. The latter two are especially important to manage the golden sailfin pleco’s high waste output as is typical of Hypostomus species. Feeding the golden sailfin pleco is typical of any omnivorous Loricariid that has a bit of an herbivorous lean. They will take to most vegetable/algae-based sinking foods such as algae wafers, larger pellets, gel foods, and fresh vegetables. More protein-heavy foods can be given as an occasional treat, but should not make up a majority of their diet. While golden sailfin plecos are mostly peaceful, they can become territorial toward conspecifics especially when feeding and spawning. If you want to keep them with other large plecos, be sure to provide ample territory space for each fish and try to spread out food when feeding. As previously mentioned, golden sailfin plecos usually are only territorial to species like them. Considering their massive size and heavily-armored bodies, they can otherwise be kept with almost any other fish that enjoys the same water parameters as them. This makes the golden sailfin pleco an excellent choice for a tank stocked with larger, more aggressive South American species like peacock bass. Smaller species are also typically safe as these bottom-dwellers are not considered predatory. Just keep in mind that the golden sailfin pleco prefers cooler water, so warm water species like discus would not be at home in the same tank as them. If well fed, they usually will leave live plants alone, however they can potentially dig them up or crush them as they swim and dig around in the substrate. For many, the golden sailfin pleco is the “holy grail” of the larger-growing Loricariid s. Whether it is due to their captivating colors, unique hue shift as they grow, or simply their blatant rarity within the hobby, pleco enthusiasts and general aquarists alike see it as a must-have species. Whatever your reasoning for seeking out these golden wonders, they are an excellent fish and an eye-catching addition to almost any South American aquarium.

Remarks: The L066 king tiger pleco is known from the same area as the L333 Gurupa pleco, the lower Rio Xingu in Brazil. Adults of both fish look heavily similar and are frequently confused for the other. The L066 king tiger pleco differs from the L333 Gurupa pleco in that their base color is much lighter compared to the yellow or tan base color of the L333 Gurupa pleco. The stripes on their fins are also more straight and uniform. The difference in color and pattern are much more obvious in juvenile fish which can sometimes be almost white with disconnected black stripes and spots. Recently in 2025, a taxonomic study was conducted on the L066 king tiger pleco along with a number of other similar looking Hypancistrus . This study determined that the plecos under the L-numbers L333, L66, L236, L399 and L400 were all just different variations/localities of the same highly variable new species. This new species name was deemed Hypancistrus seideli . They were named after professional aquarist, Ingo Seidel, who has been a great influence within the hobby and the scientific realm in regards to Loricariids . He especially made an impact in regards to Hypancistrus species so it is very fitting that he get these amazing little catfish named in honor of him. You can read more on this study by clicking HERE . The L066 king tiger pleco is a typical Hypancistrus in regards to their care in captivity. They come from rocky areas of pristine, heavily oxygenated, warm, soft, and acidic water and will gradually decline in health in the home aquarium if these conditions are not replicated. Using a high quality filter with a high flow rate along with a heater and frequent water changes will help keep these plecos happy and healthy. Like all known Hypancistrus , the L066 king tiger pleco is a carnivore so they must be fed a varied diet high in protein. Protein rich gel foods like Repashy, bloodworms, and sinking wafers are good choices to feed to meet their dietary needs. To reduce territorial fights and help the L066 king tiger pleco feel comfortable in the aquarium, plenty of snug, rocky caves should be provided for them to hide in. These caves are also where these fish will spawn if all other conditions are just right. They can be a very exciting breeding project as they are such a unique and beautiful catfish. An important thing to note, however, is that it is not wise to house the L066 king tiger pleco with other similar Hypancistrus as they can hybridize with it being near impossible to tell pure fish from hybrids. We encourage anyone who sets out to keep these fish make an effort to ensure captive populations remain pure to preserve this species in light of dam construction in Brazil destroying their natural habitat.

Remarks: Males are primarily blue with bright yellow fins. Members of the "Jake" type Aulonocara group traditionally have wide, white margins to their unpaired fins. They spend most of their time inside caves among large boulders, as opposed to open, sandy areas. Scientific Name : Aulonocara sp. Remarks : Nerite Snails are excellent algae grazers and they do not reproduce in freshwater due to their larvae requiring brackish conditions, meaning you won't be overrun with tiny snails seemingly crawling out of the substrate. They will deposit eggs on many surfaces, however, and these can be scraped off or left to naturally decay. They seem to appreciate brown algae (diatoms) most. Any tanks housing these snails should have a tight-fitting lid as they can crawl up the glass and escape. Luckily, these snails can close up their shells when out of water to slow the rate at which they dry out. Some have reported finding snails 24 hours or longer after escape that perk back up when placed back in the water. This combo pack includes 3 zebra nerite snails and 3 tiger nerite snails. B-grade snails have imperfections on their shells such as small chips or scratches but none that are a threat to the snail's health. They most likely will eventually heal and look like any other snail.

Remarks: Japanese trapdoor snails are, as their common name implies, a species native to Japan but they have also been introduced to certain parts of North America. They are very popular among those with ponds as they have a voracious appetite for algae, are very tolerant of cold weather, and are unlikely to overpopulate due to their slower reproductive cycle. Instead of laying egg clusters on surfaces, these snails keep their eggs in a brood chamber until they hatch into tiny baby snails. Their clutches are rather small for a snail, only typically having anywhere from 1 to 15 babies at a time. Whether you plan to keep this species in a tank or a pond, they make a great addition to almost any clean-up crew.

Remarks : The blue dragon blood peacock ( Aulonocara sp.) is a variant of dragon blood that has been line-bred by our farm for several generations. Their appearance is very different from them in regards to color and pattern. Dominant males display a bright, metallic blue face and reddish-pink or orange bodies with more metallic blue scales. Typically their fins are a rich orange color making for some really nice contrast. Females are usually more dull and faded. As this is a man-made line, there is some variation in color.

Remarks: Retroculus lapidifer is an absolutely stunning member of its genus that is highly sought after by cichlid enthusiasts. While young fish are mostly silver or tan, mature males and females are a rainbow of color. Their base color takes on a silvery hue covered in iridescent blue-green scales, dotted with gold speckling making them shine even more. The fins also will display orange, red, and yellow hues as a perfect accent to their body colors. Some identifying markings displayed by mature Retroculus lapidifer are the black spot on the middle back half of the dorsal fin and the two diagonal blue lines that run through and under the eye. Breeding fish get even more dramatic with their lips, underside, and ventral fins turning black. It can take up to a year for Retroculus lapidifer to mature and show full color, but it is well worth the wait. Retroculus species are rarely seen in the hobby due to a number of factors making their importation very costly. Freight from their native ranges, that of Retroculus lapidifer being the Rio Tocantins and Rio Araguaia systems in northeastern Brazil, is already very costly. Add on the fact that these fish are very sensitive to water quality and therefore cannot be packed in high densities, and it is easy to see why wild specimens carry such a hefty price tag. While captive breeding has been done, it also can be very costly as Retroculus need large aquariums due to their large size with heavy maintenance to maintain pristine conditions. As previously stated, Retroculus are not considered an easy species to keep when it comes to water quality tolerance. In the wild, they inhabit fast-flowing rocky rapids that provide them with pollutant free, heavily oxygenated, soft, acidic, water. They are highly specialized to these conditions, even lacking a functional swim bladder to instead hop around on the substrate to avoid having to swim in the fast currents. Retroculus are highly social and will live in large shoals, feeding on benthic organisms like small crustaceans and insect larvae they sift from the substrate. The best way to ensure your Retroculus are able to thrive within your aquarium, they need their natural habitat mimicked and to be treated like a rapids-dwelling Geophagus . Despite not being closely related to Geophagus and actually belonging to their own subfamily of Retroculinae , they have a similar body shape and feeding style. To avoid choking and possibly even outright refusal to eat, Retroculus should be kept on a substrate of fine, soft sand. Gravel is a potential choking risk and can damage their sensitive gills if they attempt to feed from it. The tank itself should also be very large so it can help dilute pollutants and allow for a current to be established using equipment like wavemakers. Lots of current, weekly water changes, and heavy filtration are all necessary to support the health of your Retroculus as they keep conditions pristine and dissolved oxygen levels high. Keeping your Retroculus in a larger tank is also needed to support their social nature. If not kept in groups of at least 5-8 individuals, not only will this cause your Retroculus to become stressed and skittish, it can have them kill the smaller, less dominant members of their school. Larger numbers take less of the focus off those lower in the pecking order and helps encourage more natural behaviors. Dither fish like Leporinus and larger tetras able to withstand a current make great tankmates for Retroculus and can even make them be bolder. Just be sure tankmates are not small enough to be swallowed and are not overly aggressive. While these cichlids are generally very peaceful, they still will swallow things small enough to fit in their mouths. Retroculus do not typically eat aquarium plants, but they can still present a hazard to them. This is because their earth-eating feeding style can have them uproot plants in the substrate. Instead, opt for plants that attach to structures like Anubias sp. and java fern to create a beautiful aquascape for these breath-taking cichlids.

Remarks : Regan’s dwarf pike cichlid ( Wallaciia regani ; formerly Crenicichla regani ) has many other pike cichlids beat in a few areas. They are known to be one of the smallest, most peaceful, and most widespread species of pike cichlid. With their native range being spread throughout the Amazon River basin, they can be found in a variety of habitats. Anywhere from clear waters full of aquatic vegetation to black water shallows filled with botanicals, this dwarf species has made itself at home. Such a wide distribution has made them able to tolerate a range of water parameters with the only requirement being their waters remain at least on the mildly soft and acidic side. The wide distribution of Regan’s dwarf pike cichlid not only has made them very adaptable, but it also has caused them to become a polychromatic species. What this means is that not only are there numerous different localities with different appearances, but it also means that even among a single spawn, you may find individuals that vary in color and pattern. Such differences have some researchers believing that Regan’s dwarf pike cichlid may actually represent a variety of different, closely related species but this has yet to be confirmed. While their polychromatic nature has created some exceptions, there are a few key characteristics that can help you sex your Regan’s dwarf pike cichlids. One of the first visual differences between males and females is that females typically have 1-3 black ocelli (eye-spots) rimmed with white on their dorsal fin. This can be a great indicator when determining the sex of juvenile Regan’s dwarf pike cichlids as it is a marking present even when females are young. If dealing with mature fish, you can further identify which are female by looking at the belly. When ready to spawn, female dwarf pike cichlids will get a yellow or pink hue to their bellies that also become heavily rounded. Regan’s dwarf pike cichlids are capable of growing up to 5” long, however most top out at about 3” in captivity. Such a diminutive size has resulted in a key difference from their larger relatives when it comes to their social structure. Unlike their far more solitary larger relatives, when given enough space, dwarf pike cichlids can be kept in groups rather than just as a single fish or pair. In fact, some have found that keeping them in groups often leads to stronger pair bonds forming. Their more mellow personalities also make Regan’s dwarf pike cichlids a great candidate for community aquariums. So long as a tankmate is not small enough to fit in the mouths of these pocket-sized predators, they typically are safe. Also keep in mind, being smaller and less aggressive means that overly large or aggressive tankmates should not be kept with your dwarf pikes as they may get bullied or even eaten. As previously mentioned, while they are small, Regan’s dwarf pike cichlids are still predators. In the wild, they will hunt down tiny fish, crustaceans, and insects to feed on. Within the home aquarium, they will benefit from a varied, carnivorous diet with blood worms and chopped krill being favorites. While most will eventually take to high protein pellet foods, some wild pikes might remain stubborn. You can help wean them off live and frozen foods by gradually mixing pellets/flakes in with each feeding. Whether keeping a breeding pair or as a member of a community aquarium, Regan’s dwarf pike cichlids are a joy to keep. They are a great option if one wants all the personality of a pike cichlid but are more limited on space. Care for them properly and they are sure to become a fast favorite.

Remarks: Neolamprologus brevis is one of the smallest lamprologines known to the hobby, rarely growing beyond 2” in length. What these shell-dwellers lack in size, they make up for in their feisty personalities and striking appearance. N. brevis will fearlessly defend their shells against intruders much larger than them, sometimes even nipping the hands of keepers that get too close! This amusing level of bravado combined with the electric blue markings that seem to glow on their tan or silver bodies makes N. brevis a must have for many Tanganyikan cichlid enthusiasts. In the wild, N. brevis populations can be found throughout Lake Tanganyika to which they are endemic. Each locality can differ in both color and pattern, but their habitat type choice remains the same. Being a shell-dwelling species that form monogamous pairs instead of harems, N. brevis are found in open sand where empty snail shells are scattered about with each pair controlling a territory approximately 6” in diameter centered around their chosen shell. They hover outside their shell feeding upon any passing plankton that they snatch out of the water column. A unique trait of N. brevis is that they have a far greater number of gill-rakers compared to other shell-dwellers which gives cause to their robust, frog-like heads that house them. It is suspected that having so many gill-rakers aids this species in feeding upon even the smallest of zooplankton within the lake. Within the home aquarium, it is best to attempt to replicate the natural habitat of N. brevis to allow them to thrive. They require warm, hard, alkaline water parameters, a sandy substrate, and at least one shell per pair. Their monogamous nature allows N. brevis to be comfortable if kept as a single pair with a 10-gallon aquarium being sufficient enough space. If keeping multiple pairs together as a colony or if keeping them in a Tanganyikan community, 20 gallons or more will be needed. While N. brevis are very protective of their shells, they are otherwise peaceful cichlids and thus can be kept with many other Tanganyikan species so long as enough space is provided and tankmates aren’t large enough to swallow them. Feeding N. brevis is both an entertaining and straight forward task. Being true micropredators and planktivores, they will take most small, meaty foods provided. High protein crushed flakes and small pellets, baby brine shrimp, moina/daphnia, small bloodworms, and tubifex are all great options they should take to readily. Since N. brevis usually are not very picky, you can occasionally provide them with a crushed veggie flake as a treat to aid in digestion, but majority of their diet should be high protein. Like with most shell-dwelling species, a lot of the enjoyment most find in keeping N. brevis is being able to witness their breeding and fry-rearing habits. Of course, to begin breeding your own, you will need males and females. Since it can be difficult or near impossible to sex young N. brevis , it is best to start with a group of at least 5-6 young juveniles and allow them to pair off naturally. As they mature, you can begin to spot the handful of differences between males and females. Males will get extensions on their ventral fins, have a more pointed dorsal fin, grow larger, and will have more vibrant blue markings. Females remain smaller, rounder, have smaller fins, and will get a yellow hue to their bellies. How vibrant this yellow color is depends on the locality of your N. brevis with some having very subtle yellow color while others are more intense. When ready to spawn, a pair will select a shell to breed in and use as a hiding spot when threatened. A unique behavior N. brevis display is that both males and females will hide in the same shell, something not seen in other cichlid species. While this species does not tend to bury their shells like many other shell-dwellers, they instead show off surprising strength and resourcefulness when their selected shell is not in ideal placement. By biting onto and manipulating the shell or simply ramming into it, these bulldog-like cichlids are able to move the shell around or even flip it over if needed despite the shell usually being at least twice their size. Once a shell is selected and in prime condition, the female will lay her eggs deep inside the shell with the male then fertilizing them. Both the male and female will guard the eggs and fry until they are free-swimming after which the male typically moves on to another female if one is available. The female will continue to care for the fry until they begin to leave the shell about 1-2 weeks after becoming free-swimming. So long as the fry have other hiding spots to retreat to and the tank is large enough, they typically can be safely left in the same tank as the parents to continue to grow.

Remarks : The L018 gold nugget pleco is a highly coveted species of Loricariid within the aquarium keeping hobby and one look at them shows exactly why this is. With their dark gray to black bodies decorated with contrasting bright gold/yellow seams along the edges of their dorsal and caudal fins along with similarly colored spots, they are considered one of the most beautiful plecos. These seams and spots are thicker and larger when the fish is younger, reducing in size as they grow but gaining even more of these spots. This changes their pattern from a playful polka-dot one to a more elegant speckle or starry pattern. While many would presume their common name to be derived from their gold/yellow pattern, it actually has a much more interesting story. When the gold mining industry in the native range, the Rio Xingu, of the L018 gold nugget pleco shut down, locals turned to these abundant plecos as a source of income. Young fish are collected for the aquarium trade while older fish are collected for food. Capturing these fish is far from an easy endeavor, however, as they live in some of the fastest flowing water in the Amazon and hide among the cracks in boulders where they graze on biofilm and algae as well as capture small insect larvae and crustaceans. These conditions consisting of clear, pristine, warm, oxygen-rich waters full of hiding spots should be replicated in the aquarium if one wants to keep L018 gold nugget plecos. If these conditions are not met, this sensitive species will almost certainly decline in health over time and eventually die. As this omnivorous catfish mainly feeds on algae and vegetable matter, this should consist of a majority of their diet in captivity. However, they are still omnivores so protein still should be provided. Due to L018 gold nugget plecos actually having softer teeth compared to other species, they prefer softer foods so Repashy gel foods are a great choice for feeding them. It should also be noted their metabolism is rather fast for how long their intestinal tract is so they will need to be fed more frequently than most other Loricariids. Keeping multiple L018 gold nugget plecos can be challenging as they are a very territorial species, aggressively sparring to the point of injury and sometimes even death if ample space is not provided. A 60 gallon tank can be enough for a single male and a small group of females, but a minimum of 100 gallons is needed if one plans to keep more than one male. This aggression can also be shown to conspecifics so they are best kept as the only pleco in the tank or even in a species only tank. Needless to say, this is not a beginner species of pleco and is more suited for the intermediate to advanced keeper. If well cared for, it is well worth the challenge to keep such a beautiful and unique species.

Remarks: The Gold Spot Pleco ( Pterygoplichthys joselimaianus ), commonly known as L001 or the Spotted Sailfin Pleco, is a striking armored catfish with gold-to-cream markings across a dark body and fins. Native to Brazil's Tocantins River basin, this species is distinct from Pterygoplichthys gibbiceps , which is also commonly sold as a sailfin pleco. Young fish can show larger, irregular markings that become finer as they mature. Their tall dorsal fin and attractive pattern make them an impressive addition to a suitably large aquarium. Size and aquarium requirements Plan for an adult around 12–16 inches long. A spacious aquarium of at least 150 gallons, with a footprint at least 6 feet long, provides room for an adult to move comfortably. Provide sturdy hiding places, heavy filtration, and regular water changes. These large plecos produce substantial waste and should not be purchased simply as a solution to an algae problem. Feeding and tankmates Offer a varied diet of sinking foods suitable for plecos, vegetables, and occasional protein-rich foods. Naturally occurring algae supplements their diet but should not be their only food source. They can become territorial toward other large plecos, especially as they mature, so allow ample space and separate shelters when choosing tankmates. Scientific name: Pterygoplichthys joselimaianus Common names: Gold Spot Pleco, Spotted Sailfin Pleco L-number: L001 Origin: Tocantins River basin, Brazil Never release aquarium fish into the wild. If a fish outgrows your aquarium, arrange a suitable new home.

Remarks : Black angelfish ( Pterophyllum scalare ) are a popular and elegant variant of angelfish. Their bodies and fins are almost entirely a striking jet black. Some, especially young fish, may have a few silver scales. Most start with gold or black eyes that they keep to adulthood, others have their eyes turn a deep, blood red as they mature. Angelfish are easy-going cichlids that do well in almost any community tank. Captive bred specimens can tolerate a wide range of pH values and are typically peaceful enough to be kept with most tetras and other peaceful South American cichlids. Due to their long ventral fins, we do not recommend keeping them with very nippy fish such as tiger barbs or zebra danios. Breeding Angelfish can often be achieved by giving them a vertical, flat surface to spawn on, such as a leaf of an Amazon Sword or a piece of slate leaning against the wall. Fry will be cared for until a few weeks after they are free swimming, though you can remove the fry or eggs and hatch them artificially if you wish. It is usually best to isolate breeding pairs in their own tank when spawning as they can become territorial.

Remarks: Neolamprologus sexfasciatus is a species of Tanganyikan cichlid whose coloration and even behavior varies based on what locality/population it belongs to. Most are familiar with the blue variant from the southern end of the lake that has proven to be extremely challenging to breed in captivity. They also have gained a reputation for having a nasty temperament with the males often killing any other of their kind. In contrast, the gold Kipili variant whose golden yellow coloration combined with black, vertical bars gives it a bumblebee look, are far more willing to spawn and have a more mellow temperament. The gold Kipili variant of Neolamprologus sexfasciatus can be found in the rocky shallows of the southeastern side of Lake Tanganyika near Kipili, Tanzania. There, it can be found in pairs inhabiting crevices between rocks. Gold Kipili kept within the home aquarium will thrive best when their natural habitat is replicated with a sandy substrate and plenty of rocky caves. The more caves and breaks in their line of sight, the less aggression will be displayed. While gold Kipili are far more manageable than their blue counterparts, they are still a particularly feisty cichlid. They should not be kept with more timid and slow moving tankmates, but they can get along with more robust Tanganyikans provided enough space and caves are provided. While a lone pair can be kept in a 40-gallon aquarium, 75 gallons or more is recommended if they are being kept in a community setting. Being voracious predators, gold Kipili will hunt down fish small enough to fit in their mouths so great consideration should be given when choosing tankmates. So long as these aspects of their personalities are kept in mind, unlike the blue variant, it is possible to have a gold Kipili as a member of a more robust Tanganyikan community. If looking to breed gold Kipili, they are best kept in a species only tank as a solitary pair. This is because when spawning, their aggression gets far worse with the male viciously guarding the cave in which the female chooses to lay her eggs. Of course, one must obtain a pair before they are able to breed this species which can be a challenge as just having a male and female will not guarantee they will pair off. Rather, one should get a group of at least six juveniles and allow pairs to form naturally as they grow, a process that can take up to a year. Since males and females only differ in that males are slightly larger, you will only be able to tell a pair has formed based on behavior so close monitoring is key. Once pairs have formed, they should be separated as soon as possible as the aggression of spawning pairs is far worse toward their own kind and conspecifics. After a pair has been established, the female will lay her eggs within a cave selected by the pair. Gold Kipili are notably prolific once they start spawning as eggs can number around 500 per spawn. She will tend to the eggs and fry until they are around 2-3 weeks of age while the male guards the cave. Afterwards, the male will actually chase off the female and fully take over brood care until the fry are around 4 months of age at which point they will disperse. It is very important when breeding gold Kipili that you have a back-up holding tank to place the female in as the male can get extremely aggressive with her outside of spawning or when he takes over brood care. While these feisty cichlids can be a challenge to breed, their vibrant colors and fascinating behavior make them a worthy challenge for anyone looking to keep them.

Remarks: Blue mystery snails ( Pomacea bridgesii ) have a white shell and a dark foot causing the shell to appear a pale blue. Mystery snails have been a staple part of the aquarium hobby for many years acting as great algae control. They come in many color forms and are very easy to breed. Unlike many snail species that are typically hermaphrodites, these snail are separated into male and female with the males having a second appendage beside their siphon, a structure used to get supplementary oxygen from the surface. Mystery snails lay their eggs just above the surface of the water, usually on the glass of the aquarium, in large masses that tend to look like pink styrofoam. Population control is as easy as removing any egg clusters before they hatch. As these snails lack a larval stage, they hatch out as tiny versions of the adults, ready to feast on algae and detritus.

To avoid their fins getting damaged, this species should not be kept with nippy fish like danios.

listings.description: Remarks : Odessa barbs are small, active, vibrant, shoaling fish that look fantastic in a planted aquarium. They do well in tanks with both slow or heavy flow making them excellent tankmates for many species including those requiring a hillstream set up. Male Odessa Barbs turn bright red with shiny gold scales. They may not fully color up without the presence of females. If kept in small numbers, it is likely for this fish to become stressed and nip the fins of tankmates. The best way to prevent this is to keep them in groups of 6 or more so they are preoccupied with displaying and sparring rather than harassing other species.

Hornwort ( Ceratophyllum demersum ) Pond & Greenhouse Grown • Fast Growing • Low Maintenance • Excellent Fry Cover Our Hornwort ( Ceratophyllum demersum ) is grown in our ponds and greenhouses here at Imperial Tropicals . Our Hornwort is generally very lush, with natural variations in shades of green depending on growing conditions. Hornwort is a fast-growing, low-maintenance floating aquatic plant that grows well under a wide range of lighting conditions, including relatively low light. It does not produce true roots, so there is no need to plant it in substrate. Simply allow it to float freely in your aquarium, pond, breeding tank, or grow-out system. Its dense, feathery growth makes Hornwort particularly useful for providing cover for fry and small fish . It also provides shade for fish, utilizes nutrients from the water, and produces oxygen during photosynthesis. Natural Distribution Hornwort ( Ceratophyllum demersum ) has a cosmopolitan distribution and occurs naturally across much of the world. It can be found throughout diverse regions of North America, Europe, Asia, Africa, and other parts of the world . In the wild, Hornwort commonly grows submerged in ponds, lakes, slow-moving streams, canals, and other freshwater habitats . Its ability to thrive under a wide range of environmental conditions has helped make it one of the world's most widely distributed aquatic plants. Why We Like Hornwort Fast growing and easy to maintain Excellent cover for fry and small fish Great for breeding and grow-out tanks Provides natural shade and security for fish Produces oxygen during photosynthesis Helps utilize nutrients from the water Does not require substrate No supplemental CO₂ required Tolerates relatively low light Excellent for aquariums and outdoor ponds Easily propagated from stem sections Hornwort Care Scientific Name: Ceratophyllum demersum Common Names: Hornwort, Coontail Difficulty: Easy Growth Rate: Fast Placement: Floating or submerged Lighting: Low to High CO₂: Not required Temperature: Approximately 50–86°F Maximum Length: Can reach several feet under favorable conditions Propagation: Stem cuttings and fragments Rooted Plant: No Aquarium Suitable: Yes Pond Suitable: Yes Important Information About Our Pond & Greenhouse-Grown Hornwort We HIGHLY recommend a plant dip for Hornwort to help prevent unwanted critters from making it into your aquarium. Our Hornwort is grown in our ponds and greenhouses , where it is exposed to a natural growing environment. We cannot treat these plants with harsh chemicals that could put our livestock—or our customers' livestock—at risk. We do everything we reasonably can to prevent unwanted hitchhikers from traveling with our plants, including rinsing the Hornwort before shipment. However, snails and other small aquatic organisms can be very difficult to completely eliminate. Hornwort may contain: Snails and/or snail eggs Scuds and other small aquatic organisms Duckweed ( Lemna minor ) Watermeal ( Wolffia globosa ) Please give your Hornwort a very thorough rinse upon arrival. If you do not want potential hitchhikers introduced into your aquarium, we strongly recommend using an aquarium-safe plant dip before adding the Hornwort to your tank. There are several different methods for dipping aquarium plants, and information on how to properly plant dip can easily be found online . Please research the method you choose and follow the recommended instructions carefully, as Hornwort can be sensitive to some treatments. We cannot guarantee that pond- and greenhouse-grown plants will be completely free of snails, snail eggs, scuds, duckweed, watermeal, or other small aquatic organisms. Upon Arrival Some shedding is normal during shipment. Rinse the Hornwort thoroughly upon arrival to remove loose plant material before placing it in your aquarium or pond. Once established under suitable conditions, Hornwort is a vigorous grower and may need periodic trimming or harvesting. For reference, the product picture shows a Medium Bunch of Hornwort. listings.description: Remarks : Green Texas cichlids ( Herichthys carpintis ) are found in northern Mexico. They are very similar to H. cyanoguttatus , though their spots are larger and more like blotches. They are also slightly less aggressive than H. cyanoguttatus , but still capable of owning a tank. Due to their large size and territorial nature, this species is best kept alone, in pairs, or with other large, territorial species in a large aquarium.

Remarks: The Jack Dempsey cichlid is a large, colorful, and territorial species native to Central America. They are mostly found in Mexico, but they can also be found in Belize, Guatemala, and Honduras in a variety of different habitats. This diversity in natural habitats has made the Jack Dempsey cichlid a very hardy and adaptable species when in captivity. They have been known to thrive in both hard and soft water but they usually are the healthiest and show the most amount of color when kept in neutral conditions. For many years Jack Dempsey cichlids have been a popular cichlid among aquarists due to how hardy they are, their impressive size, feisty nature, and bright colors. While juveniles only have a few metallic blue scales, they tend to get more and more as they age until it covers a large majority of their body and fins as long as they are healthy. Females will have less of these dazzling scales with some males being almost completely covered in them. The Jack Dempsey's common name comes from an American heavyweight boxer of the same name that was well known back in the 1920s. Aquarists at this time thought the strong, defined jaw and aggressive nature resembled the boxer and the name has stuck even to this day. Jack Dempsey cichlids are highly territorial and are large predators so great care should be taken if one plans to house them with other fish. Anything small enough to fit in their expansive mouths is very likely to be eaten and any fish that is timid or looks similar is likely to be a target for bullying. When keeping them with other large cichlids, plenty of space should be provided with the tank being at least 150 gallons. However, pairs of Jack Dempseys can be kept in a smaller tank with 75 gallons being sufficient for a single pair as they tend to form strong, peaceful bonds. Pairs also tend to be excellent parents, carefully tending to eggs they lay on flat surfaces and even chewing up food into smaller pieces to feed their fry when they hatch. This makes Jack Dempseys a fun fish to breed or just to simply keep and appreciate their dazzling colors and interesting behaviors.

Remarks: The featherfin squeaker cat is one of the largest species of synodontis. Hailing from multiple different rivers in West Africa, they can be found in many different biotopes resulting in a very adaptable species. As they have been bred in captivity for many years, this has made them even more hardy and tolerant of a wide range of parameters. However, this species is not suited for most community aquariums. This is due to their large size, typically reaching 8" in captivity but some reaching 12", and their territorial behavior. Despite being a shoaling species, like all synodontis, that does best when kept in groups of three or more, featherfin squeaker cats command large amounts of territory for each fish and thus can get aggressive with their own kind and conspecifics. To combat this, featherfin squeaker cats should be kept in a tank that is at least 150 gallons if keeping just one and at least 250 gallons if keeping a small group. Their large size and boisterous attitude make the featherfin squeaker cat a good choice for a bottom-dweller that can handle its own against large, African cichlids. Most large haps won't attempt to harass them as long as the catfish isn't smaller than the cichlid by much. If kept in the right conditions, these large catfish can make a beautiful and active addition for the lower levels of a large aquarium. Their flowing fins from which they derive their common name combined with their leopard pattern make them a truly amazing synodontis.

Remarks: The rainbow dace has long been a wrongfully over-looked species in the hobby due to it commonly being seen as a "bait fish." If one sees this species in the right conditions, though, it would prove to be much more than that with its vibrant red fins and head and pale blue body. This North American native has more than just color as it also has a very active and inquisitive behavior making it very fascinating to observe. This fish can be found throughout the mid-west in a wide variety of parameters making it very hardy and an excellent candidate for a native pond. It is said that they show their best colors when kept in cooler conditions, though, and require heavy aeration. Some report the rainbow dace to be a fin nipper but this can be alleviated by keeping them in large schools of 8 or more so they are preoccupied with displaying and sparring with one another. Remarks : Platinum angelfish ( Pterophyllum scalare ) are incredibly elegant with with their shimmering, platinum white scales and fins. They lack any markings and really stand out in a tank with their stark coloration. Angelfish are easy-going cichlids that do well in almost any community tank. Captive bred specimens can tolerate a wide range of pH values and are typically peaceful enough to be kept with most tetras and other peaceful South American cichlids. Breeding Angelfish can often be achieved by giving them a vertical, flat surface to spawn on, such as a leaf of an Amazon Sword or a piece of slate leaning against the wall. Fry will be cared for until a few weeks after they are free swimming, though you can remove the fry or eggs and hatch them artificially if you wish. It is usually best to isolate breeding pairs in their own tank when spawning as they can become territorial. Remarks: Discus are often referred to as the king of aquarium fish. This nickname arose from the sheer beauty of these fish along with their reputation for being difficult to care for making those who keep them successfully revered within the hobby. It being difficult to keep discus was an opinion developed when majority of specimens available were wild caught. With most now being captive bred and even line bred to produce many different color variants such as turquoise and pigeon blood, they are much more hardy. That being said, discus still require very clean, soft, acidic water with little to no nitrates and warm temperatures. These peaceful cichlids tend to be timid, especially when it comes to feeding, so they shouldn't be kept with overly boisterous or aggressive fish. Typically their mouths are very small, but once they reach adulthood they are capable of swallowing very tiny fish so this should also be considered when choosing tankmates. If attempting to breed discus, lots of vertical surfaces should be provided for them to lay their eggs on and it should be noted they can become territorial when spawning. Once the fry hatch and are free-swimming, both parents show an incredible form of parental care in which they feed their fry by allowing them to eat their slime coat. This behavior is an amazing sight and makes breeding discus very enjoyable. Remarks: Green aeneus Osteogaster ( Osteogaster aeneus ) are one of, if not the most popular Corydoradinae species in the hobby. They have been captive bred for so long that they have become very tolerant of a wide range of water parameters and come in different color morphs and fin types such as albino or long-finned making them the perfect starter Corydoradinae . These are the albino variant displaying red eyes and bodies that can vary in color from white, to light pink, to a very faded orange making them stand out very nicely against a dark substrate. It should be noted that albino animals are more sensitive to light, so these fish should not be kept under bright lighting unless they are provided lots of areas of shade to escape to. Green aeneus Osteogaster were previously classified as Corydoras aeneus , but were reclassified as Osteogaster aeneus upon publication of a phylogenomic analysis in 2024 that reclassified many species in the Corydoradinae subfamily. Corydoradinae are small, peaceful catfish that are active shoalers and will stay near conspecifics, making for a lovely sight. They feed by searching through sand with their barbels, making such a substrate necessary for their long-term health . Gravel substrates tend to be abrasive and damage the barbels, leading to infections and an inability to find food. While these friendly catfish are willing to swim with other species of Corydoradinae different from their own, this does not provide the same social need as being kept with members of their own species. Because of this, it is highly recommended to keep at least six of each species of Corydoradinae present in the aquarium and only mix species if one has the space to keep at least six of each. Corydoradinae are often looked at as "scavengers," but they should be treated in a similar fashion as the rest of your fish. They are omnivores and require a mixed diet. Sinking prepared foods are readily accepted, as are frozen and live foods such as brine shrimp, blackworms, and bloodworms.

Remarks: The peppered or salt and pepper Hoplisoma is almost as common, or is as common as the green Osteogaster in the fishkeeping hobby. They have silver or tan bodies mottled with gray and black blotches and a metallic blue-green sheen. This species has been bred in captivity for a very long time resulting in a very hardy fish that handles a wide range of water parameters, though it does fare best when kept in cooler water. Captive breeding has also resulted in there being interesting mutations such as albinism and long-finned variants. An interesting thing to note about the peppered Hoplisoma is that they were first discovered back in the 1830s by no other than Charles Darwin during his expedition in Buenos Aires aboard the Beagle. It was previously classified as Corydoras paleatus , but was reclassified as Hoplisoma paleatus upon publication of a phylogenomic analysis in 2024 that reclassified many species in the Corydoradinae subfamily. Remarks: Melanotaenia lacustris , the turquoise rainbow, has long been a staple in the hobby. Both males and females display quite a bit of color, but males show a bright gold/orange stripe from the nose to the first dorsal fin when excited. These fish are omnivorous and should be fed a quality flake food with supplemental proteins such as baby brine shrimp. They require clean water but tolerate a wide variety of water parameters. By providing frequent water changes, you will be rewarded with nearly continuous spawning attempts. Melanotaenia species deposit eggs in weedy areas (often mimicked by a yarn mop) and the eggs hatch 7-10 days later. Eggs can be harvested for hatching in separate tanks to avoid predation. Most Rainbows show their best colors at sunrise, when the males display their bright fins for potential mates. Having more females than males will allow for proper color displays and avoid any unwanted aggression towards lone females.

Remarks : Compressiceps are best maintained as a single pair, but can be maintained in groups if in large enough aquaria. It's not particularly territorial and can make a good addition to a community of Tanganyikan species, but shouldn’t be kept alongside anything small enough to be considered food. It is not recommended as a companion for Tropheus or any others species requiring a low protein diet. They grow very slowly with some taking years to reach maturity. In the wild, compressiceps are ambush predators that wait in crevices between rocks until prey comes by. Once it does, their mouth juts out to nearly the size of the tallest part of their body in one fast motion, engulfing their prey. These crevices are also where these fish spawn with both parents guarding the eggs and fry. Remarks: Amano shrimp ( Caridina multidentata ) are named after the late Takashi Amano, a famous photographer and aquascaper that introduced this species to the fishkeeping hobby. These shrimp quickly grew in popularity not because of their looks, as they typically are clear with a few black specs, but because of their voracious appetite for algae. Amano shrimp can quickly clean up many types of algae including stubborn black beard algae. An interesting thing to note is the type of things the shrimp feed on can actually alter their color, some getting a bit of a blue, green, or brown hue. While adults can live their whole life in freshwater, this species goes through a larval stage that requires brackish water conditions so they can't reproduce in the freshwater aquarium. This typically is not an issue as amano shrimp have a long life-span for a shrimp, usually 3-5 years, with some reporting having specimens for as long as 10 years. These shrimp reach quite a large size compared to other freshwater shrimp in the hobby making them more suited for being kept with small to medium-sized fish upon maturity compared to smaller species like cherry shrimp. They also differ from most other shrimps in that instead of only flopping and hopping around when out of water, amano shrimp are actually very good at crawling around on land, making them notorious escape artists. For this reason, we recommend they be kept with a tight-fitting lid.

Remarks : Dojo loaches are a very popular loach in the aquarium hobby due to their hardy nature and endearing personalities. Many become tame enough to eat right from their keeper's hand. Their other common name, the weather loach, comes from their peculiar increase in activity when a storm is on the way. These loaches tend to burrow, so a sandy substrate is best for their health. They also grow to a very large size so while a 40 gallon may work as a grow-out tank, once they begin to reach the 6 inch mark these fish should be kept in a 90 gallon at minimum. Care should be taken to not allow these fish to escape as the combination of them being able to squirm across the land into new water-ways and their wide tolerance of water parameters has made them highly invasive. Remarks : The Candy Cane Tetra is more red than the wild-type Rosy Tetra. They are tall-bodied tetras with long dorsal fins that are red with a black spot. Like any shoaling species, they prefer to be kept in groups of 6 or more. They can be told apart from the very closely related and similar looking ornate tetra ( Megalamphodus bentosi ) by a lack of a dark spot behind the gill plate. The scientific name for the candy cane tetra used to be Hyphessobrycon rosaceus "HY511". However, it was reclassified as Megalamphodus rosaceus after the completion of an intensive phylogenic study on species in the family Characidae. Remarks: The L398 Tanke tiger pleco is a native of the Rio Xingu in Brazil. They are specifically found in the lower sections of the river where fallen branches and trees litter the clear, fast-flowing waters. In the aquarium, they do best when these conditions of clean, heavily oxygenated, soft, and acidic water are imitated. As they are a xylivore (a wood eater), lots of driftwood should be provided for them to graze on along with fresh vegetables such as zucchini, carrots, and sweet potatoes. Loricariid species like the Tanke tiger pleco have fast metabolisms that result in the creation of lots of waste so to keep their water pristine and allow them to remain healthy, frequent, large water changes are a must. If one provides the L398 Tanke tiger pleco with correct parameters, plenty of hiding spaces, and a healthy diet, you will be rewarded with a truly stunning fish. Individuals at peak healthy display vibrant yellow or orange coloration that pairs nicely with the black or dark gray stripes that also cover their fins and body. As their common name indicates, this gives them a pattern similar to that of a tiger. This attractive coloration combined with their manageable size makes the L398 Tanke tiger pleco an excellent choice for many South American tanks.

Remarks : Compressiceps are best maintained as a single pair, but can be maintained in groups if in large enough aquaria. It's not particularly territorial and can make a good addition to a community of Tanganyikan species, but shouldn’t be kept alongside anything small enough to be considered food. It is not recommended as a companion for Tropheus or any others species requiring a low protein diet. They grow very slowly with some taking years to reach maturity. Once it does, their mouth juts out to nearly the size of the tallest part of their body in one fast motion, engulfing their prey. These crevices are also where these fish spawn with both parents guarding the eggs and fry. Remarks : Fossorochromis rostratus is a large Haplochromine from Lake Malawi, and it requires a tank that exceeds 100 gallons to accommodate its large size and high activity level. In the wild, many would expect them to be voracious predators due to their size (some males even exceeding 16" in length!), but they prove to be a mostly peaceful hap so long as other fish do not fit in their mouths. They actually feed by sifting the sand in search of worms and micro-organisms to feed on similar to Geophagus . An interesting thing to note is that in the wild, blue dolphin cichlids frequently follow this species around to feed on any morsels of food they stir up while sifting. The Fossorochromis rostratus makes further use of the sand by diving into it when they feel threatened as well as the dominant making massive spawning pits in the soft substrate. As it is necessary for their natural feeding and spawning behaviors, a substrate of soft sand is required for these fish to thrive. Any other substrate can results in choking, abrasions, and an unwillingness to feed. While being fairly peaceful for a hap, Fossorochromis rostratus males can show quite a bit of aggression toward one another so if one wants to have more than one, they will need to provide ample space and many females to allow them to establish separate territories. Some note having a lesser dominant male with a more dominant male and many females will result in the brightest colors from the most dominant male through this of course comes at the risk of increased aggression. Adult, dominant males show some truly striking color with iridescent blue-green fins and bodies with nicely contrasting orange accents. Some also keep the 3 large spots along their lateral line that is present in juveniles, females, and stressed fish but they are usually very faded. Lesser dominant males, females, and juveniles are usually tan or gray with the aforementioned three prominent black spots on their sides that can be used to identify this species.

Mbuna cichlids are rock dwelling fish that come from Lake Malawi in the Rift Valley. Both males and females are typically very colorful and hardy fish that are easy to keep in an aquarium. Unlike peacocks and haps, multiple breeding groups of different species can be kept together in the same tank without quite as much aggression, but there is still a possibility of hybridization. Being mainly herbivorous, mbuna should be fed a mainly vegetarian diet. Mbuna will attack young peacocks and haps which in turn, will attack mbuna upon maturity, so it is not recommended to mix these groups.

Remarks : If you're looking to maximize the color-to-size ratio of your fish, you'll be hard pressed to beat cherry barbs ( Rohanella titteya ). Males are an electric red color that can be spotted from across the room, despite their small average size of 1-1.5". Females sport golden-orange bodies and may be required for males to show their full colors. The albino variant of this species is closer to pink than red in both males and females. Cherry barbs are endemic to the rainforests of Sri Lanka where they can be found in shallow streams with plenty of leaf litter, soft sand, fallen twigs, and shade provided by overhanging vegetation. These waters are clear or mildly tannin-stained, soft, acidic, and mildly warm. Unfortunately, these fish are heavily threatened by habitat destruction resulting in wild populations being so few in number that export of wild fish is currently prohibited. This means that cherry barbs available in the hobby are captive bred and their breeding should be encouraged to have stock to replenish their natural habitats once they are restored. With cherry barbs being extensively captive bred since their entry into the hobby, they have become very tolerant in regards to water chemistry making them an excellent, hardy choice for beginners. However, despite their ability to survive in a broad range of conditions, it is best to mimic their natural habitat. Keeping cherry barbs in soft, acidic, mildly warm water with plenty of vegetation and botanicals as well as minimal light will not only have them at their healthiest, but also display their best coloration and encourage them to be out and about rather than hiding timidly. Feeding a varied and high quality diet supplemented by the occasional feeding of small, live foods such as baby brine shrimp or daphnia will also bring out the best in your cherry barbs. Cherry barbs are a shoaling species that naturally live in large groups in the wild. If kept in small numbers in captivity, it is likely for this fish to become stressed and nip the fins of tankmates. The best way to prevent this is to keep them in groups of 6 or more so they are preoccupied with displaying and sparring rather than harassing other species. When comfortable and with all their needs met, cherry barbs can make an excellent community fish with their hardy nature, active behavior, and bright colors. Cherry barbs were previously classified as Puntius titteya but after a review of the Puntius genus was finished in 2023, it was reclassified as Rohanella titteya . This makes them the only member of their genus establishing Rohanella as a monospecific genus. These barbs were not the only ones to receive a new classification as the Puntius genus had been used as a collection pot for smaller barb species until their true classification could be further analyzed. If you would like to learn more, you can find the research paper here .

Remarks: Mystery snails ( Pomacea bridgesii ) have been a staple part of the aquarium hobby for many years acting as great algae control. They come in many color forms and are very easy to breed. Unlike many snail species that are typically hermaphrodites, these snail are separated into male and female with the males having a second appendage beside their siphon, a structure used to get supplementary oxygen from the surface. Mystery snails lay their eggs just above the surface of the water, usually on the glass of the aquarium, in large masses that tend to look like pink styrofoam. Population control is as easy as removing any egg clusters before they hatch. As these snails lack a larval stage, they hatch out as tiny versions of the adults, ready to feast on algae and detritus. These B-grade mystery snails have imperfections on their shells such as small chips but none are a threat to the snail's health. They most likely will eventually heal and look like any other snail.

Remarks : Olive nerite snails are a species that can be found both in the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean typically in estuaries. They are aptly named for their olive colored shells that have a swirl pattern toward the tip of their shells. This species is noted as possibly the hardiest nerite snail so it is an excellent choice for the beginner aquarist, B-grade snails have imperfections on their shells such as small chips or scratches but none that are a threat to the snail's health. They most likely will eventually heal and look like any other snail. Nerite Snails are excellent algae grazers and they do not reproduce in freshwater due to their larvae requiring brackish conditions, meaning you won't be overrun with tiny snails seemingly crawling out of the substrate. They will deposit eggs on many surfaces, however, and these can be scraped off or left to naturally decay. They seem to appreciate brown algae (diatoms) most. Any tanks housing these snails should have a tight-fitting lid as they can crawl up the glass and escape. Luckily, these snails can close up their shells when out of water to slow the rate at which they dry out. Some have reported finding snails 24 hours or longer after escape that perk back up when placed back in the water.

Females typically remain gray or tan but can occasionally take on a little color. In the wild, these fish can be found on the edges of the rocky where males set up territories around rock piles so imitating this environment will aid in attempts to breed them.
