Remarks : Blue blushing veil-tail angelfish ( Pterophyllum scalare ) are a very uncommon color variant. They have white or silver bodies with dark colored fins similar to a Bulgarian green, but the color sheen they get when in the right light is blue instead of green. These fish also have the veil-tail gene which results in elegant, elongated fins. These longer fins are beautiful but can make these angels more of a target for fin-nippers so extra care should be taken when choosing tank mates. Angelfish are easy-going cichlids that do well in almost any community tank. Captive bred specimens can tolerate a wide range of pH values and are typically peaceful enough to be kept with most tetras and other peaceful South American cichlids. Due to their long ventral fins, we do not recommend keeping them with very nippy fish such as tiger barbs or zebra danios. Breeding Angelfish can often be achieved by giving them a vertical, flat surface to spawn on, such as a leaf of an Amazon Sword or a piece of slate leaning against the wall. Fry will be cared for until a few weeks after they are free swimming, though you can remove the fry or eggs and hatch them artificially if you wish. It is usually best to isolate breeding pairs in their own tank when spawning as they can become territorial.

Remarks: The black saddled Hoplisoma ( Hoplisoma sp. CW51), also known as the new panda Hoplisoma, is a medium-sized Corydoradinae that is found in a small creek near the settlement of Villa Bittencourt which lies on the border between Colombia, Brazil and Peru. A very similar, close relative known as the black diamond Hoplisoma can also be found here with both species sometimes being found intermingling among the fallen branches in the tannin-stained water. Both have white or tan bodies with a black mask over the eyes with the main difference between the two being the shape of the large black spot that runs from their lateral line above the pectoral fin into the dorsal fin. The black diamond Hoplisoma has a diamond shaped spot, while the black saddled Hoplisoma has a more rounded, almost semi-circle shape. Black saddled Hoplisomas were previously classified as Corydoras sp. CW051, but were reclassified as Hoplisoma sp. CW051 upon publication of a phylogenomic analysis in 2024 that reclassified many species in the Corydoradinae subfamily. Corydoradinae are small, peaceful catfish that are active shoalers and will stay near conspecifics, making for a lovely sight. They feed by searching through sand with their barbels, making such a substrate necessary for their long-term health . Gravel substrates tend to be abrasive and damage the barbels, leading to infections and an inability to find food. While these friendly catfish are willing to swim with other species of Corydoradinae different from their own, this does not provide the same social need as being kept with members of their own species. Because of this, it is highly recommended to keep at least six of each species of Corydoradinae present in the aquarium and only mix species if one has the space to keep at least six of each. Corydoradinae are often looked at as "scavengers," but they should be treated in a similar fashion as the rest of your fish. They are omnivores and require a mixed diet. Sinking prepared foods are readily accepted, as are frozen and live foods such as brine shrimp, blackworms, and bloodworms.

Remarks: The longtail spatula whiptail is a very large, uncommon Loricariid mainly found in the Rio Orteguasa in Columbia. However, there are reports of it also being found in the Rio Napo in both Ecuador and Peru. Within both rivers, they inhabit spaces with very clear, fast-flowing waters rich in dissolved oxygen and almost devoid of pollutants such as nitrates. These conditions should be simulated within the aquarium with plenty of aeration and small, frequent water changes to ensure the longtail spatula whiptail remains healthy. While this species has fairly mundane coloration of a light brown or tan body with about 4 wide, dark brown bands down the tail and one behind the head, its size, shape, and behavior are very attractive. Like all whiptails, its body is fairly thin and flat but elongated resulting in a very unique shape. Even more interesting is that it possesses very long streamers extending from the tips of its caudal fin that looks very graceful as it swims about the tank. Unlike many of its cousins, the longtail spatula whiptail is not very shy and will happily swim about the tank during the day as long as it is maintained in the appropriate conditions. This active behavior pair with its territorial habits toward conspecifics makes it where this fish should be maintained in a tank with a length of at least 5 ft to give it ample swimming space. A standard 125 gallon typically will be sufficient for 2-3 of these whiptails. All of this makes this species perfect for those looking for a very large whiptail that won't just hide away all day.

Remarks: The red striped eartheater is a rare, close relative of Geophagus sveni and looks very similar to them as well as a number of other species of Geophagus . This has resulted in them frequently getting misconstrued with one another. According to taxonomic literature, adult specimens can be identified by having four, faint, vertical, parallel bars on the body when stressed or deceased. Hobbyists have also claimed they can be identified by these fish having stripes rather than spots in their caudal fin, no dark markings on the head, and the black spot on the lateral line always being present even if just faintly. Similar to G. sveni , the red striped eartheater is a slow grower but makes it worth the wait in the end. As an adult and if in the right conditions, they display bright blue and red horizontal stripes across their bodies accented by a golden sheen. This combined with the elegant streamers the males develop results in an absolutely beautiful looking fish. Like all Geophagus , red striped eartheaters require a sandy substrate due to their earth-eating habits. They sift mouthfuls of sand through their gills, pulling out bits of food to eat. Gravel presents a very high probability of choking or refusing to eat. Also like their close relatives, these fish do best in groups of 4 or more but can also do well in single male and female pairs. Due to their large size, adult red striped eartheaters should be kept in an aquarium that is at least 90 gallons if kept as a single, breeding pair, but 125 gallons or more is needed if they are to be kept with other fish. When spawning, they can become territorial as they are protective parents and they have a good chance of swallowing tank mates that can fit in their mouths. These behaviors should be taken into consideration when planning a tank for these wonderful fish. We imported these fish as Geophagus surinamensis but it is very rare to actually get the true species due to how uncommon they are and the fact they look similar to many other species of Geophagus when young and even as adults. Due to this, we do not feel it is right to guarantee these are for sure Geophagus surinamensis at their current size. Therefore, there is NO GUARANTEE these are this exact species.

Remarks: The blue black-banded tetra ( Hyphessobrycon melanostichos ) is fairly new to the hobby, having been described back in 2006 when it was discovered in the Rio Doze de Outubro which is a part of the Rio Tapajos basin. Here, it darts in the clear waters with fairly swift currents to fight against. They are very similar in appearance to the blue ribbon tetra, Hyphessobrycon sp. , with both species displaying bright blue coloration on the top half of their bodies above a thick, black, horizontal band that extends from the back of the eye to the middle of the caudal fin. What sets the blue black-banded tetra apart is its more stream-lined appearance and the striking red coloration mostly present in courting or sparring males. This mix of blue and red looks excellent against a backdrop of green plants. This species is rather territorial with males constantly vying for dominance, and is very active. To have the most success, their habitat of fast-flowing, clear, highly oxygenated, streams should be replicated with plenty of horizontal space to swim and set up territories. These conditions are also usually preferred by most small, South American catfish , so they would be good options for tank mates. Blue black-banded tetra show behavior similar to that of barbs with them being very nippy even in regards to larger tankmates if they are not provided enough space and are not kept in large groups. Keep these fish in groups of 10 or more and tank mates with long fins should be avoided. If provided with these conditions, one will be rewarded with a truly stunning, rare fish and a more peaceful attitude.

Remarks: If you are looking for an extremely rare and almost never seen in the hobby species of tetra, Hyphessobrycon vinaceus is it. While it was described back in the early 2000s, it is brand new to the hobby. Because of this, it has yet to be given a common name and there is not much information in regards to their care. For species like this, it is best to replicate their natural habitat to have the best chance at success and maybe even get them to spawn. Hyphessobrycon vinaceus come from the Rio Pardo drainage in Brazil, specifically the Rio São João. The area of collection was specifically in a portion of rapids directly below a waterfall with a sandy bottom. From this, it can be concluded this species requires, clear, highly oxygenated water with a good amount of current. When healthy and mature, this species displays a body that varies from silver, to gold, to green and a black, horizontal bar along the lateral line that starts at the base of the caudal fin and fades up into the middle of the body. When mature and in the right conditions, below that bar and on the back half of the fish is a vibrant red patch of color and just behind the eye on the gill plate is a black spot preceded by a spot of green iridescence. Between this beautiful coloration and its rarity, this fish is a must have for tetra collectors.

Remarks: The Sertanejo pleco is a slightly smaller relative of the common pleco that comes from the Rio Umbuzeiro in Brazil. Its habitat consists of clear, fast flowing, highly oxygenated streams and rapids containing soft sand and rounded stones. As they were only described back in 2017, they are still fairly new to the hobby. Like their common cousins, this pleco is rather hardy and accommodating of a fairly broad range of water parameters compared to most Loricariidae . What makes it even better, however, is its much more attractive pattern. When young, this fish is black with many large, yellow spots while older specimens take on a more bronze or copper color with smaller but more numerous spots. This makes young Sertanejo plecos look very similar to snowball plecos with the most obvious difference between the two being their dentition. Being a voracious herbivore, they can make a great candidate for algae maintenance in cooler South American community tanks.

Remarks: A perfect starter fish! Platies are peaceful community fish that reproduce with ease. They are livebearers, meaning the females release live fry rather than laying eggs. It is recommended to keep more females than males, as males can easily harass females with relentless attempts to reproduce, leading to stress in the females. Red calico platies have reddish-orange bodies with black dots and patches.

Remarks: The red leporinus is native to Bahia, Brazil, and is rare within the hobby. Therefore, not much is known about it, especially in regards to care. It is likely they behave similar to other species of leporinus in that they can be nippy toward fish with long fins and are best kept in groups of 5 or more. Red leporinus have silver or gold bodies with three black spots along their lateral line, a larger one under the dorsal fin, a mid-sized one under the adipose fin, and then the smallest one right at the base of the caudal fin. When in the right conditions, their fins are a nice reddish-orange color that stands out nicely against a black background.

Remarks: The jewel spotted doradid, also known as the snoring catfish, is a large, rare catfish endemic to the Rio Jequitinhonha and Rio Pardo in Brazil. This rarity can be owed in part to the fact that these waters remain mostly untouched by the ornamental trade. Only once Brazilian exporter Hudson Crizanto Gonçalves began breeding these fish did they start to really appear in the trade. An interesting thing to note about them as well is that they are the only ones in their genus, differing from others in the Doradidae family in that it lacks retrorse thorns on their midlateral scutes. While the jewel spotted doradid doesn't have the most striking appearance as a juvenile, typically being a muted brownish-gray with a few white speckles, the adults really stand out especially against a black background. Upon maturity, these fish develop striking white or gold spots across their bodies which makes the wait absolutely worth it. While they also grow quite large, they are mostly peaceful toward non-conspecifics and anything that does not fit in their huge mouth. The jewel spotted doradid can be shy so keeping light low and providing plenty of hiding spots will encourage them to venture out more. With how rare this species is and their fantastic pattern, it is a must have for oddball catfish collectors

Remarks: The slate pleco is an uncommon, but amazing species of small Loricariid native to the Rio Jaguaribe. They have dark gray or black bodies mottled with white spots similar to that of L201 making for a nice contrast. As their genus, Pseudancistrus , entails, their body shape is similar to that of bushynose, Ancistrus , plecos in that they are rather short and stout. Unlike bushynose, their bristles are present on both males and females and are fairly short. Males and females are instead differentiated by head shape with the female's being shorter and more broad compared to that of a male. With a fairly brave and curious nature, the behavior of the slate pleco makes it all the better for aquarium life. If kept in the right conditions, you can find this species exploring every inch of the aquarium. They can prove to be a rather helpful addition to a peaceful South American community in that they are mainly herbivorous, happily feeding on any surface algae they can get to. Furthermore, unlike most Loricariids found in the hobby, they prefer warmer water and don't get very large so they pair nicely with species such as German blue rams or cardinal tetras. It should be mentioned, however, that they do not tolerate poor water quality so frequent water changes are a must to keep this fascinating pleco happy and healthy.

Remarks: The Atromaculatus cichlid ( Mesoheros atromaculatus ) is an uncommon South American cichlid native to coastal drainages in Columbia. Unlike other fish within their genus such as festaes, they are typically fairly docile for a cichlid as long as their territory is not intruded on and the fish in question isn't small enough to be swallowed. Usually they will alter the space they consider their territory, digging in the sand and rearranging objects to their liking. The Atromaculatus cichlid is best kept in male-female pairs as males tend to fight if kept in the same space. Once a pair has formed, they will spawn on a flat surface with the female doing most of the guarding of eggs and fry. With how uncommon they are within the hobby, we encourage anyone getting these fish to attempt to breed them. Upon maturity and if in the right conditions, these fish get bright yellow coloration on their gill plates and sometimes along their backs. Their fins also gain a yellow or orange color, some even getting an iridescent blue spot in the dorsal fin as well, that looks nice against their silver bodies and black markings. Dominant males when in breeding dress will display a nice red belly with that coloration rising up toward the lateral line. With such coloration and a somewhat more docile personality, If given enough territory, Atromaculatus cichlids can be excellent additions to a large, South American cichlid tank or in a species only tank.

Remarks: The Parnaibae sailfin pleco is possibly one of the most attractively patterned sailfin plecos known to the hobby. Their dark brown or black bodies and fins are covered in a mottled pattern of gold or tan striations and spots. Furthermore, they have endearing little "horns" on their nose and a very tall dorsal fin as is typical of their genus. This pleco is a fairly large species, sometimes reaching 15 inches in length, but most in captivity top out at around 12". In the wild, the Parnaibae sailfin pleco is only found in the Rio Parnaiba alongside the numerous other endemic species found there. Being omnivores, they will feed on anything from wood to fallen fruits, to vegetation, to insect larvae. They have proven to have quite the appetite like all sailfin plecos which results in lots of waste so frequent water changes are a must. Young specimens have a voracious appetite for algae so they can be great for cleanup in a smaller community tank until they grow large enough to go with bigger fish such as large, South American cichlids. With their thick armor and large size, they can protect themselves from these bigger, more boisterous fish.

Remarks: Chalinochromi s sp. "Bifrenatus" is a mid-sized Tanganyikan cichlid found hiding in rock piles and away from the sandy areas of the lake. Like other Chalinochromis sp., they have bridle-like markings on the face (chalina in Greek translates to bridle). What sets them apart from other species is that the markings continue down the length of their body in the form of two horizontal stripes along their lateral line rather than a series of dots. When in breeding dress, males will sometimes display striking blue coloration on the edges of their fins and a yellow body in order to catch the female's attention. Chalinochromis sp. "Bifrenatus" can be spawned by keeping a small group of fish until they pair off. Once a pair is formed, they will defend a spawning site, such as a flower pot or cave, and lay 40-60 eggs.

Remarks: Painted swordtails are beautiful variety of swordtail that sport a red or orange body with variable black spots and patches that make it look like it were splattered with black paint. This black color tends to be more concentrated toward the back end of the fish but sometimes you can get an individual that has a more scattered pattern placement. The result is that no two fish look the same adding a unique touch to an already unique fish. Swordtails are peaceful community fish that reproduce with ease. They are livebearers, meaning the females release live fry rather than laying eggs. It is recommended to keep more females than males, as males can easily harass females with relentless attempts to reproduce, leading to stress in the females. Dominant males will begin developing swords and a modified anal fin, called a gonopodium, around 1-1.5" in length. However, it is not uncommon for less dominant males to maintain the physical appearance of a female until much later in life (even as large as 4"!) Some have also reported the strange phenomenon of these fish occasionally changing gender with it typically occurring with older, large females becoming male with mixed results in regards to them remaining fertile.

Remarks: The Colombian green severums ( Heros efasciatus ) we currently offer are captive-bred offspring of wild-caught parents collected from the upper Rio Negro near San Felipe, along the Colombia–Venezuela border. While they are more adaptable and forgiving than wild-caught specimens, they retain the genetics, coloration, and natural characteristics of their wild lineage. Because they have not been subjected to generations of selective breeding or hybridization, these fish represent a pure bloodline with excellent genetic diversity compared to many severums commonly found in the aquarium hobby. Severums have been a staple of the aquarium hobby thanks to their impressive size, attractive coloration, and generally peaceful temperament. They are large enough to serve as a stunning centerpiece fish without requiring the enormous aquariums that many larger cichlids demand. While typically peaceful, they can become territorial when spawning. Very small tank mates may be viewed as food, and most aquatic plants are unlikely to survive long, as severums are known to nibble on or uproot them. The Colombian green severum is especially striking, displaying an ever-changing blend of emerald green, turquoise blue, and reddish hues that shift depending on lighting, mood, and breeding condition. Healthy specimens may also display a series of dark vertical bars along the body, with the bar at the base of the tail extending all the way to the dorsal fin. Their vibrant reddish-orange ventral and anal fins provide a beautiful contrast, making this one of the most attractive naturally occurring severum varieties available. Originating from the blackwater habitats of the upper Rio Negro, these F1 fish are particularly desirable for aquarists seeking a geographically authentic bloodline with the beauty, coloration, and adaptability of captive-bred fish.

listings.description: Remarks: Cryptocoryne wendtii "Tropica" is a variant of the ever popular Cryptocoryne wendtii. There is great variation in the colors that this plant can display, sometimes being mostly green, sometimes red, and even in rare cases, pink like the flamingo variant. Some do note that it tends to display a more obvious pattern of stripes or spots on its leaves compared to other variants. A lot of how this plant will appear depends on the conditions it is kept in, especially in regards to quality of light and substrate. Cryptocoryne wendtii is a beautiful low to medium light plant. This is a great mid-ground plant which should do well in any planted aquarium. It is relatively undemanding if left alone and will grow into a nice clump and a max size of around 8". Y ou will receive the exact fish in the photos/video. Remarks : The starry night cichlid is possibly the most popular of the cichlids native to Madagascar within the hobby. They are known for their rich, black coloration and bright white speckles that looks like the night sky which explains where their common name originates from. This striking coloration is best brought out when this species is kept on a dark substrate under dim lighting. While these fish can be rather shy for a larger cichlid, they still can hold their against most other cichlids. They usually are very peaceful except when spawning during which the pair will claim a rather large territory space. Being piscivorous, despite their typically docile temperament, eat any fish small enough to fit in their mouths. Starry night cichlids are extremely adaptable in the wild with many different populations inhabiting a wide variety of habitats from cold, high altitude waters, to hot springs, to acidic blackwater pools, to even brackish estuaries. That being said, in captivity they do best in water parameters that are fairly neutral all around. Despite their broad range, starry night cichlids are still considered critically endangered in the wild due to habitat destruction and introduction of invasive species. There is some debate whether Paratilapia polleni and " P. bleekeri " represent two species or one, based primarily on the size and frequency of the spots. It is said Bleekeri tend to be larger and have larger spots than Polleni . The most recent literature suggests that they both belong to P. polleni , but we have kept the "Bleekeri" name for those who collect the various types.

Remarks: Xenotilapia sp. "Kilesa" are a very rare species of Tanganyikan cichlid found on the western side of the lake. They aren't a very large species, with a long face used for sifting sand and a cigar-shaped body, they patrol the sandy bottom. While they are omnivores, they lean more toward being carnivores so they feed mostly on meaty foods such as tiny crustaceans and worms. Juveniles and females are silver in color while mature males show much more fantastic coloration. If in the right conditions, males display metallic blue scales on their bodies, an iridescent green sheen on their faces, yellow lips, black pectoral and anal fins, and a blue dorsal fin dotted with yellow spots. This coloration is absolutely beautiful and pairs well with the fascinating displays males put on to get the attention of females. In the aquarium, Xenotilapia sp. "Kilesa" are not the easiest Tanganyikan to care for. They do not tolerate poor water quality at all, are very skittish, and require a lot more space than one would expect such a small species would require. This is because males command large territories as they build multiple spawning pits that can span 2 feet in diameter. A tank with a footprint of at least 48" by 18," equivalent to that of a standard 75 gallon, should be considered the minimum. Xenotilapia sp. "Kilesa" also do best when kept in groups of 6 or more, preferably in a ratio of 2 males to 4 females. While males can be pretty feisty, their fights rarely become physical and they usually ignore other species that do not dwell on the bottom like they do. This makes them excellent tank mates for Cyprichromis species, though their interesting behaviors and eye-catching colors also make them a great choice for a species only tank. Due to the sensitive nature of these fish, DOA claims will only be honored if the fish are in their sealed bags. No exceptions will be made for losses that occur after opening the bags.

Remarks : Heckel discus ( Symphysodon discus ) are one of the most colorful, challenging to keep, and oldest known wild discus species. They display vibrant yellows, oranges, greens, and blues that vary in amount and pattern depending on the exact locality they are sourced from. Typically, Heckel discus are identified by the particularly wide and dark band that runs down the center of their body that is particularly round even for a discus. The Nhamunda blue face Heckel discus is a highly sought after locality as they display some of the most electric blue coloration found in any wild discus with most of it concentrated toward their heads. For some, this color is so rich it covers up the orange striping near the face. This combined with them being found in the Rio Nhamunda is where they get their common name. Care should be taken in regards to water parameters as these discus are wild and much less tolerant of incorrect water parameters. For the best chance at being successful, keep them in very soft, acidic, warm water and perform frequent water changes. Discus are often referred to as the king of aquarium fish. This nickname arose from the sheer beauty of these fish along with their reputation for being difficult to care for making those who keep them successfully revered within the hobby. It being difficult to keep discus was an opinion developed when majority of specimens available were wild caught. With most now being captive bred and even line bred to produce many different color variants such as turquoise and pigeon blood, they are much more hardy. That being said, discus still require very clean, soft, acidic water with little to no nitrates and warm temperatures. These peaceful cichlids tend to be timid, especially when it comes to feeding, so they shouldn't be kept with overly boisterous or aggressive fish. Typically their mouths are very small, but once they reach adulthood they are capable of swallowing very tiny fish so this should also be considered when choosing tankmates. If attempting to breed discus, lots of vertical surfaces should be provided for them to lay their eggs on and it should be noted they can become territorial when spawning. Once the fry hatch and are free-swimming, both parents show an incredible form of parental care in which they feed their fry by allowing them to eat their slime coat. This behavior is an amazing sight and makes breeding discus very enjoyable.

Remarks: G eophagus altifrons is a very uncommon, yet highly sought after species of eartheater. This is due in part to their fantastic coloration with healthy adult specimens displaying orange/red fins dotted with blue and bodies covered in electric blue scales. These scales practically glow especially in tannin-stained water. Both males and females can grow impressively long trailers especially on their ventral fins, but they do tend to get a bit longer on males. The native range of Geophagus altifrons spans across many tributaries in the middle to lower Amazon basin and crosses over with many other species of Geophagus . This crossing of native ranges along with how similar they are to other species has resulted in many fish being misidentified as Geophagus altifrons . It is extremely difficult if not impossible to tell them apart from some other species when they are juveniles, but adults do show some defining features. When looking to confirm if a fish is truly a Geophagus altifrons , some features to look for are as follows: an absence of vertical stress bars no matter the condition of the fish, lack of a dark spot on the gill plate, and the most defining feature of either a very small dark spot on the middle of the body only two scales in width or a complete absence of the spot entirely. Like all Geophagus , Geophagus altifrons require a sandy substrate due to their earth-eating habits. They sift mouthfuls of sand through their gills, pulling out bits of food to eat. Gravel presents a very high probability of choking or refusing to eat. Also like their close relatives, these fish do best in groups of 4 or more but can also do well in single male and female pairs. Due to their large size, adult Geophagus altifrons should be kept in an aquarium that is at least 90 gallons if kept as a single, breeding pair, but 125 gallons or more is needed if they are to be kept with other fish. When spawning, they can become territorial as they are protective parents and they have a good chance of swallowing tank mates that can fit in their mouths. These behaviors should be taken into consideration when planning a tank for these wonderful fish.

Remarks: The red Kachese tropheus is an uncommon locality of Tropheus that can be found near Cape Kachese along the southern coast of Lake Tanganyika. Upon maturity and when in the right conditions, these fish have beautiful coloration. The top half of their bodies and their faces are dark gray or black making their golden bellies, reddish-orange fins occasionally flecked with blue, and blue lips really pop. These colors are more blended together and dull in juveniles but the wait for them to grow into their true potential is worth it as it is with all T ropheus . Tropheus are obligate herbivores, and even small amounts of protein can induce bloating conditions. They form social hierarchies and should be kept in large groups, about 10 or more, to spread out any aggression. Tropheus tend to be more peaceful toward non-conspecific species so they can do well in a large Tanganyikan community tank.

Remarks: Fairy moss, also known as mosquito fern, is a fascinating species of floating plant native to the Western United States where it can be found in areas of stagnant water. It grows in a manner similar to duckweed where smaller parts of the plant will break off as it grows to become a new plant. Fairy moss is typically a vibrant green, but certain conditions such as high quality light and low nitrate levels can result in it turning a beautiful pink or red color. To remain healthy within the aquarium, this plant shouldn't be kept in areas of high flow and should be provided with medium to high light. As long as these conditions are met, this small, floating plant can be a great addition to both small and large aquariums or ponds. Photos show one portion which is approximately 2 oz. If you are only ordering plants, you are eligible for a shipping rate of $19.99. Remarks: Anubias congensis is perfect for any planted aquarium. It is relatively undemanding and is a low light plant native to Africa. What makes this anubias unique is that its leaves are fairly long and pointed compared to more common anubias such as nana. Their leaves also tend to reach up toward the surface of the tank rather than lay flat. Anubias spp. should be tied to a rock, driftwood, or other decor, not planted into the substrate. If the rhizome, the thick main stem, is buried, it will likely rot away from being smothered. It will eventually grab and propagate itself to whatever it's tied to or wedged into using its strong roots. You will receive a medium sized plant with 4-6 leaves. Remarks: Kohaku koi swordtails possess a patch of reddish-orange on their head and on their tail with a silvery-white body in-between. "Kohaku" means "amber" in Japanese which is fitting for such an intensely colored fish. Their vibrant reddish-orange patches and high contrast results in a striking fish that stands out well in just about any aquarium. Swordtails are peaceful community fish that reproduce with ease. They are livebearers, meaning the females release live fry rather than laying eggs. It is recommended to keep more females than males, as males can easily harass females with relentless attempts to reproduce, leading to stress in the females. Dominant males will begin developing swords and a modified anal fin, called a gonopodium, around 1-1.5" in length. However, it is not uncommon for less dominant males to maintain the physical appearance of a female until much later in life (even as large as 4"!) Some have also reported the strange phenomenon of these fish occasionally changing gender with it typically occurring with older, large females becoming male with mixed results in regards to them remaining fertile.

listings.commonName: L137 Blue Eyed Red Fin Pleco
listings.description: Remarks: The L137 blue eyed red fin pleco is a beautiful and uncommon species of Hypostomus from Brazil. Like others in the same genus, they have high backs, tall dorsal fins, and spoon-shaped teeth that aid them in grazing on algae and plant matter. The color of this species is variable with their bodies ranging from a soft gray to a warm brown, accented by their fins that can be anywhere from a dark brownish-red to a burnt orange. Sometimes these fins even have spots. These fins along with their striking blue eyes give them their common name. The second half of their scientific name, soniae , was given in honor of loricariid expert, Sonia Fisch-Muller who took part in its discovery. In the aquarium, the L137 blue eyed red fin pleco can be a great choice for an algae-eater to live alongside large, South American cichlids. They have a voracious appetite and can make quick work of many different species of algae but still need to have their diets supplemented with wood, fresh vegetables, and high-quality pellets. This appetite coincides with a high metabolism so frequent water changes are necessary to manage their high waste output. These plecos can be rather territorial and boisterous so it is best not to house them with other loricariids unless they are in a very large system. This behavior, however makes them very good at handling cichlids with similar demeanors so they pair well with cichlids such as Salvin's cichlids and large severums.

Remarks: The L031 peppermint pleco is an elegant loricariid from the Rio Xingu in Brazil. They live in areas with strong currents and rocky bottoms where they hide in the cracks between rocks. Most would suspect that conditions like this would result in the L031 peppermint pleco preferring cooler water, but quite the opposite is true as they prefer warmer temperatures compared to other loricariids. They do, however, still require very pristine water with a high oxygen content so heavy aeration and frequent water changes are a must. If cared for properly, this medium sized pleco can be a dazzling addition to the aquarium. Their dark brown to jet black bodies and fins look like the night sky with the white speckles that cover them. Typically these spots start out larger while the fish is younger and decrease in size but increase in abundance as they age. While they will eat algae, L031 peppermint plecos are omnivores and require a varied diet of both vegetarian and carnivorous foods to remain healthy. Providing plenty of hiding spaces will make this species feel safe enough to venture out more for you to see their beautiful patterns and fascinating behavior.

Remarks: The Xingu black neon tetra is new to the hobby and rarely imported. As their common name suggests, they are visually similar to the more common black neon tetra, Hyphessobrycon herbertaxelrodi , but they have a lot of differences. Unlike the regular black neon tetra that can be found in calmer waters in the more southern regions of South America, the Xingu black neon are found in the extreme rapids of the more northern Rio Xingu in Brazil. This species also remains a bit smaller and shows more color. Rather than just displaying the typical black and tan color with a blue stripe along the lateral line, they also have bright yellow belly when healthy. The contrast between the yellow and the blue looks beautiful and unique in the aquarium especially among green plants. As these rare tetras come from areas of high flow, it is important that they are provided plenty of aeration in the aquarium to remain healthy. Soft, clean, acidic water is also necessary. Like most tetras, Xingu black neon tetras are highly social and will become stressed if not maintained in a group of at least 6 fish with 10 or more being ideal. The larger the school, the more secure they will feel making them more likely to venture out where you can view them actively darting about the tank.

Remarks: The Tuira's whiptail is an uncommon species of whiptail not often imported into the United States. In the wild, they are actually not found in the Rio Tuira, but rather in the fast flowing section of the Rio Xingu where they get their other common name, the marbled Xingu whiptail. The Tuira part of their common name actually comes from the fish being named after a Kayapo woman that was considered a symbol of résistance in regards to hydroelectric dams being built on the Rio Xingu. Another fascinating thing to note about this species is that it ended a 70 year long time-frame in which no new species in the Spatuloricaria had been described once it was first recorded in 2014. As they are a rapids-dwelling species, Tuira's whiptails require pristine water and high levels of dissolved oxygen to thrive. They are a smaller whiptail with the males actually being the smallest of their genus, typically maxing out at 5-6" in length. Another unique aspect is that they are the only members of their genus where the females grow larger than the males, typically growing to 6-7" in length. This makes them a good choice for medium sized aquariums as they do not require quite as much spaces as other, larger whiptail species. The Tuira's whiptail can be a great choice if you are looking for an omnivorous whiptail that won't be too much competition for species like Otocinclus catfish as they tend to not care much for algae. Instead, they should be provided a varied diet consisting of both meaty and vegetable based foods. If all their needs are met, these whiptails can be fascinating talking point for your South American community tank.

Remarks: The L114 Demini leopard cactus pleco is a massive and beautiful species of Loricariid popular among those with tanks based around monster South American fish. Their common name lends credence to their yellow or tan bodies covered in black leopard spots as well as the sharp armor covering their bodies making them very prickly. This armor is made up of pointed structures called odontodes that help the pleco wedge itself in hiding spaces as well as discourage predators from attempting to eat it. Adding to their unique look, the L114 Demini leopard cactus pleco has a brilliant caudal fin and edge to their dorsal fin showing coloration that ranges from a vibrant gold to a rich orange. There are actually a few different color variations and localities of this species, each being referred to by a specific L number. This particular locality is known from the Rio Demini and is identified by how the spots on their heads are about the same size as the spots on their bodies. Within their natural range, they inhabit acidic, soft, warm, blackwater areas filled with driftwood. To have the most success with keeping them in captivity, these conditions should be replicated while also providing plenty of aeration as is needed by all Loricariids. As beautiful as these catfish are, they are not the easiest to care for. L114 Demini leopard cactus plecos can be very aggressive with other loricariids especially if not provided ample territory space and caves. It also can be a challenge to keep up with their needs in regards to parameters as while they produce a lot of waste, they do not tolerate pollutants such as high nitrate levels. Consequentially, they require large, frequent water changes to maintain the pristine conditions they need. Their diet also must be taken into account as they are omnivorous and need a varied diet to remain healthy. Repashy products can be a great option for feeding them. While typically docile toward non-conspecifics, L114 Demini leopard cactus plecos have been reported eating fish that fit in their mouths so care should be taken when choosing tank mates. Larger characins such as chalceus and headstanders can be good options for tank mates that can't be swallowed and won't take away from the beauty of this amazing catfish.

Remarks: The crystal red tetra is a beautiful gem of a nano fish native to the Rio Araguaia in Brazil. In the wild, their intensely bright red coloration helps them blend into the reddish-brown water of tannin-stained tributaries. Mature, healthy specimens in captivity display this brilliant red color more than any other tetra when in the hobby which makes them look absolutely incredible when kept among green plants. Most will note this species bears a striking resemblance to young specimens of the serpae tetra, but they can be told apart by the fact the crystal red tetra has a smaller black spot on the dorsal fin and that it has white tips on its fins. As it was only described in the past few years, is rarely imported, and is very difficult to spawn for a tetra, they are fairly rare within the hobby. Housing the crystal red tetra in a heavily planted tank will make these shy fish feel brave enough to come out more readily. Their shy nature and small size does mean care should be taken when choosing tankmates, ensuring the other species they are housed with are not aggressive or large enough to swallow them. If provided the right conditions, these little fish add plenty of movement to the tank. They will dart around exploring every corner of the tank and performing display dances as males compete for females. If you are looking to add a splash of red to your tank, these rare little tetras can be an excellent choice. The scientific name for the crystal red tetra used to be Hyphessobrycon haraldschultzi . However, it was reclassified as Megalamphodus haraldschultzi after the completion of an intensive phylogenic study on species in the family Characidae. Many other species were reclassified as well as a result of this study which can be read here: https://academic.oup.com/zoolinnean/article-abstract/202/1/zlae101/7748269 The following article also provides a good breakdown of the results of the study and does not have a paywall: https://aquainfo.org/the-end-of-the-characidae-family-as-we-know-it/

Remarks: The zebra gold mbuna is a brightly colored, medium-sized mbuna. Males are a golden yellow with black ventral fins and light blue details on their other fins. Their face and belly are black to blue. Females are gray to silver and occasionally have a few light blue markings. These fish are mainly herbivorous, feeding on algae and plankton in the wild. Zebra gold mbunas are aggressive toward similar looking species but are generally non-combative toward non-conspecifics making them a good species to keep alongside blue colored mbuna.

Remarks: Scarlet badis are a gem of a nano fish with their bright red bodies and fins accented by electric blue stripes and edges. The amount of color packed into such a tiny fish is truly impressive. Males use this bright color to court females that are notably duller, usually being mostly tan. As territorial battles amongst these tiny fish can get very violent, sometimes less dominant males will pretend to be females by also displaying muted colors so they are less likely to be attacked. In the wild, these fish can be found in shallow, blackwater pools and streams in India. The water in these pools is very warm, mildly acidic, soft, and full of botanicals such as fallen leaves and seed pods. These botanicals provide a habitat that supports a wide variety of tiny worms and crustaceans that scarlet badis feed on. While tiny, these little fish are voracious in their hunting of these small organisms so they are often referred to as micro predators. This makes them a poor choice to keep alongside cherry shrimp as they will hunt down baby shrimplets and if hungry and bold enough, occasionally take down full grown shrimp! Since they can be rather picky and have very fast metabolisms, scarlet badis should be fed small, live foods such as moina or baby brine shrimp at least daily if not multiple times a day. Care should also be taken when choosing tankmates as most fish will either attempt to eat the scarlet badis or will frighten it as they are very timid. Most do best when kept as pairs in a species-only tank. One can be kept in a 5 gallon, while a pair or more will require a 10 gallon or larger. Due to their need for live foods and cryptic nature, they are not a good beginner fish. However, for the more experienced keeper, they are well worth the effort once they begin to show their intense colors and inquisitive personalities.

Remarks: A perfect starter fish! Mollies are peaceful community fish that reproduce with ease. They are livebearers, meaning the females release live fry rather than laying eggs. It is recommended to keep more females than males, as males can easily harass females with relentless attempts to reproduce, leading to stress in the females. Fish with long fins such as guppies should be avoided as mollies tend to be fin-nippers. This line of mollies are absolutely beautiful and unique with their platinum white bodies and black spots similar to the dalmatian breed of dog. They stand out in just about any tank, but especially against a backdrop of green plants and driftwood. Using a dark substrate as well will really make their elegant color pop!

Remarks: A perfect starter fish! Guppies are peaceful community fish that reproduce with ease. They are livebearers, meaning the females release live fry rather than laying eggs. It is recommended to keep more females than males, as males can easily harass females with relentless attempts to reproduce, leading to stress in the females. This line of guppies are absolutely breath-taking with their stark white bodies that seem to glow with how pure white the majority of their bodies and fins are resulting in an elegant look. For most strains, males are very colorful while the females remain a gray or silver color. However, there are some exceptions to this rule so sexing these fish is best done by looking at the anal fin. The females will have short, rounded triangle shaped anal fins with a black spot on the body directly above it, these are her female reproductive organs. Males will have long, thin, pointed anal fins that form his male reproductive organs called the gonopodium.

It is recommended to keep more females than males, as males can easily harass females with relentless attempts to reproduce, leading to stress in the females. This line of guppies were originally produced in Israel which has gained a reputation for producing some of the most beautiful and healthy modern guppy lines. It should be noted that the original lines likely were produced by hybridizing guppies and endlers so they are most likely not a pure species but this goes for most modern strains. Now we breed them here on site to be able to offer these fish to fishkeepers in the United States. They stand out in just about any aquarium with their bodies being a bright gold and their lyretails a striking blue. For most strains, males are very colorful while the females remain a gray or silver color. However, there are some exceptions to this rule so sexing these fish is best done by looking at the anal fin. Black eye koi guppies display a form of partial albinism with their bodies lacking black pigment but still having black eyes instead of pink. They typically have white/platinum bodies and bright orange heads, tails, and fins. As these beautiful fish have pigment in their eyes, they are not as sensitive to light compared to complete albinos. For most strains, males are very colorful while the females remain a gray or silver color. However, there are some exceptions to this rule so sexing these fish is best done by looking at the anal fin. The females will have short, rounded triangle shaped anal fins with a black spot on the body directly above it, these are her female reproductive organs. Males will have long, thin, pointed anal fins that form his male reproductive organs called the gonopodium.
