Betta coccina is one of the most spectacular wild Betta species available, prized for its brilliant scarlet coloration, peaceful demeanor, and fascinating natural behavior. When provided with soft, acidic blackwater conditions and a carefully aquascaped environment, the Scarlet Betta becomes a breathtaking centerpiece for dedicated Southeast Asian biotope and blackwater aquariums.

Orange Tiger Otocinclus, Hypoptopoma sp. “Peru”, is an undescribed South American loricariid catfish native to the upper Amazon Basin of Peru. It is believed to originate from tributaries associated with the Río Ucayali drainage, where it inhabits slow to moderately flowing streams with abundant submerged vegetation, driftwood, and biofilm-covered surfaces. These habitats are typically warm, well oxygenated, and rich in algae and microorganisms that support constant grazing. Adult Orange Tiger Otocinclus typically reaches about 2 to 2.5 inches in length. The body is elongated and noticeably flatter than that of true Otocinclus, with a broad, wedge-shaped head and eyes positioned high on the skull. This unique profile allows the fish to cling tightly to leaves, wood, and other surfaces while grazing. Coloration is exceptional, featuring a vibrant orange to golden base crossed by bold black tiger-like bands and irregular markings that extend across the body and fins. The striking pattern, combined with the fish’s unusual body shape, makes it one of the most distinctive algae-eating catfish available in the aquarium hobby. A tank of at least 20 gallons is recommended for a proper group, though larger aquariums provide greater stability and more natural grazing opportunities. Orange Tiger Otocinclus are social fish and should be maintained in groups of six or more to encourage natural behavior and reduce stress. The aquarium should include abundant driftwood, broad-leaved plants, smooth stones, and mature surfaces rich in biofilm. Moderate water movement and excellent oxygenation are strongly recommended. Water conditions should remain exceptionally clean and stable. Temperatures between 72 and 79 degrees Fahrenheit are appropriate, with a pH range of roughly 6.0 to 7.5 and soft to moderately soft water preferred. This species is sensitive to deteriorating water quality and should only be introduced into mature, well-established aquariums with excellent filtration and consistently low nitrate levels. Feeding Orange Tiger Otocinclus requires more than naturally occurring algae. In the wild they graze continuously on biofilm, soft algae, diatoms, and the microorganisms growing on submerged surfaces. In the aquarium they should be provided with mature biofilm along with algae wafers, spirulina-based foods, Repashy-style gel foods, blanched vegetables such as zucchini and spinach, and other herbivore diets. Newly established aquariums rarely produce enough natural food to sustain this species on algae alone. Temperament is exceptionally peaceful and community-friendly. Orange Tiger Otocinclus coexist well with small tetras, rasboras, pencilfish, Corydoras, dwarf cichlids, shrimp, and other gentle community fish. They spend most of their day methodically grazing surfaces and rarely show aggression toward either tankmates or one another. Breeding has not yet been reliably documented in captivity, and much of the species’ natural history remains unknown due to its undescribed status. Most specimens currently available in the aquarium trade are wild collected. Hypoptopoma sp. “Peru” is one of the most spectacular algae-grazing catfish to enter the aquarium hobby in recent years. Its brilliant orange and black tiger pattern, unusual body shape, peaceful temperament, and constant grazing behavior make the Orange Tiger Otocinclus an outstanding addition to mature planted aquariums and specialized South American community setups.

Agassiz's Corydoras, Corydoras agassizii, is a South American armored catfish native to the Amazon Basin, with a natural distribution that includes Peru, Colombia, Brazil, and neighboring regions. It inhabits slow-moving rivers, forest streams, floodplain lakes, and flooded forests with sandy substrates, leaf litter, and submerged wood. These habitats are typically warm, soft, slightly acidic, and rich in organic material, providing excellent conditions for bottom-dwelling fish. Adult Agassiz's Corydoras typically reaches about 2.5 to 3 inches in length. The body is elongated and streamlined with a pale silver to creamy white base coloration. A bold black stripe runs from the tip of the snout through the eye and along the upper flank to the base of the tail, while the back and upper sides are decorated with irregular black blotches and marbled markings that create an attractive reticulated pattern. The dorsal fin usually carries a prominent black patch, and the caudal fin is marked with rows of dark spots or bars. This striking combination of facial stripe, mottled body, and patterned fins makes Corydoras agassizii one of the most recognizable and attractive Corydoras species. A tank of at least 20 gallons is recommended for a proper group. Agassiz's Corydoras are highly social and should be maintained in groups of six or more to encourage natural schooling behavior and reduce stress. A fine sand substrate is strongly recommended, allowing them to sift through the bottom naturally without damaging their sensitive barbels. Driftwood, leaf litter, plants, and shaded areas help recreate their native habitat while leaving open areas for foraging. Water conditions should remain stable and clean. Temperatures between 72 and 79 degrees Fahrenheit are appropriate, with a pH range of roughly 6.0 to 7.2 and soft to moderately soft water preferred. Good oxygenation, regular water changes, and consistently low nitrate levels are important for long-term health. Feeding is straightforward. In nature, Agassiz's Corydoras feeds on insect larvae, worms, small crustaceans, and organic material sifted from the substrate. In the aquarium they readily accept quality sinking pellets, wafers, frozen foods such as bloodworms, daphnia, and brine shrimp, along with other prepared foods. They should always be target-fed rather than expected to survive on leftover food from other fish. Temperament is exceptionally peaceful. Agassiz's Corydoras is an ideal community fish and coexists well with tetras, rasboras, pencilfish, dwarf cichlids, small gouramis, and other non-aggressive species. Their active schooling behavior and constant foraging make them an engaging addition to planted and South American community aquariums. Breeding is readily achievable in captivity. Like most Corydoras, they are egg scatterers that deposit adhesive eggs on aquarium glass, plants, or other smooth surfaces. Adults provide no parental care, and eggs should be removed or protected if fry are to be raised successfully. Corydoras agassizii is a beautiful and hardy bottom-dwelling catfish that combines intricate patterning, peaceful behavior, and constant activity. Its distinctive facial stripe, marbled body, and sociable nature make Agassiz's Corydoras an outstanding choice for planted aquariums and Amazonian community setups.

Sodalis Corydoras, Corydoras sodalis, is a South American armored catfish native to the central and western Amazon Basin of Brazil and Peru. It is recorded from the Amazon River system, including the Rio Yavarí region along the Brazilian-Peruvian border and waters of Loreto, Peru. It inhabits shallow river margins, tributaries, flooded areas, and other quiet habitats with fine sand, leaf litter, submerged wood, and gentle water movement. Adult Corydoras sodalis typically reaches about 2 to 2.5 inches in length. The body has a pale cream, silvery beige, or faintly pinkish base covered with an intricate gray to dark brown network of interconnected lines and irregular markings. This reticulated pattern extends across the head, back, and sides, creating the net-like appearance responsible for the common name False Network Corydoras. The markings are finer and more interconnected across the head and become broader and less orderly along the body. The caudal fin is usually crossed by several narrow rows of dark spots or broken bars. Unlike the very similar Corydoras reticulatus, Corydoras sodalis does not have a large, clearly defined black blotch in the dorsal fin. There is also no bold stripe running from the snout to the tail. A tank of at least 20 gallons is recommended for a proper group. Sodalis Corydoras are highly social and should be maintained in groups of six or more, with larger groups encouraging greater confidence and more natural activity. Fine sand is the ideal substrate because it allows them to search for food without damaging their sensitive barbels. Driftwood, leaf litter, plants, and shaded retreats can be added while leaving open areas of sand available for group foraging. Water conditions should remain stable and clean. Temperatures between 74 and 82 degrees Fahrenheit are appropriate, with a pH between approximately 6.0 and 7.5 and soft to moderately hard water. Good filtration, regular water changes, and adequate oxygenation are important for maintaining healthy barbels, active behavior, and long-term condition. Feeding Sodalis Corydoras is straightforward. In nature they search the substrate for insect larvae, worms, small crustaceans, and other edible organic material. In the aquarium they readily accept quality sinking pellets, wafers, frozen bloodworms, daphnia, brine shrimp, and other appropriately sized foods. They should be deliberately fed and should never be expected to survive solely on scraps left by other fish. Temperament is peaceful, social, and community-friendly. Corydoras sodalis does well with tetras, pencilfish, rasboras, dwarf cichlids, peaceful gouramis, and other non-aggressive species. Aggressive fish and overly competitive bottom dwellers should be avoided, particularly if they prevent the Corydoras from reaching food. Breeding is possible in captivity and follows the typical Corydoras pattern. Females hold fertilized eggs between their pelvic fins before attaching them individually to aquarium glass, plant leaves, or other smooth surfaces. Adults provide no parental care and may consume the eggs, so the eggs should be protected or transferred if fry are to be raised. Corydoras sodalis is an attractive and somewhat uncommon Corydoras distinguished by its detailed network pattern, softly colored body, and banded tail. Its peaceful temperament, manageable size, and beautifully reticulated markings make the Sodalis Corydoras an excellent choice for planted aquariums and South American community setups.

Peruvian Festivum, Mesonauta mirificus, is a South American cichlid native to the upper Amazon Basin of Peru, where it inhabits slow-moving rivers, flooded forests, oxbow lakes, and quiet tributaries associated with the Ucayali and adjacent river systems. These habitats are typically warm, soft, and slightly acidic, with abundant submerged roots, fallen branches, aquatic vegetation, and overhanging rainforest canopy that creates shaded conditions. Adult Peruvian Festivums typically reach about 5 to 6 inches in length. The body is tall, laterally compressed, and distinctly disc-shaped, giving the fish an elegant profile that resembles a freshwater angelfish. Base coloration ranges from pale olive to golden bronze with beautiful blue-green iridescence scattered across the scales. A bold black stripe extends diagonally from the dorsal fin through the eye to the lower jaw, creating the species' unmistakable facial pattern. The dorsal, anal, and caudal fins often develop subtle blue, turquoise, and reddish highlights, while mature specimens display elongated finnage that enhances their graceful appearance. Their habit of swimming among vertical branches and plants further adds to their elegance. A tank of at least 75 gallons is recommended for a pair or small group, with larger aquariums preferred for community setups. Peruvian Festivums appreciate heavily planted aquariums with driftwood, root structures, broad-leaved plants, and open swimming space. They naturally orient themselves among vertical structures, making tall plants and branches especially beneficial. Gentle to moderate water movement is ideal. Water conditions should remain stable and clean. Temperatures between 76 and 82 degrees Fahrenheit are appropriate, with a pH range of roughly 5.5 to 7.2 and soft to moderately soft water preferred. Regular water changes, strong biological filtration, and stable water chemistry help maintain health and encourage natural behavior. Feeding is uncomplicated. In nature Mesonauta mirificus feeds on insects, small crustaceans, fruits, seeds, and other plant material that enters the water from the surrounding forest. In the aquarium they readily accept quality cichlid pellets, flakes, frozen foods such as bloodworms, mysis shrimp, and brine shrimp, along with vegetable-based foods and occasional fresh greens. A varied omnivorous diet promotes vibrant coloration and overall health. Temperament is peaceful for a cichlid of its size. Peruvian Festivums coexist well with larger tetras, peaceful Geophagus, Corydoras, peaceful catfish, and other calm South American species. They are generally non-aggressive outside of breeding, making them excellent centerpiece fish for larger Amazonian community aquariums. Breeding is readily achievable in captivity. Peruvian Festivums are substrate spawners that lay eggs on broad leaves, driftwood, or flat rocks. Both parents actively guard the eggs and fry, displaying excellent parental care until the young become free-swimming. Their attentive breeding behavior is one of the highlights of keeping the species. Mesonauta mirificus is an elegant and underrated South American cichlid that combines graceful body shape, striking facial markings, and peaceful temperament. Its ability to thrive in planted Amazonian aquariums, along with its fascinating parental care and beautiful coloration, makes the Peruvian Festivum an exceptional centerpiece species for aquarists seeking a refined and community-friendly cichlid.

Hongslo's Apistogramma, Apistogramma hongsloi, is a South American dwarf cichlid native to the upper Orinoco River Basin of Colombia and Venezuela, particularly within the Río Meta and Río Vichada drainages. It inhabits slow-moving forest streams, flooded margins, and blackwater tributaries with soft sandy bottoms, dense leaf litter, submerged roots, and fallen branches. These waters are typically warm, soft, acidic, and stained a tea-like color from decomposing vegetation. Adult males typically reach 3 to 3.5 inches in length, while females remain considerably smaller at around 2 inches. Males develop an elongated, elegant body with extended dorsal, anal, and caudal fin rays that become increasingly pronounced with age. Their base coloration ranges from silvery cream to pale gold, overlaid with brilliant pink, salmon, and reddish-orange hues that intensify across the face, chest, and flanks. Iridescent blue scales shimmer across the head and body under proper lighting, while a bold black lateral stripe and distinct shoulder spot provide striking contrast. The dorsal fin is edged in vibrant orange to crimson, often with blue highlights between the rays, and the tail displays attractive red spotting or banding. Females are much more subdued, exhibiting tan to yellow coloration with a distinct black lateral stripe and developing a brilliant yellow breeding dress accented by bold black markings when guarding eggs or fry. A tank of at least 20 gallons is recommended for a single pair, while larger aquariums can comfortably house multiple territories when carefully aquascaped. Fine sand is essential, as these cichlids naturally sift the substrate while foraging. Driftwood, leaf litter, caves, coconut shells, and dense planting help recreate their natural habitat while providing the cover necessary for breeding territories. Floating plants are also beneficial, as they diffuse lighting and help these fish display their best coloration. Water conditions should remain exceptionally clean and stable. Temperatures between 75 and 82 degrees Fahrenheit are ideal, with a pH range of approximately 5.5 to 7.0 and soft to moderately soft water preferred. While captive-bred specimens are generally adaptable, breeding success is greatest in softer, more acidic water with consistently low nitrate levels. Hongslo's Apistogramma is an opportunistic micropredator in nature, feeding on insect larvae, tiny crustaceans, worms, and other small aquatic invertebrates collected from leaf litter and the substrate. In the aquarium they readily accept quality micro pellets, frozen bloodworms, brine shrimp, mysis shrimp, daphnia, and other meaty prepared foods. A varied, protein-rich diet produces the best coloration, conditioning, and spawning success. Temperament is peaceful but territorial, particularly during breeding. They are excellent candidates for carefully planned South American community aquariums with small tetras, pencilfish, hatchetfish, Corydoras, Otocinclus, and other peaceful species that occupy different areas of the aquarium. Males will establish territories and may display aggressively toward rival males, while females become highly protective when guarding eggs and fry. Breeding is relatively straightforward and is one of the most rewarding aspects of keeping this species. Apistogramma hongsloi is a cave-spawning cichlid, with the female depositing adhesive eggs inside small caves or crevices. She remains with the eggs and fry, providing nearly all parental care while the male patrols the surrounding territory. Under favorable conditions the fry become free-swimming after about a week and readily accept newly hatched brine shrimp and other fine foods. Apistogramma hongsloi is widely regarded as one of the most beautiful dwarf cichlids in the hobby. Its vivid pink and red coloration, shimmering blue highlights, graceful finnage, and fascinating breeding behavior make it an exceptional centerpiece for planted aquariums and authentic South American biotope displays.

The Cryptocoryne wendtii, commonly known as Wendtii Crypt, is a popular and versatile freshwater plant native to Sri Lanka. Known for its hardiness, ease of care, and attractive appearance, this plant is a favorite among aquarists, especially those with low-tech setups. It thrives in a wide range of water conditions and is well-suited for beginner and experienced aquarists alike. Physically, Cryptocoryne wendtii has long, wavy leaves that can range in color from green to reddish-brown, depending on the lighting, substrate, and specific variety. The leaves grow in a rosette pattern, forming dense clusters that can reach 6 to 18 inches (15 to 45 centimeters) in height. Its variations, such as green, brown, or red Wendtii, allow aquarists to choose the one that best fits their aquascape. In the aquarium, Cryptocoryne wendtii is typically used as a midground or foreground plant, depending on the size of the tank. It grows best when planted in nutrient-rich substrate, and its roots will anchor firmly over time. Crypts are slow growers, but once established, they form lush, bushy clusters that provide excellent cover for fish and shrimp. The plant’s adaptability makes it suitable for low-light tanks, but its colors become more vibrant under medium to high lighting. Water parameters for Cryptocoryne wendtii are highly flexible. It can thrive in a pH range of 6.0 to 7.5 and temperatures between 72 to 82°F (22 to 28°C). This plant is tolerant of both soft and hard water, making it adaptable to a wide variety of aquarium conditions. However, consistent water quality is key, as Cryptocorynes are sensitive to sudden changes, which can lead to “Crypt melt,” where the leaves deteriorate. The plant usually recovers by regrowing new leaves once stability is restored. Cryptocoryne wendtii does not require CO2 injection or frequent fertilization to grow, but both can enhance its growth and coloration. In low-tech tanks, it absorbs nutrients from the substrate and benefits from root tabs. In higher-tech setups, liquid fertilizers can promote healthier and more vibrant growth. Propagation of Cryptocoryne wendtii is simple. The plant naturally produces runners that grow close to the main plant, eventually forming new plants. These can be left to create a dense carpet or separated and replanted elsewhere in the tank. Overall, Cryptocoryne wendtii is a hardy, adaptable, and visually appealing plant that adds natural beauty to any aquarium. Its low maintenance requirements, combined with its ability to thrive in a variety of conditions, make it an excellent choice for aquascapers and hobbyists of all experience levels. Whether used as a centerpiece in small tanks or as part of a lush underwater jungle, this plant will enhance the aesthetic and ecological balance of any aquatic setup.

Rainbow Emperor Tetra, Nematobrycon lacortei , is a South American characin native to the Río Calima and lower Río San Juan drainage in western Colombia. It inhabits slow-moving rainforest streams, shaded tributaries, and quiet forest creeks with soft, acidic water, abundant leaf litter, submerged roots, and fallen branches. These blackwater environments are heavily influenced by tannins from decaying vegetation, creating dimly lit conditions that enhance the species' spectacular iridescent coloration. Adult Rainbow Emperor Tetras typically reach about 2 to 2.5 inches in length. Their body is laterally compressed and elegantly proportioned, with long, flowing fins that become especially impressive in mature males. Depending on the angle of the light, the scales shimmer with brilliant shades of turquoise, emerald green, violet, gold, and lavender, giving the fish its common name. Males develop elongated dorsal, anal, and central caudal fin rays that create the distinctive trident-shaped tail characteristic of Emperor Tetras. Their eyes are equally striking, displaying vivid ruby-red irises that contrast beautifully with the metallic body coloration. Females are slightly smaller and deeper-bodied, with shorter fins, softer iridescence, and metallic blue to blue-green eyes that make them easy to distinguish from males. A tank of at least 20 gallons is recommended for a small school, although larger aquariums provide more natural behavior and allow males to display their best coloration. Rainbow Emperor Tetras should be maintained in groups of at least six, with eight or more being ideal. A densely planted aquarium with driftwood, leaf litter, floating plants, and subdued lighting closely replicates their native habitat while encouraging vibrant coloration. Dark substrates are particularly effective at making their iridescent scales stand out. Water conditions should remain stable and exceptionally clean. Temperatures between 74 and 80 degrees Fahrenheit are ideal, with a pH range of approximately 5.5 to 7.2 and soft to moderately soft water preferred. Regular water changes, excellent filtration, and consistently low nitrate levels are important for maintaining their health and coloration. In the wild, Rainbow Emperor Tetras feed on small aquatic insects, insect larvae, tiny crustaceans, and other microscopic invertebrates. In the aquarium they readily accept quality flakes and micro pellets while thriving on regular offerings of frozen or live foods such as daphnia, baby brine shrimp, cyclops, and bloodworms. A varied diet helps maximize coloration, encourages natural display behavior, and promotes long-term health. Rainbow Emperor Tetras are peaceful schooling fish that make excellent additions to South American community aquariums. They coexist well with Corydoras, pencilfish, hatchetfish, small rasboras, peaceful dwarf cichlids, and other similarly sized tetras. Males frequently engage in harmless display behavior, flaring their fins and intensifying their colors as they compete for the attention of females, providing constant activity without serious aggression. Breeding is possible in captivity under suitable conditions. They are egg scatterers that deposit adhesive eggs among fine-leaved plants or spawning mops in very soft, acidic water. Adults provide no parental care and should be removed after spawning to prevent egg predation. The fry are tiny and require infusoria or other microscopic foods before graduating to newly hatched brine shrimp. With its dazzling rainbow iridescence, graceful finnage, vivid eye coloration, and peaceful temperament, Nematobrycon lacortei is one of the most beautiful tetras available to aquarists. The Rainbow Emperor Tetra is an outstanding choice for planted aquariums and refined South American community displays, where its brilliant colors and elegant behavior quickly make it a centerpiece of the aquarium.

Crystal Red Shrimp, Caridina cf. cantonensis , is a selectively bred freshwater dwarf shrimp that originated from Bee Shrimp ( Caridina cantonensis ) native to southern China. While its wild ancestors inhabit cool, clear mountain streams with rocky bottoms, leaf litter, and abundant biofilm, the Crystal Red Shrimp itself does not occur naturally in the wild. It was first developed in Japan through selective breeding, resulting in the iconic red and white color pattern that has become one of the most sought-after ornamental shrimp varieties in the aquarium hobby. Adult Crystal Red Shrimp typically reach about 1 to 1.25 inches in length. They possess a slender, translucent body overlaid with brilliant white and deep crimson-red bands of varying width and intensity. Higher-grade specimens exhibit solid, opaque white coloration paired with vibrant, evenly distributed red markings that create striking contrast. Their graceful legs and antennae are often lightly colored to match the body pattern, and healthy individuals display a clean, glossy appearance that stands out beautifully against dark substrates and lush green plants. Numerous grading systems exist, ranging from lower-grade banded shrimp to highly prized patterns such as Hinomaru, No Entry, Mosura, and other advanced exhibition-quality forms. A mature aquarium of at least 10 gallons is recommended, although larger aquariums provide greater water stability and are considerably easier to maintain. Crystal Red Shrimp thrive in densely planted aquariums with abundant mosses, fine-leaved plants, driftwood, botanicals, and porous rock that encourage biofilm growth. Sponge filters or other shrimp-safe filtration are strongly recommended, and plenty of hiding places should be provided for newly molted shrimp and juveniles. Water quality is the single most important factor in successfully keeping Crystal Red Shrimp. Temperatures between 68 and 74 degrees Fahrenheit are ideal, with cooler water generally promoting longevity and successful breeding. They prefer a pH of approximately 5.8 to 6.8, very low carbonate hardness, and soft water with a general hardness of roughly 4 to 6 dGH. Many successful keepers utilize remineralized reverse osmosis water and active buffering substrates to maintain the stable water chemistry these shrimp require. Sudden fluctuations in water parameters should always be avoided. Crystal Red Shrimp are constant grazers that feed primarily on biofilm, algae, microorganisms, and decaying plant material. In the aquarium they readily accept high-quality shrimp foods, algae wafers, powdered fry foods, blanched vegetables, and occasional protein-rich foods offered in moderation. A mature aquarium with abundant natural biofilm is invaluable, as it provides a continuous food source between supplemental feedings. Temperament is exceptionally peaceful. Crystal Red Shrimp are best maintained in species-only aquariums or with very gentle tankmates such as small snails and other peaceful dwarf shrimp requiring identical water parameters. Most community fish, including many small tetras and rasboras, will prey on shrimplets and may stress adult shrimp. A dedicated shrimp aquarium is the best option for establishing a thriving breeding colony. Breeding is readily achievable under stable conditions. Females carry fertilized eggs beneath their abdomen for approximately three to four weeks before releasing fully formed miniature shrimp. Unlike Amano Shrimp, Crystal Red Shrimp do not require a larval stage in brackish water, allowing young shrimp to develop entirely in freshwater. Stable water quality, abundant biofilm, and minimal disturbances are key to raising large numbers of healthy juveniles. With its stunning red and white coloration, peaceful nature, and fascinating colony behavior, Caridina cf. cantonensis remains one of the most iconic freshwater shrimp in the aquarium hobby. Whether showcased in a dedicated shrimp aquarium or a carefully planned planted aquascape, the Crystal Red Shrimp rewards attentive care with vibrant color, continuous activity, and the opportunity to establish a beautiful, self-sustaining colony.

Super Crystal Red Shrimp, Caridina cf. cantonensis , is a premium selectively bred freshwater dwarf shrimp developed from the Bee Shrimp ( Caridina cantonensis ) native to southern China. While its wild ancestors inhabit cool, crystal-clear mountain streams with rocky substrates, leaf litter, and abundant biofilm, the Super Crystal Red Shrimp is an ornamental variety that does not occur naturally in the wild. Through generations of careful selective breeding, these shrimp have been refined to display exceptionally vibrant red coloration and brilliant opaque white markings, making them one of the most prized freshwater shrimp available to aquarists. Adult Super Crystal Red Shrimp typically reach about 1 to 1.25 inches in length. They possess a slender, elegant body adorned with intensely saturated crimson-red markings contrasted by brilliant snow-white bands. Unlike standard Crystal Red Shrimp, Super Crystal Reds exhibit much higher color coverage and opacity, with clean, sharply defined patterns and minimal translucency. Premium specimens often display thick white bands and rich ruby-red coloration that extends across much of the body, creating remarkable contrast. Healthy individuals have bright white legs, clear antennae, and a polished appearance that stands out dramatically against dark substrates and lush green aquatic plants. Their exceptional coloration makes them a favorite among shrimp breeders, aquascapers, and collectors alike. A mature aquarium of at least 10 gallons is recommended, although larger aquariums provide greater stability and make maintaining ideal water conditions significantly easier. Super Crystal Red Shrimp thrive in densely planted aquariums filled with mosses, fine-leaved plants, driftwood, botanicals, and porous rock that encourage natural biofilm growth. Shrimp-safe sponge filtration is highly recommended, and plenty of hiding places should be available for freshly molted shrimp and developing juveniles. Maintaining pristine water quality is essential for long-term success. Temperatures between 68 and 74 degrees Fahrenheit are ideal, with cooler water generally promoting longevity and successful reproduction. They prefer a pH of approximately 5.8 to 6.8, very low carbonate hardness, and soft water with a general hardness of roughly 4 to 6 dGH. Many experienced keepers utilize remineralized reverse osmosis water along with active buffering substrates to maintain the stable conditions these shrimp require. Sudden changes in water chemistry should always be avoided. Super Crystal Red Shrimp spend much of their day grazing on biofilm, algae, microorganisms, and decomposing plant material. In the aquarium they readily accept premium shrimp foods, algae wafers, powdered foods for shrimplets, blanched vegetables, and occasional protein-rich treats offered in moderation. A mature aquarium with abundant natural biofilm greatly contributes to their overall health and breeding success. Temperament is exceptionally peaceful. Super Crystal Red Shrimp are best maintained in dedicated shrimp aquariums or with other peaceful invertebrates that require similar water conditions. While they can coexist with a few very gentle nano fish, most community fish will prey upon young shrimp and may stress adults. A species-focused aquarium provides the greatest opportunity for colony growth and allows their vibrant coloration to be fully appreciated. Breeding is readily accomplished under stable conditions. Females carry fertilized eggs beneath their abdomen for approximately three to four weeks before releasing fully formed miniature shrimp. Unlike Amano Shrimp, there is no free-swimming larval stage, allowing the entire life cycle to occur in freshwater. Stable water parameters, abundant biofilm, and minimal disturbance will encourage steady reproduction and healthy juvenile survival. With their extraordinary red and white coloration, peaceful disposition, and fascinating colony behavior, Caridina cf. cantonensis Super Crystal Red Shrimp represent the pinnacle of Crystal Red breeding. Their exceptional contrast and refined appearance make them an outstanding centerpiece for dedicated shrimp aquariums and high-end planted aquascapes, where they reward attentive care with vibrant color, continuous activity, and thriving generations of offspring.

Red Fancy Tiger Shrimp is a selectively bred freshwater dwarf shrimp developed from Tiger Shrimp and Bee Shrimp bloodlines native to southern China. While its wild ancestors inhabit cool, crystal-clear mountain streams with rocky substrates, leaf litter, and abundant biofilm, the Red Fancy Tiger is a man-made ornamental variety created through years of careful selective breeding. Highly sought after for its intricate patterning and vivid coloration, it has become one of the most prized Caridina shrimp among aquascapers and shrimp enthusiasts. Adult Red Fancy Tiger Shrimp typically reach about 1 to 1.25 inches in length. They possess a slender, graceful body decorated with a stunning combination of brilliant white and deep crimson-red coloration overlaid by distinctive tiger striping. Unlike standard Crystal Red Shrimp, the red markings are often broken into intricate lace-like patterns, irregular bands, or fine reticulated lines that give every individual a unique appearance. High-quality specimens display thick, opaque white coverage contrasted by rich ruby-red markings with exceptional pattern definition. Their long antennae, delicate legs, and constant grazing behavior further enhance their elegant appearance, making them a true centerpiece in any freshwater shrimp aquarium. A mature aquarium of at least 10 gallons is recommended, although larger aquariums provide greater water stability and are easier to maintain. Red Fancy Tiger Shrimp thrive in densely planted aquariums with mosses, fine-leaved plants, driftwood, botanicals, and porous rock that support abundant biofilm growth. Shrimp-safe sponge filtration or other gentle filtration is highly recommended, and plenty of cover should be available for newly molted shrimp and developing juveniles. Excellent water quality is essential for long-term success. Temperatures between 68 and 74 degrees Fahrenheit are ideal, with cooler water generally promoting longevity and breeding success. A pH between approximately 5.8 and 6.8, very low carbonate hardness, and soft water with a general hardness of roughly 4 to 6 dGH are preferred. Many successful keepers utilize remineralized reverse osmosis water along with active buffering substrates to maintain the stable conditions these shrimp require. Sudden fluctuations in water chemistry should always be avoided. Red Fancy Tiger Shrimp spend much of their day grazing on biofilm, algae, microorganisms, and decomposing organic matter. In the aquarium they readily accept premium shrimp foods, algae wafers, powdered foods for shrimplets, blanched vegetables, and occasional protein-rich treats offered sparingly. A mature aquarium rich in natural biofilm is invaluable, providing a continuous food source that supports healthy molts, vibrant coloration, and successful breeding. Temperament is exceptionally peaceful. Red Fancy Tiger Shrimp are best maintained in dedicated Caridina aquariums or with other peaceful shrimp requiring identical water parameters. While adults may coexist with a handful of very gentle nano fish, most community fish will readily consume shrimplets and may stress adult shrimp. A species-focused aquarium provides the greatest opportunity for colony growth and allows their intricate coloration to be fully appreciated. Breeding is readily achievable under stable conditions. Females carry fertilized eggs beneath their abdomen for approximately three to four weeks before releasing fully formed miniature shrimp. Unlike Amano Shrimp, Red Fancy Tiger Shrimp complete their entire life cycle in freshwater without a free-swimming larval stage. Stable water chemistry, abundant biofilm, and minimal disturbance encourage consistent reproduction and high juvenile survival. With their extraordinary combination of vivid crimson coloration, brilliant opaque white markings, and intricate tiger striping, Red Fancy Tiger Shrimp are among the most striking ornamental shrimp available today. Their peaceful nature, fascinating colony behavior, and breathtaking patterns make them an exceptional choice for dedicated Caridina aquariums and high-end planted aquascapes where their beauty can truly be appreciated.

Aurora Tetra, Moenkhausia aurora , is a South American characin native to the upper Rio Xingu Basin in Brazil. It inhabits clear, moderately to swiftly flowing tributaries with sandy bottoms, scattered rounded stones, submerged roots, and patches of aquatic vegetation. Unlike many blackwater tetras, this species is associated with clearer waters that are well oxygenated and bordered by dense tropical rainforest. Adult Aurora Tetras typically reach about 1.5 to 1.75 inches in length. They possess a sleek, laterally compressed body with a brilliant silver base that shimmers with pink, lavender, and golden iridescence depending on the angle of the light. The dorsal, anal, and caudal fins are washed with vibrant orange to reddish-orange, while the eye often glows with a reddish-gold hue that complements the warm fin coloration. Mature males are noticeably more colorful than females, developing deeper red fins and stronger iridescent highlights, whereas females are slightly deeper-bodied with a more subdued appearance. Their constantly shifting metallic colors give the impression of the northern lights, inspiring the common name "Aurora Tetra." A tank of at least 20 gallons is recommended for a proper school, though larger aquariums allow for more natural behavior. Aurora Tetras should be maintained in groups of at least eight to ten individuals, where they become far more confident and display their best coloration. A dark substrate, driftwood, scattered leaf litter, patches of aquatic plants, and open swimming space create an ideal environment while helping their metallic colors stand out. Water conditions should remain stable and exceptionally clean. Temperatures between 72 and 79 degrees Fahrenheit are ideal, with a pH range of approximately 6.0 to 7.5 and soft to moderately hard water. Good water movement, excellent filtration, and regular water changes help replicate their naturally oxygen-rich habitat and keep them in peak condition. In the wild, Aurora Tetras feed on small aquatic insects, insect larvae, tiny crustaceans, and zooplankton. In the aquarium they readily accept quality flakes, micro pellets, frozen bloodworms, daphnia, cyclops, baby brine shrimp, and other appropriately sized foods. A varied diet rich in quality frozen and live foods enhances both coloration and breeding condition. Aurora Tetras are peaceful, active schooling fish that make excellent additions to community aquariums. They coexist well with Corydoras, pencilfish, hatchetfish, peaceful dwarf cichlids, rasboras, small gouramis, and other similarly sized characins. Males frequently spar through harmless displays, intensifying their colors and flaring their fins without causing injury. Breeding is possible in captivity but is not commonly attempted. Like many characins, they are egg scatterers that deposit adhesive eggs among fine-leaved plants or spawning mops. Adults provide no parental care and should be removed after spawning to prevent egg predation. Soft, slightly acidic water and subdued lighting generally produce the best results. With its glowing metallic body, fiery orange fins, and peaceful schooling behavior, Moenkhausia aurora is one of the most elegant recent additions to the aquarium hobby. The Aurora Tetra offers a unique blend of understated beauty and constant activity, making it an outstanding choice for planted aquariums and peaceful South American community displays.

Paradise Fish, Macropodus opercularis , is a hardy labyrinth fish native to eastern Asia, with a natural distribution spanning southern China, Taiwan, northern Vietnam, and parts of the Korean Peninsula. It inhabits shallow ponds, rice paddies, marshes, ditches, slow-moving streams, and flooded fields where dense aquatic vegetation provides cover. Many of these environments experience low oxygen levels, allowing Paradise Fish to thrive thanks to their labyrinth organ, which enables them to breathe atmospheric air. The numerous color varieties available today—including the traditional wild-type, Blue Paradise, Albino, Red, Black, and other selectively bred strains—have all been developed from this naturally widespread species. Adult Paradise Fish typically reach 3 to 4 inches in length. They possess an elongated, laterally compressed body with long, flowing dorsal, anal, and deeply forked caudal fins that become especially dramatic in mature males. Wild-type specimens display alternating bands of brilliant turquoise-blue and fiery orange-red across the body, complemented by iridescent blue fins marked with red striping. Selectively bred varieties expand upon this beauty with colors ranging from brilliant cobalt blue and deep crimson to pale gold, black, and albino forms. Males develop significantly longer fins, more intense coloration, and extended filamentous fin rays, while females remain smaller, rounder, and more subtly colored. Regardless of color form, Paradise Fish are among the most striking and recognizable labyrinth fish in the aquarium hobby. A single Paradise Fish or compatible pair can be maintained in an aquarium of at least 20 gallons, although 30 gallons or larger is recommended for community aquariums. The aquarium should include dense planting, driftwood, floating vegetation, and open swimming areas that allow the fish to establish territories while providing visual barriers. A secure lid is recommended, as Paradise Fish are capable jumpers and frequently surface to breathe atmospheric air. Paradise Fish are remarkably adaptable but thrive in stable, well-maintained aquariums. Temperatures between 68 and 78 degrees Fahrenheit are ideal, making them one of the few commonly available tropical fish that also tolerate cooler water. A pH between approximately 6.0 and 8.0 and soft to moderately hard water are well accepted. Good filtration and regular water changes will help maintain excellent health, although excessive current should be avoided. In nature, Paradise Fish are opportunistic predators that feed on aquatic insects, mosquito larvae, worms, crustaceans, and other small invertebrates. In the aquarium they readily accept quality pellets, flakes, frozen bloodworms, brine shrimp, mysis shrimp, daphnia, and live foods. A varied, protein-rich diet promotes vibrant coloration, strong immune function, and successful breeding. Paradise Fish are intelligent, bold, and highly territorial. Males, in particular, can be aggressive toward one another and toward similarly shaped or long-finned fish such as Bettas and some Gouramis. They are best maintained singly, as compatible pairs, or with robust, similarly sized community fish that are not overly timid or aggressive. Their confidence and inquisitive nature quickly make them one of the most interactive fish in the aquarium. Breeding is relatively straightforward under suitable conditions. Like other labyrinth fish, the male constructs a floating bubble nest beneath broad leaves or floating plants before courting the female. After spawning, the male gathers the eggs and carefully places them into the nest, where he guards them until the fry hatch and become free-swimming. The female should generally be removed after spawning, and the male should be removed once the fry are swimming independently. With their brilliant coloration, flowing fins, fascinating bubble-nesting behavior, and engaging personality, Macropodus opercularis remains one of the classic ornamental fish of the aquarium hobby. Whether in the traditional wild-type pattern or one of the many stunning selectively bred color forms, the Paradise Fish offers a unique combination of beauty, intelligence, and hardiness that continues to captivate aquarists around the world.

Australian Amano Shrimp, Caridina typus , is a freshwater dwarf shrimp native to northern Australia, New Guinea, Indonesia, the Philippines, and numerous islands throughout the Indo-Pacific region. In Australia, it is commonly found in clear coastal streams, rainforest creeks, and small rivers where it inhabits rocky substrates, submerged wood, leaf litter, and dense aquatic vegetation. These habitats are typically clean, well oxygenated, and characterized by moderate water movement that supports abundant algae and biofilm growth. Although commonly referred to as the Australian Amano Shrimp due to its similar appearance and behavior, Caridina typus is a distinct species from the well-known Japanese Amano Shrimp ( Caridina multidentata ). Adult Australian Amano Shrimp typically reach about 1.5 to 2 inches in length, making them somewhat smaller and more slender than the Japanese Amano Shrimp, which commonly reaches 2 to 2.5 inches. Their body is largely translucent with subtle tan, olive, or smoky coloration that varies depending on diet and surroundings. Fine rows of dark brown to reddish speckles and short dashes extend along the sides of the body, while the internal organs remain visible through the transparent exoskeleton. Compared to Caridina multidentata , Australian Amano Shrimp generally exhibit finer markings, a more delicate body shape, and a cleaner, more transparent appearance that many aquascapers find especially attractive. Females are larger and deeper-bodied than males and develop a broader abdomen for carrying eggs. A mature aquarium of at least 15 gallons is recommended, although larger aquariums provide greater stability and more natural grazing opportunities. Australian Amano Shrimp thrive in planted aquariums with driftwood, rounded stones, mosses, leaf litter, and abundant biofilm. Moderate water movement and high dissolved oxygen levels closely resemble their natural habitat. Shrimp-safe filtration is essential, and plenty of hiding places should be provided, particularly during molting. Water conditions should remain clean and stable. Temperatures between 70 and 80 degrees Fahrenheit are ideal, with a pH range of approximately 6.5 to 7.8 and soft to moderately hard water. Consistently low nitrate levels, regular water changes, and stable water chemistry are important for successful molts and long-term health. Like other dwarf shrimp, they are sensitive to copper-based medications and sudden changes in water parameters. Australian Amano Shrimp are excellent scavengers and algae grazers. They spend nearly all of their time feeding on soft algae, biofilm, diatoms, decaying plant material, and microorganisms growing on hard surfaces. Like their Japanese relatives, they are highly effective at controlling soft algae and consuming leftover food, although their slightly smaller size means they are somewhat better suited to nano aquariums and more delicate aquascapes. They should also be offered quality shrimp foods, algae wafers, blanched vegetables, and occasional protein-rich foods in moderation, as no shrimp should be expected to survive on algae alone. Temperament is exceptionally peaceful. Australian Amano Shrimp coexist well with other peaceful shrimp, snails, Corydoras, Otocinclus, small rainbowfish, rasboras, tetras, and other gentle community fish that are unlikely to view them as prey. Their constant activity and tireless grazing make them one of the most useful invertebrates for planted aquariums. Breeding follows a life cycle similar to that of the Japanese Amano Shrimp. Females readily produce and carry large clutches of eggs in freshwater, but the newly hatched larvae require brackish to marine conditions to complete their development before returning to freshwater as juveniles. As a result, successful captive breeding is considerably more challenging than with freshwater-breeding dwarf shrimp such as Crystal Reds or Neocaridina varieties, and most specimens available in the aquarium trade remain wild collected. Caridina typus combines the renowned algae-eating ability of the Japanese Amano Shrimp with a more refined appearance and a size better suited to smaller planted aquariums. Its peaceful temperament, nearly transparent beauty, and tireless grazing behavior make the Australian Amano Shrimp an exceptional choice for aquascapes, community aquariums, and anyone seeking an efficient yet elegant cleanup crew.

Blue Bolt Shrimp, Caridina cf. cantonensis, is a selectively bred freshwater dwarf shrimp developed from Taiwan Bee Shrimp bloodlines. While its wild ancestors originate from cool, clean streams of southern China, the Blue Bolt is a captive-developed ornamental variety that does not occur naturally in the wild. It is prized for its icy blue and white coloration and remains one of the most recognizable high-grade Caridina varieties in the aquarium hobby. Adult Blue Bolt Shrimp typically reach about 1 to 1.25 inches in length. Their defining feature is a beautiful powder-blue to intense sky-blue coloration that spreads across a milky white to translucent body. Color coverage varies between individuals and grades, with some shrimp displaying pale blue concentrated around the head and upper body while higher-grade specimens may develop rich blue coloration extending nearly from head to tail. The combination of frosty white undertones and cool blue pigmentation gives them an almost glowing appearance, particularly against dark substrates and deep green aquatic plants. Females generally grow larger and develop a deeper, more rounded abdomen than males. A mature aquarium of at least 10 gallons is recommended, although larger aquariums provide greater water stability and are generally easier to maintain. Blue Bolt Shrimp thrive in established planted aquariums with mosses, driftwood, botanicals, porous rock, and other surfaces that encourage abundant biofilm growth. Shrimp-safe sponge filtration or protected filter intakes are strongly recommended, and plenty of hiding places should be available for freshly molted shrimp and juveniles. Water quality and stability are especially important with Blue Bolts. Temperatures between 68 and 74 degrees Fahrenheit are ideal, with a pH of approximately 5.5 to 6.5, very low carbonate hardness, and soft water with a general hardness around 4 to 6 dGH. A KH near 0 to 1 dKH is generally preferred. Many successful keepers use remineralized reverse osmosis water together with an active buffering substrate to maintain the soft, acidic conditions favored by Taiwan Bee Caridina. Sudden changes in temperature, mineral content, or other water parameters should be avoided. Blue Bolt Shrimp spend much of their time grazing on biofilm, algae, microorganisms, and decomposing organic material. In the aquarium they should also receive high-quality shrimp foods, algae-based foods, powdered foods for juveniles, and occasional protein-rich foods in moderation. A mature aquarium with abundant natural biofilm is especially important because newly released shrimplets depend heavily on microscopic food growing throughout the tank. Temperament is exceptionally peaceful. Blue Bolt Shrimp are best maintained in dedicated Caridina aquariums or alongside other peaceful invertebrates requiring similar water conditions. They can coexist with carefully selected nano fish, but nearly any fish capable of fitting a shrimplet into its mouth should be expected to eat some young. A dedicated shrimp aquarium provides the best opportunity to establish a thriving colony and fully appreciate their coloration. Breeding occurs entirely in freshwater when conditions are suitable. Females carry fertilized eggs beneath the abdomen for approximately three to four weeks before releasing fully formed miniature shrimp. There is no brackish larval stage. Blue Bolts can interbreed with other compatible Taiwan Bee and Bee Shrimp varieties, so aquarists interested in maintaining a consistent Blue Bolt line should carefully consider which Caridina varieties are housed together. Caridina cf. cantonensis Blue Bolt Shrimp are among the most visually impressive ornamental shrimp available, combining frosty white undertones with brilliant shades of powder blue, sky blue, and icy turquoise. Their extraordinary coloration, peaceful nature, and rewarding breeding behavior make Blue Bolt Shrimp an outstanding centerpiece for dedicated Caridina aquariums and high-end planted aquascapes.

Blood Parrot Cichlid is a selectively bred hybrid cichlid developed in Taiwan in the 1980s and does not occur naturally in the wild. Its exact parentage has never been officially confirmed, although Central American cichlids are responsible for its ancestry. Blood Parrots have become extremely popular due to their unusual body shape, brilliant coloration, relatively manageable temperament, and highly interactive personalities. Adult Blood Parrot Cichlids typically reach about 7 to 8 inches in length, with exceptionally large individuals sometimes growing slightly larger. They have a distinctive deep, rounded body with a pronounced forehead, large expressive eyes, and a small beak-like mouth that gives the fish its parrot-like appearance. Natural coloration ranges from brilliant orange and tangerine to deep red, with healthy mature specimens often developing incredibly saturated coloration. Juveniles may initially appear darker or display temporary black markings that generally fade as they mature. Their unusual shape, vivid color, and curious expressions make Blood Parrots immediately recognizable and give them a tremendous amount of personality. A tank of at least 55 gallons is recommended for a single adult, with 75 gallons or larger preferred for multiple Blood Parrots or community setups. The aquarium should provide substantial open swimming space along with driftwood, smooth rocks, caves, and other structures that allow the fish to establish secure retreats. Sand or smooth gravel works well as substrate. Blood Parrots frequently dig and rearrange their surroundings, so plants should be hardy, securely anchored, or attached to hardscape. Water conditions should remain stable and clean. Temperatures between 76 and 82 degrees Fahrenheit are appropriate, with a pH range of approximately 6.5 to 7.8 and soft to moderately hard water. Blood Parrots are relatively hardy, but their substantial size and appetite produce a significant bioload. Strong filtration and regular water changes are essential for maintaining excellent long-term health. Feeding is straightforward, although their unusual mouth shape should be considered when selecting foods. Blood Parrot Cichlids readily accept high-quality cichlid pellets, sinking or slow-sinking foods, frozen brine shrimp, mysis shrimp, bloodworms, and other prepared foods. Smaller pellets are often easier for them to manipulate than oversized foods. A varied, high-quality diet helps maintain their intense orange-red coloration and healthy body condition. Temperament is generally semi-aggressive but considerably more manageable than many similarly sized Central American cichlids. Blood Parrots are confident, curious, and highly interactive fish that often learn to recognize their keeper and approach the front of the aquarium for food. Individual personalities vary considerably, with some remaining extremely peaceful while others become territorial as they mature. Suitable tankmates include similarly sized peaceful to moderately assertive cichlids, larger barbs, rainbowfish, robust catfish, and other fish that are neither small enough to be bullied nor aggressive enough to injure them. Blood Parrot Cichlids frequently form pairs and exhibit typical cichlid courtship, spawning, and parental behavior. Females can produce viable eggs, but males are commonly infertile due to the hybrid origin of the fish, so many pairings produce eggs that never develop. Fertile offspring can occasionally result when females are crossed with compatible non-hybrid cichlids. Blood Parrot Cichlids combine brilliant orange-red coloration with an unmistakable appearance and an unusually engaging personality. Their curious behavior, intelligence, and tendency to interact with their owners make them much more than simply a colorful display fish. With adequate space, strong filtration, and appropriate tankmates, the Blood Parrot Cichlid becomes a charismatic centerpiece for medium to large freshwater aquariums.

Senegal Bichir, Polypterus senegalus, is a primitive freshwater fish native to tropical Africa, where it has a broad distribution across the Nile Basin and numerous river systems of West and Central Africa. It inhabits slow-moving rivers, floodplains, swamps, marshes, and shallow vegetated waters where submerged wood, aquatic vegetation, and muddy or sandy substrates provide shelter. These environments may experience low dissolved oxygen, something bichirs are exceptionally well adapted to thanks to their paired lungs and ability to breathe atmospheric air. Adult Senegal Bichirs typically reach about 10 to 12 inches in captivity, although larger individuals are possible. The body is long, muscular, and almost reptilian in appearance, covered in tough, diamond-shaped ganoid scales that give the fish an armored, prehistoric look. Coloration typically ranges from pale gray and silver to olive-gray or beige, often with a lighter cream-colored underside. Instead of a single continuous dorsal fin, the back carries a row of individual finlets, each supported by its own spine. Large paddle-like pectoral fins are used almost like limbs as the fish moves across the bottom, while the broad head, small eyes, and prominent nostrils complete its unmistakably ancient appearance. Bichirs belong to one of the oldest surviving lineages of ray-finned fishes, and the Senegal Bichir looks every bit the living fossil. A tank of at least 75 gallons is recommended for an adult, with larger aquariums preferred for multiple bichirs or community setups. Floor space is particularly important because Senegal Bichirs spend most of their time near the bottom. Fine sand or smooth substrate is ideal, along with driftwood, caves, rocks, and shaded retreats. A tightly secured lid is absolutely essential. Bichirs are remarkably capable escape artists and can squeeze through surprisingly small openings. A small air space should remain between the water surface and lid because they must periodically surface to breathe atmospheric air. Water conditions should remain stable and clean. Temperatures between 75 and 82 degrees Fahrenheit are appropriate, with a pH range of approximately 6.0 to 8.0 and soft to moderately hard water. Senegal Bichirs are hardy and adaptable, but strong biological filtration and regular water changes are important because of their size and protein-rich diet. Water movement should be gentle to moderate rather than excessively strong. Senegal Bichirs are carnivorous predators. In nature they consume insects, worms, crustaceans, small fish, amphibians, and other aquatic animals. In the aquarium they readily accept sinking carnivore pellets, shrimp, krill, earthworms, bloodworms, mussel, and other appropriately sized meaty foods. Many become enthusiastic feeders and quickly learn to emerge when food is offered. Feeder fish are unnecessary and are best avoided because of their potential to introduce parasites and disease. Temperament is generally peaceful toward fish that cannot be swallowed. Senegal Bichirs are not particularly aggressive, but they are opportunistic predators and should never be trusted with small tankmates. Any fish narrow enough to fit into a bichir's mouth should eventually be considered potential prey, particularly after the lights go out. Suitable tankmates include medium to large peaceful cichlids, larger rainbowfish, robust catfish, larger characins, and other bichirs of compatible size. Breeding is possible in captivity but remains relatively uncommon in typical home aquariums. During courtship, males use their enlarged anal fin to receive and fertilize eggs from the female before the adhesive eggs are scattered among vegetation. Adults provide no parental care and may consume both eggs and fry. Young bichirs initially possess prominent external gills, giving the juveniles an especially unusual amphibian-like appearance. Polypterus senegalus is one of the most accessible members of an extraordinary ancient lineage of fishes. Its armored scales, individual dorsal finlets, lung-breathing ability, deliberate movements, and almost reptilian appearance make the Senegal Bichir unlike virtually anything else commonly kept in freshwater aquariums. Despite its predatory nature, its generally calm temperament and impressive hardiness make it an outstanding centerpiece for aquarists prepared to provide adequate space and appropriately sized tankmates.

Threadfin Acara, Acarichthys heckelii, is a distinctive South American cichlid native to the Amazon Basin and surrounding river systems, with a natural range that includes Brazil, Peru, Colombia, Guyana, and portions of the Rio Essequibo drainage. It inhabits slow-moving rivers, flooded forests, lagoons, and quiet tributaries with extensive sandy substrates, submerged wood, roots, and leaf litter. These warm tropical habitats provide the soft substrate that plays an important role in the species’ natural feeding and breeding behavior. Adult Threadfin Acaras typically reach about 7 to 8 inches in length, with mature males often becoming larger and developing more elaborate finnage. The body is elongated and moderately deep with a warm silver, gold, or olive base covered in beautiful pearlescent blue-green spotting. A prominent dark blotch appears along the middle of the flank, while additional dark markings and vertical shading may become more pronounced depending on mood. The feature that truly sets mature Threadfin Acaras apart is their spectacular finnage. The dorsal fin develops long trailing extensions, often accented with fiery orange-red coloration and brilliant metallic blue patterning, while the anal and caudal fins can develop similar iridescent blue, red, and orange highlights. Fully mature specimens are exceptionally colorful and become increasingly impressive with age. A tank of at least 75 gallons is recommended for a single adult or compatible pair, with 100 gallons or larger preferred for groups or community setups. Fine sand is strongly recommended because Threadfin Acaras naturally sift and excavate the substrate. Driftwood, branches, rocks, and open sandy areas create an ideal environment, but structures should be positioned securely because these fish can move significant amounts of substrate. Plants can be incorporated, although delicate or poorly rooted species may be disturbed by digging. Water conditions should remain warm, clean, and stable. Temperatures between 76 and 84 degrees Fahrenheit are appropriate, with a pH range of approximately 5.5 to 7.5 and soft to moderately hard water. Strong biological filtration and regular water changes are important, particularly as these fish mature and their bioload increases. Gentle to moderate water movement and good oxygenation are ideal. Threadfin Acaras are omnivorous benthic feeders that naturally search through sand and detritus for insect larvae, worms, crustaceans, and other small organisms while also consuming some plant and organic material. In the aquarium they readily accept quality cichlid pellets, sinking foods, frozen bloodworms, mysis shrimp, brine shrimp, chopped shrimp, and other appropriately sized foods. A varied diet helps develop the intense coloration and elaborate finnage seen in mature specimens. Temperament is generally peaceful to moderately territorial for a cichlid of this size. Threadfin Acaras can be successfully maintained with other medium to large, relatively peaceful South American fish, including larger tetras, silver dollars, Geophagus and other compatible eartheaters, peaceful catfish, and similarly tempered cichlids. Territorial behavior becomes considerably stronger during breeding, and adequate floor space and visual barriers are important when maintaining multiple cichlids. Breeding behavior is particularly fascinating. Acarichthys heckelii is a substrate-spawning cichlid that naturally excavates tunnels or burrows in sandy banks for reproduction. In aquariums, pairs may dig beneath wood, rocks, or other structures and create surprisingly elaborate spawning chambers. Both parents participate in defending the breeding territory and caring for the developing young, and their normally moderate temperament can become significantly more assertive while guarding offspring. Acarichthys heckelii is an exceptional centerpiece cichlid that becomes dramatically more beautiful as it matures. Its shimmering blue-green spotting, fiery fin coloration, long thread-like dorsal extensions, sand-sifting behavior, and unusual burrow-spawning strategy make the Threadfin Acara one of the most distinctive South American cichlids available to aquarists.

Compressiceps Dwarf Pike Cichlid, Crenicichla compressiceps, is a small South American predatory cichlid native to Brazil, where it occurs in the Rio Tocantins drainage. Unlike many larger Crenicichla that inhabit slower channels and flooded forests, this species is strongly associated with clear, flowing water and rocky river habitats. Its combination of compact adult size and classic pike-cichlid behavior makes it particularly appealing to aquarists who love Crenicichla but do not have room for one of the genus's much larger species. Adult Crenicichla compressiceps typically reaches about 3 to 4 inches in length, making it a true dwarf compared with pike cichlids that can exceed a foot in length. The body is elongated and torpedo-shaped, with a relatively large head, predatory mouth, and streamlined profile. Coloration is typically olive, tan, or golden through the body with a series of dark vertical bars along the flanks. The head and gill covers can develop attractive blue-green iridescence, while mature fish may show yellow, orange, or reddish coloration through the fins and lower body. Despite their small size, they retain the unmistakable predatory appearance and attitude of a much larger pike cichlid. A tank of at least 30 gallons is recommended for a single specimen or established pair, with larger aquariums preferred for groups or community setups. The aquarium should provide numerous caves, rock piles, driftwood, and visual barriers while still leaving open areas for swimming. Sand or fine gravel works well as substrate. Moderate to strong water movement, excellent filtration, and high oxygen levels are particularly beneficial because of the species' naturally riverine habitat. Water conditions should remain stable and exceptionally clean. Temperatures between 75 and 82 degrees Fahrenheit are appropriate, with a pH range of approximately 6.0 to 7.5 and soft to moderately hard water. Crenicichla compressiceps appreciates excellent oxygenation and regular water changes, and prolonged exposure to deteriorating water quality should be avoided. Compressiceps Dwarf Pike Cichlids are micropredators. In nature they hunt aquatic insects, insect larvae, crustaceans, and small fish among rocks and crevices. In the aquarium they readily accept frozen bloodworms, mysis shrimp, brine shrimp, chopped shrimp, and quality carnivore pellets once accustomed to prepared foods. Live feeder fish are unnecessary and should be avoided because of their potential to introduce parasites and disease. Temperament is assertive and predatory despite the species' small size. Compressiceps Dwarf Pikes can be territorial toward their own kind and other small cichlids, particularly when breeding. They can be maintained with appropriately sized, fast-moving community fish that are too large to swallow, but very small tetras, rasboras, shrimp, and fry should be considered potential prey. Providing abundant structure and broken lines of sight is especially important when maintaining a pair or multiple individuals. Breeding is possible in captivity. Crenicichla compressiceps is a cave-spawning cichlid, with pairs selecting protected cavities or crevices in which to deposit their eggs. Both parents participate in defending the territory and young, and aggression can increase considerably during spawning. Once free-swimming, the fry can be raised on newly hatched brine shrimp and other appropriately sized foods. Crenicichla compressiceps packs virtually everything aquarists love about pike cichlids into a remarkably compact fish. Its streamlined predatory appearance, attractive barred coloration, iridescent highlights, energetic behavior, and bold personality make the Compressiceps Dwarf Pike Cichlid an outstanding choice for aquarists who want an authentic Crenicichla experience without the enormous aquarium required by many of its larger relatives.

Betta unimaculata, commonly known as the Howong Betta or One-Spot Betta, is a large wild Betta native to eastern Borneo, Indonesia. It inhabits forest streams, shallow pools, and flowing tributaries in Kalimantan, where it is commonly associated with clear to lightly stained water, submerged roots, leaf litter, rocks, and dense overhanging vegetation. Unlike many of the tiny peat-swamp Bettas, Betta unimaculata is a substantially larger, more powerful fish adapted to somewhat more open and flowing habitats. Adult Betta unimaculata typically reaches about 4.5 to 5 inches in length, making it one of the larger wild Betta species commonly maintained in aquariums. The body is elongated, muscular, and considerably more streamlined than the familiar domesticated Betta splendens. Mature males are especially impressive, developing rich bronze, copper, green, and blue iridescence across the scales. The head and gill plates can glow with metallic turquoise to emerald coloration, while the fins develop beautiful blue-green iridescence accented by warm reddish, orange, or brown tones. Males also develop longer, more pointed finnage and a much more intense metallic sheen than females. The overall effect is distinctly wild and predatory, with coloration that changes dramatically depending on lighting, mood, and viewing angle. A tank of at least 30 gallons is recommended for a pair, with larger aquariums strongly preferred for groups or community setups. The aquarium should provide substantial structure using driftwood, branches, rocks, dense planting, and floating vegetation while maintaining some open swimming space. Visual barriers are particularly important when keeping multiple individuals. A tightly fitted lid is absolutely essential, as Betta unimaculata is an exceptionally capable jumper. Water conditions should remain warm, clean, and stable. Temperatures between 75 and 82 degrees Fahrenheit are appropriate, with a pH range of approximately 5.5 to 7.5 and soft to moderately hard water. Unlike some highly specialized blackwater Betta species, Betta unimaculata is relatively adaptable when maintained in stable conditions. Gentle to moderate water movement and good oxygenation are beneficial. Betta unimaculata is primarily carnivorous and naturally feeds on insects, insect larvae, crustaceans, worms, and other small aquatic animals. In the aquarium it readily accepts quality carnivore pellets along with frozen foods such as bloodworms, mysis shrimp, brine shrimp, krill, and other appropriately sized meaty foods. A varied diet helps develop the intense metallic coloration and robust body condition seen in mature specimens. Temperament is confident and territorial but generally manageable with appropriate space. Males may display aggressively toward one another, and pairs can also become confrontational if adequate cover is not provided. Their relatively large size means very small fish and shrimp may be viewed as prey. When kept in a community aquarium, tankmates should be peaceful but confident species large enough not to be swallowed or intimidated. Unlike the bubble-nesting Betta species familiar to most aquarists, Betta unimaculata is a paternal mouthbrooder. After an elaborate courtship and spawning embrace, the male collects the fertilized eggs into his mouth and carries them throughout their development. After approximately two weeks, he releases relatively large, fully formed fry capable of immediately feeding on small live foods. This fascinating reproductive strategy is one of the major attractions of keeping the species. Betta unimaculata is a spectacular wild Betta that offers a completely different experience from domesticated Betta splendens. Its impressive size, metallic turquoise and bronze coloration, streamlined predatory appearance, paternal mouthbrooding behavior, and bold personality make the One-Spot Betta an exceptional centerpiece for aquarists interested in larger and less commonly kept wild Betta species.

Betta sp. Api Api ‘Jade’ is a rare wild Betta from Sumatra, Indonesia, belonging to the Betta coccina complex. It originates from highly acidic peat-swamp habitats characterized by dark tannin-stained water, dense leaf litter, submerged roots, branches, and thick forest canopy. These environments are typically extremely soft and nutrient-poor, with very little water movement and extensive organic material covering the substrate. Adult Betta sp. Api Api ‘Jade’ typically reaches about 1.5 to 2 inches in length. Mature males are exceptionally colorful, displaying a vivid scarlet to fiery orange-red base coloration across the head, body, and fins. The center and rear portion of the body is covered with brilliant metallic jade-green to turquoise-blue scales, creating a striking jewel-like patch that contrasts dramatically against the red body. This iridescence can shift between emerald, turquoise, aqua, and electric blue depending on lighting and viewing angle. The caudal fin is broad and intensely red-orange with a delicate pale blue to turquoise outer edge, while the elongated anal fin combines rich red coloration with darker inner areas and brilliant blue-green edging. The dorsal fin is similarly red-orange and may develop an especially striking turquoise-white margin. Males also display elongated red pelvic fins tipped in bright white to blue-white. Females are generally smaller and more subdued, though mature females can still develop attractive red and iridescent coloration. A tank of at least 10 gallons is suitable for a pair, with larger aquariums recommended for groups. The aquarium should be heavily structured with driftwood, fine branches, caves, dense plants, floating vegetation, and plenty of leaf litter. Subdued lighting helps the fish feel secure while also bringing out the remarkable metallic coloration of mature males. Water movement should remain gentle, and a tightly fitted lid is essential because wild Bettas are excellent jumpers. Water conditions should reflect their specialized peat-swamp origins. Temperatures between 75 and 82 degrees Fahrenheit are appropriate, with very soft, acidic water strongly preferred. A pH between approximately 4.5 and 6.5 is ideal, with very low carbonate hardness. Botanicals such as dried leaves, seed pods, and natural driftwood are highly beneficial, helping create the tannin-rich conditions characteristic of their natural habitat. Stability is especially important, and sudden changes in water chemistry should be avoided. Betta sp. Api Api ‘Jade’ is a micropredator that naturally feeds on tiny insects, insect larvae, crustaceans, worms, and other small aquatic invertebrates. In the aquarium they thrive on frozen and live foods such as daphnia, baby brine shrimp, mosquito larvae, bloodworms, and other appropriately sized foods. Some individuals will accept high-quality pellets, but regular frozen or live foods are strongly recommended to develop the intense red coloration and metallic jade-green iridescence for which this form is prized. Temperament is relatively peaceful but territorial. Males will display toward rivals and may defend preferred areas of the aquarium, particularly during breeding. Compatible pairs can be maintained together when abundant cover is provided, while larger groups require considerably more space and numerous visual barriers. They are best suited to species-focused aquariums or carefully selected communities containing very small, peaceful fish that tolerate extremely soft and acidic water. Betta sp. Api Api ‘Jade’ is a bubble-nesting species. Males construct nests beneath floating plants, leaves, or other protected areas near the surface. Following spawning, the male tends the eggs and developing larvae until the fry become free-swimming. Very soft acidic water, minimal disturbance, dense surface cover, and abundant microscopic foods for newly free-swimming fry provide the best conditions for successful reproduction. Betta sp. Api Api ‘Jade’ is an extraordinary wild Betta whose coloration rivals even the most elaborate domesticated varieties. The combination of a fiery scarlet-orange body and fins, brilliant jade-green and turquoise metallic scaling, contrasting pale blue fin edging, and white-tipped pelvic fins gives mature males an unmistakable appearance. For aquarists interested in rare wild Bettas and authentic blackwater aquariums, the Api Api ‘Jade’ Betta is a truly exceptional centerpiece species.
