Royal Acara, Aequidens diadema, is a South American cichlid native to the Amazon and Orinoco systems of northern South America. It occurs in blackwater habitats, including the upper Rio Negro region and tributaries of the Orinoco in Colombia and Venezuela, with Peruvian populations also entering the aquarium trade. These fish inhabit warm, soft, acidic waters with submerged wood, leaf litter, sandy substrates, and plenty of structure. Adult Royal Acaras generally reach about 5 to 7 inches in length, although large aquarium-raised males can approach 8 inches or more. The body is robust, moderately elongated, and laterally compressed. Their base coloration ranges from silver and olive to warm gold, with a beautiful metallic blue sheen across the scales. A large dark blotch on the flank provides strong contrast, while the face can become covered in brilliant blue-green iridescence crossed by vivid red striations. The eyes may develop a striking red coloration, and the fins are often washed with yellow, orange, turquoise, and red. Mature males can develop elegant extensions to the dorsal and anal fins. Their appearance changes dramatically with mood and breeding condition, with displaying adults developing much stronger yellow, red, blue, and black coloration than juveniles. A tank of at least 75 gallons is recommended for an adult or compatible pair, with larger aquariums preferred for community setups. The aquarium should provide plenty of open swimming space along with driftwood, branches, rocks, caves, and other structures that create territories and break lines of sight. Sand or fine gravel makes an excellent substrate. Plants can be used, but established or securely anchored species are preferable because mature fish may dig and rearrange the substrate. Water conditions should remain warm, clean, and stable. Temperatures between 75 and 83 degrees Fahrenheit are appropriate, with a pH range of approximately 5.5 to 7.2 and soft to moderately soft water preferred. Royal Acaras are particularly well suited to tannin-rich South American setups. Strong biological filtration and regular water changes are important as the fish mature and their bioload increases. Royal Acaras are omnivorous and easy to feed in captivity. A high-quality cichlid pellet makes an excellent staple and can be supplemented with frozen bloodworms, mysis shrimp, brine shrimp, krill, chopped shrimp, and other appropriately sized foods. A varied diet rich in quality ingredients helps mature specimens develop their strongest metallic blue, red, and golden coloration. Temperament is best described as semi-aggressive. Royal Acaras are generally manageable compared with many similarly sized cichlids, but they are confident territorial fish rather than peaceful community cichlids. Individual temperament varies considerably, and mature specimens can become dominant toward weaker tankmates. They are best housed with appropriately sized, confident species such as larger tetras, peaceful eartheaters, robust catfish, and other moderately tempered South American cichlids. Very small fish may eventually be viewed as prey. Breeding behavior is particularly interesting. Aequidens diadema forms pairs and displays strong parental behavior, with aggression increasing substantially once reproduction begins. Spawning and brood-care behavior can differ from the more familiar substrate-spawning acaras, and the species is notable for mouthbrooding behavior associated with care of the developing offspring. A breeding pair should be provided with ample territory and should not be expected to tolerate timid tankmates near its brood. Aequidens diadema is a spectacular and relatively uncommon South American cichlid that becomes increasingly impressive with maturity. Its metallic turquoise-blue sheen, vivid red facial markings, warm golden coloration, elegant finnage, substantial size, and confident personality give the Royal Acara a genuinely regal appearance and make it an exceptional centerpiece for a large South American aquarium.

Gold Blue Kerri Tetra, also known as the Leucistic Kerri Tetra, Inpaichthys kerri, is a striking selectively bred color form of the classic Kerri Tetra. The wild species is native to Brazil, where it occurs in the Rio Aripuanã drainage of the Amazon Basin. It inhabits small forest streams and tributaries with submerged roots, leaf litter, and overhanging vegetation. These waters are typically warm, soft, and slightly acidic, providing the conditions in which this beautiful South American tetra naturally thrives. Adult Gold Blue Kerri Tetras typically reach about 1.5 to 2 inches in length. What makes this variety special is its leucistic coloration, which dramatically transforms the appearance of the normally darker Kerri Tetra. The body develops a luminous cream to pale golden coloration with beautiful metallic blue, lavender, and turquoise iridescence across the scales. Warm yellow to gold tones can become particularly noticeable along the back and fins, while the translucent quality of the lighter body allows the blue iridescence to glow under aquarium lighting. Depending on the individual, lighting, and maturity, the fish can shift visually between gold, icy blue, violet, and silvery-white. The result is a bright, almost pastel version of Inpaichthys kerri that looks especially impressive against dark substrates and lush green plants. A tank of at least 15 to 20 gallons is recommended for a proper school, though larger aquariums provide greater stability and a more impressive display. Gold Blue Kerri Tetras are social fish and should be maintained in groups of at least six, with eight or more being preferable. In larger groups they become more confident, interact more naturally, and create a beautiful shimmering display through the midwater. Plants, driftwood, and shaded areas can be arranged around the perimeter while leaving plenty of open swimming space. Water conditions should remain stable and clean. Temperatures between 74 and 80 degrees Fahrenheit are appropriate, with a pH range of approximately 5.5 to 7.2 and soft to moderately soft water preferred. Captive-bred Kerri Tetras are relatively adaptable, but regular water changes and consistently good water quality help maintain their strongest coloration and overall condition. Feeding is straightforward. Inpaichthys kerri naturally feeds on small insects, insect larvae, crustaceans, and other tiny aquatic organisms. In the aquarium, Gold Blue Kerri Tetras readily accept quality flakes, micro-pellets, frozen daphnia, cyclops, baby brine shrimp, bloodworms, and other appropriately sized foods. A varied diet containing quality frozen or live foods helps intensify their metallic blue and golden coloration. Temperament is peaceful and community-friendly. Gold Blue Kerri Tetras coexist well with other small, non-aggressive fish including Corydoras, pencilfish, rasboras, dwarf cichlids, peaceful gouramis, and other tetras. Males may display toward one another, but these interactions are generally harmless and can actually bring out stronger coloration. Breeding is possible in captivity. Like other small characins, they are egg scatterers that deposit eggs among fine-leaved plants or spawning media. Adults provide no parental care and may consume the eggs, so breeders typically separate the adults after spawning. Because the Gold Blue coloration is a selectively bred trait, offspring may vary in appearance depending on the genetics of the breeding stock. The Gold Blue Kerri Tetra is an exceptional variation of an already beautiful South American schooling fish. Its luminous leucistic body combined with shimmering blue, turquoise, violet, and golden highlights gives it a completely different appearance from the standard Inpaichthys kerri. For aquarists looking for an unusual tetra that remains peaceful, manageable, and highly colorful, the Leucistic Kerri Tetra is a standout choice for planted and community aquariums.

Eriocaulon sp. ‘Vietnam’ is a compact rosette plant originating from Vietnam and belonging to the pipewort family, Eriocaulaceae. Plants in this group are typically associated with shallow wetlands, stream margins, marshy areas, and seasonally inundated habitats where they grow in nutrient-poor substrates exposed to clean water and strong tropical light. Unlike many Eriocaulon species known for being demanding aquarium plants, the Vietnam form has developed a reputation in the hobby for being considerably more adaptable and easier to maintain. In the aquarium, Eriocaulon sp. ‘Vietnam’ forms an attractive rosette of long, narrow, bright green leaves that radiate outward from a central growing point. The leaves have a fine, grass-like appearance but are broader and more substantial than true carpeting grasses, giving mature plants a distinctive starburst or fountain-like shape. Plants generally remain around 4 to 8 inches tall, although size varies considerably with lighting and nutrient availability. As the rosette matures, it becomes increasingly dense and symmetrical, making this plant especially attractive as a midground accent or individual focal point. A nutrient-rich substrate is strongly recommended, as Eriocaulon sp. ‘Vietnam’ develops a substantial root system and obtains a significant portion of its nutrition from the substrate. Root tabs can be particularly useful when it is planted in inert sand or gravel. Moderate to high lighting encourages compact, dense growth and helps maintain the plant’s characteristic rosette form. CO₂ supplementation is highly beneficial and produces faster, fuller growth, although this particular Eriocaulon is considerably more forgiving than many of its relatives and can be maintained without injected CO₂ in a well-balanced aquarium. Water conditions should remain stable and clean. Temperatures between 70 and 80 degrees Fahrenheit are appropriate, with slightly acidic to neutral water generally preferred. Soft to moderately hard water can be tolerated, making Eriocaulon sp. ‘Vietnam’ significantly less restrictive than some of the extremely soft-water Eriocaulon species. Consistent nutrient availability and good circulation around the plant help prevent deterioration of older leaves and encourage healthy new growth from the center of the rosette. Eriocaulon sp. ‘Vietnam’ benefits from balanced fertilization containing nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, iron, and trace elements. Although it is primarily a strong root feeder, consistent water-column fertilization can further improve growth and overall appearance. Older or damaged outer leaves can simply be removed at the base, while the central growing point should never be cut or buried. Propagation occurs through the production of side shoots or daughter plants around the base of mature specimens. Once these plantlets have developed their own root systems, they can be carefully separated and replanted elsewhere in the aquarium. Established plants may gradually form attractive clusters if the daughter plants are allowed to remain together. Eriocaulon sp. ‘Vietnam’ is compatible with virtually all peaceful aquarium fish and invertebrates. Its compact growth works particularly well alongside carpeting plants, Cryptocoryne, Bucephalandra, and colorful stem plants, where its fine bright-green foliage provides excellent textural contrast. Shrimp also frequently graze among the leaves for biofilm and microorganisms. Eriocaulon sp. ‘Vietnam’ offers the distinctive architectural appearance of an Eriocaulon without the extreme difficulty associated with many members of the genus. Its bright green starburst growth, manageable size, and relatively forgiving care requirements make it an excellent choice for aquarists looking for an unusual midground or focal plant that adds both texture and structure to a planted aquarium.

Amazon Sword ‘Compacta’, Echinodorus ‘Compacta’, is a cultivated dwarf sword plant developed from South American Echinodorus stock. Unlike the full-sized Amazon Swords that can quickly dominate an aquarium, ‘Compacta’ was selected for its shorter, denser growth and more manageable proportions. It provides the broad-leaved, lush appearance aquarists expect from an Amazon Sword while fitting comfortably into considerably smaller planted aquariums. In the aquarium, Amazon Sword ‘Compacta’ develops a dense rosette of broad, lance-shaped leaves emerging from a central crown. The foliage ranges from bright to medium green, with new leaves sometimes emerging a lighter green before darkening as they mature. Its leaves are substantially shorter and more compact than those of standard Amazon Swords, generally keeping the plant around 6 to 12 inches tall depending on growing conditions. The dense, symmetrical rosette creates an attractive bushy appearance that works exceptionally well as a midground plant or smaller centerpiece. Amazon Sword ‘Compacta’ should be planted directly into the substrate with its roots buried but the crown left exposed. Burying the crown can cause rot and eventually kill the plant. Moderate lighting is sufficient for healthy growth, although stronger lighting generally encourages denser, more compact foliage. Because of its manageable size, it works particularly well in medium aquariums where a standard Amazon Sword would eventually become overwhelming. Like other Echinodorus, Amazon Sword ‘Compacta’ is a heavy root feeder. Nutrient-rich aquarium soil provides excellent growing conditions, while plants maintained in sand or gravel benefit greatly from regular root tab supplementation. Water-column fertilization can provide additional nutrients, but maintaining a healthy root zone is considerably more important. CO₂ supplementation is not required, making this an excellent option for low-tech planted aquariums, although added CO₂ will encourage faster and fuller growth. Water conditions are flexible and forgiving. Temperatures between 72 and 82 degrees Fahrenheit are appropriate, with a pH range of approximately 6.0 to 7.8 and soft to moderately hard water. Amazon Sword ‘Compacta’ adapts well to a broad range of freshwater aquarium conditions, with stability and adequate nutrition being more important than achieving specific parameters. Growth is moderate once the plant becomes established. Newly introduced specimens may lose some older leaves while adapting from emersed nursery growth to fully submerged aquarium conditions. This is normal, and healthy plants will begin producing new submerged leaves from the center of the crown. Older or damaged outer leaves can be removed individually at their base rather than cutting the leaves midway. Propagation typically occurs through flower stalks or runners that produce small daughter plants. Once a plantlet develops several leaves and a healthy root system, it can be carefully separated from the parent and replanted. Mature specimens maintained under good conditions may produce multiple plantlets over time. Amazon Sword ‘Compacta’ is compatible with virtually all peaceful community fish and invertebrates. Its broad leaves provide excellent shelter and resting surfaces for small fish, shrimp, and bottom-dwelling species. Large herbivorous fish or particularly enthusiastic digging cichlids may damage or uproot the plant, but otherwise its sturdy foliage holds up extremely well in community aquariums. Echinodorus ‘Compacta’ is an excellent choice for aquarists who love the classic appearance of an Amazon Sword but do not want a plant that eventually takes over the entire aquarium. Its broad green foliage, compact rosette growth, easy care requirements, and ability to thrive without injected CO₂ make the Amazon Sword ‘Compacta’ a versatile centerpiece or midground plant for a wide range of freshwater aquariums.

Orange Finned Kyathit Danio, Danio kyathit, is a colorful Southeast Asian cyprinid native to northern Myanmar, where it occurs in tributaries of the upper Ayeyarwady River system, particularly in Kachin State. It inhabits clear, shallow streams and smaller flowing waterways with gravel, stones, and mixed substrates surrounded by dense vegetation. These environments experience seasonal changes in temperature and flow and are typically clean, well oxygenated, and considerably more dynamic than the still-water habitats associated with many tropical aquarium fish. Adult Orange Finned Kyathit Danios typically reach about 1.5 to 2 inches in length. The body is slender, streamlined, and built for active swimming, with a warm golden to olive-gold base coloration covered in dark blue-black spots and broken horizontal markings. What makes this form especially attractive is the intense orange to reddish-orange coloration that develops throughout the fins, particularly the dorsal, anal, and caudal fins. Mature, well-conditioned fish can develop extremely vivid orange finnage that contrasts beautifully against the dark body pattern and metallic golden background. Depending on the individual, the markings along the flanks may range from distinct spots to irregular broken stripes, giving each fish a slightly different appearance. A tank of at least 20 gallons is recommended for a proper school, with longer aquariums preferred because of their energetic swimming behavior. Orange Finned Kyathit Danios should be maintained in groups of at least six, although eight to twelve or more creates a much more impressive display and encourages natural social behavior. The aquarium should provide plenty of open swimming space combined with plants, driftwood, rounded stones, and areas of moderate current. A secure lid is strongly recommended, as these active danios are capable jumpers. Water conditions should remain clean and well oxygenated. Temperatures between 68 and 78 degrees Fahrenheit are ideal, making this species somewhat better suited to cooler conditions than many typical tropical community fish. A pH range of approximately 6.0 to 7.5 and soft to moderately hard water are appropriate. Moderate water movement, strong filtration, and regular water changes help replicate the clean, flowing streams of their native habitat. Orange Finned Kyathit Danios are omnivorous and easy to feed. In nature they consume small insects, insect larvae, crustaceans, zooplankton, and other tiny aquatic organisms. In the aquarium they readily accept quality flakes, micro-pellets, frozen daphnia, cyclops, brine shrimp, bloodworms, and other appropriately sized foods. Regular frozen or live foods help bring out the strongest orange coloration in the fins and keep the fish in excellent breeding condition. Temperament is peaceful but extremely active. Orange Finned Kyathit Danios make excellent community fish with other energetic, non-aggressive species that appreciate similar temperatures and water movement. Suitable tankmates include other danios, rasboras, small barbs, hillstream loaches, peaceful catfish, and similarly active community species. Very slow-moving or timid fish may be overwhelmed by their constant activity, particularly at feeding time. Breeding is possible in captivity and follows the typical danio pattern. They are egg scatterers that release small adhesive eggs among fine-leaved plants, mosses, or spawning media. Adults provide no parental care and will readily consume eggs and fry, so a separate breeding aquarium or protective spawning substrate is recommended when attempting to raise offspring. Fry initially require very small foods before graduating to newly hatched brine shrimp. Danio kyathit is an outstanding alternative to more familiar danio species, combining the hardiness and energetic schooling behavior of the group with an intricate spotted pattern and brilliant orange-red finnage. When maintained in a large school with clean, oxygen-rich water, the Orange Finned Kyathit Danio creates a constantly moving display of gold, dark patterning, and fiery orange color.

The Rainbow Shark, scientifically known as Epalzeorhynchos frenatum, is a popular freshwater fish prized for its striking appearance and active behavior. Native to rivers, streams, and floodplains in Southeast Asia, including Thailand, Laos, and Cambodia, this fish is known for its vibrant red fins and sleek, shark-like body. Rainbow Sharks are a great addition to larger aquariums with compatible tank mates, though their territorial nature requires careful planning. Physically, the Rainbow Shark has a streamlined body that is typically dark gray to black, contrasting beautifully with its bright red or orange fins. Some variations, such as the albino Rainbow Shark, have a pale body but retain the same vibrant fins. Adults typically grow to about 6 inches (15 centimeters) in length, requiring ample space to thrive. In the aquarium, Rainbow Sharks are bottom-dwelling fish that enjoy exploring and staking out territories. A tank of at least 50 gallons is recommended to provide enough space and reduce territorial aggression. The tank should include caves, rocks, and driftwood to create hiding spots and allow the Rainbow Shark to establish its own territory. While they appreciate some open swimming areas, they also thrive in aquariums with dense vegetation that mimics their natural habitat. Water parameters for Rainbow Sharks should replicate their natural environment. They prefer slightly acidic to neutral water with a pH range of 6.5 to 7.5 and temperatures between 72 to 79°F (22 to 26°C). Maintaining clean, well-oxygenated water is essential, as poor water quality can stress them and lead to health issues. Regular water changes and efficient filtration are crucial. Feeding Rainbow Sharks is straightforward, as they are omnivorous and will accept a variety of foods. They thrive on a diet of high-quality sinking pellets or wafers, supplemented with live or frozen foods such as bloodworms, brine shrimp, and daphnia. Additionally, they will graze on algae and enjoy vegetable matter, so offering blanched spinach, zucchini, or spirulina-based foods ensures a balanced diet. Rainbow Sharks can be semi-aggressive, especially toward fish that encroach on their territory. They are best kept with tank mates that are similarly sized and active, such as barbs, danios, or other robust species. Avoid housing them with slow-moving or bottom-dwelling fish, as Rainbow Sharks may chase or bully them. Keeping only one Rainbow Shark per tank is advisable unless the tank is very large, as they can be territorial with their own kind. Breeding Rainbow Sharks in captivity is rare and difficult. They are egg scatterers in the wild, but replicating their breeding conditions, including specific water parameters and spawning triggers, has proven challenging in home aquariums. Most Rainbow Sharks available in the aquarium trade are commercially bred. Overall, the Rainbow Shark (Epalzeorhynchos frenatum) is a stunning and energetic addition to freshwater aquariums. With its bold coloration and dynamic behavior, it can become a focal point in any setup. Providing adequate space, suitable tank mates, and a well-maintained environment ensures these fish can thrive and showcase their unique personality.

Black Ruby Barb, Pethia nigrofasciata, is a beautifully colored cyprinid native to Sri Lanka, where it is naturally found in forested streams of the island’s southwestern wet zone. It inhabits clear, shaded waterways with gentle to moderate current, sandy or gravel substrates, leaf litter, submerged wood, and dense riparian vegetation. These streams are typically cool to moderately warm, well oxygenated, and relatively soft, making the species particularly well suited to planted aquariums with clean, flowing water. Adult Black Ruby Barbs typically reach about 2 to 2.5 inches in length. Juveniles and females display a warm golden-yellow to silvery body crossed by several broad vertical black bands, giving them an attractive barred appearance even before males develop their mature coloration. Adult males become spectacular, particularly when displaying or in breeding condition. Much of the body darkens to deep charcoal or velvety black while the head, chest, and forward portion of the body develop intense ruby-red to crimson coloration. The dark vertical bands become partially obscured against the blackened body, while the fins can take on rich red, orange, and black tones. A group containing mature displaying males can produce an impressive combination of glowing ruby red and nearly black coloration. A tank of at least 20 to 30 gallons is recommended for a proper school, with longer aquariums preferred because these are active swimming fish. Black Ruby Barbs should be maintained in groups of at least six, although eight to twelve or more encourages more natural social behavior and creates a much stronger display. The aquarium should include plenty of open swimming space along with dense plants, driftwood, rocks, and shaded areas around the perimeter. A darker substrate and lush green plants provide an especially attractive backdrop for mature males. Water conditions should remain clean, stable, and well oxygenated. Temperatures between 68 and 79 degrees Fahrenheit are appropriate, with a pH range of approximately 6.0 to 7.5 and soft to moderately hard water. Black Ruby Barbs appreciate regular water changes and good circulation but do not require excessively strong current. They are relatively hardy once established and adapt well to typical community aquarium conditions. Black Ruby Barbs are omnivorous. In nature they consume algae, plant material, detritus, insects, crustaceans, and other small aquatic organisms. In the aquarium they readily accept quality flakes and small pellets along with frozen daphnia, brine shrimp, bloodworms, and similar foods. Vegetable-based foods and spirulina should also be included regularly. A varied diet is particularly important for developing the intense black and ruby-red coloration of mature males. Temperament is peaceful and social. Although they are active barbs, Black Ruby Barbs are generally much less prone to persistent fin nipping than some of their more boisterous relatives, particularly when maintained in an appropriately sized school. They coexist well with rasboras, danios, peaceful loaches, Corydoras, gouramis, rainbowfish, and other similarly sized community species. Males frequently display toward one another, intensifying their colors and spreading their fins, but these interactions are generally harmless. Breeding is possible in captivity. Black Ruby Barbs are egg scatterers that deposit eggs among fine-leaved plants, mosses, or spawning media. Adults provide no parental care and may consume both eggs and newly hatched fry, so breeders typically separate the adults after spawning. Conditioning adults with a varied diet and providing clean, slightly softer water can encourage spawning. Pethia nigrofasciata is one of the most dramatically colored barb species available in the aquarium hobby. The transformation of mature males from golden, vertically barred juveniles into intensely ruby-red and velvety black adults is spectacular, while their peaceful temperament and manageable size make them considerably easier to incorporate into community aquariums than many aquarists expect from a barb.

Licorice Gourami ‘Sentang’, Parosphromenus sp. ‘Sentang’, is a rare wild labyrinth fish from Indonesia associated with the Sentang region of Sumatra. Like other members of the genus Parosphromenus, it inhabits heavily shaded peat-swamp forests and extremely slow-moving blackwater streams where the substrate is covered with decomposing leaves, branches, roots, and other organic material. These habitats contain exceptionally soft, acidic, tannin-stained water and are among the most specialized freshwater environments in Southeast Asia. Adult Licorice Gourami ‘Sentang’ typically reaches only about 1.5 inches in length. Despite its tiny size, mature males can be spectacular. The body is slender and dark brown to nearly black, crossed by lighter cream to tan horizontal striping that can become more or less pronounced depending on mood. During display, males darken dramatically and spread their ornate fins, revealing brilliant blue-green to turquoise iridescence contrasted by deep red, burgundy, and black coloration. The dorsal, anal, and caudal fins can appear almost jewel-like when fully extended, with metallic blue-green bands glowing against the darker fin membranes. Females are considerably more subdued, generally displaying brown, beige, and cream coloration, although their pattern can change dramatically during courtship and breeding. A tank of at least 10 gallons is suitable for a pair or small group, although larger aquariums provide greater stability and make maintaining multiple territories easier. The aquarium should be heavily structured with driftwood, fine branches, leaf litter, caves, and dense plant cover. Small caves, overturned coconut shells, film canisters, or similar enclosed spaces provide important spawning territories. Floating plants help diffuse the lighting, and the aquarium should remain relatively dim. Water movement should be extremely gentle, and a tightly fitted lid helps maintain the warm, humid layer of air required by labyrinth fishes. Water chemistry is critical for long-term success. Temperatures between 74 and 80 degrees Fahrenheit are appropriate, with very soft, acidic water strongly preferred. A pH between approximately 4.0 and 6.0 is ideal, with extremely low carbonate hardness and low conductivity. Reverse-osmosis water is often the easiest starting point for maintaining appropriate conditions. Leaf litter, peat, seed pods, and other botanicals can be used to introduce tannins and humic substances while recreating the dark blackwater conditions these fish naturally inhabit. Stability and excellent water quality are essential. Licorice Gourami ‘Sentang’ is a micropredator and can be considerably more particular about food than common gouramis. In nature it feeds on tiny crustaceans, insect larvae, worms, and other minute aquatic invertebrates. Live foods such as baby brine shrimp, daphnia, grindal worms, mosquito larvae, and similar appropriately sized prey are ideal. Frozen foods may also be accepted, but many wild specimens are reluctant to recognize flakes or pellets as food. Aquarists should be prepared to provide live or frozen foods regularly. Temperament is peaceful but territorial, particularly among males. Parosphromenus are not well suited to typical community aquariums because their small size, deliberate feeding behavior, and specialized water requirements allow more active fish to easily outcompete them. Licorice Gourami ‘Sentang’ is best maintained in a species-focused aquarium or alongside only extremely small, peaceful blackwater species that will not compete aggressively for food. Multiple males can sometimes be maintained together in larger, densely structured aquariums where each can establish its own territory. Breeding is possible under appropriate blackwater conditions and is one of the most fascinating aspects of keeping Parosphromenus. Pairs typically spawn inside tiny caves or other enclosed spaces. The male establishes and defends the spawning site and tends the eggs, often maintaining a small bubble nest within the cave. After hatching, the larvae remain inside the spawning site until they become free-swimming. The fry are extremely small and initially require microscopic foods before progressing to newly hatched brine shrimp. Parosphromenus sp. ‘Sentang’ is an exceptional fish for aquarists interested in rare Southeast Asian blackwater species. Its tiny size hides an extraordinary amount of color, with displaying males transforming from understated brown fish into brilliant combinations of turquoise, blue-green, crimson, and black. The Licorice Gourami ‘Sentang’ does require specialized water and feeding compared with common gouramis, but in a carefully maintained blackwater aquarium its coloration, courtship displays, and fascinating behavior make it an incredibly rewarding species.

Licorice Gourami ‘Gelam’, Parosphromenus sp. ‘Gelam’, is a rare wild labyrinth fish from Indonesia associated with peat-swamp habitats on Sumatra. Like other members of the genus Parosphromenus, it inhabits extremely slow-moving blackwater streams and pools within lowland peat-swamp forest. These environments are heavily shaded and filled with submerged roots, branches, and deep accumulations of decomposing leaf litter. The water is typically darkly stained with tannins, extremely soft, highly acidic, and very low in dissolved minerals. Adult Licorice Gourami ‘Gelam’ typically reaches only about 1.5 inches in length. The body is slender and elongated with a dark chocolate-brown to nearly black base crossed by lighter cream to golden horizontal bands. Mature males become dramatically more colorful when displaying, darkening through the body while spreading their ornate dorsal, anal, and caudal fins. The fins develop brilliant metallic blue to turquoise-green iridescence contrasted against deep burgundy, reddish-brown, and black areas, creating an intense jewel-like appearance. The exact intensity and arrangement of these colors can vary with mood, lighting, and individual fish. Females are generally more understated, displaying softer brown, beige, and cream tones, although their coloration also changes noticeably during courtship and spawning. A tank of at least 10 gallons is suitable for a pair or small group, although larger aquariums provide greater water stability and make maintaining multiple territories easier. The aquarium should be heavily structured with driftwood, fine branches, abundant leaf litter, caves, and dense plant cover. Small enclosed caves are particularly important because they provide spawning territories for males. Floating plants help create the dimly lit environment these fish prefer. Water movement should remain extremely gentle, and a tightly fitted lid helps maintain warm, humid air above the water surface. Water chemistry is particularly important for Licorice Gourami ‘Gelam’. Temperatures between 74 and 80 degrees Fahrenheit are appropriate, with extremely soft, acidic water strongly preferred. A pH between approximately 4.0 and 6.0 is ideal, along with very low carbonate hardness and low conductivity. Reverse-osmosis water is often the easiest starting point for recreating these conditions. Leaf litter, peat, seed pods, and other botanicals can be used to introduce tannins and humic substances while recreating the naturally dark blackwater environment. Stability and excellent water quality are more important than attempting to constantly adjust parameters. Licorice Gourami ‘Gelam’ is a micropredator that naturally feeds on tiny crustaceans, insect larvae, worms, and other minute aquatic invertebrates. Live foods such as baby brine shrimp, daphnia, grindal worms, mosquito larvae, and similar small prey are ideal. Frozen foods may also be accepted, particularly after the fish become established, but many wild Parosphromenus are reluctant to recognize dry flakes or pellets as food. Aquarists should be prepared to provide live and frozen foods regularly. Temperament is peaceful but territorial, particularly among mature males. Parosphromenus are generally poor candidates for conventional community aquariums because their tiny size, deliberate feeding behavior, and specialized water requirements allow more active fish to easily outcompete them. Licorice Gourami ‘Gelam’ is best maintained in a species-focused aquarium or alongside only extremely small, peaceful blackwater species that will not compete aggressively for food. Multiple males can be maintained in larger, densely structured aquariums when enough separate territories are available. Breeding is possible under appropriate conditions and provides some of the most fascinating behavior seen among small labyrinth fishes. Pairs typically spawn inside tiny caves or other enclosed spaces selected and defended by the male. The male tends the eggs and developing larvae, usually maintaining a small bubble nest within the spawning cavity. After hatching, the larvae remain inside until they become free-swimming. The fry are extremely small and initially require microscopic foods before progressing to newly hatched brine shrimp. Parosphromenus sp. ‘Gelam’ is an exceptional licorice gourami for aquarists interested in rare and specialized Southeast Asian blackwater fish. Its understated appearance transforms completely during display, when mature males reveal brilliant turquoise-blue iridescence against deep red, burgundy, and black finnage. With extremely soft acidic water, abundant cover, and appropriate foods, the Licorice Gourami ‘Gelam’ rewards careful husbandry with extraordinary coloration and fascinating natural behavior.

Geophagus sp. “Alto Sinú” is a distinctive South American eartheater cichlid originating from the upper Río Sinú drainage of northwestern Colombia. The Río Sinú is an independent Caribbean-draining river system west of the Andes, geographically isolated from the Amazon and Orinoco basins that are home to many better-known Geophagus species. This locality makes the Alto Sinú Geophagus an especially interesting fish for aquarists interested in uncommon South American cichlids and geographically accurate biotope aquariums. Adult Geophagus sp. “Alto Sinú” can reach approximately 7 to 9 inches in length, with mature males generally becoming larger and developing more elaborate finnage than females. The body is moderately deep and laterally compressed with the sloping forehead and downward-oriented mouth characteristic of eartheaters. Base coloration ranges from silver and pale gold to warm olive, overlaid with beautiful metallic blue-green and turquoise iridescence across the scales. A prominent dark lateral blotch provides strong contrast along the flank, while the face develops brilliant blue-green lines and spotting. Mature fish can show warm orange, red, and yellow coloration through the dorsal, anal, and caudal fins, with males developing elongated fin extensions as they mature. Their coloration becomes substantially richer with age and condition, making fully grown specimens considerably more impressive than juveniles. A tank of at least 75 gallons is recommended for a small group of juveniles, with 125 gallons or larger preferred for a mature group. Geophagus are social cichlids and generally display their most natural behavior when maintained in groups rather than singly. Floor space is especially important because these fish spend much of their time foraging along the bottom. Fine sand is essential, as they repeatedly take mouthfuls of substrate, sift edible material through their gills, and discard the cleaned sand. Coarse or sharp gravel prevents this natural behavior and can damage the mouth and gill structures. Driftwood, branches, smooth rocks, and open expanses of sand create an excellent environment. Water conditions should remain warm, clean, and well oxygenated. Temperatures between 76 and 82 degrees Fahrenheit are appropriate, with a pH range of approximately 6.0 to 7.5 and soft to moderately hard water. Strong biological filtration and substantial regular water changes are particularly important because Geophagus constantly disturb the substrate while feeding and can produce a considerable bioload as they mature. Geophagus sp. “Alto Sinú” is an omnivorous benthic feeder. In nature, these fish continuously sift sand for insect larvae, small crustaceans, worms, organic material, seeds, and other edible items. In the aquarium they readily accept high-quality sinking pellets, frozen bloodworms, mysis shrimp, brine shrimp, chopped shrimp, and other appropriately sized foods. Several smaller feedings are preferable to a single large meal because their natural feeding strategy involves continuously searching the substrate for small food items. Temperament is generally peaceful for a cichlid of this size. Alto Sinú Geophagus spend much of their time interacting socially and sifting the substrate rather than aggressively defending large territories. Some dominance behavior and chasing should be expected within a group, particularly as fish mature and pairs begin forming. They make excellent companions for appropriately sized tetras, larger characins, peaceful catfish, and other relatively calm South American cichlids. Very aggressive Central American cichlids and other highly territorial species should be avoided. Breeding behavior follows the highly developed parental strategies characteristic of Geophagus. Compatible adults form pairs and become more territorial as spawning approaches. Eggs are deposited and fertilized on a carefully cleaned surface, after which the parents protect the developing offspring. Depending on the reproductive behavior expressed by this particular population, developing larvae or fry may also be taken into the mouth for protection. Both parents participate extensively in brood defense, and a breeding pair may aggressively exclude other fish from the immediate spawning territory. Geophagus sp. “Alto Sinú” is an uncommon and impressive Colombian eartheater that combines beautiful metallic coloration with the endlessly fascinating sand-sifting behavior that makes Geophagus so popular. Its isolated origin in the upper Río Sinú drainage, graceful social behavior, increasingly vivid coloration with maturity, and engaging parental care make the Alto Sinú Geophagus an exceptional centerpiece for a large South American aquarium.

Rosy Cichlid, Panamius panamensis, is a distinctive Central American cichlid endemic to Panama. It occurs in Pacific-slope river systems of central Panama, where it inhabits streams and rivers with moderate current, rocky and sandy substrates, submerged wood, and quieter areas along the margins. Its restricted natural distribution and relative rarity in the aquarium hobby make it an especially interesting species for aquarists looking beyond the more commonly available Central American cichlids. Adult Rosy Cichlids typically reach about 5 to 6 inches in length, making them considerably more manageable than many larger Central American cichlids. The body is moderately deep and robust with a rounded head and substantial lips. Base coloration ranges from silvery gray and beige to warm olive and golden tones, but mature, well-conditioned fish develop the beautiful rosy pink to reddish coloration responsible for their common name. Dark vertical barring and a prominent mid-body blotch provide contrast across the flanks, while subtle turquoise to blue-green iridescence can appear across the face and scales. During courtship and breeding, the warm pink, rose, and reddish tones intensify considerably, transforming mature fish into especially attractive display animals. A tank of at least 55 gallons is recommended for a single adult or compatible pair, with larger aquariums preferred for community setups. The aquarium should provide open swimming areas combined with substantial rockwork, driftwood, caves, and other structures that allow territories to be established and break lines of sight. Sand or fine gravel works well as substrate. Plants can be incorporated, although mature fish may dig and rearrange the substrate, particularly when preparing to spawn. Water conditions should remain clean, stable, and well oxygenated. Temperatures between 74 and 80 degrees Fahrenheit are appropriate, with a pH range of approximately 6.5 to 8.0 and moderately soft to moderately hard water. Rosy Cichlids are relatively adaptable, but strong biological filtration and regular water changes are important for maintaining excellent long-term health and coloration. Panamius panamensis is an omnivore that naturally consumes aquatic insects, crustaceans, worms, algae, plant material, and other available foods. In the aquarium it readily accepts high-quality cichlid pellets, frozen bloodworms, mysis shrimp, brine shrimp, chopped shrimp, spirulina-based foods, and vegetable matter. A varied diet containing both animal and plant-based foods supports healthy growth, rich coloration, and breeding condition. Temperament is moderately territorial but generally manageable for a Central American cichlid. Rosy Cichlids are confident and assertive, particularly toward other cichlids occupying the same areas of the aquarium, but they are not typically among the extremely aggressive species associated with some larger Central American cichlids. Appropriate tankmates include similarly sized, robust fish capable of handling normal cichlid territorial behavior. Adequate space and visual barriers become particularly important once a pair begins breeding. Breeding is readily achievable once a compatible pair forms. Rosy Cichlids are biparental substrate spawners, with pairs selecting and cleaning rocks, caves, or other protected surfaces before depositing their eggs. Both parents vigorously defend the eggs and developing fry, and their rosy coloration and territorial behavior intensify significantly during this period. Watching a pair actively shepherd and protect a school of fry is one of the most rewarding aspects of keeping the species. Panamius panamensis is an excellent choice for aquarists who enjoy the personality and parental behavior of Central American cichlids but want something less commonly encountered and more manageable than the region's giant species. Its warm rosy coloration, manageable adult size, fascinating breeding behavior, and restricted Panamanian distribution make the Rosy Cichlid a distinctive and rewarding centerpiece for a carefully planned Central American aquarium.

listings.commonName: Blue Star Endler's Livebearer Pairs-Locally Bred
listings.description: Endler’s Livebearer, scientifically known as Poecilia wingei, is a small, colorful livebearing fish native to shallow, freshwater lagoons and streams in Venezuela, particularly around the Cumana region and Laguna de Patos. Aquarists prize this species for its vibrant colors, ease of care, peaceful temperament, and lively behavior, making it highly popular in planted and community aquariums. Physically, Poecilia wingei males are notably smaller, typically reaching around 1 inch (2.5 centimeters), and display vibrant coloration, including iridescent shades of red, green, orange, black, and blue. Females are larger, reaching up to 1.5 inches (3.8 centimeters), and exhibit a more subdued coloration—typically olive-gray or tan. This sexual dimorphism makes distinguishing between sexes straightforward. In the aquarium, Endler’s Livebearers thrive in setups that closely replicate their natural habitat. A minimum aquarium size of 10 gallons is suitable for a small group, but larger tanks are advisable to accommodate their active swimming behavior. Providing ample vegetation, including dense live plants, along with open swimming areas, helps them feel secure and encourages natural behaviors. Gentle water flow and stable conditions are beneficial to their long-term health. Suitable water parameters include a temperature range of 72 to 82°F (22 to 28°C), a pH between 6.7 and 8.0, and moderately hard water. Regular water changes and good filtration are essential, as these fish are sensitive to poor water quality. Feeding Poecilia wingei is straightforward, as they eagerly accept high-quality flakes, micro-pellets, freeze-dried, frozen, or live foods like brine shrimp, daphnia, and microworms. Providing a varied diet ensures optimal health, coloration, and vigor. Endler’s Livebearers are peaceful, active fish ideal for community aquariums. Compatible tank mates include similarly sized peaceful species such as small tetras, rasboras, dwarf corydoras, shrimp, and small snails. It is advisable to avoid larger, aggressive, or fin-nipping species. Breeding Poecilia wingei is exceptionally easy and occurs naturally without special intervention. As livebearers, females give birth to fully developed fry approximately every 23 to 30 days. To improve fry survival rates, provide dense plant cover or separate breeding tanks, as adult fish, including parents, may occasionally prey on their young. Fry readily accept finely crushed flake foods, baby brine shrimp, or microworms from birth. Overall, Poecilia wingei (Endler’s Livebearer) is a colorful, hardy, and lively fish ideally suited for aquarists of all skill levels. Their attractive appearance, easy care, and lively behaviors make them a popular choice for hobbyists interested in maintaining peaceful, vibrant, and engaging community aquariums.

Limia perugiae, commonly known as Perugia’s Limia, is a colorful livebearing fish endemic to the Dominican Republic on the island of Hispaniola. It occurs primarily in freshwater habitats of the southern Dominican Republic, where it inhabits streams, rivers, springs, ponds, and other shallow waters with aquatic vegetation and areas of gentle to moderate current. Like many Limia, it naturally occurs in warm, mineral-rich water and is particularly well suited to aquariums maintained on the harder, more alkaline side. Adult Limia perugiae typically reaches about 2.5 to 3 inches in length, with females becoming noticeably larger and heavier-bodied than males. Mature males are especially attractive, displaying a silvery to pale golden body covered with numerous dark vertical bars that create a bold tiger-like pattern along the flanks. Depending on lighting and condition, the scales can develop beautiful blue, green, and golden iridescence, while the dorsal and caudal fins may show yellow, orange, and darker markings. Males also possess the modified anal fin, or gonopodium, characteristic of livebearers. Females are larger and more robust, with a softer silver-gray to olive coloration and less intense patterning. Mature males displaying together can become remarkably colorful and are considerably more striking than their relatively understated appearance in dealer tanks might suggest. A tank of at least 20 gallons is suitable for a small group, although 30 gallons or larger is preferable for an established colony. Limia perugiae is an active, social livebearer and does particularly well when maintained with multiple females for each male. The aquarium should provide open swimming space combined with dense plants, floating vegetation, driftwood, and other cover. Thick plant growth also provides important refuge for newborn fry and greatly increases juvenile survival. Water conditions should remain warm, stable, and mineral-rich. Temperatures between 72 and 80 degrees Fahrenheit are appropriate, with a pH range of approximately 7.0 to 8.2 and moderate to hard water preferred. Like mollies and many other Caribbean livebearers, Limia perugiae generally performs much better in water containing adequate calcium and magnesium than in extremely soft, acidic conditions. Salt is not required for successful maintenance. Limia perugiae is an omnivorous grazer that naturally consumes algae, biofilm, plant material, small crustaceans, insect larvae, and other available foods. In the aquarium it readily accepts quality flakes, small pellets, spirulina-based foods, frozen daphnia, brine shrimp, bloodworms, and blanched vegetables. Providing plenty of vegetable matter and algae-based foods alongside protein-rich foods helps maintain excellent body condition, coloration, and reproductive health. Temperament is peaceful, active, and community-friendly. Perugia’s Limia can be maintained with other peaceful livebearers, rainbowfish, robust tetras, peaceful barbs, Corydoras, and other species that appreciate similar water chemistry. Males frequently display toward females and one another but serious aggression is uncommon when adequate space and cover are provided. Breeding is extremely straightforward. Limia perugiae is a livebearer, with females giving birth to fully formed, free-swimming fry rather than laying eggs. Females can produce broods regularly once mature, and dense vegetation provides young fish with protection from adults. Fry are relatively large at birth and readily accept finely crushed flakes, powdered foods, and newly hatched brine shrimp. Given suitable conditions, a small starter group can develop into an active breeding colony. Limia perugiae is an underrated Caribbean livebearer that combines the ease and activity of familiar mollies and guppies with a much less commonly encountered wild-species appearance. The bold vertical patterning, metallic blue-gold sheen of mature males, peaceful personality, and easy breeding make Perugia’s Limia an excellent choice for planted community aquariums and aquarists interested in unusual livebearers.

Joka Cichlid, Coelotilapia joka, is a distinctive West African cichlid native to coastal river systems of Sierra Leone and Liberia. It inhabits clear to lightly stained forest streams and rivers with rocky areas, submerged wood, sandy substrates, and abundant cover along the banks. These tropical waterways are typically warm, soft to moderately hard, and well oxygenated. Its relatively restricted distribution and uncommon appearance in the aquarium trade make Coelotilapia joka an especially interesting species for aquarists interested in West African cichlids. Adult Joka Cichlids typically reach about 4 to 5 inches in length. The body is elongated and moderately deep with a rounded head and substantial lips. Their coloration is particularly attractive, with a pale cream, yellowish, or golden base crossed by several broad, dark brown to nearly black vertical bands. The contrasting bands extend through much of the body and create a bold, almost zebra-like appearance. Depending on mood and condition, the lighter areas can become noticeably warmer and more golden, while the dark bars intensify dramatically. Mature males generally become larger and more robust, while females remain somewhat smaller and can develop especially strong coloration during breeding. A tank of at least 40 gallons is recommended for a compatible pair, with larger aquariums preferred for community setups or multiple individuals. The aquarium should provide plenty of structure using driftwood, rocks, caves, and dense planting while still leaving open areas for swimming and foraging. Sand or fine gravel works well as substrate. Visual barriers are especially important because these fish establish territories and appreciate secure retreats. Water conditions should remain clean, stable, and well oxygenated. Temperatures between 74 and 80 degrees Fahrenheit are appropriate, with a pH range of approximately 6.0 to 7.5 and soft to moderately hard water. Regular water changes and good biological filtration are important, particularly when maintaining breeding adults. Gentle to moderate water movement works well and helps replicate their naturally flowing stream habitats. Coelotilapia joka is an omnivore that naturally feeds on algae, aufwuchs, small invertebrates, insect larvae, crustaceans, and other organic material collected from rocks and submerged surfaces. In the aquarium it readily accepts high-quality cichlid pellets, spirulina-based foods, frozen brine shrimp, mysis shrimp, bloodworms, and other appropriately sized foods. Including vegetable and algae-based foods alongside meaty offerings provides a balanced diet and helps maintain excellent condition. Temperament is generally moderate but territorial, particularly between adults and during breeding. Joka Cichlids can be maintained with appropriately sized, peaceful to moderately assertive West African and community species, but adequate space and visual barriers are important. Established pairs may vigorously defend their territory, so timid or very small tankmates should be avoided in confined aquariums. Breeding is possible in captivity and is one of the most interesting aspects of keeping the species. Coelotilapia joka forms pairs and uses protected areas among rocks, caves, and other structures for reproduction. Both parents participate in caring for and defending their offspring, becoming significantly more territorial once fry are present. Providing several potential spawning sites allows a pair to select a secure territory while reducing stress. Coelotilapia joka is an uncommon and beautifully patterned West African cichlid whose bold dark barring and warm cream-to-golden coloration immediately set it apart from more familiar aquarium cichlids. Its manageable adult size, fascinating pair behavior, and restricted West African distribution make the Joka Cichlid an excellent centerpiece for aquarists seeking something genuinely different.

listings.description: Bamboo Shrimp, Atyopsis moluccensis, is a large freshwater filter-feeding shrimp native to Southeast Asia, with a natural distribution that includes Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, and surrounding regions. It inhabits clear streams and rivers with moderate to strong current, where individuals position themselves on rocks, submerged wood, roots, and other elevated surfaces to capture microscopic food carried downstream. These habitats are typically warm, clean, highly oxygenated, and rich in suspended organic material. Adult Bamboo Shrimp typically reach about 2.5 to 4 inches in length, making them considerably larger and more substantial than common dwarf shrimp such as Neocaridina and Caridina varieties. The body is robust and usually displays warm shades of reddish brown, rust, tan, orange-brown, or earthy brown, often with a lighter cream or yellowish stripe running along the back. Coloration can change considerably depending on the individual, surroundings, diet, and molt cycle. Their most distinctive feature is the pair of specialized fan-like feeding appendages at the front of the body. When feeding, the shrimp spreads these delicate fans directly into the current, periodically folding them toward the mouth to consume the captured particles. This unusual behavior makes Bamboo Shrimp fascinating to watch even in a busy community aquarium. A mature aquarium of at least 20 gallons is recommended, with larger tanks providing greater stability and more opportunities for natural feeding behavior. Water flow is particularly important. The aquarium should include moderate to strong current along with rocks, driftwood, branches, or other elevated perches positioned directly in the flow. Once comfortable, Bamboo Shrimp often select a favorite perch and spend hours sitting in the current with their feeding fans fully extended. Caves, wood, and shaded retreats should also be provided for use during molting. Water conditions should remain stable, clean, and well oxygenated. Temperatures between 72 and 82 degrees Fahrenheit are appropriate, with a pH range of approximately 6.5 to 7.8 and soft to moderately hard water. Bamboo Shrimp are sensitive to deteriorating water quality and sudden parameter changes, particularly around molting. Copper-based medications should be avoided, as copper can be toxic to shrimp and other aquatic invertebrates. Feeding Bamboo Shrimp differs considerably from feeding typical dwarf shrimp. They are specialized suspension feeders that capture microscopic algae, microorganisms, fine detritus, and other tiny organic particles directly from the water column. A mature aquarium with abundant natural microorganisms provides an important foundation, but supplemental feeding is often necessary. Finely powdered shrimp foods, crushed flakes, powdered spirulina, fry foods, and other very fine foods can be released upstream so the current carries them through the shrimp's feeding fans. If a Bamboo Shrimp is repeatedly scraping the substrate with its fans instead of filtering from the current, it can be a sign that insufficient suspended food is available. Temperament is exceptionally peaceful. Bamboo Shrimp have no claws designed for catching fish and pose essentially no threat to healthy tankmates. They coexist well with peaceful tetras, rasboras, danios, Corydoras, Otocinclus, small gouramis, peaceful loaches, dwarf shrimp, and snails. Large or predatory fish should be avoided, particularly because Bamboo Shrimp are extremely vulnerable immediately after molting. Breeding is extremely difficult in captivity because Bamboo Shrimp have an amphidromous life cycle. Females can carry large numbers of eggs in freshwater, but the newly hatched larvae require brackish to marine conditions for development before eventually transitioning back into freshwater. As a result, establishing a self-sustaining population in a normal freshwater aquarium is highly unlikely. Atyopsis moluccensis is one of the most fascinating freshwater shrimp available, offering behavior completely different from conventional algae-grazing dwarf shrimp. Its impressive size, peaceful temperament, constantly waving feeding fans, and habit of positioning itself dramatically in flowing water make the Bamboo Shrimp an outstanding addition to mature community aquariums with good current and plenty of suspended microscopic food.

Vallisneria ‘Contortionist’ is a distinctive cultivated form of Vallisneria prized for its dramatically twisted, corkscrew-like foliage. Like other Vallisneria, its ancestry traces to freshwater habitats where these plants grow rooted in the substrates of rivers, lakes, streams, and other shallow waterways. The ‘Contortionist’ form is cultivated specifically for aquarium use and is valued for providing the durability and easy care of Vallisneria with a much more unusual appearance than traditional straight-leaved varieties. In the aquarium, Vallisneria ‘Contortionist’ produces long, narrow, ribbon-like leaves that twist, curl, and contort as they grow upward through the water column. Rather than forming uniform spirals, the leaves develop irregular waves and corkscrew-like bends that give each plant a highly textured, almost sculptural appearance. The foliage ranges from bright to deep green, and established plants form dense stands of twisting leaves that move beautifully in the aquarium current. Depending on growing conditions, mature leaves can reach approximately 12 to 24 inches or more in length, making this an excellent midground or background plant. Vallisneria ‘Contortionist’ should be planted directly into the substrate with the roots buried while leaving the crown exposed. Burying the crown can cause the plant to decline or rot. Moderate lighting is sufficient for healthy growth, although stronger lighting generally produces denser stands and more compact, strongly twisted foliage. Once established, the plant spreads horizontally through runners and can gradually develop into an impressive colony. Water conditions are highly flexible. Temperatures between 68 and 82 degrees Fahrenheit are appropriate, with a pH range of approximately 6.5 to 8.0 and soft to hard water. Like other Vallisneria, ‘Contortionist’ often performs particularly well in water containing adequate calcium and other minerals. Its adaptability makes it suitable for a wide range of community and planted aquarium setups. Vallisneria ‘Contortionist’ is primarily a root feeder and benefits from a nutrient-rich substrate or regular root tab supplementation when grown in inert sand or gravel. CO₂ injection is not required, making it an excellent choice for low-tech planted aquariums, although supplemental CO₂ and balanced fertilization can accelerate growth and runner production. Liquid carbon products containing glutaraldehyde should be used cautiously, as Vallisneria can be particularly sensitive to them and may experience significant leaf melt. Newly planted Vallisneria may occasionally shed older leaves while adapting to different aquarium conditions. Once established, fresh growth emerges from the center of the crown and the plant generally becomes extremely hardy. Older or damaged leaves should be removed at their base rather than trimmed midway, as cut leaf tips usually do not repair themselves attractively. Propagation occurs naturally through runners. Established plants send horizontal shoots beneath or across the substrate, producing daughter plants at intervals. Once the daughter plants have developed several leaves and their own root systems, they can be separated and replanted or simply allowed to remain attached and develop into a dense stand. Vallisneria ‘Contortionist’ is compatible with virtually all peaceful freshwater fish and invertebrates. Its dense twisting foliage provides excellent shelter for fry, shrimp, and timid fish while creating vertical structure throughout the aquarium. The long leaves are particularly attractive in moderate current, where their contorted shape produces considerably more movement and texture than standard Vallisneria. Vallisneria ‘Contortionist’ is an excellent choice for aquarists who want the reliability and simplicity of Vallisneria with a much more dramatic appearance. Its unusual twisting foliage, easy care requirements, rapid runner-based propagation, and ability to thrive without injected CO₂ make it a striking and practical background plant for freshwater aquariums.

Polar Blue Parrot Cichlid, commonly sold as the Polar Blue Parrot or Polar Parrot Cichlid, is a selectively bred hybrid Central American cichlid. It is generally considered to have been developed using Convict Cichlid lineage together with Blood Parrot-type hybrid stock, although the exact breeding history of the strain is not formally documented. Unlike naturally occurring cichlid species, the Polar Blue Parrot has no wild distribution and was developed specifically for the ornamental aquarium trade. Adult Polar Blue Parrot Cichlids typically reach about 4 to 5 inches in length, giving them a much more manageable adult size than traditional Blood Parrot Cichlids. Their appearance combines the compact, rounded body of a parrot-type cichlid with the bold barring of a Convict Cichlid. The body is typically icy blue, powder blue, blue-gray, or silvery blue and is crossed by a series of dark charcoal to black vertical bars. Many specimens develop beautiful turquoise or pearlescent iridescence across the scales, particularly around the face and gill plates. Their rounded forehead, large expressive eyes, short body, and small parrot-like mouth give them an unmistakable appearance, while the blue coloration and dark barring create excellent contrast. A tank of at least 30 gallons is recommended for a single specimen or compatible pair, with 40 to 55 gallons or larger preferred for groups or community setups. The aquarium should provide caves, driftwood, rockwork, and other structures that allow individuals to establish territories and break lines of sight. Sand or fine gravel works well as substrate. These fish frequently dig, move substrate, and rearrange their surroundings, particularly when breeding, so delicate plants may be uprooted. Water conditions should remain stable and clean. Temperatures between 76 and 82 degrees Fahrenheit are appropriate, with a pH range of approximately 6.5 to 8.0 and soft to moderately hard water. Polar Blue Parrots are hardy and adaptable, but good biological filtration and regular water changes are important because of their substantial appetite and cichlid-sized bioload. Feeding is straightforward. Polar Blue Parrot Cichlids are omnivorous and readily accept high-quality cichlid pellets, flakes, frozen bloodworms, brine shrimp, mysis shrimp, krill, and vegetable-based foods. Appropriately sized pellets are particularly useful because of their relatively small mouths. A varied diet supports healthy growth, strong body condition, and the best blue coloration. Temperament is best described as semi-aggressive. Polar Blue Parrots are generally confident, active, and highly interactive, but their Convict Cichlid ancestry becomes particularly apparent when they establish territories or begin breeding. They can coexist with similarly sized, robust community fish and moderately assertive cichlids, but very timid fish may be bullied. Multiple individuals should be given plenty of space, caves, and visual barriers. Unlike traditional Blood Parrot Cichlids, Polar Blue Parrots are generally fertile and can reproduce very readily in the aquarium. Compatible pairs frequently form at a young age and become devoted, highly territorial parents. Eggs are typically deposited inside caves or on cleaned surfaces, and both parents vigorously guard the eggs and fry. Once established, a pair may spawn repeatedly, and their parental behavior can be fascinating to observe. The Polar Blue Parrot Cichlid combines the unusual rounded appearance and personality of a parrot cichlid with beautiful icy blue coloration, dramatic black barring, a compact adult size, and the fascinating breeding behavior of its Central American ancestry. Hardy, colorful, and extremely interactive, the Polar Blue Parrot makes an engaging centerpiece for aquarists looking for a smaller parrot-type cichlid with plenty of personality.

Kissing Gourami, Helostoma temminckii, is a large labyrinth fish native to Southeast Asia, with a natural distribution that includes Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam, Malaysia, and Indonesia. It inhabits slow-moving rivers, floodplains, swamps, lakes, canals, and heavily vegetated wetlands where water is warm and current is generally gentle. Like other labyrinth fishes, Kissing Gouramis possess a specialized labyrinth organ that allows them to breathe atmospheric air, an adaptation that helps them thrive in shallow, oxygen-poor environments. Adult Kissing Gouramis commonly reach about 8 to 12 inches in aquariums, although exceptionally large specimens can grow even larger. Two primary color forms are commonly encountered in the hobby. The natural or green form displays a silvery green to olive-gray body, while the extremely popular pink form ranges from pale blush pink and peach to nearly creamy white. Both possess a deep, laterally compressed body with large scales, a long dorsal and anal fin, and their unmistakable thick, protruding lips. These specialized lips are lined with fine teeth used to scrape algae and other food from surfaces. The famous “kissing” behavior occurs when two fish lock mouths and push against one another. Despite its affectionate appearance, this is generally a dominance interaction rather than actual affection. A tank of at least 75 gallons is recommended for a single adult, with 100 gallons or larger strongly preferred for multiple specimens or community setups. Kissing Gouramis are active, substantial fish that require considerably more room than their small juvenile size might suggest. The aquarium should provide plenty of open swimming space along with driftwood, rocks, and sturdy plants around the perimeter. Because they naturally graze surfaces, delicate or soft-leaved plants may occasionally be damaged. Gentle to moderate water movement is appropriate, and unobstructed access to the surface must always be available so the fish can breathe atmospheric air. Water conditions should remain warm, stable, and clean. Temperatures between 74 and 82 degrees Fahrenheit are appropriate, with a pH range of approximately 6.0 to 8.0 and soft to moderately hard water. Kissing Gouramis are hardy and adaptable, but their eventual size and substantial appetite create a considerable bioload. Strong biological filtration and regular water changes are important for maintaining healthy adults. Kissing Gouramis are true omnivores with a particularly strong grazing component to their diet. In nature they consume algae, phytoplankton, zooplankton, aquatic insects, small crustaceans, and plant material while constantly rasping food from submerged surfaces. In the aquarium they readily accept quality pellets and flakes along with spirulina-based foods, algae wafers, blanched vegetables, brine shrimp, bloodworms, and other frozen foods. Providing plenty of vegetable matter is important for maintaining good long-term condition. Temperament is generally peaceful to semi-aggressive. Kissing Gouramis are not dedicated predators, but their large adult size and assertive personality can make them overwhelming for small or timid community fish. Individuals may establish dominance hierarchies, chase one another, and engage in their characteristic mouth-locking contests. They are best housed with similarly sized, peaceful to moderately assertive fish that will not be intimidated by their activity. Very small tankmates should be avoided with large adults. Breeding differs considerably from many familiar gouramis. Kissing Gouramis are egg scatterers rather than dedicated bubble-nest builders. During spawning, buoyant eggs are released near the surface, often among floating vegetation. The eggs float upward and may become trapped among plants, but the adults provide no parental care and may consume eggs or fry if given the opportunity. Fry are extremely small and initially require microscopic foods. Helostoma temminckii is one of the most recognizable gouramis in the aquarium hobby, combining impressive adult size, unusual feeding adaptations, hardy nature, and one of the most famous behaviors found among freshwater fish. Whether kept in the classic pink form or the more natural green form, the Kissing Gourami is an engaging and highly interactive centerpiece whose distinctive puckered lips and fascinating “kissing” displays make it impossible to mistake for anything else.
