Shadow Mosura Shrimp, Caridina cf. cantonensis, is a highly prized selectively bred freshwater dwarf shrimp developed from Taiwan Bee Shrimp bloodlines. This ornamental variety combines the deep, dramatic pigmentation of Shadow Bee Shrimp with the distinctive Mosura pattern, creating one of the most striking black-and-white shrimp available in the aquarium hobby. While its wild ancestors originate from freshwater streams in southern China, the Shadow Mosura is a captive-developed variety produced through generations of selective breeding for intense coloration, clean pattern definition, and exceptional contrast. Adult Shadow Mosura Shrimp typically reach about 1 to 1.25 inches in length. Their appearance is characterized by a deep black to blue-black body contrasted with brilliant opaque white markings concentrated around the head and upper body. The signature Mosura pattern features extensive white coverage over the head and thorax, often resembling a white mask or cap, while much of the abdomen remains intensely dark. Depending on the individual and breeding line, the black pigmentation may display beautiful midnight-blue, indigo, or steel-blue undertones, giving the shrimp an almost metallic appearance under aquarium lighting. High-quality specimens exhibit exceptionally clean white coverage, rich dark pigmentation, and sharply defined transitions between colors. Females generally become larger and develop a fuller, more rounded abdomen than males. A mature aquarium of at least 10 gallons is recommended, although larger aquariums provide greater stability and are generally easier to maintain. Shadow Mosura Shrimp thrive in established planted aquariums with mosses, driftwood, botanicals, porous rock, and other surfaces that encourage abundant biofilm growth. Shrimp-safe sponge filtration or protected filter intakes are strongly recommended, and plenty of hiding places should be provided for freshly molted shrimp and developing juveniles. Dark substrates and lush green plants create an especially attractive backdrop for their dramatic black-and-white coloration. Water quality and stability are particularly important for Shadow Mosura Shrimp. Temperatures between 68 and 74 degrees Fahrenheit are ideal, with a pH range of approximately 5.5 to 6.5, very low carbonate hardness, and soft water with a general hardness around 4 to 6 dGH. A KH of approximately 0 to 1 dKH is generally preferred. Many successful keepers use remineralized reverse-osmosis water along with an active buffering substrate to maintain the soft, acidic conditions favored by Taiwan Bee Caridina. Sudden fluctuations in temperature, mineral content, or other water parameters should be avoided, as these shrimp are particularly sensitive to environmental instability. Shadow Mosura Shrimp spend much of their time grazing on biofilm, algae, microorganisms, and decomposing organic material. In the aquarium they should also receive high-quality shrimp foods, algae-based foods, powdered foods for juveniles, and occasional protein-rich foods in moderation. A mature aquarium containing abundant natural biofilm is especially valuable for newly released shrimplets, which depend heavily on microscopic foods growing throughout the aquarium. Consistent nutrition supports healthy molting, strong coloration, and successful reproduction. Temperament is exceptionally peaceful. Shadow Mosura Shrimp are best maintained in dedicated Caridina aquariums or alongside other peaceful invertebrates requiring similar water conditions. Although they can coexist with carefully selected nano fish, virtually any fish capable of swallowing a shrimplet may reduce juvenile survival. A dedicated shrimp aquarium provides the best opportunity to establish a thriving breeding colony while allowing their exceptional coloration and fascinating behavior to be fully appreciated. Breeding occurs entirely in freshwater when conditions are suitable. Females carry fertilized eggs beneath the abdomen for approximately three to four weeks before releasing fully formed miniature shrimp. Unlike Amano Shrimp, Shadow Mosura Shrimp do not require a brackish larval stage. They can interbreed with other compatible Taiwan Bee and Bee Shrimp varieties, and offspring may display a range of patterns and coloration depending on the genetics of the breeding stock. Aquarists interested in maintaining a consistent Shadow Mosura line should selectively breed individuals displaying the desired pattern and pigmentation. Shadow Mosura Shrimp represent some of the finest achievements in ornamental Caridina breeding. Their dramatic black and white contrast, subtle midnight-blue undertones, distinctive Mosura pattern, and peaceful colony behavior make them an extraordinary addition to dedicated shrimp aquariums. For aquarists seeking a premium ornamental shrimp with exceptional patterning and visual impact, the Shadow Mosura is a truly spectacular choice.

The Neocaridina Shrimp, belonging to the Neocaridina genus, is a diverse and widely popular group of freshwater shrimp in the aquarium hobby. Native to East Asia, particularly Taiwan and China, these shrimp are highly sought after for their striking color variations, hardy nature, and excellent algae-grazing abilities. Their adaptability to a wide range of water conditions makes them an ideal choice for both beginner and experienced aquarists. Physically, Neocaridina shrimp are small, elongated crustaceans with a semi-transparent body structure that has been selectively bred into a vast array of vibrant colors. Some of the most well-known varieties include Cherry Shrimp (Neocaridina davidi var. red), Blue Dream, Yellow Golden Back, Orange Sakura, Green Jade, Chocolate, Black Rose, and Rili-patterned shrimp, among others. Depending on the variety and grade, individuals may display solid, gradient, or speckled coloration. Adult Neocaridina shrimp typically reach between 1 to 1.5 inches (2.5 to 4 centimeters) in length, with females being larger and more robust than males. In the aquarium, Neocaridina shrimp thrive in planted tanks with plenty of hiding spots, such as driftwood, caves, and dense vegetation. A soft, fine substrate such as sand or small gravel is ideal, as it allows them to forage safely. A tank of at least 5 gallons is sufficient for a small colony, though larger tanks provide better stability for growing populations. These shrimp are highly active and spend most of their time grazing on biofilm, algae, and organic detritus, making them excellent natural cleaners. Water parameters for Neocaridina shrimp vary slightly depending on the species, but they generally prefer neutral to slightly alkaline conditions with a pH range of 6.5 to 8.0 and temperatures between 65 to 78°F (18 to 26°C). They can tolerate a wide range of water hardness (GH 4-12, KH 2-8), making them well-suited for different tank setups. However, stability is key, as they are sensitive to sudden fluctuations in water parameters. Ammonia and nitrites should always be at zero, and they are particularly vulnerable to copper and other heavy metals, so care should be taken with fertilizers and medications. Feeding Neocaridina shrimp is straightforward, as they are omnivorous scavengers. They naturally graze on biofilm, algae, and detritus, but their diet should be supplemented with high-quality shrimp pellets, algae wafers, and blanched vegetables such as zucchini, spinach, or carrots. Protein-rich foods like bloodworms, brine shrimp, or specialized shrimp protein supplements should be offered occasionally to support molting and breeding. Calcium supplementation (such as cuttlebone or calcium-rich foods) is beneficial for healthy exoskeleton development. Neocaridina shrimp are peaceful and social, making them excellent tank mates for small, non-aggressive fish such as tetras, rasboras, and nano fish. They also coexist well with other invertebrates like snails and peaceful Caridina shrimp. However, larger or predatory fish, such as cichlids and large barbs, may see them as food. A shrimp-only setup or a densely planted tank with hiding places helps ensure their survival in a community setting. Breeding Neocaridina shrimp in captivity is extremely easy, as they reproduce readily in stable water conditions. Females carry fertilized eggs beneath their abdomen (berried) for about three to four weeks, after which the fully-formed baby shrimp hatch. There is no larval stage, and the juveniles begin grazing immediately. Given the right conditions, Neocaridina shrimp colonies can multiply rapidly, making them a great species for breeding projects. However, different color varieties will interbreed, often resulting in wild-type brown or transparent offspring over multiple generations. Overall, Neocaridina shrimp are one of the most adaptable and rewarding freshwater invertebrates in the hobby. Their vibrant colors, peaceful nature, algae-eating abilities, and ease of breeding make them a fantastic addition to planted and community aquariums. Whether kept for their beauty, breeding potential, or practical tank-cleaning benefits, Neocaridina shrimp remain a favorite among aquarists of all experience levels.

Red Fancy Tiger Shrimp, Caridina cf. cantonensis, is a highly prized selectively bred freshwater dwarf shrimp developed through the crossing and refinement of Tiger Shrimp and Bee Shrimp bloodlines. This ornamental variety combines the intricate striped patterning of Tiger Shrimp with the brilliant red and white coloration associated with Crystal Red Shrimp, producing one of the most visually impressive Caridina varieties available in the aquarium hobby. While its wild ancestors originate from freshwater streams in southern China, the Red Fancy Tiger is a captive-developed variety that has been selectively bred for exceptional coloration, pattern complexity, and contrast. Adult Red Fancy Tiger Shrimp typically reach about 1 to 1.25 inches in length. Their bodies display a spectacular combination of rich crimson-red pigmentation and brilliant opaque white markings arranged in intricate, irregular patterns. Unlike the relatively uniform bands of traditional Crystal Red Shrimp, Red Fancy Tigers develop elaborate tiger-like stripes, broken bands, and lace-like markings that create a uniquely detailed appearance. The red coloration can range from bright cherry red to deep ruby, while the white areas often develop a beautiful porcelain-like opacity. Some individuals exhibit delicate red spotting or fine reticulated patterns across the head and abdomen, giving each shrimp a distinctive appearance. High-quality specimens are particularly valued for their intense pigmentation, clean white coverage, and intricate pattern definition. Females generally grow larger and develop a broader, more rounded abdomen than males. A mature aquarium of at least 10 gallons is recommended, although larger aquariums provide greater water stability and are generally easier to maintain. Red Fancy Tiger Shrimp thrive in established planted aquariums with mosses, driftwood, botanicals, porous rock, and other surfaces that encourage abundant biofilm growth. Shrimp-safe sponge filtration or protected filter intakes are strongly recommended, and plenty of hiding places should be provided for freshly molted shrimp and developing juveniles. Dark substrates and lush green plants create an especially attractive backdrop for their vivid red and white coloration. Water quality and stability are particularly important for Red Fancy Tiger Shrimp. Temperatures between 68 and 74 degrees Fahrenheit are ideal, with a pH range of approximately 5.8 to 6.8, very low carbonate hardness, and soft water with a general hardness around 4 to 6 dGH. A KH of approximately 0 to 1 dKH is generally preferred. Many successful keepers use remineralized reverse-osmosis water along with an active buffering substrate to maintain the soft, acidic conditions favored by Bee and Tiger-derived Caridina. Sudden fluctuations in temperature, mineral content, or other water parameters should be avoided, as these shrimp are sensitive to environmental instability. Red Fancy Tiger Shrimp spend much of their time grazing on biofilm, algae, microorganisms, and decomposing organic material. In the aquarium they should also receive high-quality shrimp foods, algae-based foods, powdered foods for juveniles, and occasional protein-rich foods in moderation. A mature aquarium containing abundant natural biofilm is especially valuable for newly released shrimplets, which depend heavily on microscopic foods growing throughout the aquarium. Consistent nutrition supports healthy molting, strong coloration, and successful reproduction. Temperament is exceptionally peaceful. Red Fancy Tiger Shrimp are best maintained in dedicated Caridina aquariums or alongside other peaceful invertebrates requiring similar water conditions. Although they can coexist with carefully selected nano fish, virtually any fish capable of swallowing a shrimplet may reduce juvenile survival. A dedicated shrimp aquarium provides the best opportunity to establish a thriving breeding colony while allowing their intricate coloration and fascinating behavior to be fully appreciated. Breeding occurs entirely in freshwater when conditions are suitable. Females carry fertilized eggs beneath the abdomen for approximately three to four weeks before releasing fully formed miniature shrimp. Unlike Amano Shrimp, Red Fancy Tiger Shrimp do not require a brackish larval stage. They can interbreed with other compatible Bee and Tiger-derived Caridina varieties, and offspring may display a range of patterns and coloration depending on the genetics of the breeding stock. Aquarists interested in maintaining a consistent Red Fancy Tiger line should selectively breed individuals displaying the desired pattern and pigmentation. Red Fancy Tiger Shrimp represent some of the most beautiful achievements in ornamental Caridina breeding. Their extraordinary combination of brilliant crimson coloration, opaque white markings, intricate tiger striping, and peaceful colony behavior makes them an exceptional addition to dedicated shrimp aquariums. For aquarists seeking a premium ornamental shrimp with unique patterning and remarkable visual impact, the Red Fancy Tiger is a truly spectacular choice.

Tangerine Tiger Shrimp, Caridina mariae, is a beautiful freshwater dwarf shrimp originating from southern China, where wild Tiger Shrimp populations inhabit cool, clean streams with rocky substrates, leaf litter, submerged roots, and abundant biofilm. Unlike the heavily hybridized Fancy Tiger varieties, Tangerine Tiger Shrimp are closely associated with naturally occurring Tiger Shrimp populations and are prized for their brilliant orange coloration, distinctive dark striping, and relatively adaptable care requirements. Their combination of vivid color, active grazing behavior, and attractive natural patterning makes them one of the most desirable Tiger Shrimp varieties in the aquarium hobby. Adult Tangerine Tiger Shrimp typically reach about 1 to 1.25 inches in length. Their bodies display a beautiful translucent golden-orange to rich tangerine coloration, accented by a series of dark brown to nearly black tiger stripes running vertically and diagonally across the abdomen. The orange pigmentation can range from pale amber to deep orange depending on genetics, age, and condition, while the dark markings provide striking contrast against the warm body color. Some individuals display additional dark spotting or subtle markings around the head and tail. Females generally grow larger and develop a fuller, more rounded abdomen than males, particularly when mature. Healthy, well-conditioned specimens can develop an almost glowing orange appearance that stands out dramatically against dark substrates and lush green aquatic plants. A mature aquarium of at least 10 gallons is recommended, although larger aquariums provide greater stability and allow colonies to develop more naturally. Tangerine Tiger Shrimp thrive in established planted aquariums with mosses, driftwood, botanicals, porous rock, and other surfaces that encourage abundant biofilm growth. Shrimp-safe sponge filtration or protected filter intakes are strongly recommended, and plenty of hiding places should be available for newly molted adults and developing juveniles. Their constant activity and bright coloration make them particularly attractive in heavily planted shrimp aquariums. Water conditions should remain clean and stable. Temperatures between 68 and 76 degrees Fahrenheit are ideal, with a pH range of approximately 6.2 to 7.5 and soft to moderately hard water. A general hardness of roughly 4 to 8 dGH and low to moderate carbonate hardness are appropriate. Unlike many Taiwan Bee and Crystal Shrimp varieties, Tangerine Tiger Shrimp are often more adaptable to neutral water conditions and do not necessarily require extremely acidic water or an active buffering substrate. However, consistent mineral content and stable water chemistry remain essential for healthy molting and reproduction. Tangerine Tiger Shrimp spend much of their time grazing on biofilm, soft algae, microorganisms, and decomposing plant material. In the aquarium they readily accept high-quality shrimp foods, algae wafers, spirulina-based foods, powdered foods for juveniles, and occasional protein-rich foods in moderation. A mature aquarium with abundant natural biofilm provides an important continuous food source, particularly for newly released shrimplets. A varied diet supports healthy growth, successful molting, and strong coloration. Temperament is exceptionally peaceful. Tangerine Tiger Shrimp are best maintained in dedicated shrimp aquariums or alongside other peaceful invertebrates with compatible water requirements. They can coexist with carefully selected nano fish, although most fish will consume newly hatched shrimplets if given the opportunity. Their bright orange coloration and active grazing behavior make them particularly enjoyable to observe in species-focused aquariums. They can also be maintained alongside other compatible Caridina varieties, although interbreeding may occur and should be considered when preserving specific color strains. Breeding occurs entirely in freshwater when conditions are suitable. Females carry fertilized eggs beneath their abdomen for approximately three to four weeks before releasing fully formed miniature shrimp. Unlike Amano Shrimp, Tangerine Tiger Shrimp do not require a brackish larval stage. Under stable conditions, established colonies can reproduce regularly, with juveniles grazing on biofilm and microscopic foods throughout the aquarium. Tangerine Tigers are also valued in selective breeding projects because their genetics can contribute interesting orange coloration and tiger patterning to hybrid Caridina lines. Caridina mariae Tangerine Tiger Shrimp combine the beautiful natural striping of Tiger Shrimp with brilliant golden-orange coloration and relatively forgiving care requirements. Their peaceful nature, active behavior, manageable size, and rewarding breeding potential make them an outstanding choice for dedicated shrimp aquariums and planted aquascapes. For aquarists interested in colorful Caridina without the demanding water requirements of many high-grade Taiwan Bee varieties, the Tangerine Tiger Shrimp is an especially attractive option.

Kamaka Rainbowfish, Melanotaenia kamaka, is a beautiful and relatively uncommon freshwater rainbowfish endemic to Lake Kamakawaiar in the Triton Lakes region of western New Guinea, Indonesia. This isolated lake habitat is part of the remarkable freshwater ecosystems of the Bird's Head region, where numerous rainbowfish species have evolved in geographically restricted waters. Unlike many rainbowfish that inhabit flowing streams and rivers, the Kamaka Rainbowfish is naturally associated with a freshwater lake environment, making it an especially interesting species for aquarists interested in the extraordinary biodiversity of New Guinea. Adult Kamaka Rainbowfish typically reach about 2.5 to 3 inches in length. The body is moderately deep and laterally compressed, with mature males developing a noticeably taller, more robust profile than females. Their most distinctive feature is the beautiful metallic blue to turquoise coloration that spreads across much of the body, often accompanied by silvery, lavender, and subtle greenish highlights. Mature males can develop an especially intense electric-blue sheen, with the scales reflecting different shades of blue depending on lighting and viewing angle. The dorsal, anal, and caudal fins are generally translucent to pale blue with darker edging or subtle yellowish tones. Females are typically slimmer and display softer silver-blue coloration, while mature displaying males become considerably more vibrant and develop the impressive body depth characteristic of many Melanotaenia species. A tank of at least 30 gallons is recommended for a proper school, with longer aquariums preferred to accommodate their active swimming behavior. Kamaka Rainbowfish should be maintained in groups of at least six, although eight to twelve or more creates a much more impressive display and encourages natural social behavior. A combination of open swimming space, aquatic plants, driftwood, and shaded areas provides an excellent environment. Males frequently display toward one another, intensifying their coloration and spreading their fins, making a group containing multiple males and females particularly attractive. Water conditions should remain stable, clean, and well oxygenated. Temperatures between 74 and 82 degrees Fahrenheit are appropriate, with a pH range of approximately 6.5 to 8.0 and moderately soft to moderately hard water. Kamaka Rainbowfish are generally adaptable once established, but regular water changes, good filtration, and adequate circulation are important for maintaining excellent health and coloration. Stable mineral content and consistently clean water are particularly beneficial for long-term maintenance. Kamaka Rainbowfish are omnivorous and readily accept a wide variety of aquarium foods. In nature they feed on small aquatic insects, insect larvae, crustaceans, zooplankton, and other available organic material. In the aquarium they readily accept quality flakes, small pellets, frozen daphnia, brine shrimp, bloodworms, cyclops, and other appropriately sized foods. A varied diet containing regular frozen or live foods helps develop the brilliant blue coloration and robust body condition seen in mature males. Temperament is peaceful, active, and social. Kamaka Rainbowfish make excellent additions to community aquariums containing other similarly sized, non-aggressive species. Suitable tankmates include other peaceful rainbowfish, rasboras, danios, Corydoras, small peaceful loaches, and other active community fish that appreciate similar water conditions. Their constant movement and enthusiastic feeding behavior may overwhelm extremely timid or slow-moving species, so tankmates should be selected accordingly. Breeding is possible in captivity and follows the typical rainbowfish pattern. Kamaka Rainbowfish are egg scatterers that deposit adhesive eggs among fine-leaved plants, mosses, or spawning mops. Spawning may occur repeatedly over several days, with small numbers of eggs released during each event. Adults provide no parental care and may consume eggs or fry, so breeders often transfer spawning mops to a separate rearing aquarium. Newly hatched fry require very small foods before progressing to newly hatched brine shrimp and finely powdered prepared foods. Melanotaenia kamaka is a spectacular and geographically unique rainbowfish that combines brilliant metallic blue coloration, elegant finnage, and the lively social behavior characteristic of the genus. Its isolated origin in the lakes of western New Guinea, manageable adult size, and increasingly impressive coloration with maturity make the Kamaka Rainbowfish an exceptional choice for planted community aquariums and dedicated rainbowfish collections.

Iron is immobile in plants. This means that plants cannot divert iron from older leaves to new ones. Therefore, deficiency symptoms appear first on new or young leaves. Because plants use iron to produce chlorophyll, a lack of iron results in chlorosis, or yellowing, of the younger leaves. Stems may also appear short and slender. If the deficiency is severe and prolonged, each new leaf emerges lighter in color than the preceding leaf. When choosing an iron supplement, it is important to know the distinction between the two forms of iron. The iron will be in one of two oxidation states: ferrous having a +2 charge, or ferric having a +3 charge. Ferrous iron, the preferred iron form and is soluble in water at any pH. Ferric iron, however, is only soluble below a pH of around 5.5; but if the pH is higher than 5.5, which more than likely it will be in a planted aquarium, the ferric iron will become insoluble and precipitate, settling in the root zone. Once this occurs, foliar absorbtion becomes impossible. To overcome this precipitation, competing products employ a chelate of ferric iron: iron-EDTA. While this does keep it soluble, it has a couple of drawbacks with respect to foliar uptake of iron. (1) Iron-EDTA bonding is very strong, thus very little of the iron will be available to the plants over a given time frame and (2) Physiological energy must be expended by the plant in order to extract the ferric iron from EDTA-iron and then convert (reduce) it to the ferrous form. Our approach is different in that we use a complex (not chelate) of ferrous iron in Flourish Iron™. Flourish Iron™ is a highly concentrated (10,000 mg/L) ferrous iron gluconate supplement. Plants are able to much more easily derive a beneﬁt from Flourish Iron™ because ferrous iron gluconate is already in the ferrous form so they do not expend energy reducing it. Despite what other manufacturers may intimate, gluconate is not harmful to plants or fish. In fact, ferrous gluconate is better suited to foliar feeding than is iron-EDTA owing to the relatively weaker iron-gluconate bonding vs. iron-EDTA bonding. In addition, ferrous gluconate has the added bonus of being a source of carbon.

Melini Corydoras, Corydoras melini , commonly known as the False Bandit Corydoras, is a beautifully patterned South American armored catfish native to the upper Amazon Basin of Colombia and Brazil. It is particularly associated with the Río Vaupés and Rio Negro drainage systems, where it inhabits forest streams, shallow tributaries, and quiet river margins with fine sandy substrates, submerged roots, driftwood, and accumulations of leaf litter. These habitats are typically warm, soft, and acidic, often containing tannin-stained water from the surrounding rainforest vegetation. Adult Melini Corydoras typically reach about 2 to 2.5 inches in length. Their body is compact and gently elongated, with a pale cream to silvery-beige base coloration that provides a beautiful contrast against their distinctive dark markings. A bold black mask extends across the eyes, giving the fish the bandit-like appearance responsible for its common name. The most recognizable feature is a broad, dark diagonal stripe that begins near the dorsal fin and runs backward along the upper body toward the lower portion of the caudal peduncle. This angled marking distinguishes Melini Corydoras from the similar Bandit Corydoras ( Corydoras metae ), whose dark dorsal marking is shorter and does not extend diagonally toward the tail. The dorsal fin is marked with dark pigmentation, while the remaining fins are generally translucent. Their striking combination of a dark facial mask, pale body, and dramatic diagonal stripe makes them one of the most recognizable Corydoras species. A tank of at least 20 gallons is recommended for a proper group, although larger aquariums provide more room for natural foraging and social behavior. Melini Corydoras are highly social and should be maintained in groups of at least six, with eight or more being ideal. Fine sand is strongly recommended because these fish naturally sift through the substrate while searching for food. Driftwood, leaf litter, plants, and shaded retreats help recreate their native habitat, while open sandy areas provide space for the group to forage together. Gentle to moderate water movement and good oxygenation are beneficial. Water conditions should remain stable, clean, and preferably soft. Temperatures between 72 and 79 degrees Fahrenheit are appropriate, with a pH range of approximately 5.5 to 7.2 and soft to moderately soft water preferred. Wild specimens are particularly well suited to slightly acidic, tannin-rich aquariums, although established fish can adapt to somewhat broader conditions. Regular water changes, good filtration, and consistently low nitrate levels are important for maintaining healthy barbels and long-term health. Melini Corydoras are omnivorous bottom feeders that naturally consume insect larvae, worms, small crustaceans, and other tiny organisms found within the substrate. In the aquarium they readily accept high-quality sinking pellets, wafers, frozen bloodworms, daphnia, brine shrimp, and other appropriately sized foods. A varied diet containing both prepared and frozen foods supports healthy growth and breeding condition. Like all Corydoras, they should be deliberately fed rather than expected to survive solely on leftover food from other aquarium inhabitants. Temperament is exceptionally peaceful and social. Melini Corydoras make excellent additions to South American community aquariums containing small tetras, pencilfish, hatchetfish, peaceful dwarf cichlids, and other non-aggressive species. They spend much of their time moving together across the substrate, occasionally resting beneath wood or plants before resuming their constant search for food. Maintaining a substantial group encourages confidence and brings out their most natural behavior. Aggressive or highly competitive bottom-dwelling fish should be avoided. Breeding is possible in captivity but is less commonly reported than with some of the more frequently maintained Corydoras species. Like other members of the group, Melini Corydoras are egg scatterers that deposit adhesive eggs on aquarium glass, plant leaves, and other surfaces. Spawning may be encouraged by conditioning adults with quality live or frozen foods and performing water changes with slightly cooler water to simulate seasonal rainfall. Adults provide no parental care and may consume eggs, so the eggs should be protected or transferred to a separate rearing aquarium. Newly hatched fry can be raised on appropriately sized live and prepared foods. Corydoras melini is an exceptionally attractive and somewhat uncommon Corydoras species that combines a distinctive black facial mask, dramatic diagonal body stripe, and peaceful schooling behavior. Its manageable adult size, fascinating foraging habits, and beautiful natural patterning make the Melini Corydoras an outstanding choice for planted aquariums and authentic Amazonian community displays.

Red Devil Koi Angelfish, Pterophyllum scalare, is a spectacular selectively bred variety of freshwater angelfish developed for its intense red-orange coloration and distinctive koi-like patterning. While this ornamental strain does not occur naturally in the wild, its ancestry traces to wild Pterophyllum scalare populations native to the Amazon Basin of South America, including Brazil, Peru, Colombia, and neighboring regions. Wild angelfish inhabit slow-moving rivers, flooded forests, quiet tributaries, and vegetated waterways where submerged roots, branches, and aquatic plants provide shelter. Through generations of selective breeding, aquarists have developed the Red Devil Koi Angelfish into an exceptionally colorful form that combines the graceful proportions of a traditional angelfish with the vivid pigmentation of ornamental koi. Adult Red Devil Koi Angelfish typically reach about 6 inches in body length, with their tall dorsal and anal fins producing an overall height of 8 to 10 inches or more. Their body is strongly laterally compressed and distinctly triangular, with long, flowing dorsal and anal fins and delicate, thread-like pelvic fins. What makes this variety particularly impressive is its brilliant red to fiery orange coloration, which can extend across the head, shoulders, back, and much of the body. Depending on the individual and breeding line, the remaining body may display patches of creamy white, pale gold, or yellow, sometimes accented by irregular black marbling characteristic of koi-patterned angelfish. High-quality specimens often develop exceptionally strong red-orange coverage, creating a dramatic appearance that distinguishes them from standard Koi Angelfish. The intensity and distribution of coloration vary between individuals, making each fish uniquely patterned. A tank of at least 30 gallons is recommended for a single adult or compatible pair, with 55 gallons or larger preferred for groups or community setups. Because angelfish grow considerably taller than many similarly sized aquarium fish, vertical swimming space is particularly important. The aquarium should provide tall plants, driftwood, branches, and other vertical structures that recreate the sheltered environments favored by their wild ancestors. Open swimming areas should also be maintained, and visual barriers become especially beneficial when mature fish begin establishing territories. Water conditions should remain warm, clean, and stable. Temperatures between 76 and 82 degrees Fahrenheit are appropriate, with a pH range of approximately 6.0 to 7.5 and soft to moderately hard water. Captive-bred Red Devil Koi Angelfish are generally adaptable to typical community aquarium conditions, although consistent water quality is essential for maintaining healthy growth, finnage, and coloration. Strong biological filtration, regular water changes, and gentle to moderate water movement are recommended. Red Devil Koi Angelfish are omnivorous micropredators that readily accept a wide variety of aquarium foods. In nature, wild Pterophyllum scalare feed on aquatic insects, insect larvae, small crustaceans, worms, and other small organisms. In the aquarium, Red Devil Koi Angelfish thrive on high-quality cichlid pellets, flakes, frozen bloodworms, brine shrimp, mysis shrimp, daphnia, and other appropriately sized foods. A varied diet rich in quality proteins and natural carotenoids can help support the intense red and orange pigmentation characteristic of this selectively bred variety. Temperament is generally peaceful to semi-aggressive. Red Devil Koi Angelfish make excellent centerpiece fish in appropriately sized community aquariums with compatible tankmates. Suitable companions include medium-sized tetras, Corydoras, peaceful plecos, larger rasboras, and other calm species that appreciate similar water conditions. Very small fish and shrimp may eventually be viewed as prey, while aggressive or persistent fin-nipping species should be avoided. As adults mature, compatible pairs may form and become increasingly territorial, particularly during breeding. Breeding is readily achievable once a compatible pair forms. Red Devil Koi Angelfish are biparental substrate spawners that deposit adhesive eggs in neat rows on broad plant leaves, vertical pieces of wood, slate, or other cleaned surfaces. Both parents typically guard and fan the eggs before protecting the developing larvae and free-swimming fry. Because this variety has been developed through selective breeding, offspring may display considerable variation in red-orange coverage, white patterning, and black markings depending on the genetics of the parents. Maintaining the most desirable Red Devil Koi coloration requires careful selection of breeding stock over successive generations. The Red Devil Koi Angelfish is one of the most visually impressive selectively bred forms of Pterophyllum scalare, combining the elegance of a traditional angelfish with brilliant red-orange pigmentation and distinctive koi-like patterning. Its graceful finnage, striking coloration, engaging personality, and fascinating parental behavior make it an exceptional centerpiece for planted aquariums and carefully planned freshwater community displays.

Green Myriophyllum, Myriophyllum pinnatum, is an attractive North American aquatic stem plant native to the eastern and southeastern United States. It naturally inhabits ponds, lakes, marshes, slow-moving streams, and shallow wetlands, where it grows rooted in soft sediments and extends its delicate foliage through the water column. These habitats range from still to gently flowing freshwater environments with abundant sunlight and nutrient-rich substrates. Its finely divided foliage and vibrant green coloration make Green Myriophyllum an excellent choice for aquarists seeking a soft, feathery appearance in planted aquariums. In the aquarium, Green Myriophyllum develops slender, upright stems surrounded by delicate whorls of finely divided, feather-like leaves. Each leaf consists of numerous narrow segments arranged along a central axis, creating a soft, almost fern-like appearance. The foliage typically displays beautiful shades of bright green, emerald, and yellow-green, with healthy new growth often appearing especially vibrant. Under favorable conditions, the stems become densely covered in foliage, producing lush, bushy clusters that sway gracefully in the current. Mature stems can reach approximately 12 to 24 inches or more in height, making this an excellent background plant or a textured midground accent in larger aquariums. Green Myriophyllum is best suited for background placement, where its delicate foliage can create dense, natural-looking stands. It looks particularly attractive when planted in groups of several stems, forming soft green clusters that contrast beautifully against broad-leaved plants, rocks, and driftwood. Moderate to high lighting is recommended, with stronger lighting encouraging compact growth, shorter internodes, and fuller foliage. Under insufficient light, the stems may become elongated and sparse, with reduced leaf density along the lower portions. Water conditions should remain stable and clean. Temperatures between 68 and 78 degrees Fahrenheit are appropriate, with a pH range of approximately 6.0 to 7.5 and soft to moderately hard water. Green Myriophyllum performs best in established planted aquariums with consistent nutrient availability and gentle to moderate water circulation. CO₂ supplementation is beneficial for encouraging faster, denser growth but is not strictly required when adequate lighting and nutrients are provided. Because this species naturally occurs in temperate and subtropical environments, it generally appreciates somewhat cooler conditions than many tropical aquarium plants. Green Myriophyllum benefits from nutrient-rich substrate and balanced water-column fertilization. Consistent availability of nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, iron, and trace elements supports healthy foliage and vigorous stem development. Although the plant develops roots in the substrate, it also absorbs substantial nutrients directly through its leaves and stems. Regular liquid fertilization is particularly beneficial in aquariums with inert substrates. Maintaining stable nutrient levels helps prevent yellowing, sparse growth, and deterioration of older leaves. Growth is moderate to fast under favorable conditions, and regular trimming encourages fuller, bushier growth. When stems become too tall or begin shading neighboring plants, the upper portions can be cut and replanted directly into the substrate. The remaining lower stems will often develop new lateral shoots, gradually creating denser clusters. Propagation is straightforward through stem cuttings, allowing a small initial planting to develop into an impressive stand over time. Because the foliage is delicate, care should be taken when handling and planting to avoid unnecessary damage. Green Myriophyllum is compatible with most peaceful community fish and freshwater invertebrates. Its dense, finely divided foliage provides excellent shelter for shrimp, fry, and small fish while creating numerous surfaces for biofilm and microorganisms. It works particularly well alongside Cryptocoryne, Anubias, Rotala, Ludwigia, and other aquarium plants with contrasting leaf shapes. Large herbivorous fish, digging cichlids, and particularly boisterous species may damage or uproot its delicate stems and should be avoided. Myriophyllum pinnatum is a beautiful and versatile aquatic plant that brings a soft, natural texture to freshwater aquariums. Its vibrant green coloration, delicate feather-like foliage, graceful movement, and relatively straightforward propagation make Green Myriophyllum an excellent choice for planted aquariums. Whether used to create a dense background or as a contrasting accent among broader-leaved plants, this elegant species adds depth, movement, and a lush underwater appearance to any aquascape.

Black Morpho Tetra, Poecilocharax weitzmani , is a spectacular South American characin native to the upper Amazon and Orinoco basins, with populations recorded in Colombia, Venezuela, Brazil, and Peru. Commonly associated with the name Black Darter Tetra, this small species inhabits shaded forest streams and blackwater tributaries with extremely soft, acidic water, submerged roots, fallen branches, and thick accumulations of leaf litter. Unlike conventional schooling tetras, Black Morpho Tetras spend much of their time close to the substrate, moving deliberately among leaves and submerged structures. Their unusual behavior, remarkable coloration, and striking sexual dimorphism make them one of the most fascinating small characins available in the aquarium hobby. Adult Black Morpho Tetras typically reach about 1.5 to 2 inches in length. Their body is slender and elongated, with a distinctive pointed head and relatively large fins. Mature males are especially spectacular, displaying a dark charcoal to nearly black body accented by brilliant electric-blue, turquoise, and violet iridescence. Depending on lighting and viewing angle, the metallic coloration can produce an almost butterfly-like shimmer reminiscent of a Blue Morpho butterfly. Males develop beautifully extended dorsal and anal fins, often decorated with contrasting dark pigmentation, metallic blue highlights, and subtle reddish tones. Females are generally smaller, fuller-bodied, and considerably less colorful, displaying more subdued brownish, gray, and cream coloration with darker longitudinal markings. The dramatic contrast between mature males and females makes this species particularly interesting to maintain in mixed groups. A mature aquarium of at least 20 gallons is recommended for a small group, although larger aquariums provide more opportunities for establishing territories and observing natural behavior. Black Morpho Tetras are best maintained in heavily structured aquariums with abundant driftwood, fine branches, leaf litter, caves, and dense plant cover. Fine sand is an excellent substrate, particularly when covered with scattered botanicals that create natural hiding places. Subdued lighting and floating plants help recreate their shaded forest habitat. Unlike active open-water tetras, these fish prefer to remain near the bottom and among cover, so horizontal space and numerous visual barriers are more important than extensive open swimming areas. Water conditions should remain exceptionally clean, soft, and acidic. Temperatures between 74 and 82 degrees Fahrenheit are appropriate, with a pH range of approximately 4.0 to 6.5 and very low carbonate hardness preferred. Wild specimens are particularly well adapted to mineral-poor blackwater conditions and may be sensitive to hard, alkaline water. Reverse-osmosis water, natural botanicals, and gentle filtration can be useful for maintaining suitable conditions. Stability is especially important, as sudden changes in water chemistry can be stressful for this specialized species. Black Morpho Tetras are micropredators that naturally feed on tiny aquatic insects, insect larvae, crustaceans, worms, and other small invertebrates found among leaf litter and submerged vegetation. In the aquarium they thrive on appropriately sized live and frozen foods such as baby brine shrimp, daphnia, cyclops, mosquito larvae, and small bloodworms. Some individuals may eventually accept high-quality micro-pellets, but wild specimens can be reluctant to recognize dry prepared foods. A varied diet containing regular live or frozen foods is strongly recommended for maintaining excellent condition and developing the spectacular coloration of mature males. Temperament is generally peaceful toward unrelated species but can be territorial among males. Rather than forming tight schools, Black Morpho Tetras establish small territories and spend much of their time displaying, exploring cover, and interacting near the substrate. Mature males may flare their fins and intensify their colors when encountering rivals, making these displays one of the highlights of keeping the species. They are best maintained in species-focused aquariums or carefully planned blackwater communities with small, peaceful tankmates such as pencilfish and other gentle characins. Larger, aggressive, or highly competitive fish should be avoided. Breeding is possible in captivity but requires carefully maintained conditions. Unlike typical egg-scattering tetras, Poecilocharax weitzmani is a cave-spawning species. Males establish territories around small cavities or sheltered spaces, where females deposit adhesive eggs. The male guards the eggs until they hatch, displaying parental behavior that is unusual among small aquarium characins. Very soft, acidic water and abundant appropriately sized live foods are particularly important for breeding success. Newly hatched fry require microscopic foods before progressing to newly hatched brine shrimp. Poecilocharax weitzmani is one of the most extraordinary small South American characins available to dedicated aquarists. Its dramatic black and electric-blue coloration, elaborate male finnage, unusual bottom-oriented behavior, and fascinating cave-spawning strategy distinguish the Black Morpho Tetra from conventional schooling species. For aquarists interested in rare blackwater fish, this remarkable species offers an exceptional combination of beauty, personality, and fascinating natural behavior.

The Panda Loach (Yaoshania pachychilus) is a rare freshwater hillstream loach known for its dramatic juvenile coloration and active, playful personality. Young Panda Loaches display bold black-and-white bands that give the species its name. As they mature, the pattern gradually develops into a more intricate gold, brown, and black reticulated appearance. Reaching approximately 2 to 2.4 inches as adults, Panda Loaches remain relatively small but require more specialized care than a typical nano fish. They thrive in mature aquariums with clean, highly oxygenated water, strong current, and plenty of established algae and biofilm for grazing. 🐟 About This Fish The Panda Loach is a peaceful and highly active bottom-dweller native to fast-flowing mountain streams in Guangxi, China. Its flattened body and broad fins allow it to grip rocks and move comfortably through strong current. Juveniles display the most recognizable black-and-white panda pattern. As the fish matures, the bands become more subdued and develop into a unique spotted or reticulated pattern. Adults are social and are best kept in a small group rather than alone. 🌊 Aquarium Care Panda Loaches should be introduced only to a mature, fully cycled aquarium. They require very clean, oxygen-rich water and moderate to strong current that recreates their natural hillstream environment. Although they can tolerate some variation in water chemistry, they are sensitive to poor water quality, low oxygen levels, and unstable conditions. Regular water changes and strong filtration are important for long-term health. 🪨 Tank Setup Provide a river-style setup with smooth rocks, rounded pebbles, caves, driftwood, and open grazing surfaces. Strong lighting can be helpful because it encourages the growth of soft algae and biofilm. Hardy plants such as Anubias, Java fern, and Bucephalandra can be included and will not be damaged by these loaches. A longer aquarium with more bottom surface area is preferable to a tall tank. A 20-gallon or larger aquarium is recommended for a small group. Keep at least four together when possible, and provide multiple feeding and resting areas to reduce competition. 🍽️ Diet Panda Loaches naturally graze on soft algae, biofilm, and the tiny organisms living on rocks and other aquarium surfaces. A mature aquarium with established grazing material is essential. Our Panda Loaches are fed a combination of: • Frozen daphnia • High-quality sinking pellets • High-quality flake food Foods rich in algae or plant matter should make up a meaningful part of the diet. Frozen meaty foods can be offered for variety, but they should not become the primary food source because a diet that is too high in protein may cause health problems. 🤝 Tankmates Panda Loaches are peaceful and can be kept with small community fish that tolerate cooler, highly oxygenated water and stronger current. Good tankmates may include small rasboras, peaceful danios, hillstream loaches, freshwater gobies, and other calm species that will not outcompete them for food. They can generally be kept with dwarf shrimp, although newly hatched shrimplets may occasionally be eaten. Avoid large, aggressive, or slow-moving fish that require warm, low-flow conditions. 🐣 Breeding Notes Reliable breeding information remains limited, although successful aquarium breeding has been reported. Hobbyist observations suggest that adults may spawn beneath rocks or inside small caves. Eggs can fall into coarse gravel, where newly hatched fry remain protected and feed on microorganisms during their earliest stages. A mature aquarium with abundant natural food appears especially important for fry survival. 📏 Recommended Water Parameters Temperature: 68° to 75° F pH: 6.5 to 7.5 KH: 4 to 8 dKH Minimum tank size: 20 gallons for a small group Adult size: Approximately 2 to 2.4 inches Origin: Guangxi, China ❤️ What We Like About This Fish • Bold black-and-white juvenile coloration • Unique reticulated adult pattern • Active, outgoing, and entertaining behavior • Peaceful with most small community fish • Regularly grazes algae and biofilm • Safe with live aquarium plants ⚠️ Important Notes Panda Loaches are not ideal for brand-new or low-flow aquariums. They require a mature tank with strong oxygenation, excellent water quality, and established algae and biofilm. They should be kept in a small group and should not be expected to survive on prepared foods alone. Avoid consistently warm water and diets that rely too heavily on high-protein frozen foods.

Bring shifting color and constant movement to your freshwater aquarium with the Rainbow Stiphodon Goby (Stiphodon ornatus). This peaceful dwarf goby is known for its fascinating rock-climbing behavior, active grazing, and dramatic differences between males and females. Females typically display an elegant cream-colored body with dark horizontal striping. Mature males are the showstoppers, developing metallic shades of electric blue, emerald green, burnished gold, and red-orange depending on their mood, environment, and lighting. Native to western Sumatra, Indonesia, the Rainbow Stiphodon Goby comes from rocky freshwater streams and is well adapted to life in moving water. Its fused pelvic fins form a strong disc that allows it to grip rocks and other surfaces while grazing and exploring. 🐟 About This Fish The Rainbow Stiphodon Goby is a peaceful, active bottom-dweller with a big personality for its small size. It spends much of the day perching on rocks, climbing across hardscape, and grazing on algae and biofilm. These gobies are especially striking when kept in a mature aquarium that allows males to display their full coloration. They can be kept individually, in pairs, or in groups when enough space and grazing surfaces are provided. 🌊 Aquarium Care This species does best in a mature, stable aquarium with clean, highly oxygenated water and moderate to strong current. A newer aquarium without established algae or biofilm may not provide enough natural grazing material. Water quality should remain consistent, and excess waste or stagnant areas should be avoided. A secure aquarium lid is strongly recommended. Like many gobies, Rainbow Stiphodons may climb glass or jump through small openings. 🪨 Tank Setup Provide plenty of smooth rocks, rounded stones, driftwood, and open areas where the gobies can perch and graze. A longer aquarium footprint is more useful than additional height because these fish spend most of their time near the bottom. Allow some algae and biofilm to grow naturally across the hardscape. Hardy plants such as Anubias, Java fern, and Bucephalandra work well and will not be damaged by these gobies. When keeping multiple males, provide additional space and rockwork to create separate territories and break up sightlines. 🍽️ Diet Rainbow Stiphodon Gobies are active grazers and should have regular access to natural algae and biofilm. Our fish are currently fed a combination of: • Live baby brine shrimp • Frozen daphnia • High-quality flake food Algae-based foods, spirulina products, and quality sinking foods may also be offered. Live or frozen meaty foods should be treated as supplements rather than the entire diet. 🤝 Tankmates This goby is generally peaceful and can be kept with other small, non-aggressive community fish that appreciate similar water conditions. Suitable tankmates may include small rasboras, danios, peaceful tetras, hillstream loaches, and other calm goby species. Use caution with very small shrimp and newly hatched shrimplets, which may occasionally be eaten. Larger invertebrates such as Amano shrimp and Vampire shrimp are generally better suited because of their size. Males may become territorial with one another, particularly when displaying or competing for preferred grazing areas. Provide extra space and multiple rock piles when keeping a group. 🐣 Breeding Notes Breeding Rainbow Stiphodon Gobies in captivity is extremely difficult. Stiphodon gobies have an amphidromous life cycle. Adults spawn in freshwater, but the newly hatched larvae move downstream and develop in marine conditions before returning to freshwater as juveniles. Their tiny larvae and extended marine stage make successful captive rearing exceptionally challenging. 📏 Recommended Water Parameters Temperature: 72° to 75° F pH: 7.2 to 7.5 GH: 7 to 8 dGH KH: 3 to 4 dKH TDS: 180 to 250 ppm Minimum tank size: 20 gallons recommended Adult size: Up to approximately 2 inches Origin: Western Sumatra, Indonesia ❤️ What We Like About This Fish • Brilliant, color-changing appearance in mature males • Peaceful temperament and active personality • Fascinating rock-climbing and perching behavior • Regularly grazes algae and biofilm • Safe with live aquarium plants • Compatible with many peaceful community fish ⚠️ Important Notes This species requires a mature aquarium with strong oxygenation, consistent water quality, and established grazing surfaces. It should not be purchased as the sole solution for aquarium algae. Very small shrimp and shrimplets may be eaten. Larger shrimp are generally safer, but no small invertebrate should be considered completely protected. A secure lid is also strongly recommended.

The Red Lipstick Goby (Sicyopus rubicundus) is a rare freshwater dwarf goby prized for its bold male coloration, active behavior, and big personality in a small package. Mature males can develop striking red to orange markings on the lips and rear body, paired with a bright yellow second dorsal fin. Females are more subtle in color but remain active, curious, and entertaining to watch. Native to fast moving, clear streams in Indonesia, this goby does best in mature aquariums with excellent water quality and strong flow. It is a great choice for peaceful community tanks with small fish, hillstream species, and larger shrimp that are too big to be seen as prey. 🐟 About This Fish The Red Lipstick Sicyopus Goby is an active dwarf goby from Indonesia. Males are known for their bright red/orange markings and yellow second dorsal fin, while females have more understated coloration. Both are fun to watch and bring lots of movement to a well maintained aquarium. Great for Algae eating. 🌊 Aquarium Care This species needs a mature aquarium with clean, oxygen rich water and strong current. It comes from shallow, fast flowing freshwater streams, so it is not a good fit for low flow tanks or unstable new setups. A secure aquarium lid is strongly recommended. Like many gobies, this fish may climb glass or jump if given the chance. 🪨 Tank Setup Provide smooth rocks, driftwood, caves, and open areas where the goby can perch, explore, and establish small territories. Hardy plants such as Anubias work very well because this fish will not damage live plants. For a single fish or pair, a 10 gallon aquarium may work if water quality and flow are excellent. For groups, especially with more than one male, a larger aquarium is recommended. 🍽️ Diet The Red Lipstick Sicyopus Goby is a micropredator and should be offered small meaty foods. It typically does best with frozen or live foods such as baby brine shrimp, daphnia, bloodworms, and other appropriately sized foods. Dry foods are often ignored, so this is not a fish to buy if you need something that will reliably eat flakes or pellets. 🤝 Tankmates This goby is generally peaceful with most small, calm fish. Good tankmate options may include small rasboras, peaceful tetras, hillstream loaches, and other non aggressive community fish. Use caution with dwarf shrimp. This species may eat very small shrimp or tiny invertebrates if given the opportunity. Larger shrimp are usually safer, but tiny shrimp should not be considered fully safe tankmates. Males may show territorial behavior toward each other, especially in smaller tanks. If keeping a group, provide extra space, strong flow, and plenty of rockwork to break up sightlines. 🐣 Breeding Notes Breeding has reportedly occurred in aquariums, but raising the fry is extremely difficult. In the wild, adults spawn in freshwater, and the larvae are carried downstream to marine or brackish environments before later returning to freshwater as they mature. This complex life cycle makes captive rearing very challenging. 📏 Recommended Water Parameters Temperature: 72° to 79° F pH: 6.0 to 7.5 KH: 4 to 8 dKH Minimum tank size: 10 gallons for one fish or a pair, 30 gallons or larger for a group Adult size: 1.5 to 2 inches Typical purchase size: Around 1.5 inches Origin: Indonesia ❤️ What We Like About This Fish • Rare dwarf goby with beautiful male coloration • Active, curious, and full of personality • Great choice for high flow community aquariums • Peaceful with most small fish • Safe with plants • Can be kept with larger shrimp that are too large to be eaten ⚠️ Important Notes This fish requires strong water flow, excellent water quality, and a mature aquarium. It is not recommended for brand new tanks. It may prey on dwarf shrimp or tiny invertebrates, and it should be fed frozen or live meaty foods rather than relying on dry foods.

The Tuxedo Platy ( Xiphophorus maculatus ) is a colorful, peaceful livebearer known for its distinctive two-tone pattern. Most Tuxedo Platies feature a bright red, orange, yellow, or gold front half contrasted by deep black coloration across the rear body and fins. Exact colors and markings vary between individual fish, making every group unique. Hardy, active, and easy to feed, this platy is an excellent choice for both beginning and experienced aquarists. It does especially well in planted community aquariums with moderately hard, slightly alkaline water. About This Fish The Tuxedo Platy is a selectively bred color variety of the Southern Platy. Its bold black rear body creates the formal “tuxedo” appearance that gives this variety its name. These fish are active throughout the day and are usually found exploring the middle and upper levels of the aquarium. Platies are social and look best when kept in a small group. If keeping both sexes, maintain approximately one male for every two or three females to reduce persistent chasing. Aquarium Care Tuxedo Platies are hardy and adaptable, but they still require a fully cycled aquarium with stable water quality. They prefer moderately hard to hard water with a neutral to alkaline pH. Gentle to moderate filtration is appropriate. Avoid extremely strong currents, as platies naturally inhabit slower-moving waters. Regular water changes and consistent parameters will help maintain their health and coloration. A secure aquarium lid is recommended because active platies may occasionally jump. Tank Setup Provide open swimming space along with live plants, driftwood, rocks, and other areas where fish can rest or move out of sight. Hardy plants such as Anubias , Java fern, water sprite, and Vallisneria work well. Dense plants or floating cover are especially useful when fry are present. Tuxedo Platies are plant-safe, although they may nibble on soft algae and decaying plant material. A 15-gallon aquarium can house a small group, but a 20-gallon or larger aquarium provides more swimming room and makes population management easier. Diet Tuxedo Platies are omnivores and readily accept most appropriately sized aquarium foods. Offer a quality flake or small pellet as the staple diet, supplemented with foods such as frozen brine shrimp, daphnia, bloodworms, and spirulina-based foods. A varied diet containing both plant and animal matter helps support strong coloration, healthy growth, and successful breeding. Feed small portions once or twice daily and avoid overfeeding. The Red-Line Halfbeak “Sijuk” ( Hemirhamphodon phaiosoma ) is a rare freshwater halfbeak from Indonesia. The Pink Albino Axolotl ( Ambystoma mexicanum ) is a soft, light-colored morph with a pink to creamy white body, pale translucent eyes, and bright feathery gills. Its delicate coloring gives it a clean, luminous appearance that stands out against darker aquarium decor. Pink Albinos are frequently mistaken for leucistic axolotls, but the eyes give them away. Albino genetics remove melanin completely, leaving pale gold or clear eyes rather than the dark eyes of a Lucy. About This Axolotl Albinism removes black pigment across the entire animal, including the eyes. What remains is a pale pink, white, or cream body with gills that flush a deeper rose color when the axolotl is active or well fed. Individual animals vary noticeably. Some lean toward a warm pink, others toward an almost paper-white cream. None will develop the dark freckling seen on wild type or dirty leucistic axolotls. Axolotls are neotenic salamanders, meaning they retain their larval features and external gills for life rather than transforming into a terrestrial adult. They remain fully aquatic from hatching onward. Aquarium Care Axolotls are cool-water amphibians and must be kept in a fully cycled aquarium with stable water quality. They are sensitive to ammonia and nitrite, so the aquarium should be established and tested before an axolotl is introduced. Temperature is the single most important factor in axolotl care. They do best in cool water and become stressed once temperatures climb into the mid 70s Fahrenheit. A tank placed in a cool room is usually sufficient, although a chiller or clip-on fan may be needed in warmer climates. Keep the current gentle. Strong flow causes stress and can fold the gill filaments back against the body. A sponge filter, or a canister outlet fitted with a spray bar, works well. Tank Setup Substrate choice matters more than almost anything else in the aquarium. Use a bare bottom or fine sand only. Gravel and small stones are readily swallowed during feeding and are a leading cause of impaction. Provide caves, PVC pipe, terracotta pots, or other shaded retreats. Albino axolotls are especially light sensitive because they have no eyelids and no protective eye pigment, so keep lighting subdued and give them somewhere dim to rest. A 20-gallon long aquarium is the practical minimum for a single adult, with roughly 10 additional gallons for each further axolotl. Floor space matters more than depth. Avoid sharp decorations and any ornament with narrow openings an axolotl could become trapped in. Diet Axolotls are carnivores. Sinking axolotl pellets or soft carnivore pellets make an excellent staple diet, supplemented with earthworms, nightcrawlers, live blackworms, and frozen bloodworms. Juveniles are generally fed daily, while sub-adults and adults are fed every two to three days. Offer food at the bottom of the aquarium where the axolotl naturally hunts, and remove anything uneaten to protect water quality. Albino axolotls have poorer eyesight than pigmented morphs and often hunt more by scent and touch. Place food directly in front of them or use feeding tongs if they are slow to find it. Tankmates Axolotls are best kept alone or with other axolotls of a similar size. Anything small enough to fit in the mouth will eventually be eaten, including nano fish, dwarf shrimp, and small snails. Fish are not recommended. Many species nip at the exposed gill filaments, and most community fish require temperatures far too warm for an axolotl. When housing more than one axolotl, keep them closely matched in size and provide separate hiding places and generous floor space. Smaller individuals may lose limbs or gills to larger tankmates. Breeding Notes Axolotls generally reach breeding condition between 12 and 18 months of age. The male deposits spermatophores that the female collects, after which she lays several hundred eggs on plants, decor, and aquarium glass. Eggs hatch in roughly two to three weeks depending on temperature. Larvae need live foods such as baby brine shrimp and microworms from the moment they begin feeding. Breeding is demanding. Larvae are cannibalistic and must be sorted by size, and a single clutch can produce far more young than most keepers are able to house. Plan for the offspring before attempting to breed. Live Blackworms ( Lumbriculus variegatus ) , also sold as California blackworms, are a protein-rich live food that axolotls take readily. Their constant movement triggers a natural hunting response, which makes them particularly useful for picky eaters and for animals that need to put on size. We offer them in four sizes, from a quarter pound for a single axolotl up to a full pound for multiple animals or a breeding collection. About This Food Blackworms are a soft-bodied aquatic worm with no hard shell or exoskeleton, so they are easy to digest and suitable for axolotls at every stage from juvenile through adult. They are high in protein and moisture and are widely used as a conditioning food for animals recovering from illness, transitioning between diets, or being prepared for breeding. Because they stay alive and active at the bottom of the aquarium, blackworms encourage foraging behavior that pellets and frozen foods do not. Feeding Rinse thoroughly in clean, cold, dechlorinated water before every feeding and discard any water the worms were stored in. Offer only what the animal will finish in a single sitting, using feeding tongs, a turkey baster, or a worm feeder to keep the portion contained. Remove anything uneaten to protect water quality. Blackworms work best as a supplement alongside a staple of sinking axolotl pellets and earthworms rather than as a sole diet. Care and Storage Keep blackworms refrigerated in a shallow container holding roughly half an inch of clean, cold, dechlorinated water. Depth matters more than volume, as a shallow layer keeps them oxygenated. Change the water once or twice daily, rinsing the worms and removing any dead material or debris each time. Properly maintained, a batch will keep for one to two weeks. Healthy blackworms clump tightly together and disperse when disturbed. A batch that has gone slack, pale, or foul smelling should be discarded rather than fed. The combination produces a deep, smoky copper with dark accents and no golden warmth. MACs are one of the rarer axolotls in the hobby and are usually available only in small numbers. About This Axolotl Copper lightens the base pigment, melanoid pushes the remaining dark pigment deeper and removes reflective iridophores, and axanthic strips out the yellow. What is left is a matte, richly toned animal in bronze, charcoal, and deep taupe. Because three recessive traits are stacked, no two MACs look quite alike. Some lean dark and smoky, others hold more visible copper. Coloring typically deepens through the first year. They do best in cool water and become stressed once temperatures climb into the mid 70s Fahrenheit. A tank placed in a cool room is usually sufficient, although a chiller or clip-on fan may be needed in warmer climates. Keep the current gentle. Strong flow causes stress and can fold the gill filaments back against the body. A sponge filter, or a canister outlet fitted with a spray bar, works well. Tank Setup Substrate choice matters more than almost anything else in the aquarium. Use a bare bottom or fine sand only. Gravel and small stones are readily swallowed during feeding and are a leading cause of impaction. Provide caves, PVC pipe, terracotta pots, or other shaded retreats. Amano Shrimp Amano Shrimp Care Amano Shrimp or their scientific name Caridina multidentata, are very hardy and are great algae eaters. They are perfect beginner freshwater shrimp. These Amano Shrimp are sold at roughly 3/4" in length and can grow up to 2". They are shrimp ninjas and are known to crawl out of the water, so make sure there is the lid on your tank! Amano Shrimp can also be kept with other colored shrimp like Cherry Shrimp and other Neocaridina varieties. They are very peaceful invertebrates and won't bother other shrimp and can survive in a large range of water conditions. Amano Shrimp Lifespan Amano Shrimp lifespan is around 2 to 3 years but lifespan will vary depending on the tank conditions, specifically temperature. Most invertebrates will grow quicker in higher temperatures (above 80F-84F) but their lifespan might be shortened slightly due to the faster metabolism caused by the higher temperature. Amano Shrimp Breeding A question we get a lot is regarding Amano Shrimp Breeding. Amano Shrimp are difficult to breed in captivity. Their eggs and larvae require brackish water to survive and flourish. Some breeders have found some success but with very low survival rates. To protect our animals and to ensure they get to our customers healthy, we will only ship orders with Sulawesi Shrimp via UPS Next Day Air. These beautiful Cardinal Sulawesi Shrimp are bred by us here in the USA. Native to the lakes of Sulawesi, Indonesia, these shrimp are natural rock dwellers and feed on the bio-film and algae growing on rocks. Smaller than their Neocaridina and Caridina counterparts, these shy shrimp have been increasingly popular in the hobby due to their interesting feeding habits, distinctive white legs and beautiful Scarlet red and white spotted patterns. These shy shrimp do better in larger groups, we recommend getting at least a group of 5 or more. Sulawesi Cardinal Shrimp or White-Sock shrimp, were difficult to breed when they were first introduced to the hobby. They required a higher PH (7.5-8.5) and higher water temperatures (78-86F) for them to breed successfully in captivity. However, we have been successful in breeding them at a lower PH of 7.0-7.2 We use an inert sand along with Lava rocks in our tank setup. For our water, we remineralized RO water with Salty Shrimp GH/KH+ to a TDS of about 150 ppm. Cholla wood is the skeleton of a Cholla Cactus, it is harvested after the Cactus dies. Each piece is unique and it's distinctive holes provide great hiding spots for shrimp and provide a media for biofilm to grow on. It also releases tanins into the water which is beneficial to all shrimp types. The wood will disintegrate over many months depending on the size and thickness of the wood. We offer Cholla pieces that are 4 inches or 6 inches in length. We recommend boiling all botanicals before use in your aquarium. This is good practice when adding anything new to your aquarium, the wood will also sink a lot quicker after it is boiled. This cool looking all-natural wood is a great addition to any aquarium.

Looking for details for your planted tank? Java moss is a popular aquarium plant option among hobbyists and is loved for its deep green color and ease of maintenance. Java moss has roots in Asia, where it can be found dispersed throughout Malaysia, Java, and India. Now used by hobbyists, java moss in fish tanks has become the common option because it’s versatile, beautiful, high quality and efficient for fish and shrimp to thrive. The versatility of aquarium java moss makes it simple to mix things up in your personal hobbyist tank - attach it to hardscape, driftwood, or cholla wood, or let the java moss aquarium plant float freely for a lovely aquatic aesthetic that also serves as spots for coverage and breeding. Beyond its ability to protect shrimplets and fish fry, java moss can also help maintain high water quality. Java moss is easy to care for; its hardiness allows it to thrive in most water conditions and grow freely throughout the tank. Keep an eye on dirt buildup, excess algae growth, overgrowth and leaves that turn brown. To propagate java moss, use scissors to cut into sections. Keep each section at about two inches in length. Disperse it throughout the aquarium and watch it naturally attach itself throughout the tank. Our java moss are available in golf ball size and require low light.

Dwarf Aquarium Lily — Plant with Bulb Add an already-sprouted aquarium lily to your planted tank! The Dwarf Aquarium Lily is a freshwater aquatic plant native to India, admired for its attractive reddish leaves and compact growth habit. Unlike our Bulb Only option, this listing is for a Dwarf Aquarium Lily that has already begun growing, with its bulb attached. It's a great choice for aquarists who prefer a head start rather than waiting for a dormant bulb to sprout. What You'll Receive 1 × Dwarf Aquarium Lily Plant with Bulb A sprouted plant with existing growth The original bulb attached to support continued development Plant size, leaf count, and coloration may vary naturally. How to Plant Your Aquarium Lily Position the plant in the foreground or midground. Rest the attached bulb on top of the substrate. Do not completely bury the bulb , as this may cause rot. Allow the roots to anchor naturally into the substrate. Provide consistent lighting and nutrients for healthy new growth. Some existing leaves may adapt or decline after relocation as the plant adjusts to its new aquarium. Healthy new growth is a good indication of acclimation. Plant Care Guide Difficulty: Easy Lighting: Low to moderate CO₂ Injection: Not required Placement: Foreground or midground, depending on growth Appearance: Reddish leaves with an attractive compact form Substrate: Keep the attached bulb exposed Growth: Continued leaf and root development under suitable conditions Why Choose the Plant with Bulb? Ideal for aquarists who want an aquarium lily that has already started growing rather than beginning with an unsprouted bulb. Please note: This is a live aquatic plant. Leaf size, shape, coloration, and growth vary with lighting, nutrients, and growing conditions.

Grow Your Own Dwarf Aquarium Lily — Bulb Only Bring the excitement of growing a live aquatic plant into your aquarium with the Dwarf Aquarium Lily Bulb. Native to India, this attractive freshwater plant is known for its reddish leaves and compact appearance. This listing includes the bulb only — not an established plant with developed leaves. Watch your lily sprout, develop roots, and gradually produce its first leaves. What You'll Receive 1 × Dwarf Aquarium Lily Bulb No established leaves or visible plant growth are guaranteed at delivery A bulb to grow under suitable aquarium conditions How to Plant Your Lily Bulb Place the bulb on top of your aquarium substrate. Do not completely bury the bulb , as this may cause rot. Allow the roots to develop naturally into the substrate. Watch for shoots and leaves as the bulb begins growing. If no growth appears after approximately one week, gently rotate the bulb so another side faces upward. Sprouting times vary depending on bulb condition, temperature, lighting, and aquarium conditions. Plant Care Guide Difficulty: Easy Lighting: Low light; moderate lighting may support stronger growth CO₂ Injection: Not required Placement: Foreground or midground, depending on growth Appearance: Reddish leaves with a compact growth habit Substrate: Keep the bulb resting on the surface Why Choose the Bulb Only? Ideal for aquarists who enjoy growing plants from the beginning and watching new growth develop. Please note: This is a bulb, not a fully grown or pre-sprouted aquarium plant. Appearance and sprouting time may vary.

Anubias is an iconic aquatic plant celebrated for its broad, deep green leaves that form a striking underwater display. This robust epiphytic plant boasts a strong, structural growth habit, providing an eye-catching contrast to delicate, finer-leaved varieties while adding rich visual scale and depth to your aquascape. It will thrive comfortably under low to medium lighting conditions, making it incredibly easy to care for as it draws nutrients directly from the water column. CO2 is not strictly required, though supplementing with CO2 injection will yield significantly denser and slightly more rapid growth for this notoriously slow-growing species.
