If you are looking for a lively nano fish with personality and dazzling colors, look no further than the Emerald Dwarf Rasboras (Celestichthys erythromicron). While the fish we offer are tank-bred, they originate from Lake Inle in Burma. These colorful fish have shining, turquoise-green striations that run along the sides of their bodies. These stripes are particularly eye-catching under bright lighting conditions. They don’t grow larger than 1-1.5” , with males being slightly smaller than their female counterparts. Males have red & orange fins, while females tend to have clear, translucent fins. In terms of care, Emerald Dwarf Rasboras are relatively easy to care for; they can thrive so long as water parameters are stable and water quality is high . In terms of numbers, as shoaling fish, they do prefer being kept in small groups. One will observe dancing and sparring behavior amongst males, so the more individuals kept in a tank, the less chances of fighting will occur. Similar to other danios, they are very peaceful and can be kept with the vast majority of other peaceful nano fish and invertebrates. They will appreciate having plant cover, in addition to wood and rocks, to offer solace if need be. Spawning Emerald Dwarf Rasboras requires high-quality water and stable parameters. As egg layers, females distribute eggs amongst vegetation, which are subsequently spawned by males. Offering hiding places with plants and other aquarium hardscaping will ensure an increased likelihood of fry survival. Emerald Dwarf Rasboras can be fed prepared fish foods such as fish flakes or pellets/tablets, but they have been known to show a preference towards small live foods and frozen foods such as baby brine shrimp, daphnia, bloodworms, and tubifex worms. Dwarf Emerald Rasbora are pretty easy to care for as long as they are introduced to a mature, cycled tank. They can acclimate to a wide range of parameters. The following are the water parameters we keep at: Our Tank Water Parameters PH: 7.2 to 7.5 GH: 7 to 8 KH: 3 to 4 TDS: 180 to 250 Temp: 72 to 75 We feed them a mix of frozen brine shrimp, frozen daphnia and high-quality flake food.

One of the most commonly kept nano fish in the hobby, the Ember Tetra offers a lot of beauty in a small package; its maximum size tops out around 0.8 inches. Its dazzling red and orange body, coupled with its easy-going nature, has led to its popularity. It is particularly beautiful in a well-planted aquarium, with its fiery colors offering a nice contrast whilst swimming in front of a background of green. Originating from the Araguaia River basin in Brazil, its natural habitat is composed of acidic, tannin-rich, slower-moving waters. These fish are usually found schooling in groups , exploring the middle to top levels of the water column, at times venturing down to the lower levels to pick up any leftover food. In order for them to display their best schooling behavior, they should be kept in groups of at least 6 . Given its amiable personality, it can be kept with a plethora of similarly sized, non-aggressive fish species such as other tetras , danios, and members of the rasboras family. As it is a smaller fish, it can be kept with Neocaridinia shrimp and other small invertebrates, though some babies may end up as dinner if the fish are hungry. The Ember Tetra is easy to feed , and will readily accept high-quality flake food, pellets, and live, frozen, or freeze-dried organisms. Our Tank Water Parameters PH: 7.2 to 7.5 GH: 7 to 8 KH: 3 to 4 TDS: 180 to 250 Temp: 72 to 75 We feed them a mix of live baby brine shrimp, frozen daphnia and high-quality flake food.

Some fish need no introduction, and the Neon Tetra ( Paracheirodon innesi ) certainly falls into this category. With their eye-catching, blue, white, and neon red stripes running along their bodies, they are hard not to pay attention to! Growing no larger than 2 inches , these beauties are a great candidate for a smaller tank (we recommend 10 gallons as a minimum). These non-aggressive fish are a very popular addition to a community aquarium. Alternatively, a large school of them swimming as a unit makes them a great choice for a centerpiece fish. They look exceptionally brilliant in a densely planted tank. These fish can be sensitive to changes in water parameters; as such, special attention should be taken when acclimating these fish to ensure survival and longevity. Similarly, proper water parameters should be maintained consistently in their home to avoid illness and death. As our fish are tank-bred, their ability to acclimate to waters here in the States will be superior to those that are wild-caught. Their natural habitat consists of soft, acidic, tannin-rich waters with leaf litter . They occupy the upper and middle levels of the aquarium, seldom reaching the bottom of the tank. Being a schooling species, they should be kept in a school of at least 6 fish at the very minimum so that they will display their best colors and behaviors. One of the most popular nano fish in the aquarium hobby, the Chili Rasbora ( Boraras brigittae ), is well-known and beloved for its peaceful disposition, striking color pattern, and petite size. With shiny, iridescent blues and glowing fiery reds, the Blue Neon Rasbora Tetra is a rather rare, attractive nano fish that is extremely eye-catching. These colorful beauties originate from acidic swamps and shallow creeks in Borneo and Sumatra, with slightly warmer and softer water. The waters from which they originate have high tannin levels and leaf litter . They enjoy having open areas of water to swim in, as is found in their natural habitats. Keeping them in groups of 6 or more will encourage them to display their natural schooling behaviors. Spawning Blue Neon Rasboras has proven difficult for many, with high-quality water and stable water parameters being a must. We are proud to offer our own Shrimpy Business Premium Shrimp Food range. Shrimpy Party, Protein Party, and Snowflake Party. We created each food to provide a balanced diet for shrimp, additional nutrition for berried shrimp, to encourage breeding of the shrimp colony and to ensure shrimplets have sufficient food for growth. This pack contains 10g of Shrimp Party, 10g of Protein Party and 15g of Snowflake Party. Made from carefully chosen ingredients, we formulated Shrimpy Party to provide a balanced, nutritional diet to all freshwater invertebrates. High-quality protein content is derived from Vegetables, Algae and other natural sources. Minerals and micronutrients are also added to maintain a healthy immune system. These are the same food we feed to all our shrimp and they look like they're having Shrimpy Party during each meal! :) We formulated Protein Party to provide a balanced, nutritional diet especially for berried shrimp. High-quality protein content is derived from Vegetables, Algae and other natural sources. Minerals and micronutrients are also added to maintain a healthy immune system. Berried shrimp mommas go through a taxing time during the gestation period and need the extra protein to ensure their nutritional needs are met. Also known as the Blue-Eyed Forktail or Furcata Rainbowfish, the Blue-Eyed Forktail Rainbowfish is native to eastern Papua New Guinea, where it can be found in clear, flowing, heavily planted streams. The Blue-Eyed Forktail Rainbowfish is aptly named; its stunning eyes and yellow bands along its gray-green body make for an extremely eye-catching fish species. Their colors intensify with age , with juveniles appearing slightly duller than their grown-up counterparts. To ensure maximum color display and natural behaviors, they should be kept in schools of 6 or more individuals. While not as jumpy as other fish species, such as killifish , the Blue-Eyed Forktail Rainbowfish has been reported to jump out of its tank on occasion . A tight-fitting lid or a lower water level will ensure that this fish does not jump out of their home. Given its small size, fully grown Forktail Rainbowfish are generally considered safe to keep even a wide variety of invertebrates of varying sizes, including dwarf shrimp such as Neocaridina . They will also leave most plants alone, occasionally picking at aquarium plants with softer leaves and parts. These fish are not picky eaters and will readily accept high-quality flake, frozen, and dried foods. As they inhabit the upper levels of the water column and have smaller, slightly upturned mouths, it is beneficial to provide appropriately sized food items for them to consume. Our Tank Water Parameters PH: 7.2 to 7.5 GH: 7 to 8 KH: 3 to 4 TDS: 180 to 250 Temp: 72 to 75 We feed them a mix of live baby brine shrimp, frozen daphnia and high-quality flake food.

Long renowned as the arch nemesis of aquarium algaes, the Otocinclus Catfish ( Otocinclus macrospilus ) has been eradicating tanks of this nuisance for many years. Their sucker-mouths are perfectly equipped to tackle algae from all surfaces of an aquarium. The “Otto” or “Otto cats” as they are fondly referred to, are native to South America where they reside in fast-flowing bodies of water. As such, they enjoy aquariums with stronger water flow and good aeration. They are not large fish, maxing out around 2 inches in length. Ottos are recognizable by the mottled variety of darker colors that cover them from head to tailfin. Their skin is a mix of black, gray, and brown hues. Similar to plecos, they have rows of plating running along their bodies. Despite their relatively shy demeanor, Ottos enjoying being in groups of 6 or more as they are very sociable and and peaceful. Due to their diminutive nature, they are commonly kept with other non-aggressive fish and small invertebrates such as freshwater shrimp , snails , and crabs . Extra care should be taken when acclimating these fish, as they can be sensitive to poor water quality/parameters. Being primarily an algae eater, it is best to introduce your Ottos to a well-established tank which has algae and biofilm present. In the event that algae is not readily available in your aquarium, their diet can be supplemented with fresh vegetables (cucumber and zucchini are very popular choices), algae or kelp wafers, and vegetable-based flake food. The edible Crispy Caves contain essential natural fiber while enhancing the development of a biofilm on their surface. In particular for animals that like to graze on surfaces, such as shrimp, snails and catfish, fiber is an important part of their diet and is needed for digestion. The Crispy Caves consist largely of wood fibers (cellulose), clay and leaves, which are usually found in the natural habitats of the animals and are ingested in large numbers. Nutrients such as algae and bacteria are eaten with such fibers, which settle as a biofilm on surfaces and form the basis of nutrition. Crispy Caves are therefore the perfect addition to regular feeding with staple food, they remain dimensionally stable in the water and the nutrients have to be actively grated off with the roughage, which corresponds to the animals' natural eating behavior. Smaller animals can enter the cave and eat in peace from the inside of the cave wall. Bee-Shrimp Mineral GH+ has especially been developed for the keeping and breeding of bee shrimp, bumblebee shrimp and tiger shrimp in an aquarium, to mineralise RO water, rainwater, fully desalinated water etc. It raises the total hardness (°dH) without significantly influencing the carbonate hardness (KH). This is especially important for shrimp originating from softwater habitats (ratio of KH/°dH: 0.06/1.0). Bee-Shrimp Mineral GH+ contains all the important minerals and trace elements your shrimp need for their well-being, an intensive colouration, successful breeding and healthy growth. It also furthers plant growth and the microbial regeneration of biological filter substrates. The danger of noxious bacteria is reduced, as these salts especially further the growth of antagonistic (beneficial) microflora. Bee Shrimp Mineral GH+ does not influence the pH directly. For keeping and breeding bee shrimp, aim for a pH of under 7. As soon as biological biodegradation processes start in your tank this may happen all by itself. However, if the pH remains higher, the low carbonate hardness (KH) enables you to influence the pH very easily, e.g. by the use of black alder cones or peat (both containing fulvic acids), or with pH-reducing additives. Instructions of use Mix with water outside of the aquarium. Bee-Shrimp Mineral GH+ dissolves almost completely within seconds, and the water is ready for use at once. Please make sure that any undissolved particles go into your tank, too. Close the container tightly after use. Dosage Use Bee-Shrimp Mineral GH+ to re-mineralise RO water, rainwater, fully desalinated water etc. to reach a total hardness of about 6 °dH and/or a conductance of about 200 +/- 50 µS (Microsiemens). For this purpose, an evenly full measuring spoon (about 3 g) to 20 litres of water is sufficient. Measuring spoon enclosed. Sulawesi Mineral 7.5 is the most easily soluble variant of our Sulawesi Mineral scope. It buffers the pH at around 7.5 and serves for mineralising RO water, rainwater, fully desalinated water etc. Sulawesi Mineral 7.5 contains all important minerals and trace elements the well-known shrimp species from this region need for their health, wellbeing and colouration. Cardinal shrimp (Caridia dennerli) breeders have been using it very successfully. This mineral salt furthers the microbial regeneration of biological filter substrates. Raises carbonate and total hardness at a ratio of KH/°dH = 0.42/1.0. Note The shrimp originating from Lake Towuti on Sulawesi (e.g. the freshwater harlequin shrimp - Caridina woltereckae -, or the red-banded shrimp - Caridina striata) are still very difficult to breed in captivity. Thus we went to the Ancient Lakes on Sulawesi again in 2011 (after our initial trip in 2008) in order to have a closer look at the conditions in the habitat and to take water samples to have them analysed here. The results of these analyses show fundamental differences of the water chemistry of the Malili Lakes in comparison with generally known types of lacustrian waters. Here we had to completely rework the mineral constellation; the result of these efforts is the salt Sulawesi Mineral 8.5 Less finicky Sulawesi shrimp like the freshwater cardinal shrimp (Caridina dennerli) can be kept and bred with positive outcomes both with Sulawesi Mineral 7.5 and Sulawesi Mineral 8.5. For the more susceptible shrimps we hope to achieve long-term successful breeding by the use of Sulawesi Mineral 8.5, which is practically identical to the water chemistry of Lake Towuti. Instructions of use Add Sulawesi Mineral 7.5 to water outside of your aquarium. It will almost totally dissolve within seconds, and the water is ready for use immediately. We recommend adapting the temperature of the new water to that in your tank. Please make sure to add any undissolved particles to your tank, too. Close the container after every use. Dosage RO water, rainwater, fully desalinated water etc. is remineralised with Sulawesi Mineral 7.5 until a hardness of around 6 °dH and/or a conductance of around 270 +/- 40 µS (Mikrosiemens) is reached. This corresponds to a slightly heaped measuring spoon (around 3.5 g) to 15 litres of water. Measuring spoon enclosed. Shrimp Baby Food is a powdered rearing food for ornamental shrimp that is rich in protein, containing zooplankton, natural vitamins, minerals and high levels of Omega 3 fatty acids, providing young shrimp with everything they need for healthy growth and delivering sufficient power and energy. The content of 100 ppm astaxanthin forms especially in red, yellow and orange shrimp, the color pigments cells from the beginning good, so they may show up in a blaze of color. Highly digestible carbohydrates and polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA) deliver the necessary energy for molting. Carefully chosen algae, vegetables and herbs supply the baby shrimps with micronutrients. Green-lipped mussels are well-known for their high content of glykosaminoglykans, which form a very valuable component of the shrimp carapace. The multivitamin mixture we have also added provides your shrimps with all the vitamins they need and prevents deficiencies. This manufacturing method guarantees high digestibility. All the nutrients contained in this food are highly bioavailable. The powdery micro granules form a fine filmlike layer on all the surfaces in the tank. This is necessary as baby shrimp are quite sessile in the beginning, which means that they usually remain in the place where they hatched and that the food has to come to them. If it doesn't, they risk starvation. Shrimp Baby Food has been manufactured with the utmost care, it is a fully extruded and 100% conglomerated powdered food. Native to Papua New Guinea, the Peacock Gudgeon's intriguing behaviors and coloration is well-known in the fishkeeping community. If you’re looking for a gorgeous fish for a planted nano aquarium, one would be hard pressed to find a more striking fish than the Peacock Gudgeon ( Tateurndina ocellicauda ). Beautiful red and blue vertical stripes run along its body, with yellow tints around the edges of their fins. Their tails feature a dark, rounded “eye-spot”. Males have a rounder head than their female counterparts and can develop a nuchal hump. They can grow up to 3 inches in length, with females usually being ½ - 1” shorter. These fish have a lifespan of ~4-5 years. Breeding in captivity is not uncommon, with fish pairing up the male performing a dancing ritual to entice the female to lay their eggs. After fertilizing the eggs, the male will fiercely protect them from hungry mouths. Males can display posturing behavior with other males which can be pretty cool to watch. To optimize prime coloring and to deter territorial behavior, we recommend keeping these fish in groups of at least 3 or more. A planted aquarium with plenty of hiding spots such as driftwood and rocks will further encourage peaceful social behavior. There have been reports of Peacock Gudgeons being jumpers, but a tight lid will ensure that they don’t mistakenly leave their homes! Keeping water flow to a minimum will keep their stress levels down, as they aren’t the most powerful swimmers. Regarding compatibility, these fish are frequently kept with other similar sized peaceful swimmers. Smaller invertebrates and their offspring may end up an occasional snack for the Peacock Gudgeon. Larger invertebrates such as amano shrimp or vampire shrimp generally hold their own, given their size. Our Tank Water Parameters PH: 7.2 to 7.5 GH: 7 to 8 KH: 3 to 4 TDS: 180 to 250 Temp: 72 to 75 We feed them a mix of live baby brine shrimp, frozen daphnia and high-quality flake food.

It grows to a maximum size of just under 3 inches , and as such, care should be taken if one is to attempt to keep them with smaller invertebrates such as dwarf shrimp, and the fry will likely end up as prey. Larger invertebrates such as Vampire , Amano , and Bamboo shrimp are worth candidates for invertebrate tank mates. Feeding the Neon Dwarf Rainbowfish isn’t too finicky, as it readily accepts the large majority of dried, prepared foods such as flakes, pellets, and granules. For maximum color output, be sure to supplement its diet with nutrient-rich freeze-dried, frozen, and live foods.

Catfish and especially Plecos need a different diet. Cellulose is a part of that diet in the wild as they feed off the roots and branches of dead and live trees and shrubs. Java Moss on mat is a simple, convenient product where it can be used as a wall or floor for your aquascape. Now used by hobbyists, java moss in fish tanks has become the common option because it’s versatile, beautiful, high quality and efficient for fish and shrimp to thrive. With GlasGarten Mineral Food (cubes, hearts and leaf shapes) you can provide your favorite invertebrates in the aquarium with minerals over a longer period of time and, depending on the variety, with important additives such as fiber, proteins, vitamins, potassium, iron and tannins. Simply place a piece of Mineral Food in the aquarium and the animals will nibble on the minerals. The minerals contained in the Mineral Food are also gradually released into the water and can thus improve the microbiology in the filter and substrate. For successful molting in shrimps, crayfish and crabs and against pitting in snail shells. Snails also use minerals to repair any existing shell damage. Minerals are vital for invertebrates in the aquarium, but they cannot be produced by the respective organism itself. With Mineral Junkie Bites you can supply your animals with all the important minerals they need. The small sticks/bites contain both inorganically and organically bound minerals in order to avoid deficiency symptoms, which are often noticeable in shrimp and other crustaceans through shedding problems, weak growth and high mortality rates in young animals. With snails you can avoid pitting in the shell with Mineral Junkie Bites, they grow better with sufficient mineral supply and build an even, strong snail shell. A sufficient supply of minerals is a very important factor in keeping and breeding shrimp, crayfish, crabs and snails, they are literally “addicted” to these substances. All invertebrates have a so-called exoskeleton, which consists of minerals, among other things. However, minerals are also responsible for many more specific tasks in the organism, e.g. for stimulating muscles and nerves. As is well known, the color cells of ornamental shrimp (chromatophores) are coupled to muscles, so an optimal supplementation of minerals can have a positive effect on the species-specific colouration. Numerous hormonal processes are also not possible without minerals. In addition to minerals, Mineral Junkie Bites also contain useful vegetarian ingredients and herbal extracts with many secondary plant substances for agile and healthy animals. Protein and fat are very low, so the water quality is hardly affected and you can also use the Mineral Junkie Bites as summer or weekend food. FEEDING RECOMMENDATION Every 2 – 3 days or as needed as much as the animals eat within a few hours. COMPOSITION Minerals, Vegetable by-products, Cereals, Herbal exctracts FOOD TYPE Soft Bites (soft sticks) approx. 5 – 10 mm

Copella arnoldi, commonly known as the Splash Tetra or Splashing Characin, is a unique and fascinating freshwater fish from South America. While it is often called a "tetra" in the aquarium hobby, it is more accurately classified in the family Lebiasinidae, which includes pencilfishes, not the true tetras (Characidae). The most remarkable thing about Copella arnoldi is its breeding behavior. Breeding on a Leaf: Unlike most fish that lay eggs in the water, Copella arnoldi leaps out of the water to deposit its eggs on a leaf or other surface hanging just above the water's surface. A Coordinated Leap: The male and female will select a suitable location, often an overhanging plant leaf. They then simultaneously leap from the water and cling to the underside of the leaf for several seconds, where the female lays a small batch of eggs and the male immediately fertilizes them. This process is repeated several times until 100-200 eggs have been laid. Parental Care by the Male: After spawning, the male takes on the role of guarding the eggs. He will remain in the water below the leaf and periodically splash water onto the eggs with a flick of his tail. This keeps the eggs moist and prevents them from drying out until they hatch. Splash Tetras are pretty easy to care as long as they are introduced to a mature, cycled tank. They can acclimate to a wide range of parameters. The following are our water parameters we keep them at: Our Tank Water Parameters PH: 7.2 to 7.5 GH: 7 to 8 KH: 3 to 4 TDS: 180 to 250 Temp: 72 to 75 We feed them a mix of live baby brine shrimp, frozen daphnia and high-quality flake food.

Betta fish, also known as Siamese fighting fish, are one of our favorite fishes renowned for their vibrant colors, flowing fins, and unique personalities. Barongsai refers to the "lion dance" in Indonesian which refers to a ceremonial dance where beautiful colors and patterns are displayed on lion costumes. This name is fitting to these beautiful bettas due to their unique colors and patterns. Every color and pattern is unique to each Betta fish. Male bettas are highly territorial and will fiercely defend their space. They are known for their aggressive displays towards other bettas, which include flaring their gills, spreading their fins, and charging. Male bettas build bubble nests at the water's surface to house their eggs and fry. Each betta has its own distinct personality. Some are curious and interactive, while others are more shy and reclusive. bettas prefer warm, clean water with a temperature range of 78-80°F (25-27°C). While they can survive in small containers, a minimum of 5 gallons is recommended for optimal health and well-being. Larger tanks provide more space for swimming and exploration. The Red Lyretail Swordtail (Xiphophorus hellerii) is a vibrant freshwater livebearer known for its brilliant red coloration, flowing lyretail fins, and lively personality. These active fish are constantly exploring and bring color and movement to the middle and upper levels of the aquarium. Swordtails are adaptable and generally easy to care for once introduced to a mature, fully cycled aquarium. They are active swimmers that appreciate stable water conditions, plenty of open space, and a planted environment where they can explore and retreat. About This Fish The Red Lyretail Swordtail is a selectively bred variety of the Green Swordtail. Its bold red body and extended lyretail fins create a more dramatic appearance than the standard form. Swordtails are social, curious fish that remain active throughout the day. Males may display toward females and occasionally compete with other males, particularly when space is limited. The species can reach approximately 5 to 6 inches at full size, including the male’s extended sword. Aquarium Care Red Lyretail Swordtails should be introduced to a mature, cycled aquarium with stable water quality. They can acclimate to a reasonably wide range of parameters, but they generally do best in neutral to alkaline water with moderate hardness. Regular water changes, consistent filtration, and sufficient swimming room are important. A secure aquarium lid is recommended because swordtails are active and may jump when startled. Tank Setup Provide a planted aquarium with open areas through the middle and upper portions of the tank. Plants can be placed along the back and sides to create cover without restricting swimming space. A 30-gallon or larger aquarium is recommended for a small group. Larger tanks are preferable when keeping several males because males may become territorial toward one another. When keeping males and females together, maintain more females than males to reduce persistent attention toward any one female. A ratio of one male to at least two or three females generally works well. Diet Red Lyretail Swordtails are omnivores and should receive a varied diet containing both animal-based and plant-based foods. Wild swordtails consume small crustaceans, insects, worms, and plant matter. Our Red Lyretail Swordtails are fed a combination of: • Frozen brine shrimp • Frozen daphnia • High-quality flake food Quality pellets, spirulina-based foods, and occasional frozen or live foods may also be offered to provide variety and balanced nutrition. Tankmates Red Lyretail Swordtails are generally peaceful and work well in active freshwater community aquariums. Suitable tankmates may include: • Platies and mollies • Peaceful tetras and rasboras • Corydoras catfish • Peaceful loaches • Other similarly sized community fish Avoid housing them with highly aggressive fish or persistent fin-nippers that may target their extended lyretail fins. Male swordtails may spar with one another, particularly in smaller aquariums. Additional swimming space, plants, and visual barriers can help reduce competition. Breeding Notes Swordtails are livebearers, meaning females give birth to free-swimming fry rather than laying eggs. They reproduce readily and can quickly increase the population of an aquarium. Provide dense plants, moss, or other hiding places if you would like some of the fry to survive. Adult fish may eat newborn fry when they are able to catch them. Females may already be carrying fry when purchased and can potentially produce additional broods after being separated from males. Recommended Water Parameters Temperature: 72° to 75° F pH: 7.2 to 7.5 GH: 7 to 8 dGH KH: 3 to 4 dKH TDS: 180 to 250 ppm Minimum tank size: 30 gallons for a small group Adult size: Approximately 4 to 6 inches, including extended fins Origin: Captive-bred variety of a species native to Mexico and Central America What We Like About This Fish • Brilliant red coloration • Elegant, flowing lyretail fins • Active and entertaining personality • Beginner-friendly once properly acclimated • Works well in many community aquariums • Reproduces readily in suitable conditions Important Notes Red Lyretail Swordtails are active fish and should not be kept in cramped aquariums. Provide adequate swimming room and keep the aquarium securely covered. Males may compete with one another, and females can become stressed when kept with too many males. Maintain an appropriate male-to-female ratio and provide plants or visual barriers throughout the aquarium. Swordtails reproduce quickly, so keep males and females separately if you do not want fry.

The Blue Belly Goby (Lentipes ikeae) is a rare freshwater dwarf goby known for its vivid male coloration, active behavior, and ability to navigate rocky, fast-moving environments. Mature males can develop a brilliant blue belly, dark markings on the second dorsal fin, and a bright red band near the tail. Females are more understated but remain active and interesting additions to a specialty freshwater aquarium. Native to Indonesia, the Blue Belly Goby occurs in small, rapid mountain streams with rocky bottoms and large boulders. It does best in a mature aquarium with excellent water quality, high oxygen levels, and consistent flow. 🐟 About This Fish The Blue Belly Goby is a compact, active stream goby with striking differences between males and females. Mature males display the species’ signature blue belly, along with red and black accents that may become more intense depending on mood, environment, and lighting. This species reaches approximately 1.5 to 2 inches and spends much of its time perching on rocks, exploring hardscape, and moving through the lower levels of the aquarium. 🌊 Aquarium Care Blue Belly Gobies are manageable once established but should only be added to a mature, fully cycled aquarium. They require clean, oxygen-rich water and moderate to strong current that recreates their natural stream habitat. Although they can acclimate to a range of water parameters, stability is more important than chasing an exact number. Avoid introducing them to new, unstable, low-flow, or poorly oxygenated tanks. A secure aquarium lid is strongly recommended because small stream gobies may climb glass or escape through narrow openings. 🪨 Tank Setup Provide smooth rocks, rounded stones, driftwood, caves, and open areas where the goby can perch and explore. Multiple rock piles and visual barriers are helpful when keeping more than one male. A longer aquarium footprint is preferable to a tall aquarium because these fish spend most of their time near the bottom. Hardy plants such as Anubias, Java fern, and Bucephalandra work well and will not interfere with their natural behavior. A 10-gallon aquarium may work for one fish or a compatible pair. A larger aquarium is recommended for groups or when keeping multiple males. 🍽️ Diet Offer the Blue Belly Goby a varied diet of small, appropriately sized foods. Suitable options may include: • Live baby brine shrimp • Frozen daphnia • Frozen bloodworms • High-quality sinking micro pellets • Finely crushed, high-quality flake food A mature aquarium with natural biofilm and microorganisms provides additional grazing opportunities, but the fish should not be expected to survive on aquarium algae alone. 🤝 Tankmates The Blue Belly Goby is best kept with small, peaceful fish that appreciate clean, oxygenated water and moderate to strong flow. Suitable tankmates may include small rasboras, peaceful danios, hillstream loaches, Stiphodon gobies, and other calm community fish. Use caution with dwarf shrimp and newly hatched shrimplets. Very small shrimp or other tiny invertebrates may be eaten if given the opportunity. Larger shrimp are generally safer, but no small invertebrate should be considered completely protected. Provide additional rockwork and space when keeping multiple males so each fish can establish a preferred area. 🐣 Breeding Notes The Blue Belly Goby is presumed to have an amphidromous life cycle, like other members of its subfamily. Adults live and spawn in freshwater, while the larvae develop downstream in marine or brackish conditions before returning to freshwater. This complex life cycle makes successful captive breeding and fry rearing extremely difficult. 📏 Recommended Water Parameters Temperature: 72° to 75° F pH: 7.2 to 7.5 GH: 7 to 8 dGH KH: 3 to 4 dKH TDS: 180 to 250 ppm Minimum tank size: 10 gallons for one fish or a pair, larger for groups Adult size: Approximately 1.5 to 2 inches Typical purchase size: Varies by shipment Origin: Indonesia ❤️ What We Like About This Fish • Brilliant blue and red coloration in mature males • Rare and unusual freshwater dwarf goby • Active, curious, and entertaining behavior • Excellent choice for mature, high-flow aquariums • Remains small enough for carefully planned nano setups • Safe with live aquarium plants ⚠️ Important Notes The Blue Belly Goby requires a mature aquarium with stable water quality, strong oxygenation, and consistent flow. It is not recommended for brand-new or low-flow tanks. Keep the aquarium securely covered and use caution when housing this species with dwarf shrimp, shrimplets, or other tiny invertebrates.
